<margin>In which year of his life he died</margin>
...he was hurrying the publication of those works which he had begun. But in the year of our redemption **1494**, while he was completing his thirty-second year of age and staying in Florence, he was seized by a most treacherous fever. This illness raged so fiercely through his humors and vitals that he disregarded every kind of medicine, and it forced him to satisfy the debt of nature within thirteen days.

<margin>How he conducted himself in his illness</margin>
Although I was far from him at that time, I shall not cease to relate what I have received from very serious witnesses who were present. How remarkable was it when, after receiving the sacrament of the Eucharist, the image of the crucified Christ was offered to him! From it, he could drink full draughts of love in memory of that ineffable passion suffered for the sake of our salvation, so that before he breathed out his soul, he might take up a most strong defense against any adversity and a most powerful rampart against wicked demons.

<margin>The praiseworthy end of a Christian man is related</margin>
Soon after, he was asked by an elder whether he firmly believed that image to be of the true God and true man: who, as He is God before time and eternity, was begotten by the Father (to whom He is equal in all things), and from the Holy Spirit (who is also God), and from the Father—these three are one, remaining co-eternal.

<margin>The image of God</margin>
And that He was conceived in time in the womb of Mary, ever virgin; that He suffered hunger, thirst, labors, heat, and vigils; and finally, to wash away our filth contracted from the seed of Adam, and to throw open the great gate of heaven, embracing the human race with charity, He had poured out His most precious blood both voluntarily and most willingly on the altar of the cross; and other things of that kind which are usually recounted.

<margin>Albertus Pius, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Themistius, Averroes</margin>
He replied that he not only believed but was *certain* of it. He also spoke with Alberto Pio <note>Pico's nephew, the Prince of Carpi, a notable Renaissance diplomat and scholar.</note>, his sister's son, whom we mentioned at the beginning of this life's journey—a young man distinguished for his talent, his study of the liberal arts, and his character. Pico used the same reasoning as Alexander of Aphrodisias and Themistius in the preface of their books on <term>Auscultation</term> <note>original: "auscultatorioꝝ libroꝝ"; referring to Aristotle’s *Physics*, often titled *Physical Auscultation*.</note>, declaring that fortitude against the fear of death is drawn from physical contemplations—a sentiment which Averroes soon adopted. Attempting to make the boundaries of death more peaceful for Alberto, he expressed it in this way: that the soul is not pacified by that reason alone, nor is an end put to the torments of death, but most of all by the fact that a limit was now placed on his offenses against his God; for he did not consider his short span of life to be content with even more frequent offenses against God.

<margin>The Queen of Heaven visited the sick man at night</margin>
Furthermore, he revealed this to several most proven witnesses from the college of preachers and to the aforementioned Alberto: that the Queen of Heaven had come to him at night, fragrant with a wonderful scent, and had refreshed all his limbs bruised and contracted by that fever, promising that he would not yield entirely to death. He was found lying in bed with a cheerful and peaceful face while he was ill. And amidst the stings of death which he endured, he was accustomed to speak as if he saw the heavens opened to him. He greeted everyone, and when they offered their help—as is the custom—he received and kissed them with the most charming speech. We were also informed that he asked forgiveness from all his servants if he had perhaps been troublesome to any of them. A year earlier, he had provided for them in his will: that food be given to some and clothing to others while he lived, and money paid to others according to their merits. He appointed the poor of the Florentine <term>Xenodochium</term> <note>The Hospital of Santa Maria Nuova in Florence.</note> as his heirs for those things which could not be moved, but for his movable goods, his brother Antonio Maria.

<margin>His death caused distress to all ranks of men</margin>
How much distress his death caused to the lowest and highest ranks of all, the princes, cities, and peoples of Italy are witnesses. These kings whom we mentioned above are witnesses. Also, the kindness and grace of Charles [VIII], King of the Gauls, must not be passed over in silence. When he was arriving in Florence—intending to seek Rome and conquer the Kingdom of Naples—and it was announced that Pico was suffering from a grave illness, he immediately sent two doctors (who were then performing the duty of legates) to visit and help him. He gave letters which we have both seen and read, written by his own hand, full of both humanity and those promises which...

The most benevolent mind and remarkable virtues of the King <note>Referring to King Charles VIII of France, who was in Italy at the time and was a great admirer of Pico.</note> required this of the dying man. Indeed, Pico was already very well known to him by reputation and joined to him by a certain intimacy; for he had been honorably received by the King in France when he visited Paris. Truly, just as he showed himself to be a wonder to the whole world and to many ages while he lived, so he decreed that his death should be celebrated no less famously and in an unprecedented manner. Wherefore, I think those things should be related at present which I heard with my own ears while I was in Florence—whither I had betaken myself, though not in time, upon hearing of his illness—at the sacred church which they call Santa Reparata <note>The old cathedral of Florence, later replaced by Santa Maria del Fiore.</note>. There I heard **Girolamo Savonarola** of Ferrara <note>A charismatic and controversial Dominican friar who became the de facto ruler of Florence; he was a close friend and spiritual advisor to Pico.</note>, of the Order of Preachers, a man most learned in theology and most renowned and famous for his holiness, delivering sacred sermons to the Florentine people. But first, it is my counsel to warn those ignorant of sacred letters with the words of Apuleius: lest, 

<margin>The words of Apuleius and of Brother Girolamo.</margin>
with thick ears and an obstinate heart, they think those things to be lies which seem new to the hearing, or strange to the sight, or certainly difficult beyond the reach of thought. If they explore these things a little more deeply, they will find them not only evident to the understanding but also most easy in fact. He, therefore, declaiming from the pulpit, suggested to all who were present the things I am about to say: "A secret must be revealed to you, O Florence, which is indeed so true that if it were as common among you as the Gospel of John, I would have remained silent. But I am compelled to speak; and He who can command me has ordered that I make these things public. Furthermore, I think there was no one among you who did not know Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. He was heaped with great benefits from God and great graces, and endowed with multifaceted learning; perhaps no mortal ever possessed such a celebrated genius. The Church suffered a great loss in him. I would judge that, had his span of life been prolonged further, he would have excelled all those who have died these eight hundred years past by the monuments of writing he would have left behind. He was accustomed to frequent my company to reveal his secrets, from which I knew that he was summoned by God to a religious life <note>Meaning he felt called to join a monastic order, specifically the Dominicans.</note> through internal stirrings. Desiring to obey these inspirations, he had proposed to comply more than once. But, being ungrateful for divine benefits or called away by his senses, he shrank from the labors—for he was of a delicate temperament—or perhaps thinking that his work was more needed by religion, he deferred it to this time. I say this not as a certainty, but as my conjecture and presumption. For this reason, for two years I threatened him with a **scourge** <note>Latin: *flagellum*; a prophetic warning of divine punishment.</note> if he should negligently execute the work God had proposed for him to perform. I confess I prayed to God repeatedly that, being struck a little, he might finally take up the way that had been shown to him from on high. I did not seek this by which he was struck down; I had not thought this was decreed by God: that he should leave this life and lose a part of the glorious crown prepared for him in heaven, and that he should not fully attain the fame and celebrity of name which he would have had in the highest heap if he had lived. But the most kind Judge behaved most mercifully toward him. And on account of the alms 

<margin>Alms. The state of his soul.</margin>
distributed to the poor with a large and most lavish hand, and the prayers which were most insistently poured out to God, it was brought about that his soul neither burns in the bosom of the Father above the heavens yet, nor is it assigned to the underworld to be tortured with perpetual torments. Instead, committed for a time to the fire of **Purgatory**, he pays temporal penalties. I would most gladly say this in this place so that those who knew him—and especially those who were heaped with his benefits—might aid him with their prayers." The man of God asserted these and many other things with a clear voice. He added that it was not hidden from him that, because of lies of this sort (if any were mixed in), the preachers of the word of God are made worthy to suffer eternal punishment; adding also that for several days these things had been known to him in their entirety. But because of the words which the sick man had affirmed the Virgin had spoken to him, he had stood wavering and feared for a long time lest that had been an illusion of demons, since the promise of the Virgin was frustrated by his death. 

<margin>A double death</margin>
Nevertheless, it became known to him that the deceased had been deceived by an "equivocation of death" <note>A spiritual misunderstanding where "death" refers to the death of the worldly self rather than physical expiration, or vice versa.</note>. Since she spoke of a second death...

->### THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA<-

...had spoken of eternal things: He would have believed concerning the first and temporal things. But if anyone should say that this man <note>Referring to Savonarola.</note> had either lied out of hypocrisy, or was deceived by phantasms, or circumvented by the trickery of demons, such a person—unless they are either ill-disposed toward the faith or of a deranged mind—must necessarily admit that God has revealed, and can still reveal, in various ways to the living the happiness or misery of those who have poured out their souls. And in that same span of time, God makes those to whom these things are made manifest more certain that they are not being deluded by ghosts or specters, but that the things they perceive and see, whether with the mind or the eyes, are true.

<margin>Praise of the learning and integrity of Brother Girolamo</margin>
Indeed, no one except a malevolent person would deny that a man of such great learning and authority, and of such integrity and prudence, would have announced these things as true and held them as unshakable before so many thousands of people in the principal temple of so celebrated a city. For his short theorems on **Aristotelian** philosophy, his public warnings, his most excellent interpretations of the sacred word, and his predictions of future events—which almost all of Italy knows have happened exactly to the letter—have long since established a most well-attested faith in him. To this I add that, while I was inquiring no further into the matter, I heard from a man who had been present at the sermon that the preacher <note>Savonarola.</note> had reported more: that the deceased <note>Pico.</note> had appeared to him surrounded by fire, confessing that he was still paying the penalties for his ingratitude.

Furthermore, a certain nun, famous for many excellent prophecies and who predicted many future things during her life that happened precisely, uttered this one thing two years before she departed from life: that at the **"time of the lilies,"** by the work and encouragement of **Brother Girolamo** (whom we have mentioned), Pico would be dedicated to the college of the **Order of Preachers** <note>The Dominicans.</note>. At that same time, she predicted that a certain Florentine family (which they call the **Pazzi**) <note>A prominent noble family that had been exiled after the Pazzi Conspiracy of 1478.</note>, then in exile, would return to their homeland. Many to whom this report came wondered at this nomenclature of the "lilies," thinking she spoke of the springtime when lilies bloom. 

But it was discovered that this "Lily" was the **King of the Gauls** <note>King Charles VIII of France, whose royal emblem was the fleur-de-lis (the lily).</note> who used such insignias. On the day before Pico took his religious vows—for he had so vowed before he died—and four days after that exiled family betook themselves into their home city, the King entered Florence with a great retinue, making his way through Tuscany to claim the Kingdom of Naples by force of arms.

But before I make an end, I think it not useless to preface a few more things at the conclusion of this work. For I seem to see "Molossian hounds" <note>original: "moloſſos"; Molossian dogs were a famous breed of large guard dogs in antiquity, here used metaphorically for aggressive critics.</note> barking at these revelations as if at the shadow of the moon. Perhaps bones should be thrown to them (since they are not content with the previous ones) lest they beat the air with their barking in vain. I see also that laughter is forced from the senseless; I see the sport of those who think themselves scholars being set aside. For perhaps they will contend that souls ought not to be tortured by fire for not setting aside the world to enter religion, and that in our time men inspired by the divine spirit are not to be found who enjoy conversations with **Christ**. 

But if they considered that sins worthy not of death but of pardon are to be punished by the fire of **Purgatory**, they would not wonder that even the just pay penalties. Likewise, if they were not ignorant that the servant who knows the master's will and does not fulfill it shall, by the witness of the Truth, be beaten with many stripes <note>A reference to the Gospel of Luke 12:47.</note>, they would not be surprised that this man—who knew the will of God but delayed in fulfilling it—should suffer punishments, even if he were immune from all other faults. 

On the other hand, I cannot sufficiently marvel at the crude and dull cleverness of those who, while they believe that Christ died for men, do not believe that those same men can easily speak with Him. By a more forceful argument, it should be noticed by them that mortal men can indeed become partakers of the speech of the Virgin Mother, angels, or the spirits of blessed men. For all lower things are governed by higher things, according to the witness of **Dionysius** in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. 

<margin>Dionysius the Areopagite</margin>
Through the higher minds, the divine mysteries are drawn either from the supreme ranks or from God Himself, and thus minds of a lower grade and nature (to whom the care of men is entrusted) are illuminated. In this way, men inspired by the divine spirit receive and accept these same revelations...

<margin>
True things are sometimes predicted by false prophets
</margin>

...to receive/to reveal to the multitude of men when it is expedient, this most holy law of divinity: as we are taught by the same **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian theologian whose writings on the *Celestial Hierarchy* were deeply influential to Pico.</note> in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, so that through the first things following, one may be raised toward the most majestic light. Those who doubt are surely ignorant of divine letters, and are of an insolent and stubborn disposition; for in those letters it is seen that divine future mysteries are sometimes revealed not only through good men, but even through wicked men and false prophets. What prevents us from having faith in this man <note>Brother Girolamo Savonarola.</note> who is so powerful in both doctrine and so many virtues, and who has already predicted many future events which have now come to pass? And he did not testify to this dreamily, but affirmed it with certainty. Add to this that the **Aristotelian** philosophy <note>original: "Aristotelis phīa"</note> does not cry out against these things, and **Platonic** teachings support them—though I would not accept such a weighty testimony unless it were by the authority of the divine Scriptures. Yet, it is not absurd to cite these external sources as well, so that the web of the malevolent may recoil upon its authors with greater force than it was sent.

But we must now return to ourselves. We should not mourn so much that we have lost such a man, but rather give thanks to the King <note>God.</note> in whom all things live, for having had him and for still having him. Indeed, having completed the duty of his mortal life, let him now depart from those with whom he long dwelt—whom he had bathed in no small amount of light—and as he enters the inaccessible and infinite light of the heavenly fatherland, he shall enjoy, without end, the ineffable divinity that will bring us aid day by day.

->THE END<-

### A poem by Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, concerning the Wood of the Cross:

> There is a place which we believe to be the center of the whole world,
> Which the Jews call Golgotha in their ancestral tongue:
> Here, I remember, a tree cut from sterile oak
> Was planted and brought forth healthy fruits.
> Yet it did not offer these to those who settled there as farmers;
> Strangers possessed the blessed fruits
> Of this tree. This species rises from a single trunk,
> And soon extends its arms into twin branches,
> Just as a ship’s sails stretch out when full and heavy,
> Or like the yoke when young oxen are uncoupled from the plow.
> That which this tree bore, fallen from the first mature seed,
> The earth conceived; soon—marvelous to say—
> On the third light <note>The third day; i.e., the Resurrection.</note> it brought forth again
> A branch, fearful to both the earth and those above, blessed with the fruit of life.
> But in twice twenty days <note>Forty days; the time between the Resurrection and Ascension.</note> that branch was strengthened,
> It grew into the immense sky, and with its highest peak
> It touched the heavens, and at last joined its holy head to the heights,
> While yet it brought forth enormous branches of twelve-fold weight,
> Stretching out and scattering them throughout the whole world,
> So that for all nations it might provide sustenance and eternal life.

They might offer death and teach those how to die.
And soon, when fifty days <note>This likely refers to the arrival of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, fifty days after the Resurrection.</note> had passed,
A draught of divine **nectar** <term>nectar: In a Christian context, this refers to divine grace or the sweetness of the Spirit, borrowed from the classical term for the drink of the gods.</term>
The breeze of the heavenly **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus"</note> brought down from the highest peak into the branches.
The leaves, heavy with sweet dew, dripped on every side:
Behold, beneath the vast shade of the covering boughs
There was a **fountain** <note>original: "fons"; an allegory for the Sacrament of Baptism or the source of Life.</note>: it was serene, undisturbed by any chance,
With waters clear and bright; and the grasses around it
Cast forth joyful colors from the various dews.
Around this fountain, countless nations and peoples gathered—
Various in race, sex, age, and status.
Unmarried and married women alike, widows and daughters-in-law,
Infants, boys, men, youths, and the elderly.
Here, where the branches bent low, weighed down by many kinds of fruit,
They strove to reach the branches with eager hands.
They rejoiced in the fruit soaked in heavenly nectar.
Yet they could not pluck these with their yearning palms
Until they had scrubbed away the foul, muddy tracks of their former path
And washed their bodies in the holy fountain.
So, wandering for a long time upon the soft grass,
They gazed up at the fruits hanging from the tall tree.
Then they fed upon the husks fallen from those branches
And the sweet leaves dripping with much nectar,
Longing to partake of the true fruit.
Therefore, once their mouths tasted the heavenly flavor,
They changed their spirits and cast away their greedy thoughts.
Indeed, many whose minds were renewed often restored
Their weary souls; they endured things they once thought impossible
And began to reap the fruit of their labor.
Many, too, having dared to touch holy thoughts,
Suddenly turned away again; slipping backward,
They wallowed once more in that same filth and mire.
But many others, bearing a good heart, received it
With their whole souls and hid it deep within their very core.
Therefore, for those who are able to approach the sacred springs,
The seventh light <note>The "seventh light" may refer to the Sabbath or a final stage of spiritual initiation.</note> brings them to the longed-for waves;
They bathe their fasting limbs in the clear fountains.
In this way, they finally cast off the uncleanness of the mind
And the stain of their former life; they bring back their bright souls,
Pure from death and ready to approach the threshold of heaven.
From here, the path leads to the branches and the sweet fruits of salvation;
From there, the journey goes to heaven through the branches of the tall tree.
This is the **Tree of Life** <term>Tree of Life (lignum vitae): A central Christian symbol representing the Cross of Christ as a source of eternal life and wisdom.</term> for all who believe; Amen.

# THE SEVEN-FOLD WORK <term>Heptaplus: From the Greek 'hepta' (seven) and 'aplous' (fold). Pico uses this title because he offers seven different layers of interpretation for the creation story.</term> OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA ON THE
## SEVEN-FOLD EXPLANATION OF THE SIX DAYS OF GENESIS
### ADDRESSED TO LORENZO
### DE' MEDICI. PROLOGUE.

<margin>
The doctrine of Moses
The book of Solomon
Luke
Philo
Pythagoras
Plato
Empedocles
Democritus
Numenius
Hermippus
The origin of the mysteries; Pythagorean silence
Lysis published the Golden Verses of Pythagoras
Porphyry
</margin>
**M**y emulation of your studies, Lorenzo de’ Medici, moved me to review the secret volumes of Moses. During this past winter, I observed that whatever leisure the Republic allowed you, you spent no more willingly or diligently than in that reading. At the same time, a private reason also invited me: for some time now, under your auspices but growing in your name, I have been working on another project. In it, I attempted not only to defend the hymns of David—translated by the Seventy interpreters <note>This refers to the Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and continually sung in the Church—from all suspicion and slander, but also to illuminate them with the torches of interpretation. I found no treatment more useful, none more fruitful, and none more consistent—or to speak more truly, more necessary—than a study of those books. It happened, moreover, during these days, that I was constantly occupied with those celebrated works of the six days in the creation of the world. Great reasons suggest themselves that we should believe the secrets of all nature are contained within them. For even if I omit the fact that our prophet <note>Moses, traditionally regarded as the author of the first five books of the Bible.</note>, filled with God and by the dictation of the heavenly Spirit, the master of all truth, received these things: have not the testimonies of our own people, his own people, and finally the nations, given him to us as the most expert in all human wisdom, doctrines, and letters? 

There exists among the Hebrews a book by that most wise Solomon, titled *Wisdom*—not the one now in our hands, which is the work of Philo <note>Pico follows a common Renaissance belief that the deuterocanonical "Book of Wisdom" was actually written by the Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria.</note>, but another composed in the "Jerusalem" tongue, which they call the secret language. In this, that man, considered an interpreter of the nature of things, confesses that he received all such knowledge from the inner sanctuaries of the Mosaic law. Likewise, as far as our own people are concerned, both Luke and Philo are most serious authorities that he was most learned in all the doctrine of the Egyptians. Moreover, all the Greeks who were held to be more divine—Pythagoras, Plato, Empedocles, and Democritus—employed the Egyptians as teachers. Well known is that saying of the philosopher Numenius: "What else is Plato but Moses speaking Attic?" <note>original: "atticum Moſem". This famous quote suggests that Plato’s philosophy was simply the wisdom of Moses translated into the Greek of Athens.</note>. 

But even Hermippus the Pythagorean attests that Pythagoras transferred very many things from the Mosaic law into his own philosophy. But if, meanwhile, Moses appears unrefined in his books and popular rather than a philosopher, a theologian, or a master of some great wisdom, let us remember that it was a celebrated custom of the ancient sages to write of divine matters either not at all, or to write of them in a disguised manner. From this, they were called "mysteries" <note>original: "myſteria"</note>, and they are not mysteries if they are not hidden. This was observed by the Indians, by the Ethiopians—who are named for their nakedness—and by the Egyptians. This was also what those Sphinxes <term>Sphinxes: In the Renaissance, Sphinxes placed before Egyptian temples were believed to symbolize the guarding of sacred, "hieroglyphic" secrets from the uneducated masses.</term> before the temples suggested. 

Instructed by them, Pythagoras became a master of silence; nor did he himself commit anything to writing, except for a very few things which, when dying, he commended to his daughter Damo. For the *Golden Verses* <note>original: "aurea carmína"</note> that are circulated are not by Pythagoras, as is commonly believed even by the more learned, but by Philolaus. Thereafter, the Pythagoreans most religiously guarded that law [of silence]. Lysis complained that it was violated by Hipparchus. Finally, Porphyry is the authority that the disciples of Ammonius—Origen, Plotinus, and Herennius—swore to it. Our Plato likewise [wrapped his truths] in the covering of enigmas, fables, mathematical images, and somewhat obscure...

<summary>Pico begins his Heptaplus by dedicating the work to Lorenzo de' Medici and arguing that the Book of Genesis contains the hidden secrets of all natural and divine philosophy. He asserts that Moses was the ultimate source of wisdom for ancient Greek philosophers like Plato and Pythagoras, who hid their highest truths in "mysteries" and silence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's prologue to the Heptaplus. He is building an argument that sacred texts, specifically the books of Moses (the Pentateuch), contain deep, hidden meanings that are not immediately apparent to the casual reader, much like the secret doctrines of ancient philosophers.</meta>

## THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...he hid his own teachings behind the evidence of the receding senses, just as he himself said in his letters that no one among those who read what he wrote would properly understand his opinion on divine matters—and he proved this to those who were less believing. Therefore, if we think the reading of Moses is commonplace <note>original: "exculcata", meaning well-trodden or ordinary.</note> because it seems to have nothing on the surface that is not ordinary or crude, we would, by that same logic, condemn all the ancient philosophers—whom we venerate as masters of all wisdom—for crudeness and ignorance.

<margin>Jesus Christ</margin> 

Indeed, we see the same practice observed in the Church. Jesus Christ, the image of God’s substance, did not write a Gospel, but preached it. Moreover, he preached to the crowds in parables, but separately to a few disciples, to whom it was granted to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven openly and without figures of speech. Nor did he tell all things even to those few, for they were not capable of all things, and there were many things they could not bear until the coming Spirit taught them all truth. If the Lord's disciples, so few chosen out of so many thousands, could not bear many things, how could the whole Israeli crowd—laborers, cooks, butchers, shepherds, male and female slaves, to all of whom the law was handed down to be read—have borne the weight of the entire Mosaic, or rather divine, wisdom? 

He [Moses], on the heights of the mountain (certainly that mountain on which the Lord often spoke to his disciples), was illuminated by the light of the divine sun, and his whole face shone in a wondrous way. 

<margin>Why Moses spoke with a veiled face.</margin> 

But because the people, with their blinking, nocturnal eyes, could not bear the light, he spoke to them with a veiled face. Let us return to our own writers. Matthew was the first to write a Gospel; 

<margin>The Gospel was first written by Matthew.</margin> 

and as the prophet says, "hiding the words of God in his heart so that he might not sin," <note>A reference to Psalm 119:11.</note> he pursued only the history of those things which pertained to Christ's humanity, lest the memory of the deeds performed be lost to oblivion. This is why we understand him to be represented by the figure of the Man in Ezekiel's mystical vision <term>The Four Living Creatures: In Christian tradition, the four authors of the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John) are associated with the four creatures described in Ezekiel 1:10—the Man, the Lion, the Ox, and the Eagle.</term>. John, who more than all others revealed the secrets of divinity, was compelled to speak the things he had long kept silent—many years having passed since the Lord's crucifixion—in order to abolish the heresy of the Ebionites, 

<margin>Ebionites</margin> 

which asserted that Christ was a man and not also God. He spoke of the eternal birth of the Son, but to few, and he spoke obscurely. Thus he began: "In the beginning was the Word." 

<margin>Paul</margin> 

Paul denies solid food to the Corinthians because they still live by the laws of the flesh and not by the Spirit; he speaks wisdom only among the "perfect." 

<margin>Dionysius</margin> 

Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher who was historically (but incorrectly) identified with Paul's convert in Athens.</note>, a disciple of Paul, writes that it was a holy and established custom for the churches not to communicate the more secret doctrines through letters, but only by word of mouth to those who had been properly initiated. 

I have pursued these matters at length because there are many who, judging by the crude outer bark of the words, despise and reject the book of Moses as something common and trivial. Nothing seems less credible to them than that it holds something more divine in its inner depths than what it promises on its surface. But if this has been sufficiently refuted, then it is easy to believe that if he treated of nature and the craftsmanship of the whole world anywhere—that is, if in any part of his work, as if in some field, the treasures of all true philosophy were buried by him—it was done primarily in this part. Here, he philosophizes most profoundly, even explicitly, on the emanation of all things from God, and on the degree, the number, and the order of the parts of the world. 

<margin>Jerome</margin> 

For this reason, it was a decree of the ancient Hebrews (which Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> also mentions) that no one should touch upon this account of the creation of the world unless they were already of a mature age. Perhaps, therefore, I will seem to have done something worthwhile if, lingering longer with more exact care and more laborious study (as far as my weakness allowed), I have searched out the understanding of the Mosaic reading. 

<margin>What the commentators have explained.</margin> 

When I saw that many Latin and Greek authors had worked on its explanation—and furthermore, countless old and new Chaldean and Hebrew interpreters—I did not even dare to think of writing or commenting anything new on this matter after so many others. However, I remembered that the Mosaic law cautioned that no one should harvest their field completely and entirely, but should leave an untouched portion for the poor and the needy, who might seek out sheaves and handfuls from it to take for themselves to endure their hunger. This...

<summary>Pico defends the idea that the Bible contains hidden, mystical truths intended for the "perfect" rather than the masses, drawing parallels between Moses, Jesus, and the Apostles. He justifies his new commentary on Genesis by suggesting that even after centuries of scholarship, there are still "scraps" of divine wisdom left for him to uncover.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's prologue to the Heptaplus. In the previous section, he argued that Moses, like Christ and the ancient philosophers, hid profound mysteries within a seemingly simple narrative to protect them from those unprepared for such wisdom.</meta>

->### HEPTAPLUS###<-
->a ii<-

When it came to mind, I began to survey with sharp eyes the vast fields of the prophet <note>referring to Moses as the author of Genesis</note>, searching to see whether—since the most learned interpreters were no less "cultivators" of the law than its explainers—they might have left some part untouched according to the law’s decree, to be harvested by us, the weaker ones. From this, I too might gather a few ears of grain to place upon the altars of the Church as the first fruits of my labors, so that I might not be excluded from the privileges of the temple as if I were a false Israelite or one who contributed nothing at all. The matter succeeded according to my wish; not because I could do anything that they could not, but because they, following the law's precept, did not wish to block the path for the industry of those who came after them. Furthermore, such is the vastness of the field and its fertility that no number of "grains" <note>referring to interpretations</note> can equal it; so that although nearly infinite and most capable efforts have been exerted upon it with all their strength, we can still say that Gospel phrase: *The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few.* <note>original: "Messis multa operarii pauci," citing Matthew 9:37.</note> Therefore, what the most holy men have written on this book—
<margin>Latin interpreters</margin>
Ambrose and Augustine, likewise Strabo and Bede, and Remigius, and from the more recent ones, Giles <note>Egidius Romanus</note> and Albert <note>Albert the Great</note>; and likewise what the 
<margin>Greeks</margin>
Greeks wrote: Philo, Origen, Basil, Theodoret, Apollinaris, Didymus, Diodorus, Severus, Eusebius, Josephus, Gennadius, and Chrysostom—all these will be left entirely untouched by us. Indeed, it would be both reckless and superfluous for a weak man to exert himself in that part of the field where the most robust minds have already labored. Regarding those things also which either Jonathan or Onkelos or the elder Simeon 
<margin>Chaldeans</margin>
handed down in the Chaldean language <note>referring to the Aramaic Targums, which are paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible</note>, or what the 
<margin>Hebrews</margin>
Hebrews wrote—either the ancients Eleazar, Abba Johannes, Nehunia, Isaac, and Joseph, or the more recent Gersonides, Saadia, both Abrahams, Moses <note>likely Maimonides and Nachmanides</note>, Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, and Menahem—we shall make no mention of them for the present.

<margin>Seven new expositions</margin>
Instead, we shall bring forward, besides all these, seven other expositions of our own discovery and meditation. In these, our first care will be to overcome, if we can, three difficulties with which there seems to have been a great and difficult struggle for all those who have undertaken to explain this book. 

<margin>The first difficulty</margin>
The **first** is the danger that anything said by Moses might seem either insufficient or lacking in learning and wisdom. Some have freed themselves from this by saying that he did not speak of all things, nor bring forward grand and sublime matters, because he was speaking to an unrefined <term>rude: Pico uses "rudi populo" to describe the ancient Israelites as a simple or uneducated audience</term> people who were not yet capable of understanding everything. We can believe that the unrefined listeners were satisfied if the light of knowledge—which the wise would look into—was covered by thick words, as if enclosed in a <term>horn lantern: "cornea testa," a common metaphor for a protective casing that lets light through but softens it</term>, so that the eyes of the duller folk would not be dazzled. Let him therefore have brought the light so that it might benefit healthy eyes, yet let him have brought it enclosed and veiled so that it would not hurt those with weak sight. For he neither should, nor could, nor wanted to help the learned any less than the unlearned.

<margin>The second difficulty</margin>
The **second** difficulty is that the "tenor" <note>the flow or consistent character</note> of the interpretation should be self-consistent and fitting, and that the whole series should be referred back to that same sense from which it first proceeded, as if by a single stroke and mindful of its purpose. We should not, for instance, introduce him speaking of "Ideas" <note>Platonic forms</note> in one place and then, in the very next clause, have him dealing with physical elements or with man. This would be an arbitrary and violent kind of exposition. Yet, to avoid this in the explanation of this book has seemed to many, I will not say difficult, but certainly laborious for all. So great is the perplexity, the ambiguity, and the variety of the entire reading. 
<margin>See the labor</margin>
See how much work it is, and how not easily done is that which we have conceived in our mind (may we achieve it!): that not just in one sense, but in a **sevenfold sense**, always beginning a new work from the start, we might interpret this entire creation of the world in a continuous and unmixed order of exposition, using nothing from the works of previous interpreters.

<margin>The third difficulty</margin>
The **third** difficulty consists in this: that we must not make the prophet assert anything extraneous or monstrous, or alien to the nature of things as they are now seen, or contrary to the truth which our own people have accepted as discovered by the better philosophers. Rather, let us show that it is the Divine Spirit speaking through the prophet. For why...

# LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA
<meta>Catchword: more evidently</meta>

However, we shall make clear in the following chapter the reason why these seven expositions were undertaken by us, what our purpose was, and what necessity drove us to them. We will also reveal what is entirely new in this work we are striving to produce. In that chapter, he who is to write most perfectly about this matter—that is, the creation of the world—emulating nature itself, will attempt to paint its "Idea" <note>In the Platonic sense, an "Idea" is the perfect, eternal archetype of a thing.</note>. He will then endeavor to prove in the following sections that our prophet <note>referring to Moses</note> did not fall away from that archetype in any respect. Instead, he achieved it in every detail, so that nothing else should be set forward as the ideal for all writers except Moses himself. We can all more easily admire his greatness than estimate it according to its true worth. 

<margin>Moses as the idea of writing correctly about nature</margin> 

These works of mine, whatever these early fruits of my youth may be worth, are owed to you, most illustrious Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici (1449–1492), the ruler of Florence and Pico's patron.</note>, either because they are mine and I gave and vowed myself to you long ago, or because you yourself provided the leisure of the Fiesole retreat <note>Fiesole is a hill town overlooking Florence; Lorenzo provided Pico with a villa there to study and write.</note> in which they were born. This leisure was seasoned by the frequent, or rather constant, presence of your friend Angelo Poliziano <note>A famous Renaissance humanist, poet, and scholar who was a close associate of both Lorenzo and Pico.</note>, 

<margin>Angelo Poliziano</margin> 

whose pleasant and fertile genius, which previously produced various flowers of literature, now, I believe, promises the solid and mature fruit of philosophy. Furthermore, it is customary that when something festive or joyful happens to those we love or revere, we should not only congratulate them with words, but also favor them with some gift, so to speak, to share in their happiness and testify to the joy of our soul. Therefore, this work of my late-night studies comes to you at an opportune time, when your son Giovanni—at an age when no one before him has done so—has been designated for the highest college of the Christian orders <note>The College of Cardinals.</note> by the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII. 

<margin>Innocent VIII</margin> 

This was due to Giovanni's own character, which promises all good things, and to your merits and authority, which justly demand this for him. It remains for us to hope that he shows himself worthy of this dignity. He will do so if he takes as his model for life—that is, for prudence and all virtue—the same man he had as father and author of his status. Farewell.

-> ANOTHER PROLOGUE TO THE WHOLE WORK. <-

<margin>The structure of the three worlds: Plato</margin> 

**A**ntiquity fashioned three worlds. The highest of all is the ultra-mundane, which theologians call the "angelic" and philosophers call the "intellectual" world. Plato says in the *Phaedrus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the soul, beauty, and eros.</note> that no one has ever praised this world according to its true dignity. Next to this is the celestial world; the last of all is the sublunary <note>The region below the moon; specifically, the Earth and its atmosphere.</note>, this one which we inhabit. This is the world of darkness, while the angelic is the world of light; the heavens are tempered by both light and darkness. Here, the flowing and unstable substance is denoted by waters; there, it is denoted by fire, by the brightness of light and the high altitude of the place. 

<margin>The Angelic, Celestial, and Sublunary Worlds</margin> 

The heavens, being intermediate in nature, are therefore called by the Hebrews *shamayim* <note>original: "asciamaim"</note>, as if composed of *esh* and *mayim* <note>original: "es et maim"</note>—that is, of fire and water (which we mentioned). Here is the alternation of life and death; there is perpetual life and stable activity; in the heavens, there is stability of life but alternation of activities and locations. This world consists of the decaying substance of bodies; that one of the nature of the divine mind; the heavens consist of a body, but an incorruptible one, and of a mind, but one bound to a body. 

<margin>The sequence of motion: Moses' Tabernacle</margin> 

The third is moved by the second; the second is ruled by the first. Furthermore, there are many differences between them which it is not my purpose to recount here, where we are skimming over these matters rather than flooding into them. I should not omit that these three worlds were most evidently represented by Moses in the construction of that admirable Tabernacle of his. For he divided the Tabernacle into three parts, which represent the three worlds we have mentioned. The first part, defended by no roof or covering, was exposed to rains, snows, the sun's heat, and the cold; and this part represents our world—that is, the sublunary world—more evidently...

# HEPTAPLUS

->a iii<-

<note>Bleed-through from the reverse side is visible throughout the text block.</note>

...more clearly an image <note>original: "simulachrum"</note>. In it dwelt not only men, pure and impure, sacred and profane, but also animals of every kind. Within it, there was a perpetual succession of life and death, whether due to sacrifices or the constant slaughter of offerings. The remaining two parts were both covered and protected on all sides from every foreign injury, just as both worlds—the celestial and the supercelestial—are neither capable of injury nor subject to dishonor. Both are likewise honored with the name of holiness, yet in such a way that the one which was more secret was called the Holy of Holies; the other was graced with the title of Holy. Similarly, both the celestial and the angelic worlds are each holy, since above the moon—after the fall of Lucifer—neither stain nor sin exists or can exist; yet the angelic world is considered far holier and more enriched than the celestial. But why do we pursue these more remote similarities? For if the final part of the tabernacle was common to men and beasts, did not the middle part, which shone with the splendor of gold and was illuminated by a candelabrum distinguished by seven lamps—which all Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters say signify the seven planets—clearly represent the celestial world? In the third part, the most sacred of all, there were winged cherubim. Do these not place before our eyes the three worlds? This world, which both beasts and men inhabit; the celestial world, in which the planets glitter; and the supercelestial dwelling place of the angels. Furthermore, we are reminded from this of an even higher evangelical mystery <note>original: "sacri"</note>.

<margin>What the tearing of the veil through Christ signifies.</margin>

For since the way to the supercelestial world and the company of angels has been opened to us through the cross and blood of Christ, therefore, as He died, the veil of the temple was torn. By this veil, the Holy of Holies—which we said signifies the angelic world—was partitioned off from the other parts. This was a sign that the entrance to the kingdom of God, to God himself who "flies above the cherubim," now stands open to man—an entrance that had been closed from the beginning by the laws of justice due to the sin of our first parent <note>referring to Adam</note>. This is enough regarding the three worlds, in which this point especially must be greatly observed—upon which our entire intention depends—that these three worlds are **one world**.

<margin>The three worlds meet in one according to Anaxagoras, and the agreement of the Platonists and Pythagoreans.</margin>

They are one not only because they are all traced back to one beginning and to the same end, or because they are bound together by appropriate numbers, a certain harmonic kinship of nature, and an orderly series of degrees, but because whatever exists in all the worlds together is contained in each one individually. Nor is there any one world among them in which all things that are in the individual worlds do not exist. I believe this was the opinion of Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously taught that "everything is in everything."</note>, if we think his view was correctly explained afterward by the Pythagoreans and Platonists. Truly, the things that are in the lower world are also in the higher ones, but of a better quality; likewise, those things in the higher worlds are seen in the lowest, but in a degenerate condition and an adulterated—so to speak—nature. Heat is an elementary quality among us; in the celestial bodies, it is a heating power; in the angelic minds, it is an Idea of heat. 

<margin>An exemplar of the proposal.</margin>

Let me say something more expressively. Among us, there is fire, which is an element. The Sun is fire in heaven. In the ultra-mundane region <note>the realm beyond the physical universe</note>, there is the fire of the Seraphic intellect <note>Seraphim are the highest order of angels, associated with the fire of divine love.</note>. But see how they differ: the elementary fire burns, the celestial fire gives life, and the supercelestial fire loves. There is water among us; there is water in the heavens, the mover and mistress of this water, namely the moon, the threshold of the heavens. There are also waters above the heavens: the Cherubic minds <note>Cherubim are the second highest order of angels, associated with divine wisdom and "flowing" knowledge.</note>. But see the disparity of condition in the same nature: elementary moisture overwhelms the heat of life; celestial moisture nourishes it; supercelestial moisture understands it. In the first world, 

<margin>The ten spheres of the intellectual world.</margin>

God, the primary Unity, presides over the nine orders of angels as if over so many spheres, and being himself immovable, he moves all toward himself. In the middle world—that is, the celestial—the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most fire-like part of the heavens in medieval cosmology.</note> presides over nine celestial spheres like a leader over an army; 

<margin>The ten spheres of the celestial world.</margin>

and although each of these spheres revolves with unceasing motion, the Empyrean, imitating God, is motionless. There are also in the elementary world, after prime matter which is its foundation, 

<margin>The ten spheres of the elementary world.</margin>

nine spheres of corruptible forms. Specifically, three of bodies lacking life, which are the elements and the mixed things; then among these the middle ones, which are mixed but imperfect, such as the impressions <note>meteorological phenomena like rain or lightning</note> that occur on high. Three of a vegetative nature, which is first divided into three genera: herbs, shrubs, and trees. 

<margin>Body, Nature, Soul.</margin>

Three of the sensory soul, which is either imperfect, such as in the "Zoophytes" <note>organisms like sponges or corals that were thought to be half-plant, half-animal</note>, or perfect but within the limits of irrational imagination, or that which is highest in beasts and even capable of human training, which is like a middle ground...

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

<note>Though the header indicates a "Life" (biography), the text itself is the preface to Pico's "Heptaplus," a work of mystical philosophy. Early printed editions often combined his biography with his major works.</note>

...[is the mid]dle point between man and beast, just as the **Zoophyte** <note>original: "Zoophitum"; a term used in the Renaissance for organisms like corals or sea anemones that seemed to exist halfway between animals and plants.</note> is the middle between beast and plant. But of these things we have said more than is necessary; let us only add that the mutual containment <note>original: "mutuam continentiam"</note> of the worlds is indicated even in the Sacred Scriptures. 
<margin>In the Sacred Scriptures, there is also evidence of the worlds.</margin> For it is written in the Psalms that he "created the heavens in understanding" <note>Psalm 136:5</note>, and we read that "the angels of God are spirits and his ministers a flame of burning fire." For this reason, divine things are often given celestial names, and often even earthly ones: while they are figured now through stars, now through wheels and animals, and now through elements. Conversely, earthly things are often given celestial names. This is because these worlds are bound by the chains of harmony, and like their natures, they grant their names to one another with mutual generosity. 

From this principle (if perhaps someone has not yet noticed this) the entire discipline of **allegorical meaning** <note>The method of interpreting a text to reveal a hidden spiritual or moral meaning.</note> has flowed. Nor could the ancient fathers have fittingly represented some things by the figures of others, unless they had been taught the hidden—so to speak—friendships and affinities of all nature. Otherwise, there would be no reason why they should have represented this thing by this image, and another by that, rather than the opposite. But being knowledgeable of all things, and driven by that Spirit who not only knows all these things but made them, they very aptly figured the natures of one world through those things they knew corresponded to them in the remaining worlds. 
<margin>A fourth world is added to those above: that is, Man.</margin> Therefore, the same knowledge is needed (unless the same Spirit is present) for those who wish to correctly interpret their figures and allegorical meanings. However, besides the three worlds we have described, there is a **fourth world** in which all those things are found which are in the others. This is man himself, who, for this reason—as the Catholic doctors say—is considered in the Gospel under the name of "every creature." For while the Gospel is to be preached to men, and not to beasts and angels, Christ nevertheless commanded that it be preached to "every creature" <note>Mark 16:15</note>. It is a common saying in the schools <note>The universities of the time.</note> that man is a **lesser world** <note>original: "minorem mundum"; also known as the "microcosm," the idea that the human being is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note>, in whom is seen a body mixed from the elements, a celestial spirit, the vegetative soul of plants, the senses of beasts, reason, the angelic mind, and the likeness of God. 

<margin>That Moses treated all these worlds, and that this Scripture is the image of nature.</margin> If we establish these four worlds, it is credible that Moses, about to speak sufficiently of the world, discussed all of them. And since a writer portrays nature—if he is skilled in nature, as we believe this man of ours was if anyone was—it is credible that the doctrine concerning them was arranged no differently than the Almighty God, the Craftsman, arranged them in themselves. Thus, this writing of Moses is an expressed image of the world, just as we read that he was commanded on the mountain where he learned these things to "make all things according to the pattern he had seen on the mountain" <note>Exodus 25:40</note>. Therefore, the first thing, which is the greatest of all (as we have shown that what is in all worlds is contained in each), is that Moses, an imitator of nature, should never treat any of those worlds 
<margin>The root of the fourfold exposition.</margin> without treating all of them equally at the same time, under the same words and the same context. From this, a **fourfold exposition** <note>A method of interpretation that finds four distinct levels of meaning in a single text.</note> of the entire Mosaic reading immediately arises: so that, in the first place, we explain whatever is written there concerning the angelic and invisible world, making no mention at all of the others. In the second place, likewise, all things concerning the celestial world; then concerning this sublunary and corruptible world; fourthly, concerning the nature of man. For if the intelligible world <note>The world of ideas and angels, which can only be understood by the mind.</note>, for example, is never treated without the Scripture also warning us about the remaining worlds—just as that world contains all subsequent natures within itself—then we certainly can, and indeed must, interpret all the small parts concerning all of them. 

Furthermore, just as the natures, although they are contained interchangeably within each other, have nevertheless been allotted distinct, proper seats and certain peculiar laws; so also, if the fourfold nature is discussed in the same series of text in individual parts of the present work, it must nevertheless be believed 
<margin>The root of the fifth exposition.</margin> that the first nature is treated more specifically in the first part, and thereafter in the rest in the same order. From this, the necessity of a **fifth exposition** arises. To this is added the reason...

->a iiii<-

these things are distinct; yet, because there is no multitude which is not also one, they are bound together by a certain discordant concord and tied by multiform chains of connections.

<margin>Root of the sixth exposition</margin>
Since it is likely that Moses deals with this throughout his entire work, it calls us now, even against our will, to the sixth interpretation. In this, we will show that there are fifteen modes by which we can understand one thing as related or joined to another; and since there are neither more nor fewer than these, they are all so sufficiently and clearly expressed by the prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses as "the prophet."</note> that Aristotle never wrote anything more expressly concerning the nature of things. Finally, just as the Sabbath—that is, rest <note>original: "quies"</note>—follows the six days of creation, it is fitting that we too, after the orders of things distributed by God in the preceding sections, and after explaining their union, difference, covenants, and relationships, should touch upon some things in a seventh and "Sabbatarian" (if I may call it so) narration. This will concern the happiness of creatures and the return to God, which—through the Mosaic and Christian law—has been granted to man after his long exile due to the sin of our first parent. 

<margin>Root of the seventh exposition</margin>
Here we shall relate those things which Moses most clearly concealed in the present scripture concerning these matters: so that a most express prophecy might be read here openly concerning the coming of Christ, the progress of the Church, and the calling of the nations. Thus, this book is truly—if any other is such—"the book sealed with seven seals" <note>A reference to Revelation 5:1, implying the text contains hidden divine secrets.</note>, full of all doctrine and all mysteries. However, we will not imitate those who, having undertaken to explain this creation of the world, heaped up here everything disputed among philosophers and theologians concerning God, angels, matter, heaven, and the whole of nature. 

<margin>Isaac the Persian, Samuel Ophinides</margin>
In this, among the Hebrews, **Isaac the Persian** and **Samuel Ophinides** <note>Medieval Jewish commentators whose works Pico studied as part of his interest in the Kabbalah and Hebrew scholarship.</note> especially erred. Instead, we shall strive with all our might to declare only what the Mosaic letter itself intends, and what the context of the words either indicates or signifies. Nor, if we show that by the "firmament" is meant, for instance, the **eighth sphere** <note>In the cosmology of Pico's time, the eighth sphere was the level of the fixed stars, sitting above the seven planetary spheres.</note>, will we immediately begin a dispute about how it draws along the other spheres, by how many signs or images it is distinguished, or whether it rotates with a simple motion, or rather two, or more truly three. Or, if in any passage we say that the human soul is indicated, we will not digress to explain everything written about the soul; rather, we will note only those things about each subject, and that briefly and in passing, 

<margin>These writings are entrusted to the learned, not to those unrefined in philosophy.</margin>
of which the author seems to make express mention. I said "concisely and in passing" because it is not the aim of this work that those who have not learned these things elsewhere should first learn them here; rather, it is so that they may recognize what they already know to be true in the words of the prophet. Understanding how he has both included and concealed in a few words what they have read digested in the immense volumes of theologians and philosophers, they may hear the Lawgiver speaking with an "unveiled face." But if anyone, perhaps moved by a spirit of "holy simplicity" <note>original: "sanctae rusticitatis"; a phrase used to describe a simple, unlearned, but sincere faith.</note>, should not approve of these mysteries sought from so deep a source, but should instead wish for a simpler interpretation of the sacred context more suited to himself, I will first bid him 

<margin>Paul, Augustine</margin>
remember Paul's precept: that he who eats should not despise him who does not eat, and he who does not eat should not judge him who eats <note>Romans 14:3. Pico is using the metaphor of "eating" to refer to the consumption of complex intellectual or spiritual truths.</note>. Then I will address him not with my words, but with those of **Augustine** in his own exposition of Genesis, in this manner: 

<margin>The power of Scripture</margin>
"Grasp these things if you can; if you cannot yet, leave them to those who are stronger. But you, while the Scripture does not abandon your weakness and walks more slowly with you with a maternal step, may progress." For Scripture speaks in such a way that it mocks the proud with its height, terrifies the attentive with its depth, feeds the great with its truth, and nourishes the little ones with its affability. But let us return to our purpose; starting from this corruptible world which we inhabit, let us provide as much as we are able what we have promised. 

<margin>Pomerius</margin>
Otherwise, in great things, it is enough to have willed them; and as **Pomerius** <note>Julius Pomerius, a 5th-century Christian priest and author.</note> says, "the great effort toward great things is itself a success."

->The words of Moses to be explained.<-

These are the very words of the prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses as "the prophet," the traditional author of Genesis.</note> which we have undertaken to explain.

<margin>First day</margin> **I**N the beginning God created the heaven and the earth: but the earth was empty and void: and darkness was upon the face of the abyss: and the spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters: and God said let there be light and light was made: and God saw the light that it was good: and he divided the light from the darkness and he called the light day and the darkness night: and the evening and the morning were made one day. And God said let there be a firmament <term>firmament: In ancient cosmology, the solid dome of the sky that separated the waters above from the waters below.</term> in the midst of the waters: and let it divide the waters from the waters: and God made the firmament and divided the waters which were under the firmament from those which were above the firmament: and it was so: And God called the firmament heaven: and the evening and the morning were made the second day. And God said let the
<margin>Second day</margin> waters which are under the heaven be gathered together into one place and let the dry land appear: and it was so and God called the dry land Earth: and the gathering together of the waters he called Seas: and God saw that it was good: and he said let the earth bring forth green herbs: and those producing seed and the fruit-bearing tree making fruit according to its kind: whose seed is in itself upon the earth: and it was so and the earth brought forth green herbs and those producing seed according to their kind and the tree making fruit: and each having its own seed according to its species and God saw that it
<margin>Third day</margin> was good: and the evening and the morning were made the third day. And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven and let them divide the day and the night and let them be for signs and seasons and days and years that they may shine in the firmament of heaven: and illuminate the earth: and it was so and God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day: and the lesser light to rule the night and the stars and he placed them in the firmament of heaven that they might shine upon the earth: and rule the day and the night and divide the light and the darkness: and God saw that it was good: and the evening and
<margin>Fourth day</margin> the morning were made the fourth day. God also said let the waters bring forth the creeping thing <note>original: "reptile"</note> of a living soul and the winged creature above the earth under the firmament of heaven: And God created great whales and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth into their species: and every winged creature according to its kind: and God saw that it was good: and he blessed them saying. Increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea: and let the birds be multiplied upon the earth: and the
<margin>Fifth day</margin> evening and the morning were made the fifth day. And God said let the earth bring forth the living soul in its kind: cattle and creeping things and the beasts of the earth according to their species: and it was so: and God made the beasts of the earth according to their species: cattle and every creeping thing of the
<margin>Sixth day</margin> earth in its kind: and God saw that it was good and he said. Let us make man in our image and likeness and let him rule over the fish of the Sea and the winged creatures of heaven and the beasts of the whole earth and every creeping thing that moves on the earth: and God created man in his image and likeness in the image of God he created him.

Thus far we have undertaken to explain Moses. I have divided the whole exposition into seven books or treatises: rather to imitate Basil and Augustine <note>Saint Basil the Great and Saint Augustine both wrote famous commentaries on the creation story (the *Hexameron*).</note> than because the attention of the reader is refreshed by this frequent distinction as if by a pause. It happens that since there are seven expositions arranged in seven books and each individual book is divided into seven chapters, all things correspond to the seven days of creation. This was likewise done by us for a most fitting reason: so that just as the seventh day in Moses is the Sabbath <note>original: "sabbatum"</note> and the day of rest: so any exposition of ours in the seventh chapter may always be directed toward Christ: who is both the end of the law: and is our Sabbath, our rest, and our happiness.

# FIRST EXPOSITION ON THE ELEMENTARY WORLD.
## Book One, Chapter One.

<margin>
The principle of natural things: he places matter through three dimensions and privation.
</margin>
**N**atural Philosophers, who discourse on the nature of corruptible things <note>In this context, "corruptible" refers to everything in the physical world subject to change, decay, and death.</note>, establish their principles thus in general: that there is a raw matter, devoid of forms, capable indeed of receiving all forms, yet by its own nature deprived of all of them. Therefore, besides matter, they also make "privation" <note>original: *privationem*; a technical term in Aristotelian philosophy meaning the absence of a form that a substance is capable of having.</note> a principle of natural things. Furthermore, Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational for Renaissance thought.</note> added that matter is extended in a triple dimension of length, width, and height; so that, namely, corporeal things would not be said to arise from an incorporeal subject. Then they bring in the transmuting cause, which they call the "efficient cause." By its power, the matter being treated—which is potentially—may at some time become actually, just as soft and indefinite wax is transformed into various figures according to the whim of the one handling it, through the guidance and touch of the hand. But since nature does nothing rashly, but for the sake of achieving some good, the "final cause" <note>The purpose or "end goal" for which a thing exists or an action is performed.</note> immediately introduces itself.
<margin>
Efficient cause
End
Form
Dispositions of matter
</margin>
And the nearest end of the acting cause is the "form," which it draws out from the bosom of matter. Indeed, the agent acts and stirs with this purpose: that it may lead matter to the perfect habit of form. Whence "form" is the third principle established by Aristotle. However, this form cannot be drawn out from the womb of matter unless it is first influenced and prepared by suitable qualities. Around these, the entire labor of the craftsman and the entire duration of the action is consumed; the form itself shines forth instantly in an individual moment, like the prize for the labor. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they allegedly discussed philosophy while walking (*peripatētikos*).</note> call the craftsman himself a "cause" rather than a "principle." But the Platonists, always mindful of divine things, wish us to be warned:
<margin>
Natural agents are the organs of divine ones.
Organic and exemplary cause.
</margin>
that although natural agents alone appear to us as those which move, form, and transmute bodies, they are nonetheless not the primary causes of those things which are made, but rather instruments of the divine art, which they obey and serve. Just as the hands of a builder—even if they alone assemble, order, and transmute the house's materials of wood, stones, and cement—and nothing else is seen to be involved in the building of the house besides them; yet we know those hands are an instrument obedient and serving the art established in the mind of the architect, who, having conceived the house all at once, distributes it piece by piece and unfolds it in the unfeeling matter. Thus it happens that they add two causes: the "organic" <note>The instrument or tool used by the primary cause.</note> and the "exemplary" <note>The "blueprint" or ideal form in the mind of the creator.</note>. Nor do the Peripatetics deny this; rather, they confirm it, among whom that saying is common: "Every work of nature is a work of intelligence." These are the things they say in common regarding corruptible things; all of which Moses embraced in the work of the first day so that the most esteemed philosophers have said nothing regarding these things either more certainly or more aptly.

### Chapter Two

<margin>
The active cause is heaven; the material is earth, as said by the Stoics.
Varro said
Interpretation
Aristotle
Plato
</margin>
In the beginning, therefore, he established two causes: the agent and the matter—that is, that which is in act and that which is in potential. He calls the former "heaven" and the latter "earth." Our exposition is first attested by the authority of the Stoics, who called heaven the active cause and earth the material one, as Varro writes, not to mention the Greeks. Reason also attests to this. For matter is the most lowly of all natures, just as the earth is of all the elements; and they correspond in an entirely similar proportion: as the Peripatetics prove, heaven is the agent to matter and to the earth. But this "earth"—that is, matter—was "empty and void" <note>original: *inanis et vacua*; the Latin Vulgate translation of Genesis 1:2.</note> as Jerome translated, or "invisible and uncomposed" as the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated. All these terms indeed suit raw and formless matter, which, being devoid of all forms, is deservedly called empty and void, and is entirely uncomposed and invisible. Truly, the Hebrew words *tou* and *bou* <note>original: *tou et bou*; transliterations of the Hebrew *tohu* (formless/chaos) and *bohu* (void/empty).</note> which are read in this place are explained differently by many Hebrews. They interpret *Tou* indeed as a "brute thing," stunned or astonished. This is referred by them to the dark and deformed face of matter, for the reason that it renders us astonished when we direct our attention toward the knowledge of it; because of which Aristotle says it is known by "proportion," and Plato by a "bastard reason" <note>original: *notha ratione*; a phrase from Plato's *Timaeus* describing how we perceive prime matter, which is neither purely sensible nor purely intellectual.</note>.

<summary>Pico identifies the philosophical principles of matter, form, and cause within the opening verses of Genesis, harmonizing Aristotelian and Platonic thought. He argues that "Heaven" represents the active, formative cause and "Earth" represents the raw, potential matter (Tohu) of the physical world.</summary>
