<meta>This page continues the exposition of the first chapter of Genesis, moving from the definition of "Tohu" (emptiness) to "Bohu" (void/fullness). Pico is reconciling the Mosaic account of creation with Aristotelian physics, specifically the concepts of matter, form, and privation.</meta>

JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA

...they told us of it. But many explain **Bohu** <note>original: *Bou*; Referring to the Hebrew *Bohu* from the phrase *Tohu va-Bohu* (formless and empty) in Genesis 1:2.</note> from the power of the word’s beginning and the rudiment of form. Indeed, if we translate it word for word, it is **Bohu**, as if we were to say "in it is" or "something is in it." If we follow this, we will understand a form begun in it in potentiality, besides the subject. This is what not only <margin>Albertus, the Ancient [Peripatetics], Simeon</margin> Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who synthesized Aristotle with Christian thought.</note> and many Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked while teaching.</note> believed, but also the ancient Hebrews, as we clearly gather from the monuments of the most ancient **Simeon** <note>Likely referring to Rabbi Simeon ben Yohai, the traditional author of the Zohar.</note>. But in what way this "beginning" is to be understood, he declares by adding: *and darkness was upon the face of the abyss.* <margin>Abyss, Darkness, What Privation is</margin> He calls the **Abyss** "earth," that is, matter extended into the deepest depths by a triple dimension. Upon this is **darkness**, which is **privation** <term>Privation: in Aristotelian philosophy, this is the absence of a quality or form that a thing should naturally possess.</term>—a principle famously celebrated among the Peripatetics, to which no name is more fitting than "darkness."

<margin>The origin of form is seen from the arrangement of matter</margin> But privation, as the great Albertus most consistently maintains, differs from negation in that it is this very "beginning of form" of which we speak; a matter on which the same philosopher has discoursed copiously and subtly. Furthermore, if the earth lies beneath the waters and, being irrigated from there, brings forth what it finally gives birth to: will not the "waters" in this place signify the accidental qualities and affections of matter? These, by their own flux and tractable nature, bear the appearance of waters. By these, so to speak, the moistened matter gives birth to the **form**, which it brings forth into the light at the final moment of time. <margin>Light has its origin from the appearance of form</margin> Upon these waters the **spirit of the Lord**—that is, the power of the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being.</note>, the organ and instrument of the Lord—is deservedly said to be "carried." It is not said to be carried over the "earth" because the agent does not touch or permeate the subject except through those intervening qualities. While it turns and moves these qualities, **light** arises—that is, the appearance of form and the beauty that expels and puts to flight the darkness we mentioned (that is, privation). <margin>Evening and morning: one effect</margin> And it is done by the voice of God thus commanding: because natural causes do nothing that the order of divine art has not commanded. Then, from **evening and morning** one day is made: when, from the nature of potentiality and act, a third substance—which we call a "composite"—has leaped forth. And the reason is now manifest, according to this sense, why he said "one day" and not "the first day"; and deservedly he saw the light, because it was **good**. For the nature of form is nothing other than a thin image and shadowy likeness of the **First Good**. <margin>Epilogue. A proposition against Aristotle</margin> Thus far, we have spoken in general about corruptible substance <note>Substance that can change, decay, or die.</note>, such as everything that exists below the moon. There we have seen both the "heaven" and the "earth"—that is, the transmuting nature and that which is transmuted; and the same "earth"—that is, matter—void and empty of every specific substance and likewise of every accidental form. We saw the darkness of privation sitting upon that abyss extended in three dimensions—not indeed within the innermost part of it (for **privation** is not the essence of matter, as Aristotle proves), but occupying its outermost face. <margin>Explanation of the Spirit of the Lord</margin> We likewise saw the **Spirit of the Lord** carried over the "waters"—that is, the fluid dispositions of matter, as if present to the earth—not as the principal cause, but as the Spirit of the Lord, that is, the organ of divine art, just as our vital spirit is the organ of the soul. And immediately, as the Spirit handled those waters and pervaded the subject, by the command of God the Craftsman, **light** arose—that is, the beauty and splendor of form.

### Chapter Three.

<margin>Aristotle. What we understand by the "waters" on the second day</margin> Since, however, we correctly descend from common and general things to specific ones, as Aristotle proves, Moses, intending to do the same, after speaking of those things which are common to all elementary things, divides the entire elemental substance into three parts on the second day. First, however, it must be understood that all material forms are designated by him here under the name of **waters**; a more fitting comparison could not even be made. For in this sphere of the rule of things that are born and die, matter stands like a sea-bed, while there is a perpetual and ceasing flow and ebb of waves—the coming and going of forms. <margin>Solomon. The Platonists: imitators of the Hebrews</margin> As **Solomon** says: *one generation passes away and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever.* <note>Quoting Ecclesiastes 1:4.</note> For these forms are also called "waters" among the **Platonists**, who were always imitators of the Hebrew discipline.

<summary>Pico explains the first day of Creation as a metaphor for Aristotelian physics, where "darkness" represents privation and "light" represents the emergence of physical form from raw matter. He argues that Moses’s account follows a logical scientific progression from general principles to specific elemental divisions.</summary>

First part
Second

...of discipline, or rather generations of forms, which may more truly be said to be in a state of "becoming" than of "being." For this same reason, just as he used the name "waters" above to refer to the qualities of matter and accidental forms, he here uses it to refer to the material substances themselves. This was to remind us—not of what Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (active c. 200 AD), a celebrated commentator on Aristotle.</note> believed, namely that qualities themselves are the substantial forms for the elements—but of what the Platonists strongly affirm: that every species found in matter should be considered more as an accident <term>Accident: a property that does not belong to the essence of a thing (like being "blue" vs. being "a person").</term> than a true substance. For those things alone can legitimately claim the title of substance which stand by themselves, leaning on nothing but their own nature, and are true by their own reason, unmixed with foreign things and entirely unadulterated. Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 535–475 BC), a pre-Socratic philosopher famous for the idea that everything is in flux.</note> called the substance of sensible things "the sea," and among the poets who veil philosophy in the flights of fables: when, after the Saturnian unity <note>The "Saturnian unity" refers to the Golden Age or the intelligible world where all things are unified under Saturn (Cronus).</note>—that is, the union of the intelligible world enfolding all things within itself—they divided the sensible world into three parts, they assigned the celestial region to Jupiter, the subterranean to Pluto, and the middle region—stretching from the Moon to the Earth, which we are now discussing—to Neptune. They called Neptune the "Lord of the Sea," and among the Platonists, he is understood as the power that presides over the generations of living things.

But let us return to Moses dividing the waters from the waters by means of the firmament. For there is a triple partition of sublunary bodies <note>Sublunary bodies: objects in the region below the moon, subject to change and decay.</note>. Some are above the middle region of the air; these are the highest parts of that same element and the purest fire, all of which is designated by the name "Ether." There, the elements are pure, unmixed, and in their true state. Others are below the middle of the air, which are here with us, where no element is pure. For no pure element is perceptible to the senses; rather, all things here are mixed and composed of the drossy and thicker parts of the worldly body. The intervening region of the air is what is called here the **firmament**; hence, birds are described as flying "under the firmament of heaven." This is the region where those "sublime impressions" appear: rain, snow, lightning, thunder, comets, and others of that kind. See how rightly this firmament distinguishes and separates the upper elements from the lower, as if "waters from waters," not only by its position but by its natural property. Above it, the elements are pure; below it, they depart from elemental simplicity through a perfect mixing; within it, they are mixed but imperfectly and in a middle state, so that it may most truly be called a middle ground between the nature of elements and the nature of mixed bodies.

### Chapter Four.

<margin>
How the earth was thus separated from the multitude of waters
Why the earth produced plants
</margin>
But let us see what Moses philosophizes further. He says: *let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear.* "Dry land" is matter, as we have already established, and matter does not "appear" or become visible unless it is clothed in the appearance of forms. But it does not appear even when clothed in the form of a simple element; for, as we have said and as the philosophers prove, a simple element can neither be seen nor touched, nor fall under any sense at all. Therefore, if the earth (which was previously invisible) is to come into view, it is necessary for the waters under the heaven—that is, under the middle region of the air—to be gathered into one place; that is, flowing together into a common mass of mixture, yet bound by certain laws like prescribed shores, to coalesce into a single form of mixture. This happens to the "lower waters," as we have shown, but not to the "upper" ones, where there is either no mixture at all or an imperfect one. Since the vegetative soul <note>original: *anima uegetalis*; the lowest level of the soul in Aristotelian biology, responsible for growth, nutrition, and reproduction.</note> immediately follows this form, what else should we expect from our philosopher than that, after the gathering of those waters, he should immediately introduce the fruitful production of herbs, shrubs, and trees?

### Chapter Five.

Although from here the logical order seemed to require a transition to animals, whose soul is most closely joined to the vegetative soul, nevertheless, because one proceeds from animals to man—in whom all treatment of the corruptible world ends—Moses therefore inserted something concerning those things which occur in the firmament, and with which it is adorned, just as the earth is adorned by those things produced in it: metals, plants, and living creatures. These are those "impressions" which occur on high—that is, in the middle region of the air. Above this, the heaven...

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

<margin>What the firmament is</margin> ...what he called the firmament and what he called the sky; here, however, he calls it the "firmament of heaven," so that we might know it is not that which truly exists, but that which lies beneath heaven. For this reason, <margin>Ennius</margin> Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC), an early Roman poet often cited by later philosophers.</note> in his *Achilles* called this part "lying beneath," because it is situated closest to heaven. That these "impressions" <note>original: "impressiones" — in Renaissance science, this referred to atmospheric phenomena like comets or meteors.</note>—secondary stars, constellations, and heavenly bodies—are so named by philosophers is well enough known that it need not be proven with many arguments, nor should it seem too difficult for someone to set forth what is said here about the stars. <margin>Two primary causes</margin> But since all their diversity is referred to two primary causes, heat and cold, we shall conveniently refer those which are hot by nature to the Sun, and those which are cold to the Moon. Nor is it only for this reason that both the Sun and Moon and the other stars claim this name for themselves—that they are the same in the lower heaven as those others are in their own more divine heaven; or because they show themselves to men with a similar appearance, shining and sparkling alike; but rather because some of them follow another star in the heaven as their leader and guide. Hence, they are also signs of those things: for stars are accustomed to portend in lower things those events by which they were excited. A proof of this is that they follow the motion of the stars, by whose force and influence they consist of matter composed of earth—that is, a vaporous exhalation.

### Chapter six.

What follows regarding the production of animals and man is now manifest. For after plants, those things are mixed which feel and move; <margin>Opinion of the Pythagoreans</margin> although the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed in a universal soul and the interconnectedness of all living things.</note> also attribute a dull sense to plants: a matter we shall discuss with the help of a longer "seat" <note>A metaphor for a detailed academic discussion.</note> in that concord which we are bringing forth. Now these living things, which without any controversy participate in motion and sense, are distinguished here <margin>Timaeus</margin> by Moses and in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> as those that fly, those that live in water, and those that dwell on land. Supreme among all and the prince is man: at whom the corruptible nature of the world stops its progress and "sounds the retreat" <note>A military metaphor meaning that nature has reached its final goal in the creation of humanity.</note>.

### Chapter seven

<margin>Christ our happiness</margin> Just as man is the absolute consummation of all lower things, so Christ is the absolute consummation of all men. Because, as the philosophers say, from that which is most perfect in every genus all perfection is derived to the others of the same order as if from a fountain; there is no doubt to anyone that the perfection of all goodness is derived from Christ the man into all men. To him alone, surely, the spirit was given "not by measure," so that we might all receive from his fullness. See how undoubtedly this prerogative belongs to God and man; which also, insofar as he is man, fits him by a peculiar and legitimate privilege.

# SECOND EXPOSITION ON THE CELESTIAL WORLD.
## PREFACE.

<margin>Three reasons why Moses wrote figuratively</margin> **S**Vrgamus <note>original: "Surgamus" (Let us rise). The large decorative 'S' marks the beginning of a major new section.</note> Let us rise from the elements to the heaven; from corruptible to incorruptible bodies: so that it may be clear to all that by the same words through which the whole of nature was shown to us in the elemental world, the highest dogmas have likewise been grasped by the prophet concerning the celestial realms. When we revolve this in our mind, there will be, besides what we said in the prefaces, another reason ready at hand for us. Why, for instance, when Moses was about to speak of the acting cause and of matter, did he not call that the "acting cause" and this "matter" in express words, but called them "heaven and earth"? And the dispositions of matter, he called not "qualities" as the philosophers do, but "waters"; and he called the form "light" rather than "form." Likewise, he named comets and lightning and other things of that kind not by their own names, but called them "heavenly bodies" and "stars"; and so on with the rest. In the beginnings, indeed, it was suggested by us that both the ancient custom of writing great physical and divine matters was secret and figurative, and also the ignorance of the listeners who, since they could not bear the splendor of the Mosaic teaching, required him to speak to them with a veiled face, lest he blind with excessive light those he undertook to illuminate. Now we have the opportunity for a third reason: because, namely, if he had named matter and form and qualities and the acting cause, it might have served for treatises on the corruptible world, but not for the rest. Therefore, it is unthought...

...and the truly divine, not human, industry and **wonderful craftsmanship of Moses** <margin>Wonderful</margin> in using such expressions and <margin>Moses'</margin> arranging his discourse in such a way that the same words, the same context, and the same sequence of the whole scripture suitably fits the secrets of <margin>craftsmanship</margin> all the worlds and of all nature which are to be represented. This is that in which the book of Moses surpasses the learning, eloquence, and genius of all nations. This is that new and <margin>Most absolute</margin> hitherto untouched thing which we have attempted to bring forward: namely, to prove to our men by the thing itself that this was done by Moses. This is the idea, this is the pattern of the **most absolute writer**; not only because this kind <margin>kind of writing</margin> of writing (as we demonstrated above) portrays and emulates nature—for just as among the angelic minds, according to the authority of <margin>Dionysius</margin> Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose works on celestial hierarchies were central to Renaissance thought.</note> and Saint <margin>Saint Thomas</margin> Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note>, that [mind] is supreme in the <margin>Dionysius</margin> splendor of our theology which comprehends all things through intelligence <margin>Saint Thomas in Latin</margin> in the fewest notions and forms, while the lower minds do so through varied and multiple ones—so among scriptures, that one is supreme and <margin>Theology's</margin> <margin>brightness, not</margin> holds the peak of all perfection which embraces all things with the fewest words, as if they were individual parts, both congruously and <margin>unjustly</margin> profoundly. Yet before we hear him speaking, it will be useful to preface a few things about the tenth heaven, so that we may be more capable of receiving his words.

### Chapter One.

<margin>That there is a tenth sphere or celestial globe, which</margin> Above the nine celestial spheres—that is, the seven planets, the eighth sphere which they call the "fixed" <note>The sphere of the stars that appear not to move relative to one another.</note>, and the ninth sphere which was discovered by reason rather than the senses and is the first among moving bodies—it is believed that there is a **tenth heaven**, remaining fixed and quiet, which partakes in no motion. <margin>theologians call the Empyrean,</margin> Nor is this only believed by our men, especially the more recent ones like Strabo <note>Walafrid Strabo, a 9th-century Carolingian scholar.</note> and Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk and scholar.</note>, but <margin>according to Strabo and Bede, as well as Abraham and</margin> also by many of the Hebrews, and furthermore by certain philosophers and mathematicians. Of whom it shall be enough to bring forward two: Abraham the Spaniard <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish polymath and astronomer.</note>, the greatest astrologer, and Isaac the philosopher; both of whom attest to this. Indeed, this Isaac understands the tenth sphere to be designated by Ezekiel <margin>Ezekiel</margin> through the **Sapphire** in the likeness of a throne: so that the color of the sapphire signifies the brightness of the light, and the likeness of the <margin>Isaac through the Sapphire</margin> throne signifies its immobility. Likewise, he understands the ten spheres to be symbolized by Zechariah through the golden lampstand <margin>Ezekiel</margin> distinguished by seven lamps, and a bowl above its head, and then two olives above the bowl. For since the seven lamps indicate the seven planets, and the bowl indicates the eighth circle shining with so many lights, he wants the ninth and tenth spheres to be indicated by the two olives, because oil flows down from the olives to the bowl and the lamps for the nourishment of the light. Therefore, by an analogy of reason with the heavens that we see, light <margin>they established</margin> emanates from those highest ones and is preserved (for he who gives light also preserves it). Justly, those [higher spheres] are compared to olives, while these [lower ones] are compared to lamps and the bowl. But if <margin>Note</margin> two primary fountains of the same water cannot be established, it is necessary that one of those two highest spheres be the principle of all light. <margin>In what way light descends from the first to the lowest sphere</margin> If it is to be referred to either, it must surely be to the first—that is, the tenth—so that it is itself, as it were, the **unity of lights**; then the ninth receives the light next, in the whole essence of its substance. From there, it reaches the Sun thirdly in full participation; and from the Sun, now in the fourth and therefore final degree, it is divided among all the stars in parts. Therefore, above the nine heavens let us establish a tenth, which theologians call the **Empyrean**. Moreover, it has been doubted by some whether its nature is corporeal or rather incorporeal. For perhaps it is fitting for unity that, just as there is an analogy of nature <margin>The reason for these things</margin> corresponding to the elemental number, so it should not be of the same kind. But whatever may be decided on this question, let it remain unshaken: that there are the treasures of light, and from there whatever light is seen in physical bodies is derived, as if from a primary fountain into the others. <margin>Julian the Emperor</margin> For it does not stand in the way if someone more obstinately (or rather more truly) wishes to believe that it is not of a truly corporeal nature, since in the theology of the Phoenicians—as Julian the Emperor <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363), who wrote a Neoplatonic hymn to the Sun.</note> writes in his *Oration on the Sun*—corporeal light emanates from an incorporeal nature. This tenth heaven, therefore, presides over the nine heavens succeeding each other in a consequential series, like a leader to an army or a form to matter; and bearing the type of the **Monad** <note>The Monad (Unity) was the Pythagorean symbol for the source of all things.</note>, it completes the decade.

## Chapter Two.

<margin>
Explanation
of the words
of the prophet:
"Heaven and
Earth"
</margin>
Let us come to Moses, who, when about to speak concerning all things, deigned to use the name "Heaven" <note>original: "caeli"</note> here particularly for that which is first and principal. In the same way, although there are nine angelic choirs, we are able to call them "gods" because they participate in divinity—whence comes that phrase, *God of gods*. Nevertheless, when we say "God" in an absolute sense, we do not mean any one of them, but the undivided Trinity presiding over them, just as the **Empyrean heaven** <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the universe in medieval cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God.</note> presides over the nine orbits subject to it. But he called the eight final spheres "Earth." This was not done without cause, but because the extremes of this number claim the name of "earth" for themselves. These are the Moon and the Starry Heaven <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, the eighth sphere in the Ptolemaic system.</note>; we are compelled to call both of these "earth" both by the authority of the ancients and by reason.

<margin>
Concerning the
eighth sphere:
the opinion of
the Pythagoreans,
the Academics,
and Aristotle
</margin>
For concerning the eighth sphere, it was very frequent in the Academy <note>The followers of Plato.</note> to give it the name of "earth." Likewise, **Aristotle** said the Moon was similar to earth, imitating the **Pythagoreans**, who call it both a "celestial earth" and a "terrestrial heaven." But see what reasoning leads us to both: for if we seek the elements in the heavens, we establish the Moon as the "earth," the lowest and most ignoble of all the stars, just as the earth is of all the elements; it is likewise similar to it in its opacity of substance and its spots. Then we call **Mercury** "water," the "changing-skin" and transformable star; for this reason, in **Lucan** <note>Marcus Annaeus Lucanus (39–65 AD), a Roman poet.</note>, it is called the "ruler of the waves." We call **Venus** "air,"

<margin>
Lucan
Interpretation
of the Stars
</margin>
vivifying with temperate heat; the **Sun** is "fire" for the most manifest reason. Then, in inverse order: **Mars** is "fire"; **Jupiter** is "air," related to Venus in nature; **Saturn** is "water," an old man of condemned frigidity. It remains that we call the eighth sphere—the non-wandering one—"earth," as the very order of the calculation requires. Correct, therefore, is this whole [region] which is enclosed by two earths on either side; that above which nothing is visible to us, he called "earth."

<margin>
The light is the
receptacle of
many powers
</margin>
Then he adds: *And the earth was empty and void*—empty, that is, of light, which had not yet been propagated to it from the first heaven, and empty of the remaining powers <note>original: "virtutum", referring to spiritual or astrological influences.</note> for which light is the vehicle. Nor do we say this of ourselves, but the author himself declares of what thing he speaks regarding "emptiness," adding: *And darkness was upon the face of the abyss.* Rightly he calls such a great altitude, such a number of orbits, and such wonderful profundity the **Abyss**.

<margin>
What is the
Abyss?
</margin>
<margin>
Ephrem the
Syrian
</margin>
<margin>
Through the
crystalline: the

of the Lord, etc.
</margin>
Truly, lest we should believe there is nothing in the middle between the eighth sphere and the Empyrean seats—as many have believed, following only the evidence of the senses—he warned us of an intervening orbit. This, since he himself figured it through "the waters," has been named the **Crystalline Heaven** by more recent [thinkers]. Over this was borne—or, as the Hebrew truth has it and **Ephrem the Syrian** <note>A 4th-century theologian and poet.</note> translated, *was incubating* <note>original: "incubabat". Pico highlights the Hebrew word 'merachephet', suggesting a bird brooding over eggs to bring forth life.</note>—the Spirit of the Lord. That is, the spiritual Olympus, the seat of the spirits of the Lord, properly adhering to it, was cherishing it with its vivifying light. And it was rightly done that what is nearest to the beginning of light should drink in light with its whole body and its whole mass; it is invisible to us because it is not terminated by a more solid thickness. Therefore, the Empyrean, "incubating" first upon it, bestowed its light, which soon—at God's command—was derived into the remaining spheres which we say are designated by "the earth" and "the abyss," the darkness having been shaken off. *And there was evening and morning, one day*, because through the reception of light and supernal influx, the lower parts of heaven are allied to the first. In summary, therefore, on the first day, the eminence of the first heaven over the rest and the derivation of light to them is indicated through the names of "water" and "earth," according to the properties of the ninth orbit and the others.

### Chapter III.

<margin>
One Day
</margin>
<margin>
Epilogue: the
firmament
between the

</margin>
Now, indeed, pronouncing particularly concerning the moved orbits, he teaches that the non-wandering sphere, which we call the **Firmament**, is in the middle between two waters. The reason for this saying is manifest from what we have said; for both the ninth orbit and the planet Saturn, as we have declared, claim the name of "waters" for themselves. Therefore, the Firmament was placed by God in the midst of the waters. And *the waters which are under the heaven were gathered together into one place*, and it was done so *that the dry land*—that is, the earth—*might appear*, and all this was provided for the safety of living things.

<margin>
From which
comes the
gathering of
the waters
</margin>
Let us see what these words of Moses mean. The waters which are under the heaven are the **seven stars** [planets] which are under the firmament (which he called "heaven"), of which the first is Saturn. These waters are "gathered into one place" for this reason: because the power of all the planets is collected in the one **Sun**, which all philosophers and all mathematicians confirm with one voice...

<meta>This page continues Pico's "Second Exposition" of Genesis, focusing on the celestial world. Having previously identified the "waters" and "heavens," he now identifies the "Earth" mentioned in Genesis with the Moon and explains why Moses seemingly omits four of the seven known planets.</meta>

# HEPTAPLUS

<margin>Oceanus</margin>
If this gathering of waters is called the "sea," it is not absurd that this will be that **Ocean** <note>In Greek mythology, Oceanus was the divine personification of the sea, often called the "father of gods and men." Pico is linking this classical idea to the celestial waters of Genesis.</note> which is called the father of gods and men by those who dignify the planets with the names of gods. <margin>The Earth appears</margin> Moreover, what else shall we say the **Earth** is but the **Moon**, which was so named by **Aristotle** and the **Pythagoreans**? <note>Pythagoreans often viewed the Moon as a "celestial earth" because of its solid appearance and perceived similarities to our world.</note> While it was overwhelmed by the waves of the aforementioned sea, it was neither useful nor visible to us. But it became fit for the uses of animals and for our own needs when, withdrawing from that sea, it came more and more into view. Then it became fertile and fecund, especially in those things that arise from a vegetative nature, whose gifts are growth, nutrition, and generation. For the chief power of the Moon lies in these things, as the **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologers and sages highly regarded by Renaissance thinkers for their supposed secret wisdom.</note> have said. This is most clearly demonstrated here by Moses, since as soon as the Moon appears, he makes it the parent of grasses, shrubs, and trees. See how he has indicated the nature of the Moon and Sun to us in very few words and through figurative language.

<margin>Why there is no mention of the four planets</margin>
But why is he silent regarding the remaining planets, when we promised in our introductions to provide a sufficient and learned treatise on all of them? And why, when he mentioned the tenth, ninth, and eighth spheres, as well as Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon, did he not say even a word about the four that remain: **Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, and Mars**?

<margin>First solution</margin>
Perhaps you will say this was done because an unrefined people <note>Referring to the ancient Israelites to whom Moses was writing, who were often thought by Renaissance scholars to be incapable of understanding complex astronomy.</note> knew only the Sun and the Moon. <margin>Refutation</margin> But I have already taken this refuge away from myself; nor can I turn there without blushing, for I have attested above that almost nothing was omitted by Moses that contributes to the perfect understanding of all the worlds.

<margin>Second solution</margin>
Another might say that by dealing with the Sun and Moon, he dealt with the rest: because these two hold the kingdom of heaven, and while the power of the others is particular, these two stars prevail with a universal influence. <margin>Refutation</margin> But this does not satisfy us either; for by the same reasoning, he should have omitted Saturn, of whom we have nevertheless shown mention was made.

<margin>Third solution</margin>
I believe a deeper mystery of the ancient teaching of the Hebrews lies hidden here. Among their dogmas concerning the heavens, this is primary: that **Jupiter and Mars are enclosed within the Sun**, while **Venus and Mercury are enclosed within the Moon**. <margin>Affinity of the Sun with Jupiter and Mars</margin> Nor is the reason for this opinion obscure if we weigh the natures of these stars, even if the Hebrews themselves offer no reason for their dogma. Jupiter is hot, Mars is hot, and the Sun is also hot. But the heat of Mars is sharp and violent, while that of Jupiter is beneficial. In the Sun, we see that sharp and violent quality of Mars and the beneficial property of Jupiter—that is, a certain intermediate nature tempered from these two, so to speak. Jupiter is fortunate, Mars is unfortunate; the Sun is partly good and partly bad—good in its radiation, but bad in its close proximity. Aries is the house of Mars, and Cancer is the dignity <note>In traditional astrology, "dignity" or "exaltation" refers to a sign where a planet's influence is particularly harmonious or strengthened.</note> of Jupiter; the Sun, having attained its highest point in Cancer and its dignity in Aries, shows a manifest kinship with both stars. <margin>Affinity of the Moon with Venus and Mercury</margin> Let us come to the Moon, which clearly participates in the "waters" of Mercury; and how great an affinity it has with Venus is indicated especially by this: that the Moon is so exalted in Taurus (the domicile of Venus) that it is judged to be nowhere more happy or beneficial. <margin>Epilogue</margin> Therefore, concerning the Empyrean heaven, the ninth sphere, the firmament, the star of Saturn, and the Sun and Moon (which embrace the rest), he has spoken sufficiently so far, reminding us of this "embrace" by his very silence.

### ->Chapter Four.<-

<margin>Timaeus</margin>
It remained that after he had spoken of the nature of the stars, he should discourse on their works and office, declaring for what use they were founded and to what duty they were delegated by God. Know, however, that the discussion is still about the heaven as a luminous body; nothing has yet been said by the prophet about its intellect or its moving power, which is an order that **Timaeus** <note>A reference to Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*, which describes the creation of the physical universe.</note> also follows: first fashioning the body, then adding the soul to the completed body. Two operations of the celestial bodies are manifest in the universe: **motion** and **illumination**. <margin>Motion</margin> Motion is established as twofold: one is that of the whole world, by which the heaven and the ether are revolved through the whole space of the universe in a completed circuit in twenty-four hours. <margin>Illumination</margin> The other is the proper, manifold, and various motion of the stars, among which the principal is the motion of the Sun, which circles all the signs of the **Zodiac** in the space of twelve months. The former makes the day (whence it is called "diurnal"); the latter makes the year. The motions of the other stars are completed in various intervals of time. Rightly and briefly, therefore, Moses reminded us of all these when he said the stars were placed in the firmament for **days, years, and times**. He added **for signs**, which, because it is sufficiently explained by other interpreters, I pass over. He indicated moreover...

<summary>Pico explains that Moses omits four planets because they are "enclosed" within the Sun and Moon, and he begins discussing the functions of the heavens: motion and illumination.</summary>

# THE WRITINGS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Averroes</margin>
<margin>Abraham</margin>
<margin>Avicenna</margin>
<margin>Babylonians</margin>
<margin>Influence on lower things</margin>
...what the celestial body contributes to the other operations of the stars, which is illumination, when he [Moses] said those decrees were "to shine in the heavens and illuminate the earth." Although there are diverse opinions among the ancients regarding how the celestial bodies influence lower things, the words of Moses fit any of them clearly. For if they influence nothing other than light—which **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose physical theories dominated Medieval and Renaissance thought. He generally held that the heavens affect the earth primarily through light and motion.</note> seems to have intended, if we interpret his words with a reverent rather than a biased judgment—nothing could be thought more consistent with the Mosaic sayings. If, besides light, they also influence heat and nothing else—as **Averroes the Arab** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a Muslim philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Western universities.</note> and **Abraham the Jew** <note>Likely referring to Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a polymath and astrologer.</note> maintain—it was enough to have spoken of the light from which these same authors admit heat proceeds. Likewise, if many other and manifold powers are sent down from the heavens, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher.</note> and the **Babylonians** believe, it was not by chance that mention was made of light alone; for as Avicenna himself writes, it is light alone which carries all other powers from heaven to us. Into these ministries, therefore, the bodies of the moon, the sun, and the stars are distributed.

## Chapter Five

<margin>Signs of the eighth and ninth spheres</margin>
It remained for him [Moses] to make mention of the signs which are visible in the **Zodiac**, and those which, though invisible to us, are far more effective in the **crystalline heaven**. <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the crystalline heaven (the ninth sphere) was placed above the starry firmament to account for certain astronomical motions.</note> Concerning these things, nothing has been said until now. This, therefore, is what is meant by the "living creatures" which the waters produce and the earth produces: namely, those waters which are above the heavens and that earth which is the **firmament** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> itself, as was proven above. For the signs which are seen in those two spheres alone are in the likeness of animals—such as those noted among us by the **Egyptians** and **Indians**. <margin>Celestial signs noted by Egyptians and Indians</margin> They were able to perceive these more easily and correctly than our people, aided by the flatness of the soil and the clarity of the sky. Otherwise, the production of animals which are perishable here on earth pertains no more to these two elements, earth and water, than to the others, namely fire and air. And since he [Moses] gave the name of "water" to the crystalline sphere, he appropriately called the animals there "fish"; likewise, those in the firmament, which he calls "earth," he called "beasts" and "cattle."

## Chapter Six.

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
<margin>Timaeus</margin>
Thus far concerning the bodily nature of the heavens. Now, being about to declare that they are endowed with a rational soul, he mentions "man" allegorically—not indeed that man who is perishable and earthly and whom we see, but the one by whom, as **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who emphasized the soul's governance over the body.</note> says, the man who is seen is governed. That is the rational soul itself; since **Timaeus** <note>The title character of Plato's dialogue "Timaeus," which describes the creation of the world and the soul using the metaphor of a mixing bowl (*patera*).</note> constitutes it from the same elements and in the same mixing bowl from which he also constitutes the soul of the heavens, what is said concerning the soul of man is not inappropriately transferred also to the soul of heaven. Sacred Scripture supports our exposition, in which the whole angelic and rational nature is often designated by "man." This is most frequent in the prophets regarding good angels; and regarding the evil demon, who differs from them in nature not at all, it is written in the Gospel: "An enemy man has done this." <note>A reference to the Parable of the Weeds in Matthew 13:28.</note> God therefore added to the celestial machine a living and rational substance, a participant of Intellect. Therefore, He willed this substance, according to His image and likeness, to preside over those animals we spoke of a little earlier—that is, over all the starry signs and planets. <margin>All celestial things must obey their mover</margin> These turn at its nod and obey its word with no delay or defiance, which does not happen equally in the brute bodies of the elements. Nor will you find anything else over which the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> labor more than to prove that the celestial body does not resist its "mover" in the way our bodies resist us. Wherefore, they experience neither weariness, difficulty, nor fatigue from perpetual motion as we do. This is the "dominion over the animals" which Moses touched upon regarding the celestial man. <margin>Epilogue</margin> Nor is it without mystery that he created that man "male and female." For it is the prerogative of the celestial souls that they perform both duties at once: both contemplating and ruling bodies, without the one being a hindrance or obstacle to the other. This is used especially by the ancients; even in the **Orphic hymns**, <note>A collection of ancient Greek poems attributed to the mythical singer Orpheus, highly regarded by Renaissance Neoplatonists as "pious" secret wisdom.</note> we observe these two powers in the same substance—one of which contemplates and the other presides over the body—designated by the names "male" and "female." These things concerning the celestial world...

<summary>Pico explains that celestial influence is carried through light and argues that the "animals" mentioned in Genesis are actually the constellations of the Zodiac. He further interprets the creation of "man" as an allegory for the rational soul that governs the heavens with both contemplative (male) and active (female) powers.</summary>

...division of the body, the number of spheres, their nature and properties, and their office. Finally, they treat the moving force of the heaven—its rational substance—and its character, as handed down by the prophet.

### Chapter VII.

<margin>To what extent we should honor heaven, according to Plato</margin>
This is a noble creature, to be looked upon by us with awe and celebrated. But if we consider the opinion of **Plato** <note>The Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BC). Pico often harmonizes Platonic philosophy with Christian theology.</note>—to say nothing of the theologians—whom we just mentioned and have not forgotten, our souls were tempered by God the Maker in the same mixing bowl and from the same elements as the celestial souls. Let us take care, then, that we do not wish to be the servants of those to whom nature intended us to be brothers. Nor should we measure our condition by this weak body. For man—as written in the *Alcibiades* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato which argues that the "soul is the man," while the body is merely its instrument.</note>—is not this fragile and earthly thing we see, but is the soul; he is the intellect which exceeds the entire circuit of heaven and the whole course of time. We must therefore be careful—as many do—not to give more to heaven than is necessary, attributing so much to it that we resist both the will of the Maker and the order of the universe. In doing so, we might even displease heaven itself, which holds God's counsel and the world's order most dear, even while we strive to please it.

<margin>How Macrobius considers it to have a more divine soul and to be primarily spiritual</margin>
The **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers and astrologers often associated with the "Chaldean Oracles," a text Pico highly valued.</note> warn of this when they say: 
<margin>Chaldeans</margin>
"Do not increase fate." **Jeremiah** <note>A biblical prophet (7th century BC).</note> proclaims this as well: "Do not fear the signs of heaven which the nations fear." Our prophet **Moses** commands this elsewhere, warning that man must be careful, when looking up at the sun, moon, and stars, not to worship those things which God created for the service of all nations.

<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
But if someone does not accept the sense that those things serve us like ignoble and dead bodies, let us nevertheless understand it to mean that the author or master of our nature cannot be a substance whose even "better" part is found to be more ignoble than some "lower" part of ourselves.

<margin>Moses and Christ alone are to be worshiped, from whom comes all good</margin>
For in a finished work, nothing can or should be more perfect than those things which are in the maker. Let us, therefore, fear, love, and venerate Him in whom—as **Paul** says—all things were created, whether invisible or visible.

<margin>Paul</margin>
This is the "Beginning" <note>original: "principium". Pico is playing on the first word of Genesis, "In the beginning" (In principio), arguing that this "Beginning" is actually Christ (the Logos).</note> in which God made heaven and earth; and this Beginning is Christ. Indeed, when asked who he was, he who best knew himself replied: "I am the Beginning, who speaks to you." Therefore, let us not forge images of the stars in metals <note>A reference to "astrological talismans," common in Renaissance magic, which Pico critiques here.</note>; rather, let us reform the image of Him—that is, the Word of God—in our souls. Let us not seek from the heavens either the goods of the body or of fortune, which they cannot give. Instead, let us seek present goods (insofar as they are truly good) and the true happiness of eternal life from the Lord of heaven, the Lord of all good things, to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth.

# THE THIRD EXPOSITION CONCERNING THE ANGELIC AND INVISIBLE WORLD. PREFACE TO THE THIRD BOOK.

<margin>He desires wings in the manner described above</margin>
**H**itherto, while we have disputed concerning the celestial world, revealing the mysteries of Moses according to the strength of our own talent, we have done our best. Now, however, who will give me wings like a dove—wings covered in silver and feathers with the yellow sheen of gold? <note>A poetic paraphrase of Psalm 68:13.</note> I shall fly above the celestial region to where there is true rest, true peace, and true tranquility: a peace which this visible and corporeal world cannot give. Open my eyes, O ultra-mundane spirits, and I shall contemplate the miracles of your city, where God has stored up riches for those who fear Him—things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man.

<margin>Dionysius; the ancient dogmas of the Hebrews are to be deferred.</margin>
Since much has been handed down concerning this angelic and invisible nature by the ancient Hebrews, and likewise much by **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose "Celestial Hierarchy" described the ranks of angels.</note>, it was my intention to explain the words of Moses according to the doctrine of both "families." However, because the things said by the Hebrews are unusual among the Latins and could not be easily understood by our people unless I began from the "twin egg" (as they say) <note>A classical idiom meaning "from the very beginning."</note> and explained almost all the dogmas of the ancient Hebrew discipline, I have decided this must be deferred until I have written more extensively on these matters elsewhere and made them known to our countrymen.

<summary>Pico warns against the worship of celestial bodies and astrological determinism, arguing that the human soul is superior to the physical heavens. He then begins the third book of the Heptaplus, shifting his focus from the physical stars to the angelic, invisible realm of the "ultra-mundane" spirits.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Third Exposition" of the *Heptaplus*, Pico’s seven-fold interpretation of the creation story in Genesis. -> THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA <-

<margin>
Dionysius
Paul
Hierotheus
</margin>
...their opinions: examining how much they harmonize with Egyptian monuments, how much with Platonic philosophy, and how much with Catholic truth. If they agree with us, we shall bid the Hebrews to stand by the ancient traditions of their fathers; but where they disagree, being equipped with the Catholic legions, we shall make an assault upon them. Finally, whatever we find that is foreign to the evangelical truth, we shall refute with all our might; and whatever we find in the holy and true synagogue, we shall transfer to ourselves—the legitimate Israelites—as if taking it back from an unjust possessor. <note>Pico argues that the hidden "true" meaning of Jewish scripture and Kabbalah actually supports Christian doctrine, viewing Christians as the spiritual heirs to these mysteries.</note> Meanwhile, following in the footsteps of **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian mystic who wrote extensively on the "Celestial Hierarchy."</note>—or rather **Paul** and **Hierotheus** <note>Dionysius claimed to be a student of St. Paul and Hierotheus of Athens; Pico accepts this historical lineage.</note> whom he followed—we shall endeavor to bring light into the "darkness of the law," where the Spirit of God, the author of the law, has placed his hiding place, in consideration of our weakness.

### Chapter One.

<margin>
Unity
Number
</margin>
Whatever exists after Unity is **Number**; it is through Unity that it is perfected and completed. Unity alone is entirely simple and perfect in itself; it does not go out from itself but adheres to itself in indivisible simplicity and solitude. It is self-sufficient, lacking nothing, and full of its own riches. **Number**, being by its nature a multitude, becomes "simple" only by the benefit of Unity—at least as much as it is capable of simplicity. However, the further any number is from Unity, the more it falls into greater multitude, and the more there is in it of dissimilarity, of parts, and of composition. Yet, no number is so close to Unity that it is not still a multitude, possessing its unity as something added to it, being "one" not by its own nature, but by composition.

<margin>
The anagogical ascent to divine things. <note>Anagoge is a method of spiritual interpretation that leads the mind from literal words to heavenly realities.</note>
</margin>
Let us transfer these ideas to divine things in the manner of the **Pythagoreans**. <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe.</note> God alone—from whom all things come—is the most simple and indivisible essence. Whatever He has, He has from Himself: by the same thing that He *is*, He also *knows*, *wills*, is *good*, and is *just*. We cannot understand Him as being anything other than **Being Itself** <note>original: "ipsum esse"</note> which He is. Other things are not "Being Itself," but exist *through* it. Therefore, an angel is not Unity itself; otherwise, it would be God, or there would be multiple gods, which is inconceivable. For what would be "one" if Unity itself were not one? It remains, then, that an angel is a "Number." If it is a number, it is "one multitude" in another part of itself. Every number is imperfect insofar as it is a multitude, but perfected insofar as it is one. Therefore, whatever is imperfect in an angel we should attribute to the "angelic multitude" (from which it derives its nature as a number, i.e., a creature); and whatever is perfect, we should attribute to the "approaching unity" which it receives from its union with God.

<margin>
A double imperfection accompanies the angel
</margin>
We find a double imperfection in the angel: First, because it is not "Being Itself," but an essence to which "being" happens by participation so that it may exist. Second, because it is not "Understanding Itself," but "understanding" comes to it so that it may perceive; for by its own nature it is an intellect capable of intelligence. The second imperfection depends on the first, for that which does not exist of itself certainly does not understand of itself, since nothing can exist there where Being Itself is not present. Both of these occur in the angel because it is a "multitude." It remains that its release and consummation must come from the Unity approaching from above. God is that Unity: so that Being, Life, and all perfection may derive from Him to the angel. Just as there is a double imperfection where there is a double multitude, so let us understand a double approach of Unity to perfect both.

<margin>
The empty earth
</margin>
The first Unity is that which makes the essence. Before this, the essence is crude, formless, and devoid of life and being; this is the **"empty and void earth"** <note>original: "terra inanis et vacua" — a reference to Genesis 1:2.</note> which God created. You should not believe, as some have, that only the "formation" of essence belongs to the Maker and not also its "creation." At the same time He created the "earth," He also created the "heaven"—that is, the act of that essence and the Unity participated in the multitude; this is Being Itself. Thus, the creation of "heaven" and "earth" is the same, as it were a pairing and an embrace of two natures coming together in a similar bond.

<margin>
Xenophanes
The Saracens
</margin>
And not discordantly with the ancients, we call "Being Itself" (the participation in divinity) "Heaven"; just as **Xenophanes** <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 570–478 BC).</note> called the Archetypal World a "sphere," and the **Saracens** <note>A medieval term for Muslims; Pico often cited Islamic philosophers like Averroes or Avicenna.</note>—and indeed our own people—call God a "circle."

### Chapter Second.

Through these things we have said, the angel has now perfectly attained its nature and its intellectual property. Nevertheless, it does not yet have that by which it may fulfill its duties of understanding and contemplating, unless it is first clothed by God with "intelligible forms." For this reason, it remains...

<summary>Pico applies Pythagorean number theory to theology, arguing that God is absolute "Unity" while angels are "Numbers" (multiplicities) that require God's unity to be perfected. He interprets the "empty earth" of Genesis as the raw angelic essence before it is filled with divine light and being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's "Third Exposition," focusing on the spiritual or "intelligible" world of angels. Having established that angels represent "Number" (multiplicity) proceeding from "Unity" (God), he now interprets the specific phrases of the Genesis creation narrative as they apply to the angelic intellect.</meta>

-> HEPTAPLUS <-

...darkness was still over the face of the abyss.
<margin>Description of the abyss corresponds with the chaos of Lactantius</margin>
The intellectual **abyss** <note>original: *abyssus*; Pico defines this not as a physical void, but as the deep, searching capacity of the angelic mind before it is filled with divine light.</note> is a deep property, penetrating and scrutinizing all things. Over this, there is darkness until it is illuminated by the rays of spiritual concepts, through which it sees and perceives all things. It is written, however, that darkness was *over the face* of the abyss, not *over the abyss itself*, because light and darkness occupy the same place. For **light**—that is, the **intelligible species** <note>The "intelligible species" are the mental forms or "ideas" that an angel uses to understand reality.</note>—occupies the "face," meaning the outermost parts of the angelic intellect; because these are accidental qualities, they do not belong to its actual essence.

<margin>Spirit of the Lord</margin>
But what intervenes before the darkness is driven away and light suddenly arises? He immediately adds, saying: *And the Spirit of the Lord was hovering over the waters.* What will the Spirit of the Lord be, rather than the **Spirit of Love**? For we do not call the spirit of knowledge the "Spirit of the Lord" so properly, since knowledge sometimes leads away from God. But love always leads toward God. Unless this Spirit is carried over that abyss, light will not be made. For just as the eye is not filled with light unless it is turned toward the sun, so the angel is not filled with spiritual light unless it is turned toward God. This movement of "turning" is not, nor can it be, anything else in the nature of an angel than the movement of love. Therefore, the Spirit of the Lord was a loving spirit over the abyss—that is, over the angelic intellect (for love follows understanding)—by which, once the angelic mind is moved and excited, it is turned toward God.

<margin>Let there be light. One day. Averroes. Moses the Egyptian.</margin>
God said: *Let there be light,* and light was made in the angel—namely, through the forms of the intelligible world. And there was evening and morning, **one day**; because, as **Averroes** <note>A famous 12th-century Islamic philosopher (Ibn Rushd) whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Medieval and Renaissance thought.</note> proves, a greater unity is formed from the intellect and the intelligible than from matter and form. As the same author affirms, and as **Moses the Egyptian** <note>The Jewish philosopher Maimonides (12th century).</note> also writes, this is found to be far more true in angels than in man. Setting aside their reasons, let this one suffice for us: that the "species" (the forms of knowledge) are joined to the angelic mind in an inseparable bond, not—as happens to the human intellect—in a wandering and temporary way, but united by perpetual ties.

### Chapter Three.

We have seen the nature of the angel created by God, then turned toward God by the spirit of love, and then illuminated and perfected by the light of intelligible reasons. Let us now see in what order the angelic armies are distinguished among themselves.
<margin>Firmament in the midst of the waters</margin>
We read that a **firmament** was placed in the midst of the waters, where three angelic **hierarchies** <note>Pico adopts the traditional three-tiered structure of angels (Totaling 9 choirs) popularized by Pseudo-Dionysius.</note> (for we shall always call them by that customary name) are indicated to us. The first and last of these are designated by "waters": the first by the *waters above the heavens*, the last by those which are *below the heavens*. The middle one, dividing them, is called the "firmament." If we weigh the nature and duties of the three hierarchies, they could not harmonize better with the doctrine of **Dionysius**.

<margin>Super-celestial waters. Firmament.</margin>
The supreme hierarchy, since (as he writes) it is free for contemplation alone, is deservedly represented by the **waters** which are established *above the heavens*—that is, above every action concerning worldly things, whether celestial or earthly—and they praise God incessantly with a perennial sound. The middle order, however, being delegated to celestial duties, certainly could not be more fittingly signified than by the **firmament**—that is, the sky.

<margin>Sub-celestial waters</margin>
The last hierarchy, even if by nature it is above every body and above the sky, nevertheless cares for those things which are *under the sky*. Though it is divided into **Principalities**, **Archangels**, and **Angels**, the entire operation of all these is focused on those things under the moon: Principalities concern themselves with republics, kings, and princes (as we learn from Daniel); Archangels concern themselves with mysteries and sacred ceremonies. Angels attend to private matters, and are assigned to individual men. Correctily, then, this sub-celestial army is represented by the **sub-celestial waters**, which both preside over flowing and falling things and are subject to that order which deals with celestial things.

### Chapter Four.

What it might mean for the waters under the sky to be "gathered into one place" would perhaps be doubtful if **Paul** did not declare it to us. For in his writings, we read concerning these angels who are sent to perform duties in this world, that they are all "ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who will inherit salvation." From this we can understand that these sub-celestial waters—that is, the angelic armies—are gathered into one place: namely, for the good of one man...

...[are] gathered to provide for our health and salvation, for which they are sent to us; they appear to us at different times, in different forms, places, and moments, both while we rest and even now while we are awake. We will only truly understand how this statement is to be accepted once we have considered the manner in which it is true—as Moses says—that the **waters**, <note>In this third exposition, Pico interprets the "waters" as the lower orders of angels who are closer to the material world and human affairs.</note> namely, were gathered into one place. 
<margin>An objection that could be raised</margin>
For it is not true in the sense that waters are never found in distinct and separate places, since the Indian Sea is divided from the Hyrcanian <note>The ancient name for the Caspian Sea.</note>, the Hyrcanian from the Adriatic, and the Adriatic from the Euxine <note>The Black Sea.</note>; moreover, countless flows of rivers, springs, and lakes are separated by very long distances from one another. But the waters are said to be "gathered into one place" for this reason: because all these particular and divided collections of waters, whether of the sea or of rivers, all tend toward the primary sea—as <margin>Solomon</margin> **Solomon** says—and they unite and meet in the single place of the Ocean. In exactly the same way, we must understand those angels who care for sublunary things <note>Things on Earth, located "under the moon" in the ancient cosmological model.</note>. For different angels preside over different physical things and other matters concerning man. 
<margin>The Platonists</margin> 
Since just as the **Platonists** believed, so also our own teachers have believed that various spiritual substances were appointed by God over the various things of this corruptible world. 
<margin>Augustine</margin>

Being of this same opinion, **John Damascene** <note>A 7th-century Syrian monk and influential theologian.</note> believed that the angel who sinned <note>Referring to Lucifer/Satan.</note> was from among those of the lowliest rank who preside over the terrestrial order. Truly, just as all these things below man are referred to man, so all the care of the angels regarding these things is primarily subservient and devoted to the labor and study of caring for human affairs; by aiding our weakness, they ensure—as much as we ourselves allow—that we live a godly and happy life. 

Therefore, Moses immediately added what those collections of waters intended: that the **earth** should bring forth fruit, herbs, plants, and trees. Now, what is this earth <margin>The earth of which Paul speaks in the Gospel</margin> besides that of which it is written in the Gospel <note>Though Pico says "Gospel," he is referencing the Parable of the Sower and later quotes Hebrews.</note> that some brings forth a hundredfold fruit, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold? And let us hear the Father saying: *Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field which God has blessed.* <note>Quoting Genesis 27:27.</note> And let no one wonder that "heaven and earth" signify one thing to us on the first day, and "firmament and dry land" signify another thing now; 
<margin>
Origen
Basil
</margin> 
this is something we also observed in the previous books, since both **Origen** and **Basil** and many others maintain that in Moses' account, heaven and earth on the first day are one thing, and the dry land and the firmament on the second day are another.

### Chapter Five.

The celestial virtues <note>In the hierarchy of angels, "Virtues" are a specific rank known for governing the movements of the heavens.</note> also favor this earth of ours. For both the sun and the moon and the stars were placed in the firmament to illuminate our earth. 
<margin>Dionysian mysteries</margin> 
See how aptly these things agree with the **Dionysian mysteries** <note>The "mysteries" refer to the works of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, who wrote the definitive Renaissance guide to the nine ranks of angels.</note>. We have spoken of the lowest hierarchy, to which the care of things under the moon—that is, human affairs—was delegated. Now the middle hierarchy is discussed, to which the administration of the heavens is entrusted. Nor should it be expected that he will speak of the third [the highest] hierarchy in the same way; of that, nothing needs to be said beyond what has been mentioned: namely, that it is above the heavens—that is, above every movement of action and above the administration of all worldly things—devoted only to contemplation. ...not as physical stars, but as the rulers of the moon and sun, namely the angelic powers. And in the history of the kings, we read according to the Hebrew literature that **Solomon** prayed with these words: *Hear, O heaven* <note>original: "Exaudi o caelū"; reference to 1 Kings 8:30. Solomon addresses "heaven," but Pico argues he is addressing the spiritual ruler of that realm.</note>; where he does not mean the physical sky, but calls upon the ruler of heaven and earth, the Lord God. So also in this place, when we hear of the sun and the stars, let us understand not the celestial bodies, but the angels who preside over those stars. Although they are themselves invisible, they also illuminate an invisible "earth"—namely, the substance of our mind. Nor was it said lightly or in a common way that these were ordained *to illuminate*. But it was said so appropriately and so in harmony with what we have brought forward, that if from nowhere else, certainly from here our exposition is most strongly proven. For since (as **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined how angels were ranked in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> teaches) there are three angelic actions—**purgation**, **illumination**, and **perfection**—they are distributed such that the lowest order purges, the highest perfects, and this middle order, which we are now discussing, illuminates. Therefore, the lower waters purge our "earth," which is why it comes into view as "clean"; the celestial ones illuminate the purged earth. The "super-celestial" ones <note>The highest rank of angels.</note> perfect and make it fertile with a certain fiery and life-giving dew, often to such great happiness that it no longer sprouts merely medicinal herbs, but germinates the **Savior** himself; and not just one virtue, but Christ, the fullness of all virtues, is formed within us.

Next follows the account of the inhabitants of the elements: the multitude of fish, birds, and beasts. Here, I would certainly have been held in great distress—more than anywhere else in this whole work of ours—had I not had at hand both **Isaiah**, in whose writings we read of the winged **Seraphim**, and **Ezekiel**, in whose writings (if we believe the **Hebrews**) both birds and beasts indicate to us spiritual substances. I would also be stuck if the ancient **Hebrews** had not run to my aid, who all want the **angelic multitude** to be indicated by Moses in this place. Let us say, therefore, following in their footsteps, that the prophet here refutes the error of the philosophers. These philosophers believed that there were indeed some principal intellectual substances, but they denied that each of them (as the theologians say) presided over a numerous following and multitude, just as leaders preside over legions. Therefore, when we think of the nine angelic orders, and each order having its own leader, let us imagine in our mind that leader and prince as a "great sphere," and then the following army as the inhabitants and ornament of that sphere—just as we imagine fish in the water, birds in the air, beasts on the earth, and stars in the eighth sphere. And that saying of **Daniel** will be true: *Ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him, and a thousand thousands ministered to him.* <note>Daniel 7:10. Pico uses this to prove that the spiritual world is densely populated with legions of angels, not just a few solitary spirits.</note>

# Chapter Seven.

<margin>
Jesus Christ, the firstborn of all creation
Dionysius
Paul
</margin>
Finally, he mentions **man**, not because man is an angel, but because he is the end and boundary of the angelic world. Just as when Moses dealt with corruptible nature, he also included man—not as a part of that nature, but as its principle and head. Thus, the treatment of man belongs to three worlds: to the one that is his own, and to both extremes, namely the incorporeal and the elemental. He is so placed in the middle that he serves as the end of one and the beginning of the other. But I see a trap prepared for our exposition when they point out that man is said to "preside over the fish of the sea, the birds, and the beasts." For if those things signify the angelic nature to us, how will it be true what is written—that man presides over them—when both the philosophers know and the prophet testifies that man was *made lower than the angels*? <note>Psalm 8:5. Pico is addressing a logical contradiction: how can Man (the "lower" being) rule over angels (represented by the animals) if he is naturally below them?</note> May he be present with us and break the snare, he who also crushed Satan under our feet: **Jesus Christ**, the *firstborn of all creation*. He certainly breaks the snare and unties and snaps every knot. For not only in him, in whom the whole divinity dwelt bodily, was human nature so exalted that the Man-Christ, insofar as he is man, teaches, illuminates, and perfects the angels (if we believe **Dionysius**), having been made *so much better than the angels* (as **Paul** says) *as he has inherited a more excellent name than they*; but also all of us, to whom power was given to become the **sons of God** through the grace of which Christ is the giver, can be raised above angelic dignity.

# FOURTH EXPOSITION ON THE WORLD, THAT IS, THE HUMAN WORLD, CONCERNING THE NATURE OF MAN.
## PREFACE TO THE FOURTH BOOK.

<margin>
The Delphic letter <note>original: "Lřa delphica"; likely referring to the letter 'E' at Delphi, which was a symbol of self-knowledge and being.</note> mentioned in the margin of the book on *Being*. Plato.
</margin>
After we have sufficiently shown through the prophet <note>Moses, whom Pico considers the "prophet" and author of Genesis.</note> all parts of the world and the entirety of celestial, angelic, and corruptible nature, it remains (if we are mindful of our promise) to interpret the whole reading again as referring to Man. We shall prove by this very thing that there is no statement in this entire work which—just as it deals with the three worlds discussed above—does not also encompass hidden meanings and the deepest truths regarding the nature of Man. Nor shall we have performed a less worthy task if we are diligent in explaining this fourth exposition than we were in the previous ones. For how useful, indeed how necessary, the knowledge of oneself is (as witness that Delphic inscription <note>The famous Greek maxim *Gnothi Seauton*, or "Know Thyself."</note>), was so demonstrated by **Plato** in the *First Alcibiades* that he left nothing for those coming after him to attempt to bring forth as new on this subject. And truly, it is a wicked and reckless pursuit for one who is still ignorant of himself, and still does not know whether he can know anything at all, to nevertheless boldly seek knowledge of things that are so far removed from him. Let us return, therefore, into ourselves, and let us see (as the prophet says) what great goods God has done for our soul. Lest, perhaps, if the soul is less diligent in recognizing things within itself, it should hear the Father saying in the *Song of Songs*: *If you know not yourself, O most beautiful among women, go forth and follow the footsteps of your flocks.* <note>Reference to Song of Solomon 1:8. Pico interprets this as a warning that if humans do not recognize their own divine nature, they are exiled from God and reduced to the level of animals.</note> You see what penalty awaits us for our ignorance. We must "go away" from the Father—namely, an exile followed by disinheritance; what could be more unhappy? We must likewise "go forth"—that is, out of ourselves. For the mind is not at home when it does not see itself. But he who leaves himself is torn away from himself; what could be more bitter? Thirdly, we must go "after the footsteps of our flocks," that is, after the tracks of the brutes <note>Animals/beasts.</note> that are within us (about which we shall say enough in the exposition); what could be more miserable? What more despicable and contemptible? To become, that is, the footmen of beasts, over whom nature had appointed us the leaders. Therefore, proceeding not after the tracks of the brutes but after the footsteps of **Moses**, let us enter into ourselves; let us enter the inner chambers of the mind with the prophet himself opening the way for us, so that in ourselves we may happily recognize all worlds, and the Father, and our homeland.
<margin>
The triple penalty of self-ignorance:
Above self
From self
After self

### Chapter One.

<margin>
The rational soul. Aristotle. The Platonists. Plotinus.
</margin>
Before we more accurately arrange the exposition according to the words and order of the prophet, it is necessary to say a few things beforehand about the nature of Man and briefly explain some terms, so that the understanding of the whole sense may then be more fitting. Man consists of a body and a <term>rational soul</term> <note>The highest part of the human soul, capable of reason and connection to the divine.</note>. The rational soul is called "heaven." For **Aristotle** calls heaven a living being moved by itself, and our soul (as the **Platonists** prove) is a substance moving itself. Heaven is a circle; and the soul is likewise a circle; indeed, as **Plotinus** writes, heaven is a circle for this reason: because its soul is a circle. Heaven is moved in an orbit; the rational soul, transferring itself from causes to effects, and returning again from effects to causes, revolves in an orbit of reasoning. If these points had to be explained individually for those who have not read them elsewhere, we would no longer be interpreters of Moses, but of Aristotle and Plato. The body is called "earth," since it is a Georgeous <note>original: "terrosa"; meaning earthy or of the soil.</note> and heavy substance. Wherefore, being made from the soil (as Moses writes), it gave Man his name <note>A wordplay on "Adam" (man) and "Adamah" (earth/ground) in Hebrew, or "Homo" and "Humus" in Latin.</note>. But between the earthly body and the celestial substance of the soul, there was need for a middle link that might couple such distant natures together. Assigned to this duty is that thin and spiritual "little body" <note>original: "corpusculum"; referring to the "astral body" or the refined medical "spirits" believed to bridge soul and flesh.</note> which both physicians and philosophers call <term>spiritus</term> <note>In this context, "spirit" is not the soul itself, but a subtle physical vapor that transmits commands from the soul to the limbs.</note>. Which **Aristotle** writes is of a more divine nature than the elements and corresponds proportionately to heaven. Here it is called "light," a name which could not more suitably agree with the opinion of philosophers and physicians, for whom it is a common...
<margin>
Body. Spirit. Aristotle.
</margin>

there is a general consensus; that it [the spirit] is a most lucid substance, and that it rejoices in, is nourished by, and is refreshed by nothing more than by light. It is added that just as all the power of the heavens (as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> writes) is transferred to the earth by the vehicle of light, so all the power of the soul (which we have called "heaven")—namely all the power of life, motion, and sense—is conveyed and poured into this earthly body (which we have called "earth") through the mediation of the lucid spirit. Let us now descend to the words of the prophet <note>Moses.</note>; in whose writing we first see the creation of the heaven and the earth—that is, the extremes of our substance: the rational power and the earthly body. Finally, since there is light (that is, the lucid spirit), they are so united that from "evening and morning"—that is, from the nocturnal nature of the body and the morning nature of the soul—one man is made. And since (as we have shown) all vital and sensory power descends to our "earth" through this light, it is with good reason that before the birth of light, the earth was "void and empty." For its own heaven could not share the benefits of life and motion unless through the messenger of light. For this reason, he immediately added the cause of this emptiness: because, namely, darkness was still over it, as the light had not yet arisen.
