### Chapter Two.

But it still remains to be asked what that phrase means: *and the spirit of the Lord moved over the waters.*
Here, an indistinct and universal doctrine concerning the waters is handed down, which is more clearly distinguished on the following day: when he teaches that some are those which are above the heaven, and others are those which are under the heaven. If we desire the true sense of all these things, let us consult nature itself, which our prophet (as we have often said) mirrors and represents with great precision. We have seen mention made of a triple part of the human substance: namely, the rational, the mortal body, and the middle spirit. Two parts remain. For between the rational part by which we are men, and all that which is corporeal in us—whether it be dense or thin and spiritual—the middle part is the sensual part, by which <margin>The sensual soul</margin> we communicate with the beasts. And since our communication with the angels is no less than our communication with the beasts, just as sense is below reason (whence comes our commerce with the animals), so above reason is the intelligence, through which we can say that phrase of **John**: *Our fellowship is with the angels.* <note>Reference to 1 John 1:3: "our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son," here interpreted by Pico to include the angelic hierarchy.</note> You see what is below and what is above our reason. If, therefore, reason is called "heaven" (as we have proven), it is now manifest which are the waters above the heavens in us, and which are likewise the waters below the heavens. However, by a different reasoning, the name of "waters" fits both the intellectual part and the sensual part: to the former because it is most permeable to the rays of divine illuminations; to the latter because it gapes for and delights in fleeting and flowing things. The prophet sufficiently warns us of this diversity when he places the latter "under the heaven," where all things are flowing and falling; and the former "above the heaven," where the administration of pure and perpetual intelligence resides. Therefore, when we read on the first day that the spirit of the Lord "brooded over the waters," and they had not yet been divided into two parts, we surely shall not take this as being said of those waters which are under the heaven; for the spirit of the Lord is not carried over these, but rather the heaven is carried over them. It remains that it was said concerning those which are above the heaven. From this, a great dogma concerning the soul is reported to us. For the intellect which is in us is illustrated by a greater and indeed divine intellect—whether that be God (as some wish), or a mind most proximate and kin to man, as almost all the <margin>Reason / Intelligence</margin> <margin>John</margin> <margin>The divine intellect in the principles: Albunasar, Alpharabius, Moses the Egyptian, Abubachr</margin> Greeks, the Arabs, and most of the Hebrews wish. This substance both the Jewish philosophers and **Albunasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a Persian astrologer and philosopher.</note> and **Alpharabius** <note>Al-Farabi, a renowned philosopher and jurist of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>, in the book he writes on *Principles*, called in express words "the spirit of the Lord." Nor was it done without cause that he [Moses] mentioned this matter—that is, the moving of the spirit over the waters—before he had established man from soul and body by the bond of light; but it was done for this reason: lest we might perhaps believe that this spirit was not present to our intellect except when it was coupled to the body. Both **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> and **Abubacher** <note>Likely Ibn Bajja (Avempace) or Ibn Tufail, Andalusian philosophers.</note> the Arab, and certain others, falsely believed this.

### Chapter Three.

It remains for us to explain what is meant by saying that the "waters which are under the heaven"—that is, the sensual powers which are under the rational part—are "gathered into one place." This is most manifest to those not entirely unlearned in philosophy. For all the sensitive powers [lead] to the sense which, from the thing itself, [is called common sense].

<margin>Concerning that which we call the common sense: here, however, if we follow Aristotle, it is in the heart, where the senses flow together like rivers to the sea.</margin>
**Concerning that which** we call the common <term>sense</term> <note>The *sensus communis*, a theoretical faculty that integrates the data from the five individual senses into a single perception.</note>: here, however, if we follow Aristotle, it is in the heart; the senses flow together into it just as rivers flow to the sea. Nor would we speak absurdly if we said that from that sea, the five senses of the body—which we see as
<margin>Aristotle in the third book of *On the Soul*, extensively.</margin>
hearing, sight, taste, touch, and smell—enter the continent of the body, spread out like five Mediterranean seas. This was the clear opinion in the *Theaetetus* of **Plato**. And since we understand that from the perfection of these sensory powers—and from this collection of them toward their source—life, health, and nourishment come to the body which we call "earth," it is with good reason that immediately after that
<margin>Plato</margin>
gathering of the waters, he introduces the earth greening and flowering. For nature provided senses to all mortals for the sake of procuring the life and safety of the body, so that through them they might recognize what is harmful and what is beneficial; then, once recognized, they might reject the former and desire the latter through the <term>appetite</term> <note>The faculty of "appetite" here refers to the basic biological drive toward or away from stimuli.</note> annexed to the senses; and finally, through the joined motor power, they might flee evils and pursue useful things. The eye sees the food; the nostrils smell it; the feet approach; the hands take it; the palate experiences it. We say all these things so that we may recognize the fertile happiness of the "earth" (which for a long time has signified the "body" to us) as being aptly joined to the establishment of the "waters" (that is, the sensory powers).

->Chapter four.<-

But truly, since rational nature is distinguished by many powers and potencies, we have spoken above regarding its naked substance. Now let us speak of its ornament and, so to speak, its royal furniture.
<margin>The opinion of the modern philosophers.</margin>
This is what he writes: that the sun, moon, and stars were placed in the firmament. The <term>modern philosophers</term> <note>Pico likely refers to Scholastic thinkers or contemporary Neoplatonists who interpreted celestial bodies as psychological faculties.</note> might perhaps interpret the sun as the intellect in act and the moon as the intellect in potential; but since we have a great controversy with them on this matter, let us meanwhile explain it thus: that the part of the soul which turns toward the higher waters—toward the spirit of the Lord—is called the "sun" because it shines entirely. That part which looks back toward the lower waters—that is, the sensory powers—and from which it contracts some stain of infection, should have the
<margin>The Platonists called these *Dianoia* and *Doxa*.</margin>
name of the "moon." The Greek Platonists, following the dogmas of their own teaching, called the sun accepted in this way **Dianoia** <note>original: "Διανοιαν" - Discursive or rational thought.</note> and the moon **Doxa** <note>original: "Δοξαν" - Opinion or belief.</note>. Moreover, since we are wandering far from our own country and living in the night and shadows of this present life, we mostly use that part which turns toward the senses; hence we "opine" more than we "know." But when the day of the future life dawns, and we have turned toward divine things—the senses becoming foreign to us—we shall understand with that other, higher part. Thus it is rightly said that this "sun" of ours presides over the day, while the "moon" presides over the night. Likewise, because once we have cast off this dying garment, we shall behold that [divine] thing by the single light of the sun; whereas in this most miserable night of the body, we strive to see by many powers and potencies rather than actually seeing. Therefore, the day shines with a single sun; the night, by contrast, is composed of many stars—namely, the power of joining and dividing, of reasoning, and likewise of defining, and the rest. These help and unite with the moon as if they were auxiliary aids to a less potent power.

->Chapter five<-

So much for the cognitive powers of the soul. Now he transfers himself to those things whose work is of the appetite: namely, the seats of anger and lust (that is, concupiscence). These he designates through the "beasts" and the irrational genus of living things, because these are common to us and the beasts; and what is more wretched, they often drive us toward a
<margin>The Chaldeans, Plato, Theocritus, and Virgil mentioned this.</margin>
brutal life. Hence that saying of the **Chaldeans**: "Beasts of the earth inhabit thy vessel." And in Plato's *Republic*, we learn that we have various kinds of brutes within our home; so that it should not be a difficult paradox to believe **Pythagoras** (if he is understood correctly) when he says that depraved men migrate into brutes. For within us, and even in our very bowels, there are brutes, so that we need not wander far to "migrate" into them. Here belong the fables of **Circe**; and that saying of **Theocritus**: that those whom virtue and wisdom have looked upon cannot be undone by Circe’s cups. But let us see what the Mosaic reading suggests to us regarding the difference between these brutes. Some are produced from the waters under the heaven; others from the earth. The waters, as we have said, signify the internal sensory
<margin>The sense is called "phantasia" [imagination].</margin>
part which is "under the heaven" because it is subject to reason and serves it closely. The "earth" is this very earthly and fragile body with which we are surrounded. Let us consider, therefore, whether from the affections by which we are moved, some pertain more to the body and others to the internal sense, which the philosophers call **phantasia** <note>The imagination or "image-making" faculty that sits between raw sensation and high reason.</note>. <note>The Sevenfold Account of Creation</note>

appear to me to regard the body, which drive us either to food or to sexual love. For these were given to us by God both for the protection of the body which we nourish, and for the procreation of children: in whom we might survive when we perish in ourselves. We abuse these same things, lured by more pleasure than is fitting: through gluttony and through lust making "provision for the flesh," as <margin>Paul</margin> Paul says, "in its desires." <note>Original: *curam carnis... in desideriis*, referencing Romans 13:14.</note> In his words, it should be noted that he did not say "do not make provision for the flesh," but "do not do so in its desires": that is to say, we must use those things for necessity, and not for pleasure; much less should our happiness be placed in them. Let us, therefore, understand these affections through the cattle and wild beasts, which are called the offspring of the earth and rather of the waters: because they are both fulfilled and excited through the members of this coarser body, and were provided for us by God for its well-being: although they become the destruction of those who wither from hangovers or are dissolved by lust. But let us refer to the waters—that is, the sense of imagination—those affections which can be called spiritual rather than offspring of the flesh. These are the kinds of things that call us toward honors, toward anger, toward revenge, and other affections related to these. These are necessary and useful to those who use them moderately. For one must be angry, but within measure; and revenge is often a work of justice; and each person's own dignity must be defended; nor are honors to be refused which are obtained by honorable means. I say this for this reason: lest, when God created these brutes which indicate sensual <term>appetites</term> <note>The basic biological and emotional drives that move an animal or person toward an object of desire.</note> and blessed them once created, we should believe they are evil by their nature along with the <margin>Manicheans</margin> Manicheans <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that taught that the physical world and the body were created by an evil principle rather than a good God.</note> and created by an evil principle rather than by the good God. All those things are therefore good and necessary for man: but we ourselves, by exceeding into ambition, fury, white-hot rage, and pride, make into evils by our own fault those things which that Best of Beings had established as the best.

### Chapter six.

But see how precisely it agrees with what we have said, that which follows: that man was made by God in His own image so that he might rule over the fish, birds, and beasts which both the water and the earth had produced. Indeed, we were already discussing man above; but now for the first time we understand the image of God in him: hence his dominion over the brutes is expressed. For man was so established by nature that reason should rule over the senses, and all the fury and appetite of both anger and lust should be restrained by its law. But because the image of God was scarred through the stain of <term>sin</term> <note>In Pico’s Neoplatonic view, sin is a turning away from the divine light toward the material world, which "disfigures" the soul's resemblance to God.</note>, we have begun, wretched and unhappy, to serve our own beasts; and like the <margin>Chaldean King</margin> Chaldean King <note>Referring to Nebuchadnezzar, who, as described in the Book of Daniel, was driven from men and ate grass like an ox.</note>, to dwell among them and lie upon the ground, greedy for earthly things, forgetful of our fatherland, forgetful of our Father, forgetful of our kingdom: even though it was given to us as a privilege of our former dignity. Truly, "man, when he was in honor, did not understand: but was compared to the senseless cattle and became like them." <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 49:20.</note>

### Chapter seven.

But just as all of us in the first Adam, who obeyed Satan more than God, are deformed according to the flesh as his sons and degenerate from man into beast; so in the last Adam, <margin>Jesus Christ</margin> Jesus Christ, who fulfilled the will of the Father and by his own blood overcame spiritual wickednesses: we, his sons—the "whole Adam" according to the spirit—are regenerated and reformed through grace from man into the adoption of the sons of God: provided that as in Him, so in us, the prince of darkness and of this world finds nothing of his own.

# FIFTH EXPOSITION CONCERNING ALL WORLDS 
# SEPARATELY IN SUCCESSIVE ORDER.
## PREFACE TO THE FIFTH BOOK.

**J**ust as Moses, as we have shown in the individual parts of his text, discussed all the worlds together—the intellectual, the celestial, the elemental, and the human—imitating nature, or rather God the craftsman of nature, who has embraced all things in each individual world: so too, following the example of that same nature which distributes proper seats, proper rights, and peculiar laws to each one, our prophet, with a marvelous and perfect mastery of the divine art, [composed] the scripture...

...has thus arranged his work: so that while he might everywhere discuss all things under the same appearance and the same veil of words, he would nonetheless specifically assign individual parts of his work to individual worlds in a successive order. We shall begin this by interpreting the first part concerning the first world—that is, the angelic world—then subsequently the remaining parts concerning the others, as we sagaciously observe in the words of Moses that <term>Golden Homeric Chain</term> <note>A traditional metaphor for the hierarchy of being, connecting the lowest parts of creation to the divine.</note> and those <term>Platonic rings</term> <note>Referencing Plato's *Ion*, where divine inspiration is compared to a magnet (the Stone of Hercules) passing its power through a series of iron rings.</note> suspended from the living virtue of the Creator as if from a true <term>Stone of the unconquered Hercules</term> <note>original: *lapide indomiti Herculis*; a common name for a magnet or lodestone.</note>.

## Chapter One.

<margin>
Mind and eye are the same in logic but differ in reality
</margin>

About to speak of the angelic nature, which is pure intellect, I say we should first conceive of minds as being like certain eyes. For what the eye is in bodily things, that very thing the mind is in the spiritual category. Even if the eye possesses some light within the mixture of its innermost substance, it nevertheless requires external light to perform the duty of vision, in which it observes things, colors, and differences. Nor is it for that reason by its nature "not-sight," even if it does not see except by the benefit of light. For even the ears—not to mention inanimate things—and all other parts of the body are illuminated by light, yet they do not see. Therefore, that which has obtained the nature of seeing and is, by its very definition, "sight," is that which can see once light is received. Let us consider these same things in intellects: Intellects are the eyes, intelligible truth is the light. And since the intellect itself is intelligible, it has some light of its own within, by which it can see itself; but it cannot see other things. Rather, it requires <term>forms and ideas</term> <note>The essential patterns or archetypes of things.</note> of objects, through which, as if by certain rays of invisible light, the intelligible truth is undoubtedly perceived. Nor should it be said (as we declared through the example of the eyes) that they are not by nature intelligent, as if they obtained their intellectual property by some accidental condition similar to our own souls. Here flows the opinion of those who think the title of "Intellect" is unworthy of God. For if we take the intellect as a kind of eye that sees not from itself but by participation in light, and since God is Light (for Truth is Light), and vision is the action by which the eye reaches the light, then God does not need this operation, for He is Light itself. He is as much more remote from the ignorance of all things than the angels are, as the nature of light is further from darkness than the eye is. But let us return to the angels. The eye—that is, the intellectual substance—is not entirely simple; otherwise, it would not admit the composition of arriving light.

<margin>
Angels consist of act and potency
Averroes the Arab
</margin>

From this comes the common proverb that angels consist of <term>act and potency</term> <note>Aristotelian terms: "Act" (actus) is the full realization of a thing, while "Potency" (potentia) is the capacity to become or receive something.</note>, though there is an anxious dispute over what that "act" is, what that "potency" is, and what the reason for their composition might be. Likewise, what <term>Averroes the Arab</term> <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval university study.</note> intended when he said that both the intellect which is in act and that which is in potency exist in all intellects below God. But for our purposes here, it is enough that the common opinion be accepted in whatever way. Moses reveals all these things to us at the very beginning. For he divides the substance of the angel into a "heavenly" and an "earthly" nature: namely, the nature of act and the nature of potency. However, just as the same thing has different properties, so it has different names. Therefore, this same "act"—while it is taken as the virtue granting sight to the eye and as the fulfillment of potency—is called "Heaven," because it holds the same relationship to potency as heaven does to earth. Again, because it is in need of light and cannot perform its own duty of intelligence by itself, it is symbolized by "the waters": a body capable of light, yet by its own nature not at all shining. There is also another reason for the similarity: that this "act" of "potency" (which he calls "Earth") is as closely present to it as water is to the earth. But let us now join the words of the prophet: *God created heaven and earth*—the nature of act and the nature of potency, from which he fashions the angel. And the *earth*—that is, potency—was *void and empty*: void of act and empty of light, which it does not receive except through the intervening waters. And since contraries occur around the same thing, and it pertains to the same subject to host both light and darkness, he added: *and darkness was upon the face of the abyss.*

<margin>
What the Abyss is
James the Apostle
</margin>

He did not say "upon the earth." For the "Abyss" is nothing other (unless we misuse the word) than the depth of the waters. Over these waters the spirit of the Lord was moved—the spirit which is called by the <margin>James</margin> Apostle James the "Father of Lights," from whom soon upon them—that is, upon the angelic minds...

->HEPTAPLVS<-

...minds, the light of intelligible forms arises. Perhaps the <term>Saracens</term> <note>Pico often refers to "Saracens" when citing Islamic philosophers like Avicenna or Averroes, whose works were central to Medieval and Renaissance thought.</note> understood this clearly when they said that the angels were led by God from darkness to light and filled with eternal joy. For pleasure follows understanding; no pleasure is greater, none truer, and none more permanent.

### Chapter two.

<margin>Note</margin>
The celestial world is closest to this [angelic] world. Its primary property is that it is the <term>interstisium</term> <note>A boundary or space between two things.</note> of both the intelligible world—of which we have just spoken—and this sensible world which we inhabit. We cannot more clearly indicate the essence of any middle nature than by expressing the extremes by which it is enclosed; for a middle nature is tempered by the extremes. Therefore, [Moses] reveals the greatest knowledge of the condition of heaven to us when he speaks of the middle heaven being placed between "the waters and the waters"—that is, between the angelic and the corruptible substances—not so much by physical location as by the nature of its essence. 

<margin>For it is clear above how water is the formal cause.</margin>
By "waters," we have already said that we understand "forms," which are present in potentiality (like the "first earth") and which bring essence to perfection. However, just as there is one "earth" of the angels and another of the elements (since the potentiality in each is different), so too is there a different nature or "ratio" of the waters in each—that is, of the forms. Between these, the middle heaven has been allotted its place by the providence of the Architect: possessing divine life on one side and bodily formation on the other; incorruptible substance here, and visible substance there; the firmness of essence here, and the change of location there; and finally, whatever is simple and uniform on one side, and whatever is varied, mixed, and dissimilar on the other.

### Chapter three.

After this, he briefly reminds us of the integrity, position, and order of the elements through the "collection of the waters into one place" and the laws prescribed for the sea so that it does not overwhelm the earth. Indeed, there is nothing that indicates more clearly that there are laws instilled in the elements by an intelligent cause—by which they are ruled and kept in their seats beyond the mere inclination of their brute, bodily nature—than these barriers of the waters. By these, the ocean is restrained; though its momentum would naturally carry it across the entire circuit of the earth (just as the whole of fire rests upon the whole of the air), yet, as if warned by a <term>pedagogue’s rod</term> <note>A metaphor for a teacher's authority or guidance.</note>, it draws back its foot. It does not advance further than our safety and the life of all living creatures 

<margin>Repression of the fierce ocean's furies</margin>
demands. This cannot be attributed to the necessity of matter (which would rather incline all elements equally toward the shape of a globe), nor to the fortuitous collision of atoms as <term>Epicurus</term> <note>The Greek philosopher who proposed that the world was formed by the random clumping of indivisible particles.</note> dreams, nor to the "seed-like" force of nature as <term>Strato</term> <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a naturalistic philosopher who argued that the world functioned by natural necessity without needing divine intervention.</note> says, who was ignorant of any final purpose. 

<margin>Epicurus on atoms and indivisible bodies / Strato</margin>
Instead, it can only be referred to the <term>final cause</term> <note>The "purpose" or "end goal" of a thing, a key concept in Aristotelian philosophy.</note>, to which only a mind and intellectual providence can direct things. For this reason, it happened that Moses, when about to treat the order of the elements, mentioned only this fact; and the prophets so often bring this forward as the most powerful argument for divine power and wisdom. Hence in Proverbs: "When he fortified the abysses with a certain law and circle." 

<margin>Proverbs / Jeremiah</margin>
Hence that saying: "He who surrounded the sea with its boundary"; and in <term>Jeremiah</term> <note>original: *Hieremiam*</note>: "Will you not fear me, says the Lord, who have placed the sand as a bound for the sea?" And: "You have set a bound which they shall not pass over, nor shall the waters cover the earth." Moreover, since the entire constitution of the elements is ordered so that things—especially living things—might be mixed together, for that reason, immediately after the order of the earth and waters and the firmament, he added the command for the earth to bring forth plants. Otherwise, the treatment of that work belonged instead to the fifth day.

### Chapter four.

After he dealt with the celestial and elementary spheres, and thus with the integrity of the "wheel" of the corporeal universe, it remained to speak of the inhabitants and citizens (if I may call them that) of this worldly city. This begins with the celestial beings, as if they were the senate and officials of the city, and then the terrestrial beings, as if they were the common people and the populace. 

<margin>Comparison</margin>
Of the celestial beings, he first mentions those which God placed in the firmament to be "for signs and times," to "shine in the heaven," and to "illuminate the earth." I mean the sun, the moon, and the stars. Very deep questions would need to be examined here, each of which would require a full volume: in what way are these stars in the firmament?

He uses the metaphor of a city to transition into a discussion of the inhabitants of these realms, starting with the celestial "senate" of sun, moon, and stars.</summary>

<margin>
Eusebius
the Mede
Diodorus
Basil
Apollinaris

</margin>

...or whether they are its more noble parts, as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> believe; or whether they are like animals in their own spheres—as fish are in water or cattle are on land—which is the view held by Eusebius the Mede and Diodorus. This passage might also demand a confrontation with the <term>genethliacs</term> <note>Astrologers who cast birth charts to predict the future.</note> who use the stars to confirm the science of divination and the foretelling of future events. Although Moses said the stars were placed by God "for signs," this science is not only condemned by our own fathers—such as Basil, who rightly called it a "most busy vanity," and Apollinaris, Cyril, and Diodorus, who taxed it severely—but even the better Peripatetics reject it. Aristotle held it in contempt, and what is more, Theodoret provides evidence that it was repudiated by Pythagoras, Plato, and all the Stoics. One might also expect to find here a discussion on the nature of stars, their motion, their dominion, the spots on the moon, and all the science of the heavens. Truly, if we were to descend into these matters, as beautiful and worthy of knowledge as they are, we would perhaps hear that line of Horace: *But there was no place for these things now.* <note>original: "Sed nunc non erat his locus." A quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, used here to mean "stay on topic."</note> Therefore, we defer these matters to the work we have planned, in which we have undertaken to treat and examine the whole of philosophy by reconciling Aristotle and Plato as much as we are able.

### Chapter Five.

<margin>What he is not going to treat</margin>
Let us come, then, to Moses. After he spoke of celestial things, he mentioned terrestrial animals in a fitting order: those that inhabit the waters, the earth, or the air (if indeed birds can be said to "inhabit" the air). Let no one here expect or demand from us a dispute on how the bodies of animals are made from the elements, or what <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>Lat: *seminariae rationes*. A Stoic and Augustinian concept of "seed-principles" implanted by God in nature to govern growth and development.</note> were implanted by God into the nature of things. Nor shall we debate whether the life of "brutes" <note>In this period, "brutes" simply meant non-human animals lacking rational souls.</note> is drawn out from the "bosom of matter," or whether all life proceeds from a divine principle, as Plotinus most firmly asserts. Our friend Marsilio Ficino will soon provide a Latin translation of Plotinus for the public benefit, illuminated by his own long arguments. The Prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses here as "the Prophet."</note> might perhaps seem to support this view in this passage; for after he said, "let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of a living soul," he added later, "God created every living soul." Here, someone might observe not only that the waters bring forth at God’s command, but that God Himself also brings them forth. But there is also this: where it speaks of God’s work, it is written "God created the living soul," but where it speaks of the waters, it says not "soul," but "the creeping thing *of* the living soul." It is as if the mixture of the body (the "creeping thing") is attributed to the waters as a vehicle for the soul, but the substance of the soul itself—the giver of life, motion, and sense—shines from the outside into the now-tempered body from God, the divine principle. But more on these things elsewhere.

<margin>Plotinus</margin>

<margin>Three general differences of brutes</margin>
Among the animals of the earth, Moses mentions three: cattle, creeping things, and beasts. In these, he suggests to us the three differences of irrational brutes, for there are no more than these. First, there are **beasts**, which possess a perfect <term>imagination</term> <note>Lat: *phantasia*. The faculty of the soul that receives and stores sensory images.</note> and hold the middle place among the irrational animals, but they do not know how to be tamed or domesticated by man. Second, there are **creeping things**, which have an imperfect imagination and are situated, as it were, between animals and plants. Third, there are **cattle** (beasts of burden). Although these lack reason, they are nonetheless capable of human discipline in some way, and thus they seem to participate in something of reason, holding a middle condition between brutes and men.

### Chapter Six.

<margin>A simile commonly used by kings</margin>
Thus far we have spoken of the three worlds: the supracelestial, the celestial, and the sublunar. Now we must treat of Man, of whom it is written: *Let us make man in our image.* Man is not so much a "fourth world" (as if he were some new creature) as he is the bond and "complex" of the three worlds we have already described. It is a custom often used by the kings and princes of the earth that, if they have built a magnificent and noble city, once the city is finished, they place their own image in the center of it to be seen and admired by all. We see that God, the Prince of all, did the very same: after the whole machinery of the world was constructed, He last of all placed Man in the center of it, formed after His own image and likeness. But it is a difficult question why Man alone has this privilege of being the image of God. For if we cast aside the madness of Melito—who imagined God in a human shape—and return to the nature of reason and mind, which (just as God is an understanding...

<note>Melito of Sardis was an early Christian bishop often (perhaps unfairly) accused by later writers of "Anthropomorphism"—the belief that God possesses a literal physical body.</note>

I say "actually" because even angels and every intelligent creature contain all things in themselves in a certain way, insofar as they know all things through forms and <term>reasons</term> <note>In Platonic and Scholastic thought, "reasons" (rationes) are the formal principles or blueprints of things.</note> of all things. We cannot say this of any other creature, whether angelic, celestial, or sensible. There is, however, this
<margin>The difference between God and man.</margin>
difference between God and man: God contains all things in Himself as the source of all; man contains all things in himself as the center of all. Thus it happens that in God, all things are of a better quality than they are in themselves; in man, the lower things are of a more noble condition, while the higher things are somewhat diminished. There are fire, water, air, and earth, according to the truest property of their nature, in this thick and earthy body of man which we see. There is, besides these, another more divine spiritual body (as 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle says) than the elements, which corresponds in proportion to the heavens. Moreover, there is in man the life of plants, performing for him those same functions as for them: nourishing, growing, and generating. There is the sense of brute animals, both internal and external. There is a soul powerful in celestial reason. There is a participation in the angelic mind. There is, therefore, a truly divine possession of all these natures flowing together into one, so that one might gladly cry out that line of Mercurius:
<margin>Hermes Trismegistus, named Mercurius there, is introduced in the *Asclepius*.</margin>

For him the earth and the elements, for him the brutes are ready and serve; for him the heavens fight; for him angelic minds procure safety and good, if indeed what Paul writes is true: that they are all ministering spirits sent forth to

->Chapter Seven.<-

<margin>Man is the bond and knot of terrestrial and celestial things, as mentioned above, he is the embrace and linkage.</margin>
To man terrestrial things are enslaved, on man celestial things look with favor; for he is the bond and the knot of both the celestial and the terrestrial. Nor can both of these fail to have peace with him, provided that he himself has peace with himself—he who sanctions the peace and treaties of those things within himself. But let us take care, I pray, that being placed in such great dignity, we do not fail to understand it. Rather, let us always have this before the eyes of our mind as a certain, explored, and indubitable truth: just as all things favor us when we keep that law which was given to us, so if through the transgression of the law by sin we fall away from our course, we shall have all things as adverse, hostile, and inimical. For it is reasonable that just as we do an injury not only to ourselves, but to the universe which we embrace within us, and to the author of the world Himself, the omnipotent God—so we are also punished by all things that are in the world, with God and the most powerful things as judges and the most grave avengers of the injury received. From this let us estimate what penalties and what punishments await the transgressors of the divine law. These are they who (as the oracle said):

<margin>From here even among the poets the thresholds of creation are extended.</margin>
The unshaken justice of the entire worldly Republic strikes down and pursues these people. For they are guilty of a violated universe and of <term>lese-majesty</term> <note>Original: "laesae maiestatis." A legal term for treason or an offense against the dignity of a sovereign; here, Pico applies it to an offense against God’s supreme authority.</note> against the divine, whose image they have defiled with the foulest stain of iniquity. Perhaps it is from this that among the prophets, whenever something is promulgated by God—whether commanded or forbidden—heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses. This is because the transgression of a precept also violates them; having received a common insult, they too will receive satisfaction from the wicked while they administer punishments as ministers of God. It altogether surpasses every madness to be led to believe that someone placed in a city and decorated with the highest honors is permitted to offend with impunity against the prince, or against the whole republic which has deserved so well of him, rather than being given over immediately to be tortured and tormented by <term>lictors</term> <note>Original: "lictoribus." Lictors were Roman civil officers who carried out the punishments and executions ordered by magistrates.</note> and executioners, or to be overwhelmed by stones with the consent of the entire people.

<margin>Wicked demons. Paul. Orpheus.</margin>
Indeed, there are executioners and there are lictors in this republic of God: the wicked demons, assigned to the most vile service as punishment for an ancient crime. From this comes that saying of Paul: *I have delivered him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh* <note>Original: "Tradidi illum Sathanae in interitum carnis." A reference to 1 Corinthians 5:5.</note>. From this also comes the naming of the "avenging demon" even in Orpheus, if perhaps we trust our own scriptures less. However, just as every creature hates and execrates the crimes of men, so too is his upright life and conduct pleasing to all and satisfies all. For all things—which are entangled and joined to man by such a tight bond—cannot (so to speak) fail to be admitted into the participation of both his good and his evil. From this comes that Gospel saying: *If a sinner repents, all the angels exult with joy.* From this also comes the clear reason for that mystery which was hidden for ages: that our nature, corrupted in the first Adam and cast down from its state, might be restored through the cross of Christ. Namely, for our sake the Son of God becomes both man and is fixed to the cross. For it was also fitting that He who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation in whom all things were founded, should be coupled by an ineffable union with him <note>Referring to man.</note> who was made in the image of God, who is the bond of every creature, and in whom all things are enclosed. Nor, if all nature was endangered along with man, was its loss either to be neglected or to be repaired by anyone other than Him through whom all nature had been established.

## SIXTH EXPOSITION: ON THE KINSHIP OF THE WORLDS WITH EACH OTHER AND OF ALL THINGS.

### PREFACE TO THE SIXTH BOOK.

<margin>What a wonderful footprint of the Trinity there is in creatures.</margin>
<margin>Father, Son, Spirit: The root of all ordered charity.</margin>
God is a unity so distinct in its triad that it does not depart from the simplicity of unity. There is a manifold footprint of the divine Trinity in the creature. We shall bring forward here only this one, which as far as I know has not yet been offered by anyone: that although we see unity in creatures, we find it divided by a threefold reason. First, there is that unity in things by which each thing is one within itself and consists and coheres for itself. There is a second unity by which one creature is united to another, and through which, finally, all parts of the world are one world. The third and most principal of all is that by which the whole universe is one with its Maker, like an army with its leader. This threefold union is present in each thing through its own single, simple unity derived from that One which is both the first One and simultaneously Three and One: namely, from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the power of the Father, producing all things, bestows His unity upon all; the wisdom of the Son, rightly arranging all things, unites and couples all things to each other; and the love of the Spirit, turning all things back to God, joins the entire work of the Maker by the bond of <term>charity</term> <note>Original: "charitatis." In this context, it refers to "Caritas" or divine, selfless love that binds the universe.</note>. But just as He is more intimate, so God is more "one" to us than we are to ourselves; again, each thing is more tightly joined to itself than to other parts of the world. Thus, having been taught the order of universal charity, if we wish to follow the divine law inscribed on the tablets of nature, we shall love first God Himself above us and above all things; in the second place ourselves; and in the third place our neighbor. and what is one in itself: then he has said enough: when he has examined the nature of all things individually. But concerning that by which we are joined to God: we shall deal with it in the next treatise, where we will dispute concerning the **summit of happiness** <note>Original: "foelicitatis." In Pico’s Neoplatonic context, this refers to the ultimate state of the soul’s union with God, often called "beatitude."</note>. This remains: that by which the diverse parts are coupled to one another in a **mutual covenant**; about which we must deal for the present. <margin>Chapter One.</margin>

After we have seen the distinct natures of things and, as I might say, arranged them in separate stations, lest we believe that one universe is made from all these only because each thing is contained by another according to the condition of its nature (as we showed above), the **Prophet** <note>Pico refers to Moses as "the Prophet," the traditional author of the Book of Genesis.</note> wished also to indicate in his own narrative <note>Original: "contextu," literally the "weaving together" or context of the text.</note> how and in how many ways the natures of things were coupled among themselves. He does this not only to call us to this curious understanding, but through this to instruct and demonstrate by what path and reason we can be coupled to those things which are better than ourselves. However, as I thought before approaching the explanation of the words, about how many ways there were, or could be imagined, by which things might obtain either an affinity or a bond with each other—and as I ran through all the **doctrines of the philosophers** in which I have labored since childhood—scarcely more than fifteen genera occurred to me. These I then saw indicated by Moses so clearly and so aptly that I believe no one could be better instructed concerning them anywhere else. <margin>Chapter Two.</margin>

<margin>In how many ways something is said to be coupled to another</margin>
Immediately, therefore, on the first day—I know not whether more briefly or more clearly—he embraces **five modes** by which something can be joined to another. For that which is joined to another is either its essence, or a property of its essence; or it is in it as a **form in a subject** <note>In Aristotelian terms, a "subject" is the underlying matter, and "form" is the quality or essence that makes it a specific thing (e.g., "roundness" in a bronze sphere).</note>; or it affects it either as that which transmutes affects that which is transmuted, or as art affects the material subject to it. Similarly, we read of five things in Moses, compared and connected as it were: **heaven and earth; earth and emptiness; the abyss and darkness; the spirit of God and the waters; light and bodies.** <margin>The five Mosaic connections.</margin> 

The first mode of connection is designated for us by the **earth, empty and void**, because the earth—that is, matter—is by its nature empty unless it is filled from elsewhere by forms. The second is indicated by **darkness upon the face of the abyss**. For the abyss by its own nature is neither luminous nor dark; but darkness follows its nature unless the approaching light puts it to flight, just as the darkness of **privation** <note>Original: "privationis." A philosophical term for the absence of a quality that should naturally be present.</note> follows the formlessness and emptiness of matter until an arriving species expels it. The third is shown by **light** arising upon bodies. For light is in them as a form in a subject. <margin>How heaven is annexed to the earth.</margin> The fourth is **heaven and earth**, because heaven does not inhere in the earth as a form or accident exists in the thing it perfects; rather, it is joined to it as an **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something about, like a builder building a house.</note> to a patient and a transmuting cause to the body which is transmuted. The last example is the **Spirit of the Lord**, which moved over the waters. For the Artisan, the wisdom of the Lord and the spiritual nature—altogether removed from the commerce of the body—is understood to be joined to bodies in no other way than **art**, which is in the mind of the architect, is joined to cement, wood, and stones. 

But consider again this logic of consequence: that the earth is empty of itself and has its own domestic darkness; then it is joined most closely to light, through light to heaven, and through heaven to the spiritual substance. But let us see how these things hold themselves **within us**. The **earth** is the earthly body, empty and void of life and sense; upon which there is **darkness**: death, torpor, inefficacy, immobility, and lack of sensation. **Light** is the life which vegetates, excites, acts upon, moves it, and renders it endowed with sense. **Heaven** is the soul, the source of that light; and the **Spirit of God** is the intellect, the light of the divine countenance. And concerning these things, even more than is necessary has been said in this place. <margin>Chapter Three.</margin>

Let us examine what Moses intends in what follows, and we shall see **ten other modes** suggested by him, in which we may understand a mutual league between things. For besides those we have mentioned, there are again these which we shall number: since something is either a part of another or an effect; likewise, if it is a part, it is either an indivisible part of its whole...

We have spoken of the part and the effect, and by the same reasoning, of the whole and the cause. For these concepts correspond to one another. But we have not yet fulfilled all the categories of kinship. For there remains that species of affinity regarding the cause: in which the secondary cause obeys and is joined to the primary. Just as when God produces, the waters produce; these do so first, because they are the **proximate cause** <note>The immediate or direct cause in a chain of events.</note>, but not otherwise than by God's command, because the primary cause has more influence than the secondary. Similarly, there is a secondary end attached and annexed to the principal one; which the Prophet <note>Moses.</note> signifies cleverly by saying the stars were placed to shine in the sky and to illuminate the earth. For the benefit of inferior things is not the primary purpose of the celestial bodies. Rather, they intend this first: that they should shine for themselves;
<margin>Homer</margin> then finally that they might illuminate us. For this reason, we read in **Homer** <note>A reference to the opening lines of Book 12 of the *Odyssey*, where the sun rises to bring light to the immortals and then to mortals.</note> that both the dawn and the sun rise first for the immortals and then for mortals to bring light. Furthermore, beyond all these things, man is kin to man and lion to lion. Yet a lion is neither a part nor an effect of another lion if it was not sired by it; the Prophet signifies this when he gathers and unites the fish, birds, and beasts of the earth together. There is a final reason for affinity: which is the agreement of a **middle nature** <note>Original: "mediae naturae." ## Chapter six.

Let us again examine what the arrangement of the waters and the earth teaches us. Let us learn from the earth that we shall not bring forth the fruit we are laboring to produce unless we repress and drive back the force of the flowing and falling matter that invades us, and unless we cast out from our dwellings the whirlpools and torrents of pleasures that rush in upon us like waters. Let us learn from the waters that they were not considered fit for procreating fish until they were collected into the single integrity of their own element. For neither shall we be able to bring to light any offspring worthy of our divine nature if we are torn apart and distracted by diverse things, and if we are not carried toward a single intention with all our powers collected together. 

<margin>a mystery</margin>
There is also contained here a deeper mystery: just as it is the happiness of drops of water to reach the ocean where the fullness of waters resides, so it is our happiness that the portion of intellectual light within us should one day be joined to the first intellect of all and to the Primary Mind, where there is fullness and the entire universality of intelligence.

## Chapter seven.

<insert>NATIONAL LIBRARY VITTORIO EMANUELE ROME</insert>
But the greatest thing of all is that which the doctrine of the firmament signifies to us: where we see that the lower waters cannot be enriched by any benefit from the upper waters unless the heaven intervenes, which is placed as a medium between them. Thus, let us propose to our minds that a union of extremes can only be achieved through a nature which, being the middle between the extremes, embraces both within itself. Therefore, it conveniently unites those things—that is, the extremes—among themselves, because it first united them within itself through the property of its own nature.

<margin>Man cannot be joined to God except through Christ</margin>
From this we are reminded of that great sacrament <note>The Latin "sacramentum" here refers to a sacred mystery or "hidden truth."</note> which is *foolishness to the Gentiles and a stumbling block to the Hebrews*, but to us *the power and wisdom of God*: that man cannot be joined to God except through Him who, having joined man to God within Himself, has been made a true mediator. He is thus able to bind men to God so that, just as in Him the Son of God put on man, so through Him men might become sons of God. If what we say is true—that extremes are not joined to each other except through a medium, and that which is truly called a medium is that which has already united the extremes within itself—then surely if that ineffable dispensation <note>original: "dispensatio," referring to the "divine economy" or the plan of the Incarnation.</note> occurred in Christ alone, so that the **Word became flesh**, then Christ alone is also He through whom flesh can ascend to the **Word**. 

<margin>John Paul Christ</margin>
Nor is there (as John rightly wrote) *any other name under heaven by which it is necessary for men to be saved* <note>A reference to Acts 4:12, though Pico attributes the sentiment to "John," perhaps associating the theology with the Johannine tradition or misremembering the specific attribution in the heat of composition.</note>. Let those who say they believe with Christ, yet believe that a common religion or the religion into which each was born is sufficient for attaining happiness, take diligent notice of this. Let them believe not me, nor these arguments, but John, Paul, and Christ Himself, who said: *I am the way. I am the door; and he who does not enter through me is a thief and a robber.*

<summary>Pico interprets the separation of earth and water as a metaphor for the soul's need to repress physical pleasures and find unity. He further argues that Christ acts as the necessary ontological "medium" or bridge between the human and the divine, asserting the necessity of Christ for salvation.</summary>

# SEVENTH EXPOSITION ON HAPPINESS, WHICH IS ETERNAL LIFE.
## PREFACE TO THE SEVENTH BOOK.

<margin>Twofold happiness</margin>
**I**f we have examined the order and nature of the ranks of the whole world in the six completed expositions, as if in six days, it remains that in this seventh treatise—as if on the Sabbath of our commentary—we treat the Sabbath of the world and the rest of creatures, whose nature we established in the previous parts; that is, we shall treat their happiness. Or, to speak more correctly, let us listen to Moses treating this as a true prophet of all things to come. Now, there is one kind of happiness (as theologians proclaim) which we can attain through nature, and another through grace. They call the former "natural" and the latter "supernatural." Concerning the first, that is, natural happiness, enough has been said by Moses; for once the nature of things is known, we also know their natural happiness. It remains, therefore, for him to teach concerning the
<margin>The illusion of some</margin>
second kind, showing himself to be a prophet rather than a teacher. For when Moses wrote, grace did not yet exist, but it was to come. Truly, however, because I seem to see certain <term>sciolists</term> <note>original: "sciolos." Those who possess a superficial, "smattering" of knowledge but claim to be experts.</note>—I might better call them worthless idlers and rascals—who call themselves philosophers when they are nothing of the sort, immediately laughing at both grace and supernatural happiness as if these were empty names and old wives' tales, I wished to make a very brief dispute with them on this matter 
<margin>Definition of happiness.</margin>
as a preface to the seventh book. This is a matter useful on its own to all, and very necessary for the work we have undertaken, wherein I may clearly prove that the view of the theologians stands firm, rooted and established in the deepest foundations of philosophy. I define happiness as follows: the return of each thing to its own principle <note>original: "principium." In this context, it refers to the source or origin from which a thing began.</note>. For happiness is the supreme good. The supreme good is that which all things
<margin>What the desirable Good is according to Alexander</margin>
desire. But that which all things desire is that which is the principle of all things, as **Alexander of Aphrodisias** <note>A celebrated commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD) who emphasized the naturalistic aspects of his philosophy.</note> attests in his commentaries on First Philosophy <note>Aristotle's Metaphysics.</note>, and as the Greek interpreters attest regarding Aristotle’s *Ethics*.
<margin>The Pythagorean name for God</margin>
Therefore, the end of all things is the same as the principle of all things: the one God, almighty and blessed, the best of all things that can either exist or be imagined. Here, two names are primarily applied to Him among the **Pythagoreans**: namely, "The One" and "The Good." He is named "The One" because He is the principle of all,
<margin>Why God is called Alpha and Omega, as will be said below</margin>
just as unity is the principle of all number. He is "The Good" because He is the end of all, the rest of all, and absolute happiness. We can already see, if we are a little more skillful, the reason for the twofold happiness. For happiness is the possession and attainment of this first Good. This Good can be attained by created things in two ways: either in themselves, or in Him. For this Good is both in itself, exalted above all things and dwelling in the abysses of its own divinity, and it is found diffused through all things in all things.
<margin>Poets</margin>
In some things He is found more perfectly, in others more imperfectly, according to the condition of the things by which He is participated in. Whence (as the poets write), "Jupiter is whatever you see" and "all things are full of Jove" <note>original: "Iuppiter est quodcumque vides, & Iovis omnia plena sunt." Pico quotes classical poets like Lucan and Virgil to show that even pagans intuited God's omnipresence.</note>.
<margin>What natural happiness is</margin>
Therefore, since every nature has God within itself in some way (for it possesses as much of God as it possesses of goodness, and all things that God made are good), it follows that when a nature possesses itself in its full perfection, having attained itself, it also attains God within itself. And if the attainment of God is happiness (as we have proved), it becomes happy in some way within itself. This is **natural happiness**, which different things have obtained in greater or lesser degrees according to the diversity of their natures. 
<margin>In what way fire participates in God.</margin>
Fire is a thing lacking a soul, yet it participates in God in many ways. For first, it *is*, and each thing participates in God insofar as it exists, for He is "Being itself." Likewise, because fire is a certain species and an act, it is like God, who is the First Species and the First Act. And while fire produces fire, it imitates the divine fecundity; while it contains itself within the boundaries of its own sphere, it imitates justice; while it serves us, it imitates beneficence according to the small measure of its nature. This fire, while it acts, having attained its perfection...

<summary>Pico defines happiness as the return of a creature to its original source (God) and distinguishes between natural happiness, found within a creature's own perfected nature, and supernatural happiness. He defends these theological concepts against skeptics by grounding them in the philosophy of Aristotle, Alexander of Aphrodisias, and the Pythagoreans.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Preface to the Seventh Book, transitioning from the definition of natural happiness to the necessity of supernatural grace for true union with God. Pico is currently contrasting the views of ancient and medieval philosophers with those of Christian theologians.</meta>

->HEPTAPLUS<-

Each part is happy to the extent that it is capable of happiness. Plants are more happy, because they possess life; animals more happy still, having also been granted the power of cognition, so that as they find more perfection, so too they find more of the 
<margin>Man is in the best condition of all mortals.</margin>
divine within themselves. Man is in the best condition of all mortals: he who, just as in his nature, also excels others in natural happiness; he is endowed with intelligence and freedom of choice—the principal 
gifts and those most conducive to happiness. The angelic mind is supreme among creatures, both in the nobility of its substance and in the attainment of its goal; it is the greatest participant in the divine, because 
it is both joined and closest to it. But truly, as we said above, through this happiness, neither plants, nor beasts, nor man, nor an angel reaches God—who is the supreme good—in God himself, but rather they reach Him in themselves. For this reason, the degree of happiness varies step by step according to the capacity of their nature.
<margin>The imperfection of natural happiness</margin>
**F**or this reason, the philosophers, speaking only of this [natural happiness], placed the happiness of each thing in the best operation of its own nature. And concerning the angels, whom they call "minds" and "intellects," even if they confessed that their highest perfection was that they understood God, they nevertheless established that the knowledge they have of God is no other than that by which they know themselves; thus they understand only as much of God as the nature of God is represented in their own substance. Regarding man, even if different thinkers have felt differently, they all kept themselves within the narrow bounds of human faculty: either in the mere investigation of truth, as the <term>Academics</term> <note>Followers of the later Platonic Academy who practiced a form of skepticism, holding that the "search" for truth was the highest human activity since absolute certainty was unattainable.</note> did; or rather in the attainment of it through the study of philosophy, as <margin>Al-Farabi</margin> Al-Farabi <note>A famous 10th-century Islamic philosopher who integrated Aristotelianism and Neoplatonism.</note> said, defining the happiness of man. <margin>Averroes, Avicenna, Abubacher, Alexander</margin> Averroes, Avicenna, Abubacher <note>Ibn Bajja (c. 1085–1138), known in the West as Abubacher, an Andalusian philosopher.</note>, Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (c. 200 AD), the most influential ancient commentator on Aristotle.</note>, and the Platonists dared to give something more, fixing our reason in the "intellect in act," or in some higher intellect, yet one related to us as if in its own goal; but even these do not lead man back to his own beginning nor to the supreme good. I neither reject nor despise these disputes and opinions of theirs, if they profess only to be speaking of natural happiness. For it is certain that through it, man or angels cannot be raised higher than what they say. This is most strongly proven by this reasoning: since nothing striving by its own strength can rise above itself (otherwise it would be more powerful than itself), surely nothing striving by itself will be able to attain any happiness greater or more perfect than its own nature. But let these philosophers tell me: if this is the only happiness in things, why 
<margin>Man cannot be joined to God by his own strength</margin>
do even they admit that among animals, only man is born for happiness? For why should others besides man also reach their own ends? We can say there are other forms of happiness lesser than man's; but how shall we defend the idea that there is none at all? Rather, since other things below man never stray from the end established by nature, while man almost always goes astray, human condition would seem the most unhappy of all, unless man could boast of some other privilege. Let us therefore hear the sacred <margin>Theologians</margin> theologians, who remind us of our dignity and of those divine goods which are offered to us freely by the most liberal Father; let us not, I pray, be cruel to our own souls and ungrateful toward God our Maker by rejecting them. 
<margin>What the difference is between supernatural and natural happiness</margin>
We said above that the height of happiness is in the attainment of God, who is the supreme good and the principle of all things. But this can happen in two ways: for we reach God either in the creatures in which God shares Himself, or in God Himself. We have also shown—and it must be shown—that if we pay attention, the former is a shadow of happiness rather than true happiness, just as the creature in which you reach God is not the supreme goodness itself, but a thin shadow of the supreme, that is, the divine goodness. Add to this that through that [natural happiness] things are restored to themselves rather than to God; they have not 
<margin>Who are capable of supernatural happiness and in what way</margin>
achieved a return to their beginning, but only this: that they do not depart from themselves. But true and perfected happiness leads us back and draws us to gaze upon the "Face of God," which is "all good" (as He Himself said), and to a perfect union with that Principle from which we flowed. Angels can be lifted up to this, but they cannot ascend to it by their own power. This is why Lucifer sinned, saying: *I will ascend into heaven* <note>original: "Ascendã in cælu." A reference to Isaiah 14:13, describing the pride and fall of the morning star.</note>. Man cannot go to this; he can be drawn, which is why Christ said of Himself, who is that very...
<meta>catchword: ...way [modo]</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that while philosophers correctly define natural happiness as acting according to one's nature, this is merely a "shadow." True, supernatural happiness consists in direct union with God's essence, which no creature can achieve by its own strength, but only through being "drawn" by divine grace.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Preface to the Seventh Book of the Heptaplus. In the previous section, Pico established that natural happiness is limited by the capacity of a creature's nature. Here, he transitions to "supernatural happiness," which requires the intervention of divine grace, using the analogy of celestial motion and the "divine mover."</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

<margin>
Who are capable of supernatural happiness and in what way
</margin>
...happiness said: <note>original: "fœlícítas díxít." Pico personifies happiness, citing the words of Christ from John 6:44.</note> "No one comes to me unless my Father has drawn him." Brute animals and those things below man can neither go nor be drawn to it. Therefore, only man and the angel are made for that happiness, which is true happiness. Vapor can ascend on high, but only when attracted by a ray of the sun; a stone and every heavy substance can neither admit the ray at all, nor be lifted into the heights by it. This ray, this divine power, this influence, we call <term>grace</term> <note>original: "gratiam." In theology, grace is the free and unmerited favor of God, here described as a "divine ray" that pulls the soul upward.</note> because it makes both man and angel pleasing to God.

<margin>
An example of both kinds of happiness in physical bodies.
</margin>
The philosophers have a clear example of this doctrine in physical bodies. For among bodies, some move in a straight line, while others move in a circle. Straight motion—by which the elements are carried to their proper places—represents natural happiness, through which things are stabilized in the perfection of their own nature. Circular motion—through which a body is revolved back to the same point from which it departed—is the most expressive image of true happiness, through which the creature returns to the same Beginning from which it had proceeded. But see how all things agree on both sides. Only immortal and incorruptible bodies move in a circle. Only an immortal and eternal substance returns to God. For the elements to complete their motions, they need no other power than that which was bestowed on them from their birth, whether by the impulse of gravity or levity; in the same way, individual things are carried toward natural happiness by their own impulse and their own power. But truly, although the heavenly bodies are suited for circular motion, they are not sufficient in themselves to complete this motion; rather, they have need of a <term>divine mover</term> <note>original: "divino motore." Referring to the Aristotelian concept of the "Unmoved Mover" who initiates the motion of the celestial spheres.</note> who may turn and revolve them. Finally, those bodies are so suited for perpetual revolution that they do not *cause* it, but rather *receive* it. It happens no differently for us and for the angels. For we are such by nature that we cannot turn and reflect ourselves, but we can be turned by the moving power of grace and reflected back into God. Hence that saying: <note>Romans 8:14</note> "Those who are led by the spirit of God are the sons of God." He said those who are *led*, not those who *lead*. In this we differ from the heavens: that they are moved by the necessity of nature, but we are moved through our freedom. For the spirit-mover constantly knocks at your soul. If you refuse to listen, you will be left to yourself, to your own sluggishness, and to your own weakness, wretched and unhappy. If you admit it, being immediately filled with God, you are carried back through the circle of religion to the Father and to the Lord, to possess life forever in Him, in whom 

<margin>
The sum of true happiness
</margin>
you were life even before you were made. This is true happiness: that we should be one spirit with God; that we should possess God in God, not in ourselves, knowing "even as we also are known." <note>1 Corinthians 13:12</note> For He knew us not through us, but through Himself. So also we shall know Him through Himself, and not through ourselves. This is the whole reward; this is eternal life; this is the wisdom which the wise of this world did not know: that from all the imperfection of multiplicity, we may be reduced into unity through an indissoluble bond with Him who is Unity itself.

For this happiness, Christ prayed to the Father in this manner:
> Father, grant that even as you and I are one, so also these may be one with us. <note>John 17:21</note>
In this happiness Paul hoped, saying:
> I shall know not in part, but even as He is; <note>Paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 13:12</note>
And since he so hoped, did he not rightly say:
> Who shall separate me from the love of Christ? <note>Romans 8:35</note>
And he desired

The fall of the demon
</margin>
to be dissolved, so that he might become one with Christ. From this happiness the demon fell, because he wished to ascend to it, not to be carried up; and therefore he lost that which he would have held if he had remained.

<margin>
The lot of infants who die before being initiated.
</margin>
From this root it is known what is the fate of infants who have died before being initiated <note>original: "inítiatí," referring here to the sacrament of Baptism.</note>: namely, they remain with themselves, neither stripped of their own goods, nor enriched with divine ones. For us, we must fall into one of two parts: either the greatest misery or the greatest happiness. Since he who is the cause of not receiving the Mover not only makes himself immune to grace, but also corrupts his own nature, whose integrity depends on this: that it seeks the recognized spirit and does not refuse it. Beyond doubt, a nature cannot be right if it either rejects or despises the hope of a greater good offered to it. Therefore, after Christ has been made known, if any do not "put on Christ," they are deprived not only of the primary happiness, but also of the worldly—that is, the natural—right; because to be unwilling to receive grace belongs only to a corrupt and failing nature. <margin>Against those who think that heresy arises from the fountains of philosophy.</margin>
...because just as we love and retain that which has already been given to the human race, so also the fathers under the Old Law received Him; they believed in His future coming without doubt, hoped for it eagerly, and desired it ardently. But just as they received Him not as one already present, but as one to come, so too they did not experience the fruit of the indwelling Spirit until after He arrived. When, after the covenant on the altar of the cross—that ineffable sacrifice—Christ descended to them, they were whirled by Him, as by a mover, in the space of a moment toward liberty, and raised to the rank of the highest happiness. Religion promotes, directs, and impels us toward this happiness, just as we use <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "phīa" (philosophia). For Pico, philosophy is the handmaid to theology, preparing the mind for divine truths.</note> as a guide toward natural happiness. If nature is the first step of grace, then surely philosophy is the beginning of religion; nor is there any philosophy that moves a man away from religion. Correcty, therefore, do we also follow Moses: after we have philosophized about nature for six days, on the seventh day, being free for divine things, we shall speak of supernatural happiness.

## Chapter One.

<margin>Angelic and human nature is capable of celestial happiness.</margin>
This highest happiness (as we have shown) is capable of being received by a twofold nature: the angelic and the human. The former is called "heaven," the latter "earth," because angels inhabit heaven and we inhabit the earth. And concerning heaven there is no need to say more, because Moses was going to write the law not for angels, but for men. Descending to men, therefore, he says: *The earth was formless and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep.* <note>Genesis 1:2.</note> God does not create emptiness; He does not create darkness. But the earth (he says) *was* empty and there *was* darkness. He does not say these things were created, but that they existed. Why this was said will become clear once we recognize what this emptiness and this darkness are. Human nature, which is called "earth" in comparison to the angels, was empty and void of <term>original justice</term> <note>original: "originali iustitia." In theology, this refers to the state of perfect harmony and grace in which the first humans were created before the Fall.</note> immediately from the beginning—because it sinned immediately—and its "face" (that is, its reason) was veiled by the darkness of sin. God did not make these things, but rather the malice of man, who willingly deprived himself of those goods with which God had enriched him. Thus is the state of corrupt nature described by the prophet; in what follows, it will be demonstrated how, through Abraham, through Moses, through the prophets, and finally through His only-begotten Son, human nature was restored to its former dignity and prepared for the highest happiness. Truly, even at the time when the waters were covered by darkness—infected, that is, by the ancient filth of the original mark—nevertheless, the Spirit of the Lord cherished them. This is to be understood in two ways: first, that men were still ruled by the light of the divine countenance which is signed upon us (that is, the light of natural intelligence); and second, that the human race was not abandoned by the care of divine providence. Rather, the Spirit of the Lord cherished the waters—that Spirit <margin>The Apostle.</margin> who (as the Apostle says) <note>Referring to St. Paul in Romans 8:26.</note> intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words—and even then, He was constantly considering how He might purge those waters of the poisons with which the ancient serpent had infected them. And behold, He immediately commands light to arise: and light was made. <margin>The merits of Abraham.</margin> This light is Abraham, that most wise first founder of true religion. He was the first because he was released from the law of nature and meditated on the divine law; the first to persuade men of the worship of the one God against idols and the nations; the first who attempted to dispel the darkness of error and to declare war on the evil demons who are called the "princes of darkness." For this reason, he is worthily named "light." Because all the disciples of the Lord did this as well, they were all called "the light of the world" by the Lord. This is the first light that shone upon the world, and it distinguished between the religion of the demons and that of the true God, as if between light and darkness.

## Chapter Three.

It would have come to pass, unless some greater power and mercy of God stood in the way, that the waters which are under the heaven—that is, those serving idols—would have invaded and occupied everything. Thus the infection of the whole world from the first stain, and the empire of Satan the avenger, demanded his right over us, who were guilty of the ancient offense and nearly liable to this kind of servitude. But the always beneficent and saving providence of God willed that one part of the earth—even if a small one, as far as the laws of justice permitted—should be free from the injury of the waters. This is Judea, called the <term>Promised Land</term>, <margin>The preservation of Judea was promised to Abraham and the rest.</margin> because it was promised by God to Abraham and his posterity. All the prophets support our exposition, for among them the onslaught of the Gentiles against the Israelites is so often compared to the incursions of waters and the sea. Hence they raised the cry: "the floods have lifted up their voice," and "the wonderful surges of the sea," and "the waters thereof roared and were troubled," and "we will not fear though the earth be troubled and the mountains be carried into the heart of the sea" <note>Pico is paraphrasing Psalm 93 and Psalm 46.</note>. Indeed, the Gentiles surrounded Judea, enclosed within the boundaries of a not very large region, in no other way than the ocean now surrounds this certainly modest portion of the earth which we inhabit. But also in many places in <margin>In Christian letters, the Gentiles are designated by waters.</margin> Christian letters <note>meaning the New Testament</note>, the Gentiles are designated by "waters." For it is written: "the waters which you saw are the peoples" <note>Revelation 17:15</note>; and when the Lord Jesus made wine out of water, which had failed in the Pharisee's house, he signified figuratively (as our writers say) that the waters—that is, the Gentiles—were to be called to that faith <margin>The Lord Jesus: Why water is mixed with wine in the mysteries.</margin> which would thereafter fail among the Jews, where it had previously existed. Likewise, they hand down in the <term>mysteries</term> <note>Referring to the liturgy of the Eucharist</note> that water is mixed with wine for this reason: so that the waters—that is, the Gentiles—may draw in and drink the blood of Christ through the faith of the cross. Therefore, that part asserted from the yoke of the waters was by God’s providence: so that if the rest of the earth, overwhelmed by the waves of spiritual wickedness, was to be useless and deserted, and not fit for the fruits of true religion, this part at least would be; which, having received the light brought forth on the first day and the dew of heaven established on the second—that is, the doctrine of the Law—helped toward fertility, might meanwhile germinate as if herbs, plants, and trees: the judgments, ceremonies, and good morals; until, when the <term>fullness of time</term> had come, it might germinate that very Savior <margin>Isaiah</margin> whom Isaiah also desired.
