<margin>Jesus Christ, the splendor of the paternal substance.</margin>
...that is, of the true religion, which He had brought into the world to be spread most widely through the whole circle of the earth by the <term>Sun of Righteousness</term><note>A reference to Malachi 4:2, often interpreted by Christians as a prophecy of Christ.</note>, by the true light that illuminates all men. He saw Jesus Christ, the <note>original: "splendor paternae substantiae"</note> splendor of the paternal substance <note>A phrase from Hebrews 1:3, describing Christ as the "radiance of God's glory."</note>, shining upon those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death; and he saw the prince of darkness, the prince of this world, being cast out and banished from the minds of men. He saw these things and rejoiced; he saw the fourth day and was glad. This is the day the Lord has made; on which the Lord becomes man, on which God dwelt among us: let us, too, exult and rejoice in it. I ask you, Christian brothers, to consider a little more carefully how true and solid the reasoning of our exposition is. From this, they will supply you with the most powerful weapons against the stony heart of the Hebrews, fetched from their own armories. We will prove this, first, from the testimonies of the Jews: that the coming of Christ is signified to us through the works of the fourth day. Second, we will show that the <term>Messiah</term> is represented to us by nothing more fittingly than by the sun; and we will gather most evidently from the logic of the times that the Christ is not to come in the future, but that Jesus of Nazareth, the son of the Virgin, was the Messiah promised to the Hebrews.

<margin>Dogma of the Hebrews</margin>
It is among the decrees of the ancient Hebrew discipline that the six thousand years of the world are designated by the six days of Genesis: so that what are called here the works of the first day are a prophecy of those things which were to happen in the first millennium of the world; likewise the works of the second in the second, and so on, with the same order of succession always preserved on both sides. To this opinion, <margin>Moses of Girona</margin> <term>Moses of Girona</term><note>Also known as Nahmanides or Ramban (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar.</note>, a theologian of the highest celebrity among the Hebrews, bears witness among the more recent authors. <margin>Saint Jerome</margin> Saint Jerome also mentions this in his exposition of that psalm which is inscribed to Moses <note>Psalm 90:4</note>; <margin>A day of God is a thousand years.</margin> and this opinion seems to rest chiefly on that foundation: that "a thousand years" (as the prophet says) "are as one day" before God. Therefore, if this doctrine is true, the fourth day is a prophecy of those things that were to happen in the fourth millennium of the world. Come now, let us show that according to the annals of the Hebrews, and the calculation of years which they themselves approve, <margin>At what time Jesus appeared according to the annals of the Hebrews.</margin> Jesus appeared in the fourth millennium of the world. They compute from Adam to the flood 1,556 years; from the flood to Abraham 292 years; and so from Adam to Abraham 1,848 years are collected. But from the birth of Isaac to the ruin of the second Temple, which was after the death of Christ, they count about 1,660 years. For they calculate 430 years from Isaac to the exit from Egypt; from the exit to the temple which Solomon built, almost the same number; from Solomon to the desolation of the temple by the Babylonians, 410 years; and from the restoration of the temple under Ezra to this captivity under Titus, 420 years. Therefore, if you collect all these together, you will calculate from the beginning of the world to Christ, according to the mind of the Hebrews themselves, 3,508 years; so that Christ arrived in the very middle of the fourth millennium, and within the same millennium—as if within the boundaries of the fourth day—the light of the moon (that is, the Church) shone upon the whole world; and an innumerable multitude of martyrs, apostles, and doctors, all of whom became famous within five hundred years after the death of Christ, illuminated the obscurity of the <term>firmament</term> (that is, the Law) and the darkness of our night. But the Hebrews will say: "Granted that Jesus arrived during these times. You still do not have proof that he was the Christ, unless you show it was believed by our people that Christ would come during those times." The matter stands well, and they ask for what is fair; and we can easily provide what they rightly demand. <margin>The oracles of Elijah</margin> For manifest, common, and public oracles of Elijah are circulated among them, which expressly state, without any figure or veil, that the Messiah would come in the fourth millennium of the world; and lest these seem either invented by me or interpreted according to my own will, I shall bring forward the testimonies of the <margin>Talmudists</margin> <term>Talmudists</term><note>The rabbinic sages whose discussions are recorded in the Talmud.</note> themselves, with whom we must deal.

<summary>Pico argues that the creation of the sun on the fourth day symbolizes the coming of Christ in the fourth millennium of world history. He uses Jewish chronological sources and the "Oracles of Elijah" from the Talmud to demonstrate that Jesus of Nazareth appeared exactly when Jewish tradition predicted the Messiah would arrive.</summary>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

<margin>In the <term>Avodah Zarah</term><note>Pico writes 'Anodazara', referring to a tractate of the Talmud concerning 'Foreign Worship'.</note>, how the future coming of the Messiah is described</margin>
...there is a controversy: they even make mention of these things and, compelled by the truth itself, they confess that the time predicted by Elijah for the coming of the Messiah has already passed. These words are found in the section titled *Avodah Zarah*, in the chapter <note>original: "libne edeē"</note> of the <term>Tanna Debei Eliyahu</term><note>A rabbinic midrash; Pico transcribes it as 'Tana dbe elihau'.</note>: <note>original Hebrew: "seseth alaphim sana ha ue haola. Sene alaphim tohu: usnæ alaphim thora: usnæ alaphim iemoth hamassihi uba hauonothema serabu ias hu meon maseias."</note> "The world is six thousand years. Two thousand are void; two thousand are the Law; two thousand are the days of the Messiah; and because of our sins, which are many, those years that have passed, have passed." Thus they say. Come now, with these very words placed before the eyes of all—since I can bring forward nothing fabricated or arbitrary—let us discuss and examine the words of the oracle, and we shall immediately achieve our purpose. "The world is six thousand years," it says. We may interpret this to mean that after a circuit of six thousand years (as many of our own people have also believed), the consummation of the world will occur like a <term>Sabbath</term><note>The idea that the world lasts 6,000 years, followed by a 1,000-year "rest" or end-times, mirroring the six days of creation and the Sabbath.</note>. Or, more truly, we may take it in this sense: that no prophecy in the Law extends to a further time. But this does not pertain to the question at hand. Let us see what follows: "Two thousand void; two thousand Law; then the Messiah."

<margin>Hebrew interpreters</margin>
It is called "void" (as all Hebrew interpreters say) to describe the time before any law was given by God to men. But I see the mocking Jew saying: "If there are two thousand years before the Law and two thousand of the Law, then the Messiah is not to come on the *fourth* day (that is, while the fourth millennium is acting), but rather on the *fifth* day, because it is after the fourth millennium." But the response is easy, as the spirited truth itself supplies it. For what is said by Elijah—"two thousand void, two thousand Law"—is not to be understood as if the world were to be without law for a full two thousand years, and similarly that the Law would remain for exactly two thousand years. Rather, it means that the time of the law of nature would reach into the second millennium, and the time of the [Mosaic] Law would reach unto the fourth. But even before the second millennium is finished, there is the Law; and before the fourth passes away, there shall be the Messiah.

<margin>Elijah and the Talmudists</margin>
I do not fashion or dream up this exposition for myself; rather, Elijah himself teaches it to me, and the <term>Talmudists</term><note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> teach it. This will soon be manifest to you, Jewish <term>asp</term><note>A common, though harsh, Renaissance polemical metaphor for an opponent who 'plugs their ears' to the truth.</note> (unless you close your ears). Elijah says: "two thousand void, and two thousand Law." Let us see in what sense what is said about the "void" was true; from that, let us learn the method for explaining what is said about the Law.

<margin>How the beginning of the Law ought to be understood</margin>
We must take the beginning of the Law either from Moses or from Abraham. It cannot be taken from Moses, because then the "void" would have lasted more than two thousand and three hundred years, or thereabouts—for that is roughly the span from Adam to Moses. Therefore, the beginning of the Law must be taken from Abraham, to whom was given the covenant of circumcision, the root and foundation of the entire ancient Law. But if the Jews consult their own histories, they find that from Adam to Abraham, a full span of two thousand years had not passed, but only one thousand, eight hundred and forty-eight years had flowed by. Thus it happens that the fullness of the Law succeeded the "void" not *after* the second millennium, but *within* its boundaries. For the same reason, the evangelical fullness [of the Messiah] ought to succeed the "void" of the Law not *after* the fourth millennium, but while the fourth was still acting.

<margin>Talmudists</margin>
If they should impudently and obstinately persist in denying this, let them hear their own Talmudists, who most strongly reinforce our opinion. For they themselves confess that even at the time they were writing, the time predicted by Elijah for the coming of the Messiah had already passed, and they attribute this to their own sins. If the words of Elijah were to be understood as meaning that Christ was to come *after* the fourth millennium and not within the limits of that fourth itself, the Talmudists would not have said—nor could they have said—that the time promised by the prophets for the Messiah had passed; for at the time the Talmudic doctrine I have cited was written, four thousand years had not yet passed from the beginning of the world. He appeared...

<meta>catchword: ...appeared</meta>

<summary>Pico uses a famous prophecy from the Talmud (the prophecy of Elijah) to argue that the transition between the three great ages of the world—Void, Law, and Messiah—occurs within the specified millennia rather than after them. He calculates that the Messiah must have appeared during the fourth millennium of world history, aligning with the birth of Jesus.</summary>

# HEPTAPLVS

<margin>Jerusalem <term>Talmud</term><note>The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of discussions on Jewish law and tradition.</note></margin>
<margin>Babylonian <term>Talmud</term></margin>
...appeared. For as we showed above, Jesus appeared three thousand five hundred and eight years after the beginning of the world, according to the Hebrew reckoning. Moreover, they themselves hand down that the Jerusalem Talmud was written in the three-hundredth year after Christ’s death, and the Babylonian Talmud in the hundredth year after the Jerusalem one <note>The Jerusalem Talmud was compiled around 350–400 CE; the Babylonian around 500 CE. Pico is using these dates to show they were written within the "fourth millennium" of their calendar.</note>. Therefore, both were composed within the boundaries of the fourth millennium. And yet, they both confess and lament that the time spoken of by Elijah regarding the coming of Christ has already passed. Where will they hide themselves? Or what lurking places will they seek, so that they might not see our Sun <note>A metaphor for Christ.</note> shining throughout the whole world, even against their will?

The <term>Talmudists</term> confess (even if they do not believe the ancients) that the times predicted by the prophets for the coming of Christ have passed. They confess that the prophets believed He would come during those very times in which they acknowledge Jesus did arrive. Nor are their own teachers entirely untruthful when they say that the Messiah did not come because of their sins. For indeed, He did not "come" to those who did not recognize Him. Nor is He the Messiah—that is, the redeemer, the avenger of the most wretched captivity, the beneficent king, the granter of the promised land (which is the heavenly Jerusalem)—except to those who have confessed Him as the Messiah. But if He came unto His own and His own received Him not, those who were once His are no longer His; instead, they come from the east and from the west to lie in the bosom of Abraham, while the children of the kingdom <note>original: "filii aut dılectıonıs", likely "filii autem dilectionis" or "filii regni"</note> are cast into the outer darkness. From this, their persistent question is resolved: that the Messiah would be for the salvation of the Hebrews, but Christ was for their ruin and destruction. For they are not truly Hebrews who not only fail to follow the King and Lord promised to the Hebrews from the seed of David, but who also—as if He were a thief, a sacrilegious man, and a profane person—affixed Him to the Cross with every injury and insult. If they were children of Abraham, they would persist in the institutions of Abraham; and they would have received His coming with joy, just as Abraham, foreseeing this "fourth day," rejoiced. But—

<margin>What the coming of Christ brought to the human race.</margin>
The Messiah brought peace to men, but not to all. For it was not said simply by the angels, "and on earth peace to men," but it was added, "to men of good will" <note>A reference to the Latin Vulgate translation of Luke 2:14: "pax hominibus bonae voluntatis."</note>. Certainly, the same sun that illuminates healthy eyes blinds and darkens those that are sick and weak. It is consistent with right reason that what is healthy for the good should be harmful to the evil; and He who blesses His friends, being powerful and not ungrateful, should also strike and scatter His enemies with lightning. If it had gone poorly for the Jews after accepting Christ, He would not have been the Christ. But if it went poorly for them because they crucified Him, then He certainly was the Christ. For even when affixed to the Cross, at the very moment He appeared most defeated, He triumphed over His conquerors with such slaughter and calamity for them. Why then, O blind ones, do you wait for the sun? The Sun is here and it shines; but it shines in the darkness, and your darkness does not comprehend it. The fourth day has passed, in which the Sun rose. He did not abolish the Law, but perfected it—just as the sun does not destroy the firmament, but adorns, completes, and illustrates it.

<margin>The Sun as an image of Christ.</margin>
We have proven from the order of the "fourth day" and the time of His arrival that the things said here must be understood as referring to Christ. Let us prove the same from the likeness of the figure: for there is no other thing through which we can more fittingly imagine Christ than the sun.

<margin>Plato in the *Republic*.</margin>
For "He set His tabernacle in the sun" <note>A common medieval Latin reading of Psalm 19:4.</note>, and He came from the tribe of Judah, whose sign is the Lion, a solar animal. And since Plato, in the *Republic*, calls the sun the "visible son of God," why should we not understand that it is an image of the invisible Son? If He is the true light that illuminates every mind, He has His most expressive likeness in this sun, which is the imaginary light illuminating every body. But why do we seek other things? Let us ask the sun itself: which, by failing through the opposing moon while Christ was suffering, clearly showed us its natural sympathy with Him <note>Referring to the solar eclipse/darkness reported during the Crucifixion.</note>.

<margin>The Day of the Sun is the Lord's Day.</margin>
Thus, by the best right—not to touch upon a deeper cause—we have called the day which the astronomers call the "Day of the Sun" the "Day of the Lord" <note>Pico is explaining why Christians worship on Sunday (the Day of the Sun) rather than the Sabbath (Saturday).</note>, and we have dedicated it entirely to His worship. Even from this, we show there is no reason to worship the physical sun any longer (as the pagans once did) as the king of heaven and lord, now that the invisible Sun—co-eternal and co-equal with the Father, through whom both heaven and earth were established—has illuminated men sitting in the shadow of death.

<summary>Pico argues that the timing of Jesus's life corresponds to the "fourth day" of creation and uses the sun as a primary symbol for Christ, noting that even the Talmudic tradition inadvertently supports this timeline. He further justifies the Christian shift from the Sabbath to Sunday by identifying Christ as the "True Sun."</summary>

# JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA

# Chapter five.

But let us now examine whether the works that follow the fourth day correspond to those things known to have happened after the arrival of Christ; so that we may finally accept this exposition of ours as true and established, once we recognize that everything from every side bears witness and harmonizes with it. Let us see what happens after the fourth day. The waters produce fish and birds; the earth produces cattle and beasts of burden.

<margin>The Gentiles are symbolized by the waters, the Israelites by the earth</margin>
Let us recall to mind what we said above was signified by the waters: those which, located under the sky, were gathered into one place; and likewise what was signified by the earth: that which was made immune from their flood. We said that the Gentiles <note>In this context, "Gentiles" refers to all non-Jewish nations and peoples.</note> are symbolized by the waters and the Israelites by the earth; this we proved through many testimonies of the prophets as well as by logical similarities. We saw, however, that before the rising of the sun, the sterile waters produced nothing that was good. The earth, meanwhile, was indeed fertile, but only with the meager fruit of greens and herbs. After the sun appears, the waters—with even greater fertility than the earth—bring forth two kinds of living creatures: birds and fish. The earth, no longer content with trees and shrubs, produces both great cattle and beasts of burden.

<margin>Simeon</margin>
Do you not see, even if I remain silent, that the word of the good Simeon has been fulfilled? That this sun of ours should be <note>original: "lumen ad revelationem gentium et gloriam plebis tuae Israel"</note> "a light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel" <note>This is a reference to the 'Nunc Dimittis' (Luke 2:32), the song of the priest Simeon upon seeing the infant Jesus.</note>. Do we not have before our eyes a clear expression—even if we intended nothing else—of both the calling of the Gentiles and the transformation of the earthly Jerusalem and the shadowed synagogue into the true Church and the eternal, heavenly city of God? Before the sun rises, the waters produce nothing. The earth produces something, but it is thin and meager.

<margin>For by the intervention of the sun, plants, sentient beings, and rational beings are generated, as Aristotle says.</margin>
For before the arrival of Christ, there was no sign of life among the Gentiles, no fruit of true religion. Among the Israelites, there was indeed some hope of life, and they knew the way of light in part and worshipped the true religion—but it was incipient and imperfect until He came, who is the way, the truth, and the life. And unless we return to this mystery, let someone offer me a reason why Moses divided the adornment and offspring of the earth in such a way that it brought forth some things before the sun, and others after the sun. Why, likewise, do the waters produce nothing before the sun, while the earth produces something? Why are two kinds of living creatures produced from the waters, while only one kind is produced from the earth? Why is the bird, an animal of the air, ascribed to the waters? For (to deal with the first point) it is not enough to say, as some have, that herbs and plants were brought out of the earth before the making of the sun so they would not be seen as created by its power. For by that same reasoning, the fish and birds and all the adornment of the elements much more ought to have been made before the sun, so they would not be believed to be made by its power.

<margin>Moses recorded everything skillfully</margin>
Moses would have left behind a suspicion: even if the light of the sun were not needed for producing plants (as they are more imperfect), it might have been necessary for producing animals, which are more perfect. For it follows that if more perfect things came into the light without the sun's help, those things which are less perfect could also be made without it. The logic does not work the other way: if the more ignoble things were made without it—such as plants, the lowliest kind of living thing—it does not follow that the entire nature of animals could also be produced without the sun's intervention.

Therefore, the intention of the author is more truly investigated from the perspective we have stated. Similarly, if someone says that the living creatures related to the waters are those that live in the water, he will see that only one kind belongs to them, while two kinds ought to have been referred to the earth, because the home of birds is the earth rather than the water. And beyond all controversy, if we consider the nature of the animal, a bird is either a terrestrial or an aerial animal; it is in no way an aquatic one.

<margin>The highest reasons of Aristotle</margin>
But hear the highest reasons of all, drawing us—even against our will—to the mysteries of Christ and the Church. And indeed, if all things (as Aristotle says) harmonize with the truth, then all things must especially harmonize with Christ, who is Truth itself. It was not for nothing or out of vanity that He said so often to the Hebrews: "Search the scriptures, for it is they that bear witness..." <note>original: "Scrutamini scripturas: ipsae sunt quae testimonium"</note>

<summary>Pico argues that the creation of life following the sun's creation allegorically represents the spiritual fruitfulness of both Gentiles and Jews after the arrival of Christ. He challenges literal biological interpretations of Genesis, suggesting the text's structure is designed to point toward Christian mysteries.</summary>

->## HEPTAPLUS<-

which bear witness of me: and so many things predicted about himself. Indeed, he affirmed all things in the law, the psalms, and the prophets. But we are often blind to such great light; nor can we consider the wonders of his law unless he reveals our eyes <note>A reference to Psalm 119:18: "Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law."</note>. Let us come, with him bringing us help, to the revelation of mysteries and figures. He produces two kinds of animals from the waters, but only one from the earth: because the fullness of believers from the Gentiles was greater than from the Jews. Yet the earth, even if it produced fewer, produced more perfect living beings than those which the waters produce—namely cattle and all four-footed beasts. Although more from the ethnic peoples <note>original: "ethnicis", meaning non-Jews or Gentiles</note> believed than from the Hebrews, those from the Hebrews were nonetheless more perfect: from these came the apostles, the founders of the whole religion. Likewise, the water brings forth two different kinds and a double nature—of birds and of fish—while the earth brings forth only one. This is because from the Gentiles, some are transferred to Christ from the service of demons, while others come from the law of nature. Every Hebrew, however, is only a Hebrew because it was not permitted for him to live within the limits of nature; to him was given the specific law of God, which was his alone and not shared with the rest of the nations. For "he has not done so for every nation, and he has not manifested his judgments to them" <note>Quoting Psalm 147:20.</note>. 

Therefore, the fish signify for us those who came to us from the cult of demons—not only because the waters (as we showed above) represent the impiety of the nations, but because through these animals that live in the waters, <margin>Jonathan the Chaldean</margin> Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Ionethes caldeus refers to Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets.</note> attests that wicked demons are often signified in the sacred scriptures. The birds signify those who were translated from the institutions of nature to grace. The clear reason for this comes from the things we wrote abundantly in the preface of this book concerning natural and supernatural happiness <term>happiness: fœlicitate, referring to "eudaimonia" or the ultimate fulfillment of the soul</term>. For we showed that the sky is the most expressive image of supernatural happiness, and that natural happiness is a certain secondary and imaginary thing rather than true happiness. Therefore, those who pursue this using the laws of nature are most fittingly denoted by birds—inhabitants not of the first and true sky, but of the air, which by a certain secondary and imaginary reason also claims for itself the name of "sky." Hence they are so frequently called "fowls of the sky" and "birds of the sky" in the divine scriptures. 

Observe, however, how it was done with deep counsel: so that birds are referred not to the air, but to the water. Since those who lived according to nature were nonetheless counted as a people of origin [Gentiles]. For they both called themselves Gentiles and lived among Gentiles—such as perhaps Socrates and many of the philosophers. For that reason, both kinds were referred in common to the waters.

<margin>Paul, Gospel, Christ</margin> 
But how much this exposition agrees with evangelical and apostolic doctrine is easy to show. Since indeed the apostles converted from the Hebrews are represented as "oxen" (terrestrial animals) by Paul <note>In 1 Corinthians 9:9, Paul interprets the law about "not muzzling the ox" as referring to those who preach the Gospel.</note> and by our doctors in the commentary on the Gospel where those selling in the temple are cast out; and Christ calls the Israelites "sheep." But the Apostles, to whom the conversion of the nations was commanded, are called "fishers" by the Lord—the prince of whom was Peter, who at Rome, the mistress of the nations, was to be a fisher, as it were, of the ocean of the rest [of the nations]. But Christ—who said he was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel—claimed for himself the name not of a fisher, but rather of a shepherd.

### Chapter six.

<margin>Why on the second day it was not said "that it was good"</margin> 
From here also is the clear resolution of the question that has long perhaps disturbed interpreters of this book: Why on the second day it was not said, "and God saw that it was good." For if we say what is usually said—that it was because the work of the waters was not completed on that day, but on the third, when the waters under the sky flowed together into one place—it will hardly seem a full satisfaction. For the proper work of the second day is not the arrangement of the waters, but the arrangement of the firmament, by which it was strengthened in the middle place between the waters. It was...

<summary>Pico explains why the waters produce two types of animals (fish and birds) while the earth produces one (land animals), linking them to the conversion of Gentiles from paganism or philosophy versus the Jews' focus on the Law. He also contrasts the roles of the Apostles as "fishers of men" for the Gentiles and Christ as the "shepherd" for Israel.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's allegorical interpretation of the Genesis creation narrative. Having previously discussed the distinctions between Jews and Gentiles in the context of the fifth and sixth days, he now moves toward the fulfillment of the Law in Christ and the significance of Baptism as the ultimate "re-creation" of man.</meta>

-># GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-
<meta>catchword: re lectoribus (to the readers)</meta>

on that same day as the creation of the firmament: when God said "Let there be a firmament," and the separation of the waters was sufficiently completed. However, the gathering of the waters which is called the "sea," the revelation of the dry land, and the production of plants possess the character of another work entirely. Thus, they were completed on another day—that is, the third day—to which they belonged. We must therefore seek the reason for this higher mystery. The firmament (as we showed above) symbolizes the Law. And the firmament was as if unformed and not simply perfect until it was furnished with the sun, moon, and stars; in the same way, the Law was neither
<margin>Manichaeus</margin>
<margin>Christ fulfilled the Law</margin>
bad (as the Manichaeans <note>Followers of Mani who believed the material world and the Old Testament God were evil.</note> say), nor was it simply good—that is, perfect—until Christ came, who fulfilled the Law. If the firmament had been evil, it would not have received the sun; if it had been good, it would not have needed the sun. But the firmament was good only insofar as it was capable of containing the sun and the other stars; just as the Law was good insofar as it was a tutor <term>pedagogus: in the ancient world, a slave who escorted children to school; Pico uses it here in the Pauline sense of the Law leading humanity to Christ</term> for us in Christ, and Moses permitted many things because of the hardness of the people’s hearts which the Gospel later did not permit. That we cannot call the Law
<margin>Mani</margin>
evil, as Mani believed, but can nevertheless call it "not good," the prophet most clearly teaches, through whom God, speaking of the Hebrews, says: "I gave them precepts that were not good" <note>original: "dedi eis precepta non bona," quoting Ezekiel 20:25.</note>. He did not say "evil precepts," but "not good precepts"—that is, not perfect, not absolute, not completed. This is confirmed by the
<margin>Ancient Hebrews</margin>
ancient Hebrew teachers, who, interpreting that passage of Ecclesiastes, "Vanity of vanities and all is vanity," say: even the Law is "vain" until the Messiah comes. And enough regarding these things for now.

## Chapter seven.

<margin>What the power of baptism performs</margin>
Furthermore, since the supreme benefit of the Word made flesh was that through the sacrament of baptism—through which the power of Christ is poured into us—we are reborn as children of God, born not of blood but of God; Moses finally indicates this to us when, after the sun has risen and been shown to the world, and after the fertility of the waters and the earth, he makes man in the image of God—not an earthly man, but a heavenly one. For once the Gentiles and Jews had turned to Christ, this remained: that through the most holy washing, conforming themselves to the cross of the Lord, they might be reshaped into the image of God. For if baptism makes us children of God, and the Son is the image of the Father, is it not the power of the entire Trinity working in baptism that says: "Let us make man in our image"? If, therefore, we are in the image of God, we are also sons. If sons, then we are heirs: heirs
<margin>Paul</margin>
of God and co-heirs with Christ. But who are the sons? It was written by Paul that we cry "Abba, Father" <note>A reference to Romans 8:15.</note> in the Holy Spirit. Those who live by the Spirit are the sons of God; these are the brothers of Christ; these are destined for the eternal inheritance which they will happily possess as the reward for both faith and a well-lived life in the heavenly Jerusalem.

### EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST WORD
### THAT IS, "IN THE BEGINNING"

<insert>I</insert> <note>This 'I' refers to the historiated woodcut initial beginning the word 'Iam' (Now). It depicts a scholar at a desk, signifying the scholarly nature of the commentary.</note> have now come to the heel <note>original: "calcem," an idiom meaning the very end or finish line of a task</note> of the work, having run through the exposition of the seven-fold context of the universe. But I recognize that something still remains untouched and undiscussed by us, which indeed seemed necessary to explain in the first place: namely, what that first word of the Law signifies, which is "In the beginning." <note>original: "in principio," the Latin translation of the Hebrew 'Bereshit'.</note> Not by chance or without cause did I wish to speak of this "beginning" at the end of the whole work. I am not going to dispute here about the Son, who is the "Beginning" through whom all things were made (for He is the wisdom of the Father); nor am I going to prove that the ancient Hebrew doctors feel the same as we do on this point, which we shall do elsewhere. Instead, we intend to give a taste through another method of interpretation...

-># HEPTAPLUS<-

to the readers of the Mosaic depth. We shall not do this before we have tasted a few things concerning a certain doctrine—which is truly a paradox <note>original: "paradoxon"; here meaning a statement contrary to common belief but potentially true</note> of the more ancient Jewish discipline <margin>The author promises to set forth a doctrine that is according to the paradox of the ancient Jewish discipline</margin>. It is the firm opinion of all the ancients, which they confirm with one voice as beyond doubt: that the complete knowledge of all arts, and of all wisdom both divine and human, is included in the five books of the Mosaic Law. They say this art is disguised and hidden in the very letters with which the words of the Law are woven, in the manner we shall now declare. Let us take, for example, the first small portion of the book of Genesis—namely, from the beginning up to the place where it is written: *and God saw the light, that it was good.* That entire scripture is joined together from one hundred and three elements <term>elementis: in this context, the individual letters of the Hebrew alphabet</term>; these are arranged in such a way that the words they constitute, which we read, display nothing but what is common and trivial. This order of letters constitutes the "husk," <note>Pico uses the metaphor of "cortex" (husk/bark) for the literal meaning and "medulla" (marrow) for the hidden spiritual meaning</note> while this text contains the marrow of hidden mysteries within. But if we take those same elements, once the words are dissolved and the letters divided, and properly join them together according to the rules they themselves hand down regarding what words can be formed from them, they say it will come to pass—if we are capable of this locked-away wisdom—that wonderful and most secret doctrines concerning many things will shine forth to us. And if this were done in the whole Law, then finally from this arrangement and connection of elements (if properly established), every doctrine and the secrets of all liberal disciplines could be brought into the light. Now, I said "if we are capable of this locked-away wisdom." For it can happen that as we handle, dissolve, and compose certain words, many vocabularies and a multiple series of discourse may be produced which teach great things and signify great things; but unless one has obtained the doctrine concerning that matter from elsewhere, they will not understand what those things signify, and cannot help but despise them as useless and accidental. For we cannot *learn* dogmas and doctrines there, but we can only *recognize* them. I do not assert or attest to these things as if I have proven them—since I have neither made a trial of them, nor do I trust that I am able to do so—yet I neither deny nor despise them. This is partly because this opinion has great authors, and partly because concerning Moses, who was faithful in all the house of God <margin>Moses was faithful in all the house of God</margin>, even greater things can easily be believed.

As for me, though I do not enter those abysses but only graze the shore of this sea, I have encountered such riches of gems as neither the Hermus nor the Pactolus <note>Rivers in Asia Minor famous in antiquity for their gold-bearing sands</note> are said to carry among the poets. I thought it would not be unwelcome to our people if I made them public. I chose to take a risk with the first word of the work, which among the Hebrews is *Bereshit* <note>original: "Brefit"; the first word of Genesis, usually translated "In the beginning"</note> and among us is read as *In the beginning*, to see if I too, using the rules of the ancients, could bring something worthy of knowledge into the light from it. Therefore, beyond my hope and beyond my expectation, I found—what I myself could hardly believe when I found it, and others could not easily believe—the entire logic of the creation of the world and of all things opened and explained in that one word. I speak of a thing marvelous, unheard of, and incredible. But soon you will believe it if you pay attention, and the reality itself will prove me true. That word among the Hebrews is written in this way: <note>The Hebrew letters בראשית (B-R-A-Sh-Y-T) were intended to be here.</note>

From this word, therefore, if we join the third letter to the first, it becomes the word *Ab* <note>Hebrew: אב; meaning Father</note>. If we add the second letter to the first doubled, it becomes *Bebhar* <note>Hebrew: בבר; interpreted by Pico as "in the Son"</note>. If we read all except the first, it becomes *Reshit* <note>Hebrew: ראשית; meaning Beginning or Principle</note>. If we connect the fourth to the first and the last, it becomes *Shabat* <note>Hebrew: שבת; meaning He rested or Sabbath</note>. If we set down the first three in the order they lie, it becomes *Bara* <note>Hebrew: ברא; meaning He created</note>. If, omitting the first, we take the three following, it becomes *Rosh* <note>Hebrew: ראש; meaning Head</note>. If, omitting the first and second, we take the two following, it becomes *Esh* <note>Hebrew: אש; meaning Fire</note>. If, omitting the first three, we couple the fourth to the last, it becomes *Sheth* <note>Hebrew: שת; meaning Foundation or Six</note>. Again, if we put the second before the first, it becomes *Rab* <note>Hebrew: רב; meaning Great</note>. If after the third we place the fifth and then the fourth, it becomes *Hish* <note>Hebrew: איש; Pico likely refers to "Ish," meaning Man</note>. If we join the first two to the last two, it becomes *Berith* <note>Hebrew: ברית; meaning Covenant</note>. If we join the last to the first, it becomes the last word and <margin>In the first word of the work is contained the entire logic of the whole world</margin>...

-># THE SEVENFOLD EXPOSITION OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...the twelfth, which is "good" <note>Hebrew: *Tob*</note>, considering that among the Hebrews the letter *Tav* is very frequently <margin>A faithful interpretation</margin> substituted for the element <term>elementum: here meaning a letter of the alphabet</term> *Teth*. Now let us see what these terms signify first in Latin, and then what mysteries concerning the whole of nature are revealed through them to those not ignorant of philosophy. **Ab** signifies Father. **Bar** signifies in the Son and through the Son (for the preposition *Beth* signifies both). **Reshit** signifies the beginning. **Sabbath** signifies rest and the end. **Bara** means he created. **Rosh** means head. **Esh** means fire. **Sheth** means foundation. **Rab** means of the great. **Ish** means man. **Berit** means by a covenant. **Tob** means in a good way. And if we weave the whole speech together in successive order, it will be as follows: *The Father, in the Son and through the Son, created the beginning and the end (or rest): the head, the fire, and the foundation of the great man by a good covenant.* This entire sentence leaps forth from the breaking down and re-assembling of that first word. How deep and how full of every doctrine its meaning is cannot be obvious to everyone. But let us immediately open some things—though not all things to everyone—which are signified to us through these voices. It is known to all Christians what it means for the Father to have created in the Son and through the Son. Likewise, it is known how the Son is the beginning and the end of all things: for he is the Alpha and the Omega <margin>John</margin> <note>original: "α & ω"</note> (as John writes), and he called himself the "Beginning." We ourselves have demonstrated that he is the end of all things, so that they may be restored to their own source. The rest is a little obscure: namely, what those terms "head," "fire," and "foundation of the great man" mean, what that "covenant" is, and for what reason it is called "good." For it is not immediately clear to everyone that the entire logic of the four worlds <note>Pico previously defined four levels of existence: the angelic, celestial, sublunary, and the human world</note> about which we have treated is explained here—likewise their kinship and happiness, about which we have recently disputed.

First, therefore, it must be noted that the world is called a "Great Man" by Moses. For if man is a "little world" <note>The "microcosm" (man) vs. the "macrocosm" (the universe)</note>, then <margin>The Great World (which was called the fourth above) is Man</margin> certainly the world is a "Great Man." Taking this opportunity, he most aptly represents the three worlds—the intellectual, the celestial, and the corruptible—through the three parts of man. At the same time, he indicates by this figure not only that all worlds are contained within man, but he briefly declares which part of man corresponds to which world. Let us therefore consider three parts in man: the highest is the head; then that which extends from the neck to the navel; and the third, which extends from the navel to the feet. For these are also separated and distinguished in the human figure by a certain variety. But it is wonderful how beautifully and precisely they correspond in proportion to the three parts of the world through an exact logic. In the head is the brain, the <margin>Which part in man corresponds to which world</margin> source of knowledge. In the chest is the heart, the source of life, motion, and heat. In the lowest part are the genital members, the principle of generation. Likewise in the world: the highest part, which is the angelic or intellectual world, is the source of knowledge, because that nature was made for understanding. The middle part, which is the heavens, is the source <margin>Knowledge, Motion, Generation</margin> of life, motion, and heat, in which the sun rules just as the heart does in the chest. Below the moon is that which is known to all as the source of generation and corruption. You see how aptly all these parts of the world <margin>See the author's mystical investigation.</margin> and of man agree with one another.

Now, Moses designated the first part by the proper name of "Head" <note>Hebrew: *Rosh*</note>. The second part he called "Fire" <note>Hebrew: *Esh*</note>, both because the heavens are judged to be such by many, and because in us this portion is the source of heat. The third he called "Foundation" <note>Hebrew: *Sheth*</note> because through it (as is known to all) the whole body of man is founded and sustained. Moreover, he added that He created these things "by a good covenant," because among them a covenant of peace and friendship has been sanctioned through the law of God’s wisdom, arising from the kinship of their natures and mutual consent. This covenant is "good" because it is so directed and ordered toward God—who is Goodness itself—that just as the whole world is one within itself, so also it might ultimately be one with its Author. Let us also imitate this most holy covenant of the world, so that we may be one with each other through mutual charity, and at the same time, through a true love of God, we may all happily become one with Him.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s prayer to God in elegiac verse.

**A** <note>The original Latin begins with a decorative woodcut 'A' for "Alme Deus."</note> Bounteous God, to be revered for your supreme majesty,
Who truly possess one divine power in a threefold divinity,
Whom the blessed throng of the angelic choir serves
Above the flaming walls of the high world;
Whose omnipotent right hand once created this
Immense work, visible to our eyes;
You who turn the heavens, who direct the world with a nod,
From whose command the hurled thunderbolts fall:
Spare, I pray, the wretched; wash away our filth, I pray,
Lest the just punishment of your fury drive us to ruin.
But if our debts are weighed on an equal scale,
And if the standard of your judgment be severe,
Who could endure the horrific whip of the living
Avenger? And who could withstand the heavy blows?
The very Fabric of the World <term>Machina: literally "machine," a common Renaissance term for the universe as a divinely engineered system</term> would not withstand your angry right hand—
That Fabric not destined to perish until the final day.
What mind is not condemned by the origin of the first sin? <note>A reference to Original Sin inherited from Adam.</note>
Or what mind is not made guilty by its own crime?
Or surely you are that very one whose nature it is always to spare,
And who holds justice with equal mercy:
You who repay rewards far greater than merits deserve,
And punishments for sins committed far lighter than the evils.
For your clemency is greater than our sins,
And to give to the unworthy is a thing more worthy of God.
And yet they are worthy enough, if he deigns to love them—
He who, finding them unworthy, makes them worthy himself.
Therefore, pitying us, I pray look upon your own with a peaceful face—
Whether you prefer us to be servants, or rather, the accused:
Accused indeed, if you look at the crimes of our life,
The work of an excessively ungrateful mind:
But if instead you perceive your gifts in us,
Gifts ennobled by exceptional blessings,
We are those whom nature once made your servants,
And whom holy grace <note>original: "gratia sancta"</note> soon after made your children.
But (alas!) the privilege of such a lot weighs upon the wretched:
Those whom grace made children, sin made defendants.
Sin made them defendants, but let grace conquer sin,
So that your honor may grow through our crime:
For whether your wisdom or your power could otherwise
Make known its riches to the world,
The glory of your goodness is greater in our errors,
And that love shines forth, to be loved above all things:

### Roberto Salviati sends greetings to Lorenzo de' Medici.

Since I was born with such a disposition, most illustrious Lorenzo, and was so trained by nature that nothing is more important to me than to love, cherish, and venerate those who excel in talent or are singular in learning: I could not help but love your Pico della Mirandola above all others and admire a man truly most worthy of all admiration.

Since he recently dedicated to you the book on the sevenfold explanation of the six days of Genesis <note>The *Heptaplus*, the very book this letter introduces.</note> as the first fruits of his studies—a work not only in my judgment, but in the judgment of all, most excellent—I wished to take care that it be published at my expense in a corrected edition. I did so doubting not that I would simultaneously satisfy both my love for him and the public usefulness of studies. Furthermore, I hoped I would be doing something not unwelcome

# APOLOGIA FOR THE QUESTIONS OF MIRANDOLA
<page-num>35</page-num>

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

I have dedicated my *Apologia* <note>The "Apologia" is Pico’s formal defense of the 13 controversial propositions from his 900 Theses which were condemned by a papal commission.</note> to you, Lorenzo de’ Medici, as a thing—I call God to witness—that does not seem to me worthy of so great a man, but is nevertheless owed to you by that right by which I realize I have long since owed you all my works. For you may be most well-assured that whatever I am, or am to be in the future, is yours, Lorenzo, and shall remain so forever. I say less than I would wish, and these words are altogether too faint to sufficiently express what I feel: that is, with what love, what faith, and what respect I shall follow you—and indeed have followed you for many years now. I am moved both by the many kindnesses you have bestowed upon me, which clearly testify to your most loving spirit, and by your own qualities—not so much those of fortune as of the mind—those same rare virtues peculiar to you, which your own modesty prevents me from recounting at present. I return to the *Apologia*: I ask that you receive it with a cheerful countenance. It is indeed a small gift, but a significant testimony of my faith and of my truly great respect for you at all times. If it should happen that you touch upon this work amidst the great affairs with which you are always most busily occupied, remember that this work was produced in haste rather than being a polished labor, and that the subject of the work had to be taken from the judgment of others, not my own. I did not dedicate it to you so that you might recognize in me a' excellence of talent or learning—which I do not possess—but so that you might know (for I shall say it again) that whatever I am, I am most devoted to your greatness.

### APOLOGIA OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, 
### COUNT OF CONCORDIA.

<margin>
Pope 
Innocent VIII
</margin>
When I recently arrived in Rome to kiss the feet of the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII <note>Pope Innocent VIII (reigned 1484–1492) initially permitted Pico’s debate but later suspended it and formed a commission to examine the theses.</note>—whose name is most deservedly earned from the innocence of his life—and so that I might not depart from my usual custom of studying and always treating something of a literary nature, I sought to do something worthy of the city of Rome according to my strength: something pleasing to a Christian prince, and useful to myself and to scholars. I proposed nine hundred questions <note>The famous "900 Theses," intended to cover all known branches of philosophy and theology to prove their underlying harmony.</note> concerning divine and natural things, which I intended to answer in a public assembly of most learned men. Scarcely had these reached the public when—even if there were some who approved of my talent, learning, or at least my study of the liberal arts—a <margin>Detraction</margin> multifaceted crowd of detractors arose against me. And although I saw that the distastes, the sneers, the censures, and the judgments of each individual were varied—as always happens when we attempt something new and not trivial—there were roughly five main points that these censors condemned in me. For some altogether plucked at philosophy and literature; they saw these as the trifles of "know-it-alls" <note>Original: *scioli*, a derogatory term for those with superficial or "smattering" knowledge.</note>. Sometimes they added that Adam was cast out of paradise because, through the "knowledge of good and evil," he wished to make himself equal to the gods. They argued that those who wish "to know more than is proper" <note>A reference to Romans 12:3, often used in the Middle Ages to discourage over-curious intellectual inquiry.</note> should be banished from the court of Christ by a similar example. Others did not so much disapprove of philosophy as this very style of disputing and this custom of public debate on letters; they barked that it was for the pomp of talent and the ostentation of learning rather than for the acquisition of erudition. Some called me bold and rash: <margin>At what age he would dispute</margin> who, at this age—not yet twenty-four years old—would not hesitate to propose a disputation on the highest points of philosophy, on the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, and on unknown disciplines, in a most celebrated city and in a most ample assembly of learned men. <margin>He had maintained.</margin> Many accused me not so much for being in Rome, or for being a youth, but for the sheer number—that is, that I was going to dispute nine hundred questions—claiming that this was done superfluously, ambitiously, and beyond my strength. Among those who professed the "wisdom"—that is, the study of theology—there were some who, perhaps not content with lighter insults, no longer called me merely bold...

# APOLOGIA

## APOLOGIA

[They] proclaimed me not merely rash or boastful, but a magician, impious, and a new arch-heretic <term>arch-heretic (haeresiarcha)<gloss>a leader or founder of a heretical movement</gloss></term> in the Church of Christ. I was (God is my witness) long in doubt whether I should wash away these objections or if they should rather be passed over in silence. Two things especially moved me to be silent: 

<margin>Two obstacles to writing</margin> 

First, because I, abhorring both contention and quarrels, have always loved peace and that most placid tranquility of life which my studies have provided me. Nor do I hate any task of writing more than one set in debate or bitter altercation, of whatever kind; for I have never considered it the part of a good man, nor of a philosopher, to either inflict or return an injury or insult. The second reason was this: I was content with the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff <note>referring to Pope Innocent VIII</note> (whose memory I must always celebrate) and many from the most holy apostolic senate [the College of Cardinals], whose kindness and most benevolent spirit toward me I can and should never forget. I seemed able easily to disregard the hatred and insults of wicked men; and indeed, regarding the rest, I was of the opinion that they were unworthy of a response. 

But regarding this one charge of heresy brought against me, I feared that if I did this [remained silent], I might seem to acknowledge a crime I did not clear away. 

<margin>Rufinus</margin> 

Indeed, Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–411 AD), a monk and scholar known for his translations of Greek Church Fathers.</note> writes most wisely that it is glorious to endure injuries patiently following Christ’s example. But he who bears or ignores the mark of heresy is no Christian. 

<margin>Jerome</margin> 

And our Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Vulgate Bible and a fierce defender of orthodoxy.</note>, with the greatest possible mental effort, cries out with a very clear voice: "I do not wish anyone to be patient under the suspicion of heresy." <note>original: "Nolo in suspitione haereseos quēq̄ esse patientem"</note> Therefore, Jerome does not wish me to be silent; he draws and impels me, a reluctant and idle man, to write by his great authority. 

Therefore, if there are any who perhaps wish I would remain silent, let them know they have a controversy not with me, but with Jerome, who does not wish me to be silent. Who can fail to listen to Jerome without a sense of shame? Therefore, with him persuading—even compelling—me, I have set out to write a brief defense: not to tear into or accuse anyone, but to rightfully excuse myself from the greatest crime of impiety which is unjustly charged against me. This I ask my detractors to endure with the same spirit with which I have always endured their unfair offense. 

Let them endure, I say, so that I, a Christian born of Christian parents, who bear the banner of Christ Jesus on my forehead <note>a reference to the sign of the cross made at baptism or confirmation</note>, who for the faith of Christ would also gladly die, may—with them listening fairly—cry out with the voice of 

<margin>Paul</margin> 

Paul <note>The Apostle Paul.</note>: "I am not a magician, not a Jew, not an Ishmaelite <note>original: "Ismaelita"; a term used in this period for Muslims</note>, not a heretic. But I worship Jesus, and I carry the cross of Jesus in my body; through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world." <note>original: "p̄ qué mihi mūdus crucifixus est/ & ego mundo"; a reference to Galatians 6:14</note> Finally, while I neither claim for myself nor take away from them titles of holiness or wisdom and such excellent honors, I ask that they not strip me of this one title, for which I would even willingly shed my blood: namely, that I may call myself a Christian. If they concede this, I do not write for them, for I have already obtained from them what our entire defense strives for.

<margin>The burden of this defense was undertaken to abolish the name of heresy.</margin> 

I write for others who believe or suspect that I am or have been at some time a heretic. Although the principal purpose is this: to show that it is not I, but those who slander me as a heretic, who deviate from the orthodox and catholic path; nevertheless, since I must write, we shall also say something about those things which were first charged against us, lest our detractors be able to misuse my silence as if it were a conscience of guilt. 

Now, there were many who first turned this philosophizing of mine into a vice. To whom I will answer nothing in this place, because it is my plan to plead the cause of philosophy separately in a specific work <note>likely referring to his "Oration on the Dignity of Man"</note>; and if it is altogether shameful to devote oneself to letters and to cultivate the good arts and disciplines, I would rather acknowledge this "fault" than beg for forgiveness. To those also who detest this kind of disputing and this method of publicly debating about God, nature, and morals, I will not say much, since this crime—if it is a crime—is shared with great men, indeed with the most approved philosophers of almost all ages, for whom it was most certain that nothing is more vital for attaining...

He passionately asserts his Christian identity, rejecting labels like "magician" or "Ishmaelite," and defends the value of philosophical disputation.</summary>

# OF THE QUESTIONS

->DISPUTATIONS<-

<margin>He sets forth the utility of debate.</margin>
...the knowledge of truth for themselves, rather than being very frequent in the practice of disputation. For just as physical strength is made firmer through <term>gymnastic exercise (gymnasticam)<gloss>referring to the classical Greek tradition of physical training</gloss></term>, so in this, as it were, <term>literary wrestling ground (literaria palaestra)<gloss>a metaphor for a school of debate or intellectual arena</gloss></term>, the powers of the mind emerge far stronger and more vigorous. 

Nor would I believe that the poets meant anything else by the famous arms of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, usually depicted with a helmet, shield, and spear</note>, or that the Hebrews—when they say that "iron" is the symbol of the wise—meant anything other than that these most honorable contests of this kind are entirely necessary for attaining wisdom. By chance, it also happens that the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologers and sages</note>, in preparing the <term>nativity (Genesi)<gloss>an astrological birth chart</gloss></term> of one who is to be a philosopher, require this: that <note>original: "Mars Mercurium triquetro aspectu"</note> Mars look upon Mercury in a trine aspect. This is as if to say that if you take away these meetings, these "wars," all philosophy will become sleepy and nodding off. 

But as for these things, as I said, I prefer to defend myself with the authorities and previous judgments of great men rather than with reasons. It is a task of greater effort to satisfy those who say that, in age, talent, and learning, I am unequal to so great a province <note>meaning a vast field of study or responsibility</note>, and that, according to Horace, I have not consulted my shoulders as to what they can bear and what they refuse. 

<margin>Horace</margin>
Truly, here I find a difficult path of defense; for if I call myself equal to the task, I seem immodest and of too high an opinion of myself; if I confess myself unequal, I seem rash and ill-advised, destined to suffer a mark of shame. I have fallen into grave straits, as I cannot promise something about myself without fault, nor fail to provide it without fault. And I could bring up that passage of Job—that he is "simple in all things"—and perhaps hear with Timothy: <note>original: "Nemo contemnat adolescentiam tuam"</note> "Let no one despise your youth." 

<margin>Job</margin>
<margin>Timothy</margin>
But I shall say this more truly from my own conscience: there is nothing in us that is great or singular. I am perhaps studious and a lover of the <term>good arts (bonarum artium)<gloss>the humanities and liberal sciences</gloss></term>, which I do not deny; yet I neither claim nor arrogate to myself the name of "learned." For as my friend Hermolaus—the delight of the Roman tongue, the splendor and glory of our age—once wrote: <note>original: "non potest non indoctus esse qui se doctum credit"</note> "He who believes himself learned cannot be anything but unlearned." 

<margin>A saying of Hermolaus</margin>
Therefore, the reason I placed such a heavy burden on my shoulders was not that I was unaware of my own weakness. Rather, it was because I knew that this kind of "battle" (that is, literary debate) has a peculiar quality: that there is a benefit even in being defeated. Thus, even the weakest man can and should not only not refuse these contests, but should seek them out by right. For he who succumbs receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury; for he returns home enriched—that is, more learned—and better equipped for future battles. 

Animated by this hope, I, a weak soldier, did not fear to decide upon so grave a battle with the strongest and most strenuous of all men. Whether this was done rashly or not, it is better to judge by the outcome of the battle than by my age. It remains for me to respond to those who are offended by the sheer number of the proposed subjects, as if this burden rested on their shoulders and not rather upon me alone, who must exhaust myself in whatever labor there is. 

It is truly unseemly and overly peevish to wish to set a limit on another's industry, and—as Cicero says—to desire a "middle ground" in a matter that is better the greater it is. It was entirely necessary for me, in such great endeavors, either to succumb or to satisfy. If I satisfied the requirements, I do not see why what is laudable in performing ten questions should be considered blameworthy in performing nine hundred. If I succumbed, they would have grounds to accuse me if they hate me, or grounds to excuse me if they love me. Indeed, in a matter so grave and so great, for a young man of slender talent and meager learning to have failed was worthy of pardon rather than accusation. 

<margin>Cicero</margin>
<margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin>
As the poet says: <note>original: "si deficiant vires audacia certe laus erit, et in magnis voluisse sat est"</note> "If strength fails, daring will surely be praise; and in great things, to have willed is enough." Moreover, if in our age many have imitated Gorgias of Leontini <note>A famous Greek Sophist who claimed he could answer any question on any subject</note> by accustomed to proposing a disputation not just on nine hundred, but on all questions of all arts (and not without praise), why should I not be allowed to dispute—even if without fault—concerning many, yet certain and determined things? 

<margin>As the Pythagoreans, Epicureans, and likewise the Thomists and Scotists say.</margin>
But they say this is "superfluous and ambitious." I, however, contend that this was done by me not in a superfluous manner, but out of necessity. Even they, if they consider my method of philosophizing, must clearly admit this, even if unwillingly. For those who have devoted themselves to any one of the families of philosophers—namely to Thomas or Scotus <note>Referring to Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus, the leaders of the two dominant and often conflicting schools of medieval scholasticism</note>, who are now most frequently in people's hands—can indeed make a trial of their doctrine even in the discussion of a few questions. But I have so established myself that I swear by the words of no [master]...

# APOLOGY

<margin>
Latin philosophers
</margin>
...I thought that I should spread myself through all the masters of philosophy, examine every page, and recognize every school. For this reason, since I had to speak concerning all of them, I did not want to appear bound to any one of them, as if I were a defender of a private dogma who had neglected the rest. Nor could a few things be proposed about each individual without there being many things which were brought forward at once concerning all of them. And let no one condemn me for the fact that *wherever the tempest carries me, there I am brought as a guest.* <note>original: "quocūq ferat tēpestas deferar hospes" — a famous line from Horace (Epistles 1.1.15), signaling intellectual independence.</note> For this was observed by all the ancients, that in unfolding every kind of writing, they would pass over no interpretations they could find. This was especially true of Aristotle, whom for that reason Plato used to call the **Reader** <note>original: **αναγνωστης** (anagnōstēs)</note>. And surely it is the mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single Porch <note>referring to the Stoic school</note> or Academy. Nor can one have rightly chosen a path for oneself from among all of them if one has not first become familiarly acquainted with them all. Add to this that in every single school there is something distinguished that is not common to the others.

And so, to begin now with our own people, to whom philosophy most recently arrived: In <term>John Scotus<gloss>Johannes Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Scholastic philosopher known for his complex "Subtle" reasoning</gloss></term> there is a certain vigor and divisiveness. In <term>Thomas<gloss>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential Catholic theologian, known for his systematic clarity</gloss></term>, something solid and balanced. In <term>Egidius<gloss>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316), a student of Aquinas</gloss></term>, it is polished and exact; in <term>Francis<gloss>Francis of Meyronnes (c. 1280–1328), a student of Duns Scotus</gloss></term>, sharp and acute. In <term>Albert<gloss>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), the teacher of Aquinas who sought to synthesize Aristotle and faith</gloss></term>, it is ancient, ample, and grand. In <term>Henry<gloss>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), known for his "Sublime" and difficult metaphysical questions</gloss></term>, as it has always seemed to me, it is sublime and venerable. Among the Arabs, in <term>Averroes<gloss>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Andalusian commentator on Aristotle</gloss></term>, it is firm and unshakeable. In <term>Avepace<gloss>Ibn Bajja, 12th-century polymath</gloss></term> and <term>Alfarabi<gloss>9th-century philosopher known as the "Second Teacher" after Aristotle</gloss></term>, it is serious and meditated. In <term>Avicenna<gloss>Ibn Sina, the 11th-century Persian physician and philosopher</gloss></term>, it is divine and Platonic. Among the Greeks, philosophy is generally bright and chaste. In <term>Simplicius<gloss>6th-century Neoplatonist commentator</gloss></term>, it is rich and copious. In <term>Themistius<gloss>4th-century commentator</gloss></term>, elegant and concise. In <term>Alexander<gloss>Alexander of Aphrodisias, the definitive Aristotelian commentator</gloss></term>, consistent and learned. In <term>Theophrastus<gloss>Aristotle's successor</gloss></term>, it is weightily elaborated. In <term>Ammonius<gloss>Ammonius Hermiae, 5th-century head of the school in Alexandria</gloss></term>, it is clear and graceful.

And if you turn to the Platonists—to review a few: in <term>Porphyry<gloss>3rd-century student of Plotinus</gloss></term>, you will be delighted by the abundance of matter and the many-layered religion. In <term>Iamblichus<gloss>4th-century mystic</gloss></term>, you will venerate a more secret philosophy and the mysteries of the "barbarians." In <term>Plotinus<gloss>The founder of Neoplatonism (3rd century)</gloss></term>, there is nothing in particular to admire, because he shows himself admirable in every way; the sweating Platonists can scarcely understand him when he speaks of divine things divinely, and of human things in a learned, indirect way far above man. I pass over the more recent ones: <term>Proclus<gloss>5th-century systematic Platonist</gloss></term>, luxuriant with Asiatic fertility, and those who flowed from him: <term>Hermias</term>, <term>Damascius</term>, <term>Olympiodorus</term>, and many others, in all of whom that **Divine** <note>original: **Τοθειον** (To theion)</note>—the peculiar symbol of the Platonists—always shines forth.

Add to this that if there is any sect which attacks truer dogmas and mocks good causes of the intellect with slander, it actually strengthens the truth rather than weakening it; just as a flame is stirred up by movement, not extinguished. Moved by this reasoning, I wished to bring into the open the opinions not of one school only (as some would have liked), but of every kind of doctrine. I did this so that by this comparison of many sects and this multifaceted discussion of philosophy, that "shining forth of truth" which Plato mentions in his letters <note>A reference to Plato's Seventh Letter, describing the spark of truth that leaps across minds in dialogue.</note> might shine more clearly upon our minds like a sun rising from on high. 

What would it be if only the philosophy of the Latins—namely Albert, Thomas, Scotus, Egidius, Francis, and Henry—were treated, while the Greek and Arab philosophers were omitted? For all wisdom flowed from the barbarians to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to us. Thus our people have always thought it enough to stand on foreign discoveries in their way of philosophizing and to cultivate what belongs to others. What would it be to have dealt with the <term>Peripatetics<gloss>Followers of Aristotle</gloss></term> on natural matters unless the <term>Academy of the Platonists<gloss>The followers of Plato</gloss></term> were also summoned? Their doctrine regarding divine matters has always been held as the most sacred among all philosophies, as <term>Augustine<gloss>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430), who highly valued Platonism as a precursor to Christianity</gloss></term> testifies. And now for the first time by me—let there be no envy in my words—after many centuries, this doctrine has been brought out into the public for the examination of dispute. 

What would it be to have treated the opinions of others, however many there were, if we—approaching like guests at a <term>symposium of the wise<gloss>a banquet or intellectual gathering</gloss></term>—brought nothing of our own that was ours, born of us and worked out by our own talent? 

<margin>Seneca</margin>
Surely it is ignoble, as <term>Seneca<gloss>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (4 BC–65 AD), Roman Stoic philosopher</gloss></term> says, "to be wise only from a commentary," as if the discoveries of our ancestors had closed the way to our own industry, or as if the force of nature in us were exhausted, unable to produce anything from itself that might, if not demonstrate the truth, at least point to it or hint at it from afar. For if a farmer hates sterility in his field, or a husband in his wife, surely the divine mind joined and associated with the soul will hate an unfruitful soul all the more, since a far nobler <meta>catchword: offspring</meta>...

He lists the unique strengths of various thinkers and emphasizes that relying solely on past commentaries is an "ignoble" sign of intellectual laziness.</summary>

# OF QUESTIONS

<margin>Note what we have proposed</margin>
...progeny is desired. Therefore, not content with common doctrines, I have added much from the ancient theology of **Hermes Trismegistus**, much from the teachings of the **Chaldeans** <note>ancient Babylonian astronomers and sages</note> and of **Pythagoras**, and much from the more secret mysteries of the **Hebrews**. We have also proposed for dispute many things discovered and meditated upon by us concerning natural and divine matters. We first proposed the harmony of **Plato** and **Aristotle**, which has been believed by many before now, but proven sufficiently by no one. **Boethius**, among the Latins, promised he would do this, but he is not found to have ever performed what he always wished to do. **Simplicius**, among the Greeks, professed the same; would that he had provided it as well as he promised it.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
**Augustine** also writes in the *Academics* <note>specifically his work *Contra Academicos*</note> that there were many who attempted to prove the same through their most subtle disputations: namely, that the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle is one and the same.

<margin>John the Grammarian</margin>
Likewise, **John the Grammarian** <note>also known as John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator</note>, although he says that Plato differs from Aristotle only for those who do not understand Plato's words, nevertheless left the proof of this to posterity. Furthermore, we have added several instances where we assert that the opinions of **Scotus** and **Thomas** <note>Duns Scotus and Thomas Aquinas, the two giants of medieval scholasticism</note>, and several where those of **Averroes** and **Avicenna** <note>famous Islamic philosophers</note>—which are considered to be in discord—are actually in accord.

<margin>Note the new dogmas devised</margin>
In the second place, we have placed those things which we ourselves have devised in both Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, as well as **seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas**. If anyone holds to these, they will be able (unless I am mistaken) to resolve any proposed question concerning natural and divine things by a far different reasoning than that taught to us through the philosophy read in the schools and cultivated by the doctors of this age. Nor should anyone wonder that I, in my early years and tender age—during which it was hardly permitted, as some boast, to read the commentaries of others—should wish to bring forth a new philosophy, rather than merely praising it if it is defended or condemning it if it is rejected. Finally, since these are our writings, the youth of the author should not be judged; rather, one should count their merits or demerits.

<margin>A new method of philosophizing</margin>
Besides that, there is another new method of philosophizing through numbers that we have introduced. This is indeed an ancient method, observed by the earliest theologians, especially by **Pythagoras**, by **Aglaophamus**, by **Philolaus**, and by **Plato** and the earlier Platonists. But in this time, like other noble things, it has so faded away through the neglect of posterity that scarcely any traces of it can be found.

<margin>Plato</margin>
Plato writes in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue often attributed to Plato or his student Philip of Opus</note> that among all the liberal arts and contemplative sciences, the science of numbering is the principal and most divine. Seeking also why man is the wisest animal, he answers: because he knows how to count. **Aristotle** also mentions this opinion in his *Problems*.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Albumasar</margin>
**Albumasar** <note>a famous Persian astrologer</note> writes that it was a saying of **Avenzoar** the Babylonian that he knew all things who knew how to count. These things can in no way be true if by the art of numbering they understood that art in which merchants today are most skilled.

<margin>Plato</margin>
Plato also testifies to this, warning us with an exerted voice not to understand this divine arithmetic as the arithmetic of merchants. Since I seem to myself, after many sleepless nights, to have explored this arithmetic which is so highly extolled, I have promised to give a public trial of this matter by answering through numbers seventy-four questions which are considered principal among physical and divine matters.

<margin>Twofold magic</margin>
We have also proposed magical theorems, in which we signify that there are two kinds of magic. One consists entirely of the work and authority of demons, and is, by God <note>original: "mediusfidius" — an oath to Sancus or Fides, common in Latin prose</note>, an execrable and monstrous thing. The other is nothing else, when well-explored, than the absolute consummation of natural philosophy. While the Greeks mention both, they in no way deem the former worthy of the name of magic, calling it <term>Goeteia</term> <note>original: γοητειαν — sorcery or witchcraft</note>; the latter they call by its own peculiar name <term>Mageia</term> <note>original: μαγειαν</note>, as if it were the perfect and highest science.

<margin>What a Magician is according to Porphyry</margin>
For, as **Porphyry** says, the same word "Magus" in the Persian language means what "interpreter and worshiper of divine things" means among us. There is, however, a great—indeed, the greatest—disparity and dissimilarity between these arts. Not only the Christian religion, but all laws and every well-ordered republic condemn and execrate the former. The latter, however, all wise men and all seekers of heavenly and divine...
