# ->APOLOGIA<-

<margin>
The authority of **Plato** in the *Alcibiades* and *Charmides* concerning magic.
</margin>
...nations studious of divine things approve and embrace it. The former <note>sorcery or "goetia"</note> is the most fraudulent of arts; the latter <note>natural magic</note> is a higher and holier philosophy. The former is fruitless and vain; the latter is firm, faithful, and solid. Whoever practiced the former always did so in secret, for it brought ignominy and reproach upon its author. From the latter, however, the highest literary renown and glory have been sought since ancient times and almost without interruption. No man of learning or philosopher eager to study the good arts was ever a devotee of the former; yet **Pythagoras**, **Empedocles**, **Democritus**, and **Plato** all traveled abroad to learn the latter. Once they returned, they preached its merits and held it as a chief among their secrets. While the former is supported by no reason and no certain authors, the latter is honored by the most illustrious "parents," as it were, and possesses two primary founders: **Zamolxis**, whom **Abaris** the Hyperborean imitated, and **Zoroaster**—not perhaps the one people imagine, but that son of **Oromasdes**. 

<margin>
Who the magicians were: **Pythagoras**, **Empedocles**, **Democritus**.
</margin>
If we were to ask **Plato** what the nature of each magic is, he would answer in the *Alcibiades* that the magic of **Zoroaster** is nothing other than the science of divine things, in which the kings of the Persians educated their sons so that they might be taught to govern their own republic according to the model of the republic of the universe. He would answer in the *Charmides* that the magic of **Zamolxis** is the "medicine of the soul," through which temperance is achieved in the soul, just as health is acquired for the body through medicine. 

<margin>
**Plato**, **Zamolxis**, **Abaris** the Hyperborean, **Zoroaster**, **Charondas**, **Damigeron**, **Apollonius**, **Ostanes**, **Dardanus**, **Homer**, **Eudoxus**, **Hermippus**, **Al-Kindi**, **Roger Bacon**, **William**, **Antonio**.
</margin>
Later, **Charondas**, **Damigeron**, **Apollonius**, **Ostanes**, and **Dardanus** followed in their footsteps. **Homer** also persisted in this; we shall one day prove in our *Poetic Theology* that he disguised this magic, like all other forms of wisdom, under the wanderings of his **Odysseus**. **Eudoxus** and **Hermippus** followed it, as did almost all who have searched into the **Pythagorean** and **Platonic** mysteries. Among the more recent thinkers, I find three who have had a scent of it: **Al-Kindi** the Arab, **Roger Bacon**, and **William of Auvergne** <note>Bishop of Paris</note>. In our own time, I have seen **Antonio Vinciguerra** <note>original: "Antonium cronicum," a Venetian diplomat and author</note>—who, although deeply occupied in the greatest affairs and distractions of state, possesses such sublimity and elegance of intellect that he has touched upon this art most beautifully, just as he has all other liberal arts. 

**Plotinus** also mentions it where he demonstrates that the magician is a servant of nature and not its master. This most wise man approves and asserts the value of this magic, while so abhorring the other <note>sorcery</note> that when he was invited to the rites of evil demons, he said it was more fitting for them to come to him than for him to go to them—and rightly so. For just as the former magic makes a man a slave and a bondman to wicked powers, so the latter makes him their prince and lord. Finally, the former cannot claim the name of either art or science. The latter is full of the loftiest mysteries and involves the deepest contemplation of the most secret things, and ultimately, the knowledge of all nature. 

Calling forth into the light, as if from hiding places, the virtues scattered and sown in the world by the kindness of God, this magic does not so much work wonders as it diligently serves nature as she works them. Having searched more inwardly and deeply into that universal consensus which the Greeks more expressively call <term>sympatheian</term> <note>original: "συμπαθειαν"; the concept of "cosmic sympathy" or the interconnectedness of all things</note>, and having a clear perspective on the mutual knowledge of natures, it applies to each thing its own native charms—which the magicians call <term>iynges</term> <note>original: "ιυγγεσ"; mystical "attractors" or "links" used to draw down celestial influences</note>. Thus, it brings forth into the public eye the miracles that lie hidden in the recesses of the world, in the lap of nature, and in the storehouses and secrets of God, as if the magic itself were the artisan. And just as the farmer marries elms to vines, so the magician marries the earth to heaven—that is, he marries lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher. 

<margin>
What leads us to religion and the contemplation of God.
</margin>
Consequently, while the former magic appears monstrous and harmful, the latter is seen to be divine and salutary. Above all, while the former surrenders man to the enemies of God and calls him away from God, the latter excites in him an admiration for the works of God, which is most certainly followed by a ready charity, faith, and hope. For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the constant contemplation of God's wonders. When we have well-explored these through this natural magic of which we speak, we are animated more ardently to the worship and love of the Creator, and we are compelled to sing: "The heavens are full, and all the earth is full of the majesty of your glory." <note>original: "Pleni sunt caeli..." from the Sanctus of the Mass</note> And this is enough regarding magic, of which we have said these things because there are many who, like dogs always barking at strangers, often condemn and hate what they do not understand. I come now to those things which have been unearthed from the ancient mysteries of the **Hebrews**...

<summary>Pico defines "Natural Magic" as a noble, scientific pursuit of nature's secrets and God's wonders, sharply distinguishing it from the "fraudulent" and "evil" practice of demonic sorcery. # ON QUESTIONS

...I have brought these things forward to confirm the most holy and Catholic faith. Lest they be thought—by those to whom they are unknown—to be made-up trifles or the tall tales of charlatans, I want everyone to understand what they are, where they were sought, and by which illustrious authors they are confirmed. These are recondite, divine matters, necessary for our people to defend religion against the persistent slanders of the Hebrews. Not only do famous Hebrew doctors write of this, but also our own <margin>Esdras, Hilary, Origen</margin> **Esdras**, **Hilary**, and **Origen**. They write that **Moses** received on the mountain from God not only the Law—which he left to posterity inscribed in five books—but also a more secret and true explanation of that Law. God commanded him to publish the Law to the people, but he was neither to commit the interpretation to writing nor make it common. Instead, he was to reveal it only to **Joshua**, who would then reveal it to the succeeding high priests under a great religious obligation of silence. And this was rightly done. For it was enough for the common people to recognize—through simple history—God's power, His anger toward the wicked, His mercy toward the good, and His justice toward all. Through these divine and salvific precepts, they were instructed in living well and happily and in the worship of true religion. But to make public to the common people the more secret mysteries and the secrets of the highest divinity, which lie hidden under the shell of the Law and the rough pretext of words—what else would that be <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6</note> than to give what is holy to dogs and to scatter pearls among swine?

->Therefore, to keep these things hidden<-

from the common crowd and to communicate them only to the perfect—among whom alone **Paul** says he speaks wisdom <note>1 Corinthians 2:6</note>—was a matter not of human counsel but of divine command. The ancient philosophers also observed this custom most religiously. <margin>The same regarding Pythagoras in the Heptaplus</margin> **Pythagoras** wrote nothing except a few trifles which he entrusted to his daughter **Dama** as he lay dying. The sphinxes carved in Egyptian temples warned that mystic dogmas should be kept inviolate from the profane multitude through the knots of riddles. <margin>Plato</margin> **Plato**, writing certain things to **Dion** <note>Plato’s 13th Letter is addressed to Dion of Syracuse</note> concerning the highest substances, said: "I must speak in riddles, so that if the letter should happen to fall into the hands of others, what we write to you may not be understood by them." <margin>Aristotle</margin> **Aristotle** used to say that his books on First Philosophy <note>What we now call the *Metaphysics*</note>—in which he treats divine matters—were both "published and not published." What more? He asserts that Jesus Christ, the master of life, <margin>Origen</margin> as **Origen** notes, revealed many things to his disciples which they refused to write down, lest they become common to the crowd.

<margin>Dionysius</margin> This is most strongly confirmed by **Dionysius the Areopagite**, who says that the more secret mysteries were poured from the authors of our religion <margin>that is, from the soul</margin> into the soul without writing, through the intervening medium of the Word. In this very same way, when that true interpretation of the Law divinely handed to **Moses** was revealed by God's command, <margin>What Kabbalah is</margin> it was called <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>original: "Cabala"</note>, which among the Hebrews means the same as "reception" among us. It is called this because one person received that doctrine from another—not through written records, but through a regular succession of revelations—as if by a hereditary right. But after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity by **Cyrus**, and the temple was restored under **Zerubbabel**, they turned their minds to repairing the Law. **Ezra**, then the head of the Church, after correcting the book of **Moses**, realized that because of the exiles, slaughters, flights, and captivity of the Israelite people, the custom established by the ancestors of handing down doctrine by hand <note>i.e., orally</note> could not be preserved. <margin>What the priest Esdras did</margin> He saw it would happen that the secrets of celestial doctrine divinely granted to them would perish, for their memory could not long endure without the intervention of commentaries. He decreed that the wise men who then remained should be called together, and each should bring forward what he remembered about the mysteries of the Law. Notaries were employed to compile seventy volumes—for there were about that many wise men in the Sanhedrin. Regarding this matter, those who do not believe me may hear **Ezra** himself speaking thus: <margin>The words of Esdras</margin> "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: 'The first things you wrote, place in the open for the worthy and unworthy to read. But the last seventy books you shall preserve, to deliver them to the wise...'" <note>A quotation from the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra) 14:45–46</note>

<summary>Pico argues that Moses received a secret oral tradition (Kabbalah) on Mount Sinai alongside the written Law, intended only for the spiritual elite. # DEFENSE

<margin>
Mirandola was urged by Sixtus to prepare certain questions
</margin>

...to the <unclear>wise</unclear> among your people. For in these books is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge. And so I did: these are the words of **Esdras** <note>Esdras is the Latin form of Ezra; here Pico refers to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras, which describes the recovery of lost scriptures</note> exactly. These are the books of the science of **Kabbalah** <note>A Jewish mystical and contemplative system of interpreting the Hebrew Bible</note> in which Esdras—with good reason—clearly proclaimed with a loud voice that there was a "vein of understanding" (that is, the ineffable theology of the substantial deity from above), a "fountain of wisdom" (that is, an exact **metaphysics** <term>metaphysics</term>—the branch of philosophy dealing with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, and identity—of the intelligible and angelic forms), and a "river of knowledge" (that is, the most solid philosophy of natural things).

The Supreme Pontiff **Sixtus IV** <note>Pope from 1471 to 1484</note> (whose successor, **Innocent VIII**, we now happily live under) took the greatest care and study to ensure that these books were translated into Latin for the public benefit of our faith. By the time he passed away, three of them had reached the Latin world. Among the Hebrews today, these books are revered with such religious devotion that no one is permitted to touch them unless they are forty years old. When I had acquired these books for myself at no small expense, and had read through them with the greatest diligence and tireless labor, I saw in them (God is my witness) a religion that was not so much Mosaic as it was Christian. There I found the mystery of the **Trinity**; there the **Incarnation** of the Word; there the divinity of the **Messiah**; there I read about **original sin**, its expiation through Christ, the heavenly Jerusalem, the fall of the demons, the orders of the angels, purgatory, and the punishments of hell. I read the very same things we read every day in **Paul** and **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian and philosopher</note>, in **Jerome** and **Augustine**. 

Indeed, in those parts which concern philosophy, you may plainly hear **Pythagoras** and **Plato**, whose decrees are so closely related to the Christian faith 

<margin>
Augustine
</margin>

that our **Augustine** gives immense thanks to God that the books of the Platonists came into his hands. In short, there is hardly any point of controversy between us and the Hebrews that cannot be so refuted and conquered by the books of the Kabbalists that not even a corner remains for them to hide in. I have a most weighty witness to this fact, **Antonio Cronicus**, a most learned man, who with his own ears (when I was with him at a banquet) heard **Dattilus the Hebrew**, a man skilled in this science, yield entirely—hand and foot <note>An idiom meaning to agree completely or surrender an argument</note>—to the Christian opinion on the Trinity.

And to review the remaining chapters of my disputation: I have also brought forward my own opinion on interpreting the poems of **Orpheus** and **Zoroaster**. Orpheus is read among the Greeks almost in his entirety; Zoroaster is read among them in fragments, but more completely among the Chaldeans. Both are believed to be the fathers and authors of ancient wisdom. 

<margin>
Zoroaster, Orpheus, who were considered most wise in antiquity. Iamblichus. Note.
</margin>

I will say nothing of Zoroaster, whose mention is frequent among the Platonists and always with the highest veneration. **Iamblichus** of Chalcis writes that Pythagoras took Orphic theology as a model upon which he shaped and formed his own philosophy. Indeed, they say the sayings of Pythagoras are called "sacred" for this very reason: they flowed from the institutions of Orpheus. From there came the secret doctrine of numbers and whatever great and sublime things Greek philosophy possessed, flowing from that first source. 

But as was the custom of the ancient theologians, Orpheus so wove the mysteries of his dogmas into the wrappings of fables and disguised them with a poetic veil, that if anyone reads his hymns, they would believe nothing lies beneath them except the most trivial trifles and stories. I wanted to say this so it might be known what labor and difficulty it was for me to draw out the hidden senses of secret philosophy from the intentional riddles of knots and the hiding places of fables—especially in a matter so grave, so hidden, and so unexplored, without the help and diligence of other interpreters. 

And yet, my "barking dogs" <note>A common metaphor for his critics and detractors</note> grumble that I have accumulated certain tiny and trivial things to make a show of numbers—as if these were not the very questions that are most ambiguous and highly controversial, over which the principal academies fight. As if I have not brought many things to these very people who carp at me (and who believe themselves the princes of philosophers) that are entirely unknown and untried. 

Indeed, I am so far from that fault that I have taken care to compress my disputation into as few chapters as possible; if I had wished to divide and cut it into its members as others usually do, it would certainly have grown to an innumerable number. To say nothing of the others, who does not know that one dogma out of the nine hundred—namely, that of reconciling the philosophy of **Plato** and **Aristotle**—

<header>OF THE QUESTIONS</header>

<term>Philosophy</term> <note>original: "phīa"</note> could have allowed me, without any suspicion of affected complexity, to have divided these topics into six hundred or even more chapters, enumerating in detail all the points in which I believe others disagree and I agree. Why not instead come to the very thing for which this entire work was undertaken: to prove—as clearly as light, and beyond all controversy—that not only am I not impious, but that those who do not blush to say that I am or have been a heretic are themselves the impious ones and the heretics. Afterward, other learned and distinguished men in our own and foreign Universities will examine these things; the Holy See will judge, and on that See <margin>The Holy See. Innocent VIII.</margin> **Innocent VIII** <note>Pope from 1484 to 1492, who initially commissioned the inquiry into Pico's theses</note> shall judge. To neglect or violate his judgment is a sin and a crime. He is the supreme judge on earth who represents Him who is the judge of the living and the dead. For my discourse is now with "barbarians," <margin>A witty proverb</margin> and as the witty proverb goes, "the stammering are understood only by the stammering." <note>original: "balbi nō nisi balbos intēlligunt." Pico is taking a sharp jab at his Scholastic critics, implying their Latin is crude ("barbarous") and their logic is clumsy compared to his refined Humanist style.</note>

# FIRST QUESTION: CONCERNING CHRIST’S DESCENT INTO HELL.

The **FIRST conclusion** from my propositions which those men condemned was this: *Christ did not truly and regarding his real presence descend into hell, as **Thomas** and the common way posit, but only regarding the effect.* <note>Pico is challenging the view of Thomas Aquinas (the "common way" of the schools) that Christ's soul literally and locally traveled to the underworld (the Harrowing of Hell), arguing instead that Christ remained in heaven and only His power or "effect" reached hell.</note> Regarding this conclusion, I first wish to declare my meaning and what my mind and opinion were concerning the descent of Christ, which it was my intention to explain in the proposed conclusion; I will show it to be not only Catholic—and believed and approved by many Catholic doctors— <margin>How he intends to proceed in declaring the conclusion.</margin> but even much more probable than its opposite. Second, I will declare how the proposition itself, by the virtue of the discourse and the force of the words, should by no means be judged as heretical or simply "savoring of heresy" by learned men. Third, I will declare that they themselves err in the faith if they persist in the opinion that I cannot defend my conclusion from heresy in the sense that the force of the words allows. Fourth and finally, I will show out of an abundance of caution that they can in no way excuse themselves for the fact that their condemnation was made without due consideration.

However, before I set forth the manner in which I hold that Christ descended into hell, I wish to premise this: although we are bound to believe explicitly and in particular that Christ descended into hell as an article of faith handed down and promulgated to us by **Philip** <margin>The descent of Christ was given to us by Philip</margin> <note>Traditional belief held that each of the twelve Apostles contributed one clause to the Apostles' Creed; the clause "He descended into hell" was attributed to St. Philip</note>, so that my protestation or anything like it would not save someone who proposed the opposite of that article. Yet, it does not seem that every faithful person is bound to believe a *determined manner* of that descent explicitly and in particular. Rather, it suffices for a Christian man to believe that Christ descended into hell not according to his body, nor according to body and soul together, but according to his soul alone; and that he should believe this descent according to the soul was done in a manner possible, fitting, expedient, and opportune. This is because the determined manner of that descent is not found expressly, nor can it be proven, from Holy Scripture, nor from any determination of the universal Church, nor from special revelation of God, nor from the faithful report of the Apostles. <margin>**Scotus**. **Francis of Meyronnes**.</margin> Indeed, what is more, **Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus, a major medieval philosopher and theologian</note>—who was no little practiced in the sacred letters—says that it is not found in Holy Scripture that Christ descended into hell, as **Francis of Meyronnes** <note>A 14th-century follower of Scotus</note> reports in the fourth book of his *Sentences*. How much less, then, can we say that a certain and determined manner of Christ’s descent is found in Scripture? Hence, there has been no lack of doctors...

<summary>Pico begins his formal defense by addressing the first of his condemned theses: the nature of Christ's descent into hell. He argues that while the fact of the descent is an article of faith, the specific "manner" of it (physical presence vs. spiritual effect) is not dogmatically defined.</summary>

# APOLOGIA

<margin>
Hence, it is not a true theological proposition concerning God’s being everywhere through presence, power, and essence. 
**Thomas Aquinas**. 
What does it mean "to penetrate"?
</margin>

From this, it appeared probable to someone whose condemnation I have never read regarding this article <note>the specific article or "thesis" on trial</note>: it seemed to him that the article was defensible—namely, that the soul of Christ was not presentially <note>term: <term>presentially</term>; meaning to be physically or substantially present in a specific location</note> in hell. All the authorities that **Francis of Mayronnes** <note>a 14th-century Franciscan theologian</note> cites in the fourth book and other theologians cite in the third: it might appear to someone that these could be interpreted as a descent "by effect" just as much as by "real presence." This follows the very way of interpreting Scripture used by the doctors who hold the opposite view. For we read in **Ecclesiasticus 24**: *I will penetrate all the lower parts of the earth.* In explaining this, **Thomas Aquinas** says in the third part of the *Summa* <note>The *Summa Theologiae*, Aquinas's most famous work</note> that this should be understood as being "by effect." Therefore, someone might perhaps say by analogy that the authorities who say He "penetrated" into **Limbo** or the **Bosom of Abraham** <note>traditional terms for the place where the righteous dead waited before Christ's resurrection</note> could be explained in the same way. For "to penetrate" is the same as to enter deeply and within; it is even more than simply "to descend." Therefore, if He is said to have not only entered, but to have entered deeply and within the lower parts of the earth, not because He was really present there, but because He was there only "by effect," then it could likewise be said that He was in the Bosom of Abraham and entered the Bosom of Abraham only by effect and not by real presence.

However, I do not say these things because I have ever believed that Christ, while existing presentially elsewhere, was said to be in hell only because He worked something there—in the way a king staying in his palace is said to be in another place in his province where he effectively accomplishes something by the authority of his power and command. For that was never my opinion, as will soon be clear in the declaration of my views. Rather, I firmly hold and have held, and have always said both publicly and privately, that just as the soul of Christ was in the three days <note>the time between the Crucifixion and Resurrection</note>, it was truly present in hell.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
But I wanted to say these things for a fuller examination of this matter, so that we might see the truth of that saying of **Augustine** in his *Book on Heresies*: that nothing is more difficult than defining what is or is not "heretical." This is why he says it happened that when two very famous writers, **Epiphanius** and **Philastrius**, wrote about heresies, they disagreed greatly in counting them, for no other reason than that what seemed heretical to one did not seem so to the other. But now I come to manifest my opinion on the manner of Christ’s descent and to perfectly declare my conclusion. First, I will set forth its meaning in summary. Second, I will explain and prove it more broadly.

<margin>
Note: Twofold opinion on separated substances
</margin>
The summary sense of my conclusion is this: Because Christ descended to hell according to his soul only, and since it seems that being located in a place or moving locally does not belong to a soul—just as it does not belong to any **separated substance** <note>term: <term>separated substance</term>; a being that exists without a physical body, such as an angel or a human soul after death</note>—except by reason of its "operation" <note>its action or influence</note>. Therefore, I say that to have descended to hell, or to have been in hell locally, does not seem to have applied to Christ except by reason of his operation. This is so even though the soul of Christ was truly presentially in hell, yet his substance itself was not the reason for his presence, but only his operation. 

So that these words may be more fully understood, it must be noted that among those who posit that separated substances are not in a place except through a "transient operation," there is a twofold opinion. For some say that to incorporeal substances, by reason of their substance, a location is in no way owed—just as a soul is never truly white or black. And so, according to them, it can be said not irrationally that the soul is not in a place and is "nowhere," just as it is truly said to be neither hot nor cold. The authorities and scriptures that seem to give a place to angels when they say they are in heaven, or sent to this place or that, are to be understood thus: not that they themselves are here or there (since they are not properly in a place), but that they "operate" here or there, or begin to operate where they were not operating before. 

<margin>
The first: Gregory of Nyssa
</margin>
And these thinkers rely heavily on the words of **Gregory of Nyssa**, who says that when we ought to say "the spirit operates here," we say "the spirit is here" as a figure of speech <note>original: *abusie*, meaning an improper use of a term or catachresis</note>. And so this opinion holds that the substance of an angel or a separated soul can never be said to be present to this or that place except in a "negative" sense (that is, not-distant). But if it is ever said to be or to have been somewhere, it is the same as saying it operates or has operated somewhere. They add that this way of speaking is borrowed from physical things.

<summary>Pico defends his thesis on Christ's descent into hell, arguing that while Christ was truly present there, the philosophical nature of a soul's presence is defined by its "operation" rather than physical occupancy. He cites Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa to show the complexity of defining heresy and the nature of spiritual substances.</summary>

Here, he explores the philosophical "mode of being" in a place for things that don't have bodies, like souls and angels, contrasting the "common opinion" with his own preferred "Second Opinion."</meta>

# ON THE QUESTIONS

temporal things; because we see that these cannot act unless they are present, at least <margin>See the false [view]</margin> according to common opinion. Therefore, believing the same regarding incorporeal <note>non-physical</note> things, they conclude that where they operate, and where their operation is found to be, there also their substance exists locally through its presence. They conclude finally that it is a dullness of mind and a lack of imagination not to be able to understand that something can be a being and yet not be in a place; and that the argument of those who say "to be" presupposes "to act" is frivolous. For that proposition is true in the sense that a non-being cannot act. For it is necessary for an agent to be "in act" <note>actually existing/functioning</note>, according to the principle that "some moving species will always be reckoned." But it is not true in the sense that acting in a place presupposes being in a place, since the one acting may be of such a nature that local presence or distance is no more owed to it than whiteness or blackness. Those who hold this opinion would say that the soul of Christ, when separated from his body according to its substance, was neither in hell nor outside of hell: but truly was nowhere. It is said, however, to have been in hell because it acted in hell; and it is said to have been most principally in that part of hell where it principally acted. However, although many <term>doctors</term> <note>highly learned theologians and scholars of the Church</note> hold this opinion regarding the mode of being presentially in a place, I nevertheless do not hold it, nor have I followed it in my conclusion; but I held that which I shall immediately subjoin. 

There is, therefore, another opinion which says that a separated substance—such as an angel or a <margin>The second opinion, which the author held</margin> soul not united to a body—is truly in a place. And thus it is truly <term>definitively</term> <note>term: <term>definitively present</term>; meaning to be in a place by being restricted to it, but without occupying physical space or having dimensions</note> present locally, just as a corporeal thing is <term>commensuratively</term> <note>term: <term>commensuratively present</term>; meaning to occupy a place such that the object’s dimensions match the space it fills</note> present locally. And in this, this path agrees with the common one, which is the path of **Duns Scotus** and all the **Scotists** <note>followers of the 13th-century philosopher John Duns Scotus</note>. But they differ in this: the Scotists say that the "definition" and limitation of the essence—and finally the intrinsic determination of its substance—is the reason for a separated substance being in a place. But this opinion, which I have followed in my conclusion, says that just as a corporeal substance is commensuratively in a place, yet the reason for its being so in a place is not its "substantiality" but its quantity (which is extrinsic and foreign to the nature of its substance); so too, although an incorporeal substance is truly definitively in a place and present locally, the reason for its being in a place is not its substance, but its <term>operation</term> <note>action or effect</note> passing from it to the outside. I judge this <margin>Declaration of the opinion</margin> opinion should be understood in this way, and so understood, I judge it not only not heretical, but even more probable than its opposite. And it is this: even if the finiteness or limitation of a separated nature is the reason for it not being everywhere, or the reason why if it is in one place it is not simultaneously in another in its entirety (and in both by nature), nevertheless that is not the reason for the substance itself being "simply" in that place. Rather, its effect or operation—taking "operation" for every relationship to a body or place that functions by way of an active or passive operation—is the reason. This is distinct from the relationship of "local presence" [in the physical sense], and this is understood as a matter of fact, not denying another possible mode of descent or location for a separated soul (as I say in the following conclusion), which mode is nonetheless unknown to us. Following this opinion in my conclusion, I say that Christ was in hell only by effect; since he was not there except according to his soul. It must be said, according to this opinion, that just as it is not fitting <margin>He shows the necessity of his opinion</margin> for a corporeal substance to be anywhere commensuratively except through quantity, so it was not fitting for that soul to be in hell (where it is believed to have been) except through effect and operation. But just as the reason for the presence of the souls of the holy fathers <note>the Old Testament patriarchs waiting in Limbo</note> was their relationship to that place, which functioned by way of a "passing operation" (such as their detention and binding to that place until the door was opened and they were drawn out by the Redeemer), so the reason for the presence of the soul of Christ was the operation that he worked there. And that this was my mind, and that the words of my conclusion intend this, I shall manifest below, where the conclusion itself will be declared; and it will be judged not heretical by the virtue of the discourse and according to the force of the words. Which of the two opinions is truer regarding the mode of being in a place for substances... <margin>Note</margin>

<summary>Pico explains his philosophical view on how Christ's soul was present in hell, arguing that while it was "truly" there, its presence was defined by its actions and effects rather than by physical location. He distinguishes his view from the Scotists, asserting that his position is both more probable and entirely orthodox.</summary>

Whether I followed theirs, I do not determine; I say only this: that my opinion has been believed and held as most true by so many and such great masters and Catholic doctors, most celebrated in both teaching and holiness. Thus, if there are any who dare to judge the opinion of such proven doctors as heretical or "savoring of heresy," they should be considered far more reckless than I, who prefer the authority of those ancient theologians over the determinations of the younger ones. For this opinion which I follow is held assertively not only by Durandus, but also by **Bernard of Gannat** in his *Impugnations of Hervaeus*, in the second "Quodlibet" <note>A "Quodlibet" was a public academic debate on "whatever you please"</note>. **Thomas of England** holds it in his *Quodlibets*. **Herveus the Breton** holds it in his second book on the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* by Peter Lombard was the standard textbook of medieval theology</note>. **Blessed Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> also held it in his first book on the *Sentences*, although elsewhere he may then seem to follow another opinion. The **Archbishop of Amalfi** holds it in his second book. **John of Paris** holds it in his *Corrective of the Corruptor*. And why should I number more? I believe more than a hundred proven Catholic doctors held this opinion. Their books have not only not been rejected by the Church, but are celebrated and publicly read in all the schools of the Christians. If anyone wishes to consult them, they will be able to see the foundations of the opinion and recognize its probability; I do not intend to do that here. I only act to declare the conclusions proposed by me in such a way that the simple may not have cause for scandal, nor detractors (if there be any) have anything to slander.

<margin>Arguments against this opinion</margin>
<margin>First</margin>
<margin>Second</margin>
<margin>Third</margin>
<margin>Fourth</margin>
However, for the sake of exercise, I will bring forward certain arguments that I have heard against this opinion. **First**, it is argued through the 204th Parisian Article <note>Refers to the Condemnations of 1277, where the Bishop of Paris listed 219 "errors" taught at the university</note>, which says: *to say the substance of an angel is not in a place without operation is an error*. **Second**, it is argued that it is possible for a separated substance <note>an angel or soul</note> to perform no external work; if this is granted, the question is whether it is somewhere, or nowhere, or everywhere. Not "nowhere," because even then it remains a part of the universe; and thus it would be true to say it is in the world. Not "everywhere," because that is unique to God. Therefore, it must be "somewhere." **Third**, because angels are said to be in the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual heaven</note>, and yet they have no transitive operation <note>direct physical effect</note> acting upon that heaven. **Furthermore**, the Master General <note>The head of a religious order</note> insisted chiefly on two reasons: the first is that, setting aside any external operation, the essence of an angel is still finite; therefore, it is still "defined" by place. The **second** is this: if place is denied to an angel because it lacks extension <note>physical size</note>, this is no obstacle; for even if a "point" were given separate from a line, it would still have a position, yet a point has no extension.

<margin>The first solution is manifold, and an explanation of the Parisian article.</margin>
To the first, a manifold response is evident according to the aforementioned doctors. For there are some who, wishing to save the Article while keeping their position, say the "mind" <note>intended meaning</note> of the Article is this: the opinion stating that a separated substance is not in a place except through operation (meaning external local motion or real alteration) is an error. That this is the "mind" of the Article is clear because Article 78 says, as if explaining this one: *to say that if there were some separated substance that did not move some body in this world, it would not be included in the universe, is an error*. Behold! Just as in the article cited by the arguer, it says it is an error for an angel to be in a place *only* by operation, so in this one it says it is an error to say a separated substance is not included in this universe except through the motion of a body. Whence it seems to understand the same thing by "operation" in Article 204 as it does by "motion" in Article 78. But this position does not hold that an angel is in a place *only* by operation taken in that way, as will be clear in the response to the third point.

<margin>Second [solution] - Godfrey of Fontaines</margin>
<margin>Note</margin>
<margin>Henry</margin>
Likewise, the "Solemn Doctor" **Godfrey of Fontaines** says that these Articles require great correction; for some are false, and some contradict each other. And certainly in this matter it is necessary either that the Article be explained in the manner just proposed, or that there be a manifest contradiction within the Articles themselves. Which I prove thus: for there is Article 218, which says: *if it is understood that the substance of an angel is not the reason for its being in a place, it is true to say that it is nowhere according to its substance*. And **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent</note> testifies in his second *Quodlibet*, question 9, that all...

He cites the famous "Articles of Paris" (the Condemnations of 1277) to show that his view is not heretical.</meta>

<header>QUESTIONS</header>

# QUESTIONS

All the masters of theology, gathered together, have unanimously agreed on this: that the substance of an angel is not the reason an angel is in a place. Henry <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major scholastic philosopher and theologian</note> says that he himself was among those masters who made this determination. And Henry adds in the same place that, by a similar logic, it is undoubtedly true that if an angel—through its power, namely through its intellect and will—does not apply its strength to a place by working upon it, then its simply intellectual and volitional power is not the reason for it being in that place. This is because its power is no less abstract than its substance. Therefore, it follows that one must either concede that the reason for being in a place is something existing by way of a "second act" <note>In scholastic philosophy, "first act" is existence or essence, while "second act" refers to an operation or activity performed by that essence</note> passing into a body—whatever that might be (which is the position I follow)—or there will be a manifest contradiction within the articles <note>The 219 articles condemned by the Bishop of Paris in 1277, which set the boundaries for academic theology</note>. Thus, Henry confesses in the same passage that he cannot understand how a separated substance <note>A "separated substance" refers to a being that exists without a physical body, such as an angel or a human soul after death</note> can be in a place unless it acts upon something or is acted upon by the place, or by a thing existing in that place.

<margin>Third</margin>
<margin>Giles</margin>
<margin>Note</margin>
However, Giles <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316), a pupil of Thomas Aquinas and a major theologian</note> and many others say that one should not worry about those articles, because they were made without summoning all the Parisian doctors, but rather at the request of certain leaders <note>original: "capitoforū," likely referring to the heads of the university chapters</note>. Whatever the truth of that may be, I wish to say two things: First, that Article 218 supports our position no less than Article 204 might seem to oppose it. Second, it is certain—and the Parisians themselves admit this—that those articles do not bind all the faithful. Nor are we held to believe them except insofar as they rely on Holy Scripture or the determinations of the universal Church. Hence, the English are accustomed to saying that those articles "do not cross the sea" <note>A common medieval saying meaning that the local rulings of the University of Paris did not have legal or theological authority in England</note>.
<margin>Saying of the</margin>
<margin>English</margin>
Therefore, if we may joke in such a serious matter, we can say that they do not cross the Alps either. Thus, even if my conclusion were against an article, let those who condemned me remember that they were entirely wrong to condemn me: for they claimed my conclusion was against the Apostolic Creed <note>The fundamental statement of Christian belief</note>, when they ought to have said it was against the "Parisian Creed"—and even that is false, as we have shown before.

<margin>Declaration</margin>
<margin>of the</margin>
<margin>articles</margin>
However, it seems to me that the true understanding of those articles is as follows: in Article 204, if the discussion is about "operation" in the sense mentioned before, the intent is that even if every operation were set aside, the finiteness or limitation of a separated nature would still be the reason it is not "everywhere"—or the reason why, if it is in one place, it is not simultaneously in another whole place, both by its nature. In Article 218, however, I believe the intent is that the substance (or the finiteness of the substance) is not the reason for an angel being simply in a place. By explaining it this way, there is no contradiction in the articles. And understood thus, the articles are not only not against my position, but they confirm it entirely on both sides, as is clear from the declaration of the position set down above.

<margin>Solution of the</margin>
<margin>second argu-</margin>
<margin>ment ac-</margin>
<margin>cording to</margin>
<margin>many</margin>
Regarding the second point, it is said by many—conceding that it is possible for an incorporeal substance to exist without an operation passing outside of itself—that the argument seems to suggest one of three "inconveniences" <note>In logical debate, an "inconvenience" is an absurd or unacceptable consequence of a premise</note> follows. The first is that since it is a part of the universe, it is "inconvenient" for it not to be "in" the universe. To this, they would say that the person arguing is using the word "part" in two different ways. For if by "part of the universe" one means that which has a fixed position in the universe, then they say an angel cannot be called a "part of the universe" whether it is operating or not. But if one means being a "part of beings"—that is, one 
<margin>Part is</margin>
<margin>taken in</margin>
<margin>two ways</margin>
of the beings and natures of the universe—then they concede it is a part of the universe, and indeed one of the more noble parts. But it does not seem to follow from this that it must have a location or a physical definition in a place.

<margin>Being everywhere</margin>
The second "inconvenience" is that it could not then be said to be "everywhere," because that is unique to God. To this, it is said that to be "everywhere" in the way theologians say God is everywhere—namely, by essence, power, and presence—is unique to God and cannot belong to any created nature.
<margin>Henry</margin>
<margin>Double</margin>
<margin>limitation</margin>
But as for being "everywhere" in the sense of being "here" or "there" by indifference, or "everywhere" by "indistance" <note>A technical term meaning the lack of spatial distance between a spiritual substance and a physical place</note>—that is, truly existing according to a substance that is not distant from any place—you should hear what Henry says in his *Quodlibet* 11, question 9. He says: "In a creature, a double limitation can be understood. One is in its nature and essence..."

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense concerning the location of incorporeal beings. He is elaborating on the arguments of Henry of Ghent and St. Thomas Aquinas to prove that angels are not "in a place" by their essence, but only through their actions or "operations."</meta>

# APOLOGIA

...which is finite and contained within certain limits; and in this way, God alone is unlimited and infinite in nature. Another kind of limitation of nature can be understood: which is limitation to a <term>site</term> <note>original: "situ"; referring to a specific spatial position</note> by which a thing is so finite and contained within certain limits that it must be somewhere—not nowhere, nor everywhere—but in such a way that it is here and not there; or even if it is not determinately here or there, it is still under the determination of being either here, or there, or somewhere. This limitation belongs to the <term>category of 'Where'</term> <note>original: "prædicamentũ ubi"; one of Aristotle's ten categories describing the location of an object</note>. I see clearly that every creature differs from God by that first limitation of their nature. However, whether it is necessary for every creature to differ and be distant from Him by the second limitation—namely, because He is everywhere, while every creature is necessarily somewhere but not everywhere—I say that "I am completely ignorant of this." These are Henry’s literal words. From these words, we have it clearly enough that Henry cannot understand why that which they <note>Pico's critics</note> bring forward as an "inconvenience" <note>An "inconvenience" in scholastic logic is a point that leads to a logical absurdity or contradiction</note> should actually be considered unsuitable. The third "inconvenience" they cite is that unless it is conceded that an angel is somewhere, it must be conceded that it is nowhere.

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
To this, you should hear the Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian</note> in his commentary on the *First Book of the Sentences*, distinction 37, responding thus: "I say," he says, "that I do not consider it unsuitable that an angel can be without a place and not in a place when it has no operation regarding a place; nor is it unsuitable if it is then said to be 'nowhere' or in no place. But nonetheless, this is not imaginable, because the imagination does not transcend the <term>continuum</term> <note>The physical, material world which is continuous in space</note>." These are Thomas’s literal words.

<margin>Operation can be understood in two ways</margin>
To the third point, I say that their argument proceeds from an incomplete understanding of our position. For our position, by "operation" (through which an incorporeal thing is said to be located), does not understand only that operation which is an external local motion or a real alteration <note>i.e., physically moving or changing something</note>, as we also touched upon somewhat in the response to the first point in the exposition of the <term>Articles of Paris</term> <note>The 1277 condemnations mentioned on the previous page</note>. Rather, it takes "operation" broadly for every motion or influence or relationship signified by the manner of an operation passing into a body and proceeding from the angel, or vice versa.

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
And that this is the intended meaning of the position is clear from the words of Thomas in the *First Book of the Sentences*, distinction 37, question 1, article 1, where he seems to follow this opinion, saying: "It remains, therefore, that an angel cannot be defined and determined to a place except through action or operation. I speak of operation commonly, according to how an angel relates to a body contained in a place by way of presiding over it, or ministering to it, or in some way acting or being acted upon." These are Thomas’s words verbatim. From these words, the answer to the argument is clear: for although angels do not have an operation toward the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, purely spiritual part of the heavens</note> that is a local motion or a real alteration, they nevertheless have something that functions by way of a "transient operation," such as "presiding" or something similar.

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
Regarding the fourth point, upon which that <term>Master General</term> <note>Likely referring to a specific high-ranking critic within the Dominican or Franciscan orders</note> relied so heavily: what needs to be said can be made clear enough from the words of Henry alleged above in the solution to the second point. Nevertheless, let us also hear what Saint Thomas says about that line of reasoning. "Some say," he says, "that an angel is not in a place <term>circumscriptively</term> <note>Occupying space so that every part of the angel matches a part of the space</note> but <term>definitively</term> <note>Being limited to a certain area without occupying volume</note>, because it is determined to some place such that it is in this place and not in another, since its essence is finite. For because it is a created thing, they say one must understand that it is determined to some place."

<margin>Limit can be understood in two ways</margin>
But this is a very crude proof, because it proceeds from an <term>equivocation</term> <note>A logical fallacy where the same word is used with different meanings</note> of the word "limit" <note>original: "finis"</note>. For when the essence of an angel is said to be "finite" <note>limited</note>, "limit" is taken as the limit of essence and power—just as a definition is called a "term"—and not as a limit of physical dimension. A place, however, is called "finite" according to the three dimensions of quantity. A limit according to these two different meanings has no shared measurement or proportion. Therefore, it is not necessary that what is finite in essence be limited by the boundaries of a place. These are Thomas’s literal words. From which it follows that, if Thomas is not lying, this Master is "crude," since he called his own crude proof a "demonstration."

<margin>What is a point?</margin>
Regarding the other argument about a "point," I say that it is even cruder than the first. For a point is a thing in the category of <term>quantity</term>, having a location by its very nature. An incorporeal thing, however, is entirely abstracted from location; and truly it is great crudity to imagine the same thing concerning the <term>indivisibility</term> of an incorporeal thing and the indivisibility of a point. To make this even clearer

->to this master<-

### OF THE QUESTIONS.

<margin>Argument against the opponent</margin>
To **this master**. Let him tell me, I ask: if **unity** were separate, would it have a determined **site**? <note>Pico is using a mathematical analogy: "Unity" (the number one) is a concept that doesn't exist in a specific physical spot.</note> Certainly, it is clear that it would not, since a **unity** is distinguished from a **point** by the fact that a **point** has a position, but **unity** does not. But it is manifest that an angel—and indeed any incorporeal substance—is even more abstract than any quantity, whether continuous or 
<margin>Point</margin>
discrete. For **Metaphysics**, as is clear to everyone, deals with things more abstract than **Arithmetic**, 
<margin>Unity</margin>
which is one of the mathematical sciences. Therefore, it is much less possible to say of an angel that it has a **site**. If **this master** cannot imagine the abstraction of an angel, he should at least consider the abstraction of **unity**. Let him hear what should be said about this according to **Henry**. For he, in the
<margin>Henry</margin>
place cited above speaking on this matter, says: "Those, therefore, who cannot understand an angel according to the nature of its substance as a **unity** without the concept of a **point**, are those of whom the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, known in the Middle Ages simply as 'The Commentator' on Aristotle.</note> speaks in the second book of the *Metaphysics*, in whom the **imaginative power** dominates over the **cogitative power**." And therefore, as he says, we see that such people do not believe in demonstrations unless their **imagination** accompanies them. Whatever they think of, they imagine as a quantity or as having a site in space, like a **point**. Hence, such people are **melancholic** and become excellent **mathematicians**, but they are naturally inept at **natural philosophy** <note>Physics or the study of nature.</note>. These are **Henry’s** words exactly. From which it follows that, according to **Henry**, **this master** is ill-disposed for the study of natural philosophy, worse for the study of **metaphysics**, and worst of all for the study of **theology**, which deals with the most abstract things. There remains to him only an aptitude for **mathematics**; since he has not exercised himself in those, he himself may judge what judgment should be made of him. After these reasons—which are commonly brought against the foundations of the position I followed in my conclusion regarding the manner of **Christ’s descent** <note>Referring to Christ's descent into Limbo.</note>—have been refuted, I wish also to bring forward the words of **our Albert**, a man no less great in learning than in his name 
<margin>Albert the Great</margin>
**the Great**. I remember reading his thoughts on this matter in his book on the *Physics*. Specifically, in the first tractate of the fourth book, in the first chapter, after he explained that passage where **Aristotle** says the ancients were deceived—believing that just as that which is not in a place is nothing, so too nothing is a being unless it is in a place—he then says the following regarding that passage: "There are, however, many moderns who grant the consequence of this argument, even though they know the logical sequence is invalid." For we know from **logic** that a consequence is not valid when it proceeds from the destruction of the antecedent to the destruction of the consequent <note>A logical fallacy: "If A, then B. Not A, therefore not B." Just because physical things are in a place, it doesn't mean non-physical things are "nowhere" in a sense of non-existence.</note>. And therefore, although it is true that "that which is nowhere does not exist," it does not follow from this that "that which exists is somewhere." And although this does not follow from what was said, there are still many who say that everything that exists is in some place, using this reasoning: "Everything that exists is a particular thing. A particular thing is 'here and now,' and what is 'here and now' is somewhere. Therefore, everything that exists is somewhere." Furthermore: "Everything that has a defined essence is limited, because it is confined within the terms of its own nature; and what is of a defined essence is defined in a place; and what is defined in a place is in some place." These people distinguish, according to **John Damascene**, 
<margin>John Damascene: To be in a place in two ways</margin>
saying that "to be in a place" is said in two ways. For something can be in a place **circumscriptively** <note>original: "circumscriptíue"; meaning the object is contained by the place, with its own boundaries matching the container's boundaries, like water in a cup.</note>, to which a beginning, middle, and end are assigned in that place; and in this way, they say bodies are in a place. Also, something can be in a place **definitively** <note>original: "defínítíue"; meaning the being's presence is limited to a certain area even if it doesn't have physical parts like a beginning or end.</note>, whose essence is so finitely enclosed in one place that nothing of it is found outside that place; and in this way, they say indivisible things are in a place, and similarly **intelligences** <note>Angels.</note> and **souls**, etc. But we do not believe these things; for even the **outermost heaven** is not 
<margin>Clarification of the words of the conclusion regarding the force of the argument</margin>
defined nor circumscribed by a place, because everything that is in a place is enclosed and contained by the place in which it is; and an **intelligence**, by its nature, is not in a place nor in any spatial distinction. These are **Albert’s** literal words. He does not approve of that common distinction of being in a place "definitively" and not "circumscriptively"—a distinction which some masters thought it an absolute sin to deny. Now, finally, it remains for me to show how the words of my conclusion are to be understood, and to declare that, by the weight of its argument, it is **Catholic**...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his theological theses. He is currently addressing the controversy surrounding his conclusion on Christ’s descent into Hell, specifically defending his use of logical phrasing to distinguish his view from that of Thomas Aquinas and the "common way" of the Parisian theologians.</meta>

<page-num>79</page-num>
# APOLOGIA

...Thus the conclusion states: Christ did not truly and in terms of **real presence**, as **Thomas** and the **common way** posit, descend into the underworld, but only as far as the **effect**. <note>Pico is defending a specific theological thesis: whether Christ’s soul was physically present in Hell or if "descending" simply meant his power and authority (the "effect") were felt there.</note> Here it must be noted that the word **"and"** where it is said **"and in terms of real presence"** is held **conjunctively**; and the word **"as"**, when it says **"as Thomas posits,"** is held **specifically** and **determinatively**, as I shall soon declare. From these things it is clear that the aforementioned conclusion is a single **negative copulative proposition**, or a negation of a joined extreme placed before a copulative conjunction. <note>In Scholastic logic, a "copulative proposition" is an "A and B" statement. Negating it (Not [A and B]) is different from negating each part individually.</note> Its sense is: "It is not the case that Christ truly and in terms of real presence, in the manner that **Thomas** posits, descended into the underworld, etc." And that copulative is equivalent to a single **affirmative disjunctive** of contradicting parts; namely, this one: "Either Christ did not descend truly into the underworld, or he did not descend into the underworld according to a **real presence**, etc." From which it follows that by inferring from the said conclusion that "Christ did not truly descend into the underworld," one is arguing from a whole affirmative disjunctive to one of its parts determinately. Such an argumentation, however, fails as a **fallacy of the consequent**. <note>A logical error where one assumes that because the whole "either/or" statement is true, one specific part must be the reason why.</note> For an affirmative disjunctive is the consequence of one of its parts. It follows further that by reason of the falsehood of the aforementioned part, the whole aforementioned disjunctive ought not to be falsified. Thus, in a similar case, this proposition is true: "Socrates is a man." And this one is false: "Socrates is a man and God is not God." From which to argue "Therefore Socrates is not a man" is surely **childish**. By similarity, from that negative copulative—"Christ did not truly and in terms of real presence, as Thomas posits, descend, etc."—to argue "Therefore Christ did not truly descend" is **childish**, and belongs to a man utterly ignorant of logic and philosophy, let alone theology.

<margin>
Scotus
St. Bonaventure
Nominalists
St. Thomas
Common way
University of Paris
</margin>

Not only do I not intend in my conclusion that this proposition is true—"Christ did not truly descend into the underworld"—but neither do I intend this one: "Christ, or the soul of Christ, was not presentially in hell and by a real and true presence of his substance." Rather, I only intend that he was not there by **real presence** in the manner that **Thomas** and the **common way** posit. Therefore I said that the word **"as"** is held **specifically** and **determinatively** regarding the term **"real presence."** Therefore, it is not valid to say: "He was not there really present in the way that such a Doctor says; therefore he was not there really present."

The **common way**—that is, the way of **Scotus**, **Bonaventure**, and nearly all the **Scotists** and almost all the **Nominalists**—holds that he was present there in such a way that his substance itself was the reason for his presentiality and locatability; <note>The "Nominalists" and "Scotists" were rival schools of thought to the "Thomists" (followers of Thomas Aquinas). Pico is navigating the complex academic politics of his day.</note> which opinion even **Thomas** seems to me to follow in this matter. Therefore I said, "**as Thomas and the common way posit**," calling the "**common way of theologians**" that which is commonly held now at **Paris**, where the study of theology especially flourishes. There, almost everyone proceeds in this matter concerning the presentiality of the soul to a place along with the **Scotists** and **Nominalists**; and for this reason alone—that is, out of **reverence** for the **University of Paris**—I did not wish to posit this conclusion of mine except as **probable**, even though I saw that it could also be posited **assertively** according to the way of many most approved doctors. 

<margin>
Scotus
Thomists
</margin>

That the word **"as"** can be held in the common way of speaking **determinatively** is clear. For if someone says, "The **attributes** are not distinguished, as **Scotus** says," among everyone that proposition would have a double proper sense. One would be by taking the word **"as"** **relatively**, and it would be equivalent to this expression: "That which Scotus says—namely, that the attributes are not distinguished—is true." And that proposition would be false even according to the **Thomists**, because even they grant that the attributes are in some way distinguished. The other sense would be by taking the word **"as"** **determinatively** and **specifically**, and it would be equivalent to this expression: "The attributes are not distinguished in that mode of distinction by which **Scotus** says they are distinguished." And then, among the **Thomists**, the proposition would be **true**. And thus it is in any proposition where, after an opinion is recited, the authority of someone is placed, joined by this word **"as."** If therefore this mode of speaking is both proper and most common among everyone...

<summary>Pico uses formal logic to defend his thesis on Christ's descent into Hell, arguing that his critics misinterpreted a specific qualified statement as a general denial of the doctrine. He highlights his respect for the University of Paris while distinguishing his views from the specific spatial theories of Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s logical and theological defense regarding the manner of Christ’s descent into Hell. Having previously argued that his proposition was a formal negation of a specific scholastic definition, he now clarifies that his use of the phrase "by effect" does not deny Christ's real presence, but rather explains the metaphysical reason for that presence.</meta>

# QUESTIONS

...all theologians might concede: it is necessary that they also concede that in our proposition in which it is said **"Christ did not descend as Thomas says,"** the word **"as"** <note>original: "ly ut"; "ly" is a technical term in scholastic logic used to point to a specific word as an object of analysis</note> can be held **relatively**, so that the sense is: "Christ did not descend [in the way] which, namely, **Thomas** says Christ descended." It can also be held just as well and just as properly **specifically**, being equivalent to this: "Although Christ descended **presentially**, he did not do so in that presential manner which the **common way** <note>The "common way" (communis via) refers to the prevailing theological consensus in the universities of the time, largely following the Thomist school.</note> describes," and this is the sense that I intend.

<margin>Objection</margin>
But perhaps someone would still say: "You do not escape [the charge], because you then add: **'but only as to the effect.'** Therefore, you do not only exclude **real presence** in the way the **common way** posits it, but you simply exclude *all* **real presence**, since you say **'only as to the effect.'** Thus, the proposition you stated is not a **negative copulative** (as you claim by negating presence in the manner of Thomas, etc.), but it is also **affirmative**, stating affirmatively that Christ was in Hell **only as to the effect**."

<margin>Solution</margin>
But this objection is crude. For this word **"but"** is an **adversative** word, and by its power, it introduces through the words following it an **affirmative truth** opposed to the statement which the superior part of the conclusion negates. To this [negation], it stands in opposition. If, therefore—as was proven in the superior part—only the presentiality of the soul **by substance** is negated (not as to the "what" but as to the "by what"; <note>original: "non quantum ad quid sed quantum ad quo"</note> that is, it does not negate that the substance was present, but that the substance was the *reason* for the presentiality), so also in this final part, which posits an affirmative precisely opposed to that [negation], **"to have been in hell by effect"** is to be understood not as to the **thing located**, but as to the **reason for its being located**. Briefly, the sense (which can be clear even to the unlearned) is this: since the finitude of the [soul's] substance was not the reason for its local presence, the **effect** alone was such a reason for it.

<margin>Epilogue</margin>
Recollecting briefly, therefore, I say that **Christ truly descended to the underworld**, and that he was in Hell by **real presence**.

<margin>Of the conclusion</margin>
But I say that he was not there truly and presentially in the manner that **Thomas** and the **common way** describe, because his substance was not for him the reason for being in that place (as they posit), but rather his **operation** <note>In this context, "operation" refers to the active power or influence of the soul.</note> was. And that this opinion is probable and believed by many Catholic and most excellent doctors has already appeared enough above. We have also sufficiently explained that, according to the literal force of the words, it is true and not to be judged heretical. For we know that this statement is true: **"Christ did not, as God and man, as Arius posits, satisfy for us."** <margin>Arius</margin> <note>Arius was a 4th-century priest whose teachings (Arianism) claimed that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father. Pico uses him as a logical example: one can agree with a premise (Christ is God and man) while rejecting a specific person's definition of it.</note> For although it is true that he satisfied as God and man, it is nevertheless false that he did so existing as "God and man" in the way that **Arius** posits. Likewise, although it is true that Christ was truly and presentially in Hell, it is nonetheless probable and believed by many that he was not there truly and presentially in the way that **Thomas** and the **common way** describe, in the manner explained above.

<margin>Objection</margin>
But one scruple seems to remain: that this was not my intention when I set down the conclusion. For if **Thomas**, in the first book of the *Sentences*, <note>Referring to Thomas Aquinas's commentary on Peter Lombard's *Sentences*, an early work.</note> holds this way himself—namely, that **operation** is the reason for an angel being in a place—it seems that the conclusion would also be true according to **Thomas**. Therefore, when I say **"not as Thomas posits,"** it seems I must have intended something else regarding that descent than what I have said.

<margin>Solution</margin>
However, one would not have this scruple if they had well considered my conclusions. For I am of this opinion: that **Thomas**, in this matter of the manner of being in a place <margin>Diverse opinions of Thomas on this question; he is a Scotist</margin> <note>Pico is provocatively suggesting that in his later works, Aquinas shifted toward the views of Duns Scotus, the great rival of the Thomist school.</note> for separated things <note>i.e., souls or angels without bodies.</note>, held diverse views and did not follow the same opinion everywhere. Therefore, although in the first book of the *Sentences* he seems to hold this way which I follow in the conclusion, nevertheless elsewhere—as in the fourth book of the *Sentences* and especially in the **Third Part of the Summa** (where he treats this descent and from which his opinion should be judged rather than from his [early] writings)—he seems to agree with the opinion of the **Scotists**: that [the soul] was there through **essence** in such a way that its essence was for it the reason for its locatability, and not **effect** alone or **operation**. For **Thomas** says there that the soul of Christ was by **effect** in other parts of Hell, but by **essence** in **Limbo**, etc. From this statement, I argue thus: Wherever something is by that which is for it the reason of locatability, there it is by its **substance** and **real presence**. Therefore, if **effect** was the reason for the locatability of Christ's soul wherever it was by effect, then it was there by the real presence of its substance. But according to **Thomas**, he was in some places by effect where he was *not* by his real presence. Therefore, according to [Thomas]...

<summary>Pico clarifies that his thesis does not deny Christ's real presence in Hell, but argues that the "reason" for this presence is Christ's active power (operation) rather than his substance's location. He also points out inconsistencies in Thomas Aquinas's writings, claiming Thomas later incorrectly separated essence from effect.</summary>
<keywords>Christ's descent into Hell, Real Presence, Thomas Aquinas, Limbo, Scholastic Logic, Essence vs. Operation, Arius, Scotists, Metaphysics of Place</keywords>
