<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his thesis on Christ’s descent into Hell. Having argued that his "negation" of Thomas Aquinas's position was logical rather than heretical, he now addresses the technical nuances of how incorporeal beings (like souls or angels) exist in a physical location.</meta>

# APOLOGIA

<margin>Dissension among the Thomists</margin>
For **Thomas**, "effect" was not his reason for **locatability** <note>The metaphysical capacity of a being to be assigned to a specific place.</note>. This moved me to believe it probable that **Thomas** "walked" with the **Scotists** <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus, who often disagreed with Thomas Aquinas on how angels and souls relate to physical space.</note> on this point. But whatever **Thomas’s** opinion may be, it is irrelevant to the present matter, because to err regarding the opinion of **Thomas** is not to err in faith. Indeed, there is often a multiple of opinions among the **Thomists** themselves regarding his actual opinion. It is enough that this clearly appears: that when I proposed the conclusion, I believed this to be **Thomas’s** opinion, and that I am not now twisting the proposition to a meaning alien to the one I held then. That I believed this from the beginning—and that this was my judgment of **Thomas's** opinion when I posed the conclusions—is most clearly evident from this: that I proposed the conclusion that **Thomas** and **Scotus** do not differ regarding the way **angels** exist in a place. It should be known, however, that **Scotus** explicitly says that even excluding all **operation** <note>In this context, "operation" refers to an angel or soul acting upon something in a location, such as moving an object or exerting power.</note>, a place is still owed to **incorporeal substances**. Therefore, I had to believe that **Thomas** was of this same judgment. Thus, although I firmly held that **Christ** was truly and presentially in **Hell**—and in this I agreed with **Thomas** and all **Catholics**—I nevertheless thought **Thomas** believed his substance itself was the reason for his locatability, rather than his operation.

<margin>Note.</margin>
<margin>
That Saint Thomas sometimes held different views on the same matter.
</margin>
Therefore, I said in my conclusion: "not in the way **Thomas** and the **common way** <note>The *communis via* or the standard theological teaching of the time.</note> posit." Nor should it seem strange to anyone that **Thomas** follows one opinion in one place and another elsewhere. For in the first book of the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard was the standard textbook for medieval theologians; Thomas wrote a famous commentary on it.</note> he follows the opinion of the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher widely cited in medieval universities.</note> regarding things generated from decay <note>Pico refers to "spontaneous generation," the medieval belief that certain life forms arose from rotting matter.</note>, which he later rejects in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* and elsewhere. Likewise, in the second book of the *Sentences* he follows the **Commentator's** opinion on the matter of the heavens, which he later rejects in the second book of *On the Heavens* and in the *Summa*. Likewise, in the fourth book and in the questions on **Boethius’s** *On the Trinity*, he holds the **Commentator's** view on **indeterminate dimensions**; yet in his own specific booklet (it is believed) and in many other places, he does not hold it. Likewise, in the first book of the *Sentences* he says that by the same action one understands the object of thought and the act of thinking itself. Yet in the first part of the *Summa* and the third book of the *Sentences*, he holds that the **reflexive action** differs from the **direct** one. Likewise, in his writings, he holds that the soul of **Christ**, insofar as it was joinable to a body, was like the soul of a "wayfarer" <note>A living person still on the journey toward God.</note>; but insofar as it was joinable to the **Word**, it was like the soul of a "comprehensor" <note>One who has reached the destination of heaven and "comprehends" the divine essence.</note>. In the *Summa*, however, he holds that the soul of **Christ** was totally and in all respects like the soul of a "comprehensor," and that it did not overflow the gift of clarity and impassibility <note>The state of being unable to suffer or change.</note> into the body by divine dispensation. Likewise, he feels differently about the **knowledge of Christ** in his writings and in the *Summa*, and so it is with many other things where one can see that he followed different opinions in different places. If those men contend that the opinion regarding the way of being in a place according to operation is also **Thomas’s**, they will have nothing more against me except that my opinion on the manner of **Christ’s descent** is even more probable—and should be judged less heretical—insofar as it is true even according to the opinion of **Saint Thomas**. On account of this, I wonder even more that these **Masters** condemned my conclusion.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Before they judged that conclusion heretical, I had not only declared my intention to them in these words, but I had even dictated them to be written down and noted, saying: "Let no one understand me to say by this conclusion that the soul of **Christ** did not descend to the underworld,

<margin>
Words of the printed conclusion
</margin>
and that the soul of **Christ** was not in **Hell** during the three days; indeed, I confess both. But I say that neither **local motion** nor being **located** anywhere fits any **separate substance** <note>A "separate substance" is a philosophical term for a being without a physical body, like an angel or a human soul separated from its body after death.</note>—such as the soul of **Christ** was—except by reason of **operation** alone." These exact words, and no others, I pronounced for them to note as a brief declaration of this conclusion. How they can still judge it heretical after this, when they could already hold it as **Catholic** <note>Meaning "orthodox" or "universal" church teaching.</note>, I do not see.

<margin>
He argues against the opponents
</margin>
And to show briefly, by way of recapitulating the argument, that those who believe my proposition cannot be defended from heresy are themselves erring in faith, I argue thus: he who posits a conclusion that is heretical in itself can be accused of...

<s>
fari de <note>Catchword: "accused of..."</note>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's logical defense of his thesis. On the previous page, he established that his disagreement with Thomas Aquinas regarding how spirits occupy space was a matter of philosophical interpretation, not religious dogma. He now moves to a formal logical proof to demonstrate that his specific conclusion about Christ’s descent into Hell cannot be classified as heresy.</meta>

# ON THE QUESTIONS

<margin>
Subtleties:
by which
the conclusion
is
defended
</margin>

...to speak of heresy insofar as heresy exists in the intellect. But one who posits my aforementioned conclusion cannot, by the act of positing it, be accused of heresy; therefore, the aforementioned conclusion is not heretical in itself. They concede the major premise; the minor premise I prove as follows. Whenever someone posits everything from which a proposition *a* necessarily follows, that person cannot be accused of heresy, and the person positing proposition *a* cannot be accused. But someone positing everything from which the position of my conclusion follows—in the manner in which it was posited by me—cannot be accused of heresy; therefore, the one positing the proposition itself (as I have posited it) also cannot be accused.

I prove the minor premise thus: 
1. The contradictory of this statement—*the reason for existing in a place (that is, "here" or "there" in the manner declared above) for separate substances <note>In medieval philosophy, "separate substances" refers to beings that exist without physical bodies, such as angels or human souls.</note> is their operation, not the limitation of their nature*—is not a matter of faith <note>original: "de fide"; this refers to established Church dogma that must be believed for salvation.</note>. 
2. And the contradictory of this statement—*it is not permitted to argue from a whole conjunction to one of its parts*—is not a matter of faith. 
3. And the contradictory of this statement—*if someone, having posited some negative or affirmative assertion, adds the authority of some Doctor <note>A "Doctor of the Church," such as Thomas Aquinas or Augustine.</note> with a proposition such as "as it can be held," it can be taken just as well in a definitive sense as in a relative sense*—is not a matter of faith. This is because "just as well" can be equivalent to the word "in the same way as," which similarly is not a matter of faith. 
4. And the contradictory of this statement—*through the "common way" <note>original: "communem viam"; the standard or majority opinion held by a particular school of thought.</note> in theological matters, we can appropriately understand the way which is commonly held in that university where, at the time of the speaker, the study of theology most flourishes*—is not a matter of faith. 
5. And the contradictory of this statement—*at this time, the study of theology flourishes more in the University of Paris than elsewhere*—is not a matter of faith. 
6. And the contradictory of this statement—*in the University of Paris it is now commonly held that the limitation of nature is the reason for the locatability of a separate substance*—is not a matter of faith. 
7. And the contradictory of this statement—**Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan theologian.</note> and the majority of the **Nominalists** <note>A school of philosophy that argued "universal" concepts are just names, not real things. They often clashed with "Realists" like the followers of Aquinas.</note> hold the aforementioned opinion, and **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note> seems to hold it in the third part of his *Summa* where he treats the descent of Christ—is not a matter of faith.

The logic then stands: if the contradictories of these statements are not matters of faith, it follows that to posit, believe, and dispute these statements is not in itself heretical or against the faith. Nor can the person who posits, holds, and disputes them—whether individually or collectively—be accused of heresy. But from these statements, when posited together and collectively, the position of my conclusion follows precisely as it stands; therefore, the one positing my conclusion precisely as it stands cannot be accused of heresy. 

The proofs of all the aforementioned points are found in the writings above. For regarding the first statement, it is clear that it is not only not heretical, but is more reasonable than its opposite, and is believed and approved by many Catholic Doctors. In the second, all logicians and all theologians who ever knew logic agree. So it is with all the others; even if someone might doubt whether they are true or false, no one is so unrefined, so lacking in all learning, so ignorant of the faith and those things which pertain to the faith, that they would say those things cannot be believed without heresy—and thus that their contradictories are matters of faith. 

Then let it be argued further: whoever believes this conclusion ("Christ, etc.")—based on the force of the words and according to proper and non-deviant usage of speech—cannot have a Catholic meaning, believes the contradictory of one or more of the seven statements above to be a matter of faith. But those who hold something to be a matter of faith which is *not* a matter of faith have a wrong understanding of the faith. For this goes against the word of the Lord in Deuteronomy 4: *You shall not add to the word that I speak to you, nor shall you take away from it.* Therefore, regarding my conclusion, those who feel poorly about it (as described above) have a poor understanding of the faith.

->See, O Supreme Pontiff! See, O senators of the august apostolic order! See, all of Rome, indeed all of Italy, indeed the whole Church of Christians!<- 

<margin>
Exclamation
</margin>

Let it be seen how they are refuted in this first proposition, in which they most heavily attacked me, and in which they seemed to many to have some handle—not so much for accusing me, but for excusing themselves for their condemnation of me. Regarding the other conclusions, it will appear clearer than light that they could have had no occasion, not even the slightest, for condemnation.

<summary>Pico uses a rigorous logical syllogism to argue that his thesis is not heretical, listing seven philosophical premises that are not matters of dogma and showing that his conclusion follows naturally from them. He ends with a passionate appeal to the Pope and the Roman elite to recognize the intellectual validity of his defense.</summary>

# APOLOGIA

<margin>Finally, he defends his conclusion using the authority of Durandus out of an abundance of caution.</margin> 
...regarding those charges of heresy; and concerning this first point, in which they felt strongest, it is seen whether it was condemned by them rightly or wrongly, especially now that I have explained to them the sense I intended and the words of the conclusion, without any abuse or distortion of terms or speech. And although this should suffice for the defense of my conclusion, yet for a fuller discussion of this matter, I say that even interpreting the conclusion in the way they themselves interpreted it—namely, that Christ was in hell <term>effectually</term><note>To be present "effectually" means to be present through one's power or influence rather than one's physical or spiritual substance.</note> only and not <term>presentially</term>—it might still seem to have been determined by them as "simply heretical" in a presumptuous manner. This is because **Durandus**, a greatest theologian of the **Order of Preachers** <note>The Dominicans</note> who perhaps exceeds these masters in learning no less than I am exceeded by them, held that opinion to be probable and well-defensible alongside the truth of the Article of Faith. For he writes as follows in the third book of the *Sentences*: <note>The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard was the standard textbook of medieval theology; Durandus’s commentary on it was widely studied.</note>

<margin>The words of Durandus</margin> 
Regarding the third point, it proceeds thus: and it seems that Christ, according to his soul, did not descend into hell, because the same finite thing cannot be in different places at the same time. But the soul of Christ, since it was a finite creature, was immediately after death in paradise with the soul of the thief, to whom it was said in Luke 23: *Today you shall be with me in paradise* <note>original: "Hodie mecum eris in paradiso"</note>; therefore, at least at that time, he could not be in hell. Likewise, those things which Christ did and suffered in his assumed human nature were ordained for human salvation. But it would not have benefited this salvation for Christ to descend to the underworld, because through the passion which he sustained in this world, he liberated us from all guilt and punishment; therefore, it seems that Christ did not descend to the underworld. To the contrary is what is said in the **Creed**: *He descended into hell.* And the Apostle says in Ephesians 4: *But that he ascended, what is it but because he also descended into the lower parts of the earth?* The <term>gloss</term><note>A standard marginal or interlinear commentary on the Bible.</note> says: "that is, to the underworld." I respond that since the Article of Faith states that Christ descended into hell, and this cannot be understood by reason of his divinity (according to which he is everywhere), nor by reason of his body (according to which he was in the tomb), it remains that it be understood by reason of the human nature of the soul. Regarding this, two things must be seen: first, by what mode the soul of Christ descended into hell; second, to which hell he descended.

<margin>How angels are moved to a place</margin> 
Regarding the first, it must be known that since a separated soul is not a body, nor a power within a body, it cannot be said that the soul of Christ descended to the underworld by that kind of motion or descent by which bodies are moved. It is not clearly evident if it is by that kind of motion by which angels are moved. For angels are said to move from place to place insofar as they operate successively in different places. A separated soul is not said to have any operation regarding a place or regarding a body existing in a place, because since by its nature it is determined to a specific body, it cannot move or act upon another thing except by means of its own body; but it lacks that while it is separated. Therefore, the soul cannot be moved from place to place by reason of an operation which it has regarding a place or a body existing in a place. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this, a separated soul can be said to have descended into hell in two ways. 

<margin>The descent of separated souls to hell is understood in two ways. A double assignment. Note the duality of effect.</margin> 
In one way, according to **assignment**; and thus the souls of the damned are said to descend into hell simply, because they are simply assigned so that, having resumed their bodies, they may be in hell, on account of which they are said to be there because they are simply assigned to it. However, the souls of the holy fathers <note>The righteous figures of the Old Testament.</note> are said to be in **Limbo**, or to have descended to Limbo, on account of an assignment that is not simple but conditional: namely, that they would remain there unless they were liberated by the Redeemer after resuming their bodies. But Christ’s soul is not said to have descended into hell in this way—namely, on account of assignment—because all such assignment is on account of guilt contracted or committed, which was not in Christ. In another way, a separated soul can be said to descend into hell according to **effect**; and in this way the soul of Christ can be said to descend into hell on account of the double effect which he had upon those who were in hell. One...

<summary>Pico defends his thesis by citing the prominent Dominican theologian Durandus, who argued that Christ's "descent into hell" should be understood as an exercise of power or effect rather than a literal movement of his soul's substance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical theological argument borrowed from Durandus of Saint-Pourçain. Having established that the "descent into hell" can be interpreted as an extension of Christ's power rather than a physical movement of his soul, Pico now explores the mechanics of how a spiritual substance acts and the definition of "paradise" and "hell" in this context.</meta>

<page-num>43</page-num>
<header>QUESTIONS</header>

## QUESTIONS

The effect was the presentation of the divine vision <note>The "beatific vision," or the direct sight of God, which is the source of eternal happiness.</note> which they lacked. Toward this, the Passion of Christ stood as a form of merit; and because all merit depends principally on the action of the soul, therefore this effect is attributed to the soul as the primary source of meriting. Likewise, by appropriation <note>A theological term for attributing a specific quality or action to one person of the Trinity or one part of Christ's nature that technically belongs to the whole.</note>, just as Christ was blessed in his soul, so through his soul he is credited with being the cause of blessedness in others. For it is fitting that a being in potentiality be brought to actuality by that which is already in actuality. 
<margin>Whence it is said that something is brought from potentiality to actuality through a mediating act.</margin>
Another effect, according to some, was one toward which the soul of Christ stood directly as an agent: namely, to enlighten the souls of the holy fathers <note>The righteous people, like Abraham or David, who died before Christ's sacrifice.</note> who were in Limbo, and concerning the mysteries that fall under revelation. For according to 
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian.</note> in the seventh book of *The Celestial Hierarchy*: Christ, according to his soul, has the task of teaching the angels; and by reason of this twofold effect, the soul of Christ can be said to have descended into hell. This is confirmed by a threefold reason. The first is because movement or
<margin>First reason</margin>
descent belongs to a <term>separated soul</term> <note>A soul that has been separated from the body after death.</note> not in the manner of the movement of bodies, but in the manner that movement belongs to a spiritual substance. However, for other spiritual substances—such as God or an angel—it is not fitting for them to move from place to place through a movement that exists within them as subjects, but rather through the effect they have on other things; therefore, it belongs in the same way to a separated soul, and belonged to the soul of Christ. 
<margin>Second [reason]</margin>
The second reason is this: Christ is said to have descended into hell to enlighten the souls of the holy fathers to see God. At the very instant Christ died, the holy fathers saw God. At that same instant, the soul of Christ could not have been in hell by means of movement; therefore, he did not descend there by a movement within himself, but by the effect he had on others. 
<margin>Third [reason]</margin>
Likewise, just as in those three days Christ's soul is said to have been in hell with the souls of the holy fathers, so in those three days (or part of them) he is said to have been in paradise with the soul of the thief, to whom it was said in Luke 23: *Today you shall be with me in paradise.* But this cannot be understood as a physical location reached by movement, since according to those who hold that a spirit is in a place <term>definitively</term> <note>Meaning its presence is limited to a specific boundary or "definition," unlike God's presence, which is everywhere.</note>, the same spirit cannot be in multiple places at once, nor move simultaneously in multiple directions toward multiple places. Therefore, it must be understood in terms of effect. For if anyone should say that "paradise" is used in two ways: in one way as a physical place, namely the
<margin>Paradise is spoken of in two ways</margin>
Empyrean heaven <note>The highest part of heaven, believed to be the dwelling place of God.</note>, and in this sense, Christ's soul was not in paradise until after the Ascension. In the other way, paradise is called the vision of the divine essence; and in this way, Christ's soul was in paradise from the moment of conception, and the thief's soul on the very day of the Passion. By this means, it is not contradictory for Christ's soul to have been simultaneously in paradise in that sense (meaning he saw God) and locally in hell. If this were said, I say it is not valid, because just as paradise is spoken of in two ways, so is
<margin>Hell is spoken of in two ways</margin>
hell. In one way, hell is called the place corresponding to the area beneath the earth. In the other way, it is the lack of the divine vision. Just as the soul of the thief is not said to have been with Christ's soul in paradise except because, by the merit of Christ's Passion, the thief's soul saw God, so too Christ's soul is not said to have been with the souls of the chosen fathers in hell except because their souls—which lacked the divine vision and thus were said to be in hell—were cleansed of this lack through the merit of this Passion. Therefore, both should be understood equally in terms of effect, not in terms of place or local movement occurring within the soul itself. And although this is said as a probability and seems sufficient to preserve the article of faith and the words of Scripture, nevertheless, because divine power is not fully grasped by human reason, therefore one should not stubbornly assert that Christ could not have descended into hell by some other way unknown to us. To the first argument, it must be said that the same finite thing cannot be in several places at once <term>definitively</term> or <term>circumscriptively</term> <note>Occupying a space such that its boundaries match the boundaries of the place.</note>, nor is it claimed in this way that Christ's soul was in paradise and hell at the same time. But regarding effect, nothing prohibits the same finite thing from being said to be in multiple places when the effects are present...

<sig>e iiii</sig>

<summary>Pico argues that Christ's descent into hell and presence in paradise should be understood "effectually"—through the power of his merit—rather than through physical movement. He explains that "heaven" and "hell" can refer to the presence or absence of the divine vision rather than just physical locations.</summary>

# APOLOGY

...at the same time they are subject to the power of the same agent; and thus the soul of Christ is said to have been in paradise and in hell simultaneously. This is because, by merit, the soul of the thief <note>The "Good Thief" crucified alongside Jesus, to whom Christ said, "Today you will be with me in Paradise."</note> saw God—which is what it means to be in paradise—and the souls of the holy fathers <note>The righteous people of the Old Testament.</note>, who lacked the divine vision and were for this reason said to be in hell, were liberated from this lack and consequently from hell. 

Indeed, according to one and the same effect—namely, the liberation of the fathers—the soul of Christ could be said to be simultaneously in paradise and in hell by considering the point of departure <note>original: *terminum a quo*</note> and the point of arrival <note>original: *ad quem*</note> of that effect. For by reason of the lack of divine vision, from which they were liberated through Christ’s passion, the soul of Christ could be said to have been in hell; but by reason of the divine vision to which they were admitted, it could be said to be in paradise. 

To the second point, it should be said that by the very fact that we were liberated from guilt and punishment through Christ’s passion, Christ is said to have descended into hell, because by the merit of his passion some have been rescued from the punishments of hell. For that descent is not considered according to **local motion** <term>physical movement from one place to another</term> existing in the soul, but according to the effect he had on those to be saved. These are the words of Durandus, verbatim.

Anyone who is never found to have retracted such an opinion—if that opinion is simply heretical and consequently against what has already been determined by the Church—it follows that Durandus died a heretic. 

<margin>Exclamation</margin>
O noble **Order of Preachers** <note>The Dominicans, the religious order to which Durandus and Thomas Aquinas belonged.</note> and greatest splendor of our religion! Can you suffer this: that your teacher—perhaps the first after Thomas [Aquinas], or undoubtedly among the first—whose books are held, read, and honored daily in your schools, your cloisters, and your libraries, is now pronounced a heretic? You must plead the cause of your teacher; I have pleaded mine. Nay, O Church, you must plead your own cause, you who have permitted for so many years, and now permit, Durandus to be read publicly. Either through ignorance you never recognized such an abominable heresy (according to these masters) or through negligence and contempt for divine matters you failed to condemn it once recognized. 

If they say there was no need for a new condemnation, since this opinion is among those already condemned: First, it follows from this (as I said above) that Durandus died a heretic. Second, it follows that Capreolus and Durandellus and many other doctors who recite Durandus's opinion and yet do not accuse it of heresy were ignorant and unrefined in the faith, not knowing how to distinguish a heretic from a non-heretic. Third, let these fathers tell me where they have read a condemnation of this opinion. As for myself, I confess I do not remember ever reading it. They certainly cannot bring forward any determination of the Councils against Durandus. Not only was this opinion never condemned in Councils, but there isn't even a mention of it in any of them. Likewise, I do not know how they will be able to allege passages of Holy Scripture against him, 

<margin>Francisco</margin>
unless Scotus <note>Duns Scotus, a major scholastic philosopher.</note> is lying, who says (on the testimony of Francisco <note>Likely Francesco di Meyronnes, a student of Scotus.</note>) that regarding the descent of Christ itself—let alone the *manner* of the descent—there is no express mention in the Gospel teaching and in the things set forth by us at the beginning. 

This is clear from the way Durandus would perhaps use to explain authorities of Scripture that might seem to be against him. Concerning the authorities of the Saints <note>The "Church Fathers" such as Augustine or Jerome.</note>, they could perhaps bring forward many who say Christ's soul was in hell for three days just as his body was in the tomb, and similar things. And whatever comes from Durandus’s imagination—namely, the way he would explain the aforementioned authorities, perhaps by saying this is said of the soul and not of the **whole composite** <note>The human being as a union of body and soul.</note> because he operated those things principally through the soul—whatever he might say (and I do not hold his opinion, nor have I ever held it), I say this and firmly assert that this consequence is not valid: "This opinion is against the sayings of Augustine or Jerome or Gregory, and so on for the other doctors of the Church; therefore it is heretical." 

<margin>Note that Durandus's opinion is against Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory</margin>
And the truth of this statement, as it is believed by all good and subtle theologians, so it will be clearly proven by me. For although the writings of the holy doctors placed outside the biblical canon are to be handed down and read and received with due reverence, nevertheless their sayings are not of such firm authority and immutability that it is not permitted to contradict them or to doubt them, unless [they are confirmed] by...

<center>e iiii</center>

...unless it is clearly and expressly proven otherwise through Holy Scripture, or firmly determined by the authority of the Church itself that those writings contain firm and indubitable truth. Therefore, a heretical opinion cannot be precisely and manifesty convicted solely through the sayings of the Saints <note>In this context, "Saints" refers to the "Doctors of the Church," the authoritative early Christian theologians like Augustine or Jerome.</note> outside the canon of the Bible. For where there is no infallible truth, there is neither certain nor indubitable faith. Since

<margin>Reason</margin>

certain faith relies upon infallible truth; indeed, regarding such matters, there is neither infallible assent nor firm adherence. From this, it follows that because there is no certain truth and indubitable faith there, one does not always assent to it

<margin>Augustine</margin>

without doubt and fear of falsehood. As **Augustine** says in his *Letter to Jerome* and in Book 11, Chapter 8 of *Against Faustus*, and again in Book 16 of the same work: if Scripture does not contain infallible truth and is found to be false in any part of itself, there does not remain in it a certain faith by which one might firmly believe it; because of a falsehood discovered in one part, the whole is held suspect, and thus faith would stumble. For as Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*, Chapter 7: faith stumbles if the authority of the Holy Scriptures wavers. However, regarding the fact that there is no infallible truth in the sayings of the Saints outside the 

<margin>First proof that there is no infallible truth in the sayings of the Saints outside the canon of the Bible</margin>

canon of the Bible, three proofs occur to me for the present purpose. The first is that these very Doctors doubt their own sayings—whether they have erred in them or not. Whence Augustine says in the first book of *On the Trinity*, Chapter 1: "I will not be slow to search if I hesitate anywhere, nor will I be ashamed to correct myself if I err anywhere." And in Chapter 2: "Therefore, let anyone who reads this where he equally hesitates, seek with me; where he recognizes his error, let him return to me; where he recognizes mine, let him call me back." Hence also Augustine’s book of **Retractions** <term>original: *retractationum*; a late-life work where Augustine reviewed his earlier writings and corrected his own errors</term>, in which he condemns and retracts many things from his previous sayings. Whence also in the second book of *On the Trinity*: "I would rather be rebuked by anyone than be praised by someone who is either erring or flattering. For the erring praiser confirms the error, while the flatterer entices one into error. But the righteous man will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; the oil of the sinner shall not anoint my head." And as **Guido the Carmelite** <note>Guido Terreni (c. 1270–1342), a philosopher and theologian known for his work on heresy.</note> says in 

<margin>Guido the Carmelite</margin>

his *Book on Heresies*: although Augustine speaks humbly in these sayings, he nevertheless speaks truthfully. Whence Augustine himself says to Vincent: "I cannot, nor ought I, deny that just as in the works of the elders, so too in my own many small works there are many things which can be rebuked with righteous judgment and without rashness." And in the book *On True Religion*, he says: "Whatever error is found in my books is to be attributed to me alone; but whatever is true or well-explained, let that be attributed to the one rewarder and giver of all, God." Therefore, the sayings of the eminent and divine doctor Augustine may not always contain indubitable truth in all things, since he himself doubts whether he has erred or not; and what has been said of Augustine should be understood similarly for other Doctors. The second proof is taken from the discord

<margin>Second</margin>

that exists among the authors themselves. For discord among writers is a testimony of falsehood, since it is necessary that at least one of the disagreeing parties says what is false, because necessarily one side of a contradiction is false. Therefore, Augustine, in Book 16 of *The City of God*, proves the truth of Holy Scripture from the mutual harmony of its writers, in which all agree and none disagrees with another—which testifies to the indubitable and infallible truth of the Holy Scriptures. For to the true and to the truth, as **the Philosopher** <note>Pico is referring to Aristotle.</note> says in the first book of the *Ethics*, 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

all things are in harmony—which does not happen in other writings. For how great the discord is in the sayings of the Saints outside the canonical scriptures, no one remains ignorant of, unless he has not read their books. Augustine disagrees with the other holy Doctors regarding the understanding of the **works of the six days** <note>The creation story in Genesis.</note>. For others posit that God made those works of the six days according to a succession of time; Augustine disagrees with them, positing that all things were made at once, according to that text: "He who lives forever created all things at once." Whence Augustine was moved to number those six days not according to a succession of times, but according to the distinction of angelic knowledge of things in their own kind and in the Word <note>Augustine's theory of "simultaneous creation" suggests the "days" were spiritual stages of knowledge rather than 24-hour periods.</note>; and yet, neither these nor those are called heretics, though it is certain that one opinion...

Similarly, **Jerome** and **Augustine** disagree because **Augustine** considers **David** the author of all the Psalms, which **Jerome** denies. They similarly disagree regarding **Paul’s** rebuke of **Peter**, specifically whether it concerned a mortal or a venial sin on **Peter’s** part. This refers to the debate over when the requirements of Jewish Law, like circumcision or dietary restrictions, officially became "deadly" for Christians to practice.</note>; thus, by contradicting each other, one necessarily speaks a falsehood, and yet neither of them is considered a heretic because of this.

<margin>**Jerome** agrees with **Bede** on this question</margin>

Furthermore, **Jerome**, in the first book of *Against Jovinian*, says it must be recognized that **Samuel** was a Levite, not a priest nor a high priest; therefore, he is not named among the priests, but among those who call upon the name of the Lord. <margin>Aristotle</margin>

Here, **Augustine** clearly says the priesthood was transferred to **Samuel**, so that **Samuel** was as truly a priest as **David** was truly a king. Regarding this same **Samuel**, as to whether he was truly 

resuscitated, **Augustine** seems to disagree with himself. However, in his book *On the Care to be Had for the Dead*, he posits that the soul of **Samuel** was truly summoned by a demon through magical arts and spoke to **Saul**. **Jerome** also, on the question of whether "Sale" <note>likely a reference to Salem/Jerusalem</note> was Jerusalem, seems to contradict himself in one of his letters, the title of which I do not recall. He also holds a contrary opinion to 

<margin>Discord between **Gregory** and **Dionysius the Areopagite**</margin>
**Augustine** regarding the seventy translators <note>The "Seventy" refers to the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. Likewise, **Gregory** and **Dionysius** disagree regarding the orders of angels; and **Jerome** alone stands against the others regarding the promotion of a twice-married man <note>original: "bigami." In early church law, a man who had married a second time, even after the death of a first wife, was often barred from the priesthood.</note>. For he himself holds and writes in his *Letter to Oceanus* that a twice-married man may be promoted to the priesthood if the marriages occurred before and after baptism, provided he has not known multiple wives after his baptism. The others contradict him, saying that a twice-married man cannot be promoted whether before or after baptism; and in this, the others are considered to have spoken better, as **Augustine** writes in *On the Good of Marriage* and **Ambrose** in *On Duties*. Furthermore, **Jerome**, writing to **Marcella** on five questions, says that the saints who are found at the end of the world will not die but will be taken up alive; **Augustine**, however, in the book *The City of God*, affirms that everyone then will die. Likewise, **Jerome**, in his commentary on **Matthew**, says that the statement of the Psalm, *Their sound has gone out into all the earth*, etc., and that saying of **Christ**, *This gospel shall be preached in the whole world*, was fulfilled by the Apostles. **Augustine**, however, in his *Letter to Exitius*—with whom **Origen** agrees in his commentary on **Matthew**—holds that this has not yet been fulfilled. Likewise, **Jerome**, on the *Epistle to Titus*, holds that the angels existed and served God for many ages before the visible world; **Ambrose** also holds this in the *Hexameron* <note>A treatise on the six days of creation.</note>. **Augustine**, however, in his literal commentary on *Genesis*, holds that they were created at the same time as the empyrean heaven. Likewise, **Jerome**, in the prologue to the *Book of Wisdom*, holds that the book is by **Philo** and is not to be counted among the Holy Scriptures. **Augustine**, however, in the third book of his *Retractions*, shows that he once held it was published by **Jesus son of Sirach**, which he retracts there; and although he does not express who published it, nonetheless in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, he numbers it among the sacred books. Likewise, **Jerome**, in his book of *Hebrew Questions*, says that before God made heaven and earth, he had previously established Paradise, because of the text which says *God had planted a paradise from the beginning* <note>original: "a principio."</note>. **Augustine**, however, in his literal commentary on *Genesis*, explains it differently.

But as for the writings of others, I read them in such a way that, no matter how much they excel in holiness and learning, I do not therefore think a thing is true because they thought so, but because they were able to persuade me—either through other passages of Holy Scripture or by probable, i.e., evident reason—that it does not abhor the truth. <meta>This page continues the author's argument that the writings of the Church Fathers and later Doctors are not beyond criticism, unlike the Holy Scriptures. The previous page listed specific contradictions between Jerome, Augustine, and Bede to show that even the most "holy doctors" can err or disagree. This page extends that logic to scholastic theologians like Robert Holcot, William of Ockham, and Duns Scotus.</meta>

<header>DEFENSE</header>

# DEFENSE

Neither should we hold the writings of any men, however Catholic and praised they may be, as we do the canonical scriptures. We are not forbidden—out of the respect due to those men—to reject or disapprove of something in their writings if we find they have sensed something other than the truth. And in the book *On One Baptism*, it is said that we know the holy canonical Scripture of the Old and New Testaments is contained within its own fixed limits, and it is placed so far above all later letters of bishops (so that it is impossible to doubt whether whatever is established as written in it is true or right). However, the letters of bishops which were written after the canon was confirmed, or are being written now, may be corrected—if perhaps there is something in them that deviates from the truth—either by the speech of someone wiser, or by the weightier authority and more learned prudence of other bishops, or by councils. <note>The author is quoting or paraphrasing St. Augustine's famous distinction between the absolute authority of the Bible and the fallible authority of later Church leaders.</note> Infinite examples of this kind could be brought forward. From these it would be clear that the sayings of the saints do not rest upon infallible truth precisely because they are the sayings of saints. This is why you will often find modern doctors departing from the sayings of the holy fathers.

<margin>Robert Holcot</margin>
For **Robert Holcot** <note>An English Dominican theologian (c. 1290–1349) known for his work on wisdom and logic.</note> says that the holy man **Anselm** was deceived in many things because of his ignorance of logic.

<margin>Ockham</margin>
And **Ockham** <note>William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347), a pioneer of nominalism.</note> does not agree with **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential 5th-century mystical theologian.</note> regarding hierarchical acts.

<margin>Scotus</margin>
And **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), the "Subtle Doctor."</note> in his commentary on the third book of the *Sentences* almost destroys the entire line of reasoning used by **Anselm** in his book *Why God Became Man* <note>original: "Cur deus homo"</note>. And you will frequently find the same in other doctors. I wanted these examples brought forward here not so much for the sake of the opinion of **Durandus**—which I neither hold nor have ever held—but because of what will be treated shortly at the beginning of the second question.

<margin>He concludes that **Durandus** erred</margin>
From all these things, I conclude that if an express determination of either Holy Scripture or the universal Church is not found against the opinion of **Durandus**, it is presumptuous to call it simply "heretical." If, however, such a determination is found, **Durandus** must patiently endure this mark of error.

<margin>Objection</margin>
But someone might say: "Granted that the meaning you declared you intended by that proposition is Catholic; and granted that the force of the words allows it; can your proposition not also produce that sense of **Durandus** which you yourself detest? And therefore you erred by putting forward a conclusion that could cause scandal in the minds of the faithful."

<margin>First Response</margin>
To this I say first: there is one logic for things put forward for debate <note>original: "disputanda"</note>, and another for things handed down in writing to be read as doctrine. For when something is proposed for debate, the proposition is brief, concise, and unexplained; in itself, it involves multiple difficulties of words and meanings that are meant to be untangled in the heat of the debate itself. Otherwise, if everything were explained there, no room would be left for the dispute. Therefore, one who puts forward an ambiguous, obscure, or equivocal proposition for debate is excused, because it will be distinguished and clarified during the discussion. However, those who commit something to writing for teaching do through writing what is done here through debating. Therefore, in that case, everything ought to be clear, lucid, and settled.

<margin>Second [Response]</margin>
Second, let these most fickle censors consider that it is not only difficult but almost impossible to so weigh and examine the words of every proposition one puts forward that no ambiguity can exist in the meaning and no erroneous opinion can be drawn from it. Indeed, I do not wish to claim for my propositions what many Evangelical and Apostolic

<margin>Note where the heresies of heretics sprout from</margin>
propositions do not have. For among those, one may find many that have multiple interpretations and can be transferred to an erroneous sense—indeed, some which at first glance seem to sound like heresy. This is where all heresies have sprouted: namely, when some people did not look into the depth of the meaning so much as they grasped at what the "bark" or surface of the Gospel words sounded like. From this, **Arius**, hearing "The Father is greater than I," <note>John 14:28</note> believed the Father was greater than the Son and said the Son was a creature. From this, **Helvidius**, hearing that **Joseph** did not "know" **Mary** *until* she brought forth her firstborn, <note>Matthew 1:25</note> attended more to the grammatical force of that word "until" and doubted the truth of the Gospel sense regarding the perpetual virginity of **Mary**. From this, **Marcion**, reading **Paul's** statement "The law entered that sin might abound," <note>Romans 5:20</note> believed the Law of Moses was evil and from an evil principle, following **Mani**. And **Basilides**, reading "I once lived without the law..." <note>Romans 7:9. original: "ego aliquando sine lege uiuebam"</note>

<summary>The author argues that because even revered Church Doctors like Anselm and Dionysius can be criticized or corrected, the theologian Durandus should not be labeled a heretic unless his views explicitly contradict Scripture or Church decree. He further defends his own use of complex language by noting that even the Bible can be misinterpreted by heretics who look only at the literal "bark" of the words rather than their deep meaning.</summary>

<header>QUESTIONS</header>

### QUESTIONS

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, discussing the transmigration of souls.</note> ...believed that the soul of Paul lived at some point in another body. From this, **Eunomius** <note>A 4th-century bishop and advocate of extreme Arianism, which argued Christ was not of the same substance as God the Father.</note> hearing Christ answering the Jews—who were accusing him because he called himself the Son of God—where it is written: *I said, you are gods and all of you are sons of the Most High* <note>original: "ego dixi dii estis & filii excelsi omnes"</note>, attended to what was said rather than the intention and purpose of the one responding. He believed that Christ is called the Son of God in the same way that any holy person is called a son of God. Similarly, the proposition that *the Son does not know that day* <note>A reference to Mark 13:32 regarding the end of the world.</note> has been an occasion for many to believe the Father understands more than the Son; for if we interpret it according to the common sense that the words produce, it seems to suggest that, even if the truth of a hidden meaning is different. I could bring forward infinite similar propositions from the canon of the scriptures. 

<margin>Hilary</margin>
Therefore, **Hilary** <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a leading Latin theologian.</note> rightly said: "The understanding of things said must be assumed from the causes of the saying, because the matter is not subject to the speech, but the speech to the matter." 

<margin>Gloss</margin>
And the **Gloss** <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries.</note> upon this text says: "We ought not always to understand words as they seem to sound at first glance, especially where they are ambiguous, but we ought to return to the intention of the speaker." 

<margin>Gregory</margin>
And **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> says: "Frequently, while the literal property of words is attended to, the sense of the truth is lost." And Gregory, in the twenty-sixth book of the *Morals*, says: "One should not consider the words, but the will and the intention; because the intention should not serve the words, but the words the intention." 

<margin>Jerome</margin>
And **Jerome**, in his commentary on the *Epistle to the Galatians*, testifies: "The Gospel is not in the words of the scriptures, but in the meaning; not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of the speeches, but in the root of the reason." 

<margin>Ockham</margin>
Because of this, **Ockham** <note>William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347), a pioneer of nominalist philosophy.</note> in his *Dialogue* falsifies this common proposition: "Words are to be accepted not from the opinions of individuals, but especially from common usage," specifically in the second part. For he says that in ambiguous and multifaceted words, one should not return to the common understanding, but rather to the intention of the speaker. And thus, when there is ambiguity in the doctrine of anyone speaking or writing, one must similarly return to the speaker's intention so that he may explain himself and express the true meaning which the force of the words allows. Nor is he to be rejected unless it can be proved that such a true meaning is contrary to his other sayings or is impertinent to his purpose. 

And so also in simple speech, the same <term>Doctor</term> <note>A title for a recognized authority in theology or law.</note> says one must return to the intention of the speaker, and one must stand by his interpretation unless it is certain or probably/strongly presumed that he used such an ambiguous way of speaking to deceive or for some other evil end. 

<margin>Epilogue</margin>
From all of this, I conclude that I have not erred. During the dispute, I put forward a multifaceted proposition to be declared with a <term>protestation</term> <note>A formal legal or theological declaration of intent meant to clarify one's orthodoxy.</note> of probability. This proposition cannot produce any sense that some Doctor (who has not been rejected or declared as such by the Church) has not held. Rather, those have erred who judged a proposition to be simply heretical when it has a Catholic meaning allowed by the force of the words—especially since it had already been declared by the proposer in that Catholic sense. 

Even if they had made this judgment before my sense was declared, they might perhaps have erred more excusably; however, because they are truly learned, they were able to recognize by themselves that the proposition had a double meaning. Seeing this, they ought not only to have refrained from simply condemning it, but rather should have interpreted it in a good sense. 

<margin>Augustine, Book 2, Chapter 18</margin>
For **Augustine**, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, explaining that passage of Matthew, "Judge not and you shall not be judged," says: "In this place, I think nothing else is commanded but that we should interpret in the better part those deeds which are doubtful as to the spirit in which they are done." For regarding neutral deeds, which can be done with a good or evil mind, it is rash to judge, especially to condemn. 

Therefore, let us understand that what Augustine says about things that are *done* applies equally to things that are *said*. Thus, applying Augustine’s sentence more speculatively, let us conclude: in those sayings which can have a good and an evil meaning, it is rash to judge, and especially rash to condemn.

He cites major authorities like Hilary, Gregory, Jerome, Ockham, and Augustine to argue that ambiguous statements should be interpreted favorably rather than condemned.</summary>

# SECOND QUESTION ON THE PUNISHMENT FOR MORTAL SIN.

The second conclusion which these men <note>The author's critics or inquisitors.</note> have condemned is this: **for a mortal sin of finite duration, an infinite punishment in terms of time is not owed, but only a finite one.**

And because, when I set forth this conclusion in my little book, these words were prefixed: "Unless there were sayings of the Saints <note>original: "sanctorum"; here referring to the Church Fathers and established authorities.</note> which in the plain sense of their speech seem to say the opposite, I would firmly assert the following conclusions. I assert, however, that they are probable and can be reasonably defended." The first of these is: **Mortal sin is in itself a finite evil.** The second is this: **For a mortal sin of finite time, etc.** <note>Referencing the main conclusion mentioned above.</note> A certain Master, holding a disputation with me regarding this conclusion, said: "What else is your conclusion but the first evidence that you are a heretic? Since you yourself clearly say it is against the sayings of the Saints. For the logic holds: it is against the sayings of the Saints, therefore it is heretical."

I showed him then, as I will show below, how my conclusion was in no way repugnant to the opinions of the Saints, and how the words were to be understood. But even if it were the case that the conclusion was against the sayings of the Saints, how much his logic was worth—and how unworthy it was of a doctor of theology, as he boasts himself to be—can be clear to anyone from what was said above regarding the first conclusion. I know what I would say here about this Master. He is the one who so many times sent letters to our homeland about me, as if promising a trophy and a triumph. But I wish, as I promised from the beginning, to plead my case with reasons, not with insults.

I come to the conclusion. And because these Masters judged the conclusion itself, and the responses I gave them when they questioned me on it, to be false, erroneous, and heretical, I wish first to declare the conclusion itself to be Catholic <note>meaning "universal" or "orthdox" in the theological sense.</note> and in harmony with the sayings of almost all doctors. I call it "my" conclusion, however, because if you take it in a sense other than the one I intend by it, it is no longer my conclusion which I proposed. For a proposition is manifold; there are many propositions. Next, I wish to declare that these responses of mine are such, both regarding the conclusion itself and the responses, by always clarifying my meanings—that is, those I intend through them—as far as the force of the words permits. For the declaration of the conclusion, five things are to be noted.

<margin>
The first thing to be noted in sin: namely, "turning toward" and "turning away."
</margin>
**First**, it must be noted that in sin two things can be considered: the *turning toward* a created good and the *turning away* from the unchangeable and uncreated good <note>God</note>. In the first way, sin is a finite evil according to all the doctors. In the second way, sin is an infinite evil according to the common path; and because the turning toward a created good (which the sinner abuses by sinning) is of the intrinsic <term>nature</term> <note>original: "ratione"</note> of the sin itself, it is therefore said that sin is intrinsically a finite evil. However, the turning away from the uncreated good makes it extrinsically infinite; for it is only called an infinite evil insofar as it is a turning away from an infinite good, and therefore it only remains that it is an extrinsically and objectively infinite evil.

<margin>
The second thing to be noted regarding "time."
</margin>
**Second**, note that by "time" we can understand only the "time of the way" <note>The theological term for human life on earth (the "way" to the afterlife).</note>; and in this way it is certain that neither sin nor anything else pertaining to man can be infinite according to time, since the "time of the way" for any traveler <note>meaning any living person.</note> is not only finite in duration but also brief. In another way, we can understand by "time": the time of the "way" and of the "end" <note>Eternity or the final state.</note>; and it is in this way that it is taken in the conclusion. And thus something in a person can endure for an infinite time, as is evident.

<margin>
The third thing: "sin" can be taken in two ways.
</margin>
**Third**, note that <term>mortal sin</term> can be taken in two ways. In one way, for the prohibited act or the omission of an act commanded by God. In another way, for the <term>guilt</term> <note>original: "reatus"; the state of being liable for punishment.</note> left behind from the aforementioned prohibited act or said omission of an act. This guilt is indeed called "sin" in many places of Holy Scripture; and by such a "sin" someone is denominated a "sinner" even when the act of sin (taken in the first way) has ceased or passed away. From this third point to be noted, it is clear that it is reasonable to say that although in one who is damned for mortal sin, the sin for which he is damned might at some point end—insofar as the intrinsic entity of the act itself, which is called sin in the first way—it does not end, however, in terms of the guilt; indeed, if it ended in that way, eternal punishment would not be owed to him. And...

...finite. And thus, a sin to which an infinite punishment is **owed** is infinite in terms of time as far as **guilt** <note>original: "reatum"; in medieval theology, this refers to the legal liability or "debt" of punishment one carries after committing a sin.</note> is concerned.

<margin>Fourthly, "to be owed" is understood in two ways</margin>
Fourthly, it must be noted that "to be owed" is understood in two ways; or, it can be understood in two ways that a certain punishment is "owed" to any given sin. In **one way**, that is said to be owed to someone which will **actually be rendered** to them at some point. In this sense, it is said reasonably and according to Catholic teaching that for a sin of finite time—as far as its intrinsic nature and guilt are concerned—an infinite punishment in terms of time is **not** owed. And it is in this way that the present conclusion is understood: that for a sin of finite time, etc. <note>The author is arguing that if a person repents, they are no longer "owed" eternal punishment because they will not actually receive it.</note> For every sin to which [punishment] is owed in this way—that is, for which an infinite punishment will eventually be rendered—is "infinite" in the sense already described. Nor is anyone ever damned unless the sin for which they are damned is infinite in that way regarding its duration.

However, the conclusion also has **another** Catholic sense, namely: that eternal punishment is never "owed" in such a way that it is actually rendered to someone unless that person is **finally impenitent** and ceases to repent without end for that sin which they omitted or committed in life. Thus, for a temporal sin, an infinite punishment is "owed" in the aforementioned way only if the sinner does not return to justice. For just as repentance ends a sin as far as God's rejection is concerned—according to the saying: *in whatever hour the sinner shall groan* <note>original: "quacuq́ hora ingemuerit peccator"; a common paraphrasing of Ezekiel 18:21-22, suggesting that God forgives the moment a sinner truly repents.</note>, etc.—so impenitence regarding a sin perpetuates that sin in its guilt and rejection toward an infinite punishment. Thus, an infinite punishment is never owed to anyone in that first sense unless they possess a sin that is infinite in terms of time.

<margin>Note on vengeance</margin>
For the **vengeance** which God seeks from a sinner is that the sinner should return voluntarily to the duty of obedience, grieving for his contempt. Otherwise, he will be tormented as long as he chooses to remain in that state.

In **another way**, something can be understood as being "owed" to someone because they are **deserving** of it (whether by merit or demerit), and it is that which *would* be rendered to them if they were to die in that state. In this sense, an infinite punishment **is** owed for a mortal sin of finite duration, because whoever sins mortally in the span of a single hour is **deserving** of infinite punishment. And that punishment will indeed be rendered to him if he finally dies in that state, even assuming he has no other sin that is infinite in terms of time. This distinction regarding the word "owed" is in frequent use among theologians. Hence, according to this distinction, the **doctors** <note>The "Doctors of the Church," or established theological authorities.</note> say that for one who is **foreknown** <note>original: "præscito"; someone God knows will ultimately be damned.</note>, eternal life is not "owed" for a meritorious act performed while they were in a state of grace—taking "owed" in the first sense—because it will never actually be rendered to them. Similarly, it is said that for one who is **predestined** <note>original: "prædestinato"; someone chosen by God for salvation.</note>, while they are in a state of mortal sin, eternal punishment is not "owed," because it will never be rendered to them, since that sin will be brought to an end, and they will not die in it but in a state of grace.

<margin>Epilogue</margin>
From the foregoing, it is clear that my conclusion itself has a Catholic sense and follows the customary way of speaking used by Catholic doctors. It should not have been condemned as heretical, false, and erroneous, since its opposite is rather the thing that is false and erroneous.

<margin>Note</margin>
Furthermore, it was the height of ignorance to believe that by the aforementioned conclusion I intended to **deny** the eternal punishment of the damned. On the contrary, my conclusion provides an examination of the **cause** for which the damned are punished eternally. This cause, I have stated, is the **perpetuation of guilt** in the soul of the sinner through his final impenitence and the perpetual failure to groan for his sin. This opinion not only appears not to be heretical, but is so Catholic that no one, if he be a Catholic and trained in the **Sacred Letters** <note>The Bible and official scripture.</note>, could rightly and reasonably deny it. That the proposition, by the very force of its terms, carries this meaning is clear.

<margin>He declares that the conclusion is not heretical based on the force of its terms</margin>
For the proposition says: *For a mortal sin of finite time, an infinite punishment in terms of time is not owed.* In this proposition, I take "owed" to mean that which will eventually be paid out—which has already been shown above to be a most common usage among the doctors. And I take "sin" to mean the offense and the guilt; this usage is not only not improper or abusive, but is frequent in the Sacred Letters.

<margin>The Master of the Sentences</margin>
For after the **Master of the Sentences** <note>original: "magr̃ sententiar̃"; referring to Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose book was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> inquires in the second book whether, once the act of sinning has passed, the sin remains in the one who sinned until he repents, he responds thus: "It must not be ignored that sins exist in someone in two ways and pass away in two ways: namely, in **act** and in **guilt**."

<margin>Durandus</margin>
**Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a famous philosopher and theologian.</note> also says in the same place that the "ending" of a sin is understood in two ways. In one way, by the cessation of the act alone. In another way, by the forgiveness of the sin. That guilt is also sometimes called...

-># DEFENSE<-

<margin>Thomas</margin> Thomas expressly calls [liability] "sin," saying in that same place: "The <term>liability</term> <note>original: "reatus"; the legal or moral obligation to undergo punishment for an act.</note> mediating between fault and punishment takes the name of both extremes." But is not "sin" also understood as liability in that passage: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the deceased, that they may be loosed from their sins"? <note>original: "Sancta ergo & salubris est cogitatio pro defunctis exorare ut a peccatis solvantur"; a reference to 2 Maccabees 12:46.</note> For those deceased for whom we must pray to be loosed from sins are not in "sin" if we take "sin" to mean <term>mortal fault</term>; <note>If they were in a state of unrepented mortal sin, they would be in Hell, where prayer cannot help them.</note> nor are they loosed from such sin after death, but only from "sin" understood as the punishment or the liability for punishment. In this same way, "sin" is also understood in the passage: "Redeem your sins with almsgiving"; <note>original: "peccata tua elemosynis redime"; from Daniel 4:24.</note> and likewise in many other passages of Scripture. If, therefore, both the sense of my proposition is Catholic and the use of the terms in the proposition is Catholic and most highly proven: <margin>Responses which the author had given: First, Second, Third</margin> why was there any reason for them to condemn this conclusion of mine as heretical?

Now I come to my responses. First, I said that if someone persists only for a finite time in mortal sin, he will not be punished except for a finite time; a statement which is verified in three ways. **First**, when we take "mortal sin" for the liability and not for the act of commission or omission, as was said in the declaration of the conclusion. **Second**, it must be noted that the term "mortal sin," according to logical rigor, is taken generally rather than specifically. <note>The author is using a technical logical distinction (confused vs. determinate) to argue that "mortal sin" can refer to the general state of the sinner rather than a single specific act.</note> **Third**, because it is true that if the one who sinned persisted only for a finite time in a specific sin—for instance, in the omission of repenting for his sin—so that at some point he did repent of it, he would not be punished for it except for a finite time. 

That I intended these Catholic senses and nothing discordant with the faith is clear from what I subjoined in the response when I said it stands with the truth of the conclusion that anyone dying in mortal sin will be punished forever. When it was further asked of me whether someone who sins only for a finite time with one mortal sin and dies unrepentant is punished forever, <margin>Question, Response</margin> I responded: "Yes." But I said that such a person is not punished for that act alone—which was a true response to the question asked. For although it is true that if he had sinned only by that act he would be punished eternally, yet because the question posits that he dies unrepentant, he would also be punished for that very impenitence. Indeed, he would be punished for the infinite omissions of repenting and for the infinite other evil acts, total or partial, in which the damned person persists. For just as the damned person continually wills evil, so he continually sins and demerits—not that there would be different essential punishments, <margin>Note</margin> at least not those which are not the fault itself, but rather the same punishment is multiplied. Thus he will be punished for those evil acts in which he continues. 

Because, however, this seems to be against the common way of speaking used by the Saints <note>The "Saints" here refers to the established Church Fathers and authoritative theologians.</note>—though not against the substance of what they said and their intended sense—I stated both in writing and in speech that I do not assert this opinion (that is, this specific way of speaking) out of reverence for the Saints; but I said it could be defended as probable. Finally, beyond what was said above, I added: that anyone dying in mortal sin is punished forever because of the liability of that sin. This is because by the fact that he dies in that state of liability, he is placed in a state that necessitates sinning forever—at least with the sin of the perpetual omission of repenting and of disposing himself toward grace. 

But these Masters said that my aforementioned responses were not satisfactory for their arguments and inquiries. On the contrary, they said I added error upon error through such a response; for which reason they declared both the responses and the clarifications to be false, erroneous, and heretical. But who cannot see that they themselves are adding error upon error in this most reprehensible condemnation of theirs—unless it be someone who hates Catholic truths along with them, or does not understand them?

Nevertheless, if a mortal sin is finite according to time—not only regarding its intrinsic positive entity as an act prohibited by God (or the privative omission of an act commanded by God), but also regarding its imputation, its rejection, and also the liability and the stain, which in many places of Scripture and in...

For if the said <term>imputation</term> <note>The legal or moral assignment of guilt to a person.</note> or <term>stain</term> <note>original: "macula"; the spiritual blemish left on the soul by sin.</note> did not remain, a debt would never be owed for the sin, and at some point the eternal punishment would be fully paid. And so it is clear that the infinity of the duration of this sin in the one who is damned—I mean infinity regarding the liability of imputation or the stain, and the impenitence or omission of repenting—is the cause why eternal punishment will be owed and will one day be paid. # THIRD QUESTION: ON THE ADORATION OF THE CROSS AND IMAGES.

<margin>Disagreement among authors</margin>
**T**he third conclusion which they condemned was this:
Neither the cross of Christ nor any image is to be adored with the adoration of <term>latria</term>, <note>original: "latria"; the highest form of worship, which Catholic theology teaches is reserved for God alone, as opposed to "dulia," which is honor given to saints.</note> even in the manner that Thomas [Aquinas] posits.
This conclusion, though condemned by them, I believe to be not only Catholic but even truer than its opposite, which is this:
The cross of Christ and images are to be adored with latria in the manner that Thomas posits. For the opinion of Thomas in this matter seems to me less reasonable than the opinion of Durandus, Henry of Ghent, John of Guarra, Robert Holcot, Peter of Aquila, and many others whom I follow in this conclusion. To make this manifest, I will first set down the opinion of Thomas, which I do not hold. Then, I will set down the opinion of the doctors whom I follow. From this, it will be clear that the determination of those masters regarding my conclusion is neither right nor just, and that it assumes the exact opposite of what I intend in the conclusion. Thomas says, therefore, that just as <margin>Thomas</margin> the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>original: "ph'us" (philosophus); referring to Aristotle.</note> says in the book *On Memory and Reminiscence*, there is a twofold movement of the soul toward an image: one toward the image itself as it is a certain thing, and another way toward the image insofar as it is the image of another. Between these two movements there is a difference, because the first movement, by which one turns toward the image as it is a certain thing, is distinct from the movement which is toward the reality of which that is an image. The second movement, however, which is toward the image insofar as it is an image, is one and the same as that which is toward the reality. And therefore he concludes that although adoration is not owed to the image of Christ as it is a certain thing in itself, nevertheless, as it is an image, the same reverence is owed to it as is owed to Christ himself, which is the adoration of <term>latria</term>. This is the method of Thomas, which to other doctors rightly seems strange and dangerous. For the image itself, even as an image, is distinct from the thing imaged; for as such, it refers to the thing imaged as to something distinct from itself. Wherefore, if even as such it terminates the adoration of latria, it seems to follow that something other than God will be adored with latria, which is absurd. Nor can it be said, as Capreolus says <margin>Against the response of Capreolus</margin> wishing to save the statement of Thomas, that the image itself is not adored separately, but that the image and the thing imaged are one total object of adoration. Because either one part of this total object is the image itself (which is a created, relative being) or it is not. If not...
