-># DEFENSE<-

Therefore, it should not be said that from those two <note>Referring to the image and the person depicted.</note> one total object is made, because from such a statement it follows that each of them would be a partial object, even if one of them were more principal. If this follows, it means that some created thing of the genus of relation would, at least partially, be the end point of the <term>adoration of latria</term>, <note>original: "adorationem latriæ"; the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone.</note> which certainly seems poorly Catholic. This is even more true because not only can this not be said of a created thing, but even the persons in the divine nature, by reason of their relative properties, <margin>Against the foundation of the opinion.</margin> are not the formal end point of adoration. However, the foundation of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> seems to have little effect. For when the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says that the movement of the soul toward the image and the thing imaged is the same, he does not mean it in such a way that the soul declares the image, insofar as it is an image, to be the same as the original model—and thus that whatever is owed to one is also owed to the other. Rather, the Philosopher only intends this: that the movement of memory, by which the soul is moved toward the image as an image, also terminates at the thing imaged. It also has another true sense: that if I have a definitive concept of one relative thing, I also understand the other. But the Philosopher in no way intends that every movement of the soul—and especially of the will—is the same toward the image and the thing imaged. This is clear by a similar example even according to the way of speaking used by Thomas himself. For he often says that the movement of the will is the same when the will is carried toward an end and toward those things which lead to the end, when it wills them for the sake of the end. And yet it is certain, even according to him, that <margin>Opinion of other doctors.</margin> that movement, insofar as it reaches the end, is "enjoyment," <note>original: "fruitio"; a technical term for the soul's delight in its ultimate goal, God.</note> but insofar as it reaches the things leading to the end, it is "use" <margin>Opinion of Durandus.</margin> and not enjoyment. Therefore, it seems to other <term>doctors</term> <note>Theological authorities.</note> that it should in no way be said that we adore the image of Christ—even as it is an image—with the adoration of <term>latria</term>. For, as such, it is a created thing not united to the divinity; and what is more, as such, it is a "relative entity" <note>An entity that exists only in relation to something else.</note>. For this reason, Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain.</note> says that this proposition—"the cross of Christ is adored with latria"—is false in its proper sense, but it has a true improper sense. And it is this: Christ, as remembered through the cross, or as present in the cross just as the thing imaged is present in its image, is adored with the same adoration as if he were <margin>Opinion of Robert Holcot, Henry, John of Guarra, and Peter of Aquila.</margin> present in himself. And according to this sense, I also concede this proposition: "The Cross is adored with the adoration of latria." This is what Durandus means when he says it is adored "commemoratively." Robert Holcot intends the same meaning when he says that the more proper way of speaking is to say "we adore *before* the cross" rather than "we adore the cross." Finally, Henry <note>Henry of Ghent.</note> and John of Guarra intend the same meaning when they say it is adored "incidentally" <note>original: "per accidens"; indirectly or by association.</note>, and Peter of Aquila says the same. Truly, that which Henry and John of Guarra add, who speak more completely on this matter, is this: They say that the honor which is owed <margin>What Henry and John of Guarra add.</margin> "of itself" to the thing imaged and remembered is owed to the image "incidentally" or "commemoratively." However, it is certain that there is nothing to which <term>latria</term> is owed "of itself" except the Triune God, and Christ by reason of the unity of the person of God; otherwise, it cannot be an image. It remains that if there is any image to which <term>latria</term> is owed incidentally and commemoratively, it is the image of Christ. Truly, because such an image principally represents to us the humanity of Christ, but secondarily his divinity, it seems that <margin>Agreement of Francis with Henry and the Scotists.</margin> primarily and incidentally, such honor is owed to it as is owed "of itself" to the humanity of Christ. But the humanity of Christ, taken by itself, is only adored with <term>hyperdulia</term>; <note>original: "ypdulia"; the special veneration given to the highest of creatures, here applied to Christ's human nature as distinct from his divine nature.</note> therefore, even to such an image, primarily and incidentally, only the adoration of <term>hyperdulia</term> will be owed. Secondarily and incidentally, however, the adoration of <term>latria</term> will also be owed in the manner described: because the image itself also secondarily represents and reminds us of the very divinity of Christ. And in this, Francis of Mayronis and all the <term>Scotists</term> <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus.</note>—who say that <term>latria</term> is not owed to the humanity of Christ—agree with Henry. But Thomas, because he seems to hold the opposite regarding the adoration of Christ's humanity, would perhaps disagree with Henry in this case as well. And truly, the opinion of Thomas, as it is stated <margin>And Thomas is condemned by Francis and by Capreolus.</margin> also by Francis in the third book, is somewhat dangerous; and in this matter of adoration, his way does not seem to me to be very safe. ...all theology, because it [the Cross] cannot in itself be a subject capable of holiness or virtue, it cannot be the endpoint of any adoration. Even Johannes Capreolus, <note>Johannes Capreolus (c. 1380–1444) was known as the "Prince of Thomists" for his extensive defense of Thomas Aquinas's theology.</note> the defender of Thomas, admits that this statement of Thomas cannot be defended; nor does he have any other way of saving Thomas’s reputation except by saying that Thomas himself seems to have later thought differently in his *Summa*. From these points, therefore, it can be clear that my conclusion is Catholic and more reasonable than the opposite view, and more in harmony with the common path of theologians. 

<margin>Recapitulation of the meaning of the conclusion</margin>
In briefly summarizing the meaning of this, I say that this proposition—"the Cross of Christ is adored"—can have two meanings. One is the **proper** meaning: namely, that the Cross of Christ, whether as a physical thing, as an image, or as a partial or total object, is adored as the endpoint of the adoration. This is the sense that Thomas intends and which I deny. The other is the **improper** <note>In medieval logic, "improper" refers to figurative or non-literal usage rather than something "wrong."</note> sense of the stated proposition: "the Cross of Christ is adored," meaning that Christ is adored *in* it as in his reminder, as if he were present in himself. This sense I grant, and I pray with the Church, saying:

> Hail, O Cross, our only hope; and we adore your Cross, O Lord. <note>original: "O crux ave spes unica. et cruce tua adoramus domine." These are traditional liturgical antiphons used during Holy Week.</note>

From what has been said, many things can now be clear. First, it is clear what 
<margin>Many things are deduced. First:</margin>
I intended when I said elsewhere that, following the opinion of Henry <note>Likely Henry of Ghent, a major 13th-century theologian.</note> and Johannes de Guarra, the image of the Crucifix is owed <term>hyperdulia</term> <note>original: "ypdulia"; a level of veneration higher than that given to saints (dulia) but lower than that given to God (latria). It is usually reserved for the Virgin Mary.</note>. This was to be understood by reason of that which it primarily brings to our memory, which is the humanity of Christ. I said this briefly because I was referring to those authors, whom I considered to be veteran masters for these students—read and re-read ten times over. Second, it is clear that they 
<margin>Second:</margin>
falsely claimed that I deny every mode of the <term>adoration of latria</term> <note>original: "adorationis latriae"; the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone.</note>. For I expressly say in my conclusion that I deny Thomas's *method*; even if I had not said that, but the proposition simply stood as "neither the Cross nor any image is to be adored with latria," yet by the power of the words, that proposition would not deny every mode of the adoration of latria. For it is clear according to good logic that the negation or distribution of a term with multiple meanings does not negate or distribute it for every possible meaning. Otherwise, this proposition—"Every dog is a star"—would have to be simply granted or simply denied. <note>The author uses a classic logic puzzle: in Latin, "canis" (dog) can mean a barking animal, a "sea-dog" (shark), or the "Dog Star" (Sirius). Because the word has multiple meanings, you cannot make a simple "all or nothing" claim about it.</note> Therefore, just as one does not say collectively that every heavenly dog, every sea dog, and every barking dog is a star (though it might be said of each individually), so in this negative—"the Cross is not adored with the adoration of latria"—where the word "adored" is equivocal (referring either to adoration as an endpoint or adoration as a reminder), it does not negate every mode of adoration collectively, but only individually. Third, it is
<margin>Third:</margin>
clear that this proposition could be stated thus, absolutely and without distinction: "The Cross is not to be adored with the adoration of latria," because in the proper sense it is true (or at least more probable than its opposite). The proper sense of a word is more to be observed in the rigor of speech than the improper sense, in which the statement is false. Just as 
<margin>Note</margin>
an analogous term placed by itself stands for its most famous meaning, so a statement having both a proper and an improper sense, if spoken without specification, is to be taken according to the proper sense rather than the improper. Therefore, as I said, I could have posed it without distinction, intending to declare the sense in which I understood it during the debate. From this I infer that although in a proposition with multiple meanings it is perhaps better to do as I did—namely, to determine the sense in which it is posed—nevertheless, it is a greater defect to condemn a proposition simply and without distinction when it is true in its proper sense, just because of the falsity of its improper sense. I wanted to note this here not only for this conclusion (in which I specifically deny Thomas's method), but because of many other propositions which, although they have a Catholic sense that I have always promised to declare (as I am declaring now), were nevertheless condemned simply and without distinction. But however it may be regarding my conclusion, they cannot excuse their condemnation of it from error. I declare this clearly: this was formally their determination, because [the opponent] denies every mode of the adoration of latria toward the Cross according to the way of Catholic doctors and the prayer which the universal Church offers to the Cross. ...we say that the aforementioned conclusion is scandalous, an offense to pious ears, and against the custom of the universal church. This was precisely their judgment. First, let them tell me where it appears to them that I deny every mode of <term>latria</term> <note>From the Greek *latreia*; this is the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone, as opposed to *dulia*, which is the veneration given to saints.</note> toward the Cross according to the way of Catholic doctors. They certainly do not have this from my conclusion, in which I expressly and specifically say that I deny the way of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the highly influential Dominican theologian.</note>—unless perhaps, which I cannot believe, they have seen no other doctor and therefore estimated that the way of Thomas is the only way. Furthermore, they could not have gathered from my response that I deny every mode of divine worship according to the way of Catholic doctors, since I expressly say in my response that I grant that mode which 

<margin>Teacher of Scotus</margin> John de la Ware, <note>John de la Ware (active late 13th century) was a Franciscan theologian and teacher of Duns Scotus.</note> who was the teacher of [Duns] Scotus, and the solemn doctor Henry of Ghent <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293) was a major philosopher at the University of Paris.</note> grant. This is true unless they perhaps wish to say that both Henry and John are not Catholics, which necessarily follows from their statements. For since I told them that I follow Henry and John, and they then say that I do not follow Catholic doctors, who would not infer from this that those whom I said I followed are not Catholic doctors? But who would bear this? Who could endure with an equal mind that Henry and John, such illustrious and excellent doctors of the Church—the lights of the faith and its bulwarks—be rejected as non-Catholics and, consequently, as heretics and infidels? I cannot help but be indignant at times, but yet I shall restrain myself. 

Let us attend, however, to the second error. They say that my conclusion is scandalous, an offense to pious ears, and against the custom of the universal church. O most damned judgment! Let them see that they cannot escape these snares. For either my conclusion denies nothing except the "way of Thomas" in the manner explained above, and then it is clear that my conclusion is not against the custom of the church, as has been most extensively declared; or, as they wish, it denies every mode of adoration and denies that images are to be adored in the customary form of the church, and then the conclusion is not merely "scandalous" or "offensive to pious ears," but simply **heretical**. 

<margin>John of Damascus</margin> For, according to John of Damascus, <note>Saint John of Damascus (c. 675–749) was a key defender of the use of holy images against the Iconoclasts.</note> the honor shown to an image according to the rite of the church passes to the **prototype** <note>Original: "ptothīpon" (prototypon). In icon theology, the image is not the thing itself; honor given to a portrait of Christ goes to Christ himself.</note>. Therefore, he who does not observe the custom of the church in adoring images—which is to adore that which is imaged and represented, which is God, with divine worship—is to be called a heretic. Why then do they judge a conclusion that denies this as "scandalous" and not "simply heretical"? They themselves should be called heretics for such a judgment.

### FOURTH QUESTION: WHETHER AN IRRATIONAL 
### NATURE CAN BE ASSUMED BY GOD.

**The fourth conclusion** condemned by these men is this: *I do not assent to the common opinion of theologians who say that God can assume any nature into a personal union, but I grant this only concerning a rational nature.*

By this conclusion, I do not intend to deny that God *could* assume any nature into a <term>suppositum</term> <note>The term *suppositare* (to assume a nature into a personhood) refers to the mystery of the Incarnation, where the Divine Word took on human nature. The author is debating whether God could, in theory, take on the nature of a plant or animal.</note>. I only intend to deny a particular and explicit assent to this assertion: "God can assume any nature into a person." Between these two intentions, there is a great difference. For even if this were among the things possible according to the **absolute power of God**, nevertheless a proposition which, by the force of its words, only denies a positive and explicit assent in the particular case of that saying, does not derogate from the omnipotence of God, nor does it taste of any heresy. 

The reason is because not every believer is bound to assent explicitly and in particular to all things possible according to the absolute omnipotence of God, nor to profess these things explicitly and in particular. Rather, it is sufficient to believe some such things in general and implicitly, and to stubbornly disbelieve nothing. Therefore, it was not without mystery <note>Likely meaning "not without a specific, hidden purpose" or "not without careful thought."</note> that I did not phrase the conclusion in these terms: "God *cannot* assume any nature"; but rather in these: "I *do not assent* to the opinion saying that God can assume any nature." <margin>The words of Henry.</margin>
From the conclusion regarding the literal force of the word, it cannot be inferred that God cannot do this. Nor can it be said that this is asserted by me in the conclusion. For it is not in the first part, which is negative, nor in the second, from which it only follows that a grant of action belongs to a rational nature in a distinct way—namely, specifically and in particular. I therefore deny any particular and explicit assent on my part to this assertion: "God can <term>supposit</term> <note>From the Latin *suppositare*; in scholastic theology, this means to take a nature into one's own personal existence, as when the Word became flesh.</note> any nature whatsoever." I can reasonably deny this, both because the opposite might be true—since it can only be unknown to us in particular—and because I do not see that I am explicitly obliged to believe it. This is especially true because it is not easy to falsify or disprove that assertion "God cannot, etc." without derogating from the omnipotence of God. This is most strongly confirmed by the authority of the solemn doctor, **Henry of Ghent**, who, after previously holding the opposite opinion—namely, that any nature could be assumed—later leaned toward the view that only a rational nature can be assumed. For Henry writes thus: since there is no doubt about the possibility of the nature to be assumed—whether God can assume any assumable nature to himself—therefore the whole difficulty of this question turns on the possibility of the nature being assumed. And there are two solemn positions concerning this. For he says there is a more common and more solemn position.

<margin>The first position which Henry recites</margin>
<margin>Against this position.</margin>
<margin>That God is in creatures in two ways</margin>
To this [first position] I have sometimes been accustomed to assent somewhat: that any nature subsisting among creatures can be assumed. Those who hold this maintain that some nature is "elevatable" even if the corresponding power is not "elevatable"—a view that does not seem to me to be reasonably held. To understand this, one must note that God has existence in creatures in two ways. One way is naturally and in a manner agreeable to nature; the other way is voluntarily and in a manner exceeding the limits of nature. In the first way, He has existence through <term>influx</term> <note>Latin: *illapsus*; the way God "flows into" or sustains all created things at every moment.</note> in every nature and creature. In the second way, He has existence only in an assumed nature through <term>circumincession</term> <note>Latin: *circumincessio*; usually refers to the mutual indwelling of the Trinity, but here used to describe the profound intimacy between the divine and human natures in Christ.</note>. And although through influx God is intimate to every creature—more intimate than the creature is to itself, or than form is to matter—nevertheless, through circumincession He becomes most intimate of all to the assumed nature, and more intimate than He would be to any nature through influx alone. For through the intimacy of circumincession with the assumed nature, the Assumer is united ineffably and incomprehensibly to the nature assumed. It is necessary for the assumed nature to lose its own existence of subsistence <note>The nature stops existing as its own separate "person" or independent thing.</note> if it had such before the assumption; or, if it never had it, to enter into the existence of the subsistence of the nature into which it is assumed, so that there is the same <term>supposit</term> <note>A "supposit" is the individual subject or person that "owns" the nature.</note> subsisting in a double nature. For each of those natures in their union retains its own existence of essence. Through influx, however, God is made intimate to every creature naturally and in a manner agreeable to nature for two purposes: first, for the "first act" of nature, which is to be stabilized so that it persists; and second, for the "second act" of nature, which is to work and produce so that it exists in action.

<margin>Being made intimate through influx according to Gregory.</margin>
<margin>To be Absolutely and Principally</margin>
Without that influx, a creature can neither persist in being nor draw forth its own operation. Because through influx, God conserves the creature in being and, by cooperating, provides it with all its action or operation, as **Gregory** says in the 16th book of the *Moralia* <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Pope and foundational Latin Church Father. His *Moralia in Job* was a standard theological textbook.</note> on that passage of Job 23: *He is alone.* <note>original: "ipse solus est"</note> Is it not the case that there are angels, and men, and heaven, and earth? Certainly. But it is one thing to *be* absolutely, and another thing to *be* principally. For these things exist, but they do not exist principally because they do not subsist in themselves. Since they were created, all things were indeed made from nothing, and their essence would tend back toward nothingness unless the hand of the Ruler of the realm held it. This is the first of the sayings. And it follows concerning the second: they would be able neither to subsist nor to move by themselves. They subsist only insofar as they have received that they ought to be; they move only insofar as they are disposed by a hidden instinct. The earth dries up, the sea is shaken, the air catches fire, the sky grows dark, men burn with passion, the angelic virtues are moved. Are these not agitated by their own institutions, or rather by divine impulses?

<margin>To whom God is made intimate through circumincession</margin>
Through circumincession, however, God is made intimate only to the nature which He voluntarily assumes, but in a supernatural way. And this is similarly for two purposes: namely, for elevating the nature to the "first act," which is the existence of the subsistence of the divine <term>supposit</term>, and the power to the "second act," which is to perform the beneficial act of understanding and willing. For without the said circumincession, nature could not be elevated into the existence of divine subsistence, nor...

# APOLOGY

...I seem to perceive a difference of operations—namely, in loving the divine essence in a manner suitable to a creature.

<margin>Damascenus</margin>
But through <term>perichoresis</term> <note>original: "circuincessio"; a theological term describing the mutual indwelling or interpenetration of the divine and human natures in Christ.</note> God raises the assumed nature to the divine being of his own existence and promotes it to divine operation, as **John of Damascus** says in Book 3, Chapter 17: "the flesh of the Lord is said to be deified." <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749) was a Syrian monk and a key authority on the nature of Christ's two natures.</note> And this is therefore in a shared, indivisible way, not according to a change of nature, but according to the "dispensation of the union," by which the flesh was indivisibly united to God the Word through that mutual indwelling of the natures. And so, the divine flesh was enriched with divine actions because of its most pure union with the Word. Here, "flesh" is used to represent the whole of human nature. From these points

<margin>Henry's argument</margin>
I argue as follows: just as God exists in every creature through a natural "in-flowing" regarding those two aforementioned actions that exceed the limits of nature—as is already clear from the words of Damascus—a similarity cannot be denied in some respects. For just as that in-flowing is meant to operate in that into which God flows, so this mutual indwelling is meant by its very nature to always perform those two things. But no creaturely nature is capable—nor can it be capable—of this "in-flowing" of God to receive within itself (in a manner suitable to its nature) that first operation of God mentioned before, unless it is also capable of

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
the second operation. For no creature can exist as a substance if it cannot also perform some operation through its power. As the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), often called simply "the Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> says at the end of the fourth book of *Meteorology*: all things are defined by their function and exist for the sake of their operations. They exist only as long as they can perform their proper operations; when they cease to be able to perform them, they simultaneously cease to exist. As **Damascus**

<margin>Damascenus</margin>
says in the same place, Chapter 18: "An intellect that is foolish and deprived of knowledge will not exist at all." For if it is incapable of operation and immovable, it is entirely non-existent. By this, he clearly suggests that if a substance could not be "raised up" by means of its intellect, then the substance of the intellect itself would not be "assumable" <note>Capable of being taken up by God into a union of persons.</note>, nor would the man himself be. For he would not be a man, according to what was said previously: "Since he is rational and intellectual, otherwise how could God have become man if he had assumed soulless flesh or a soul without a mind?" <note>original: "anoin" (from the Greek 'anous'); meaning without intellect or mind.</note> This would not be a man. Therefore, likewise, no creature's nature is capable (nor could be capable) of the mutual indwelling of God to receive within itself the first operation of God above the limits of nature, unless it is also capable of the second operation. But it is not capable of the second operation except through the powers of intellect and will; therefore, etc.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Therefore, although the argument of **Augustine** mentioned in the first reason does not hold in its logical form, it does not fail in its subject matter. It follows that if this nature (say, of a man) can be elevated according to its essence, it must necessarily also be elevated according to its power. And if it cannot be elevated according to power, then not according to essence either. This is just as it follows that "if the soul of Socrates is immortal, then the soul of every man is immortal; and if it is not so for every man, it is not so for Socrates," because the reason for immortality or mortality is the same in all. Therefore, such an argument holds well because of the nature of the material, just as if it held by logical form. Indeed, it holds by virtue of its form when looking at the common reason that belongs to a certain nature (for instance, the immortality of the soul, which is the same in every soul). Let us see, therefore, the possibility and impossibility of this "assumption." On the part of God, as we said, there is no doubt.

<margin>Another position recited by Henry</margin>
But because it is unknown to us on the part of the one receiving the union, the understanding of the truth in this question is difficult for us. Therefore, there is another position besides the one mentioned, although it is less common. However, it is more applicable to the mind; though it might not seem as true because of its unfamiliarity, it is perhaps truer: namely, that "no nature is capable of being assumed by God through the aforementioned mutual indwelling except for an intellectual nature." This pleases me more. Holding this opinion for the present, I say in response to the first opposing point: the "susceptible" thing is the incorporeal rational soul (or an angel) and, in man, the nature of the body insofar as it is ordered toward the soul—like something "perfectible" ordered toward its "perfection." In this state, the soul performs its intellectual operation more effectively (once all accidental hindering conditions are removed) than when it is separated. Thus, the whole composite of body and soul, with its intellect, is the thing that is assumed; the body is assumed through the mediation of the soul's substance and in relation to that substance, as the soul is the

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding which types of created natures can be "assumed" (taken into a personal union) by God. It focuses on the "image of God" found in the intellectual soul as the necessary foundation for this union.</meta>

# OF THE QUESTIONS

...intellectual power, so that in no way is that which lacks intellectual power capable of receiving this union. In this context, "intellectual power" encompasses everything in which the <term>reason of the image</term> <note>The "reason of the image" (ratio imaginis) refers to the specific qualities of the human soul—memory, understanding, and will—that make it a "mirror" of the Trinity.</note> primarily consists within the substance of the soul. Thus, nothing is capable of this union except by reason of the image of God which is within it, whether through <term>mutual indwelling</term> <note>original: "circumincessio"; also known as perichoresis, this describes the interpenetration of the divine and human natures.</note> according to both substance and power simultaneously (as in Christ alone), or according to power alone (as in all of us). In these cases, the image of God is, as it were, imprinted back upon its own <term>prototype</term> <note>The original model or "master version" of the image.</note>, just as a coin is shaped by the figure from which its image was pressed.

<margin>John of Damascus</margin>
Hence, **John of Damascus** says in the aforementioned chapter that "according to the image" exists in the one who wills; the willing God, the Word, was made man; the image of God is according to the intellect. Why then would he assume anything except the intellect? Therefore, if you abandon what is better [the intellect], you assume what is worse. It is as if he were saying that this is not at all possible except by reason of the order that the nature has toward the intellect. He is speaking here against those who claimed that the human body was assumed in Christ without a rational soul. He also includes the very substance of the soul under the term "intellect," showing its force and power in the act of assumption, adding: "For the intellect is in the middle between God and the flesh; it is the inhabitant of the image of God." Therefore, intellect is mixed with intellect, and the intellect serves as a mediator between the purity [of God] and the thickness of the flesh. 

By this "mixture," I mean the union through the mutual indwelling of the divine intellect with the human intellect. This human intellect exists with its three powers—memory, intelligence, and will—and is united to the soul. 

<margin>Note the powers</margin>
It is united through a certain mutual indwelling to the Trinity of Persons in the unity of the divine nature. Thus, the primary and most immediate reason why something is capable of being assumed by God is the "reason of the image" of God, which exists only in intellectual substance. Therefore, only intellectual substance is capable of this union. 

According to this, in the glorious "assumption," through the mutual indwelling by which the divine nature enters the assumed nature, the "Image" (which is the assumed intellectual nature) is intimately united to that which is in the divine nature. It is just as if a seal were reapplied to wax in which the figure of the seal had already been impressed, entering into all its corners in the same way it first made the impression. This could not be applied to something in which its figure had not been previously impressed, but which only possessed some vague likeness—such as the <term>trace of God</term> <note>original: "vestigium dei"; Scholastic theologians distinguished between the "image" of God found in humans and the "trace" (footprint) of God found in animals, plants, and inanimate objects.</note> found in every non-intellectual creature. Thus, no non-intellectual nature can be assumed except through the mediation of an intellectual one.

Regarding the second point—that assumption to God can occur because in Him is the reason for "being" and "subsistence" found in the assumed nature—I say it is true as a contributing cause. For if that were not the case, nothing could be assumed by God, just as one creature cannot be assumed by another. But this is not the *total* cause. Although it is the cause on the part of the one assuming (God), it is not the cause on the part of the thing to be assumed. In the latter, the total cause of "assumability" is the "Image." It is only through this that a nature can be interpenetrated by God and elevated to the said union in the divine essence in the unity of the Person. 

Therefore, there is no final cause or purpose for which God would assume another nature instead of an intellectual one. The assumption of a nature exists ultimately only for the promotion and perfection of that nature in its elevation—something that only an intellectual nature can possess.

These are the words of **Henry of Ghent**, almost word for word. It was not correctly determined, therefore, that my conclusion—according to the literal sense of the words—savored of heresy simply because it denies positive assent to those contradicting **Henry**. 

<margin>Authors who agree with Henry</margin>
I have never read of a condemnation of Henry's opinion, nor do I believe those critics have ever read one. I know this: neither **Duns Scotus**, nor **Godfrey of Fontaines**, nor **John of Wales**, nor **Durandus of Saint-Pourçain**, nor **Thomas the Englishman**, nor **Robert of Cowton**, nor **Bernard of Gannat**—all of whom I have seen reciting Henry's opinion—ever judged it to be heretical or to "savor of heresy."

<margin>Two arguments against Henry</margin>
So that these men do not seem to have acted unreasonably, I wish to briefly set forth the way in which Henry seems to defend his position. There are, however, two primary arguments against Henry. The first argument stands on this: that in God is every reason for "substantiality," because He is the fullness of all being...

...it seems that any nature could be <term>substantialized</term> <note>Given substantial existence.</note> and <term>suppositated</term> <note>To "suppositate" (suppositare) means to provide the personal "who" for a nature; in this context, it refers to the Divine Word acting as the person or subject of a created nature.</note> by God. The second reason is because, during the <term>three days</term> <note>The "triduum," the period between Christ's death on the Cross and His Resurrection.</note>, God "suppositated" the body that was in the sepulcher, even though it was not then a "rational" being <note>Because the soul had departed, leaving only the corpse.</note>. And just as He suppositated it for three days, He could have done so for as long a time as He willed. These are the two primary foundations of the opposing opinion. And as was seen in the recitation of his opinion, **Henry** brings these very points against himself. To the first 

<margin>Solution to the first</margin>
reason, as we have seen, he responds that it is true that the fullness of all being is in God, and the entire principle of substantializing and suppositating is found most fully in Him. However, this is not the *total* cause of a nature’s "assumptibility" <note>The capacity of a created nature to be taken up into union with God.</note>; rather, it is a co-cause. For unless God were the one assuming, the nature could not be assumed. But beyond this, something is required in the thing being assumed by which it is made "assumptible." This is the <term>reason of the image</term> <note>The "ratio imaginis," or the specific way humans are made in the image of God via their intellect and will.</note> and, ultimately, the aptitude for a supernatural elevation to <term>beatific operation</term> <note>The activity of "seeing" and enjoying God in heaven.</note>. Since this is found in intellectual nature alone, it seems appropriate that only such a nature is capable of being assumed. For it seems reasonable that a nature which cannot be elevated to the "second act" <note>The "second act" refers to operation or activity (like thinking or loving), while the "first act" refers to the basic existence or union of the nature itself.</note> could not be elevated to the "first act" either. From this response, it seems **Henry** wishes to maintain that nothing is taken away from divine omnipotence. For everything that those opponents claim to be in God, concluding that He *could* thus suppositate a nature, **Henry** also attributes to God. He does not deny that, regarding what is required on the part of the Assumer, God possesses the most full power to assume any nature. Rather, he says this limit exists because an irrational nature itself is not capable of being assumed—not due to a defect in divine omnipotence, but rather due to the excellence of the divine nature and the "deformed deficiency" of irrational nature. To the second reason, 

<margin>A manifold solution to the second: First</margin>
it seems several things can be said. First is the response of **Henry**, who says that God assumed the nature of that body [in the tomb] insofar as it was ordered toward the intellectual soul; by reason of that ordering, the body itself can be called "intellectual" in a ministerial and preparatory sense. To respond more completely, it must be said that when it is stated that nothing can be assumed by God except an intellectual nature, it is understood that nothing *other* than that can be assumed in such a way that it is the "primary" thing assumed and the "totally adequate" subject of assumption. As is clear, the body in the three days of burial was not assumed in that way, but only as a *part* of the rational nature, which was the total and primary thing assumed. Furthermore, someone might perhaps 

<margin>Second</margin>
say that the body was not properly "suppositated" during those three days, because a body is not a nature capable of being its own "supposit" <note>The individual, self-subsisting subject.</note>. From this, it could be argued not improbably that "terminating the dependence" of the nature of that body is not the same as "suppositating" it. Otherwise, everything that terminates the dependence or leaning of a part would be said to "suppositate" it, which is not said. Thus, although the Word in those three days terminated the dependence of the body—the same dependence that the whole of humanity would have terminated—and by virtue of this, the body in the three days communicated to Christ its "property" of lying in the sepulcher, the Word did not strictly "suppositate" the body in the same way He would "suppositate" a human nature. The most evident sign of this is that the nature of that body did not communicate to Christ the "property" of being a "body" during those three days in the same way that human nature had communicated (and still communicates) to Him the concrete name "man." Thus the response to the aforementioned objections against the opinion of **Henry** is clear. Regarding other irrational natures, he seems to say that the Word could not assume them through <term>mutual indwelling</term> <note>original: "circumincessio"; the interpenetration of the two natures.</note> or "suppositate" them, especially since there is no final cause for it. For he says himself: no end or purpose could exist for the assumption of any nature other than an intellectual one, because assumption exists 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
only for the "promotion" (elevation) of the assumed nature, which only an intellectual nature can receive. Hence **Augustine** says in his commentary *on John*: "The Word willed to be born from man, so that you might be born securely from God." <note>original: "verbum voluit nasci ex homine: ut tu securus nascereris ex deo."</note> Thus it seems that concerning any other nature which is not "born from God" through grace, God would have been born as it in vain. From these points, it can be clear that I am not acting irrationally if I do not have an explicit act of contradicting this opinion in particular.

-># QUESTIONS<-

...specifically. And because these masters were also particularly insistent on this point—that such conclusions should at least not be debated because of the potential for <term>scandal</term> <note>In a theological sense, "scandal" refers to an action or word that leads others into spiritual confusion or sin.</note>—I want to say this regarding that conclusion: even if its opposite were truer and more in line with the common path, if it were publicly debated, it would be more scandalous among the common people and offensive to "pious ears."

For what unrefined and simple person would not be offended if they heard someone saying it is possible for these propositions to be true: **God is a donkey, God is wood**? What if they heard those which many following the aforementioned opinion concede: **God can be damned to hell; God could be tortured by the devil in hell; the devil can be God**?

<margin>
The difference between learned and common people
</margin>

While these things might cause no scandal among many learned men when speaking of God's <term>absolute power</term> <note>A distinction in medieval theology (potentia absoluta) referring to what God could theoretically do, as opposed to what He has actually ordained to do.</note>, the common and simple people would certainly be much more offended than if they heard that a donkey cannot be united to the divine nature in the unity of a <term>person</term> <note>The Latin 'suppositum' refers to the individual subject or 'person' that carries a nature. Here, the author argued God cannot 'suppositate' or be the person of an animal.</note>. Yet these fathers said my conclusion, by the literal force of the words, derogates from divine omnipotence and through this "savors of heresy"—relying I know not on what logic, or rather, what theology.

For let them say, I pray, whether he who says he does not assent to some proposition is saying—by the strictness of the words—the opposite of that conclusion to which he does not assent? Let them say whether this consequence holds: "I do not assent to (or I have no assent for) this conclusion: *The Pope is sitting*; therefore, I believe this: *The Pope is not sitting*." Would the first part not be true of a sleeping man? A person who is sleeping has no act of assent at all, yet the conclusion "The Pope is not sitting" could be false.

Furthermore, if the present conclusion derogated from divine omnipotence according to true theology, it should not only "savor of heresy" but be judged as heretical. Indeed, even a sleeping Catholic or a small child lacking the use of reason—who would not have assent to that proposition: **God can sustain any created nature in His own person**—would be a heretic, or at least would be erring in the faith, which no one would say.

From these points, it is clear that their condemnation is not correct. For this was formally their determination, considering the response of the one proposing it and the opinion, motives, and reasons of **Henry**, upon whose opinion the person posing the conclusion relies: *It has seemed to us that the aforementioned conclusion, by the literal force of the words, derogates from divine omnipotence, and through this savors of heresy.*

First, they were deceived because when I said I followed **Henry** in this, they did not understand that by the pronoun "this" I was denoting the very conclusion they were asking to be explained. Therefore, "in this"—that is, in the conclusion itself, in not assenting to the phrase "**God can [take on] any nature, etc.**"—I said I followed Henry. I did not denote by "this" the opinion that says, "**God cannot [take on] any nature.**"

But they perhaps believed there was no difference between one statement and the other; yet, if they are learned theologians, they ought to know the difference between *not explicitly believing* something is possible by the power of God and *explicitly disbelieving* it.

<margin>
Why Henry is called the Solemn Doctor
</margin>

Second, they ought to remember that from their statements it follows that the famous **Henry**—who is called the **Solemn Doctor** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major figure in scholastic philosophy.</note> because of the excellence of his teaching—died a heretic. As was seen above, in his old age he declined toward this opinion and remained in it: that not every nature can be <term>suppositated</term> by God.

Third, just as in the condemnation of the previous conclusion, so also in this one: regardless of the status of the conclusion, they are entirely in error. For if it is true, as they say, that the conclusion is against the omnipotence of God, then the conclusion is simply heretical, and not merely "savoring of heresy" as they claim.

Fourth and finally, they erred because even if Henry's opinion were entirely heretical, the conclusion by the literal force of the words would not be heretical, because by that force it does not imply that opinion, as has been most extensively declared. And yet they specifically condemned it by the literal force of the words.

# FIFTH QUESTION REGARDING NATURAL MAGIC AND THE CABALA OF THE HEBREWS.

The fourth conclusion condemned by those men was this: **There is no science that makes us more certain of the divinity of Christ than magic and <term>Cabala</term>** <note>Cabala (Kabbalah) refers to a tradition of Jewish mysticism and scriptural interpretation. Pico believed its ancient secrets actually pointed toward Christian truths.</note>. 
In clarifying this conclusion, I stated that among those sciences which are "sciences" in such a way that they do not rely on revelation—neither in their method of proceeding, nor in their principles, nor in their conclusions—there is none that makes us more certain (in the way that sciences discovered by human effort can provide certainty) than that magic about which these conclusions are proposed (which is a part of natural science) and that part of Cabala (which is a science and is not revealed theology). These masters said that my clarification did not match the intent of the words of the aforementioned conclusion, and that the aforementioned conclusion was false, erroneous, and heretical <term>by the literal force of the words</term> <note>original: "de virtute sermonis" — a technical scholastic term meaning the meaning of a statement based strictly on its grammatical structure, regardless of the author's intent.</note>. Let us see, I pray, how many things in their condemnation must themselves be condemned.

<margin>First</margin>
First, let them tell me how my clarification could be more to the point of my conclusion's words. For what else is in that clarification than to explicitly declare the power of each individual term placed in the conclusion? For there, I first explain what I understand by "science" when I say "no science," and what I mean by "to certify," what by "magic," and what by "Cabala." I do not see what further remains to be clarified.

<margin>Second</margin>
Second, I want to show that not only is it not false and heretical "by the force of the words," but rather its opposite is false—and according to them, entirely heretical. For the said conclusion is a negative one, which is explained disjunctively through three categories: **No science not revealed, etc., other than magic and Cabala, certifies the divinity of Christ;** or **magic and Cabala do not certify, etc.;** or **magic and Cabala certify us more regarding the deity of Christ than any other non-revealed science.** This disjunctive statement is true and Catholic, because at least one part of it is true. And so it is already clear that by the literal force of the words it is not false. But it is clear that its opposite, according to them, would be heretical. For the opposite of "no non-revealed science, etc., certifies more, etc." is this: **Some non-revealed science certifies more regarding the deity of Christ than magic and Cabala.** From this, it follows by the literal force of the words that magic and Cabala *do* certify the divinity of Christ, which they themselves regard as heretical. Thus, it is clear that while they wish to condemn this negative statement—"no science certifies more regarding the divinity of Christ than magic and Cabala"—they are forced by their own judgment to hold this affirmative one as Catholic: "Magic and Cabala certify us regarding the divinity of Christ." However, how true the conclusion is in itself can certainly be demonstrated most evidently. For although there is no science discovered by human effort that can certify us of the divinity of Christ (since we have no certainty of his divinity, as we said in the preceding conclusion, except from the manner of performing the miracles he did—and we know those miracles were both done by him and done in such a manner only from the testimony of Scripture), nevertheless, if human sciences can help us in this regard—just as they help in the knowledge of many supernatural truths—there is none that can help us more than the magic and Cabala we have mentioned.

<margin>How many things are required to recognize the divinity of God.</margin>
To this end—so that the miracles of Christ may testify to his divinity to us—it is necessary first to know that they could not have been performed by natural power, but only by the power of God. Second, it is necessary to know that Christ had that power from himself and not from elsewhere. In the first part, no human science can help us more than that which knows the powers and activities of natural agents, and their applications and proportions to one another and to their natural subjects, and what they can do by their own power and what they cannot. Among human sciences, this is best known by that science which I call **natural magic**, regarding which...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense against his accusers. On the previous page, he began clarifying his terminology to prove his theses were not heretical. Here, he specifically defends his use of the word "Magic," arguing that it historically refers to natural wisdom rather than demonic sorcery.</meta>

# APOLOGY

<margin>Second objection</margin>
Even if they wanted to, they cannot say that this is against the faith. But they will say: "We rebuke you for this—that you call these things **magic**; by using a word with multiple meanings, you cause a scandal in the minds of the faithful. Likewise, we have it from our own doctors that all magic is prohibited; if all is prohibited, it follows that none is allowed. Yet you say that some magic is not prohibited; therefore, you are speaking in contradiction to the doctors of the Church."

<margin>Response</margin>
The ignorance of those speaking this way is truly remarkable. First of all, the assignment of names is not something we are doing just now; rather, we use names and their meanings based on the custom of the ancients. If they, therefore, chose to call this part of natural science "magic," why do you want me to invent new names? Do you want what they called magic to be called geometry or arithmetic by me? I am not the first, nor am I a newcomer, to call this science magic. Many holy and learned men did so before me. Let them be dragged into court; let them be condemned—if it is indeed a damnable thing for this science to be called by this name.

<margin>The word "Magus" is proper to that nation. Consider how the name of a wise man is given to a shape-shifter.</margin> <note>Pico is likely referencing how the term "magus" has been transformed or "shifted" from a title of honor to a term of sorcery.</note> However, we can easily understand that the naming was rightly established if we correctly consider Paul <note>Pico may be referring to St. Paul’s discussions on worldly vs. divine wisdom.</note>. For this word *magus* is neither Latin nor Greek; it is Persian. In the Persian language, it means the same thing as "Wise Man" does for us. Among the Persians, "Wise Men" are the same as those called "Philosophers" among the Greeks (so named by Pythagoras, though they were previously called "Wise Men"). Indeed, among various nations, their wise men were called by various names: for instance, **Druids** among the Gauls; **Prophets** or the **Sanhedrin** <note>original: "fenedrim," referring to the Jewish council of sages</note> or **Pharisees** or **Cabalists** among the Hebrews; **Gymnosophists** <note>literally "naked philosophers" of India</note> among the Indians; **Priests** among the Egyptians; **Philosophers** among the Greeks; **Magi** among the Persians; and so on for others.

Just as royal dignity has specific names among various nations, such as the King of the Egyptians who was first called **Ptolemy** and later **Pharaoh**; the **Artaxerxes** of the Persians; the **Caesar** of the Romans; the **Prester** of the Indians (who is now called by our common people by the corrupted name **Prester John** <note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in medieval European lore</note>); and so on for others.

If, therefore, "magic" is the same as "wisdom," they rightly wished to call this practical branch of the natural sciences—which presupposes an exact and absolute knowledge of all natural things and is the peak and summit of all philosophy—by the peculiar and appropriate name **Magic** (that is, Wisdom). This is just as we call Rome "The City," Virgil "The Poet," or Aristotle "The Philosopher." If we shrink from this name "Magi" so much, then we certainly could not patiently listen to the Gospel saying: *that the Magi came from the East to adore Christ.* Those were not necromancers or people in league with demons; they did not come to adore the enemy of demons—indeed their Lord, who would soon triumph over them. Rather, they were wise men instructed in the science of celestial and earthly things, who worshiped and venerated that very Wisdom of the Father made visible in a human body.

St. Jerome makes this distinction very clearly in his *Letter to Paulinus*, in which, mentioning Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous 1st-century Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note>, he says: "Apollonius of Tyana was either a **Magus** (as the common people say) or a **Philosopher** (as the Pythagoreans say)." In these words, Jerome expressly signifies that what is true philosophy is sometimes believed by the common people to be what they call magic. Therefore, I am not to be rebuked because, following the proper and customary manner of speaking—not only of the doctors of the Church but even of the Gospel itself—I have called this natural wisdom "magic."

<margin>Note</margin>
Nor have I caused a "scandal" to the faithful by the ambiguity of the word, because in my conclusions I did not use this name indistinctly or vaguely. Instead, to remove any occasion for a sinister opinion, I distinguished **lawful magic** from **unlawful magic**, and **natural magic** from **superstitious magic**. I declared what that natural magic is and what it can do, and what it cannot do, so that even the simple and unlearned cannot suspect anything impious or erroneous in faith from my conclusions. In those conclusions, utterly rejecting and detesting prohibited magic, I placed this first conclusion precisely in these words:

**"All magic which is in use among modern people, and which the Church rightly exterminates, has no firmness, no truth, no foundation; because it depends on the hand of the enemies of the first truth—those powers of darkness which strike the darkness of falsehood into poorly disposed intellects."**

And after that conclusion, I place the second, which says that **natural magic is lawful and not prohibited**; and I testify concerning these things...

He distinguishes between "natural magic," which is the study of God's creation, and "superstitious magic," which he condemns as demonic.</summary>

Here, he distinguishes between "natural magic"—the science of understanding nature's hidden powers—and "superstitious magic" or necromancy, which involves demons. He cites the Three Magi and the theologian Albert the Great to support his use of the term.</meta>

<page-num>56</page-num>
<header>QUESTIONS</header>

...only to speak. Once this is done, what further suspicion can remain? Or what scandal could arise through the **equivocation** <note>original: "æquocationẽ"; meaning the use of a single word ("magic") to refer to two very different things.</note> of this name **magic**? To have distinguished it in this way—rejecting that superstitious and diabolic form while approving this natural form—cannot lead the simple-minded into scandal, but rather toward edification.

<margin>Note</margin>
For I have seen many people who, hearing that the **Magi** came to adore Christ, believe that this name "magi" signifies nothing other than **necromancers** <note>Those who claim to communicate with the dead or work with demons.</note>. From this, they take up the argument that magic is not prohibited nor against the faith of Christ, since practitioners of magic were the first to adore Christ himself. It is therefore useful to have taught the faithful that when they hear the word "magus," they should not always understand it to mean a worshipper of demons. And when they hear that among the Persians the Magi were held in the highest honor and reverence because of their learning and wisdom, they should know that those men were **philosophers**, not necromancers. For all nations have always pursued and detested necromancers as destructive and harmful—indeed, as a plague—casting them out and treating them poorly.

<margin>For this was commonly rumored about Albert</margin>
Similarly, when they read that **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prominent Dominican friar and bishop who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note> consumed much time among "experiments of magic," they should understand this to mean **natural magic**, not the forbidden kind. This prevents people from devoting themselves to forbidden acts by following the example of such a great man, presuming that what was permitted to him must also be permitted to them. Therefore, my conclusions on magic remove scandals from the minds of the faithful; they do not generate them. Furthermore, if they ever read in the works of the Doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church," authoritative theological teachers.</note> that "all magic is prohibited," they will immediately understand from the reasons for that prohibition that those authors are speaking only of that which has commerce with demons, and that they intend nothing regarding natural magic.

<margin>Hilary</margin>
For as **Hilary** <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century theologian.</note> says, the understanding of what is said must be derived from the reasons for saying it. But if they wish to return to the literal force of the words, they can learn from **logic** <note>original: "dialectica"</note> that the negation or distribution of a term with multiple meanings does not negate or distribute that term for every possible meaning or every thing it might represent. Therefore, since this term "magic" is **equivocal** <note>Having more than one meaning.</note>—referring to both the superstitious and the natural—a rule applied to it does not apply to every possible meaning joined to it. Rather, from the statement that "all magic is forbidden," it will be understood only that all types of *superstitious* magic are forbidden, as they all share one name and one definition. For there are many prohibited forms. All these things are clear and lucid even to the moderately educated. In no way, therefore, should my magical conclusions have been suspect to these masters; for as I said in my first conclusion, I refute all magic prohibited by the Church, damning and detesting it, making it clear that I speak only of natural magic. I declared this even more expressly through a special conclusion, stating that through this magic we perform nothing except by activating or uniting natural virtues.

> For so says the 11th of the magical conclusions: The wonders of the magical art exist only through the union and activation of those things which are [contained] **seminally** and separately in nature. And it is the same as what I said in the 13th conclusion: **to perform magic is nothing other than to marry the world.** <note>original: "maritare mundum"; this is one of Pico's most famous phrases, suggesting the magician acts as a "matchmaker" who brings together complementary forces in nature to produce effects.</note>

Furthermore, I intend for the aforementioned specification and restriction of my meaning—limiting it to natural magic in these conclusions—to be applied to every particular conclusion. Thus, when I speak of the activity of **characters** <note>Symbols or written signs believed to hold power.</note> and **figures** in a magical work, I am speaking of their true and natural activity. It is clear that they possess such power according to all philosophers, both in their action and in their manner of acting and receiving. And although according to the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, who focused on physical, material explanations.</note> these things are of much less activity and power than material qualities, nevertheless the **Pythagoreans** would say otherwise. 

<margin>Pythagoreans.</margin>
I call their philosophy "more secret philosophy" in conclusion 24, because it is less known and less in use. They argue that just as mathematical things are more **formal** <note>Related to the "Form" or essential pattern of a thing rather than its raw matter.</note> than physical things, they are also more active; and just as they are less dependent in their being, so too are they less dependent in their operation. Thus, what I said about their greater power—though the disagreement between the Pythagoreans and Peripatetics is indifferent to the faith—I did not state as something absolutely true in itself, but as a consequence of the "secret philosophy" of the Pythagoreans, understood in the manner described above. It is also their opinion that among all mathematical things, numbers are the most formal and thus the most active—and among the odd numbers, the **number three** <note>original: "ternarium"</note> is foremost.

<summary>Pico defends his use of the word "magic" by distinguishing natural science from demonic sorcery, arguing that "marrying the world" through natural forces is a legitimate philosophical pursuit. He also introduces Pythagorean views on the power of numbers and mathematical forms as being more active than simple physical matter.</summary>

<header>DEFENSE</header>

# DEFENSE

Because the first is unique <note>original: "spar," likely a typo or variant for "par" or "super"; the sense is that the number one is the unique source of all things.</note> and the first in every category is the most perfect in that category, and among even numbers, the number ten <term>denarius<gloss>the number ten</gloss></term> is the most complete, as is evident. For beyond ten, we only count by repeating. This is what I intended by what I said concerning the number three and the number ten in my work on natural magic. Indeed, the Catholic doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church" are authoritative theologians such as Augustine or Jerome.</note> also attribute efficacy and power both to good and to evil through numbers. 

<margin>Hilary</margin>
Hence **Hilary** <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a leading Latin theologian.</note>, in his commentary on the Psalms, inquires why the order of the Psalms is not according to history, but often a Psalm composed earlier is placed in a later position. He says: "It must be known that among the Hebrews, the number of the Psalms is not fixed and they were written without any notation of order. For they do not mark them as first, second, third, fiftieth, or hundredth; rather, they are mixed together without any assigned order. 

<margin>Ezra</margin>
For **Ezra** <note>original: "Hesdras"; the biblical scribe credited with reorganizing the Hebrew scriptures after the Babylonian exile.</note>, as ancient traditions hold, collected them into one volume after they had been scattered and composed at different times and by various authors. But the seventy elders <note>The "Septuagint," the seventy Jewish scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note>—who, according to the tradition of Moses, remained in the synagogue as guardians of the law and doctrine—were later commissioned by King Antiochus to translate the whole Law from the Hebrew into the Greek language. Through spiritual and heavenly science, they understood the powers <note>original: "uirtutes"; here meaning inherent spiritual energies or hidden properties.</note> of the Psalms and restored them to a specific number and order. They assigned each individual number according to its own efficacy and perfection, matching the numbers to the sequence of the most perfect and effective Psalms." Thus says Hilary, word for word. From this, it is perfectly clear that number bestows power and efficacy. 

<margin>Jerome</margin>
**Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> also, writing against Jovinian, says that the number twenty-one is unfavorable, for it was the length of time Jacob served, and when Joseph was sold, and the number Esau loved when receiving certain gifts. In the same passage, he praises the number ten, saying he has spoken of its praises quite often. And in Chapter 8 of the same book, he says that on the second day of creation, it was not said "and God saw that it was good," because the number two <term>binarius<gloss>the number two, or duality</gloss></term> is evil. 

<margin>Passage from the Heptaplus</margin>
Indeed, he takes an argument from the number two against those who marry twice <note>Pico refers to Jerome’s ascetic argument that the "binary" represents a departure from the "unity" of God or a first marriage.</note>, and because of this, he says all the unclean animals entered Noah's ark in pairs (twos), while the clean animals entered by sevens. 

<margin>Basil, Nazianzen, Ambrose, Origen, Augustine, Rabanus</margin>
You will find such things a hundred times in the works of **Basil**, **Gregory Nazianzen**, **Ambrose**, **Origen**, **Augustine**, and others. Furthermore, **Rabanus Maurus** <note>A 9th-century Benedictine monk and influential scholar.</note>, a distinguished doctor of the church, composed a special book on the powers of numbers. You will find the ecclesiastical doctors always observing the properties of these numbers everywhere—sometimes even to the point of "curiosity," if it may be called that. At one moment, they refer the number two to the two Testaments, the two Cherubim, the two commandments of charity, the two primary dignities, or the two primary peoples. 

<margin>Note on numbers.</margin>
At another moment, they contemplate the mystery of the number three <term>ternarius<gloss>the number three</gloss></term> in the substantial divinity, in the three days in the tomb, in the three theological virtues <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity.</note>, in the three ages (of Nature, of Law, and of Grace), and in the three states of perfection. Again, they maintain that it is not without mystery, but because of a hidden property of the number itself, that **Moses** fasted for forty days, **Elijah** for forty, and **Christ** for forty; and that Christ ascended forty days after the resurrection; and was among the dead for forty hours; and that after forty days Nineveh—which is a figure of this world—would be subverted; and the Lord sent rain upon the earth for the same number of days and nights. They also say it contains a great sacrament that the Holy Spirit descended in the number fifty, in which the remission of sins occurs. And in that same number is placed the Psalm *Miserere mei Deus* <note>Psalm 50 in the Vulgate numbering (Psalm 51 in modern Bibles), the great prayer of repentance.</note>, which Hilary and Origen particularly note. 

<margin>Hilary, Origen</margin>
<margin>Note</margin>
And the mysteries of the **Kabbalists** <note>original: "cabaliſtaR"; practitioners of Jewish mysticism whose methods Pico integrated into Christian theology.</note> agree perfectly with these things in all respects; they attribute the number fifty to the Holy Spirit, which among them is also signified by fire. In this form and in this number of days, the Spirit descended upon the apostles. Among them, the Holy Spirit is the third person or property in the divine realm, proceeding from the first and the second. The second is called **Wisdom**, and it proceeds from the first. The third differs from both only by the nature of its "procession"—just as that which proceeds differs from those from whom it proceeds—though it is nonetheless the same with them in substance and essence. 

<margin>What the sin against the Holy Spirit actually is.</margin>
The Kabbalists say these things expressly. Yet these masters of mine <note>The ecclesiastical critics who attacked Pico’s theses.</note> loathed their sayings, which I brought forward against the Jews, as if they were suspicious regarding the faith. They also call this same third property **Penitence**, which agrees with what was just said: that the same number is attributed to the Holy Spirit as is attributed to peni-

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "Apologia," specifically his defense of the "natural magic" of numbers (arithmology). He is transitioning from a discussion on the significance of the number ten to a broader exploration of how numbers and names hold inherent spiritual power, citing both Hebrew tradition and Church Fathers like Augustine and Jerome.</meta>

# QUESTIONS

...concerning the sacred mystery of penitence. From this we can also gather that the "sin against the Holy Spirit" <note>original: "peccatum in spiritum sanctum"</note> is properly the sin of **impenitence**, which is not forgiven in this world nor in the future; but more on these things elsewhere. We see two denarii <note>A reference to the two coins given by the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:35), often interpreted numerically or allegorically by theologians.</note> and a certain secret property observed in the **twelve tribes of Israel**, in the **twelve apostles**, and in the **twelve stones** of the heavenly Jerusalem. It is believed, and not without cause or by chance, that the number ten <term>denarius<gloss>the number ten</gloss></term> coincides with the precepts of the Law <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> and the ten strings of the psalter. Among the Hebrews—as is held in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A Jewish commentary on the Psalms.</note>—there are ten singers of the Psalms: **Adam, Abraham, Melchizedek, Moses, Asaph, David, Solomon,** and the **three sons of Korah**; although they are enumerated differently by our own writers.

<margin>Singers of the Psalms</margin>
And these correspond to ten "organs"—that is, ten instruments or ten modes of music by which they are sung, which are named thus among the Hebrews:

1. *Nesa* <note>original: "nesa," likely *Nitzachon* (Victory/Ode).</note>
2. *Nieum* <note>original: "nieum," likely *Niggun* (Melody/Instrumental).</note>
3. *Mizinor* <note>original: "mizinor," *Mizmor* (Psalm).</note>
4. *Sir* <note>original: "sir," *Shir* (Song/Canticle).</note>
5. *Thephila* <note>original: "thephila," *Tefillah* (Prayer).</note>
6. *Beracha* <note>original: "beracha," *Berakhah* (Blessing).</note>
7. *Alel* <note>original: "alel," *Hallel* (Praise).</note>
8. *Odaya* <note>original: "odaya," *Hodayah* (Thanksgiving).</note>
9. *Asre* <note>original: "asre," *Ashrei* (Happiness/Beatitude).</note>
10. *Alleluia* <note>Praise to God.</note>

I have observed these to be distinguished such that through the first, an **ode** is sung. The second is the same as an **instrument** <note>original: "organum"</note>. Through the third, **psalms**. Through the fourth, **canticles**. Through the fifth, **prayers**. Through the sixth, **blessings**. Through the seventh, **lauds**. Through the eighth, **thanksgivings**. Through the ninth, the **happiness** of someone. Through the last, **praises of God alone**. You may also add *Maschil* <note>original: "meschíl"</note>, by which **contemplations** are sung; and there will be an "Alleluia" when you do not include the *Ein Sof* <note>original: "eísoph." In Kabbalah, the Infinite/God before manifestation. Pico is discussing how to count the modes of song depending on whether the Infinite is included.</note> in the number with the others. They also add the **ten days** during which the Spirit descended after Christ’s ascension, and the **ten curtains** in the Temple, and countless similar things, always saying that nothing happens by chance, but that "God disposed all things through His wisdom in weight, and measure, and number" <note>A famous quote from the Wisdom of Solomon 11:20.</note>. 

I shall remain silent on how many things are observed in the number **nine**: such as the hierarchies of angels, the nine degrees of the Beatitudes according to Matthew, and the length in cubits of **Og, king of Bashan** <note>A giant mentioned in Deuteronomy 3:11.</note>, who is a type of the devil—they do not believe these to be accidental or without mystery. They also observe that the Lord cried out at the **ninth hour**. And do they not also consider the perfection of the number **four** in the four Gospels, the four rivers of Paradise, and the four living creatures of Ezekiel? Or the number **six** in the six days of the world's creation and the six ages? Whether the future life will be the **seventh** age (as **Augustine** wishes) or the **eighth** (as **Jerome** wishes), they do not overlook the fact that the Lord suffered on the **sixth day** <note>Friday.</note>. 

<margin>Augustine. Jerome.</margin>
What of the number **seven**? They say much worthy of great attention: that on the **seventh day** the Lord rested; that there are **seven gifts** of the Holy Spirit; and in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, **seven seals** of the book, **seven horns**, **seven eyes**, **seven angels**, **seven churches**, **seven lampstands**, **seven stars**, **seven spirits** of wickedness, and (according to Solomon) **seven abominations**. Also, the prophet David sings to God **seven times a day**. Furthermore, we see the number **fourteen** observed by Matthew in such a way that, in order to maintain it throughout the generations of Christ, he even omitted several generations. 

I bring nothing here from physicians, astrologers, or philosophers (especially the **Platonists** and **Pythagoreans**), but only from our own **Ecclesiastical Doctors**. The question at hand is whether believing that there are properties in numbers and certain natural virtues in some way contradicts the truth of the Catholic faith. Since we see these things observed by Catholic authors—perhaps even to the point of curiosity—I see no reason why we should doubt that such an opinion is *not* to be rejected as heretical. 

Therefore, when I speak in my "Conclusions" about figures and numbers, I do not speak regarding their **superstitious use** through pacts and conventions with demons, for I have rejected all such things in my first Conclusion. Similarly, it is known to all that **names** possess a certain natural activity. Indeed, they do not have this natural activity merely as signs chosen by whim, but as they are in themselves certain natural things. Therefore, I said those names have power in **natural magic**, not as they are significations, unless perhaps they are those whose significance is natural—just as the **Stoics** say of all names (which the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed names were arbitrary conventions.</note> oppose), and as **Plato** agrees in the *Cratylus* regarding those names that are correctly assigned. 

<margin>Stoics. Peripatetics. Plato. Origen.</margin>
**Origen**, however, feels this way about **Hebrew names**. He says that certain Hebrew names in Holy Scripture—such as *Hosanna*, *Sabaoth*, *Alleluia*, and the like—were preserved and not changed into another language because they would not have retained their natural significance and, consequently, their virtue <note>original: "uirtutem," meaning power or efficacy.</note>...

<summary>Pico defends the use of numerology and the inherent power of names in theology by citing Church Fathers, Hebrew tradition (including the Midrash), and classical philosophers. He argues that numbers like 10, 7, and 4 carry divine significance and that certain Hebrew names possess a "natural power" that is lost in translation.</summary>
