<meta>This page continues Pico's defense, moving from a discussion of the "virtue" or power of names and numbers in natural magic to a specific defense of Kabbalah. He begins by addressing the ignorance and fear his critics have toward the term "Kabbalah."</meta>

# APOLOGIA

[...virtue]. And this alone I intended to say while comparing meaningful names with meaningless ones, and Hebrew names with others regarding their efficacy in natural magic, and so forth. I wish also to say something more broadly about this Kabbalah, although we have already said many things above in the first part of our Apology; but those things are perhaps no better understood by these masters <note>Pico refers to the scholastic theologians and inquisitors who criticized his 900 theses.</note> than foreign languages are understood by the unlearned. Therefore, here also we shall say something about this Kabbalah in this Parisian style <note>The "Parisian style" refers to the rigorous, logical method of the University of Paris, the center of scholastic theology.</note>. For this name seems terrifying to those fathers of yours, and to be feared from its very sound; so much so that there are perhaps some among them who suspect Kabbalists are not men, but rather "goat-stags" <note>original: "hircocervos," a mythical creature used in logic to represent something that can be imagined but does not exist.</note> or centaurs, or something entirely monstrous. Nay more, hear a ridiculous thing: when once one of them was asked what this Kabbalah was, he replied that it was a certain treacherous and diabolical man called "Kabbalah," and that he had written many things against Christ, and thus his followers were called "Kabbalists." Who, I ask you, could hold back laughter at this?

It must therefore be known that it is the opinion not only of Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Moses of Egypt <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the famous Jewish philosopher.</note>, Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish, Rabbi Ishmael, Rabbi Judah, and Rabbi Nachman,
<margin>Hebrew authors</margin>
and many others among the wise men of the Hebrews, but also of our own doctors—as I shall show below—that besides the Law which God gave to Moses on the mountain and which he left written down, contained in five books, there was also revealed to the same Moses by God Himself the true explanation of the Law, with the manifestation of all the mysteries and secrets contained beneath the "bark" <note>original: "cortice," a common metaphor for the literal surface of a text.</note> and rough outward appearance of the words of the Law. Finally, that Moses received a twofold Law on the mountain: the literal and the spiritual. The former he wrote down and, by God's command, communicated to the people. Regarding the latter, however,
<margin>A twofold Law given to Moses</margin>
he was commanded by God not to write it down, but to communicate it only to the seventy wise men who existed, whom Moses himself had chosen by God’s command to guard the Law; and he commanded them likewise not to write it down, but to reveal it to their successors by living voice; then they to others, and so in perpetual order. From this manner of handing down this science through successive reception <note>original: "receptionem"</note> of one from another, the science itself was called the "Science of Kabbalah," which is the same as the "Science of Reception"; for "Kabbalah"
<margin>Whence Kabbalah is derived and why it is so called</margin>
signifies among the Hebrews the same thing as "Reception" signifies among us. Later, however, these mysteries were committed to letters at a time and for a reason to be mentioned below, and those books were called the "Books of Kabbalah." In these books, many—nay, almost all—things are found to be in harmony with our faith. For they were handed down from the mouth of God and written by the Jews before Christ, at a time when they could not be moved by any passion to taint or corrupt the truth itself. From these books and authors of this science, I proposed many conclusions for the confirmation of our faith against the Jews; which, because these masters perhaps did not consider them well, they claimed were suspicious in faith and savored of Jewish treachery.
<margin>Note</margin>
Yet, after they later understood what Kabbalah actually was, many of them were ashamed of what they had said.

That it is indeed as we said above—that God, besides the literal Law which he himself wrote,
<margin>Ezra, Paul, Origen, Hilary, the Gospel</margin>
gave and revealed to Moses the mysteries contained in the Law—I have five witnesses from among our own: Ezra, Paul, Origen, Hilary, and the Gospel. First, we have this from the text of Ezra, where the Lord, speaking, says thus: "Revealing, I was revealed upon the bush, and I spoke to Moses when my people were serving in Egypt. And I sent him and led him out of Egypt, and I brought him upon Mount Sinai, and I kept him with me for many days. And I told him many wonders, and showed him the secrets of the times and the ends; and I commanded him, saying: 'These words you shall make public, and these you shall hide.'" <note>A paraphrase of the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) 14:1–6.</note> Second, we have the authority of Origen, whose testimony is most powerful in those matters for which he is accepted by the Church; for where he is good, no one is better. He, therefore, commenting on that passage of Paul in the third chapter of Romans: "What advantage then do I see, or what is the profit of circumcision? Much in every way: first, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them." <note>Romans 3:1–2.</note>
<margin>Origen</margin>
Origen says: "It must be considered that he did not say the letters <note>original: "litteras"</note> were entrusted, but the oracles <note>original: "eloquia," i.e., the spoken or divine utterances.</note> of God." From this statement of Origen, you have evidence that besides the literal Law, something else was handed down to the Jews, which he calls here—

<summary>Pico defines "Kabbalah" as a divinely revealed oral tradition (Reception) given to Moses alongside the written Law. He mocks the ignorance of his critics who think Kabbalah is a diabolical person and cites Christian authorities like Origen and Ezra to support the existence of hidden spiritual mysteries.</summary>

# OF QUESTIONS

<page-num>53</page-num>

Paul calls these the "divine utterances" <note>original: "eloquia dei." Pico refers to Romans 3:2, where Paul discusses the advantages of the Jews.</note>. For no one denies that the "letters"—that is, the literal law—were handed down to them. But he does not credit this to them as a special privilege, because the "letter" by itself kills <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note>; and unless the vivifying spirit is present, it is entirely a dead thing on its own. But besides these letters, the divine utterances were handed down to them, in which they rightly glory, and which are nothing other than what the Hebrews call **Kabbalah** <note>The word Kabbalah literally means "reception" or "tradition."</note>. This is the true sense of the law received from the mouth of God. Hence, among the Hebrews it is sometimes called [the Oral Law], which is the same as the "law born from the mouth." Because of that successive reception, it was thereafter called **Kabbalah**. And that Moses then communicated this knowledge, once received from God, only to the seventy elders, is openly testified by Hilary.

<margin>Hilary</margin>

Hilary <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), an influential bishop and theologian.</note>, in his exposition of Psalm 2, "Why have the nations raged," etc., writes as follows: "It had already been instituted by Moses that there should be seventy teachers in every synagogue. For although this same Moses had preserved the words of the Old Testament in letters, he had nevertheless separately disclosed certain more secret mysteries from the hidden parts of the law to the seventy elders, who were to remain teachers thereafter." The Lord also mentions this teaching in the Gospels, saying: "The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses. Therefore, do and observe all things whatsoever they tell you, but do not act according to their deeds" <note>Matthew 23:2–3.</note>. Indeed, their doctrine remained for posterity. These are Hilary's words verbatim.

Behold how Hilary expressly testifies that besides the written law, there was a certain other more secret doctrine which Moses disclosed to those seventy wise men. Moreover, that this more secret and truer exposition of the mysteries of the law was not made public to everyone everywhere, but was revealed only to Moses specifically by God, and by him only to the seventy wise men, Origen also testifies in the previously cited passage, saying this of Moses, the prophets, and others like them: "These things are to be understood as being said to those to whom the divine utterances were entrusted." Add also: "if anyone among them was a wise and understanding listener and a wonderful counselor." These are Origen's words <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar who often sought deeper, allegorical meanings in scripture.</note>.

By these "wonderful counselors" are understood those whom the Hebrews call the **Sanhedrin** <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the Jews.</note>, that is, those seventy elders whom Moses chose by the Lord's command.

<margin>Sanhedrin</margin>

Their place, it seems to me, is held by the **Cardinals** in our Church. And in imitation of the number of those seventy elders, as we shall now declare, the mysteries of Kabbalah were compiled into seventy principal books in the time of Ezra. For until the time of Ezra, nothing of this doctrine had been written down; but, as I said, it was handed down only by successive reception, from which it took the name "Kabbalistic."

After they were restored from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus, and the temple was restored under Zerubbabel, then Ezra—who was the leader of the synagogue—after he had restored the written law of Moses and corrected the Old Testament, wished also that those secret divine utterances, which until that time had not been written down, should be recorded in writing. This was because, due to the nation's captivity, they could not maintain that order of handing down the doctrine "by hand" <note>original: "per manus," referring to oral transmission from teacher to student.</note>; and there was a justified fear that because of their dispersion, if the teachings were not found in writing, they might eventually perish.

<margin>Concerning this elsewhere</margin>

Ezra therefore decreed that they should be written down, employing scribes specifically for this purpose. And because there were seventy elders or counselors among whom this doctrine resided, he ordered that all those secrets be compiled into seventy principal volumes, which, however, were only to be shared thereafter with the wise. And this is what is read in the book of Ezra <note>Pico quotes the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra) 14:44–46.</note> in these words: "When the forty days were ended, the Most High spoke, saying: 'Make public the first things you wrote, that the worthy and unworthy alike may read them; but the last seventy books you shall preserve, to hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge.' And so I did." These are Ezra's words verbatim.

Moreover, there is a broad and extensive mention of that council in which these books were written among the Hebrews in the book called *Seder Olam*, that is, the "Book of the Ages."

<margin>*Seder Olam*—what it means in Latin</margin>

In that book is recorded who sat in the council, and finally the acts and order of the whole council. From all these things it can be sufficiently clear that it is not a fiction of my own making that, besides the written law, Moses also received a true exposition of the law from God; and through that exposition, subsequently by succession from Moses to the seventy elders, and from them...

<margin>Paul the Apostle</margin>
...they believe. For their foolish heart was darkened <note>original: "Obscuratum est enim insipiens cor eorum." A quote from Romans 1:21.</note>. And concerning those utterances of God—which we have declared above to be this very Kabbalistic tradition—Paul speaks in this manner: "What if some of them did not believe? Has their unbelief nullified the faithfulness of God? God forbid. For God is true, and every man a liar" <note>original: "Quid. n. si quida illorū nō crediderūt... Est. n. deus uerax. oīs aut homo mendax." Pico quotes Romans 3:3-4.</note>. So we also say: what if many do not believe? Does their unbelief nullify the truth and nobility of this science? God forbid.

Indeed, Christians are most worthy of this science because, just as the law itself is spiritual and not carnal, so we are spiritual Israelites, not carnal ones. Furthermore, the spiritual law pertains to him who, according to Paul, is a Jew in secret, not to him who is a Jew outwardly <note>Pico refers to Romans 2:28-29, contrasting the "circumcision of the heart" with outward ritual.</note>. As for the claim that the teachers of the Church wonder why no mention was ever made of this doctrine, we have shown sufficiently above that Hilary, Origen, and Ezra—and alongside these, Paul and the Gospel—recall this science.

<margin>Why no mention seems to be made among us</margin>
It must also be noted that you will never, or very rarely, find any of our teachers—I speak of the ancients—citing any of the Hebrews by name; rather, you will see them speak only in general terms, saying: "the Hebrews say this," or "this is the opinion of the Hebrews." Indeed, I do not remember finding this but once in Origen, who cites the patriarch Huillus <note>likely referring to Hillel II, a 4th-century Jewish leader, or "Jullus" as mentioned in Origen's commentaries.</note>, his contemporary. Therefore, it is no wonder if you never hear the authors of Kabbalah cited by them by name.

<margin>Jerome, Eusebius, Origen, Clement</margin>
But since we see our teachers occasionally rely on the testimony of the Hebrews—as our Jerome says: when they wish to prove what they say, especially Eusebius, Origen, and Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD), an early Christian theologian who often integrated Greek philosophy and Jewish tradition.</note>, and many others—they always refer back to the Hebrews, saying: "a Hebrew told me," "I heard from a Hebrew," or "this is the opinion of the masters." There can be no doubt that they mean the teachers of Kabbalah; this can be demonstrated by clear reason.

<margin>Division of the Hebrew Schools</margin>
For the entire school of the Hebrews is divided into three sects: the Philosophers, the Kabbalists, and the Talmudists <note>The Talmudists focus on the "Talmud," the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note>. That the Talmudists were cited by our ancient teachers is not to be believed,

<margin>Clement</margin>
both because Clement and many others who cite the Hebrews lived before the composition of the Talmud itself (which was more than 150 years after the death of Christ), and because the Talmudic doctrine was fabricated by the Hebrews entirely against us, while they were already fighting against Christians. Therefore, our teachers would not have paid such honor to that doctrine, nor would they have considered anything said by them to be firm simply because it was corroborated by the testimony of [Talmudic] Jews. It is equally certain they do not cite the Philosophers, because those who began to explain the Bible according to philosophy began only a short time ago.

<margin>Rabbi Moses the Egyptian, first biblical expositor</margin>
For the first was **Rabbi Moses of Egypt** <note>Better known as Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note>, in whose lifetime **Averroes of Córdoba** <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an influential Al-Andalus Muslim philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> flourished.

<margin>Note the era of Averroes</margin>
Not yet three hundred years have passed since the death of Averroes. It remains, therefore, that this doctrine of the Hebrews—to which the Catholic teachers, by Jerome’s testimony, defer so much, and which they approve of to such an extent—is that which our own teachers confess and believe was revealed by God to Moses, and from Moses by succession to other wise men. It is this which, because of this method of handing down, is called **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah (Hebrew: "Reception") <explanation>The term for the Jewish mystical and oral tradition believed to be handed down alongside the written law.</explanation></term>, and which I often see designated by our authors in this way: "as the ancient tradition says."

<margin>Conclusion on Kabbalah</margin>
This is the first and true Kabbalah, of which I believe I was the first among the Latins to make explicit mention. It is the one I use in my conclusions, which I put forward expressly against the Hebrews for the confirmation of our faith; I do not know how those masters could hold them as suspect in the faith. However, because this method of handing down by succession (which is called Kabbalistic) seems to suit every secret and mystical thing,

<margin>The Hebrews' usurpation</margin>
hence it is that the Hebrews have usurped the term, calling every science they consider secret and hidden "**Kabbalah**." Every bit of knowledge obtained from any source through a hidden path is said to be held "by way of Kabbalah." In general, they have honored two sciences by this name: one which is called the "**art of combining**" <note>likely referring to the Kabbalistic techniques of Gematria or Temurah, where letters are rearranged or substituted to find hidden meanings.</note>, which is a certain way of proceeding in the sciences and is something similar to...

The other type is concerned with the powers of superior things which are above the moon, and this is the highest part of natural magic. Both of these are also called Kabbalah among the Hebrews for the reason already stated: and we have also made mention of both of these at various times in our conclusions. For that "combinatory art" is what I call in my conclusions the <term>alphabetical revolution</term> <note>A method in Kabbalah, often called "Tseruf," involving the permutation of Hebrew letters to gain spiritual insights.</note>. It is this latter one of which I speak in the present conclusion, saying that it aids us in our knowledge of the divinity of Christ in the manner already declared. And although the name "Kabbalah" might not suit these two sciences by their primary and proper definition, it could nevertheless be applied to them figuratively.

However, just as once only the wise were called "magi," but later necromancers and diabolical men—falsely claiming the name of a wise man for themselves—called themselves magi; so too certain people among the Hebrews, polluting divine things with false and vain superstitions (indeed, in truth differing almost nothing from necromancers), have said they possess secrets regarding names and powers with which demons might be bound and miracles performed.

They even claimed that Christ performed His miracles by no other way. ### SIXTH QUESTION CONCERNING THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST.

**I**f the common path is held regarding the possibility of "assumption" <note>original: "suppositionis". In scholastic logic and theology, this refers to how a person (like the Word) takes on a nature (like humanity or, hypothetically, bread).</note> with respect to any creature, I say that without the conversion of the substance of the bread into the body of Christ or the annihilation of the "bread-ness," it can happen that the body of Christ is present in another way, according to the truth of the sacrament. This is said regarding what is *possible*, not regarding *how it is*. By this conclusion, I do not intend to say that the bread is *not* converted into the body of Christ, or that the body of Christ is present in the sacrament—as actually instituted by Christ—in this other way, or that the actual truth of that sacrament is the presence of the body of Christ alongside bread actually assumed or sustained by the Word. For I expressly reject these as claims of *fact* in the conclusion where I say: "this is said regarding what is *possible*, not regarding *how it is*." I want the term "possible" to refer not only to the preceding statement about the "assumption" of the bread by Christ, but to the truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist and even to the sacrament itself; indeed, even to the presence of Christ’s body simultaneously with the assumed bread. So that perhaps it would not be necessary that, by virtue of this assumption of the bread by the incarnate Word, the bread would be the body of Christ which He already took from the Virgin along with the bread. But nevertheless, it is possible that it would be on the altar together with the bread if it were assumed by Christ. I speak, therefore, in the present conclusion about a *possible* sacrament and its *possible* truth and the *possible* presence of Christ's body together with this bread capable of being assumed. Therefore, I wonder why the present conclusion was condemned as erroneous on the grounds that the aforementioned things are false regarding the sacrament of the Eucharist as already instituted (of which they say I am speaking), when I expressly speak and profess in the conclusion regarding a *possible* sacrament and its *possible* truth. Therefore, let them consider the words of the conclusion more carefully before they condemn a conclusion that so expressly refutes the sense they are condemning. Indeed, let them consider that the determination...

## OF THE QUESTIONS

...that his own determination can hardly be defended from the charge of error. For if it were the case that the conclusion intended to preserve the truth of the sacrament according to the institution of Christ which the Church holds—as they themselves say—then it would be not only erroneous but simply heretical. However, if the meaning of the conclusion is that which I have explained, then it is not only not erroneous in faith, but indeed it is erroneous to say the opposite. For there are many things which, in terms of **actual fact** <note>original: "de sic esse"</note>, are heretical, but whose opposite, in terms of **possibility** <note>original: "de possibili"</note>, would be heretical. For example: to say that the Father was incarnated is heretical as a statement of fact; yet to say that the Father *could* be incarnated is not only not heretical, but it is heretical to claim the opposite <note>Scholastic theologians argued that while only the Son became human, all three persons of the Trinity possess the power to take on flesh.</note>. Let these things suffice for the declaration and defense of that conclusion.

But for the sake of scholastic exercise, let us set aside my conclusion and see whether it might be true that the body of Christ could be present on the altar through a different mode than the <term>conversion</term> <note>The Catholic doctrine of Transubstantiation, where the substance of bread changes into the body of Christ.</note> of the bread into Him. Specifically: through the <term>sustenance of bread-ness</term> <note>original: "substentatio paneitatis." This is the theory of "impanation," suggesting the substance of the bread remains and is "assumed" by God.</note> in the Divine Person <note>original: "supposito." A technical term for the individual substance or "personhood" of the Word.</note> alongside the assumed humanity. Thus, there would be one Person in three natures: namely, divinity, humanity, and "bread-ness." By reason of this one Person, each nature could be predicated of the other in their union—a <term>communication of properties</term> <note>original: "comunicatio idiomatum." A theological rule where the attributes of Christ's human and divine natures can both be attributed to his person (e.g., "God died" or "the man Jesus created the world").</note>—so that God is bread and man, and vice versa; and Christ as man is on the altar just as Christ as bread is on the altar, and so on. This would occur sacramentally or by the power of the sacrament, if such power were divinely given to the sacred word. We need not concern ourselves here with whether the phrase "This is my body" would suffice for this by the aforementioned power, or if it would require something else.

<margin>
John Damascene
</margin>
<margin>
First argument for the affirmative side
</margin>
First, one argues for the affirmative side that this position should be held because <note>John</note> Damascene <note>A 7th-century Syrian monk and Church Father whose "De Fide Orthodoxa" was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages.</note> seems to hold this as a matter of fact: namely, that this sacrament exists through "assumption." For he speaks thus: "And now you ask how the bread becomes the body of Christ, and the wine and water become the blood of Christ? I say to you: the Holy Spirit comes upon them and performs that which is above reason and understanding." He continues: "But the bread and wine are assumed." And further in the same place: "Just as in baptism—because it is human custom to be washed with water and anointed with oil—God joined grace and the Holy Spirit to the water and made it the bath of regeneration; so, because it is human custom to eat bread and drink wine, God joined His divinity to them and made them His body and blood." And further in the same chapter, speaking of this sacred altar, he says: "Isaiah saw a coal. But a coal is not simple wood, but wood united to fire. So also the bread of communion is not simple bread, but bread united to the divinity."

<margin>
Dionysius
</margin>
Moreover, Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential mystical theologian thought at the time to be the convert of St. Paul.</note> in the third chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* calls this sacrament an "assumption." Since these doctors seem to say this regarding the **actual fact**, it can much more easily be held regarding **possibility**.

<margin>
Second: Augustine
</margin>
Second, it is argued that—according to Augustine in his letter to Volusian—in miraculous matters, the entire reason for the deed is the power of the Doer. To thus restrict this miraculous sacrament to a determined mode of defense which is not expressly found in the canon of Scripture or the determination of the Church is to restrict the divine power to the capacity of our own intellect. This is dangerous and goes against what Augustine says in the same place: "If a reason is sought, it will not be a miracle; if an example is provided, it will not be unique. Let us grant that God can do something which we must admit we cannot investigate."

<margin>
Third
</margin>
Third, it is argued: that whose opposite is not clearly held as a matter of fact from the sayings of the saints can, much more strongly, be held as a matter of possibility. But the opposite of this—that the substance of bread remains on the altar, sustained by the Divine Person—is not clearly held from the sayings of the saints; therefore, etc.

<margin>
Gregory
</margin>
This is proved because that statement of Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (6th century).</note> in his Easter homily, saying "the appearance and likeness of those things are the names of things that were before" (namely, bread and wine), is explained by those holding this opinion as meaning "those things which were *only* bread and wine before." Now, however, they are not *only* bread, because the body of Christ is hidden there.

<margin>
Ambrose
</margin>
Likewise, the statement of Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose, 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> that "the power of God, which creates creatures from nothing, here changes the creatures," and other statements saying that bread and wine do not remain after consecration but are converted, are explained as meaning that the bread does not remain *as it was* before, even though the same "bread-ness" remains...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his thesis on the Eucharist. He is arguing that while the Church teaches "Transubstantiation" (where bread becomes Christ's body) as a matter of fact, it is logically possible for God to have chosen "Impanation" (where the Word of God assumes the nature of bread). He uses historical confessions and the writings of Peter Lombard to support the logical consistency of his view.</meta>

<header>DEFENSE</header>

# ## DEFENSE

another person <note>original: "suppositum"; in scholastic philosophy, this refers to an individual substance or person that acts as the subject of properties</note>. However, this word "bread" signifies a person in the nature of bread-ness, and this does not remain. Yet there is a great difference between saying that the bread-ness remains **hypostatized** <note>personally united to the Divine Word</note> in the divine person, and saying that the bread-ness remains in its own proper person. This is because, in this second way, there would be no **communication of properties** <note>original: "communicatio idiomatum"; the theological principle where attributes of one nature, like humanity, are predicated of the person, like the Word of God</note>, which does occur in the first way. I entirely believe that these authorities are against those who propose such things as a matter of **actual fact** and of **how things are**, and not merely as a matter of **possibility**. <margin>Fourth</margin> Fourth, it is argued as follows:

This opinion—regarding "how things are"—is approved in the confession of **Berengarius** <note>Berengar of Tours (d. 1088), a theologian who was forced to recant his views on the Eucharist and affirm a very literal, physical presence of Christ</note>, which was approved by Pope Nicholas in Rome before 114 bishops. Therefore, it can much more easily be held as a matter of **possibility**. The premise is deduced thus: <margin>Berengarius</margin> Because Berengarius confesses that after the consecration, there is not only the sacrament, but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ on the altar. He confesses that it is handled by the hands of the priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful, **sensually**, not only sacramentally, but in truth. These words seem impossible to accept in a clear and unencumbered sense—as the words of a confession so solemnly approved ought to be—unless by the **sustenance of bread-ness** in the person of God along with the body of Christ in the aforementioned manner. 

Thus, it would be the same body of Christ, of the man, and of the bread. It would be whole insofar as it is the body of a man, and ground insofar as it is bread; just as Christ on the cross died and yet lived, but he died as a man and lived as God. That some have understood the words of the aforementioned confession in this way is clear from the **Master of the Sentences** in Book 4, Distinction 12. <margin>Master of the Sentences</margin> <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose "Sentences" was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages</note> His words are these: 

*Others hand down that the body of Christ is essentially broken and divided, yet remains whole and incorruptible. They assert that they gather this from the confession of Berengarius, who confessed before Pope Nicholas and many bishops that the bread and wine placed on the altar after consecration are not only the sacrament, but also the true body and blood of Christ; and that they are sensually, not only in the sacred rite but also in truth, handled by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful.*

Behold, the confession of Berengarius, heard and examined by the Church, contains the idea that the body of Christ is ground by the teeth of the faithful not only in the sacred rite, but in truth. This, if taken plainly, would have truth through the **communication of properties**; for it is ground by the teeth according to the bread-ness, and remains whole according to the humanity. 

If someone wishes to explain the said confession by saying that the phrase **in truth** and **not in the sacrament only** refers only to the immediate verb—that is, "handled by the hands of the priests"—and the following words refer to the **species** <note>the outward appearances of bread and wine</note> or the external sacrament (under which, when broken and ground, the whole body of Christ is received), it seems they are not accepting the words of the confession plainly as they lie and as they sound on the surface. Yet the words of a confession so examined ought to be accepted without violent interpretation and extortion, according to the sense they make openly. 

<margin>The first argument for the opposite. Primary reasoning.</margin> But it is argued to the contrary because this opinion—that the substance of bread remains on the altar—is condemned by the Church; therefore it must be avoided as heretical. Those who hold this opinion respond to this first: that it was condemned as a matter of **how things are**, not as a matter of **possibility**. <margin>Second</margin> Second, the condemned opinion differs from this one, which posits that the bread-ness remains **hypostatized** <note>united in one person</note> by the Word-man. <margin>Differences between this opinion and the condemned opinion</margin> For that condemned opinion posits that after the consecration there are multiple **persons**—of the man Christ and of the bread. This view posits one person in three natures, just as in the Divine Trinity there is one nature in three persons. That view posits that the substance of bread remains after the consecration; this view, however, does not posit it remaining by way of **substance**, but by way of **accident** <note>in this context, an assumed quality</note>, just as it is with the assumed humanity. That view posits that the bread and wine remain; this view does not, but rather says it is a *different* bread, even though it is the same bread-ness. From that view, it follows that the body of Christ cannot truly be in the altar under the sacrament, since the bread is changed in nothing. But from this view, it does not follow, since it posits the bread is changed even in its bread-ness as far as its **being** <note>existence</note> is concerned. From that view, the statement "the bread is the body of Christ" is not verified, since there are two persons. From this view, it is verified due to the unity of the person, which is one in two natures. From that view, it follows that whatever is in this sacrament is not to be adored with **latria** <note>the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone</note>, since there are two persons of Christ and the bread. This...

<summary>Pico argues that his theory of "Impanation" (the Word assuming the nature of bread) is logically consistent with historical Church confessions, specifically the realism of Berengarius's recantation. He distinguishes his view from condemned heresies by emphasizing that he is discussing divine possibility and the personal union of natures, not the simultaneous existence of two separate substances.</summary>

<header>OF DISPUTED QUESTIONS</header>

# ## OF DISPUTED QUESTIONS

bread: this indeed posits that it is to be adored with a single act of adoration <note>original: "unica adoratione"; refers to *latria*, the highest form of worship reserved for God alone</note>: whatever is under the sacred [species] because of the unity of the **subject** <note>original: "suppositi"; the underlying person or substance that possesses the nature</note>.

<margin>Second</margin> Secondly, it is argued that it can in no way be maintained that the body of Christ could be on the altar through that mode. For when it is asked whether the body of Christ can be on the altar, etc., it is not understood as the "body" which is Christ himself and is taken as a **genus** <note>In scholastic logic, "body" can mean a general category of being (a physical substance) or a specific anatomical "part"</note>. Rather, it is understood as the "body" which is a **part** and is not predicated of the man in the direct sense. Such a body, which is a part, does not share the **properties** <note>original: "idioma"; the specific characteristics or attributes of a nature</note> of the nature assumed with it, neither to the subject nor vice versa. For although God is man and vice versa, nevertheless God is not the "head of Christ" and vice versa. And although Christ as man is everywhere by reason of the divine subject, nevertheless the head of Christ as man is not everywhere, because the parts of the assumed nature do not communicate their properties to the subject, nor are they predicated of it, or vice versa. ¶ Therefore, although "bread-ness" <note>original: "paneitas"; the essential nature of bread</note> might be assumed by the Word along with "body-ness," it still could not be said that the body of Christ *is* bread, or that the body of Christ is on the altar simply because bread is on the altar. This is so even though it could be said and verified that the bread is the "body" which is Christ, according to the sense in which "body" is taken as a general category. ¶ That it is not understood otherwise in this question and in the sacrament is apparent: both because the "body-as-genus" which is predicated directly of Christ is not called the "body of Christ"—just as the animal or man that Christ is, is not called the "animal of Christ" or "man of Christ"—and because the form of words in which this sacrament was instituted is this: **This is my body.** It is certain that the truth of that word is not preserved if "body" refers to the general category. For the animal which is predicated of me in the direct sense is not "my animal," but rather the animal that I am. Furthermore, if the sacrament had been consecrated during the three days of Christ’s death, there would have been on the altar not the "body-as-genus," but only the "body-as-part." For a "body" [in the general sense] is an animated body, which he was not then. Therefore, the body of Christ as it is asked here, and which is dealt with in the sacrament, is the "body-as-part" only, which is not predicated of the bread, or of God, or of man. Nor does it share the properties of other natures. Therefore, it would not be true to say that the body of Christ was on the altar in the aforementioned way by reason of the bread or the subject.

<margin>Third</margin> Furthermore, granted that by reason of the said **sustentification** <note>original: "substentificationis"; the act of a subject providing existence/support to a nature</note> in a single subject the bread were the body: nevertheless, it would not follow that wherever the bread is on the altar, there is the body of Christ. Rather, the bread on the altar would be the body of Christ which is in heaven—just as during the three days [of death] the soul and body were sustained in the subject [of the Word], yet because of this, the soul was not in the tomb with the body, nor the body in hell with the soul.

<margin>Fourth</margin> Furthermore, if there were this sustentification, it would terminate at that which we say the conversion of the bread terminates—namely, the body of Christ. But the sustentification of a foreign nature cannot terminate at that. For this is proper to the uncreated subject alone according to the common way. Therefore, the sustentification of "bread-ness" in the subject of another nature cannot happen in this sacrament.

<margin>Fifth</margin> Likewise, it is argued thus: because according to the aforementioned mode of the sustentification of "bread-ness" in the Word together with the body of Christ assumed long ago, the body would not *begin* to be on the altar; rather, something new would begin to be the body of Christ.

<margin>Sixth</margin> If, however, it does not "begin," since it was not there before, it follows that it will not be on the altar. Likewise, it is argued that although the subject of the Word could assume "bread-ness" (which in assuming it, he would create, as we hold regarding the humanity of Christ), nevertheless he cannot assume a "bread-ness" already existing in its own proper subject; for this would be to destroy the bread-ness, not to assume it.

<margin>Seventh</margin> Furthermore, it is argued that power cannot be conferred upon the Word regarding the union of "bread-ness" to the Word, because the assumption of bread-ness into the subject of the Word is of greater difficulty than creation. This is because divine being is more distant from the nature of bread-ness (to which it is said to be communicated in assumption) than being is from non-being. And yet <margin>Thomas</margin> the power of creation cannot be communicated to a creature by operating or cooperating; therefore, neither can the power of assumption.

<margin>Eighth</margin> This is confirmed by the authority of **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in the third part [of the *Summa Theologiae*], who says that a creature cannot cooperate toward the [hypostatic] union.

<margin>Ninth</margin> Furthermore, that being granted, after the consumption of the sacred...

<summary>Pico presents a series of scholastic objections to the theory of "Impanation," arguing that logically and theologically, the "body" present in the Eucharist is a specific part of Christ's nature, not a general category that could simply be applied to assumed bread. He cites St. Thomas Aquinas to argue that a creaturely nature (like bread) cannot cooperate in being personally united to the Divine Word.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense regarding the Eucharist. He is addressing scholastic objections to his theory that the substance of bread could potentially be "assumed" by the Divine Word (the Son of God) rather than being entirely destroyed or converted, similar to how the Word assumed human nature.</meta>

-># APOLOGIA<-

<margin>Response to the second opposing argument</margin>
...[the priest] would not be fasting and there would be not only spiritual food there, but also physical food, which is contrary to the dignity of the sacrament. Also, Christ would "dismiss" or let go of something after he had assumed it into the unity of the **subject** <note>original: "suppositi"; in scholastic theology, this refers to the underlying person (the Word) who "owns" or sustains a nature</note>, because he would assume the **bread-ness** <note>original: "paneitatem"; the essential essence of bread</note> which he would then let go of once the bread was converted into his limbs. To these points, however, it might perhaps be said first—saving the claim that it is possible for Christ’s body to be on the altar without the conversion of the bread in the aforementioned way—by the **substentification** <note>original: "substentificationem"; the act of the Divine Word providing the "standing-under" or existence for the bread's nature</note> of the bread-ness in the Word, together with the humanity long ago assumed. This is from the "body" as it is a **genus** <note>a general category of physical substance</note>, not as it is a **part** <note>an anatomical limb or piece</note>; and thus regarding the "body" which is Christ, it is derived from "corporeity" which is a nature and can be predicated in the nominative. And when it is argued that the body of Christ would not be spoken of as a "body as a genus," it is replied that, on the contrary, it would be. Just as we speak of the "creature of salt," that is, that which is salt; and the "Word of God," that is, that which is God; just as it is said, "By the Word of the Lord"—that is, by the Word who is God—"the heavens were made" <note>A reference to Psalm 33:6</note>. And we say the substance of matter remains through every natural transformation—that is, the substance which *is* matter. Just as it is also said by our opponents that the substance of bread is converted into the body of Christ—specifically the substance which *is* bread, not that which is a *part* of bread.

<margin>Damascene</margin>
Thus also John of Damascus <note>An 8th-century Church Father</note> in Book IV, chapter 17, takes "Christ’s flesh"—that is, the flesh which *is* Christ—as a **genus**, saying that the Lord's flesh is said to be "deified" and **consubstantial** <note>of the same essential substance</note> with God. And when it is argued that the form of the words would not be fitting—since "This is my body" would mean "This body is a part of me"—it would be replied that perhaps it is not achieved through such a form of words, and perhaps a sacramental power would be given by God to any word whatsoever. And perhaps also, every power that God could give to any word, he could give to this word: "This is my body" <note>original: "Hoc est corpus meum"</note>, or even to a non-significant word, by his **absolute power** <note>the theological concept of "potentia absoluta," referring to what God can do by his sheer might, regardless of the current laws of nature</note>, because the power of God is not restricted to the linguistic meaning of words.

<margin>Response to the third</margin>
And when it is argued that, even granted that bread is the body and vice versa, it still does not follow that where the bread is, there the body is on the altar; it is replied that, on the contrary, it does follow. For whatever is said of the predicate is also said of the subject. For because God is man and God is everywhere, it follows that the man Christ is everywhere just as God is; and that God is enclosed in the cradle, and is the son of the Virgin, and sucks the breasts just as the man Christ does. Thus it follows that if the man Christ is bread and vice versa, if the bread is on the altar, then the man Christ is there too—not only by the reason that he is everywhere insofar as he is God, but because the bread is on the altar. For the **properties** <note>original: "idiomata"; the specific attributes of a nature, such as "mortality" for humanity or "omnipresence" for divinity</note> of the assumed natures are shared on the part of the subject, especially because in the subject it is held as the person. It is said "on the part of the subject" because on the part of the predicate, the properties are perhaps not necessarily shared, because there it is held as the "nature." Hence, perhaps it is not necessary that Christ-as-man be everywhere, even though he is God-everywhere; although on the part of the subject, the man Christ is everywhere. Nor is the argument valid regarding the soul and body during the three days [of Christ's death], because they were not so united in the person that they were predicated of the person or of each other, since they were united as parts of a single nature. Therefore, it is not necessary for them to share properties among themselves like those natures which are spoken of in relation to each other.

<margin>Responses to the fourth</margin>
It is certain that if it does not follow by necessity, it follows at least by possibility. As for the claim that if there is a **substentification** of bread-ness, it must terminate at that at which we say "conversion" terminates—namely, the body—it is replied that this has no necessity. Rather, we can say that the "sustenance" happens in the **subject** <note>the person of the Word</note> simply, even though those who posit "conversion" say it terminates at the "body" as a part. It could also perhaps be said, as will be discussed below, that substentification can terminate at the body not as "human" but as "united." For if the divine subject can sustain another nature in itself insofar as it draws that nature to its own being, then to whichever nature it communicates its infinite being, it could also communicate the ability to sustain another nature united to itself in that same being. More on this below.

<margin>Response to the fifth</margin>
When it is objected that according to this mode, the body of Christ would not "begin" to be on the altar, but rather something would "begin" to be the body of Christ or the body-Christ; it would be said that just as if bread-ness were to come to Christ (who was already man), Christ-the-man would "begin" to be bread. Thus, he begins to be on the altar in a new way **accidentally** <note>original: "per accidens"; a change in circumstance or attribute rather than a change in core essence</note>, because what happens to the bread itself begins to happen to Christ-the-man.

<summary>Pico defends the possibility of Christ being present in the Eucharist through "substentification," where the Divine Word sustains the nature of bread rather than destroying it. He uses the doctrine of the communication of properties to explain how the attributes of bread and Christ could be shared through their union in a single divine person.</summary>

# QUESTIONS

...[Christ] as man is visibly on the altar, and as the food of the faithful by reason of the assumed **bread-ness** <note>original: "paneitatis"; the essential substance or "being-bread" of the host</note>, just as Christ as God began to be in the womb or uterus of his mother in a new way by reason of the assumed humanity. Regarding what is said about the assumption of a pre-existing bread-ness in its own **subject** <note>original: "supposito"; in scholastic terms, the individual "person" or foundation that "owns" a nature</note>: 
<margin>Response to the sixth proper [argument].</margin>
It is replied that God can assume every assumable nature that pre-exists in its own subject and, in the act of assumption, deprive it of its own subject-hood and draw it into His own being. For it is certain that the Word could let go of human nature, which would immediately have its own personal subsistence and the character of a subject and person—even though it does not have this while united to the Word—and it would be the same humanity in essence that was previously united. Therefore, He could in a similar way assume a humanity previously existing in its own subject in the manner just stated, and it would be the same nature now assumed that was previously not assumed. When, however, it is argued that 
<margin>Response to the seventh.</margin>
a power cannot be conferred upon the [sacramental] word for this purpose, perhaps it can and perhaps it cannot. And if an inherent power cannot be given because such a power would be created, perhaps an "assistant" power can be given because such would be uncreated and not created. In this way, there would be a sacramental assumption of the bread-ness by the power of the Word, in the same way that great men <note>likely referring to Thomas Aquinas or Bonaventure</note> posit that power is conferred upon the sacraments of the New Law. And perhaps if an inherent power can be conferred upon the sacramental word to convert the whole [of the bread] into the whole [of Christ]—and especially into that which pre-exists without increasing it—it can also be conferred for the aforementioned effect; for it might seem to someone that this is of the same level of difficulty as the other. 

Regarding what is said about the breaking of the **fast** <note>The "natural fast" required of a priest before Mass</note>: 
<margin>Responses to the eighth</margin>
one might respond that the rule about not breaking the natural fast follows the commonly held view, namely, that the substance of bread does not remain. But if we posit that the substance remains, we shall say something else; or perhaps it will be said that a priest is not called "fasting" after receiving the host not because the substance of bread is absent—for however much the substance of bread is not there, if a Jew or a Christian were to consume the sacramental species as physical food and with the intention of eating, they would break the fast—but rather because the priest does not receive it as physical food, but as a sacrament. Therefore the fast is not broken. And it would be similar if the substance of bread remained: he would still not break the natural fast, provided it was not received as physical food. 

As for the claim that Christ 
<margin>Responses to the ninth</margin>
does not let go of what He has once assumed, this is said by presupposing that He is held to have assumed only human nature, just as in fact He assumed only that. However, He could assume another nature and let it go. It can also be said that if bread-ness were assumed by the Word, He would never let it go of His own accord and on His own part; but "accidentally," due to the condition of the assumed nature with its natural defects, He would let it go because of the corruption of the assumed nature—just as He "let go" of His humanity during the three days [in the tomb]. 

But let us inquire again through disputation whether the 
<margin>Argument for the affirmative part.</margin>
body, which is a part of existence, can truly be on the altar without the conversion of the bread into it. And it seems so: because just as color is sustained in a substance as in a subject by means of another **accident** <note>a quality or property that does not exist by itself but in something else</note>—for example, a surface—not indeed that the surface is the "subject" of the color (for one accident is not the subject of another, because, as is said by **the Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note>, "there is no quality of a quality"), but because color does not exist in a subject except in relation to the surface; so bread-ness can be sustained in the Word by means of the body. Not indeed that the body is the immediate sustainer and "grounder" of the assumed bread-ness and the Word the first, but because bread-ness is not sustained in the subject of the Word except in relation to the body of Christ as a part. For God can establish this order between assumable natures, even if they do not have that order in their own nature, just as He can take away from some things the natural order they have among themselves—as He did between heat and the act of heating in the **furnace of the Chaldeans** <note>A biblical reference to the Book of Daniel, where the fire did not burn the three youths</note> and in many other cases. Therefore, just as color, because it exists in a substance in relation to the surface, is spoken of as the surface in a "concrete" sense, in the manner of an accidental quality...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his "third way" regarding the Eucharist. Having previously discussed how the Word of God might assume the nature of bread, he now explores the metaphysical mechanics of how "bread-ness" and the "Body of Christ" relate to one another, using the philosophical framework of subjects and accidents.</meta>

# DEFENSE

<meta>Catchword: But if</meta>
<meta>Signature: ij g</meta>

By saying a surface is colored, so the **bread-ness** <note>original: "paneitas"; the essential quality that makes bread what it is</note> which is the substance will be said of the **body of Christ** taken in its concrete sense through the mode of a quality—or in the same way that we say the Son of God is bread and vice versa. This is just as humanity is spoken of regarding the **subject** <note>original: "supposito"; the underlying person or foundation of a nature</note> when we say the Son of God is man and vice versa. Therefore, just as God is man and vice versa, they share their **attributes** <note>original: "idiomata"; the theological concept where the properties of the divine and human natures are both attributed to the one person of Christ</note> so that where God is, there is man; and similarly regarding the surface and the white color, so it is with the bread and the body.

<margin>
The dogma
of the
ancient
theologians
</margin>
For if the bread is on the altar, the body of Christ is on the altar. Perhaps it should be stated differently: that the assumed natures have the mode of an **accident** <note>original: "accidentis"; a non-essential quality that exists within a substance, like color in an apple</note> as the ancient theologians used to say, insofar as they come to a subject already subsisting in act and do not constitute that subject themselves, but are rather constituted in being through it. Just as among accidents one being is found to be the subject of another (though not in the ultimate sense)—as we say the power of the soul is the subject of virtues and habits insofar as it is sustained by the soul, and similarly a surface is said in some way to be the subject of color—so although one assumed nature cannot by itself and primarily sustain another nature, nevertheless, insofar as it is united to the **Word** <note>the Logos or Son of God</note> and sustained in Him, it can sustain another nature in itself. It can have the mode of a subject in respect to that other nature, and the other can have the mode of an accident in respect to it, solely in this regard: that one is sustained in the other as it is united to the Word and sustained by Him. For if the subject does not give subsistence to the assumed nature except by reason of its own infinite being (to which it draws the nature united to it), then to whatever nature it communicates its infinite being, it also communicates the power to sustain another nature united to it.

<margin>
In what
way an
accident is
called a
being
</margin>
Thus also substance, insofar as it draws an accident to its own being—because an accident is not a "being" except because it belongs to a "being"—gives it enough so that it can sustain another accident coming to it (as an act coming to a potentiality) within itself and within its own being. Therefore, the Body, accepted as a part that is united and sustained by the Word in its own being (which is the being of the Word communicated to it), can give subsistence within itself to the nature of the bread which is capable of being assumed and which has the mode of an accident. For this is assumed: that just as God gives to accidents the mode of a substance, so He can give to bread-ness the mode of an accident by sustaining it in another thing which will relate to it as a subject. Nor does it differ in this regard whether that thing is perfect in its species or not, because sometimes the subject of an accident is imperfect in its species, such as a head or a hand. Just as God produces some creatures immediately and others through the mediation of others, and just as He terminates some creatures in Himself as their end through others, so also can the Word terminate a creature in Himself as the sustaining subject through the mediation of another creature. And just as the creatures through which God produces things are called "producers," and the creatures through which He terminates things in Himself as an end are called "ends" or "sub-ends," so the creature through which the Word gives subsistence to another will be said to "give subsistence." By reason, therefore, of such subsistence-giving in the body of Christ as a "quasi-subject" and immediate support, it will be said in a concrete sense that "the bread is the body" and vice versa, just as "the Son of God is man" and vice versa. And they will share their attributes in the manner previously described, like a surface and that which is colored.

<margin>
Aristotle.
Damascene.
</margin>
For "bread" stands for that which supports bread-ness, just as "white" stands for that which supports whiteness. For just as the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Topics* that "white" is a body having such a color, so **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian</note> says in Book III, Chapter 11, that "God" is He who has the divine nature, and "man" is he who has the human nature, and so on for the rest. And just as it makes no difference to something being "white" whether the thing in which the whiteness is sustained is perfect in its species or not, so it makes no difference to something being called "bread" whether that which is the bread-ness—that is, the "quasi-subject" in which the bread-ness is immediately given subsistence—is perfect in its species or imperfect, whether it is a whole nature or a part of a nature.

<margin>
Doubt
</margin>
**On the contrary**: because an assumed nature (or a part of an assumed nature) does not have the character of a subject, nor does it have the being of subsistence in itself. Because although the being of the Word is communicated to it, nevertheless, as it belongs to the nature, it is not the being of subsistence, but of existence in another. Therefore, an assumed nature, as it is united, cannot sustain another nature in itself, nor draw it to the subject, since it does not itself have the character of a subject.

<summary>Pico argues that the Body of Christ can act as a "subject" that sustains the "bread-ness" of the Eucharist, much like a surface sustains color, allowing the two to share attributes. He supports this by citing Aristotle and John of Damascus while addressing the metaphysical difficulty of one nature supporting another.</summary>

But against this, it is still argued: the Word assumed flesh by means of the soul <note>original: "mediante anima"</note>; yet because of this, the soul is not said of the flesh, nor vice versa. <meta>This page continues the scholastic defense of the "Assumption" theory of the Eucharist (the idea that Christ assumes the bread) as an alternative to "Conversion" (transubstantiation). # APOLOGY

<margin>Fourth</margin>
<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>Fifth</margin>
...[things are done] without a multiplication of miracles. **Fourth**, because of what **Paul** says in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 10: "The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord?" <note>original: "Panis que frāgimus nōne participatīo corporis dñi est."</note> **Fifth**, because Christ is sacramentally present where he is directly through the power of the sacrament. But Christ becomes present on the altar more directly through **assumption** <note>the act of a divine person taking a nature to himself</note> than through **conversion**: because the "form" <note>the spoken words</note> of this sacrament, which works by signifying, more directly effects that which it more properly signifies. And this is the union through assumption, by which the **communication of properties** <note>original: "cōicant idiomata"; a theological term meaning that the attributes of the assumed nature can be spoken of as belonging to the person</note> occurs, so that "This is my body" sounds exactly like what the formal words mean. This is not the case with a union of conversion: because through conversion, the bread is not Christ, nor vice versa; rather, the bread *becomes*

<margin>Sixth</margin>
Christ or is *converted* into Christ. **Sixth**, because that method of conversion is intricate and holds many difficulties; this method, however, is clear and straightforward. For we already believe in **Assumption** through another article of faith <note>the Incarnation, where God became man</note>. Whatever things are identical in their **subject** <note>original: "supposito"; the individual person or thing in which properties exist</note> are limited such that wherever one is, the other is also. Just as wherever there is loud music, there is also the "whiteness" of the musician <note>a standard medieval example: qualities of the same person exist in the same place</note>. I say "limited" because if one were limited and the other unlimited, where the limited was, the unlimited would be, but not necessarily vice versa. But if the bread were assumed, the human body of Christ and the body of the bread would be one in their **subject**, and both would be limited. Therefore, since the assumed bread would be on the altar, the body of Christ would consequently be there as well. Likewise, the medium is closer than the extreme. But if Christ were to assume the bread or **bread-ness** <note>original: "paneitatem"; the essence of being bread</note>, he would do this by means of his own bodiliness: because a less worthy thing to be assumed is taken up by means of a worthier thing, according to the fitness of assumption. Therefore, since the **subject** of Christ which assumes would be on the altar with the assumed bread, much 

<margin>Finally</margin>
more so would the body of Christ be there, which would be the "medium" of the assumption. **Finally**, it seems that the authorities of the holy Fathers regarding "conversion" can nonetheless be upheld while holding to "assumption": since **being** <note>original: "esse"; existence</note> differs from **essence**, one can be assumed while the other is not. Thus, the Word "impaneated" <note>original: "inpaneatum"; the Word becoming bread</note> is not exactly like the Word "incarnated" <note>the Word becoming flesh</note>, because in that [human] assumption, the essence was assumed before it had its own being. Hence, the human nature never had a "being" other than the divine being communicated to it, which is why that was an assumption without any conversion of the assumed into the assuming, or vice versa. Thus the Church says "not by conversion of the divinity into flesh," and nor—supply the opposite—"vice versa," but by "the assumption of humanity into God." Pre-existing bread has both **being** and **essence**, and the assumption into the **subject** of the person consumes its own independent existence—not through **annihilation**, but by the assumption of the substantial essence, they fulfill this mystery. And so, all authorities speaking of **transubstantiation** and **conversion** can be referred to the "being" and not the "essence." Authorities saying that after the consecration "bread does not remain" are correct regarding its **being** <note>its independent existence</note>: because it remains only according to its **essence**. From these points, it seems that the body of Christ can just as truly be sacramentally on the altar without conversion, through the assumption of bread-ness, as is now commonly held through conversion; indeed, regarding these terms:

<margin>Assumption.</margin>
<margin>Annihilation.</margin>
<margin>Conversion</margin>
...**assumption**, **conversion**, and **annihilation**, a good distinction cannot be understood except by presupposing the method of this opinion. We say that something is **assumed** which, having previously had its own independent existence, is taken into a new **subject**. That is **annihilated** which simply ceases to be, such that its reproduction would be a new creation; it is entirely irrelevant to this whether something succeeds it or nothing succeeds it, because that is entirely external to the thing which ceases to be. However, that thing is **converted** which, remaining according to its **essence**, loses its own independent **being** and passes into the **being** of another subject, and truly becomes that subject. And this is the true logic of conversion, in which two things are understood in the thing converted: first, that it remains through its essence (and by this it differs from what is **annihilated**); and second, that it becomes something else

<margin>Logic of conversion</margin>
by reason of the **subject** (by which it differs from what is **not converted**). And while it becomes another by reason of the subject, it sets aside its own subject-hood, and by this it differs from what is **assumed**. However, if one holds the common method of conversion, the bread is not converted, but rather **annihilated**. And those who do not wish to preserve...

It defines key metaphysical terms—assumption, conversion, and annihilation—to show how Christ can be present without the bread's essence being destroyed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate between "Conversion" (transubstantiation) and "Assumption" (the idea that Christ assumes the bread as a new nature). # OF QUESTIONS

...saving [the bread] so that there is a conversion rather than an annihilation seems to satisfy words rather than reality. Wherefore many from that school of thought granted that it is an annihilation, etc.

<margin>The first argument of Durandus for the [other] side</margin>
On the opposite side, for the true part, it is argued that the opinion positing that the sacrament of the Eucharist is actually completed through the **assumption** <note>The theological concept where a divine person takes a nature to himself, as in the Incarnation</note> of the bread is inconvenient and irrational. First, **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a famous Dominican philosopher and theologian known for his independent thought</note> argues thus: that it is ridiculous that every day one nature—indeed many—should be assumed by a divine **person** <note>original: "supposito"; the underlying subject or personhood</note> and then put down every day. This would be the case if the substance of bread were newly assumed in this sacrament; for there would be as many assumptions as there are consecrations, and as many depositions as there are takings of the sacrament. But perhaps this "ridiculousness" does not demonstrate the falsehood of the premise.

<margin>Second</margin>
Second, it is argued because it seems impossible that such an assumption could happen by means of something created, as the aforementioned opinion posits. For that medium either behaves as the **efficient cause** <note>the agent that brings something about</note> of such an assumption or as the **terminating** <note>the end point or sustainer</note> cause. But nothing created can relate to an assumption in either of these ways; therefore, etc. The minor premise is proven: that nothing created can be the efficient cause of such an assumption is clear, because such an assumption happens by a thing losing its own natural way of being and putting on another. This, it seems, can be done by no one except the Author of Nature, who alone instituted the natures of things; thus, He alone seems able to change them.

<margin>Response</margin>
This argument of Durandus perhaps shows that a created thing cannot be the primary efficient cause. By the same logic, it seems that nothing created can "terminate" such an assumption, because nothing can be granted to a nature that is above nature and the entire course of nature. This [act], however, is to give **substantial existence** <note>original: "substātificare"; to provide the foundation for a thing's existence</note> to another nature that is born to subsist in itself. And perhaps this erroneous opinion mentioned above would think it avoids [this] through certain points mentioned earlier. Indeed, a falsehood is not always easily convinced of its own falsity through evident reasons; the light of our intellect is so weak, being the very last in the order of intellectual natures.

<margin>Third: Saying man is from body and soul; the former by way of definition, but from the body, etc., in reality</margin>
Furthermore, Durandus argues as follows: whatever may be said of the position of such an assumption, it is nonetheless entirely inconvenient that it should happen by means of the **body-as-part** <note>the idea that the "body" is just one component of the human being, rather than the whole person</note>. For the body, when taken as a part of human nature—assuming there is only one **form** <note>the soul or organizing principle</note> in a human—cannot name matter alone. Instead, it must necessarily name the composite of matter and the form that gives "bodily-being." It is necessary that the human body refers to the whole in reality, and not just a part; although according to reason it can name a part because the soul gives all the perfections that lower forms give. And therefore, if one considers the composite of matter and form (which is the soul) insofar as it gives bodily-being only, and compares it to that same composite insofar as it has not only bodily-being through the soul but also sense, life, and reason: then the "body" in the first sense is taken as a part, and in the second sense as a whole. But since this difference is only a **distinction of reason** <note>a mental distinction rather than a physical one</note>, it does not support their proposal when they say a real assumption of bread happens by means of the "body-as-part." A distinction of reason does nothing for the distinction of a real assumption.

<margin>Response</margin>
Whatever may be the case regarding the effectiveness of this argument against those who posit a single form, it is clear that it does not proceed against those who do not hold to a single form.

<margin>Fourth</margin>
Likewise, he argues thus: this position fails in that it posits that through such an assumption, the body of Christ taken from the Virgin is in this sacrament through the **communication of properties** <note>original: "cōicationē idiomatū"; a doctrine where attributes of one nature are predicated of the whole person</note>, because one is predicated of the other. For by the same reasoning that the body of Christ would be in the sacrament of the altar through the assumption of the substance of bread, by that same reasoning the blood would be in this sacrament through the assumption of the substance of wine. But this is not true, as will be proven; therefore, etc. The premise is proven: for if the blood of Christ were in this sacrament through the assumption of the substance of wine, just as it is posited for the body of Christ through the assumption of the substance of bread, then it would be necessary that just as bread is assumed by means of the body (which belongs to the unity of the assuming **person** <note>original: "supposito"</note>), so wine would be assumed by means of the blood belonging to the unity of the person. But it is well known that the blood of Christ does not belong to the identity of Christ's person, since blood is not yet under the "human form," but is a **humor** <note>original: "humor"; in medieval medicine, a fluid that has not yet been fully transformed into the specific tissue of the body</note> on the way to conversion so that it may come under the human form. Therefore, it [the wine] cannot be assumed by the person of Christ by means of the blood.
