# DEFENSE
Page 70

<margin>Response</margin>
...unless perhaps you were to say that in any consecration of this sacrament there was an **assumption** <note>The act of a divine person taking a nature to himself</note> of Christ's blood immediately, and an assumption of the wine mediated through the blood. In this way, every day there would be an assumption of a new nature—namely, the blood—without any relationship to the assumed nature of the bread (which others deny), and through that [blood] there would be an assumption of the wine. But in this, perhaps many would not only reject **Durandus's** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, the theologian whose arguments are being analyzed</note> reasoning, but would rebuke him no less than the aforementioned opinion. That is, regarding the non-assumption and the lack of a **hypostatic union** <note>The union of divine and human natures in the one person of Christ</note> of the blood of Christ shed on the cross and presented in the sacrament to the **person** <note>original: "suppositum"; the individual substance of a rational nature</note> of the Son. For according to this, that blood would not have been a sufficient price for the redemption of the human race, since it would not have been united to the hypostatic divinity. 

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
Wherefore **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Catholic theologian</note> in his *Miscellaneous Questions* <note>original: "vi. quolibet. q. vi."; referring to his Quodlibetal Questions</note> says: "The blood of Christ shed in the Passion sanctified the human race," according to the last chapter of Hebrews: *Jesus, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.* Also, the humanity of Christ held a life-giving power 

<margin>Damascene</margin>
from the power of the **Word** <note>The Logos, the second person of the Trinity</note> united to it, as **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Church Father who wrote "On the Orthodox Faith"</note> says in his fourth book. From this it is manifest that the blood shed in the Passion, which was the greatest means of salvation, was united to the divinity. And therefore it was necessary 

<margin>Another argument of Durandus</margin>
that in the Resurrection it be joined to the other parts of his humanity, etc. These are his words. **Durandus** follows against the aforementioned position because the body of Christ is on the altar or in the sacrament of the altar through the true existence of its own nature, and not solely because of the **communication of properties** <note>original: "comicatione idiomatũ" (communicatio idiomatum); a theological principle where properties of the human nature are attributed to the divine person and vice versa</note> as this opinion posits. This is clear because a [demonstrative pronoun] always refers to the same numerical thing that preceded it. But Christ, instituting this sacrament, spoke these words in Luke 22: *This is my body which will be given for you,* etc. And *This cup in my blood which will be shed for you.* Therefore, it is that same numerical body which was afterward given to the apostles in the sacrament to be eaten. But the body which was given to be crucified was not of the nature of bread, but was the body belonging to the nature of humanity. Therefore, the body given to the apostles in the sacrament of the altar was truly of the nature of humanity; and by the same reasoning, in our sacrament, the body of Christ is present belonging to his humanity, and it is not there solely through the **communication of properties** 

<margin>Removal of an objection</margin>
arising from the assumption of "bread-ness." Now, if someone should say that the relative pronoun refers to the same thing according to the **person** <note>supposito</note> and not the same according to the **nature**, and thus it could be said—having pointed to the assumed bread—"This is my body which will be given for you," because it is the same person who possesses the assumed "bread-ness" and the "body-ness" later given up [on the cross]; and thus the same person was first pointed out and then given up, even if according to different natures—this is not valid. Because when it is said, "This is my body," "body" cannot be taken there for the person possessing "body-ness," but rather for the **nature** possessed, as noted by the possessive pronoun added to it when it is said *my body*; this is that which I 

<margin>Response</margin>
possess. But perhaps this [argument] would have greater efficacy among grammarians than among theologians. 

<margin>Another argument of Durandus</margin>
Furthermore, he argues thus: the said "assumption" does not suffice for the body of Christ to be on the altar either **really** or according to the **communication of properties**. Not really, because the assumption of two natures by one person does not suffice for one nature to be where the other is. For if the person of the Son had from the beginning assumed the humanity of Peter in Rome and of Paul in Judea, it would not follow that where Peter was, there Paul would be, and vice versa—except in regards to the **person**, which is predicated of both, and of whom both are predicated in the concrete. Similarly, granted that the person of the Son assumed humanity and "bread-ness," it does not follow that where the nature of bread is, there the nature of humanity must be. Nor by reason of the person could it be said that where the bread is, there the body of Christ is on account of the **communication of properties**; because according to that opinion, the name of the person does not receive the predication of the assumed bread nor the parts of the body. For it is not true to say, according to them, that the Son of God is "bread" or a "body" (which is a part). Therefore, by reason of a common person, one cannot be predicated of the other so that it is said one is the other, or one is where the other is. Nor is it similar to the case of an Ethiopian's tooth and his whiteness <note>A classic logic puzzle: an Ethiopian is black, but his teeth are white; this does not make the "black man white" in total</note>.

It also uses St. Thomas Aquinas and John of Damascus to emphasize that the blood in the sacrament must be the same blood shed for salvation on the Cross.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the "Assumption" theory of the Eucharist. The previous page discussed whether Christ's blood is truly united to his divinity and referenced Thomas Aquinas’s rejection of certain views held by Durandus. This page introduces arguments from Peter of the Palude against the idea that the bread is "assumed" by Christ’s person, favoring instead the doctrine of transubstantiation.</meta>

# ON QUESTIONS
Page 65

...because a tooth is called white and white is called a tooth. Where one is, the other is, because they are one in subject; and consequently, they are indistinct in subject and location. However, this cannot be said of the human body and the assumed "bread-ness." Whatever may be the case regarding this argument, it is true that although it does not follow by necessity, it follows as a possibility, etc. 

<margin>Response: The first argument of Peter of the Palude</margin>
**Peter of the Palude** <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a prominent Dominican theologian and canon lawyer</note> argues as follows: Either Christ would assume the substance of the bread with its **accidents** <note>term: accidents (physical properties like color, taste, and size that exist in a substance)</note> or without them. Not without them, because that is impossible; for that which is not able to be made or sustained by itself by any power—such as a **relation** <note>The category of being that refers to how things are connected</note> or something of that kind—is not able to be assumed by itself. Moreover, a physical substance cannot exist without **quantity** <note>The physical dimension or size of an object</note>, because quantity (or figure) is its own limit and proper characteristic. However, many would deny this. If, on the other hand, the substance is assumed with its accidents, then Christ would not be on the altar **sacramentally** <note>Present through the sign of the sacrament rather than physical location</note> but **locally** <note>Occupying physical space in the way an object sits in a room</note> through the quantity [of the bread] along with the assumed substance on the altar. Nor would he have moved from there, just as he was locally in the womb through his quantity along with the human nature assumed there.

<margin>Response</margin>
And perhaps this concludes that it is not in the sacramental manner described by the **Thomists** <note>Followers of Thomas Aquinas</note> through **conversion** <note>The change of one thing into another; specifically transubstantiation</note>. They say that Christ is not present there through his own quantity, but through the quantity of the bread. If he were to assume that quantity along with the bread, it would then seem that he is there through a quantity that is his own. However, the manner proposed by the Thomists is not held by many.

<margin>Second: Genus</margin>
Secondly, Peter argues that this cannot be understood as "body" meaning a **genus** <note>A general logical category, like "physical object"</note>, but only as "body" meaning a **part** <note>A specific component, like a limb or flesh</note>. This is because a genus is not predicated "possessively" of its lower members, whereas a part is predicated of the whole. For example, when I say "my humanity" and "my hand," it is correct; but I do not say "my animal" nor "my human" of myself. This is also apparent in the consecration of the blood, where it is said, *this is the chalice of my blood*. "Blood" is not an **equivocal** <note>A word with multiple unrelated meanings</note> term referring to both a genus and a part, as "body" is; it is taken only as a part. Therefore, granted that the "body" which is Christ were present on the altar by the power of the sacrament through assumption, it would still not be the "body of Christ" which is a part, except by natural **concomitance** <note>The doctrine that where Christ's body is, his blood, soul, and divinity must also be present</note>. This is because through "assumption," a union would not occur in the natures, but only in the **person** <note>original: "persona"; the individual identity of the Son of God</note>.

<margin>Response</margin>
Wherefore, through that assumption, it would result that the bread was the "body" that is Christ, but not the "body of Christ," just as the divinity is not currently the humanity. Enough has been said about this above regarding the "body as a part" and the "body as a genus."

<margin>Third</margin>
Thirdly, he argues: just as the assumed body of a man ought not to be corrupted or rot, neither in its substance nor in its quantity, so too the bread ought not to decay if it were assumed. However, perhaps this similarity does not hold by necessity.

<margin>Response: To the first argument for the opposing side</margin>
To the arguments for the opposing side, a response is given to the authority of **Damascene** <note>St. John of Damascus (c. 675–749), an influential Eastern Church Father</note>. It is said that just as it is certain that the water of baptism is not assumed into the unity of the divine **person** <note>original: "suppositum"</note>, nor is the grace of the Holy Spirit united to it so as to make one person, similarly the bread and wine are not assumed into the divine person, nor is the divinity joined to them in unity of person. Rather, just as the water there is taken up as a permanent material of the sacrament, so the bread and wine are taken up as a passing material. This is because the material of the sacrament is converted into the body of Christ, and consequently it is said to be "united" to the divinity in some way—not by assumption while the nature of the bread or wine remains, but through **transubstantiation** <note>The change of the whole substance of bread into the substance of the Body of Christ</note> into the previously assumed human nature. This is clear from what follows, where it is said: *just as naturally, through eating, bread and wine and water are transformed into the body and blood of the one eating and drinking—and it does not become a different body than before—so too the bread, wine, and water of the offering are supernaturally transformed into the body and blood of the Lord through the change and the coming of the Holy Spirit, and therefore they are not two, but one and the same.* From these points, it seems that it is not Damascene’s intention that the substance of the bread and wine remain and be assumed by the divine person, but rather that they pass into the body and blood of Christ and are thus united to the divinity.

<margin>Objection</margin>
However, those people object by asking how that which is **annihilated** <note>Reduced to nothing</note> is "united"—that is, how it truly ceases to be in itself. They also object regarding that similarity of the **coal** <note>An analogy used by John of Damascus to describe the Eucharist</note>, in which it is said that just as a coal is not simple wood but wood united to fire, so the bread of communion is not simple bread but bread united to the divinity.

# APOLOGIA

[coal] and fire are not the same in one **subject** <note>original: "supposito"; in scholastic philosophy, the "suppositum" is the individual substance or "person" that acts or possesses natures</note>, yet one passes into the other through its own corruption. In the same way, the bread of communion is not one with the divinity in its subject; rather, by its own ceasing to be, it passes into the 
<margin>Objection</margin>
body of Christ, which is united to the divinity. But an objection is raised against this: for then the bread of communion would be likened to the fire into which the 
<margin>Response</margin>
coal has passed through its own corruption, and not to the coal itself, in which the nature of fire is found simultaneously with the preservation of the nature of the wood. Therefore, look for the response. 

Perhaps the answer is this: that the likeness does not hold in all respects, and perhaps it would 
<margin>Damascene</margin>
have been better if **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and Church Father whose writings on the Eucharist were central to medieval debates</note> had not proposed that likeness. And when the same Damascene says that "God coupled the divinity to the bread," it must be said that this was not through **assumption** <note>The act of a divine person taking a created nature into themselves, as in the Incarnation</note>, though it is like food being joined to the one who eats because it is converted into him. Let that likeness which can apply there be accepted between this conversion and that one.

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
**St. Thomas** in his *Commentary on the Fourth Book of Sentences* (distinction 11, question 1) says that Damascene’s word is to be understood regarding the **species** <term>species (the outward appearances of bread and wine—such as color, taste, and smell—that remain after the substance has changed)</term> through which the body of Christ, united to the divinity, is joined in an ineffable manner. This is his view; and since this manner is ineffable, one ought not to inquire further regarding it. 

In the third part of the *Summa* (question 75), he says God coupled His divinity—that is, the divine power—to the bread and wine: not so that they remain in this sacrament, but so that from them He might make His body and 
<margin>Gloss on the authority of the Apostle</margin>
blood. Regarding the authority of the Apostle <note>St. Paul (specifically referencing 1 Corinthians 10:16)</note>, it is said that his speech is figurative, both on the part of the subject and the predicate. For "bread," as the subject, stands for the sensible sacrament—namely, the species of bread. "The body of Christ" is also taken figuratively. Hence, according to the **gloss** <note>A standard biblical commentary used by medieval scholars</note>, that phrasing does not mean that the substance of the bread or the species of bread is truly and really Christ or the body of Christ; nor that "body of Christ" is predicated directly of the substance or species of bread. Rather, the sense is that the bread which we break in the sacrament—that is, the participation in the broken bread at the altar—is the participation in the divine body; that is, it makes us to be one with Christ. 

Let the masters who were condemning my views remember this: that if the words of Damascene and Paul in this matter were accepted as they 
<margin>The first solution to another point</margin>
seem to sound at first glance and superficially, they could create an erroneous sense of the faith for many. 

When it is said that fewer difficulties follow from this "Assumption" position, it must be said that in those things which belong to faith, one should not always choose that to which fewer difficulties follow, but rather that which is more in harmony with Apostolic traditions and ecclesiastical dogma, even if more difficulties occur. For it is necessary to "capture the intellect in obedience to the faith" and to commit oneself in humility to the obedience of the traditions of the Fathers—as 
<margin>Plato</margin>
**Plato** also says, very well and most religiously, in the *Timaeus*. 

<margin>Second</margin>
Likewise, someone will say that although that "Assumption" theory might better preserve the appearance to the senses, **conversion** <note>Transubstantiation</note> better preserves the 
<margin>Instance</margin>
appearance to the intellect—that is, the words of the Gospel, which it is better to preserve because they cannot lie, whereas the senses can be deceived. 

But it is argued further for the opposite side: that if this does not happen through "assumption"—so that it would be included in the article of the Incarnation (since the belief would be the same)—it would be necessary for there to be a special article in the Creed regarding this conversion, yet there is none. 

<margin>Response of Peter of the Palude and St. Thomas</margin>
Some, like **Peter of the Palude**, say that the article on the Eucharist is perhaps a special part under that phrase, "the communion of saints," etc. **Saint Thomas** says in the *Secunda Secundae* that two things can be considered in the sacrament of the Eucharist: one is that it is a sacrament, and this has the same rationale as other effects of sanctifying grace; the other is that the body of Christ is contained there miraculously, and thus it is concluded under the article on the **Omnipotence** [of God], just as all other miracles attributed to omnipotence are. However, in his *Commentary on the Sentences*, he says that faith regarding the body of Christ and all the sacraments and "keys" and all such things is 
<margin>Gloss on the confession of Berengarius</margin>
included in the article regarding the effect of grace, which is "the holy Catholic Church," etc. 

Regarding the confession of **Berengarius** <note>Berengarius of Tours (d. 1088), a theologian who sparked controversy by arguing for a more symbolic presence of Christ in the Eucharist</note>, it must be said, as the gloss there states, that unless you understand the words of Berengarius soundly, you will fall into a greater error than he himself held. It says then...

<meta>This page continues a scholastic discussion on the Eucharist, specifically addressing the views of Peter of the Palude regarding the "Assumption" theory versus transubstantiation. It then transitions into a famous and controversial debate of the Renaissance: whether the early Christian theologian Origen was saved or damned.</meta>

<header>QUESTIONS</header>

<margin>Peter of the Palude</margin>
**Peter of the Palude** <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342) was a prominent French Dominican theologian and Archbishop of Mainz</note> says that when it is said that the "body of Christ is broken," it must be interpreted to mean that he remains under the **species** <note>In Eucharistic theology, "species" refers to the outward appearances of bread and wine—the taste, texture, and shape—that remain even after the underlying substance has changed</note> which are broken, so long as he remains in whatever part remains. Furthermore, Peter adds these words: "Thus I say that God could **assume** <note>The "Assumption" theory suggested God could take the bread into his divine personhood like he took on human nature, rather than changing the bread into his body</note> bread and wine just as he could convert them, and that he could have instituted words that, when spoken, would result in this assumption—just as now, through the speaking of these words, conversion follows. However, he did not give this power to these words, nor could the understanding of the moderns be preserved if assumption occurred without conversion." These words are most effective for the truth of my conclusion, which is entirely about what is **possible** <note>original: "de possibili"; a logical distinction between what God could do by his absolute power versus what he chose to do</note>, not about how things actually are, etc.

<margin>To the other point</margin>
To the argument that whenever there are two things identical in their **subject** <note>original: "supposito"; in scholasticism, the "suppositum" is the individual substance or "person" that acts or possesses natures</note> and limited in space, wherever one is, the other must be: It is said that this rule holds only for those things that are in a place **accidentally** <note>original: "per accidens"</note>. It is different for those things that are in a place **through themselves** <note>original: "per se"</note>. 

<margin>To the last point</margin>
And when it is said that these statements—namely, "the bread is the body of Christ" and "the body of Christ is the bread"—cannot be verified unless the bread remains, it must be said that it should be interpreted as: "where the bread was, there the body of Christ becomes." And let it suffice to have disputed this question. From all these points, I hold those which are in harmony with the declaration of my conclusion explained above. Those which are discordant, I judge should be rejected and condemned.

# SEVENTH QUESTION: ON THE SALVATION OF ORIGEN

<margin>The process regarding Origen's salvation proceeds in seven articles</margin>
**I**t is more reasonable to believe that **Origen** <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was a massively influential but controversial early Christian thinker. His theories on the pre-existence of souls and the eventual salvation of all beings led to his posthumous condemnation</note> is saved than to believe he is damned. These masters have said that this conclusion is rash, blameworthy, and **savoring of heresy** <note>original: "haeresim sapiens"; a technical ecclesiastical term for a statement that sounds heretical even if not explicitly condemned</note>, and contrary to the determination of the universal Church. I, however, to speak of them more modestly, wish to show that their judgment is not correct; that this conclusion is not against the determination of the Church; and further, even if everything they bring against me were true, it still cannot be said that this conclusion is heretical or savors of heresy. 

For a fuller declaration of this matter, there will be seven articles. In the first, we shall see whether Origen ever wrote or believed any heretical opinion regarding matters of faith. In the second, granted that he wrote them, whether he wrote them **dogmatically** <note>As fixed truths</note>, or with **adherence** <note>Personal belief</note>, or merely **inquisitively** <note>Exploring ideas as a seeker</note>. In the third, granted he wrote with adherence, whether he sinned mortally in writing them so that he could be called a heretic. In the fourth, granted he wrote such things and erred in writing, whether he ever repented for them. In the fifth, granted that neither his repentance nor his lack of it is certain, whether it is more reasonable to believe him damned or saved. In the sixth, what should be judged from the decrees regarding what the Church has determined about Origen. In the seventh, to what extent the determination of the Church obliges our belief in this matter.

<margin>Regarding the first article</margin>
Regarding the matter of the first article, there was a bitter contention between **Rufinus** and **Jerome** <note>Rufinus of Aquileia and St. Jerome were once close friends who became bitter enemies over the legacy of Origen in the late 4th century</note>. To them (as **Augustine** says, who deplored the dissension that arose between them), God had granted that they might together lick the honey of the Holy Scriptures as the closest of friends. Rufinus is of the opinion that the heretical dogmas found in Origen's books were falsely inserted by heretics who corrupted his books, and that they did not reflect Origen's mind. Jerome feels the opposite. But let us see what probability each opinion holds, and it will perhaps appear that—saving the faith and the full satisfaction of those things we are bound to believe for the necessity of salvation—it can still be freely and probably believed that those principal heresies for which Origen is convicted of sin and consequently damned were not from Origen’s mind, but were falsely attributed to him by treacherous heretics corrupting his books. 

<margin>Pamphilus the martyr</margin>
On this side, there is first the authority of **Pamphilus the martyr** <note>Pamphilus (d. 309 AD) was a scholar and martyr who wrote an 'Apology for Origen' to defend him against charges of heterodoxy</note>, whose book is put forward in defense of Origen, in which the most glorious martyr, using the words of Origen himself from his books there cited...

# APOLOGIA

<margin>
Jerome's testimonies indicating Origen's heresy
</margin>
...showed that he thought in an orthodox <note>original: "catholice"; here meaning in accordance with the universal Church's teaching</note> manner in those matters for which he is accused as a heretic. However, **Jerome**, denying that this book belongs to **Pamphilus** in his responsive *Apology to Oceanus and Pammachius*, speaks thus: "If you say Origen's books were violated by his enemies so that he might be driven mad, why should I not be allowed to say that a volume was composed by his friends and readers under the name of Pamphilus, which would vindicate him from infamy by the testimony of a martyr?" From these words, it can be sufficiently noted that Jerome proposes both as probable, hinting that just as **Rufinus** cannot be convinced that those books were not corrupted, so too he himself cannot be convinced that the book is by Pamphilus. And below, Jerome adds: "The very name of an 'apologetic' <note>A formal defense or justification of a position or person</note> shows an excuse. For it defends nothing except what is under accusation." But perhaps someone might say then: since Jerome himself marks this very treatise in which he writes these things with the title of *Apology*—in which he defends himself, saying he followed Origen's learning but not his **dogma**—he likewise shows himself to be guilty of a crime, since he defends nothing unless it is under accusation. Thus no one could be justly excused if an excuse always presupposes a just accusation. 

But let us see then by what conjectures Jerome is moved to believe the book is not by Pamphilus. The first thing that moves Jerome is that the same things are read in the first book of **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History"</note> among those six that he wrote in favor of Origen. The second is that Eusebius himself, writing the *Life of Pamphilus*, said that Pamphilus wrote no work of his own. For Jerome speaks thus in the first book *Against Rufinus*, addressed to Pammachius and Marcella: "Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, formerly the standard-bearer of the **Arian faction** <note>Arianism was a major 4th-century heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ</note>, wrote six books for Origen—a very broad and elaborate work—and by many testimonies he approved Origen to be orthodox <note>original: "catholicum"</note> according to him—that is, according to us, an Arian. You translate the first of these books under the name of the martyr." And below: "If that book is by Pamphilus, which of the six will be Eusebius’s first?" And below: "Likewise, Eusebius—the lover, herald, and companion of Pamphilus—wrote three most elegant books containing the *Life of Pamphilus*, in the third of which he says of Pamphilus: 'He himself indeed wrote nothing at all of his own work, except for letters which he perhaps sent to friends.'" To such an extent did the defender of Origen and praiser of Pamphilus humble himself by his humanity that he says Pamphilus composed nothing at all of his own speech; and he said this after Pamphilus was already crowned with **martyrdom**, lest you have the refuge of saying Pamphilus wrote this after the books were published by Eusebius. 

And below: "What will the letters of Bishop **Theophilus** do, or those of **Pope Anastasius**, who pursue the heretic throughout the whole world? Since your book, issued under the name of Pamphilus, fights against their letters." And in the second book, Jerome writes thus: "When nearly ten years ago, my friend **Dexter**, who administered the **Praetorian Prefecture** <note>One of the highest administrative offices in the Roman Empire</note>, asked me to list the authors of our religion for him, I placed this book among the other treatises, thinking it was issued by Pamphilus, just as it had been spread by you and your disciples. But since Eusebius himself says Pamphilus wrote nothing except letters, etc., and the first book of Eusebius’s six volumes contains the same things and in the same words which were faked by you under Pamphilus’s name, it is clear that you wanted to spread this book for this reason: so that you might introduce heresy under the persona of a martyr. Since you have even perverted many things from the one you pretend is Pamphilus, and it is one way in the Greek and another in the Latin." 

In the responsive *Apology to Oceanus and Pammachius*, in which he shows he followed the learning of Origen and not his dogma, Jerome says this while speaking of that same book of Pamphilus: "It seems to have been a minor work of either **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a prolific Alexandrian theologian</note> or someone else. If we redundantly concede it to be by Pamphilus, it was not yet by the martyr; for he wrote it before he underwent martyrdom. And how great a martyr he was worthy to be—namely, so that he might erase his error by martyrdom." These are Jerome's words, verbatim, in various places as they are cited concerning that book of Pamphilus.

<margin>
Rufinus’s opinion against Jerome
</margin>
**Rufinus**, however, proving the book to be by the martyr Pamphilus and to serve as a defense for Origen, says in his second book of invective against Jerome, after he said that it could easily be said of any work that it is not by the author to whom...

<header>QUESTIONS</header>

<margin>Pico here refutes the statements of Jerome</margin>

to whom he ascribes it, then he says: "But let us suppose that this booklet is not by the martyr but by any single person from the church; did that writer use his own words, whoever he is, so that it would seem we must yield to the merits of the author?" He places examples from the volumes of *Origen* themselves. And what he feels about individual points, he shows not with his own defensive words, but with the words of the very man who will be accused. Therefore, a <term>question</term> <note>original abbreviation "qō" for "quaestio"</note> about the author is superfluous where such a defense exists that needs no advocate. These are the words of *Rufinus*. 

However, to those things which *Jerome* says, someone might perhaps respond on behalf of *Rufinus* in this way: First, when he says that *Eusebius* wrote six books in which he proves *Origen* was an *Arian* <note>A follower of Arianism, a 4th-century belief that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father</note> and that the first of these was translated by *Rufinus* under the name of *Pamphilus*—how can this stand? For the book of *Pamphilus* is the first by *Eusebius* when entirely different and conflicting goals are intended in those books. For *Eusebius*, according to you, O *Jerome*, tries in his books to prove that *Origen* was an *Arian*. Yet in the book of *Pamphilus*, he does nothing else than try to prove that *Origen* was not an *Arian*. Rather, he argues that whatever things confirming the heresy of *Arius* are found in his books were inserted by the *Arians* themselves—of which kind *Eusebius* was, as were many others. Therefore, it is necessary that this book be entirely different from that one, as it pleads a completely different, indeed contrary, cause. 

Nor is it sufficient if someone says that those things pertaining to the *Arian* heresy were changed from the book of *Eusebius*. For *Jerome* cannot say that *Eusebius* showed the books of *Origen* were corrupted regarding other heresies. Because he himself says in the second book against *Rufinus* that, except for what pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit, in other dogmas *Eusebius* and *Didymus* most clearly concede to the sect of *Origen*. Therefore, it cannot be well understood how the same things read in the book of *Pamphilus* could be read in the first book of *Eusebius*, unless perhaps some common points about *Origen* were there that do not pertain to the point of this conclusion being discussed. Nor does it seem so marvelous (as *Jerome* marvels) that *Pamphilus* and *Eusebius* wrote similar things, since, as *Jerome* himself says, they had been <term>companions</term> <note>original: "contubernales"; literally "tent-mates," meaning close associates or colleagues</note>. What *Eusebius* set down was either read in *Pamphilus's* work and reported in his own books, or, as happens daily, he discovered and thought it out by a similar movement of the mind. And this concerns the first book of *Eusebius*.

Regarding what *Jerome* says—that *Eusebius* wrote in the *Life of Pamphilus* that because of his humility he [Pamphilus] wrote nothing of his own work except letters—and he adds that *Eusebius*, a defender of *Origen* and a praiser of *Pamphilus*, says this. Perhaps *Rufinus* would respond that this does not do much against him. First, because even that little treatise of *Pamphilus* leans more toward the brevity of a letter than to the magnitude of a proper book. Second, because that brief apology for *Origen* perhaps cannot rightly be called a "work of his own," since *Pamphilus* does not dogmatize there; indeed, no question is treated there concerning a thing in general, but it deals briefly only with a particular man, namely *Origen*. Whether his books were corrupted or not is not to "found" <note>original: "condere"</note> something of one's own work. It was necessary out of his humility that he, avoiding the name of a dogmatist or author, should raise himself up. Third, it is possible that even this book did not come to the notice of *Eusebius*: both because of the smallness of the book and because of the author’s humility (which he himself mentions), writing nothing great and hiding even those thin and tiny things he did write rather than showing them off. Fourth, *Rufinus* will say it is also possible that *Eusebius*, as a defender of the *Arian* treachery, wished not only to hide the book of the martyr—which deprived his own sect of *Origen's* testimony—but also to act through this indirect testimony of his so that posterity would believe it was not by *Pamphilus*. Therefore, what *Jerome* says (as if to corroborate his reason) that the "defender of *Origen*" says *Pamphilus* wrote nothing, etc., is rather against him than for him. Because from the moment *Eusebius* defended *Origen* not as a Catholic but as an *Arian*, he could justly be suspect in this matter, as I said. But why is it necessary to labor in these things? Or how can *Jerome* at all prove from the testimony of *Eusebius*...

### APOLOGY

<meta>catchword: that it may be otherwise</meta>

...the matter that the *Apology for Origen* is not by *Pamphilus*, even though *Eusebius* himself, in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, says that the *Apology for Origen* was written by the holy martyr *Pamphilus*. When *Jerome* adds: "What will the letters of Bishop *Theophilus* do? What of Pope *Anastasius*?" and so on—*Rufinus* would perhaps respond that the book of *Pamphilus* does not conflict with their primary intention. For their purpose was to eradicate from the world those most wicked heresies and poisonous doctrines, regardless of who authored them, because this concerned the faith and the strengthening of religion and the stability of the church. 

However, whether those doctrines belonged to *Origen*, as many believed, or did not, those most religious <term>pontiffs</term> <note>Original: "pontifices"; here referring to the Popes and high-ranking bishops</note> would have cared very little. Rather, it would perhaps have been desirable and most welcome to them if it could have been proven by certain and valid arguments that those heretical opinions were not actually believed by *Origen*. This would be acting in favor of the faith, not against it; it would be against heretics, and not for heretics—who relied not a little on the testimony of such a great man, so praised by Catholics, and defended their own error with his authority. 

Therefore, the book of *Pamphilus* would only "fight" against those letters if it tried to excuse the very heresies they were accusing. But it does not do so, if its whole strength is directed toward ensuring that the supporters of those heresies are deprived of such a good <term>patron</term> <note>A legal or spiritual protector; in this case, the authority of Origen</note> whom those letters pursue. It is certain that they only pursue him as the <term>heresiarch</term> <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect</note> of those believed opinions. 

Regarding the points that *Jerome* brings forward in the second book, one might perhaps respond like this: First, when he says that he himself once believed and even wrote that it was *Pamphilus’s* book, before he read in *Eusebius* that *Pamphilus* wrote nothing, and so on. From this statement of his, *Rufinus* might argue thus: "If you, O *Jerome*, having read the book of *Pamphilus*, once both believed and wrote that it was by *Pamphilus*, tell me, I pray: did you recognize the things you were reading in it as lies and heresies, or as favoring heresy? Or were they rather true or probable things that in no way harmed the Catholic faith? 

And if they were heretical, how could you be led to believe the author of the book was a Catholic martyr? For no one could suspect anything sinister in a martyr's testimony and words without it being a disgrace. But if the contents were both Catholic and worthy of a Christian martyr, why do you now condemn them and call them fabricated, and spread abroad to introduce heresies? In short, why do you now judge as unworthy of a martyr the very things you then judged worthy of a martyr? For they are the same things you read now and read then, even if we set aside the title of the author. 

Let us consider the things said there in defense of *Origen* on their own merits. If they are bad, why did you then judge them to belong to a holy martyr? If they are good, why are they even now not accepted as good, regardless of whose they are? Furthermore, how can you say, O *Jerome*, that I distributed the book to introduce heresies? For in that book, as stated above, nothing else is done except ensuring that heretics cannot strengthen themselves with *Origen’s* testimony; this works to uproot heresy, not to spread it. 

Moreover, this book is found not only in Latin but in Greek. I, *Rufinus*, made it Latin by translating it from the Greek. Who published the Greek if not *Pamphilus*? Certainly not I, *Rufinus*—according to you, who accuse me of ignorance of Greek letters—for I could not have written a book so eloquently in Greek as to equal the style of *Eusebius*. If someone else is suggested, *Jerome* responds that it belongs to <term>Didymus</term> <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a famous Alexandrian theologian who, despite his blindness, was highly esteemed by Jerome before their later falling out</note> or someone else. *Rufinus* will persist: 'Whoever that other person may be, I, *Rufinus*, am no longer the one held guilty of this crime, but another.'

And if it is *Didymus*, then according to you, *Didymus*—your own teacher, O *Jerome*!—is a liar and a deceiver. Yet in your books, you called him a "seeing prophet," the "eye of the Bride" from the <term>Song of Songs</term> <note>original: "cantico canticorum"</note>, and an "apostolic man." He is the liar, I say, who by publishing the Greek version falsely attributed it to *Pamphilus*. Not I, who communicated it to the Latins by translating it under the title of the same author as I found it in the Greek. Nor should it be surprising to you that I believed *Didymus* in this matter, since you believed him in the explanation of the Scriptures." 

Regarding what he says, that it is one way in the Latin and another...

...it might not be otherwise in the Greek. <note>The text continues a debate about whether translations from Greek to Latin accurately reflect the original source.</note> Rufinus would say: "Why, O Jerome, do you not put forward the poorly translated passages? Is it so that I cannot defend my own fault? You do the same when **Augustine** writes to you that certain parts of your translation from the Hebrew are condemned, yet he does not cite the specific passages." You say this was done so that you could not defend yourself and prove the truth of your translation. Therefore, what Rufinus said to you was permitted regarding Augustine; let it also be permitted for me to suspect the same of you, O Jerome. These things are said concerning the disagreement between Jerome and Rufinus over the book of **Pamphilus**; in this, as in all other matters, I always place Jerome's judgment above the judgment of Rufinus.

<margin>He proves by the example of other authors that Origen's books were corrupted.</margin>
Secondly, regarding the possibility of asserting that **Origen's** books are corrupted: we see that this has similarly happened to many other books by <term>Catholic doctors</term> <note>Orthodox Christian teachers and theologians recognized by the Church.</note>. For **Clement**, the disciple of the Apostles, who was Bishop of Rome and a martyr after the Apostles, published books which they call the *Recognitions*. In these, while he explains truly Apostolic doctrine in the persona of Peter, in some places the <term>Eunomian dogma</term> <note>A heresy started by Eunomius of Cyzicus which claimed the Son of God was a created being, not of the same substance as the Father.</note> is inserted so that one would believe no one else but Eunomius himself was arguing that the Son of God was created out of nothing. 

Likewise, in the writings of **Clement of Alexandria**, a priest and a Catholic man, it is found written that the Son of God was created. And in the four books of **Dionysius**, Bishop of the city of Alexandria, where he argues against **Sabellius**, there is a confirmation of the <term>Arian</term> <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus was a created being subordinate to God the Father.</note> dogma. And why is it necessary to bring up Apostolic men, when we know that even the Gospels themselves and the sayings of the Apostles have often been corrupted by heretics? This can be established by anyone, especially from the book of **Tertullian** against **Marcion**. 

If this happened to their books, why could it not also have happened to the books of Origen? And in an altogether similar case, why is a similar excuse not accepted in every respect? This excuse seems even more acceptable regarding Origen's books because he himself, while still living, complained about this in his letters (as will appear below): namely, that his books were being corrupted and depraved by heretics. 

But if Jerome holds this to be impossible, asserting that if we allow this, then anything found in anyone's books could be claimed by others to be corrupted, and that it is difficult for all copies to be spoiled—I do not know how he himself will be able to answer the Eunomians who prove their dogma by the testimony of Clement, the disciple of the Apostles, in whose works it is found expressly written that the Son of God was created. For if Jerome himself recurs to the argument that Clement's books were corrupted by those same heretics, they will argue using Jerome's own words that this is "impossible." They would say exactly what he says: that anything found in anyone's books could be called "corrupted" by others, and it is impossible for all copies to be corrupt. 

Therefore, perhaps we must be careful that, while we wish to make Origen a complete heretic, we do not also make the Apostles and the disciples of the Apostles heretics. For since no less detestable and cursed heresies and no less impious dogmas are found in their books than in the books of Origen, I do not see why they should not be similarly accused, or Origen similarly excused. 

Jerome, however, responds to the corruption of the books of Clement and others with these words: "And if," he says, "there are some faulty things in their books, if I respond that I do not know the causes of the faults, I will not immediately judge them to be heretics. For it is possible that they simply erred, or wrote with another meaning, or that their writings were gradually corrupted by unskilled scribes, or that they spoke some things innocently and with less caution, which could not avoid the <term>calumny</term> <note>False and malicious accusations.</note> of perverse men." 

To this response of Jerome, Rufinus would perhaps answer: "If you do not wish to immediately judge them heretics because there are some faults in their books—even if you do not know the causes of the faults—why then do you immediately judge Origen a heretic for certain faulty things in his books, even though you read Origen contradicting those very things elsewhere? What is the cause of this disparity?" Especially since you yourself knew, wrote, and preached that in Origen there was such loftiness of genius, such zeal for the faith, and such great study of the Scriptures, that it is not without merit to believe the fault was in the <term>codices</term> <note>Early manuscript books.</note> from wherever they came, rather than in his mind.

-> # APOLOGY <-

...you might suspect. Furthermore, just as it could have happened, according to you, that those others [the Church doctors] either simply erred, or wrote with a different meaning, or spoke innocently and with less caution, why could it not similarly have happened that **Origen** either simply erred, or wrote with another meaning—as <margin>Didymus</margin> **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a prominent Alexandrian theologian who defended Origen.</note> contends—or spoke certain things innocently and with less caution which cannot escape the slander of perverse men? 

And just as you say their writings could have been corrupted by wicked copyists, why could Origen's writings not similarly have been corrupted either by wicked copyists or by treacherous heretics? No reason for such a distinction appears at all. 

<margin>Examples from Rufinus</margin> **Rufinus** also relates that a book by **Hilary** the Confessor <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a leading Latin theologian who fought against Arianism.</note> was falsified by heretics after the Synod of Ariminum <note>A church council held in 359 AD where many bishops were pressured into accepting an Arian-leaning creed.</note>; and that for this reason, when a question was raised against him in a council of bishops, he ordered a book to be brought from his own house which, unknown to him, a heretic was keeping in his own chests. And he says that when it was produced and judged heretical by everyone, the author of the book, Hilary, left the council excommunicated. 

<margin>Jerome</margin> **Jerome** says this is false and a fiction created for the slander of Hilary, offering nothing else as proof. But whether it was true or not cannot be well known, nor does it pertain much to the defense of Origen. This much is true, however: that Rufinus, being about to recite this about Hilary, prefaced it with these words: "And lest anything be lacking for open belief, I will re-examine matters which are still within our memory, so that the truth of the testimony may be hidden from no one." Therefore, either it was true, or great was the impudence of Rufinus to weave a fitting lie and a new fable in a matter of such recent memory. 

But whether it be true or false, it does not seem to have been invented or recited for the slander of Hilary, because he slanders those who had corrupted Hilary's book rather than Hilary himself, whom he attests was innocent of heresy, unjustly excommunicated, and craftily deceived. 

After this, Rufinus relates that a book by **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220) from Carthage.</note> whose title is *On the Trinity* was being read in Constantinople under the name of **Cyprian** the Martyr by heretics of the <term>Macedonian party</term> <note>Followers of Macedonius I of Constantinople, who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>. Jerome says that the book is not by Tertullian, nor is it called Cyprian's, but rather **Novatian's** <note>Novatian was a 3rd-century scholar and antipope; the work *De Trinitate* is indeed now attributed to him.</note>. Neither of them brings forward anything else for his case, except that Jerome says the author's eloquence demonstrates the specific nature of his style. Although in many cases it is often possible to detect a similar appearance and tenor of style. But these things have nothing to do with Origen. 

However, Rufinus himself shows that this same thing happened to Jerome as to the books of Origen. For he relates that when ecclesiastical letters were handed to him by **Damasus**, Bishop of the city of Rome, to be transcribed, the **Apollinarists** <note>Followers of Apollinaris of Laodicea, whose Christological views were later declared heretical.</note> took a book of **Athanasius** <note>Saint Athanasius (c. 296–373), the chief defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy.</note> where "the Lordly man" <note>original: "dominicus homo" — a controversial phrase in early debates about how to describe the humanity of Christ.</note> had been written, and they corrupted it so that they wrote again in the book that which they had erased, specifically so that it would be thought not falsified by them, but added by Jerome. 

<margin>Note.</margin> And take note that Jerome, responding to Rufinus in this part, although he says, "He forces my own little story upon me," nevertheless does not deny that it was true. But at the end he says this: "It can happen, Rufinus, that even if you heard the truth from me, another who is ignorant of this matter might say it was composed and feigned by you." 

The third thing that makes it probable that Origen's books were corrupted is that he himself complained of this while he was alive. <margin>Note the words of Origen.</margin> For there exists in the fourth book of Origen a letter of his to certain dear friends of his in Alexandria, in which he complains in these words: 

"But it seems no wonder to me if my doctrine is adulterated by enemies, and is corrupted by such adultery as the epistle of Paul the Apostle was corrupted by. For certain people wrote a false epistle under the name of Paul to disturb the **Thessalonians**, as if the day of the Lord were at hand, and to seduce them. Because of this epistle, therefore, in the second epistle which he wrote to the Thessalonians, he said these things: 

'Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together unto him, that you be not soon shaken in your mind, nor be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as if sent by us, as if the day of the Lord were at hand. Let no man deceive you by any means.' <note>A translation of 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3.</note> 

Therefore I see certain such things happening to us. For a certain author of a heresy, when in the presence of many it had been held..."

# QUESTIONS

<margin>Letter of Origen to the brothers in Palestine regarding the falsification of his books</margin>
...our discussion had been, taking the writings from those who had transcribed the volume, he added what he wished, removed what he wished, and changed what seemed fit to him; and he circulates it as if in our name, mocking us and presenting what he himself wrote as ours. Because of this, the indignant brothers who are in **Palestine** sent a man to me in **Athens** <note>Palestine and Athens were major centers of early Christian scholarship; Origen often traveled between such hubs.</note> to receive the authentic copies from me, which had not even been re-read or reviewed by me before; indeed, they lay so neglected that they could hardly be found. I sent them nonetheless, and I speak with God as my witness: when I confronted that very man who had adulterated the book, asking why he had done this, he responded as if to satisfy me that he "wanted to improve and purify the discussion." See with what kind of "purification" he purified our discussion! Surely the same kind of purification with which **Marcion** <note>Marcion of Sinope (c. 85–160 AD), a famous heretic who edited the Gospel of Luke and the letters of Paul to remove Jewish influences.</note> purified the Gospels or the Apostle, or the kind his successor **Apelles** <note>A disciple of Marcion who further altered scriptures to fit his own theological system.</note> used after him. For just as they subverted the truth of the scriptures, so this man, having removed what was truly said for the sake of accusing us, inserted what is false. These words are read verbatim in **Origen's** letter. Now, if heretics did not hesitate to corrupt his books while he was still living, how much more must we believe they dared to do this after his death? He also complains about a certain other heretic in Ephesus who attributed many false things to him; and there even exists in another of his letters a complaint about the falsification of his books.

Fourthly, that which provides the greatest proof of this matter—namely, that those heretical ideas are not Origen's but were inserted by heretics—is that one finds **Origen** elsewhere determining those same points in a pious and catholic <note>In this context, "catholic" refers to the universal, orthodox teachings of the Church.</note> manner. From this, it follows that if those heretical things were Origen's, he would be contradicting himself. One may see many places where he acts in a catholic manner in the *Apology* of **Pamphilus**. This is what **Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410), the scholar who translated Origen into Latin and defended him against charges of heresy.</note> says: that there is no need to worry about the name of the author of that book <note>Referring to the Apology for Origen.</note>, because that defense is valid in itself regardless of who wrote it, since it proves Origen's catholic and orthodox dogma using his own words and sayings. By this, a certain saying of **Jerome** against Rufinus also seems to be answered. For when Rufinus said the same thing—namely, that Origen had determined those matters catholically elsewhere—Jerome said this against him: "Where is that confidence with which you used to sound off so frequently with puffed-out cheeks, claiming you had corrected in the books of the **Periarchon** <note>Greek: *Peri Archon*; Latin: *De Principiis*; English: *On First Principles*. This was Origen's most controversial work on systematic theology.</note> those things you had read in Origen's other books? And that you had restored his own things to him? From such a great forest of books, you cannot even produce a bush or a twig." For perhaps Rufinus would respond that he did not need to produce twigs from that forest from which **Pamphilus** had already produced many entire trees. For Pamphilus recites those passages most copiously, and with that already presupposed, Rufinus acts in his own little book (which he adds to Pamphilus's book) to show how it happened that contradictions are found in Origen's books; and he assigns the cause to falsification by heretics. 

Fifthly, and this does much to assert that those heresies are not from the mind of Origen, is that from the testimony of many to whom we are rightly bound to give faith, we hold that Origen held catholic views on the principal opinions in which he is said to have erred.

<margin>Which principal heresies are attributed to Origen; Defense of the first heresy; Didymus; Athanasius</margin>
For there are two principal heresies which are charged against Origen. The first concerns the Trinity: that he thought poorly regarding the Son and worse regarding the Holy Spirit. The second concerns the salvation of the devil: that is, that his punishment and the infernal suffering will not be eternal, but that he must be delivered from it at some point. From this second one, many other errors ascribed to him seem to depend: namely, that for the sake of the salvation of these demons who are to be saved, Christ must be crucified again in a higher element; and that all things are to be restored into one; and that the devil can repent; and that the punishment of the damned is not eternal. Regarding these two heresies, there appear to be evident arguments that they were not in the mind of Origen. For concerning the Trinity, not only does **Didymus**—of whom **Jerome** boasts so much as his teacher—say that Origen held catholic views, and proved it in his own published commentaries on the *Periarchon*; but even **Athanasius** <note>Saint Athanasius the Great (c. 296–373), the chief defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy against Arianism.</note>, the defender of the Council of Nicaea, called this man a witness to his own faith with a clear voice in his own books against the Arians.

<summary>This page argues that Origen's alleged heresies were actually the result of heretical forgeries and provides historical testimonies from Didymus and Athanasius to defend Origen's orthodox views on the Trinity.</summary>

# DEFENSE

<margin>Sayings of Origen by which he is judged not a heretic, but most Christian.</margin>

And we read that **Methodius** <note>Methodius of Olympus (died c. 311 AD), a bishop and martyr who was an early critic of Origen but, as the text suggests, was believed by later scholars to have retracted his harsher condemnations.</note> repented of having condemned **Origen**. He says that Origen was ultimately found to believe nothing wrong concerning the Holy Trinity. Indeed, Origen’s own words concerning the Trinity do not differ at all from the Catholic faith. For regarding that passage of Paul to the Romans, *and the Spirit helps our infirmity* <note>Romans 8:26</note>, he expressly holds that the Holy Spirit is not a created being. And regarding the passage, *He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him give us all things?* <note>Romans 8:32</note>, Origen explains: "For there is nothing, either of visible or invisible creation, that can be made equal to the Son. For in no way can a creature be compared to its Creator. And if the Creator himself was given to us, how shall not every creature be given to us with him?" 

Further down, regarding Paul’s words, *who is over all things, God blessed forever* <note>Romans 9:5</note>, Origen says: "That Christ is one thing according to the flesh and another according to the spirit, he [Paul] already designated in the earlier parts of this same epistle, where he says he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, and was destined as the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness." We have fully explained there, to the best of our ability, how he is the Son of God according to the spirit and the son of David according to the flesh. Therefore, the one whom he called the Son of God according to the spirit, he now—following the order of doctrine for those making progress as listeners—pronounces to be the very God who is over all things. 

I wonder how certain people, reading what the same Apostle said elsewhere—*There is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things* <note>1 Corinthians 8:6</note>—can deny that they ought to profess the Son of God as God, lest they seem to profess two Gods. What will they do with this passage of the Apostle in which Christ, through whom are all things, is openly described as being *God over all*? But those who feel this way do not notice that just as he said Jesus Christ is the "one Lord" in such a way that God the Father is not thereby excluded from being called Lord, so also he said God the Father is the "one God" in such a way that the Son is not believed to be anything other than God. For the Scripture is true which says: *Know that the Lord himself is God* <note>Psalm 100:3</note>. Yet both together are one God, because there is no other beginning of divinity than the Father; rather, as Wisdom says, the Son is the "purest emanation" <note>original: "purissima emanatio"</note> of that one paternal fountain. 

Therefore, Christ the Son is God over all things—all those things, without doubt, which we said a little earlier are above principalities, powers, virtues, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come. But He who is "over all" has no one above Himself. For He is not *after* the Father, but *from* the Father. This same point regarding the Holy Spirit ought to be understood from the Wisdom of God, where it is said: *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 1:7</note>. If, therefore, the Son of God is said to be "over all," and the Holy Spirit is recorded as "containing all things," and God the Father is He "from whom are all things," then the nature of the Trinity and the single substance <term>substantia</term> <note>The underlying essence or reality of God; the "stuff" God is made of, which is shared by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> which is over all is clearly shown. 

These are Origen’s words, verbatim. And elsewhere, regarding Paul’s question, *How shall they preach unless they are sent?* <note>Romans 10:15</note>, he says: "There are some who indeed announce and preach concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but not sincerely or completely. Such are all the heretics who announce the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but do not do so well or faithfully. For they either wrongly separate the Son from the Father, saying the Father is of one nature and the Son of another, or they wrongly confuse them, making God a composite of three or merely a triple naming." But those who "announce good things" will give to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit their own specific properties, while confessing that there is no diversity in substance or nature. 

These are Origen's words. What could be more Catholic? What could be more explicit? It is necessary, therefore, that if anything is found written otherwise in the books of Origen, it is not 

<margin>Defense of the second heresy by Origen himself.</margin>

Origen's work, but the work of heretics who wanted to have Origen as a patron of their error through the corruption of his books. Regarding the second heresy, however, such evident testimony exists that, in my judgment, it can hardly be denied. For in his own letter, Origen even according to...

<meta>This page continues the systematic defense of Origen, specifically addressing the accusations that he believed in the eventual salvation of the devil and the subordination of the persons of the Trinity. It then moves to the most difficult charge: his views on the pre-existence of souls.</meta>

<page-num>70</page-num>
<header>[ON] QUESTIONS</header>
<sig>h iiii</sig>

# [ON] QUESTIONS

<margin>The truth of Origen’s testimony</margin>
In **Jerome’s** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate, who was initially an admirer of Origen but later became one of his most famous critics.</note> translation, which expressly mentions Origen's epistle, he denies that the devil can ever be saved, saying that no one, unless they have lost their mind, could say such a thing. Furthermore, there exists a dialogue between **Origen** and **Candidus**, a follower of the **Valentinian** <note>A prominent Gnostic sect in the early Church that Origen frequently argued against.</note> dogma, in which Candidus tried to attribute this same error to Origen; Origen refuted him and denied that he held such a view. Moreover, regarding that passage of **Paul**, *Did they stumble so as to fall?* <note>Romans 11:11</note>, Origen, looking at this fall, says that Israel did not fall permanently. For their conversion will occur at the end of the age when the fullness [of the Gentiles] has entered, and so all Israel will be saved. But regarding him who is said to have fallen from heaven <note>The devil/Lucifer.</note>, there will be no conversion, even at the end of the age. These are Origen's words. It is also clear that the heresy attributed to him—that the Spirit does not understand the Son and the Son does not understand the Father—is falsely attributed. This is evident from what he himself says regarding Paul’s words: *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!* <note>Romans 11:33</note>. For Origen says that while this depth of God is "unsearchable" to every creature, he could not say such a thing about the Son or the Holy Spirit; for the Son says to the Father in the Gospel, *Father, all mine are thine and thine are mine* <note>John 17:10</note>. And concerning the Holy Spirit, Paul himself proclaims: *For what man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him? Even so, no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.* <note>1 Corinthians 2:11</note>. Therefore, when Paul says, *Who has known the mind of the Lord?*, he is speaking of created beings, but the nature of the Trinity is excepted. These are Origen’s words.

<margin>Defense against the heresy concerning the creation of souls.</margin>
One heresy attributed to Origen seems to remain: namely, his opinions concerning the soul—that they were created from eternity and "slid down" from heaven into bodies. Regarding the soul, Origen himself writes in his commentaries on Paul’s **Epistle to Titus** that he can receive nothing as determined from Church dogma, except that all souls are of the same species, that they possess free will, that they are rational, that they are immortal, that they were created by God, and that they will have punishments for evil and rewards for good. He says he only affirms these things about the soul because evident testimonies for them are found in the Scriptures. In other matters concerning questions of the soul, he says he speaks of what seems more probable to him, proceeding by way of inquiry rather than by way of determination, because nothing has been determined about those things in Church dogma. However, that which seemed most likely to Origen—that souls were created before bodies and lived in the heavens—is a point upon which everyone agrees [that he taught].

<margin>What Rufinus ultimately felt about the soul</margin>
And **Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), a monk and translator who defended Origen and translated many of his works into Latin.</note>, in his apology to **Anastasius**, the Bishop of the city of Rome, after he had recounted three opinions concerning the soul, said at the end: "I indeed, having read each of these, say with God as my witness that until the present I hold nothing certain or defined regarding this question; rather, I leave it to God to know what is true, and to whom He himself deigns to reveal it. I do not deny, however, that I have read each of these views, and I confess I am still ignorant—except for this which the Church clearly hands down: that God is the creator of both souls and bodies." Also, in the book of **Pamphilus** <note>St. Pamphilus (died 309 AD), a martyr and scholar who wrote an influential defense of Origen while in prison.</note>, he does not deny that Origen adhered to that opinion, but he writes this in his defense: "Now, however, since there is diversity among churchmen and some feel one way and others another about the soul—and everyone differs—how is this man [Origen] to be blamed more than the others?" Then, after these words, the opinions concerning the soul that existed at that time are recited, among which is the one now held by Catholics. And when it is shown that manifest proofs from the Holy Scriptures cannot be applied to them, and that great difficulties occur even for the authors of those opinions, he finally concludes: "What we wish to show from all of this is that just as those who think any one of these opinions we set out above is true are not rightly called heretics—because nothing certain or manifest seems to have been said about them in the Divine Scriptures, nor are they thought to be contained in the Church’s preaching—so it is not just to blame this man [Origen] for discussing what seemed most likely to him." This is found there.

<margin>First position</margin>
From all the things said above, I infer two propositions. The first is that if Origen is shown by testimonies to have thought in a Catholic <note>original: "catholicē", meaning universally orthodox or in line with the general Church.</note> manner regarding both the Trinity and the salvation of demons, we cannot convict him of heresy based on his erroneous opinion regarding the soul.

<summary>This page defends Origen against charges of heresy concerning the Trinity and the devil's salvation by quoting his own commentaries, then argues that his controversial views on the pre-existence of souls were speculative inquiries in an era before Church dogma was strictly defined.</summary>
<keywords>Origen, Jerome, Rufinus, Pamphilus, pre-existence of souls, Trinity, universalism, heresy defense, free will, early church dogma</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen, specifically addressing the theological ambiguity surrounding the origin of the soul during the early centuries of the Church to argue that Origen cannot be labeled a heretic for views that were not yet dogmatically settled.</meta>

<page-num>62</page-num>
<header>APOLOGIA</header>

# APOLOGIA

<margin>
That Augustine
was always
doubtful
concerning
the creation
of the soul.
</margin>
...condemnation. Because **Origen** was not bound to believe all things explicitly concerning the creation of the soul that we are now bound to believe; for it was neither clearly contained in **Scripture**, nor had it been determined by the **Church** then as it was later. Indeed, not only in the time of Origen, but even in the time of **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note>—who lived two hundred years after Origen—nothing had yet been determined by the Catholics (that is, by the Universal Church) regarding the soul. For Augustine himself was doubtful in his opinion on the soul, as is evident from his letter to **Jerome**, namely: whether individual souls are created for individual people, as the **orthodox** tradition now holds. From one perspective, it seemed to Augustine to follow that God would be unjust <note>Augustine struggled with "Creationism" (individual creation of souls) because it made it hard to explain how original sin was passed down without making God responsible for a "soiled" soul.</note>; or whether it followed from that one soul which was made by God in **Adam**, and thereafter, just as body comes from body, so souls were propagated from the soul <term>Traducianism<gloss>the theory that the soul is transmitted through biological generation from the parents, rather than being created individually by God.</gloss></term>. Nor should you believe that Augustine doubted this matter only in his youth; for even in the first book of his *Retractions* <note>Augustine's *Retractationes*, a late-life work where he reviewed and corrected his earlier writings.</note>, which was among his last works, he doubts this question. For he writes thus in the first book: "Without controversy, therefore, God is a certain original kingly source of the soul's happiness, who did not beget the soul from himself, but created it from no other thing, just as he created the body from the earth. For as pertains to its origin, by which it is in the body—whether it be from that one soul which was first created when man was made into a living soul, or whether individual souls are similarly made for individuals—I did not know then, nor do I know now." These are Augustine’s words, verbatim. From this it is clearly evident that because of the aforementioned erroneous opinion on the soul, Origen can in no way be called a **heretic**.

<margin>
The second
proposition
of St. Thomas.
</margin>
The second proposition I state is this: that if it is true what **Thomas [Aquinas]** says in his *Quodlibeta* <note>Disputed questions on various topics; here Pico refers to Book VII.</note>, as will be shown more widely in the seventh article of the *Defense of Origen*, and if sound theology says we are not bound by the necessity of salvation to believe not only the **Doctors of the Church**—such as Jerome, Augustine, and the like—but not even the Church itself except in those things which pertain to the **substance of faith**; and if we add that it pertains nothing to the substance of faith whether Origen was the author of those heresies, or someone else (so long as we confess those heresies to be impious dogmas), then it seems to follow that a faithful man and a true Christian is not bound by the necessity of salvation in this question to side with Jerome—even if the Church inclines more toward him—rather than with **Athanasius**, **Didymus**, **Methodius**, or **Rufinus**. Rufinus's faith was proven by his exiles; rather, we should believe Origen's own words, especially since in many 

<margin>
Jerome is
not always
to be believed,
for he is
often condemned
for the vice
of sarcasm.
</margin>
other matters which pertain even more to the substance of the faith, we do not approve of Jerome. Such is the case in the matter of ceremonies, and it is more pious not to believe Jerome where he calls **Ambrose's** commentaries on Luke "nonsense," and calls Ambrose himself now a "crow" and now a "jackdaw." <note>Jerome was known for his polemical and often insulting style, even toward other respected Church Fathers like St. Ambrose.</note> And where, damning Ambrose's book on the **Holy Spirit**, he says he has seen "bad Latin made from good Greek." And where he taxes **Basil the Great** with pride; and where in the letters of Augustine he says he has read certain heretical things; and so perhaps here too. In this matter, he would rather have it that those writings which show Origen to be a Catholic are forgeries and adulterations, rather than admitting that the things which prove him a heretic do not belong to him at all. It is neither impious, nor does it appear ruinous to the faith, to offer a defense for Origen; rather, it seems to strengthen the faith and take testimony away from the heretics, according to what is written in the book of **Pamphilus** <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD), a scholar who wrote an influential "Apology for Origen."</note> in these words: "They ought to have contemplated how much material for laughter they provide to the heretics when they see those whom they think to be the assertors and defenders of Christian dogma now being refuted and repelled by their own people; they rejoice in this civil war, attacking him whom they themselves could not attack as enemies."

Whence **Aymo** <note>Haymo of Halberstadt (d. 853 AD), a Carolingian scholar and bishop.</note>, one of the noble and ancient Doctors of the Church, in his book *On the Memory of Christian Affairs*, says: "Indeed, concerning the man Origen, so illustrious a man of most continent and chaste life and clear doctrine..."
