<page-num>71</page-num>

<header>OF THE QUESTIONS</header>

...and of clear speech, saving the faith of the fathers, I might say that he did not write these things at all, but they were maliciously invented and written by heretics to obscure his famous name, and titled with his name. These are his words, verbatim. These things were said concerning the first article to be examined and inquired into: whether those two opinions of Origen were heretical or not; in which matter, as in all others, I always place the judgment of the Church before the judgment and reasons of all others.

<margin>Concerning the second article.</margin>
Regarding the second article, it seems more reasonable that Origen should be excused because, if he wrote anything not accepted by Catholics, he did not proceed dogmatically or assertively in those writings, but always doubtfully and inquiringly. Therefore, just as although there are many things in **Augustine’s** books *On Genesis* that are not accepted, they are nevertheless excused by us because, as he himself says in his book of *Retractions* <note>Augustine’s *Retractationes*, a work where he reviewed and corrected his earlier writings late in life.</note>, more things were "searched for" in that book than "found." So also many things in Origen's books may be rejected and condemned, but because he said them by inquiring rather than determining, he is not for that reason to be called a heretic.

<margin>What true heresy is.</margin>
"Heresy" is properly called an assertion of a dogma against the express truth of either Scripture or the determination of the Church. <margin>Note the words of Origen</margin> That Origen always spoke in this way is clear from many places. For even after a discussion about the soul, he says: "Let these things, according to our opinion, not be dogmas, but only things sought and proposed so that they would not seem entirely unaddressed." And elsewhere, speaking of the resurrection, he says: "If these things are not contrary to the faith, etc."; and below: "Therefore a triple suspicion <note>Here, "suspicion" (Latin: *suspicio*) carries the sense of a tentative opinion or hypothesis.</note> is suggested to us concerning the end, from which the reader may inquire which is true and better." Then he joins three opinions concerning the resurrection.

And in the preface of his books *On Genesis*, he says: "If anything profound occurs, it must indeed be spoken of, but not affirmatively"; and below: "Regarding great matters that are above us, we are not ignorant of our own ignorance." And on the *Epistle to the Romans*, book II: "Let these things be said by us on the condition that if anyone says something better and more reasonable, those things should be held more than these of ours." And in book IV: "These things, as far as we were able, have been brought forth in places so steep and difficult: if anyone perhaps considers the zeal of our mind, he will be able to embrace it. But if he wishes to note the weakness of our perception, we ask for pardon, and we freely yield to him who is able to discuss or explain these things better." And elsewhere: "Let whoever reads this prove which of these fits more with the apostolic sense and hold to that." And in book V: "These things, for now, were able to occur to us in the present place. But if anyone perceives something better, let it not be a burden to disregard these and look to those."

And why say more? Let the book *On First Principles* <note>original: *Periarchon*</note> be read. We will see him proceed in this order: first, he sets down those things which seemed to him to be expressly determined in Scripture; and in those, he deviates nothing from the Church. Other things he says are doubtful to him and he wishes to inquire about them, asserting concerning all things that only that truth is to be received which in no way opposes apostolic and ecclesiastical dogmas.

<margin>Concerning the third article.</margin>
For the third article, which is as it were a confirmation of the second, I state this proposition: <margin>A proposition to be noted.</margin> that if there is someone having an erroneous opinion concerning matters of faith not yet determined by the Church, provided that there is no stain in his will but rather a firm purpose to always believe in harmony with Scripture and the Church, that person neither sins mortally nor is properly to be called a heretic.

<margin>A corollary.</margin>
From this proposition it follows as a corollary <note>A natural consequence or logical conclusion.</note> that it is possible for holding a certain opinion at one time to be a mortal sin <note>A grave sin that, in Catholic theology, cuts the soul off from God’s grace.</note>, which would not be so at another time. And this is because someone can believe something without obstinacy <note>original: *pertinacia*</note> at one time which they would not believe without obstinacy at another time—for instance, after a determination of the Church or a clarification of Holy Scripture. Regarding the opposite of what is believed, the opinion of all the Doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church," respected authoritative teachers.</note> bears witness, saying that it is not precisely an error of the intellect that makes a man a heretic, but there must be malice and perversity in the will. Therefore <margin>Augustine</margin> **Augustine** used to say: "I can err, but I cannot be a heretic."

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
This is confirmed by the determination of the Universal Church, which has canonized many who nevertheless persevered until death in erroneous opinions...

<summary>This page argues that Origen should not be considered a heretic because his controversial ideas were presented as philosophical inquiries rather than dogmatic assertions. The author defines heresy as a willful, obstinate rejection of established Church doctrine, rather than a simple intellectual error on undecided matters.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen by drawing a parallel between him and other early Church Fathers who held views later declared heretical, yet were still canonized as saints. It transitions into a philosophical argument about the difference between intellectual error and malicious intent (pertinacity).</meta>

-># APOLOGIA<-

<margin>Those who were heretics and were afterwards canonized</margin>
...opinions concerning the faith, and were then reproved by the Church as heretical, which opinions it is nowhere read were retracted by them. Such were **Papias**, bishop of Hierapolis; **Victorinus** of Poitiers; **Irenaeus** of Lyons; the Blessed **Cyprian**; and many others whom we know to have erred in the faith and whose opinions were condemned as heretical. And yet, they are nonetheless held in the canon of the saints. From this, it follows that it must necessarily be said either that they, <margin>Papias</margin> even though they passed away while holding those erroneous opinions in faith, did not however pass away in <margin>Victorinus</margin> mortal sin; or that the Church erred in their canonization. If they should say—as <margin>Irenaeus</margin> indeed one of those who were attacking me said—responding that perhaps they were not well-canonized, then it is not I, but they themselves who feel against the determination of the universal Church. <margin>Cyprian</margin> From this proposition, I infer the following regarding the case of **Origen**: that even given that Origen held many and numerous erroneous opinions in faith, if there was no stain in his will in any way, this precisely cannot be an argument that his soul is damned. Thus I argue: either a great error concerning any matters of faith in the intellect of someone—provided there is no stain in the will—does not impede his salvation; or even a small error regarding any matter does impede it; or some errors impede and some do not. If a great error does not impede it, then even if Origen erred in many and even in the most principal matters, provided his will was well-disposed and in no way stained, it did nothing to impede his salvation. And so, for those who wish to prove his damnation, it is not enough for them to show his errors and his perseverance in them; rather, they must show his perseverance coupled with <term>pertinacity</term> <note>Pertinacity: A theological term for stubborn persistence in an error even after being corrected by the Church's authority.</note> or negligence, or other malice of the will. If even a small error suffices to impede salvation, then the error concerning the re-baptizing of heretics <note>Cyprian famously argued that those baptized by heretics must be baptized again, a view the Church later rejected.</note> ought to have impeded the salvation of **Cyprian**, and the heresy of those who are called <margin>Chiliast heretics.</margin> **Chiliasts** <note>Chiliasts: Also known as Millenarians, these early Christians believed in a literal 1,000-year reign of Christ on earth before the final judgment.</note> ought to have impeded the salvation of **Papias**, who was the author of that heresy and passed away with it. And if so, then they were wrongly canonized by the Church. If some errors impede and some do not, those who say so must specify which errors those are that impede and which do not. And where is such a distinction ever found to have been made by the Church? For example, to say that having an error in things pertaining to such or such an article—even if it is precisely a weakness and defect of the intellect and there is no perversity, nor negligence, nor pertinacity, nor any other malice in the will—is a mortal sin; but to have an error in things pertaining to another kind of matter is not <margin>Objection</margin> a mortal sin unless there is a defect in the will. If such a distinction is not found to be made either by the Church or by the Doctors, nor does it seem possible for it to be made reasonably, then the claim of certain people appears invalid when they say there is one rule for **Cyprian** and **Papias** and their like, and another for **Origen**, because Origen erred in "principal" matters. For however great the error may be, as long as it is only an error in the intellect and there is no malice in the will, it does not seem that one so erring sins mortally. Wherefore, since we do not read that there was such malice in the will of **Origen**, even granted that he erred in the principal mysteries of the faith with a most grave error—one deservedly condemned by the Church—it cannot be proven that he himself is damned in his soul. But if someone should say there are many degrees of propositions to be believed besides this degree of propositions (namely, those determined by the Church), and that even if there is no pertinacity, it is still a sign of pertinacity to assert things whose opposite is held by the person asserting them to be held by explicit faith; and that an error is not only mortally <margin>First response to the objection.</margin> culpable because of pertinacity, but is also sometimes blamed because of negligence in seeking the truth—which negligence is not pertinacity, at least properly speaking—it seems a reasonable response can be made to this. First, that **Origen** cannot be blamed for negligence in seeking the truth in this matter <margin>Second</margin> because, as **Jerome** well says, he "sweated through days and nights" in the searching of the Scriptures. Second, that...

<summary>The author argues that Origen should not be considered damned because his errors were intellectual rather than malicious, comparing him to canonized saints like Cyprian and Papias who also held erroneous views. He posits that without "pertinacity" (stubbornness of will), intellectual error in faith does not constitute a mortal sin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen, specifically addressing the legal and theological definitions of heresy. It moves from general principles of intellectual error to specific evidence of Origen's repentance, citing Saint Jerome and contemporary debates.</meta>

# QUESTIONS

<margin>Notes on the reasons why someone is called a heretic</margin>
Secondly, **Origen** did not err in this, because at that time he did not hold it necessary to believe with explicit faith; for one who asserts the opposite—not dogmatically, but as it seemed more probable to him—cannot be called a heretic. I prove this clearly from a certain saying of **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Bible into Latin.</note> cited above. For where **Jerome** says that even if certain faulty things are found in the works of **Clement** <note>Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian teacher.</note>, the disciple of the Apostles, and others like him, one should not immediately judge them as heretics for that reason. He adds a fourfold reason. First, that the books might be corrupted. Second, that they wrote in a different sense. Third, that they simply erred. Fourth, that they spoke less cautiously. 

In these words, we must notice that even if **Clement's** book (in which he says the Son of God is a creature) is not corrupted, and even if the author did not intend another meaning, **Clement** is still not to be immediately judged a heretic, because he could have simply erred. What does "simply erred" mean, if not to have erred from a defect of the intellect and an erroneous judgment of reason, rather than from malice or perversity of the will? 

If one can "simply err" even in that heresy regarding the Son being a creature—which is the greatest charge brought against **Origen**—it is because there was not yet a determination of the Church on the matter, nor a more certain verification through greater clarification of the Scriptures, after which such an error would no longer be possible. If **Clement** was not then bound under pain of mortal sin to believe with explicit faith, how can we say that **Origen** was obliged to believe explicitly in those matters in which he is said to have erred?

<margin>Note on Augustine and Jerome</margin> 
It must be noted, however, that because heresy can exist both in words spoken badly or inordinately (as **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note> says) and in the underlying meaning, the Master **Jerome** gives a way of excusing one who has erred in either or both. This excuse applies when the error stems from a defect of the intellect alone and not the will. He says one may have "spoken less cautiously" if the heresy appears in the words, or "simply erred" if the meaning is heretical but produced by a simple and upright will through a weak and wandering intellect. These words of **Jerome** are to be well noted and weighed, because in them a useful and healthy <term>dogma</term> <note>A principle or tenet laid down by an authority as incontrovertibly true.</note> concerning <term>heretical pertinacity</term> <note>Stubbornly holding onto an error even after being corrected by the Church.</note> is rightly founded.

<margin>Regarding the fourth article.</margin> 
Regarding the fourth article, some who say that **Origen** repented cite the *Lament of Origen*, but that book is considered <term>apocryphal</term> <note>A work of doubtful authenticity, not accepted as part of the official canon.</note> as is noted in the decrees <note>original: "xv. di." referring to the Decretum Gratiani.</note>. 

<margin>Apocryphal book</margin> 
Instead, I cite the testimony of **Jerome** himself, which cannot be held as apocryphal, who expressly testifies that **Origen** repented of his errors. I do not assert this because it is reasonably necessary to believe in **Origen’s** salvation (as will be clear in the following article), but because these masters never cease shouting: "I show you that **Origen** erred; you show me that he repented! You will never show this; you will never find it written that **Origen** repented of what he wrote." 

Let these reverend fathers, therefore, hear **Jerome** himself—by whose authority they strike down **Origen**—in his *Apology to Pammachius and Oceanus*, in which he shows that he followed **Origen’s** scholarship but not his dogma. After reciting **Origen’s** errors, he adds these words: "**Origen** himself, in the letter he wrote to **Fabian**, Bishop of the city of Rome, expresses repentance for why he wrote such things, and he blames his rashness on **Ambrose** <note>Ambrose of Alexandria, Origen's friend and patron, who published Origen's notes without his permission.</note>, because he brought into the public sphere things that were edited in secret." These are **Jerome’s** words, verbatim. What could be clearer? What more express? With what face can they now say it is nowhere found that **Origen** repented?

I will also mention what happened to me these days regarding a similar topic with two of those who were condemning this conclusion. 

<margin>Note the wit</margin> 
When I—in order to defend **Origen** against the charge of <term>pertinacity</term>—was speaking to a certain man who insisted that the Church had determined **Origen** was damned in his soul for pertinacity, I said that according to Greek histories, **Origen’s** dogmas were condemned many years after his death. I referred him (if he did not have the books at home) to the **Bishop of Trogir** <note>A city in modern-day Croatia.</note>, a man no less outstanding in learning and character than in his dignity, at whose house I had seen a Greek book in which many things concerning the councils were collected. That good father said: "Why do you refer me to the Greeks? You know I [don't know] Greek..."

He further provides historical evidence from Jerome that Origen actually repented of his controversial writings, blaming their premature publication on his friend Ambrose.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of Origen, shifting from abstract theological definitions to a narrative account of his debates with critics. ### THE APOLOGY

...completely ignorant of these letters. "Let us look for Latin ones," he said. "Do we not have the *Bundle of Times* <note>original: "fasciculū temporum"; a famous world chronicle by Werner Rolevinck, first published in 1474.</note> which treats these matters most elegantly?" I said, "Let that bundle be brought," although I added: "If you prepare a fire for me as if for a heretic by placing this bundle beneath me, I will immediately send both you and your bundle to the gallows <note>original: "in malam crucem"; literally "to the evil cross," a common Latin idiom for a shameful death or a curse.</note>! For there is no trust to be placed in it." He flared up as if I had blasphemed the Trinity. "Do not be so angry," I said. "Let the bundle be brought. And do not think I will yield to you now just because your bundles <note>A pun on "fasciculus" (small bundle/book) and "fasces" (the bundles of rods symbolizing Roman magisterial authority).</note> are untied." It was brought, and in it we read these things concerning **Origen**: "**Origen**, an outstanding doctor and incomparable in the holiness of his life, most famous in the Church of God." And a little later at the end it says: "A great labyrinth is woven by various authors concerning **Samson**, **Solomon**, **Trajan** <note>The salvation of the pagan Emperor Trajan was a popular medieval legend.</note>, and this **Origen**—namely, whether they were saved or not. Because these things can be left unknown without danger, and because the Church has not certified anything regarding them, they must be committed entirely to the Lord." This was a "good bundle" indeed! When he had read this and heard that the Church was not certain about the damnation of **Origen**, it is amazing how pale he turned. And for a man upon whom the most proven 

<margin>Note another point</margin>

authorities had no effect, this "bundle" alone had such power that he changed his opinion on the spot. On the following day, another man approached me more sharply, carrying a rather large book in his hand. "By what way," he said, "or by what means at all do you dare to defend **Origen** from the eternal punishment of fire? Look, I will show you a testimony you cannot contradict, which says that **Origen** cannot be defended." "Produce your witnesses, venerable man," I said, "if you have them." Then he said, "Here is a certain great witness," and he added the name. I, however, wish to remain silent about the name. These are his sermons and preachings. Then I said, "What sermons, what trifles are you bringing me?" "Trifles?" he responded, now completely enraged. "Trifles," I said, "in which—if he even has sermons on this matter (for heaven forbid I should ever read such things)—unless some most manifest error is found, I am willing to break **Origen's** head on **Ixion's** wheel <note>A mythological reference to eternal punishment; Ixion was bound to a perpetually turning fiery wheel.</note> along with you." Now impatient and boiling with bile, he opened the book and began to read, raging in a very loud voice: "Wednesday, Sermon 11: On the Origenists." Then, in his persecution of what was written, he shouted at every single word: "Is this not an error?" And while he was shouting thus to the envy of **Stentor** <note>A Greek herald in the *Iliad* known for having a voice as loud as fifty men.</note>, he read these words written in the book: "Finally, **Jerome** confesses that he himself read six thousand books of **Origen**." And as soon as he had read this, he shouted again: "Is this not an error?" "This," I said, "is an error, and a great one indeed! This is an open lie; this is a manifest falsehood!" And to restrain the man on the spot, I ordered **Jerome's** letters to be brought. Running immediately to the second book of his *Invective Against Rufinus* <note>Rufinus was a friend-turned-rival of Jerome; their bitter dispute over Origen's orthodoxy dominated early 5th-century theology.</note>, I showed him **Jerome** responding to **Rufinus** (who had claimed that **Pope Epiphanius** boasted of reading six thousand of **Origen's** books) with these words: "As for the six thousand books which you pretend were read by him: who will believe either that you are telling the truth or that he could have lied so much? For if **Origen** had written six thousand books, it might have been possible for a learned man, instructed in sacred letters from infancy, to have read the works of others out of curiosity and knowledge. But since **Origen** did not write them, how could he have read them? Count the index of his books, which are contained in the third volume of **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the first great historian of the Church.</note> where he wrote the *Life of Pamphilus*, and you will not find—I do not say six thousand—but even a third of that number." These were **Jerome's** words verbatim. 

<margin>Conclusion</margin>

He blushed, and my case was saved. But let us return now to the point, concluding that either with **Rufinus** and others whom we cited above in the first article, we must concede that **Origen** never sinned; or, if with **Jerome** we contend that he did sin, let us know that we must also grant that **Origen** repented of his sin by giving a personal pamphlet to the Bishop of Rome. For my part, after I have carefully weighed and examined those things which are said about **Origen** by **Eusebius**, **Rufinus**, and **Jerome**, I conjecture that **Origen**, laboring long in the scrutiny of the Scriptures, was ambiguous concerning many difficult and principal questions of theology since he did not [state] with certainty and without doubt to himself...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen’s orthodoxy, shifting from general arguments to a detailed chronological analysis of his life and works. Pico uses the testimony of Eusebius and Jerome to argue that Origen's most controversial ideas were private intellectual exercises from his youth, published against his will by his friend Ambrose.</meta>

### OF QUESTIONS

...he himself saw that he was able to assert something regarding those matters from the testimony of the Scriptures. For this reason, regarding many mysteries of the faith, he perhaps said many things by way of inquiry and dispute in the earlier years of his age which the Catholic faith would not receive. Therefore, **Origen**—who, as he himself says, was "not ignorant of his own ignorance" and clearly recognized that he had not yet attained the truth of those questions—never wished to be taken down by shorthand writers <note>original: "notariis"; these were scribes who used a form of shorthand to record live speeches or dictation.</note> in public before his sixtieth year, even regarding those things he preached in the churches, as **Eusebius** reports.

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
Let us note, therefore, what **Eusebius** writes in the twenty-sixth chapter of the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*: that **Origen**, in the third year of the reign of Emperor **Philip** and under Pope **Fabian**, when he was already reaching his sixtieth year, began to commit his words to public writing. And let us note what he says above in the seventeenth chapter: that under Pope **Urban** (who was succeeded by **Pontianus**), already before the time of **Fabian**, **Origen** took up the beginning of writing commentaries on the Holy Scriptures at the urging of **Ambrose** <note>This is Ambrose of Alexandria, Origen's wealthy patron, not the famous Saint Ambrose of Milan.</note>, who compelled him with many prayers and entreaties. **Eusebius** says that **Ambrose** seemed most worthy of having this duty bestowed upon him, and to him whatever was secret and hidden, covered within the sacred letters, should be opened. From these two passages in **Eusebius**, in which an apparent contradiction is found, it is clearly gathered: that at the urging of **Ambrose**, he dictated certain things in his earlier years before he had yet discovered any truth, intended to be communicated privately to **Ambrose** alone and not to be published to the public—as things he did not yet know to be safe and in harmony with Apostolic truth. **Ambrose**, however, brought those things, which had been produced in secret, into the public. Later, when the Catholic truth was discovered by **Origen** (now a sixty-year-old), he began to write boldly, because he was writing both Catholically and publicly. He grieved vehemently that those things he had written for **Ambrose's** private use had already been published through him. To clear his name <note>original: "purgationē"; a legal or formal clearing of one's reputation.</note>—as is conjectured from the words of **Jerome** and **Eusebius** regarding the sequence of the whole matter—he wrote to **Fabian**, the Bishop of Rome, providing testimony of his Catholic faith and explaining that the things found written by him earlier were not written for publication, as he himself was doubtful whether they were Catholic or not.

<margin>Jerome</margin>
But it was **Ambrose** who published them. This is indeed what **Jerome** says: **Origen** himself, in the letter he wrote to **Fabian**, the Bishop of the city of Rome, performs penance for why he wrote such things, and he refers the causes of this rashness to **Ambrose**, who brought into the public those things produced in secret. **Eusebius**, however, narrating what he wrote after his sixtieth year—after he enumerated the book *Against Celsus*, twenty-five books of *Commentaries on Matthew*, and twenty on the Prophets—adds: "He also wrote to **Fabian**, Bishop of the city of Rome, and to very many other leaders of the churches concerning his Catholic faith." Thus says he.

Let it be true, then, that before his sixtieth year **Origen** was doubtful concerning many mysteries of the faith. And let it be true that he communicated many things in writing secretly to **Ambrose**, which he then held not by firmly adhering to them, but by inquiring doubtfully—opinions which are now not to be received by Catholics. Thus **Jerome** speaks the truth: that what is found in many of **Origen's** books that is not Catholic belongs to **Origen**, because they were truly dictated by him—though not as things believed, but as things sought rather than found. Consequently, they are not to be culpably ascribed to **Origen**, to whom the Catholic truth was later revealed. Furthermore, in these works, many things were also devised by heretics, according to **Rufinus**.

We can also accept as truth that **Origen** himself complained most especially about this while he was still alive. Let it be true then, according to **Eusebius** in his *Ecclesiastical History* (approved as true by **Jerome**), that **Origen** does not acknowledge as his own works—namely, those in which he says anything definitively and with adherence—except those he wrote after his sixtieth year. And let it be true also according to **Jerome** that he repented of the earlier writings rashly published by **Ambrose**, and consequently died a Catholic.

<margin>Concerning the fifth article. First proposition.</margin>
Thus, not only according to **Rufinus**, **Pamphilus**, and **Eusebius**, but even according to **Jerome**, it is more reasonable to believe that he is saved than to believe he is damned. For the fifth article, I state this proposition: however much anyone may sin gravely and mortally in life, and it is established that he sinned mortally...

<summary>Pico argues that Origen's controversial writings were youthful private inquiries published without his consent by his patron Ambrose, and that Origen later retracted them and died a faithful Catholic.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of Origen. Having previously discussed the timeline of Origen's writings, Pico now moves into a theological and legal argument: that it is impossible for humans to certain of anyone's damnation without divine revelation, using historical biblical figures as precedents.</meta>

-># APOLOGIA<-

...unless his <term>final impenitence</term> <note>The theological state of dying in a state of mortal sin without repenting, which according to Church doctrine results in eternal damnation.</note> is certain, it is rash to truly assert that he is damned. The truth of this proposition is clear from the common opinion of all the <term>Doctors</term> <note>Authoritative theologians of the Church whose teachings are considered particularly reliable.</note> who agree on the said proposition. From this proposition, I infer two corollary propositions. The first is this:

<margin>First corollary proposition</margin>
It is not because someone has lived in mortal sin—and it is not certain to us that he did not repent—that we must firmly judge him to be in hell. This is clear because, even if a mortal sin is granted, that which leads to eternal damnation is not yet fully established. Rather, beyond the sin, it is necessary to establish and be certain of **final impenitence**. Nor do I, who deny that we must firmly believe him to be in hell, have to show you his repentance. But you, who assert that he is damned, must provide certainty regarding his impenitence. For this reason, the statement of **Henry of Hesse** <note>original: "Héricus de aslia"; a 14th-century German theologian and mathematician.</note> carries much weight; in his exposition of the fourth chapter of the book of Genesis, he says these formal words: 

"If, therefore, the argument of some were effective—by which they persuade us that someone is damned (as they do regarding **Solomon**) because Scripture records his sin and makes no mention of his justice or repentance—then it would likewise prove that the first man [Adam] was damned for his sin, just as the first angel was."

Thus says **Henry**. For nowhere is mention made of the repentance of **Adam**, but only of his sin. Similarly, in the eighth chapter of Judges, one reads of the sin of **Gideon** and not of his repentance; and yet it is well believed by the Doctors that he was saved. You can also say that by this same argument, some were erroneously deceived into saying that **Moses** was damned, because his sin at the "waters of contradiction" <note>A reference to Meribah (Numbers 20), where Moses struck the rock in anger.</note> was read about, and nothing was expressly held regarding his repentance. And yet God said to **Joshua**: "*Moses my servant is dead.*" 

The second corollary proposition is this: 

<margin>Second corollary proposition</margin>
No one can be certain that anyone is damned to hell unless he has this from a special revelation of God, or from those to whom it is believed God has revealed it. The truth of this is clear from the preceding propositions, because no one can be certain of final repentance or impenitence except He who knows the secrets of the heart and to whom He has wished to reveal them. Since, indeed, no one is as certain of another's state as he is of his own—because "no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him," as is said in the second chapter of **Corinthians**—and since a man cannot be certain of himself "whether he be worthy of hatred or love," as **Ecclesiastes** 9 says, how much more will he be unable to be certain of another unless he has a special revelation regarding this. 

From this principal proposition with its corollaries, I infer for the purpose of my conclusion that, even granted that **Origen** sinned mortally by erring in those errors, nevertheless, since we are uncertain of his final impenitence or repentance, to assert that he is damned is an altogether rash judgment and is to be rejected. Since, therefore, we can be certain of neither his salvation nor his damnation, it is nonetheless pious and very reasonable to believe, as I have said, that God saved him—a man of such great and immense knowledge. 

Regarding him, **Jerome** says in his preface to the *Song of Songs*: "While in other matters he surpassed all others, in this he surpassed himself," and that verse is verified of him: "*The king brought me into his chamber.*" 

<margin>Jerome's words</margin>
And elsewhere, wishing to partially imitate **Origen**—whom no one but the unskilled denies was the master of the churches after the Apostles—**Jerome** says that **Origen** toiled with such labor over the Scriptures that he justly received the name **Adamantius** <note>A Greek nickname meaning "Man of Steel" or "Unbreakable," referring to Origen's legendary stamina and productivity.</note>. 

<margin>Origen is justly called Adamantius</margin>
And after certain other things, he adds this: "Who can ever read as much as he wrote?" And for this toil, what reward did he receive? He was damned by Bishop **Demetrius**, with the exception of the priests of Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, and Achaia. The city of Rome itself consented against him; it assembled its senate not because of the novelty of his dogmas, nor because of heresy (as rabid dogs now falsely pretend against him), but because they could not bear the glory of his eloquence and knowledge. 

"Why I have written this," **Jerome** says, "and why I dictated it by the fire of a poor lamp with a quick but not cautious speech, you can understand if you consider the followers of **Epicurus** and **Aristippus**." 

These are the words of **Jerome** verbatim. Which individual words, I ask you, O ingenious reader, to diligently...

<summary>Pico argues that judging Origen (or biblical figures like Solomon and Moses) as damned is "rash" because humans cannot know a soul's final state without divine revelation. He cites Saint Jerome to suggest that Origen's historical condemnation was fueled more by professional envy than by genuine heresy.</summary>
<keywords>final impenitence, damnation, Origen, Jerome, Henry of Hesse, Solomon, Moses, Adamantius, divine revelation, judgment</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of the early Christian scholar Origen. Following the previous page’s legal argument regarding the impossibility of judging someone's "final impenitence" without divine revelation, Pico now provides historical and patristic evidence—quoting Jerome, Augustine, and others—to show that Origen’s devotion and suffering for the faith should weigh more heavily than his suspected errors.</meta>

# QUESTIONS

...reader, attend diligently: and through them understand for yourself the things I do not express. In the preface to his *Hebrew Questions*, speaking of the same Origen, **Jerome** says this: "I say this one thing: that I would wish to have his knowledge of the Scriptures even with the envy attached to his name." He valued at a straw the images and shadows of ghosts whose nature, he says, is to terrify children and chatter in dark, shadowy corners. I pass over what Jerome proclaims about him: that he trampled on avarice; that he castrated himself out of zeal for God—though not according to knowledge <note>A reference to Romans 10:2 and Origen’s famous literal interpretation of Matthew 19:12, for which he was later criticized by the Church.</note>—and that he sweated day and night in the explanation of Scripture. Those who illuminate it shall have eternal life, as the Wise Man says. And as he writes to Vigilantius, he explained the obscurities of the prophets. And yet I know he revealed the greatest mysteries of the Old Testament. 

<margin>Note.</margin>
I pass over that he was not only the son of a martyr, but he himself was barely short of the merit of martyrdom. 

<margin>Origen eager for martyrdom</margin>
For **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the primary historian of the early Church.</note> says that even as a young boy he burned with such a great fire for attaining martyrdom that he voluntarily thrust himself into dangers. Later, in the time of the **Decian persecution** <note>The persecution of Christians under Emperor Decius, c. 250 AD, known for its intensity.</note>, he endured new crosses, new types of punishments, and torments unheard of in all ages, so that—as Eusebius says—he was harassed by "a thousand deaths," lest even that one death which he hoped for should happen to him, with the persecutor working with the greatest effort so that neither should death be granted nor should the punishment cease. 

See how little he lacked the praise of martyrdom, which so many of his disciples achieved with him as their leader and encourager. I say he lacked little; indeed, he clearly did not lack the praise of martyrdom; rather, he earned a merit almost equal to it. For **Augustine** also says in the book *On the Good of Marriage*: "The merit of martyrdom is not unequal in John, who did not suffer, and in Peter, who did suffer." 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Note these words of Augustine well. Thus, just as **John**, although he did not pass through the sword, was nevertheless prepared to endure martyrdom when he was sent into the vat of boiling oil; so also Origen, although he did not undergo death by martyrdom, was nevertheless prepared; indeed, he was most greedy to undergo it. And he suffered as many torments—as Eusebius says—as if he underwent a thousand deaths for one. And this is what **Bernard** says in his sermon on the holy martyrs: that there is a **triple martyrdom**: 

<margin>Bernard: Triple Martyrdom</margin>
martyrdom of the will only; martyrdom of the work only; and martyrdom of both work and will. John the Evangelist suffered the martyrdom of the will only, to whom it was said (along with his brother): *You shall drink of my cup* (Matthew 20). 

<margin>Cyprian</margin>
Whence **Cyprian** says: "Among the servants of God, where martyrdom is intended and the mind conceives it, the soul devoted to good is crowned by God the Judge. For it is one thing for martyrdom to be lacking to the soul, and another for the soul to be lacking to martyrdom." If, therefore, the soul of Origen was never lacking to martyrdom, and he underwent a thousand deaths for one, how can we not believe him to be crowned by God the Judge, unless the martyr Cyprian is lying? 

And if he is damned, I ask: who damned him to the death of Gehenna <note>The biblical term for hell or eternal punishment.</note>? Was it Jesus Christ, for whom he himself wished to die so many times? Rather, as Augustine says of Cyprian himself, the blood of martyrdom washed away every stain of heresy in him. 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
So too of Origen: let us piously believe that the blood of martyrdom—poured out by him, not so much outwardly upon the earth as inwardly upon his heavenly soul burning with zeal for God and charity—washed away every stain of heresy. Let us say with **David**: "Blessed is Origen, who, although he sometimes went into the counsel of the erring, nevertheless did not stand in the way of sinners through impenitence, and never sat in the chair of pestilence through stubbornness; but his will was in the law of the Lord, and in His law he meditated day and night." <note>Pico is here adapting the language of Psalm 1:1-2 to Origen’s life.</note> Blessed is Origen, whose iniquities were forgiven through baptism and whose sins were covered through repentance, and to whom the Lord did not impute sin because of martyrdom. 

Finally, such a man and so great a man—even if he sometimes erred in the mysteries of faith out of a defect of intellect and not from any malice of will—let us believe that he was not abandoned by the Lord in his final moments. But rather, by the visitation of His most merciful mercy, he was illuminated regarding the secrets of faith (if he erred in any) and called back from the erroneous way to the way of salvation. And this I understood in my brief response when I said elsewhere: "Since he is not found to have been stubborn, it is likely to believe that God saved him"—that is, by visiting him with the visitation I mentioned...

<summary>Pico argues that Origen’s extreme sufferings during the Decian persecution constitute a "martyrdom of the will" that, according to Church Fathers like Augustine and Cyprian, would wash away any accidental errors or "stains of heresy."</summary>
<keywords>Origen, martyrdom of the will, Decian persecution, Jerome, Augustine, Bernard of Clairvaux, Cyprian, heresy vs. error, final salvation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s legal and theological defense of Origen, specifically addressing whether the Church has ever officially declared Origen’s soul to be in hell. It follows the previous discussion of Origen's zeal and asceticism as evidence of his character.</meta>

# APOLOGIA 9

...most mercifully placed him in a state worthy of salvation: and, illuminating him regarding the secrets of the faith in which he had erred, called him to a saving repentance for them. Whether this truly happened or not, no one can know with certainty unless it has been revealed to them from above. But to believe that it was so, rather than that it was not, is more consistent and thus more reasonable to anyone considering the life and deeds of Origen. For it is also reasonable that in doubtful matters, one should always adhere to the more favorable side. Let these things be said so they may have weight even if Origen’s repentance were not certain—though we have most clearly shown it to be certain in the preceding sections, based on the testimony of the most blessed **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), though later a critic of Origen, often praised his immense learning and early piety.</note>.

<margin>Regarding the sixth article.</margin>
Regarding the sixth article, I say that it is not to be believed that the Church ever determined that the soul of Origen was damned to hell. I prove the truth of this proposition by two reasons.

<margin>The first reason.</margin>
The first reason is this: regarding a matter where one side or the other cannot be determined with certainty except by being rash, it ought not to be believed that a determination was made by the Church. But regarding this question of whether Origen is saved or damned, neither side can be determined without being rash, at least without a special revelation from God. Therefore, since no such revelation is established, it ought not to be believed that a determination on this matter was made by the Church. The major premise is well-known: and to believe the opposite would be injurious to the Church—namely, that anything could be judged by her without consultation and rashly.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
The minor premise is clear from the articles mentioned above. It is confirmed because the Church could not be made certain of Origen’s damnation except through a special revelation made concerning him. But of such a revelation, no mention is made anywhere; therefore, etc.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
The second reason is this: if there is anything that persuades people that the Church determined Origen's damnation, it is certain texts of the decrees which seem to sound that way to those who interpret them in a crude <note>original: "grosso modo" - meaning a simplistic or literalistic interpretation that misses the technical legal nuance.</note> manner. Yet, when they are rightly examined, they act against those people rather than for them. These are the texts they usually bring forward: First, that in the **Decretals** <note>Canon law collections.</note>, distinctio 15, chapter *Sancta Romana Ecclesia*, as written by **Pope Gelasius**: "Also, we accept some small works of Origen which the blessed Jerome does not reject for reading. But all the rest, we say, are to be renounced along with their author." Also, in causa 24, quaestio 3, chapter *Sane*: "Also, if anyone goes back to the times of **Theophilus** <note>Theophilus of Alexandria, a fierce opponent of Origenism in the late 4th century.</note> of holy memory or earlier, they will find Origen anathematized after his death—which your Holiness and Julius, the most religious man of ancient Rome, also do." And the gloss there says: "Since he was damned, are not his writings also excluded?" And regarding heretics, in the chapter *Fraternitatis*, it is written: "Since Celestinus and Pelagius were damned in the **Synod of Ephesus**, how can the chapters of those whose authors are damned be received?"

<margin>Synod of Ephesus.</margin>
From these authorities, some believe that the damnation of Origen’s soul to hell is proven. I, however, say that nothing more is contained in these premises except that the Church condemns both the opinions and the dogmas attributed to Origen as heretical, and condemns and detests him as a dogmatizer <note>In this context, one who formulates or spreads unofficial or unauthorized doctrines.</note>—intending nothing at all regarding the damnation or salvation of his soul. That this is true is clear for many reasons.

<margin>The first reason against the doctors condemning Origen; Gelasius.</margin>
First, because it does not pertain to the Church to damn or save the souls of men; that belongs solely to Him who is the Judge of the living and the dead. Therefore, it is ridiculous if one reads in the decrees, "We damn Origen," to interpret it as, "We damn his soul with the damnation of hell." This is also evidently clear from the way of speaking used by Gelasius himself, who says: "his other works are to be renounced along with their author." For this word "renounce" can in no way carry the meaning that they intend. Rather, the Pope intends nothing other than this: namely, that his works are not accepted as authentic in the Church, nor is he himself received as an approved teacher whose sayings are to be believed in the Church. Even if the Pope had not only said "we hold back" but "we damn," it would be of no use to them, because we are also accustomed to speak this way: "In this matter **Scotus** damns **Thomas**," or "**Hervaeus** damns Scotus," <note>Pico refers to the famous intellectual battles between scholastic theologians Duns Scotus, Thomas Aquinas, and Hervaeus Natalis. To "damn" a person in an academic context meant to reject their arguments or doctrines, not to judge their eternal soul.</note> and so on for the rest. In these phrases, we must always understand the "damnation" of the doctrine and not the soul, according to the common and proper way of speaking.

<summary>Pico argues that the Church's historical condemnation of Origen refers to his heretical writings and status as an unapproved teacher, not a final judgment on his soul's salvation, which only God can determine. He explains that medieval academic language often used "damn" to mean the refutation of ideas rather than eternal punishment.</summary>
<keywords>Origen, Pope Gelasius, salvation, damnation, Church authority, heresy, scholasticism, Duns Scotus, Thomas Aquinas, canon law</keywords>

--- Page 148 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s Apologia, specifically the defense of Origen. He is currently arguing that the Church's condemnation of a teacher’s writings does not necessarily mean the Church has judged that teacher’s soul to be in hell.</meta>

### OF QUESTIONS

<margin>Second [reason]</margin>
Second, I argue against those based on the gloss <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria" was the standard medieval commentary on Canon Law or the Bible, often cited as an authority in legal and theological disputes.</note> which they themselves cite, which says: "If he himself is damned, are not his writings also damned?" I ask these people how the consequence—"Origen himself is damned, therefore his writings are also damned"—is to be understood. How is the term "damned" <note>original: "ly dānatus"</note> taken in the first part of the statement? If it is taken to mean "not approved in his doctrine" and "not accepted as a teacher of dogma" <note>original: "dogmatistes"</note>, then I have proven my point. But if it is understood that he is damned in his soul to the punishment of hell, then the logic does not hold. For it is possible for many teachers whose writings are Catholic—and are read daily as Catholic works—to be in hell. This is because it is possible for someone to err in no part of the faith and to hold correct views on all the articles of belief, yet still be in another mortal sin and die in that state. The damnation of the soul is entirely irrelevant <note>original: "imptinens" (impertinens)</note> to the condemnation of a person's doctrine, because the former depends on the malice of the will, while the latter depends on a defect of the intellect. Therefore, this argument is also invalid: "This person is in paradise, therefore his sayings are Catholic." For **Papias** <note>An early Christian author (c. 60–163 AD) whose works are mostly lost; he was a millenarian, a view later rejected.</note> is in paradise, as are **Irenaeus**, **Victorinus**, **Cyprian**, and many others, whose sayings are nevertheless rejected as heretical in many matters which they are never recorded to have revoked. I confirm this from the saying to which the gloss refers concerning heretics, in the chapter *Fraternitatīs* <note>A reference to the Decretals of Gregory IX, a core part of Canon Law.</note>, where it says: "**Celestinus** and **Pelagius** <note>Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD) and his follower Celestius were leaders of the Pelagian movement, which the Church condemned for denying original sin.</note> were condemned in the Council of Ephesus; how then could those chapters be received whose authors are condemned?" It is certain,

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
however, that in that council Celestinus and Pelagius were not damned in themselves (that is, in their souls), but in their doctrine. This is both because, as was said above, the Church is neither accustomed to nor able to damn men in that way, and because we must understand the judgment to be about the matter that was first investigated and disputed. But in that council, as is clear from the acts of the council, the question was not whether the souls of Celestinus and Pelagius were in paradise or in hell, but whether their sayings and dogmas were Catholic or non-Catholic. Therefore, we must understand the judgment to be about this—that is, about the truth of their dogmas and the approval or rejection of their authors as people teaching those dogmas.

<margin>Third [reason]</margin>
Third, it is foolish to say that the Church has determined Origen's soul to be damned, because the Church does not have a custom of damning people in the same way it has a custom of canonizing them—that is, by decreeing through a sentence that they are in hell. The reason why it is accustomed to do the latter but not the former is because, to decree that someone is saved, we must be certain that they died in a state of grace. While we can have signs of this, though not certain ones, from what they did in life (which are not enough, since as long as someone is "on the way" <note>The theological term "viator" (one on the way) refers to a living person who still has the capacity to merit or sin.</note> there is always room to merit or demerit and to change from one purpose to another), we do have signs after death, such as miracles or something similar. However, such a sign by which we could be convinced of someone's damnation after their death is not possible to have, nor is it easy to find. Indeed, without doubt, no other sign can be had except a special revelation regarding the matter. If such a revelation were occurring or had occurred, surely the Church—just as it testifies to miracles and other things that moved it toward canonization—would also make mention of a special revelation having been made when it condemned someone; it would not appear to have decreed such a thing rashly or unadvisedly. Yet the Church nowhere tells such a story regarding Origen. We must therefore understand Origen to be "damned" by the Church in the same way that he is shown to be damnable based on the life he lived: but the Church reports nothing about him except that he erred in the mysteries of the faith. Absolute damnation of Origen in himself does not follow from this error, but only the damnation of his writings and doctrine, as is clear from what was said before; and thus we must judge him to have been damned by the Church and not otherwise. Furthermore, we know that he was not "pertinacious" <note>In canon law, "pertinacity" is the stubborn persistence in error required for a person to be legally considered a heretic.</note> against the Church's determination in those opinions, because the councils in which those opinions were condemned took place long after Origen's death, as is clear from Greek and Latin histories. And whether he was unrepentant of them, we cannot know in any way; indeed, we have proved above from **Jerome** that he either did not write those things or, if he did, he repented of them.

<summary>Pico argues that the Church condemns Origen's specific doctrines as heretical but has never formally decreed that his soul is in hell. He distinguishes between intellectual errors in writing and the moral state of a soul, noting that the Church lacks a formal "damnation" process equivalent to canonization.</summary>
<keywords>Origen, Canon Law, canonization, heresy, Pelagius, Council of Ephesus, St. Jerome, pertinacity, damnation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his controversial "Conclusion on Origen." He concludes his argument that one can question whether a specific person is in hell without being a heretic, then transitions to his eighth disputed conclusion regarding the nature of belief and the human will.</meta>

->APOLOGIA<-

<margin>
Regarding the seventh article. Saint Thomas.
</margin>
Regarding the seventh article, I state this proposition: that according to the doctrine of **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval philosopher and theologian.</note>, it is not held that every member of the faithful is required, as a necessity of faith, to believe that a person whom the church has judged and sentenced is in hell. The truth of this proposition is derived as follows: the same degree of faith is to be given to the church in the damnation of someone as is given in the canonization of saints. But Thomas says in the last article of his *Quodlibeta IX* <note>original: "quolibet .noni." A "Quodlibet" was a public theological debate where the speaker answered "any question" posed by the audience.</note> that we are not bound by the necessity of faith to believe that saints canonized by the church are in glory, but only by a **pious belief** <note>original: "pietate fidei." This refers to a belief held out of religious devotion and respect for Church tradition rather than a strictly required dogma.</note>. Therefore, we are also not necessarily bound to believe those damned by the church are in hell, but it is only to be believed piously. The foundation of Thomas's view is that we are only bound by the necessity of salvation to believe those things in the church which pertain to the **substance of faith** <note>The essential, unchanging core doctrines of Christianity.</note>. This is because, in those matters, the Spirit who comes teaches the church all truth. However, whether the soul of this or that person is in hell or in paradise has nothing to do with the substance of the faith. Nevertheless, because the honor we show to saints is a certain profession of faith by which we believe in the glory of the saints, even if we are not bound to this by the necessity of salvation, it is still to be believed piously. From this proposition, I infer for the purpose of my conclusion that even if the church had determined **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar whose salvation was a subject of intense debate in the 15th century.</note> to be damned, we would still not be bound by the necessity of the Catholic faith to assent that it is so. From this, it is clear that even if what they allege against me were true—namely, that the church had determined the opposite of my conclusion—it would still have been poorly judged by them that my conclusion "savored of heresy" <note>original: "hæreſim ſaperet." A technical legal term for a statement that sounds like heresy even if it hasn't been officially condemned.</note>. Therefore, let these masters see that their determination against my conclusion is not correct, even if the things they bring against me are true. Let them beware lest they establish new things to be believed by the faithful on their own authority, and determine them to be "of the faith." Let them hear that prohibition of the Lord in **Deuteronomy 4**: "You shall not add to the word that I speak to you" <note>original: "Non addetis ad uerbū qđ ego loquor uobis."</note>. This saying condemns not only those who, by their own authority, add new beliefs to previous ones, but also those who reject Catholic truth as if it were heretical.

# QUESTION EIGHT: CONCERNING THE FREEDOM OF BELIEF.

<margin>
Proof of the conclusion for its first part. Aristotle.
</margin>
**J**ust as no one holds an opinion precisely because they *wish* to hold that opinion, so too no one believes something is true precisely because they *wish* to believe it. From this conclusion, I infer this corollary: it is not in the free power of a human being to believe an article of faith to be true whenever they please, and to believe it is not true whenever they please. These masters judged that this proposition, along with its corollary, was erroneous and savored of heresy. I, however, consider the principal conclusion to be not only Catholic but most true, and far truer than its opposite. And I say the same regarding the corollary when understood correctly; its sense, if taken according to my mind, is not to be understood otherwise than as it follows from the principal conclusion, of which it is stated to be a corollary.

<margin>
Proof for the second [part]. Augustine.
</margin>
That the conclusion is not only Catholic but also most true is clear. For regarding its first part—which is that no one holds an opinion on something precisely because they want to—there is **Aristotle** in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de aīa" (De Anima)</note>, commentary text 254. There, Aristotle distinguishes between imagination and opinion. This sentence of Aristotle has not only not been rejected but has been unanimously approved by all our theologians. Regarding the second part of the conclusion—which is that no one believes something is precisely true because they want to believe it is true—there is **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for Western Christianity.</note> in several places. He says quite often that no one can believe by free will alone—that is, by a mere command of the will without the persuasion of reason or a motive.

<margin>
Peter d'Ailly.
</margin>
And my entire conclusion, in which this opinion is summarily held—that when some doubtful proposition is proposed, a mere apprehension of the terms and a mere command of the will is not sufficient for someone to believe it or disbelieve it—is held by **Peter d'Ailly** <note>original: "Petrus de alliāco" (1351–1420), a prominent French theologian and cardinal.</note>... 
<meta>catchword: Henricus (referring to Henry of Ghent on the next page)</meta>

->QUESTIONS<-

<sig>i ii</sig>

<margin>Doctors by whom this conclusion is proven.</margin>
<margin>Declaration of the correlation.</margin>
<margin>Something is said to be in the freedom or free power of the will in two ways.</margin>
<margin>First.</margin>
<margin>Second.</margin>
**Henry of Oyta** and **Henry of Hesse** <note>Henry of Oyta (d. 1397) and Henry of Langenstein (also called Henry of Hesse, d. 1397) were influential 14th-century theologians whose works bridged late medieval scholasticism and early modern thought.</note> agree. Indeed, when I was in Paris, almost the entire **University of Paris** <note>The intellectual center of Western Christendom during the Middle Ages, where Pico’s ideas were heavily scrutinized.</note> held this view. Many Catholic doctors consider it so true that they regard the opposing view as impossible. In fact, I have not yet read a doctor who contradicts this opinion. However, the corollary <note>A logical consequence of a previously proven statement.</note> or proposition should not be understood or accepted otherwise than with the restriction or determination placed in the antecedent <note>The first part of a logical argument.</note>. Specifically, it is not within the free power of the will to believe an **article of faith** <note>A fundamental point of Christian dogma.</note> is true whenever it pleases, or to believe it is false whenever it pleases. Thus, the intellect does not believe simply because it pleases the will that it should believe. Such a connection between the intellect and a proposition is not unusual; indeed, in **Sacred Scripture**, the meaning of the letter is often understood by what precedes or follows it. This is exactly what must be done in our case: since this statement "it is not in our power," etc., is not presented as a separate conclusion but as a corollary to what came before. If it does not please my critics to accept the meaning of this corollary from the principal statement to which it is linked and concatenated, let them observe that something is said to be "in the freedom or free power of the will" in two ways. **In one way**, because once an idea is grasped by the intellect, no other intellectual act is required—it is within the commanding power of the will to place that act of belief. In this conclusion, I deny that the **act of believing** <note>original: "actus credendi"</note> is in the free power of man in this way. Nor is it necessary for every commanded, meritorious, or demeritorious act to be in a person’s power in this manner. For the mere grasping of the terms of an article is not sufficient for belief; rather, persuasion or some other probability is required, as is cited from **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD), who famously argued that "no one believes unless they are first persuaded."</note>. **In the other way**, something is said to be in the free power of the will because, once all other requirements for that act are present, the will has the power to bring it into being or not. In this sense, the will is not forced into the act, even when all other conditions are met. In this second way, the act of believing an article is indeed in the free power of the will. This is the true meaning of the corollary proposition, and from what has been said, anyone with understanding can see that those masters were not correct to say absolutely that the view is erroneous or "smacks of heresy."

<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>First argument.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>Second argument.</margin>
<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
That the opinion of those doctors I follow is probable and reasonable—namely, those who say that to cause the **assent of faith** <note>The mental act of accepting something as true.</note>, the mere grasping of terms combined with the command of the will is not enough—can be seen not only by the authority of **Augustine**, who affirms this in many places as I have said, but also by very effective reasons. **First**, it is argued as follows: It is not in the free power of a man to form an opinion that this or that is the case simply when he wants to. Therefore, it is not in the free power of a man to *believe* that this or that is the case simply when he wants to. The logic follows because if something (belief) seems more likely to be under our control than another (opinion), yet it is not, then the conclusion holds. It is less difficult to adhere to something with a fear that the opposite might be true <note>This is the definition of "opinion" in scholastic thought—holding a view while acknowledging you might be wrong.</note> than to adhere to it without such fear <note>This refers to "faith" or "certainty," where one has no doubt.</note>. This antecedent is expressly stated by **Aristotle** in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "ii. de anima," text of commentary 153.</note> and is clear from experience. For anyone can experience within themselves that when a doubtful proposition is offered, they are inclined to neither side by assent until some new appearance comes to them—either through a logical argument, or through intuitive knowledge, or through the testimony of many, or through the authority of the speaker, or something similar. **Second**, it is argued thus: It is not in the free power of a man to make something *appear* true to his intellect, or to make it *appear* false. Therefore, it is not in the free power of a man to believe something to be true or false in this way. The logic holds because it is a contradiction for someone to believe and assent to something if it does not "appear" true to them. This premise is proven because for something to "appear" such-and-such to the intellect is for it to be represented in a certain way to the intellect, and this cannot depend on a command of the will, because the representation precedes the act of the will. This is confirmed because something appearing a certain way to the intellect happens because the object represented is such, and the evidence (or whatever makes it credible or incredible) is such, and the intellect itself is such. But to make the object such, or the intellect such, is not within the choice of the will...

<summary>Pico defends his eighth conclusion, arguing that faith is not a simple choice made by the will, but requires intellectual persuasion and the "appearance" of truth. He distinguishes between the will's power to command an act and the intellectual conditions necessary for that act to occur.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his thesis that belief is not purely a matter of will. Having established that the intellect is a distinct faculty from the will, he now employs formal Scholastic logic to argue that while the will can direct the mind to think about a subject, it cannot force the mind to accept something as true without sufficient reason or evidence.</meta>

# DEFENSE

<margin>Thirdly</margin>
Thirdly, it is argued thus: Whenever there is a power that is merely neutral and indifferent toward two opposite **second acts** <note>original: "actus secundos"; in Scholastic philosophy, a "first act" is a capacity or habit, while a "second act" is the actual performance of a function, like the act of thinking itself.</note>, it cannot perform either of them unless it is first determined by something that is a **primary act** <note>original: "actus primus"</note>, or which stands in the place of a primary act in respect to those two secondary acts. But the fact is that the intellect is a power that is merely neutral and indifferent regarding the **specification** <note>The "specification" of an act refers to its specific content—what is being thought—as opposed to the "exercise" of the act, which is simply the fact that the mind is thinking at all.</note> of any of its secondary acts. Therefore, it cannot be determined to any such specification unless something else arrives which is either a primary act or stands in its place. Based on this reasoning, I assume this consequence: a mere act of the will cannot serve as the primary act regarding the specification of the intellect’s acts; therefore, the intellect cannot be determined to such a specification solely by the command of the will. This consequence is well-known from the aforementioned reasoning, and the **antecedent** <note>The first part of a logical proposition.</note> is clear from the common opinion of all **doctors** <note>Learned theologians and scholars of the Church.</note>, who agree on this: although the act of the intellect depends on the will regarding its **exercise** <note>The choice to perform the action of thinking.</note>, it does not depend on it regarding its **specification** <note>The content or conclusion of that thinking.</note>.

With these points accepted, I argue as follows regarding the proposal: The act of assenting and the act of dissenting are acts that have opposite specific characters. Therefore, the intellect cannot be determined toward assent or non-assent simply through the command of the will. Thus, the fact that someone believes an **article of faith** <note>A fundamental tenet of Christian dogma.</note> to be true or does not believe it through the intellect is not precisely because they wish or do not wish to believe, but because of something else determining the intellect, which is neutral in itself, toward such a specification.

<margin>Fourthly</margin>
<margin>Our theologians assign eight reasons why we ought to believe the Gospel.</margin>
Fourthly, it is argued thus: A person is not determined to believe something precisely through an act of the will if, when asked why they believe it, they do not assign that belief to a precise act of the will. But it is the case that if someone is asked why they believe in the **Christian faith** <note>original: "fidei christianae"</note> rather than the **faith of the Muslims** <note>original: "fidei maumethensium"</note>, they will not assign it precisely to an act of the will. Therefore, they were not inclined to believe by a precise act of the will. That a mere act of the will is not assigned is clear from experience and from the sayings of our theologians, by whom these eight reasons are commonly alleged for why we ought to believe the Gospel: 

1. The pronouncement of the prophets; 
2. the harmony of the Scriptures; 
3. the authority of the writers; 
4. the reasonableness of the contents; 
5. the unreasonableness of [competing] contents <note>The Latin here repeats "irrationabilitas contentorum," likely a scribal error or OCR duplication, but it traditionally refers to the irrationality of opposing doctrines.</note>; 
6. the unreasonableness of individual errors; 
7. the stability of the Church; 
8. the clarity of miracles.

Fifthly, it is argued: Whenever two people are determined to believe opposite things, and each of them is determined precisely because they wish to be so determined—indifferent to any judgment or persuasion of reason—it cannot be said that one is moved more reasonably to believe than the other. But given two people, one of whom wishes to believe a thing is true and the other does not wish to believe it, we do say that this one or that one wishes more reasonably and the other more unreasonably. Therefore, they are determined to wish this or that not precisely because they simply want to.

<margin>Albertus</margin>
The **major premise** <note>The first part of a syllogism or logical argument.</note> of this reasoning is well-known because, as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prominent Dominican friar and philosopher who taught Thomas Aquinas.</note> says in the fourth book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>, when the will acts precisely because it wants to act that way, it is likened to a **tyrant** <note>original: "tyranno"</note>. In a tyrant's action, no reason is sought for the deeds, because his acting is not acting according to reason, but acting according to his whim. The **minor premise** <note>The second part of a syllogism.</note> is manifest because we say every day that Muslims or Jews act unreasonably in not believing, and we act more reasonably because we do believe. If the precise cause of why I believe and he does not believe were simply because I willed it and he did not, both would be a "tyrannical" act of the will, and in neither would a greater or lesser reasonableness appear. In fact, in neither would there be reasonableness, but mere power and the tyrannical command of the will. From what has been said in this argument, the truth will be clear to those masters of few words concerning what I said in my response about the "tyrannical act of the will." Many other reasons could be brought forward for this opinion. However, it is not my purpose here to treat these matters or discuss the proposed questions at length, but only to show that the determination of my conclusions is not heretical.

<summary>Pico argues that belief is not a choice made by the will alone, but requires rational determination; otherwise, faith would be a "tyrannical" whim rather than a reasonable act.</summary>
