He moves from his own logical arguments to citing established theological authorities—specifically the English Dominican Robert Holcot—to demonstrate that his position has historical and orthodox precedent.</meta>

<page-num>77</page-num>
<header>OF THE DISPUTATIONS</header>

## OF THE DISPUTATIONS

<margin>Praise of Robert Holcot</margin>
Let these things suffice for the defense of my conclusion. However, I also wish to say this: there was a certain doctor—and I must confess that I have never yet read of his condemnation on this point—who held simply that the act of believing was not free. Indeed, Robert Holcot <note>Robert Holcot (c. 1290–1349) was a famous English Dominican theologian and philosopher known for his "subtle" logic.</note>, a most **subtle doctor** of the **Order of Preachers** <note>The Dominicans.</note>, held this assertively in his first book on the *Sentences*. And when it is argued that it would follow that the act of believing or not believing would not be **meritorious** <note>Deserving of a spiritual reward from God.</note> or demeritorious, he says this objection is null and frivolous. For an act is not meritorious because it is free, but because it conforms to some law promising a reward to the one performing that act for himself or another. Consequently, he says the act of believing is not meritorious because it is free, but because it conforms to the divine law which promises such a reward—namely, eternal life—to anyone who believes. He adds that God could change this law and decree that whoever should happen to fall upon a **cornerstone** <note>original: "lapidem angularem"; likely a metaphor for Christ or an arbitrary physical test of faith.</note> unawares tomorrow should be saved; in that case, that accident would be meritorious of eternal life. For our acts are not meritorious because they are free, but because they are accepted by God for eternal life; and God can accept natural acts just as he accepts voluntary acts. Thus, He seems to have accepted the death of the **Innocents** <note>The "Holy Innocents," the infants killed by Herod in the Gospel of Matthew, who could not exercise free will but are considered martyrs.</note> for eternal life, in whom there was no use of free will. Nor in doing so does God act unreasonably, because His will is a sufficient reason for all those things which He establishes or ordains.

Hence Holcot concludes that if we take "to believe" to mean adhering with firm assent to things whose truth is not evident to us except by the testimony of others—according to the way **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the most influential Western Church Father.</note> defines it in a homily on John, saying: "What is faith but believing what you do not see?"—then such an act of believing is not in the free power of man. But if "to believe" is taken to mean assenting to whatever is revealed by God and witnessed by miracles, and wishing to live and work according to them, then because this "believing" includes both an act of the intellect and the will, he concedes that it is free. It is in this way that Augustine, defining it in a homily on John, says: "To believe in God is, by believing, to love; by believing, to go into Him; by believing, to adhere to Him and be incorporated into His members." And of this kind of belief it is said: "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." But of the first kind it is said: "The demons believe and tremble." The first <note>In the sense of the second definition provided—living faith.</note> is meritorious; the second <note>Bare intellectual assent.</note> is not meritorious. 

And when it is said that "faith exists only in those who will it," Holcot says this must be understood regarding **formed faith** <note>Faith animated by charity/love, as opposed to "unformed" or bare belief.</note> according to this second mode, which is "faith working through love," but not concerning faith taken in the first mode. For he maintains that a believer can be necessitated to believe by seeing miracles. I do not believe this opinion to be true. However, after his **quodlibet** <note>A formal academic debate on any subject ("quodlibet" means "whatever you please").</note>, the same doctor, re-examining several of his opinions, says that although the will is necessitated to believe even when there is evidence in reason that something should not be believed, nevertheless, because he was himself the cause of such necessity, it is imputed to him as a sin. He says the cause was that he neglected to consider and persevere diligently and to discuss those things which created a false evidence for him; had he done so, it would not have appeared so to his intellect. Therefore, he concludes that whenever someone believes or disbelieves wrongly, his first sin is **negligence**. This is the opinion of Robert Holcot on the freedom of belief, which never seemed good or probable to me. Let these Fathers consider whether they should also anathematize <note>Formally curse or excommunicate.</note> this doctor as a heretic along with Durand, Henry, and the others.

<margin>Belief is spoken of in two ways, according to Augustine.</margin>

<margin>Augustine.</margin>

<margin>Holcot</margin>

If one says that an **accident** <note>In Scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a quality (like color or taste) that exists in a substance but is not the substance itself.</note> cannot exist unless it "in-exists" in the **Eucharist** <note>The Sacrament of the altar; the bread and wine.</note>, one could hold the Sacrament while also holding that the substance of the bread does not remain.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his controversial theses. Having discussed the nature of belief, he now transitions to a technical defense of his conclusion regarding the Eucharist—specifically, how the physical properties (accidents) of bread can exist when the substance of the bread is gone. ->APOLOGY<-
[iii i]
<meta>catchword: cundum</meta>

...arguments that I have seen. I say, however, for the clarification of my conclusion, that by this conclusion I do not intend to say categorically and absolutely that an **accident** <note>In medieval philosophy, an 'accident' is a property like color, smell, or taste that cannot normally exist without being 'in' a substance (the 'subject').</note> cannot exist without a **subject**, or that in the Holy Sacrament they are, in fact, in a subject. On the contrary, I hold firmly with the Church that the **sacramental accidents** <note>The appearance of the bread and wine.</note> are, in fact, without a subject. But I say that someone who might say that accidents cannot exist without a subject—and who held, with **Thomas**, the real distinction between the existence of bread and its essence—
<margin>Thomas Aquinas</margin>
could say that it does not contradict divine omnipotence to preserve the **existence** of the bread without its **essence** <note>Thomas Aquinas argued that 'what a thing is' (essence) is distinct from 'that a thing is' (existence). Pico suggests God could keep the 'existence' of the bread to hold the properties, even if the 'essence' of the bread is gone.</note>; just as God preserves an act, whether substantial or accidental, without its own power. Consequently, in that 'existence' of the bread, the accidents could be hosted even though the substance of the bread does not remain. Toward these accidents, the Body of Christ could have a real presence, just as it now has toward accidents that are hosted in no subject at all. And whatever the case may be regarding the Sacrament of the Eucharist—as in fact instituted by Christ and believed by the Church, in which it is agreed that nothing of the bread remains, so much so that its reproduction would be a new creation—nevertheless, by holding the aforementioned opinion of Thomas regarding the real distinction of essence from existence, and by taking the Sacrament of the Eucharist in a broad sense (to mean that which is or can be, as it is taken in my conclusion, which is a **modal divided** one), not only is the present conclusion probable and not erroneous, but rather it is erroneous to say that there cannot be some Sacrament of the Eucharist in which the accidents would be in a subject. Nor do I know by what logic those masters saw fit to condemn
<margin>Note.</margin>
a **divided proposition concerning possibility** <note>A logical statement about what *could* happen.</note> because of the falsehood of a **proposition concerning fact** <note>A statement about what *is* happening.</note> composed of the same terms. I wonder that they do not know what a **fallacy of the consequent** <note>A logical error where one wrongly assumes that if the current state of affairs is X, then any other possibility is impossible.</note> is: arguing from the less inclusive to the more inclusive while destroying the more inclusive. It is as if someone were to say, "No man is in the house, therefore no man *can* be in the house." They argue similarly in the condemnation of this proposition: "In no Sacrament of the Eucharist which exists in fact, or was in fact instituted by Christ, are the accidents in a subject; therefore, in no Sacrament which is or *can be* or *could be* instituted by Christ, can accidents be without a subject." From these words, it is clear how wrongly the present conclusion concerning possibility was condemned as erroneous by those fathers who ought to have remembered better.

<margin>The opinion of certain theologians which Peter of Palude recounts.</margin>
There have been among Catholic doctors those who held that, in fact, the accidents in the Sacrament of the Altar are hosted in the **existence** of the remaining substance. This is one way of the theologians, as **Peter of Palude** <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a prominent French theologian and bishop.</note> relates in his fourth book, distinction twelve, question three. They say that just as a quality remains here naturally because its immediate subject (which is quantity) remains—even if its remote subject (the substance) is removed, and thus the quality itself does not subsist on its own but adheres—so too the quantity lacks its remote subject (the essence of the substance), but it has its own proper and proximate subject: the **existence** of the substance. Through this existence, it is present in the substance, because it is possible for that existence to remain while the essence does not. Indeed, they say it is *necessary* for it to remain, considering the way he defines 'existence' here. And indeed, they say it is clear that this is possible; for although essence is prior to existence (from which it would seem that the prior could be separated from the posterior, and thus essence could exist without existence more easily than the reverse), yet considering from the other side that essence relates to existence as **potency to act** <note>Potentiality vs. Reality.</note> and as **matter to form**, because the 'act' depends less on the 'potency' than vice-versa, it seems more feasible for existence to be without essence than the reverse. But God, in the **Incarnation of the Word** <note>The birth of Jesus, where God became man.</note>, made the essence of humanity exist without its own human 'existence' (as is said by many doctors). Therefore, He can much more easily make the 'existence' of the substance of bread here without the essence; so that, just as there the essence was assumed and remains but the existence does not, so here, conversely, the existence can be preserved and remain while the essence does not. Secondly, they show that this is not only possible, but necessary, because nothing created can be converted into the Uncreated <note>God.</note>, but one created thing can be converted into another when they share in matter and genus; otherwise an accident is not converted into a substance, nor into an accident of another category...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's complex logical defense regarding the Eucharist. In the previous section, he discussed how the accidents (physical properties) of bread might be sustained by the "existence" of the bread even after its "essence" has been changed. Here, he moves into the nature of that change and the specific linguistic function of the words spoken by the priest during the Mass.</meta>

->QUESTIONS<-

### QUESTIONS

...according to common opinion. However, the essence of the bread agrees with the essence of the body of Christ in its matter and its **genus** <note>In Aristotelian logic, a 'genus' is a broad category or class of things.</note>. Hence, one could be converted into the other even through nature if the body were mortal; but the **existence** <note>original: "esse"</note> of the bread does not share in matter nor in genus with the substantial existence of the body of Christ, since the latter is uncreated and divine, being the **divine person** <note>original: "suppositum divini"</note>, as in Christ there is only one existence of actual substantial existence. Therefore, they argue it is impossible for the existence of the bread to be converted, and it is necessary for it to remain.

<margin>The author's opinion</margin>
I am of the opinion that it is not necessary for it to remain: for although it cannot be converted, it can nevertheless be annihilated, or it can be corrupted by yielding into the potentiality of matter. Just as the human nature [of Christ] could be assumed without the "existence" being assumed, but remaining in the potentiality of matter, so too can the essence be converted without the "existence" being converted, but rather reduced into the potentiality of the essence—although, to tell the truth, these "reductions" are more easily said than understood. Furthermore, although the existence of the bread cannot be converted into uncreated existence, it can nevertheless be converted into a created essence, because things that share in matter are mutually transmutable—granted that they do not share in **proximate matter** but only in **remote matter** <note>'Proximate matter' is the specific substance (like wood), while 'remote matter' is the underlying 'prime matter' that makes up all physical things.</note>, just as an element can be converted into a living soul and vice versa. Now, the existence of the bread and the essence of the body of Christ agree in **prime matter**, which is the remote potentiality of both, even if they do not agree in the proximate. For matter is pure potentiality, while essence is potentiality with act. Indeed, if that reasoning were valid, it would conclude that of all the food which Christ consumed before his Passion, only the essence would have been converted into him and not the existence; rather, it remained, or else was corrupted by something other than conversion. For the substantial existence of Christ was uncreated before the resurrection just as it was after. 

Furthermore, some say that just as water—which by **ordained power** <note>A theological term referring to the way God chose to set up the laws of the universe, as opposed to his 'absolute power' to do anything.</note> cannot be converted into the blood of Christ—is first converted into wine and afterwards the whole is converted into blood, so too existence, which cannot be converted into something of Christ by **absolute power**, is by nature first converted into its own essence, passing into it like a form that yields into the potentiality of matter. And after that, the whole essence is converted into the [divine] essence, and thus it is not necessary for the existence to remain. But just as it seems to me erroneous to say that it is *necessary* for the existence to remain, so it is no less erroneous to say that it *cannot* remain.

## TENTH QUESTION CONCERNING THE WORDS OF CONSECRATION.

<margin>Note</margin>
Those words **this is my body**: which are spoken in the consecration are held **materially** and not **significatively**. <note>Pico is making a linguistic distinction. To take words 'materially' means you are quoting them or referring to the words themselves (e.g., 'The word "bread" has five letters'). To take them 'significatively' means you are using them to refer to their actual meaning in the world.</note>
These masters [my critics] said that this conclusion is scandalous and against the common opinion of the saints and doctors, and that the opinion of the **Glossator** <note>Likely referring to a standard legal or biblical commentator of the time.</note> does not hold in this case. I, however, say that their determination is scandalous and against the common opinion of many doctors, and that the opinion of the Glossator rather than theirs ought to be held in this; and that this is so will appear evidently once the meaning of the conclusion is understood. First, therefore, it should be noted that I do not intend for those words to have been taken materially when they were uttered by <term>Christ</term> <note>original: "xp̄o"</note>, but only when they are uttered by the Gospel priest while consecrating. And for that reason, I said in my conclusion "the words which are spoken *in the consecration*," that is, those which are now uttered by those who consecrate. 

For it is certain that the priest in consecrating recites the aforementioned words of Christ, so that the prayer uttered by such a priest stands for the person uttered by <term>Christ</term> taken significatively. And such an opinion is not only not erroneous or scandalous, but rather the opinion opposed to the aforementioned sense seems to be contrary to the form of consecration in which the priest speaks those words recitatively. For the consecrating priest recites that Christ said to the apostles: <term>Take and eat, etc.</term> <note>original: "Accipite & māducate & c."</note> The consecrating priest, however, neither speaks to the apostles nor says to them "take and eat," except recitatively. For he alone receives the sacrament, nor does he say "take and eat" to those standing by. Similarly, when he says **this is my body**, that which is recited by the priest is that prayer **this is my body** taken materially in place of a similar prayer...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense regarding the Eucharist and the nature of Christ's power. On the previous page, he was discussing the transformation of the bread and wine. Here, he focuses on the linguistic nature of the words spoken by the priest during the Mass and begins a new inquiry into how miracles prove the divinity of Christ.</meta>

...consecration and composed of similar words uttered significantly by Christ. This is also clear through those words which are said before or after the consecration of the blood, namely: "which will be shed for you and for many" <note>original: "qui pro uobis & pro multis effundetur"</note>, etc. For these would be false if they were taken significantly <note>In this context, 'significantly' means the words are performing the action in the present moment.</note> because the blood of Christ will no longer be shed in that manner; therefore those words are only taken recitatively <note>'Recitatively' means the priest is quoting or reenacting Christ's historical words rather than speaking as himself.</note>. For what is recited but a voice uttered by another, for which the voice of the person reciting stands in? And therefore, this voice is to be taken materially <note>A logical term meaning the words are treated as an object of study or a quote, rather than for their direct meaning.</note> as a recitation of another’s voice. Furthermore, if these words were taken not recitatively but significantly, they would denote that the blood of Christ is shed for others and not for the priest consecrating, since it is said: "which will be shed for you and for many." For it ought rather to be said: "which [is shed] for us" <note>original: "qui pro nobis"</note>, etc. I do not say these things because I believe the opposite opinion cannot be defended, but so that it may be clear that my conclusion is not only Catholic, but more probable than its opposite. From this it is clear that the present conclusion is not scandalous but probable; and the opinion of the Solemn Glossator <note>Likely referring to a famous commentator on Canon Law, such as Johannes Teutonicus.</note> regarding the *Consecration*, distinction II, chapter *Timorem*, is not to be rejected in this matter but approved, just as it has never been rejected by the Church until these times.

# ELEVENTH QUESTION ON THE MIRACLES OF CHRIST.

### The miracles of Christ are the most certain proof of his divinity, not by reason of the thing done, but by reason of the manner of his doing them.

[Q] In explaining this conclusion, I said that it is the firm knowledge of theologians that those miracles which Christ performed could be done by a mere human through the power of God. For Christ says in John 14: "Amen, I say to you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do, and greater than these will he do" <note>original: "Amen dico uobis qui credit in me opera quæ ego facio ipse faciet & maiora horum faciet"</note>. Therefore, it is even unanimously concluded by these same theologians that the factor from which we can conclude Christ was God is not the work itself that was performed, but the manner of doing it. For he acted in such a way as those act who act by their own power and not by power received from elsewhere—which is proper to God alone: to act independently and not by another's power. This manner of acting cannot be communicated to a creature. Since, therefore, Christ did many things in such a way—not by praying or asking, but by commanding and ordering as one having authority—it is clear that he operated as being God himself and not as a man existing within the power of God. 

Having seen this explanation of mine, they said: "this conclusion can be drawn toward a bad sense, because it is contained among the magical arts" <note>Critics accused Pico of implying that Christ’s miracles were a form of natural magic rather than divine acts.</note>, even granted that his explanation is true. Concerning this judgment of theirs, I wonder so much that I cannot wonder more. First, let them tell me: can my conclusion have any meaning to anyone interpreting my words correctly and according to the upright and usual way of speaking, other than the one I have stated? For what is clearer or more expressive than these words: "The miracles of Christ are the most certain proof of his divinity, not by reason of the thing done, but by reason of the manner of doing"? 

Second, let them tell me whether this is the judgment of an upright judge: "this conclusion, although it is true and Catholic, is nevertheless to be condemned because it can be drawn toward a bad sense." Therefore, should this also be condemned: "Christ cast out demons," because the Jews drew it toward a bad sense, saying that "by Beelzebub, the prince of demons, he casts out those demons" <note>original: "in belzabu principe dæmoniorum eiiciebat dæmonia"</note>? And should this be condemned: "The Father is greater than I" <note>original: "pater maior me est"</note>, because Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336 AD) was a priest who taught that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note> devised from it an inequality between the Son and the Father? And should this be condemned: "He did not know her until she brought forth her firstborn son" <note>original: "non cognouit eam donec pepit primogenitum filium suum"</note>, because Helvidius <note>Helvidius (4th century AD) used this verse to argue that Mary did not remain a virgin after the birth of Jesus.</note> thought up a heresy against the perpetual virginity of Mary from it? And should this be condemned: "Concerning that day, not even the Son knows" <note>original: "illam diem neque filius nouit"</note>, because from it some want to know more things as the Father than the Son knows? Indeed, almost all Gospel propositions could be condemned, since they could be drawn toward a bad sense by heretics. Since I have put my proposition in these same terms in which it is put by many Catholic doctors, why must we condemn it even though it is true, just because some can draw it to a bad sense? Surely, if any interpret it badly, it is their sense, which is bad, that is to be condemned.

...is to be condemned, not mine which is holy and Catholic. Third, let them tell me what this evil sense <note>In this context, a "sense" refers to a specific interpretation or meaning of a proposition.</note> is that it could produce. Let them say if they know: certainly it is not possible to say if anyone wants to or thinks of an evil sense from that proposition. For if there were one, it would perhaps be that someone might suspect me of wanting to say that the same miracles which Christ performed could be done through magic, as far as the physical act is concerned. But this is not allowed to be suspected of my conclusion, because immediately before it I placed another conclusion: that the miracles of Christ could not be done through the way of magic or the Kabbalah <note>The Kabbalah is a tradition of Jewish mysticism; Pico was one of the first Christian scholars to suggest it could prove Christian truths.</note>. Now let those keep silent who say that judgment cannot be passed on the unknown, since it has already been decreed that those things are especially to be condemned which are especially unknown. But let us return to the matter at hand: "It is among the magical ones," they say, "therefore it is to be condemned." Let them tell me themselves whether magical conclusions are good or evil. If they are evil, they have still judged poorly. For Christ suggested in the parable of the weeds <note>original: "zizania." Referring to the Parable of the Tares in Matthew 13:24-30.</note> that not only should the wheat <note>original: "triticum"</note> not be rejected because of the mixed-in weeds, but rather for the sake of saving the wheat, he suggested that the weeds should not be uprooted before the harvest. If they are good, why should they have condemned a good conclusion placed among good ones, if they are good men?

## TWELFTH QUESTION: WHETHER GOD UNDERSTANDS.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>Augustine, Jerome</margin>

**I**t is more improperly said of God that He is "understanding" or "intellect" than of an angel that it is a "rational soul." <note>This was Pico's 12th thesis. He argues that human language is too limited to describe God, so even the word "intellect" is an understatement.</note>
In explaining this conclusion, I said that the conclusion relied on the manner of speaking used by Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian mystic and philosopher who argued that God is beyond all human categories.</note>, who often says of God that He is not "intellect" nor "intelligible" <note>Something that can be understood by an intellect.</note>; and likewise I said my words were to be taken in the same way that the words of Dionysius were taken. They said that the conclusion was false and could be transferred to a heretical sense, and that my explanation did not satisfy them. Regarding their determination, I wonder not a little; I wonder, I say, if they are wise, that they say a conclusion is false which is not mine, but Dionysius's conclusion. And so they may more clearly understand my mind, I will briefly explain the foundation of both the conclusion and the speech of Dionysius himself. It should therefore be noted that just as "reason" <note>original: "ratio"</note> refers to the discursive knowledge <note>Knowledge gained through a step-by-step process of reasoning, rather than direct intuition.</note> proper to men,
<margin>
Man is born rational, just as an Angel is called intelligence.
</margin>
which "reason" would indeed be improperly said to be in God; so likewise Dionysius says that "to understand" is the knowledge appropriated to an angel, caused by the angel and the angelic intellect, both informing it and changing it in such a way, and such "understanding" he says is not in God. Nor, by taking "understanding" in this way, can the conclusion be pulled toward an evil sense: for Dionysius does not therefore deny that there is knowledge of all things in God. But this [divine knowledge] is further distant from "intellection" properly taken in the aforementioned way than a man is from an angel. When, however, it is said "God understands," "to understand" is taken generally for all knowledge; and briefly let them know this: that through this conclusion I do not intend to deny the most perfect knowledge of all things to God, just as I do not deny any perfection simply; indeed, I do not even intend to deny that God "understands" by taking "understanding" in the common sense. But I deny that "understanding" which, according to Dionysius's way of speaking, refers to the knowledge appropriated to an angel, just as 
<margin>Objection</margin>
"reason" refers to the knowledge appropriated to man, according to which it will also improperly be said that there is "reason" in God. But they say: "You say it is more improperly said of God that He is intellect than of an angel that it is a rational soul." This, however, is false, because no one would ever say of an angel that it was a [rational] soul; of God, however, it is very often said that He is intellect. Therefore, that [the former] is a more improper expression.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s Apologia, where he defends his theological and philosophical theses against the charges of a papal commission. In the previous section, he argued that his views on magic and miracles were not heretical. Here, he moves into a defense of his terminology regarding God’s intellect and the nature of the soul’s self-knowledge.</meta>

# DEFENSE

<margin>Of Augustine.</margin>
I wonder at the learning and the extensive reading of sacred matters of those fathers who say that it is never said of an angel—neither properly nor improperly—that it is <term>rational</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "rational" usually referred specifically to human reasoning, while angels were "intellectual," possessing immediate knowledge without the need for step-by-step logic.</note>. But let them read **Augustine** in the book *On Music*, in the book *On True Religion*, in the *Acts Against Fortunatus*, and in the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*. For in all these places, I remember that angels were called by Augustine by the name of "souls" <note>original: "animarum nomine"</note>; yet I have not seen everything, nor can I remember every place where I may have read in the sacred doctors that angels were called by this name. Indeed, there is nothing which, when read, is not worthy of great attention. 

However, when I said that it is more "improperly" said of God that He is "intellect," I intended nothing else except that angelic knowledge—which claims the name of "intellectual knowledge" for itself—is further removed from the infinite knowledge of God (by which He knows all things through His essence) than it is from the <term>discursive reasoning</term> <note>discursive reasoning: The human process of moving from one thought to another to reach a conclusion, as opposed to the immediate "intuition" of higher beings.</note> of the rational soul, or that which is proper to man. But if it is inferred from the present conclusion that God is "improperly" said to understand—just as a comparative implies a positive—let the resulting consequence be accepted only in this sense: God is not said to be "intellect" according to the proper or appropriated acceptance of this word as we understand it, etc., but according to the common, less proper way, as was evident from the manner of speaking used by **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist who emphasized that God is beyond all human names and categories.</note>.

<margin>Note.</margin>

## QUESTION XIII. CONCERNING THE HIDDEN INTELLIGENCE OF THE SOUL.

<margin>Augustine. Hericus.</margin>
**A**nima <note>The historiated woodcut 'A' depicts a scholar or geometer with measuring instruments, signaling the beginning of this philosophical investigation into the soul (Anima).</note> The soul understands nothing actually and distinctly except itself. In declaring this, I said that I understood it as the "hidden understanding" <note>original: "intelligere abdito"</note> which **Augustine** mentioned in his book *On the Trinity*, and **Hericus** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a prominent Scholastic philosopher.</note> in his *Quodlibets*. These masters said that my conclusion did not match the understanding of the doctors whom I cited in my response; I do not know how they can say this if they have actually seen those doctors. And because this matter of "hidden understanding" is subtle and profound, I do not wish to explain it more broadly here. 

Since they do not condemn the conclusion on other grounds, I wish to say only two things. First, I do not intend to universally deny that the soul, in any state whatsoever, has some distinct knowledge of things other than itself. For I concede that the soul of Christ understands other things actually and distinctly, and similarly the souls of the blessed through revelations or infused species <note>Infused species: knowledge put directly into the mind by God rather than learned through the senses.</note>. Second, I say that I am speaking of that "hidden understanding" which exists without a <term>phantasm</term> <note>phantasm: A mental image or impression derived from the senses. Pico argues the soul has a deep level of self-awareness that doesn't rely on seeing or touching physical things.</note> or the assistance of the senses or imagination—and not just any such understanding, but a "direct and permanent" hidden understanding. Regarding this, I placed a conclusion next to this one, saying: "The soul always understands itself, and in understanding itself, it understands all beings in a certain way." And so, in all my conclusions, there is always a certain hidden concatenation <note>concatenation: a chain or linked series of ideas.</note> which perhaps they themselves do not notice. 

But returning to the point, I say that the soul, through such direct and permanent "hidden understanding," understands nothing actually and distinctly except itself. From this, it is clear that the present conclusion, so understood, should not have been indistinctly condemned as erroneous, even if in some sense it were not true. For in that way, many propositions of both philosophers and theologians, and even of Holy Scripture, would be condemned. Such as this from **Habakkuk** 1: "Your eyes are too pure to behold evil, and you cannot look on iniquity" <note>original: "Abachuh primo mundi sunt oculi tui ne uideas malum & ne despicias iniquitates."</note>. And similarly this from **Matthew** 25 concerning the foolish virgins: "I do not know you." For although the vision of God or His knowledge is unique and most simple, the said propositions would seem to universally deny such vision or knowledge even to God in respect to evil, because of the negation placed before the verb "to see" or "to know." They are, however, explained by the doctors specifically as referring to God’s "approving" vision or knowledge, and the negation in them is not taken to deny every mode of God’s vision or knowledge. Because that saying of the **Psalmist** is also true: "My sins are not hidden from you." Therefore, if many such sayings are distinguished by the commentators and doctors and drawn toward a true sense rather than being condemned, I do not know what this [thesis of mine] has done to deserve being so simply condemned, even after it had been explained and declared to the condemners in the manner aforesaid.

<margin>Habakkuk. Matthew.</margin>
<margin>Psalms.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense (Apologia) of his 900 Theses. Having addressed specific philosophical and theological points, he now discusses the circumstances of the work's composition, his submission to the Church, and a warning to readers about how to interpret his controversial propositions.</meta>

<page-num>80</page-num>
<header>OF THE QUESTIONS</header>

# QUESTIONS

These things have been dictated by me with a hurried pen, though I might write more—and perhaps better—at another time with greater leisure and care. This work itself, such as it is, was composed by lamplight over twenty nights; in its publication, speed was more desirable to me than diligence. For it was necessary that friends have something to throw like a morsel to the barking enemies, as if to Cerberus <note>Cerberus: The three-headed dog of the underworld; Pico compares his critics to this beast, suggesting they are mindlessly aggressive.</note>, and so to immediately counter the disease of unjust infamy coming upon me. <margin>Note.</margin> However, whatever we have written and shall write in the future are always said with this preface: that only that which the Supreme Pontiff <note>Supreme Pontiff: The Pope.</note> and all those whose judgment he approves shall decree as valid and holy, should be held as valid and holy. And I wish that he had already decreed something concerning these opinions of ours that have been called into doubt, according to his wisdom and authority. This work would not have been undertaken by me, since it would have been reckless to defend what he had condemned, and superfluous to defend what he had approved. Therefore, while we are not yet able to utilize the sentence of such a great judge, let us write these things, lest there be a reason for malicious detractors to speak, or for the unrefined and simple to suspect anything concerning the questions I have proposed for debate.

For it can happen that when someone less learned comes upon them, he might read this proposition: *Christ did not truly, and as far as real presence goes as the common way posits, descend into hell*, and be immediately offended by that phrase "not truly." He might believe the meaning of the proposition to be that the article of faith concerning the descent of Christ is not true <note>Pico is clarifying a technical philosophical distinction regarding "presence" that could be easily misinterpreted as denying the biblical account of Christ's descent into hell.</note>. Likewise, when he reads: *An infinite punishment is not owed to a mortal sin of finite time*, he might suspect me of harboring the heresy that the punishment of hell is not eternal. And when he understands that I think well of the salvation of Origen <note>Origen: A 3rd-century theologian whose views on the ultimate reconciliation of all souls with God (apocatastasis) were controversial and later condemned; Pico's defense of him was a major point of contention with the commission.</note>, he might suspect that it is not so much the life, character, teaching, and penance of Origen that I love, but rather Origen's believed dogmas.

It is similar regarding many other propositions which perhaps might have on their first appearance something that offends "holy simplicity"—that is, ears that are as pious as they are unlearned. For that reason, just as we have written these things so that no one thinks ill of us or of the orthodox dogma of our holy religion, I would not want those raw and unexplained propositions—if I may put it that way—to be read by our people unless they have first reached this defense. For from those propositions, they could conjecture many things as foreign to the Catholic faith as they are to our own mind—especially those who are duller, unrefined, and unaccustomed to the distance of these doctrines. <margin>Note.</margin>

Therefore, I pray, I beseech, and I implore friends and enemies, the pious and the impious, the learned and the unlearned, by the bowels of Jesus Christ our Lord, by the wonderful mystery of His descent into hell, by the eternal fire of the damned which is not extinguished—owed especially to heretics and enemies of the most holy Roman Church—by the sacrament of the true and mystical body and blood, by the omnipotence of God, and by the reverence deservedly to be shown to the images of His Son and his co-heirs: let them read without malice and without envy what we now write; and let them not read the earlier things—that is, the propositions themselves—unexplained and unclarified. For we proposed them to be debated among the learned; we did not publish them to be read everywhere by everyone. For there are also many impious <margin>Averroes Alexander</margin> dogmas of the ancient philosophers **Averroes** and **Alexander** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and Alexander of Aphrodisias: Mentioned here because their views on the soul and the eternity of the world were often seen as conflicting with Christian doctrine.</note> and many others. Although we have always professed, asserted, and preached publicly and privately that these are no less foreign to true and right philosophy than they are to the faith, nevertheless, intending a <term>scholastic exercise</term> <note>scholastic exercise: A formal academic debate or disputation common in medieval universities where speakers argued various sides of a question to sharpen their logic and find the truth, often playing "devil's advocate."</note>, we undertook to debate them in a private gathering among a few learned men, according to the custom of the universities.

Truly, he who reads the booklet of propositions to be disputed—as he could be warned by the title itself—while I distinguish what is said according to our opinion from what belongs to others, will see that those are not proposed by me as my own true opinions, but as believed by those others. Thus he might also suspect that even if they are called the dogmas and inventions of others, both these and those seem true and probable to me. Therefore, let those who hate me not read them because they are ours; let those who love me not read them because from those things which are mine, they might imagine many things which are not ours.

->THE DEFENSE OF THE QUESTIONS ENDS.<-

<meta>This page lists a series of formal "Conclusions" through which Pico della Mirandola defends his orthodoxy. After having apologized for the speed of his writing in the previous section, he now provides a systematic list of propositions concerning two main theological issues: the nature of Christ’s descent into the underworld (the "Harrowing of Hell") and the definition of mortal sin and its eternal punishment.</meta>

# THE CONCLUSIONS WHICH I DEFEND IN THIS WORK AS CATHOLIC ARE WRITTEN BELOW.

## First conclusion.
The soul of Christ descended to the <term>underworld</term> <note>original: "inferos"; in a theological context, this refers to the place of the dead, often called Limbo or Hell.</note> by a true and real descent. Thus, Christ was in the underworld during the three days [between his death and resurrection] according to the true and real presence of his soul.
**Corollary.** I do not approve of the opinion of <term>Durandus</term> <note>original: "Durandi"; Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334) was a philosopher and theologian who suggested Christ's descent was not a physical presence of the soul, but rather a descent by "effect" or power.</note> regarding the descent of Christ to the underworld.

## Second conclusion.
Although this is the case, the reason for the true and real descent and the true and real location of Christ’s soul in the underworld was not its essence or substance—as is held by the common way of the <term>Scotists</term> <note>Followers of the philosopher John Duns Scotus.</note> and the <term>Nominalists</term> <note>A school of thought that emphasized individual things over universal essences.</note>, which is commonly held at **Paris**, and which **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> seems to adhere to in the third part of the <term>Summa</term> <note>The *Summa Theologiae*, Aquinas's most famous work of systematic theology.</note>—but solely its effect or operation.

## Third conclusion.
The meaning explained through the conclusions written above is the meaning I intended by this proposition: "Christ did not truly descend to the underworld in terms of real presence, as Thomas and the common way posit, but only in terms of effect."

## Fourth conclusion.
The question of whether the aforementioned proposition, according to the rigor of logic and the force of the words, allows for that specific meaning is not a question of faith.

## Fifth conclusion.
One who believes that this proposition, by the virtue of the language itself, permits that meaning does not err in faith.

## Sixth conclusion.
He who believes something to be a matter of faith which is not a matter of faith does not judge correctly concerning the faith.

## Seventh conclusion.
One who puts forward a proposition having a double meaning, if he asserted and continues to assert it in a Catholic sense, is not bound to revoke the proposition, but only to clarify it.

## Eighth conclusion.
Given the aforementioned case and the multiplicity of meanings itself, we ought to judge the proposition according to the sense intended by the proposer rather than according to the sense that the words more strongly sound like.

## Ninth conclusion.
<term>Mortal sin</term> <note>In Catholic theology, a grave sin that destroys the relationship with God.</note> is demeritoriously worthy of eternal punishment.

## Tenth conclusion.
Anyone departing this life in mortal sin, even if they depart in only one, will be punished for eternity.

## Eleventh conclusion.
Unless the guilt of mortal sin were to persist eternally in the soul of the sinner, the punishment of the sinner would not persist for eternity.

## Twelfth conclusion.
Just as this term "mortal sin" is sometimes taken for the act of sinning (whether of omission or commission), so also is it frequently and properly taken among Catholic doctors for the <term>guilt</term> <note>original: "reatu"; the state of being liable for punishment due to sin.</note>.

## xiii. conclusion.
When we say that a punishment or a reward is "owed" in some case, we can understand it in two ways: either that one is demeritoriously or meritoriously worthy of such punishment or reward, or that such punishment or reward is actually being paid out to them.

## xiiii. conclusion.
The distinction of this term "owed" as placed in the preceding conclusion is not erroneous in faith.

## xy. conclusion.

Regarding the question of whether an irrational nature <note>For example, an animal or an inanimate object.</note>, due to a defect in its own nature, is incapable of being assumed into the divine nature in the unity of a <term>person</term> <note>original: "suppositi"; in scholastic logic and theology, a "suppositum" is a distinct, individual substance or person.</note>—as **Henry** believed—or whether it is not incapable—as the common way holds: a Catholic may be so uncertain that they need not take a positive action of contradicting **Henry’s** opinion.

A position that denies assent to a particular statement does not, by the force of the words themselves, imply a positive assent to the opposite statement.

All magic that is commonly called <term>necromancy</term> <note>original: "necromantia"; In this era, the term referred broadly to any magic involving communication with spirits or demons.</note>, and absolutely any art or science—if such things should even be called arts or sciences—which involves a pact or communion with demons in any way, whether explicit or implicit, whether as a primary part or an accessory, whether coming before, alongside, or after, or in any way at all, is a prohibited and superstitious thing and is rightly condemned by the Church.

### 29. conclusion.
The act of believing is a free act.

### 30. conclusion.
The act of believing is not in a person's power in such a way that, in a purely doubtful proposition, the intellect can adhere to one side rather than the other by the mere and sole command of the will.

### 31. conclusion.
One who believes this proposition—that it is not in the free power of the will to believe an article of faith is true whenever one pleases, or to believe it is false whenever one pleases (allowing for the sense explained in the preceding conclusion)—does not err in faith.

### 32. conclusion.
The <term>accidents</term> <note>In scholastic philosophy, "accidents" are qualities like color, taste, or smell. Usually, these must exist within a "substance" (like bread), but in the Eucharist, it was argued they exist on their own.</note> in the sacrament of the altar exist in no subject.

### 33. conclusion.
It is possible, by God’s absolute power, for the <term>existence</term> of bread to remain without its <term>essence</term>, and for the accidents of the bread to be grounded in that existence; this assumes a real distinction between essence and existence.

### 34. conclusion.
One who believes this proposition—that whoever says an accident cannot exist unless it exists [in a subject] could uphold the sacrament of the Eucharist even while holding that the substance of bread does not remain (which can be verified by what was said in the previous conclusion)—does not err in faith.

### 35. conclusion.
<term>Breadness</term> <note>original: "Paneitas"; a technical scholastic term for the essential "bread-nature" of the host.</note> does not remain in the sacrament of the Eucharist as assumed by Christ, God and man, but through conversion passes into the essence of the body of Christ.

### 36. conclusion.
If one holds the common view that God can <term>hypostasize</term> <note>original: "suppositare"; this refers to a divine person (like Christ) taking on a nature as his own, as he did with human nature.</note> any possible nature, it is possible that Christ assumes "breadness" into the unity of the divine person; and it is possible that through such an assumption, Christ is present on the altar where the bread is. Thus, without the conversion or annihilation of the "breadness," Christ could be on the altar according to a possible truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist—not indeed the one instituted by Christ, but one that *could* have been instituted.

### 37. conclusion.
One who believes this proposition—namely: if the common view regarding the possibility of God assuming any creature is held, I say that without the conversion of the substance of bread into the body of Christ or the annihilation of "breadness," it could happen that the body of Christ is on the altar according to the truth of a sacrament (speaking of what is possible, not what is actually the case, allowing for the sense explained in the preceding conclusion)—does not err in faith.

### 38. conclusion.
These words, "This is my body," etc., when they were spoken by Christ, were meant <term>significantly</term> <note>In logic, "significantly" (significatiue) means the words point to the actual thing (the body), whereas "materially" (materialiter) means the words refer to themselves as sounds or signs.</note>, not materially.

### 39. conclusion.
These same words, when they are uttered by a Gospel priest during consecration, are meant <term>materially</term>—that is, they are used as a recitation—not significantly. <note>This was one of Pico's most controversial points, suggesting the priest merely recites Christ's original act rather than "performing" the miracle himself.</note>

### 40. conclusion.
The miracles of Christ, regarding the thing performed, are an argument that they were done by divine power.

### 41. conclusion.
The miracles of Christ, regarding the manner of their performance, are an argument that Christ himself, in performing divine power, possessed it from himself and not from elsewhere.

**xlii. conclusion.**
God knows both himself and all things other than himself in the most perfect mode of knowledge.

**xliii. conclusion.**
Therefore, he is every perfection in a simple sense <note>In scholastic philosophy, "simpliciter" (simply/absolutely) refers to a quality that exists in its purest form, without composition or limitation.</note>.

**xliiii. conclusion.**
If we use this name "intellectual" according to the manner of **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian who argued that God is beyond all human categories, including "intellect."</note>, as he says that "knowledge" is appropriated to the angelic nature just as "rational" says that knowledge is appropriated to the human nature, then we say improperly that God is "intellectual" or that he "understands."

The soul, through that hidden understanding which is direct and permanent—without the aid of sense or imagination—understands only itself actually and distinctly.

**xlvi. conclusion.**
Through its manifold and various other acts, the soul understands various and manifold things other than itself.

# A Brief of Alexander VI, Supreme Pontiff, to John Pico of Mirandola, Count of Concordia.

->TO OUR beloved son, the noble man John Pico, Count of Mirandola.<-

# POPE ALEXANDER VI.

BELOVED Son, greeting and apostolic blessing. As far as it is permitted with God, we take care for the peace of all Catholics and for the reputation of those especially whom nobility of birth, the discipline of letters, and integrity of life and orthodox faith commend. A while ago, indeed, when you first presented yourself to our predecessor of happy memory, Pope **Innocent VIII** <note>Pope from 1484 to 1492; he originally condemned several of Pico's 900 theses.</note>, and to the Roman Curia, you had posted nine hundred conclusions in theology and other faculties to be publicly debated (as is the custom) with the permission of the aforementioned predecessor, which you offered to defend under the correction of the Apostolic See. And the said predecessor had understood from some people that among those conclusions were several contrary to our faith and religion—erroneous, scandalous, ill-sounding, and suspected of unsound doctrine. Then, wishing to safeguard the integrity of the faith, lest the minds of the faithful (and especially the simple, who are accustomed to flocking to public debates of this kind) be corrupted, he commissioned and commanded several venerable brothers—then his bishops, now ours—and other professors of sacred theology and of **both laws** <term>utriusque iuris</term> <note>This refers to the study of both Canon Law (church law) and Civil Law (Roman law).</note>, named by him through his letters in the form of a brief, to examine the contents of the said conclusions: [to see] whether any of them, by the force of the words, were discordant with the Catholic faith, or **savored of heresy** <note>A formal theological category (haeresim sapientes) for propositions that seem to lead toward heretical belief even if they don't explicitly state it.</note>, or were doubtful and ambiguous such that they could be drawn toward an erroneous sense. They were to report back to the predecessor himself, as is more fully contained in the said brief, so that, having received a faithful report from them, he might provide appropriately. Indeed, these bishops and professors reported to the same predecessor that certain conclusions seemed suspicious to them and, as they asserted, savored of heresy. You had, however, published these conclusions only for the sake of scholastic debate and to be disputed under the correction of the Apostolic See; and you finally professed that you would hold them to be such as they were judged to be by our same predecessor, promising under oath to assent to whatever declaration the predecessor himself might happen to make regarding this. Then truly, it was received by the said predecessor that you had published a certain other book, an **Apology** <note>Pico's *Apologia*, published in 1487, was his defense of the thirteen disputed conclusions. It backfired, leading to his total condemnation and flight to France.</note>, in which you interpreted and declared those same conclusions in a better and Catholic sense, and explained the understanding of the sincere faith concerning them. The same...

You persisted in the aforementioned promise and your oath, just as you intend to persist and now promise anew. 

Therefore, embracing with fatherly affection your good and whole mind, your sincerity of faith, and your devotion and obedience toward us and the Apostolic See—and [embracing] you, whom divine generosity has illustrated with various virtues—as a greater precaution for you, we absolve you and decree you to be absolved from all guilt of perjury, if perhaps you had indirectly incurred any by contravening your said oath in any way (the form of which we wish to be held as if expressed here). Taking up the cause of this commission against you and its specific status as if expressed, and <term>as far as</term><note>original: "quatenus"</note> it may be pending before any judges, even Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, we—by our own accord and from certain knowledge <note>In Latin "motu proprio et ex certa scientia," a legal formula indicating the Pope is acting on his own initiative with full information.</note>—extinguish the case. 

We decree and declare through these presents, by the same accord, knowledge, and authority mentioned before, that you, persisting in your oath according to the form of the letters of the predecessor himself, have incurred no mark of ill-repute at all on account of the preceding matters. Nor, on account of the publication of such declarations and the "Apology" or otherwise, have you incurred any appearance or suspicion of heresy or any sinister mark, nor have you fallen into the crime of real or feigned relapse <note>A "relapsed" heretic faced much harsher penalties, often death.</note>, nor incurred penalties or censures in law or otherwise against heretics or those suspected of heresy. 

We prohibit and strictly command, by virtue of holy obedience, local bishops, commissioners, and all officials, including inquisitors of heretical depravity, that they should not presume to molest or investigate you in any way on the occasion of the preceding matters. We decree it to be null and void if anyone, by any authority, knowingly or unknowingly, attempts to act otherwise regarding these things, notwithstanding any apostolic constitutions and ordinances or anything else to the contrary, of which special mention would otherwise have to be made here.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter's, under the Ring of the Fisherman <note>The official seal used for papal briefs.</note>, on the 18th day of June, 1493, in the first year of our pontificate.

->EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE, BOOK ONE.<-

# EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE, BOOK ONE.

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON BEING AND THE ONE TO ANGELO POLIZIANO, THE PREFACE.

<margin>The very sharp intellect of Lorenzo</margin>
**Y**ou were telling me recently, Angelo, about the discussion Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and a great patron of the arts and philosophy.</note> had with you regarding being and the one. This occurred while he was disputing against Aristotle—whose *Ethics* you are teaching publicly this year—relying on Platonic arguments. He is a man of such effective and versatile talent that he seems made for all things. In him, I especially admire this: that although he is always very busy in the Republic <note>Meaning the government of Florence.</note>, he is always either speaking or thinking about some literary matter. And since those who think Aristotle disagrees with Plato also disagree with me—as I make the philosophy of both concordant—you asked how Aristotle might be defended in this matter while also agreeing with his master, Plato. I said what came to my mind then, 
<margin>The harmony of Aristotle and Plato</margin>
confirming the points you had answered to Lorenzo during the dispute rather than bringing forward anything new. But this was not enough for you; for you demand that, although I intend to write more extensively on this in the very "Harmony of Plato and Aristotle" which I am currently laboring to produce <note>Pico spent his final years working on a massive project to prove the underlying unity of all philosophical systems, which remained unfinished at his death.</note>, I should nevertheless briefly touch upon for you in a short commentary the things I spoke to you about in person regarding this question. Indeed, Domenico Benivieni <note>A Florentine theologian and close friend of Pico and Savonarola.</note> happened to be present, a man very dear to both of us for his learning and integrity. Truly, what can I deny you, especially in a literary matter, being a companion I might almost call inseparable? However, let me—as a defender of the more polished tongue <note>Pico is being modest about his Latin style compared to Poliziano, who was the era's greatest Latin stylist.</note>—be permitted to use certain words that have perhaps not yet been granted the right of Roman citizenship <note>Pico means technical philosophical terms (scholastic Latin) that might seem "un-classical" or "barbaric" to a humanist like Poliziano.</note>. The novelty of the subjects and a certain necessity have forced them out; do not look for the charms of an elegant style. For as Manilius <note>Pico writes "Malius," likely referring to the Roman poet Marcus Manilius.</note> says: *The matter itself refuses to be adorned, content to be taught.* These, then, if I remember correctly, were the things we were talking about.

### Chapter 1: The assertion by the Platonists that the one precedes being.

---

Aristotle says in many places that these terms respond to one another and are equal in scope: namely, "the one" and "being"; and likewise "the true" and "the good"; but of these we shall speak later. The Academy <note>Referring to the Neoplatonists.</note> resists this, for they believe that "the one" is prior to "being"—prior in the sense that, as they say, it is understood to be more simple and more universal. For this reason, they say that God (who is supreme simplicity) is "the one," but is not "being." They also claim that "prime matter"—that is, the raw and unformed stuff of the universe—is included within the boundaries of "the one," yet it is outside the limits of "being." Then they assert that that which is opposed to "the one" is not the same as that which is opposed to "being"; for nothing is opposed to "being," but "multitude" is opposed to "the one." Therefore, by the same law by which opposites are judged, those two—being and the one—are not interchangeable <term>convertant</term>, nor should they be thought to correspond to each other.

### Chapter 2: That Plato nowhere considers the one higher than being, but rather that they are equal.

**T**hey rely on these arguments. Before we dismantle them, it will not be irrelevant to bring into the open what I have found expressed by Plato on this question. I find Plato disputing about "being" and "the one" in two places: namely, in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist*. The Academics <note>Neoplatonists like Plotinus or Proclus.</note> contend that in both places, "the one" is placed above "being" by Plato. I, however, will first say this about the *Parmenides*: that in that entire dialogue nothing is asserted as a certainty; and even if it were most strongly asserted, nothing could be found clearly enough for us to ascribe a dogma of that kind to Plato. Certainly, the book is not to be counted among the dogmatic ones, since it is entirely nothing other than a kind of dialectical exercise. Our opinion is so far from being contradicted by the words of the dialogue themselves that there exist no interpretations more arbitrary or violent than those brought forward by those who wanted to interpret Plato's *Parmenides* in another sense. But let us disregard all the interpreters. Let us look at the sequence of the dialogue itself: where it begins, where it tends, what it promises, and what it carries out. For...

<margin>k</margin> <note>A printer's signature mark used for binding the book.</note>

<summary>Pico begins his treatise by addressing Angelo Poliziano, aiming to reconcile the views of Plato and Aristotle on the relationship between "Being" and "the One." He challenges the Neoplatonic view that "the One" is superior to "Being," arguing instead for their equality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's examination of Plato's "Parmenides." Having established in the preface his intent to reconcile Plato and Aristotle, Pico now begins a close reading of the Platonic dialogues to prove that Plato did not actually intend to place "the One" in a category higher than "Being," a point of major contention between different schools of philosophy.</meta>

->EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE<-

...when Socrates had turned toward the ideas <note>The "Theory of Forms," Plato's central doctrine that abstract concepts have a higher reality than physical objects.</note> and asked many things of Parmenides concerning them, regarding that dispute of whether all things that exist are one or many. Parmenides responds 

<margin>Words of Parmenides</margin>
that he is pleased by that impulse and the inclination toward defining the highest things; but, he says, "Pull yourself together and exercise yourself more diligently while you are young in that faculty which seems useless to many, 

<margin>The utility of logic</margin>
and which is called 'trifling' or 'garrulity' <note>Parmenides is referring to dialectic, or formal logic, which critics often dismissed as mere empty talk.</note> by them; otherwise, the truth will escape you." It is admitted by all, as the following points make clear, that by these words he [Parmenides] means <term>dialectic</term><note>The art of logical investigation; Pico argues here that the dialogue is a logical exercise, not a theological revelation.</note>. After this, when Socrates asks what the method of this exercise is, Parmenides responds first with the one he had heard from Zeno <note>Zeno of Elea (c. 490–430 BCE), famous for his paradoxes.</note>, and then, teaching more particularly on this matter, he advises that he should look around with sharp skill not only at what follows if a certain thing *is*, but also what follows if it *is not*. Then he should see: what follows for that thing which we posit as being or not being in relation to itself and in relation to others; likewise, how other things relate to themselves and to it. When he had said much more to this effect, Socrates said: "You propose a difficult task, and I do not entirely understand you. But why 

<margin>From this we conclude it is shameful for an old man to speak or debate about dialectics</margin>
do you not yourself posit something and treat it in that manner which you approve, so that my understanding of this matter might become clearer?" Parmenides responds that for him, as an old man, this would be laborious. Finally, Zeno says that this should be done by Parmenides since they are in a meeting of only a few people; otherwise, he says, it would be unseemly for such things to be discussed in a large crowd by an old man, since few would know that such discussion and wandering is necessary for attaining the truth. These words of Zeno give full credit to what we have said. For the matter that Parmenides is about to treat is of such a kind, if we believe Zeno, that it should not be treated openly in a large gathering by an old man. But if, as they [the Neoplatonists] wish, he were dealing with the divine orders and the first principle of all things, what treatment would be more fitting for an old man, or less to be ashamed of? But it is beyond all controversy, unless we wish to deceive ourselves, that the business Parmenides was about to engage in was a dialectical one, and Socrates had asked for something else from him. Zeno had judged that task to be the duty of a youth rather than an old man. If we do not believe these testimonies, let us run through the dialogue itself. We will see that nowhere is anything affirmed, but everywhere it is only asked: "If this is so, what will follow?" and likewise, "What if it is not so?" The Academics <note>Followers of the later Platonic Academy who leaned toward skepticism.</note> seized the occasion for their opinion on being and the one from this: because in the first position he exercises himself with this problem, to see if all things are one, what might follow. And he responds that it would happen that the "one" which we posit to exist would be indivisible, would be infinite, would be nowhere; and since he enumerates many things of that kind, he brings this among others: namely, that it would happen that the "one" is not "being." But take note: if this is not a dialectical exercise, but a dogma handed down concerning being and the one, how much these things differ—namely, to assert that the "one" is above "being," and to assert that *if* all things are "one," that "one" would not be "being." Enough about Parmenides. Truly, in the *Sophist*, he speaks rather toward this opinion: that "the one" and "being" are equal, rather than "the one" being higher than "being." 

<margin>What he says in the Sophist about being and the one</margin>
For I do not find where he might explain that [the latter]. He signifies the former in many ways, as through these words: "For in so considering, you will admit that it is necessary that he who says 'something' says 'some one thing'..." and soon: "Truly, he who does not say 'something' must necessarily say 'nothing' at all." These are his words. Therefore, in his view, "not one" and "nothing" are the same and equal; likewise "one" and "something" are equal. After this, he likewise proves that it cannot be said that "non-being" is "one." And thus he concludes: "Being does not happen to non-being; therefore the one does not happen to non-being." <note>original: "Ens nō enti nō accidit: ergo unū non accidit nō enti"</note> But he speaks of the "one" which he had said above was equal to that which is "something"; he seems, therefore, to take it as granted that the "one" is "being." But so be it; let us grant that Plato affirmed this, which certainly he nowhere affirmed. Come, let us examine in what sense it could have been truly said, first laying the foundations of the Aristotelian opinion in this manner.

# BOOK ONE.

k ii

<meta>catchword: being</meta>

**H**aving said these things, the word "Being," about which there is a doubt as to whether it is equal to "the One," can be understood in two ways. The first is that when we say "Being," we understand everything that is "not-nothing." This is the way 
<margin>The two ways of "Being"</margin>
Aristotle used it when he made Being equal to the One. Nor did he use the word this way without reason: for as it is truly said, we ought to *think* as the few do, but *speak* as the many. For we perceive and form opinions for ourselves, but we speak to others—that is, to the multitude—and therefore we speak so that we may be understood. The common people, and anyone from the general public, take "Being" to mean everything that does not lack existence, and which cannot truly be called nothing. But we find that even those who are held to be the wisest among the very people who disagree with us have used the word in this way. 

<margin>Parmenides the Pythagorean when he said</margin>
For Parmenides the Pythagorean, when he said that the One is that which *is*, he understood it to be God. If we believe Simplicius 
<margin>Simplicius</margin>
and many others who wish to defend Parmenides against those who misrepresent him—as if he had said that *all* things are one—they answer with one voice that it was never believed by Parmenides that there is no division, multitude, or plurality in things. Indeed, he openly admits this elsewhere in his poems. But when he said "that which is, is one," he judged that the name "Being" truly fits only that which is One: and that which truly "is," is only the One, which is God. Therefore, if we believe Parmenides and his defenders and the Platonists, the One cannot be "above" Being unless it is "above" God; and Parmenides is so far from denying that God is "Being" that he concedes the true name of "Being" to God alone. And thus, the solution to the first argument of the Platonists <note>The Platonists argued that the One is superior to Being; Pico argues here that they are merely being restrictive with their definitions.</note> occurs to us in passing. 

But even Dionysius the Areopagite—whom those who dispute against us claim as a supporter of their own opinion—will not deny that it was truly said by God to Moses, "I am who I am," which 
<margin>Dionysius the Areopagite</margin>
we read in Greek as *ego eimi ho on*, that is: "I am Being" <note>Exodus 3:14. Dionysius was a Christian Neoplatonist whose works were foundational for medieval theology; Pico points out that even he uses "Being" as a divine name.</note>. Furthermore, since they themselves say that "nothing" or "non-being" is opposed to Being, just as "multitude" is opposed to "the One," they must necessarily concede that what is *not* Being is nothing or non-being. Just as what is not one is many, or a multitude. Therefore, if they observe the same law of speech, they must admit either that God is nothing (which the ears themselves dread to hear) or that He is Being. In this way, when "Being" is accepted, we establish that first axiom and universal statement: that of any thing, it must necessarily be said that it either *is* or *is not*; and regarding nothing can it be said or thought that it both is and is not at the same time. Since, therefore, there is nothing outside of all things except "nothing" itself, if "Being" understood in this way excludes only "nothing" from itself, it must without a doubt encompass all things. Therefore, "the One" cannot encompass more things than Being does, unless it encompasses "nothing"—which Plato denies in the *Sophist* <note>One of Plato's later dialogues where he investigates the nature of "Non-being."</note>. When he says that "non-being" or "nothing" cannot be called "one," if it does not encompass fewer things (as they wish), then both Being and the One are equal.

## Chapter four: in what way something can be said to be higher than Being is declared.

**W**e have explained one of these ways in which we said "Being" could be understood. Those who use it this way—and they can use it most rightly—truly affirm that nothing is more common than Being. It remains for us to explain the other way, according to which it will be manifest that it can nonetheless be truly said that there is something placed above the eminence of Being. 

<margin>What is an abstract and a concrete name</margin>
Some names are concrete, others are abstract. Concrete names are "hot," "shining," "white," "man." Abstract names are "heat," "light," "whiteness," "humanity." Now, the power and diversity of these is such that what is called "abstract" signifies that which is such of itself, not from another. On the other hand, the "concrete" signifies that which is such not from itself, but by the benefit of another. Thus, a "shining thing" shines by light. A "white thing" is white by whiteness, and a "man" is a man by humanity. Since truly nothing participates in itself, the same condition cannot exist in the same thing both from itself and from the participation of another. 

<margin>The rule of naming</margin>
It follows that what is called "abstract" cannot be named from the "concrete." Therefore, it is not fitting to say "whiteness is white," or "blackness is black." Indeed, one who says such things would be ridiculous—not because whiteness is black or heat is cold, but because whiteness is as far from "being white" as heat is from "being cold." This is because whatever things are white are white by *that* whiteness, and whatever things are hot are hot by participation in *this* heat. 

<margin>Two ways in which something is denied to be in a thing</margin>
Therefore, we deny that certain things are in a certain subject in two ways: either because the subject does not have it (as when we say a black thing is not white) or because it has it in a more excellent way and by a more perfect principle than we can express by such a word...
