<margin>
How God is said not to be Being but above all Being, as Dionysius and Damascene intended.
</margin>
We mean: as when we deny that whiteness is white, not because it is black, but because it is not only not black because it is white (which is the same as saying it *has* whiteness), but because it *is* whiteness itself. Let us come to our own terms: "Being" <note>original: *ens*</note> has the form of a concrete noun. For "Being" and "that which is" <note>original: *id quod est*</note> mean the same thing. Its abstract counterpart is this word "To Be" <note>original: *esse*</note>; so that "Being" is said of that which participates in "To Be." Just as a "shining thing" is so called because it participates in light, and a "seeing thing" is one in which the act of seeing resides. Therefore, if we look at this exact meaning of Being, we will deny that God is "Being"—not only because he is not a thing, or because he is nothing, but because he is such that he is "To Be" itself, which is from itself and by itself, and by participation in which all things exist. Just as we would deny that heat itself is "hot," not because it lacks heat, but because it is heat itself. Such a thing is God, who is the fullness of all Being; who alone is from himself, and from whom alone, with no intermediate stepping in, all things proceeded into existence. By this reasoning, we will truly say that God is not Being, but "Above Being," and that there is something higher than Being—namely God himself. Since the name "The One" follows the same condition, we must confess that the One is above Being. But then we call God "One," not so much declaring *what* he is, as *how* he is all the things he is, and how other things come from him. For Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose writings were highly influential in the Middle Ages</note> says God is called "One" because he is all things uniquely. Again, he is called "One" because he is the principle of all things that are, just as unity is the principle of all numbers. Therefore, if, as the Academics want, Plato affirms in the first hypothesis of the *Parmenides* that the One is superior to Being, that One will be nothing other than God; which they themselves admit, asserting by common consent that Plato is there treating the first King and Principle of all things. But someone will say that at least in this part, Aristotle will be discordant from Plato: because Aristotle never takes "Being" in such a way that it falls under "the One," nor does he exclude God from it, as Plato does. Those who say this have not read Aristotle; for he does this too, and far more clearly than Plato. For in the sixth book of his *First Philosophy* <term>First Philosophy: Aristotle's own term for what we now call Metaphysics</term>, he says that Being is divided into "being through itself" <note>original: *ens per se*</note> and "being by accident" <note>original: *ens per accidens*</note>. Since "being through itself" is divided into ten categories <note>original: *x. genera*, referring to Aristotle's Categories</note>, there is no doubt among

<margin>
As Thomas explained in *On Being and Essence* and also *On the Nature of the Genus*.
</margin>
good interpreters that God is not contained under this "Being," for he is neither "being by accident" nor is he contained under any of the ten categories into which "being through itself" is divided. Also common among the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: The school of philosophers who followed Aristotle</term> is that division by which Being is said to be divided into substance and accident. Since this is so, we take "Being" such that God is *above* Being, and is not *under* Being, just as Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> teaches in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences* <note>Sentences: The *Sententiae* of Peter Lombard, the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages</note>. I will add this: certain Platonists boast wrongly, as if they possessed a mystery unknown to Aristotle, when they say there are two names proper to God, namely "The One" and "The Good," and thus that "The Good" and "The One" come before "Being." For just as we have shown that the Peripatetics are not unaware of how God can be understood as above Being, we can also show that Aristotle gave these two names, "The Good" and "The One," to God in the first place. For in the twelfth book of the *First Philosophy*, after he disputed concerning the whole of being and separated minds, he asks finally (as if having turned, after all else, to investigating the properties of God alone) whether, besides the good which is, as it were, in the ranks of the universe of beings, there is some separate Good, like a leader of this army; and he determines that this is so, because God is the Good. Concerning whom, in the same chapter, he subsequently proves his unity, citing for its testimony (after strong arguments) that line of Homer: **Let there be one lord, one king.** <note>original Greek: εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω, εἷς βασιλεύς. From the *Iliad* II, 204-205</note>. Where, then, is Aristotle false? Where is he discordant with Plato? Where is he profane? Where does he think of God less honorably than is fitting?

# BOOK ONE
k iii

...is all things and most eminently and perfectly is all things. Which will not be the case unless he so encloses in himself the perfections of all things that he rejects from himself whatever pertains to imperfection in things. Moreover, we can define whatever holds the logic <note>original: "rationem" - the defining principle or essence</note> of the imperfect in these things that exist under two heads. 

<margin>Imperfection in things is twofold</margin>

One is when there is something in a thing that is less perfect within the genus of that thing. The other is when it is indeed perfect in its own genus, but for that reason not simply perfect: because it has the perfection of only one genus, and there are many genera outside of it, honored by their own perfections, which are not included in it. 

<margin>Example of that which is not perfect in its own genus</margin>

Example of the first: sensory cognition is not only imperfect because it is only cognition and not appetite, but because it is also an imperfect cognition. This is both because it requires a brute and bodily organ, and because it only touches the surface <note>original: "extrema" - the outer limits or accidents</note> of things; it does not penetrate to the innermost parts, that is, to the substance. 

<margin>Note. How human cognition is imperfect</margin>

Likewise human cognition, which is called rational, is an imperfect cognition because it is wandering, uncertain, mobile, and laborious. Add to this the intellectual cognition of divine minds—which theologians call angels—and even this is an imperfect cognition. It is so at least for this reason: that it seeks outside itself what it does not fully possess within itself—namely, the light of truth which it needs and which perfects it. 

<margin>How angelic cognition is imperfect</margin>

Take life: that life which is in plants, or rather, which is in every body. It is not an imperfect life only because it is life and not cognition, but because it is not pure life, but rather a certain "enlivening" <note>original: "vivificatio"</note> derived from the soul into the body, always flowing, always mixed with death. Finally, it should rather be called death than life. For we begin—if perhaps you do not know—to die at the very moment we begin to live; and death is extended along with life. We first finish dying when we are released from the body of this death through the death of the flesh. 

<margin>When we begin to die [and] when to live</margin>

But neither is the life of angels perfect: for unless a perpetually life-giving ray of divine light cherished it, it would slip away entirely into nothingness. The same reasoning applies to the rest. Therefore, when you consider God to be a living God, first see to it that the life and cognition ascribed to him are understood as free from all these detriments. 

But this is not enough. For there remains the other type of imperfection, of which this is the example: Conceive of a most perfect life <note>OCR: "uirā" corrected to "vitam"</note> which is entirely life and pure life, having nothing mortal, nothing mixed with death, which needs nothing outside itself through which it may endure stable and remain. Conceive likewise of a cognition which knows all things at once and most perfectly. Add to this that the knower knows all these things in himself, so that he does not seek the truth he knows outside himself, but is himself that very truth. Yet even if both of these were most perfect in their own genus and such that they could not exist outside of God, yet if they are accepted thus as distinct from each other, it is unworthy of God. 

For God is all-encompassing and infinite perfection; but he is not all-encompassing and infinite just because he contains all such particular and infinite perfections within himself. For then he would not be most simple <note>In philosophy, "simplicity" means being non-composite, or not made of parts</note>, nor would the things in him be infinite; rather, he would be one infinite thing collected from many infinite things—finite in number or perfection—which it is profane either to say or think about God. 

But truly, if life were indeed a most perfect life, but were only life and not cognition; and likewise if appetite or will were indeed a most perfect will but only will and neither life nor cognition—if such similar things were placed in God, it would clearly result that the divine life would be of finite perfection, since it would have the perfection of life but not the perfection of cognition or appetite. Therefore, let us take away from life not only that which makes it an imperfect life, but also that which makes it *only* life; and similarly from cognition and other names by which we call God. Then, what remains from all these will necessarily be what we want God to be understood as: namely, one, most perfect, infinite, and most simple. 

<margin>How God is Being itself</margin>

And since life is a certain being, wisdom likewise is a certain being, and justice equally; surely if you take away from these the condition of particularity and limitations, what remains will not be this or that being, but Being itself—simply being, universal being, not by universality of predication <note>Logical categorization</note>, but of perfection. Similarly, wisdom is a certain good because God is the good which is wisdom and is not that good which is justice. 

<margin>Augustine</margin>

Take away, as Augustine says, "this," take away "that"—that is, the particular—take away this limitation through which wisdom is a good in such a way [that it is not another]...

Yet it is not only intimate to all things, but more "one" with all things than they are with themselves. Truly, words fail, and they are altogether less than what is conceived. never to find what we seek, rather than to possess through love that which, without love, would be found in vain. But let us return to our subject. It is now clearly evident to you by what means God is sometimes called Mind and Intellect and Life and Wisdom, and yet at other times is placed above all these things. Both views are proved to be both true and consistent. Nor does Plato disagree with Aristotle 
<margin>Plato.</margin>
because, in the sixth book of the *Republic*, he establishes God (whom he there calls the "Idea of the Good") above intellect and intelligible things, giving to the former the power to understand and to the latter the power to be understood. For this man, 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle, often calls God both Intellect and that which understands, and the Intelligible itself. For even Dionysius 
<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
the Areopagite, though he says the same as Plato, will not deny (even with Aristotle) that God is not ignorant of himself and of other things. Therefore, if he understands himself, he is both intellect and intelligible. For he who knows himself necessarily knows and is known. And yet, if we take these perfections as "particular" (as I said), or if when we say "intellect" we signify a nature that tends toward an intelligible thing as if toward something else outside itself, then Aristotle would deny—no less than the Platonists—that God is either intellect or intelligible. In the 
<margin>Third degree.</margin>
third degree, something more shone upon us as we approached the darkness, so that we do not merely imagine in our thought some imperfect or, as it were, mutilated being for God (such as he would be if he were called a body, or the soul of a body, or an animal composed of them), nor likewise some particular genus (however perfect we make it, such as human wisdom, or if we say he is "life" or "mind" or "reason"), but even better than those things which universal names indicate—which encompass everything—namely, "True Being" and "The Good." In the 
<margin>Fourth degree.</margin>
fourth degree, we knew that he himself is not only above those things, but above every name that can be formed and above every notion that can be conceived by us. Then, for the first time, we knew him in some way when we did not know him at all. From this can be gathered that God is not only—as 
<margin>Anselm.</margin>
Anselm says—"that than which nothing greater can be thought," but he is that which is infinitely greater than everything that can be 
<margin>Psalm.</margin>
thought. So that the prophet David truly said, according to the Hebrew text: "To you, silence is praise" <note>original: "Tibi silentium laus" — from Psalm 65:1 (64:2 in Vulgate), reflecting the idea that God's greatness surpasses all language</note>. Let us say these things for the solution of the first reasoning; from which a great window is opened for the legitimate understanding of the books of Dionysius which are inscribed *On Mystical Theology* and *On the Divine Names*. In these, one must be careful: neither to make the things he wrote less than they are (for they are the greatest things), nor, while we think everything we understand is small, to devise for ourselves dreams and inextricable commentaries.

<summary>Pico reconciles Plato and Aristotle by arguing that God is both the source of all perfections (like intellect and life) and yet transcends those very categories. He introduces the concept of apophatic theology, where God is ultimately praised through silence because his nature exceeds all human thought and naming.</summary>

# EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND UNITY

### Chapter six, in which he solves the second argument of the Platonists concerning prime matter.

<margin>This is the matter which is called *hyle* <note>original: "hyle"; the Greek term for primordial, formless matter</note> by another name, about which I wrote in the *Heptaplus* <note>Pico’s work on the six days of creation</note>, because according to Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, multitude arose from unities.</margin>
The objection they raise regarding prime matter is frivolous. For insofar as it is a being, to that extent it is one. Indeed, if they wish to follow Plato’s words to the letter, they must grant that it has less the character of the "one" than it does of "being." For Plato does not want matter to be absolutely nothing; otherwise, how would it be a "receptacle of forms," how a "nurse," how a "certain nature," and the other things he confirms it to be in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the physical world</note>? It is not, therefore, nothing—that is, it is not entirely deprived of being, if we believe Plato. Yet, in the *Philebus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on pleasure and the good</note>, they call this same matter not only "multitude" (which, as they would have it, is opposed to the one just as nothing is opposed to being) but "the infinite." However, if a multitude is finite, it does not entirely escape the definition of the one, for insofar as it is finite, it is one. But an infinite multitude lacks the nature of the one just as it lacks a limit. Therefore, according to Plato, prime matter is more a "being" than it is "one." Those who argue to the contrary, in order to prove the "one" is higher than "being," used to say it was "not being" and yet "one." Furthermore, Iamblichus the Platonist, in the book he wrote on the Pythagorean sect, calls prime matter "duality" because duality is the first multitude and the root of all other multitudes. Therefore, according to him—who is so great among the Platonists that he is called "divine"—prime matter is not only not "one," but is multitude itself, the very root of all multitude found in things. We have said these things by turning their own arguments against them. Otherwise, that matter is not entirely devoid of unity, just as it is not devoid of being; however, it receives its perfected unity from the same source as its being: from "form." I pass over the disputes concerning its unity, whether affirmative or negative, all of which are very well known to those who have spent even a little time walking with Aristotle <note>original: "iunculam fecerint"; literally "made a little rush-mat," meaning to have even a basic acquaintance</note>.

### Chapter seven, in which he solves the third argument of the Platonists concerning multitude; and shows that those who say the "one" is more common than "being" must concede something which Plato denies.

<margin>Solution to the third argument.</margin>
<gloss>f</gloss>They are most greatly deceived in their third argument. For multitude is not opposed to the "one" in the same way that "non-being" is opposed to "being." The latter have a contradictory opposition, while the former have either a privative or contrary opposition <note>A technical distinction in logic: "non-being" is the simple absence of "being," but "multitude" is a specific state of having many parts, which still requires those parts to exist</note>, a matter extensively discussed by the Aristotelians in the tenth book of the *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*</note>. But let the Platonists see what ruins they fall into when they say the "one" is higher than "being." It is certain that whenever two categories are related such that one is more common than the other, it is possible for something to escape the scope of the lower one while still falling under the higher one. This is why the higher one is said to be "more common." A ready example is that "animal" is more common than "man"; it can happen that something is "not a man," yet it is still an "animal." By the same logic, if the "one" were more common than "being," it would be possible for something to be "non-being" or "nothing," yet still be "one." Thus, "one" would be predicated of "non-being," which Plato expressly refutes in the *Sophist* <note>Plato’s dialogue exploring the nature of being and the definition of a philosopher</note>.

### Chapter eight, in which he declares how these four—namely the one, the true, and the good—are in all things that exist after God.

<margin>The followers of Avicenna established six terms.</margin>
<margin>He bit Avicenna for opposing Averroes.</margin>
The truest opinion, therefore, is that there are four things which encompass everything: Being, One, True, and Good. These are understood such that their negations are: Nothing, Divided, False, and Evil. To these four, two others were added—namely "Something" and "Thing"—by later thinkers following Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath whose interpretations of Aristotle were central to medieval philosophy</note>, who in many places updated the philosophy of Aristotle. From this arose the great battles fought by Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd, the Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle</note> against him, though as far as this matter is concerned, the disagreement is over a small thing. For these thinkers divide what is understood under "one" into "one" and "something" (which does not disagree with Plato, who in the *Sophist* lists "something" among these most common terms), and they divide what is contained under "being" into "being" and "thing." But regarding these matters, we shall speak elsewhere. To follow what we have begun, these four are in God in one way, and in those things which come after God in another; for God has these from Himself, while others have them from Him. Let us see first how they are in created things. All things that exist after God have an efficient, exemplary, and final cause <note>Aristotelian causes: the maker, the model, and the purpose</note>. For all things are from Him, through Him, and toward Him. If, therefore, we consider things as they are established by God as the "efficient cause," they are called "beings" because they participate in being through His action; if we consider them according to their "exemplary cause," which we call the "Idea" according to which God founded them, they correspond to <note>Catchword: correspond to and...</note>

<summary>Pico refutes the Platonic idea that "the One" is superior to "Being" by arguing that even prime matter must have some unity to exist, and that making "the One" more common than "Being" would lead to the logical absurdity of "nothing" being "one." He introduces the four transcendental properties—Being, One, True, and Good—shared by all created things.</summary>

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>The order among these four</margin>
They square and correspond: they are called true. For it is said that a "true image of Hercules" is one which is indeed conformed to Hercules. If they tend toward him as to the ultimate end, they are called **good**. But if each thing is taken absolutely according to itself, it is named **one**. However, the order here is that first, each thing should be conceived under the aspect of "being" <note>original: "entis ratione"; the most basic category of existence</note>, since an agent first brings it about that each thing exists before it is anything in itself; otherwise, it would not be from the agent according to the whole of what it is. From this it follows that there is nothing after God which, when we conceive of it, we do not understand as "being from another": finite being, participated being. The **one** succeeds **being**. The third is **truth**, because after something exists in itself, it must be seen whether it is such as the exemplar to which it was formed: if it is found similar, it follows that it turns itself toward that thing—as if toward its kin and relative—through **goodness**. 

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Who would not see that these things are equal in scope? Grant that something exists, and certainly it is also one. For he who says "one" does not say "nothing," as Plato says in the *Sophist* <note>A dialogue by Plato exploring the nature of being and non-being</note>. For whatever exists is undivided from itself and divided from others which are not itself. When we say this, we understand "the one," or to use Plato's words, it is "the same to itself and other from others," which he himself confirms applies to every single thing in that same dialogue.

<margin>Truth is converted with being; really, from Augustine.</margin>
It is also necessarily **true**. For if it is a man, then he is certainly a "true" man. It is the same thing to say "this is not true gold" and "this is not gold." For when you say "it is not true gold," you mean this: it looks like gold and is something similar to gold, but it is not gold. Therefore, Aurelius Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD)</note>, defining it in the *Soliloquies*, says: "that which is true, or truth, is that which is" <note>original: "id quod est"</note>. This should not be taken to mean that "being" and "truth" are the same thing. For although they are the same in reality, they are different in reason and definition. Therefore, one should not be defined by the other, but Augustine wanted to express this: I would call it "true" when it is that which it is called and said to be; just as gold is "true gold" when it is gold and nothing other than gold. This is what he meant by "truth is that which is." Some people, failing to notice this, bring a false charge against the definition. 

<margin>Goodness is converted with being. He disputes against Olympiodorus.</margin>
Similarly, it is also **good**, because whatever is, insofar as it is, is good. In my opinion, Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that the Good is superior to Being</note> is far mistaken in believing he could prove that "the good" and "being" are different. His argument is that we desire "the good" simply. However, he claims that to exist "simply" is not the goal, but to exist "well" <note>original: "bene esse"</note>; therefore, it can happen that if things go badly for us, we might desire not to exist. Setting aside whether those who are in a bad and miserable state can, by a right and natural desire, seek not to exist, he failed to notice that just as "being" is manifold, so too is "goodness" manifold. 

<margin>Just as there are different kinds of being, so there are different kinds of good.</margin>
For first, there is the "natural being" of things, such as for a man to be a man, a lion to be a lion, or a stone to be a stone; natural goodness follows this being indivisibly. There are other ways of being which can be called "accidental" <note>original: "adventitia"; literally "coming from outside"</note>, such as for a man to be wise, beautiful, or healthy. Just as wisdom and beauty are different "beings" from humanity, so they are different "goods." For the goodness of humanity by which a man is a man is one thing; the goodness of wisdom, by which he becomes not just a man but a wise man, is another. Just as these are different beings, they are also called different beings. 

Therefore, just as all things seek "the good," so all things seek "being." First, they seek that goodness which follows natural being, because this is the foundation of the goodnesses that follow; all the others are added to it such that they cannot stand without it. For how can someone be happy <note>original: "felix"</note> if they do not exist at all? Truly, that goodness they obtain when they first exist does not suffice for them; they desire to attain the remaining ones as well, which complete and adorn that first one. Just as we truly say they seek other goods beyond the first goodness, so we can truly say they desire other ways of being beyond the first being. 

<margin>The error of Olympiodorus</margin>
For it is one thing to be happy and another to be a man. And if someone grants that it is possible for someone to not want to exist if they are not happy, it does not follow (as Olympiodorus thinks) that "the good" is one thing and "being" another. Rather, it follows that being a man is one thing and happiness is another; and likewise the goodness of a man is one thing and the goodness of happiness is another. I will omit for now whether, by the same logic, something is called "simply good" and "simply being"... for this is not the place to dispute all things. Therefore, we were saying truly that each thing...

<summary>Pico argues that Being, the One, the True, and the Good are "convertible" terms that refer to the same reality from different perspectives. He refutes Olympiodorus's claim that the Good is superior to Being by explaining that there are different levels of both existence and goodness.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic reconciliation of Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy regarding the four "transcendentals": Being (Ens), the One (Unum), the True (Verum), and the Good (Bonum). Having previously established their definitions, he now discusses their "convertibility"—the idea that they are all essentially the same thing viewed from different angles—and how they apply to God.</meta>

# EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE

<margin>Evil and nothingness are interchangeable. Against the error of the Manichaeans. Nothingness and the divided are interchangeable. Aristotle.</margin>
That which exists is good to the extent that it exists. Indeed, "God saw everything that he had made, and they were very good" <note>Genesis 1:31</note>. Why shouldn't they be? They are from a good craftsman, who impresses his own likeness upon all things that are from him. In the "being" <term>entitate: the quality of existence or being a specific thing</term> of things, therefore, we can admire the power of the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into existence</note>; in the "truth," we can venerate the wisdom of the craftsman; in the "goodness," we can proclaim the generosity of the lover; and in the "unity," we can embrace the unique simplicity of the Creator, so to speak. This unity has joined each thing to itself, then all things to one another, and finally all things back to God himself; thus calling each thing to the love of itself, of others, and finally of God. Let us examine their opposites to see if they are similarly equal in scope. What we said above shows that the "false" and "nothingness" are the same. If we say "evil" and "nothingness" differ, both philosophers and theologians alike will protest. Therefore, "to do evil" is "to do nothing" <note>A standard philosophical argument: since God created all things as good, "evil" has no substance of its own; it is merely the absence or "nothingness" of good</note>; and it is customary to say that evil is not an efficient cause, but a "deficient" one. From this, the insanity of those who established two principles—one of good and one of evil—is refuted <note>Referring to the Manichaeans, a dualist sect that believed evil was a primary, creative force</note>, as if there were some efficient principle of evil. But to divide a thing is the same as to destroy it; nor can we take away from any thing its own natural unity without its existence in its integrity ceasing to remain. For the whole is not merely its parts, but that "one" which results from the parts, as Aristotle teaches in the eighth book of the *First Philosophy* <note>original: "primæ phiæ"; referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>. Therefore, if you divide the whole into parts, the parts indeed remain, but the "whole" which is divided does not remain; it ceases to exist "in act" <term>actu: being fully realized or functioning as a whole</term> and is only "in potentiality," just like the parts, which previously in the whole did not have their own unity in act, but first obtain it when, separated from the whole, they subsist by themselves.

## Chapter 9. In which he declares how those four are in God.

<margin>Three conditions of the good according to Plato</margin>
<margin>Pythagoras.</margin>
<margin>By what path these terms apply to God through those four causes.</margin>
**L**et us examine again how these are in God, in whom they do not exist in respect to a cause—for he has none. He himself is the cause of all and is from no one. These can be considered in God in a twofold way: either insofar as he is the cause of others (a distinction which does not apply to created things as far as the present business is concerned, since God can be such that he is not a cause <note>Pico is arguing that God's internal nature is distinct from his role as Creator</note>); or that other things cannot be such that they are not from him. Therefore, we first conceive of God as the universality of all "act," the fullness of "being" itself. Intelligence follows this so that he is "one," such that not even an opposite can be conceived. See how much they wander from the truth who imagine many first principles or many gods! Immediately, it is also most true: for that which has the appearance of being and is not, is certainly followed by "being" itself, so that it is also "truth" itself; but it will also be "goodness" itself. For there are three conditions of the good, as Plato writes in the *Philebus*: it must be perfect, sufficient, and desirable. This which we conceive as such will be "perfect" because nothing will be lacking to him who is all things; it will be "sufficient" because to those possessing it, nothing will be lacking in which all things are found; it will be "desirable" because from him and in him are all things which can be desired for any reason. God, therefore, is the fullest "being," indivisible "unity," most solid "truth," and most blessed "goodness." This, unless I am mistaken, is that **Tetraktys** <note>original: "Tetraktys" ($T\epsilon\tau\rho\alpha\kappa\tau\upsilon\sigma$); the Pythagorean "four-fold" number (1+2+3+4=10), which they considered the foundation of the universe</note>, that is, the "quaternity" by which Pythagoras swore and which he called the "principle of ever-flowing nature." For we have demonstrated that these things, which are the one God, are the "principle" of the being of all things. Moreover, we swear by those things which are holy, firm, and divine; what is firmer, holier, or more divine than these? But if we assign these four names to God insofar as he is the cause of things, the whole order is inverted. For first, he will be "one," because he is understood in himself before he is understood as a cause. Second, he will be "good." Third, "true." Fourth, "being." For since the cause which is called "final" <term>the purpose or end goal</term> is prior to that which is "exemplary" <term>the blueprint or idea</term>, and the exemplary is prior to the "efficient" <term>the builder</term>—for first, we desire to have something by which we are protected from the injury of storms [the end], then we conceive the idea of a house in the mind [the exemplar], and finally we form it in matter by acting from without [the efficient]—therefore, if (as we defined in the previous chapter) the "good" relates to the final cause, the "true" to the exemplary, and "being" to the efficient, then God, insofar as he is the cause, will have the character first of the "good," then the "true," and finally of "being." All of these things we touch upon briefly here, though they are otherwise teeming with many and great questions.

## Chapter 10. In which he turns the whole dispute toward the instruction of life and the amendment of morals.

# BOOK ONE

<margin>Note.</margin>
**B**ut let us not debate for the sake of others rather than for ourselves; we must take care that, while scrutinizing the highest things, we do not live in a lowly—that is, an unworthy—condition relative to these matters. It is granted to us by heaven that we are able to investigate even the reasons of celestial things. But we must constantly meditate on this: that our mind, to which even divine things are accessible, cannot be of mortal seed, nor will it be happy anywhere except in the possession of divine things. The more it raises and enflames itself toward divine things, having set aside the care of earthly ones, the more it—as a stranger and a pilgrim here—approaches happiness. Indeed, the presiding spirit of our discussion seems to warn us in the first place that if we wish to be blessed, we should imitate the most blessed God of all, possessing within ourselves unity, truth, and goodness.

Ambition disturbs the peace of unity; it snatches the soul, which should cling to itself, and drags it outside itself, tearing and rending it apart into diverse directions. Who would not lose the splendor and light of truth in the filth and darkness of pleasures? The most thievish desire—that is, greed—steals goodness from us; for it is the unique quality of goodness to share the goods you possess with others. For this reason, when <margin>Plato's inquiry</margin> Plato asked why God founded the world, he answered himself: "He was good" <note>A reference to Plato’s *Timaeus* 29e, a foundational text for Renaissance thinkers explaining that the Creator made the world because He was free from jealousy and wished all things to be like Himself.</note>. These are those three "superiors"—that is, of life: the "lust of the flesh," the "lust of the eyes," and the "pride of life" <note>original: "concupiscentia carnis & concupiscentia oculoz̃ [et superbia vitae]"</note>, which, as <margin>John.</margin> John writes, are of the world and are not of the Father, who is Unity itself, Truth itself, and Goodness itself <note>1 John 2:16</note>.

<margin>Note</margin>
Let us flee from here, therefore—that is, from the world which is steeped in wickedness—and let us fly away to the Father, where there is unifying peace, where there is the truest light, and where there is the best pleasure. But who will give us wings to fly there? The love <margin>Note</margin> of those things which are above. Who will take them away? The lust for things which are upon the earth. If we pursue such things, we suffer the loss of unity, truth, and goodness. For we are not "one" if we do not bind together our crooked senses and our reason (which looks toward heavenly things) by the covenant of virtue. Instead, there are two princes reigning in us, as if at intervals: while now we follow God through the law of the mind, and now Baal <note>A biblical name for a false god, used here by Pico to represent the "law of the flesh" or idolatry of physical pleasure.</note> through the law of the flesh; and "our kingdom, divided against itself, is surely laid waste" <note>Luke 11:17</note>.

If we should be "one" in such a way that reason is enslaved to the senses and only the law of the members <note>A Pauline reference to the conflict between physical desires and moral reason.</note> commands us, this unity will be false, because we will not be true. For we shall be called men, and appear to be men—that is, <term>rational animals: a standard definition of humanity in Scholastic philosophy</term>—and yet we shall be brutes, for whom sensory appetite stands in place of law. We will be putting on a deceptive show for those who see us and among whom we live. The image will not correspond to its archetype. For we are in the likeness of God, but <margin>Paul</margin> God is Spirit. We are no longer "spiritual" (to use Paul’s words), but "animal" <note>original: "animales." In this context, it refers to being governed by the lower soul or physical nature rather than the higher spirit.</note>. However, when we do not deviate from our Archetype through truth, it will remain for us to be joined to Him at last, tending toward Him through goodness. But if these three follow Being in a perpetual bond—namely, Unity, Truth, and Goodness—it follows that when we are not those things, we also essentially *are not*, even if we seem to be; and although we are believed to be living, we are dying continually rather than truly living.

### ->THE FIRST OBJECTIONS OF ANTONIO FAVENTINO<-
### ->AGAINST THE TREATISE ON BEING AND THE ONE.<-

<margin>First objection.</margin>
**I**f any little book deserves to be titled *On Being and the One*, it is necessary that it explain the nature and properties of Being and the One. Yet in this little work, which recently came into my hands and which is titled *On Being and the One*, several things are treated that are almost foreign to the title and inscription. For the principal purpose of the author is to dispute whether, according to Plato, Being and the One follow one another mutually, or whether, as the Academics <note>The "Academics" refers to followers of the Platonic Academy, whose views on whether "The One" is superior to "Being" were a major point of debate.</note> think, the One is more common than Being. But this is not to treat "Being and the One" absolutely, but rather the mutual convertibility of Being and the One, and not even entirely in an absolute sense, but only according to Plato. For if any philosopher were to agitate only that question of whether the soul is immortal, he would not therefore be disputing "On the Soul," but would have a treatise solely on the immortality of the soul.

<margin>Second.</margin>
Furthermore, the author of the work says that the Academics think that God, according to Plato, is not truly and properly Being; which I wonder at greatly in him. For if all the Academics, or the Platonists...

The page then introduces the critiques of Antonio Faventino, who argues Pico's work is too narrow to justify its broad title.</summary>

...understands them: just as the speech seems to signify; otherwise it would not be pronounced absolutely. 

<margin>Themistius</margin>
The claim that the Academics <note>Followers of the skeptical school of philosophy in the tradition of Plato's Academy.</note> feel this way is perhaps not without falsehood. For Themistius <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle and Plato.</note>, a nobly regarded author among the Platonists, testifies that according to Plato’s opinion, the Idea—which is the principle of things—is truly and properly Being and the One. However, most or all Platonists do not consider the Idea to be one thing and God the Craftsman <note>Referring to the "Demiurge," the divine creator figure in Plato’s Timaeus.</note> another. He continues by saying:

<margin>Third Objection.</margin>
If it can be defended in any way according to Plato that the One is more universal than Being, it should be judged thus: words which (on Latin pages) are called "concrete"—such as "white," "shining," or "being"—signify something external <note>In medieval logic, a "concrete" term implies both a quality and the subject that possesses it (e.g., "white" implies "whiteness" in a thing).</note>, by whose presence things receive the name of the word. Indeed, "whiteness" is one thing, and "a white thing" is another; "man" is one thing, and "humanity" another. Therefore, that in which "to be" is one thing and that which "subsists" is another will be called "being." Therefore God, who is Being itself, cannot be considered "being," but rather "the One," since He contains and encloses all things. But is not this sort of defense inconsistent with itself? For by the same reasoning that "white," "man," and "being" signify something external, the One, the Blessed, God, and many such things would also signify something external.

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
It must be so: therefore God, who is Unity, Blessedness, and Deity all at once, could neither be called "the One," nor "the Blessed," nor "God" at all. How then is He not "being" but only "the One"? Furthermore, a thing is called "being" because it exists. Just as it cannot happen that one who sits is not "sitting," it also cannot happen that He who truly and properly exists is not "being." For He says: "I am who I am" <note>Original: "ego sum qui sum," the name of God revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14.</note>.

<margin>Fourth Objection</margin>
It may seem even more remarkable that he [the opponent] tries to defend the idea that God is not "being" not only according to Plato, but also tries to pull Aristotle himself into the same opinion. For he says that in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*, Aristotle divides being into <term>being through itself (ens per se): something that exists by its own nature</term> and <term>being through accident (ens per accidens): something that exists only coincidentally or as a property</term>. He says that "being through itself" is divided into the ten categories <note>Aristotle’s classification system for all types of existence, such as substance, quality, and quantity.</note>, yet God can be placed in no category, as he believes Blessed Thomas [Aquinas] has demonstrated. Therefore, if God is not "being through itself" nor "being through accident," as is established according to Aristotle, He will not be "being." Furthermore, being is separated into substance and accident according to the most common division; but God is neither an accident nor a substance (for he says God is above these). God exceeds the limits of any category. But truly, I do not see by what reason the author of this work ascribes a Platonist opinion to our Aristotle—if indeed it is even Plato’s opinion.

<margin>St. Thomas, Aristotle.</margin>
For the division of being into "being through itself" and "being through accident" is a division of "complex being" <note>Logical propositions where a predicate is joined to a subject, such as "Socrates is white."</note>, as Blessed Thomas—to whom he gives great authority—writes subtly in that place. The same is clear from examples: for "being through accident" according to Aristotle is threefold: either an accident is predicated of a subject, or a subject of an accident, or an accident of an accident—all of which pertain to a "complex" proposition. In the same way, those things are called "through itself" in which something is predicated that pertains either to substance, or to quantity, or another category, provided that what is predicated belongs to the subject through itself—such as "white" of Socrates, or "man" and "animal" of a horse. However, the division of being into "substance" and "accident" also encompasses God. For it is a division made through affirmation and negation: for "substance" is that which relies on nothing but exists through itself, while "accident" is that which is in another as if in a subject. Between these, there is no middle ground, as Blessed Thomas thinks.

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
Since indeed no middle point can be imagined between "having a subject" and "not having a subject." Therefore, "substance," which is the opposite of "accident," will not be a category <note>Original: "genus."</note> if God is contained in no category. Furthermore, it is not the undisputed opinion of Aristotle that God is contained in no category through Himself; for there are some followers of Aristotle who think that God is placed through Himself in the categories. And I indeed think that this was the opinion

<margin>Boethius, Augustine.</margin>
of the distinguished philosopher Boethius <note>A 6th-century Roman philosopher whose work "The Consolation of Philosophy" was a bridge between Antiquity and the Middle Ages.</note>; and I would show, if it were necessary, that this can be aptly gathered from the words of Boethius as well as Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo.</note>.

<margin>Fifth Objection</margin>
Again, he says that the "divided" is the negation of "the one." He proves this because a thing is destroyed when it is pulled apart and divided. But how can "the divided" be opposed to "the one" as a negation? For between an affirmation and a negation there is a contradiction; yet a chimera <note>A mythological monster, used here as a standard logical example of a non-existent thing that cannot be categorized.</note> is neither one nor divided, nor is the idea that "a diagonal is commensurable" <note>A mathematical impossibility used to represent something that is logically "nothing."</note> either one or divided. He also thinks that "the false" is the negation of "the true":

<margin>Sixth Objection.</margin>
...which, even if it could be defended in some way, is nevertheless a contrary rather than a negation.

<summary>Pico rebuts several arguments claiming God is "the One" but not "Being," using Thomas Aquinas and Aristotle to show that if God exists, He must be categorized as Being. He specifically challenges the misuse of the Aristotelian categories and the definition of substance to exclude the divine.</summary>
<keywords>Themistius, Platonism, concrete terms, Being vs. the One, Aristotle's Metaphysics, Thomas Aquinas, substance and accident, Boethius, Augustine, logic of negation</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page where Antonio Faventino’s objections were being listed, this page concludes the series of objections—specifically citing Thomas Aquinas, Aristotle, and Boethius—and begins Pico della Mirandola's formal response in the form of a letter to Antonio.</meta>

<header>OBJECTIONS, BOOK TWO</header>

<margin>Sixth: Blessed Thomas.</margin>
...negation: just as Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian whose work Pico often seeks to reconcile with Platonism.</note> demonstrates. For a chimera <note>A mythological creature; in logic, it refers to an impossible concept that has no basis in reality.</note> is not true or false unless we utterly misuse the term. For "true" is that which is; this is as he himself explains it: that which is exactly what it appears and is said to be. It follows, therefore, that "false" will be that which is not what it appears and is said to be—like a false coin. Therefore, nothing happens to be false except that which appears to be something other than what it is. Between that which is seen to be what it is and that which is not what it is seen to be, there is no contradiction. Therefore, truth and falsehood do not oppose each other by any opposition of affirmation and negation. He also considers evil to be a negation of good.

<margin>Seventh: Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle, however, affirms in the *Categories* <note>Original: "praedicamentis." One of Aristotle's logical works concerning the classification of things.</note> that good and evil are distinct classes of contraries. But what is a mere negation cannot be a class. Furthermore, good is to be sought for the reason that it is good, while evil is to be avoided. To seek and to avoid are themselves contraries, just as gathering and scattering are; therefore, good and evil will be contraries. Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524), whose translations and commentaries were central to medieval logic.</note> also asserts this in his commentary on the *Categories*, whatever others may have said about it.

<margin>Confirmation</margin>

->Response to the First Objections.<-

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ANTONIO OF FAENZA, GREETINGS.

<margin>Solution to the first objection.</margin>
I read your questions against that little book I recently published *On Being and the One* with as much pleasure as they were written by you with both affection and frankness. I owe you much for this service. If we either bestowed such frankness more freely upon our friends, or demanded it more willingly from them, we would certainly be far more learned and better than we are. But a deadly persuasion has seized the minds of men: that we do not think people like us if they do not like our errors. We interpret the free judgment of friends as either hatred or grumpiness, while we interpret flattery as love and natural goodness. Thus it happens that while we prefer to be praised undeservedly rather than be mocked for being corrected when we deserve it, we may always be praised, but we never deserve it. See how much we err! For almost all praise is always useless, and often even harmful. For if it is true, what utility does it bring? If it is false, it surely makes us who are praised insane, and those who praise us ridiculous. Reproof is certainly always useful: if it is just, it rouses us to knowledge; if it is less than just, it rouses us to the defense of the truth. Finally, what else is it to be corrected but to be made better by another's labor? Or what else is it for a friend's book to shine under the file <note>A common metaphor for the polishing and refining of a literary work.</note> but for you to benefit from his sleepless nights while you yourself were sleeping? I cannot, therefore, as I was saying, not owe you very much. For you have freely signaled to me what you felt about those things in my book which pleased you less. I recognized in your writings, besides your benevolence, that dexterity of wit already known to me for a long time. I immediately began to examine whatever you had noted, not as a father <note>Meaning he did not view his own work with parental bias.</note> but as a judge, and more severely, since those things had already come under suspicion of falsehood for me based on your testimony. But as I was thinking, several things occurred to me by which those points seemed able to be defended and cleared of fault. These things I wanted to write to you freely, lest I myself should fail to embrace the very virtue I praise in you; so that if I do not imitate your judgment in criticizing those points, at least I might imitate your frankness in defending them. You say it is not right for the book to be titled *On Being and the One*, since you do not deal in it with all the natures and properties of "being" and "the one," but only with their convertibility <note>The philosophical idea that "Being" and "One" refer to the same thing and are interchangeable.</note>. To me, Antonio, it 

<margin>What a title and a preface are.</margin>
usually seems that two "vestibules," as it were, are placed before books: the Title and the Preface. What is a title but a short preface? A preface is a title poured out and explained. The title promises a treatise on being and the one; the preface explains that it is the *relationship* between being and the one that is to be treated. If this were done in the title itself, there would be a fear that the title of the book would become a book itself! This could be defended by the precedent of a thousand authors, the titles of whose books would be subject to the same calumny. But this question is not of such weight that either I or you should be occupied with it for long. You wonder, furthermore, why it is believed by the Platonists...

<meta>This page continues the "Expositions" by Pico della Mirandola, where he defends his treatise *De Ente et Uno* (On Being and the One). Having listed objections in previous pages, he now begins his "solutions," specifically addressing the Neoplatonic view that God is "The One" and is situated above the category of "Being."</meta>

<header>EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE.</header>

# EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE.

<margin>Second solution</margin>
<margin>Syrianus, Proclus, Plotinus</margin>
...that I said God is not properly "being." Do not be amazed at me, but at those whom I—along with you—do not approve of in the assertion of this dogma. However, I want you to see that they held this view (which seems almost incredible to you) and left it written for posterity; it is very well known to all who have read the Platonic works. Syrianus, Proclus, Plotinus <note>Major philosophers of the Neoplatonic school who lived between the 3rd and 5th centuries AD.</note>, and finally all extant interpreters of Plato confirm this with one voice. But, you say, Themistius <note>A 4th-century commentator who sought to reconcile Plato and Aristotle.</note>—no noble figure among the Platonists—asserts that according to Plato's opinion, that which is truly and properly "being" is also "one." Most or all Platonists think the "Idea" <note>The eternal, perfect forms or patterns of things in the divine mind.</note> is no different from God, the maker of things. Therefore, if the Idea is properly called "being," God himself would also properly be called "being." You argue this cleverly enough, but see if you do so with enough piety.

<margin>Plotinus' opinion on the Ideas.</margin>
For they—namely Proclus and Plotinus—confess that an "Idea" is "being" and is called such, but they contend that God is above ideas just as He is above all beings. For Plotinus placed all the Ideas in that Mind which is closest to God—which he also calls the first being, the first intelligible thing, and the first life—so that God is not the "womb" of the ideas but their source; not their receptacle, but their principle <note>original: "principium," meaning the fundamental source or origin.</note>.

<margin>Proclus' opinion on the Ideas.</margin>
Proclus makes not just one, but many orders of intermediate minds between God and the Ideas, whose fullness—imitating Plato's words in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the world; the "Perfect Living Being" refers to the model used by the Creator.</note>—he called the "Perfect Living Being." I pass over Syrianus, Amelius, Iamblichus, and many others who feel the same way.

<margin>St. Thomas, First Part, sufficiently</margin>
These are the basics and, so to speak, the cradle of that doctrine which is considered "Platonic."

<margin>Another solution</margin>
But if someone grants you that in reality the "Idea" and God are not different, you will not deny that they are nevertheless different in "reason" <note>In scholastic logic, "reason" (ratio) refers to a conceptual distinction rather than a physical one.</note>. This diversity will sufficiently allow God, insofar as He is the exemplar <note>The perfect pattern or model.</note> of man, horse, or lion, to be truly called "being." Yet, insofar as He looks at nothing outside Himself and has no relationship to created things, but remains solitary in the recesses of His divinity, He exceeds every name of "being." As Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a mystical theologian who emphasized God's transcendence beyond all language.</note> says, He has neither name nor opinion.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
Therefore, it is most manifest that even among the leaders of the Academy <note>The school of Plato.</note>, God cannot be properly called "being." Even if one grants that the "Idea" and God are the same thing in reality, it does not immediately follow that if the Idea is "being," God must also be properly called "being." Let us pass to other matters, among which this might displease you most: that I said there is a certain way of speaking which, if we follow it, allows us to truly say that "The One" is higher than "Being." Indeed, we give God the name of "The One" while not giving Him the name of "Being," because "being" has the appearance of a "concrete name" <note>In Latin grammar, a "concrete name" (nomen concretum) like *ens* (being) implies a subject participating in an attribute, rather than the pure essence itself. Pico argues God is the essence itself, not a "thing that has being."</note> (for so we may speak in English). It signifies that which participates in existence from another, which cannot be said of God (who is existence itself). You say that by the same reasoning, God could not be called "The One," because "The One" is also a concrete name just like "Being." I saw this question while I was writing and I resolved it: for as soon as I proved that "Being" cannot be predicated of God (because it signifies that which is not of itself, but participates in another), I added that for God, the name of "The One" is given as a consequence. From there, we must confess that "The One" is above "Being." Immediately after this, meeting your objection, I added: "However, we call God 'The One' then not so much declaring *what* He is, but *how* He is all things that He is, since in whatever way they are, all things are from Him." For Dionysius says God is called "One" because He is all things uniquely; again, He is called "One" because He is the principle of all things that exist, just as Unity is the principle of all numbers. I wrote these things there word-for-word.

<margin>Third solution</margin>
If, therefore, when we call God "One," we wish to declare *what* He is, I agree with you that by the same reasoning He cannot be called "One" any more than He can be called "Being," because both are concrete names. Indeed, I was the first to assert this very thing clearly in that same book with these words: "These names—Being, True, One, Good—are what they call 'concrete' and, as it were, 'participated.'" Therefore, we say again that God is above Being, above Truth, above The One, and above Good, because He is Existence itself, Truth itself, Unity itself, and Goodness itself. These are my words there.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
It did not escape me, therefore, when I was writing, that "Being" and "The One" are equally concrete, and by reason of that concreteness, either neither or both should be removed from God. But as I had warned above: when we call God "One" but not "Being," we do not signify *what* God is, but *how* He is that which He is—namely, because He is most primarily and simply all things. This "mode" can in no way be indicated or figured through the name of "Being," but it can be through the type and naming of "Unity." For beings relate to one another as numbers do, as Aristotle writes, and of numbers, the most [primary...] <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "palissima," likely continuing as "principalissima" (most primary).</note>.

<summary>Pico defends the Neoplatonic view that God transcends "Being," arguing that while both "Being" and "The One" are limited "concrete" terms, "The One" better describes how God acts as the simple source of all things. He distinguishes between God's role as a model for creation (where He can be called Being) and His solitary, absolute nature (which is beyond all names).</summary>
<keywords>Pico della Mirandola, Neoplatonism, Being and the One, Plotinus, Proclus, Dionysius the Areopagite, metaphysics, divine names, concrete vs abstract, transcendence</keywords>

<meta>Pico continues his defense against the objection that he claimed God is not "being." Having previously cited Neoplatonic authorities, he now turns to the heavyweight of Medieval Scholasticism, Thomas Aquinas, to show that even in the Aristotelian tradition, there is a sense in which God is described as being "above" the categories of being.</meta>

<page-num>90</page-num>
<header>OBJECTIONS. SECOND BOOK.</header>

...most [perfect] and simplest unity. You add that you wonder that I wish to defend—not only according to Plato but also according to Aristotle—that God is not being. But if you have run through the book more attentively, in this whole work I principally strive to show that God both is and is called properly **being**: not only from Aristotle’s dogma but also Plato’s, and consequently that the "one" is not superior to "being." Truly, lest those who said God is not being but "above being" should seem entirely insane:

<margin>Aristotle. Fourth solution according to Aristotle.</margin>
Among those authors, if it were neither Plato nor Aristotle, there is certainly Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian mystic whose writings, then thought to be by a convert of St. Paul, heavily influenced medieval theology regarding the "unknowability" of God.</note>, who is greater than both. I have attempted to prove that there is a certain way of speaking which, if we follow it, will not be discordant with the truth: that God is greater than the name of "being." This way of speaking is even sometimes used by the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>; although you may shrink from applying it to God, you cannot deny it unless you deny their authority, to whom even in your opinion the first place in that family of thinkers is owed.

<margin>Plato. Dionysius.</margin>
For who does not know that the division of being into **substance** <note>The underlying reality or "thing-ness" of an object.</note> and **accident** <note>A quality that exists in a substance, like its color or shape, but is not the substance itself.</note> is frequent among the Aristotelians? However, when being is so divided, it is the opinion of your own Thomas [Aquinas] that God is not being but "above being." Regarding him, you used to say: "Take away Thomas, and Aristotle will become mute." The words of Thomas are roughly these:

<margin>The immortal glory and praise of Thomas</margin>
> God is neither an accident, nor can He properly be called a substance: both because a substance is called a substance because it "stands under" [original: *substat*], and because substance indicates a quiddity <note>The essence or "what-ness" of a thing.</note> which is something other than His being.

Therefore, that division of being into substance and accident is the division of *created* being. Thus says Thomas. Furthermore, when Aristotle says the "first philosopher" <note>The metaphysician.</note> deals with being insofar as it is being, and with the causes and principles of being, there are many among the Peripatetics who want God not to be placed there by Aristotle among "beings," but among the "causes of being." Moreover, that He can also be properly called being in another way of speaking, I have not only not denied but asserted and confirmed by many reasons in the third chapter of the same work.

<margin>Confirmation of the solution. Boethius. Fifth solution.</margin>
I do not know why you, always an imitator of illustrious authors, now defect from the most famous Peripatetics to those who place God under a "genus" <note>A general category or class.</note>—among whom I have no doubt Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher and statesman whose work bridged the gap between Classical and Medieval thought.</note> would in no way wish to be numbered. Finally, you contend that the "divided" is not the negation of the "one," nor the "false" the negation of the "true," nor the "evil" the negation of the "good." Indeed, regarding the oppositions of these things, I know the controversy among great authors is not easy, and for that reason I ended the book in which these were treated in passing with this clause: "All these things we touch upon briefly here, which otherwise would make for many and great questions." But that the opinion I have followed is less probable or true—so that I should doubt—nothing you object moves me. You say a **Chimera** <note>A mythical beast; in philosophy, it represents an impossible thing that cannot exist because its parts are contradictory.</note> is neither one nor divided. I, however, say that the Chimera we conceive in the mind does not exist for the reason that the parts from which we understand it to be combined are, in the nature of things, divided and not united. And just as that thing does not exist whose parts (from which it would be constituted if it did exist) are divided, so too it not only does not exist but is impossible [original: *necesse poteat*] whose parts are neither united nor can be united by the force of nature. Therefore, for no other reason do we say the Chimera does not exist—and believe it cannot even come to be—than because it is not credible that the brute parts from which we fashion it could ever come together into a single animal composition. Again you insist that the diameter being incommensurable <note>Referring to the mathematical proof that the diagonal of a square cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of its sides.</note> is neither one nor divided. You are mistaken, in my opinion. For by whatever reason something is false, it is by that same reason necessarily divided in itself. For something is detected as false insofar as it fights with itself and includes a contradiction. And what else is it to include a contradiction than to be divided within oneself?

<margin>Sixth solution</margin>
Therefore every true thing is one, because it is consistent and harmonious with itself; every false thing is divided, because it fights with itself and is not coherent with itself. That the false is the negation of the true many have believed, which is not hidden from you either. Nor do the arguments you bring forward stand in the way. For as I said, we call "false" that which is not what it seems to be: such as false gold, which seems to be gold but is not. Although false gold is not gold but something other than gold, nevertheless, insofar as it is false...

<summary>Pico defends his view that God is Being by reconciling Aristotelian and Platonic perspectives, using Thomas Aquinas to show that God transcends the standard categories of substance and accident. He also argues that truth is synonymous with unity, while falsehood and impossibility (like a Chimera) are synonymous with internal division and contradiction.</summary>
<keywords>Being, The One, Thomas Aquinas, Aristotle, Dionysius the Areopagite, Substance, Accident, Chimera, Contradiction, Metaphysics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's defense of his work "On Being and the One." In the previous section, Pico argued that God can be described as "above being" without contradicting the idea that He is the source of all existence. Here, he concludes his argument on the nature of truth and falsehood before transitioning to a letter from his friend and critic, Antonio Faventinus (Antonio Cittadini), who raises specific objections to Pico's definitions and his interpretation of Plato.</meta>

...it happens that being is something other than gold: but it is false for the reason that it is not the gold which it nevertheless appears to be. Gold, therefore, is false because it does not match the **idea** <note>In this context, an "idea" refers to the perfect, divine archetype or blueprint of a thing in the mind of God.</note> of gold; but because it matches the idea of brass or silver, it is not entirely false, but only false gold—just as it is not entirely non-being. For although it is not that which is gold, it is nevertheless something else, such as lead or silver. <margin>what absolute falsehood is</margin> However, that which corresponds to no idea is entirely and absolutely false, just as it is entirely non-being; such is the thing we call a **chimera** <note>A mythical creature composed of parts from different animals; used by philosophers to represent something that is logically impossible or has no basis in reality.</note>. <margin>Seventh solution</margin> See, therefore, that they proceed with an equal pace: non-being, the divided, and the false; and every false thing might deservedly be called divided. Evil, indeed, does not oppose good by a contrary opposition as you think, and as Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant medieval philosopher and teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note> teaches when explaining Aristotle’s <margin>Albert. Thomas.</margin> **categories** <note>Aristotle's "Categories" is a fundamental text classifying all things that can be said to exist.</note>; and as Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential Scholastic theologian.</note> teaches most safely in the first question *On Evil*: all of which I believe have long been very well known to you. FAREWELL.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA. ANTONIO OF FAENZA.

<margin>Let the <unclear>gloss</unclear> hold for the one and the many <unclear>likewise</unclear></margin>
**Q**uantum I have loved you and always honored you, most excellent man, you yourself are witness; you can easily recall, if you wish, how diligently and exceptionally I have worked on your behalf. But if you now either doubt that you are loved by Antonio, your old friend and godfather, or do not believe it at all, by Hercules, you have little memory of my respect toward you. For how could it happen that I, who loved and honored you when you were scarcely initiated into philosophy, would not love and admire you now that you are distinguished in learning and integrity? Would that all those with whom you have been familiar had embraced you with as much goodwill as your godfather has always pursued his dear Pico. But let us now come to our business: You say that your little book *On Being and the One* could be correctly titled, even if the title of the work is short; and though it promises a treatise on being and the one, the preface (which is more expansive than the title) explains what kind of treatise it promises: namely, the mutual **conversion** <note>In logic, "conversion" refers to the idea that "being" and "the one" are interchangeable terms for the same reality.</note> of being and the one. But see, I pray, whether this <margin>First objection</margin> defense of yours is sufficient: by the same reasoning, if a book were published in which only the immortality of the soul was asserted by the author, the book could deservedly be titled *On the Soul*. For an author entering upon a dispute might soon propose a question, asking whether the soul be immortal or not. Truly, this objection was almost entirely explained in my previous letter, but you answered nothing to my judgment. Furthermore, if a question were made regarding the velocity of motions—whether it follows an arithmetic or geometric proportion—and at the beginning of the work the author promises to take many things from geometry, could the book be titled *On Geometry*, since it would be concerned with motions? But let us omit these things as if they were frivolous. In another book, I have written on this opinion. <margin>Second objection.</margin> No one, I say, says that the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, particularly the Neoplatonists who emphasized the "One" above all else.</note> feel otherwise unless all or most of them feel that way. If, however, Themistius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Aristotle who tried to harmonize Aristotelian and Platonic thought.</note>—no ignoble man among the Platonists—affirms from Plato’s opinion that the **Idea**, which is the principle of things, is truly and properly **being**, it should not have been pronounced absolutely that the Platonists (following Plato) think God is not truly and properly being: for the Idea is God. You, however, answer that the Idea is one thing and God is another; and if it were granted that the Idea is God, it would not follow that God is properly and truly being; for God and the Idea, even if they do not differ in reality, nevertheless differ in **reason** <note>A technical distinction meaning they are the same thing in existence, but we understand them through different mental concepts.</note>. But I would not wish to dispute in this place whether the Platonists think God is one thing and the Idea another, since that question is far removed from the purpose; although very many authors, Greek and Latin alike, place Plato’s Ideas in God. I seem to have done enough for the purpose by imitating Plato, demonstrating that a certain Platonist—and by Hercules, not an ignoble one—asserts that according to Plato, the Idea, and therefore God, is truly and properly being. Nor does the discrepancy of reason to which you flee do anything in this matter: for the "Idea" is relative, while "God" is an absolute thing.

Antonio challenges the title of Pico's book and disputes Pico's claim that Platonists view God as being "beyond" existence, arguing instead that God and the "Idea" of Being are essentially the same.</summary>
