# OBJECTIONS: SECOND BOOK

If, therefore, God is truly and properly **being** <term>ens: a philosophical term for anything that exists</term> in that respect where he relates to things outside of himself, how much more should he be considered **being** by that reason by which he is God and consists in his own nature? For why is an **idea** <note>In Platonic thought, an Idea is the perfect, eternal form of a thing.</note> truly and properly **being** by the very reason that it is an idea? I say that no reason can be assigned for this unless it is said to be truly and properly being because it truly and properly *is*. Therefore, God, by the reason that he is God, will be even more truly and properly **being**. For he said: <note>original: "ego sum qui sum"</note> "I am who I am." Furthermore, the objection stands in this way: if the Platonists can be rightly defended when they say God is not truly and properly **being**, but rather **the One**, because the name "being" is a **concrete** <note>A "concrete" name refers to a subject possessing a quality (like "white thing"), whereas an "abstract" name refers to the quality itself ("whiteness"). Pico's critics argued "being" was too concrete for God.</note> name which signifies something other than that which is "the One," or because he is uniquely all things: by the same logic, it could be concluded that God is not "the One." For "the One" is also a concrete name. Indeed, he would be neither blessed nor God, as both terms are concrete. But you respond that you do not call God "the One" as if the **substance** <term>substantia: that which exists in itself rather than in another thing</term> of God were shown by the name of "the One," but rather to explain how he is that which he is. But I ask: to what end is this? For the objection is not yet resolved. You say God is not **being**, but **the One**, because the name of "being" is concrete. If, therefore, "the One" is also concrete, must it not be concluded by the same reasoning that God is not "the One," nor is he "God" (which name pertains to substance, just as "being" does)? Furthermore, if he is "the One" because he is uniquely that which he is, why should he not also be called **being**? For to be one is to be all things: namely, he is wisdom, and goodness, and power. For he is not called "One" because he is the only one who is one; therefore, by the same reasoning, he can be called **being** even if he is not the only being; for he is, in the highest degree, **being**. Furthermore, that reason has not yet been resolved which stated: God is truly and properly **being**, for he said, "I am who I am."

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
Again, I wondered that you would defend the idea—following Aristotle as well—that God is sometimes not considered by the name of **being** at all, because he is not being **through himself** <note>original: "per se ens"</note> nor **by accident**, nor **substance**, nor **accident** <term>accidens: a property that exists only within a substance, like color or shape</term>. For I have shown that God is neither being through himself nor by accident, and that nothing can be thought of as a medium between substance and accident. But you offer no response to the first objection. Against the second, however, you allege only one interpreter of Aristotle, namely Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian and philosopher.</note>, who says that God is not properly a **substance** because he does not "stand under" any accident, nor is the essence of God anything other than God himself. But see, most excellent man, whether Thomas does not bear witness against you. For if the division of **being** into substance and accident is, according to Blessed Thomas, a division of *created* being (as you report), how can it be ignored that there is some *uncreated* **being**, which is God? By what reasoning, then, can you maintain, according to the interpretation of Blessed Thomas, that Aristotle thought God is not properly and truly **being**? As for the fact that Blessed Thomas seems to deny in a certain place that God is properly a **substance**, imitating the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose "Sentences" was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> because God does not "stand under" any accident: it is not therefore false what we wrote in the previous letter, that there is no medium between substance and accident. Blessed Thomas proves this in many places with effective arguments, and you have not solved a single one of the points written to you. If, therefore, he sometimes denies that God is a substance, the very words you bring forward clearly reveal the man's mind. For **substance** can be spoken of in many ways, which he himself explains more extensively in the first part <note>A reference to the "Prima Pars" of Aquinas's "Summa Theologica."</note>. For sometimes it is properly called "substance" because it "stands under" accidents; for this reason, he denies God is a substance—not simply and absolutely, but he says he is not *properly* a substance because he stands under no accident. However, "substance" is sometimes said to be that which exists through itself and does not need a subject, in which way Blessed Thomas sometimes—and indeed frequently—uses the name of substance. Thus, no middle ground can be thought of between substance and accident; for it is a division based on affirmation and negation of the other. As for the fact that I affirmed, led by no necessity but of my own accord from the opinion of Boethius and Augustine, that God is placed in a **predicament** <term>predicamentum: one of Aristotle's ten categories of being</term> "through himself," I did not say this because I do not highly value, venerate, or approve of Blessed Thomas. But I said it because the authority of Blessed Thomas alone is not sufficient to show that either Aristotle or the Aristotelians thought God is in no way placed in a predicament. Nor do we, for that reason, desert the best authors for those who are wicked or common. I follow and approve the best; do you ever make Blessed Thomas equal or superior to Boethius or Augustine? Indeed, I have read them all in the past and read them daily; nor do I think anyone's mind is so vigorous that those things which were said by our Britons... <note>The text cuts off here, but likely refers to "British" or "English" scholastic philosophers like Duns Scotus or William of Ockham, who were highly influential in logical and metaphysical debates.</note>

->## ON BEING AND THE ONE<-

...and similar things thought out, he either ignores or neglects. I certainly do not approve and admire everything they have written; indeed, I am often accustomed to weaken several—and by Hercules, not a few—based on the opinion of Aristotle and worthy authors. Yet, I cannot help but admire the immense **subtlety** <note>Pico refers to the "subtlety" of the Scholastic philosophers, whose intricate logical hair-splitting was both admired and criticized during the Renaissance.</note> of these men and their most acute reasoning in physical matters. Even Aristotle himself, if he were to rise from the dead, would admire and extol this subtlety in a marvelous way, approving at least of their ingenuity in many cases, even if not always their truth. 

Furthermore, you defend the idea that the negation of "the One" is "the divided." For you say that the **chimera** <term>chymera: a mythological creature made of disparate parts; in logic, it represents an impossible concept that cannot exist.</term> is "divided" because the parts of which it would consist, if it were to exist, are divided from one another and cannot be united. Likewise, you think the **commensurable diameter** <note>This refers to the "incommensurability of the diagonal," a classic Greek mathematical proof showing that the diagonal of a square cannot be expressed as a simple fraction of its side. Thus, a "commensurable diameter" is a logical impossibility.</note> is "divided" because it is divided from itself and is discordant. These are the very words you use: "For a thing is found to be false to the extent that it fights with itself and includes a contradiction." 

But what else is it to "include a contradiction" than to be divided within oneself? Therefore, every **truth** is **one** because it is consistent and harmonious with itself; every **falsehood** is **divided** because it fights with itself and is not coherent with itself. But see how you can sustain your position: for if something is "one" because it is harmonious with itself and undivided from itself, then **falsehood** itself and the **impossible** will be "one" and "true." I do not mean that this falsehood—the chimera or the flying stag—actually exists, but I am considering the very nature of "falsehood" and "impossibility." I will prove that this nature is one and true. 

According to your dogma, the chimera is "divided" because its parts are always divided from each other, and also because it is divided from itself—for a chimera is not a chimera. By that same reasoning, the commensurable diameter is "divided." For it cannot be understood otherwise than that both of these things are discordant with themselves and fight with themselves. But if you look at the **false** itself separately, the false is false and the impossible is impossible; neither fights with itself; neither is discordant with itself. By the same logic, the **dead** do not fight with themselves at all; for they are dead, those who are already dead. Therefore, any of these is "one" and "true" if a thing is "one" because it is undivided from itself. 

Furthermore, how is it true that everything false "encloses a contradiction"? Are there not many things that are false which could be true either by the power of nature or of man? Again, you try to defend the definition of **truth** provided by you, saying that the "true" is that which seems to be what it is, while the "false" is that which seems to be what it is not. Now, for this reason, you think it follows that falsehood is not the negation of truth. But, by your leave, I would say you have so far responded nothing to my argument. My argument is this: if the "true" is that which seems to be what it is, and the "false" is that which seems to be what it is not, then since there is no contradiction between "seeming to be what is" and "seeming to be what is not," falsehood will not be the negation of truth. 

For if neither man nor God existed in the nature of things, Socrates would not exist; thus, he would not seem to be what he was, nor what he was not. Therefore, he would be neither true nor false. He would, however, be **non-being** <term>non ens: that which does not exist.</term>. Thus, "non-being" and the "false" sometimes differ. Even **Blessed Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theologian of the Catholic Church.</note>, whom you do not oppose, pronounces that truth and falsehood are contraries to one another if they are referred to the mind—upon which your opinion of the nature of truth and falsehood depends. He says that true and false estimations are contrary to one another, just as **Aristotle** says.

Lastly, you deny that **good** and **evil** are contraries to each other, but you do not respond to the reasoning by which it was proved they are contraries, nor do you explain how evil is a negation of good. For I said this: no negation—especially one that encompasses those things which are not—can be a **genus** <term>genus: a general category or classification in logic.</term>. Indeed, it is said by Aristotle in the *Topics* that of "non-being" there are no genera nor species. Therefore, **evil**, which encompasses all non-beings, cannot be a genus. How then did Aristotle, that most eminent man, say in the **Categories** <note>original: "in predicamentis", referring to Aristotle's work *Categories*, which classifies types of being.</note> that good and evil are the genera of contraries? 

You also say that **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), teacher of Aquinas and a massive authority in science and philosophy.</note>, who I believe carries weight with you, denies that good and evil are contraries to each other; and you say Blessed Thomas feels the same in the first question of *On Evil*. But you do not respond to how **Boethius** <note>Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a Roman philosopher whose translations of Aristotle were the foundation of medieval logic.</note> either spoke the truth or lied when he says in the *Categories* that good and evil are contraries to each other—not in the way that white and black or hot and cold are (which are all truly qualities), but in the way that healthy and sick, strong and weak, rare and dense, beautiful and ugly, and many similar things are. Nor does Blessed Thomas deny this; but that most eminent man...

...as we did in the first question concerning evil, regarding the solution of the second argument, it shows how good and evil, even if they oppose each other by the opposition of privation and habit <note>In Scholastic logic, "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present (like blindness), while "habit" (habitus) is the presence of that quality (like sight).</note>, are nevertheless usually counted among contraries. ### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ANTONIO OF FAENZA, GREETINGS.

<margin>He lightly censures Antonio</margin>
**A**lthough my prior letter was far too brief or certainly more obscure in solving your questions regarding that booklet I recently published *On Being and the One*, you doubt the same questions and the same points in these letters. Indeed, I will not deny that in the first letters certain things were omitted to which no answer was given, lest I waste words on trivial matters; some things were treated briefly by me because I believed they should be judged by a man of philosophy rather than fully explained. Now, since you demand this of me, we shall pursue even every tiny detail, and through each chapter of your questions, I will bid you remember those things we wrote previously; I will stir you up where necessary toward a deeper understanding of them. Furthermore, since you have not yet touched upon either the Platonic commentaries or the Greek **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophy, so named because Aristotle was said to teach while walking (peripatōn).</term> due to an ignorance of the Greek language, I shall lead you through the lines and decrees of the Latins, especially Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, whose synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy and Christian theology was the standard for Latin "Scholastic" thinkers.</note>, who is more familiar to you for the purpose of grasping the meanings of those things discussed in my book. But as to what affects you first: by what reasoning do the Platonists place God above **Being**? For if God truly *is*, you say, He surely truly and properly *is* Being, and is so called; just as someone sitting is truly said to be "sitting" because he sits. You add: insofar as He is an "Idea," He is Being; much more so, insofar as He is God, will it be that He is and is called Being. Even if not all Platonists concede that the Idea and God are the same, you say it is enough to oppose me if even a single person like **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century statesman and philosopher who wrote influential paraphrases of Aristotle.</note> did not say what I have ascribed to the Platonists in common. You likewise cannot understand how I can say God is called "the One," since by this I have signified not *what* He is, but *how* He is the being which He is. For if He is "the One" in the sense that He is uniquely all things, why should He not also be called "Being," since He is all things with the One? For He is not called "One" because He is only one. Therefore, He could likewise be called "Being," even if He is not the only being. These are the first things from which you cannot extricate yourself; but in a few words, and just as I promised, I will remove every pebble of doubt from you using even those things known to you. You know that in Thomas's view, the **Essence** of a thing is one thing,

<margin>He reviews those things about which he doubts again</margin>
and **Existence** <note>original: "existētiā"</note> is another. The existence of a thing is that by which a thing *is*—that is, it exists; the essence is that by which a thing attains a certain species, whether of a horse, or a stone, or a shrub. Therefore, what is called "Essence" is also called **Quiddity** <term>Quiddity: from the Latin "quid" (what); the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</term> by the younger thinkers, because from the notion of essence, we know *what* a thing is. Since, therefore, as Aristotle teaches in the second book of the *Posterior Analytics*, one question is asked when we inquire whether, for example, a rose *exists*, and another when we wish to know *what* a rose is. The first belongs to

<margin>How Essence and Existence are understood in Thomas</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Something through itself</margin>
the existence of the thing. The second to the essence, or, to use the words of the more recent thinkers, to the "quiddity." Again, remember that according to the opinion of Thomas, all things below God which exist in act are composed of essence and *esse* (for so he calls existence); but God Himself is not composed of essence and existence, nor again is He an essence, but He is pure existence itself, from which thereafter all other things [derive]...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's response to the objections raised by Antonio Cittadini regarding the relationship between "Being" (Ens) and "the One" (Unum). Pico is specifically addressing the distinction between existence (that a thing is) and essence (what a thing is), using the authority of Thomas Aquinas and the Platonists to support his claim that God transcends the category of "Being."</meta>

# ->ON BEING AND THE ONE<-
## ii

<margin>Third, Thomas</margin>
...derives the existence of created things: namely, as it is communicated to created essences. Add to this that by this word **being** <term>ens: a philosophical term for "that which exists" or a thing's substance</term> essence is mostly indicated; however, by this word **is** existence is indicated, not essence. <note>Pico is making a technical distinction: "Being" refers to *what* something is (its nature), while "is" refers to the fact *that* it exists.</note> This is exactly what Thomas teaches you in the first question of *On Evil* <note>Referring to *De Malo* by Thomas Aquinas.</note>: where he says: when we say this or that is a **being**, the question of *what the thing is* is answered (for this question, as we said above, looks to the essence of the thing); but when we say "this is" or "is not," we satisfy the question of *whether the thing is*: which, as we were saying, pertains to existence. Now, I believe the opinion of the Platonists and the solution to your objection is open to you. 

<margin>
Solution of the argument according to the opinion of Thomas. Thomas.
</margin>
For if God is existence, but not essence, just as we truly say that God **is**, so we truly deny that God is **being**. Nor can I help but wonder that, even if you have not read the Platonic works, you still insist so frequently on this argument in your reading of Thomas: "God is, therefore He is being": when Thomas himself says, word for word, that "to be" and "to be being" do not follow each other mutually, but pertain to entirely different and unrelated questions. However, what need is there here for the authority of Thomas? Who but a fool doubts *whether God is*? Who, on the other hand, but a fool presumes to know even in the smallest part *what God is*? Since knowing *whether* God is and knowing *what* God is are the most diverse things, the statements will also be most diverse: that which says "God is" from that which says "God is being": since the former asserts that God exists—than which nothing is more certain—while the latter would dare to pronounce some part of what God is—than which nothing is more uncertain.

<margin>
Note. Poliziano; Simonides the poet.
</margin>
For this reason, when you were asking during our dispute what God might be, our most learned friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a famous humanist scholar and Pico's close friend.</note> answered you most correctly by citing the opinion of the poet Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BC). When asked by King Hiero to define God, he kept asking for more time, eventually saying the longer he thought, the more obscure the answer became.</note>: that he grew old trying to discover what He was. Yet the example you bring forward about "sitting" is far removed from this purpose: for "to be sitting" and "to sit" do not vary in the same way as these two: "to be" and "being." 

<margin>
Solution of the confirmation: he shows the example does not hold.
</margin>
For I answer the same question when I say "Socrates sits" as when I say "he is sitting"—namely, whichever question asks me about Socrates's posture. Just as when we say "Socrates is white" and "Socrates is pale," the same question is satisfied: namely, that which asks *of what sort* Socrates is. But the same logic does not apply between "being" and "is": one of which, to hammer home the same point, manifests *what* a thing is, and the other *whether* it is to those who ask. From this it is also clear:

<margin>
Solution of another Platonic argument.
</margin>
...if God is called "being" as an "Idea," it does not follow that insofar as He is conceived as absolute in Himself, He should have the name of "being." For just as He takes on the role of an Idea, so too He takes on the role of an Essence; but as He is understood above all essence and relationship to created things, He is greater than the name of "being." For that He is not called "being" is not due to a deficiency, as you believe, but due to His eminence <note>original: "eminentiae" — God is "above" being, not "less" than being.</note>. Therefore, He is pronounced by the Platonists to be "above being" rather than "not being."

<margin>
That Themistius is not a Platonist but a Peripatetic. Hermolaus.
</margin>
I truly do not know why you so obstinately strive to count Themistius <note>Themistius (c. 317–388 AD), a statesman and philosopher who wrote commentaries on Aristotle.</note> among them. If you ask the ancients, they will all reply that Themistius is a Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle.</note>, not a Platonist. If you ask the man himself, I think he would call himself a paraphraser and follower of Aristotle, not of Plato. But perhaps (allow me to joke) you drag him into the Academy <note>The school of Plato.</note> even against his will so that you do not seem entirely ignorant of Platonic and Greek matters, since you have at least read Themistius through the benefit of our friend Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), who translated Themistius into Latin.</note> having made him Latin. But let Themistius be a Platonist. Let it also be entirely true—we have already declared abundantly enough in both this and the previous letter that nothing he says contradicts our opinion, because the Platonists will say one thing about God as He is God, and another as He is an Idea.

<margin>
Solution of another argument.
</margin>
Let us come to why God is called "the One," even though He is not called "being." Recall to your memory what we wrote to you in our first letters. When the Platonists call God "the One," they are not stating *what* He is, but *how* He is that which He is. But you do not quite understand this. I will say it more aptly. If you ask a man of the Academy what God is, he will reply not only that he cannot answer you, but that you have no right to ask: that this is an unworthy question about Him. For He who is above all essence and above all that can be understood, can only be asserted by him to be most similar to "Unity." For just as this [Unity] is the principle of numbers, so He is the ruler of all things that are. Just as Unity embraces all numbers, both even and odd, while being itself neither even nor odd in its individual simplicity, so He...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense against Antonio Cittadini. Having previously argued that God transcends the category of "Being" (Ens), Pico now addresses specific objections regarding whether God belongs to a "genus" (a logical category) and how "the One" relates to truth and falsehood.</meta>

# ->OBJECTIONS. BOOK TWO<-

...encloses and contains all things in His impartible <note>original: "impartibili" — meaning something that cannot be divided into parts.</note> infinity. Do you not see what is being said? That by the name of **the one**, it is not indicated *what* God is, but rather the *manner* in which He is that which He is. Finally, if we say: "God is like unity," we are expressing what we mean when we give Him the name of **the one**. We will certainly be truthful; however, if we were to say to our listeners: "God is like being," we would surely move them to laughter. But why should I apply more arguments to you? For he <note>Likely referring to a source like Dionysius or Thomas Aquinas.</note> says these things are enough, or I know not what words could ever be enough.

<margin>Why God is under no genus.</margin>
It is also gathered from here why God is under no genus <term>genus: a general category or class in logic, such as "animal" or "substance"</term>. For the genera of things are their essences; but God is neither an essence nor does He have an essence. For this reason, since **being** <term>ens: a philosophical term for "that which exists"</term> is sometimes understood by the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> as encompassing only the ten genera, it is manifest that under the name of **being**—which even the followers of Aristotle sometimes use—God is not contained. But you insist that by Thomas [Aquinas] and others from the same family <note>The Dominican Order, whose members followed the teachings of Thomas Aquinas.</note>, both **substance** and **being** are often used in such a way that God is called both a substance and a being. As if I were ignorant of this, which no one fails to know! Or as if it were not enough for me that they occasionally do otherwise; I have said that they were accustomed to using this expression in that way not always, but only sometimes.

<margin>Solution to another objection, namely the third principal one.</margin>
Let us move on to those things which you object regarding the opposition of **the one** and the **divided**. Here, I think, you are playing with me and testing me with childish quibbles. For you say, "if the false is surely divided, then a 'falsehood that is false' is not false." For a falsehood is not divided from itself, because a falsehood is a falsehood. Likewise, you say that the dead do not fight among themselves, for those who are dead are already dead. Furthermore, Antonio <note>Antonio Cittadini, the scholar to whom Pico is writing.</note>, when I said that things which are false "fight with themselves," I admit that if this "fight" must be with fists or even with a weapon, then the dead do not fight among themselves, nor are they false. And just as a falsehood is a falsehood, so for a "falsehood to be a falsehood" is not false, but true; therefore, it is not divided, but **one**.

<margin>Solution to another.</margin>
You add that it is falsely said by me that a falsehood "encloses a contradiction." This is because there are many false things which, either by the power of nature or of man, could be true. But consider this: everything that is false, for as long as it is false, encloses a contradiction. But just as some things are false in such a way that they *could* become true, others are false in such a way that they can *never* be true. So there are some things so contradictory and "fighting with themselves" that they can never return to friendship and concord. Some things hate each other in such a way that they can, nevertheless, return to favor.

<margin>Example</margin>
This will be manifest by an example: to say "a human is a lion" is always false, because it always encloses a contradiction; and just as it can never be brought to union, so it can never be brought to truth. But "that I am sitting" is neither true nor false <note>Pico means this as a neutral proposition until the action occurs.</note>. If, however, you add that I am sitting while I am standing, you immediately introduce falsehood. In that case, you also bring in a contradiction. For "that I am sitting while I am standing" includes a contradiction; and as soon as it ceases to be false—as when I actually begin to sit—it immediately returns from division to unity.

<margin>Solution to another.</margin>
Furthermore, those things which you object regarding the opposition of the false and the true have already been resolved in my earlier letter. For you say: "If it is true that what is seen, is; and false that what is seen, is not—since there is no contradiction between 'seeming to be what is' and 'seeming to be what is not'—then the false will not be the negation of the true." I, however, do not accept the definition of the false as merely "seeming to be something that is not." Rather, I want its definition to be this: that it **is not** that which it is said to be. For "false gold" is false because it is not gold; and as far as the definition of the false is concerned, it happens to it either to "seem to be" or "to be" something other than gold.

<margin>Solution to another</margin>
As for your claim that I have not solved your argument by which you prove that **good** and **evil** are contraries, I will speak frankly. I did not think a solution was needed where there was no knot. Your argument is of this kind: "Good is to be sought, but evil is to be fled. Seeking and fleeing are contrary motions. Therefore, good and evil are contraries."

<margin>Note.</margin>
To me, indeed, this reasoning of yours seems so effective and of such great strength that it proves not only that good and evil (about which someone might perhaps doubt) but even **being** and **non-being** (which everyone knows are contradictories) are contraries. For we would conclude thus: "Being is to be sought, non-being is to be fled. Seeking and fleeing are contrary motions. Therefore, being and non-being are con—"

He mocks his opponent's syllogisms, showing that if they were valid, they would lead to the logical absurdity of "Being" and "Non-Being" being simple contraries.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic rebuttal of his critic, focusing on the metaphysical nature of "Good" and "Evil." In the previous pages, Pico argued that God is beyond "Being"; here, he addresses whether Evil can be considered a real, existing opposite to Good.</meta>

# DE ENTE ET VNO
# ON BEING AND THE ONE

3 i

<margin>Solution of the other. Aristotle.</margin>
...contraries. Therefore, either you must grant me that "being" and "non-being" are contraries, or I will not grant you that good and evil are contraries? But, you will say, another reasoning must be resolved. For "non-being" is not a genus <term>genus: a general category or class in logic</term>; how then is evil "nothing," when Aristotle says in the *Categories* <note>original: "praedicamentis" — one of Aristotle's logical works</note> that good and evil are the "genera of contraries"? All the interpreters of Aristotle are full of solutions to this question, to whom I directed you in my previous letter, so that I would not involve myself and you in superfluous labor.

<margin>Simplicius</margin>
To pass over what Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> does not dislike: that Aristotle spoke there in the manner of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who organized the universe into pairs of opposites.</note>, who establish two orders of things, one contained under the good, the other under the evil. He [Aristotle] often, in logical discussions, uses examples from the opinions of others rather than from his own. I reply with what you could also read in Simplicius: that good and evil are called "genera of contraries" because one side of the contraries has the nature of evil and deficiency—as black is compared to white, or bitter to sweet. In this way, all contraries are reduced to good and evil: insofar as every defect has the nature of evil. On this account, even in the first book of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle's work on the principles of nature.</note>, it is said that contraries are always compared according to the respective nature of the "better" and the "worse."

<margin>Porphyrius</margin>
I pass over the many other solutions of Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> and even more recent authors.

<margin>Thomas</margin>
But I cannot wonder enough that you say Thomas [Aquinas] also descends into this opinion: that good and evil oppose each other by "contrary opposition." You add that he confirms this very point by the authority of Simplicius. Yet, your entire first question concerning evil opposes this opinion of yours with all its might. For what else does that dispute primarily aim to do than to prove that **evil is nothing**? Now, if evil is nothing, it cannot be a contrary to the good, since the nature of each of the contraries is *something*. And this is precisely what Thomas confirms to you by the authority of Simplicius. See how far you wander! You believe an opinion is confirmed by the testimony of Simplicius which he himself weakens by the testimony of Simplicius. Perhaps you would not have fallen into this error if you had at some point read Simplicius's book itself, in which no mention is ever made of the contrary opposition of good and evil. If you should object to me the cases of ophthalmia <note>An inflammation of the eye.</note> and sickness, in which Thomas seems to recognize contrariety, I will bid you to look more closely into his words. For he does not say these *are* contraries, but that since they are privations <term>privation: the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, such as blindness being the absence of sight</term>, they are nevertheless sometimes *called* contraries.

<margin>Note.</term>
If you attend to why he wishes this to be done, you will see that evil itself is entirely ignorant of the property of a "contrary." For he allows that these things can in some way obtain the name of "contrary" only insofar as they do not possess the full nature of evil, but retain something of the goodness they have not yet lost. Therefore, they are in some way contraries only insofar as they are not entirely evil. But if I were to set death or blindness against you, and I were to ask whether these are "true evils" according to the opinion of Thomas, and again whether they oppose one another by that "species of contrariety" you speak of, I do not see at all what you would answer. For if these are evils—and in that very place where you bring forward testimony from Thomas for your side—he would contend with great assertion that these can in no way be contraries by that very species of contrariety you bring into the middle. With what mind, then, do you affirm that according to Thomas’s opinion, good opposes evil by some opposition of contrariety? Certainly, you ought to have considered this: that what is granted concerning certain *imperfect* evils, because of the mixture of goodness they still retain, must not be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself.

OBJECTIONS, BOOK TWO

# ANTONIO OF FAENZA SENDS GREETINGS TO GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA.

<margin>
Do not doubt, dear friend <note>original: "compater" — literally "godfather," a term used between close associates or colleagues</note>, I have not forgotten. I remember everything clearly: you will plainly see it, even if it is no great loss if the things we discussed in person should slip away. For all these matters with which you occupy yourself—and with which you keep me, a man not at leisure, occupied—are very light. But lest you think I am imitating Nicoletto <note>Nicoletto Vernia (c. 1420–1499), a prominent Aristotelian philosopher at Padua who had a public dispute with Pico</note>, who did not deign to reply at all to you when you wrote against him, I will briefly note the solutions to your doubts. God is: I said it is truly said "God is." Likewise, according to the opinion of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who argued God is beyond all names</note>, God is greater than every name, even this name "God," as he writes in the book *On Mystical Theology*. You have not yet moved Dionysius from his position with your strikes. And it is no wonder, for he stands far stronger than you, even though you might despise his authority while I was using it against you. I also said that by those who deny God is "being," it is sometimes conceded that God is "One"; I declared the reasoning for their opinion both in my own commentaries on *Being and the One* and in two letters to you. But you might say: I said in the last letter that there is no one who does not know that among Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> and other Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, both "being" and "essence" are so often accepted that both are said of God. But it is enough for me that sometimes one uses "being" and "essence" in such a way that they cannot be said of God; that is...
</margin>

The conclusions once granted in speech—unless perhaps you have forgotten—were: God is; God is one; "God is not God" <note>This refers to the law of non-contradiction; Faventinus is arguing that denying God's existence while speaking of Him is a logical impossibility</note> involves a contradiction. For God to be—that is, to be the first being <term>being: *ens* in Latin; the most basic category of existence</term>—and yet not to be, and to be increased—against these I formed several objections and gave them in writing. I was expecting you to finally answer these objections, since you have been silent for four months, perhaps entangled in greater business. 

But you respond only to the first ones, which I had previously formed against the solutions of certain arguments. You speak first in this way: "I will show you through the decrees of the Latins, and especially of the blessed Thomas, that although God truly and properly *is*, He is not, however, properly *being*." For you say that according to Thomas, God is not an "essence" <term>essence: *essentia*; the "whatness" or definition of a thing</term>. Likewise, according to the same Thomas: the word "being" usually signifies essence and answers the question "What is it?" <note>original: "quid est"</note>; but the word itself, "to be" <note>original: "esse"</note>, is usually returned to the question "Is it?" <note>original: "an est"</note>. Therefore, you conclude that according to Thomas, God is not "being" if He neither "is" <note>in the sense of common being</note> nor has an "essence," but merely exists.

But tell me, I ask, where in Thomas did you learn that God is not an essence? For the whole of Thomas cries out against this opinion. In the first part of the *Summa*, in the *Against the Gentiles*, in the *Disputed Questions*, in the booklet *On Being and Essence*, in the commentaries on Aristotle—in all places, finally, where the matter requires it—he holds and proves that God *is* essence. Nor is there any need to cite the words of the man in so clear a matter; if you deny it, I will recount more than is necessary. 

Furthermore, in your own booklet *On Being and the One*, unless it has slipped your mind, you previously said: the reason God is not "being" according to the Platonists is that God’s "to be" is nothing other than His essence. How then do you now, following the same men and defending them, deny that God is essence? 

Likewise, tell me: from what place in Saint Thomas did you gather that the word "being" usually signifies essence and not also "to be"? Since in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* and the first question of *On Truth* and elsewhere, he says that a thing is called "being" (*ens*) because it *is* (*est*), but a "thing" (*res*) because it is an essence or has an essence. 

Likewise, tell me: where in Thomas could you have learned that to the question "What is it?" one may reasonably answer "It is being"? For it is foolish to ask "What is it?" unless one knows the thing exists, as Aristotle in the second book of the *Posterior Analytics* and Thomas aptly testify. But I understand "to be" <note>original: "esse"</note> just as substances and accidents exist, in which there is both essence—not as privations <term>privation: the absence of a quality that should be present, like blindness</term> and negations exist, in which Thomas seems to deny that which is usually answered to the question "What is it?" can be found, whether that be true or false, which is omitted for the present. 

The words of Thomas in the first question of *On Evil*, which if I am not mistaken provided you the occasion for error, and which you also seem to invoke, are these: "Being is spoken of in two ways: in one way according to what signifies the nature of the ten categories <note>Aristotle's classification of all things that exist</note>; and thus..." which you should not reject. Nor will you ever bring more to this matter than is necessary. Furthermore, in your booklet, there is a crude objection: for the Platonists, when they say this, do not mean there is essence and "to be" in God, but that in Him they do not differ. But "to be" holds that place in God which essence holds in other things, so that for Him, there is nothing else for an essence than "to be" itself.

Likewise, tell me: read your earlier letters and you will see. For it is a foolish, or rather a most tasteless argument, since it is one thing for a thing "to be" (that is, to exist) and another to be "being" (insofar as "being" is an essential predicate). Even if it were true, you would have to admit it is true unless you disregard the words of Thomas. These are the things which, if you had seen them earlier, perhaps you would not have erred.

<meta>This page continues the debate between Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and his critic, Antonio of Faenza. Having previously discussed the nature of God and the authorities of Dionysius the Areopagite, Antonio now turns to a rigorous analysis of how Thomas Aquinas defines "Being" and "Something." He challenges Pico’s claim that God cannot be called "Being" by distinguishing between different ways the term is used in Scholastic philosophy.</meta>

->iiii 1<-

# ON BEING AND THE ONE

<margin>
It is demonstrated. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the Dominican theologian whose works were central to these late 15th-century debates</note>. I wonder that you always dwell on these same points. Has it not been said a thousand times that "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> can be understood such that it is predicated of it: namely, when it signifies *that it exists* <note>original: "quod est"</note>; but again it can be understood such that it is not predicated: namely, when it signifies *essence* <note>original: "essentiam"</note>, which is distinct from existence.
</margin>

Evil and other privations <note>term: "privation" — the absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness in an eye</note> are not "being," nor are they "something." In another way, according to that which answers the question *is it?* <note>original: "an est"</note>; and in this way evil is, just as blindness is; however, evil is not "something" <note>original: "aliquid"</note>, because to be "something" signifies not only what responds to the question *is it?* but also what responds to the question *what is it?* <note>original: "quid est"</note>. But I pray you, repeat more carefully the words of such a great philosopher; for they bear judgment against you, which is demonstrated thus. Thomas clearly says that "being" and "something" are said in two ways. One way is that which has the nature of some category <note>term: "category" (genus) refers to the ten Aristotelian classifications of reality, such as substance, quality, or quantity</note>. In another way, that which answers the question *is it?*. Now, the question *is there a God?* is answered, nor is the response a lie; therefore God is "being." If we must proceed further, let us say this, departing not at all from Thomas: what is rightly answered to the question *is it?* is "being"; therefore, what is answered truly and properly to the question of whether a thing truly and properly exists, is truly and properly "being." For as "God simply is" relates to that which truly and properly is: to one asking whether [God] truly and properly is, the answer "God" is reasonably given; therefore, God is truly and properly "being."

<margin>
"Something" and "being": See how you are deceived. According to Thomas, evil is not such that to one asking *what* God is, we can respond "something" or "being"; and yet to one asking "what is sin?", we can answer: "it is evil." Furthermore, will you dare [to deny this]? When "Being" is converted with "the Good" <note>term: "convertibility of transcendentals" — the medieval philosophical doctrine that Being, Goodness, and Unity are co-extensive and refer to the same reality under different aspects</note> in Thomas, it is not taken in the same way as when he denies it is located in God. You joke against yourself; for this is exactly what I am saying: and either you do not wish to understand it, though it has been repeated a hundred times, or you cannot. In the first way, God is not "being," although in the second way—namely, so that "being" answers the question *is it?*—he is called "being." For I was saying that not in every way, but in some way even in Thomas, God cannot be called "being"; but it is permitted to argue thus, colleague <note>original: "compater" — a term of endearment or professional respect</note>: God is not "being" in the first sense, therefore in some sense he is not "being." *Constrained:* These are your constraints, not Thomas's. *Ridiculous:* What is not asked ridiculously, he does not solve ridiculously; although many things are asked ridiculously, which are solved ridiculously: namely, when they are solved lest they seem unsolved because they cannot be solved.
</margin>

Furthermore, Thomas calls "something" and "being" according to the first way that which answers the question *what is it?*; but to one asking "what is it that preserves and moves the world?" and "what raises the dead?", "God" is reasonably answered; therefore, in both the first and second ways, God is "being" and "something." Furthermore, will you dare, according to Thomas, to deny that God is "good" or "one"? Since, therefore, "good," "being," and "one" are mutually convertible, how can it be said or touched upon according to Thomas that God is not "being"? But you, unless I am mistaken, seem to argue from these words in this way: "being" is said in one way as signifying the nature of the ten categories; but God is in no category, as Thomas himself testifies. Therefore, God is neither "being" nor "essence." But you ought to have noticed (permit me to joke) that if the reasoning is effective that God is not "being" in the first way: for although he is in no category, nothing prevents him from truly and properly existing in the nature of things, and the question *is it?* being answered truthfully. How then could it be unknown that he is "being" in another way? Furthermore, the reasoning has no strength. For the sense of Thomas’s words is this: "being" is said in one way as signifying the nature of the ten categories; that is, it signifies substance and accident, and all positive things entirely which are contained in the ten categories: either through themselves, like species and genera, or as certain principles, whether constrained or not, like prime matter and fortune in the category of substance; and God and all substantial differences. In which way, certainly, negations and privations cannot belong to the category. In another way, "being" is said as that which can be answered to the question *is it?*, whether it be a true and positive being or not; wherefore adding an example, he says: "and thus evil is, just as blindness is"; that is: "and thus evil is being, just as blindness is being"; for in Thomas there is no difference in words whether it is said "is" or "is being."

<margin>
To one asking, therefore, whether the moon is "being," it will be rightly answered that it is "being." But to one asking further "what sort of being is it?", it is certainly ridiculous to answer "it is being."
</margin>

What he adds indeed, that "to be something" does not only signify etc., does not tend toward the meaning that to one asking "what is the moon?" or "what is thunder?" it is reasonably answered if it is said "it is being" or "something," as you seem to have thought. For such a solution is ridiculous. But it is of this sort: "to be something" signifies, especially according to the first way, that which can reasonably be answered to the question *what is it?*; for example, it signifies that it is a substance, or an accident, or an animal, or a color, or something

<summary>Antonio of Faenza defends the Thomistic view that God can be called "Being," arguing that Pico confuses the definition of Being as a category of nature with Being as a response to the fact of existence. He asserts that since God truly exists, God must be considered "Being" and "Something" in the highest sense.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical debate between Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and his opponent (Antonio of Faenza) regarding the interpretation of Thomas Aquinas and the nature of God as "Being" or "The One." They are specifically dissecting the definitions of existence used in the Scholastic and Platonic traditions.</meta>

<header>OBJECTIONS: BOOK TWO</header>

<margin>
To be something: You say nothing. For who does not know that it is not "something" because it is neither substance nor accident? He says: These same points are those made in the first question about evil, and they favor me just as those did.
</margin>
...or something of this sort: which could be rightly answered to someone asking "what is it?" Blindness and evil, however, are none of these. But <term>Thomas Aquinas</term> <note>original: "B. Tho."</note> himself explains in the First Part, Question 48, Article 2—where it is asked whether evil exists in things—that he does not wish for the first part of the division to be interpreted in that way. For responding to the second argument, he says: "As it is said in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, 'Being' <note>original: "Ens"</note> is spoken of in two ways. In one way, according to what signifies the entity of a thing as it is divided into the <term>ten categories</term> <note>Aristotle’s classification of everything that exists, such as substance, quality, and quantity</note>; and in this way, 'being' is interchangeable with 'thing.' In this sense, no <term>privation</term> <note>The absence of a quality that should naturally be present</note> is a 'being,' and thus neither is evil. In another way, 'being' is spoken of as that which signifies the truth of a proposition, which consists in composition, the sign of which is the word 'is'; and this is the 'being' that answers the question 'does it exist?' <note>original: "an est"</note>. In this way, we say blindness 'is' in the eye, or any other privation; and in this way, even evil is called 'being.'" Thus says <term>Thomas</term>.

<margin>
A real thing: In that way, God is both spoken of and denied to be a "thing," just as He is with "being."
</margin>
Do you not see, then, how he declares the first part of the division to be interchangeable with "thing"? Truly, he does not deny that God is a "thing," nor whatever else is good; for by that argument and by the first question on evil, he confesses that every good is a "thing."

<margin>
Because if: I have shown just now that they are not true; therefore, the reasoning is dissolved.
</margin>
Because if these things are true, the argument I stated against the <term>Platonists</term> has not yet been refuted: "being" is named for that which "is," just as "a seated person" is named for "one who sits." God, however, not only "is," but He "is" properly and truly; therefore, He is "being" truly and properly.

<margin>
But from Thomas: But you, holding the words of Thomas and explaining them above, have fallen into our opinion when you said God is called "being" insofar as He answers the question "does He exist?" through "being," but not insofar as He signifies the essence of things.
</margin>
For in this way, you wished to solve the argument not from the Platonists, but from <term>Thomas</term>, attributing things to Thomas that anyone who has read Thomas would know are utterly foreign to the man’s thought.

<margin>
Not to attribute those things to Thomas; false things about Thomas because I do not imitate you, my dear colleague, who say that according to the opinion of Thomas, good and evil are properly and truly contraries, and that this is even confirmed by the authority of <term>Simplicius</term> <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note>. Regarding this, when I showed that not a single word of this is in Simplicius, you respond that you inferred it was said by Simplicius. But the book is in our hands, colleague. Simplicius does not say it; therefore, you have inferred it poorly.
</margin>
Hence, that other argument of mine has not been refuted: if God is "being" by that part which is the "Idea," much more is He "being" by that part which is "God." For the latter is something absolute, while the former is relative. For it is not true, as you just responded, that God is essence by that part which is the "Idea" but not by that part which is "God."

<margin>
Now indeed demonstrated: It has also been demonstrated that you have not demonstrated well.
</margin>
For it has now been shown that He is both "being" and "essence." Furthermore, if God is "being" and "essence" by that part which is the "Idea," it is necessary for there to be <term>composition</term> <note>The state of being made of different parts or aspects, which contradicts the idea of God’s absolute simplicity</note> in God, which is easily proved in this way: for you said previously that according to the Platonists, God is not "being" because the existence of God is not distinct from God.

<margin>
For previously: God and the Idea are the same. Nor is the being of the Idea different from the being of God; but because their rational definitions are different, some things are pronounced of God as He is God, and others as He is the Idea.
</margin>
If, therefore, the Idea is "being," this will be because the being of the Idea is something other than the Idea itself. However, the being of the Idea cannot be located or imagined outside of God; if, as has been granted, God is the Idea, then it is necessary that there be composition in God.

<margin>
Composition: This composition is according to reason, not according to the reality of the thing.
</margin>
You say, furthermore, that God is called "The One" <note>original: "unum"</note> by the Platonists because He is similar to Unity; which, although it contains all numbers in its power (namely even and odd), is itself neither even nor odd.

<margin>
Subtle: So subtle that you now surely could not understand it even if repeated; as will soon be clear from how you present your knowledge to us.
</margin>
By Hercules, what a subtle reason for naming! Aside from the fact that God cannot be "similar" to things—as <term>Cicero</term> says, and <term>Thomas</term> too—for the pattern of the world is not similar to the world, nor is a man similar to a painting of him; no other cause can stand. For that which takes a name from another due to similarity or <term>analogy</term> is usually called by the proper name of that same thing: for we call a statue "a man" based on the man it imitates, not "human-like." Or because there is a difference in the types of propositions, or because of an analogy of natural place, we do not call a place "local."

<margin>
Not possible: I do not wish to speak with you except within defined limits. But you should know this kind of speech is often used by excellent and sacred authors, such as that regarding the likeness of <term>Melchizedek</term> <note>A biblical priest-king; the author is likely referring to the "likeness" between him and Christ mentioned in the Book of Hebrews</note>.
</margin>
Therefore, if God received His name from Unity because of similarity, He should not be called "One," but rather "Unity" itself. Furthermore, if every concrete name signifies one thing and another, why do the Platonists not call God "Likeness" rather than "Like"?

-># ON BEING AND THE ONE<-

<margin>Furthermore if: The "One" that the Platonists predicate of God is not denominative <note>A term derived from a noun, such as "brave" from "bravery."</note> but substantive: this is because you are entirely ignorant of Platonic thought and cannot understand the Greek language. See then how subtle this method of naming is.</margin>
Furthermore, if matter, according to the Platonists, is "one" as you write, and the unity of matter is not one thing and matter itself another—which I do not think can be abstractly denied—by what reasoning can its unity be defended? For it is not similar to Unity itself; otherwise, it would also be similar to God.

<margin>Furthermore: It is clear from this how matter is called "one" in one sense, and God is called "one" in another.</margin>
Furthermore, you previously said that God is "one" because he is all things uniquely. But now you seem to approve of the reasoning of the Platonists and rather that of <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose works were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>, perhaps casting aside your earlier view. If you still hold it, it remains for you to respond to the arguments that have been written. For the "root" you lean on to solve my objections—namely, that God is neither being nor essence—is not true, as I have already nearly demonstrated.

<margin>Of the Platonists: How can you say I follow the reasoning of the Platonists rather than Dionysius, when you boast with a loud voice that you have never even read the Platonists or Dionysius? But you should know that among the Platonists, unity is the type of God, and according to Dionysius, God is uniquely all things.</margin>
But let us now come to the definition of "the true" provided by you. You said in your earlier booklet that "the true" is defined by <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential 4th-5th century theologian.</note> in this way: *the true is that which is*. And lest the definition of "the true" and "being" appear the same, you say it must be added in this way: *the true is that which is what it says*. I therefore opposed this definition in this way: "being what it says" seems to signify nothing other than "being that which it is named." For a thing to be called by this name or that is simply for it to appear as this or that. Therefore, it finally seemed to be concluded that "being what it says" is nothing other than "being what it appears to be." Since there is no contradiction in appearing to be what one is and appearing to be what one is not, I therefore proved that "the false" is not simply the negation of "the true," if the definition held firm.

<margin>The root you lean on: See how firm that root is—one that you can neither conquer with any strength nor tear up with hard iron.</margin>
But since you have now explained your definition more clearly, many more points occur to me that seem to disprove your formal definition. For you say "the true" is that which says [what it is]. That is, the true is that which is what it itself is: for example, gold is "true gold" because it is gold. But on the contrary, if God did not exist and gold still existed, gold would be what it itself is, and it would be "true," yet it would not exist—because it would correspond to no <term>Idea</term> <note>In this context, the perfect archetypes or "blueprints" of things existing in the mind of God.</note>.

<margin>I therefore: All these points were satisfied in the previous letters.</margin>
For later you say that things are "true" because they correspond and answer to the Ideas. If the true definition of a human is a "rational animal," it is a contradiction to think that if God did not exist and a human were a rational animal, that human would not be a human. Nor can that be answered which was said elsewhere: namely, that it involves a contradiction for God not to exist and gold to exist. For there is no contradiction here, as theologians themselves and philosophers and logicians openly confess. For one can imagine gold existing while God does not—neither the first cause of all nor the first being. For those who judge that there are infinite worlds, or that the heavens are infinitely multiple, or other things of this sort, do not because of that deny that gold is what is seen with the eyes and handled with the hands.

<margin>This is true: You love gold too much, my friend <note>original: "compater," a term of familiar address.</note>, to attribute so much to it that it is believed it can exist even if God does not.</margin>
<margin>They judge worlds: Those who say these things—and say that gold exists [without God]—say contradictory things and are ignorant of their own words.</margin>
<margin>If God did not exist: If God did not exist and gold existed, gold would be gold and gold would not be gold; for an impossibility gives birth to an impossibility.</margin>
Furthermore, whether there is a contradiction or not, the argument is not yet resolved. For I say this: If God did not exist and gold existed, gold would be gold, but it would not be "true." Therefore, "being what it itself is" is not the formal definition of "the true." Just as the definition of a human would not be formal if I said: "If God did not exist and a human were a rational animal, he would not on that account be a human." For nothing can be deprived of its own definition, nor can a definition apply to anyone to whom the defined name cannot be fitted.

<margin>In the absolute: This is not an accidental relation distinct from the gold, but a substantial one, regarding which see <term>Henry of Ghent</term> <note>original: "Herichum Gandauensem," a 13th-century Scholastic philosopher known for his work on "intentional" existence.</note>...</margin>
Furthermore, you cannot deny that gold is, by nature, gold before it corresponds to God's Idea; for the absolute is prior to the relative. Gold, therefore, even if it is gold, cannot be "true" unless some likeness comes to the nature of gold by which it answers to its archetype—whether that likeness is something different from the gold or not (which is a separate question). Furthermore, you seem to put forward a definition of "being" in this way: "being is that which is." Otherwise, you would not say that Augustine's definition must be completed in this way: The True...

<meta>This page continues a philosophical dispute, likely directed at Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s "De Ente et Uno" (On Being and the One). The author of these objections is scrutinizing the definition of "Truth" and its relationship to "Being," specifically challenging the notion that something is "true" simply because it is identical to itself.</meta>

-># OBJECTIONS: BOOK TWO<-

<margin>We have said the same things: Everything that exists is exactly what it is. For this reason, every being is true, and every true thing is a being. However, the reasoning <note>original: "ratio" — here meaning the conceptual definition</note> for each is different.</margin>
...to fulfill. It is true that "truth" is that which is itself, lest we seem to have given the same definition for "truth" and for "being" by only saying "that which is." If, therefore, the definition of "being" is "that which is," by that same reasoning—insofar as a being is what it is—it is also itself a being. Therefore, by the same reasoning that something is a "being," it must also necessarily be "true." But this is utterly false. Furthermore, if "truth" is simply that which is itself, then blindness would be true, as would death, and falsity, and even non-existence. For blindness is blindness, death is death, falsity is falsity, and even non-being is non-being. Each of these would be "true" even if no intellect were thinking of them at all. But if any of these are true, they must necessarily be "one" <note>In Scholastic philosophy, Truth, Being, and Unity are "transcendental" properties that convert with one another.</note>. But I know what you will say next: "Did I not concede that each of these *is*, and is therefore true, in the words I wrote to you?" Just as "falsity is falsity," so the fact that falsity is falsity is not false, but true, because it is not divided, but one. But against this is the principle that everything that is "one" is "good," and in the same way, it is "true." Blindness, however, is not only evil, but according to your own writings, it is entirely evil and tastes of nothing good. The same applies to death. For you seem to call the nature of blindness and death a nature of absolute evil, unmixed with any good. Therefore, none of these things is "true," nor are they "one," especially when the soul is not thinking of them.

<margin>Regarding blindness: It is one thing for "blindness" to be true, and another for it to be "true that blindness is blindness." Therefore, you labor in vain with many words to show that blindness itself is not true.</margin>
Furthermore, "truth" is that which corresponds to an <term>Idea</term> <note>Referring to the Platonic or Augustinian "Ideas" in the mind of God which serve as the blueprints for reality.</note>, but blindness and death have no Idea. Furthermore, if God did not exist, nor anything else capable of intelligence, non-being would nonetheless be non-being, and nothing would be nothing. For it would be either something or nothing; certainly not "something," as is evident, therefore it would be "nothing" and "non-being." It would be that which it is now, and would be so then. If, therefore, "truth" is "that which is what it is," then non-being and "nothing" would be true—which is impossible. For it would correspond to no Idea. Therefore, the <term>formal definition</term> of truth is not simply "to be that which it is." You attempt, moreover, to defend what you said previously: that every false thing contains a contradiction. You say that everything false contains a contradiction as long as it is false. You add these words: "But for me to be sitting is neither true nor false. If, however, you add 'I am sitting' while I am standing, you immediately find a contradiction as well as a falsehood." For "me sitting while I stand" contains a contradiction; and that which is first defined as false, as soon as I begin to sit, returns from division back to unity.

<margin>Regarding "Indeed, true": For me to sit is always either true or false, because I am always either sitting or not sitting. As for the claim that "me sitting" is neither true nor false, this means that this proposition does not determine truth or falsity from its own nature, unlike <term>necessary propositions</term> <note>Statements that must be true by definition, like 2+2=4.</note>. But since it is possible for it to be true (namely, when I sit) and false (when I do not sit), it is of itself undetermined toward either. But without a doubt, my fellow-father <note>original: "compater" — a familiar or collegial address</note>, you have an abundance of paper and leisure to stoop to these things that are known even to schoolboys.</margin>
But I ask you to see if you are consistent with yourself. For you think that "true" and "false" are opposed, not indeed as contraries, but as affirmation and negation. How then can a "middle ground" be found, unless there is a middle between affirmation and negation? Furthermore, every <term>enunciation</term> <note>A logical statement or proposition.</note> is either true or false, unless you deny the first principle <note>The Law of Excluded Middle: for any proposition, either its positive or negative form is true.</note>, which is that in any contradiction, one part is true and the other is false. How then is "you sitting" neither true nor false? Indeed, I do not see by what reasoning you can maintain this unless you do away with all philosophy and every concept of opposites. Furthermore, if every falsehood contains a contradiction as long as it is false, then the statement "God does not exist" (which is false) would contain a contradiction as long as God exists in the nature of things. If, therefore, God did not exist, the statement "God does not exist" would be neither false nor a contradiction. If, then, "false" is the negation of "true" as you posit, it will be "true" that God does not exist if God were not to exist. But every "true" thing is "good," as you grant; therefore, if God did not exist, it would be a good thing...

He further debates the logical status of false propositions and the Law of Excluded Middle, mocking the opponent's "schoolboy" errors in logic.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a philosophical critique of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s "De Ente et Uno" (On Being and the One). The author is specifically attacking Pico's logic regarding the unity of truth and the nature of falsehood. There is visible bleed-through from the reverse page on the left margin and a catchword "Sed mirum" (But it is a wonder) at the bottom.</meta>

-># ON BEING AND THE ONE<-

<margin>
But the truth is: Good and evil are in things, while falsehood and truth are in the soul. Therefore, a true proposition can signify a bad thing, although the proposition itself—insofar as it is true—is to that extent good; and the thing itself, insofar as it is evil, is to that extent false. However, it is one thing to say, "it is true that Judas sins"; it is another to say, "Judas’s sin is true."
</margin>

<margin>
Furthermore, every: Every falsehood is divided, as we said in the previous booklet. But "being false" is not equally "being false"; therefore, "not being false" is not equally "divided," as we said in the letters to you. For those things which are necessarily false and always false are not equally false compared to those which are not necessarily false or always false. For this reason, neither the former nor the latter have the same quality of division. See if there is anything here that I ought to have said truly or that you can refute.
</margin>

...it would be that God does not exist, which seems absurd; for He would neither be simply good nor good to anyone, but entirely non-being. Furthermore, in your previous letter, you said that every falsehood is "divided" from itself for the reason that it contains a contradiction. If, therefore, not every falsehood simply and absolutely contains a contradiction, but only remains "divided" as long as it is false: to whatever the definition and cause of "being" does not apply, neither does that which follows from that definition. And if "the One" <note>In this philosophy, "the One," "Being," and "Truth" are considered interchangeable or "convertible" terms; to exist is to be one thing and to be true.</note> does not apply simply, neither does the other. Therefore, not every falsehood is simply divided—which is an impossible position—for every falsehood is simply and absolutely non-being. Indeed, both terms are rather interchangeable; by the same reasoning, therefore, it is simply "divided" if "divided" and "non-being" coincide. 

Furthermore, every truth is simply one; therefore every falsehood is simply divided. For one is the negation of the other. Furthermore, if I demonstrate that every falsehood is absolutely divided, what reason was there for you to not dare to state simply and absolutely that every falsehood is divided, but only when there is opposition? We demonstrate the "division" of falsehood in this manner: "Socrates is sitting" is false; but "Socrates sitting" is not "Socrates sitting," therefore it is divided from itself. For if "Socrates is sitting" is "Socrates is sitting" and "Socrates sitting" is "Socrates sitting"—since both are conjoined—then if "Socrates sitting" is indeed "Socrates," then by simple logical conversion, "Socrates is Socrates." Therefore, "sitting" is "sitting." Therefore, he sits—which is false! 

By the same reasoning, I will prove that a **chimera** <note>A mythological beast; in logic, it is used as the standard example of an impossible object that can be thought of but cannot exist.</note> is not a chimera, nor is "being a chimera" the same as "to be a chimera." For if a chimera exists, a chimera is an animal. For we understand a chimera to be an animal consisting of a goat and a servant <note>original: "seruo" — likely a transcription error for "serpente" (serpent), as a chimera is traditionally part snake.</note>, or something of this sort. But if it is an animal, it can live and die—which we do not agree upon, since we posit that a chimera can by no means be produced by nature, just as a **golden mountain** <note>Another classic example of a "non-being" that exists only in the imagination.</note> cannot be generated. 

Furthermore, if a chimera is an animal, then some animal is a chimera. But no animal is a chimera. For every animal exists, and lives, and is simply a "being" and "something"; for that which does not exist is not an animal, except in name only <note>original: "æquiuoce" — equivocally, meaning the word is used but the reality is absent.</note>. Therefore, a chimera is not a chimera by the same reasoning, nor is "being a chimera" the same as "being a chimera." For if "to be generated" is "to be moved," then "generation" is "motion." Therefore, if generation is not motion, neither is "to be generated" "to be moved." 

By a similar logic, if "to be a chimera" is "to be a chimera," then "a chimera is a chimera." For both are conjoined. But a chimera is not a chimera, as has already been proven; therefore, neither is "to be a chimera" the same as "to be a chimera." Furthermore, no chimera is a chimera. Therefore, the statement "no chimera is a chimera" is true; therefore, it is false that "any chimera is a chimera." 

By the same reasoning, it will be shown that a **vacuum** is not a vacuum because it does not exist, nor is blindness "blindness." Even if it is always non-being, nonetheless "non-being" is "non-being." For "not to be" is "non-being" and is true, just as "that a chimera is not" is both true and necessary. Why then was it necessary to fear that you might be refuted if you stated simply and absolutely that every falsehood is divided within itself? Thus, there was no need to flee to the concept of contradiction. 

Finally, you frankly confess that my argument—by which I proved that good and evil are mutual contraries—is not resolved. But you say it is not resolved because no <term>nodus</term> <note>literally "a knot"; a difficult problem or crux of an argument</note> was present. By Hercules, what a clever excuse!

<summary>The author uses logical puzzles involving non-existent things, like chimeras and golden mountains, to argue that falsehood implies a lack of internal identity (being "divided"). He mocks his opponent's refusal to admit that all falsehoods are inherently self-contradictory and "non-being."</summary>
