<header># OBJECTIONS, BOOK TWO</header>

<margin>
But it is a wonder: You ought to have said how you have now solved it; for it is no wonder not to solve what has no knot <note>A "knot" (*nodus*) refers to a difficult philosophical problem or entanglement.</note>. Therefore, marvel at me for what I have solved in which there was no knot.
</margin>

...you say it was not solved because there was no knot present. A clever excuse, by Hercules! But it is a wonder, if no knot were present, how you were able to untie the knot: the words of my argument which were written to you in my first letters are as follows: "The good is to be sought for the reason that it is good. But evil is to be avoided. Now, seeking and avoiding are mutually contrary, just as gathering and scattering are. Therefore, good and evil will be mutually contrary," which Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose commentaries on logic were standard textbooks in the Middle Ages.</note> also had affirmed in his commentary on the <term>Categories</term> <note>original: "praedicamentis." This refers to Aristotle's *Categories*, a work that organizes all possible things into ten types or "categories."</note>.

<margin>
To be similar: Why not similar? Since just as these things have no virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to logical force or strength.</note>, neither do those. For if the good is to be sought for the reason that it is good, and evil is to be avoided, and seeking and desiring are contraries, how do you prove from this that good and evil are contraries? This is what you must prove; yet you never said a single word to prove it before, nor do you do so now. Rightly, therefore, I said there was no "knot" in your argument: because you not only fail to prove strongly what you must prove, but you do not prove it in any way, nor even attempt to prove it.
</margin>

But you respond in this way: "to be" is to be desired, "not to be" is to be avoided; however, it does not follow that they are contraries. But I ask you, do you not see that your argument is similar to mine? You might say it this way: "to be" is to be desired for the reason that it is "to be"—that is, the proper nature of being is something to be desired; "not to be" is something to be avoided by its own nature; therefore, they are contraries. You will gather a beautiful argument! For by this form, we have demonstrated that hot and cold, and white and black, are contraries. For the nature of the hot is to separate heterogeneous things, but the nature of the cold is to gather them; likewise, the nature of white is to disperse the eyes, and of black to gather them.

When you responded to my argument in person, you said that the proper nature of the good is not that it is "something to be sought"—which, however, is conceded by all philosophers, especially the Latins; and Aristotle in the first book of the <term>Ethics</term> <note>original: "ethicorum." Referring to the *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> says they defined the good correctly by saying it is: "that which all things desire." This also seemed wonderful to those listening. And when the definition of the good was asked of you, you said that a thing is good because it is ordered toward God. But I immediately added: therefore, God is not good. It was said that God is not good, but you added "goodness" <note>The author is mocking a subtle distinction: saying God is not a "good thing" (an adjective) but "Goodness itself" (a noun).</note>; therefore, there is something intermediate between good and evil. For God is not "good," nor is He "evil." How, then, can it be defended that evil is the negation of good, if some intermediate is conceded?

Furthermore, if evil is the negation of good, then "evil" and "not good" are the same. For there is only one negation of one thing. It follows then: "it is not good, therefore it is evil." Thus, an affirmation can be gathered from a negation. Furthermore, it does not follow: for if evil is either a <term>privation</term> <note>Privation is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note> or something deprived. If it is "something deprived," it is some subject; therefore, it is also good. If it is a "privation," it is in a subject, and therefore it exists; but whatever is a being is in some way also good; therefore, it is not "not good." Furthermore, you deny that what Aristotle says in the *Categories* is true—namely, that good and evil are genera of contraries—which, however, neither Boethius nor the Latin commentators dare to deny.

<margin>
But you: Or are you, who are usually a follower of Boethius and a mocker of "barbarians" <note>This likely refers to the "barbarous" Latin of the Scholastic philosophers, whom Pico often defended against the more elegant Humanists.</note>, now laughing at those who, setting aside Latin interpreters, follow the Greek interpreters? But even your Thomas [Aquinas] is not only Latin, but the chief among the Latins, and he not only relates Simplicius’s exposition but also approves it. You, however, not only do not agree with Simplicius or Thomas, but you also say that the Latin commentators do not dare to deny it. You are a strange man.
</margin>

But you, having set aside the Latin interpreters, flee only to Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note>, who says that for this reason good and evil are the genera of contraries: because of contraries, one is always good (that is, it is "better") and the other is evil (that is, it is "worse"). Blessed Thomas [Aquinas] also relates this from Simplicius. But if one may oppose Simplicius: against this is what Aristotle says in the same place, that not only is good contrary to evil, but sometimes "evil is contrary to evil" <note>In Aristotle's view, a virtue (good) is a mean between two vices (evils), such as courage being between cowardice and recklessness. Thus, two evils can be opposites of each other.</note>. If, however, Aristotle calls "good" that which is "better" and "evil" that which is "worse," then good will always be contrary to evil. Furthermore, if the good and evil which Aristotle says are the genera of contraries are "better" and "worse," then good and evil are placed in the category of relatives, since "better" and "worse" are relatives. Aristotle, however, says that good and evil are not *in* a genus, but *are* genera.

# ON BEING AND THE ONE

<margin>
You wonder: Who would not wonder? I wondered then, when I had not yet perceived your sharpness; now I do not wonder, for many things are similar.
</margin>
Finally, you wonder that I affirm good and evil to be contraries, even according to the opinion of Thomas [Aquinas]; and what is more, you say I am in error because you claim I falsely cite Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note>; and that I falsely said Blessed Thomas proves by his testimony that good and evil are mutually contrary. But take care lest you be the one in error,

<margin>
That I cite falsely? And you yourself admit below that you cited falsely; but you say this is of no consequence: how then does your mind escape me? That I admit escaped me, that it is of no consequence to ascribe things to Simplicius which he does not say. For I believed that he was in error who would say: "Simplicius says this," which Simplicius nevertheless would never say.
</margin>
you who have poorly weighed my mind or my words: indeed, the words written to you in the second letter are read in this sequence. I say therefore again: and I approve that good and evil are mutually contrary: not indeed in the way that white and black, or hot and cold are, which are all truly qualities; but in the way that healthy and sick, strong and weak, rare and dense, beautiful and ugly, and many similar things of this kind are. Nor does Blessed Thomas deny it; but that most eminent man, in the first question "On Evil" <note>Referring to Aquinas's *Quaestiones Disputatae de Malo*.</note>, around the solution of the second argument, shows how good and evil—even if they are opposed as <term>privation and habit</term> <note>original: "privationis et habitus." In scholastic logic, a "habit" is a positive quality, and "privation" is the lack of a quality that should naturally be there, like blindness in an eye.</note>—are nevertheless accustomed to be counted among contraries; and he confirms this by the authority of Simplicius.

Remember, therefore, that Aristotle in the <term>Categories</term> <note>original: "praedicamentis." A foundational text for medieval logic.</note> assigns four kinds of opposition. Likewise, remember that Aristotle separates these kinds of genera from one another. Again, note that healthy and sick are numbered by him among contraries: for this reason, therefore, Aristotle separates contraries from the remaining kinds of opposition.
<margin>
For if: Why must you pervert the whole of Thomas to explain yourself, and fashion for yourself some sort of "half-full" <note>original: "semiplenas." Referring to partial privations that do not totally remove a quality.</note> privations, and deny that Thomas there properly accepts privation and habit when he says evil is privatively opposed to good? Does he not prove in the whole question that evil is nothing? And he concludes from this that evil is a privation, but not a contrary. Or is a privation which is nothing a "half-full" privation? Likewise, we say that blindness has the perfect nature of an evil, not because it takes away every good—for who does not know this?—but because it takes away that entire good of which it is called the privation, that is, sight, which ophthalmia <note>Inflammation of the eye; here used as an example of a "partial" evil compared to the "total" evil of blindness.</note> does not do. These are the things, therefore, which Thomas by no means wants to be called contraries, since they have the true nature of evil; certainly, he who says evil is a contrary according to the opinion of Thomas errs no less than that godfather <note>original: "compater meus." Likely a sarcastic reference to a colleague.</note> of mine would err, who said Simplicius says things which he does not say.
</margin>
I have affirmed that good and evil are contraries, and I confess it again. And also what Saint Thomas said in the first question "On Evil": Good and evil are contraries, just as healthy and sick, but not as sight and blindness. But you say: "I will show you how evil is entirely ignorant of the property of a contrary." For although a certain evil may seem contrary to a certain good, as the sick to the healthy (because it leaves behind something of the good), I will nevertheless offer a certain evil which can by no means be opposed to good in this way: for instance, death and blindness. But indeed, I do not know if you are pretending. For if you have read the words of Thomas more accurately, it can be clearly understood how neither blindness nor death nor any other evil can take away the good entirely. Blindness indeed takes away sight, and the whole of it; but not life, nor the body. Death takes away life entirely; but neither the body nor primary matter. What deceived you, therefore, is this: that blindness is certainly the privation of sight, and death the privation of life; but it ought not for that reason be believed to be a perfect privation of the good. Does not Thomas openly admit and say there that evil is contrary to good, just as the sick is to the healthy, not as blindness is to sight? Blindness, therefore, insofar as it is evil, leaves behind something of the good upon which it leans; but insofar as it is blindness, it permits no sight to be present. That which Blessed Thomas says—that good and evil are opposed like habit and privation—is most true. For in that place, Blessed Thomas properly calls those things "habits" and "privations" not only which are perfect habits and perfect privations (which alone Aristotle calls habit and privation in the *Categories*), but he pronounces more broadly that all things of which one is a habit and the other a privation—whether it be complete or "half-full"—are opposed as habit and privation. As for what I said, and what was confirmed by the authority of Simplicius, it is this: Simplicius says...

# BOOK TWO OF THE OBJECTIONS

...Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says in his commentary on the *Categories* <note>original: "p̄dicamentis"; referring to Aristotle’s work on the classification of things.</note> that those things are properly called contraries of which each is a distinct thing. Aristotle, however, numbers health and sickness among the contraries, but not blindness and sight. Therefore Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note>, who interprets Aristotle, must necessarily provide a reason why Aristotle did not compute all privations <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness (absence of sight).</note> among the contraries; indeed, he cannot explain the reason except for what has been stated. Therefore, Blessed Thomas—who says Simplicius claims those things are properly called contraries of which each is a distinct thing—explains the reason why health and sickness are numbered among contraries while blindness and sight are not. It is necessary to gather this from Simplicius, who expounds on Aristotle: whether that reasoning be true or false, it is a matter of no small importance to wander through.

<margin>Whether true: Why then do you not frankly admit that you have erred? For it is no wonder; you are a man.</margin>
Since, however, in your last letters you seemed to call "evil" that which you think is a negation of "good"—meaning an evil that is entirely evil—and in the same way you ask about the "false" as divided from the one "true," I wish to ask you:

<margin>Is it a chimera? In that chimera of yours, you fashion many chimeras <note>Here "chimera" refers both to the mythical beast and to a logical absurdity or a "non-thing."</note>.</margin>
Whether you think a chimera is entirely a "non-being." If you deny it, you must necessarily contradict yourself, for you previously said a chimera is entirely non-being and false. But if you grant that it is entirely non-being, I shall proceed in this manner: "non-being" and "entirely evil" are equals; a chimera is entirely non-being; therefore, it is also entirely evil. But this cannot be.

<margin>To be created: If a chimera can be created by God, this power is not in the chimera, but in God.</margin>
For a chimera does not involve a contradiction; therefore, it can be created by God. Whatever can exist, however, is a good. Therefore, what can be created can be a good. But the potentiality for good is itself good. Therefore, a chimera is not entirely evil.

<margin>Furthermore, the Chimera: The notion I form of a chimera: as it is "something," it is good; but the chimera itself, as it is "nothing," is neither good [nor bad].</margin>
Furthermore, a chimera can be understood both by God and by us. Therefore, it can exist in our mind and soul. Therefore, it can exist in some way; and whatever can exist in some way participates in goodness in some way. Therefore, a chimera is not entirely evil. Furthermore, nothing can be evil unless it is to be avoided; but nothing can be fled from or avoided unless it is known, either by the one who flees or by God, who implanted the natural instinct for flight. It is necessary, therefore, that every evil be known in some way. But knowledge is a certain good; therefore, the ability to be known is also a good. For the potentiality for a good is itself a certain good.

<margin>Aristotle, *Metaphysics* Book 4: Good and evil, according to you, are contraries, and each of the contraries is something positive; therefore, that which is good is something positive and that which is evil is something positive. And according to you "non-being" is good, therefore according to you "non-being" is something positive. And some being is converted; therefore according to you "non-being" is a positive being. See where your chimera has led us!</margin>
Furthermore, Aristotle says in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* that negations and privations are, in a certain way, beings. Indeed, he even says that "non-being" itself is in a certain way "being," the sign of which, he says, is that we say "non-being" is "non-being." That which is in any way "being" is in some way "good." Therefore a chimera, in which it is true to predicate the name of non-being, is in some way a being and a good.

<margin>Furthermore, evil is: But according to you it is a contrary, not a privation.</margin>
Furthermore, evil is a privation of good. Every privation, however, is a negation of a form in a subject naturally suited to have that form and habit <note>A "habit" (habitus) in this context is a stable quality or state of being.</note>. Therefore, nothing can be evil which is not capable and suited for good. But the capacity and aptitude for good is good. Therefore, evil cannot be entirely evil.

<margin>Augustine says: He did not say evil is good, but [that it is] in the good.</margin>
Whence Augustine says that evil is always in the good.

<margin>Furthermore, if evil: It is a privation insofar as it is a privation. Formally, it is a negation.</margin>
Furthermore, if evil is a privation of good as you say, how can it be a negation of good? For the opposition between privation and habit is one thing, but the opposition between affirmation and negation is another. Furthermore, it is your part to show that the reason you previously made was valid, by which you proved from Aristotle and Thomas that God is not a "being" <note>This refers to the core of the controversy: whether God is "Being" (*Ens*) or "Above Being."</note>. For I have weakened both, and it is not enough to say: "I know that sometimes the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> call God a 'being,' but I also know that among those same men, God is sometimes not included in the naming of 'being'."

<margin>Show: For you should reread your earlier letters, and you will see this was shown to you in them, perhaps even more than you might desire.</margin>
I ask you, show me in what place either Aristotle or the Aristotelians do not consider God under the name of "being."

<summary>The author argues that "evil" cannot be an absolute "non-being" because even a "chimera" (a non-existent thing) participates in goodness by being thinkable or potentially creatable. He concludes by challenging his opponent to prove that Aristotle or Aquinas ever excluded God from the category of "being."</summary>

<margin>
Furthermore: Take note, I will soon explain that when you conceive of "God" <note>original: "deus"</note> only as what is signified by the name, this word does not function as a predicate <note>The part of a sentence that says something about the subject.</note> but as a subject. For it is that about which it is asked what can or should be declared of it; it is not that which is declared about another. Therefore, this was not unknown to Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos, a Greek poet who famously delayed answering a tyrant's question about the nature of God because the more he thought, the more difficult it became.</note> nor to the tyrant who consulted him. Likewise, when you ask whether God can be called "God," or if He is something other than God, I ask you what you conceive by this word "God" which you declare of God. If you conceive nothing, you do not err, because you say nothing. If you conceive something, I say that God is something other than what you conceive and what you explain through this word "God," since He is above everything that can be conceived by us. Regarding "God does not exist": Let us come then to your gold, which you do not wish to lose at all, even if God were lost. It is impossible for anything to be if "Being" itself <note>original: "ipsum esse"</note> does not exist; therefore, it is impossible for gold to be if God is not. Furthermore, if God is not, then the "infinite" exists; if the infinite exists, then nothing exists, because if it is infinite, it is not finite. But if it is infinite, then it is not even infinite, because the infinite destroys itself, just as other things which imply a contradiction. If "nothing" exists, then gold does not exist. I believe these points are sufficient for you, as ingenious a man as you are. 
**Farewell.**
</margin>

# EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE <note>original: "DE ENTE ET VNO"</note>

Furthermore, if there is time, explain how you defend that God is and is One, yet God is not "God." For if the word is understood, it is necessary that some description be formed by the mind; once this is given, it follows that God is God. Nor would the poet Simonides have asked the tyrant for time to respond to the question "What is God?" unless he had conceived an interpretation and a notion of the word in his mind. In every question, the first thing is the meaning of the word. Furthermore, if God is "One," then God is "another One," which can be nothing but God. Likewise, if God exists and is not "God," He is something other than God; therefore, it is necessary that He be other than Himself. Furthermore, if God is not "God" because the name of God is a concrete term <note>A term that implies both a quality and the subject possessing it, like "white" vs "whiteness."</note> signifying one thing, and another thing should not be conceded to be God, then "God is One" means nothing; for there is nothing in the nature of things that could be God by participating in divinity. Finally, you will show how you either prove or defend that it implies a contradiction for God not to be and for gold to be. A dispute of this kind will be pleasing to me, nor should it be troublesome to you; for a dispute is the sieve of truth—the sweetest food for the soul, having nothing unpleasant about it. **Farewell.**

---

### Fourth Objections.

**N**on-being was not said of God because "to be" exists in God as His essence, but because "being" <note>original: "esse"</note> is not distinct from essence—which is a very different thing. Otherwise, the very being of a stone, which serves as its essence, would be neither "a being" <note>original: "ens"</note> nor "good." For the being of a stone is not its essence, but it is itself to itself: both its "being" and its essence. If, in negations and privations <note>A "privation" is the absence of a natural quality, like blindness being the absence of sight.</note>, it cannot be asked "what they are" <note>original: "quod sint"</note>, then since they exist, it is not enough for the question "what is it?" to know the thing about which "being" is asked. Rather, one must know more: both "that it is" and "that it is something." Therefore, to one asking "what is it?", it is replied ridiculously and irrationally that it is "a being" or "something," whether "being" is taken in the first or second sense. But if it is asked what "sin" <note>original: "peccatum"</note> is, the question is about the word rather than the thing. If something is "a being," then according to your position it is a being because "being" <note>esse</note> is distinct in reality from its essence. You say humanity is one thing, and a man is another; white is one thing, and whiteness another; a white thing is another. Therefore, if an "Idea" <note>Referring to the Platonic Ideas or Forms.</note> is a being, it will be a being because the being of the Idea is distinct from the Idea. But God is an Idea; therefore the being of the Idea is distinct from God. There is therefore in God a composition <note>A mixture of different parts or aspects, which contradicts the theological idea that God is "Simple" or without parts.</note> according to reality, not just according to reason. According to the definition of denominatives <note>Words derived from others, like "brave" from "bravery."</note>, "one" is a denominative from "unity." But God, according to your position, is called "one" by a similarity to unity; therefore, the declaration by which the Platonists say "God is one" does not pertain to the substance of God. Furthermore, when we say "God is one," you think it signifies not *that* He is, but *how* He is. However, the "how" or mode belongs to the category of accidents <note>Non-essential qualities.</note>; therefore the word "one" in God is not substantive, nor does it pertain to the thing itself. Perhaps I have either not learned the Academic sect <note>The skeptical school of philosophy following Plato.</note> or I am ignorant of the Greek language, for that is not enough to protect the discipline of the Academics. If God were not and gold were, gold would be in... <note>unclear text follows</note> gold and would not be gold; therefore it would be gold. If, therefore, the definition of the "true" stands, no quarter of an Idea will be true. If "Socrates is sitting" is neither true nor false because it is not necessary, then I shall defend that a true affirmation or negation does not exist in every case; for in every case, one or the other does not necessarily have truth. If good and evil are in things, but the true and the false are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation? For a negation posits nothing. How can a Chimera <note>A mythological creature used here to represent something that is "non-being" or logically impossible.</note> exist both in things and in the soul, if it is entirely non-being and false, since you think non-being and evil are mutually interchangeable? If "blindness is blindness" is true, who does not see that blindness is "true"? For they are the same; for by blindness alone...

<meta>This page continues a dense scholastic debate regarding the nature of being and negation. The author is responding to a critic (likely a fellow philosopher or theologian) regarding how we define "the good" and how "evil" or "non-being" (represented by the mythical chimera) fits into a universe created by God. It specifically tackles the technical definitions of "privation"—the idea that evil is not a substance but a lack of something that should be present.</meta>

<header>OBJECTIONS: BOOK TWO</header>

When a quality is established, its essence is established. That which is blindness is established as being blindness; and when it is taken away, it is removed. By that same logic, "Socrates" and "Socrates being Socrates" are the same thing, and both are brought into being by the same act of generation. In himself, God and "God being God" are also the same; for both are eternal and the primary truth.

If everything false is simply "divided" <note>In scholastic logic, "divided" often refers to the separation of a predicate from a subject, or a thing from its existence.</note>—as you do not deny has been proven—then one should not say that "something false" exists only under the condition "as long as it is false." For if every man is simply and absolutely "risible" <note>A classic logic example: "risible" means "capable of laughter," an essential property of being human.</note>, it is not necessary to add a condition that restricts it, saying: "Every man is capable of laughter as long as he is a man." Nor should such a restriction be added just because not all false things are equally divided; not even all beings are equally good, yet all things are absolutely good in their existence.

As for how one concludes that good and evil are contraries: if "pursuing" and "fleeing" are contraries, it will be easily established, provided that the logic of contrary motions has been sufficiently understood by you. Why do you wonder if I say the Latin scholars do not deny Aristotle? Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note> denies him now, but Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century Roman philosopher who translated Aristotle into Latin.</note> does not. Is it because of this that I either fail to imitate Boethius or instead exalt the "barbarians"? Do you call me a "wonder" <note>The author is likely using "wonder" sarcastically here to mirror his opponent's phrasing.</note>? Indeed, I call you "wonderful," for while I am imitating Boethius and setting Simplicius aside for the moment, you think I despise Boethius and follow the barbarians.

If good and evil are contraries, you wish to use the "chimera" <note>A mythological creature used in logic to represent an "impossible" or "non-existent" thing.</note> to prove that something exists within the nature of things. But if it were understood by what logic I called good and evil contraries—which you either do not yet wish to understand or are unable to—you would have proven nothing using the chimera. 

You marvel greatly that certain "privations" <term>privatio</term> <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that a being should naturally possess, like blindness in an eye.</note> are called "half-full" <note>original: "semi-plenas"</note> by me, and you try to prove they do not exist in this way: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not a half-full privation." But I, following your own argument, would say: "Sickness is evil; therefore it is nothing, and therefore it is not a half-full privation." Yet sickness *is* a certain kind of privation. Therefore, it is not a "half-privation" of health or of some good, but rather a "full" and "perfect" one? That is impossible. Therefore, privations are "half-full," such as sickness, rarity, or ugliness. Blindness is a "perfect" <note>Here, "perfect" means "complete" or "total."</note> privation of sight, but an "imperfect" privation of the Good; for the Good that exists in the one who sees is not entirely taken away by blindness.

If it is true, as you write, that every evil leaves some good behind, then the chimera—which is entirely "non-being" and evil—also retains some good. But if it preserves some good, it is not entirely evil, nor is it entirely "non-being." Even though the "potency" <note>The capacity or power to be created.</note> by which it can be created and exist is in God, and the "notion" by which it can be understood is in the mind, this does not prevent the chimera from being "potentially good" and a "being." For the power of God and the chimera exist by different logics. We do not deny that the Antichrist is "potentially good," since the power by which he can exist is partly in matter, partly in the heavens, and in man. Furthermore, how can the Chimera—if all thought and the power of God are excluded for a moment—be entirely "non-being" and evil? For if it does not exist, it certainly cannot be evil. Evil is a privation that exists in a subject, and that subject must necessarily participate in goodness; otherwise, it could not be a "subject" at all. That which entirely does not exist cannot be a subject for anything.

You have not yet disproven what I said, and you confirm it with the authority of Simplicius, except you claim Simplicius does not say it. But there was no reason to boast in this; for I did not say Aristotle felt that every single being exists either "through itself" <note>Essential existence.</note> or "by accident," <note>Incidental existence.</note> nor did I falsely attribute anything to Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> because of it.

Although every privation is a kind of negation, it is not yet established that there isn't one kind of opposition for "affirmation and negation" and another for "privation and habit" <note>In logic, "habit" (habitus) is the possession of a quality, while "privation" is its absence.</note>. Nor is it necessary, if evil is the privation of good, that "evil" and "not-good" are interchangeable terms.

As for your defense, by which you wish to protect the idea that "God is not God," I consider it consistent with neither the truth nor with Blessed Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian famous for "negative theology," which argues we can only say what God is NOT.</note>. Blessed Dionysius never denied that God is God.

# ON BEING AND THE ONE

But just as **Blessed Thomas [Aquinas]** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian.</note> interprets it, no name can fully explain the nature of God; nor for any other reason does he believe that affirmations about the gods are "uncompacted" <note>original: "incompactas." A term from Dionysian theology suggesting that human descriptions of God are loose or fragmentary rather than solid definitions.</note>. You, however, say that the name of God, if it has a description, holds the status of a subject and not a predicate. But even if this is granted, the argument stands: For let *a* be the definition of the name, and let it be said in this way: "God is *a*." For the definition of anything is predicated of that which it defines. Therefore, by simple conversion, "*a* is God." Therefore "God is God." 

Likewise, you say that when it is asked whether God is something other than God or not, one must know what is conceived by the name of God. Whatever other thing is given, you say, "I will call it God," for He is above everything that can be conceived. But does not this sort of solution contradict itself? For if you admit this proposition—that God is above that which can be conceived—do you not openly affirm something about God? Let the definition of the name then be that statement: "He who is above that which can be conceived," and the argument will still hold. Furthermore, it follows that "God is above everything that can be conceived"; therefore God cannot be conceived, otherwise He would be above Himself. If so, He cannot be loved or worshipped <note>A common Scholastic principle: "Nihil volitum nisi praecognitum"—nothing can be loved or willed unless it is first known/conceived.</note>. 

Finally, you must think the power of "gold" is so great that, whether we like it or not, it necessarily drags God along with it, either in reality or in the mind, in this manner: "Gold exists; therefore Being itself exists; therefore God exists." Likewise: "God exists; therefore the infinite exists. The infinite exists; therefore it is nothing." If an infinite being exists, you say, the finite does not exist—as if you were arguing "the finite is not, therefore it is nothing." Then you say: "the infinite exists, therefore the infinite is not," for you claim the infinite destroys itself. 

Truly, I think if someone had written such arguments to **Nicoletto** <note>Likely Nicoletto Vernia (c. 1420–1499), a prominent Aristotelian philosopher at Padua.</note>, he would have offered no response. Nor will I oppose them further, lest I seem to doubt a matter that appears clearer to me than light—though if you try to prove your position with these same arguments, I fear you will "lose your gold" <note>A play on words: likely meaning both losing the logical argument and a literal wager.</note>. If you wish, my excellent **colleague** <note>original: "compater," literally godfather, but used here as a warm term for a close intellectual associate.</note>, I shall respond to these objections so that we may finally end this disputation; for we have played enough. Moreover, I would not want you to think I turned to these matters out of hatred or ill will. I know you remember that before I wrote anything to you, I asked if you were willing. Indeed, I call God to witness that I love and venerate my **Count of Mirandola** <note>Referring to his uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> as my companion; if you ever care to put me to the test, you will find I have told no lie.

->GIANFRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ANTONIO<-
->FAVENTINO, DISTINGUISHED PHILOSOPHER, GREETINGS.<-

Although all the vigor and hope of my studies—which had been almost entirely placed in him—withered upon the death of my uncle **Giovanni Pico**, I had hoped while he lived that the study of **philosophy** <term>philosophia: the pursuit of wisdom, here implying a return to pure, uncorrupted ancient sources</term> would be recalled to its ancient purity, but enriched with great resources. I hoped the Christian faith, with errors utterly eliminated and heresies driven out, would be fortified with the strongest towers against its enemies. 

Yet I was not so dismayed in spirit that I did not labor with all my might to ensure that the vigils and the begun works that had flowed from that man—so admirable in every branch of letters—should not perish entirely. Therefore, looking out for myself and for all men, I hurried to **Florence** by the fastest possible routes. I took every care I could to ensure that whatever he had noted down, even if unpolished and unexamined, should be placed in our power. Our efforts were not entirely in vain. For even if the boards <note>Refers to book covers or binding boards.</note> were not yet fitted, nor the heir known, his cabinets were such that I could inspect and turn over all his commentaries. In those scattered paper codices, we saw the man's incredible industry, a range of reading beyond the grasp of the human mind, and truly admirable insights. But in the organizing of his writings, there was a lack of care that cannot be praised: everything was scattered and dissipated here and there. But more on this elsewhere. While I was unfolding these with diligent care, I found his little work *On Being and the One*, published about four years before his death...

->## OBJECTIONS, BOOK TWO<-

<warning>Translator's Note: The following text is a letter or preface by Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola regarding the publication of his uncle's philosophical debates.</warning>

...sent out together with three letters written by you and their responses, fell into my hands. Because of the novelty of the matter, I did not merely read them through, but drank them down—almost, as they say, **devoured them** <note>original: "deuoratis." A metaphor for reading with extreme eagerness or speed.</note>. (For I had recognized by rumor that this had been done, but I did not yet have enough information on what weight of argument had been brought forward.) I began to consider and debate with myself whether I should give that work to the printers to be published along with other works which I had gathered into one volume and intended to release, making no mention of your objections; or whether it would be more advisable if it went out into public fortified on this side by "stumbling blocks" <note>Attacks or objections.</note> and on that side by "bulwarks" <note>Defenses or responses.</note>. 

After a long discussion of the matter, a final decision at last settled in my mind. Indeed, it seemed that it might bring marks of infamy upon learned men if the work appeared to fear its accusers so much that it did not even dare to summon them to judgment, as if lacking confidence in its own conscience. Likewise, it seemed appropriate that the work should go out accompanied by responses, as if with witnesses to defend the cause of innocence. I did not doubt that our plan would be praised by upright men. For I either had to allow my deceased **paternal uncle** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher.</note>—a man who certainly deserved the best from me—to be defrauded in some part of his celebrated learning by not publishing such a booklet; or, if it proceeded alone, I would leave a handle for the most wicked detractors to constantly bring accusations, since the arguments that had been composed on both sides in many letters, both by objecting and by refuting, had not been summoned into the "forum" <note>The public sphere or the court of scholarly opinion.</note>. 

However, when some letters were presented by our fellow citizen and physician, **Christopher Saxolus**, signifying to us that you had composed a **fourth letter** regarding this business which (as you said) had lacked a response, the matter was called back into doubt. Again, I became of two minds, thinking I should more exactly weigh the judgment I had already freed, since the last accuser was pressing the case and there was no one to act as patron for the defense. Then a certain "tickle" or urge to undertake the defense entered my mind, though it was not immediately clear how I might turn myself toward a protective silence.

<margin>Plato</margin>
The man's modesty, his kindness toward all, and also the skill and sharpness of his genius moved my mind. He was adept at untying and dissolving even difficult knots and "inexplicable riddles" <term>riddles: "scyrpis," literally "bulrushes," a Latin idiom for a complex or knotty problem.</term> on the spot. Thus, I suspected that your last letter had not been safely delivered. I thought it might easily have happened that he *had* written back, but if your letters were indeed delivered to a faithful messenger, the response might have perished on the journey through the negligence of the couriers (as often happens) or some other accident. 

Finally, it occurred to me that in the explanations of your earlier questions, you had frequently complained that the same things were being repeated by you and doubted by you. Because of this, I immediately ran through the main points of your entire controversy to see if anything could be found in the first responses that might show the fourth letter had been partially satisfied before it was even written. The matter succeeded according to my wish; I found so many things relevant to the purpose that, although I did not respond to the objections of the final letter word-for-word as much as might be done, I nonetheless showed that you can recognize the "knots" of those objections as being largely opened by the solutions to your previous questions. 

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
We have added many things sought as testimony even from great authors. I would wish you to think that I have done all this for no other reason than to meet the judgments of those who are ignorant and unaccustomed to philosophy, and the malevolent. For if the rumor reached them that you had given a fourth letter to my uncle on that controversy to which he had not responded, they would have immediately passed judgment (as is the habit of windbags and the envious) that he had cared not to write back for some reason other than a just one. 

<margin>Thomas</margin>
Otherwise, my dear **Antonio**, I would have most willingly omitted the work I undertook from the beginning. First, so that I might not seem to be initiated into controversies—which I abhor even if I were pleading a most just cause; and second, so that I might not deviate from the true path of philosophy. 

<margin>Pico</margin>
I began to measure this path after **"horses and arms"** <note>Referring to the typical life of a nobleman or soldier, which Gianfrancesco left to pursue scholarship.</note> (although I had smelled some "little flowers" of literature as a boy) under the guidance of my uncle **Giovanni Pico** and our **Giovanni Mainardi**. For the knowledge of nature is ordained not for sweating in literary agonies, but for recognizing the Creator of nature Himself.

...and philosophical commentaries by their very nature should always spontaneously invite us to investigate the most profound meanings of the divine words; this is the end of all studies, and by these the path to heaven is revealed to us—provided, however, that we do not cultivate them for the sake of hunting our own glory, but so that we may be able to both know our God more easily and love Him more fervently. Thus, we may more promptly follow what He has commanded to be done, and flee from what He has taught to be avoided. 

Behold, the reason for this burden I have undertaken and the business with you has been explained; it is most just, as it seems, that it should be borne by you with an even mind, since I could perhaps think that I might use these works of ours as intermediaries in confirming the benevolence already auspiciously contracted with you in Ferrara. For when I arrived there in recent days, you deigned to visit me with your typical kindness. And while talking about literature, the death of my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous Renaissance philosopher.</note>, and his many works—some begun but not finished—you showed that you were so far from being offended by the opinion I formed for responding (that is, for solving your arguments) that you even praised what I was going to do. But now, entering the business itself, let us first apply our hands to dissolving the first objection. It is of this sort:

<margin>
The First Objection
</margin>
It was not said that God is not "being" <term>Ens (Being): A technical term for anything that exists. In this context, the debate is whether God is "Being itself" or "above Being."</term> because in God "being" <term>Esse (to be/act of being): The act of existence itself.</term> stands for essence; but because "being" is not different from essence, which is a far different thing. Otherwise, the "being" of a stone—which is its essence—would be neither "being" nor "good." For the "being" of a stone is not its essence, but its "being" is both its very self and its own essence. 

To which we will respond very easily. But I will bid you first to remember those things which were written by him <note>Giovanni Pico</note> for this very purpose, lest he should seem to have brought forth conflicting words. Indeed, in that commentary *On Being and the One* (which he mentioned for the sake of your objections), he not only approved of Amelius, Iamblichus, Syrianus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who argued that the "One" (God) is superior to and beyond "Being."</note>, and several Platonists who said that God is not "being," but in the whole treatise he primarily acted to show—not only from Aristotle's but also from Plato's doctrine—that God both "is" and is properly called "being."

</margin>
But he also demonstrates by some reasoning of speech that although it follows, it was not discordant with the truth that God is greater than the name "being." And for this reason, this was practiced by him so that both the authority of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a mystical theologian who emphasized God's transcendence.</note> and the reasoning of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the great Scholastic theologian.</note> might be maintained, lest—to use his words—those most learned and holy men who said God is not "being" but "above being" should seem to be entirely insane. One of them <note>Dionysius</note> repeated this opinion a thousand times; the other <note>Thomas</note> used it occasionally. 

But let us return to ourselves. When, therefore, it is said in this way that God is not "being," we assert it for this reason: that "being" in God is for His essence. You oppose this, saying it is asserted not for that reason, but because "being" simply is not different from essence, thinking these two things are entirely different. I, however, contend that one is the opening and clarification of the other saying. For when it is said that God is not "being" because in Him "being" is not separated from essence, nothing else is asserted than that "being" in God is for Him in place of essence. Nor is it judged by us through this statement—that is, "being in God is not different from His essence"—that there is an essence in God <note>as a separate component</note>.

<margin>
Of the objection
</margin>
As is clearly seen from the words of that person against whom you argued; for my uncle refuted your objection which concerned this very matter. For the Platonists, when they say this, do not mean that there is essence and "being" in God and that they do not differ. Rather, they mean that "being" holds that place in God which essence holds in other things, so that for Him nothing else is "for essence" except "being" itself. 

But if you think it entirely incongruous that the "being" of a stone cannot be called "being" and "good," you will perhaps change your mind if you consider what is said by Thomas Aquinas—

<margin>
Thomas
</margin>
—who was called upon by you as if a judge of the controversy, in the First Part of the *Summa*, Question 45, Article 4. You will clearly recognize that "being" itself, which falls into the composition of essence, should be called neither "being" nor "created," since he pronounces that all non-subsisting forms and other accidents of that kind can be called "co-existing" and "co-created" rather than "created" and "beings." Wherefore, among his followers, especially Capreolus <note>Jean Capreolus, known as the "Prince of Thomists."</note>, when the question is about the distinction of "being" and "essence," the "being" of created things is received neither into the number of true beings nor into the number of creatures. If it does not receive the name of "being," it undoubtedly does not receive the name of "good," since "being" and "good" preserve one another and reciprocate with an equal embrace.

-># DEFENSE<-

...and concerning <term>privations</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, a "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, such as blindness being the privation of sight.</note>, what they are, since it is not possible [to define them as positive things]. Therefore, since they exist, it is not enough to form the question "what is it" simply by knowing that the object of the inquiry exists. Instead, one must know more: both that it exists and that it is "something" <note>original: "aliquid"</note>. It is, therefore, ridiculous and irrational to answer "it is being" or "it is something" to the question "what is it," whether "being" is understood in the first or second sense. But if it is asked "what is sin," that is a question of the name rather than the thing itself. To this objection, we respond: he never said that one could not ask what privations and negations were.

<margin>*His solution*</margin>

Rather, he said that an answer could not be given to the question "what is it?" He brought forward the authority of <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian.</note> Thomas, whom he cited to you in previous letters—when you were doubting whether this was true or false—with these words: "you must confess it to be true unless you abandon your own Thomas."

<margin>*Giles*</margin>

We have also found this asserted by <note>Egidius Romanus (Giles of Rome), a prominent medieval philosopher and pupil of Aquinas.</note> Egidius Romanus in his second book of commentaries on the theological "Sentences." For it is enough to form the question "what is it" if one simply knows that the thing being asked about exists; it is not necessary for the person investigating what a thing is to know that it is "being" or "something" in the primary sense, but only in the secondary sense—that is, simply that it exists. 

If you were to contend that you understood the question could be formed only when an affirmative and correct answer can be given: first, if you think that a question cannot be correctly formed unless the thing being asked about is such that a response can be given through it, I do not agree with you. For it is the opinion of <note>The Greek philosopher Aristotle.</note> Aristotle that one can ask whether a <term>centaur</term><note>A mythical creature, half-man and half-horse; used here as an example of something that exists as a concept but not in reality.</note> exists or not, even though a centaur is not the kind of thing that allows the question "is it?" to be answered [affirmatively], since it is a mere fable and a total figment. 

Likewise, I oppose you if you believe that the seeker must already know this same thing; for he does not need to know more (as we have shown) than that the thing he is asking about actually exists. Therefore, although he knows the thing is "something," it is not a ridiculous answer to tell someone who does not know and is asking about it that it is "something." I ask: when we are asked "what is a thing," are we not accustomed to teaching that it is "being" or "something" so that we might provide a complete answer? For having established that it is "something," they would still search for what *kind* of being it might be. Therefore, we satisfy not only their explicit request but also their desire for investigation when we dissolve their questions—both those conceived in the mind and those spoken aloud—by anticipating them with our responses. 

However, those words—that if one asks "what is sin," the question concerns the name rather than the thing—which were part of the objection made against you, seem to carry little weight. For you had previously argued from the opinion of Thomas: namely, that "being" in the first sense is the answer given to the question "what is it?" When someone asks what it is that preserves and moves the world, the rational answer is "God." From this, you concluded that God is "being" and "something" in the primary sense. 

<margin>*Showing the error*</margin>

But he responds: see how much you are deceived! According to Thomas, evil is not the kind of thing that allows us to answer "it is something" or "it is being" to one who asks what it is; and yet, to one asking "what is sin," we can answer "it is evil." Therefore, your response does not help you at all—namely, that if one asks what sin is, the question is of the name rather than the thing. For the question "what is it that governs the world?" is no more a question of a name than "what is sin?", since the one who governs the world is God. That is, He does not have a <term>quiddity</term><note>The "what-ness" or essence of a thing that defines what it is.</note>, as the more recent thinkers say; this is most clearly confirmed by everyone except those who place Him in a <term>category</term><note>In logic, "categories" are classifications of types of being; Pico argues God transcends these classifications.</note>. And as the most holy <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian mystic and theologian.</note> Dionysius says—the prince of our theology after the Apostles—there is neither a name nor a definition for Him. 

<margin>*Dionysius*</margin>

This response of yours does not even harmonize with what you said before, when you previously claimed that evil itself is not "nothing" but something positive; yet now you admit that the question is formed only regarding the name.

<margin>*Third Objection*</margin>

You object a third time with these words: if "something" is being, then according to your position, it is being because its "to be" <note>The act of existence.</note> is a different thing from its essence. Humanity is one thing, a human is another; whiteness is one thing, a white object another. Therefore, if an <term>Idea</term><note>In this context, a Platonic Idea or a divine archetype in the mind of God.</note> is being, it will be being because the "to be" of the Idea is different from the Idea. But the Idea is God; therefore, the "to be" of the Idea is something other than God. Therefore, there is a "composition" <note>A mixture of different parts or components.</note> in God according to the thing itself, and not only according to our reason.

<margin>*His Solution*</margin>

To which we say an answer has already been given. For when you argued with almost the same means you are using now in the third letter, he responded that the composition of "being" and "essence" in divine matters exists according to reason, not according to the reality of the thing.

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of Pico della Mirandola's "On Being and the One." The author is refuting an opponent (likely Antonio Civitella) who argued that God cannot be called "One" in a substantial way because the word "one" is derived from the concept of unity, making it an accidental description rather than a name for God's actual essence.</meta>

-># ON BEING AND THE ONE<-

Regarding this <term>hypothetical syllogism</term><note>A logical argument based on "if... then" statements.</note> you bring forward: we deny that the first proposition is true. For even if in created things <term>essence</term><note>The nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</note> differs from <term>existence</term><note>original: "esse" or "existentia," the actual state of being.</note>, it does not necessarily follow that whatever can be called "being" must be composed of essence and existence as if from parts. Therefore, in the <term>Idea</term><note>In the Platonic sense, an "Idea" is the perfect eternal pattern of a thing in the mind of God.</note>—which is the pattern for created things—essence and existence do not come together as distinct things. But this composition is made by us in our minds; we weigh that Idea as the "pattern-cause" of essence and existence found in created things. We apply this composition and distinction even to the simplest things; we call it "conceptual" (according to reason) when our intellect has fashioned it. 

<margin>Usage of the Peripatetics; Seneca</margin> This distinction was most frequently used and popularized by the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, repeated by Antipater, mentioned by Posidonius, and cited in the letters of Seneca. For this reason, we can say in this manner that the Idea is "composed" of essence and existence conceptually, and we can call it "being"—specifically as the pattern of creatures. We are considering them as composed of existence and essence that are truly different [in the physical world]. However, we do not place this composition in God when we contemplate Him not as the pattern of others, but as He who enjoys Himself in the innermost retreat of His divinity.

<margin>Fourth objection</margin> Fourthly, you say that according to the definition of <term>denominative</term><note>A word derived from another, like "brave" from "bravery." The opponent argues "one" is just a label derived from "unity."</note> terms, "one" is derived from "unity." But according to your position, God is called "One" because of a likeness to unity. Therefore, you argue, the predication by which the Platonists say "God is one" does not concern the substance of God. Furthermore, you think that when we say "God is one," it signifies not *what* He is, but *how* He is. You argue that "how" (mode) belongs to the category of <term>accidents</term><note>Non-essential qualities, like color or shape, that can change without the thing itself disappearing.</note>; therefore, you claim the word "one" is not <term>substantive</term><note>Naming the actual thing or essence.</note> in God. You suggest I say this either because I have not learned the Platonic sect or because I am ignorant of the Greek language—for you say my knowledge is not enough to defend the teaching of the <term>Academics</term><note>The followers of Plato's Academy.</note>.

But the response is easy. It has been rightly asserted by 

<margin>His solution</margin> the Platonists that the "One" which is predicated of God is substantive and not merely denominative. And again, since it has been asserted that He is called "One" because He is like unity, this is not inconsistent. Nor can it be said for that reason not to be substantive. For even if a name is adapted to something from the property or likeness of some other thing, it does not necessarily follow that the name is not substantive—provided it is taken as a substantive name that signifies the thing standing by itself, rather than as an "adjacent" attribute. Indeed, it is clear that the "One" predicated of God is understood not as a quality clinging to Him, but as His very "standing" or being, so that it needs no proof. 

You see, therefore, that the property from which a name is taken does not strip away its status as a substantive name. 

<margin>Thomas</margin> For your <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century Dominican theologian.</note> Thomas—rather *our* Thomas—reports both in other places and in the first part of his *Summa* that the thing a name is intended to signify differs from the source from which the name is derived. For example, he explains that the name "stone" <note>original: "lapis"</note> is applied to signify that specific substance, but the name itself is derived from a related property—namely, that it "hurts the foot" <note>original: "laedit pedem." This is a classic medieval etymological pun: la-pis from laedere-pedem.</note>. 

<margin>John Scotus</margin> From this, he teaches in another place that grammarians use nouns to denote "substance with quality," which <note>John Duns Scotus, the influential Franciscan philosopher.</note> John Scotus also affirms in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences*.

Therefore, my dear Anthony, when we predicate "one" of God, we predicate it truly and as a substantive name, because we both conceive and predicate it as "standing" by itself. Again, when we say it is applied from a likeness to unity and its properties, we approach the truth as much as is permitted to us, because we use a suitable word to indicate that deity which is far ineffable above all created things. He is the principle of all things that are, just as unity is the principle of all numbers. 

And from these words, you will also gather the solution to your other argument about "mode," which you claim belongs only to the category of accidents. Namely, that in this predication, "God is One," it signifies *how* God is one, and nonetheless the word "one" in God is substantive. [Considering] by what origin the name is made and what it is meant to

# APOLOGIA

<margin>A brief solution from the words of the fathers.</margin>
If you consider what is attributed to the notation of the thing, you can recognize the solution to your doubt even more briefly from the words of my uncle <note>The "uncle" refers to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494); the author of this defense is his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola.</note>: when he says, "Why do you say I follow the reasoning of the Platonists rather than <term>Dionysius</term><note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th century.</note>, when you have never read either Dionysius or the Platonists—even though you boast of them with a great voice?" But you should know that the same thing exists among the Platonists: the pattern of God is Unity, and in Dionysius, God is uniquely all things. No one could rightly desire a more efficient solution. For when it is said that the pattern of God is Unity, it refers to the likeness and manner; but when it is said that God is uniquely all things, it must be referred to <term>substance</term><note>The fundamental reality or essence of a thing.</note>. However, it has been asserted that these are entirely the same, since even in the Greek language (which he knew well), the <term>abstract and the concrete</term><note>For example, "Unity" (abstract) vs. "The One" (concrete).</note> can sometimes be signified by the same word.

<margin>Solution to the fifth objection.</margin>
There is no need for many words to bring a solution to your fifth doubt. He says: "If God did not exist and gold existed, gold would be gold and gold would not be gold." You add these words: "Therefore gold would exist; because if the definition of truth stands, it will be a truth corresponding to no <term>Idea</term><note>In this context, the eternal blueprint in the divine mind.</note>." I beg you, add also these few words which followed from his speech, and you will recognize how it will be a truth corresponding to no Idea. What do I mean? He produces an impossibility, and therefore it is no wonder if you make whatever you wish follow from your impossible proposition. For if God did not exist and gold existed, there would be a truth corresponding to no Idea, since from the impossible, the impossible is born—not only the <term>dialecticians</term><note>Logicians who use formal debate and reasoning.</note> but also the theologians agree with this. For if you ask <margin>John of Baconthorp</margin> <term>John of Baconthorp</term><note>original: "Ioannem de bachone," a 14th-century English Carmelite monk and philosopher known as the "Doctor Resolutivus."</note>, the Carmelite, whether it is possible for gold to exist and God not to exist, he will answer you in the first [book] of the *Sentences* that no thing at all, of whatever kind it may be, can be understood unless God is understood first. Since he is of the intellect of all things, you will gather whether it can be pronounced—even among novice dialecticians—that it is impossible for gold to be and God not to be, beyond all controversy. But we will speak of this again at the end of the work if you later consult <margin>Cardinal of Cambrai</margin> the <term>Cardinal of Cambrai</term><note>original: "Cardinalis cameracensis," referring to Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous theologian and logician.</note>. You will hear a man practiced in all philosophy saying in his first commentary on the *Sentences* that a contradiction follows from any impossibility.

<margin>Sixth objection</margin>
In the sixth place, you said that if it were neither true nor false that "Socrates is sitting" (which he had asserted because it was not necessary), you could defend that it is not the case that in every instance either the negation or the affirmation is true, since in every instance one or the other does not have a necessary truth. 

<margin>Its solution</margin>
Solving this objection, we respond that this speech—namely, "Socrates is sitting"—does not necessarily determine truth or falsehood for itself insofar as it is itself; nor does it follow from this that there is not a true affirmation or negation for every instance. Yet, if you understand it in the way he teaches, you will also be able to deny in every instance that an affirmation or negation is true such that one part is *necessarily* true. For he says: "That I sit is always either true or false, because I always either sit or I do not sit." And what is said—that "me sitting" is neither true nor false—means that this proposition does not determine truth or falsehood for itself from its own nature, which is what <term>necessary propositions</term><note>Statements that must be true by their very nature, like 2+2=4.</note> do. But since it can happen that it is both true (when I sit) and false (when I do not sit), it is by itself indeterminate toward either. Furthermore, against certain of his words concerning good and evil, truth and falsehood,

<margin>Seventh objection</margin>
which he had claimed exist in things and in the soul, you insist in this way: "If good and evil are in things, and truth and falsehood are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation? For negation posits nothing; whereby even a <term>Chimera</term><note>A mythical beast used in logic to represent a thing that cannot exist in reality.</note> is in things and the soul. <margin>Aristotle</margin>

Rather, it is observed and considered regarding the things themselves—that is, insofar as a thing is deprived of its perfections, which results in things not being "good." A <term>Chimera</term><note>A mythical creature composed of parts from different animals; in logic, it is often used as a standard example of an impossible or non-existent thing.</note>, however, is not among real things because it is entirely "non-being" and entirely "bad." Nevertheless, if it were possible by nature for it to be a real thing, it would be both a thing and good. Yet it is "false" insofar as it is entirely non-existent and corresponds to no <term>Idea</term><note>In the Platonic tradition, an "Idea" or "Form" is the eternal, perfect blueprint of a thing that exists in the divine mind.</note>. Nor do we even affirm that the Chimera itself is in the soul, but rather the *notion* of the Chimera; that notion, as it is a certain "thing," is good and true, but it is "false" insofar as it represents a Chimera, since the Chimera itself is both nothing and bad.

<margin>Eighth objection</margin>
After this, you believed you could prove that **blindness** is true, which he <note>Pico the Elder</note> had denied—even though he would neither have denied nor granted that "blindness being blindness" is true. But he would have said these two things are far different. You argued in this manner: if "blindness being blindness" is true, then who does not see that "blindness is true" is the same thing? For if blindness alone is posited, then this fact—that "blindness is blindness"—is also posited; and if it is taken away, the fact is taken away. Hence, by the same reasoning, **Socrates** and "Socrates being Socrates" are the same, and both are produced by the same <term>generation</term><note>The process by which something comes into being.</note>. Likewise, **God** and "God being God" are the same—

<margin>Its solution</margin>
for both are eternal and the <term>First Truth</term><note>A theological term for God as the ultimate source and standard of all truth.</note>. But I, my dear Antonio, contend the opposite and deny that these things you bring forward are the same. For when one of those things you offer is posited, the other is not necessarily posited. For if blindness alone were posited with no intellect considering it, there would indeed be blindness, yet there would not be this "complex" fact which is "blindness being blindness." For this reason, the argument concerning God and the generation of Socrates is also dissolved. For Socrates is generated in himself, but the proposition "Socrates is Socrates" is not generated, since <term>complexes</term><note>In medieval logic, a "complex" refers to a proposition or sentence (a combination of terms), whereas a "simple" is a single term like a name.</note> are not generated. Even if I were to grant you that they are the same, it still does not follow as you were concluding, because of the different way of signifying—namely, *complexly* and *incomplexly*. Indeed, this argument would have no value: "Blindness and 'blindness being blindness' are the same; but this one is true, therefore that one is true," because in the same way it would follow: "This one is a complex proposition, therefore the other is too," which is absurd. Since "blindness" is a simple name and not a complex sentence or any kind of <term>enunciation</term><note>A formal statement or proposition that can be true or false.</note>, it is therefore one thing for "blindness to be true" and another for "it to be true that blindness is blindness." And although these points would suffice for my uncle's defense, nevertheless, do not believe that other

<margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin>
ways of guarding and defending are lacking. So that a more complete response may reach you, know that I could have spoken according to the opinion of **Gregory of Rimini**<note>An influential 14th-century Augustinian theologian and logician known for his work on the objects of knowledge.</note>: even if positing blindness alone posited "blindness being blindness," it does not therefore necessarily follow that they are the same. He 

<margin>Cardinal of Cambrai</margin>
denies this consequence, as well as many of this kind: "Everything other than God being set aside, God exists; therefore 'God exists' is 'God being God'." The **Cardinal of Cambrai**<note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous theologian and philosopher. He argued that infinitive propositions (like "to be") shouldn't be treated as objects that things are predicated of.</note> also denies all sentences in which something is enunciated about an infinitive phrase used significatively; he asserts they are both false and incongruous,

<margin>Ninth objection</margin>
as can be seen in his first book on the *Sentences*. Next, you complain that the word "false" should not have been pronounced as "divided" with this condition: "so long as it is false." You explain it in these words: "If everything false is simply 'divided'—which you do not deny has been proven—it should not have been said that 'a certain false thing is divided only with this condition, namely, so long as it is false'." For if every man is simply and absolutely capable of laughter, one should not have to add a condition by which you restrict it, saying "every man is capable of laughter so long as he is a man." Nor should the restriction have been added 

<margin>Its solution</margin>
for the reason that not all false things are equally "divided" or false. For not all beings are equally good, yet all are absolutely good. But consider his words carefully; from them you will be able to cast away every scrap of doubt. He says: "Every false thing is divided," yet not every false thing is "equally" false, because they are not "equally divided." For those things are not equal which are not necessarily and always false, compared to those which are always and necessarily false. Therefore, Antonio, that phrase "so long as" was rightly added for the sake of those things which are not always and necessarily false—things which, though false, can become true and be "unified" either by the work of nature or an artist. You also said this in your second set of objections: however, as long as they are divided, they are false; but those things are always false

# APOLOGIA

which can never return to friendship <note>The author uses "friendship" here as a metaphor for logical compatibility or reconciliation between propositions.</note>: as you have seen abundantly in the response to the second objection. Nor does the similarity concerning <term>beings</term><note>Latin: *entia*. In medieval philosophy, "being" refers to anything that exists.</note> and **risibility** <note>The "ability to laugh," traditionally used in logic as the quintessential "proper" attribute of human beings—something that is not part of the definition of "man" but belongs to every man and only to men.</note> support you at all. For beings are always and absolutely good. Although they are not equally good and some participate in the nature of "good" more than others, they are nevertheless always and necessarily good. For insofar as they are beings, they are good, and they cannot become non-beings and non-good unless they are reduced to nothing. But it can conveniently happen that a "false and divided" thing—which consists in a complex proposition—becomes "undivided and true." Therefore, the comparison does not fit. For although not all false things are equally divided, they are nevertheless false insofar as they are not united and not true. Add to this that this objection should have troubled us very little. For who would doubt that a man (who is absolutely and always capable of laughter) can be pronounced "risible" with this condition: "as long as he is a man"? Or will this expression be disapproved of by learned men: "A man is risible as long as he is a man"?

<margin>Solution to the tenth objection.</margin>
The tenth head of your objections brings nothing else against him except that what you said could have easily been established if the logic of **contrary motions** had been sufficiently understood by him. But he—unless he has failed—complained that you did not prove what you so often said would follow: namely, that from the contrariety of "pursuing" and "fleeing," the contrariety of "good" and "evil" is inferred. He asks: by what reasoning is the good to be sought because it is good, and the evil to be fled? And even if "fleeing" and "seeking" are contraries, how do you prove from this that "good" and "evil" are contraries? This is what you had to prove; however, you never spoke a single word to prove it, nor do you do so now. He denies this—namely, the form of your argument—perhaps for this reason: because "seeking" and "fleeing" are not properly contrary motions from which it could be gathered that their terms are contrary. Indeed, even by **Aristotle** himself, some contrariety of changes is assigned in the sixth book of the *Physics* <note>Latin: *Physica Auscultatio*, Aristotle's foundational work on nature and motion.</note>, where the terms are not **contraries** but **contradictories**: namely, "being" and "non-being," since generation proceeds from non-being to being, while corruption falls from being into non-being. You, however, have treated this contrariety of good and evil again, yet you brought no other proof. Furthermore, you should not doubt that he [Pico the Elder] looked into the logic of contrary motions diligently and "from the very fingernails" <note>An idiom meaning "from the earliest stages" or "thoroughly."</note> as they say. On the contrary, he very often not only repelled your arguments against him regarding this contrariety, but also acted against you when, in the second letter, he deduced that your proof would not only infer that evil and good are contraries, but that **contradictories** are contraries. Secondly, he turned your own weapons back against you in this way: "According to you, good and evil are contraries; and each of two contraries is something positive; and according to you, non-being is good; therefore, according to you, non-being is something positive. And since 'something' and 'being' are interchangeable, then according to you, non-being is something positive."

<margin>Eleventh objection</margin>
When you said in the third letter that he had fled to **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Greek philosopher and one of the last great Neoplatonists, famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, abandoning the Latin interpreters regarding the opposition of good and evil, he replied as if in wonder: Why would you—who used to be a follower of **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century Roman philosopher who translated Greek logic into Latin; Pico calls him a "mocker of barbarians."</note> and a mocker of "barbarians"—now mock those who follow Greek interpreters instead of Latin ones? He was suggesting most aptly that you feel wrongly if you think the Greek philosophers should not be magnified, whom Boethius (whom you hold in great esteem) always held in the highest honor, and whom he used as both teachers and guides. To these points you reply that the matter is not worthy of wonder, since you said the Latins do not deny Aristotle, whom Simplicius does not deny, etc. 

<margin>Its solution.</margin>
But it does not seem to me that Simplicius denies Aristotle when he interprets him correctly, nor does it appear that the Latin interpreters vary from the opinion of Simplicius. Indeed, they embrace it with their whole mind and execute it in their works. If he [Pico the Elder] was amazed that you claimed the Latin expositors do not follow Simplicius, he would perhaps have fallen into a greater stupor if he had understood you to say that the Latins do not deny Aristotle, while Simplicius (whom you said they follow) does deny him. 

<margin>Simplicius's task</margin>
Furthermore, Simplicius and those who followed him clearly elucidate the mind of Aristotle when he said that good and evil are contraries for this reason: that one of the contraries always has the nature of evil and deficiency. Wherefore, in the first book of the *Physics*, contraries are always [determined] according to the "better"...
