The doctrine of the Pythagoreans
</margin>
Pythagoras also taught, imitating this same reasoning, that things are compared by a "worse" ratio: he established two principles, one of which was contained under **good** and the other under **evil**. He frequently used this exposition in his exoteric <note>original: "externis." Referring to works intended for a general audience rather than specialized students.</note> books with examples, as your beloved **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian.</note>—who is not only a Latin author but the most eminent among the Latins—not only reports but also approves. To him we also add **Giles** <note>Egidius Romanus (Giles of Rome, c. 1243–1316), a student of Aquinas.</note> in his second book on the *Sentences*, and many others such as **Burley** <note>Walter Burley (c. 1275–1344), an English logician.</note> and **Esculanus** <note>Cecco d'Ascoli (1257–1327), an Italian encyclopedist and poet.</note> who hold the same view.
<margin>
Thomas
Giles
Burley
Esculanus
John Duns Scotus
</margin>
Even **John Duns Scotus** <note>A major Franciscan theologian (c. 1266–1308).</note>, in his explanation of Aristotle’s *Categories*, supports this opinion of ours, stating that if **good** is taken as being interchangeable with **being**, then **evil** is nothing, and thus it is not contrary to good. For since it is beyond controversy that both sides of a pair of contraries must be something positive, it follows that something which is "nothing" in the nature of things—which is what evil is—cannot be declared a "contrary." 

And although you have denied that evil is nothing, appealing to Thomas, he not only fails to support your opinion but abundantly refutes it. My uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> also showed this sufficiently in the margin of his third letter. However, we do not think it out of place to touch upon a few points in passing for the sake of my uncle's opinion, and to show that not only was Thomas of the opinion that **evil is nothing**, but that many other illustrious philosophers and theologians have followed this path with "hands and feet" <note>An idiom meaning "wholeheartedly" or "completely."</note>. 

We find **Augustine**
<margin>Augustine</margin>
discussing the *Customs of the Manichaeans*, saying that no nature is evil; and shortly after, lest there be any ambiguity about what he meant by "nature," he added: "and nature itself is nothing other than that which is understood to be something in its own genus." We have seen that **Giles of Rome**
<margin>Giles</margin>
left written in his first commentary on the *Sentences* of the Fathers that evil, insofar as it is evil, is <term>pure privation</term> <note>original: "puram esse privationem." In medieval philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness in an eye.</note> and not "something." In this way, it can be pronounced to be "something" only in the same way that "nothing" itself can be called "something"—insofar as both can be designated by a name. In the second book of those same commentaries, he affirms that evil does not have (to use his words) <term>quiddity</term> <note>original: "quidditatem." The "whatness" or essence of a thing.</note>, and for that reason, the question "What is it?" cannot be answered regarding it. He says that there is nothing else to it but the name. He likewise interprets Aristotle’s words on the opposition of evil and good according to my uncle’s mind, and agrees with the doctrine of **Simplicius** 
<margin>Simplicius</margin>
and other upright interpreters of Aristotle. Namely, he pronounces that they are not "proper genera," but that "genera" should be said only of other contraries where one has a positive nature and the other does not. For no contrary is "non-being" in itself, but rather some nature and existence. 

**Gregory of Rimini**
<margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin>
testifies to this same thing in his commentaries on the second book of the *Sentences*: that evil itself is not (to use his speech) an <term>entity</term>, but pure privation. 
<margin>Robert Holcot</margin>
The man of most perceptive intellect, **Robert Holcot**, felt this same way in the first question of his commentaries on the second book of theological *Sentences*. Many others have judged the same, whom it might bring weariness to me in writing and to you in reading to bring forward at present. It will be enough for the current business to have numbered these, especially since it will be necessary to speak of this again when resolving other objections where mention of evil occurs. 

But to return to where we digressed: if you seem to judge that **Boethius** alone among all the Latins should be cited against Simplicius and the other illustrious interpreters—and if you deign to count only him among the Latin expositors—then he will be the *only* one among the Latin expositors (not "the Latin expositors" in general) who will seem to support your opinion. Add to this that even he, if his mind is properly searched, does not reclaim our opinion; he does not weigh this question exactly, nor does he search it out to the final judgment. He only declares what Aristotle’s words, strictly and at face value, seem to demand. This was his most familiar custom in his first editions: to leave the various opinions of the Greek interpreters for a second edition, where they would be examined scrupulously and anxiously.

## ->DEFENSE<-

By whatever reasoning you have called good and evil contraries, you bring nothing else forward. Therefore, I will do nothing against you except to note that he <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the author’s uncle.</note> both saw and perceived everything you had written, and when it pleased him, he reviewed many things I had said concerning contraries. For my plan in this matter is to dissolve your final objections against my uncle; however, those to which he himself had responded in some way, I shall pass over in silence. Nevertheless, if anything seems to you not fully clarified by him, and you both desire and demand that it be opened up by me, we will attempt to satisfy your desire. Through these efforts, we will wander through your arguments, both by dissolving and responding to them as much as we are able; for he judged it inconsistent for even the smallest of your words to lack a response. He admits in his first letters that some things were omitted to which no response was given, lest he waste words on trivial matters; some things were treated lightly, as he thought that to a philosopher, things ought to be indicated rather than explained. I would wish these words to be interpreted by you in this way: that for some matters—the controversies of which are well known even to common philosophers—it was not worthwhile for a noble philosopher like yourself to be led against a man most celebrated in both learning and fame, who held discourse on the highest things. For he would not descend to discussing these lowliest matters without a loss of the contemplations he had conceived concerning the most difficult subjects. However, concerning this "contrariety" of yours, we shall say something in the following response when we speak of "incomplete privations." <note>original: "semiplenis priuationibus." A technical term in logic referring to a partial lack of a quality.</note>

<margin>Solution to the thirteenth objection.</margin>
Furthermore, you wonder that he marveled at your invention of "incomplete privations." I believe his wonder was turned toward this matter not so much at that time, but after you proved that you were attempting it again (if indeed your final objections were seen by him). He had said against you: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not an incomplete privation." You, however, pursue his argument in this manner: "Sickness is evil; therefore it is nothing. Therefore, it is not an incomplete privation. But sickness is a certain privation; therefore, it is not the incomplete privation of health or of any good, but rather a good and perfect one <note>Meaning a "complete" or "total" privation.</note>—which cannot happen. Therefore, imperfect privations are incomplete, such as sickness or rarity; foulness or blindness are perfect [privations] of a good, [while] these [others] are imperfect." These are your words verbatim. But I, my dear Antonio, would say freely that these words of yours either do nothing against him, or (so that you may see this more clearly) I will review them individually. You say first, from his own words: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not an incomplete privation." You walk correctly there. Again: "Sickness is evil; therefore it is nothing; therefore it is not an incomplete privation." Thus far you proceed well, because sickness, insofar as it is evil, is to that extent nothing. Again you say: "Sickness is a certain privation, therefore not health, etc." right to the end—in which words, by your leave, a falsehood is asserted in my judgment, which we shall endeavor to show. For blindness is not only a perfect privation of sight, as you say, but it can also be called a perfect privation of a good, because it takes away that entire good which it is by nature meant to take away—namely, sight. Ophthalmia <note>term: <term>ophthalmia</term> — a general historical term for severe inflammation of the eye.</note> does not do this, although it also oppresses the good which it is born to take away; however, it can in no way be called a privation of that which it is not fit to destroy, whether you call it an incomplete or a full privation. For privation is considered either absolutely—that is, as it regards a "habit" <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "habit" (habitus) is a positive quality or state of being, the opposite of a privation.</note> in general—or it is restricted to a certain and limited kind of being, such as to the health

<margin>Privation is considered in two ways. Dionysius.</margin>
of the whole body, to the eye, to beauty, and other things of that kind. Taken in the first way, it does not deprive any particular habit, because an all-encompassing privation, as **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian philosopher.</note> says in the book *On the Divine Names*, fails entirely in its powers. Taken in the second way (which is called "singular" by Dionysius, distinguishing it against the universal), it deprives that habit which it regards. And in this way, this kind of habit—which the privation is naturally meant to oppose—is a full privation, and not an incomplete privation of some other thing. For who would dare to say that blindness is an "incomplete privation" of a man, or of any other good that might be in a man? Therefore, absolute privation regards a habit absolutely, and proper and particular privation regards a proper and particular habit; and it does not exceed those limits. For this reason, sickness is a full privation, not an incomplete one, whether you ascribe it to the whole body or to a particular member. For a fever is a perfect privation of that [healthy] temperature which it is born to corrupt; ophthalmia, even if it is not a privation of all the good that is in the eye, is nevertheless a privation of some good...

He argues that any specific ailment, like blindness or fever, is a "perfect" or complete privation of the specific health or function it affects, rather than a partial lack of general goodness.</summary>

Having previously discussed whether good and evil are true contraries, Gianfrancesco now addresses the specific logical category of "privation"—the absence of a quality that should be present.</meta>

# ON BEING AND THE ONE

<margin>The destruction of Antonio’s arguments through examples</margin>
...a perfect and proper <term>privation</term> <note>In scholastic philosophy, a "privation" is not just the absence of something, but the absence of a quality that ought to be present by nature, like blindness in an eye.</note> is that which destroys all that good which it is meant to destroy; just as it destroys the perfect health of the eye, yet does not take away sight entirely unless the <term>ophthalmia</term> <note>An inflammatory eye disease used here as an example of a partial loss of function.</note> does nothing else. So too with ugliness: because it takes away that whole good which it can take away—namely, the perfect composition of parts which is called beauty—it is a perfect privation. Consider this also in other cases. We have said this even in excess: blindness, insofar as it is blindness, is an evil; and insofar as it is an evil, it is nothing, and it is a "nothing" that is not a semi-complete privation. For if it were semi-complete, it would leave behind something positive, which evil does not do. Furthermore, no privation in itself actually deprives one of all good; therefore, all privations would be "semi-complete" privations, which goes against your own position, for you contend that some are full and others are semi-complete. This is an excellent and necessary connection, and we prove what we have assumed by this argument: no good would ever be found if a certain total and universal privation were discovered in the nature of things, as we indicated a little while ago from the words of <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian theologian who argued that evil has no independent existence but is a lack of good.</note>. For evil deprives a particular good, since evil exists within the good; and a universal evil would destroy universal good—if indeed it could be found, which is impossible. Thus, you may gather that privations of their proper <term>habits</term> <note>In this context, a "habit" (habitus) refers to a stable quality or state of being, like sight or health.</note> are always found to be full, not semi-complete.

<margin>Solution to the fourteenth objection</margin>
To the fourteenth objection, which contains several questions, I respond individually: first, that not every evil leaves something of good, unless you understand this to be within some <term>subject</term> <note>The "subject" is the underlying thing (like a body or a soul) in which the evil or privation exists.</note> which the evil itself does not regard, or you take it to be that subject whose habit is destroyed by the evil itself. Nor should you accept that opposite habit which you nevertheless impose upon it and try to catch as a hypothesis. For Dionysius abundantly testified that some evil is found which entirely takes away every good born from it; when he addressed you on this in the response of the second letter, he wrote in this way: "You certainly ought to have considered this: that what is granted concerning certain imperfect evils, due to that mixture of goodness they still retain, must not be transferred to the absolute and unmixed nature of evil itself." And so that you may perceive the truth more clearly, it will not be a burden to explain the force of this distinction.

<margin>Evil understood in two ways</margin>
Evil can be considered in two ways: first, absolutely and according to its own proper definition of evil—that is, insofar as it is nothing; and second, insofar as it is a privation of a certain good—that is, a particular evil. When accepted in this second way, evil leaves behind only the good of the subject. This does not make evil anything other than a complete non-entity and a "nothing," just as we call a <term>Chimera</term> <note>A mythological creature used in logic to represent an impossible or non-existent concept.</note> a nothing, since it does not regard any subject or habit. For this reason, total evil is called by Dionysius the "absolute and unmixed nature of evil." This evil, to use the words of Dionysius from his book *On the Divine Names*, is "in no way, nowhere, and is nothing existing," because it lacks a subject.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
Indeed, even if a Chimera could be called "potentially" good because of the power to produce it which exists in God, it nevertheless can be named neither a being nor a good. For if this connection were valid—namely, that if something is potentially good, it is therefore good—the opponent would be able to turn that blow back upon the author. I would think it would lead him to confess that all things which ought to be created by God, but are not yet made by the force of nature, and even those things which have been destroyed, both "are" something and "are not" something. For if, according to him, they were both beings and good things because they are "potentially" created, then they would necessarily be "something," since "something" and "good" are interchangeable terms and are entirely of the same scope.

That it could not be "something," I shall argue as follows: something cannot be made out of nothing. Before a Chimera is created, it cannot "be" according to you unless it is created; it is created, therefore, out of nothing. Therefore, before it was created out of nothing, it was not "something." Therefore, because of the power of goodness which is in the Creator, a thing cannot be called absolutely good [before it exists]; otherwise, to use the language of our logicians, the fallacy of <term>moving from a qualified statement to an absolute one</term> <note>original: "fallacia secundum quid ad simpliciter." This is a logical error where one assumes that because something is true in a specific case (it is *potentially* good), it is true in all cases (it *is* good).</note> would be committed. I deliberately set aside those things which might be brought against that opinion concerning "eternal essences" and "objective potentiality," even if your opinion could perhaps be weakened by those same reasons. For it is enough for our purpose if we have proven that a Chimera cannot be called good. 

<margin>Averroes</margin>
Add to this that we can also say, imitating <term>Averroes</term> <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Western scholasticism.</note> in this part, that a being in potentiality is not a being.

<summary>Gianfrancesco argues that evil is a "perfect privation" (a total absence) of a specific good, rather than a positive substance. He uses the logical example of a "Chimera" to demonstrate that "potential" goodness or being is not the same as actual existence.</summary>

<margin>Albert the Great; Aristotle.</margin>
...one opposition is of a different kind than the opposition of negation: and that he did not prefer that opposite: but for this reason it still follows that if evil is opposed to good through <term>privation</term><note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality in something that normally possesses it—like blindness being the privation of sight.</note>, then it is necessary that "evil" and "non-good" are <term>convertible</term><note>In logic, terms are "convertible" if they mean the same thing and can be swapped in a sentence without changing its truth.</note>. For as **Albert the Great** says in the first book of the *Physics*, insofar as privation is not "of itself" or "by itself," it has no existence of its own; indeed, it has even been asserted by **Aristotle** in his *Metaphysics* <note>Original: "prima philosophia" (First Philosophy), the traditional name for Aristotle's Metaphysics.</note> that privations belong to the category of non-beings, since privation of itself is the other extreme of a contradiction. Therefore, since evil is the privation of good, and consequently is "non-being" insofar as evil is evil, "evil" and "non-good" are convertible. For evil and "nothing," as has been proven, are the same; "nothing" and "non-being" are the same; and "non-being" and "non-good" are the same, because "being" and "good" are the same. Wherefore my uncle <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> most correctly said that negation is a privation to the extent that privation is formally a negation. For although they differ in this—that one (namely contradiction) has no middle ground, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, while the other might have one in a certain way since it occurs simultaneously with the opposite regarding the same subject—nonetheless, as far as the present purpose is concerned, they would be the same. This is because privation of itself is negation and non-being and posits nothing, just as **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> proves in many places, especially in the treatise *On the Four Opposites*. If indeed non-beings are evil, and evil things are non-good, from these points you can conclude that evil and non-good are entirely

<margin>Thomas; Aristotle; Anselm.</margin>

Therefore, add by the rule of contradictories that "evil" is said of "non-being." Listen to the most celebrated theologian **Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury**, in his book *On the Fall of the Devil*, uttering these words: <note>original: "malū nō est aliud q nō bonū"</note> "evil is nothing other than non-good," from which it is gathered most

<margin>He reproves Antonio for his little diligence.</margin>

of darkness. Even if I were to set aside the theologians, philosophers of right sentiment would affirm this. Since this name "God," which performs the office of a <term>predicate</term><note>In the sentence "God is God," the second "God" is the predicate—the part that says something about the subject.</note> in the proposition "God is God," not only fails to explain and declare the divine essence and nature, but is even infinitely surpassed by it, he denied that it could be affirmed of God, keeping that fourth step of darkness in mind. Come then, let us examine the words themselves which will testify to the man's mind; afterwards we will bring forward several points so that it may be seen more clearly whether and how God can be spoken of by us. Then we will show that your arguments against his words—even as they lie apprehended—conclude nothing. He had said that "God is God" can be said in different ways; likewise, that according to the opinion of **Dionysius**, He is greater than every name, even this name of "God," just as was held in the book *On Mystical Theology*. He had said in another place that when you conceive through this word "God" only that which is signified by the name, this word does not have the nature of a predicate, but of a <term>subject</term><note>The "subject" is what the sentence is about; the author argues that "God" is always the subject we wonder about, but never a label we can fully apply.</note>, since it would be that concerning which it is asked what could or should be stated about it, but not that which is stated about another. Wherefore this was not unknown to **Simonides** <note>A Greek poet who, when asked by King Hiero to define God, kept asking for more time because the more he thought, the more obscure the subject became.</note> nor to the Tyrant who consulted him. When you likewise asked whether, if God could not be called "God," He were something other than God, I would ask you what you conceived through this word "God" which you were stating about God. If you conceived nothing, you would not err: because you would be saying nothing. If you conceived something, you would be saying that God is "other" than that which you conceive and explain through this word "God": since He would be above all that which is [conceived] by us.

...could be conceived by us, as he said. I believed it was evident to you from those words the very truth of your doubts regarding this resolution: You, however, contend that it is not denied by **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose "Mystical Theology" argued that God transcends all human categories.</note> that "God is God." 

<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
Read, I pray, **Dionysius** in the last chapter of the book *On Mystical Theology* and the first letter to **Gaius**, and it will become plain to you that God is greater than every name or title. Read also the same author in the second chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, and you will understand that this divine man teaches us that the likeness of divine truth transcends all underlying life and every life; no light expresses it, and every word, every mind, and every reason is, without any comparison, inferior to the likeness of Him. From these things, I thought you could weigh the mind of my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> so that, namely <note>Original: "scilicet" (abbreviated as .f.).</note>, it cannot truly be said in this way: "God is God," as if by this name "God" acting as a <term>predicate</term><note>A predicate is the part of a sentence that says something about the subject. Here, the author argues that the word "God" cannot fully "explain" the subject "God."</note>, it might declare that which we strive to conceive through the subject. It is not that it cannot be said in *some* way that "God is God," just as it is said "God is good," "God is wise," and other <term>predications</term><note>Assertions or descriptions applied to a subject.</note> are granted with which the sacred books are full, in which something is enunciated about God in some manner. But His nature is not explained, since He stands at an infinite distance from those concepts: just as that uncle of mine quite clearly taught in the fifth chapter of the book *On Being and the One*, where he spoke not upon those words of **Dionysius** which **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> brings forward, as you supposed, but upon those which were cited a little earlier.

<margin>Damascene.</margin>
Furthermore, **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century Syrian monk and Church Father.</note> writes in the first book of the *Sentences* of his theology that there are certain things said affirmatively about God which have the power of a "super-excellent" negation. For the sake of a word, if we speak of "darkness" in God, we do not understand darkness, but rather that He is not light <note>Meaning He is not "light" in the limited way humans understand light.</note>. Indeed, we say He is "super-light" and "above light" when darkness is absent. This opinion the most learned and devoted former Chancellor <note>Referring to Jean Gerson, Chancellor of the University of Paris.</note> handles, saying:

<margin>Jean Gerson</margin>
Thus: "Whatever we say affirmatively about God includes some negation," and a little later he says that for this reason **Dionysius** denies that God is "being," but affirms that He is "super-being." **Giles** says that God is wise

<margin>Giles. Averroes.</margin>
in the first book of the *Sentences* <note>Referring to Giles of Rome (Egidius Romanus), a prominent medieval theologian.</note>, but not in that way of being "wise" which we understand. Hence he says this is the reason why **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note>, in the 12th book of the *Metaphysics*, pronounces that these predications which we attribute to God are similar to mathematical propositions; in their manner, the things which we understand are indeed in the things themselves, but not in the way that we understand them, just as we do not understand a line which is in matter by the same logic as the matter itself. But why should I delay you with many words when I can make you more certain of this truth we assert with even a few? Namely, that you may know that whatever we predicate of God signifies something far different than what we conceive and enunciate. **Jesus Christ** himself, 

<margin>Christ.</margin>
the power of God and the wisdom of God and the truth, says—witnessed by the Gospel of **John**—"God is a spirit." 

<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
**Dionysius**, in the book *On Mystical Theology*, speaking of God and contemplating the ineffable deity, removes many of those predicates which we attribute to Him, saying: "He is not even a spirit, insofar as we are able to know." See, therefore, that **Dionysius** does not wish "spirit" to be enunciated of God in the way that we can know it. Reading these final words teaches that it is true that God is a spirit, so that he might agree with Christ's Gospel, and yet He is not a spirit in the way we understand "spirit," lest we believe that the nature of God could truly be expressed by us through any name. Truly, how great the authority of **Dionysius** is, and how much his most sacred dogmas have been extolled and celebrated with praise by all theologians who have frequented the schools of Paris! Although I thought this was not hidden from you, yet when my uncle found in the responses to your objections that you did not very willingly admit **Dionysius's** sayings during the dispute, you should know that he was that most faithful disciple of the **Apostle Paul** in the faith of Christ. **Damascene** and many others have extolled him with the highest praises. <meta>This page continues the "Solution to the Eighteenth Objection" regarding the defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s work. The discussion focuses on the limits of human reason and language in describing the Divine. It transitions from a defense of Dionysius the Areopagite's authority to citations of classical philosophers like Apuleius and Themistius to prove that God is fundamentally "ineffable" (beyond words).</meta>

-># ON BEING AND THE ONE<-

<margin>Solution to the eighteenth objection.</margin>
...had committed to memory; for if **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a foundational figure for Christian mysticism who argued God is best described by what He is not.</note> had been held by more of the Fathers who fought great wars against the heretics and enemies of the most holy Catholic Church, they would have achieved a triumph over those enemies much more quickly and easily (which was later done by the same men only slowly and with great, exhausting labors).

But when you intend to prove that God can be called "God" because of the definition of the name which is predicated of the name, I say to you, my dear **Antonio** <note>Antonio Cittadini, the philosophical opponent to whom this defense is addressed.</note>, that you labor in vain. For you do not announce anything concerning God, but rather concerning this name "God." To be understood more clearly, I will explain this more broadly: for I will ask you what you conceive by "water" according to the definition of the name. If you conceive nothing, you do not err (to use the words of my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note>). If you do conceive something, I ask again if you conceive it as that of which something can be predicated. If in this way, you also do not err, because again that "something" will hold the place of the **subject** rather than the **predicate** <note>In logic, the subject is what we are talking about, and the predicate is what we say about it. The author argues we can name God as a subject, but no word we use as a predicate can fully encompass His nature.</note>. If you were to conceive that which is announced concerning Him, you would wander far astray, since God Himself is infinitely greater than all that you are able to conceive. 

<margin>Apuleius</margin>
Even the Platonist **Apuleius** <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and author. Though best known for *The Golden Ass*, he also wrote on Platonic philosophy.</note>, in his book *On the Dogma of Plato*, calls Him "unspoken" and "unnameable." The words of **Plato** himself on this matter were rendered into Latin by Apuleius: *To find God is indeed not easy; to understand Him is impossible.* <note>Original Latin: "Deum quidem invenisse haud facile est intellectu impossibile."</note> Therefore, let us say that all affirmations concerning God are improper, since whatever we wish not only to say but even to conceive, He exceeds it by infinity. Not only are we held in this earthly prison of ignorance and misery, but even in that very enjoyment of God by which we are perfectly blessed in the heavens, the faculty will be granted to us to **apprehend** <note>To "apprehend" means to reach out and touch or experience the reality of God.</note> God, but not to **comprehend** <note>To "comprehend" means to fully grasp or contain God within the mind—which the author argues is impossible for a finite creature.</note> Him (to use the words of our theologians).

Furthermore, you believe these propositions fight against one another: namely, "God is above that which can be conceived" and "nothing can be affirmed of God." And you say: "Let the definition of the name be 'above that which can be conceived,' and the argument will hold." But it is resolved: for when it is said that proper affirmations cannot be brought toward God, it is understood that no predicate is found that represents the nature of God in its integrity. Indeed, this statement—namely, "above that which can be conceived"—signifies nothing other than that God cannot be conceived and what God is cannot be known. Therefore, these words say not only what God is, but that it cannot be known what He is. Thus, they possess the power of **negating** rather than **affirming**. 

But although they may seem to affirm in that place, your argument will not hold for that reason. Otherwise, if someone wished to know about some unknown thing and asked us about its essence, and we were able to respond to the seeker: "It is that which we do not know, which we have not recognized, which we have not yet conceived in the mind, nor are we able to conceive," it would not seem that his request was satisfied. He would not be able, having received this teaching, to announce anything affirmatively about that thing, but only negatively. Unless, perhaps, someone were found who could intimate to others what that thing was, which—as it would be entirely unknown to men and above the grasp of all thoughts—could not be known or conceived even by himself. Thus, both **Simonides** <note>A Greek poet famous for his reply to Hiero of Syracuse; when asked "What is God?", he kept asking for more time to think, eventually concluding that the more he meditated, the more obscure the answer became.</note> and the Tyrant consulting him knew the greatest name of God that could represent Him, and yet one of them desired to know what God was, while the other denied that he knew.

Furthermore, you use such a connection: "God is above all that can be conceived, therefore God cannot be conceived; otherwise He would be above Himself; therefore He cannot be loved or worshipped." I respond: God can be conceived in His integrity only by Himself as He is, and by no other intellect. Nor does it follow from this that He cannot be loved or worshipped. For we conceive the Godhead to be so great, endowed with omnipotence, surpassing all creatures in every kind of virtue, that we cannot conceive Him except from His **effects** <note>We cannot see God's essence directly, but we can see what He has done in the world.</note>. Excited by this admiration and warmed, we burn with love for Him. We conceive the effects, and that He is the supreme good.

<margin>Themistius</margin>
We admire, and worship, and love: for having known these perfect things which God made (to use the words of **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher and rhetorician who commented extensively on Aristotle.</note>), He turns the minds and faces of all toward admiration and praise of Himself. Likewise, we read those things which have been divinely revealed, and being endowed with His grace, we conceive through faith that which...

<summary>The author argues that God is "ineffable" and beyond human comprehension, citing Plato, Apuleius, and Simonides to show that we can only know God through His effects and through negation. He refutes the idea that God's unknowability prevents Him from being loved or worshipped, suggesting instead that this mystery inspires deeper devotion.</summary>

## DEFENSE

...that which we cannot by our nature fully conceive—at least we ought to love Him above all things, so that finally, once the riddle of this flesh <note>original: "carnis enīgmate"; a reference to the veil of mortality or the "glass darkly" mentioned in 1 Corinthians 13:12.</note> is broken, we may contemplate Him as He is, to the highest joy of both the inner and outer man, which is our true happiness. Furthermore, for us to love something, it is not necessary that it be perfectly seen, known, or conceived by us; it is enough if we know that He exists, or is such a being, even if that knowledge is confused and obscure, derived either from faith or from His effects. Therefore, even a modest knowledge—whatever its quality—is enough for us to love such a thing. For we can love any thing at all, provided we are not entirely lacking in knowledge of it. For from those things <margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin> which the mind knows, it learns to love the unknown, as **Gregory** <note>Gregory of Rimini (c. 1300–1358), a prominent Scholastic theologian and philosopher.</note> says. **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> also, in the first part of the second book <note>The *Prima Secundae* of the Summa Theologica.</note>, proves that something can be loved perfectly even if it is not perfectly <margin>Thomas</margin> known, and he proposes God as an example of this, among other things.

<margin>Solution to the final objection</margin> Finally, you say that my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> thought the power of gold was so great that, whether we willed it or not, it would by necessity drag God along with it, either in reality or in the mind. But I would believe, my dear **Antonio**, that he did not think this was due to the power of gold, but rather its impotence <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "impotence" here refers to the lack of independent existence; gold cannot exist on its own.</note>; he was made certain that gold itself could neither exist nor be understood if God were removed. And although I could refer you to **John of Baconthorpe** <note>An English Carmelite philosopher (c. 1290–1347) known as the "Prince of Averroists."</note>, in whose <margin>John of Baconthorpe</margin> work we have already mentioned the dismantling of such a great objection, I will say this: when you recounted my uncle’s arguments—by which he had asserted that the statements "God does not exist" and "gold exists" are mutually contradictory—you said you did not wish to respond, lest you seem to be groping in the dark in a matter clearer than light. Yet it is my intention to show (perhaps even in your judgment) that it would have been worthwhile for you to undertake the dismantling of those arguments if you were able; or if not, at least to apply your hands to the work or frankly confess that his assertions were true. My uncle’s arguments are these, which I shall presently explain: It cannot happen that anything exists if **Being itself** <note>original: "ipsum esse"; the philosophical concept that God's essence is the very act of existing.</note> does not exist. But God is **Being itself**. Therefore, it cannot happen that gold exists if God does not exist. Furthermore, if God does not exist, then the **Infinite** exists. If the **Infinite** exists, then nothing exists; for if there is an **Infinite**, there is no **Finite**, because the **Infinite** destroys itself <note>original: "infinitū seipsum pímit" (likely *perimit*); the logic suggests that an unbounded "infinite" without the structure of God would result in a void where distinct finite things cannot exist.</note>, just as in other cases that involve a contradiction. If "nothing" exists, then gold does not exist. It cannot happen that anything exists if **Being itself**—which is God—does not exist, etc. Since **Being itself**, which is God (as no one denies), is not only that by whose participation all things that are exist, but all things also depend upon Him and are preserved at every moment, as all theologians—especially **Thomas**—teach most abundantly. <margin>Thomas, Plato</margin> But it was also asserted by **Plato** in the *Timaeus* that it is impossible for gold to exist except by the grace of **Being itself** and by participation in Him. Furthermore, if God does not exist, then the **Infinite** exists. All beings except God are finite and contained within certain limits. There is no doubt that they possess this limited nature by the work and grace of God. For this reason, the followers of **Plato** say that he called God "the Limit" in the *Philebus*, because He limits all things by distributing forms like measures everywhere. <margin>Plato. Book of Wisdom.</margin> And the *Book of Wisdom* also says that all things were established by Him in weight, number, and measure. If, therefore, God does not exist, by whose cause all things are finite, nothing will be finite; therefore, all is infinite. If the **Infinite** exists, nothing exists; for if the **Infinite** exists, the **Finite** does not exist, because the **Infinite** destroys itself, just as in other cases that involve a contradiction. Since it has been proven that there is one certain thing from which all things receive their existence, and that it is finite <note>The author argues created things are finite precisely because God limits them; without God's limiting power, they would lapse into a non-existent "infinite" chaos.</note>, with that thing removed, nothing exists and nothing is finite. For if it is "infinite," this means it is not limited or made finite by that First Principle by whose help all things both exist and are finished and bounded. It follows that the "infinite" does not exist. Therefore, the infinite destroys itself, since to say that the infinite exists (in the way it is taken here) is nothing other than saying that nothing exists; for if there is neither the finite nor God, it is beyond controversy that there is nothing at all. These, **Antonio**, are the things I have brought forward to grasp my uncle’s opinion, which perhaps contains other dogmas as well; for it is not for everyone to follow all that he had conceived. But I believe these meanings have remained hidden from others under the "bark" <note>A common metaphor for the literal or superficial meaning of words.</note> of the words. I am moved by the words with which he concluded his response: "These things, I believe, are enough for you, a man however talented; but let us leave the inaccessible things and hold to those which we have written while performing the duty of an interpreter." Since these things are satisfactory, they shall also close my response, after first bringing forward certain points that both strengthen my uncle’s opinion and my own in his defense...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s "De Ente et Uno" (On Being and the One). Having previously established that God is the source of all existence, the text now uses both Aristotelian logic and theological authority to prove that if God (the "First Cause") were removed, all truth and all existing things would necessarily vanish into nothingness. The page concludes with a personal letter from the scholar Antonio Faentino to Gianfrancesco Pico, acknowledging the defense and calling for an end to their public dispute.</meta>

# ON BEING AND THE ONE

<margin>Reasons to demonstrate the proposition from Aristotle.</margin>
The reasons for the words we previously offered in our interpretation confirm and clarify it equally. For when the First is lacking, it is necessary that all those things which proceed from it perish: as is gathered from the eighth book of **Aristotle’s** *Physics* <note>Aristotle’s *Physica*, a foundational work on the nature of change and motion.</note>. Furthermore, God—witnessed by the same philosopher—is the "First Truth": from whom all other true things exist. Therefore, if God is removed, it is necessary that all true things perish. But if truths tend toward nothingness, then beings <note>original: "entia"; things that exist.</note> are likewise not saved from destruction, since they move within an equal scope <note>This refers to the Scholastic doctrine that "Being" and "Truth" are convertible or co-extensive terms; whatever exists is true, and whatever is true exists.</note>.
Likewise, if one removes Him who communicates both existence and life to things, who would not see those very things as nothing but mere paintings?
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
That God grants this to the things themselves is the opinion of **Aristotle** in the first book of *On the Heavens*, where he adds that this existence is communicated more clearly to some and more obscurely to others. Furthermore, whatever is ruled by the art of the First Cause <note>The "First Cause" is a philosophical term for God as the ultimate origin of all effects.</note> falls if that Cause perishes. That this entire machine <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a structured system.</note> is governed and ruled by the First Cause is testified by
<margin>Averroes</margin>
**Averroes** <note>The influential 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note> in the second book of the *Metaphysics*, under which no one can doubt that all things are contained and grasped. I could bring many other things into the open from the sacred books, such as much from the Gospel itself, much from the most sacred dogmas of the Apostle **Paul**, and very many from others, such as from **Gregory** 
<margin>Gregory, Augustine, Thomas, John Scotus</margin>
who said that all things fall into nothingness unless they were preserved by Almighty God. Also from **Augustine** in his commentary on Genesis, from **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note>, and from **John Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Scholastic philosopher.</note> in his treatise *On the First Principle*. I deliberately pass over these, however, since it is enough to have proved it by the natural reasons which you seemed to demand, and by the teachings of the Gentile philosophers—which you did not believe could be proved by him at all.

Regarding all these things which we have prefaced, I would think that among good minds it will be beyond controversy that all my uncle's <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> opinions have been sufficiently defended, and perhaps even in your judgment. We wrote these things, however, not to fight with you; indeed, we wrote them unwillingly, as our **Giovanni Mainardo** <note>Giovanni Manardo (1462–1536), a famous physician and scholar from Ferrara.</note> and **Cristoforo Sassi** of Mirandola <margin>Ioannes Mainardus, Christophorus Saxolus.</margin>—our citizen, physician, and formerly your pupil—can testify. We also wrote without hatred, the greatest proof of which for you is that if you judge anything committed to these papers to be detracting from your honor in any part, I am ready to strike it out and remove it at your discretion before it passes into the hands of others. I would do this most gladly, since I love you as a man, observe you as a philosopher, and honor you as a Christian. If it should please you to put my soul's disposition toward you to the test, you will perceive that my deeds outweigh my words.

->To the illustrious prince and singular lord, Count Gianfrancesco, Antonio Faentino sends many greetings.<-

I have read the defenses sent to me regarding your uncle’s writings, in which I clearly perceived a great learning of things and an admirable skill of mind. I was wonderfully delighted by your discoveries, not only because I see that the liberal arts will finally have the best tutors and patrons by whom they may be rescued from darkness and barbarism, but even more because I easily promise myself something great and grand from you if you continue to philosophize. Posterity will see that I have told no lie if you live; may God only grant a longer life. As far as I am concerned, I certainly do not disapprove of the things you wrote subtly and sharply in defense of your uncle. For even if your uncle had lived, I would not have drawn out the already begun dispute any further, just as I clearly testified to him in my last opposition; he responded through a messenger that he too would write nothing further. Therefore, let those who read be the judges of the cause. But if you have decided that those things which you have carefully meditated upon should be given to the printers, let it be done with the honor of a friend safe and intact, as you promised. There are, however, some words in the booklet which have a bit of a sting, and not just a little; from these you can easily abstain if you wish, with the meaning of the things unchanged. If you do this, as I hope, it will not be ungrateful. I seem to myself to have protected my case sufficiently and abundantly, and could have easily continued to protect it day by day. But let there now be a limit to the disputation. For the rest, illustrious Count, I wish you to think of me as your own, now and always, to be used at your discretion. Farewell. From Ferrara, the 16th day of December, 1491.

# Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola to the distinguished philosopher Antonio Faentino. Warmest greetings.

**S**atisfaction <note>The original text begins with a decorative woodcut initial 'S'.</note> has been abundantly granted to your wishes; my promises to you have been fulfilled, as I have removed all words from our dictates that seemed to carry any sort of sting. One must restrain the impulse of the mind, even if at times it has acted more sharply than was proper. Something must be forgiven for the sake of a just defense—and all the more so since it is a common fault among those who, in their commentaries, either accuse someone or defend themselves or their friends, to pursue those to whom they write with insults, to attack them with slanders, to provoke them with reproaches, and to commit other such acts foreign to the duty of a good man. From these things (I appoint you as my witness and judge), we have entirely abstained; and at your hint, we have removed about ten stinging words, or thereabouts—though the meanings remain intact.

I would not wish you to believe there was any other purpose for laboring over this little commentary <term>commentatiuncula</term> <note>A modest term for a scholarly treatise or "small work of commentary."</note> than that we might defend my uncle Pico <note>original: "Picum patruum"; referring to the famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494).</note> without causing you offense. Indeed, I would have preferred that there had never been any dispute between you at all, so that every entrance to my writing on this matter would have been closed and every occasion removed. For the business of letters cannot be conducted, or can be only with the greatest difficulty, when it is placed in the midst of an altercation—even when all the honor otherwise due to those addressed is maintained during the writing. Add to this that one can hardly perform this duty without a certain swelling of the spirit <note>A reference to the sin of pride or intellectual arrogance.</note>, which must be avoided with great effort.

What you say regarding the protection of your own cause, we say regarding ours. But let there be an end to the controversy (as you rightly wrote); let those who read be the judges, provided they are learned and not biased toward either side—or, if they are held too ardently by love for either of us, let that love at least not cast a spell over their eyes.

Furthermore, you attribute much to me, perhaps more than I deserve, and you promise great things from me if only I continue to philosophize. But I fear, my dear Antonio, that I may grow entirely lukewarm toward this study of philosophy you mention, or perhaps even abandon it. I will tell you what I feel: that this business, to those of us who pursue it too eagerly, brings much harm and little benefit. I do not say this to condemn or disparage the many truths—or at least the likenesses of truth—which we acquire the knowledge of through philosophizing. Rather, I blame the common use or (to speak more significantly) the abuse of it. Unless we strive greatly to avoid this, and unless we examine our thoughts constantly and with the greatest diligence, ambition—the poison of the Christian soul—creeps into the heart, later giving birth to deadly pride.

From this it often happens that the lovers of this wisdom in which we are daily engaged—swollen and elated by fleeting glory—entirely neglect that Wisdom which is unbegotten but eternal, from which all this flowing and temporary wisdom is derived. But let us see, I pray, why we are so carried away in spirit; why we value ourselves too highly? For how small is our knowledge, since we possess the least science of natural things? And even those things of which we are ignorant—which are both many and great—silently cry out that we either profess or believe ourselves to be learned in vain and falsely. 

Undoubtedly, even an unrefined man, a little-skilled person, or a farmer entirely ignorant of letters, could ask many questions even about things placed before our sight and eyes, for which a philosopher, otherwise the greatest, would be unable to give a certain reason. Indeed, in perceiving the very substances that are entirely separated from sensible matter, how far do we proceed in our knowledge? Do we see them with anything but bleary eyes, or the eyes of a mind suited only for the night? <note>A common philosophical metaphor comparing human intellect to an owl's eyes: able to see in the "dark" of material things, but blinded by the "light" of divine truths.</note>

But what shall we say of divine things? Toward them, we direct our sight—not only to know them but even to track them down—gasping and anxious, yet blinking and dim-sighted, covered by almost the thickest clouds. Furthermore, have we not received this knowledge of ours either from books or from a teacher? What need is there, then, to boast? To have learned the meditations of others is as if we had drunk in a narrated history. But it is a history of nature, placed through diverse studies in bitter altercations, tossed about by various opinions, and for that reason, uncertain. This is most aptly revealed by the very name of "opinion": if anything...

I too will strive to do the same. Meanwhile, do not be reluctant to experience the love with which I regard you: perhaps I shall provide what you asked more abundantly than I promised at the end of the defense. For nothing is so difficult that I would not do it for the sake of more readily earning your favor (for you are truly a most serious philosopher).

->Gianfrancesco Pico of Mirandola, Count of Concordia, to the reader. Greetings.<-

Accept, reader, these "midnight labors" <term>lucubrationes</term> <note>Scholarly works produced by intensive study late into the night.</note> of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, works of lighter concern: which perhaps he himself would not have published while alive, nor would we have, had we not been stirred by the frequent encouragements of celebrated men. 

You will read first the most elegant *Oration*, dictated indeed with youthful alacrity but often admired by teachers for its height of learning and eloquence. Do not be troubled if many things are seen at its conclusion which are also inserted in the preface of the *Apology* <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico's defense of his 900 Theses which had been challenged by the Church.</note>; for while he published the latter abroad, he always kept the former at home, making it common only to his friends. You will see many of the secret doctrines of the ancients, previously hidden in riddles and the wings of fables, most ingeniously unlocked. You will see his effort to show, with both strength and oratorical charms, how the poetic theology of the ancient sages served the mysteries of our own theology; and, having untied the knots of both, he invites men to the "literary wrestling mats" <note>A metaphor for the public arenas of academic debate.</note>. 

In these pursuits he was most frequent during that time. Later, leaving behind these "playful battles" as if they were mere preludes to more serious studies, he turned his mind to the labor of those works which we have already released and those we shall release in the future. You will also read several letters (for it would be most laborious to collect them all), some familiar ones written both in his tender youth and in more mature years, others written after he dedicated his whole heart to God, filled with most holy advice. You will find that the former smell most copiously of learning and eloquence; the latter you will perceive to taste of both in abundance, and beyond this, to breathe most richly the love of Christ.

# THE ORATION OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA.

<margin>Note the great proposition of Abdala and Mercury.</margin>
**I** have read, most venerable fathers, in the records of the Arabs, that when Abdala the Saracen <note>likely referring to Abd Allah ibn al-Muqaffa, a famous 8th-century Persian/Arabic translator and thinker</note> was asked what he found most worthy of wonder on this world’s stage, he replied that nothing is more wonderful than man. This opinion is supported by that saying of Mercury <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic</note>: “A great miracle, O Asclepius, is man.” When I pondered the reason for these sayings, I was not entirely satisfied by the many arguments usually offered for the excellence of human nature: that man is the intermediary between creatures, the familiar of the higher beings, the king of the lower ones; by the sharpness of his senses, the inquiry of his reason, and the light of his intelligence, he is the interpreter of nature; the interval between stable eternity and flowing time, and (as the Persians say) the bond, or rather the marriage-song of the world, and—by David’s testimony—just a little lower than the angels.

<margin>The dignity of man</margin>
These reasons are great, indeed, but they are not the principal ones—that is, those which can rightly claim for themselves the privilege of the highest admiration. For why should we not admire the angels themselves and the most blessed choirs of heaven more? At last, I seemed to understand why man is the most fortunate animal and thus worthy of all admiration, and exactly what that condition is which he has been allotted in the order of the universe—a condition to be envied not only by the brutes but by the stars and even by minds beyond this world. It is a thing beyond belief and wonderful. And why not? For it is for this reason that man is rightly called and considered a great miracle and a truly admirable animal. But listen, fathers, to what this condition is, and grant me your attention with favorable ears, according to your kindness.

<margin>The constitution of the world</margin>
Now the Supreme Father, God the Architect, had already built this world-house we see—this most august temple of divinity—by the laws of His secret wisdom. He had adorned the super-celestial region with minds <note>referring to angels</note>; He had animated the celestial spheres with eternal souls; and He had filled the excrement-ridden and drossy parts of the lower world with a diverse crowd of animals of every kind. But, when the work was finished, the Craftsman desired that there be someone to weigh the reason of such a great work, to love its beauty, and to admire its magnitude. 

<margin>Moses and Timaeus</margin>
Therefore, when all things were already finished (as Moses and Timaeus <note>referring to Plato’s dialogue, the "Timaeus," which discusses the creation of the universe</note> testify), He finally thought about producing man. But there was nothing left in the archetypes from which He might fashion a new offspring, nor in His treasures what He might bestow as an inheritance upon a new son, nor in the seats of the whole world where this contemplator of the universe might sit. Everything was already full; all things had been distributed into the highest, middle, and lowest orders. 

<margin>The production of man</margin>
But it was not in the nature of the Supreme Power to have failed, as if exhausted, in His final birth; it was not in the nature of His Wisdom to have wavered for lack of a plan in a necessary matter. It was not in the nature of His beneficent Love that he who was to praise divine liberality in others should be forced to condemn it in himself. 

<margin>Free will in man</margin>
At last, the Best of Craftsmen decreed that to whom nothing of his own could be given, everything that was private to each individual should be common. Therefore, He took man as a work of indeterminate form and, placing him in the middle of the world, addressed him thus: 

<margin>From this, that migration of souls from bodies into bodies seems consistent with this opinion, as the Pythagoreans believed.</margin>
"We have given you, O Adam, no fixed seat, no form of your own, nor any peculiar gift, so that whatever seat, whatever form, whatever gifts you yourself shall desire, these you may have and possess according to your own wish and judgment. The nature of all other beings is limited and constrained within the laws prescribed by us. You, constrained by no limits, shall define your nature for yourself according to your own free will, in whose hand I have placed you. I have set you in the center of the world so that from there you may more easily gaze upon whatever is in the world. We have made you neither heavenly nor earthly, neither mortal nor immortal, so that as if you were your own free and honorable sculptor and molder, you may fashion yourself into whatever form you shall prefer. You shall be able to degenerate into the lower things, which are brutes; you shall be able to be reborn into the higher things, which are divine, according to the judgment of your mind."

<margin>Lucilius</margin>
O the supreme generosity of God the Father! O the highest and wonderful happiness of man! To whom it is granted to have what he chooses, to be what he wills. Brutes, at the moment of their birth, bring with them from their mother’s womb (as Lucilius <note>a Roman satirist</note> says) everything they will ever possess. The highest spirits <note>angels</note> were from the beginning, or soon after, what they will be for...

<summary>This page introduces the "Oration on the Dignity of Man," where Pico argues that man's unique excellence lies in his lack of a fixed nature. Unlike animals or angels, humans possess the free will to choose their own place in the cosmic hierarchy, whether descending to the level of beasts or ascending to the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's seminal argument on human nature. He has just explained that God gave man no fixed form or function, but rather the power to choose his own nature. This section explores the consequences of that freedom—how man can become a brute, a plant, an angel, or even unite with God.</meta>

...ty into perpetual eternities. Upon man, at his birth, the Father bestowed seeds of every sort and germs of every kind of life. Whichever of these each man cultivates will grow and bear their fruit in him. 

<margin>Note.</margin>
If they are vegetative, he will become a plant. If they are sensual, he will become brutish. If they are rational, he will turn into a heavenly being. If they are intellectual, he will be an angel and a son of God. And if, content with the lot of no creature, he withdraws into the center of his own unity, he will become one spirit with God, and in the solitary darkness of the Father—which is set above all things—he will surpass all.

<margin>Asclepius the Athenian.</margin>
Who would not admire this chameleon of ours? Or who would admire anything else more? Not without reason did Asclepius of Athens <note>Likely referring to the title character of the "Asclepius," a key text in the Hermetic tradition which Pico studied deeply</note> say that man was symbolized by Proteus <note>a Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will</note> in the mysteries, because of his changing and self-transforming nature. Hence those metamorphoses celebrated among the Hebrews and the Pythagoreans. For the more secret theology of the Hebrews transforms now the holy Enoch into an angel of divinity <note>The archangel Metatron</note>, <gloss>now into other things</gloss> and others into different divine beings. 

<margin>Empedocles Note.</margin>
And the Pythagoreans <note>followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed in the migration of souls</note> deform wicked men into brutes, and—if Empedocles <note>a pre-Socratic philosopher</note> is to be believed—even into plants. Imitating them, Muhammad <note>original: "Maumeth"</note> often had this on his lips: that he who falls away from divine law becomes a brute; and rightly so. 

<margin>Into what a man can be transformed</margin>
For it is not the bark that makes the plant, but its mindless and insensitive nature; not the hide that makes the beast of burden, but its irrational and sensual soul; not the spherical body that makes the heavens, but right reason; and it is not the separation from the body, but spiritual intelligence that makes an angel. For if you see someone crawling on the ground, devoted to his belly, it is a shrub you see, not a man. If you see someone blinded by the vain illusions of fantasy, as if by Calypso <note>the nymph from the Odyssey who detained Odysseus with charms</note>, and ensnared by enticing allurements, enslaved to his senses, it is a brute you see, not a man. If you venerate one who discerns all things by right reason, he is a heavenly animal, not a terrestrial one. If you see a pure contemplator, unaware of the body, withdrawn into the inner chambers of the mind, this is neither a terrestrial nor a heavenly animal; this is a more august divinity clothed in human flesh. 

Who would not admire man? Who is not undeservedly designated in the sacred Mosaic and Christian writings <note>the Bible</note> sometimes by the name "all flesh" and sometimes "every creature," since he fashions, fabricates, and transforms himself into the appearance of all flesh and the character of every creature. 

<margin>Evantes the Persian</margin>
Therefore, Evantes the Persian <note>a source Pico cites for Chaldean/Zoroastrian wisdom, possibly referring to a lost or apocryphal text</note>, where he explains Chaldean theology, writes that man has no image of his own that is native to him, but many that are foreign and adventitious. Hence that saying of the Chaldeans: 

-> that is, man is an animal of a varied, multiform, and self-dissolving nature <-

But to what end is all this? So that we understand that, having been born with this condition—that we may be whatever we want to be—we ought to take the greatest care that it is not said of us that, while we were in a place of honor, we did not realize we had become like the brutes and foolish beasts of burden. 

<margin>Asaph the prophet</margin>
But let us rather remember the saying of the prophet Asaph: "You are all gods and sons of the Most High" <note>Psalm 82:6</note>. Let us not abuse the most indulgent liberality of the Father, who gave us this free choice, lest we make the gift that was for our health harmful to us. Let a certain sacred ambition invade our soul, so that, not content with mediocrity, we pant for the highest things and strive with all our might to attain them (since we can, if we will). Let us disdain earthly things, despise the celestial, and finally, putting aside whatever belongs to the world, let us fly to the court beyond the world, closest to the most eminent divinity. 

<margin>The depiction of the super-celestial Choirs Note.</margin>
There, as the sacred mysteries relate, the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones <note>the three highest ranks of the celestial hierarchy of angels</note> hold the first places; let us, incapable of yielding and impatient of second place, emulate their dignity and glory. When we wish it, we shall be in no way inferior to them. But by what means, or by doing what? Let us see what they do, those who live that life. If we also live that life (and we can!), we shall already have equaled their lot. 

The Seraph burns with the fire of charity; the Cherub shines with the splendor of intelligence; the Throne stands with the firmness of judgment. Therefore, if dedicated to an active life, we undertake the care of lower things with right judgment, we shall be established with the steady solidity of the Thrones. If, being at leisure from actions, meditating on the Creator in his work and the work in the Creator, we occupy ourselves in the peace of contemplation, we shall glitter on all sides with Cherubic light. If we burn with love for the Creator alone, by his consuming fire we shall suddenly burst into flame in the likeness of a Seraph. God, the judge of the ages, sits upon the Throne—that is, the just judge. He flies above the Cherub—that is, the contemplator—and warms him as if by brooding over him. For the Spirit of the Lord...

<summary>Pico explains that man is a "chameleon" whose nature is determined by his will, allowing him to descend to the level of plants and beasts or ascend to the divine. He calls for a "sacred ambition" to emulate the highest angels—the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones—through love, contemplation, and justice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s "Oration on the Dignity of Man." Having established that humans have no fixed nature and can choose their own path, he now begins to argue that we should choose the highest path—imitating the celestial hierarchies (Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones) to achieve union with God.</meta>

<page-num>110</page-num>
->ORATIO<-

# ORATIO

<margin>That we can be placed above the celestial beings</margin>
The spirit of the Lord is moved almost "above the waters": those waters, I say, which are above the heavens, which in the book of Job praise the Lord with rhythmic hymns. The Seraph <note>The highest rank of angels, associated with fire and love</note>—that is, the lover—is in God, and God and he are one. We may attain the great power of the Thrones <note>The third rank of angels, associated with divine justice and stability</note> by judging, and the highest sublimity of the Seraphim by loving. But in what way can anyone either judge or love things that are unknown? Moses loved the God whom he saw, and he administered judgment among the people as a judge, based on those things which he had first seen as a contemplator on the mountain. Therefore, the middle rank, the Cherub <note>The second rank of angels, associated with wisdom and light</note>, prepares us with his light and the Seraphic fire, and equally illuminates us for the judgment of the Thrones. This is the knot of the ancient minds: the "Palladic" order <note>Referring to Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom; here, the order of wisdom or philosophy</note>, the presiding spirit of contemplative philosophy. This is what we must first emulate, desire, and eventually comprehend, so that we may be snatched up to the heights of love and descend well-instructed and prepared for the duties of action. But indeed, it is worth the effort—if our life is to be formed according to the model of the Cherubic life—to have before our eyes and ready at hand what that life is, what its nature is, and what its actions and works are. Since it is not permitted for us to attain this by ourselves—for we are flesh and savor the things of the earth—let us go to the ancient fathers. They can provide us with the most abundant and certain faith regarding these matters, as if they were their own household and kin. 

<margin>The elevation of Paul</margin>
Let us consult the Apostle Paul, the "chosen vessel," as to what he saw when he was elevated to the third heaven and witnessed the moving hosts of the Cherubim. He will surely answer, through his interpreter Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian whose works on the "Celestial Hierarchy" were a primary source for Pico</note>: they are first purged, then illuminated, and finally perfected. Therefore, we too, emulating the Cherubic life on earth—by restraining the impulses of our passions through **moral science**, and by dispersing the darkness of reason through **dialectic** <note>The art of logical argument and investigation of truth</note>—let us purge the soul, washing away, as it were, the filth of ignorance and vice. We do this so that our passions do not rage blindly, nor our imprudent reason occasionally wander into madness. Then, let us flood the well-composed and purified soul with the light of **natural philosophy**, so that finally we may be perfected by the divine knowledge of things. And lest we suffice for ourselves, let us consult the patriarch Jacob, 

<margin>Note</margin>
whose image shines sculpted on the seat of glory. That wisest father will advise us—he who sleeps in the lower world but watches in the upper world. But he will advise us through a figure (for all things happened to them in figures <note>original: "per figuram"; referring to the biblical practice of typology where Old Testament events foreshadow spiritual truths</note>) that there are scales <note>Jacob's Ladder</note> stretched from the lowest ground to the highest point of heaven, divided by a series of many steps, with the Lord sitting at the summit. The contemplating angels ascend and descend by these steps in alternating turns. If we, who aspire to the angelic life, must do this same thing, I ask: who would touch the ladder of the Lord with a dirty foot or with poorly cleansed hands? As the mysteries say, it is a sacrilege for the impure to touch the pure. 

<margin>The foot of the soul</margin>
But what are these feet? What are these hands? Surely the "foot" of the soul is that most despicable portion which rests upon matter as if on the soil of the earth—I mean the nourishing and feeding power, the fuel of lust and the teacher of voluptuous softness. 

<margin>The hand of the soul</margin>
Why should we not call the "hand" of the soul its irascibility <note>The spirited part of the soul that deals with anger and courage</note>, which fights as the champion of desire and snatches things away while toiling under the sun and dust? Let us wash these hands and these feet—that is, the entire sensual part in which the allurements of the body reside, and which (as they say) holds the soul by a twisted neck—in moral philosophy as if in a living stream, so that we are not rejected from the ladder as profane and polluted things. But even this will not be enough if we wish to be companions of the angels scurrying on Jacob’s ladder, unless we are first well-fitted and instructed to be promoted rightly from step to step, never to deviate from the path of the ladder, and to undertake the back-and-forth excursions. When we have attained this through the "sermocinal" <note>The arts of language: grammar, rhetoric, and logic</note> or rational art, already animated by the Cherubic spirit, philosophizing through the steps of nature and pervading all things from center to center, we shall now descend, tearing the "one" apart into a multitude with Titanic force—like Osiris <note>In Egyptian myth, the god Osiris was torn into pieces; Pico uses this as a metaphor for the philosophical analysis of a single truth into many parts</note>—and now we shall ascend, gathering the multitude, like the limbs of Osiris, into one by Phoebean <note>Solar/Apollo-like</note> power, until finally resting in the bosom of the Father who is above the ladder, we shall be consumed by theological happiness. Let us also question the just Job, who entered into a covenant with God before he himself entered into life. What does the highest God desire most among those ten hundred thousands who assist Him? He will surely answer: "Peace," according to what is read in his book: "He who makes peace in the high places." And because the middle order interprets the mandates of the highest order to the lower ones, let Job the theologian interpret for us...

<summary>Pico explains that humans can ascend the celestial hierarchy by purifying the soul through moral philosophy, illuminating it through logic and natural philosophy, and perfecting it through theology. He uses the metaphors of Jacob's Ladder and the myth of Osiris to describe the soul's journey toward divine unity.</summary>
