<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "Oration on the Dignity of Man." He has just finished describing how humans can emulate the celestial hierarchy (Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones). He now moves into the practical application of this by explaining how different branches of philosophy—Moral, Dialectic, Natural, and finally Theology—serve as stages of purification and ascent for the soul, drawing on the wisdom of Empedocles, the Greeks, and the Mosaic law.</meta>

->ORATIO<-

# ORATIO

<margin>Empedocles</margin>
The words of Empedocles the philosopher <note>original: "Empedocles phūs [physicus]"</note>: He indicates to us that a double nature is situated in our souls: by one we are raised upward toward celestial things; by the other, we are thrust downward toward the lower regions, through strife and friendship—or war and peace, as his poems testify. In these, he complains that he is tossed on the high sea, driven by strife and discord and a raging tide. Truly, there is a manifold discord within us; we have heavy and intestinal conflicts at home, and "wars more than civil." <note>A reference to Lucan's "Pharsalia," describing the Roman civil wars</note> If we do not wish for these, if we strive for that peace which raises us so high that we are established among the exalted of the Lord, philosophy alone will utterly restrain and calm them within us.

<margin>Discord within us, which must be calmed</margin>

<margin>First is Moral Philosophy, by which that [discord] is broken apart</margin>
First, if our "inner man" <note>The rational part of the soul</note> seeks at least a truce from his enemies, **Moral Philosophy** will restrain the unbridled rages of the many-headed beast <note>original: "multiplicis bruti"; a common Platonic metaphor for the appetites or passions</note> and the lion's brawls, angers, and high spirits. Then, if we take better counsel for ourselves and desire the security of perpetual peace, she will be present and generously fulfill our vows. Indeed, once both beasts have been slain—as if a sow were sacrificed <note>Refers to an ancient Roman ritual for sealing a treaty or peace (foedus)</note>—she will establish an inviolable treaty of most holy peace between the flesh and the spirit. **Dialectic** will calm the turmoils of reason as it anxiously struggles amidst the conflicts of discourse and the deceptions of syllogisms.

<margin>Second is Dialectic</margin>

**Natural Philosophy** will calm the strifes and disagreements of opinion which vex, distract, and tear the soul apart from every side. But she will calm them in such a way that she commands us to remember that nature, according to **Heraclitus**, was born of war, and for that reason was called "Strife" by **Homer**. Therefore, in natural philosophy, true rest and solid peace cannot be offered to us; this is the gift and privilege of her mistress, most holy **Theology**. 

<margin>Third is Natural Philosophy</margin>

<margin>Heraclitus, Homer</margin>
Theology will both show the way to that peace and lead us as a companion. Seeing us from afar as we hasten toward her, she will cry out: "Come unto me, you who labor; come, and I will refresh you; come unto me, and I will give you the peace which the world and nature cannot give you." <note>Pico is paraphrasing Matthew 11:28 and John 14:27</note> Summoned so gently and invited so kindly, flying with winged feet like "earthly Mercuries" into the embrace of our most blessed mother, we shall enjoy the longed-for peace: a most holy peace, an indivisible bond, a unanimous friendship, by which all souls not only agree in one Mind which is above every mind, but in an ineffable way become utterly one. 

<margin>The ultimate end of philosophy according to the Pythagoreans</margin>
This is that friendship which the **Pythagoreans** say is the end of all philosophy; this is that peace which God makes in His heavens, which the angels descending to earth announced to men of good will, so that through it, men themselves, ascending into heaven, might become angels. Let us wish for this peace for our friends, for our age, for every house we enter; let us wish it for our soul, that through it she might become the house of God. Thus, after she has shaken off her filth through **Moral Philosophy** and **Dialectic**, and has adorned herself with manifold philosophy as if with courtly splendor, and has crowned the gables of her doors with Theological garlands, the King of Glory may descend, and coming with the Father, make His dwelling with her. 

If she shows herself worthy of so great a guest—such is His immense clemency—she will be surrounded by a golden garment as if by a wedding gown, and with a manifold variety of colors. She will receive her beautiful guest no longer as a guest, but as her very self. From Him she will never wish to be separated; she will desire to be "dissolved" <note>An allusion to Philippians 1:23: "having a desire to depart [be dissolved] and be with Christ"</note> from her people and her father's house. Nay, forgetting herself, she will desire to die in herself that she might live in her Bridegroom, in whose sight the "death of His saints is precious" indeed—that death, I say, if it should be called death, which is the fullness of life, the meditation of which the sages said was the study of philosophy. 

Let us also cite **Moses** himself, who was made a little lower than the angels by the fount-like fullness of sacred and ineffable intelligence, from which the angels are inebriated with their own nectar. We shall hear the venerable judge proclaiming laws to us who dwell in the desert solitude of this body: 

<margin>As if proclaimed by Moses, the study of philosophy is to be embraced</margin>
"Those who are still polluted and in need of **Moral Philosophy** should dwell with the common people outside the tabernacle, under the open sky, like Thessalian priests <note>Pico likely refers to those undergoing preliminary purification before being allowed into sacred mysteries</note>, purifying themselves in the meantime. Those who have already composed their conduct, being received into the sanctuary, should not yet touch the sacred objects, but first as diligent Levites <note>The tribe of Israel responsible for assisting the priests and maintaining the Tabernacle</note>, they should serve the sacred rites of philosophy through the ministry of **Dialectic**. Then, having been admitted to these rites, they may contemplate now the multicolored—that is, the starry—courtly ornament of the palace of the higher God, now the celestial candelabrum distinct with seven lights, and now the skin-covered elements in the priesthood of philosophy. Thus, at last, through the merits of **Theological** sublimity, received into the inner recesses of the temple, with no image intervening..."

<summary>Pico outlines a hierarchical path to divine union, where moral philosophy, dialectic, and natural philosophy purify the soul of internal strife before Theology leads to a mystical "death" and union with God, paralleling the structure of the Mosaic Tabernacle.</summary>
<keywords>Empedocles, moral philosophy, dialectic, natural philosophy, theology, peace, mystical union, Pythagoras, Moses, Tabernacle, Heraclitus</keywords>

Now, he explains the progression from Moral and Dialectical philosophy into the higher "mysteries" of Natural Philosophy and, ultimately, Theology, using a blend of Mosaic, Platonic, and Pythagorean traditions.</meta>

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...through the intervening veil, they may enjoy the glory of divinity. These things Moses certainly commands us, and by commanding he admonishes, excites, and exhorts us that, through philosophy, we should prepare a way for ourselves toward future celestial glory while we are still able. Indeed, it is not only the Mosaic or Christian mysteries, but also the theology of the ancients that shows us the benefit and dignity of the liberal arts about which I am here to dispute. For what else do the levels of initiation mean in the 
<margin>Secrets of the Greeks</margin>
secrets of the Greeks? First, for those who had been purified through those arts which we might call "cleansing"—namely, Moral Philosophy and Dialectic—there followed the reception of the mysteries. And what else can this be but the interpretation of the more hidden parts of nature through philosophy? Then, at last, to those so prepared, there came the <term>Epoptia</term> <note>original: "εποπτεια"; in ancient Greek mystery religions, this was the final stage of initiation, a "direct seeing" or revelation of the sacred objects</note>, that is, the inspection of divine things through the light of theology.

Who would not long to be initiated into such sacred rites? Who would not desire, setting aside all human concerns, despising the goods of fortune, and neglecting the body, to become a guest of the gods while still living on earth, and, drenched in the nectar of eternity, to be gifted with the prize of immortality while still a mortal animal? Who would not wish to be so inspired by those "Socratic frenzies" sung by Plato in the *Phaedrus* <note>In this dialogue, Socrates discusses divine madness or "frenzy" as a way the soul recovers its wings to fly back to the divine</note>, that by the 
<margin>For Socrates is said to be the first of men to have brought Ethics down from heaven</margin>
rowing of wings and feet, he might swiftly flee from here—that is, from this world which is set in wickedness—and be carried in a most rapid course to the celestial Jerusalem? We shall be driven, fathers, we shall be driven by these Socratic frenzies, which so place us outside of our own minds that they place our minds and ourselves in God. We shall be driven by them indeed, if we have first done what is in our power. For if, through Moral Philosophy, the forces of our emotions have been so stretched through proper proportions to their correct measures that they harmonize with one another in an unshakeable consistency; and if, through Dialectic, our reason has moved toward its goal in rhythmic progression, then, stirred by the frenzy of the Muses, we shall drink in the celestial harmony with our innermost ears. 

Then Bacchus, the leader of the Muses, in his own mysteries—that is, in the visible signs of nature—showing the invisible things of God to us as we philosophize, will intoxicate us from the richness of the house of God. In this house, if we are faithful as Moses was, sacred Theology will approach and animate us with a double frenzy. For standing on that most eminent watchtower of sublimity, measuring from there all things that are, will be, and have been in the indivisible age <note>original: "insectili metientes æuo"; referring to eternity as a single moment that cannot be cut into past or future</note>, and gazing upon their primal beauty, we shall be the winged lovers of those Phoebian prophets <note>Apollo, often called Phoebus, was the god of prophecy and light</note>. And finally, stirred by an ineffable charity as if by a gadfly—like burning Seraphim—placed outside of ourselves and full of divine power, we shall no longer be ourselves, but rather He himself who made us.

The sacred names of Apollo, if anyone explores their meanings and the hidden mysteries they contain, show clearly enough that this god is no less a philosopher than a prophet. Since 
<margin>Ammonius</margin>
Ammonius <note>Likely referring to Ammonius Hermiae, a Neoplatonist commentator</note> has sufficiently followed this path, there is no reason for me to treat it differently now. But, fathers, let the three Delphic precepts 
<margin>Three Delphic precepts</margin>
command the soul, for they are exceedingly necessary for those who are about to enter the most holy and august temple of the true (not the feigned) Apollo, who illuminates every soul coming into this world. You will see that they admonish us to do nothing else but embrace with all our strength this tripartite philosophy about which we are now disputing. That famous saying, <term>Nothing in excess</term> <note>original: "Μηδεν αγαν"</note>, rightly prescribes the norm and rule of all virtues through the principle of the "Mean," which is the subject of Moral Philosophy. Then that saying, <term>Know thyself</term> <note>original: "γνωθι σεαυτον"</note>, excites and exhorts us to the knowledge of all nature, of which the nature of man is the connector and, as it were, the blend. For he who knows himself, knows all things in himself, as 
<margin>Zoroaster, Plato</margin>
Zoroaster first, and later Plato in the *Alcibiades*, have written. Finally, illuminated by this knowledge through natural philosophy, being already close to God, we shall address the true Apollo with the theological salutation "Thou art" <note>Pico is referencing Plutarch’s essay on the "E at Delphi," where the greeting "Ei" (Thou art) recognizes God’s eternal existence</note>, and thus we shall call upon him as friends and with success.

Let us also consult the most wise Pythagoras, who was especially wise because he never thought himself worthy of the name of a wise man. He will first command us: "Do not sit upon a bushel" <note>A Pythagorean "symbolon" or maxim</note>; that is, do not let that rational part by which the soul measures, judges, and examines all things, lose its edge through idle laziness. Rather, let us direct and stir it up constantly by the exercise and rule of Dialectic. Then he will indicate two things we must especially avoid: "not to urinate against the sun," and "not to cut our nails during a sacrifice." But after we have, through Moral Philosophy, passed out the flowing desires of overflowing pleasures, and have pruned the "growth of the nails"—that is, the sharp bits of...

<summary>Pico explains the soul's ascent through three stages: Moral/Dialectical purification, Natural Philosophy (the mysteries), and finally Theological revelation. He links these stages to Greek traditions, specifically the "Socratic frenzy," the Delphic precepts of Apollo, and the symbolic maxims of Pythagoras.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's discussion on the purification of the soul. He has just referenced the Greek "mysteries" and now moves into Pythagorean and Chaldean (Zoroastrian) imagery to explain how the soul ascends through different stages of knowledge—from moral discipline to the heights of theology.</meta>

<header>GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA</header>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...having pruned away the excesses of anger and the stings of the soul, only then may we participate in the sacred—that is, the mysteries of Bacchus <note>original: "bacchi myſteriis"; Pico uses Bacchus, the god of wine and ecstasy, to represent the divine frenzy or "holy drunkenness" of a soul filled with God.</note> of which we have made mention—and begin to devote ourselves to our contemplation, whose father and leader is rightly called the Sun.

<margin>See the multifaceted cleansing of the cock</margin>
Lastly, he will admonish us to nourish the cock—that is, to feed the divine part of our soul with the knowledge of divine things as if with solid food and heavenly ambrosia. This is the cock <note>original: "gallus"; in Pythagorean symbolism, the rooster represents the vigilant, divine spark within man that wakes up to the spiritual "dawn."</note> at whose sight the lion—that is, every earthly power—trembles and shows reverence. This is that cock to whom "understanding was given," as we read in the Book of Job. When this cock crows, the straying man regains his senses. This cock, in the morning twilight, daily harmonizes with the morning stars as they praise God. This is the cock that the dying Socrates—when he hoped he was about to join the divinity of his soul to the divinity of the greater world—said he owed to Aesculapius <note>original: "Aeſculapio"; the god of medicine. Socrates' final words were "Crito, we owe a cock to Aesculapius," often interpreted as a thanks for the "cure" of death.</note>, the physician of souls, now that he was placed beyond all danger of sickness. Let us also review the monuments of the Chaldeans, and we shall see (if they are believed) that the way to happiness is open to mortals through these same arts.

<margin>What Zoroaster's opinion was concerning the soul</margin>
The Chaldean interpreters write that it was a saying of Zoroaster that the soul is winged, and when the wings fall off, it is carried headlong into the body; then, when they grow back, it flies back up to the heights. When his disciples asked him how they might make their souls' wings flourish with well-plumed feathers, he said: "Water the wings with the waters of life." When they asked further where they might seek these waters, he answered them through a parable (which was the man's custom): "The paradise of God is washed and irrigated by four rivers." From there you may draw the waters of salvation for yourselves. The name of the one from the North denotes "the Right"; the one from the West signifies "Expiation"; the one from the East sounds of "Light"; and the one from the South we can interpret as "Piety."

Pay attention, Fathers, and consider diligently what these dogmas of Zoroaster mean: surely nothing else than that we should wash away the filth of our eyes with moral science, as if with western waves; then, with dialectic <note>The art of logical reasoning.</note> as if with a northern ruler, we should align our vision toward "the Right." Then, in natural contemplation, let us accustom ourselves to endure the still-weak light of truth, like the cradle of the rising sun, so that finally, through theological piety and the most sacred worship of God, we may—like celestial eagles—bravely endure the most brilliant radiance of the midday sun. These are those morning, midday, and evening cognitions first sung of by David and more widely explained by Augustine. This is that midday light which inflames the Seraphim <note>The highest rank of angels, associated with burning love.</note> to their very core and likewise illuminates the Cherubim <note>The second rank of angels, associated with divine wisdom.</note>; this is that region toward which our ancient father Abraham was always traveling.

<margin>Note: Jeremiah</margin>
This is that place where both the Kabbalists and the dogmas of the Moors <note>original: "Mauroꝝ"; referring to Islamic philosophers such as Averroes or Avicenna.</note> taught that there is no place for impure spirits. And if it is permitted to bring any secret mysteries into the public view, even under a riddle: after the sudden fall from heaven turned the head of our man into a dizzy whirl, and according to Jeremiah, "Death entered through the windows" and afflicted the liver and the heart, let us call upon Raphael <note>Raphael means "God heals" in Hebrew.</note>, the celestial physician. May he set us free through morality and dialectic as if with health-giving medicines. Then, when we are restored to good health, the strength of God, Gabriel <note>Gabriel means "Strength of God" in Hebrew.</note>, shall dwell in us. He will lead us through the miracles of nature, everywhere pointing out the virtue and power of God. Finally, he will hand us over to the High Priest Michael <note>Michael means "Who is like God?" in Hebrew.</note>, who will mark those who have served their time in philosophy with the priesthood of Theology, as if with a crown of precious stones.

<margin>The great weakness of our time is argued, which has always despised the study of philosophy</margin>
These are the things, most venerable Fathers, which have not only encouraged but compelled me to the study of philosophy. I certainly would not have said these things if I were not responding to those who are accustomed to condemn the study of philosophy, especially for princes or for those who live in moderate circumstances. For now (such is the unhappiness of our age), this whole pursuit is held in contempt and insult rather than honor and glory. This deadly and monstrous persuasion has invaded the minds of almost everyone: that one should philosophize either not at all or only a little. As if to have before our eyes and in our hands the exploration of the causes of things, the ways of nature, the reason of the universe, the counsels of God, and the mysteries of heaven and earth were a thing of no value. They think nothing is worthwhile unless they can either hunt for some favor or acquire profit for themselves. It has come to such a point—oh, the grief!—that they no longer consider anyone "wise" except those who make the study of wisdom a mercenary trade. One can see the modest Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom.</note>, who wanders among men as a gift of the gods...

...she <note>Philosophy</note> is cast out, exploded, and hissed at. She has no one to love her, no one to support her, unless she—as if receiving a meager reward for her hard-won virginity <note>original: "prestante et praestolatae virginitatis"; Pico uses the metaphor of a woman who has preserved her virtue but receives only a pittance, suggesting philosophy is undervalued by those who seek only profit.</note>—brings back a tiny, poorly gained chest from her lover. <margin>Note</margin>

It is as if they do not show by this very fact that they are not philosophers. Since their whole life is placed either in gain or in ambition, they do not embrace the knowledge of truth for its own sake. I will grant this to myself, and I will not blush to praise myself in this regard: I have never philosophized for any other reason than to be a philosopher; nor from my studies or my late-night labors have I ever hoped for or sought any other reward or fruit than the cultivation of my soul and the knowledge of the truth I have always so greatly desired. I have always been so greedy for this truth and so deeply in love with it that, leaving behind all care for private and public affairs, I gave myself entirely to the leisure of contemplation. From this path, no slanders of the envious, no insults from the enemies of wisdom, have been able to deter me in the past, nor will they be able to deter me in the future. Philosophy herself has taught me to depend upon my own conscience rather than on

# ORATION

If you take away these encounters—these battles—all philosophy will become drowsy and dormant. But truly, with those who say I am unequal to this task <note>original: "provinciae imparem"; Pico uses the word "province" in the Roman sense of a specific duty or office assigned to a person.</note>, the path of my defense is more difficult. For if I say I am equal to it, I may be seen as immodest and thinking too highly of myself; if I confess I am unequal, I seem likely to be branded as reckless and ill-advised. See the narrow straits into which I have fallen, the position in which I am placed: I cannot promise things about myself without fault, yet I cannot soon fail to provide them without fault as well. Perhaps I could bring forward that word of Job: "the spirit is in all people" <note>Job 32:8</note>, and hear with Timothy: "let no one despise your youth" <note>1 Timothy 4:12</note>. But from my own conscience, I will more truly say this: there is nothing in us that is great or singular. I do not deny 
<margin>See in what manner he defends himself</margin> 
that I am perhaps studious and eager for the noble arts, but I neither take nor claim for myself the name of a "learned man." Therefore, as for why I have placed such a heavy burden on my shoulders, it was not because I was unaware of my own weakness. Rather, it was because I knew that in this kind of battle—that is, literary ones—it is a peculiar feature that there is profit in being defeated. Because of this, even the weakest person not only can, but rightly should, seek them out of his own accord. For he who yields receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury; he returns home richer, that is, more learned, and better prepared for future battles. Encouraged by this hope, I, a weak soldier, did not fear to decide upon such a heavy battle with the strongest and most vigorous of all men. Whether this was done recklessly or not can be judged more rightly by the outcome of the battle than by my age. 

It remains for me, in the third place, to respond to those who are offended by the sheer number of proposed topics, as if this burden rested on their shoulders and the labor—however great it may be—was not instead to be exhausted by me alone. It is truly indecent and excessively grumpy to wish to set a limit on another person’s industry. As Cicero says, 
<margin>Cicero</margin> 
in a matter which is "the better the greater it is," one should not desire "mediocrity" <note>Cicero, *De Finibus*. Pico argues that intellectual inquiry is a pursuit where "the more, the better," and thus should not be restricted by the usual Greek ideal of "moderation."</note>. In such grand attempts, it was necessary for me either to fail or to satisfy the requirement. If I satisfy it, I do not see why what is praiseworthy to perform in ten questions should be considered blameworthy to have performed in nine hundred. If I should fail, those who hate me will have a reason to accuse me, and those who love me will have a reason to excuse me. Since in a matter so heavy and so great, undertaken with thin talent and meager learning, it will be more worthy to grant a young man pardon than to bring an accusation. Indeed, as the poet says, "if the strength fails, the daring will certainly be a credit; in great things, even to have willed is enough" <note>Propertius II.10.6</note>. But if in our age 
<margin>An excuse for the multitude of conclusions</margin> 
many have imitated <term>Gorgias of Leontini</term> <note>A famous Greek Sophist (c. 483–375 BC) who claimed he could answer any question on any subject.</note> and have been accustomed—not without praise—to propose a dispute not just on nine hundred, but on all questions of all arts, why should I not be allowed (even without blame) to dispute on many topics, yet topics that are certain and determined? 

But they say this is superfluous and ambitious. I contend, however, that this was done by me not in a superfluous way, but necessarily. If they themselves would consider the method of philosophizing with me, they would be forced to admit it, even against their will. 
<margin>This multifaceted collection of sects can be seen at the front of the book of questions, where this same point is repeated from here until the end of this speech.</margin> 
For those who have devoted themselves to any one of the families of philosophers—such as <term>Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas, the giant of Dominican Scholasticism.</note> or <term>Scotus</term> <note>John Duns Scotus, the influential Franciscan theologian.</note>, who are now most often in the hands of students—can indeed put their own learning to the test in a discussion of even a few questions. But I have so trained myself that, sworn to the words of no single master, I have poured myself through all the masters of philosophy, examined every page, and recognized every family. Therefore, since I had to speak regarding all of them, I would have seemed bound to one if, as a defender of a private dogma, I had neglected the rest. Even if they had proposed only a few items regarding each school, the things being brought forward regarding all of them together could not help but be very many. And let no one condemn me for being "carried as a guest wherever the storm takes me" <note>Horace, *Epistles* I.1.15. Pico turns a potential criticism of inconsistency into a virtue of intellectual openness.</note>. For this was observed by all the ancients: that in rolling through every kind of writer, they passed over no commentaries they could read. This was done especially by <term>Aristotle</term>, who for that reason was called the <term>Reader</term> <note>original: "anagnostes"</note> by <term>Plato</term>. Truly, it is a mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single Porch <note>The Stoa, referring to the Stoics.</note> or Academy. Nor can one rightly choose a path for oneself from among all of them if one has not first become familiarly acquainted with them all. Add to this that in each school...

In every single family <note>By "family," Pico means a school of philosophical thought.</note> there is something distinguished that is not shared with the others. And to begin now with our own thinkers, to whom philosophy most recently arrived: In **John Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major High Scholastic theologian known for his complex "Subtle" style.</note> there is something vigorous and analytical. In **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the "Angelic Doctor," known for the clarity and systematic nature of his work.</note> there is a solid and balanced quality. In **Giles** <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316).</note> there is a polished and exact style. In **Francis** <note>Francis of Mayrone (c. 1280–1328).</note> it is sharp and keen. In **Albert** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), the teacher of Aquinas.</note> we find the ancient, the ample, and the grand. In **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293).</note>, as it has always seemed to me, there is something sublime and venerable. Among the Arabs: in **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Spanish-Muslim philosopher who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> there is something firm and unshaken. In **Avempace** and **Al-Farabi**, it is serious and thoughtful. In **Avicenna**, it is divine and Platonic. Among the Greeks, philosophy is generally clean and pure: In **Simplicius**, it is rich and abundant. In **Themistius**, it is elegant and concise. In **Alexander**, it is consistent and learned. In **Theophrastus**, it is weightily elaborated. In **Ammonius**, it is smooth and pleasing. And if you turn to the **Platonists**, to review but a few: In **Porphyry**, you will be delighted by a wealth of material and diverse religion. In **Iamblichus**, you will venerate a more hidden philosophy and the mysteries of the barbarians <note>In the Renaissance, "barbarian" often referred to ancient non-Greek cultures like the Egyptians, Chaldeans, or Hebrews, whom Pico believed possessed primeval wisdom.</note>. In **Plotinus**, there is nothing in particular to admire because he offers himself as admirable from every side; the sweating Platonists <note>A famous reference to the difficulty of understanding Plotinus, whose prose is notoriously dense and "oblique."</note> can hardly understand him when he speaks in his learned, indirect way—divinely about divine things and far above human reach regarding human things. I pass over the more recent ones: **Proclus**, flourishing with Asiatic fertility <note>A term for a rich, flowery rhetorical style.</note>, and those who flowed from him: **Damascius**, **Olympiodorus**, and many others, in all of whom that "divine" <note>original: "to theion"; the Greek term for the divine nature.</note> quality, the specific mark of the Platonists, always shines. It must be added that if there is any sect that attacks truer dogmas and mocks good causes with clever slander, it actually strengthens the truth rather than weakening it; it stirs up the flame as if by movement, rather than extinguishing it. Moved by this reasoning, I wished to bring into the open the opinions not of just one school (as some preferred), but of every kind of doctrine. I did this so that, through this comparison of many sects and the

<margin>

What would it be if only the Latin thinkers—namely **Albert**, **Thomas**, **Scotus**, **Giles**, **Francis**, and **Henry**—were studied, while the treatises of the Greek and Arab philosophers were omitted? For all wisdom flowed from the barbarians to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to us. Thus our own thinkers have always considered it enough to stand by foreign discoveries in their way of philosophizing and to cultivate the ideas of others. <meta>This page continues Pico’s discussion of the various philosophical schools. He is moving from a general appreciation of different traditions toward his own specific project of synthesis—reconciling seemingly contradictory thinkers like Plato and Aristotle, and introducing his own unique "dogmas" and his system of "philosophizing through numbers."</meta>

->ORATION<-

...those who have attempted to prove through their most subtle disputations that the philosophies of **Plato** and **Aristotle** are the same. **John the Grammarian** <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), a Byzantine philosopher and scientist.</note> likewise says that Plato and Aristotle only seem to disagree to those who do not understand Plato’s words; nevertheless, he left the proof of this to posterity. We have also added several points where we assert that the opinions of **Scotus** and **Thomas**, and several where those of **Averroes** and **Avicenna**, which are considered discordant, are in fact in agreement.

<margin>Note</margin>

In the second place, we have set down the things we ourselves have thought out in both Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, as well as **seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas**. If someone holds to these, they will be able—unless I am mistaken, which will soon be made clear—to resolve any proposed question concerning natural and divine matters by a far different reasoning than that taught to us by the philosophy read in the schools and cultivated by the doctors of this age. 

<margin>Note on the number of Pico’s dogmas</margin>

Nor should anyone wonder, Fathers, that in my first years, in a tender age at which it was hardly permitted (as some boast) for me to read the commentaries of others, I should wish to bring forth a new philosophy—as if I were either praising it if it is defended, or condemning it if it is rejected—and finally, when they are to judge these findings of ours and our writings, they should count not the years of the author, but rather the merits or demerits of the works themselves.

<margin>A new method of philosophizing through numbers: Plato</margin>

Furthermore, there is another new method of philosophizing through numbers which we have introduced. It is indeed an ancient one, observed by the **Ancient Theologians**, especially by **Pythagoras**, by **Aglaophemus**, by **Philolaus**, by **Plato**, and by the earlier **Platonists**. But in this day and age, like other noble things, it has grown so obsolete through the neglect of later generations that hardly any traces of it can be found. **Plato** writes in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato, serving as an appendix to the *Laws*.</note> that among all the liberal arts and contemplative sciences, the most principal and most divine is the science of numbering. Likewise, seeking to know why man is the wisest animal, he answers: because he knows how to count. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

**Aristotle** also mentions this opinion in his *Problems*. **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a leading Persian astronomer/astrologer.</note> writes that it was a saying of **Avenzoar the Babylonian** <note>Likely referring to a Babylonian sage or a misattribution of the Andalusian physician Avenzoar.</note> that he who knew how to count knew all things. These sayings cannot be true in any way if by the "art of numbering" they understood that art in which merchants are now primarily most skilled; Plato also testifies to this, warning us with an uplifted voice not to understand this "divine arithmetic" to be the "merchant's arithmetic." Having therefore, after many sleepless nights, explored that arithmetic which is so highly extolled, I have publicly promised that I will respond through numbers to **seventy-four questions** which are considered principal among physical and divine matters.

<margin>Pico’s expertise in magical theorems is not obscure</margin>

We have also proposed **magical theorems**, in which we have indicated that magic is of two kinds. One of these consists entirely of the work and authority of demons—by my faith <note>original: "medius fidius," a Roman oath.</note>, a thing to be cursed and monstrous. The other, when well explored, is nothing other than the absolute consummation of **Natural Philosophy**. When the Greeks mention both, they do not deign to call the former by the name of magic, but term it *Goeteia* <note>original: "γοητείαν" (goēteia); meaning sorcery or black magic.</note>. The latter, they call by the proper and peculiar name of *Mageia* <note>original: "μαγείαν" (mageian); meaning the wisdom of the Magi.</note>, as if it were the perfect and highest wisdom. For as **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305) who wrote on the history of philosophy and religion.</note> says, in the language of the Persians, "Magus" means the same as what we call an "interpreter and worshiper of divine things." 

<margin>In the question of magic and Cabala, see more points.</margin>

There is, however, a great—no, the greatest—disparity and dissimilarity between these arts. Not only the Christian religion, but all laws and every well-ordered republic condemns and curses the former; but all wise men and all nations studious of celestial and divine things approve and embrace the latter. The former is the most fraudulent of arts; the latter is a deeper and holier philosophy. The former is vain and empty; the latter is firm, faithful, and solid. Whoever cultivated the former always concealed it, because it would bring ignominy and insult upon the author; but from the latter, the highest clarity and glory of letters has been sought of old, and almost always. No man who was a philosopher and eager to learn the good arts was ever a student of the former; but to learn the latter, **Pythagoras**, **Empedocles**, **Democritus**, and **Plato** traveled across the seas. This they preached upon their return, and held it as the chief among their secrets. Just as the former is proven by no reasons, so it is supported by no certain authors; the latter, however, is honored by the most illustrious fathers...

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...honored [with this name], has two primary authors: **Zalmoxis** <note>A legendary social and religious reformer of the Getae, often mentioned by Greek writers as a student of Pythagoras or a shamanistic figure.</note>, whom **Abaris the Hyperborean** imitated, and **Zoroaster**—not the one you perhaps believe, but that son of **Oromasius**. If we ask **Plato** what the magic of each is, he will answer in the *Alcibiades* that the magic of Zoroaster is nothing other than the science of divine things, in which the kings of the Persians educated their sons, so that they might learn to rule their own commonwealth according to the model of the commonwealth of the universe. He will answer in the *Charmides* that the magic of Zalmoxis is the medicine of the soul, through which temperance is produced in the soul, just as health is acquired for the body through it. In their footsteps later followed **Charondas**, **Damigeron**, **Apollonius**, **Hostanes**, and **Dardanus**. **Homer** also persisted in this; we shall one day prove in our *Poetic Theology* that he, like all other forms of wisdom, also disguised this one under the wanderings of his **Ulysses**. **Eudoxus** and **Hermippus** persisted in it. Almost all who have searched into the Pythagorean and Platonic mysteries have persisted in it. Among the more recent men who have caught the scent of it, I find three: **al-Kindi** the Arab <note>Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi (c. 801–873), known as the "Philosopher of the Arabs."</note>, **Roger Bacon**, and **William of Auvergne**. **Plotinus** also mentions it, where he demonstrates that the magus is the minister of nature and not its artifice. This most wise man approves and asserts this magic, while so abhorring the other <note>Pico is distinguishing between "Natural Magic"—the study of the hidden powers of nature—and "Goetia" or black magic/sorcery.</note> that when he was called to the rites of evil demons, he said it was more right that they should come to him than he to them—and rightly so. For as that first kind of magic makes man a subject and a slave to wicked powers, so this second kind makes him their prince and master. Finally, that first kind can claim for itself the name of neither art nor science; this kind, full of the highest mysteries, embraces the deepest contemplation of the most secret things, and ultimately the knowledge of all nature. This magic, calling forth into the light as if from hiding places the virtues sown in the world and scattered by the favor of God, does not so much perform miracles as it zealously serves nature as she performs them. Having more searchingly probed the harmony of the universe—which the Greeks more significantly call *sympathy* <note>original: "σ’υμ πα θειαν" (sympatheia), the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and "feel" together.</note>—and having looked into the mutual knowledge of natures, applying to each thing its own inherent attractions (which the magi call *iynxes* <note>original: "ἴυγγεϛ" (iynges), referring to "charms" or "wheels" used to draw down celestial influences.</note>), it brings forth into the public eye, as if it were itself the artisan, the miracles hidden in the recesses of the world, in the lap of nature, and in the storehouses and secrets of God. And just as the farmer marries the elms to the vines, so the magus marries the earth to heaven—that is, the lower things to the endowments and virtues of the higher. Wherefore it happens that as the former magic appears monstrous and harmful, so this latter appears divine and salutary. This is chiefly because the former, by subjecting man to the enemies of God, calls him away from God; but this latter excites in him an admiration for the works of God, 
<margin>Note</margin>
from which a ready charity, faith, and hope most certainly follow. For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the persistent contemplation of the wonders of God. When we have well explored these through this natural magic of which we are treating, we, being more ardently animated to the worship and love of the Creator, shall be compelled to sing: "The heavens are full, all the earth is full of the majesty of your glory." <note>A reference to the *Sanctus* in the liturgy, based on Isaiah 6:3.</note> And this is enough regarding magic, about which I have said these things because I know there are many who, just as dogs always bark at strangers, so they too often condemn and hate what they do not understand. 

I come now to those things which, unearthed from the ancient mysteries of the Hebrews, I have brought forward to confirm the most holy and Catholic faith. Lest these things should perhaps be thought by those to whom they are unknown to be fabricated trifles or the stories of charlatans, I want all to understand what and of what kind they are, from where they are sought, by which and how famous authors they are confirmed, and how recondite, how divine, and how necessary they are to our men for defending religion against the persistent calumnies of the Hebrews. Not only famous Hebrew doctors write of this, but also from among our own, **Ezra**, **Hilary**, and **Origen**: 
<margin>Doctors of the Hebrews</margin>
that **Moses** received on the mountain from God not only the Law, which he left recorded for posterity in five books, but also a more secret and true explanation of the Law. It was commanded to him by God that he should indeed make the Law public to the people, but that he should neither commit the interpretation of the Law to writing nor make it common knowledge. Rather, he himself should reveal it only to **Joshua**, and he then in turn to the others who succeeded as heads of the priests, with a great religious duty of silence. It was enough to recognize through the simple history now the power of God, now his wrath against the wicked, his mercy toward the good, and his justice toward all...

<summary>Pico distinguishes between "natural magic," which harmonizes the earthly and divine through the study of nature, and "goetia" or sorcery. He then introduces the Kabbalah as an oral tradition given to Moses on Sinai, essential for a deeper understanding of the Law and for defending Christianity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's transition from discussing natural magic to the Hebrew mystical tradition known as the Kabbalah. He justifies his use of these "secret" sources by arguing that all great spiritual traditions—from the Pythagoreans to the early Christians—purposely hid their deepest truths from the uneducated masses to protect them from desecration.</meta>

# ORATION

...to know; and to be instructed by divine and health-giving precepts for the purpose of living well and blessedly, and for the worship of the true religion. But to make public to the common people the more secret mysteries and the secrets of the highest divinity hidden under the "bark" of the law and the rough pretext of words—what else was that than to "give what is holy to dogs" and to "scatter pearls among swine"? <note>Pico quotes Matthew 7:6 to justify the tradition of keeping religious secrets away from those who might disrespect or misunderstand them.</note> Therefore, it was a matter of divine command, not merely human counsel, to keep these things hidden from the common crowd and to communicate them only to the "perfect," among whom **Paul** says he speaks a wisdom that is not of this world.

<margin>This same thing is said at the front of the Heptaplus of Plato</margin> <note>Pico likely refers to the preface of his own work, the *Heptaplus* (1489), where he discusses the esoteric meanings of the Creation story in Genesis, linking it to Platonic thought.</note>

The ancient Philosophers observed this custom most holily. **Pythagoras** wrote nothing except a few trifles which, as he was dying, he entrusted to his daughter **Dama**. The **sphinges** carved on the portals of Egyptian temples warned that mystical doctrines should be kept inviolate from the profane multitude through the "knots" of enigmas. **Plato**, writing to **Dion** regarding the supreme substances, said: "One must speak through enigmas, so that if the letter should by chance come into the hands of others, what we write to you might not be understood by them." <note>A reference to the *Second Letter* attributed to Plato.</note> **Aristotle** used to say that his books on *Metaphysics*, in which he treats divine matters, were "published and yet not published." <note>Aristotle reportedly told Alexander the Great that although his lectures were published, they were incomprehensible to those who had not heard his oral explanations.</note>

<margin>Jesus Christ</margin>

**Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) who believed the Bible had deeper, allegorical meanings beyond the literal text.</note> asserts that **Jesus Christ**, the master of life, revealed many more things to his disciples than they were willing to write down, lest they become common to the crowd. 

<margin>Origen</margin>

This is most strongly confirmed by **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A Christian theologian of the late 5th century whose writings on "mystical theology" were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note>, who says that the more secret mysteries were transmitted from the authors of our religion

<margin>Dionysius</margin>

<margin>Kabbalah</margin>

"from soul to soul," <term>without the mediation of letters</term> through the intervening word. He says they were "poured across" in this same way; and when that true interpretation of the Law given to **Moses** by God was revealed, it was called the **Kabbalah**—which is the same among the Hebrews as our word for "reception." <note>The Hebrew word *Kabbalah* (קַבָּלָה) literally means "receiving" or "tradition."</note> This is because one man received that doctrine from another, not through written monuments, but by an orderly succession of revelations, as if by a right of inheritance.

However, after the Hebrews were restored from the **Babylonian captivity** through **Cyrus**, and the temple was restored under **Zerubbabel**, they turned their minds to repairing the Law. **Ezra**, then the head of the Church, after correcting the book of Moses, clearly recognized that through the exiles, slaughters, flights, and captivity of the Israelite people, the custom established by the ancestors of handing down the doctrine by hand could not be preserved. It would happen that the secrets of celestial doctrine granted to them by God would perish—for their memory could not last long without the intervention of written commentaries. He decreed that the wise men who then remained should be called together, and each should bring into the open what he held by memory concerning the mysteries of the Law; and with scribes employed, these were reduced into **seventy volumes**. (For there were roughly that many wise men in the **Sanhedrin**).

<margin>Ezra</margin>

Concerning this matter, do not believe me alone, Fathers; hear **Ezra** himself speaking thus: "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: 'The first things you wrote, set in public: let the worthy and unworthy read them: but the last seventy books you shall preserve so that you may hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding and the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge.' And thus I did." <note>Quoting from the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) 14:44–47.</note> These are the words of Ezra to the letter. These are the books of the science of the **Kabbalah**. In these books, Ezra rightly proclaimed with a clear voice that there is a "vein of understanding"—that is, an ineffable **Theology** concerning the supersubstantial deity; a "fountain of wisdom"—that is, an exact **Metaphysics** concerning intelligible and angelic forms; and a "river of knowledge"—that is, a most firm **Philosophy** concerning natural things.

<margin>Sixtus IV / Innocent VIII</margin>

**Pope Sixtus IV**, who immediately preceded this **Innocent VIII** under whom we happily live, took the greatest care and zeal so that these books might be translated into Latin for the public benefit of our faith. And already when he died, three of them had reached the Latins. These books are cherished among the Hebrews in this time with such great religious awe that it is not permitted for anyone to touch them unless they are forty years old. I have prepared these books for myself at no small expense. When I had read through them with the greatest diligence and untiring labor, I saw in them (God is my witness) a religion not so much Mosaic as Christian. There is the mystery of the **Trinity**, there the **incarnation of the Word**, there the **divinity of the Messiah**; there I found information concerning **original sin**, its expiation through **Christ**, the heavenly **Jerusalem**, the fall of the demons, the orders of **angels**, and concerning purgatory and the...

<summary>Pico explains the origins of the Kabbalah as a secret oral tradition given to Moses and later recorded by Ezra, arguing that these Hebrew texts actually contain the core mysteries of Christian theology.</summary>
<keywords>Kabbalah, Ezra, Moses, secret wisdom, esoteric tradition, Sixtus IV, Origen, Dionysius the Areopagite, Christian Hebraism</keywords>

--- Page 228 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico's famous defense of his 900 Theses. He is finishing his argument that the Hebrew Kabbalah and the "ancient theology" of the Greeks and Persians (Orpheus, Zoroaster, Pythagoras) are fundamentally in agreement with Christian doctrine. He then transitions into the first book of his personal correspondence, beginning with a letter to his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico.</meta>

...penalties. I read the same things there that we read daily in **Paul** and **Dionysius**, in **Jerome** and **Augustine**. But in those matters which look toward philosophy, you would hear **Pythagoras** and **Plato** directly, whose decrees are so close to the Christian faith that our **Augustine** gives immense thanks to God that the books of the Platonists came into his hands. In short, there is almost no controversy between us and the Hebrews concerning any matter, about which they cannot be so refuted and convicted out of the books of the Kabbalists <note>The Kabbalah is a tradition of Jewish mysticism. Pico was one of the first Christian scholars to argue that it contained hidden proofs of Christian dogmas like the Trinity.</note> that not even a remaining corner is left for them to hide in. Of this thing, I have a most serious witness: **Antonio Chronico**, a most learned man, who with his own ears heard—when I was with him at a banquet—the Hebrew **Dactylus**, <note>Likely a reference to a Jewish scholar or convert skilled in these "secret" sciences.</note> skilled in this science, descend "with hands and feet" <note>original: "pedibus manibusque descendere" — a Latin idiom meaning to agree or commit entirely and enthusiastically.</note> into the Christian opinion concerning the Trinity. 

But to return to the chapters of my disputation: we have also brought our own opinion regarding the interpretation of the poems of **Orpheus** and **Zoroaster**. Orpheus is read almost complete among the Greeks; Zoroaster is mutilated among them, but among the Chaldeans <note>Here referring to the Neo-Babylonian or Persian traditions.</note> he is read more fully. Both are believed to be the fathers and authors of ancient wisdom. For—not to mention **Zoroaster**, of whom frequent mention is made among the Platonists, always with the highest veneration—

<margin>**Iamblichus** of Chalcis regarding **Pythagoras**.</margin>

**Iamblichus** of Chalcis <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the life and teachings of Pythagoras.</note> writes that **Pythagoras** had Orphic theology as a model, according to which he shaped and formed his own philosophy. For this reason, they say the sayings of **Pythagoras** are called "sacred" only because they flowed from the institutions of **Orpheus**; from there came the secret doctrine of numbers and whatever great and sublime thing Greek philosophy possessed, as if flowing from a primary source. But (as was the custom of the ancient theologians), **Orpheus** so wove the mysteries of his dogmas into the "wrappings" of fables and disguised them with a poetic veil, that if anyone reads his hymns, they would believe nothing lies beneath except the most unmixed trifles and nonsense. 

I wanted to say this so it may be known what labor and difficulty it was for me: to pull out the hidden senses of secret philosophy from the affected thickets of enigmas and the hiding places of fables—especially in a matter so grave, so hidden, and unexplored, without the help and diligence of other interpreters. And yet my "dogs" <note>Pico's term for his critics and detractors.</note> barked that I had accumulated certain minor and light things for a show of number—as if I had not brought many things to these very people who carp at my work (and who believe themselves the princes of philosophers) that were previously unknown and unattempted. I am so far from that fault that I took care to compress the disputation into as few chapters as I could. If I had wished (as others are accustomed) to divide it into its own members and tear it into shreds, the number would surely have grown to an infinite count. To say nothing of the others, who is there who does not know that one single dogma from the nine hundred—namely, the one concerning the reconciliation of the philosophy of **Plato** and **Aristotle**—I could have deduced into six hundred chapters (if not more) without any suspicion of "affected numbering," by enumerating one by one all the points where others think they disagree but I believe they agree? 

But I will say it certainly (though neither modestly nor according to my character), I will say it nevertheless: because my envy and my detractors force me to say it. I wanted to prove in this meeting of mine, not so much that I know many things, but that I know things which many do not know. 

To make this now openly clear to you in the matter itself, most worshipful Fathers, and so that my long speech does not further delay your desire, most excellent Doctors—whom I see with great pleasure prepared and girded, waiting for the contest—may it be happy and auspicious; let us now, if it is permitted, join hands in battle. 

END.

# THE LETTERS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...and the deceitful world and the evil demon would cease to be, or as if you were not still in the flesh, which desires against the spirit <note>original: "concupiscit aduersus spiritum" — a reference to Galatians 5:17, describing the internal conflict between physical desires and spiritual life.</note>; and unless we look out watchfully for our salvation, that alluring world deforms those drunk on Circean cups <note>A reference to the sorceress Circe from Homer's *Odyssey*, who turned men into swine with a magical drink; Pico uses it as a metaphor for how worldly pleasures strip humans of their reason and dignity.</note> into the monstrous appearances of beasts. But James the Apostle <margin>James</margin> affirms that you should rejoice, writing: "Rejoice, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations." <note>James 1:2.</note> And not without reason: for what hope of glory can there be if there is no hope of victory? Or what place can there be for victory where there is no battle? He is called to a crown who is provoked to battle, and especially to that battle in which no one can be conquered against his will; nor do we need any other strengths to conquer than that we ourselves wish to conquer. 

<margin>The happiness of a Christian is to be noted</margin> **Great is the happiness of a Christian**, since victory is placed in his own judgment, and the future rewards will be greater than every wish and every expectation of the victor. Tell me, I pray, dearest son, is there anything in this life among those things for which lust agitates earthly minds, for the obtaining of which many labors must not first be undergone, and many unworthy and wretched things endured? A merchant thinks it has gone well for him if, after ten years of sailing, after a thousand inconveniences and a thousand dangers to his life, he has acquired a slightly more abundant wealth for himself. Regarding military service, clearly there is nothing for me to write to you, whose miseries experience itself has taught and continues to teach you sufficiently. In earning the favor of princes, in reconciling the friendships of equals, or in seeking honors, what a mass of troubles, how much anxiety, how much intense worry there is! I could rather learn this from you than teach it to you—I who, content with my books and my leisure since I was a boy, have learned to live within my fortune, and as much as I can, dwelling within myself, I sigh for or desire nothing outside myself. 

Therefore, these earthly things—fleeting, uncertain, vile, and common to us with the beasts—we shall scarcely attain even by sweating and panting; yet toward the heavenly and divine things, which "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered the heart," <note>1 Corinthians 2:9.</note> we are drawn by God as if drowsy, sleeping, and almost against our will—as if without us either God could not reign or those heavenly citizens could not be blessed. Truly, if earthly happiness were provided for us while we were idle, someone refusing labor might choose to serve the world poorly rather than God. But if we are weary no less in the way of God—nay, far more in the way of sinners, from whence comes that cry of the damned: "We are wearied in the way of iniquity" <note>Wisdom of Solomon 5:7.</note>—it cannot but be the height of madness to be unwilling to labor there where one goes from labor to reward, rather than where one goes from labor to punishment. 

<margin>Expression of the passions</margin> I pass over how great is that peace, how great the happiness of a soul conscious of no wrong and growing pale at no fault; which undoubtedly far outweighs all the pleasures that can be possessed or desired in life. For what is desirable in the pleasures of the world? While they are sought, they weary; when they are acquired, they infatuate; when they are lost, they torment. Do you doubt, son, that their minds are agitated by perpetual cares? It is the word of God, which can neither be deceived nor deceive: "The heart of the wicked is like a raging sea that cannot rest." <note>Isaiah 57:20.</note> For nothing is safe for them, nothing is peaceful; all things threaten fear, all things threaten cares, all things threaten death. Shall we then envy these? Shall we emulate them? And, forgetting our own dignity, forgetting our own heavenly Father, shall we who were born free voluntarily make ourselves slaves of these? And living wretchedly together with them, and dying more wretchedly, shall we at last be afflicted by eternal fires? 

<margin>Exclamation</margin> O blind minds of men, O blind hearts! That they do not see, even clearer than light, that all these things are truer than truth itself; yet we do not do what we know ought to be done; but up to this point, we desire in vain to pull our foot out of the mire. Countless obstacles will meet you, my son—doubt not—especially in those places where you live, at every single hour, which may deter you from your purpose of living holily and well, and unless you take care, drive you headlong. But among all things, that pestilence is most fatal: to dwell day and night among those whose life is not only in every part an enticement to sin, but is entirely set upon the destruction of virtue; serving under the commander the devil, under the banners of death, under the wages of hell, it campaigns against heaven, against the Lord, and against his Christ. 

<margin>The saying of the Prophet</margin> You, however, cry out with the Prophet:
> "Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast away their yoke from us." <note>Psalm 2:3.</note>

...against them. For these are they whom God handed over to passions of ignominy and to a reprobate sense, so that they do those things which are not fitting, full of all iniquity, full of envy, homicides, contention, deceit, and malice; detractors, hateful to God, insulting, proud, puffed up, inventors of evil, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy <note>This entire list is a direct quotation from Romans 1:26–31, where St. Paul describes the moral decay of those who abandon God.</note>. Who, although they see the justice of God daily, do not understand; yet since those who do such things are worthy of death, not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those doing them. You, therefore, son, do not wish to please those whom virtue itself displeases. But let that word of the Apostle <margin>The Apostle</margin> always be before your eyes: *that one must please God more than men* <note>Acts 5:29.</note>; and that other: *If I were to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ* <note>Galatians 1:10.</note>. Let a certain holy ambition invade you, and may you disdain to have those as masters of your life who rather stand in need of you as a teacher. For it is far more becoming that they themselves, by living well with you, begin to be men, than that you should wish, through the omission of your good purpose, to become shamefully brutish with them.

A kind of ecstasy and stupor sometimes takes hold of me (God is my witness) when I begin to consider the pursuits of men—or as I should say, the goals of their insanity <margin>Note</margin>. I know not whether to think rather than to grieve, or whether to wonder or to deplore. For truly it is a great insanity not to believe the Gospel, whose truth the blood of the martyrs cries out, the apostolic voices resound, miracles prove, reason confirms, the world testifies, the elements speak, and demons confess. But it is a far greater insanity if, while you do not doubt the truth of the Gospel, you nevertheless live as if you did not doubt its falsehood. For if those things are true—that it is most difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven—why do we pant daily for the accumulation of riches? And if it is true that glory should be sought not from men, but that which is from God, why do we always depend on the judgments of men?

There is no one who cares to please God. And if there is a firm faith in us that the Lord will one day say: *Go, you cursed ones, into eternal fire*, and again, *Come, you blessed ones, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world*, why do we fear nothing less than hell <note>original: "gehēnnā"</note>, or hope for nothing less than the kingdom of God? What else can we say than that there are many Christians in name, but in reality very few. You, indeed, son, strive to enter through the narrow gate, and do not attend to what the many do; but what ought to be done, the law of nature itself, reason itself, and God himself will show you. For your glory will not be less if you are happy with the few, nor will your punishment be lighter if you are miserable with the many. 

Moreover, there will be two especially effective remedies <margin>Two remedies</margin> for you against the world and Satan, by which you may be lifted on high from the vale of tears as if by two wings: namely, <term>almsgiving</term> <note>Acts of charity or giving to the poor.</note> and prayer. For what can we do without the help of God? Or how will He help if He is not invoked? But certainly He will not hear you when you invoke Him, you who previously did not listen to the poor man when he invoked you. For it is not fitting that God should not despise you, a man, when you, a man, have previously despised a man. It is written: *In what measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you*; and elsewhere: *Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.* 

But when I invite you to prayer, I do not invite you to that which consists of much speaking, but that which, in the secret retreat of the mind, in the inner chambers of the soul, speaks to God with the heart's own affection. And in the most lucid darkness <note>original: "lucidissima... tenebra" — Pico refers to a concept from mystical theology where the presence of God is so bright it appears as "darkness" to the limited human intellect.</note> of the highest contemplation, it does not just present the mind to God, but unites it by certain ineffable modes, which only those who have experienced them know. Nor do I care how long your prayer is, but how effective, how burning; interrupted rather by sighs than spread out in a certain perpetual series of words and rhythmic numbers <margin>The manner of prayer</margin>. If your salvation is at heart, be safe from the snares of the devil, from the storms of the world, from the ambushes of enemies. 

If you desire to be pleasing to God and finally happy, let no day pass in which you do not approach your God through prayer at least once; and prostrate before Him with the humble affection of a pious mind, cry out—not from the tips of your lips, but from the depths of your heart—with the Prophet: *The sins of my youth and my ignorances remember not; but according to your mercy, remember me for your goodness' sake, O Lord* <note>Psalm 25:7.</note>. The Spirit himself, who intercedes for us, as well as necessity itself at every hour, will suggest to you what you should ask from your God. Sacred reading will also suggest it; I ask you again and again that, having now set aside the fables and trifles of the poets, you always have it in your hands. You can do nothing more pleasing to God, nothing more useful to yourself, than if you do not cease to turn over the sacred letters with your hand by night and by day. For there lies hidden in them a celestial...

But I have already exceeded the limits of a letter, as the material itself draws me on, along with a wonderful charity which I have always felt for you, especially from that hour when I was informed of your most holy purpose. Finally, I would wish you to be admonished of that which I often spoke of with you even when you were here with me: that you do not forget these two things: both that the Son of God died for you, and that you also, even if you live long, are shortly to die. With these as twin spurs—one of fear, the other of love—urge your horse through the short racecourse of this momentary life toward the rewards of eternal happiness, since we neither ought nor can set any other end for ourselves than that we may enjoy the infinite good without end in the perpetual peace of both the inner and outer man. Farewell. And fear God. May 15, 1492.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Filippo Beroaldo, Greetings. II.

I received from you, most learned Beroaldo, a letter both amiable and erudite, and many verses that undoubtedly challenge antiquity itself. This was a most welcome gift to me. Therefore, because of you, I have spent my leisure hours well in good business; I could not have spent them more pleasantly or more honorably in any other thing. I would truly act as a very ungrateful man if I wished to repay your excellent things with my own, which are the worst, and to exchange the poisons of Suffenus for Catullian wit <note>Suffenus was a poet famously mocked by the Roman poet Catullus for being a charming man who wrote terrible poetry. Pico is self-deprecatingly comparing his own work to Suffenus'.</note>. For I am no better in poetic style, except perhaps in this: that I recognize myself to be a Suffenus, and I see "what is in the bag on my back" <note>An allusion to Aesop's fable that people carry their own faults in a bag on their back where they cannot see them, while seeing the faults of others in a bag in front of them.</note>. Nevertheless, you demand that I give you something of my own writings. And you demand it so that, in asking, you seem unlikely to bear a refusal with a calm mind. Therefore, I must satisfy you, even at the cost of whatever reputation I have with you. Take, therefore, two letters: one to Lorenzo de' Medici, the other to Ermolao <note>Ermolao Barbaro, a famous humanist scholar.</note> on the style of philosophers. To these I have added certain verses which escaped me during these days while I was doing other things. You will read these in such a way as to remember that in these humanistic studies I am engaged with hurried care and in stolen moments, as I have applied my primary effort and "burned the midnight oil" <term>lucernas | literally "lamps," a common idiom for late-night study</term> (as they say) seriously to philosophy. Among those philosophers, if I have achieved what you have among the rhetoricians and poets—among whom (I speak from the heart) I see no reason why you should not rightly claim the first place. Your Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano, the renowned scholar and friend to both Pico and Lorenzo.</note> is entirely yours; he loves you as much as anyone can. Regarding me, you can promise yourself anything I can do. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Lorenzo de' Medici, Health and Hearty Greetings. III.

I have read, Lorenzo de' Medici, your verses which the vernacular Muse suggested to you in your tender age. I recognized the Muses and the Graces—a legitimate offspring—but I did not recognize the work of a tender age. For who would not perceive the Graces dancing to the numbers in your verses and their harmonious connection? Who would not hear the Muses singing in your melodious and modulated style? Who—in that unforced charm, cheerful wit, honeyed humor, fitting enticements, wonderful brilliance, prudent arrangement, and the weightiest meanings drawn from the innermost shrines of philosophy—would recognize a young man? I know certainly that I am not on this list <note>original: "in hoc albo," referring to a white tablet or register of names.</note> of judges, nor am I one to ascend to the judgment of kings. But I would wish it were possible to say what I feel about them without suspicion of flattery. I would say indeed that there is no ancient writer whom you do not surpass by a long interval in this genre of speaking. Lest you think this is said to curry favor, I will bring you my reasons for this opinion. There are among you two especially celebrated poets of the Florentine tongue: Francesco Petrarch and Dante Alighieri. Of whom I should first say generally: there are those among the learned who find substance lacking in Francesco [Petrarch] and words lacking in Dante. In you, whoever has a mind and ears finds nothing lacking. In you, one cannot see whether the substance is more illustrated by the speech or the words by the ideas. But let us weigh the merits of each one individually, as if on a balance scale. Indeed, if Francesco were to return to life, regarding the meanings, who doubts he would willingly "give you the herb" <note>original: "herbam tibi datu[m]." To "give the herb" is an ancient Roman idiom for admitting defeat or yielding the victory to another.</note>? So sharp, always grave, and subtle are you; he, however, is mostly from the common...

# BOOK ONE

Seizing for the most part the middle ground, he colors his sentiments with words and makes common things extraordinary by his style of speaking, in which we may see what he provides to you, and what you provide to him; in certain parts he may have appeared sweeter. But to me, his sweetness—if I may say so—strikes me as "sweetly" and "pleasantly austere." He is expansive and smoothly soothing. You, by your majesty and a certain lively light of speech, seize the minds of your audience. In him, there is an ambitious and excessive diligence; in you, a diligence that is neglected rather than affected. He is restrained and soft; you are masculine and muscular. He is fluent and tuneful; you are concise and full, but you are more vigorous. In him, there is something one might prune away; in you, nothing is redundant and nothing is cut short. But perhaps I was a bit bold to say that something should be removed from him. It is certainly so in the eyes of many whose judgment I trust. For in my own view, it is often possible to see him erring as the <term>Asiatics</term> <note>original: "asiatíci." Referring to "Asianism," a rhetorical style characterized by florid, ornate, and often excessive ornamentation, contrasted with the simpler "Attic" style.</note> used to err: inserting words as if to fill up cracks, and employing full and neat voices not to adorn the work, but to support it, like <term>flute-players</term> <note>original: "tíbicínes." A reference to a common rhetorical metaphor where unnecessary words act like the props or flute-players that keep a theatrical performance moving even when the substance is lacking.</note> so the song does not limp. In you, all words are no less necessary to the matter than they are pleasing in their ornament, so that whoever takes away from you, mutilates the work; but whoever shears from him, merely cleanses it. And even if we grant (which I never will) that the things he wrote are more charming and more elegant than yours, it was easy for a man to excel when he faced no struggle or battle with the senses themselves. But those sharp and subtle "Laurentian" <note>original: "laurétianae." Referring to the works of Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> sentiments of yours—to use two words—it can scarcely be said how they reject the <term>curling-irons</term> <note>original: "calamíſtros." A metaphor for artificial or overly-refined rhetorical embellishments.</note> and do not willingly admit those dyes; if he had handled these matters—he whom we read as soft, shining, and pleasant—we would surely read him as thorny, squalid, and unpleasant. For we see that whenever he attempts something sharp, involved, or knotty, he falls as much in style as he rises in thought. But when he displays that furniture of his words, his ointments, curls, and flowers, 
<margin>Castricius</margin>
<note>Titus Castricius was a teacher of rhetoric in the 2nd century AD, known for his critiques of overly rhythmic or "round" oratory.</note> Castricius—if he were present—would often warn, as he warned in the case of Gracchus: let us not be deceived by the rounded sound and the flow of the verses. Rather, we should inspect what lies beneath: what seat, what firmament, what foundation there is to the words. If you do this, you might see something as empty as Epicurus's <term>void</term>; either no sense lies beneath, or it is cold and trivial. In that part which is the greatest—and if you do not excel him there—I do not see at all why he should excel you in the grace of speaking. Since words cannot be more illustrious than they are with you, 
<margin>Note</margin>
and the arrangement of them is so fit that they could not cohere better, nor flow more roundly, nor fall more rhythmically in any way. 

But now let us weigh Dante with you, about whom perhaps more people are likely to make a controversy. For there are many who, in the comparison of writers, do not so much weigh merits as count years; they command others to read the ancients with reverence, while they themselves cannot read their contemporaries without envy. Certainly, as far as style is concerned, I think no one will deny you the prize; for Dante is sometimes so horrid, harsh, and lean, that he seems quite crude and unpolished—even his own admirers admit this. But they cast the blame upon his age and that century; certainly, you are more refined in speech, and he is not more grand. Yet in his sentiments, he is vastly more grand and sublime. I ask you: what wonder is it that he speaks of physical things, with nature itself compelling this and providing an abundance of sentiments? If he treats of God, of the soul, or of the blessed, he brings forward what Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> and Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo.</note> wrote of these things. 
<margin>Note</margin>
And he was as frequent as he was assiduous in treating and meditating upon these; whereas you are occupied in the conduct of the greatest public and private affairs. It was not so much a matter of praise for Dante to have done this well, as it would have been a disgrace not to have done it. But it was, without doubt, the work of a supreme genius—which you yourself provide—to make physical things out of those which are amatory, and to make those which are somewhat austere in their severity lovable by the introduction of <term>Venus</term> <note>original: "uenere." Meaning charm, grace, or the theme of love.</note>. Thus in your words, serious matters are so well mixed with the playfulness of lovers that the latter gain dignity from the former, and the former gain cheerfulness and grace from the latter; so that both, by this coupling, have both retained what was their own and shared themselves with each other, so that both possess individually what were previously the shared traits of both. But this is not so much to be admired as that which moved me most: these things were introduced by you not as if brought from outside, but as if dug out from the bosom of the material itself about which you treat; and from that very soil, as if you were irrigating it, they bloom...
