# OF THE LETTERS

...they seem to be born, appearing natural, not acquired; necessary, not merely brought in; entirely genuine, not grafted. This is what I cannot sufficiently admire: how you seem to me to have surpassed Dante. For even if he flies sublimely, he is lifted by the wings of his subject matter; you, even when the subject resists and pulls you down, are raised on high by the wings of your genius. And you are raised in such a way that you do not leave the subject behind, but carry it up with you, deserving as much from the subject itself as the subject once deserved from Dante. Now one may see what the difference is between you and Francesco <note>referring to Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374)</note> and Dante. To this I would add that Francesco sometimes does not live up to his promises, having that which attracts at first glance but does not satisfy further. Dante has that which sometimes offends at the first encounter, but it is more pleasing to penetrate his inner depths. Your works have no less in their depths to hold the reader than they have on the surface to captivate them. Add to this that they wrote their poetry in seclusion, in the shade, and in the greatest tranquility of study; you sang yours amidst tumult, the noise of the court, the shouts of the marketplace, the greatest cares, and the most turbulent storms of a very busy life. For them, the Muses were their ordinary and principal business; for you, they are a game and a certain relaxation from cares. For them, it was the height of exhaustion; for you, a rest when exhausted. Finally, by relaxing your mind, you reached that point which they, perhaps, did not reach even while straining every nerve of the soul. But what shall I say of "my" <term>paraphrase</term>? <note>original: "paraphrasi." Pico refers to Lorenzo’s "Comento de' miei sonetti," a philosophical commentary Lorenzo wrote on his own poems.</note> For why should it not be called mine by right of title? Why should it not be mine, since even if I venerate it as yours, I love it as my own? I admire it indeed, and you in it; from this I gather how much I wandered from the true praise of your verses, in which there were many great and illustrious things that I, with the eyes of a night-owl, had not looked into. I then saw them revealed by you, which only you could and should have done: you owed it to yourself and to us, lest you defraud yourself of much glory and us of much pleasure. I read it (God is my witness), most excellent Lorenzo, not so much for delight as for learning. For how many things are there from Ari-

<margin>
Aristotle
Plato
</margin>
-stotle, specifically from the *Physics*, from the books *On the Soul*, *On Ethics*, *On the Heavens*, and from the *Problems*? How many from Plato’s *Protagoras*, from the *Republic*, the *Laws*, and the *Symposium*? All these things, even if I have read them elsewhere in those authors, I read in your work as if they were new, as if they were better, and transformed by you into a certain form that makes them seem yours rather than theirs; and in reading, I feel I am learning something. This is the greatest proof

<margin>Note.</margin>
that you know these things not so much from a commentary as from within yourself. For many are accustomed to put more effort into their letters than into their deeds, and when they are about to write, they treat philosophers like <term>advocates</term> <note>original: "pragmaticos." In this context, it refers to professional legal assistants who supplied speakers with facts or precedents.</note> who suggest dogmas to them, which they then thrust into their little books to appear as philosophers. But you can easily catch them out. For you see those points are neither rightly arranged nor coherent, and not explained by the authors themselves, but rather entangled. Men who are otherwise eloquent appear like infants when speaking of those matters. But who would not see that you do not hold these things on loan, but as if you have the right and power to turn, move, and handle them at your will? You (O happy genius!) attained these things in the heat of the Republic and in an active life—things that we, who are not disciples of philosophers but merely lodgers in a life of shadows and sedentary study, pursue rather than attain. But what shall I say of the most sweet style of your paraphrase? It seems to me entirely like that of

<margin>Caesar</margin>
Caesar in the Latin language. For it is a speech not manufactured, not gilded, not twisted, but upright by its own nature, clear and solid; neither running out rashly but keeping its pace; neither luxurious nor meager, neither wanton nor unpleasant; sweetly serious, seriously lovely. The words are chosen and not hunted for, illustrious and not faked, necessary and not <insert>affected</insert>, not merely explaining the matter but placing it before the eyes. I pass over how you always remember your own character, and how seeds and traces of that wisdom of yours are scattered everywhere. These things I and many others have noted, and each has seen even better qualities. But two things in particular I saw besides these, which perhaps not many, even the sharp-eyed, might see. The first is how it conceals its own riches, so that it may avoid envy; it keeps its flowers in its bosom and does not show them off; it does not rise up on its toes but settles naturally so as to appear lesser. The other thing is—I do not quite see it, for I am not so skillful—but I see there is "something," if I may say so, that is most distinctively "Laurentian." For if anyone should see the gifts, the genius, and the excellence of Lorenzo, he would see the whole Lorenzo.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Ermolao Barbaro. Greetings. Letter IIII.

**I** indeed, my dear Ermolao, am neither able to keep silent about what I feel concerning you, nor am I able not to feel those things which ought to be felt about a man in whom all virtues are found in the highest degree, as if they were individual qualities. But would that I possessed such a grasp of mind that I could perceive your merits as they deserve; would that I had such power of speech that I might one day express what I always feel. I know that the conceptions I have formed of you fall infinitely below the heights of your learning. And you should know that whatever we say is far less than what we conceive; know that words are as lacking to the soul as the soul is lacking to the reality of things. And yet, do you believe I would dare so much as to hope I could imitate your works, whose greatness I cannot even estimate? All can admire you; so few can imitate you that no one can find fault. And would that I had such good fortune that the things I write might, in some part, reflect the image of my Ermolao. For, to say nothing of the rest, your very style—which you yourself favor so little—affects me wonderfully: how much it delights me! It is so learned, grave, composed, erudite, polished, and ingenious; in it, nothing is left unrefined, nothing is trivial, whether you look at the words or the meanings. Often I and our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the famous humanist poet and scholar</note> read whatever letters of yours we have, whether addressed to others or to us. Thus the following letters always compete with the previous ones, and new graces bloom fruitfully while reading, so that we have no room to catch our breath amidst a certain perpetual acclaim. But it is miserable to say how persuasive you are, and how you drive the reader's mind wherever you wish. I have experienced this many times, but especially in this most recent letter of yours to me, in which you mock those "barbarian" <note>A term used by Humanists to describe the medieval Scholastic philosophers whose Latin was considered crude and unclassical</note> philosophers whom you say are commonly held to be filthy, dull, and uncultured—men who did not even live while they were alive, let alone now that they are dead; and if they live now, they live only for punishment and disgrace. Thus was I moved, and thus did I feel shame and regret for my own studies.

<margin>
Thomas
John Scotus
Albertus
Averroes
</margin>

For I have now spent six years among them. I could wish I had done no less than if I had spent that time in such a laborious struggle over a thing of no value. I have lost, I say, my better years among Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, John Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note>, among Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus</note>, and among Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note>—spending such long vigils during which I might perhaps have become something in "good letters" <term>bonis literis</term> <note>Classical literature and humanities</note>. I thought to myself, in order to console myself: if any of them should now return to life, they would certainly have no lack of arguments with which to defend their cause, if indeed they are men who otherwise uphold reason. Finally, it occurred to me that one of them, slightly more eloquent than the rest, might defend his "barbarism" in a manner as little "barbarous" as possible, perhaps in this way: "We lived famous, O Ermolao, and we shall live hereafter, not in the schools of grammarians and pedagogues, but in the circles of philosophers and the assemblies of the wise. There, we do not dispute about the mother of Andromache, or the children of Niobe <note>Classical mythological trivia often mocked by philosophers as being frivolous</note>, or light trifles of that sort, but about the reasons of human and divine things. In meditating upon, inquiring into, and unraveling these matters, we were so subtle, sharp, and keen that we may perhaps seem to have been sometimes too anxious and fastidious—if indeed anyone can be fastidious or too curious in the pursuit of truth. And if anyone should charge us with dullness or slowness in these matters, come now, let whoever he is step forward; he will find that the 'barbarians' had Mercury <note>The god of both eloquence and intellect/wit</note> not on their tongues, but in their hearts. He will find that wisdom was not lacking to them, even if eloquence was absent. To have not joined eloquence with wisdom is perhaps so far from being a fault that to have joined them would be an impiety." For who

<page-num>2</page-num>
# LETTERS

...by your words, you claim to be able, at your whim, to turn white to black and black to white. You claim to be able to take away, cast down, amplify, or diminish whatever you wish by speaking—in short, to transform the very reality of things into whatever face or habit you please through those "magical powers of eloquence" <note>original: "magicis... uiribus eloquétiæ"</note> which you boast of. Thus, things do not remain what they are by their own nature, but become whatever you wish—or rather, they do not actually become so, but even though they are not, they appear so to the listeners. This whole business is nothing other than pure lying, pure imposture, and pure trickery.

Since it always either exceeds the truth by exaggerating the nature of a thing or falls short by diminishing it, it mocks the minds of listeners by flattering them, holding out a deceptive harmony of words like masks and phantoms. 

Shall there be any affinity between this and the philosopher, whose entire study is devoted to knowing and demonstrating the truth to others? Add to this that no trust will be placed in us if we affect the finery and charms of words, as if we were distrustful of the facts themselves and, lacking a reliance on truth, sought to draw men to our opinion through such enticements. 

For this reason, it is better to read sacred matters written crudely rather than elegantly. Nothing is more unbecoming or harmful in any subject where the goal is the knowledge of truth than this whole elaborate style of speaking. This belongs to legal disputes in the courts, not to natural and celestial inquiries. It does not belong to those in the Academy <note>The school of philosophy</note>, but to those involved in the Republic, where the things done and said are weighed in the "popular balance" <note>original: "populari trutina"; judged by the common crowd</note>, and where flowers far outweigh the fruit. Do you not know that "not all things fit all people with the same thread"? Eloquence is an elegant thing (we admit this), full of allure and pleasure. But in a philosopher, it is neither decorous nor pleasing. Who would not approve of a soft gait, nimble hands, and playful eyes in an actor or a dancer? But in a philosopher, who would not disapprove, rebuke, and abominate them? If we see a young girl who is charming and witty in her manners, we will praise and kiss her. But we would condemn and pursue these same traits in a matron. 

Therefore, it is not we who are foolish, but those who celebrate the *Bacchanalia* <note>wild, drunken festivals of Bacchus</note> at the feet of Vesta <note>the Roman goddess of the hearth and domestic purity</note>. They <margin>Synesius</margin> dishonor the gravity and purity of serious matters with playfulness and, as it were, curling irons <note>original: "calamistris"; symbols of excessive, feminine vanity</note>. Indeed, what Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene, a 4th-century philosopher-bishop</note> said of a youth can aptly be said of an oration: "a well-groomed oration is always a lewd one." Why should we prefer our speech to be—oh, the evil of it—rough-haired, sturdy, and unencumbered, when a well-groomed one comes with the mark or suspicion of impurity? 

And even if there were nothing else, this is most true: nothing is more contrary to the philosopher's purpose in any matter than that which tastes of luxury or pride. <margin>Socrates</margin> Socrates used to say that Sicyonian shoes <note>famed in antiquity for being luxurious and ornate</note> were comfortable and fit the foot well, but they did not suit Socrates at all. The same reasoning applies to civil dress and the dress of a philosopher, just as it does to their tables and their speech. The philosopher uses these things only for necessity; the citizen uses them for grace. If the citizen neglects grace, he is not "civil"; if the philosopher affects it, he will not be a philosopher. 

If Pythagoras could live without food, he would even spare the vegetables. If he could explain his thoughts by a look, or by some means less laborious than speech, he would not speak at all. He is so far from polishing and adorning his tongue; indeed, we must take care lest the reader, enticed by the "painted skin" <note>the outward style</note>, lingers there and does not penetrate to the "marrow and blood" <note>the essential truth</note>, which we have often seen to be diseased beneath a face whitened with lead-paint <note>original: "cerusato ori"; a common ancient cosmetic used to whiten the skin</note>. 

We have seen it, I say, in all these people, for whom it has become a habit: since there is nothing within them that is not empty and vain, they detain the reader on the surface with various melodies and harmonies. <margin>Musonius</margin> If a philosopher does this, Musonius <note>Gaius Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher</note> will cry out that it is not a philosopher speaking, but a flute-player performing for you. Therefore, let it not be held as a fault in us that we have failed to do what it would have been a fault to do. 

We seek *what* we should write, not *how*. Or rather, the "how" we seek is this: that it be without pomp or any floral display of speech. We do not want it to be delightful, charming, or witty, but useful, grave, and reverend—so that it attains majesty through a certain ruggedness rather than grace through softness. We do not expect the applause of the theater, where ears are soothed by a smooth or rhythmic closing phrase, or where people say "this is false, but that is clever." Instead, we expect the silence of a few who, out of admiration, look more deeply into something—something either unearthed from the inner shrines of nature or brought down to men from the court of heaven. We seek something so sharp that there is no room to defend against it, and so well-defended that there is no room to argue against it. Let them admire us, moreover, for being sagacious in our path, circumspect in...

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s 1485 letter to the humanist Ermolao Barbaro. Pico, writing in the persona of a "barbarous" medieval philosopher, defends the unpolished but intellectually rigorous style of the Scholastics against the purely aesthetic focus of the new Italian humanists.</meta>

-># BOOK ONE<-

...keen in exploring: subtle in contemplation: grave in judging: intricate in binding, easy in unraveling: Let us be admired for the brevity of style we have sought for many and great matters: under unpolished <note>original: "expolítis" — Likely a transcription error for "incomptis" (unadorned), as the argument favors plainness over ornament.</note> words, the most profound meanings, full of questions, full of solutions. How fit we are, how well-instructed to remove ambiguities, to dissolve difficulties, to unroll what is tangled: and with soul-bending syllogisms both to weaken what is false and confirm what is true. By these titles, O Hermolaus, we have claimed our memory from oblivion until now, and we do not doubt we shall claim it hereafter. If we are held by the common crowd, as you say, to be squalid, rude, and uncultivated, this is a glory to us, not a reproach; we do not write for the crowd, but for you and those like you. Not otherwise than the ancients, who by their riddles and the wrappings of myths kept ignorant men away from the mysteries, we too have been accustomed to frighten those people away from our feasts—which they could not help but pollute—with a somewhat bitter crust of words. Those who wish to hide treasures also tend to set them apart in the mud, or cover them with scales or rubble, so that passersby do not discover them unless they are judged worthy of that gift by the owners themselves. If it is the constant study of philosophers to hide their affairs from the people—from whom it is proper for them not only to be unapproved but also misunderstood—it cannot but be unbecoming for them to have anything in their writing that is theatrical, plausible, or popular: anything that might eventually seem to accommodate itself to the judgment of the multitude. But if you wish, I will shape for you the ideal

<margin>Alcibiades</margin>
of our speech. It is the very same as that of the Sileni of our Alcibiades <note>A reference to Plato's *Symposium*, where Alcibiades compares Socrates to Silenus statues: ugly and "rough" on the outside, but containing divine images of gods within.</note>. For there were statues of these with a rough, foul, and despicable face. But inside they were full of gems, of rare and precious furniture. Thus, if you look from the outside, you would see a wild beast; if you look within, you would recognize a divinity. But you will say that ears cannot bear a texture that is now harsh, now gaping, and always dissonant. They do not bear barbarian names, almost terrifying in their very sound—O delicate one, when you go to flute-players and harpists, keep your ears. But when you are called away from the senses to the philosophers, return to yourself, into the inner chambers of the soul and the secessions of the mind.

<margin>Apollonius of Tyana</margin>
Assume those ears of the Tyanean <note>original: "Thianeus"; referring to Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century mystic philosopher.</note>: with which, when he was not in his body at all, he heard not the earthly Marsyas <note>Marsyas was a satyr who challenged Apollo to a musical contest and was flayed for his hubris; his music represents lower, earthly sensations.</note>, but the celestial Apollo, tempering the melody of the universe with a divine lyre in ineffable ways. If you taste the words of philosophers with these ears, they will seem honeyed to you, even to the envy of Nestor <note>Nestor was the oldest and wisest Greek at Troy, famous for speech "sweeter than honey."</note>. But let us leave these matters, which rise up far too much. Truly, to feel disgust at a philosopher who disputes most subtly because his elocution is less harmonious is the mark not so much of a delicate stomach as of an insolent one. It is no different than if someone, while Socrates was teaching about morals, should point out either a loose shoe or a poorly fitting cloak, or should be terribly annoyed by a fingernail.

<margin>Cicero</margin>
Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> does not require eloquence in a philosopher: but only that he satisfy the requirements of facts and doctrine. That man, as prudent as he was learned, knew that our task is to compose the mind rather than the diction. We must take care that reason does not stray, not the oration. It pertains to us to have internal discourse <note>original: "en diathesei logou" (εν διαθεσει λογου); the internal rational thought as opposed to its outward expression.</note> and not to care for elegant delivery <note>original: "kompsen prophoran" (κομψην προφοραν)</note>. It is laudable in us to have the Muses in the soul and not on the lips, lest anything in the soul sound too harsh through anger, or be weakened through lust; finally, lest

<margin>Plato</margin>
there be anything discordant from the genuine tempered harmony of the Muses themselves. Since Plato understood that these theatrical and poetic things often corrupted the state, he banished all poets from his republic. But he left it to be governed by philosophers. Certainly, if by a lust for speaking they should imitate poets, they too would be

<margin>Lucretius</margin>
condemned to exile. But Lucretius will persist: even if philosophical meditations do not lack charm of speech for their own sake, yet through its application the austerity of the subjects themselves must be disguised. Just as wormwood <note>original: "absynthia"</note> by itself expels diseases, yet people smear the cup with honey so that the improvident age of children may be played upon. This, perhaps, was what you had to do, O Lucretius: if you were writing your works for children; if for the crowd, you certainly had to do it: for you were serving up not just wormwood, but the most unmixed poisons. But our reason is far different: we who, as we said before, seek not to allure the crowd, but to frighten them away. Nor does the earth produce wormwood 

<margin>Lactantius</margin>
but we serve up nectar. Yet Lactantius <note>original: "Firmiane"; Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero" for his polished style.</note> will contend that it is well established that truth flows more powerfully into the minds of auditors, even the older ones, when it is both equipped with its own strength and adorned with the light of oratory. If you had been as frequent in sacred letters, O Firmianus, as you were in fictitious lawsuits, you would not have said this, and you would have perhaps confirmed our views no less well than you destroyed those of others. Tell me, I pray, what moves...

<summary>Pico defends the "rough" style of Scholastic philosophers, arguing that profound truth is intentionally hidden behind unadorned language to protect it from the vulgar crowd. He uses the metaphor of the Silenus statues and critiques the need for rhetorical "honey" to sweeten the bitter but medicinal truth of philosophy.</summary>

--- Page 237 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of "barbarous" medieval philosophers. Here, he argues that the power of truth does not depend on beautiful language, citing the raw power of the Bible and the simple words of Socrates over elaborate oratory. He challenges the humanist obsession with "correct" Latin, suggesting that technical philosophical language (like that of the University of Paris) is its own valid "language" with its own rules of correctness.</meta>

-># LETTERS<-

Nothing persuades more strongly than the reading of the sacred scriptures: they do not just move or persuade. They compel, they stir, they bring force. You read words that are rude and rustic, but living: but animated: fiery, stinging, penetrating to the depths of the spirit: transforming the whole man with a wonderful power. Alcibiades says that he was moved by nothing in elaborate and brilliant orations, but rather by the naked and simple words of Socrates. He adds that even if they were clumsy <note>original: "inepta" — here meaning lacking in formal rhetorical polish</note>, he was snatched away into a frenzy, placed outside himself, and whether he willed it or not, he had to do what that man [Socrates] commanded. 

But why do I waste words on an admitted fact? If the listener is not foolish, what else does he expect from painted speech <note>original: "fucato sermone" — speech that is artificially colored or deceptive, like makeup</note> except a trap? 

<margin>One is persuaded most by three things.</margin> 
One is persuaded most by three things: the life of the speaker, the truth of the matter, and the sobriety of the speech. These are the things that will gain credit for a philosopher: if he is good, if he is truthful, if he seeks that kind of speaking 

<margin>Heraclitus</margin>
which flows not from the pleasant woods of the Muses, but from that dread cave in which Heraclitus said truth lies hidden. 

But someone will say: "Come, friend, let us examine these things, setting aside our dispute. Wisdom is something revered and divine in itself, nor does it need any foreign ornament. But what harm is there if ornament is added? Who denies that things which are fitting by themselves become more fitting if they are adorned?" Friend, I deny this in most cases: there are many things whose splendor you would dim and not brighten if you added anything. They are in their best state by nature, such that they cannot be changed by 

<margin><unclear>Alcibiades</unclear></margin>
anyone <note>likely "a billo" in OCR is "a quovis" or similar; the context implies any external change</note> except for the worse. A marble house does not accept a painting. If you apply a layer of white plaster <note>original: "opus albarium" — stucco used for wall decoration</note> over it, you take away from its dignity and beauty. It is no different with wisdom and the things treated by philosophers: they are not made clear by a veneer but are obscured. Why say more? Is it not common knowledge that beautiful faces are made ugly by white lead <note>original: "cerussa" — a toxic lead pigment used in cosmetics in antiquity</note>? In general, whatever beauty you place on top of something, it hides what was there before; it shows only what it brings with it. 

Therefore, if what was there before is better than what is added, whatever it is will have suffered a loss, not a gain. For this reason, philosophy presents herself naked, conspicuous from every side; she longs to come entirely 

<margin><unclear>Philosophy</unclear></margin>
under the eyes and under judgment. She knows she has that by which she might please completely from every side. As much as you might want to add of caution or beauty, you would take away just as much from her praise. She wants to be held sincere and unmixed. Whatever you mix in, you will have stained, adulterated, and turned into something else. She stands at a point that is unchangeable and indivisible <note>original: "puncto infectili et individuo" — a mathematical or metaphysical point that cannot be colored or broken apart</note>. 

For this reason, one must not play with tropes or words, nor be overly lush, nor sport with metaphors, nor dare to use artificial terms in such a serious matter—one of such critical importance that to take away, add, or change anything would be a disgrace. "But," you will say, "come, we grant you this, that ornate speech is not your concern. But it is certainly your duty—which you do not fulfill—to explain things at least in Latin, using its own words, even if they are not flowery." 

<margin><unclear>Latinity</unclear></margin>
"I do not demand from you a polished oration, but I do not want it to be filthy; I do not want it perfumed, but neither should it smell like a goat. It should not be overly chosen, but neither should it be neglected. We do not ask that it delight, but we complain that it offends." This is well said; you are now coming over to our side. But, please, let us recognize what this "Latinity" is, which you say philosophers alone ought to use and yet do not pay out. 

If, for example, it occurs in speaking that "man is produced by the sun," our people will say "the sun *carit* <note>original: "carit" — a Scholastic technical term for 'produces' or 'creates' that humanists found un-classical</note> man." 

<margin><unclear>Arab</unclear></margin>
You will shout immediately: "This is not Latin!" So far, you are right. It is not spoken in the Roman way; that is even truer. "Therefore, it is not correct," you say—but the argument fails. An Arab will say the same thing, an Egyptian will say it; they will not speak in Latin, but they will nonetheless speak correctly. For names of things are established either by choice or by nature. If by chance placement—as when a community of men agrees on the same meaning, decreeing what each thing should be called—then among them it is called correctly. What prevents these philosophers, whom you call "barbarians," from having conspired together into one norm of speaking, which is just as sacred among them as the Roman norm is among you? Why should you not call their way correct, and call yours your own? There is no reason, if this naming of things is entirely arbitrary. 

If you do not wish to dignify it with the name of "Roman," call it French, British, Spanish, or what the common folk are accustomed to say, "Parisian" <note>Referring to the style of the University of Paris, the center of Scholasticism</note>. When it happens that they speak to you, they are mostly laughed at and mostly not understood; the same thing would happen to you speaking among them. 

<margin><unclear>Anacharsis</unclear></margin>
As the saying goes: "Anacharsis commits a solecism <note>a grammatical error or social impropriety</note> among the Athenians, but the Athenians do so among the Scythians." <note>Anacharsis was a Scythian philosopher; Pico uses this to show that "correctness" is a matter of local convention.</note> But if the correctness of names depends on the nature of things, should we consult rhetoricians or philosophers—who alone have the nature of all things clearly seen and explored—about this correctness? Perhaps those things which...

<summary>Pico argues that philosophical truth is best expressed through plain, unadorned language rather than deceptive rhetoric. He defends the technical, "barbarous" Latin of the Scholastics as a legitimate professional language, arguing that linguistic correctness is a matter of convention among specialists.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s famous 1485 letter to Ermolao Barbaro. Pico continues his rhetorical defense of the "barbarous" medieval Scholastic philosophers (like Duns Scotus) against the critiques of the humanists who prized elegant Latin above all else.</meta>

<page-num>120</page-num>

# BOOK ONE

The ears reject [these words] as if they were splinters; reason accepts them as things more akin to reality. But why should they have had to innovate their language, and even if they were born among Latins, not speak in the Latin style? They could not, O Hermolaus, while they were reading the laws of fate and the order of the universe in the heavens, or reading the cycles of birth and death in the elements, the powers of simple things, and the temperaments of mixtures. They could not, I say, at the same time annotate the properties, laws, and observations of the Roman tongue in Cicero, in Pliny, or in Apuleius. They were seeking what was abhorrent [to nature] and what was accepted in nature; meanwhile, they did not care for what had died out among the Romans. 

But truly, now I place you in a better position: I grant you that eloquence and wisdom have conspired together in a mutual bond. But the philosophers have unyoked wisdom from eloquence, just as the historians, rhetoricians, and poets have unyoked <margin>Philostratus</margin> eloquence from wisdom. You do not doubt that the latter will live on with celebrated fame; as for the former, see that you do not view them only as objects of punishment and insult. Cicero prefers an unpolished wisdom to a talkative folly. 
<margin>Cicero</margin> 
When it comes to money, we do not ask which mint struck the coin, but what material it is made of. Nor is there anyone who would not prefer pure gold under a Germanic stamp <note>original: "sub nota teutonum" — Pico is defending the "Teutonic" or Northern European Scholastic thinkers</note> than counterfeit gold under a Roman symbol. They sin who create a divorce between the heart and the tongue; but those who are all tongue and no heart are not real men; they are, as Cato says, 
<margin>Cato</margin> 
"mortuary glossaries" <note>original: "mortuaria glossaria" — a collection of dead words, like a funeral dirge with no substance</note>. We can perhaps live without a tongue, though not conveniently; but we cannot live without a heart in any way. It is not human to be a stranger to a more refined nature; he is not a man who is devoid of philosophy. The dullest wisdom can be of use, but a foolish eloquence is like a sword in the hand of a madman. 

"Therefore," you will say, "a statue is not commended by its material, but by its shape. And if Choerilus had sung the same things as Homer, and Maevius the same as Virgil, they would have been received among the poets as equals to the former." Do you not see the disparity in this comparison? We too assert that a thing is judged by its form, not by its subject matter. For a thing is what it is because of its form. But one form is required to be received among philosophers, and another among poets. 

Let Lucretius write about nature, about God, and about providence; and let one of our own write about the same things. Let John Scotus <note>Johannes Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major medieval philosopher often mocked by humanists for his "barbarous" Latin</note> write, even if he is clumsier in verse. Lucretius will say that the principles of things are atoms and the vacuum; that God is corporeal; that he is ignorant of nature; and that all things are carried along by the chance collision of little bodies. But he will say these things in Latin and with elegance. John will say that nature consists of its own matter and form; that God is a separate Mind, knowing all things and providing for all. Nor, because he sees and governs all things, is he moved in the least from his own peace. But he says what is commonly said: "That which descends does not descend" <note>original Greek: "κάτιοντα μηκατιεναι" — likely a reference to divine emanation where the source remains stable even as its influence "descends" to lower things</note>. Yet he will speak dully, rudely, and not in Latin words. 

I ask: who could doubt which is the better poet and which is the better philosopher? It is beyond all controversy that Scotus is as much more correct as the other is more ornate in speech. But see how they differ: this one has an unclouded mouth but a scattered mind; the first knows nothing of the decrees of grammarians (not to say poets), but the other knows nothing of the decrees of God and nature. The first is most "speechless" <note>original: "insantissimus" — likely a play on "infantissimus," meaning unable to speak eloquently</note> in his speaking, yet he feels those things which cannot be sufficiently praised by speaking; the second, most eloquent in his speech, speaks of abominable things.

Perhaps they will offer these arguments in defense of their "barbarism," my dearest Hermolaus, or perhaps they have arguments much better in their subtlety. I do not entirely agree with their opinions, nor do I think any noble or liberal mind should. But I have exercised myself willingly in this subject matter, as if it were an "infamous" cause—much like those who praise a quartan fever—both to test my own talent and with the intention that, just as Glaucon 
<margin>Glaucon</margin> 
in Plato's work praises injustice not from his own judgment but to stimulate Socrates to the praise of justice, so too might I hear the cause of eloquence pleaded by you. For a little while, I have attacked it, pushing against my own feelings and nature. If I truly thought eloquence should be neglected or postponed to the barbarians, I would not have almost totally defected from them to it, as I recently did: turning to Greek letters and to your never-sufficiently-praised Themistius. 

Yet I will say freely what I feel: certain small-time grammarians move my stomach to bile; when they have mastered the origins of two words, they show themselves off, they sell themselves, they carry themselves about so boastfully that they think philosophers are worth nothing compared to themselves. "We do not want," they say, "this philosophy of yours." And what wonder? Neither do dogs want Falernian wine. 

But let us close the letter at this point. If those barbarians earned any glory for their name by the knowledge of things alone, it is not easy to say what place, what praises you should claim for yourself, you who are the most eloquent among philosophers and the "most philosophical" <note>original Greek: "φιλυποτατοσ" — a typo for "φιλοσοφώτατος"</note> among the eloquent.

Florence, June 3rd, 1485.

---

->To the Reverend father in Christ, Brother Battista Mantuanus, of the Order of Carmelites, poet<-

<summary>Pico della Mirandola concludes his defense of Scholastic "barbarism" by arguing that truth and matter are superior to style and form, though he admits his defense is a rhetorical exercise to provoke his friend Ermolao Barbaro into a deeper defense of eloquence. He compares the "clumsy" truth of Duns Scotus with the "elegant" errors of Lucretius, ultimately seeking a union of both wisdom and beautiful speech.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his defense of Scholastic philosophy to specific scholarly discussions with his contemporaries: the poet Angelo Poliziano, the printer-scholar Aldo Manutio, and the diplomat Ermolao Barbaro.</meta>

<page-num>021</page-num>

# LETTERS

To a distinguished philosopher and theologian, etc.

->To his son Giovanni [Pico] of Mirandola<- <margin>V.</margin>

<margin>A most beautiful exposition</margin>
**G**reetings, my most beloved father: Regarding Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note>, I feel no differently than you do; I shall write more to you on this matter when I have leisure and things that might not be unpleasing to you. Concerning the difference between our translation and the Hebrew text in the third chapter of the book of Genesis, where it deals with Eve and the serpent, this is indeed what I think: in the Hebrew, it is as you write, "he shall crush your head" <note>original: "ipsum conteret caput tuum"</note>, and it refers to the seed of Eve, of which it had been said, "I will put enmity between your seed and her seed." However, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and Jerome translated it as "she shall crush your head" in both places. Either way, the meaning is the same; for when it says "he shall crush," it does not look so much at the person of Eve herself as at her posterity. It says she will do this because she is to do it through her seed. But as for why they preferred to translate "she" rather than "he," I believe the cause was to signify that since not only females but also males were to be propagated from Eve, that which was said of the seed was to be referred to the female seed alone. These are the things that come to mind at present on this matter. I am diligently working on the *Harmony of Plato and Aristotle* <note>Pico's unfinished masterwork intended to prove that the two rival philosophies were actually in agreement</note>. I give it its due time every morning; after the midday hours, I give time to my friends and my health, and sometimes to the poets and orators; and if there are any lighter studies, the Sacred Letters share the night with sleep. Please do not let me lack your company any longer. Greet Beroaldo <note>Filippo Beroaldo the Elder, a famous Bolognese humanist</note>. Your Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, the great Renaissance poet and Pico's close friend</note> is entirely yours. Farewell, and pray to God for me. Florence, March 20, 1490.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Aldo Manutio. Greetings. VI.<-

<margin>The same elsewhere</margin>
**I** am sending the Homer that you desired; however, it is later than you wished and than I ought to have sent it. I am so distracted by business, my dear Aldo, that there is no room even to catch my breath. I have long since bound myself (as you know) to letters in a kind of servitude. They demand such a severe task of reading and dictating for their own sake that I can scarcely recover my health. As for what you write you will do: equip yourself for philosophy; but on this condition, that you remember there is no philosophy which calls us away from the truth of the mysteries. Philosophy seeks the truth; theology finds it; religion possesses it. Farewell. Florence, the eleventh day of February, in the 1490th year of grace.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Ermolao Barbaro, Patriarch of Aquileia. Greetings. VII.<-

<margin>Three kinds of life</margin>
**I** hear that you have been elected Patriarch of Aquileia. I congratulate those people on an excellent pastor, the whole Church on a most strenuous soldier, and you on the opportunity given to illustrate and amplify your virtue. There are generally three kinds of living: the civic, the contemplative, and the religious. In the first, we require prudence; in the second, learning; and in the third, as if at the summit of the whole life, we require holiness in addition to those two. Your city has previously experienced you as most diligent and prudent in conducting the republic and handling its great affairs, and all scholars love and admire you as a patron and champion of the good arts. As for what remains, we know without doubt that you will do this, and we rejoice so seriously that the Church should owe no less to you in the future than both your city and letters have owed you until now.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his friend Ermolao. Greetings. VIII.<-

**W**hat shall I say this is, my dear Ermolao, that you burden me daily with new favors as if you owed me something—you, to whom I have long owed everything? My brother Antonio came here in recent days, returning to his homeland. I asked what Ermolao was doing; he replied: "This is what he does. He loves you, praises you, and carries you to the heavens before me, before others, and before the Pope himself; and he does this so constantly and so vigorously as if he had nothing else to do." Likewise, friends whom I have there sometimes write to me—one especially, Cosimo Pazzi, a man worthy of your unique love, to embrace his merits once and for all. Indeed, as often as he writes, he writes of your kindnesses toward me, of your love, and of a certain wonderful inclination of mind, so that I perceive you always speak of me most honorably. O, this unheard-of humanity of yours, which is never satisfied with itself toward men...

<page-num>151</page-num>

# BOOK ONE

...you think I am a man of such words, and if you are so disposed toward me that you make me more your own and more obliged to you, you are "doing what has already been done," <note>A Latin idiom, *actum agere*, meaning to labor in vain or repeat something unnecessary.</note> as they say. I cannot owe more or love more than I already do. But in this way, you surpass all other men in wisdom, character, learning, and humanity—and you even surpass yourself. Farewell: and I ask that you praise me moderately, provided that you love me immoderately. Poliziano greets you; in loving and praising you, he is always sincere and always immoderate. Florence, the last day of July, 1490.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Hieronymus <note>Likely the humanist Girolamo Donato or possibly Girolamo Savonarola, though the tone suggests a fellow scholar.</note>, Greetings. Letter IX.<-

**U**nless our "Angel" <note>A play on the name of Angelo Poliziano.</note> were writing to you, I would have written more. But I do not wish my "magpies" <note>original: "picas"—a pun on his own name, Pico, suggesting his words are like the chattering of magpies.</note> to drown out his Muses, nor do I want to be the rude intruder who disturbs your pleasure. But if he has conferred a benefit by refraining from the injury he could have inflicted, you cannot help but credit me for this brevity of letters as a favor; you will reward me most beautifully if you return very long letters in exchange for these very short ones. For nothing is more pleasing to us than your letters; I beg you not to defraud me of them, for otherwise, if you remain silent, I shall "repay like with like." <note>An old Greek and Latin proverb for retaliation.</note> For then I shall especially not keep silent: for in that way I shall retaliate against you quite finely. Farewell: and greet our Ermolao <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a famous Venetian scholar and diplomat.</note>, the delight of the Roman tongue, most warmly in my name.

---

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico, Greetings. Letter X.<-

**T**he reason I have not replied to your letters until now was that certain Hebrew books fell into my hands, upon which I have been focused day and night for an entire week. They have nearly made me blind. For a certain Sicilian Jew, <note>Likely the convert and scholar Flavius Mithridates, who taught Pico Hebrew and Aramaic and translated many Kabbalistic texts for him.</note> who brought the books here, is set to depart in twenty days; therefore, until I have untangled myself from them, do not expect even a syllable from me. I cannot depart from them for a moment, lest perhaps they depart before I have examined them all. When I am free from this care, I will overwhelm you with letters, although you know I have a most occupied mind. If, however, you are ever going to do anything for my sake, take care by whatever means you can that the Prince of Bari <note>Ludovico Sforza, "Il Moro," the powerful ruler of Milan.</note> does not require my presence there; for it would disturb all my studies, to which you know how devoted I am and how I care for nothing besides them. It is not at all clear to me whether it would be more troublesome to displease him or myself. Farewell; fear God and think daily that you are going to die. <note>The classic *memento mori* (remember you will die).</note> Ferrara, 30 May 1490.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino <note>The head of the Platonic Academy in Florence and translator of Plato’s works.</note>, Greetings. Letter XI.<-

**W**hen friends contend for what they desire with too many words, they do an injury to friendship, as if friendship itself could not achieve what the allure of a speech can. Therefore, I shall deal with you simply, as the benevolence that has long existed between us requires. At this time, the Platonist Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) whose works were essential to the Renaissance understanding of ancient "theurgy" or divine magic.</note> is very necessary for my studies. If you send this book to me, you will bind me to you in perpetual obligation. It will be here for twenty days, or at most a month, and will then be returned immediately by courier. In the meantime, use my library and all my things as if they were your own. Farewell.

---

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings. Letter XII.<-

**M**y "loves" <note>Pico likely refers to his poems or his specific intellectual pursuits here.</note> declare that they have never been received more urbanely or more cheerfully than they were at your house in these past days; and indeed they have confessed so amiably that while they congratulate themselves greatly, they owe very much to you. For who would not wish to die by that sword of yours? They grieve that it was done more indulgently than was proper, and they are at the point of doubting whether Love himself made you blind toward my loves. And they doubt it so much that they do not sufficiently trust your judgment—otherwise most grave—in their own cause. Nevertheless, they do trust it, and now they are freeing themselves from their chains; they do not know how to stay at home, but securely demand liberty and the public eye. # LETTERS
SIG: E. XIII.
<meta>catchword: corum</meta>

...joked so elegantly: we certainly held back our weapons, both against the one who had threatened he would repay the injury and against the one whose skin had become so calloused that it would not admit such light blows. Therefore, with all the veneration we owed, we took our leave of the old man. As soon as he sat down with us, he began to speak <note>Original "phari," likely a variant or OCR error for "fari" (to speak), though it could allegorically refer to a "Pharos" or lighthouse/guide.</note> about morals. He did so in Latin, not so much because he was among Latins—for there were those in that gathering who knew Greek—though he himself, by your benefit, knew Latin more brilliantly. Yet he did not waste his effort, since he did not stop speaking until he had turned us from Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> into Stoics.

We all approved of that *apatheia* <note>original: "apathiā"—the Stoic ideal of being undisturbed by passion or external grief.</note>; it is now possible to see how men who, just a little while ago, were delicate have now become the most tolerant of all things. We can indeed be provoked by others, but we shall never be harmed by ourselves, no matter how much we might struggle against fate. We now wish for those things which are not ours to happen exactly as God wills; we shall never blame nor accuse them, we shall grieve for nothing, and we shall demand nothing, for we do not know how to submit to servitude. We are grasped by reality rather than by theory; and because we are novices, we observe ourselves as if we were our own adversaries. Let us neglect the opinions of others about us and other external things of that kind, rather than rejecting them. Let us care for each day as travelers care for an inn; let us possess things, but let us not be possessed by them.

Let us love silence, so that the mouth does not vomit up what is not yet digested. Let us rarely cause laughter in others, and never in ourselves. To embrace it in a single word: we have abundantly learned the whole of Epictetus <note>A famous Stoic philosopher who taught that one should only worry about what is within their own control.</note>—both to endure adversity and to abstain from pleasures. See how, point by point, we have modeled our lives after your Epictetus. See how quickly we have done so, lest in this part also we should fail to be Stoics, who wish us to be warned that a man fails for as long as he does not improve.

Though I have admired this in others, I admire it in myself most of all. I, who have always spent my time in the Lyceum or the Academy <note>The schools of Aristotle and Plato, respectively.</note> and never in the Portico <note>The "Stoa," the porch where Stoic philosophers taught.</note>, was so conquered by the old man's speech that I moved over to his opinion not just with my feet, but with my hands and my whole body. I am sending you the index of Greek books which are kept here with me, along with the letter from Manuel <note>Likely referring to Manuel Chrysoloras or a contemporary scholar.</note>, as your correspondence requested. I likewise desire the index of your own books. Give my greetings to young Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger.</note> in my name; I was going to write to him, but shame deterred me, lest I seem to trouble the man with letters. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Thomas Medius <note>Tommaso Mezzo, a Venetian humanist known for writing Latin comedies.</note>, Greetings. Letter XIII.<-

The fact that you dedicated your little story—and a festive and elegant one at that—to my name was a sign to me both of your learning and of your singular goodwill toward me. Both are weighty reasons which urge and impel me to love you; I know not which more so. For as in love (as the proverb goes) it is a disgrace not to have returned mutual affection, so it is the mark of either a rustic or a truly wicked mind not to have loved a most praiseworthy man, even if you are not provoked to do so.

See, therefore, how you not only call but drag me toward friendship with "twin ropes" (as they say), since there is nothing in that little book that does not smell of learning and genius. Nor could you have deserved better of me more splendidly than to consult so friendlily and so liberally for my name by dedicating this excellent little story to it. Its subject matter is so far from being something I would neglect or accuse, that I even approve of it with the greatest effort. For it has always been my opinion—and I think no learned person will disagree—that it takes a sharper genius to write these jests and little stories (provided it is done as you have presented it, most abundantly, learnedly, and elegantly) than to have discussed the weightiest matters with oratory. 

Just as we think a craftsman has fashioned a far more beautiful statue if he makes it from mud rather than from bronze or gold, why will it not be the same to have spoken something remarkable from humble material as from the sublime? It is certainly a matter of more effort, and therefore even more laudable. The dignity of the subject matter lends charm to those serious works; but whatever these lighter works bring that is worthy is drawn entirely from the writer's own store. The material itself contributes nothing, as if providing no "contribution to the feast" <note>original: "asymbola"—referring to a guest who pays nothing at a potluck dinner; here, the subject matter doesn't help the author.</note>. Nature zealously assists the former; the latter certainly contend against nature. Even if this is so, I will not deny that among these humbler materials I have mentioned, some surpass others in a wonderful way; there are several of that kind so flat and tasteless that they cannot be sufficiently raised or skillfully seasoned by any force or majesty of words. This fault can never be found in these [your stories], which...

# BOOK ONE

...are mended by their wit. But indeed, I believe those compositions should be placed on the highest benches <note>referring to a hierarchy of literary quality</note> which have a graphic description of ages and characters mixed with the charm of wit; for they have everything that belongs to comic poets, and you have most beautifully imitated this in that little play you sent to me. How much cleverness is there! How much opportunity for wit and ingenious mixing! How it delights, how charming, how complete it is on all sides! And if any part appeared a bit "dirty" <note>unrefined</note> or weak due to the lowliness of the subject matter, it raises itself up by the light and dignity of the speech, assuming brilliance and strength. It is truly that which (to speak briefly) clearly demonstrates it was perfected by a most literate man. 

But among all other things, that exquisite and fitting observation of characters, ages, and persons is especially dear to me; in which I see your prudence—and no mediocre prudence at that—as if from a high watchtower. I wish you could see what a laugh the eighty-year-old prelate causes me; who, however everything else turns out, continuously wants this: to scrape together money from somewhere—a vice that has always been innate and familiar to old men. What shall I say of our Palitus, who, disguising himself, extorts a "Salic feast" <note>original: "cœnā saliarē" — a proverbially lavish banquet, named after the Roman priests of Mars</note> from the wretched old man? Who, so to speak, fleeces him <note>original: "punice emungit" — literally "wipes his nose in the Punic fashion," an idiom for cheating someone using Carthaginian-style trickery</note> most singularly. 

There is no word in that play, my Thomas, that does not claim a certain prize for itself. But it is not my place to report everything I have "smelled out" <note>sensed or detected</note>; nor do I have the kind of nose that smells everything. Let this be certain to you: nothing more pleasing or more joyful has ever happened to me. And so, I have received the work itself within these walls, and you yourself within my soul. You have, my Thomas, what was to be sought from me (if you seek it): a mutual friendship which you yourself (as becomes a most excellent man) began under the auspices of the Muses. It remains that whenever you find my affairs or my help worthy, you test my goodwill toward you. For I will not (if any occasion is given) omit any kind of duty toward you, just as you did first toward me at the threshold of friendship.
-> Farewell. <-

-> Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, Count of Concordia, to his Nicolaus Leonicenus, Greetings. No. 23. <-

I would have spoken with you more often and at greater length by letter, my sweetest Nicolaus, if your whereabouts had been known to me by messenger, letters, or rumor. I anxiously asked many people about it, but I received a doubtful answer from all. Finally, in recent days, a letter from Antonio of Faenza <note>Antonius Faventinus</note>, a very serious philosopher, to Tommaso Frignano fell into my hands; from it, I learned you were in Florence, which was then most pleasing to me. As soon as I understood this, I sent a letter to you in Florence by courier. The journey was in vain, for it did not find you there. I grieved greatly; today Thomas indicated you had left Florence and were in Bologna; I ordered these letters to be delivered to you there. 

In these, I will not strive to open my benevolence or singular love for you at greater length, for you must not doubt my goodwill toward you even a little bit, unless you thought me forgotten—which is not my nature—of your excellent virtue and your services to me. I could not but wonder greatly that, when you snatched yourself from the city's turmoils to seek a place where you could live both calmly and pleasantly, you either forgot or looked down upon this little town of ours. You seemed, Nicolaus, to distrust either my will or my resources; but while the latter are smaller than your merits, the former is greater than your opinion of it. Nothing will be more pleasing than if you advise me of your plans; it would be most pleasing of all if you do not disdain my home as common to you, to rest with me while others deal with Mars <note>an allegory for war or political strife</note>. 

I am sending the rest of John the Grammarian <note>original: "Io. grammatici" — referring to John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> to you, which was not found for many days but has now been recovered. I am yours and I wait for you. Farewell, at Mirandola, July 20, 1487. If you love me, take care with all diligence to have an index of all the books found in the library of Saint Dominic. Send it or bring it with you.
-> Farewell again. <-

I have built a pleasant suburban villa, suitable for the condition of the place and region. I have composed a long poem about it; the house will be sweet to you and the poem will not be unpleasant.
-> Farewell. <-

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his friend Angelo Poliziano. Greeting. XV.

<insert>Q</insert>uite apart from the fact that you praised me so highly in your recent letters, I owe you as much as I am far from deserving such praise. For one owes a debt for what is given for free, not for what is paid as a due reward. Therefore, I owe you entirely for what you write about me, since there is nothing of the sort in me. Since you owed this to me in no way at all, it was entirely the result of your kindness and your singular goodwill toward me. For the rest, if you examine me, you will find nothing but what is thin, humble, and narrow. We are but the smoke of novices and mere recruits <note>original: "tiruculi"</note> who have barely moved our feet out of the darkness of ignorance; we have progressed almost not at all. It is a kindness to us if we are even counted among the ranks of students. The title of "scholar" <note>original: "docti nomen"</note> possesses something else entirely, which is peculiar to you and those like you; such heights do not suit me. Regarding those things which are foremost in the study of letters, not only do I have nothing fully explored, but I have not even seen them yet except through a lattice <note>original: "per transennam" — a phrase meaning to see something only partially or indirectly</note>. I shall certainly strive (as I am doing now) to one day be the kind of man you now proclaim me to be, and which you either judge me to be, or certainly wish me to be.

Meanwhile, I shall imitate you, Angelo, who excuses yourself to the Greeks because you are a Latin, and to the Latins because you are a Greek <note>A reference to Poliziano’s legendary mastery of both languages, which was rare even among the highest scholars</note>. I shall use a similar refuge: I shall approve myself to the poets and rhetoricians because I am called a philosopher, and to the philosophers because I cultivate the rhetoricians and the Muses. Yet, for me, the situation is far different than it is for you. For while I wish to sit on two stools (as they say), I am excluded from both; and so it happens (to put it briefly) that I am neither a poet, nor a rhetor, nor a philosopher. You, however, fulfill both roles so well that it is hardly clear to which you belong more, since you embrace both the Greek and our own Minerva <note>original: "nrām mineruā" — referring to Latin wisdom and literature</note> so beautifully that you are like a swan of both languages; one cannot easily discern which is acquired and which is your natural tongue. For to say nothing of the Latins (among whom you yield to no one in the first rank), who would believe—as was said of Hadrian—that a Roman man could speak so "Greekly"? Emanuel <note>likely Emanuel Adramyttenos, a Cretan scholar and friend of Poliziano</note> used to swear, while reading your works, that Athens itself was not so Attic <note>referring to the pure, classical style of ancient Athens</note>. You are such a man, my Angelo (away with flattery!), that among our people only one or two—I might even say no one—can be compared to you. If there were more such men, this age would have no reason to envy antiquity. 

Apply yourself, I beg you, and rescue literature as much as you can from neglect, so that the brilliance of the Roman language does not utterly fade away through the injury of time. Always forge something new that may assist and illuminate the Latin cause. And those works you have at home, let them finally come forth for the common benefit of students. For my part, just as I love you yourself, I love and desire all your works—all the more because I have set you before me as the model into which I might be molded, even if you are one whom all ought to follow, yet few are able to catch. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his friend Paolo Cortesi. Greeting. XVI.

<insert>B</insert>eneath your thoughts, Paolo, lies a good plan. Let us send letters frequently so that we, who are divided by the distances between places, may certainly be joined by the exchange of letters; this usually lightens the longing of those who are absent. If you had a statue or an image of a friend at home, you would value it; but to me, there seems to be this difference between a physical image and a letter: the latter portrays the mind, the former the body. The statue outlines only the outermost parts, but the letter clearly expresses and fashions the innermost parts. That is like the cloak and garment of a friend; this represents the true friend to us. That emulates the colors and shape of the flesh as best it can; this represents the thoughts, the plans, the sorrows, the joys, the cares—in short, all the emotions. And those secrets of the soul which a person present hardly speaks even to himself, he transmits most faithfully to an absent friend. The letter, finally, is a living and effective thing; the statue is a dead and mute likeness. 

Let us, therefore, send these images of our souls to one another: you indeed may send ones that are golden and silver (as you are able), while I shall send ones of bronze or even clay <note>Pico is being humble about the quality of his own writing compared to Cortesi's</note>. In this way, we shall be beyond all injury of space and time, just as the power of the soul itself knows neither the distances of place nor the delays of time. But truly, how much I owe you, most dutiful Paolo, because you were the first to call me to this duty with such a letter—one which held and delighted me so much that for many days now no reading has delighted me more. For it is full of eloquence, full of graces, full of love and goodwill; perhaps you were expecting me to say "full of my own praises." I was indeed about to say that as well. For I am not so iron-hearted—or if you prefer it said this way, so...

...I am a philosopher <note>original: "philosophus"</note>, so I am not delighted by the praises of friends. If they are true, they commend me to myself; if false, they commend their love and goodwill toward me. Therefore, I will easily obtain from my philosophy the permission to read your letters frequently and with pleasure, even the parts where they praise me. But it will not be so easy to appear sufficiently courteous or not ungrateful in returning this exchange of letters. -> Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Troilo Malvezzi. Health. XVII. <-

**Y**our little book on brave men <note>original: "de fortibus"</note> affected me with as much pleasure as usually affects one to whom the best fortune has happened. I give you great thanks for making me a participant in your labors, especially such as these: in which both the subtlety of your arguments and your multiple and varied knowledge of things are easily apparent. One of these deserves praise for genius, the other for diligence. Our "trifles" <note>original: "nugas," a humble term for his own writings</note> which you desire, I shall give to you shortly. For it is uncertain whether it is more unfitting for you, a most busy legal expert, to be detained by reading them, or for a most friendly man to be kept in suspense by his desire for them. Farewell and love me. May 29, 1492.

---

-> Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Thadeo Ugolino. Health. XVIII. <-

**I** held your letters most welcome, full of love, faith, and charity, not only because you remembered me, but because in them you friendly advise me to remember myself—that is, to remember the study of good arts and the expectation I have set for myself to maintain. Indeed, conscious of my weakness, I would not dare to promise anything even mediocre about myself. But He from whom every good comes, the most merciful Father of lights, as He has previously given that by which men might distinguish us, so He will give in the future, so that we may not hold such a well-conceived opinion in vain. I hasten to Rome, 
<margin>A hastening to those nine hundred conclusions</margin>
where we shall put our studies to the test, even at some risk <note>Pico is referring to his "900 Theses," which he intended to defend in a public disputation in Rome, leading to conflict with the Church</note>. If we achieve anything, it is God's gift; to Him be praise and thanks. If we fail in anything, it is our own weakness; let it be imputed to us. For the rest, I am yours, as one who, because of the integrity of your life and character, would hardly yield the first place in loving you even to our Jerome. Farewell, from Fratta.

-> Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Tommaso Mezzo. Health. XIX. <-

**I** do not remember ever being so thoroughly delighted as recently, while I was reading your *Epirota*, a little play undoubtedly most witty. With both the joy of the plot and the erudition of the style, it even challenges ancient comedies. For why should I mention these modern ones, which are clearly inept and witless, and easily declare the lack of skill of their authors? It was truly worthy to be dedicated to Ermolao Barbaro—I know not whether he is more your friend or mine—more especially marked. To him alone I think all men of letters owe as much as they hardly owe to antiquity itself. That you did not cheat me of it, you did through your most well-proven benevolence toward me. Nor is there anything with me of such value that, even if I gave it to you in exchange, I would think the favor was abundantly returned. The new comedy which you promise me, I am now waiting for with open mouth. Nor is there anything I desire more than that, except for your arrival to see us. Which, unless I had to depart from here within ten days (as I think you have learned from my letter), I would certainly have obtained from you by entreaty. For it is possible to gather from what you wrote what delightful pleasantness there would be in our association, in living together, and in the living voices, which certainly possess a latent energy <note>original: "energiam"</note> that affects the mind more deeply with pleasure in wonderful ways, far outweighing all writings. But since this is not allowed, do not expect again from me the material for a comedy. I prefer that you produce both parts from your own store, so that the little story may taste of "Tommaso Mezzo"—not "half" <note>Pico plays on the name "Mezzo," which means "half" or "middle" in Italian</note> but the whole man. For I fear lest, by following your lead, the dullness of my own genius might cause me to fall short. And if anything of mine were admitted, the work would degenerate from its maker. With me, there is nothing that is not unpolished, tasteless, foolish, or common. But these comedies require I know not what secret things—sarcastic, biting, elegant, sharp—which are the peculiar pleasantness of you and your genius. Therefore, the matter...

## Farewell. Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings. 20.

<margin>Speed of intellect</margin>
**Y**ou could not have requested your "Latin Muhammad" <note>Likely a reference to a translation of an Arabic philosophical or religious text</note> at a more opportune time than this, for very soon I will be hearing "Muhammad" himself speaking in his native tongue. I hope—after having kept watch day and night for a whole month over the Hebrew language—that now that I have devoted myself entirely to the study of Arabic and Chaldean <term>Chaldean: In this period, this usually referred to Aramaic or Syriac, which scholars believed held the secrets of ancient "Chaldean" wisdom</term>, I shall fear no less progress in them than I have made in Hebrew. In that language [Hebrew], I can already dictate a letter, not yet with great praise, but certainly without fault. See what the impulse of the mind can do! See what labor and diligence can achieve, even where the strength is somewhat weak. However, while I was occupied with other things, a certain force compelled me to learn the literature of the Arabs and Chaldeans: namely, certain books in both languages which came into my hands, surely not by chance or accident, but by the counsel of God and the favor of the divine power toward my studies. Hear the titles, and you will recognize a prophecy. These are Chaldean books (if they are books and not rather treasures!): first, the oracles of Ezra, Zoroaster, and Melchior the Magi, in which those same things that are circulated among the Greeks in a corrupt and mutilated state are read in their whole and perfect form. Then, there is a commentary by those Chaldean sages, brief and rugged indeed, but full of mysteries. There is likewise a small book on the dogmas of Chaldean theology, as well as divine and most rich explanations by the Greeks and Chaldeans upon it. See, Marsilio, what unexpected goods have crept into my bosom! Why should I not think that I have now obtained a "Horn of Plenty" <note>original: "Cornucopiā," a symbol of abundance</note> for myself? But what about the Arabic books? Among them are letters of Muhammad of Toledo, and of Abugale <note>likely the philosopher Avempace</note>, who heard Averroes <note>The famous Andalusian Muslim philosopher</note>; and (what will touch you more) many questions by a certain Adeladus, who prophesied in Egypt under Ammonius, the teacher of Plotinus <margin>Ammonius, teacher of Plotinus</margin>. Good God, how Pythagorean <note>Referring to the mystical and mathematical philosophy of Pythagoras</note> they are, how full of the dogmas of the ancients and of the most secret investigations of discipline! I wish I could effectively unroll and scrutinize these by myself without an interpreter. And this is what I am doing now; I am turning this stone <note>A metaphor for a heavy or monumental task</note> untiringly and assiduously. This, my dear Marsilio, is my desire; these are my fires, which promise me—and now even provide—a pleasure that is not fleeting and vain, but firm. It is a true image of that future glory which shall be revealed in us. But I return to your letter. Your "Muhammad" is at Perugia; when I return there (for I am currently away due to a suspicion of the plague), he will go to you immediately. Regarding what you write about Plotius, I do not quite understand; I only know that I have not forgotten Plotinus, whom I have always thought (and still think) should not only be kept in one's hands but even learned by heart. If you have complained about me either to Mithridates <note>Flavius Mithridates, Pico’s teacher of Hebrew and Arabic</note> or to Pierleone, it cannot be but that an injustice has been done to you on my part, for I have never been an injustice to you or your affairs in any way. What that matter might be, I still do not know; I am a Pythagorean, among whom nothing is more sacred than friendship; and if there is anything that could either weaken or diminish it between us (as they say), let it be carried away by the west winds. Farewell, and love me as your own, just as I have been and always was. From Fratta.

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Girolamo Donato sends many greetings. 21.

**F**or a long time, such is my negligence, I have written nothing to you. That was the sole cause of this silence of ours. I fear being judged by you for this crime—negligence, I mean. Otherwise, I am neither a man prone to forgetting nor a deserter of friendships. For I establish friendships with men of such genius as Donato not as temporary things, but as entirely perpetual.

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his Hermolao [Barbaro] sends many greetings. 22.

**I** sent a letter to you in recent days via our friend Sita. I do not know if it was delivered. Why you have not received the commentaries on Aristotle you requested, I have no doubt you understood from him. They will come as soon as I return to my library, for I have come here to explore other things for the present. Nor is there any reason for me to regret the journey, so many things have I found here, both Greek and Latin, pertaining to humane letters and learned philosophy. On this very day on which I am writing this, there fell into my hands a fragment of Apuleius <note>Author of 'The Golden Ass'</note> on interpretation: it is a learned work, and one you would clearly recognize as being by Apuleius, but it is mutilated...
