<margin>He doubts whether the text of Apuleius is mutilated or incomplete</margin> ...mutilated and maimed. Whether you have it as it is out of your own choice, or whether you have it whole so far as you know. Although when you have published your own works, which you currently have under the anvil <note>A common metaphor for a work in progress being refined</note>, there will no longer be any reason for us to miss Apuleius. As for my own studies, I have nothing to write to you except that I am a constant companion to Jerome and that I spend the greatest part of my nights keeping watch over your Themistius <note>Themistius was a 4th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were highly valued in the Renaissance</note>. I recently turned away from Aristotle toward the Academy <note>The "Academy" refers to the school of Plato</note>. But I did so not as a deserter, as that famous man says, but as an explorer <note>original: "non transfuga... sed explorator." This is a reference to Seneca the Younger, who said he visited other philosophical schools like a scout, not a defector</note>. I seem to recognize (I will tell you what I feel, Ermolao) two things in Plato: first, that Homeric faculty of eloquence which raises itself above ordinary speech; and second, if one looks more deeply into his meanings, a total commonality with Aristotle. So much so, that if you look at the words, nothing seems more combative, but if you look at the substance, nothing is more in accord. If I am ever given the chance—which is the sum of my prayers—we will spend several days together at the lighthouse <note>Likely a reference to a specific villa or study retreat</note> to discuss these things more broadly in person and make a test of this opinion of mine. Farewell, the glory of our age. Florence, December 6, 1484.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his brother Battista Mantuano, the Carmelite. Greetings. Letter 23.

Greetings, best of fathers. I have not written to you for some time, but in the meantime I have read those divine and most holy poems you have written. In them, there is such kingly majesty and such splendor of eloquence that the words and the meanings seem to compete to claim the prize for themselves. Happy are you who wish for the best things and are able to achieve them; happy are we to whom it is given not only to read what you have written, but also to love you, to see you, and to speak with you. This is a rich subject for me, and one that would fill not just a letter but a full volume, if either my own weakness or your modesty allowed me to wander at length in praising your poems. I will say this one thing: I am so delighted by the reading of your verses that almost every day, when either weariness or fatigue takes hold of me, I am accustomed to withdraw into them as if into a garden. From there, such great pleasure always arises in my mind that it desires nothing more than to be fatigued again, so that it may be refreshed in the same way. If you are finished with it, I miss the *Life of Apollonius* by Philostratus, and also Zacharias the Philosopher <note>Probably Zacharias Rhetor, a 6th-century Christian author</note>, whose copy you said you obtained in Rome; take care that I may have them at some point. Furthermore, I would like an index of your library at Bologna, if that can be done at your convenience. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to C. F. Greetings. Letter 24.

**I** wondered for a long time whether I should deal with you through silence or through letters. Since the matter seemed to have handles on both sides, and my judgment shifted now to this side and now to that, it was the reason why I have remained silent with you until this time. For it seemed no less shameless than troublesome to interrupt with these light trifles the ears of a man who is, above all, most occupied; and there was nothing at all worth writing to you. On the other hand, in the case of a man as distinguished in dignity as you are, who has deserved the best from me, I was undoubtedly failing in my duty by not venerating you through letters when I could not do so in person. After my mind had wavered for a long time between these thoughts, my devotion finally conquered my shame. It persuaded me that I should rather undergo the mark of being a bit bold and reckless than the mark of being a man who is either forgetful or negligent. Receive therefore, C. P., my letters with that cheerful and open brow with which you always used to receive me when I was there. They are indeed foolish and disorganized, but they are a most serious testimony of my loyalty toward you and of a will completely devoted to you. Through these letters, I wish this one thing to be signaled to you above all: there is nothing I desire more than that an occasion be given to me to leave behind with you some clear evidence of my loyalty, devotion, and respect. In these matters, if you ever put me to the test, you will recognize me to be as superior among those who are devoted to you as you yourself surpass the other prelates <term>antistites: high-ranking clergy or overseers</term> of your order in virtue, learning, and holiness.

A man was about to go to you on almost the same days I received yours; he was a truly honest man, but previously unknown to me. He said he was doing business in Milan. I thought his departure a timely opportunity for me, so that my letters might be delivered to you by a faithful messenger and, what I especially desired, without delay. But by postponing his departure for a month, he...

<header>OF THE LETTERS</header>

...it finally happened, but with me being utterly unaware. For my part, since I had already become somewhat negligent in writing letters <note>original: "litterarum"</note> in the hope of a certain messenger, forgetfulness had almost crept upon me. Now at last, when your letter fell into my hands, it instantly roused me as if from sleep, and it warned me of the time that had passed without my fulfilling my duty. I grieved (God is my witness) no small amount, and even now I grieve; nor would I wish to say these things to excuse myself, but rather to accuse myself. I will easily allow myself to be condemned of negligence, or to be called to whatever punishment you prefer. 

Now to your letters. I received no small pleasure both from the letters themselves and from the Greek books, the abundance of which you so liberally and so amicably made available to me; not so much because the use of them would contribute greatly to my studies, but because we have laid the foundations of a perpetual friendship <term>necessitudo</term> <note>A Latin term implying an unavoidable or sacred bond of intimacy and mutual obligation</note> between us. I value this one thing more than the entire library of either Synadius <note>Likely referring to a known collector or a specific Byzantine source</note> or Ptolemy <note>The Library of Alexandria</note>. For I am so far from neglecting the friendships of learned men that nothing is more of a concern or more to my heart. 

I know, however, what place you claim for yourself among learned men, since indeed your letter was the most evident proof to me of your teaching, erudition, and humanity. Therefore, unless I should love you most dearly, I would truly have forgotten myself and would act far differently than I am accustomed. I love you, therefore, uniquely, although I have never seen you; I love you so much from my soul that I love few more from my soul, so that finally it might be possible to add something to our familiarity, but not to our love. And if anything could be added, it would all come with your arrival here, which you have of your own accord promised in your letters, and which we seek so ardently that we desire it with impatience. If you would obtain for me John the Grammarian <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note> on the *Physics* and Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, you will have bound me to you in perpetual debt. For I do not have them, and I am in great expectation of them. Farewell.

---

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Giacomo Feltrino, Greeting. [Letter] XXVI.<-

**Y**our letters, if ever at any other time, have now delighted me most of all; through them I have learned that you hold such an estimation of me that no better could be imagined even in a prayer. One thing alone disturbed me: since you noted nothing [to critique] in those things which I wrote to you, you have created a suspicion that you did not think the whole work worthy of note. For I would have believed that many things pleased you then, if you had indicated that some things displeased you. Thus it happens that I do not sufficiently trust your testimony in my case, however highly esteemed it may be otherwise. For you love all our things just as you love us; and since from the innate ease of your character you praise everyone, this happens to you especially in our affairs, because all that is in us has flowed from your own fountain. Indeed, I do not cease, nor will I cease, to emulate you and to stand in your footsteps. Would that I might catch up to you one day. But I grieve that because of the distance between places, I am prevented from hearing you in person <note>original: "coram"</note> as you treat the deepest points of philosophy with your usual gravity. Although those same things which you say can be sent by letter—which I would most especially wish to obtain from you—nevertheless, I know not what power the living voice <note>original: "viva vox"</note> has to more greatly affect and mold the student. Farewell.

---

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Girolamo Donato. Greeting. [Letter] XXVII.<-

**I** received your letters, truly both sweet and learned, by which I was delighted no differently than I used to be by your company when I was in Padua, as often as the occasion of enjoying it was offered to me; for I was both eager for it and most desirous of it, even beyond your own opinion. For it was not hidden from me how sweet and pleasant was the genius of Donato, which is overflowing and filled on all sides with every good discipline and every virtue. But so it is indeed, my dear Girolamo: it very often happens to me that the free and easy opportunity of obtaining that which we most desire makes us sluggish and negligent. For while we hope that what we neglect today will be done quite conveniently tomorrow, it finally happens that from this sluggish delay of ours, an entire year slips away while we are blinking. But since the matter has turned out this way, you have done quite beautifully in that you have now roused me with your letters, as I was sleeping regarding this kind of duty. I shall use this against you more often in the future, and I would most greatly wish to ask you to do the same. As for what pertains to your poems, I had them with me for several days when I was in Padua, and I remember being captivated by the pleasantness and the most charming wit of the little book...

<header>BOOK ONE</header>

...delighted very much by the most rhythmic composition of the verses. But unless I am mistaken, before I departed from there, those things were returned to Ramusio <note>Girolamo Ramusio (1450–1486), a physician and humanist from Rimini</note> regarding the other matters that concern either me or my affairs. You should consider it settled that you may use them as your own; otherwise, you would certainly be doing an injury to both me and our friendship. Farewell.

-> **Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Angelo. Greetings. XXVIII.** <-

Since I have organized into five small books my slender muses <note>original: "tenues musas meas"</note>, with which I trifled concerning my loves for as long as my age permitted, I am sending them to you. I send these first, and shall send the rest later; in this one matter, I shall test whether you are a friend or a flatterer. For they come to you on the condition that they be corrected and even "flogged" <note>He invites harsh criticism, using the metaphor of a schoolboy being beaten for mistakes</note>, so that they may pay the penalty for their errors by both the fingernail <note>original: "ungue" – referring to the practice of running a thumbnail over a surface to check for smoothness</note> and the critical marks <term>obeliscis</term> <note>In ancient philology, an "obelus" was a mark (—) used to indicate suspected or spurious text</note>. Therefore, present yourself to them as a fair judge, not an unfair one—that is, be severe, not indulgent. For what greater unfairness is there than to deceive a friend who expects everything of you? I am not of such a delicate disposition that I would loathe the corrections of another, nor do I seem so beautiful to myself that I would either ignore or blame a censor. Indeed, perhaps neither you nor anyone else would believe how much these works of mine fail to satisfy me; I fear that even in those parts which please me more, I may be like that "Suffenus" mentioned by the poet <note>A reference to Catullus’s poem about Suffenus, a man who thought he was a great poet but was actually terrible</note>. We are all deceived all too often, and we do not see the knapsack of faults that hangs on our own backs <note>A reference to Aesop's fable where people carry their own faults in a bag behind them, but others' faults in front</note>. Therefore, do not deny your labor in an honorable and noble matter to a man who is most friendly to you, especially one who begs for it with such great zeal and from the bottom of his heart. If I were a man who could return the favor to you in such a matter, I would not keep silent about that Greek saying that Lysippus used the work of Apelles, and Apelles that of Lysippus, in turn <note>original: "Lysippum apellis & apellem liisippi" – Lysippus was a sculptor and Apelles a painter; Pico suggests they refined each other's art</note>. Farewell.

-> **Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano. Greetings. XXIX.** <-

When I was in Florence in previous years, I left four love elegies with you, which I had composed almost as a boy for the sake of exercising my mind, as is often the case. They were somewhat dull, unlearned, and trivial, easily revealing the age and ignorance of their author. You, however, approved of them—not because of the merit of the work, but out of your own kindness and indulgence. For that very reason, to prove that you approved of them, you requested copies. Surely you were not unaware that such things are very sharp incitements <note>original: "incitabula"</note> for the minds of youths toward virtue, so that, enticed by the desire for praise, they might soon strive to taste more deeply the glory they have only sipped. For just as strength lies down and grows cold through despair, so there is no one who doubts that it is raised up and set on fire by hope. But now the defense of my age is gone; those errors which I previously signed my name to will now be considered a vice, since I, now more mature in years, have neither cleansed them better nor deleted them. Therefore, regarding whichever of my poems are in your possession, if you love me, you should either send them back to me, or tear them up, or commit them to the fire. All these, more highly polished, along with many others which have flowed from me during my leisure since I left that place, will shortly be entrusted to your "file" <note>original: "limae" – the humanist metaphor for the final polishing and editing of a literary work</note>. Meanwhile, let those which cannot live without detriment to a friend be condemned by a "capital vote" <note>A legal metaphor meaning they should be sentenced to death/destruction</note>. Furthermore, I would entirely wish for you to send me your translation of Epictetus, and whatever of Homer you have translated to this day; likewise, what you composed concerning Giuliano de' Medici in our native tongue <note>Italian</note>, and whatever else you have written in the Latin language. I ask this of you as one who asks most urgently, for I desire them as one who is most impatient. There is no reason for you to refuse on the grounds that they have not yet been "brought to the navel" <note>original: "ad umbilicum" – an ancient expression meaning "to the very end," referring to the rod at the end of a scroll</note>; for I already announce and promise you that all these things shall remain secret with me, if that be your wish. Farewell.

-> **Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino. Greetings. XXX.** <-

<margin>Who Hermes Trismegistus is</margin>
It has always been my judgment, most learned Marsilio, that one must labor at nothing more than that we should in no way degenerate through laziness and sluggishness from the nobility of the mind—by which (as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed; Ficino was his most famous translator</note> testifies) we are considered next after Jupiter <note>Used here to mean God</note>. This has always been my chief aim: to acquire for myself the cultivation of the mind and the disciplines of the noble arts from wherever I could. Although this plan of mine has been most constant since my childhood, nevertheless, your exhortations when I was with you in previous years greatly aroused and inflamed me; nor ever more ardently than from that time until this...

# LETTERS

...day I have devoted myself entirely to letters. For three years now I have been occupied with the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> under Marsilio’s guidance; nor have I omitted anything, as far as I was able, so that I might be admitted into the house of the Aristotelians as if I were a not unworthy member of their family. And although I have not achieved this abundantly—indeed, I have barely crossed the threshold—nonetheless, I have advanced so far that if I do not yet claim the name of a learned and erudite man (which my age does not yet allow), I would not hesitate to claim the title of a student. But since it has always been your opinion, and that of the most learned men, that Academic <note>Platonic</note> philosophy should be mixed with Peripatetic—and that both schools would thus be better maintained and more enriched—I thought I should undertake this task: that now, according to the strength of my talent and with the greatest possible diligence and industry, I might compare Plato with Aristotle, and in turn, through alternating studies, Aristotle with Plato. But just as I previously needed you as a monitor, so now I need you as a helper; and it will be a mark of your humanity and benevolence toward me not to fail my purpose, especially one so honorable and noble. I believe this would be most fully accomplished by you if you were to send me your book *On the Immortality of Souls* <note>Ficino's masterpiece, the *Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum*</note>. With this book as a kind of guide, I trust I shall make the progress in Platonic discipline that I desire. For who—if the opinion of the Pythagoreans were true that Plato had been reborn in Ficino—would not promise himself the greatest things in that kind of learning? Only do not fail me. I would plead for this more extensively, were it not that the very reason of honor, which you value most highly, pleads this same thing from you. For if our friend Cicero, the wise Chilo, and the most grave philosopher Theophrastus thought one should deviate somewhat from the path for the sake of friends, would it not be a disgrace to fail a most dear friend in such an honorable request? Act, therefore, so that through your help I may finally achieve what I have long pursued by your encouragement. For I have no one else who can assist me in this matter besides you, since—just as many other beautiful things have faded—so the care for noble Platonic matters has almost entirely died out among the men of our age. Farewell.

-> Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Hermolaus. Greetings. XXXI. <-

**A**lthough I have nothing worthy of you to write, I write to you anyway; but for this reason alone: so that you may write back. Otherwise, I have neither any necessity nor any subject for writing. For I have always condemned the opinion of those who feel one must write to friends as if this were a debt to be paid to friendship. Indeed, this whole business of writing and sending letters back and forth belongs to a friendship that is weak and somewhat chilly—one that does not stand firm supported by its own strength and seeks from elsewhere a way to sustain itself. But for a friendship that has already taken root deep in the very recesses of the soul, why, I ask you, does it need the support of letters? I will therefore give you my letters, Hermolaus Barbarus, for this reason: to entice yours, which I desire most greatly. You, in turn, lest I desire yours in vain, shall return them most abundantly. For while it is the mark of a weak mind to use letters as if they were "props" <note>original: "tibicines" — literally 'flute-players' or 'supports/buttresses' used to keep a building from falling</note> for friendship so it doesn't waver, it is nonetheless a mark of singular liberality and benevolence to show oneself easy and beneficial to friends. Farewell. And please send me Ptolemy’s *Harmonics* <note>original: "muficam Ptolomæi" — a Greek treatise on music theory</note>, if it is not an inconvenience, to be here for a few days. For what might I not boldly ask of you, to whom I have long since vowed and dedicated all my things?

-> Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Hermolaus. Greetings. XXXII. <-

**I** have never either pleased myself more or owed more abundantly than at this time, when my single letter to you has called forth from you letters so sweet, so erudite, and so much like yourself. Because if your being away in Padua while I was there, and my missing your company for two years, was the reason why you wrote these things to me, it cannot be anything but pleasant to me now. Your single letter has not only abundantly fulfilled my every wish but even exceeded it. For—to say nothing of the elegance, pleasantness, erudition, and sweetness of the letter, the reading of which demands a great deal in return—how much do you think I value the fact that you give yourself to me as a friend so lovingly, so kindly, and so truly from the heart? And that you so liberally promise your effort in every way to honor me, which is something I could not have dared to hope for? Indeed, I frankly confess, without blushing in your presence, that this kind of service is not merely to be accepted but to be sought after by me. For, as you know, not even the Stoics themselves approve of *apathy* <note>original: "ἀπάθειαν" (apatheian) — the state of being free from all passion or emotion</note>, nor...

# BOOK ONE

...nor among these affections, which the Greeks call <term>passions</term> <note>original: "πάθη" (pathe)</note>, can any be more praiseworthy or more honorable than this: if indeed there is among them that which is called a desire for name and glory. Indeed, this can be provided to me more abundantly by no one than by yourself, in whom all the virtues, as if individually, compete to claim the palm of victory for themselves; and certainly I have no one to whom I would more gladly owe a debt. Therefore, this promise of yours is as pleasing and desirable to me as it is honorable, in which I rejoice most greatly because it provides proof of your extraordinary love for me and your most affectionate goodwill. I have at last what I long desired before now; thus I now truly triumph. I have, I say, Hermolaus Barbarus—the delight of the Latin language and a distinguished storehouse of all the fine arts—who is not only well-disposed toward me but most friendly. You likewise have Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, so devoted to you, so studious of your interests, that one could not be more devoted or more studious. In mutual duties toward you—since he can provide nothing either grand or worthy of Hermolaus—he will be unequal; yet if you look upon his humble spirit, he will certainly be either equal or superior.

->Farewell.<-
->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, etc. [space] Letter XXXIII.<-

---

<margin>Plato and Aristotle said that the soul is the seat of friendship</margin>
**N**othing was sweeter to me while you were here with us than your company; likewise nothing was more useful, such is the sweetness of your character and such is your learning. See, however, how sweet and how pleasing you were to me while I enjoyed your presence, since now that you are absent, nothing is sweeter to me than the memory of you. But truly, if the seat of friendship is the soul, and we are most especially that soul—as Plato and Aristotle write—there is no reason why any distance of places or long intervals of time should be able to create a separation between us. I was thinking just now whether there might be any other way I could achieve being with you, and nothing else came to mind except that my late-night work on the sevenfold narration of the six days of Genesis <note>This refers to Pico's work, the *Heptaplus*, a mystical commentary on the creation story</note> should come to you. For if we give birth to books as if they were children, and the greatest part of the father is in the son, I too shall come to you in that which I have fathered. Receive, therefore, my little son coming to you, as you were used to receiving me, cheerfully and gladly; it will please you, I know, because you love me. I know it will also displease you, for the same reason: because you love me. For it is the nature of such devotion both to look closely into the errors of those we love so that we may correct them, and to indulge lightly in those errors once seen so that we do not cause distress.

---

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola [to] F. B. C. Th. [space] Letter XXXIIII.<-

**G**reetings, most beloved father. Here is Apollonius for you; if I did not owe him to your virtue and your services to me, I would certainly owe him because of those letters in which you requested him with such love and such kindness. For it is a mark of the highest love to call me to that place where you have already arrived—namely, to the <term>purification of the soul</term>, which is true happiness—and it is a mark of the highest kindness to exhort me as an equal, when you could dictate the law to me as a son. But I hope it may happen some time in practice that we can speak piously together in some retreat. You will see that for me nothing is more important than to join piety with wisdom. You will see that I am most convinced that no wisdom exists which should blot out the image of eternal wisdom within us and make us like foolish beasts. I have my guardian angel as a witness that I count as profit in my daily studies only as much as I emerge better equipped and stronger for the struggle of purifying the soul. This all-embracing handling of disciplines and whatever letters <note>In the sense of "humanistic studies" or "literature"</note> can promise us merely colors the skin, and makes us more beautiful as if with a painted face. But we cannot hope for a healthy, firm, and robust mind from any other source than from integrity of life, from morals, and finally, from divine religion. Therefore, you compel one who is willing (if I may say so) to be even more willing. But also help me with your sacred prayers so that I may be able to do what I myself wished and what you so greatly desire me to wish. Farewell, most loving father, whom I love uniquely, whom I hold dear as my own eyes. Florence, January 14, 1490. I await all your news. My Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the prominent Renaissance scholar and poet</note>, the delight of all literature, bids me send you his greetings.

# Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Ermolao Barbaro, Greetings. Letter XXXV.

<margin>Ermolaus is honored by his translation of Themistius</margin>
**I** remember when I was deliberating which of the Italian gymnasiums <note>The word "gymnasium" here refers to a university or center of higher learning.</note> I should choose as my seat for the study of philosophy, and though many things called me to Padua, I sought to go there primarily so that my love for you, which I had long nourished in my heart, might be made plain to you through mutual association. I was in Padua for two years; yet—who would believe it?—I neither saw Ermolao, nor did I know him except by the reputation he had gained long before. Thus it often happens that while we look down upon an offered opportunity with a certain lazy procrastination, it slips through our hands like something slippery. I have regretted this matter vehemently and continue to regret it, and all the more so because the learning in all subjects for which I had previously known you only by rumor, I have now recognized with these very eyes and ears, while I heard the "Roman" Themistius <note>Ermolao Barbaro had recently translated the works of Themistius, a 4th-century Greek commentator on Aristotle, into Latin.</note> discoursing through your mouth on the genius of philosophy, on the first beginnings of things, and on the science of reasoning. Good God, what depth of learning! What riches of expression! What brilliance! What purity of speech! O most distinguished power! O vivid image of antiquity! It was my frequent prayer that the writings of Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar considered the most learned man of antiquity.</note> on divine and human matters might one day live again, so that we might have someone from whom we could learn the principles of physics in Latin. Indeed, you, reflecting both him and all the most approved authors, have shown yourself to us such that nothing else remains for us to desire, except that by translating other Greek works, you might both prepare more abundant praise for yourself and deserve even better from natural history and all students of letters. All these things, most learned Ermolao, look to nothing else than that you may understand me to be most friendly to you: your virtues so kindle me toward loving and observing you that I would yield to no one, even from your own kin, in my love for you. Let this letter sanction the treaty of friendship between us, so that we may continually engage in a most honorable contest of mutual affection.

---

# Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Andrea Corneo of Urbino, Greetings. Letter XXXVI.

**T**he letters you recently sent me on the Ides of October <note>October 15th.</note> I have received. As for those you say you sent previously, they did not arrive; I would have replied immediately if I had received them, for I am not lazy in writing, and in this duty—whether by study or by nature—I am least of all a loiterer. Yet there was no reason that our friendship could be weakened by an old and even long-standing silence; I am a perpetual friend, not a temporary one. Nor is a friendship firm enough if it requires these letters like "props"—returning the favor of letters—which (to use a word from Plautus) might "support" <note>original: "furcillent," a rare verb from the Roman playwright Plautus meaning to prop up or support something weak.</note> it as if it were tottering and somewhat infirm. <margin>Plautus</margin> But to come to the matters you write of: you exhort me to an active and civil life, saying that I have studied philosophy for so long in vain and almost to my ignominy and disgrace unless I eventually sweat in the arena of conducting and managing affairs. And indeed, my dear Andrea, I would have lost the oil and labor of my studies <margin>Note</margin> if I were now of such a mind that I could side with you and agree with you on this part. This is that fatal and monstrous persuasion which has invaded the minds of men: either that the studies of philosophy are not to be touched by leading men, or that they should be tasted only with the tips of the lips for the sake of intellectual display, rather than for the cultivation of the soul, and even then only in leisure. They hold that decree of Neoptolemus <note>A character in a lost play by Ennius who famously said one must philosophize "only a little."</note> as an absolute rule: one must philosophize either not at all, or only a little. They now receive the sayings of the wise as trifles and mere fables—that firm and solid happiness lies in the goods of the soul, and that these external things of the body or of fortune pertain to us either little or not at all. But you will say: "I wish you to embrace Martha in such a way that you do not meanwhile desert Mary." <note>A traditional allegory where Martha represents the active life of service and Mary represents the contemplative life of prayer and study.</note> On this part I do not fight you, nor do I damn or accuse those who do so. But it is far from the truth that it is an error not to have passed from the life of contemplation to the civil life; nor do I think that not passing over should be considered a disgrace or altogether marked with the brand of fault or crime. Therefore, let it be turned to a vice if a man affects and pursues virtue itself for the sake of virtue, seeking nothing outside of it, while he enjoys this leisure, scrutinizing divine mysteries and the counsels of nature, looking down upon and neglecting all other things, since those former things are enough to satisfy the prayers of their followers. Would it then be illiberal, or not at all the part of a prince, to pursue the study of wisdom for its own sake rather than for pay? Who could endure or listen to such things with a calm mind? Certainly, he was never a philosopher who became a philosopher so that one day he might...

<header>BOOK ONE</header>

...when he either can or will not philosophize. He practiced trade, not philosophy. You write that you desire me to give myself over for a time to some of the greatest princes of Italy. You do not yet know the opinion of those who philosophize about themselves:
<margin>Horace</margin>
Who, according to Horace <note>original: "iuxta horatium"</note>, think of themselves as kings of kings; they do not know how to endure the manners of others or to serve. They live with themselves and, content with their own tranquility of soul, they are sufficient unto themselves. They seek nothing outside themselves; things that are in honor among the common people are dishonored among them. And indeed, whatever human lust thirsts for or ambition sighs for, they neglect and despise. This should be done by everyone, and without doubt especially by those to whom Fortune has so indulged that they can live not only elegantly and comfortably, but even splendidly. These great fortunes certainly elevate and show off, but often, like a fierce and bucking horse, they throw the rider. Certainly, they always trouble and vex rather than carry. That desirable **golden mean** <note>original: "Aurea illa optanda mediocritas"; a reference to the classical ideal of moderation found in Horace’s Odes</note> which carries us as if by hand more steadily, and which is patient of our lack of wealth, truly serves us and does not rule over us. Staying in this opinion, I place my little cell, my studies, the delights of my books, and the peace of my soul before royal courts, public business, the hunting of favors, and the honors of the court. Nor do I expect such fruits from my <term>literary</term> <note>original: "literarii"</note> leisure that I should be tossed and fluctuate in the heat and tumult of public affairs. But rather, that I might finally give birth to those children I labor over, and—may it be happy and auspicious—put something forth in public: if not learning or genius, then at least diligence that "smells of the lamp" <note>An ancient idiom for a work produced by long nighttime study.</note>. And lest you believe our industry and labor has slackened: know that after much work devoted to constant and tireless nightly studies, I have learned the Hebrew and **Chaldaic** <note>original: "hebraicã linguã chaldai/cã"; Chaldaic was the contemporary term for Aramaic.</note> languages;
<margin>Study of Languages</margin>
and I have even now applied my hands to overcoming the difficulties of Arabic. These are the things I have always thought, and now think, to be worthy of a leading man. But though I say this truly and severely, I do indeed cherish and revere those most excellent princes, and especially the magnanimous Ludovico, Duke of Bari <note>Ludovico Sforza, known as "Il Moro," then Duke of Bari and regent of Milan.</note>, more than anyone among the princes of Italy. I understand that I owe him much for many reasons; and there is nothing so heavy, nothing so arduous that (if the opportunity were given to me) I would not do for the sake of deserving his favor. But such is their greatness and my insignificance: just as I cannot help but need them, they can in no way need either my labor or my arrival there. I shall depart for Rome shortly to spend the winter there, unless some sudden accident or new intervening fortune draws me elsewhere. From there, perhaps you will hear what your Pico has accomplished in his shadowy and sedentary life of contemplation; or what at last (I will say it, however arrogantly) he needs of others' labor in <term>literary</term> matters—he for whom you promised a wealth of teachers upon arriving there. In Rome and wherever on earth I shall be, those princes will have someone they can command; whom, as Plautus says, they may turn at their whim like a **revolving millstone** <note>original: "trusatilem... molam"; a reference to manual slave labor, used here as a metaphor for a courtier's lack of freedom.</note>.
<margin>Plautus</margin>
<margin>The wit of Terence should be noted</margin>
As for what you write regarding the matter of a wife: I do not think it was said rashly or for no reason. But I am **Davus, not Oedipus** <note>A famous line from Terence’s play *Andria*. It means "I am a simple man, not a solver of riddles." Pico is politely declining to engage in the complexity of a marriage proposal.</note>; nor if I were, would I wish to be. Whatever it is, if it seems right, explain it more broadly; if not, let it be **Harpocrates** <note>The Greco-Roman god of silence.</note>. I take counsel as things present themselves. There is no reason for you to desire my **Tuscan rhythms** <note>original: "Rhythmos meos hetruscos"; referring to his early Italian love poetry, which he later renounced.</note>. We have long since sent a message of divorce to those amorous trifles; we are meditating on other things. But I want you also to be warned: if you are going to publish your "Laura," suppress it for a few more days. For perhaps soon our people will read things about love (see what I say!) which they have not yet read. And you will be able to note many things that will be of great use to your work. Concerning that librarian, although he is not worthy of me speaking about him: I would only say that he has returned the favor poorly to a master who deserved better. There is no reason for him to cast or derive his flight onto anyone else but himself, since he owes no less to my household—which he cannot deny—than he does to me. But this is not the first time, as you know, that he has broken faith or mocked his master. I know that after he fled, he spoke against me;
<margin>Wittily said</margin>
but **the elephant does not care about the gnat** <note>original: "non curat culicem elephas"; a proverb meaning the great are unbothered by the insignificant.</note>. And I want whatever that light-headed man has sinned heretofore to be forgiven by you. But let him not abuse my patience in the future, lest I be forced to eventually show myself to him in the same way he deservedly showed himself to me. As for that friend of yours whose love affair turned out poorly...

<header>OF LETTERS</header>
<meta>Catchword: Among</meta>

<margin>Note.</margin>
You have excused our Florian <note>Florian was likely a member of Pico's circle or household who had committed a moral lapse, possibly involving a woman</note> from his duty; he has means from history, from 
poets, and even from philosophy itself to clear himself from the mark of crime. He has the 
precedents of great men to protect him—David, and especially Solomon—not to mention 
Aristotle, who, while he often fell desperately in love with several harlots, remembered nothing of 
his own moral precepts when he performed sacrifices to his beloved woman as if to Eleusinian Ceres <note>Aristotle was famously accused of offering sacrifices to his mistress Herpyllis or Hermias’s concubine Pythias, as if she were a goddess</note>. But he [Florian] does not embrace these defenses and, as it were, ramparts 
of his deed; he does not love them, but hates, rejects, and refuses them. He laments his own 
ruin; he does not plead against his fault. He grieves that he has sinned; he does not defend it. 
And to me, he seems for this reason alone worthy of excuse by others, because he does not 
excuse himself at all. Nothing is weaker than man; nothing is more powerful than love. 
That invincible and unshaken mind of Jerome <note>St. Jerome, a 4th-century Church Father, famously wrote about being tempted by memories of dancing girls while living as a hermit in the Syrian desert</note>, while it clung entirely to heaven, wasted 
away among the dances of girls. What plague could infest him that love will not tame? 
Thus love was able to do this in the desert, on ground where his limbs were crushed, and 
amidst the fasting of weeks. What will it not be able to do in soft feathers, in the 
shade, in the abundance of all delights? It happens that he has now fallen for the first time, 
otherwise unaccustomed to and ignorant of such a ruin. He can complain of Neptune <note>A metaphor for a sudden, overwhelming misfortune or temptation</note>, who 
suffered shipwreck only once. If he should strike against the same stone a second time, let no 
one stretch out a hand; let no one take pity. Now, he cannot rightly be refused excuse, 
he who so repents of the deed that he does not think himself worthy of the benefit of an 
excuse. But even these words are too many, since your friend desires that the memory of such 
a deed not only be recorded in letters in some way, but that his subsequent life may cause it 
to be entirely blotted out. Farewell. Christopher was not present when I received your 
letters. You will commend me in no common way to your lord and to the entire Borromeo 
family, which I have always loved and now love most greatly. At Perugia, October 15, 1486, the year of grace.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his nephew Giovanni Francesco. Greetings. XXXVII.<-

Your letters were most pleasing to me, not only because I had heard nothing of you for a 
long time, but also because they signaled things to me in which I was wonderfully delighted; 
because those same things are pleasing to you, I do not doubt they are most pleasing to God. 
You also should not doubt that if you only proceed in the way you have begun, your reward 
will be abundant in heaven. I do not yet have it sufficiently explored whether I must go to 
Rome or not. And as far as I can follow by a conjecture of future things, I rather believe 
that I must go there; you know the cause. As soon as I have this as a certainty, I will 
inform you immediately, lest if you come here (which otherwise I would greatly wish), you 
either do not find me here, or you must return to your own country immediately upon my 
departure. Meanwhile, you can be at home unless you feel otherwise. But remember also 
this: that you have a wife to whom you owe your body no differently than you owe your 
soul to God. Her desire must be satisfied in some part; and you must consider what she, 
from the condition of her body and from her age, either desires or could desire; and what, 
<margin>Paul</margin>
out of modesty and virtue, she does not ask for. For why should it shame me to write these 
things which the Apostle Paul also writes? <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 7:3-4, regarding the "marital debt" owed between spouses</note> There is almost no matter in which I suspect 
you could err more. And indeed, our men are very much mistaken who think their wives 
are bound and addicted to them, while they owe nothing to their wives; but they think they 
can decide about themselves whatever they judge at their own whim. Finally, you cannot be 
entirely your own, you who, once subjecting yourself to the laws of marriage, wished to 
belong to a wife. You can nonetheless be entirely God's, whom you deserve for yourself 
while you obey His law, even if in these things which are of God you obey yourself less. 
But I have spoken with you about these things in person at another time. As soon as the air 
turns to spring, that is, during the first days of Lent, when I have extricated myself 
from these bundles of Greek books <note>Pico was a prolific collector and student of Greek manuscripts, many of which were rare in Italy at the time</note>, I will immediately come to Ferrara. Meanwhile, 
give yourself to sacred letters, especially the reading of the Gospels, which may repeatedly 
lead the soul back to God, whom the world and that demon do not cease to lead away 
from there, day and night, with allurements and deceits. Farewell, half of my soul, and 
pray to God for me. As soon as I have decided anything concerning my journey toward 
Rome, I will inform you. Florence, November 27, 1492.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his friend Iacopo Antiquario. Greetings. XXXVIII.<-

# BOOK ONE

**A**mong the pleasures I most enjoyed from the company of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant poet and scholar, and a close friend of Pico</note> while I was in Florence—a man who is, in my opinion, the most learned of all in our age—it was no small delight that your letters to him, which were always weighty and elegant, he would immediately give to me to read as soon as he received them. I was greatly delighted in them both by a certain singular wisdom—for you are commended by the most prudent men even in the handling of great affairs and business—and by the refinement and restraint of your style. Furthermore, because you made honorable mention of us in several of them, not only did your letters please me, but I even began to please myself in them! Naturally, with my conscience yielding to the testimony of such a great man, it did not much hide what it felt; if it betrayed itself, it did not fight much against the feeling and was, in a way, willing to be deceived. Thus, I was bound to you by a double name: first by your virtue, and second by this kindness so often bestowed upon us. I thought more than once of giving you thanks through a letter, lest I should seem perhaps ungrateful or uncouth toward you. But since you and our Poliziano were carrying out such a beautiful commerce of letters between yourselves, I did not wish to disturb the Muses with the importunate chattering of a 
<margin>Note the simile.</margin>Magpie <note>original: "Pica". Pico is making a pun on his own name, "Picus," which sounds like "Pica," the Latin word for magpie. He contrasts the chattering magpie with the "swan-like" elegance of his friends</note>—which, like a poorly-voiced goose, might disrupt the swans singing alternately to each other. Otherwise, I knew my heart was open to you through our Poliziano; and being conscious of my own speechlessness, I used him as a most eloquent interpreter. Now, your letters have been sent to us by him, which you recently gave to Riccio, an ingenious young man; in these, you attribute to me more than I would dare to hope for, let alone believe I deserve. The magnitude of this obligation has broken my silence—which has been, I know not if uncivil, but certainly not proud—and I could not fail to give you immortal thanks. This is not because you overwhelm me with immoderate praises (which I do not recognize as true), but because you love me so much that your judgment, otherwise so constant and robust, has nevertheless wavered so much in my case under the weight of love. I owe you more, therefore, than I could ever repay, or than you might easily believe; nor is there anything so arduous or difficult that I would not do it for your honor as readily as for my own safety. As for what you possessed of me through Poliziano until now, now with nothing changed in the matter, you will simply find the name of Pico listed among your own accounts. Farewell. From the Ferrarian countryside, the 28th day of June, 1494.

->To the excellent and most learned man, Lord Jacobus Antiquarius <note>Jacobus Antiquarius (c. 1444–1512) was a high-ranking secretary to the Dukes of Milan and a central figure in Italian literary circles</note>, as if to a father.<-

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Andrea Corneo <note>Andrea Corneo was a nobleman from Urbino and a friend of Pico</note>. Greetings.<-

->E. XXXIX.<-

**M**y wishes have been fully and abundantly satisfied, dearest Andrea. For I have learned from your letters to Christopher (our very dear friend) that you are living there with both comfort and dignity. Indeed, this is and always has been my greatest wish: that you should be well and happy, and I have nothing greater to say in view of your merits. I never doubted that this would be the outcome. One thing has always been clear to me: as long as you have a tongue to speak, wherever in the world you might be, you would be held in high esteem. I know—and let this be said without flattery—the generosity of your spirit, which will suffer nothing humble or common. I know your virtues, your learning, your character, and your wisdom; all these things will easily lead you wherever you aim. Yet I fear for your health, which has been oppressed by so many illnesses from an early age (as you used to tell me), and though weakened, it is more tired than broken; indeed, your spirit has so moved your nature that it knows not how to be defeated, but with a certain perpetual solidity of its own, it fights strenuously against the blows of fortune. I beg you, take no less account of your health than of your fortunes; for these are nothing when life fails. As for the fact that you speak of me honorably before everyone, you do so indeed out of your kindness and long-standing benevolence toward me, and for that, I owe you as much as one can possibly owe. But I fear you may be unravelling your own web <note>A reference to Penelope’s web from the Odyssey; here meaning undoing his own reputation for good judgment</note> while you call into public view my ineptitudes and those trifles that flowed from me in my more tender age. For all those things are crude and unlearned; though one might judge them most kindly, they are certainly not the things that can sustain the opinion those men have perhaps already conceived of me through your speech. However, whatever they may be, I thought they should be sent to satisfy you, even at the cost of my entire reputation. Yet I would ask you to consider all these as lighter matters; for if the business at last...

<header>LETTERS</header>

...you will miss mine; and we have weightier matters in hand which have not yet been brought to a conclusion <note>original: "ad umbilicum... ducta", a classical metaphor referring to finishing a scroll by reaching the "umbilicus" or central stick</note>. And even these very things which we have sent were requiring a more perfect polish. But both the times and these studies, over which I keep watch most intensely, have diverted me from the work. We shall return, however, at some point to the Muses: and if we should strike out anything worthy of your ears, we will take care that it be brought to you immediately. Farewell.

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to R. C. <note>likely a Reverend Cardinal</note>, Greetings. Letter 40.

**M**atthew, our most dutiful man, gave me many greetings in your words and most aptly declared with what love and benevolence you follow me. He promised, moreover, in your name, your zeal and labor if ever it should happen that I might use them. Would that I were equal to this, O most kind one. For I have always both desired and hoped to be received into your protection and to be numbered among your friends. But that you should come to meet me of your own accord, approaching me so kindly with such friendly and liberal promises, and calling me—as if to a friendship, if it is allowed, but rather to your fatherly care—surpassed all my hope and every vow. For what is more pleasing than to be invited by him from whom it would have been enough not to be excluded? Although you have done a thing worthy, if not of me, then certainly of yourself. For I could have been not admitted due to my merits; yet I could not, given your humanity, fail to be called. Therefore, how much I rejoice for myself, or how much I owe to you, I cannot explain, for I cannot even conceive it. Certainly, I owe you all the more because you owe these things to me in no way (having no obligation on your part). For those things are not too grand or too many which Matthew and other friends have reported back, estimating me from goodwill rather than from judgment. <margin>Note</margin> But whatever sort of person I am, or how great I am, allow me also to be among all those who—to say nothing of the rest—cherish and admire your virtues, which are so evident in you that they both surpass antiquity and cannot be surpassed by posterity. I might say this deservedly, since in you nothing is found wanting that is placed in either honor or wisdom or learning. This one thing ought to be desired by all: that through you, at some point, according to **Plato's wish** <note>Pico refers to the famous "Philosopher King" concept from Plato’s Republic, where the state is best governed when power and wisdom are united</note>, the highest power might be joined with the highest wisdom. But these things are from God. Meanwhile, I ask and request this of you: that you provide me an opportunity—not for returning thanks, for there is no room for that either given your greatness or my insignificance—but for testifying to my mind toward you, and for testifying to my loyalty and respect. You shall find Giovanni Pico to be a man dedicated and devoted to you beyond all expectation; I cannot promise more for him. But you can use all those things, of whatever sort they may be, which are in him; and when you yourself use them, you will bring something of your own splendor to them, and they will become great when they begin to be yours, which while they are mine cannot be great. Farewell.

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his Alexander Cortese <note>Alexander Cortese (1460–1490) was a humanist poet and apostolic protonotary</note>, Greetings. Letter 41.

**Y**our letters were most pleasing to me, which you recently gave—not, as you think, as one unknown to another unknown, but as a friend and indeed an old friend, even if not yet as one known person to another. For you also knew me before, as you write, and you judged me worthy of your love. I likewise have heard very often of your learning and virtue, both from many people and from our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the brilliant scholar and poet who was a central figure in the Medici circle</note>; and who would not trust his judgment? He created in me a faith in your integrity, and he acted as a father in making me receive your benevolence long ago. Although that benevolence was already very great, know that your letter added such heaps to it as few could even conceive in their mind. For what is more pleasing than that letter? What is more learned? How scholarly it is, how lovable, as you most generously subscribe to what our friend Puccio <note>likely Puccio Pucci, a Florentine official</note> said of me, speaking more out of friendship than truth. Truly, nothing more pleasing than that could have happened to me from you, nor anything more honorable than your opinion of me. For all these things I give you the greatest thanks, and I confess that whatever is mine, or is in me, I owe to my Alexander. I am sending to you the letter which you requested, addressed to **Lorenzo de' Medici** <note>The ruler of Florence and great patron of the Renaissance</note>.

I am anxious about your health, not only for its own sake and because I love you—for I love you vehemently—but also because...

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Andrea Corneo. Greetings. Letter 43.

<margin>Commentaries on Plato's Symposium</margin>
**E**ven if I have sent letters to you rarely or never, I have nevertheless thought of you and your affairs often and constantly. But I do not wish to sell you hope, nor will I write to you what I am doing for your benefit until I can write what I have accomplished. For if it should never happen, due to your misfortune or mine, I prefer you to believe that I did nothing rather than that I labored in your affairs in vain. But perhaps fortune will be more joyful for you than either hope itself or she is accustomed to be. There is no reason for our poems to delay your "Laura" <note>likely a reference to Petrarch's muse, or a specific poetic project</note>, since they have been brought back to the anvil <note>a classical metaphor for revising a text</note> to be more perfectly shaped, nor do they dare to go out into public with the face they now have. A pressing reason and the urgency of a new work which I have in hand at the encouragement of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>The de facto ruler of Florence and a great patron of the arts</note> delays the correction; in this work, I not only illuminate the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms of King David</note> with a longer 
<margin>Hymns, interpretation</margin>
interpretation, but because those which the Church sings were translated by the "Seventy" <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>—and the Hebrews prove that translation to be unfaithful in more than six hundred places—I, relying on the propriety of the Hebrew and Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note> literature, both assert and defend them from every calumny of the Jews with the integrity of their meanings. There is nothing else to write, except that you should commend me to Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro, a famous Venetian scholar</note> as often as you see the man, and not in an ordinary way. Likewise, see that the learned and grave man Jacopo Volterrano understands that he is vehemently loved by me; if I might obtain from him the letters of Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a 4th-century Roman statesman known for his elegant letters</note> for a few days until they are transcribed, he will bind me to him by a perpetual benefit. Farewell. 1489.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Battista Guarino, his teacher. Greetings. Letter 44.

**W**hy do you knit your brow? Is it because I have inscribed you as "teacher" contrary to what you commanded, and therefore did you an injustice? If you are not a teacher, I am not rightly bound by your commands. If you are a teacher, I rightly call you teacher. But why do you reject the disciple whom you have praised for so long? These things conflict with one another, unless perhaps one belongs to love and the other to judgment: and while you proclaim his praises out of benevolence, you fear his errors out of conscience, lest, namely, they cause you shame—that you might perhaps be able to be his praiser but not his teacher. Receive me, I pray, even on this condition: into a partnership of learning, so that I may admit you into a partnership of our little glory (if there shall be any), while I alone sustain the blows. 

But why do I delay with cold jests the ardor of my joy, which I conceived from your letters and from your so grave and honorable praise? Now at last my *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's work "Heptaplus," a seven-fold explanation of the seven days of creation</note> smiles upon me. Now it is pleasing to me, since under your public praise, as if under the shield of Pallas <note>Athena's shield, signifying protection</note>, it now shows itself invulnerable to rivals. You encourage me to other writings of this kind, which you would do in vain unless, while you subscribe such full approval to me, casting sparks of good hope, you had made me far stronger for writing than I was before. Indeed, I trust myself so much by your judgment that I shall now bear the burden I took up of explaining the whole "Old Instrument" <note>The Old Testament</note>—to which I am entirely unequal—far more strongly than usual. Regarding the books, I would perhaps satisfy you better if I had an index of those books which are with you, since many could serve your purpose which you nevertheless might not lack. Your aforementioned virtue has made you most highly commended to Lorenzo de' Medici; nor is mention ever made between us of the learned men of this age without "Guarino" being frequently on our lips, especially when our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, a brilliant poet and scholar in Lorenzo's circle</note> intervenes (and he intervenes always), who [thinks] so much of you...

<summary>In these letters, Pico della Mirandola discusses his ongoing scholarly projects, including a commentary on Plato's Symposium and a philological defense of the Psalms against Jewish critiques using Hebrew and Aramaic sources. He also engages in warm, professional correspondence with his teacher Battista Guarino and mentions his famous work, the Heptaplus.</summary>

->**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Antonio Pizzamano. Greetings. Letter 45.**<-

<margin><unclear>Mogm? zionais ...</unclear></margin>
**N**othing in my whole life has been more pleasant to me than these letters which I recently received from you, full of love, duty, and kindness. As I hope to be happy, I do not deceive you: unless perhaps that day was more pleasant on which you and Grimani <note>Domenico Grimani, a Venetian nobleman and future Cardinal</note>—I know not whether he is more yours or mine—both arrived as friends and greeted me honorably. Although you both, as if borrowing a mask, were not who you seemed, but presented yourselves to me under some charmingly invented names, nevertheless your most sweet character, your singular learning, your lovable gravity, your liberal modesty, and your most charming wit and speech represented the true and fitting Grimani and Pizzamano to me. Therefore, even if I could be deceived by the naming itself and defrauded of the truth, I could not be deprived of the pleasure I owed to you. You were able to disguise your names, but you could not disguise your virtue, which betrays itself by its own brilliance and knows not how to remain hidden. That serious treatment of physical matters, those sharp and intricate arguments, those most refined judgments—whom else could they announce to me but your very selves? I congratulated myself silently as I heard you, that our age had produced not just one Grimani and one Pizzamano, as I had thought, but (being more fertile) two Grimanis and two Pizzamanis. However, when our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, the famous humanist scholar and poet</note> indicated to me who you really were, I began to congratulate not so much my own age as my own judgment, for I seemed to have recognized in you all those qualities which I had found in them—that is, in you yourselves—by the most constant testimony of everyone. But see how these praises of you draw me away from your letter; although that letter also calls me to the same place, and I follow willingly. But I will restrain myself, lest I seem to wish to satisfy your praises with my own, as if by a mutual exchange, for you have heaped many upon me. Whether these come from a leaning of the heart or from judgment, I know not whether they bring me greater honor or pleasure. I owe much to you, my dear Pizzamano, for this spirit of yours toward me. But I ask that you also, if ever the opportunity arises, take a risk on my behalf—that is, on my goodwill. You will find a man so loving and studious of your virtue that I will not yield even to your friend Grimani in loving you. Farewell. 9 July 1489.

->**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to an Unknown Friend. Greetings. Letter 46.**<-

**W**hoever you are, you shall be ours, since you are most closely joined to our friend Roberto Salviati, as I have learned from his written word. I read your letters to Mithridates <note>Flavius Mithridates, a Jewish convert and scholar who taught Pico Hebrew and translated Kabbalistic texts for him</note>, which I could not deliver to him in his absence. I began to love you in those letters, not so much because Roberto loves you, but because you love literature <note>original: "litteras"</note> and (which is the principal thing) because I recognize you are a student of sacred things and of the Law <note>The "Law" here refers to the Torah or Hebrew scriptures</note>. And since I felt I could satisfy you in some part regarding those things you requested, I wished to signal my feelings to you so that I might auspiciously begin our friendship. I would certainly do this much more richly if I had here those friends of all men—that is, my books—which I might consult; but they have already preceded their master to Rome as if they were couriers. And I myself, already wearing my traveler's hat and boots <note>original: "petasatus iam & caligatus," meaning ready for a journey</note>, gave these words to you as familiarly as I did hastily. Regarding what you ask about Josephus <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note>, know that the "just" Josephus is not found among the Hebrews. Instead, there is a certain "epitome" <note>an abridgment or summary</note> of Josephus in which there are many fabrications. Several Hebrews have confessed to me that the things read there concerning the Ten Tribes (who did not return after the Babylonian captivity) are counterfeit and adulterated. Therefore, no credit at all should be given to them regarding Josephus. In the Greek Josephus, I know there are certain things that make honorable mention of Christ and the faith; but these are entirely the same as those read in the Latin manuscripts. I would not assert this unless I had recently read the Greek copy, of which I have no supply here. And to come to those things which you desire concerning the letters <note>meaning alphabets or scripts</note> of the Chaldeans and Hebrews: I have often questioned Mithridates and many Hebrews about those things read in Jerome's "Helmeted Prologue" <note>original: "galeato prologo," Jerome's famous preface to the Books of Kings, which discusses the Hebrew canon and script</note>, where he writes that the Samaritan and Hebrew characters were once the same.

characters. Ezra, however, after the restoration of the temple under Zerubbabel, is said to have discovered other letters which are now in use; yet almost all others, unaware of this change, claim and (what is more) take it for certain that both Moses and all the ancient patriarchs used these same strokes in Hebrew literature that we use now. The science of Kabbalah <term>Kabbalah: A Jewish mystical and esoteric tradition that Pico sought to reconcile with Christianity</term>, whose writers were in the synod with Ezra himself, gives the greatest credit to this opinion (as it occurs to me now); they prove and wish it to be so, that Moses concealed divine mysteries under these very letter characters and figures in which we now have the law described, which could in no way be the case if Moses had used other characters from these which we now use. However, to protect the saying of Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate, who believed Ezra had changed the Hebrew alphabet from an older Phoenician-style script</note>, I have this one thing which I recently read in the commentaries on the book which the ancient father Abraham published concerning creation <note>The Sefer Yetzirah (Book of Formation), an early and influential Kabbalistic text</note>: for while the authors interpret those thirty-two gates which he mentions, they say that number consists of the ten numerations and twenty-two letters. But as for the remaining letters which are called "double"—*mem, tsade, pe, kaph,* and *nun*—their characters were added by the overseers or prefects. Perhaps Jerome understood this, whose testimony ought to be held, and is indeed held by me, as most holy in all things among all people. Look at the Chaldean <term>Chaldean: Historically used to refer to the Aramaic language</term> help you seek; you would not have obtained it from Mithridates <note>Flavius Mithridates, a Jewish convert and scholar who taught Pico Hebrew, Aramaic, and Arabic, but was known for his volatile and secretive nature</note>, for nothing is permitted through him, whereas you can obtain everything from me through the gods, from whom you can do all things. For he was unwilling to teach me the Chaldean language by any reasonable humanity unless I was first sworn—and indeed with solemn words—not to hand it over to anyone else. Our friend Girolamo Benivieni <note>A Florentine poet and close friend of Pico</note> can bear witness to this: for when he happened to be present while he was teaching me, the "thievish" Mithridates threw the man out. But lest you have written entirely in vain, you may have the Arabic alphabet as a substitute for the Chaldean, which is sent to you noted by my own hand. There is nothing else for me to write, except that whoever you are, I cannot be anything but most loving toward you, if I understand you to be most loving of the noble arts. Farewell, from Fratta, 10 November 1486.

->**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico. Letter 47.**<-

<margin>An example of living well</margin>
**Y**ou are happy, my son, when God grants you not only that you live well, but that, while living well, you are nevertheless spoken of ill by evil men for that very reason—because you live well. For it is equal praise to be praised by the praiseworthy and to be disapproved of by the wicked. But I do not call you happy for this reason, because this slander is glorious to you, but because the Lord Jesus, who is truthful—nay, Truth itself—affirms that our reward will be plentiful in heaven when men speak ill of us and say all manner of evil against us falsely for his sake. If you do not know it, this is apostolic dignity: you were worthy yesterday to be defamed by the impious for the sake of the Gospel name. Since we read in Luke of the apostles departing from the sight of the council rejoicing because they were held worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus. Let us therefore also rejoice if we are worthy of such great glory before God, so that His glory may be manifested in our ignominy. And if we suffer anything harsh and troublesome from the world, let that most sweet voice of the Lord console us: "If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you." If the world hated Him through whom the world was made, should we—most vile little men, and if we repent of our crimes, most worthy of all reproaches—take it poorly if someone detracts or speaks ill of us, so much so that we ourselves begin to act badly just to avoid ill speech? Let us rather receive these insults eagerly, and if it is not our happiness to endure beatings, chains, prisons, and swords for virtue and truth as our heroes once did, let us consider it handled well enough with us if we suffer at least the taunts of wicked men, detractions, and hatreds, lest, with every occasion of earning merit taken away, no hope of reward remains for us. If men praise you for living well, then this virtue of yours, insofar as it is virtue, is similarly of Christ...

<meta>This page continues the spiritual and philosophical correspondence of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. # OF THE LETTERS

<margin>Note</margin>
...he does this: but insofar as it is praised, it makes him unlike the one who received the reward of his virtue from men by the **death of the cross**; on account of which God, as the Apostle says, **exalted him and gave him a name which is above every name.** <note>original: "exaltauit eū/& dedit illi nomē qđ est sup oē nomē" — a quote from Philippians 2:9</note> It is therefore more desirable to be crucified by the world so that you may be exalted by God, than to be exalted by the world so that you may be judged by God. For the former is crucified unto life, the latter is exalted unto glory; the former is exalted unto a fall, the latter is judged unto hell. Finally, if the world applauds you, it can hardly happen that virtue—which, being totally upright, ought to have God alone as the one whom it seeks to please—does not lean slightly toward the favor of men while they applaud. And even if one does not lose one's integrity, one nevertheless loses something of the reward; for when the reward begins to be paid on earth, where all things are small, it will be less in heaven, where all things are immense. **Happy are the insults** which keep us safe, lest the flower of justice wither by the pestilential breath of empty glory, or lest the eternal wages due to us be diminished by the vain pledge of popular rumor. Let us embrace these insults, my son, and with a most holy ambition let us take pride in the faithful service of the sole ignominy of the Lord’s cross. **We preach,** says Paul, **Christ crucified: a scandal to the Hebrews, folly to the Gentiles, but to us the power and wisdom of God.**

<margin>What wisdom is</margin>
This wisdom of the world is folly before God, and that "folly" of Christ is what overcomes worldly wisdom; through it, it pleased God to save those who believe. If you do not doubt that those who disparage your virtue are insane, and that they call the Christian life—which is true wisdom—insanity, then consider how great your own insanity would be to be moved from the path of a righteous life by the judgment of the insane. For every error ought to be removed by correction, not increased by imitation. Let them gape, let them howl, let them bark; <note>The author uses vivid animal imagery here—*baubentur* and *allatrent*—comparing critics to baying dogs.</note> proceed on the journey you have begun without fear. Weigh carefully how much you owe to God for their wickedness and misery—He who illuminated you as you sat in the shadow of death, and translated you from the company of those who, in the thickest darkness, rave here and there without a leader, and associated you with the sons of light. Let that sweetest voice of the Lord sound always in your ears: **let the dead bury their own dead; you, follow me.** <note>Matthew 8:22</note> For those who do not live for God are dead, and in this span of temporary death, they most laboriously acquire eternal death for themselves. If you were to ask them where they are heading, to what end they direct their studies, works, and cares—in short, what goal they have set for themselves in the attainment of which they will be happy—they will either have nothing at all to answer, or they will speak words that conflict and disagree with themselves, like the ravings of madmen. For they do not even know what they are doing, but in the manner of those who swim in rivers, they are carried along by the force of poorly-acquired habit, as if by the rush of a torrent. From this point, their wickedness having blinded them, they rush headlong into every crime at the prompting of **Satan**, blind leaders of the blind, until unforeseen death seizes them and says to them: **Friend, this night they require your soul from you; these things which you have prepared, whose will they be?** <note>Luke 12:20</note>

<margin>Note</margin>
Then they envy those whom they once despised; they praise those whom they mocked; and they wish they could imitate those whom they preferred not to follow when they were able. Therefore, my dearest son, **plug your ears with wax** <note>A classical allusion to Odysseus, who plugged his crew's ears to resist the Sirens' song.</note> and, holding as nothing whatever men say or think of you, look only to the judgment of God. He will render to each according to his works in His revelation from heaven with the angels of His power, in a flame of fire taking vengeance on those who did not know God <margin>The Apostle</margin> nor obeyed His gospel. These (as the Apostle says) shall suffer the penalty of eternal destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of His power, when He comes to be glorified in His saints and to be made admirable in all who have believed. It is written: **do not fear those who can kill the body**, but Him who can send the soul into hell. How much less should you fear those who can harm neither your body nor your soul? If they now disparage you for living according to reason, they will disparage you no less if you abandon virtue and are overwhelmed by vices; not because vice displeases them, but because the vice of disparagement always pleases them. Flee, if your salvation is dear to your heart; flee as much as you can from their company, and returning often to yourself, pray in secret to the most merciful Father, crying out with <margin>Words of the Prophet</margin> the Prophet:

> To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust, I shall not be ashamed, even if my enemies mock me. <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 25:1-2.</note>

It draws heavily on Pauline theology and Gospel warnings about the suddenness of death and the vanity of human praise.</summary>

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

...my enemies, and so on. For truly all who hope in you shall not be confounded; let those be confounded who act unjustly in vain. Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and in you will I hope all the day long. <note>original: "inimici mei... tota die" — these are verses adapted from Psalm 25 (Psalm 24 in the Vulgate), a prayer for guidance and protection.</note> See to it also that you always contemplate imminent death, and that the time we live is but a brief point—and indeed, less than a point. Consider then how evil is the **ancient enemy** <note>The "ancient enemy" (antiquus hostis) is a traditional Christian epithet for the Devil.</note> who promises us the kingdoms of the world so that he may snatch from us the kingdoms of heaven; how false are the pleasures which do not embrace us except to strangle us; how deceitful are the honors which elevate us only to cast us down afterward; how delightful are the riches which, the more they feed us, the more they poison us. How brief, uncertain, shadowy, false, and imaginary is everything that all these things together can provide us, even if they flow to us according to our wishes. How great are the things promised and prepared for those who, despising present things, sigh for that fatherland **whose king is divinity, whose law is charity, and whose measure is eternity.** Occupy your soul with these and similar thoughts; let them rouse you when you sleep, kindle you when you are lukewarm, strengthen you when you waver, and provide wings of divine love to you as you strive toward heaven. Thus, when you come to us—which we all expect with great longing—we may see you not only as the one we want, but also in the manner we desire. Farewell, and love God, whom you long ago began to fear. Ferrara, July 2, 1492.
