# THE FIRST BOOK OF LETTERS.

Brother Baptista of Mantua, Carmelite, <note>Baptista Mantuanus (1447–1516) was a famous Neo-Latin poet and head of the Carmelite order.</note> sends greetings to John Francis Pico, Count of Mirandola and Concordia.

<margin>
John Pico <note>original: "Io. Picus"</note>
</margin>
<note>Decorative woodcut initial I showing floral motifs</note> Illustrious Lord: Having recently heard of the death of **John Pico**, your uncle—that most distinguished and learned man—I was so struck with consternation in my soul that neither my feet nor my mind could sufficiently perform their office. I was very nearly moved to complain against both God and Nature: that they should have removed such a light from the world so quickly, such an ornament of Italy, such a glory of our age. It is as if they were envious of the goods of the earthly republic and, having no regard for us, they cut him down—cut him down while he was growing, while he was flourishing, while he was nourishing everyone with the most abundant fertility of his genius. But remembering the sentiment of Paul, who says, **"The judgments of God are a great deep,"** <note>A reference to Romans 11:33 and Psalm 36:6.</note> I restrained myself, lest I should think impiously or rashly concerning God and His works. At the passing of this man, the study of letters, the knowledge of things, and the integrity of morals suffered a great eclipse. For there was (as you know) in your uncle such a union of linguistic erudition with holiness of life, and such a knowledge of human and divine things, that in one and the same man it seemed that **Jerome and Augustine** <note>St. Jerome and St. Augustine were the two most influential Latin Church Fathers; Baptista is suggesting Pico was their intellectual and spiritual equal.</note> had lived again. But would that he had finished that work **On the Harmony of Plato and Aristotle** <note>Pico's unfinished project "De Concordia Platonis et Aristotelis" aimed to prove that the two greatest Greek philosophers were fundamentally in agreement.</note> before he departed! For its title promised a fitting together of all ancient philosophy, both most recondite and most worthy of being known. All his short works, both those he completed and those he left unfinished, must be sought out with all zeal and diligence; for since they flowed from such a happy genius, they cannot fail to be most worthy of being read, loved, and adored by all posterity. I would urge you to this duty, were I not certain that you were already sufficiently persuaded and minded to do so. This immortal honor was missing from your family: that alongside your most ancient nobility, your abundance of riches and wealth, and your glory in military affairs, there should be placed the excellence of such great wisdom—so that all things which among mortals are worthy of the highest praise might flow together into your single house. Indeed, it befits you, **John Francis**, <note>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), the nephew of Giovanni Pico, who eventually published his uncle's works.</note> to strive with all your might to possess your uncle's virtue as an inheritance, and that his spirit might be doubled in you, just as the spirit of **Elijah was in Elisha**. <note>A biblical reference to 2 Kings 2:9, where Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah’s prophetic spirit.</note> This we expect from you; this we require. When you have collected his works, I pray that you would make me a sharer in them as well; it will be worth the effort for me to apply myself to such great pleasure once I know of it. I subjoin a distich in his praise, composed on the spot, even if it might not please you. Farewell, best of princes, and love me. Mantua, November 27, 1494.

> John Pico, learned in the heavens, the elements, 
> and God, died sanctified while still a youth.

<header>LETTERS</header>

# Brother Baptista Mantuanus, Carmelite, to Giovanni Francesco Pico of Mirandola, Count of Concordia, sends greetings. [Book II, Letter II]

<margin>
Who was the teacher of the Carmelite
</margin>
<note>This likely refers to Giorgio Merula, mentioned later in the text as the author's teacher.</note>

**I**llustrious Count Giovanni Francesco, the very honorable delay of your reply had made me believe that my letters had perished on the road. While I was preparing to send new ones for that reason—and had indeed already begun to write them—your most longed-for, most ornate, and most pleasant letter arrived. In the night that followed, I believe because I had been thinking of him during the day, the image of your late uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher who died at the young age of 31.</note> seemed to come to me while I was sleeping, near dawn—the time when dreams are usually found to be true. He seemed to arrive and discuss many things with me concerning the nature of angels, and of spirits—aerial, terrestrial, and aquatic—their species, names, and duties, to the greatest pleasure of us both. And when I asked him why he stuttered (for he appeared to be a stutterer <note>original: "balbus"</note>), he replied that this was a sign of the imperfect and incomplete discourse which he had begun long ago concerning the nature of things and philosophy. I seemed to be struck by a desire to inquire about many occult matters which are wondrous and unknown to us mortals; and I know not how, but the first thing that occurred to me was whether amulets were of any use to infants—and coral, and other things of that kind which are tied around the necks of children. He replied that there is sometimes some virtue in these things and that this pertains to <term>natural magic</term> <note>Natural magic was the study of the hidden powers within nature (like magnetism or medicinal herbs), distinct from "black" or demonic magic.</note>, but for the most part, they are condemned customs and superstitions. Having said these things, he vanished. 

And I, having been awakened, thought long and hard about what we had discussed in the dream, for these did not seem to be vain things, but appeared to have some weight. I write this not because I place any faith in dreams—for that is foreign both to my profession <note>As a friar, he must officially distance himself from the superstition of "dream-reading."</note> and my nature—but because I cannot sufficiently marvel at how it happens that those who sleep may dispute, teach, and learn, and frequently do those things which are impossible, or certainly difficult, for those who are awake. Our souls certainly possess something of the divine; and if we lived holily and piously, and were not driven about by the many intricacies of business, our souls would have great commerce with separated spirits. But enough on these matters. 

As for your wish to write the life of your uncle: I both praise it and urge and beseech you to do so more promptly. Indeed, that duty most suits you, and must be undertaken by you for many reasons. For you are very strong in style and eloquence, which is a gift of nature, industry, and God. Likewise, because you are his kinsman and closely related by blood to such a miraculous man, you cannot help but share in his glory. Nor should you allow your most famous family to lose any of such ornament and splendor. Added to this is the fact that his life should be known to no one more than to you, since you had long ago proposed to imitate him—and most wisely so, for he was an outstanding exemplar of sanctity and religion, in whom the light of all wisdom appeared. I will say to you, therefore, what Christ said to the apostles: 
> Gather up the fragments, lest they be lost. <note>John 6:12. Mantuanus uses this biblical quote to urge the preservation of Pico’s intellectual and biographical legacy.</note>

And this must be done all the more studiously because it will be of greater benefit to us who survive and to future posterity. Without a doubt, although I see he is more to be congratulated because, after such a short voyage, he has nonetheless gathered so many spiritual works and reached the port so happily, I cannot help but grieve with you over the loss of such a man. The death of **Giorgio Merula**, <note>A prominent Italian humanist who died in 1494.</note> first my fellow student and later my teacher (for we served together under **Gregorio Tiphernate**), affected me with sadness; but he was already aged, and with his old age weighing upon him, he was already infirm and had fulfilled his duty. The lamented passing of **Hermolaus** and **Politian**, <note>Ermolao Barbaro (d. 1493) and Angelo Poliziano (d. 1494), two of the era's greatest scholars.</note> two illustrious men, brought heavy grief to me and to all lettered men. But this wound sits deeper, and the world of letters has suffered a far greater loss in our Pico. The heads of eloquence mourn; the studies of the mathematical arts have fallen. All of philosophy, and the highest speculations of metaphysics and theology, which he had already begun to amplify and illustrate, will henceforth be silent. 

But I stop now, lest I indulge too much in just grief. We must take care rather that we turn out like him, through the study and exercise of the sciences and through integrity of character and religion, so that, enriched by a similar trade as his, we may one day arrive where he now rejoices to have arrived. As soon as I can, I will come so that I may see and adore the immortal remains of his divine genius which are in your possession. Meanwhile, apply yourself to writing his life, and love me. Farewell. Your lordship’s servant, to whom I commend myself. Mantua, the 4th day of January, 1495.

<sig>P</sig>

->BOOK ONE<-

## Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, Sends Best Greetings. Letter III.

**Y**ou, indeed, Pico, owe me absolutely nothing, either by way of silence or any duty of mine toward you. In fact, your letter brought me a great deal of shame, as you apologize to me for your "negligence" toward me, when both of us should have been willing to pay any price to redeem my own neglect of you first. Such is the goodness of your character, your talent, and your fairness: you acknowledge a fault that belongs to someone else <note>Barbaro is gracefully insisting that he, not Pico, was the one who had been slow to write</note> when you could have either avoided it or certainly shared it. You are anxious over a mutual offense, though you could have been secure with both a better category of defense and a better cause. Either we are both guilty, or you are not. In any case, as far as it concerns you, you have already cleared yourself. It remains for me to make satisfaction as well.

But as for what I can most importantly write to you: I shall exhort you to continue loving letters, in which you are most eminent. I shall advise you to devote yourself to virtue and good morals, in which you have made such progress that it is difficult to know upon which part of philosophy you have spent more effort: that which contains the vessels and instruments to be observed <note>original: "spectari vas & instrumenta", referring to logic and the tools of intellectual inquiry</note>, or that which encompasses the dogmatic and the parenetic <note>original: "dogmatice paraneticeque"; parenetic philosophy is the branch of ethics concerned with practical advice and moral exhortation</note>. Entirely, it is a supreme thing and greater than human capacity—something you owe either to your own genius or certainly to your Creator—that you have attained at such a tender age what would be the height of impudence for a man to even wish for in extreme old age. These gifts are not yours, Pico; they belong to nature; they belong to God; yet if anything is truly "yours," these things are most especially so. 

Consider how much less your nobility, fortune, health, and beauty can be called "yours"—goods in which you yield to no one, just as you yield in those things that are more truly your own. I exhort you to turn yourself toward this: ponder this day and night, thinking of how great a name you may leave for Him who has enriched you so far that you will never be able to pay back or even calculate what you possess. Think of what He is capable of, He who willed that you be capable of these things. Think of how much He loves you, He who chose you for Himself out of many thousands, so that as almost a boy you might surpass old men, and while not yet a youth <note>original: "ephebus", a Greek term for a young man entering adulthood</note>, you might turn the circles of learned men toward admiration of your doctrine. 

Unless you see this, unless you value it, I affirm to you right now and proclaim with a free voice: you are not yet as great as you truly are. What I have long promised myself about you, and what I still promise, is immense and infinite. But no speech or proclamation can catch up to my preconceived opinion. I act as people usually do: the more they admire someone and wish to explain what they feel, the less they achieve what they want. Just as they conceive something great in their mind, words nevertheless fail them, and they seem to have been capable of effort rather than speech. Therefore, do not listen to these things I am writing to you now for the public eye, but rather understand those things which I speak of you when I am alone and silent—which are, by Hercules, as much greater as thought is greater than this speech. 

Greet Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence</note> and your friend Salviati. Regarding Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the famous poet and scholar</note>, there is no need for you to go to any trouble, because I hear he will be with me shortly. Nothing more pleasant could have happened to me in this entire embassy. I am so glad that the library there <note>The Medicean library in Florence</note> is being furnished more elegantly and extensively every day that I cannot express it. Letters owe much to the Florentines, and among the Florentines to the Medici, and among the Medici to Lorenzo, who fosters this ancestral honor of his family with no less care than he does the Republic, which he has the right of administering and establishing. 

Farewell. From Milan, on the Kalends of January, 1497 <note>original: "Mcccclxxxxvii". Note: Barbaro died in 1493; this date likely refers to the year of the book's printing or a posthumous editorial dating.</note>.

## Ermolao Barbaro to Roberto Salviati, Sends Best Greetings. Letter IV.

**Y**ou are mistaken, Salviati, if you suspect it was anything other than my preoccupations that prevented me from responding to you until now. This is a common and well-worn excuse for silence; but by Hercules, it is so true that if you did not grant it to me, you would seem to have deserved poorly of my love, faith, and devotion toward you. All your letters are always most welcome to me, but those especially so in which there is name and mention of my "man of Mirandola" <note>A pun on Pico's name; "Mirandulanus" sounds like "the wonderful one"</note>. Nothing is more wonderful in letters than he; there is no one whom I would rather see praised, honored, and raised to the heavens; no one from whose praise I could less easily depart. In this matter, I am perhaps unrestrained, though I seem so to no one. There is so much praise in him, and so without limit, that there is no longer room for either ambition or flattery. 

I have read his *Apologia* <note>Pico's 1487 defense of his controversial "900 Theses," which had been challenged by a papal commission</note>. Why does he attribute so much to me in it, I who deserve so little? Why does he announce me with such an honorable preface—not to say a common or rank-and-file witness—in that work, especially since nothing is more subtle, more vehement, or more acute than that book? Nevertheless, it is better that I defer my judgment for a while, until clearly...

<header>EPISTLES BOOK II</header>

...I am weaving the whole thing together. As for what you desire to know regarding what I am doing: what else can I say than that I am studying? Public duty <note>Barbaro served as a diplomat for the Republic of Venice, which often interrupted his scholarly work</note> indeed takes away some of my persistence—or rather, it takes away from my studies, not my persistence, for I press on more sharply and demand a task from myself more harshly because what these greater matters have stolen from me, I repair with a diligence as great as the business that has increased upon me. The more business I have, the more greed and eagerness for study have been driven into me. Thus, all those holidays which a private man would give to his health, I distribute to public affairs; and so, what I lose for one cause, I gather back by another means. 

I believe I have written to you at other times, or said to those who heard it from me, that the *Instrument of Aristotle* <term>the Organon: the collection of Aristotle's works on logic</term>—for that is what the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy</note> generally call logic—likewise the eight books of *Physical Lectures* <note>Aristotle's *Physics*</note> and his three books on *Rhetoric*, were translated by me into Latin some time ago. My work on *Dioscorides* <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, the ancient Greek physician and botanist; Barbaro's commentary on him was a major scientific achievement</note> is now finished; the final hand is being laid to it by me. It is ready: it is a daughter's dowry <note>A common metaphor meaning the book is finished and ready to be "married" to the public through printing</note>; it will be settled very soon. 

Then, relieved of that burden, I shall devote myself entirely to Aristotle. Unless God calls me elsewhere, it will be published within two years of the edition of *Dioscorides*, certainly finished in the logical works, and with them the commentaries which I have already completed on the *Posterior Analytics*. After these are released, I shall enter into natural and divine matters, likewise *Rhetoric* and *Poetics*, equipping all the volumes of that philosopher with my commentaries and annotations to the best of my ability. For there are some things in the *Problems* and the *History of Animals* that desire clarity and light; these I will pass through briefly, with the light of short annotations. I am prepared to undertake nothing else new in my whole life; for I must restrain this greed—or rather, this wickedness—of my talent, lest it seem to want to be too busy and ambitious. Daily I experience more truly than is usually said that "to embrace all things is to embrace nothing." Farewell. From Milan, the 12th day before the Kalends of November <note>October 21</note>, 1488.

->Hermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico. Sends best greetings.<-
->Letter V.<-

<margin>
The 54 volumes of Plotinus
</margin>
**T**he day before yesterday, your *Hexameron* <note>Pico's work on the six days of creation, usually titled *Heptaplus*</note> was brought to us by the efforts of Salviati. I read it so greedily that on the very first day, and not without a single breath, I drained the whole thing. Three things in it delight me wonderfully: first, that your speech teaches and moves—something which it is well known the ancient theologians in the sacred letters, and the Pythagoreans and Platonists in natural philosophy, observed, while more recent writers merely sweat over teaching alone. Second, that in such a great abundance of material and such freedom to plunder, you have such chaste and innocent hands that in this genre of writing, you seem to have followed yourself and no other. This is not common either with the ancients or the moderns, but is peculiar and your own. In this matter, I will open my mind to you: I am so affected that since those earlier men did not say what you have said, they seem to me to have said almost nothing. Third, I see that you have been initiated into the sacred mysteries not so much of Aristotle as of Plato and his sect, and have brought full draughts from there into this late-night study. I pass over how many excellent things from Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> you have touched upon elegantly and in passing; it seems you have not so much read as learned by heart almost everything contained in his fifty-four volumes, arranged into six "nines" <term>the Enneads: the collection of Plotinus's writings arranged by his student Porphyry</term> by Porphyry. 

Nor can I pass over this: that you conduct yourself as a middle ground between the new and old theologians, so that you neither hate the simple majesty of the former, nor are you carried away by the ambitious subtlety of the latter. Thus it happens that while you wish to imitate the one, you are able to do so for the other; you have gathered the best of both kinds, which we hope you will do also in the narration of the Davidic poem <note>The Psalms</note>. Farewell. Venice, the day before the Nones of September <note>September 4</note>, 1479 <note>Though the text says 1479, historians believe this letter dates to 1489, following the publication of the Heptaplus</note>.

->Hermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico of Mirandola. Sends best greetings.<-
->Letter VI.<-

<margin>
Plato
Aeschylus
Menander
Euripides
</margin>
**G**reetings, most kind-hearted Mirandola. I truly speak of you so willingly everywhere that I do nothing with greater pleasure; not only because nothing is more pleasant to hear (as Plato says) than the truth, but also because, as Palaemon says, it is much more pleasant to speak the truth than to hear it. It happens that with no labor—as is often found in Aeschylus, Menander, and Euripides <note>Three of the greatest Greek dramatists</note>—the truth comes forth even when not sought; it even expresses itself from a man who is most unwilling, not by any questioning, but by its own power alone. This is that "tyranny" which you, following your own candor, interpret as humanity and goodness; and...

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

...and by Hercules, you are now so great that anyone who does not praise you detracts from their own judgment and reputation. They are acting for their own benefit; they consult their own interests; they redeem their own fame—those who favor and desire yours. There are many names in their ledger which you do not know; your creditors owe you. Many follow the counsel of Prodicus <note>A Greek philosopher known for the idea that people should do favors for those who can return them</note>: they give so that they may receive; "hand scratches hand" as <margin>Epicharmus</margin> Epicharmus <note>A Greek comic poet and philosopher</note> sang out. Indeed, by as much as you owe less to your creditors—that is, your praisers—than to me, by so much more do you make them your creditors, whether they will or no. O unheard-of kind of debt: for the creditors to exist without there being a debtor! But I am more occupied <term>than</term> <gloss>than</gloss> that I might be able to play with you any longer. But you, good gods, how free <term>than</term> <gloss>than</gloss> [how free] you are, that you allow anyone to be idle! I pray you have borne me thus far; I do not ask that you admit some longer joke, but I ask for a brief little yawn <note>original: "oscitaciunculam." A playful humanist way of asking for a moment of his friend's time or a brief indulgence in his jesting</note>. Farewell, with my Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano, the renowned scholar and close friend of Pico</note>. From Rome, on the Ides of August [August 13], 1490.

->Ermolao Barbaro, Venetian orator and Patriarch of<-
->Aquileia, sends greetings to Giovanni Pico.<-

<insert>B</insert>ene is it: it is very fitting that you, who love much, should congratulate me much on the patriarchate of Aquileia <note>Barbaro was appointed Patriarch of Aquileia in 1491, a move that caused significant political tension between the Pope and the Venetian Republic</note>, and that you should grant and prophesy even much greater things for me <term>than</term> <gloss>than</gloss> I could either wish for, were I most greedy, or deserve, were I most modest. I know your devotion toward me; I see how much you value me. I recognize the force of your love; I have nothing more certain. Would that it might sometime be that I could live with you, to philosophize about nature, about God, and about holy morals. How much I desire this, and how much of an addition to my prosperity I judge it would be if this should happen, I can neither express, nor if I could, would I wish to do so <term>certainly</term> <gloss>certainly</gloss> in this place. I pray that if you have ever thought me worthy of your benevolence, I may be counted by you in the same rank—or even a better one, if possible. As Ermolao <note>Abbreviated "Her." in the original</note> and as a priest, may you more closely cherish and hold dearer the one whom you loved as a secular layman, now that he has become a soldier of Christ. I am as unable to not proclaim, not admire, and not extol you and your most brilliant virtues, as you are unable to not increase them. If I flatter or lie to you, may I be an object of contempt to all learned men; for a long time I have been held <term>above</term> <gloss>above</gloss> [concerning] you and your affairs. Now there is wonder and an ecstasy of knowledge. You will read these things patiently, and your heart shall not be exalted, nor shall you have haughty eyes. For why should you be pleased with yourself, you who know that these good things which you possess are not your own, nor are they from your own savings <note>original: "peculio," referring to the private property of a slave or child</note>, but are granted and belong to the Lord? Forgive me. The north wind of truth and the west wind of charity have snatched me up and carried me away. Farewell. Rome, the day before the Kalends of April [March 31], 1491.

->Brother Baptista the Carmelite to Gianfrancesco Pico. E. VIII.<-

<insert>I</insert>llustrious Count and Lord: I have read your uncle’s <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> apology—or rather, the prologue to his apology <note>Pico's defense of his controversial 900 Theses which were investigated for heresy</note>. I read it with as much pleasure of mind as it is supported by truth, as much as it shines with brilliance, and with as much love and reverence as I have always pursued its author. But in reading it, while I desired to slake my thirst, another thirst grew: namely, the desire to see the rest. When I have attained this through the gift of your favor, I shall consider myself to have reached a great part of happiness. Your uncle Giovanni Pico has, in my judgment, surpassed all the philosophers of our age, chiefly for these reasons: <term>because</term> <gloss>because</gloss> while others spend their lives solely on the dogmas of Aristotle and the Peripatetics <note>The traditional followers of Aristotle's school</note>, he himself, with Herculean audacity, has scrutinized the sects and families of all philosophers, ancient and modern, with a wondrous vigor of intellect. And <term>because</term> <gloss>because</gloss> while the moderns <note>original: "neothericis," referring to the scholastic philosophers of the university, often criticized by humanists for their lack of literary style</note> pursue no flower of speech, he himself has so [joined] philosophy with eloq[uence]...

[...he] conjoined with such sequence: that he can be said to have restored the ancient and true Academy <note>The "Academy" refers to the school of Plato; humanists like Pico sought to revive this ancient Greek philosophical tradition</note>: which things are worthy of all the greater admiration, the more he ascended to such a height of virtue and glory with swift study and in fewer years. Nor does he seem to have sought knowledge, as others do, through labor and study and many late-night sessions, but rather to have found it all at once by chance—as usually happens to those who, while doing something else entirely, unexpectedly stumble upon a treasure. Happy, therefore, is your family for such a student; happy is our age, illuminated by the great splendor of this man. Farewell, most worthy prince, and remember how much you ought to strive so that you may be considered a worthy imitator of your uncle. I hate these distances between places. For I desire to be with you, so that we might each share in the other's studies. Again, fare well and fear God. At Mantua, the 29th day of October, 1494.

## Matteo Vero, regular canon of the Holy Savior, sends greetings.

<margin>Letter 9.</margin>
<margin>A display of Mirandola's genius</margin>
The interpretation of the six days in which God created all things, written by our Giovanni of Mirandola—which you sent to me as a gift—is titled and marked by him as the *Heptaplus* <note>original: "Heptaplus," from the Greek for "sevenfold." This was Pico’s work explaining the creation story in Genesis through seven layers of meaning</note>. Although it is clearly of such a nature that it cannot easily be both skimmed and understood by a reader at the same time, the beginning of the work so inflamed and drew me in that, eager for the end and holding my breath, I did not so much taste it as certainly devour it—though it must finally be chewed over with more piercing study and a longer lamp <note>The "longer lamp" refers to burning the midnight oil or studying late into the night</note> during a time of leisure. It seemed to me that our Giovanni here is not only skilled and wise in all philosophy and whatever is contained in the laws of nature, but he even raises himself above human things. He flies through the sublime, turning the secret mysteries and celestial sacraments toward mystical senses and allegories—things which those of our time who are considered wise and learned scarcely notice or pass by entirely untouched. He explains here the most difficult and celestial matters, and insofar as the subject allows, he opens, reveals, and illustrates them more splendidly than the sun. And what is wonderful is that, while still a youth and living in the world <note>original: "in saeculo agens," meaning he was not a monk or priest but a secular nobleman</note>, he joins himself closely to the likes of Dionysius, Hilary, Damascene, Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome <note>These are the "Church Fathers," the influential early Christian theologians</note>, and other such most holy and rare men of old. All posterity shall admire him once envy has grown quiet and the passage of time has established his authority. What should we think that supreme God will give him if a life equal to his spirit is granted to him? Even with his first beard <note>A poetic way of saying he is still very young</note>, he is already most learned in Latin and Greek letters—at which antiquity marveled in Origen and Jerome—and he is not ignorant of Hebrew. Furthermore, in sacred matters, he can indeed do as much as is scarcely believable for anyone else to do. Truly, we expect whatever delights are next from the Psalms and songs of David which he has been treating, interpreting, and explaining for a long time now. He has searched with infinite labor into what all the Latins, Greeks, and Hebrews have left written about them. I am glad that for the completion of this business, he chose for himself leisure in our monastery at Fiesole <note>The Badia Fiesolana, a monastery near Florence supported by the Medici, where Pico often studied</note> in my own time. To clearly see and hear him is happiness itself. And so I give you, my Roberto, as many thanks as I possibly can, for having looked after the printing of such a work so diligently and correctly. This looks toward the common benefit and the praise of your noble soul. Since you then gifted it to me immediately—so that I might appear grateful to you in whatever way I can—accept this bit of something of ours, which you may read in turn and perhaps "taste." Otherwise, farewell, and live happily in Christ. From the abbey of Fiesole.

## Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico. Sends greetings.

<margin>Letter 10.</margin>
It does not escape me, nor did it ever escape me while you were living a private life, Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, how great was the excellence of your genius and how great your eloquence. You have shown this in many things always, but most especially in this, your most learned [work]...

# BOOK TWO

...you have shown more clearly in your explanation. Indeed—to speak for myself—regarding the excellent opinion I had long ago conceived of you, you have not only confirmed it, but have also nourished and increased it in a wonderful way, and even raised it to the very peak. Truly, I was so delighted in reading this work of yours that I think nothing more excellent or worthy could be produced; it is something that ought to be read or heard by everyone. 

For while many things worthy of praise are recognized in this most brilliant work—which would be highly valuable whether taken together or even individually—that which seems most divine is that you have spoken "not with a human mouth" (as the poet says) but with a divine one. <note>original: "ut inquit ille" (as he says); likely a reference to Virgil's Aeneid, describing a voice that sounds more than mortal.</note> Furthermore, you have achieved such facility in explaining the enigmas of Moses <note>Referring to the Book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note> that Jesus Christ seems to have granted it to you alone, as one who otherwise deserves well of him. I am well aware that this is a gift of some celestial nature rather than one comparable to any lower nature; indeed, it would be impossible for any human talent, through these few years of yours, to run through three languages <note>The "three languages" (trilinguis) were Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, the mastery of which was the hallmark of the "Renaissance Man."</note>—let alone to be as sufficiently skilled in them as you are. 

Then, having mastered them, to be able to equally solve and interpret such abstruse and, as it were, hidden meanings of Moses—and finally, to speak and write about these things you have undertaken not in a crude or barbaric way, but in the Roman and Latin tongue. For indeed, it happens that only a few "whom impartial Jupiter has loved" <note>A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (6.129), referring to those favored by the gods.</note> are able to write as you have written. Therefore, posterity will commend you as a second Jerome, <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the most famous scholar of the "three languages" in the early Church and translated the Bible into Latin.</note> most expert in the three tongues. 

Accordingly, I congratulate you for making your name eternal and everlasting. For by this most useful labor of yours, all students of literature will owe you as much—since you have given it to be read by all—as they confess they owe to Plato, Aristotle, and the entire school of the Peripatetics. <note>The Peripatetics were the followers of Aristotle, so named because they allegedly walked about while debating.</note> I wish to be enrolled in their number, since I am most fond of you and most devoted to your studies, and indeed have always been. Farewell; I commend myself greatly to your excellence. September 20th, 1489. Venice.

-> Yours, in whatever capacity he may be, Sebastian Priuli, <-
-> son of the most distinguished Peter, Procurator of Saint Mark. <- <note>The Procurators of Saint Mark were among the highest-ranking officials in the Republic of Venice.</note>

## Girolamo Donato sends greetings to Roberto Salviati. Letter 11.

I was challenged by you in love a little while ago by the most sweet gift of the *Heptaplus*. <note>The *Heptaplus* is Pico della Mirandola's sevenfold explanation of the creation story in Genesis.</note> Then, I was moved by your most recent, kind, and elegant letter; either one by itself could have been enough to encompass all the measures of friendship. Added to this was our friend Seratico, <note>Likely Girolamo Seratico, a mutual acquaintance in humanist circles.</note> a man as upright in character as he is elegant in letters; for his sake also, I cannot help but love you exceedingly. Regarding how much I owe to your kindness, I prefer to be conscious of it within myself than to write of it to you. 

Pico’s goodwill toward me, already perceived before, deserves an even more grateful judgment in my mind through the trust of your testimony. I know how much I ought to value being loved and praised by that man in whom the prizes of learning and character harmonize with the highest glory of our age. It is more fitting to admire his *Heptaplus* than to judge it. That style of writing delights me wonderfully, for I see no more fertile field for both doctrine and erudition than from sacred literature. But such boldness is successful in very few—among whom is my friend Pico. Bid him greetings in my name as much as you can; I am especially dear to myself for this very reason: that I love him vehemently. You, my Salviati, shall promise yourself as much from me as is fitting to be provided by a most friendly and well-wishing man. 

Farewell. Milan, the 25th day of October, 1489.

->OF THE LETTERS<-

Battista Guarini to the most learned prince Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, greetings. ->EPISTLE XII<-

# Our
friend Vittorio, with his usual brisk pace, brought your little gift to me in recent days. Oh, why did I say "little gift" because of the number of pages? It is rather a massive gift because of the wide and manifold knowledge and the eloquence of your booklet. What point is there in me writing much about it, since it has already achieved such status through the opinions of all those whose judgments are recorded in the Register <note>original: "Albo"; a reference to the 'Album' or list of esteemed scholars and critics.</note> that it can neither be increased by praise nor diminished by blame? I will conclude with one word: from being your teacher (since you wish it so), I have become your disciple. Therefore, beware of calling me by any other name hereafter. Throughout the "halcyon days" <note>original: "halcedonia"; a period of peace and calm, here referring to a break in his teaching schedule.</note> of our lecture hall, I have read everything, re-read it, and learned much. I had learned most of it before, and I loved you then as much as anyone possibly could. Now, because of this gift, I love you even more—that is, beyond my strength—and I look up to your genius. Do so, my dear Pico. Continue through these monuments of yours to deserve well, not only of other men of letters but also of the study of sacred philosophy—which is to be considered the true and genuine philosophy—and to rescue yourself from the teeth of devouring time. Know, however, that the greatest things are expected of you, so that everyone may understand that in you, a refined elegance of humanity is joined with a deeper philosophy than these times can bear. If there is any good book there which you think would interest my studies, let my mind also share in that food. You know the scarcity of books in this city. You know also my stomach: new things please me, yet they satisfy me with a great "appetite for new things" <term>νεωφαγια</term> <note>neophagia; from the Greek for 'eating new things' or a craving for novelty.</note>; you understand what they are. To the wise, a few words suffice. I ask that you commend me to the Magnificent Lorenzo de' Medici, if any small opportunity is given, provided it can be done without troubling you. For I admire the virtue of that man in such great fortune and learning, and I venerate him in silence. Farewell, glory of the Muses. Ferrara, the Kalends of November, 1489.

Cristoforo Landino to Roberto Salviati, greetings. ->EPISTLE XIII<-

# I 
am confident that not even another Iliad would be enough to express, in proportion to the magnitude of the matter, how grateful and how pleasant your most excellent gift was to me. For what could have proceeded more appropriately from you—a man both most generous and most learned—or what could have been brought more expectantly to me, who am most greedy for letters, than that "Heptaplus" <note>The "Heptaplus" (Sevenfold Explanation) was Pico's work on the seven days of creation, published in 1489.</note> of our Pico? He is easily the leader of our age in all literature and doctrines, and this is his exact work on the Genesis of Moses, wonderfully composed. For although we see this matter treated so learnedly, distinctly, and eloquently by almost countless Hebrews, many Arabs, and not a few Greeks and Latins, such that I believed not even a word could be added; yet he himself, beginning the whole matter with an almost new argument and arriving by an unusual path at things which already seemed most worn and common to everyone, has described them in such a way that even those who are most learned marvel at them as if they were new and unheard of. For this reason, he has carried me—who until now have never stepped outside the borders of Tuscany—through all regions and tracts of the lands, <margin>Note the simile</margin> conveyed by no horse and carried forward by no beasts of burden, but drawn by the constant vehicle of his reasoning; he moved me forward with no trouble. And then, leaving the continent behind, he led me through all the seas by his narration, as if carried on Neptune’s chariot—not by the dolphins of Arion, <note>Arion was a mythical Greek poet saved from drowning by dolphins who were charmed by his music.</note> let alone by human ships. These things could certainly seem great and incredible to everyone. But there are other things greater and worthy of greater admiration. For, raised up from the waters—I know not whether by swan’s feathers, or by the wings of Daedalus and Pegasus—he led me through all the air and all the ether, even to the highest point of...

# BOOK TWO

I reached the peak of perceptible things, with him not only leading me but carrying me upward. It is truly a matter worthy of extreme amazement to have traversed this lower and elemental world. But it is a far greater thing to have reached the celestial realm: to have penetrated first the orb of the moon, then Mercury’s, and next Venus’s; to have seen the rays of the sun; to have felt the fires of Mars; and finally to have recognized the health-giving rays of Jupiter and the heavy rays of Saturn. Then, at last, to have noticed that eighth sphere shining with burning stars, and how all these heavens rotate not with a simple and uniform motion, but with a triple and triform one—yet who is ignorant that all these things fall within our senses? However, he granted me a third world to fly toward in such a way that, with all senses lulled to sleep (for these hinder rather than help such an inspection), I might have both seen and clearly perceived it by the mind alone—for only by the mind are such vast spaces traversed. But the mind's sharp vision, like an owl's eyes blinding at the sun's rays, could not endure such great splendor. Therefore, whatever in such a journey—or, to speak more truly, in this return to the homeland <note>The author uses "return to the homeland" in the Neoplatonic sense, where the soul returns to its divine origin.</note>—remained hidden from me or escaped our eyes, the guide himself is not to blame, if he to whom it was shown is easily caught in fault. For the divine genius of <term>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</term> both promises and provides that he will demonstrate everything.

What is there then, my dear <term>Robert</term>, that I should not confess I owe to you, having been enriched by you with such a gift? Indeed, as soon as I began to taste it, such a greed was once excited in me, and such a love of feasting from the sweetness of the food, that, impatient of any delay, I ordered nothing else to be chewed, but like a most greedy youth, I devoured all the solid parts. But when I had gone through the whole thing in continuous reading, and then, gathering it into my stomach like a beast <note>original: "pecudis"; a reference to ruminant animals like cows that chew the cud, a common metaphor for deep meditation and re-reading.</note> and bringing it back to the mouth, I chewed it over more carefully; then indeed a wondrous sweetness appeared; then such an amazement as never before came upon me. 

But you will say: "Did you not admire the man's learning before?" I did indeed admire that he was so engaged in all disciplines that he seemed to excel in each one. <margin>How well Pico is praised here</margin> No topic escaped him when debating in physics, none in mathematics; but in metaphysics and in every kind of theology—whether you seek that which was stirred up by Mercury <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure associated with ancient Egyptian wisdom.</note> and perfected by Plato, or our own Christian theology, the most excellent and truest of all—these our ages, and even several previous ones, have seen nothing more learned than him. But lest you think (a fault which most of us have labored under) that he separated eloquence from wisdom: does he not describe everything most weightily, most copiously, and furthermore most elegantly, so that he can now be rightly mixed with those ancient orators? Thus, I admired these things about him so far that I thought nothing could be added to such a discovery. 

But having read through his <term>Heptaplus</term> <note>Pico's seven-fold commentary on the six days of Creation in Genesis.</note>, I have now begun to wonder at it even more than I wondered at those previous things. Therefore, we should believe it happened neither rashly nor by some chance, but by God so commanding, that this divine man emerged distinguished by these three names. For <term>Giovanni</term> is interpreted either as "grace of the Lord," or "in whom is grace," or "to whom a gift was made by God." Who does not see that he could not have attained the learning he achieved without the special and greatest grace of God? In the <term>Picus</term> <note>The Latin word for "woodpecker." The author is using wordplay on Pico's family name.</note>, however, we know there is such hardness of beak and strength of head that you will find no wood, no matter how "bony" (so to speak) or stony, that this bird does not pierce; and in it, he skillfully carves out a hiding place to retreat into and builds a nest. In the same way, nothing from all the disciplines is so difficult for human genius to know that he himself, pecking at the hardest parts, has not penetrated, nested in, hatched, and brought forth young. Since indeed all things in that man are to be wondered at, who would not call him <term>of Mirandola</term> <note>Another pun: "Mirandula" sounds like "miranda," meaning "wonderful" or "to be wondered at."</note>?

# LETTERS

SIGLA: E. XXIV.

...think praiseworthy. For this reason, I congratulate you for enjoying his constant friendship; thus I grieve for myself—for myself, I say—who consider myself unfortunate in this regard: because on account of my many and necessary occupations, I am not permitted to stick to him day and night as I most ardently desire. For if it were permitted, I would never leave the side—I do not say of an old man—but of a youth; I say a youth in whom is all wisdom, and all the learning of old age and gray hair. You, however, to whom fortune has offered far greater leisure, and to whom nature has given an excellent talent (which, thereafter, your long practice in all the good arts and frequent use has increased and polished), enjoy this good that has fallen to you from heaven. Drink from this most fertile fountain, or rather this immense ocean; and drink as much as can be enough to quench not only your present thirst but every future thirst as well. Reflect then, calculate, debate with yourself, how few mortals have ever received so much good. Alexander the Great boasted that he happened to live in the times of so great a philosopher as Aristotle. But to you it has been given by your most happy lot to have lived familiarly with both Aristotle and Plato at once—and such an Aristotle and Plato that in them, besides the ancient doctrine of the <term>Academics</term><note>The followers of Plato’s school of thought.</note> and <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The followers of Aristotle’s school of thought.</note>, we see our Pauls, Johns, Dionysii, Augustines, Jeromes, Thomases, and other lights of this kind shine forth. Therefore, conclude from these things how much you ought to love yourself, or him for this reason, best Robert: to whom fortune itself has offered him, and you have advanced by your own foresight so that you have made yourself particularly close to this man.
->Farewell. November 22nd.<-

->Alessandro Cortesi to his dear Pico, Greetings.<-

### E. XXIV.

<margin>Someone praises him highly</margin> **I**n my whole life I have received no greater pleasure than recently from your letters; and although I had believed everything highest about you, you have nevertheless (I confess) surpassed my opinion; and you have surpassed it in such a way that I now consider the boundaries of your glory to be narrow, even though they are spread far and wide. Let us speak more openly and far from the flattery from which illustrious souls have always shrunk: What in you is not extraordinary? What is not worthy of admiration? Individual qualities could honor anyone, which in you have all been brought together equally. From everyone (so to speak), you alone have stolen away all the graces. And although your ancestors reached such a height that no one but those born from them could easily attain, you have nevertheless emerged so great that you seem to return a greater grace to them than you received. And while old age brings authority to others, youth exalts your dignity—which you have overcome by invincible virtue, whereas others do so by time. In my judgment, you are placed beyond all risk of talent, and even if I search through Greek praises, I find no one to whom I may deservedly compare you; and in short, while one may believe that someone equal to you existed at some time, it is not possible to see one in this time. Let all the gifted men forgive me: all are far surpassed by this one Pico. Nature's kindness has so cherished him that such a great abundance of all praises seems to have been gathered into one man. Why do you blush? Do you think I am false? Indeed, I will yield if you attribute this to love, which is painted as blind. But I have witnesses in my dear <term>Poliziano</term><note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a renowned poet and humanist scholar close to Pico.</note>, who is only deceived concerning me; witnesses who are more reliable, even if he (as I hear) daily increases his riches of gold no less than those of speech. And for that reason, I congratulate him as much as I thank him; would that he might possess a horn of plenty, since he is unmindful neither of his guest nor of our old friendship. Concerning Puccio, however...

-># BOOK SECOND<-

->SIGLA: E. XXIV.<-

...to the most loving of men at other times: who would not wish to be indebted to him? But I delay you too long as you lean over deeper studies. I see **Marsilio Ficino**, the prince of the philosophers of our age, laughing at these trifles. And why should he not laugh? He who values all mortal things no less than he despises them. You, meanwhile, gather from these scraps the fruit of my love; do not think it a small thing to be loved by me, but return the favor in turn. For this hope of a mutual bond—one in which I may entirely rest—is able to soothe my longing for you when I am gullible. Be happy, prince of Latin youth, and live mindful of me. December 26th <note>original: "vii. Kalen. Ianua." The 7th day before the Kalends of January.</note>. I have almost unlearned my letters in such a long seclusion, as you see; and unless I were compelled by the desire to contract and confirm our goodwill, I would not abuse your humanity and gentleness to such an extent. ### Girolamo Donato to his friend Giovanni Pico, Greetings. Letter XV.

<margin>Praise of Marsilio</margin>
All those parts which ought to have been mine, most learned Pico, you have taken for yourself: accusing yourself of negligence toward me, and seeking an excuse for that crime of which I am most guilty toward you. It seems too little to you to excel others in talent and erudition, unless you also surpass not only others but even yourself in modesty and humanity. But indeed, I pray that you embrace the gifts of these virtues in such a way that you leave us also some occasion for performing our duty, lest while you claim all these roles for yourself, we be held as inhuman and useless. In this matter—such is my impudence—I no longer excuse my negligence, but I accuse your humanity. Because you write that you have established not a temporary but a perpetual friendship with me, I understand that I owe you very much, not for that cause alone, but you also seem to me to have correctly defined friendship; for when it is temporary, it can no longer be friendship. Know this: I have set it aside among my most choice honors. For what more distinguished thing can happen to me than to be not only praised but also loved by such a man? I see that our **Hermolao** <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a prominent Venetian scholar and diplomat known for his work on Aristotle and Dioscorides.</note> is learned with an incredible tranquility of learning and a care for the <term>love of labor</term> <note>original Greek: "philoponia", meaning industriousness or diligence.</note>—a greatest and rare thing for which literature can hope while he is safe. I keep his companionship, which you so greatly envy me, in the same storehouse where I keep your friendship. Furthermore, I judge nothing to be so <term>marvelous</term> <note>original Greek: "thaumaston"</note> that you cannot attain it through talent and erudition, especially since I hear you have moved there; a plan I praise so much that I could not praise it more. For <term>nothing is sweeter than knowing everything</term> <note>original Greek: "ouden glykyteron e pan eidenai"</note>. I envy you for **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent poet and scholar of the Medici circle.</note>, a man of the most fertile and eloquent talent, whose *Rustic* I recently read; he seemed to me the splendor of our age. I ask from you, in my own words, those things which I might promise about myself to a most friendly man. I use you as a messenger in beginning my goodwill with him, relying on your humanity, since it is fitting that I be reconciled through you—who are most learned—to that <term>Leader of the Muses</term> <note>original Greek: "Tōn mousan Korypha..."—a high compliment to Poliziano’s poetic status.</note>. Farewell, and consider nothing more pleasant to me than your letters. I shall write more to you with more relaxed leisure. Venice, December 16th, 1484.

# OF THE LETTERS

About to dine at the home of Minus Roscius <note>Minus Roscius was a refined Roman aristocrat and senator associated with the humanists of the late 15th century.</note>—who is most polished in the study of letters and the greatest ornament of our senate—I was reading the plays of Plautus, which overflow with the most sophisticated wit. Just then, your letter was brought to me, which was remarkably literary, terse, and refined. Immediately, setting aside that comic charm, we began to read your most delightful writings with great haste. Good gods, what grace, what learning, what majesty we recognized within them!

Great fame had preceded **Giovanni Pico**; he was found to be even greater. Your writings resonate with nothing worn out, nothing trivial. Words match things and things match words precisely. You speak in Latin and use a style of speaking that is pure, splendid, and magnificent. Your way of speaking is full of pleasure and openness; you possess a most abundant supply of the best words. Your thoughts are so frequent and well-rounded, and you bring forth the feelings of your mind so clearly and elegantly, that the immortal gods seem to have given to you alone what they have granted to very few: namely, to think the best things and to say the best things.

And you encompass this no less in verse than in prose. Livy and Homer write, almost divinely, that the gods did not grant all things to one man. Hence it is that we often read of some who flourished by being outstanding in eloquence, while others were gifted in learning; but very few have emerged who were both eloquent and learned at the same time. For this reason, the two peaks of the Roman language, Terentius Varro and Marcus Cicero, are cited; from the former, the knowledge of things was sought, and from the latter, the knowledge of words. One is called the most learned in every respect by Terentianus; the other is called the most eloquent by everyone. As Seneca says so well, that "happiness of genius" failed Virgil in prose; Cicero wrote poems with no beauty and no charm, the Muses being—it goes without saying—unwilling and resistant.

But you are both most learned and most eloquent. You are powerful in prose and in verse. You write things worth reading, and you are skilled in things that must be written.

<margin>See Apuleius, book four of the *Florida*.</margin> 
You can deservedly be called a student of the Muses. You have not, like so many others, drunk only one or two cups of the Muses' wine; instead, like another Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), author of *The Golden Ass*, was a key figure for Renaissance humanists because of his "florid" and diverse style.</note>, you have drained every cup—and especially that clear and nectar-like cup of philosophy, which very few touch even with the tips of their lips, and which they hardly greet from the doorway.

O great fertility of mind! O most blessed abundance of immortal genius, which has forged such virtues in **Pico della Mirandola** while he is still a boy, still a youth! It pours in such diverse disciplines and has planted such gifts of mind. He who is a raw recruit in age is a veteran in learning.

Proceed, most learned man, as you have begun. Ensure that with increasing years your knowledge may grow; may your genius mature, and your memory become more vigorous and supportive. You who are the glory of our age and an example of virtue in your youth—what will you be in old age? Papinian is named by Spartianus as an "asylum of law" and a "treasury of legal learning"; you shall be called by us the "asylum of the liberal disciplines." You will be a treasury for us whenever something hidden occurs in the deeper study of letters—or rather, to speak more truly, you are already a treasury. 

Everything, even the most deep-seated matters in literature, is at your hand; all things meet you readily. That "circle of learning" <term>encyclopedia</term> <note>original: "orbis ille doctrinae." The writer is translating the Greek *enkyklios paideia*, describing the complete system of a liberal education.</note> which is praised by the learned seems to be in your service. To you, Greek and Latin letters act as handmaidens. You are permitted to invigorate your genius now with this meditation, now with that, for one is the seasoning for the other. And just as various and changed seeds recreate and restore the lands, so the change of studies refreshes and delights the mind. You are permitted to cheer your genius with the sweeter studies of poetry whenever it grows weary from the more austere dogmas of philosophy. 

You, finally, stand in the citadel and at the summit of the good disciplines, while we barely sweat on the first slope. You, with a giant's stride, have climbed the narrow path of virtue; we attempt to climb with the gait of a tortoise or an ant, and we labor on the rugged paths thereafter...

<meta>The text cuts off with the catchword "subinde" (thereafter/repeatedly).</meta>

# BOOK THE SECOND

...then wavering, now nodding and stumbling. I write what I feel; I feel what I write; my pen is in harmony with my mind. I am moved by an incredible desire to see you together with **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Italian humanist and poet.</note>; a desire I shall satisfy within a very few days. For Minus Roscius—who is the most loving of all men of letters and who pursues both of us with wondrous love—is coming there during these Easter holidays to fulfill his vows. I shall accompany the man. Then it will be possible to join right hands in turn and enjoy mutual conversation. Then I, a mere man of letters and grammarian, will approach, address, and greet you most learned men. Then I, who seem wise here, will perhaps whisper there—or like a goose among swans, I will sound out with a noisy squawk. Meanwhile, farewell, refuge of letters; love me in return, and greet the most longed-for Poliziano in my name. 

Bologna, the sixth day before the Ides of March [March 10], 1486.

### Bartholomew Fontius to Roberto Salviati. Letter XVII.

Greetings, for indeed I read your **Pico** <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's work, specifically the "Heptaplus."</note> with the greatest pleasure last night, Robert. I read it for two reasons: because it was sent by you, a most dear friend, and because I loved the author of the work for his own sake, whom I thought it would be shameful for me not to have read yet. Indeed, through your kindness, I have achieved what I most desired. I give you thanks for such a gift, and I heartily congratulate him for publishing such a great work, to be celebrated by all of Christendom. In it, I am uncertain whether to marvel more at the invention of so many great things, or at such incredible order in so much variety, or at such great elegance of speech in such laborious descriptions. For why should I mention in the <term>Heptaplus</term> <note>original: "heptaplo"; Pico's work published in 1489, which provides a seven-fold mystical explanation of the six days of creation in Genesis.</note> those things which the authors of the greatest works commend: that there is no wordiness, no swelling pride, and a singular modesty in all things without any suspicion of envy. 

I wish indeed that I could have returned a similar gift to this most sweet and desired present of yours, so that you might see my feelings toward you more clearly. But as I could do, I have just now sent you, before all others, a speech I recently delivered to King Matthias Corvinus <note>Matthias Corvinus (1443–1490), the King of Hungary and a famous patron of Renaissance humanists.</note>. When you have read it yourself, you will give it to your Pico to read as well. I judge him to be the most outstanding in every kind of learning among all those of our age whose writings I have yet seen. Farewell, and love me in return as you do.

### Battista Guarino to the most learned Prince Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Greetings. Letter XVIII.

I do not yet concede that the dispute should be settled in your favor. For I can easily turn those captions of yours back upon you, <term>reciprocally</term> <note>original: "αντιστρεφοντα" (antistrephonta); a term from Greek logic referring to an argument that can be inverted or turned back against the opponent.</note>. If I am your teacher, why do you not obey me? If I am not, why do you call me teacher? Nor do I refuse this name because I look down on you as a disciple—whom I assert is a teacher to me—but because I both venerate and proclaim your learning. In which I am conscious that neither my talent, nor my wishes, nor the mark of a slanted pen, nor small wax tablets, nor finally an <term>obelisk</term> <note>original: "obelisco"; a critical mark (†) used by ancient grammarians to indicate suspected or spurious text.</note> or an <term>asterisk</term> <note>original: "asterisco"; a mark (*) used to highlight noteworthy passages.</note> have advanced you so much. 

But we seem to have fallen into a certain new kind of judicial case: while you strive to claim for me that possession which I try to claim for you. What orator's case ever had a plaintiff or defendant of this kind? My dear Pico, I will never "reach out the herb" <note>An ancient Roman idiom (herbam porrigere) meaning to admit defeat or surrender.</note> to you in this arena unless we first settle on good terms: that since you will not yield otherwise, each of us should be judged as both teacher and disciple to the other. 

But joking aside, let us deal with serious matters. Both your <term>Heptaplus</term> and you yourself can rightly be pleased with you. Since you have won all the votes of learned men so completely that not even in a hidden corner of the tablet does any envy appear. It is to be hoped that the same will be granted to you more easily in your remaining writings, once experience has also been added—which is usually considered the best master in writing. As far as I am concerned, I rejoice greatly that I am on the lips of Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (the Magnificent), the de facto ruler of Florence and a major patron of the scholars mentioned here.</note>, a man praised by everyone and everywhere. Especially with the addition of Poliziano's judgment, whose abundant and secret knowledge of manifold discipline I...

...I embrace [your writing] so much that I admire it, and I admire it so much that I will not stop praising it. <margin>Note.</margin> Thus, I consider myself placed beyond the risk of ignorance by him, as if in a triumph. As for your request for a list of my books, that is laborious and useless for me. It will be enough if you assist my requests according to the time. Now I wish for Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century author of a famous encyclopedia on the liberal arts.</note> and Seneca’s *Natural Questions* <note>A significant work on the physical world by the Roman Stoic philosopher.</note>: provided the manuscripts are corrected. If I can buy them in print, it will be more pleasing to me. If not, they will return to you after a short absence. Farewell, my hope, and continue to love me and the noble disciplines. Ferrara, the Nones of December [December 5], 1489.

## Angelo Poliziano to his Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Greetings. Letter XIX.

<margin>Allusion to the Fable</margin>
**I** have burned—perhaps too shamelessly—but I have always burned with a zeal for your lasting fame: so much so that I would consider it nothing to compare it to any surviving glory. But since the things I wrote were scarcely promised a long life through my own name, you have appeared, Pico, to achieve what I could not: by dedicating to me your commentary *On Being and One* <note>original: "de uno & ente"; a philosophical treatise attempting to reconcile the views of Plato and Aristotle.</note> (for so you titled it). In this work, you call back the streams flowing through the Lyceum <note>The school of Aristotle.</note> and the Academy <note>The school of Plato.</note> to a single source. And since philosophy is one rather than twofold, you also join our theology to it. Why then should I now seek the grass of Glaucus <note>A reference to the mythological fisherman who became immortal after eating a magical herb.</note> to live forever through you? Rather, I shall live *with* you. Posterity will one day tell how there once lived a certain Poliziano whom the great Pico—himself the light and learning of all—esteemed so much that he did not hesitate to address to him his most beautiful book on the highest matters. Therefore, I give you thanks for this immortality: but let them be immortal thanks. Farewell.

## Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Germain de Ganay, President in Paris. Greetings. Letter XX.

**Y**ou wish to be more certain about the death of Pico della Mirandola, about which you seem still uncertain; and certainly, Germain, you wish to grieve more heavily. For while you have grieved heavily until now over this ambiguous loss, once you are made certain, I believe you will soon grieve most heavily indeed. Perhaps it was better to mourn a doubtful loss than to be tortured by a certain one. Alas, what do you ask, my most longed-for brother? I too wish the evil were still ambiguous. I cannot at present make you more certain without tears. Last November, on the very day that Charles, the great King of the Franks, entered our city of Florence [November 17, 1494], our Mirandola left us. He affected men of letters with almost as much grief as the King, meanwhile, brought joy to the city. Thus, the provident guardian spirit of the place compensated for the people's joy with the groans of scholars; and for the sake of the extinguished philosophical light, he meanwhile kindled a royal light. Lest Florence should perhaps seem too dark on that day, the Mirandolan light was extinguished on earth only to be returned to heaven. For Pico migrated from this shadow of life with such cheerful security that he seemed, without a doubt, to be returning from a kind of exile to his celestial fatherland. You desire, moreover, to know what Pico once composed, or what he was recently composing: he wrote the *Heptaplus* (on the six days of creation) <note>original: "Exameron".</note>, the *Apology*, and *On Being and One*, as well as several letters. Whatever he had composed regarding love during his still-fervent youth, he later condemned with more mature judgment and wished to be utterly destroyed; nor can they be published without injury to him. Indeed, I knew the last will of that pious man. For Pico was a son to me in age, a brother in familiarity, and in love, a second self. He was laboring daily on a triple concord between Aristotle and Plato; on commentaries on the sacred scriptures; and on the refutation of astrologers. All these were disputed with as much eloquence as subtlety. But those things which were brilliant in style were sketched out in such new and obscure characters that they could scarcely be read even by him. Therefore, they have not yet been revised by him in finished form, nor can they be transcribed by others unless perhaps by divination. For if they could be, we would not miss our Pico so much as if he were absent, nor would we ever suspect he was gone. But his pious nephew, Giovanni Francesco, who is also powerful in intellect, strives daily to rescue them from the shadows into light, and he is writing the life and deeds of his uncle. Finally, receive this meager epigram of ours: High priests very rarely reveal the more secret mysteries to the eyes and then immediately hide them away; so God [gave] to mortals the divine philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in the thirtieth year of his age...

...would happen. However, so that the rest of the loss to literature <note>original: "litterarum iactura"; referring to the death of great scholars as a loss to the "Republic of Letters."</note> made this autumn in Florence may be known to you: our Angelo Poliziano, most learned in the Latin and Greek languages, passed from this life this past September before the death of Pico, in the fortieth year of his age. He had long since published his *Miscellanea* <note>A collection of philological notes</note>, his *Silvae* <note>A collection of poetry</note>, and certain declamations and several epistles, all composed with both sharp insight and elegance. Every day he also noted down many things necessary for elegance in uncertain characters <note>original: "incertis characteribus"; likely referring to Poliziano’s notoriously difficult handwriting or his use of personal shorthand</note>, just as Pico did; thus a heavier loss to literature has befallen us in both men. March 24, 1494. <note>In the Florentine calendar, the year began on March 25th, so this date corresponds to 1495 in modern reckoning.</note>

->## Letter XXI.<-

->Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia. Greetings.<-

**I** sent a brief letter regarding the death and praises of Pico to France after your departure. However, one may collect long and singular praises of Pico from many of my writings scattered here and there, especially from the later books of my letters. For there are twelve now printed: from the preface to Plotinus, from the book *On the Sun*, and from the commentaries on the *Timaeus* and *Parmenides*. Accept this epitaph for him: "The high priests of the more secret mysteries grant them to our eyes very rarely, and immediately hide them away again. Thus God showed to mortals the divine philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, mature in the thirtieth year of his age." Thus far the epitaph. God seems to have given all the most abundant goods of mind, body, and fortune to Giovanni Pico, if only He had granted a longer span of life. But it is not right to accuse Providence in this. For if God had led him beyond the powers of nature to the very summit in a very short time, perhaps he could not have progressed toward anything better. Indeed, the mobility of nature does not allow one to remain in the same state, and perfected virtue does not permit a slide back toward the worse. But you yourself have written these and other things of that kind better and more extensively in the *Life of Pico* <note>Gianfrancesco wrote the first major biography of his uncle, Giovanni Pico</note>, not so much to bring him fame—for who could add light to the sun?—but so that you might brighten his hidden works, which are most worthy of light, by dispelling the clouds. Therefore, mortals will wonderfully commend your piety <note>original: "pietatem"; here meaning familial duty and devotion</note> toward your uncle, and God will judge it worthy of no small rewards. Farewell. November 1, 1495.

->## Letter XXII.<-

->Baccio Ugolini to Roberto Salviati. Greetings.<-

**L**earned men rightly love you, Roberto, whom you have always cultivated with a certain wonderful ardor; and all students love you, whom you assist not only with effort but also with expense, so that they may progress more conveniently. Indeed, although I am not to be numbered among either the learned or even the studious, I nevertheless confess that I owe you much, because through you a copy has been made available to us—even those of us further away—of a truly divine work recently published by Pico della Mirandola, a man certainly to be admired above all who are or ever were. My friend Poliziano, another miracle of our age, rightly calls him no longer "Pico" but "his Phoenix," nesting in the sacred laurel of the Physician <note>original: "medicu lauro"; a complex pun on Lorenzo de' Medici: "Lauro" is the Laurel (Lorenzo) and "Medicu" refers to the Medici name (Physician)</note>. You have seen to it that his book on the <term>Heptaplus</term> <note>The "sevenfold narration of the six days of Genesis," Pico's mystical interpretation of the creation story</note>—an increase for both true philosophy and the Christian religion, dedicated to my patron, the great Lorenzo de' Medici—was not only very diligently printed but also sent to diverse and distant places, and given freely to many who were most eager for that reading. Among these, it fell to me to obtain this desired gift through your friend Vittorio Caiano, a man sprinkled with much jest and sweetness and wit. Who would not praise this zeal of yours toward famous men, and this dutiful liberality toward all lovers of virtue, and follow it with a most grateful affection? Such a person should undoubtedly be considered discordant with all humanity and a stranger to the custom of letters. For public utility could not have been consulted more lovingly, correctly, or swiftly. Therefore, I would wish this to be especially well-known to you: that you have undertaken a task of this kind for no small reward, since you have followed it with the gratitude of good men and no mediocre glory. Farewell. Naples, April 25, 1490.
