### Junianus Maius to Roberto Salviati. Greetings.

**Q**uince you have taken care to print the divine work of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola with no less diligence than he himself used in composing it, I believe that great thanks are owed both to your industry and to his divine learning. To you, because you did not allow such a sublime work to remain hidden among the shadows of oblivion; by this one effort, you have looked after both the enduring memory of a friend and the common benefit of all. To him, however, because he was not deterred by the authority or holiness of the ancient men who explained these same matters; nor did he simply follow in the footsteps of others, but illuminated those same things with a certain light of his own. For as soon as this work—so profound and removed from the knowledge of the many—came into my hands, I began to read it quite diligently. It brought me pleasure not only through my admiration, but it also lifted my mind to such a height of contemplation that I have never seen or heard anything more admirable or more clearly explained. Truly, his intellect stands above the sharpness of others; he is skilled in an incredible investigation of the sciences <note>original: "scientiarum indaginem"</note> and possesses a knowledge of all things beyond what might be believed. This is especially true at his current age, for having only just moved past his youth, he has attained such knowledge of matters as even the most learned and those advanced in years have not been able to reach. On this account, I shall never fear to call him the sacred home of all the liberal arts <note>original: "bonarum artium," referring to the humanities</note> and the miracle of our age. This is especially true when I read more closely the profound meanings of the work—the progressions of things devised by only a few men, the revealed hiding places of nature and of God, and finally the secret riches of the supreme Creator <note>original: "summi opificis"</note> now brought out into the open. I know not what I have ever heard that is more admirable, nor what I have read that is deeper. Between the philosophers and Moses—who each wove the creation of the world by a different path—a peace has now been entered into, and certain joined covenants of nature and of God are understood without controversy. But I reserve this for another time, to be sought more deeply and explained more wordily.

I come now to you, my excellent Roberto, whom I love uniquely because of your writings; although they are few, they show such a specimen of your virtue that they promise a no less fruitful harvest of intellect than they now offer a most pleasing hope of blossoms. Thus, know that your Junianus—if you should hereafter give me anything of your writings—will be no less a herald of your affairs than a lover of you for that very reason. Our friend Victorius <note>likely referring to a mutual scholarly acquaintance</note> speaks highly of the excellence of your talent and your learned refinement <note>original: "humanitatem," referring to the "studia humanitatis" or classical education</note> in these letters, so that I am provoked to desire and praise the same. Yet I ask one thing: that you do not cease to pursue with that kindness you profess and embrace the man whom Victorius has invited to love you with his flattering encouragements. By this, you will stir my laziness so that I may write to you more often, provided you do not despise our efforts. And if, based on the words of our friend Victorius, you do not disregard my friendship, you will provoke me to follow you with every duty by a bond of necessity. For there is nothing I would prefer more than to contend in mutual love and the exchange of letters with honorable and learned men. To your friend Pico of Mirandola—whom you herald as the pillar of refinement—I even dare to call him the "delight of nature." Since I desire to be loved by him, pray return him to me as a friend, and give him greetings from me.

Farewell. Naples, the day before the Nones of June, 1490. <note>June 4, 1490</note>

->EPITOME OF THE TWELVE RULES FOR LIVING WELL<-
->e<-

# EPITOME OF THE TWELVE RULES FOR LIVING WELL

**The first rule:** If the path of virtue seems hard to a man because we must continually fight against the flesh, the devil, and the world; let him remember that whatever life he chooses, even according to the world, he must suffer many adversities: sadness, inconveniences, and toil.

**The second rule:** Let him remember that in worldly matters, the fight is longer, more laborious, and more fruitless; in these matters, labor is the only end of labor, and the final result is eternal punishment.

**The third rule:** Let him remember that it is foolish to believe one can reach heaven except through such a fight, just as our head, Christ, did not ascend into heaven except through the cross; nor should the condition of the servant be better than the condition of his master.

**The fourth rule:** Let him remember that this fight should not only be endured with patience, but even desired, even if no reward were to come to us from it, solely so that we may be conformed to Christ our God and Lord. <note>This refers to 'Imitatio Christi'—the practice of modeling one's life and sufferings on the life of Jesus.</note> Every time you resist a temptation and do violence to one of your senses, think to which part of the cross of Christ you are being made conformable. When resisting gluttony you afflict your sense of taste, remember Him given gall and vinegar to drink <note>original: "felle potatum & aceto"</note>. When you pull your hands back from stealing something that pleases you, think of His hands fixed for you to the wood of the cross. If you resist pride, remember Him who, though He was in the form of God, took the form of a servant for you and humbled Himself even to death on the cross. When you are tempted by anger, remember Him who was God and the most just Lord of men, yet saw Himself treated like a thief, mocked, spat upon, scourged, afflicted with every reproach, and counted among thieves; yet He never showed any sign of anger or indignation, but bearing all things most patiently, He replied most gently to everyone. Thus, by running through each example, you may find that there is no passion which does not make you conformable to Christ in some part.

**The fifth rule:** Trust neither in those twelve weapons <note>A reference to Pico’s related work, *The Twelve Weapons of Spiritual Warfare*.</note> nor in any other human remedy, but only in the power of Jesus Christ who said: "Have confidence, I have overcome the world" <note>John 16:33</note>. And elsewhere: "The prince of this world is cast out" <note>John 12:31</note>. Therefore, let us also trust only in His power to be able to conquer the world and overcome the devil. For this reason, we must always seek His help through prayer and through His saints.

**The sixth rule:** Remember that when you have overcome one temptation, another is always to be expected; because the devil always circles about seeking whom he may devour. Therefore, it is necessary to always serve in fear and to say with the prophet: "I will stand upon my watch."

**The seventh rule:** Not only should you not be conquered by the devil when he tempts you, but you should conquer him; and this occurs when you not only do not sin, but from that very thing with which he tempted you, you take the opportunity for some good. For example, if he offers you some good work of your own so that you might fall into vainglory, you should immediately think of it not as your own work, but as a gift from God; humble yourself and judge yourself to be ungrateful to God for His benefits.

**The eighth rule:** When you fight, you should fight as if by winning you will then have perpetual peace; because perhaps God will give you this by His grace, and the devil will no longer return, confused by your victory. But when you have won, behave as if you are about to fight again immediately, so that in the fight you are always mindful of victory, and in victory always mindful of the fight.

**The ninth rule:** However much you feel yourself well-fortified and prepared on all sides, you should always flee the occasions of sin; because as the wise man says, "He who loves danger shall perish in it."

**The tenth rule:** In temptations, you should always meet them at the very beginning and "dash the little ones of Babylon against the rock." <note>A quote from Psalm 137:9. In medieval theology, this was interpreted allegorically: the "little ones" are sinful thoughts, and the "rock" is Christ. One should kill sinful impulses while they are still small.</note> Now the rock is Christ; for medicine is prepared too late <note>A paraphrase of the Roman poet Ovid: *Principiis obsta; sero medicina paratur* (Resist at the beginning; the medicine is prepared too late [when the disease has grown]).</note>.

**The eleventh rule:** Remember that although the fight may seem bitter in the very conflict of temptation, yet it is far sweeter to overcome the temptation than to give in to the sin to which you are inclined. In this, many are deceived, because they do not compare the sweetness of victory with the sweetness of sin; instead, they compare the struggle to the pleasure. Yet a man who has a thousand times experienced what it is to yield to temptation should at least once experience what it is to overcome temptation.

<summary>This page contains the first eleven of Pico della Mirandola’s twelve rules for spiritual life, emphasizing the necessity of struggle, the imitation of Christ's suffering, and the psychological tactics needed to resist temptation.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual warfare, Pico della Mirandola, temptation, Christ's Passion, asceticism, virtue, Twelve Rules, spiritual discipline</keywords>

# EXPOSITION
<meta>visible bleed-through from the reverse side of the page</meta>

### The twelfth rule

The twelfth rule: if you are tempted, do not believe yourself to be abandoned by God, or that you are not pleasing to Him, or that you are not just and perfect. Remember that after Paul saw the divine essence, he suffered the temptation of the flesh. God permitted him to be tempted so that he would not be tempted by pride; in this, a person ought to consider that even Paul—who was a "vessel of choice" <note>original: "uas electionis," a reference to Acts 9:15</note> and was caught up to the third heaven—was still in danger of becoming proud of his own virtues. As he himself says of himself: "lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh <note>original: "stimulus carnis meæ"</note> to buffet me." For this reason, above all temptations, a person must especially fortify themselves against the temptation of pride; for pride is the "root of all evils" <note>original: "radix omnium malorum"</note>. Against this, the sole remedy is to reflect always that God humbled Himself for us even unto the cross, and death humbles us (even against our will) to such an extent that we become food for worms.

Twelve weapons of spiritual combat which ought to be kept ready at hand when the lust for sinning subdues the mind:

| | |
|---|---|
| Pleasure is brief and slight. | Eternal reward: eternal punishment. |
| Its companions are disgust and anxiety. | The dignity and nature of man. |
| The loss of a greater good. | The peace of a good mind. |
| Life is a dream and a shadow. | The benefits of God. |
| Death is imminent and unforeseen. | The cross of Christ. |
| The suspicion of impenitence. <note>The fear that one might not have enough time or will to repent before death.</note> | The testimony of martyrs and the examples of saints. |

->**The twelve conditions of a lover.**<-

1. To love one alone and to despise all things for His sake.
2. To consider unhappy anyone who is not with the beloved.
3. To suffer all things to be with Him, even death. <gloss>To adorn oneself so as to please Him.</gloss>
4. To be with Him however one can: if not in reality, then at least in thought.
5. To love everything that belongs to Him: all friends, the house, clothes, and images.
6. To desire His praises and to be unable to endure any shame directed at Him.
7. To believe all the highest things of Him, and to desire that everyone else believes the same.
8. To wish to suffer some inconvenience for Him, and for that inconvenience to be sweet.
9. To weep with Him often: either from sorrow if He is absent, or from joy if He is present.
10. To always languish and always burn with desire for Him.
11. To serve Him while thinking nothing of a prize or reward. We are usually led to this service especially for three reasons. The first is when the service itself is desirable for its own sake. The second is when the one whom we serve is, in himself, truly good and lovable—just as we often say we serve someone on account of their virtues. The third is when He has bestowed many benefits upon you before you even began. All three of these are found in God: for through His service, nothing is newly received that is not good for us, both for the soul and the body; for to serve Him is nothing other than to strive toward Him, which is to say, toward the Highest Good. Likewise, He is the best, the most beautiful, and the wisest; He possesses all the conditions that usually move us to love someone and serve them freely. Furthermore, He has bestowed the greatest benefits upon us, since He created us from nothing and redeemed us from hell through the blood of His Son.

->**Protect me, O Lord.**<-

<margin>Note</margin>
If any perfect man wishes to examine his own state, he faces one danger: that he might become proud of his own virtue. Therefore David, speaking in the person of a just man about his state, begins with this word: "Protect me" <note>original: "conserua me," from Psalm 16:1</note>. If rightly considered, this removes every occasion for pride. For whoever can acquire something by his own power can also preserve it for himself by his own power. Therefore, he who asks to be preserved by God in a state of virtue signifies by this that he did not acquire that virtue by himself from the beginning. He who remembers that he obtained virtue—not by his own power, but by the power of God—cannot be proud of it, but rather is humbled before God according to...

<meta>catchword: that of the Apostle.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual commentary attributed to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from the "Rules of Spiritual Combat" into a formal exposition of Psalm 15 (Psalm 16 in modern numbering). # EXPOSITION OF PSALM 15 OF DAVID.

That saying of the Apostle: "What do you have that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" <note>original: "Quid habes quod non accepisti? et si accepisti quid gloriaris? quasi non acceperis." See 1 Corinthians 4:7.</note> There are, therefore, two phrases which we ought always to have in our mouths: one, namely, "Have mercy on me, O God" <note>original: "miserere mei deus"</note> when we remember our sins; the other is, "Preserve me, O God" <note>original: "Conserua me deus"</note> when we remember our virtues.

**BECAUSE I have hoped in you.**
<margin>Just and good things are to be sought</margin>
This is the one thing that causes us to obtain from God what we seek: namely, when we hope that we will obtain it. And if we observe these two conditions—that we never seek from God anything except those things which are healthy for us, and that we seek what we ask for ardently with a firm hope that God will hear us—our prayers will never be in vain. Therefore, when we do not obtain what we seek, it is either because the thing is harmful to us—for we do not know what we should ask for, as Christ says—and Jesus said, "whatever you ask in my name will be given to you" <note>original: "quicquid petieritis in nomine meo dabitur uobis"</note> for this name "Jesus" signifies "Savior"; and therefore nothing is asked for in the name of Jesus unless it pertains to the salvation of the one asking. Or else He does not hear because, although we seek good things, we do not seek them well—that is, with little hope. For he who hopes timidly, asks coldly; therefore James said: "but let him ask in faith, doubting nothing." <note>original: "postulet autem in fide nihil hæsitans." See James 1:6.</note>

**I SAID to the Lord: You are my God.**
<margin>To whom it is fitting to say "Lord"</margin>
After he has fortified himself against pride, he begins to describe his state. Moreover, the entire state of the just man consists in this phrase: "I said to the Lord: You are my God." Although this phrase seems common to almost everyone, there are few who can truly say it. For a person considers that to be their "god" which they hold as their <term>highest good</term> <note>original: "summum bonum." The ultimate goal or source of happiness in classical and medieval philosophy.</note>; and we hold that as our highest good which, if we possess it alone even if all other things are lacking, we consider ourselves to be happy; and which, if it alone is missing even if we have all other good things, we consider ourselves to be miserable. Thus, the greedy man says to his money: "You are my god," because even if he lacks honor, health, virtue, and friends, so long as he has money, he is content. And if he has all those good things we mentioned but lacks money, he considers himself unhappy. Likewise, the gluttonous say this to their excess, the incontinent to their lust, and the ambitious to their power or glory: "You are my god." See, therefore, how few can say: "I said to the Lord: You are my God"; for only he can do so for whom God alone is sufficient, such that if all the kingdoms of the world, all celestial things, and all earthly goods were offered to him—but on the condition that to obtain them he must offend God even once—he would refuse. In this saying, therefore, consists the whole state of the righteous man.

**BECAUSE you have no need of my goods.**
<margin>Whence that saying of Plato: that we are not born for ourselves</margin>
He gives the reason for his proposition: namely, why he says to the Lord alone: "You are my God." The reason is that God alone does not need our goods. For there is no creature that does not need other creatures that are more imperfect than itself, as philosophers and theologians prove; for if those things were not, these things would not be. Because if one part of the universe is destroyed, the whole universe is destroyed; and if the universe is destroyed, all parts are destroyed. All creatures are parts of one universe; of which universe God himself is not a part, but the principle, depending on nothing. For God acquired nothing from the fact that He created the world, and He would lose nothing if the whole world were annihilated. Therefore, God alone does not need our goods.
<margin>Why the sayings of the Saracens fall apart</margin>
We ought to be ashamed to hold that being as "god" who needs our goods, which is true of every creature. Furthermore, we ought not to hold anything as "god"—that is, as the highest good—unless it is that in which the entirety of good resides; but in no creature is there every good. Therefore, to the Lord alone should we say: "You are my God."

**TO THE SAINTS who are in his land.**
After God, we ought most to love those who are most closely joined to God, such as the angels and the blessed in the fatherland <note>original: "patria." A common theological term for Heaven, the true homeland of the soul.</note>. Therefore, after he said to the Lord: "You are my God," he adds what God did.

**He has made his will wonderful to mine.**
That is, He made his loves and his desires wonderful toward the saints who are on the earth.

Signature mark: e ii

<summary>This page provides a philosophical and theological commentary on Psalm 15, defining God as the "highest good" (summum bonum) and arguing that true righteousness involves finding total sufficiency in God alone, who—unlike His creatures—needs nothing from us.</summary>

<header>EXPOSITION.</header>
<meta>catchword: As if to say</meta>

## EXPOSITION.

<margin>Metaphorically, the heaven of the saints is called "earth" for us</margin>
...of Him: <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion of God's dwelling.</note> that is, in the heavenly homeland which is called the land of God and the land of the living. Truly, if we consider how great the happiness of that homeland is, and how great the misery of this world—how great the goodness and brightness of those citizens—we will always desire to depart from here so that we may dwell there. However, when we meditate on these and similar things, we must always take care that our meditations are not fruitless. Instead, we should always acquire some virtue from every meditation. Specifically, from this meditation on the goodness of that higher homeland, we ought to acquire the virtue of bearing death not only bravely and patiently when our hour comes (or if we must undergo it for the faith of Christ), but even seeking it out willingly. That is, we should desire to depart from this valley of miseries <note>original: "ualle miſeriary" (valle miseriarum)</note> so that we may reign in that happy homeland with God and His saints. Therefore, when the just man has described his state—which is entirely focused on God—and looks down from on high, despising the state of evil men, he says:

### THEIR infirmities were multiplied; afterwards they hurried.
By "infirmities," he means <term>idols</term> <note>The commentator notes that the Hebrew text uses a word for "sorrows" or "weaknesses" that was often interpreted as referring to false gods.</note>; and this is how the Hebrew text has it. For just as a good man has one God whom he worships, so the wicked have many gods and idols because they serve many pleasures, many vain desires, and various passions. They seek many pleasures precisely because they find none that can satisfy them, and therefore they wander around the circuit of their own empire. He adds "afterwards they hurried" <note>original: "acclamauerunt" / "accelerauerunt"</note> because they rush headlong and thoughtlessly after their desires. From this we are taught that we should run no less quickly toward virtues than they run toward vice, nor should we serve our Lord less diligently than they serve their lord, the devil. The just man, considering the state of the wicked, firmly resolves—as we always ought to do—that he will in no way follow them, and says of them through my lips:

<margin>The custom of idolaters</margin>
### I WILL not gather their meetings of blood, nor will I be mindful of their names.
He speaks of "blood" for two reasons: first, because idolaters used to collect blood and perform their ceremonies around the victims; and second, because the entire life of the wicked, having abandoned reason, follows sensuality, which is situated in the blood. He says that he not only refuses to sacrifice to idols, but will not even name them. This shows that a perfect man ought to abstain not only from illicit pleasures but even from <term>licit</term> <note>Lawful or permitted pleasures.</note> ones, so that he may be carried more fully toward heaven and be more purely free for the contemplation of divine things. And because someone might believe it to be folly to deprive oneself of every pleasure, he adds:

<margin><unclear>The Way of Life</unclear> for us saints</margin>
### THE Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup.
As if to say: do not be surprised if I leave everything else behind to possess God, in whom all other good things are ultimately possessed. This ought to be the voice of every good Christian: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance." Because we Christians are promised God Himself as our inheritance, we should be ashamed to desire anything besides Him. And because it might seem like presumption to anyone to dare to promise these things to himself, he adds:

### IT IS You who will restore my inheritance to me.
As if to say: "Lord my God, I know well that since I am nothing in respect to You, I cannot ascend to possess You by my own strength. But You are the one who will draw me to You through Your grace, and You are the one who will give Yourself to me to be possessed." Let the just man then consider how great this happiness is, that God has fallen to him as an inheritance; he adds:

<margin>The allotments of the ancients</margin>
### THE lines have fallen for me in excellent places.
For in ancient times, portions and <term>lots</term> <note>original: "sortes"</note> were divided by <term>lines</term> <note>original: "funes," literally "ropes" or "measuring cords" used to survey land.</note>. And since there are many who, although called to this happiness—as all Christians are—nevertheless treat it as nothing and often trade it for some slight pleasure, he therefore adds:

### FOR INDEED my inheritance is excellent to me.

It encourages the reader to focus entirely on God, using the metaphor of ancient land measurement to describe the "excellent" spiritual portion God provides through grace.</summary>

<page-num>141</page-num>
->THE PSALMS OF DAVID, PSALM 15<-

## THE PSALMS OF DAVID, PSALM 15

As if to say: just as the inheritance itself is excellent, so do I consider it excellent, and all other things in comparison to it—as the Apostle Paul used to say—I consider as dung <note>A reference to Philippians 3:8, where Paul counts all things as loss or "refuse" compared to Christ.</note>. For to possess this light of the intellect, so that a person recognizes the happiness given to them as a gift of God, is a great thing; and therefore he adds:
**I WILL bless the Lord who has given me understanding.**
Since, however, a person often judges according to reason that they should serve God, yet sensuality and the flesh rebel, a person is only truly perfect when not only the soul but also the flesh is directed toward God, according to that saying: *My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God* <note>Psalm 84:2.</note>. Therefore he adds:
**MOREOVER, even until the night, my kidneys have corrected me.**
<margin>Just as night is the deprivation of light, so affliction is the cause of the deprivation of pleasure</margin>
That is, the <term>kidneys</term> <note>original: "renes." In biblical thought, the kidneys (often translated as "reins") were considered the seat of the most secret and powerful human emotions and impulses.</note> themselves, in which there is usually the greatest inclination toward lust, do not only incline me toward evil but rather "correct" or "rebuke" me. This means they pull me back even until the night—that is, to the point that they even willingly afflict their own body. For affliction is often signified by the "night." He then shows what the root of such self-denial is, and says:
**I FORESAW the Lord always in my sight.**
For if anyone always had God before their eyes as the rule for all their actions, and in all their operations sought neither their own utility, nor glory, nor pleasure, but only to please God, they would shortly become perfect. Whoever acts this way always prospers in all things; therefore he says:
**BECAUSE he is at my right hand, lest I be moved.**
He shows then how great the happiness of the just man is: because he will be happy forever in both soul and body. Therefore he adds:
**BECAUSE of this, my heart has rejoiced and my tongue has exulted.**
That is, my soul is joyful, knowing that heaven is prepared for it after death.
**MOREOVER, my flesh also shall rest in hope.**
<margin>Wherefore (as Thomas witnesses) blessedness arises</margin> <note>Likely referring to Saint Thomas Aquinas, who wrote extensively on the "beatitude" or ultimate happiness of the soul.</note>
That is, although the flesh itself does not rejoice as if it were to receive its heavenly state immediately after death, it nevertheless rests in the grave with this hope: that it will rise again on the day of judgment with its soul, immortal and most radiant. He declares all this in the following verse. For since he had said that the soul rejoiced, he adds the reason:
**FOR you will not leave my soul in hell.**
And because he had said that the flesh rested in hope, he adds the reason, saying:
**NOR will you allow your holy one to see corruption.**
<margin>See what those are</margin>
Because whatever was corruptible shall rise again incorruptible. And because Christ was the first who entered paradise and opened the way of life to us, and was the first who rose again—and his resurrection is the cause of our own resurrection—therefore these things we have said about the resurrection are understood principally concerning Christ, as the Apostle Peter declared <note>Acts 2:25-31.</note>, and secondarily they can be understood concerning us, insofar as we are members of Christ. He alone did not see corruption, because his body did not decay in the tomb. Since, therefore, the way of living well leads us to the everlasting life of soul and body, he adds:
**YOU have made known to me the ways of life.**
And because the total happiness of this life consists in the direct vision and enjoyment of God, he adds:
**YOU will fill me with joy with your countenance.**
And because happiness will endure forever, he adds:
**DELIGHTS are at your right hand even unto the end.**
He says "at your right hand" because our happiness is completed in the vision and enjoyment of the humanity of Christ, who sits at the right hand of majesty on high, according to that saying of John: *This is the whole reward, that we may see God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.* <note>A paraphrase of John 17:3.</note> **The End.**

<meta>This page marks a transition from the biblical commentary of the previous pages to a collection of "Eulogies" or praises written by famous contemporaries about the author, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. These letters serve as a testament to his reputation as a "prodigy of nature" in the late 15th century.</meta>

# PRAISES OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA BY MOST DISTINGUISHED MEN.

## From a letter of Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico.

Your genius is brilliant and clearly divine, Pico: for although the things you write are of the highest quality, you nevertheless express and shape the works of others—even those that are of the poorest quality—in such a way that they seem to be your own, which are the best. For I consider it a greater feat to humble oneself and descend than to strive for the heights; while the latter is more honorable, the former is certainly more laborious and requires greater effort. Therefore, whether you truly believe our works to be worthy of the effort you spend imitating them, or whether you do this for the sake of earning my favor, I am deeply indebted to you in either case. I do not wish to say I will return the favor when I am able (for I shall never be able), but rather when you yourself, or your people, believe that I can. For the goodness and kindness of your whole family is so great that you are accustomed to counting as a favor even that which is not a favor. Therefore, I will be acting in my own interest if I leave the manner and time of repaying my remaining gratitude to you, so that in the settling of accounts, any <term>paralogism</term> <note>A reasoning that is unintentionally false or a mathematical error in calculation; here used metaphorically regarding a debt of gratitude.</note> or error in the balance may proceed not from me, but entirely from you. 

As for what you wrote regarding the plan of your studies, and your desire to share it with me, it has affected me with the greatest pleasure. I have congratulated this century for having a man of such great learning that he knows almost nothing of which he is ignorant, yet possesses such great care that he seems to know nothing at all. I see that you are an extraordinary poet and a most eminent orator. I notice that you were previously an <term>Aristotelian</term> philosopher, and now you have become a <term>Platonist</term> as well. I see that you have not only learned but have truly drunk in Greek literature—which was the only thing lacking in you, and without which you would have been nothing—and you did so with such ease and speed that you yourself do not remember, nor could you persuade others, that you were ever ignorant of Greek letters. I proclaim this of Girolamo Donà <note>original: "Hierõ. Donato." A Venetian humanist and diplomat.</note> no less gladly than I do truly. I would urge you toward these letters so that you might hold them as clearly and familiarly as you do Latin, but you do not need spurs; and so forth.

## From another letter of the same man to the same.

In a certain corner of my letters to you, acting as if I were doing something else and in passing, I had attacked the "barbarian" philosophers <note>In the Renaissance, "barbarian" was a derogatory term used by humanists to describe the medieval Scholastic philosophers (like Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus) because of their unpolished Latin style.</note> of our age. You wrote back that you too had become hostile to them and had sent them a formal "notice of dismissal" <note>A legal or formal term for breaking off a relationship or alliance.</note>. Taking this opportunity, you sent us a "dispute" and an old controversy between us and them regarding the style of speech used by philosophers. It is a work of many thousands of lines, elegant, erudite, and carefully crafted. It was completed with such speed that, had I not known the most perfect resources of your genius, I would have believed you had this argument ready for a long time so that you could bring it forth at the first opportunity. But so that the matter might turn out both more festive and more pleasant for me, you—a most witty, refined, and Latin-literate man—defend a barbarian against a barbarian! You play the part of standing and acting as an advocate: an enemy for an enemy, an ally against an ally, and yourself against yourself; and so forth.

## From the same letter, further down.

Now, if there is anyone in that flock <note>Referring to the "barbarian" philosophers.</note> who is able to grasp the things you have said, which are endowed with such great refinement, and which strike the eyes of those approaching with so many "lights" <note>Stylistic ornaments or rhetorical highlights.</note> and so many "emblems." Add to this so many stimulating thoughts, so many histories, and examples of deeper learning, which are like little flowers—and altogether <insert>to which, if there are any among them who are a little less [like]</insert> asses, I was going to say <note>original: "ὄνου ὦτ'" (onou ot')</note> "donkey's ears," they only twitch their ears. The rest scatter, reject it, detest it; and so forth.

## From another letter of the same man.

Greetings. I have received Pico’s book on the narration of the seven days <note>This refers to Pico’s famous work, the *Heptaplus*, a mystical and philosophical commentary on the Book of Genesis.</note>, a copy of which Jacopo da Volterra <note>original: "Iacobus uolaterranus." Jacopo Gherardi da Volterra, a papal secretary and diarist.</note>, the messenger of the Supreme Pontiff, had also sent to me not long ago. I have run through the work as far as was permitted amidst the heat and the dust. It is a work worthy of a divine and admirable genius; the laws and the hurried nature of the work, prepared for the present moment, do not demand formal sentences...

demands. But at the same time, it can be said that for Pico to have attained everything expected of a learned, eloquent, and Christian man at such an age is almost a miracle: I am deeply in your debt.

### From another letter by the same author to the same man.

ALTHOUGH I love these letters of yours because they flow freely and are not affected—because they do not merely lack care, but seem to reject it; that is, they purposefully do not admit artificiality, and they shut it out even when it tries to creep in—nevertheless, traces of careful diligence are indeed present in them, though they are somewhat restrained and pushed back. I am not so skillful that I can look into the depths of your genius and estimate its magnitude and fruitfulness, yet I seem to see this (and perhaps I am not mistaken): the direction in which you are aiming, and where you are destined to arrive, and indeed very soon. 

Nothing is more noble than that natural talent of yours, nothing more delightful; and to put it somewhat more boldly, nothing is more full of promise—if indeed it should be called "natural talent" when it has already produced fruits that even the most mature ages and most practiced learning would not look down upon. Come now, how great is your spirit in poetry (as I hear)! What happiness, what vigor, and finally, what nobility and splendor in every pursuit of letters, especially the most distinguished. And when you act the <term>philosopher</term> <note>original: "phum", an abbreviation for "philosophum".</note>, what memory, what subtlety, what speed of mind, all in harmony with the vigor of your whole body! But I am carried away into your praises against my will—or rather, most willingly. For everyone desires most that which turns them toward itself by an invincible and even reluctant force. Time more suited to this duty of praise will certainly be given, if you even desire to be praised by those of little learning. Now I come to this point, and the rest.

### From a letter of Angelo Poliziano to Giovanni Pico regarding the dispute with Ermolao.

THEREFORE, my dear Pico—more learned than all, the most learned of all—you must now be called upon by me, not as a judge, but as an honorary arbiter, so that you may settle the dispute between friends who are in disagreement.

### From the preface of the *Miscellanea* by the same author.

FOR my expectation regarding that man—who is to be wondered at above all others, and whom I now call not "Pico" but rather a "Phoenix" <note>A mythological bird that is unique and reborn from its own ashes; a common metaphor for Pico's singular genius.</note> who now nests in your laurel <note>A play on the name of Lorenzo de' Medici ("Laurentius"), Pico's patron, whose name derives from the laurel tree.</note>—is so great that I dare to sing along with Propertius: *Yield, you Roman writers; yield, you Greeks.* <note>original: "Cedite romani scriptores cedite grai." A famous line from the poet Propertius suggesting that a new work surpasses all classical predecessors.</note>

### From Chapter 14 of the same work.

AS the same Giovanni Pico of Mirandola—my friend, and of all men surely the most blessed in every respect—both demonstrates and shows in a singular and admirable work: in which he teaches that the Hebrew truth corresponds to the [Greek] translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament.</note> in a psalm of sixty verses, using that specific argument of notations. This is so that no Jew can henceforth mock us or object that we sing things in the Temple every hour which we ourselves do not believe to be translated faithfully enough.

### From Chapter 80 of the same author.

SUCH also is this Giovanni Pico of mine, of the princes of Mirandola, a most perfect work of nature; I believe that <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "phiā", an abbreviation for "philosophiam".</note>, which is now learning to speak Latin through him, will reach its highest summit.

### From Chapter 89 of the same author.

SOMETIMES Pico of Mirandola and I—a man who can never be praised enough—run through the ancient commentators of the Old Testament in our spare hours, especially the Greeks: Diodorus, Philo, Gennadius, Aquila, Origen, Basil, Didymus, Isidore, Apollinaris, Severian, and many others of that kind. He, comparing all the opinions of the Latin authors with the views of the Jewish and Chaldean interpreters with the utmost diligence, sifts and weighs everything. From this, either truth can be elicited, or obscurity removed, or faith strengthened, or impiety refuted.

### From the conclusion of the same work.

UNTIL he returned to this city, especially with the goodwill of Lorenzo de' Medici...

# EULOGIES

...brought together. Attracted by a similarity of virtue and talent, this most noble prince Giovanni Pico of Mirandola—a man alone, or rather a hero, most richly endowed with all gifts of fortune, body, and soul—is a youth of almost sovereign beauty and eminent physical majesty. He possesses a most piercing wit, a singular memory, and tireless zeal, along with a brilliant and polished eloquence. It is truly doubtful whether he is more admirable in his judgment or in his character. He is already most expert in all philosophy, as well as in the varied literature of languages. He is fortified and equipped with honorable principles and actions beyond belief; in short, to embrace it all at once, he is greater than any praise, etc.

### From the Second Commentary of Filippo Beroaldo on Propertius, regarding the verse "Not with so many Achaemenians." <note>original: "Non tot Achemeniis". Filippo Beroaldo (1453–1505) was a famous Italian humanist and editor of classical texts.</note>

I read "SUSA" written in place of "ethrusea" in the manuscript of Giovanni Pico of Mirandola. He is a man worthy of the memory of ages, endowed with many disciplines. He adorns the glory of our age, to whom that which Terentianus wrote about Varro can be applied: "*Pico is a most learned man from every side.*" <note>original: "Vir doctissimus undecunq; Picus"</note> He not only esteems you, my Micius <note>A term of endearment for his correspondent.</note>—as the most learned man esteems a scholar, and the most noble a nobleman—but he loves you vehemently; he speaks of you honorably and thinks the best of you. After his more serious studies, he is accustomed to rest in the reading of Propertius as if in a most pleasant lodging-house. He agreed with me as I was reading this passage and showed me that in his own manuscript, "Susa" was written, not "ethrusea," etc.

### From the book of Johannes, Abbot of Sponheim. <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German Benedictine abbot and polymath known for his work on cryptography and history.</note>

GIOVANNI Pico, an Italian by nation, Count of Mirandola and Lord of Concordia: a man most studious of all good literature, and just as he is noble by distinguished blood, so he is most noble by a truly divine genius. Surrounded by a great crowd of every kind of art within his household, he is worthy and most well-deserving; the Muses follow his progress. He is the most learned <term>philosopher</term> <note>original: "philosophus"</note> of our age and a most sharp debater. He has written several works in a most elegant style, which our age will both approve of and greatly admire, through which he has rendered the memory of his name and glory everlasting, and not unworthily.

### From the preface of the "Book of Recoveries" by Matteo Bossi.

WITH that same Poliziano, the distinguished and most famous Giovanni of Mirandola read—not unwillingly—once and many times even to the very end. All are amazed at his genius, which is beyond human capacity, and his multi-faceted learning. From his integrity and the brightness of his soul, all hallucination and fawning confession are absent.

### From a letter of Jacopo Antiquario to Angelo Poliziano.

DO NOT, therefore, make us waste away in expectation with the brooding of a long incubation, but rather—having accepted Pico as a guarantor for the security of your name, whose whole life is full of glories—I desire with all my prayers that I may be received by him into the flock of your friends on your behalf. I always adore his footsteps. Whatever you send out from your mistress-like flock of fattened birds <note>A metaphorical reference to Poliziano’s refined literary works; "altilium" refers to specially fed or "fattened" fowl, suggesting high quality.</note> to be looked at, read, and learned by heart, you will hold all those in your strings <note>likely referring to the strings of a lyre, meaning his audience.</note> who are led by some image of virtue or harmony.

### From the "Compendium of Revelations" by Brother Girolamo Savonarola. <note>Savonarola was a famous Dominican friar and reformer in Florence who was a close associate of Pico in his final years.</note>

COUNT Giovanni of Mirandola, a man singular in our times for his genius and manifold learning.

# PREFACE TO THE WORK OF DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY
## PREFACE BY GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA, TO THE DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS.

<margin>Homer, Caecilius</margin>
**H**omer and Caecilius, <note>Caecilius Statius (c. 220–166 BC) was a Roman comic poet; only fragments of his work remain.</note> the most ancient bards, proclaim that the worst and most dangerous enemies are those who surround us under the appearance of friends. No truer sentiment could be uttered, nor any more beneficial advice given. Although why should we need the testimony of poets when Divine Truth itself—the mistress of our life and conduct—has warned us to avoid wolves in sheep's clothing <note>A reference to Matthew 7:15.</note> and not to judge by appearances? Indeed, this is the one kind of enemy that can neither be turned away nor overturned; one that we ourselves do not wish to overcome, but instead we run toward, embrace of our own accord, and welcome. We stand with it against ourselves, rather than standing against it as we ought. Certainly, this deception <note>original: "præstīgiū". In this context, Pico uses it to mean a "magical trick" or "illusion."</note> comes at a great cost. It must be looked into more deeply and examined more longly; it should neither be admitted rashly nor driven away instantly. But once the fallacy is detected, it must be exploded all the more fiercely the more secretly it was creeping toward our ruin under the pretext of beneficence. Nor should those evils be thought any less because they do not seem at first to be the worst; since they are mixed with good things, they harm more fatally. For through the appearance and mixture of good, they are more easily admitted, and once admitted, they hold on more tenaciously and retain their grip more powerfully than what they first persuaded us of. In the same way, if poison is served with pure wine—even though the wine is by its nature most healthy—the vigor of the wine drives the malice of that poison, now disguised by its flavor, more deeply and swiftly into the veins. This must also be observed in every way of life, but especially in the arts and disciplines: those are most ruinous which, while being illusions or vanities of some other kind, nevertheless hold out some allure of falsehood, so that they claim for themselves the name of "science" or "art." Whether that allure is sought from the authority of antiquity and fictitious authors, or is an enticement to human curiosity and greed through great promises. Or whether it comes from some smear and appearance of probability—since, as Aristotle testifies, <margin>Aristotle</margin> false things are sometimes more probable than the truth, <note>A reference to Aristotle's *Rhetoric* or *Poetics*, discussing how a "convincing impossibility" is better than an "unconvincing possibility."</note> especially to the common people and the multitude, whose lot it has always been to err and be deceived, and to know nothing. What is more fatal? What is more impregnable? Than when error insinuates itself into us under the title of wisdom, so that we give our labor to what that man said: "to go mad with reason." <note>original: "cum rōne īsaniamus". A reference to Terence's play *The Eunuch*, meaning to try to handle an irrational thing (like love or, here, astrology) with logic.</note> This is nothing other than to dismiss the counsel and the mind—whose power alone was born in us to drive away falsehood—so that the lie itself emerges more honorable by its testimony, more robust by its authority, and better fortified by its protection. Furthermore, there is no hope beyond for health when nature itself aids the disease. This, as I was saying a moment ago, happens through the madness which hawks and sells itself to the people under the guise of either art or science; it is no less insane because it feigns wisdom on its surface, but the more deceptive it is, the more destructive. Just as among physicians, none are more delirious (if I may say so) than those who maintain a serious face during their delirium. But this is the characteristic stain of all superstitions, whose only profession is to hand down the rules for going mad. Yet, above all, astrology has claimed this <margin>Resolution of sayings</margin> title for itself; just as among superstitions themselves, it is deservedly considered the mother and the queen, and it holds the leadership. But when I say "Astrology," I do not mean that <margin>Distinction of Astrology</margin> which measures the sizes and movements of the stars by mathematical reason—a certain and noble art, most honorable in its own merits, and greatly approved by the authority of the most learned men. <note>Pico is distinguishing between Astronomy (which he respects) and Divinatory Astrology (which he attacks).</note> But I mean that which announces future events from the stars by the fraud of mercenary lying—an art forbidden by both civil and pontifical laws, retained by human curiosity, mocked by philosophers, cultivated by charlatans, and suspected by every excellent and most prudent man. In the past, its professors were called "Chaldaeans" <margin>Its professors</margin> by their ethnic name, or "Genethliaci" <note>original: "genethliaci". From the Greek *genethlios* (birthday); those who cast birth charts or horoscopes.</note> from the profession itself; soon, so that they might ennoble themselves by a shared name, they called themselves "mathematicians" and "astrologers," as if this too were one of the liberal disciplines...

<summary>In this preface, Pico della Mirandola begins his famous critique of divinatory astrology, distinguishing it from the legitimate science of astronomy. He warns that astrology is a dangerous "madness" that deceives the public by masquerading as a noble, ancient science.</summary>
<keywords>astrology vs astronomy, superstition, Chaldaeans, Genethliaci, logic and madness, deceptive arts, Aristotle, Homer, Caecilius Statius</keywords>

# PREFACE

...it <note>This likely completes a verb like "discusses" or "relates" from the previous page.</note> would discuss those things regarding the stars with reason: yet separating itself from that true mathematics by this distinction: that they give the name **astronomy** to the former, and **astrology** to the latter. This was done out of an excessively wicked zeal for an unearned title. Indeed, "astrology" is the name of another art <note>Pico argues that the word "astrology" (the study of stars) should technically refer to the same thing as astronomy, but has been hijacked by fortune-tellers.</note>, as we shall declare; yet that divinatory art, always struggling with this ambition to be named after the stars, we shall deign to call by both names, but in no other way than this: following the lead of those who treat the motion of the stars, we shall appropriately call **astrology** "astrology" and **astronomy** "astronomy" according to their merits. 

Regarding this matter, however the name is decided, I—relying on reason and the judgments of the wisest men—would not hesitate to affirm that among the deceptive arts <note>original: "artes præstīgiōsas". These are arts based on illusion or sleight of hand.</note>, there is none that more greatly deceives the gullible and the unskilled, nor any which, by deceiving those it has persuaded, does more harm. It is all the more fatal compared to other superstitions the closer it seems to approach the truth. For while other superstitions display signs of their madness and levity on the very surface and hardly trick anyone except the completely blind, this one—nurturing its insanity in its very heart and bosom—puts on the appearance and habit of wisdom. If you look at it from a distance or through a lattice-window, you might be captured by its form; but if you move closer with a searching eye, you will see only a shadow or a sort of ghost <note>original: "laruam". A mask or a specter.</note>; and in the open light, you will loathe its fallacy and darkness. 

So it is certainly; and thus through the most manifest reasons it shall become clearer than light that there is no greater fallacy, no more ruinous one. From afar, it displays the heaven and the planets, whence you might easily believe that in such a sublime and shining spectacle, nothing could fail to be most truly foreseen. But soon, when you consider it more attentively, you see that the mirror is so high that the images of earthly things do not ascend to it; and it is so bright that the weakness of the eye grows dim at its splendor. Then, when you have come closer, you will see woven 

<margin>
Regarding this matter, before all others, Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus (c. 64 BC – AD 17), a Roman author whose "De Astronomica" linked the constellations to Greek myths.</note> shows the signs of the Greeks in fables.
</margin>

into its robe <note>original: "peplo". This refers to the embroidered robe of Athena, used here as a metaphor for the constellations draped over the sky.</note> monstrous images instead of heavenly ones, and stars transformed into animals, and a heaven full of fables—nay, instead of the true heaven, a fabricated one, a heaven not made by God but feigned by astrologers. Thus, it seems equipped with every foundation of proven dogma, while simultaneously carrying about books entitled with great names, and so many reasons for its decrees, and—beyond reason—experiments corroborated by such long-lasting observations and such diligent annotations; then, received by the usage of so many centuries and the approval of so many ages. 

It is a marvel how, through these glooms and mists, it represents to eyes struck by ignorance a beautiful, venerable image full of serious authority. But once you have dispelled these shadows and illusions with the ray of reason and diligent treatment, you will see that in those books there is nothing balanced <note>Pico uses a play on words here: "in illis libris nihil esse libratum."</note>; in the authors, no authority; in the reasons, nothing rational; in the experiments, nothing consistent, nothing constant, nothing true, nothing credible, nothing solid—but only things fighting amongst themselves: false, vain, and ridiculous. You would hardly believe that those who wrote them had any faith in what they were writing. 

Indeed, regarding vanity, you would not easily find anything that proposes more hope to its wind-bags <note>original: "aurariis". Literally "goldsmiths" or those seeking gold, but here used metaphorically for those seeking empty riches or "puffing" up the art.</note>, or which promises greater or more desirable things. It makes itself the preserver of prudence, whose conjecture about the future it would stabilize with certain foreknowledge; and it even claims to be the preserver of philosophy, the greatest part of which—concerning the heavens, as they wish it—is supposedly explained clearly through heavenly influence. 

Regarding medicine, it is not even worth speaking; nor of navigation, nor of agriculture. For it not only foretells the future for these, but even draws down the powers of the heavens to earthly things; from which the works of all arts might be most effectively achieved, and the masters of all arts might easily attain what they wish. And it has persuaded not only the ancients, but even the moderns <note>original: "neotericis".</note> that it—if it please the gods—contributes a great deal of authority and benefit to religion, both universal and Christian. To put it simply, imitating its master [the Devil], it promises the kingdoms of the world to those who worship it, and to those who taste of its tree <note>original: "suum lignum". A reference to the Tree of Knowledge in Eden.</note>, it promises a likeness to divinity and the knowledge of good and evil. Not only does it promise these things as conveniences for use in life...

<summary>Pico criticizes the deceptive nature of astrology, arguing it hijacks the terminology of astronomy to present fables and superstitions as scientific truth. He asserts that while it promises divine knowledge and earthly success, a rational examination reveals it to be inconsistent, unfounded, and spiritually dangerous.</summary>

# PREFACE TO THE DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

...be convenient for use: but it is the most pestilential fraud of all: since it is that very thing—as we shall demonstrate—which corrupts all philosophy, adulterates medicine, weakens religion, gives birth to or strengthens superstitions, fosters idolatry, takes away prudence, pollutes morals, slanders heaven, and makes men wretched, anxious, restless, and slaves instead of free; it makes them plainly unfortunate in almost all their affairs. When I seemed to have this explored and discovered for myself, I thought I would be committing a crime <note>original: "piaculum", a religious transgression requiring a sacrifice for atonement</note> that no sacrifice could expiate, if I remained silent, if I feigned ignorance, and did not attempt, according to my strength, to wrench this poison completely from the hands of the gullible, especially in this age when, if ever, every age, rank, and sex is blinded by this fraud. Yet one must fight all the more for the truth the more opponents it is known to have: since we desire to benefit everyone, yet to please only the good; nor does the judgment of the multitude have weight where reason and the consensus of the learned stand against it; nor do we look for the popular breeze, but for the light of truth and public utility. ->The Preface ends.<-

->Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola to the Most Holy Father Oliviero Carafa,<-
->Bishop of Sabina and Cardinal of Naples. Greetings.<-

**W**e read, most distinguished Prelate, that while Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century philosopher and traveler whose biography by Philostratus was popular in the Renaissance.</note> was about to undertake that pilgrimage later made famous by Philostratus for the sake of acquiring learning, he wished that he might both find and recognize good men; and he also entreated the Sun with many prayers that this would be granted to him. This vow certainly cannot be greatly praised without fault, just as the prayer to the sun itself cannot escape blame <note>Gianfrancesco Pico, writing as a Christian humanist, acknowledges Apollonius's search for virtue but critiques his pagan worship.</note>. For the unlearned and rude common people, by the innate light of knowing the truth, proclaim this everywhere—to omit the most powerful reasons and the testimonies of divine eloquence. But if that gift is to be wished for and even demanded from God the Best and Greatest <note>term: "Optimo Maximo" – a title originally for Jupiter, here reclaimed for the Christian God.</note>, then those must undoubtedly rejoice exceedingly who have not only happened to recognize good men, but to have discovered rather than "found" those very men within their own family and bound to them by the bond of blood, and thence to follow some of those fruits which the friendship of good men produces. 

I neither deny nor hide that this divine beneficence has happened to me, since I discovered within my own domestic walls Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the brother of my father Galeotto—a man indeed worthy of being eagerly searched for by Apollonius beyond the Caucasus and the Brahmans <note>referring to Apollonius’s legendary travels to India in search of wisdom.</note>, and even to the opposite side of the world—and I have emerged enriched by many benefits from him. While I had judged that I should return like for like to him while he lived, as far as I was able, I decided after his death that the duties undertaken ought to be repaid all the more, because his glory and the utility of studies were at risk, and the Church was suffering no small loss. For this reason, I have committed several things on his behalf to writing, and through his long-lasting work and anxious investigation, I have taken care to pour them into many copies to be spread abroad. 

But I have labored most greatly in repairing the books that utterly overthrow all divinatory astrology; for they were sketched in such characters <note>i.e., handwriting or shorthand symbols.</note>—which was the man’s habit due to the speed of writing and dictating—that they seemed to present the appearance of any language other than Latin. They were so smeared with many crossings-out that it was not easy to discern what should be considered deleted and what corrected; they were, moreover, mangled and torn in so many parts that it was judged they could scarcely be transcribed by the author himself. As I reflected for a long time on whom I should destine and dedicate these books (if they are not treasures rather than books), now revived and recently recalled from destruction by us, you occurred to me, most holy prelate, from whom I could in no way turn aside. For to whom...

# PREFACE TO THE DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY
<sig>ii</sig>

...could I dedicate the literary monuments of this most learned man and kinsman more appropriately or honorably than to you? This is especially true of these writings, which refute errors opposed to our Christian religion. You are a man of great learning, and through Giovanni Tommaso Carafa, Count of Maddaloni—my father-in-law, to whom you are bound by the closest kinship—you are also connected to me by necessity. Furthermore, among the people of this same religion, you hold a position that is second only to the Supreme Pontiff. Receive these works, then, with a willing heart. I pray that when you steal a bit of leisure from your most important affairs, you will read them through. In the reading itself, you will both learn and rejoice that the art of astrology—or to speak more correctly, that plague—is being extinguished. This pestilence, which has recently been emboldened by a savage madness and masks its poison behind a deceitful facade to rage against our destruction, has been most powerfully defeated by the efforts of my uncle, Giovanni Pico.

->Farewell, most distinguished Father. Mirandola, June 28.<- <note>original: "iiii. Kal. Iulias," the fourth day before the Kalends of July.</note>

---

->Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola to the lovers of truth.<-

<margin>A</margin>**Rejoice**, lovers of truth, and let your spirits be lifted, you who toil with the desire to illuminate and expand it! Behold, the *Disputations* of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola against the astrologers are now coming forth into public view. These are the works of that great Pico whose sublimity of mind and all-encompassing learning have already left nearly the whole world in awe. I say these *Disputations* will compel the haters and attackers of truth to grieve; they will force those who devote their labor to astrological vanity for the sake of swindling money <note>Gianfrancesco highlights the financial exploitation common in Renaissance astrology.</note> to either wail and be torn asunder, or to abandon their error. Nor should it diminish your solid joy that he, called to God by a death that was premature for us though timely for him, neither scrubbed and polished these books with a final filing, nor brought the final epilogue (intended to conclude the whole work) from the anvil <note>original: "ab incude," a metaphor meaning the work did not receive its final finishing touches.</note>. Perhaps that is lacking for the more exuberant decoration of the work, but not for the perfect benefit of the readers.

In other times, this tree of vanity and all superstitions has been blasted and detested by the oracles of the prophets; it has been stripped of its leaves and hissed at by our theologians and philosophers—Greek, Latin, and Barbarian alike—and even struck, at least in part, by axes. Likewise, it has been uprooted and cast out by imperial laws and papal sanctions. Yet, by human curiosity, it has often been brought back and replanted in its original pit, propped up and strengthened. Thus, it was never entirely eliminated or brought to utter destruction by the strongest instruments of reason—until now. Our Pico has cast out this ill-omened tree and reduced it entirely to ash by the scorching fire of true philosophy and true theology, and by the unique discoveries and meditations of his incomparable genius. He has destroyed it from root to trunk, trunk to branches, and branches to leaves. He has scattered the remains with such a rapid blast of eloquence that any supporter or promoter of that art (unless they be of a disturbed mind) must either cry out in grief over its demise or exult in joy at the casting away of such despised vanity. 

Come then, literate men of all nations, arm your minds with these reasons! Support yourselves with these testimonies, both human and divine. Use them like the heaviest of double-edged axes and flaming torches to strike down, crush, tear up, and exterminate any sprouts of this extinguished tree that might, by the fault of a poorly cultivated field, happen to sprout again from deep within the bowels of the earth.

## TABLE OF DISPUTATIONS

### THE SUMMARY TABLE COLLECTED HERE BEGINS, SHOWING WHAT IS CONTAINED IN EACH OF THESE TWELVE VOLUMES.

<margin>Homer</margin>
**F**irst, the preface: likewise, how astrology has been condemned by philosophy, by the prophets, by the emperors, and by the popes; and what sort of men they were who wrote on astrology.

<margin>But not only:</margin>
Second, the uselessness and falsity of the profession in general: the ignorance and negligence of the practitioners of our time; also, why they occasionally speak the truth when the profession itself is false.

<margin>We have solved:</margin>
Third, the arguments approving the truth of astrology are brought forward; afterwards, they are dissolved and turned back against them.

<margin>Our man here.</margin>
Fourth, that the things astrologers believe are not caused by the heavens; likewise, that things not caused by the heavens are not signified by them; and that "interrogations" <note>The practice of asking specific questions to a chart for immediate answers.</note> are empty.

<margin>But many:</margin>
Fifth, "great orbits," "Saturnian revolutions," and "great conjunctions" <note>Significant celestial alignments believed to signal historical shifts or disasters.</note> are eliminated.

<margin>We have departed:</margin>
Sixth, the destruction of houses, signs, aspects, <term>obsessions</term> <note>Planetary positions that "block" others.</note>, and combustions; retrogradations; the head and tail of the dragon <note>The lunar nodes where eclipses occur.</note>; <term>antiscia</term> <note>Symmetrical points in the zodiac across the solstice axis.</note>; precipitating and obedient signs; <term>exaltations</term> <note>Specific degrees where a planet is thought to be most powerful.</note>; <term>triplicities</term> <note>Groups of three signs sharing an element like fire or water.</note>; faces; terms; <term>dodecathemoria</term> <note>The division of each zodiac sign into twelve sub-parts.</note>; novenae; <term>monomiriæ</term> <note>Properties assigned to single degrees of the zodiac.</note>; the properties of degrees; "parts"; and <term>climacteric years</term> <note>Critical turning points in a person's life, often every seven or nine years.</note>.

<margin>Thus far:</margin>
Seventh, it is contained that the beginnings of fate—whether particular or universal, and whether of a man or any other thing—are not well grasped; likewise, that the time when something is to happen is erroneously defined by "directions" <note>A mathematical method used to predict the timing of life events.</note> or by any other way; and the manifold error regarding the fixed stars.

<margin>Among all</margin>
Eighth, that the number of the spheres is uncertain; and whatever is established is the certain error of the astrologers. Likewise regarding errors over the difference between images and signs; also concerning invisible images.

<margin>Demonstrated</margin>
Ninth, it contains the uncertainty of the hour of birth and other beginnings, and concerning the errors in the division of houses, signs, places, and planets; the motion of the eighth sphere and of directions.

<margin>Already for many</margin>
Tenth, the arguments of the astrologers by which they strive to strengthen their dogmas; to which categories they are reduced; all these are shown to be ineffective and utterly ridiculous.

<margin>If the nature</margin>
Eleventh, that knowledge cannot be obtained through experience; or if any experience could be gathered, it has not yet been obtained.

<margin>If by fables</margin>
Twelfth, that no revelation has been received; likewise where astrology was born, increased, nourished, and in what way it was propagated.

**The first book** is not divided into several chapters, but in a single chapter, it casts down astrology by the authority of philosophers, prophets, emperors, and popes.

**In the second book** are contained the uselessness and falsity of the profession, and the ignorance and negligence of its practitioners.
**Chapter 1:** That this art is uncertain even by the judgment of its own founders.
**Chapter 2:** That the "auspices," which they call "elections," <note>Choosing an auspicious time to start an endeavor.</note> are useless by the testimony of a single astrologer, by reason, and by experience.
**Chapter 3:** That astrology is not useful in deciding what should be done or what should be avoided.
**Chapter 4:** That astrology is not useful to religion, as **Roger Bacon** and **Pierre d’Ailly** <note>Two medieval scholars who famously attempted to use astrology to explain religious history.</note> believed.
**Chapter 5:** How harmful and how pestilential astrology is to the Christian religion.
**Chapter 6:** That this art is deceptive; if anything happens, it is due either to many other causes or because of the differing opinions among astrologers.
**Chapter 7:** On the ignorance of the astrologers of our age.
**Chapter 8:** On the negligence of the astrologers of our age, which is so great that even if—

### The third book contains the arguments favoring the astrologers, which are then refuted.

**Chapter 1.** What was handled in the preceding book, what must be done next, and in what order.
**Chapter 2.** Whatever reasons by which astrology seems to be strengthened.
**Chapter 3.** The first reason is turned back against them, and it is shown that the heaven is a universal cause and that the variety of individuals is not to be attributed to it.
**Chapter 4.** How the heaven acts through motion and light, and how it is the universal cause of meteorological elements, minerals, and living things.
**Chapter 5.** That besides the common influence of motion and light, there is no power peculiar to the celestial bodies.
**Chapter 6.** That the light of the moon, just like that of the sun, is vital; and that neither causes cold or moisture except by accident <note>original: "per accidens"; referring to indirect effects rather than an inherent quality of the light itself.</note>.
**Chapter 7.** That the dogmas of the astrologers cannot be defended—as <term>Avenazra</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar whose astrological works were widely cited in the Middle Ages.</note> thought—if all stars are assumed to be hot.
**Chapter 8.** An objection against those things which have been said.
**Chapter 9.** The objection is resolved, and it is shown that neither the specific nor the individual differences of things depend on the motion of the heaven.
**Chapter 10.** That the stars other than the sun and the moon either do nothing to us, or certainly very little.
**Chapter 11.** In what way the same stars can act on us differently at different times.
**Chapter 12.** What variety of effects can be traced back to the heaven and what cannot.
**Chapter 13.** That the sun performs many things which astrologers believe are done by other stars.
**Chapter 14.** How the power of the moon varies, and that certain days of the moon are observed without superstition.
**Chapter 15.** That the tides of the sea can be attributed to another cause than the moon; and even if they are attributed to it, astrology is not helped by it.
**Chapter 16.** The opinion of <term>Galen</term> <note>Claudius Galenus, the foundational Roman physician whose medical theories dominated for over a millennium.</note> concerning "critical days" <note>Days in the course of a disease when a change was expected, often linked by ancients to lunar cycles.</note>, referring them to the moon, is refuted.
**Chapter 17.** That the periods of the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health and temperament.</note> are not to be referred to the motions of the stars.
**Chapter 18.** That the misfortune of an eight-month birth is not to be ascribed to <term>Saturn</term> <note>A common ancient belief held that babies born in the eighth month of pregnancy were unlikely to survive, a "malice" often blamed on the influence of the planet Saturn.</note>.
**Chapter 19.** Why sailors, doctors, and farmers predict the truth more often than astrologers.
**Chapter 20.** That not everything predicted by astrologers depends on the primary qualities <note>The basic building blocks of the physical world: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>.
**Chapter 21.** That neither the harms of the elements nor the injuries to our bodies come from the heaven.
**Chapter 22.** That the variety of human talents and character does not depend entirely on the primary qualities.
**Chapter 23.** That neither wars nor external events depend on the primary qualities.
**Chapter 24.** That hidden powers are not present in the celestial bodies through which they produce the hidden properties of lower things, but only heat and life-giving light.
**Chapter 25.** If a specific and proper power is granted to each star, it is nonetheless a universal one.
**Chapter 26.** The epilogue of this book, with the rejection of certain arguments used by the astrologer when arguing against these points.

**Chapter 2.** That chance events are not caused by the heaven.
**Chapter 3.** How God is the cause of chance things; how the angels are; how the heaven is; how we are; and how fortune is.
**Chapter 4.** That it is not to be referred to the heaven if anything is done by us that seems to exceed our powers.

**Chapter 17.** Concerning "feminine," "bright," and "dark" degrees, and other things of that kind: that Ptolemy disregarded them, nor do other astrologers agree on them.
**Chapter 18.** From where the <term>Parts</term> <note>Calculated mathematical points in a chart, such as the "Part of Fortune."</note> originated, and how much the astrologers fight with one another in measuring them.
**Chapter 19.** The theory of the <term>twelfth-parts</term> <note>The division of each zodiac sign into twelve smaller parts (Dodecatemoria).</note> is exploded, and their Egyptian authors are rejected along with their <term>climacteric years</term> <note>Critical or dangerous years in a person's life, often multiples of 7 or 9.</note>.

**The Seventh Book** contains a discussion of the initial hour, directions, and the fixed stars.
**Chapter 1.** What has been discussed so far, and what is to be discussed in this book.
**Chapter 2.** That the "fatal hour" is ambiguous, if such a thing exists in all matters that are not completed in a moment but over a long time; and in humans especially, among whom the <term>nativity</term> <note>The birth chart or moment of birth.</note> seems to have little strength.
**Chapter 3.** That Ptolemy attributed more to conception than to the birth; yet Ptolemy's own reasoning proves that nothing should be attributed even to that.
**Chapter 4.** By what methods astrologers track "universal events," and how little they are based on reason.
**Chapter 5.** That an astrologer cannot predict in which region of the world a certain fate will occur, since they themselves are uncertain which region is subject to which sign or planet.
