DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY. BOOK FIRST.

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA, AGAINST ASTROLOGY BEGIN. BOOK FIRST.

---

**F**irst of all, I want the reader to know: it was not by our own bold invention that we decided to reject and refute astrology. Rather, from the earliest antiquity, it has always seemed to the judgment of good men that this was not a legitimate profession, but one that introduced so many inconveniences and so many insanities to mankind everywhere under the pretext of science and utility. Hence, by the laws of Emperors <note>original: "Caesarum," referring to Roman imperial law which often banned "mathematicians" or "Chaldeans" (astrologers) from cities for fear of political unrest.</note> and the wise, it was banished from cities as harmful to civil life. Hence, by the oracles of the prophets, the decrees of popes, and the voices and teachings of the holiest men, it is condemned as a pestilence to morals and piety. Hence, by philosophers and mathematicians—those who have learned to think from books and not just talk—it is either generally despised or refuted as false, useless, impossible, and unfriendly to philosophy. Before I address the matter with logic, I will declare this in this book: that after such accusers, this accusation of ours might not be seen as a work of malice, but rather as a defense that people of good character can uphold without shame.

<margin>Testimonies of philosophers</margin> We shall begin with the philosophers, whose authority is greater than that of the prudent, and whose way is usually more common than that of the prophets. <margin>Theodoretus</margin> That Pythagoras did not grant his trust to astrology is shown by <margin>Laertius</margin> Theodoretus, <margin>Diogenes</margin> as well as Diogenes Laertius and <margin>Plutarch</margin> Plutarch. <margin>A saying of Democritus</margin> Here is the saying of Democritus regarding the one who gazes at and scrutinizes the regions of the sky while ignoring what is at his feet. <margin>Favorinus</margin> Favorinus the <term>Academic</term> <note>A follower of the skeptical school of philosophy founded by Plato's successors.</note> and <margin>Panaetius</margin> Panaetius the <term>Stoic</term> <note>A member of the school of philosophy that emphasized logic and ethics; Panaetius was notable for being one of the few Stoics to reject astrology.</note> attacked it; <margin>Seneca</margin> Seneca laughed at it and <margin>Cicero</margin> Cicero refuted it. But who is ignorant of Carneades' dispute against it, or the philosopher Bion, who was hostile to diviners? If astrology contains so much insanity that even the "mad" Orestes <note>A figure from Greek mythology driven to madness by the Furies; Pico uses him as a benchmark for extreme irrationality.</note> would not approach it, then certainly Epicurus could not agree with its many ravings. Plato and Aristotle, the princes of philosophy, thought it so unworthy that they never spoke a word of it in their entire philosophy, condemning it more by their silence than anyone else did with voices or writings.

For those who think otherwise, I ask them to answer: why, in the whole course of their commentaries—where they had to explain the properties of the heavens or seek the causes of lower things from above—did they never bring in anything astrological? Did they think these first and most noble parts of the universe—the moving bodies that move others, the most effective causes without which nothing in nature can happen or be known—did not concern a philosopher? If they believed these causes were such as the astrologers make them out to be, then to know only generalities about them (as their leaders write) while more specific things could be understood, is the mark not of a philosopher, but of an imperfect one. Why then did Aristotle leave his books *On the Heavens* so meager, where he could have said so many splendid things? If he could have, he should have told us about the stars and planets, indicating their effects and properties. Why, in his books on *Meteorology*, when scrutinizing the causes of comets and winds, does he always forget astrological matters? Why, in his books *On the Generation of Animals*, does he never mention—even in passing—that twins, or monstrous and portended births, or the number and sex of offspring, or their form and qualities, should or could be referred to the stars? Why do Plato and his <margin>Plato</margin> *Timaeus* do the same? Why even before Plato did Timaeus the Pythagorean himself, in his book *On Nature* (a man who was, as Plato says, a supreme philosopher and astronomer), or Ocellus Lucanus in his book *On the World* (also a most eminent man in philosophy by Plato's own testimony), do the same? Did they despise these things as small? If they were true, nothing could be greater. Or did they not despise them, but were simply ignorant of them—having lived in Egypt and Babylon and yet been unable to understand these things that were chanted among those peoples and known even to the common man? Certainly, they did not think it was outside their profession (as we have said) unless they were ignorant of their own profession; for it would be a strange philosopher who believed his duty was to seek the minute properties of bees and ants, but not those of Jupiter and Saturn—especially if the truth about them is shown not only by observation but by reason.

<summary>This page serves as the introduction to Pico's critique, arguing that astrology has been historically rejected by the greatest emperors, prophets, and philosophers. He specifically points out that intellectual giants like Aristotle and Plato intentionally ignored astrology in their scientific works, suggesting they viewed it as a baseless superstition rather than a serious field of study.</summary>

<header>DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.</header>

...which astrological writers especially contend. What then else can be said, except that Plato and Aristotle held the opinion that the celestial bodies are not the causes of those things which the astrologers claim? Nor is astrology an art or a science; had it been so, they would have mentioned it alongside others. Instead, it is one of the diversions—or rather, the frauds—of itinerant charlatans <term>circulatorum</term> <note>Literally "those who form a circle"; refers to street performers or quacks who gathered crowds to sell remedies or tell fortunes.</note>. It belongs to the same class as geomancy <note>divination by patterns in earth or soil</note>, hydromancy <note>divination by water</note>, sleight of hand, and incantations; none of the ancient philosophers counted these among the sciences and arts. For if astrology were an art, it would depend on natural science, just as medicine does. For just as a physician borrows the knowledge of the nature of shrubs, herbs, and animals from the [natural] philosopher to use in restoring health to bodies, so should the astrologer learn the powers and properties of the stars from the philosopher, which he might then use and teach others to use for the purpose of predicting. 

As for those who think that divinatory astrology is a part or a goal of mathematical astronomy, and that it has more in common with it than with natural philosophy—

<margin>What the natural philosopher, the astronomer, and the astrologer can achieve regarding the stars.</margin>
—we shall later declare how far they are deceived. For now, we only advise that it is an established fact among the learned, beyond controversy, that it pertains to the philosopher to know whatever concerns the substance and order of the stars. The measuring of their movements and masses is delegated to the astronomer, while the foreseeing of the future from their condition and positioning is left to the astrologer. If one were to concede that the astrologer is indeed a craftsman, then the silence of Plato and Aristotle would be utterly drowsy and inexcusable, as they failed to even mention matters that they should have treated with the utmost exactness. 

One may marvel at this silence both throughout the works of Plato, who dealt with a miscellaneous and universal range of doctrine, and especially in the *Problems* <note>A work attributed to Aristotle consisting of questions and answers on various scientific and everyday topics.</note> of Aristotle. In that book, though he proposes questions concerning mathematics and all arts and disciplines, and offers solutions from every kind of doctrine—even the most ancient—the word "astrological" is never heard to breathe a sound. The same is true in the *Eudemian Ethics* where he discusses good fortune. If we are not sufficiently moved by this judgment, let us hear the disciples of both philosophers, who testify to that opinion which their masters expressed to us through silence. 

<margin>Porphyry</margin>
Plotinus is held to be of almost the highest authority in the Platonic family. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> writes that after Plotinus had devoted diligent effort to astrology and had finally grasped the vanity of the art and the falsehood of its predictions, he revoked all credit from the astrologers. Consequently, in the book he dedicated to the subject—titled *On the Influence of the Stars* <note>original: "de stellaz effi- / -cientia"</note>—he resolutely mocked and refuted the dogmas of the astrologers. 

<margin>Maternus</margin>
Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century author who wrote a famous defense of astrology titled 'Mathesis'.</note> took this badly and told many lies regarding Plotinus’s death, claiming that fate took vengeance upon him. However, that this claim is utterly false is easily understood from Porphyry himself, the disciple of Plotinus, who plainly and faithfully describes both the nature of the disease from which he died, its cause, and why he departed from Rome. 

<margin>Origen</margin>
Origen "the Adamantine," <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian; "Adamantine" refers to his unbreakable endurance.</note> most eminent in the philosophical sect as in all disciplines, frequently and with many reasons mocked astrological vanity—unless perhaps superstitious men give his testimony less weight because he was also a Christian. But Eudoxus was not a Christian; he was a student of Plato, spent time in Egypt, and was considered the prince of astronomers in his time. 

<margin>Eudoxus</margin>
<margin>Alexander</margin>
Yet he left it in writing that nothing should be believed of the astrologers who predict the fates of men from their births. Alexander of Aphrodisias, the greatest authority in Aristotelian philosophy, in writing his book *On Fate* to the Emperors Severus I and his son Antoninus, both rejected the necessity of fate and remained silent regarding astrological matters—even though the mention of "fate" usually draws men into such topics. Perhaps his only purpose in laboring over that commentary was to use philosophical reason to correct the mind of Emperor Severus, who was leaning toward such superstition.

<margin>Averroes</margin>
Averroes <note>The Latin name for Ibn Rushd, a famous 12th-century Andalusian philosopher.</note>, a celebrated philosopher in that same family and a weighty judge of natural things, everywhere tears apart, condemns, and attacks astrology. In his *First Philosophy* <note>His commentary on Aristotle’s 'Metaphysics'.</note>, he calls the opinion of astrologers concerning the "celestial images"—which they think terrestrial figures and animals resemble—a "fabulous" <note>meaning "mythical" or "legendary"</note> story; yet if this idea is removed, the greatest part of astrological superstition collapses. Likewise, in explaining the *Canticles* <note>The 'Poem on Medicine' by Avicenna (Ibn Sina).</note> of Avicenna, he says in one place that these dogmas are contrary to philosophy, and in another that almost all the teachings of astrologers are false, and finally that the art itself is entirely vain and weak. Also, in his books against Al-Ghazali <note>Specifically 'The Incoherence of the Incoherence'.</note>, regarding the artificial images into which they claim the virtues of heaven...
-> ...derive themselves <-

He supports this by citing major thinkers like Plotinus, Eudoxus, Alexander of Aphrodisias, and Averroes, who either explicitly rejected or ignored astrology as a fraudulent practice.</summary>

<page-num>149</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE</header>

...which the astrologers think they can derive from the stars, [the philosopher] previously declared to be ineffective. <margin>Avicenna</margin> Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential thinkers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>, a great man in all disciplines, proved by many reasons in the last book of his *First Philosophy* <note>original: "primæ phīe" (primae philosophiae), referring to his Metaphysics.</note> that the future cannot be foreseen by astrologers. Therefore, no faith should be placed in their predictions. I pass over Henry of Hesse <note>A 14th-century German theologian who wrote against astrology.</note> and many other illustrious modern scholars in the University of Paris who devoted their efforts to pursuing this vanity; although the greatest part of philosophers have despised it rather than refuted it, just as they do other charlatan arts <term>circulatrices</term> <note>Arts practiced by itinerant performers or "quacks."</note>, old wives' tales, and the ravings of tricksters.

But this is worthy of notice: that the astronomers themselves have also rejected this profession. This could not have happened unless they were conscious of its corrupt falsehood, especially since those most practiced in the celestial motions would have gained so much in knowledge, glory, and profit if astrology were granted any faith or authority. But that man whom we recently cited, Eudoxus of Cnidus <margin>Eudoxus</margin>, was the greatest in mathematics, and Aristotle relied on his judgment in astronomical matters. Yet this most prudent legislator—for he wrote laws for his fellow citizens—and a distinguished physician under Philistion, and a philosopher under Plato, warned us and left it in writing that we should not believe astrologers. Thus, mathematical reason had demonstrated it to him, and his master Plato had persuaded him. According to <margin>Panaetius</margin> Panaetius, Cassander and Archelaus, though they excelled in astronomy, never used this kind of prediction. Hypsicles of Halicarnassus <margin>Hypsicles</margin>, though most learned in all mathematics, rejected this entire genus of divining through the stars.

Let us come to the moderns: Nicole Oresme <margin>Nicole Oresme</margin> <note>c. 1320–1382, a significant French philosopher and mathematician.</note>, both a most acute philosopher and a very skilled mathematician, attacked astrological superstition with indignation in a specific commentary, thinking nothing more fallacious, nothing more detestable, and nothing more poisonous to all ranks of people, but especially to princes. Giovanni Marliani <margin>Giovanni Marliani</margin> in our time was and was held to be the greatest in mathematics. He not only always abstained from these predictions, but had also begun to write about their falsehood in his final years; although he was long-lived, he was cut off by death before he could finish it. A man not at all given to boasting, he used to say he possessed the most certain demonstrations against the astrologers. Our friend Luchino, himself an excellent mathematician, and others close to him have reported this to me more than once. Paolo of Florence <margin>Paolo of Florence</margin> <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), the famous mathematician and cosmographer.</note>, most learned in medicine but especially in mathematics, in both Greek and Latin, whenever he was asked about that profession, always asserted it was uncertain and fallacious. Among other things, he offered an evident experiment regarding himself: although he had already completed eighty-five years of life, he had found no "vital" constellation in his own birth chart, which he had examined most diligently. I could bring forward many of those who are still living, both philosophers and astronomers, who feel the same. But I do not know if they wish to provoke the envy of those men who claim power over heaven and fate.

Furthermore, our Marsilio <margin>Marsilio</margin> <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence and Pico's close friend.</note> wrote against them, aptly following in the footsteps of Plotinus. In interpreting and explaining Plotinus, he greatly helped, increased, and illustrated the Platonic cause. If, while looking out for the health of men, he occasionally requests certain "aids" from the heaven for himself, he *wishes* that such a thing were possible rather than *believing* it. I can most faithfully testify to the mind of this man, with whom I am on familiar terms; I have had no one who exhorted me more often or more effectively to expose this fallacy. Whenever we joke together, there is no more abundant occasion for us to laugh than at the vanity of astrologers—especially if Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the renowned humanist poet and scholar.</note> intervenes, who is a wonderful mocker <note>original: "exibilator", literally one who hisses someone off a stage.</note> of all superstitions.

Perhaps the judgment of our Niccolò Leoniceno <margin>Niccolò Leoniceno</margin> <note>1428–1524, a famous physician and humanist.</note> on this matter should not be hidden. While he possesses a faithful grasp of mathematics, as he does all the liberal arts, he nevertheless judges this prophetic astrology so vain that he thinks even those who wrote about it—especially the more learned ones—did not believe the things they were writing. If you ask the reason why they wrote it, he responds that it was done partly out of greed and partly due to the ignorance of princes. For, he says, when those men who excelled in astronomy labored day and night in measuring the motions and bodies of the stars (which mathematics does), they received no payment for it from the princes, who cared nothing for how large a body a star had, or how swift its motion was through the space of heaven...

<summary>Pico lists numerous historical and contemporary scholars—including Avicenna, Nicole Oresme, and his own friend Marsilio Ficino—who rejected astrology. He argues that even great astronomers dismissed it, suggesting that those who did write about it were often motivated by the need for financial support from ignorant princes.</summary>

### DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS

<margin>
The cause for the invention of divination
</margin>
...they were considering. When they saw this—lest by scrutinizing the heavens they should remain destitute of earthly goods—they devised a clever deception to bind the minds of princes to themselves and make them lovers of their profession. They claimed that the fortunes of all, but especially of princes, depended on these stars: namely children, life, victories over the impious, and health. They claimed that because they had observed the long-term movements and natures of the stars, they had deep and explored knowledge of what good things were promised or what adversities were threatened for each person. Furthermore, they claimed to have remedies at hand by which they could repel foreseen evils and confirm the good ones. For if a "lucky hour" <term>fœlix hora</term> <note>This refers to "electional astrology," the practice of picking the best astrological moment to begin an undertaking.</note> were noted, images could be forged from a certain material more akin to those celestial natures. To these images, power drawn down from the stars by wonderful devices would make men most fortunate and powerful in those affairs; whatever they sought by touch or by wearing the image, they would easily attain. To gain more trust in all these things, they added that the more secret mysteries of this art had been divinely revealed to them—just as one reads in [Firmicus] Maternus <note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who later converted to Christianity.</note> that Petosiris and Aesculapius received many things from the most powerful divinity of Mercury <note>original: "mercurii numine." This refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical Egyptian sage to whom many occult works were attributed.</note>. Then indeed, illiterate and curious princes, most greedy for the things promised, were easily led to believe, to support the practitioners, and to incite these studies daily with more and more rewards. Our Leonicenus <note>Niccolò Leoniceno (1428–1524), a contemporary of Pico and a famous physician who criticized traditional authorities.</note> speaks and feels this seriously and not far from the truth regarding astrologers.

We must take special care, however, lest the astrologers creep into our trust by ascribing forged volumes to great authors—a practice they share with every superstition. Since the things they put forward cannot be confirmed by reason, whether they believe them true themselves or want others to believe them, they attribute books of such fables to the most famous and ancient men, and they hunt for credibility for their errors from these fictional authors. 

<margin>
Which books are falsely attributed to Aristotle, Plato, and Zoroaster
</margin>
Of this kind is the book *On the Properties of the Elements* <note>original: "Aristoteli pprietatibus elemētoꝝ" (Aristotelis proprietatibus elementorum). A medieval pseudo-Aristotelian work that mixed natural philosophy with astrology.</note> attributed to Aristotle, which deals with "great conjunctions" and secrets addressed to Alexander. Through no fault of that good philosopher and by no demerit of his, they attribute these to him; just as magicians circulate books of Plato *On the Cow* <note>original: "Platonis de uacca." The *Liber Vaccae* (Book of the Cow) was a notorious medieval grimoire of "experiments" and necromancy falsely attributed to Plato.</note>, and those they call the *Institutions*, which are stuffed with execrable dreams and fabrications and are no less alien to Plato than these medicines are far from Plato's integrity and wisdom. Thus, in the past, the heretics called Gnostics showed off books of Zoroaster to make their heresy venerable by his antiquity. Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist who famously argued that the Gnostic "Books of Zoroaster" were recent forgeries.</note> demonstrated with many arguments that these were new and invented, not by Zoroaster. Those who are unrefined in humane letters <note>original: "humaniorū lŕaꝝ" (humaniorum literarum), the classical education known today as the "humanities."</note>, though otherwise learned, can easily be deceived and circumvented by these lies. It is primarily through those letters that we immediately recognize the style and character of authors and distinguish forged works from legitimate ones. However, the fabrications of our astrologers and those superstitious arts currently in use are so far from any resemblance to the truth that they are obvious to anyone.

<margin>
Note: Roger Bacon
</margin>
For who could be led to believe that the *De vetula* <note>An influential 13th-century Latin poem, "On the Old Woman," which claimed to be Ovid’s autobiography but was actually an astrological-mathematical treatise.</note> is by Ovid? In it, wonders are pronounced regarding great conjunctions and the Christian law—so much so that Roger Bacon, a man greatly prone to astrology, uses the testimony of no writer more willingly. Unless perhaps he prefers Artephius <note>A legendary medieval author of alchemical and occult texts, often claimed to be over a thousand years old.</note>, who betrays countless other secrets. Such as that claim that by inspecting not a star, but urine <note>original: "lotio." Pico is mocking the leap from celestial observation to the "base" medical practice of uroscopy.</note>, a man's life, character, and condition—in short, everything—can be known beforehand. So too did he place great faith in the "Ethic Philosopher" <note>This likely refers to Aethicus Ister, the purported author of a bizarre early medieval Cosmography.</note>, whose book on *Cosmography* is said to have been translated by Jerome. The reading is so ridiculous that none could be more so, yet it is frequently cited by our Roger in his *Letter to Clement* <note>Referring to Bacon's *Opus Majus*, addressed to Pope Clement IV.</note>. He almost goes so far as to include a certain booklet composed by him titled *On the Errors of Students of Theology*. In that volume, the primary error he accuses our theologians of is that they confirm the mysteries of religion from Aristotle and other philosophers, rather than from the authors we just named: the Ethic philosopher, Artephius, Ovid in *De vetula*, and similar poets. The book is indeed ascribed to Albert [the Great], but most falsely, since he never mentioned these dreams in his theological writings. Rather, it seems it should rightly be referred to Bacon, whose other writings easily show he held that opinion, teeming with the testimonies and oracles of those authors...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology began as a fraudulent way for poor scholars to gain patronage from gullible princes, and he warns against "pseudo" texts falsely attributed to giants like Aristotle, Plato, and Ovid to gain legitimacy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the false authorities cited by astrologers. <page-num>150</page-num>

# BOOK ONE

...opinion. If they could believe these things, it is no wonder if they could also believe in astrology. Indeed, this superstitious class of men has so shamelessly cast off all restraint <note>original: "frontem perfricuerunt" – literally "rubbed their foreheads," a Latin idiom meaning to behave without shame or to lose one's modesty.</note> that they even circulate books on necromantic images under the title of "the relatives of Thomas" <note>This refers to apocryphal works falsely attributed to the family or school of St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>; thus it is less surprising that they forge certain books 

<margin>See the annotations</margin>

of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Tetrabiblos" became the foundational text for Western astrology.</note> concerning rings, or even attribute astrological books to Aristo which Ptolemy never wrote. With similar recklessness or ignorance, many refer to a certain short work by a man of York <note>original: "Eboracensis." Likely referring to a medieval English scholar whose work was misattributed.</note> and record it as being by Albert [Magnus]; they also cite books by Hippocrates on the prognosis of illnesses from the course of the stars—which I believe Hippocrates was ignorant of when he wrote his books of *Prognostics* which were explained by Galen and celebrated throughout all of Greece. Or, if he did know of them, he kept them as secrets to be communicated only to those who were pure and properly initiated. 

I pass over what Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindus." A 9th-century Arab philosopher known as the "Philosopher of the Arabs."</note> and others record concerning rains and [astrological] "interrogations" following Pythagorean and Aristotelian lines. They even speak of a book inscribed to Aristotle "on governments" <note>original: "de regiminibus." This likely refers to the "Secretum Secretorum," a widely circulated medieval forgery attributed to Aristotle.</note> regarding celestial matters in this way. I only wish they had not attributed such profane things to holy men, and had not made the divine Jerome the translator of a certain book on incantations. Although, if they have slandered the angels, they can easily do the same to men, since they say these delirious Ravings were handed down by the angel of Adam, others by the angel of Solomon, and others by the guardian angel of Tobit <note>Raphael</note>. But let us return to the astrologers, leaving aside the magicians, to whom a shared error has led us as if to neighboring territories. 

Aristotle showed what he thought of this kind of men in a single word when, in his *Problems*, he categorized the astrologer alongside the mime and the prestidigitator <note>A juggler or sleight-of-hand performer.</note>. But you will say: even if those great philosophers did not write such things, those who did write them were upright men, such as Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Albumasar," a famous Persian astrologer.</note>, Ptolemy, Haly Abenragel, Julius Firmicus, and countless other Latin, Greek, and "barbarian" <note>In this context, meaning non-Greek or non-Latin, specifically Arabic and Persian authors.</note> authors of astrology—men outstanding in both learning and genius. 

You have helpfully reminded me, sir, that I should not merely say that astrology was neglected by the philosophers, but that even if they had written about it, they either philosophized about nothing or philosophized badly. Therefore, let us leave behind—if the gods permit—Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle; and for your part, you may keep your Abu Ma'shars, Al-Qabisus <note>original: "Alchabitios."</note>, Ibn Ezras <note>original: "Auenazras."</note>, and Abenragels. How far they were from a philosophical spirit will be openly demonstrated when we show that they turn to the most fabulous things, assert what has no basis in reason, say contradictory things, and overturn their own positions. These habits are utterly alien to a philosopher, whose most specific duty is to believe nothing and affirm nothing that cannot be demonstrated by either evidence or reason. 

But come, let us say something here to establish that the authors of astrology philosophized either too little or poorly. 

<margin>What kind of man Ptolemy was in his writings</margin>

Furthermore, they will easily concede that Ptolemy is the prince of the others. For he is the most learned of the astrologers and, as far as mathematics is concerned, a man of the greatest genius. However, regarding the casting of nativities <note>original: "genethliacos." The practice of casting birth charts.</note>, he is, as they say, "the best of the worst." How he treated philosophical matters with his judgment, he sufficiently indicated both in the introductions to that great composition which they call the *Almagest* <term>Almagestum</term> <note>Ptolemy's 2nd-century mathematical and astronomical treatise.</note> and in his books on *Judicial Astrology* <term>apoteleſmato</term> <note>Referring to the "Tetrabiblos."</note>. 

<margin>Ptolemy’s opinion from Aristotle’s 6th book of Metaphysics</margin>

For beginning his mathematical books by dividing contemplative philosophy according to Aristotle’s opinion into three kinds—theological, natural, and mathematical—he then explained the reason for this division, saying that all things that exist consist of three things: matter, form, and motion. These can be separated from each other in thought, but not in reality. From these three, therefore, those three kinds of philosophy are derived: from motion, the theological; from matter, the physical; and from form, the mathematical. 

This is Ptolemy's opinion, in which any person with even a little learning would not doubt there are as many errors as there are words. For not all things consist of those three. 

<margin>Against Ptolemy</margin>

But even if, in saying "all things," he understands only natural things, around which philosophy itself—divided into those three kinds (physical, divine, and mathematical)—is occupied: yet nothing among natural things "consists" of motion, even though nothing is made or remains without motion. But let us grant him this turn of phrase. Aristotle himself, whom he approves, how will he grant him that the theological category arises from motion? Since even God himself, insofar as he is the author and cause of the first motion, is investigated not by the theologian but by the physicist. The rest of his points are either false or easily seen as the utterances of a man little skilled and knowledgeable in philosophy. Now truly, from the books on *Judicial Astrology* which they call...

<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic debunking of the leading authorities in astrology. Having previously discussed the general dishonesty of the craft, he now moves into specific scientific and historical errors made by figures such as Ptolemy, Albumasar, and Guido Bonatti.</meta>

<page-num>190</page-num>

<header>DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS</header>

<margin>Against the same [Ptolemy]</margin>
...more notable and more evident errors, as when he believes the **moon is more humid** <note>original: "lunam humidíorem"</note> because he thinks humid vapor ascends from the earth to it—since it is closer to the earth than the other stars—and for the same reason he believes **Saturn is dry** because it is further removed from these vapors. He also claims that Saturn is cold because it is far from the sun’s heat, and that **Jupiter is temperate** because it is positioned in the middle between icy Saturn and fiery Mars. These and many other things of this kind regarding the properties of the stars are matters that philosophers will **hiss at** rather than bother to refute. And although the Arab commentator <note>Averodan, or Ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos.</note>, blushing at his master’s error, tries to twist Ptolemy’s words into another meaning, Ptolemy does not allow himself to be defended or excused in this part; he asserts, affirms, and repeats these things so often that no doubt remains about his meaning. From this one example, learn about them all; and from the best of them, judge those who are worse.

Almost first after Ptolemy they rank **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), one of the most influential Persian astrologers in the Latin West.</note>; he was neither a philosopher nor a logician, and he was unskilled in mathematics. He was, in fact, a professor of the art of grammar;
<margin>See the errors of the astrologers and the time of Ptolemy</margin>
and from writing histories (as Averodan tells it), he turned to astrology. You may recognize how "truthful" he was in this profession by the fact that he thinks **Ptolemy the astrologer** was one of the **kings of Egypt** who succeeded Alexander the Great—even though more than five hundred years intervened between them! The Ptolemaic kings flourished for four hundred years before Christ, while Ptolemy the astrologer wrote under the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus. Behold this "wonderful king," this "seeker of the highest things" and "faithful observer," who, in a matter so obvious, showed such sleepiness or slowness of mind. We shall later declare how much he erred in astrological matters and how he insisted on such obvious and admitted lies as if they were truths.

Why should I mention **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and author of the astrological work "Mathesis."</note>, who hallucinates so much even in the basics of arithmetic? He writes about what **Mercury** decrees when it occupies the middle of the sky in a "nocturnal birth"—as if Mercury could ever be more than forty degrees (or thereabouts) away from the sun, or as if the sun at night were not always more than seventy degrees away from the midheaven <note>Pico is pointing out an astronomical impossibility: Mercury is always close to the sun and cannot be high in the sky (the midheaven) if the sun is deep below the horizon at night.</note>. I pass over many other things in which you will find him to be a man of much talk but little wisdom.

As for **Mallius** <note>Marcus Manilius, author of the 1st-century astronomical poem "Astronomica."</note>—good God!—if he weren't a poet, how we would mock him! He says those celestial images he imagines are sketched with only a few stars rather than being complete, for fear that if more fires were lit there, the world would catch fire and burn.

I will not descend to the more recent men, common and ignorant, to whom the whole profession has now devolved as if to its "rightful owners." Among them, **Bonatus** <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century, whom Dante placed in the Eighth Circle of Hell.</note> is of the highest authority. He is not merely ignorant of philosophy, but plainly rages and raves. Read his first book on *Judgments*, in which he writes a preface about his own work. I lie if you do not judge the man worthy of **hellebore** <note>A plant used in antiquity as a cure for madness; to say someone "needs hellebore" is to call them insane.</note>. In the parts where he raves less, he constructs certain arguments to prove astrology is true; I should not just call them false, but childish and ridiculous beyond words. The argument he thinks most effective is that the **Quadrivium** <term>Quadrivium: The four mathematical sciences of the medieval curriculum: Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy.</term> would be destroyed if astrology were removed. For he says it is one of the four mathematical arts. See how he does not even know what the very thing he professes is! For this **divinatory astrology** which we are refuting is as far from the mathematical science <note>i.e., true Astronomy.</note> as light is from darkness, or as truth is from a lie. And indeed, this divinatory art, which usurps the prediction of the future, cannot stand if the former and truer mathematical science is removed; but the reverse does not hold: if the divinatory art is removed, the mathematical one is not also taken away. This is so clear even to those who have touched the first elements of these arts that it would be superfluous to explain it further. Ptolemy himself, in the introduction to his *Apotelesmatika* <note>original: "apotelesmaton" – The Greek title of the Tetrabiblos, meaning "Effects."</note>, after speaking of the twofold nature of astronomy, says this, referring back to the first and mathematical kind:

->Even if perhaps this profession did not occasionally displease some men of good judgment, a thing is not immediately good just because someone good did not disapprove of it; for even good men are not always good in every respect, and few achieve the distinction of being learned in all accounts. And if something must be said: not all learned men are philosophers <note>original: "philosophi sp [semper] sunt"</note>. But it is also necessary to remember that there are certain truths against which our desires struggle, and others against which none struggle. In the first class are all things concerning morals and many theological matters; in the second is the greatest part of what concerns physical and mathematical things.<-

# BOOK ONE

Furthermore, it is clear that this truth we are discussing regarding the **vanity of astrology** belongs to the first kind [of truth]; for the innate vice of human curiosity <note>original: "curiositatis vitium"</note> resists it. Since curiosity is among the most powerful of forces—being specific to man insofar as he is man—it results in many people either not taking the time to investigate this truth or, even if it is discovered, refusing to accept it. Just as many people, after hearing the most evident reasons philosophers provide against **greed**, still gape at the accumulation of wealth, so too many people, after it has been established that nothing the astrologers say can be entirely true, still find their innate curiosity difficult to tear away from them. And if we are greedy for news and listen to fables willingly, so we, curious about the future, find pleasure even when we sense the astrologers are lying to us.

Added to this is that a misguided self-love <note>original: "infatuat nimius amor nostri"</note> often makes us easily hope for prosperity and easily fear adversity; it agitates us with a blind desire for things we know cannot be found. What of the fact that this widespread, long-standing consensus creates a prejudice? Many think there must be something to astrology, and it never occurs to them to look deeper into what foundation <note>original: "fundus"</note> or what solid support might lie beneath it. Therefore, you will find that almost everyone held by this vanity was either a poor philosopher or certainly a poor astrologer; the former prevents them from seeing errors, and the latter prevents them from judging them. Finally, a "taste" of it might have pleased some by chance, but it never satisfied the palate of a true philosopher once fully "drunk." For they have something on the surface that allures—something that seems great, likely, and useful—but when you look deeper, you see everything is **false, uncertain, and legendary**, born of either no conjectures at all or the weakest ones. We will discuss these matters abundantly and at length in the following books.

<margin>
Erring through the similarity of names
</margin>

However, it may be that someone is deceived by the fact that certain philosophers and astrologers share similar names, leading to the belief that the same person wrote both philosophical and astrological works. For there is an **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), the most famous Persian astrologer in the Middle Ages.</note> among the philosophers and likewise one among the astrologers. But although the Latin language has confused these names, they are recognized as distinct among the Arabs. For the one who is a philosopher is **Albumasar**, while the astrologer is called **Aboasar**. Likewise, an **Abubater** <note>Likely Abu Bakr al-Hassar or Ibn Bajja (Avempace).</note> wrote on "nativities" (astrological predictions based on birth); yet another of the same name wrote philosophical works, especially a book on how a man may become a philosopher, which I translated from Hebrew into Latin this past year. But that man was **Al-Tabihi**, while this one was the **son of Tripidis**. There is a similar affinity of names in many cases, even though there is a great disagreement in their times and professions.

<margin>
Testimonies of the prophets
</margin>

Enough concerning the philosophers. Let us pass to the prophets—that is, to the oracles of the Old and New Law—beginning with **Isaiah**. He, when he threatened the future destruction of the Babylonians (among whom this sect flourished most, which is why astrologers were even called "Chaldeans"), and while he was summoning **Cyrus**, King of the Persians, with trumpets to fight against them—calling him "Anointed" <note>referring to the Hebrew "Messiah"</note> two hundred years before he was born—addressed the desolate city of the Chaldeans thus:

<margin>
The words of Isaiah
</margin>

*Stand now, and let the augurs of heaven save you, who gazed at the stars and counted the months to announce what was to come to you. Behold, they have become like stubble; fire has burned them. They shall not deliver their own soul from the hand of the flame.* <note>Quoting Isaiah 47:13-14.</note>

And a few verses before this, he had taxed them for this celestial observation: *This wisdom and your science will deceive you; evil shall come upon you, and you will not know its origin; and calamity shall fall upon you which you will not be able to atone for.* In these words, the divine prophet accuses the twofold rashness of astrologers: first, thinking they can foresee the future from the sky; second, thinking they can either ward off predicted evils or secure goods. *Evil shall come,* he says, *whose origin you will not know*—that is, which neither Mars nor the cold star of Saturn signified to you. Then you will not be able to "atone" for the falling calamity—that is, to repel it from you through the "election of hours," astrological images, or other superstitious machinations.

It is worthy of notice that the responses of those who wish to be both Chaldeans and Christians at the same time are refuted by this. For they are accustomed to saying that astronomy is not simply condemned by the saints and prophets, but only insofar as they attribute all vices or virtues to the sky, or bind human events to fatal necessity. They argue that since good astrologers also refute these errors, the prophets do not loathe the science of astrology, but only the errors of certain astrologers. Let **Pierre d'Ailly** <note>Petrus Aliacesis (1351–1420), a French cardinal and theologian who famously attempted to use astrology to predict the end of the world and reconcile it with theology.</note> and whoever follows this path tell me...

-># DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

they defend it with a defense: whether it pertained to morals that the king of those people brought war against the Assyrians? Even if it did not pertain to morals, why did the prophet <note>Likely referring to Isaiah or Jeremiah, whom Pico cites frequently as the chief opponents of Babylonian star-gazing.</note> believe that it could not be foreseen by the highest astrologers? For if they had been in that error—thinking that things which were to happen would necessarily come to pass—the prophet would not have reproached them with a coming calamity that they could not atone for through their own efforts; for they themselves would not even hope it could be atoned for, since they would think everything happened by necessity.

But by no right judgment are good arts condemned simply because some evil men abuse them. Otherwise, the reading of the Sacred Scriptures would have to be condemned first of all, since the unlearned and the proud have confirmed so many heresies and so many of their own insanities from them. Likewise, philosophy would have to be condemned: because this philosopher says the soul is mortal, and that one says there is only one soul in all beings; some deny that God provides for men, and others say there is no religion at all. By this reasoning, all good things would be overturned, since there is nothing so good that human nature cannot abuse it. Therefore, those who defend themselves in this way—by appealing to the judgment of the Church, which they are ashamed to despise—are indirectly and severely slandering it. But they can be compelled entirely to repudiate this vanity, unless they wish to deviate to the left <note>A biblical metaphor for straying into error or heterodoxy.</note> from their elders, that is, the leaders of the Church.

<margin>Objections</margin>
For by whatever reason those leaders condemned astrology, I ask: did they condemn it justly or unjustly? They do not wish to say "unjustly"; if they say "justly," why do you not also condemn it equally with them? "But," they say, "we also condemn those errors on account of which astrology was displeasing to them." But I ask this: why does it not displease you for those same reasons? For it is plain to see that they did not forbid astrology only to a certain extent, but pursued and abominated it entirely and in every form, as we shall soon show. You contend that they did so because of certain errors; fine. But answer this: is the whole thing rejected by a right judgment on account of those errors? If it is a right judgment, why do you not do the same? On the contrary, you approve what they condemned; you defend what they attacked; you spread what they forbade; you teach publicly what they wished not to be known. 

Or perhaps you say, as Pierre d'Ailly <note>A 14th-century cardinal and scholar who tried to reconcile astrology with theology.</note> does, that astrology could have hindered the growing faith, and therefore the first doctors of the nascent Church pursued it; but now that the faith is adult, it does not harm, but rather profits it greatly. This will be refuted later; for we shall demonstrate clearly that it is just as pestiferous now as it was then, as experience itself now demonstrates. But it was not 

<margin>Whether philosophy like astrology should be condemned</margin>
the art that was to be condemned, but its abuse. Why then did they not condemn philosophy, but only the impiety of certain philosophers—yet they condemned not just the astrologers, but astrology itself? In both cases, the reason is that in philosophy, if anything is in error, it is a fault of the professor; in astrology, the profession <term>profession: the "art" or "vocation" itself as defined by its rules</term> itself is the fault. Following their authority together with reason, we also, in disputing against the philosophers, have refuted not philosophy but the errors of philosophers. Here, however, we refute not the astrologers, but astrology, because astrology itself is an error. 

But let us return to the testimonies of the prophets. God speaks to us through Moses in this way: "The nations listen to soothsayers and diviners; but you have been instructed otherwise by the Lord your God." <note>Deuteronomy 18:14</note> In place of what we read as "soothsayers," in the Hebrew it is:

<margin>Achinas</margin>
*Me'onen* <note>original Hebrew: עוֹן</note>, which Achinas <note>Pico's name for the Jewish scholar Ibn Ezra.</note>, the greatest teacher of the Hebrews, says refers to those who calculate times and observe lucky and unlucky hours; for that word is derived from *on* <gloss>עוֹן</gloss>, which signifies "hour." Jerome translated it as "soothsayers" [augures]. But we have seen that in Isaiah, astrologers are called soothsayers. Indeed, the name of "astrologers" is not used throughout the Sacred Letters. For that superstition has various ways of speaking and has been allotted various names at different times. Formerly they were called Chaldeans and casters of nativities <note>original: "genethliaci"</note>; in Augustine's time, "mathematicians" and "planet-gazers"; now they are commonly called "astrologers." But Jerome, in that place and often elsewhere, translated 

<margin>Avenazra. Jeremiah.</margin>
"diviners" for what in Hebrew is *qesem* <gloss>קֶסֶם</gloss>. Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazra"</note> himself—though he was an astrologer—says this is a term common to all diviners, but is more properly the name for astrologers. Who is ignorant of that saying of Jeremiah? "Do not fear the signs of heaven, which the nations fear." <note>Jeremiah 10:2</note> Why then should a Christian man either rejoice or be saddened by the judgments of astrologers? From them, Isaiah says nothing is to be hoped, and 

<margin>Ambrose. Job.</margin>
Jeremiah says nothing is to be feared; rather, through both of them, Divine Truth affirms this to us. For as Ambrose says, to seek all that they profess is absurd, since the things they promise are impossible. Hence the Ruler of Heaven says in Job: "Do you know the order of heaven, and will you set down its reason on the earth?" And further: "Who shall declare the reason of the heavens?" <note>Job 38:33, 37</note> For the error of astrologers is twofold: one, that they subject many things to heaven which do not depend on it; the other, that even those things which heaven does effect cannot be foreseen by them as they think; because...

...can be answered: as the words from the book of Job, brought into our discussion, show us. And since the doctors of the Church equally refute both <note>Likely referring to the two types of astrology: the "natural" and the "divinatory" or judicial.</note>, how can it be said that they only disapprove of that which takes away free will or introduces the necessity of fate? Does not that famous argument of Augustine regarding twins <note>Augustine’s "argument of the twins" (Jacob and Esau) notes that although born nearly at the same time under the same stars, their lives were vastly different, which he used to disprove astrological influence.</note> tend toward removing all 
<margin>Testimonies</margin>
foreknowledge of the future from them? Likewise, in his *Enchiridion*, does he not say that the very observation of times—so that we consider these moments lucky and those unlucky—pertains to a great sin? Yet, in this choosing of hours and days, we are exercising our freedom rather than having it taken away. 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
But it is certainly true that astrology displeased them in every respect, though especially in that part which subjected religion and morals to the heavens. For this reason they cursed it everywhere and refuted it everywhere; for this very reason they judged it everywhere to be vain, here blasphemous, there superstitious, here abominable, and everywhere ridiculous.

Wherefore Augustine, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, said that those who are called <term>genethliaci</term><note>From the Greek "genethlios" (pertaining to birth); these were astrologers who specialized in casting birth charts or horoscopes.</note> belong to a pernicious superstition, not only because they think our actions, but even the outcomes of our actions, proceed from the stars. And in explaining that passage of Moses: *Let the stars be placed for signs and seasons*, he says it does not mean "signs" which it is vanity to observe, but rather those necessary for the uses of life, such as those observed by sailors, 
<margin>Basil</margin>
farmers, and craftsmen of that kind. In the same place, 
<margin>Ambrose</margin>
<margin>Theodoret</margin>
<margin>Chrysostom</margin>
Basil said it was a most busy vanity; Ambrose called it useless and impossible; Theodoret said it had even been refuted by the pagans; and Chrysostom called it vain, false, and ridiculous. Let us read Bardesanes, Enselaus, Didymus, Apollinaris, Tertullian, and countless other apostolic men. Furthermore, we see that the Hebrews, the heretics, and the gentiles—indeed, this whole class of men—were pursued by this censorial rod. 

This led Augustine to wonder why, while these testimonies rebuking the astrologers were read with such fame in the churches, the meeting-places were nevertheless full of our own people, who would receive the timings for their affairs from 
<term>mathematicians</term><note>In the medieval and Renaissance periods, "mathematician" was a common synonym for "astrologer."</note>. In the book *On the Nature of Demons*, 
<margin>Jerome</margin>

<margin>Severianus</margin>

Severianus, in the book *On the Seven Arts* (which he falsely cites as being by Cassiodorus), says to Roger after speaking of true astronomy: "You ought to be so ignorant of those things which pertain to foreseeing the future that they do not even seem to have been written; for they are, without doubt, contrary to our faith." These are his words, verbatim.

If the opinion of so many and such excellent men moves no one, let at least the Papal authority deter them, which so forbids this profession to our people that Pope Alexander IV willed that a certain priest should abstain from the ministry of the altar for an entire year because he had investigated something by searching with an astrolabe for the theft of a certain church; even though, as the same Pope testifies, no magic or other superstition had been admitted there. <margin>Synod of Martin</margin>

<margin>Gregory</margin>

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine teaches in the book *On the Nature of Demons*, to be designated among our people under the name of "soothsayers"—those who guard days and hours in conducting business and works. Here, that part of astrology which is called "elections" <note>The practice of "choosing" (electing) the most astrologically auspicious moment to begin a task, like a wedding or a voyage.</note> seems especially noted. <meta>This page continues the first book of Pico della Mirandola's "Disputations Against Divinatory Astrology." Having previously cited the Church Fathers, Pico now addresses potential counter-arguments involving respected scholastic theologians like Albertus Magnus and Pierre d'Ailly, before turning to the legal prohibitions of the Roman Empire.</meta>

<page-num>188</page-num>
<header>DISPUTATIONS</header>

[...condemned by] the prophets, mocked by the saints, and forbidden by the high priests and the most holy synods. But if you oppose me with Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath who sought to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with Christian faith.</note>, that most outstanding theologian and yet a supporter of astrologers, I will first remind you that many things are attributed to Albert which are not his own, as we touched upon above. If you should perhaps object to me his book *On Licit and Illicit Things* <note>Referring to the *Speculum Astronomiae*, a 13th-century treatise often attributed to Albertus Magnus which defended certain forms of astrology as compatible with Christianity.</note>, in which he indeed rejects mages but approves of astronomical authors, I will respond that this work is thought by many not to be Albert’s.
<margin>Defense of Albert</margin>
Neither Albert himself nor the inscription of the book signifies this anywhere, especially since the author, whoever he may eventually be, deliberately and perfectly conceals his name. Furthermore, many things are read in it that are unworthy of a learned man and a good Christian—such as the claim that "images" <note>Astrological talismans or "seals" intended to capture the power of the stars.</note> can be made by which not just one man, but an entire city might become either unhappy or unfortunate. Then there is the claim that books of magic should not be discarded because they might one day be useful to the Church. This is plainly contrary to the judgment of the Church itself, which commands that such books be utterly destroyed wherever they are found. For by what reason would it be useful to preserve intact books that it would have been most useful never to have written? Either Albert did not write these things, or if he did, one must say with the Apostle: *in other things I praise him, but in this I do not praise him* <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 11:22.</note>. Just as it is the mark of envy to seek out what to condemn in great men rather than what to extol, so it is the mark of madness to wish to imitate them where they have failed rather than to condemn it.
<margin>The disgrace of Pierre d'Ailly</margin>
I will praise in Pierre d'Ailly <note>Petrus Aliacensis (1351–1420), a French cardinal and scholar who famously attempted to use astrology to explain historical cycles and the coming of the Antichrist.</note> his zeal for letters, his experience in affairs, his wide reading, and the fact that he wrote and treated certain theological matters with skill and subtlety. But as for the fact that in one short work he wished to reconcile astrology with history, and in another with theology—as if he could prove it true in the former and pious in the latter—I plainly do not praise him; rather, I condemn, execrate, and detest him. For we can uphold no position that is more false or more opposed to religion. We shall discuss this matter extensively in the following books, so nothing more needs to be said here. There, we shall leave it abundantly testified even to his own supporters that those booklets are enemies to religion and full of so many historical and astrological errors that our common saying might be applied: "if you wish to remove the error, remove the book." 

We have spoken of the philosophers and the prophets; there remain the civil laws—that is, the commands and judgments of the emperors and the legal experts.
<margin>Testimonies of civil law.</margin>
Their goal is primarily to look after the interests by which the life of men may be conducted well and happily. Since among all things, life is aided most by the good arts and disturbed by the harmful ones, they took the greatest care that the former should abound and the latter should (as far as possible) be non-existent in the cities. To achieve this, they decreed rewards and honors for the professors of the good arts. But for the harmful arts, they decreed public 
<margin>Justinian</margin>
disgrace and punishments, which were more severe the more harmful they judged those arts to be. What they thought of astrologers, therefore, no one is ignorant who has read the legal codes of the Emperor Justinian <note>Byzantine Emperor (r. 527–565) whose *Corpus Juris Civilis* formed the basis of medieval and Renaissance law.</note>. In these, the "art of mathematicians" (for so the astrologers called themselves) <note>In Roman law, the term *mathematici* specifically referred to practitioners of astrology, distinguishing them from those who studied geometry or arithmetic.</note> is forbidden as abominable. The Emperor commanded that no one should consult a mathematician, and that the curiosity for such judging must be silenced forever by all. If anyone should consult a mathematician, the penalty of death (which is the highest punishment) is pronounced against him. Surely the most wise Emperor would not have established this—supported by the usage, laws, and judgment of so many wise men—unless experience had demonstrated that profession to be not only useless for life, but ruinous to men. The most fortunate Justinian himself so abhorred this race of men that if any mathematician were caught in his company, he would pay the penalty for his rashness with the highest tortures, even unto the rack. Then finally, speaking of this superstition, the Emperor pronounces that those who teach it and those who learn it are tied to the same guilt. 
<margin>Conclusion of this book</margin>
Even before Justinian, do we not read that all mathematicians were frequently expelled from the city of Rome? This we shall aptly demonstrate at the conclusion of these disputations. If all right reason—whether perfected by the prudence of kings or by philosophy, or illuminated by the rays of divine splendor—prevails, then astrology will surely be driven out by every right judgment; for the most prudent lawmakers have exterminated it, the most learned philosophers have refuted it, and the divine and most holy men have abominated it.

<summary>Pico dismisses the authority of Albertus Magnus and Pierre d'Ailly regarding astrology, arguing that their support was either misattributed or a grave theological error. He concludes the book by citing Roman civil law, specifically Justinian's code, which treated astrology as a capital offense.</summary>
<keywords>Albertus Magnus, Pierre d'Ailly, Justinian, Roman Law, Mathematici, Astrology, Speculum Astronomiae, Legal Prohibition</keywords>

<header>AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS. BOOK TWO</header>

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS. THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS.

## Chapter One: That this art is uncertain, even by the judgment of its own founders.

<margin>
Words from the
Quadripartitum
of Ptolemy
</margin>
**B**ut so that we do not fight by authority alone, we shall demonstrate throughout this entire work, by certain reasons, that this superstition has been rightly rejected by the saints because it is most opposed to religion; that it is usefully forbidden by laws because it is useless to life—indeed, it is exceedingly harmful; and that it is reasonably refuted by philosophers as something they recognized as false and uncertain. And although it seemed we should begin by demonstrating it to be false (since that would immediately render it useless), I have nevertheless thought it best to act otherwise: namely, that before I dispute its falsehood, I should show the lovers of astrologers that even if this profession were what they claim it to be, no benefit comes from it to the <term>outer man</term><note>The "outer man" refers to one's physical circumstances, wealth, and social status.</note>, while to the <term>inner man</term><note>The "inner man" refers to the soul, intellect, and moral character.</note> it brings not only the greatest damage, but even destruction. Before we approach this, we must state certain things as a preface, from which we may understand how much the very princes of the astrologers themselves attribute to their own profession.

Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note>, therefore, in the first book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "Apotelesmaton," better known as the *Tetrabiblos* (The Four Books), the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, after saying that the judgments of astrologers are often lies due to the fault of the practitioner, adds the following, which we have chosen to translate word-for-word. These words are poorly rendered in the common translation, and even worse in the translation of Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle and Ptolemy were central to medieval thought.</note>, by whom they are poorly explained; but when they are faithfully translated, they will need no explanation:

"Truly, this much is clear: even if one investigates these disciplines properly and follows their tracks as much as possible, it is still necessary that he should very often fall into error. This is not because of the reasons we stated above, but rather because of the very nature of the matter, or because our own weakness is too great to be equal to the magnitude of such a profession. For indeed, since every contemplation that deals with the conditions of matter seeks the <term>probable</term> rather than anything it can decree with certainty, this is especially true of that study which is composed of many dissimilar parts and depends upon the ancient figures and aspects of the wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets.</note>. For those events which were observed by the ancients, we adapt to our own age whenever the circumstances are the same. Yet who does not see that it can happen that the figures and aspects themselves may be more or less similar to one another through the long windings of time? But as for a completely identical harmony of all things in the heavens—especially if you add the Earth as well—it is not even to be hoped for, unless someone perhaps boasts vainly and gloriously of comprehending and knowing things which either cannot be understood at all by their own nature, or certainly not within that space of time granted to human senses. Thus it happens that when dissimilar examples are proposed, the foreknowledge of things often goes astray."

And in looking at those things which happen regarding the nature that surrounds us, nothing is more difficult than in the cases of births and in the private comparisons of individuals. For causes that are neither small nor light occur by which each person's character is shaped. For the "dominion of the seeds" <note>An early reference to what we might call genetics or hereditary nature.</note> has great power over the property of the species; for even if the surrounding atmosphere and the horizon are the same, each seed has a great deal of weight in the universal formation of its peculiar shape—for instance, in a man, a horse, or others. The locations of birth also bring no small difference. For even if the type of seed is the same (namely human) and the state of the atmosphere is the same, those who are born differ greatly in body and mind due to the diversity of regions. Furthermore, it matters greatly for varying the acts of life—even if all else be equal—what food one uses or what customs one follows. Unless each of these things is contained within the cause of the surrounding atmosphere (which would be the most powerful force), so that there is some other cause for why things are as they are, then these factors can have a very great effect against the stars. In this matter, those who believe they can know everything are in error, since all things are clearly not the same...

<summary>Ptolemy, the father of astrology, admits that the art is inherently uncertain due to the complexity of the heavens and the influence of non-astrological factors like genetics, geography, and diet.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument by citing the admissions of astrologers themselves regarding the limitations of their art. He transitions from quoting Ptolemy's "Centiloquium" to discussing the general consensus among Arab and Hebrew authorities before launching into a specific critique of "elections"—the practice of choosing auspicious times for actions.</meta>

...to discern from the motion of the celestial bodies. Thus says Ptolemy in the first and second proposition of the other book, which is entitled *Fruits* <note>original: "fructus"</note>, commonly called the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy, though now considered apocryphal.</note>, speaking of the science of the astrologer: he says it is impossible for one who is knowledgeable to pronounce the particular forms of things, just as the sense does not receive a particular form of a sensible thing, but a certain general one; and it is necessary for one treating these things to use a conjecture of things, but only those inspired by the deity predict particulars. These are his words verbatim, although they are held otherwise, erroneously and depravedly, in the common manuscripts.

But it is also the indubitable opinion of the Arabs and Hebrews who write on astrology that whatever the star has promised may nevertheless not happen: both because the matter is not suitable for receiving the influence, and because human affairs depend greatly on our free choice; and because a particular fate can be overcome by the power of a more universal opposing fate; and because divine providence—more powerful than all fate and greater than the heaven—sometimes ordains things to happen differently than the ordinary revolution of the heaven would have effected. While these things are scattered everywhere among astrologers, you will read all these rules together in Abraham ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazram"</note> in the first chapter of his book *On Nativities*.

### Chapter II. That the divinations they call <term>elections</term> are useless: by the testimony of one astrologer, by reason, and by experience.

<margin>
That divinations are useless.
</margin>
**F**or if these things are true, let the astrologer bring forward what benefit life attains from his predictions. He will perhaps respond that it is twofold: the one, he says, is that we are taught the hour in which we ought to begin our actions <note>This practice is known as an "election."</note>, so that what we are about to do may happen fortunately; the other, when he predicts what is to come, is of this use: that we might abstain from those things in which we have known ourselves to be unfortunate, and conversely, that we might undertake those in which the hour of our birth promises us happiness. 

But come, let us examine both, starting from what was proposed in the first place. And since our dispute is with the astrologers, let us use those assumptions especially which are considered most true among them. Either, therefore, in the matter you are about to do by divination, the natal constellation has made the heaven favorable to you, or adverse: if adverse, the divination is of no use according to the opinion of Ptolemy; for you will always undertake that thing unhappily, and you will always happily abstain from it. If favorable, there is no need for any "picking of hours," but your own choice suffices for you; because you will then undertake that matter most happily when your mind invites you to it. 

For being fortunate (if anyone is fortunate from the heaven) is nothing else than our imaginative power, the servant of reason, being so moved by the heaven that we undertake each thing to be done in such modes and times that our wish can be most happily fulfilled. 

<margin>
Aristotle.
Haly.
Experience.
</margin>
Therefore Aristotle said that counsel is of no use to the fortunate—specifically in that matter for which nature formed him—lest perhaps counsel distract and lead you away to something else than where that established impulse of the soul was calling you. I pass over that Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Arabic commentator on Ptolemy.</note>, the interpreter of Ptolemy, says that this part of astrology concerning elections is frivolous and ineffective. I pass over the evidence of experience itself, than which nothing is more certain, nothing more constant; for it daily makes manifest that those are especially unhappy in conducting their affairs who observe this vain distinction of times.

<margin>
To whom happiness is clear and to whom unhappiness is brought from astronomy.
</margin>
On the contrary: far more fortunate are those who, having rejected that superstition, use only choice and prudence as their guides. For who in our age was more fortunate than Francesco Sforza <note>The mercenary general who became Duke of Milan in 1450.</note>, who by military luck prepared for himself a wide and most flourishing empire in Lombardy <note>original: "Insubrium"</note>, and left it increased and confirmed to his descendants? To him, nevertheless, all astrologers were always either objects of hatred or contempt; much less did he use them as advisors in his military or domestic affairs. Who among the ancients was more powerful than Zoroaster in astrology, in magic, and in every superstition? And yet Ninus, who was neither an astrologer nor a mage, conquered and killed him in war. Pompey placed the greatest faith in the responses of diviners; Caesar placed none. The former had adverse fortune, the latter happy and joyful fortune. Who is ignorant that the Emperor Justinian, the exterminator of astrologers as we have seen, was most happy at home and in war? On the contrary, the Emperor Julian, an enemy of the Christian name and a most curious observer of all superstitions, how quickly and unhappily he lost both his life and his empire! I could nevertheless [mention] one or another...
