->ADVERSVS ASTROLOGIAM LIBER SECVNDVS<-
->AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK TWO<-

...or another: for I could name learned astrologers who were my own friends, to whom faith in this vanity—according to which they had instituted their way of life—was either a source of destruction or of no small detriment. But I do not wish to defame men who are otherwise good, nor to violate the laws of holy friendship in a matter where the truth is not strictly necessary <note>Pico is tactfully avoiding naming specific friends who were ruined by astrology to preserve their reputation, even though their failures prove his point.</note>. Yet, I wish that it had not taken away the inheritance of one, the homeland and life of another, or made many fools and madmen with vain hope, and many others miserable with fear. So may God not look upon my sins, for I have seen no one more destitute of those things which astrology promises to its followers than those who have devoted themselves entirely to astrology and who hunt for the favor of heaven hour by hour through it. 

A certain great man known to me <note>This likely refers to a contemporary figure in the Italian courts, possibly even a member of the Medici circle, who made disastrous life choices based on horoscopes.</note> changed his way of life as a result of this counsel, with no small loss of his previous fortune, being especially warned by astrological hope that in his new profession he would attain great happiness through celestial favor. But indeed, as he experienced every day more adverse fortune in that path, he was accustomed to say that he had been deceived by Mars, being unwilling to say what was more true: that he had been deceived by astrological vanity. The same man died a little while later a very miserable death, which he himself had not foreseen from the heaven; for he was preparing many things and striving for great goals, as one who had established for himself a long limit of living. 

I could enumerate many cases of this kind, but my mind shrinks from the narration of those things which I can hardly remember without tears, and which, because they happened to very dear friends, demand compassion from me rather than a reprimand. But I hope that this rebuttal—carried out with names hidden—against the life of old friends may benefit living friends. By all the laws of friendship that exist between me and them, by their fortunes, and by their hopes of happiness, I warn and ask them again and again: let them never commit themselves in their affairs to the counsel of this vanity. Let them hold it (if they like) as a sort of poetic fable over which they may laugh, play, and joke; but let them not hold it as a guide or a mistress of life. 

Rather, when they must consult for the health of the body, let them consult physicians; when they must look out for external affairs, let them use the eyes of prudence and reason. Divine wisdom teaches us both of these things: it says that the physician was created by the Most High for our necessity <note>A reference to the Biblical book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1: "Honor the physician... for the Lord created him."</note>, and it says that prudence must be kept by a man so that he may be rescued from the evil path <note>A reference to Proverbs 2:11-12.</note>. We find nothing of the sort written about astrology. We have proven its profession to be so useless that even if we granted it as much as the astrologers think should be granted, it would still fail. For when it is later proven that it contains no truth at all, it will be beyond all controversy—as we have attempted to prove here—that it is most dangerous to entrust our affairs to the counsel of astrologers. If ever anything happens correctly as a result of their predictions, it should be attributed not to their method (which is non-existent) but to rashness and chance.

### Chapter III. Astrology is not useful in deciding what should be done or what should be avoided.

<margin>Note on the dismantling of arguments</margin>

**A**nother benefit of astrology could be imagined—namely, that we should pursue a matter which the astrologer has commanded us to follow, and conversely flee those things which he forbids. We have demonstrated that this is either superfluous or harmful; for what he predicts pertains either to those things which belong to the body, or to things external and accidental. In those matters which belong to the body, if they look toward health, I ask whether the judgment of the physician agrees with the judgment of the astrologer, or if it is instead different. If both feel the same way, the astrologer brings you nothing that the physician could not provide alone. If they disagree, I ask you, which one do you think should be followed? Surely, if you reject the physician and commit yourself to the astrologer, you will pay the penalty for your insanity. 

In the conduct of affairs, I similarly ask whether prudence suggests the same thing that astrology advises. Do these judgments utterly oppose each other? If they harmonize, why should we seek in the heaven for what is so uniquely within us? If they disagree, who could defend as right or reasonable an action that abandons prudence—which is nothing other than the right reason for doing things—in the conduct of affairs? But these things will be clearer with examples. Suppose, then, that an astrologer has predicted that Mars threatens you with a tertian fever <note><term>tritē</term>: Likely referring to a "tertian" fever, one that recurs every third day, traditionally associated with an excess of yellow bile and the planet Mars.</note> this year. For he says it will stir up bile from the part he holds in the annual revolution; therefore, you should use cold remedies and a way of life suited to...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument against the practical utility of astrology. He is currently illustrating how astrological predictions are inferior to the specialized knowledge of physicians and the practical prudence of rulers.</meta>

->DISPUTATIONS<-

...turned toward a life to be established by the heat of Mars. Whether the sky itself foretells this, or the signs themselves will demonstrate it—those signs which are sought from the dispositions of your body and on which the physician's conjecture relies—either they will demonstrate it or they will not. If they demonstrate it, this will be sufficient evidence for you to take precautions against future ill health. If they do not demonstrate it, I ask: do you think it is rightly done that when there are no indicators of boiling bile, but rather white and thick urine, slow pulses of the veins, a face deformed with paleness, sluggishness of the limbs, and others of that kind which physicians use as pre-noted signs—[these signs] will indicate not bile, but the dominance of phlegm? Yet you would evacuate bile because an astrologer from the heavens fashioned a threatening Mars for you? Indeed, no prudent astrologer would advise you thus; for even if he speaks truly of Mars, your natural temperament, the universal disposition of the year itself, or the way of life you have long followed could have turned you toward the opposite. Finally, the astrologer sees only one thing that could effect this, and that a remote and universal one. The physician judges not only from proper and nearby causes, but perceives the thing itself by sense; and that which results from the complex of all causes together, he holds by the evidence of present nature showing it. I pass over that they <note>Referring to physicians.</note> also favor the judgments of astrologers; yet they are not so insane as to think that one is less deceived by the judgments of physicians. 

<margin>An example in external matters.</margin> Let us propose a similar example in the handling of external affairs: for instance, if a mathematician <term>mathematician: In the medieval and Renaissance periods, "mathematicus" often referred specifically to an astrologer or one who calculated planetary positions for divination.</term> should advise a prince not to enter into war with enemies because Mars is not sufficiently favorable to him. I ask: at the time they gave him this advice, was there no just cause for the prince to wage war? Or if there was a cause for war, was there no occasion or opportunity for winning? Or rather, did a just cause for war not fail him, and were all the instruments for victory at hand? If you grant the first, he will rightly not wage war, but with prudence alone as his leader, even if the mathematician were completely silent. If the second, not even the astrologer himself, unless it were in his own interest, would judge that he should abstain from war; and if he should abstain, what would that be other than to abandon sense and evidence for the sake of reason and conjecture?

### Chapter IV. That astrology is not useful to religion: which Roger Bacon and Pierre d'Ailly believed for a twofold reason.

<margin>Reasons for which Pierre d'Ailly affirmed astrology to be necessary.</margin>
**B**UT if it is useless for life, is it perhaps useful for religion? This is what both Roger Bacon <note>An English philosopher and Franciscan friar (c. 1214–1292) who advocated for the study of nature through empiricism and was interested in astrology.</note> and Pierre d'Ailly <note>A French cardinal and theologian (1350–1420) who attempted to harmonize astrology with history and theology.</note> seem to have thought. And the latter, indeed, for two main reasons: one, that through the astrological calculation of the "Great Conjunctions" <term>Great Conjunctions: Rare alignments of Jupiter and Saturn which astrologers believed signaled major shifts in history, such as the rise of new religions or empires.</term>, the truth of the number of years from Adam to Christ could be known—concerning which there is such great debate among ecclesiastical texts. The other, that the oracles of the prophets could be confirmed if the testimony of astrological prediction were added to their prophecies. For since all truth is consistent with all truth, the truth of astronomical science must necessarily be in accord with theological truth; indeed, it should serve it like a handmaid to a mistress, since "the invisible things of God are seen through those things which have been made visible." Nothing among those things is more noble than the sky; hence that saying of David: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands.* <note>original: "Cæli enarrāt gloriā dei & opa manuū eius annūciat firmamētū." From Psalm 19:1.</note> As if to prove this opinion, he wrote a small work divided into twenty theorems, which he calls "words," in which there are plainly as many errors as words. The title is *On the Concordance of Astrology and Theology*. He clearly had not read Paul exclaiming: *What fellowship has light with darkness? Or what part has Christ with Belial?* <note>2 Corinthians 6:14-15. Pico is arguing that divine truth and pagan/occult "science" cannot mix.</note> He strives in that work to achieve those two things we mentioned: namely, that those things which the prophets predicted by divine inspiration should also be shown as pre-signified by celestial constellation; and then that the computation of years from Adam to Christ be investigated from the dogmas of astrologers. He adds another small work to this one, *On the Concordance of Astronomy and History*, in which he strives to relate seven "Greatest Conjunctions" from the beginning of the world to those famous and wonderful things collected from histories in the intervening times. Here he intends to confirm the dogma of astrologers who wish that from those Great Conjunctions great changes of laws and kingdoms always occur in human affairs. And indeed, I would have preferred that he had written things which I ought to praise rather than refute; since, as he possessed talent, I love him for his letters and his person...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is inferior to practical medical observation and political prudence, then begins a critique of theologians like Pierre d'Ailly who tried to use "Great Conjunctions" to validate biblical history and prophecy.</summary>

->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY. BOOK TWO<-

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY. BOOK TWO

<margin>The nature of the error in Pierre d'Ailly may be forgiven.</margin>
I love the man and venerate the personage he represented in the Church <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420) was a famous French cardinal and theologian.</note>. But perhaps I shall even do him a kindness if—should I find that what he wrote to the Church with little caution or truth is undoubtedly false and harmful—it is erased through this just refutation, as far as lies in our power. What led this otherwise learned man into this error was, above all, an ignorance of astronomy. Having practiced himself in the most celebrated University of Paris in the study of theology, he began as an old man to taste a little of this art. He was enticed by that magnificent appearance of the art which discusses the greatest matters—things which human curiosity desires to know above all else. Before he reached the point of detecting the weakness of the dogma through deep examination, he wrote too hastily those two small works which he later retracted when he became a little more skilled. Then he wrote many things in that booklet which he calls the *Elucidarium* <note>Latin: "The Elucidator" or "The Bringer of Light."</note>, although there is much darkness within it. If anyone unlearned in astronomy reads these booklets, he will marvel at them all the more, the less he understands them.

<margin>The sources of d'Ailly's dogmas and his ignorance.</margin>
But anyone who has made even moderate progress in that art will judge him to have been more of a writer than an astrologer; whatever he says seems to have been read by him rather than produced from his own deep understanding. Almost everything he writes is taken word-for-word from Roger Bacon, Abraham the Jew <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century scholar.</note>, Henry Bate of Mechelen, Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note>, and some "Summa" by a certain John the Briton. That he himself was merely a listener and lacked skill in astronomical matters is proven by what he says in the *Elucidarium* itself (which is his most polished work) in chapter eleven. He says that in the year of Christ 1444, we would be in the "airy triplicity" <note><term>triplicity</term>: a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note> for another sixty-one years, until the year 1505 was reached. He claimed there would then be a "great conjunction" of Saturn and Jupiter during the change from the airy to the watery triplicity. In truth, that change had already occurred nearly forty years earlier, in the year of Christ 1365. At that time, on the twenty-ninth day of October, Saturn and Jupiter were together in the seventh part of Scorpio; and from then on, they always joined in the watery signs up to these times. Yet d'Ailly was still waiting for something to happen that had already occurred nearly a hundred years before.

<margin>Book on the true calculation of times.</margin>
Another "utility" that this same man thought came from astrology—namely, gathering the true number of years—we have abundantly refuted in that book we wrote called *On the True Calculation of Times*. Even if astrology helped the Christian state in this regard, it would not pertain to the part we are refuting here, which deals with the prediction of the future. Rather, it would belong to true astronomy, which is one of the liberal disciplines, and whose task is to calculate times and measure the movements of the stars by mathematical reasoning. But this is not the place to refute his errors; I shall do that in the following books. There, regarding the harmony of philosophy and theology, we shall show that those things announced by the prophets are neither caused nor signified by the heavens. Thus, even if astrology were true, the prediction of those events would not belong to it. As for those who exempt matters from the heavens insofar as they are "above nature," but contend they are caused and foreseen by the heavens insofar as they are "natural," we shall show they say nothing, even though they seem to say something. It is so far from the case that prophetic oracles are usefully confirmed by the decrees of astrologers, that nothing could be more powerful or effective for weakening religion. Furthermore, those who have tried to do this are always found to be liars and ignorant of astronomy, erring greatly in their historical profession. In general, not only regarding laws and divine miracles, but also regarding other changes in human affairs which many have wished to foretell from "great conjunctions," we shall expose their vanity and the falsity of their dogma. There, we shall contend for the truth against Albumasar (the author of that error), against Hermann his interpreter, against Abraham the Israelite, and against John of Exeter.

<margin>D'Ailly on the harmony of astrology and history.</margin>
We shall so thoroughly unweave d'Ailly's book, in which he wished to do the same regarding the "harmony of astrology and historical narrative," from the very beginning, that—running through it from that first "great conjunction" <note>The "Great Conjunction" of Jupiter and Saturn was believed by medieval astrologers to mark major historical shifts, such as the rise of new religions or empires.</note> he notes to the last—we shall show that nothing he said regarding either heavenly or earthly matters is sound or close to the truth. Nor is one of those...

He argues that true astronomy is a mathematical science, whereas predictive astrology undermines religious truth.</summary>

->DISPUTATIONS<-

the seven conjunctions he notes <note>In medieval astrology, "conjunctions" are the meeting of two or more planets in the same sign of the zodiac, believed to cause major historical shifts.</note> and the time he thinks they occurred; but it is greatly different from the very narration of the times—that is, the history of deeds done—and from true calculation. But let us see if those things he later brought forward have any truth: namely, that all things harmonize with each other, and that "the heavens declare the glory of God." <note>original: "caeli enarrant gloriam dei," a quote from Psalm 19:1.</note> Certainly, that first point is most true; but it should then have been assumed that since astrology is false, it cannot harmonize with theological truth. The apostle Paul teaches that this testimony of David <note>Referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> refers to the celestial minds of the Apostles, who announced that glory of God; of whom it is written afterward: "the law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls." But even if it refers to the visible sky, what kind of logic is this: if the heavens declare the glory of God, do they therefore support the "glory of God" about which astrologers babble from the sky? But he says that "His invisible things, and His power and divinity, are understood through visible things." <note>A reference to Romans 1:20.</note> Yet this is the task of the philosopher, whose proper role is to proceed from the order, motion, and nature of the heaven to the invisible, divine Architect of the heaven. If the astrologer sees anything, he sees it with his eyes; and he turns his eyes from the sky down to the earth. Only the philosopher contemplates invisible things from the visible.

### Chapter V. How harmful and pestilential astrology is to the Christian religion.

<margin>Praise of the philosopher</margin> Truly, as I survey everything on all sides and scout the enemies of the Church, I do not see any source from which more plenty or more weapons are supplied against the truth than from this profession of astrology. For from here, it is a headlong and very easy slide into impiety, into bad religion, into heresies, into vain superstition, and into ruined morals and irrecoverable malice. For from where will impiety arm itself better against the weapons of religion than to claim that divine miracles—by which all religion is chiefly confirmed—must be referred to the sky? If you offer the example of martyrs despising death; if you offer the few, poor, and unlearned apostles subjecting the world to the law of the Gospel; even if you offer men recalled from the dead—as being greater deeds than human power can achieve and better than what can be done by a demon—they will strip away the power in them, unless they can claim that nothing but the course of a star and a celestial "breath" <note>original: "afflatus," meaning a divine or celestial influence or inspiration.</note> could do it. If someone says this, is it not the same as putting an axe to the roots of religion? If he persuades others, does he not undermine and entirely uproot it? Now, if you say this is not a fault of the art itself but of its practitioners who err in their own profession, I will admit that is so. For I was not saying that this error *is* astrology, but that it is easy to fall from astrology into this error. Nor, even if astrology were true, should we stop this work of turning men away from that danger; for no truth is to be confirmed by lies. But since astrology is false, its falsehood will be usefully exposed, for if it were thought true, it could generate such a grave pestilence in the minds of the impious. Although, if you see all practitioners of some art holding the same vanities, it is hardly the case that the blame should not truly be referred to the art itself. Indeed, I have read no one among the principal writers of astrology who does not subject religion and all laws—just like all other human affairs—to the constellations of the stars.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin> Ptolemy, in the second book of his <term>Apotelesmaton</term><note>original: "apotelesmaton," better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational textbook of ancient astrology written by Claudius Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD.</note>, understands that the reason this nation worships one deity and that nation another is born from nothing other than the varied nature of the stars and signs presiding over those peoples and nations. Not far from that passage, a certain Greek interpreter of Ptolemy says that the miracle of Moses—when he crossed the Red Sea on dry feet with his people—was done because he observed the ebb and flow of the tide. As if the Hebrew people did not cross unharmed through those same waters at the same time that Pharaoh, with his astrologers, was submerged! And as if Joshua did not cross the Jordan on dry feet, in which no tide and no reciprocity of waves is imagined by them! But these and similar trifles we have sufficiently refuted elsewhere.

<margin>Albumasar</margin> Albumasar the Arab <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a Persian astrologer whose work *On the Great Conjunctions* argued that religions were born under specific planetary alignments.</note> derives the law of the Saracens, his own law, our law, and all laws equally from the sky in such a way that he predicts from the constellation itself which constellation made which law, and for how many years each one is to remain. We shall declare later how little of both astrology and truth is found in these matters.

<margin>Henry</margin> His interpreter, Henry of Mechlin <note>Henry Bate of Mechelen (c. 1246–1310), an astronomer and theologian.</note>, raved so much that he even "found" a ship in the sky, according to which Noah was to build that ark of his—an "invention" which d'Ailly greatly admired as if it were divine. Finally...

He cites and refutes the claims of Ptolemy, Albumasar, and Henry of Mechlin, who subjected even Moses and Noah to the stars.</summary>

->AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK TWO<-

<margin>Abraham</margin>
That the Law <note>In this context, "the Law" refers to a religious system or dispensation, specifically the Jewish or Christian faiths.</note> is reduced by them to an order of things that happen by natural course and the changing of the sky can be known from this: they want the revolutions of the years, from the rise of a Law to its very fall, to be known from the heavens. Haly Abenzagel <note>Also known as Albohali (c. 8th-9th century), an Arab astrologer whose works were highly influential in Medieval Europe.</note>, to say nothing of the others, predicts the prosperity and sterility of a year from this: that if the ascendant of the Law reaches the place of Jupiter or Venus, it will be a fertile year; conversely, if it reaches the places of unlucky stars. Abraham the Jew—whom the Alliacensis <note>Pierre d’Ailly (1351–1420), a French cardinal and scholar whom Pico frequently critiques.</note> falsely believed was called Avenezra, but whom they call <term>Nasi</term> <gloss>original: "nafi" (Nasi); a Hebrew title meaning "Prince" or "Patriarch," used for leaders of the Jewish community</gloss>—did he not attempt, quite foolishly and ridiculously, to refer the Mosaic law, the departure of the Jews from Egypt, and whatever happened to that people under the Law, to various conjunctions?

But if only those we mentioned had failed to see the light of this truth amidst the darkness of a bad religion! If only our own people <note>Referring to fellow Christians.</note> were not so blinded in the splendor of the Gospel, thinking no better of our religion than those others did of theirs. That insane Bonatti <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), perhaps the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century.</note> says the Lord Jesus used the <term>election of hours</term> <gloss>the practice of choosing a specific moment for an action based on the positions of the stars for a favorable outcome</gloss> when the apostles consulted Him about not returning to Judea; He replied that there are twelve hours in a day. For he says He chose an hour in which they could not harm Him—as if He could not have struck them down when He wished, or as if, passing through them in the light of day, He had not been hidden from them. I pass over what rash and blasphemous things he says about the divine family of Francis <note>Referring to the Franciscan Order; Bonatti claimed its rise was due to planetary alignments.</note>, and his fable that the miracle of divine love was the work of Mars.

But why look for distant examples? In those things that are daily published abroad in public prophecies about the year's events, is it not said that the Christian law was perfected by the doctrine of Christ and Mercury? And that the religion of Jupiter and the purity received from a Virgin [belong together]? Thus Christian men read these things with eyes that are not indignant. And in the prefaces of some theoretical work or other disputing much against Gerard <note>Likely referring to Gerard of Cremona, a prolific translator of Arabic scientific texts into Latin.</note>, is it not even written—when the election of a new Pope was being discussed—that one should pray devoutly so that the "Mercurial star" might temper with its holy ray? For they say our Law is under Mercury, and therefore he called the men of Christ "men of Mercury"—something I do not know how any Christian could hear with fair ears.

<margin>Roger Bacon.</margin>
Roger Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1220–1292), the English friar and philosopher known for his interest in the natural sciences and astrology.</note> was carried so far that he did not hesitate to write that Christians err because they do not rest on the Sabbath and refrain from work in the Jewish rite; since that is the day of Saturn, a star considered poorly suited and unlucky for conducting business. In these words, he accuses not only us, but Moses; indeed, he openly turns the prophet into an astrologer, teaching that the rules Moses established for the Sabbath rest were not based on some divine mystery, but on astrological dogma.

If anyone weighs all this with a correct judgment, they will see that the piety of true religion is offended by no error more than this; for it is equally impious to think there is no religion at all, as it is to derive it from the sky by some fatal necessity.

<margin>What the heresy of the Manichaeans is</margin>
For if an astrologer must embrace any religion, to which will he be more inclined than to idolatry, so that he might worship and revere those gods especially from whom he thinks all things, both good and bad, come to men? Now, as for the heresies of the Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious movement that Pico here links to the denial of free will, a key problem he sees in astrology.</note> taking away the freedom of the will—from where else do we think they emanated than from this false opinion of the astrologers regarding fate?

<margin>See the superstition of Varro</margin>
There is no controversy that all superstitions come from astronomy; and Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a Roman scholar and writer.</note> confirms they are contained by it as if they were its nurslings. All writers call <term>geomancy</term> <gloss>a method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand</gloss> the daughter of astrology. The Magi <note>Practitioners of magic or occult wisdom.</note> think the use of this art so necessary to them that they call astrology the "key to magic." <term>Chiromancers</term> <gloss>palm readers</gloss> fashion seven mounds in the palm of the hand according to the number of the planets, from which the future might be foreseen through the lines seen there. But we will pursue these follies one by one when, after the mistress and queen <note>Astrology itself.</note> has been overthrown, we trample the entire remaining crowd of superstitions in our path. But it is clear enough that they all are born from her and cannot stand without her: for there is no superstition that does not use the selection of days and hours, about which only astronomy instructs them. Thus, that word from Ecclesiastes <note>original: "vanitas vanitatum..." - a paraphrasing of Ecclesiastes 1:2.</note> can be said of it: "Vanity of vanities, astrology and all superstition is vanity."

It is not necessary to say more about morals, since it is clear enough that a greater patronage cannot be given to vice than if they think they have a heavenly author [for it]; and nothing...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology undermines true religion by attributing divine laws and miracles to planetary movements, citing errors by Roger Bacon and others. He concludes that astrology is the "queen" and source of all other superstitions, like palmistry and geomancy, which rob humans of free will.</summary>

->AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK TWO<-

...that it would make us fear hell less or hope for happiness less. If these things are undoubtedly true, then even if this profession [astrology] were true, would it not be more useful for the truth to be ignored? And since it is false, is it not more useful that this falsehood be attacked? Truly, I wish I could fulfill this duty as many times as I have embraced it out of a desire to help religion and protect the truth.

### Chapter 6: That this art is deceptive—if indeed it is an art—both because of many factors and because of the conflicting opinions of astrologers.

Up to this point, we have shown that it is useful to refute astrology and that defending it is unworthy of both a philosopher and a Christian. Now, before we engage in hand-to-hand combat with the astrologers, let us see how much the outcomes of events themselves refute their claims. How few predicted things actually happen? Or if something does happen, why did this specific thing occur? For this reason, I am usually amazed by those who, when arguing against this art, always raise the objection: "If their art is not true, why then are their predictions true?" Indeed, the astrologer thinks he is doing very well for himself if, when we object to the falsity of his predictions, he can provide some excuse; he is far from being able to take an argument against us from this point, even if he thinks he can. 

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
We have cited above the words of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity, whose "Tetrabiblos" was the standard textbook for the field.</note> attempting to resolve this question. In those words, we saw that he cast the blame for the lies of astrologers not only upon the astrologers themselves for being insufficiently skilled or diligent but also upon the art itself, which he claimed is uncertain and can frequently be deceptive. 

<margin>Porphyry</margin>
Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the nature of demons and oracles.</note> himself says that the responses of oracles were found to be false because those deities pronounced them based on celestial causes they had explored. Yet the pronouncement is deceptive because even the demons themselves, from whom nothing regarding celestial matters is hidden, are deceived when they look into the future from that source. If so, what shall we judge regarding men? Even those who are and have been the most excellent in this art (if there is such a thing) have never reached even a thousandth part of it. 

Finally, among all the arts—where it is common to all to sometimes miss the truth—the judgment of none is more uncertain than this one; and I believe the astrologers themselves will not deny it. For they say that human <term>choice</term> <gloss>original: "arbitrium"; the capacity of a person to decide their own actions</gloss> makes many things happen differently, and that the flow and instability of matter often frustrate the work of celestial actions. One <term>fate</term> <gloss>original: "fatum"</gloss> is turned or hindered by another. 

If you examine human affairs diligently, you will find almost nothing in which one of these factors we have mentioned does not change what was foreseen and truly signaled from the sky. For it is characteristic of humans to arrange their affairs by choice and reason; and that which is connected and bound to matter on all sides is vehemently subject to its changeability. Furthermore, since nothing exists in isolation, almost all people depend on one another in such a way that there is no one whose fortune cannot be harmed or helped by another's. Thus, a lucky son will experience an unhappy outcome from his father's misfortune, and a lucky one will inherit happiness from a parent's good fate. A servant who is naturally unlucky in his birth will fare well with a lucky master. So too, the fate of a soldier will be determined by the fate of his commander; the fortune of a patient by the doctor; and conversely, the doctor's by the patient—things will happen in various ways. 

From all this, it is clear how often it is necessary for what a mathematician <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematicus" often referred specifically to an astrologer or caster of horoscopes.</note> has predicted not to happen, even if this profession were true—let alone that the truth of the profession could be proven by the "true" predictions of its practitioners. 

<margin>Strange and many disagreements among astrologers.</margin>
What of the fact that there is such great disagreement in dogma among the authors of this art that it is necessary for either all or the greatest part of them to be speaking lies about the future? They themselves greatly admire and venerate certain Egyptians, Persians, Indians, and Babylonians as if they were priests of celestial mysteries, and they sound their names into the ears of the unlearned with puffed-out cheeks like deities. But you, O astrologers, cannot tell the truth about those ancient masters, since you only possess the books of the more recent ones whom you imitate, and you disagree with that ancient discipline in every way. For Ptolemy, your father, everywhere censures and tears apart the astrology that belonged to the Egyptians, sometimes calling his own version more consistent with reason, other times attacking them with other proofs—which is easily established for anyone reading his books on *Judicial Astrology* <note>original: "apoteleſmaton" (Apotelesmatika); referring to Ptolemy's "Tetrabiblos."</note>. Nor did Ptolemy only differ from them, but they likewise disagreed among themselves: the Indians from the Chaldeans, and the Egyptians from both and from...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence, leading into a discussion on the specific regional disagreements between different astrological traditions (Indians, Chaldeans, Egyptians).</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is inherently unreliable because human free will and the interconnectedness of people's lives disrupt celestial influence. He further notes that even the "founding fathers" of astrology, like Ptolemy and the Egyptians, constantly contradicted one another.</summary>

-># AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK TWO<-

<margin>First disagreement</margin>
...in turn, and [they are] judged by these and others, and by all of them. Nor is Greek astrology any less discordant among itself than the barbarian <note>In this period, "barbarian" often referred to non-Greek and non-Latin authors, particularly Arabic and Persian sources.</note> versions. Ptolemy rejects what Dorotheus <note>Dorotheus of Sidon (1st century AD), an influential astrologer who wrote a famous instructional poem on the stars.</note> embraces; Paul <note>Paulus Alexandrinus (4th century AD), author of an introductory text to astrology.</note> thinks one thing, Hephaestion <note>Hephaestion of Thebes (5th century AD), who attempted to synthesize earlier traditions.</note> another, and others think and believe still different things. Yet you will not find a single one among them who does not claim to have confirmed the reliability of his views through the authority of experience and outcomes. Do the Arabs not also fight amongst themselves as well as with the Greeks? <margin>Second disagreement</margin> Furthermore, just as Ptolemy rejects the ancient astrology, so Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), the most influential astrologer of the Islamic world, known to the West as Albumasar.</note> casts aside the astrology of Ptolemy—to the point that he says nothing can be read in Ptolemy's books that is consistent with either reason or experience. On the other hand, Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198 AD), the great Andalusian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> says that no one has spoken with reason in astrology except Ptolemy; he claims that if you look at the sayings of others, you will find them far removed from the truth, whereas the words of Ptolemy can in no way be found false. The Hebrews also disagree: the foremost of the Hebrews, Abraham <margin>Third disagreement</margin> Avenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167 AD), a multi-talented scholar whose astrological works were widely translated into Latin.</note>, disagrees with Ptolemy and often tears into Albumasar. Indeed, they [Avenezra and others] cast aside and repudiate his entire book, which in Latin is titled *On the Great Conjunctions*. If, therefore, the followers of Ptolemy are right, must not the ancient Arabs and their followers necessarily be liars? And if those books which they boast about were admired by everyone, why did they predict the truth? Was not Ptolemy necessarily an object of laughter in his own century, and Albumasar in his, and others who deviated entirely from their decrees? And yet, you will find it has always been the case that in every nation and every age, there have always been men who said that the truth was predicted by astrologers. This happened not by the truth of their dogmas, but by chance. Nor have there ever been lacking those who held this deception in mockery and contempt, or even in hatred. But whatever may have been the case in previous ages, certainly in our own time the truth of their dogma cannot be confirmed by the profession of its practitioners. They follow mostly bad authors and do not understand the good ones; moreover, they perform their duty so negligently that they are ignorant of many things they ought to know. They omit even more things that should be considered, sparing themselves the labor and hurrying toward the pursuit of money. If I had intended to teach astrology here rather than refute it <margin>Note</margin>, I would pour out a handbook of the errors of the younger men professing this art. But that is not my plan. However, it may be worthwhile to note a few things, so that it might become more manifest that they cannot predict the truth even if the dogmas of the astrologers were absolutely true.

->### Chapter VII. On the ignorance of the astrologers of our age.<-

These predictions of men are either universal—as when future good or evil is predicted for the whole world from the chart of the year, from eclipses of the sun and moon, or from the meetings of the superior planets—or they are particular, such as when something is divined about a person's fate from their own individual birth chart <term>genitura: a birth chart or horoscope used to predict an individual's life</term>. In the first category, nothing is more effective than an eclipse of the luminaries, from which, as the most universal causes, the most universal changes of inferior things occur. In the second category, nothing has greater weight than the calculation <note>original: "aequatone"</note> that is usually made concerning the span of life and the number of years. In both cases, it is wretched how much the modern and barbarian writers wander from the path. Their authority and usage are most powerful among our astrologers. Ptolemy writes in the second book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "apotelesmaton," referring to Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos* or *Judicial Astrology*</note> that in an eclipse of the sun, two places must be observed above all: namely, the <margin>Ptolemy</margin> place in which the sun is eclipsed, and the angle that most closely *follows* that place. For example, if an eclipse occurs in a new region of the sky, the angle of the tenth house should be observed; if in the eleventh or twelfth house, the angle of the east <note>The Ascendant</note> should be observed. This is because it is written there in Greek as "the *following* angle." However, in the common [Latin] translation, it is held as "the *preceding* angle." From this, a completely contrary sense is derived, which gave the barbarians an occasion for error. Thus, John of Eschenden <note>John of Eschenden (14th century), an English astrologer famous for his "Summa Anglicana." Pico uses a variant spelling "Astendensis."</note> <margin>John of Eschenden</margin> in that work which is commonly called the *Summa Anglicana*—which is held in the highest trust among our people—after he twisted himself in a long and argumentative question, finally defined according to the "opinion of Ptolemy" that the angle to be observed is not the one that *follows*, but the one that *precedes* the place where the eclipse occurred. That this is entirely contrary to the opinion of Ptolemy is clear from what we have said, because <margin>Error in Ptolemy</margin> it was written in Greek as "of the following," not "of the preceding." But because shortly after, Ptolemy...

<summary>Pico highlights the deep disagreements between major astrological authorities like Ptolemy, Albumasar, and Ibn Ezra, arguing their occasional successes are due to luck rather than science. He then points out a specific technical error where a mistranslation of "following" as "preceding" led modern astrologers to calculate eclipse effects incorrectly.</summary>

-># OF THE DISPUTATIONS<-

...you yourself explain how these angles are: he named the solar meridian and the eastern angle. Here the Greek interpreter <note>This likely refers to a commentator on Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, such as Porphyry or the anonymous Scholiast.</note> reminds us that the western angle is omitted because it cannot follow the location of an eclipse unless the sun is obscured beneath the earth; when that happens, they do not believe it has the power to effect future events. But if the preceding angle were to be observed, the eastern one ought to have been omitted by Ptolemy, which cannot precede the eclipsed sun unless it is beneath the earth; and the western one should be counted, which—whether the eclipse occurs in the eighth or ninth heavenly house <note>Astrological 'houses' are twelve divisions of the sky; the 8th and 9th houses were considered significant for death and travel/wisdom respectively.</note>—will always be found to precede and go before it. From this error, however, the whole method of predicting is changed, since nothing in predicting is more respected than the nature and status of the stars, both the place of the luminaries and that dominant angle; when one angle is exchanged for another, there will also be a different ruler. And through the diverse nature of the dominant star, the pronouncement about future events will always be varied, or rather, contradictory. Regarding the foreseeing of the span of life—in which these little diviners see nothing—

Abenzagel.
</margin>
I will show in a few words. Haly Abenzagel <note>‘Ali ibn Abi al-Rijal (d. 1037), a famous Arab astrologer whose work *The Complete Book on the Judgment of the Stars* was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages.</note>, the oracle of the astrologers of this age, says in the fourth part of his work that, according to the opinion of Ptolemy, there are five *Hylegh* <term>Hylegh: a Persian-derived term for the 'Giver of Life' point in a horoscope</term>. For so they speak:

Besides these, five planets are to be considered in those five places, holding right and authority. In the next chapter, speaking of what he calls the *Alchochoden*—

An 'aspect' is a specific angular relationship between stars that astrologers believe transmits influence.</note> it or not; and thus he repeatedly says many things about this *Alchochoden* according to the opinion of Ptolemy. Our astrologers, who follow him and other barbarians, are mired in the same error. They investigate what the *Hylegh* is

</margin>
and what the *Alchochoden* is, according to the opinion of Ptolemy, in every birth chart <term>genitura: a birth chart or nativity</term>. But in truth, in Ptolemy himself, this *Alchochoden* is as much a nothing as a "goat-stag" <note>A classic philosophical example of a mythical creature that does not exist in nature.</note> or a chimera. Read all his books, read all the interpreters, read even the barbarian <note>Again, referring to Arabic and Persian sources.</note> translations, and you will not find the word, nor any word corresponding to it, in his work. For this opinion—making one thing in the birth chart the *Hylegh* and another the giver of life and years, which he calls the *Alchochoden*—belongs to later authors. Neither Ptolemy nor those more ancient than him ever held such an opinion. He himself first lists the places which he calls *aphetic* <note>From the Greek 'aphetes,' meaning 'releaser' or 'sender forth.'</note>, which the Arabs call *Hylegh*; in Latin we can call them "dismissory" <note>original: 'dimissoria'</note>, so called because from there the course of life takes its beginning, as if from the starting gates <note>original: 'carceribus'. This refers to the starting stalls in a Roman chariot race.</note>. And those known places are above the earth or connected by some affinity to the setting point or the horoscope. Then he establishes the *aphetas*—that is, the releasers themselves—who, as if from those starting gates, bestow the impulse of life by their own "breath," so to speak; these he wants to be the Sun, Moon, Horoscope, the Part of Fortune, and the wandering stars [planets] ruling in those places. Besides these, by which all the *Hylegh* points are numbered, he makes no other distributor of years—though he thinks that what these "releasers" bestow can be either increased or diminished by the influence of fortunate or unfortunate stars. Yet the barbarians and our own people believe, supposedly following Ptolemy, that besides these "releasers" which they call *Hylegh*, there is another that determines the spans of life, which they call *Alchochoden*. Concerning this matter, as I was saying, Ptolemy himself says absolutely nothing;

<margin>
Haly
</margin>
yet, based on his supposed opinion, they seek, dispute, and define many things about it. And they err not only in this, upon which the whole sum of the matter depends, but also in the numbering of the *Hylegh* points themselves, since Haly says that the place of the preceding new or full moon is placed among them by Ptolemy. Yet whether the birth chart is nocturnal or diurnal, Ptolemy never thinks this should be done. What of the fact that this Haly accuses Ptolemy of contradicting himself, while greatly boasting about this "correction" of Ptolemy, in which he says no one has ever opposed him? He even gives great thanks to God, the revealer of secrets.

<margin>
Error of
Haly
</margin>
He says Ptolemy contradicts himself because he does not count the eighth house among the *Hylegh* positions because it does not "look at" [aspect] the horoscope. Yet in selecting the *Alchochoden*, Haly thinks it makes no difference whether it aspects the *Hylegh* or not. Why are you so foolish, you barbarian? Or what are you dreaming? Where

# AGAINST ASTROLOGY: BOOK TWO

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
...denials: Where in Ptolemy have you read about the <term>Alchochoden</term> <note>A Persian term adopted by medieval astrologers to mean the "giver of years," a planet thought to determine the specific length of a person's life.</note>? But I know what deceived him and the rest. Ptolemy places among the <term>Hylegiacal</term> <note>From the Greek 'hylech', meaning the 'releaser' or 'giver of life'; it refers to the specific point or planet in a birth chart that carries the life force.</note> planets those that rule in the other hylegiacal places; these men, however, think they are something different from the Hyleghs. They mistakenly added the new moon and full moon to the other four—the sun, the moon, the <term>horoscopus</term> <note>The Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>, and the <term>part of fortune</term>—believing only these should be considered for the Hylech, while the planets ruling those places should determine the years. And since Ptolemy never said it was necessary for the ruling planets to "look at" <note>An 'aspect' or specific angular relationship between planets.</note> the Hyleghs, they wondered why he did not think those two things—which they themselves consider to be two separate things: the Hylech and the Alchochoden—should be joined by the partnership of an aspect. Yet there is no fault in Ptolemy if he did not seek a partnership of aspect between things that are actually one. For in his work, whenever the sun or moon are hylegiacal, there will not be another planet besides them as the disposer of life; rather, the ruling planet is then used when the other Hyleghs have no authority in the granting of years. When this happens, no "commerce" can be left for the vital planet with any of the Hyleghs, because (to be sure) none other can be found. I do not know how these men failed to understand this from Ptolemy's words, or why none of them grasped it. Instead, they have all gone astray into this error in droves, so that there is no one who does not go looking for an Alchochoden and a Hylech according to what they *think* is Ptolemy's opinion. 

See how "true" the dogmas of the astrologers are, and how they are supposedly able to predict the truth about the span of life! Especially when the greatest error of all is added to those we have mentioned: they prescribe a number of years even from "Ptolemy’s opinion" for the planet that is the giver of life. According to that common saying among them, the sun has so many "greater" years, so many "lesser," and so many "middle"; the same for the moon, Mars, and the other stars. Yet Ptolemy rejects that Egyptian opinion, saying it has no rational basis. When he speaks of the span of life, he does not count years from the nature of the planets, but from the number of parts of the equatorial circle, according to the place of life—that is, the <term>divisor</term>—and another lethal or "interfecting" <note>Killing or life-ending.</note> point, which the course of an already failing life first strikes heavily. For example, when the <term>aphetes</term> <note>original: "aphetes"; the Greek term for the "releaser" or planet that carries the life force.</note> is placed between the boundary and the heights of heaven, that "walking" follows which the Greeks call 

-> <term>projection of rays</term> <-
<note>original: "radíosam proíectíonē"; a technical method of "directing" a planet to calculate time.</note>

But when it has declined from the peak toward the west, we use a progression drawn in both directions which we can call 

<term>hourly</term>. 

Our astrologers are so ignorant of all these things that even if they read them, I have no doubt they would think they were hearing monstrous tales. And yet we are miserably credulous of their predictions! While they promise us a "matted-grass" <note>A metaphor for a long, dry, or perhaps humble old age.</note> old age, we forget the Lord's voice commanding us to be ready, since we do not know the day of our death. If they threaten a short life, we are tortured with anxiety day and night, and the voice of a single "ranter" <note>Latin: "rabulae"; a brawling advocate or petty orator.</note> snatches all the joy of life away from us. <term>Halys</term> <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> says: if a fortunate planet is in the horoscope, it adds its "lesser years" to the years of life according to Ptolemy’s opinion. And yet, as I just said, in Ptolemy there are no "years of the planets," whether greater, middle, or lesser. When Ptolemy speaks of adding years, he follows an entirely different path, using the division of hours, which I think that man [Haly] did not understand. But one should not pursue every single point of Ptolemy, otherwise the book would grow to an immense size. 

Now, in those very questions which they call "interrogations" <note>Horary astrology, where a chart is cast for the moment a question is asked.</note>, do they not also err so signally that the entire reasoning of the answer is overturned by a single mistake? It is a common "preface" among them that the seventh place of the theme—that is, the <term>descendant</term>—is given to the matter being discussed. And yet Ptolemy prescribed that this place should be given not to the consultant or the matter, but to the <term>Mathematician</term> <note>i.e., the Astrologer.</note> being consulted. This is also what the Indian mathematicians observed; so much so that when the western angle and its lord were in bad condition, they would not answer the question, fearing an error. I could cite six hundred errors of this kind, were I not focused instead on declaring the entire profession to be in error. For recently, when I was comparing the books of Ptolemy with barbarian <note>In this context, Pico means Arabic or non-Latin/non-Greek sources.</note> and Latin authors, almost everything had to be "pierced with spits" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to be marked as false or censored.</note>.

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

### Chapter VIII. Concerning the lack of diligence among the astrologers of our age, which is so great that even if astrology were true, they themselves could not be true.

<margin>Bonatus</margin>
Indeed, how great is their negligence! You will find few even among those who have the method for calculation (which the greatest part of them lack) who do not flee to <term>ephemerides</term> <note>Tables showing the predicted positions of celestial bodies at regular intervals.</note> to obtain the true position of the stars. <margin>original: "Bonatus"</margin> <note>Guido Bonatti, the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century, whom Pico frequently targets.</note> Bonatus testifies to this in a certain place with these words: "the wise men of this art use the <term>Almanach</term>," for that is what the Arabs call the ephemerides. But those who do this must necessarily say many things incorrectly and omit many necessary things, which weakens the truth of all their predictions. For in those tables, there is almost never any indication of the <term>latitude of the planets</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic (the sun's apparent path). Without this, the exact time a planet rises or sets cannot be known.</note>. If this is ignored, where will the astrologer not err? Where will he not lie? 

If we consider the true decrees of this art, they believe the stars have the greatest power when positioned at the beginnings of the twelve celestial houses, especially the <term>cardinal points</term> <note>The most important houses: the 1st (Ascendant), 4th (Imum Coeli), 7th (Descendant), and 10th (Midheaven).</note>. Yet he will think they are in those places when they are not, and think they are not when they are, if he only observes the forward movement in a straight line and does not look at the lateral <term>declination</term> <note>The distance of a star or planet north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the stars. For when a star turns toward the north or the south, it both rises later and always moves more quickly than that part of the sign in which it is located. Thus, you will sometimes think a planet is above the earth when it is actually below it, and that one has already set which will still be clearly visible above the <term>finitor</term> <note>The horizon.</note>. 

While this creates error in every prediction, it makes them fall away from the truth even more when they investigate the hour of birth from the hour of conception. For if the moon happens to be near the west, it might be thought to have already set when it is still above the earth; and conversely, that it has not yet submerged when it is hidden below the east. This will cause one to wander from the truth by many days starting from the hour of conception. Who can rightly determine the "radiations" <note>The rays or aspects sent from one planet to another.</note> of the planets if the latitude is unknown? Who will rightly measure the "walking" of a star—which is called *peripatos* in Greek and commonly named <term>direction</term> <note>A technique used to "advance" a planet's position over time to predict when life events will occur.</note>? 

Since the declination of a star to either side of the sun’s path always makes the event of a matter either faster or slower by several years, how great is the slip in arranging the fixed stars! They commonly place them at the point to which they are carried in a straight line, but they completely fail to consider with which part of the sky they rise or set in different regions, or at the beginnings of which other houses they shine. Furthermore, ephemerides often show the position of the planets with little reliability, not only through the fault of the copyists but often because the author was insufficiently diligent or insufficiently <term>skilled</term> <note>original: "pītus" (peritus).</note>. 

I pass over the fact that different astronomers use different tables, sometimes poorly executed; even when a man has made his own diary, they often wander far from the truth in this current age. Everyone now rejects the tables of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The 2nd-century foundational authority.</note>; a great many of the more learned follow those of <term>Alphonso</term> <note>The Alfonsine Tables, commissioned by King Alfonso X of Castile in the 13th century.</note>, in whose "roots" <note>The base data points used for calculation.</note> it is now evident there is falsehood. 

But they are no less sleepy in choosing the <term>horoscopus</term> <note>The Ascendant.</note> and in grasping the beginnings of the twelve remaining celestial places. I have seen many of no small skill and good reputation in this profession use some sort of table of their own for distributing the twelve houses (as they call them), regardless of the latitude where the person was born whose <term>genitura</term> <note>A birth chart or nativity.</note> they were going to inspect. If they ever wish to be diligent by noting the difference in "climate" <note>The geographical latitude or zone.</note> (which only Alfonso shows them), they will hardly search out anything more exact beyond that. 

As for the declinations from the equator, the circumferences of the planets, their various sublimities in the shorter circle, or the fluctuations of latitudinal motions in eccentric orbits—who observes these now when judging birth charts? How many things do the younger ones not know about "equating the days" <note>The Equation of Time, correcting the difference between apparent solar time and mean time.</note>, and how many things do they say rashly? 

We have said all these things so that it might become manifest that this art of foretelling cannot be confirmed by the reliability of its predictions. Even if the theory were established as perfectly true, the truth about the future still could not be known because of the fault of the practitioners—that is, either their ignorance or their negligence. So, if this does not persuade you that no faith should be placed in astrology itself, let us at least persuade you, as it is said in the epigram, that "no faith should be placed in these astrologers."

->**BOOK TWO**<-

### Chapter IX. It rarely happens that what astrologers say comes true, which he shows by both external and domestic examples.

<margin>Interpretation of the fable of Icarus against astrologers</margin>
If these men were sane, if they were truthful—and I do not say entirely, but even for the most part—they would not only have avoided being cast out of cities and held in mockery by every prudent man, but they would have been held in the highest honor by every age and every nation. Such is the curiosity of men to know the future, especially concerning things that affect them; and for those who can provide this, there is naturally a great deal of respect and high opinion. Yet, while we read of statues being erected and public honors decreed for philosophers, doctors, poets, and generals, we never read of such things for astrologers. Instead, we read of them being expelled and laughed at, turned into a public fable. Indeed, the fables and allegories which are mostly drawn from common sense and life experience contained, among the ancients, a condemnation of this very vanity. For those who interpret Homer allegorically through the fable of Icarus <note>original: "Ichari." Pico references the myth of Icarus, who flew too close to the sun with wax wings and fell.</note>—who, committing himself to the thin air with manufactured wings, was cast headlong into the sea—say that the astrologers are meant by this. For, lifting themselves into the heavens on the wings of a reckless profession, while they are about to predict what will happen from their celestial dogmas (by which they seem to be raised up), they tumble into a sea of lies.

Why do we need other testimonies or conjectures when daily experience itself testifies to this? This is especially true in the one area where, if it could do anything at all, astrology ought to be most effective: predicting the changes of the air—namely, rain, drought, heat, cold, winds, hail, and earthquakes. In these matters, they are caught in falsehood so daily that the state of almost no day ever corresponds to their predictions.

<margin>Giovanni Pico's observation regarding the failed rules of astrologers</margin>
During this winter, in my small suburban villa where I have written these words, I observed every significant change in the weather day by day, while having the decrees of the astrologers right before my eyes. Meanwhile, the heavens favored me with such healthy weather everywhere that, in a continuous observation of over one hundred and thirty days, I saw no more than six or seven days that were such as I had foreseen in their books. I believe my friend Pandolfo Collenuccio <note>A famous humanist lawyer and historian from Pesaro, and a close friend of Pico.</note>—a man learned in the law but also most ingeniously educated in all literature—still remembers how much laughter a certain mathematician <note>The term "mathematicus" was frequently used in the Renaissance to refer to astrologers.</note> gave us in Bologna on this subject. He commanded us to expect copious rains on a day which the sun rendered entirely bright, clear, and serene.

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
Ambrose, in the *Hexameron* <note>St. Ambrose's "Six Days of Creation," a commentary on the Book of Genesis.</note>, says that when there was talk some days prior about a rain that was said to be useful, someone remarked: "Behold, the <term>new moon</term> <note>original: "neomenia." The first appearance of the crescent moon.</note> will provide it." Yet no rain fell until it was granted by the prayers of the Church, making it manifest that rain is not to be hoped for from the beginnings of the moon, but from the providence and mercy of the Creator. These are his words, by which both the vanity of astrology and the efficacy of religion are proven by the facts themselves.

<margin>Healthy teachings</margin>
Therefore, those who are less capable of reasoning and have enslaved their faith to these men can assert themselves into freedom by this path: let them repeatedly ask these men about the state of the weather. When they find that they almost always say false things about this, they will easily perceive that if these scoundrels <note>original: "nebulones." A harsh term for deceivers or "worthless fellows."</note> lie so much about the clouds, they will predict even more false things in judging the fates of men and peoples. For in the latter case, they are predicting things that are less subject to the heavens and far more difficult and laborious to foresee. 

Furthermore, if anyone examines the stories they daily fabricate about the <term>birth charts</term> <note>original: "genituris." The astrological configuration at the moment of birth.</note> of men for a mercenary fee, he will see that they lie much more than when they answer regarding the quality of the air. Unless I were to fear the fault of being inept myself while pursuing the ineptitudes of others in too much detail, I could bring forward many birth charts of both the living and the dead: the unhappy charts of the fortunate, and the exceedingly fortunate charts of the unhappy. In this matter, I surely tell no lie, for I know that the Divine Truth—under whose banner this present expedition fights—neither needs nor is delighted by our lies. But I will be content with certain domestic examples, by which I would especially wish to warn those who, having a promise of a long life from the "mathematicians," forget the voice of the Gospel warning us to "Watch..." <note>A reference to Matthew 24:42 or 25:13, "Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour."</note>

<summary>Pico argues that astrology's failure to predict simple weather patterns proves it cannot predict human fate. He uses the myth of Icarus as a metaphor for astrologers' hubris and cites personal observations and Church fathers to debunk their claims.</summary>

->**DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY**<-
->**II**<-

<margin>
Since he has given examples of many people regarding the follies of astrologers thus far, he now examines those of his own relatives.
</margin>

...lest the day of the Lord catch them unprepared <note>original: "dies domini occupet imparatos." A biblical reference to being ready for death or the second coming, used here to suggest that trusting an astrologer's timeline is spiritually dangerous.</note>. First, let us look at Pino Ordelaffo, the prince of Forlì, whom my sister Lucrezia had married. Girolamo Manfredi—the most singular astrologer of our age—had promised him total safety and a long life in the very year that he died. Yet it is hardly surprising that Manfredi failed to foresee the death of others, as he could not even foresee his own. Although he died this past summer, in the public almanac <note>term: "vaticinio." Specifically refers to the annual "prognostications" or almanacs published by Renaissance astrologers predicting the year's events.</note> for that same year—which proved fatal to him—he repeatedly promised that he would have many wonderful things to say in the following year. I do not know how he might now redeem his pawned credit, unless perhaps he looks down upon earthly things more truly from heaven than he once looked up from earth toward the celestial bodies. 

Then there is Pietro Attendolo, an ingenious youth who married Eleanor, the daughter of my brother Galeotto. He died last year, killed by the distress of a sudden and unexpected disease, though his astrologer—whom he trusted above all others—had predicted nothing of the sort, but had instead promised him a secure life. 

Consider also Costanza, the most beloved wife of my brother Antonio. When she departed this life in Rome two years ago, amidst the public grief of nearly the entire city, did she not testify to the vanity of this art? In the very year she left us mourning, she had received from an astrologer a promise not only of prosperous health but of a most happy and long life. Forgetting nothing of this, while she was drawing her final breaths and holding the hand of her weeping husband (whom she loved uniquely), she said: "Look, see how true the prophecies <note>original: "vaticinia."</note> of the astrologers are!" 

On the other hand, dear God, what evils, what heaps of trouble, and how many dangers did astrology threaten my brother Antonio himself with during that same year! And yet, having experienced no injury from the heavens, he lived with his family safe, his property intact, and his health sound—tossed by no storm of misfortune or danger.

And lest you think we are only measuring our modern astrologers, you should know that the same thing happened to the ancients. Seneca, in a certain passage mocking the most wicked Claudius Caesar, introduces Mercury among the gods arranging for Claudius's death. To tear down this vanity in passing, among other reasons Mercury uses to persuade the gods to allow the Emperor's death, he says:

<margin>
See the ridiculous.
</margin>

"Out of pity, you should let this happen for the sake of the Chaldeans <note>term: "chaldaeorum." A common Roman term for astrologers, referencing their supposed Babylonian/Chaldean origins.</note>, who for so many years now have been 'burying' him." That is, the mathematicians <note>term: "mathematici." In this context, it refers to astrologers who used mathematical charts for horoscopes.</note> were predicting every single year that Claudius would die, yet he did not die. When I read this, it brought to mind our own little diviners who say every year that the Roman Pontiff himself is about to die.

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
Cicero writes that the Chaldeans predicted to Pompey, Crassus, and Caesar that not one of them would die except in old age, at home, and in glory. For this reason, that most prudent orator says it seems a wonder to him that anyone exists who believes those whose predictions he sees refuted every day by reality and events.

### Chapter X. Why astrologers sometimes predict the truth.

<margin>V</margin>
But it does happen, occasionally, that what they predicted comes to pass. Yet, since there are many more things that do *not* happen, why should we not judge that they stumbled into the truth by sheer chance? What if there is no art so old-womanish, or of such vain superstition, that it could not be proven "true" by the same argument—simply because something predicted from it occasionally happens? Indeed, there is no art that does not achieve this, even one you might foolishly and randomly invent for yourself. 

Therefore, let those who are moved by such things tell me: do they think every divining art is true, or rather that many are vain and false? If they admit many are false, I will prove those "false" arts are "true" by the same argument: namely, that what they foretold sometimes happens. If they say *all* are true, I will demonstrate they are believing contradictory things, because different divining arts do not give the same answer about the same matters. 

For I have often—hundreds of times, in fact—tested this. When I had marked out a geomantic figure <note>term: "geomanticam." Geomancy was a method of divination involving the interpretation of markings on the ground or dots on paper.</note> for myself on a question and then drew an astrological chart for the same thing, one outcome appeared to me in the signs and another in the stars. If anyone does not believe this, let him test it himself and consult a Chiromancer <note>term: "Chiromantem." A palm reader.</note>, an Astrologer, and a Geomancer about the fate of the same man. You will see that almost always, the same thing is not designated in the lines of the hands as will be pronounced from the geomantic marks or the astrological planets. And if he looks at the actual outcome of the matter, he will find the truth more often where he least expects it—either because chance has more power where there is less reason, or because spiritual wickedness more willingly mocks us in those matters.

<summary>Pico provides several personal and historical anecdotes of failed astrological predictions (including those involving his own family and Roman Emperors) to argue that astrology is a fraudulent practice. He concludes that when astrologers are right, it is due to random chance rather than any genuine scientific or divinatory power.</summary>
