-># BOOK TWO<-

Furthermore, a multifaceted deception aids the predictions of astrologers, which is why their astrological judgments <term>apotelemata</term> <note>original: "apotelematō." Technical Greek term for the "outcomes" or effects produced by the stars.</note> seem to many to be proven by events more often than they are proven by truth. For if they must speak of the past—in order to show that such things happened as the heavens signified—nothing is lacking to them to ensnare ignorant minds. This is because there is no position of the stars, no birth chart <term>genitura</term>, in which a multifaceted constellation of both prosperous and adverse significance is not found. This is especially true since they have fashioned no fewer things for themselves in the heavens than the stars God formed there from the beginning. 

Therefore, they will always have a basis in past events from which to defend their positioning. It is rare, indeed, that they will not find in the planets whatever they wish; nonetheless, they make men both happy and unhappy in many ways, having more jurisdiction in celestial matters—that is, in their own rules—than in earthly ones. Thus, the location of the sky, or the goodness or malice of a sign, or the radiation of another star, or "love" with the sun, or "hatred" or "friendship" with the horoscope <note>In this context, the "horoscope" refers to the Ascendant, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> will always support them. Or, if these finally do not suffice, they will implore help from the stars—not the "wandering" ones <note>The planets</note>, in which they themselves never cease to wander—and if these do not suffice either, there will be plenty of "images of idols" ready for them, or Egyptian parts <term>partes aegyptiae</term> <note>A system of dividing zodiac signs into specific degrees assigned to planets, used in ancient Egyptian astrology.</note>, or the <term>antiscia</term> of Firmicus <note>A system of "shadow" points in the zodiac used by the 4th-century astrologer Firmicus Maternus.</note>, or the <term>dodecathemoria</term> <margin>The cunning of the Chaldeans</margin> of the Chaldeans <note>A technique where each sign is divided into twelve 2.5-degree segments.</note>, or some other entirely fictional thing of theirs. In these, they glory all the more as if they were secret dogmas, the more false and fabricated they actually are. 

In predicting the future, they have less opportunity for deception, although they do not lack for it even here. For they guess many things by observing the earth—as the saying goes—rather than the sky, bearing well in mind that saying of Euripides: <margin>The opinion of Euripides</margin> "The best prophet is the one who guesses well." <note>original: "qui coníícet ís uates optímus eſto." Pico translates a famous Greek fragment from a lost play of Euripides into Latin.</note> Generally, they announce certain things which almost cannot fail to happen, or at least cannot be thought to have failed. They put things forward ambiguously, in the manner of oracles. They say much, but always except something by which that which was predicted might be diminished, increased, or hindered. Thus, if it happens, you cannot say it was not predicted; if it does not happen, they are nonetheless considered truthful. 

You will rarely hear anything from them that is specific and certain; and when they dare such a thing, they either prove it by chance (which is very rare) or they are refuted by experience (which is very frequent). But it happens as that man said of the temple of Apollo: <margin>A note concerning the temple of Phoebus</margin> people remember and celebrate the successes, but no one recalls the errors. For those who favor them do not want these errors to be known, and those who despise them are entirely ignorant of both the successes and the failures. 

Yet it must not be overlooked what Augustine says—and reason persuades us—that through a hidden inspiration of demons, which they undergo without knowing it, they sometimes achieve a truth they would not otherwise reach. This should be considered the case if they announce some fact or word with a miraculous and specific prediction, which <margin>Ptolemy</margin> Ptolemy himself testified that the art of astrology could not provide. 

But someone will wonder how they can undergo this without knowing it, and yet we should think that whatever they predict is predicted through demonic inspiration. Indeed, this can happen in many ways, about which I will advise astrologers by using a similar case. It is admitted among them that one astronomer is "luckier" than another in attaining the truth, even if both have equal genius, learning, and diligence. Let them tell me then: what is this "luck"? If they do not track the truth by any other way than the dogmas of the art, and both have held those dogmas equally or better, one will not be equally lucky in predicting the truth. 

Furthermore, this is nothing other than this: since various constellations usually occur at the same time, and conflicting or diverse opinions of authors occur regarding the same constellation, the mind of the predictor is bent from heaven <note>Meaning, by a higher spiritual influence.</note> so that, in trying many things, he inadvertently falls upon the truth. This, therefore, could be a hidden and latent inspiration of a demon, by which someone is acted upon but does not perceive himself being moved. Since this is so, how it happens need not be explained more extensively now. 

But divine power and wisdom do not permit demons only this; they also permit that, through their own work, they make true what had previously been falsely predicted. Nothing is more fitting than that supreme justice exacts a punishment: that those proud minds who do not submit to divine truth should then bind their faith and their liberty to the lies of a single scoundrel and sycophant. 

But I think we have said enough now as to why these triflers sometimes seem to blurt out and scatter some truths. Nevertheless, as we said from the beginning, one should not labor too much over this matter, since those things which they predict as true—whether by chance or by cunning—are so few compared to those in which they lie that, <margin>Favorinus</margin> according to Favorinus <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who wrote a famous critique of astrology.</note>, that portion of truth is never found to be one in a thousand. 

**End of the second book.**

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA 
# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS.

### Chapter I. What was done in the preceding book: and what must be done hereafter: and in what order.

<margin>A</margin>
We wished to resolve the question of the people who repeatedly ask regarding astrologers: whence comes the credit given to their responses, if there is no solidity to their profession? I have called it a question because the more accurate and learned do not raise it. To them, it is well known that what astrologers say does not happen more often than not; rather, it happens rarely and whatever they might say is by accident. Nor, if a prediction comes true, can it be concluded that the art is necessarily true; just as it is not necessarily false simply because they lie most frequently in their predictions. For indeed, false things can be pronounced from true principles—not from the total falsity of the art, but due to an uncertain and conjectural opinion, or if the practitioner fails through ignorance or negligence. Just as, conversely, true things are pronounced from false ones—not through the truth of the dogma, but through cunning, or luck, or chance, or the hidden motion of foreknowing spirits <note>demons or spiritual influences</note> which predict, or from other causes which we sufficiently explained in the previous book. 

But if anyone cannot be persuaded, let him recall to memory how much we discussed a little while ago regarding the carelessness and lack of skill of the astrologers of our age—would that it were without hatred or envy. Nor could he (unless he desires to be deceived) be led to think that whenever they attain the truth, it was found by them rather than stumbled upon. This whole dispute will be settled by the following treatise, in which it shall be demonstrated that those things they predict from the heavens have no causes or signs there by which they are effected or indicated. Or if they are indeed done, they are nonetheless done differently than the astrologers think; or if even in that way, it is not from these causes in heaven nor from these beginnings of things on earth; then finally, even if all these things were certain, those causes cannot be grasped by men. Or if they can be grasped, perhaps they have not yet been grasped. When all this, I say, has been demonstrated, I think it will be beyond controversy for good minds that if an astrologer ever stumbles upon the truth, this can be attributed to no cause more truly than to anything but the truth of the profession.

<margin>Note</margin>
Which will clearly appear false for so many reasons, leaning on no true rational principles, but being fictional, deceitful, and therefore lying by its very nature. Therefore, let us now approach the refutation itself, examining first what constitutes the sum of the whole business: whether the heavens effect what these diviners pronounce from the heavens. This will be treated by us in such a way that in this book we maintain that the heavens act upon us only through motion and light; beyond these, it is futile to imagine other more hidden influences <term>afflatus</term> <note>original: "afflatus." Literally "breaths" or "inspirations," referring here to the "occult" or hidden spiritual forces astrologers claimed the stars emitted.</note>. Then, from that light and motion of the stars, nothing else is communicated to the "passive matter" <note>The physical matter of the Earth which receives celestial influence.</note> than motion, light, and heat—heat, I say, that consumes bodies in its general influx, and disposes those capable of life toward life and its functions. This flows from all stars; although it is not admitted that the "outflows" <note>effluvia</note> of all planets reach us. Indeed, that the stars bestow anything beyond this on lower things can neither be proved by reason, nor demonstrated by experiments, nor persuaded by the authority of the leaders of philosophy. Rather, all these things stand in the way, and we cannot understand that the power of celestial things pertains to sublunary <note>Everything below the moon; i.e., the Earthly realm.</note> bodies in any way beyond these common influences. Therefore, the particular properties of things—whether bodily, or those following the species, or the individual thing—do not have their origin from the stars (except by way of a universal principle), but from the proper nature of the things themselves and from their proximate and related causes. And we shall make this very opinion of ours asserted and probable by no other arguments more than those which the astrologers use against us. When that has been sufficiently explained, we shall then come to that treatise in the fourth book: that even if we grant astrologers that hidden powers exist in the rays beyond the effect of light and heat—whereby humans and the rest of nature might uniquely receive various gifts and powers—nevertheless, these are not the powers they think they are; and through the most suitable reasons and the consensus of all upright theologians and illustrious men, we shall cast doubt on what they divine from the heavens. When that work seems sufficiently finished, having reviewed the individual things they prophesy from the stars, we shall add and

### Chapter II. Five reasons by which astrology seems to be able to be strengthened.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
**T**he reasons by which astrologers attempt to persuade us that any changes of the sublunary world <note>the earthly realm "below the moon"</note>—and indeed the diversities of all things, as well as fortuitous events and the characters and talents of men—depend on the stars, are these principal ones. There is a single voice among theologians and philosophers that the inferior world is governed by the heavens. This most common opinion of Aristotle teaches that it is necessary for this lower world to be contiguous <note>touching or connected</note> to the superior motions: so that all its power may be governed from there. Thus Aurelius Augustine also said that these grosser bodies are ruled and moved through more subtle bodies. Who then, they ask, would doubt that any changes in earthly things are caused by the motions of the superior bodies? Who is ignorant of the power the moon has over all bodies, especially more fluid ones? ...extrinsic, but have an affinity with them, just as a wife’s resources have with the body, or dignity and honors with the soul. For this reason, he brings forward no other causes for why Saturn performs these things, Jupiter those, and Mars truly others, except that Jupiter is a hot and moist planet; Saturn is dry and cold; Mars is more dry and burning. He feels this way regarding the "wandering stars" <note>the planets</note> and the fixed stars alike: judging the fixed stars from the nature of the planets, and the planets from the nature of the primary qualities. Indeed, others might leave behind these primary qualities and flee to occult <note>hidden or non-obvious</note> powers and more eminent forces; it would not be fitting to doubt that many such highly effective powers exist in the celestial bodies. 

<margin>The Fourth Reason.</margin>
If we behold any singular and excellent gifts in earthly things, we are accustomed to consider them the gifts of heaven; these do not follow from the elementary qualities from which those bodies are composed, but rather from a virtue infused into them from heaven. How much more, then, will those most noble bodies not lack such powers and properties—bodies of such clear light, such vast bulk, and such rapid motion? Or in what way, if they transmit [influence] to the earth along with their motion and light, will they not be the producers of marvelous effects among us?

<margin>The Fifth Reason.</margin>
Finally, there is the course of human affairs, about which the divination of astrologers most especially seems to persuade everyone—even the unwilling—of the power of heaven and fate. In this, the variety itself is familiar and most frequent; then we see many things happen beyond the powers of our mortality, many things contrary to reason and merit, and most things outside the order and established condition of human life. It seems these can have no causes elsewhere than in heaven. This man is fit for philosophy; that one is born for poetry; another, scorning letters, handles either civil business or arms more willingly and successfully. From where does that variety of talents come? There is one who makes nothing of riches; there is another who sells his soul for profit; this one is sober, that one is not; this one is bold, that one is fearful. From where comes such great dissimilarity in character?

<margin>Alexander</margin>
Alexander the Great conquered the East as quickly as he saw it; from where came the impulse of such great success? What force first unlocked the secrets of nature for Aristotle, his teacher? What force did so for Plato, and before him for Pythagoras, Socrates, and the rest? This reasoning is too great for them to be believed to have sprouted from the earth. 

<margin>The course of fortune must be observed.</margin>
Again, who would not ascribe those things to the fortuitous courses of the stars? That an innocent man is condemned, while the guilty is gifted with rewards; that the industry, skill, talent, and learning of many are left to wither; while otherwise, idleness and wickedness are enriched. That a pirate, bloodied by slaughter, after a thousand perils of sea and land, finally dies at home among his own in old age; while a most mild and patient man is slaughtered by the swords of those who did not even wish it? Then there are certain portents and monsters of intellect, either those rejoicing in foul things or, to put it simply, those wandering outside the laws of humanity. Do they not seem to testify to that force and necessity of a fatal power? These are the things with which the lives of mortals are filled, persuading many that these vicissitudes of good and evil—deserved or undeserved—and such a great variety of things are caused by the motions of the stars, by whose impulses fragile and fleeting mortality can only with difficulty, or never, resist.

## Chapter III. The first reason is turned back and it is shown that heaven is a universal cause and not to be referred to the variety of individuals.

<margin>The first retortion of the reason.</margin>
<insert>W</insert>e have been careful not to weaken these reasons of the astrologers, but rather to strengthen them, so they might not complain that they have been defrauded. However, we first wish the reader to know that even if these reasons were granted, it does not therefore follow that any "astrology" <note>meaning the practice of predicting specific human fates</note> could exist, which will become known in the following books. But we do not grant them these points; indeed, we take from these very same places valid arguments against them. For regarding the first reason: as soon as the astrologers have said that every inferior motion depends on the motion of heaven, they immediately contradict their own dogma. For from that, it follows (a common saying among philosophers) that heaven is the **universal cause** of inferior effects. But a universal cause does not distinguish effects, nor is it asked why *this* happens or *that* happens; rather, that is asked of the **proximate causes**, which are varied and... <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "universal cause" like the sun provides the energy for growth, but the "proximate cause," like the specific seed, determines if a lily or a weed grows. Pico argues the stars are too general to be responsible for specific human choices.</note>

# BOOK THREE

<margin>Of individuals</margin>
<margin>Astrology</margin>
<margin>Gemini</margin>
<margin>By itself</margin>
<margin>not by force</margin>
...are different <term>through</term> <note>original: "per"</note> the difference and variety of their effects; and since among these things one cause does one thing and another does another, the universal cause does all things with all things. Although this appears clearly in things of diverse nature and <term>species</term> <note>the general category or "kind" of a thing</note>, it is a wonder how they do not understand that the same must be believed much more regarding the variety of <term>individuals</term> <note>specific, singular beings within a species</note>. For the more a thing is particular and draws its origin from matter, the less it can be referred back to a cause that is chiefly formal and universal. And who does not see that heaven generates a horse with a horse, and a lion with a lion? Is there any position of the stars under which a lion is not born from a lion, or a horse from a horse? Why, by the same reasoning, will heaven not produce different sons with different parents, even if under the same or a similar constellation? This is proven by experience itself: for we see those born at the same hour and under the same inclination of the heavens are nevertheless most different in fortune, character, and body. At this point, the astrologer cannot avoid a blow. For they are accustomed, when the birth of <term>Gemini</term> <note>twins</note> is cast against them, to flee to the <term>Nigidian wheel</term> <note>A famous argument by the Roman scholar Nigidius Figulus, who used a spinning potter's wheel to argue that even a tiny delay between births results in a massive change in the heavens' position</note>. In this, it is not possible to mark the same place twice with ink; but here they explain themselves poorly, since they cannot grasp that difference of a rapid moment from which they nevertheless want there to be such great "lordship of fate." Wherefore, while they try to defend the efficiency of heaven, they fall into other snares, so that they must confess they cannot have knowledge of that efficiency in detail. Furthermore, we do not only throw twins in their faces—where the tiny delay that occurs after one comes out after the other offers them a small handle for responding—but rather those born at the same moment from different parents, yet within the same latitude and longitude of the same region. For these births, the astrologer must describe the same "theme of heaven" <note>a horoscope or natal chart</note> and pronounce the same things, both regarding what will happen after the hour of birth and what happened to them even within the mother's womb—since he thinks that just as they were born at the same hour, so they were conceived at the same hour. What will the astrologer answer regarding these? For since the constellation is entirely the same, yet the fate of each will not appear the same. Or will he be able to say anything else—unless he be insane—than that those celestial influences, though universal in power and strength, are determined and distinguished by <term>proximate and secondary causes</term> <note>immediate physical factors like genetics, environment, or human choice</note>? But if this is so, how do they promise that they will give the cause of all the variety of individuals from the exposed hour of the stars at birth? Why this one is snowy white, that one black; this one with a short body, that one tall; this one with a slow wit, that one clever; this one pleasing to all, that one troublesome; this one born for <term>philosophy</term>, that one for trade; this one rich, that one destitute; this one short-lived, that one long-lived? All this variety of individuals under the same species is far less caused by heaven than is the diversity of species under the same genus—as when now a lion, now a man, now a donkey, now an elephant is born. For just as these [species] follow the specific difference of proximate causes, so those individuals follow either the difference of seeds (if we consider bodily qualities or wit), or education and will (if we consider the soul), or the faculties of parents and one's own choice, prudence, and opportunities (if we consider external and fortuitous things).

### Chapter IIII. How heaven acts by motion and light, and how it is the universal cause of meteorological elements, minerals, and living things.

<margin>What heaven is</margin>
**Q**uickly then, as much as a universal cause is more divine and eminent than particular causes, so much more truly and honorably do we think of heaven than the astrologers do. To make the reason for its universal efficiency shine more brightly, and to explain more clearly what heaven does and does not do, we must begin from a deeper starting point: to speak of the nature of heaven and its actions toward inferior <note>earthly</note> bodies. Heaven is a natural body, the most perfect of all natural bodies. Both motion and sensible quality follow a natural body; therefore, the most perfect motion and the most perfect of sensible things belong to the most perfect of natural bodies. No motion is more perfect than <term>orbicular</term> <note>circular</note> motion; no quality perceptible by sense is more perfect than light. These, therefore, will be the properties of the celestial body.
<margin>Perfection in circular motion</margin>
For which reason, heaven is also of an unfading substance, since its motion and quality have no contrary; but also because, as the most perfect body, it must also be in the first place—that is, the highest—to which the first motion must also be owed. For what is first in each genus is the cause of the rest contained under that series...

He then begins a physical description of the heavens as a perfect body characterized by circular motion and light.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
...although not all things have the same relationship to their cause. Therefore, that which is moved by the <term>first motion</term> <note>The "Primum Mobile," the outermost sphere in ancient cosmology that sets all other spheres in motion</note> moves the rest; if that motion were to cease, the others would not continue. Just as in the <term>smaller world</term> <note>The microcosm, or the human body</note>, if the motion of the heart were to stop, all the motions of the animal would necessarily perish. For this reason, Aristotle rightly said in the eighth book of his *Physics* <note>original: "physicae auscultationis"</note> that the motion of the first heaven is the life of all things, since the most evident and common operation of life is internal motion. Therefore, this single dignity and efficacy of the heaven toward the lower world is such that by its tireless agitation, all other motions are both ordered and excited.

<margin>The action of the heaven is a universal motion.</margin>
That this efficiency is <term>universal</term> <note>meaning it acts on everything generally rather than specifically</note> and does not distinguish between lower motions by this reasoning is clear enough; for just as it acts upon a clod of earth falling downward, so it acts upon a flame moving itself upward. One and the same celestial motion cooperates equally with all motions of every kind. Another of its prerogatives comes from light; for since light is the highest quality of bodies, it is the first grade of life for corporeal nature.

<margin>How the heaven acts upon us through light.</margin>
And since the highest order and the lowest extremes of the superior order almost touch, it necessarily follows that light possesses a certain perfecting power over bodies and holds something of a vital nature—not that light itself lives or brings life, but it prepares and disposes the body capable of life for living. This is because its proper quality, heat, follows light. This is not a "fiery" heat, nor an "airy" heat, but a celestial one, just as light is the proper quality of heaven. This heat is most effective and most healthy, penetrating all things, nourishing all things, and moderating all things. This is the chief gift of the heaven by which bodies are perfected and living things are disposed toward life, in addition to the agitation of <term>circular motion</term> <note>The paths of the planets and stars</note>, which is necessary not only to bring that light and heat down to us and to impart it to the earth in more or less quantity with wonderful opportuneness, but also so that we, being moved, might be rendered more receptive to the heat that flows perpetually from a body in constant motion. We perceive the power of this most beneficial heat in the entire world of <term>corruptible things</term> <note>The earthly realm where things are born and die, unlike the eternal heavens</note>, both in things just beginning and things completed, in things with souls and things without. Indeed, it contains and preserves the elements just as their location and form do; like a craftsman, it is absent from nothing, but diffuses itself intimately through all things. And just as it is the privilege of the first motion to turn the rest of the motions (which could not move without it), so it is the privilege of this perceptible quality that without it, other qualities can do nothing. Therefore, if they were deprived of celestial heat, coldness could not act as cold, nor could heat act as heat. For that stellar heat is not contrary to cold in the way that fiery or airy heat is; rather, it contains all elemental qualities by a "simple eminence," just as the nature of the heaven contains every body, and just as circular motion contains all motions.

<margin>For Pythagoras was diligently engaged in mathematics and especially in arithmetic.</margin>
It is just as light contains all heats, and as the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the essence of all things</note> would say, just as unity contains all numbers. Thus, those who deny that cold elements can be preserved by the heavens—unless the stars also influence them with coldness in addition to heat—are deceived. For they would say that the heaven preserves hot things by heat of the same nature and reason, but in truth, it preserves all things equally—hot, cold, moist, and dry—by that quality of its own which, while it is none of those four qualities, nevertheless encloses them all within itself. They are not present as they are in the elements, but in the way that a "multiplicity" is concluded within "unity" by a principal power. Through this power, it rules them so that it unites each thing to itself by preserving it, and preserves the whole within them by moderating all of them, and produces other things from them by mixing them all. But the name "heat" is deceptive; when we hear it, we immediately understand something opposed to coldness. Yet, elemental heat is indeed closer in nature to that celestial heat than elemental coldness is, just as it is also more perfect.

<margin>Whence the deception came.</margin>
But this in no way prevents the celestial heat from being exalted above the properties of both elements, encompassing the power of both.

<margin>A suitable analogy.</margin>
When we say "brightness," we seem to mean something opposed to dark or black color. Yet no one would deny that black color is preserved and made effective by the brightness of light just as much as white is, even though one is closer to the nature of light and even shares a common name with it (as it is sometimes called "bright"). Finally, if the substance of the heaven, as the <term>first body</term> <note>In Aristotelian thought, the "fifth element" or ether that makes up the heavens</note>, contains every body most perfectly and in power, then its proper quality must necessarily contain every corporeal quality in power and perfection. This is what we call "celestial heat," the offspring of light; we call it heat because it warms vitally, and through all the properties of the elements, that heat approaches them...

<summary>Pico explains that the heavens influence the earth through universal motion and a "celestial heat" that transcends the four basic elements. He argues this celestial heat is not the opposite of cold but a perfecting force that sustains all physical qualities, much like mathematical unity contains all numbers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument from Book 3 of his "Disputations Against Astrology." Having established that celestial motion is a universal cause, he now focuses on "celestial heat" as the primary tool by which the heavens influence the four elements, specifically addressing the formation of meteorological phenomena and critiquing astrological overreach.</meta>

# BOOK THREE

It is most closely associated with it; thus, when it degenerates from its celestial condition, it operates through this <margin>Celestial heat</margin> celestial heat above all other qualities. Together with their proximate causes, it both generates and nourishes them. Just as the heat itself is the proximate and essential cause—for although it is heat and is called such—it nevertheless rules, digests, preserves, shapes, and moderates all the matter of the offspring, whether that matter be hot or cold.

Therefore, if anyone should ask me whether the heaven produces coldness by its own nature <note>original: "per se"</note> or only incidentally <note>original: "ex accidenti"</note>, I will respond: if you ask what the heaven does by itself with no intermediate cause, I say it produces nothing except heat through its light. Other qualities are produced incidentally, just as heat itself produces coldness by accident, as we shall declare in the following chapter. However, if you ask what it does as a universal cause acting with secondary causes, it produces coldness as much as heat, and dryness as much as humidity. It no more generates water with water than it generates fire with fire; nor could water generate water, nor fire generate fire, any more without the heaven. When it generates the elements, it also generates those following properties. Therefore, it produces coldness with water and heat with fire. 

If we were to deny that anything other than heat is produced by the heaven in this way, those absurdities would follow which <margin>Thomas is argued against</margin> **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> mentions: that coldness, dryness, and humidity would not exist in the universe by their own nature, but only incidentally, and that not all substantial forms of the lower bodies would be contained within the power of the celestial bodies. These consequences do not follow at all when we deny that the heaven, by itself and from itself, makes the air or other lower bodies cold. For this reason, those arguments of **Thomas** prove not what we deny, but what we assert.

<margin>How celestial heat produces meteorological phenomena</margin>
We have seen what the heaven does in the elements, and here we have first confirmed its efficiency. Let us descend to other things which are made from the elements. Therefore, that same heat, the <term>son of light</term> <note>A poetic term for celestial heat, which Pico identifies as the active force derived from starlight</term>, stirring up vaporous breaths from earthly bodies, thinning the thick and dissolving the dregs, creates those things which occur on high. These vary according to the diversity of the matter that is raised upward. For if vapor is raised from a fluid body, it creates <term>moist impressions</term> <note>Atmospheric phenomena like rain, clouds, or mist</note> in the middle or lowest region of the air. If it is raised from a dry and terrestrial body, it is a fiery evaporation which, rising to the upper regions adjacent to the <term>ether</term> <note>The "fifth element" of the heavens; Pico refers to the friction between the elemental sphere of fire and the rotating heavens</note>, necessarily grows hot from the proximity of the motion and fire. 

The celestial heat operates all these things, whether they are cold or hot, since they all come from vapors which heat alone draws out. Therefore, heat produces everything, and universally all things—not through a variety of constellations as the <margin>Aristotle</margin> astrologers <margin>Plato</margin> falsely claim—but according to the matter and the place in which they are generated. This is made known from the books of **Aristotle** on *Meteorology* <note>original: "metheorologis"</note> and the *Timaeus* of **Plato**. 

For this reason, when **Aristotle** was about to treat this part of nature, he brought forward that common saying: that the lower things are continuous with the higher ones so that all their power might be governed from there. This can be truly accepted as a universal principle from what we have said regarding celestial motion and heat, by which all things are moved and cherished. However, this was said by **Aristotle** specifically regarding meteorological impressions, which he was then primarily discussing. To prove or explain what he had said, he added this: that the lower things are the matter of all things, while the heaven is the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The force that acts to bring something into being</note>.

<margin>Weariness of the interpreters</margin>
I wonder, however, that certain interpreters labor so hard to defend **Aristotle** from the accusation that he said every lower power is governed by the heaven—as if our human liberty were endangered by these words! They do not see from the context of the words that what is said about the "world" refers only to the elements. For it is most evidently clear from the sequence of the speech; after he said that he had determined in his previous four books that there are four bodies below the heaven (Fire, Air, Water, Earth), he then adds: "Since, therefore, this whole world around the earth consists of these bodies, whose affections we are about to discuss, this world is by necessity continuous with the higher motions, so that all its power may be governed from there." 

Therefore, the "world" whose entire power he said is governed by the higher body is this very mass of the four elements. No other world is continuous with the higher motions, nor was he about to discuss the "affections" of any other world in that book. Certainly, there is no mention there of plants or animals, but of those things which occur in the elements, such as comets and other impressions, and whatever common passions of air and water there are, as he himself prefaced in the introduction shortly before. Therefore, let our "diviners" <note>A mocking term for astrologers</note> cease to use this philosopher in their annual prophecies...

<summary>Pico argues that celestial influence acts as a "universal cause" primarily through heat and motion, rather than through specific astrological dictates. He clarifies that Aristotle's claim about the heavens governing the lower world refers specifically to physical meteorological phenomena and the four elements, not to human fate or biological specifics.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<note>The first word is likely 'Philosophers', but only 'losophers' is visible due to cropping.</note>
[Phi]losophers offer testimony as a sort of veneer and support for their deception—and yet, in that very book, the most prudent Aristotle <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, which discusses the formation of the natural world.</note> detracts from astrology, since he seeks the causes of neither rain, nor earthquakes, nor other effects of this kind in the stars, but in matter. Because of the variety of that matter—and not because of the diversity of the constellation—the heat of the sun affects things in different ways. Thus it is <margin>The heaven as the cause of minerals</margin> in meteorological impressions <term>meteorological impressions: in the Renaissance, this included not just weather, but any phenomenon in the "sublunary" sphere, including the formation of minerals and metals</term>. Perfect bodies lacking life, such as gems and metals, just as they coalesce from inferior matter, are also refined and formed by the power of that radiant heat. Nor does it stand in the way that we said this heat proceeds from light, and yet light <margin>Objection</margin> does not reach certain subterranean places in which these kinds of most precious mixtures are generated. For if <margin>Solution.</margin> that opinion of certain Platonists is not true—that light penetrates all bodies <margin>Opinion of the Platonists.</margin> because of a "diaphanous" quality, even if it is not seen in the densest bodies where it is packed tight or in the thinnest where it is dispersed—certainly it should not be denied that the heat diffused from light can reach where the light itself does not penetrate. Just as the heat of a fire can be felt through a wall although the flame itself cannot be seen, so there is nothing to prevent the light, poured into the movements and caverns within the earth, from being repelled from entering by the opacity and density of the body (which are not suitable conditions for receiving light), but nevertheless sending its heat inside. For although such bodies cannot be illuminated, they can nevertheless be heated, and even more so than those which are thin and transparent. How truly the mixture of these things is made by the heaven, and how again by secondary causes, <margin>On the solution regarding living things</margin> we shall say in the solution to the fourth reason.

The remaining things are those that are said about the breath of this heat, by which power <margin>The heaven as a cause of living things.</margin> [living things] are [governed]. Almost as we gathered a little while ago, since that quality holds the highest rank in bodies, the heaven possesses it so that it may perfect the bodies we have described, so that it is placed most closely beneath life. It joins the extremes together: life to the body and the body to life. Wherefore, in all living things, between this <margin>The spirit is the medium between what is seen and the soul.</margin> coarser dwelling place that is seen and the soul, the fountain of life, there is a medium which we call "spirit" <term>spiritus: a subtle, invisible substance, akin to a "vital breath," that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</term>. It is a very thin and invisible body, most closely related to that celestial light and heat. Life is present in it primarily, and through it, life explains and diffuses its powers into this visible and earthy body. Thus, in the seminal matter, there lies hidden this kind of spirit, whose mystery is used especially by that more divine power, the Architect of vital works. Acting in place of the soul, it flows down into the water <note>original: "aqua"</note> and propagates the species of the generator into the matter it has occupied. However, these spirits are not useful for either generating bodies, or preserving them, or performing the duties of the senses, if they are destitute of the work of the celestial spirit (that is, the heat of which we spoke). Because it is more mobile, purer, and more effective—and therefore closer to life—it strengthens the weakness <margin>The heaven is not proven to be alive because it enlivens living things</margin> of the inferior spirit and, by its commerce, restores the kinship to the soul. Thus, it is no longer an argument that the heaven is alive because it enlivens those things which live by its rays; for all these things live, indeed, through their own souls. They propagate through the power of the soul implanted in the seeds, with the heat of the heaven favoring them—not as if it were the giver of life, but because it disposes them most conveniently and closely toward life for the reason we have stated. No one would say that the power of seeing, which comes from the soul, is in the light or exists through the light, even though we cannot see without light. This could also be proven by other reasons for the non-life of the heaven, as discussed by us in the *Concord of Plato and Aristotle*. Thus it is clear that in the corporeal world nothing indeed happens without the heaven; nevertheless, that this or that thing happens is not from the heaven, but from secondary causes. With all of these, the heaven produces such things as the causes themselves were born to produce, whether they pertain to the species or to the individual.

### Chapter V. Beyond the common influence of motion and light, no special power resides in the celestial bodies.

<margin>Whether the celestial spheres act on us by heat.</margin>
The effusion of this heat is common to all stars, since it follows the entire celestial nature just like light. But whether it belongs to the spheres is doubtful; for if they are not luminous, they are not propagators of this heat. If they are luminous, it may be that because of their thinness, the light becomes invisible, or it becomes very little effective toward us, as Avicenna writes in the *Book on the Heaven* regarding those stars which come under our sight. It cannot be doubted unless we equally take away from them their celestial nature and the gifts of light. Therefore, besides motion and light (which through said light is life-giving heat), what other powers...

# BOOK THREE

...that influences reach us from the stars; nor does any experience show us—as we have seen and will see more aptly in what follows—that other corporeal or effective qualities are present in them. It appears that the heaven is able to fulfill its office everywhere enough through its motion and heat-producing light. <margin>Aristotle</margin> Thus, Aristotle said nothing else except that we are affected by the heaven through motion and heat; this is what Averroes and Plotinus—great men, each in his own school <note>Averroes was the preeminent commentator on Aristotle (Peripatetic school), while Plotinus was the founder of Neoplatonism.</note>—most firmly asserted. Indeed, as far as "cold-producing" influences are concerned, reason seems to strongly deny them. <margin>The Opinion</margin> For those who hold the opposite view, when they are convinced that all light is a producer of heat, are accustomed to decree that all stars that shine are productive of heat by a certain general property common to all; but then, through their own specific powers, it is granted to them that this star bestows dryness, that one cold, and another moisture. Thus, they say nights during a full moon are warmer because the more abundant light heats more. Yet they claim this does not prevent the moon, by its own specific influence, from either cooling or moistening the air.

I therefore ask them: do they believe this heat, which they admit is common to all stars just like light, is the kind we have described—containing <term>eminently: a philosophical concept where a higher cause contains the powers of lower effects in a superior, unified way</term> most eminently all **four qualities** <note>The four qualities of classical physics: hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note>? And therefore, do they believe it is productive of all things through secondary causes, but by itself is only diffusive of itself? Or rather, do they believe that other conditions are not contained in it, but only heat? And that cold, as a thing different from heat, flows from some other particular power of a certain star? Whichever they choose, they fall, unless I am mistaken, into no small difficulties.

If they answer the first, I will press them thus: it is not consistent with any specific reason—and if they wish it to agree with the specific nature in the stars—to say that something is more imperfect than that which belongs to it from its more common nature. This is because a specific difference always adds a degree of perfection to the common definition. But a quality that contains every quality is more perfect than one that is only effective of cold. <margin>An effective reason</margin> Therefore, if that [perfect quality] must be granted to all stars by a common and general condition, a cold-producing influence will not be granted to any star from its own specific nature.

Therefore, the other part of the division remains, in which they must necessarily be no less stuck. Indeed, nothing belongs to a thing from its specific nature that is repugnant to those properties belonging to it from its common nature. For example, if it belongs to a human insofar as they are an animal to have sense, "stupidity" <note>In this context, a lack of sensory perception or "insensibility."</note> cannot belong to that same human insofar as they are human. Or, if it belongs to a thing insofar as it lives to have an internal principle of motion, it could not happen that, insofar as it is this or that living thing, some reason for innate immobility should apply. Rather, a particular degree distinguishes that which is in the common definition. For instance, if it is the nature of a living thing absolutely to be moved not just from without but from within, it must be the nature of an animal (which is a species of living thing) to be the internal principle of some operation; and again, the nature of a rational being (which is another species) to be the principle of another internal operation.

Therefore, by a similar example: if that life-giving heat follows the celestial nature insofar as it is celestial, then an effective power of coldness and dryness—which are qualities contrary to life—will not follow the peculiar nature of any star. This is how we argue against them.

<margin>Solution to the arguments of the opposing side.</margin> The reasons for the opinion of the opposing side have been partially solved, and will be further dissolved in their own places later. For they thought it followed that cold elements could not be preserved by the heavens, and that the other qualities would only exist in the universe by "accident" resulting from heat. Furthermore, they thought it would not be true (as is believed) that all **substantial forms** <note>The essential nature or "soul" of a material thing that makes it what it is.</note> of bodies are contained in the power of the celestial nature. All these things we have already dissolved in the preceding sections.

There is also the point that in these places many things are generated by celestial action to which the light of heaven nevertheless does not reach. Two points remain: one, that the air cannot be changed so suddenly from heat to cold—and intense cold at that—as experience shows, unless it is believed to be the work of a coldness coming from a new **constellation**. The other point is how the moon, when it is moved below the earth, and even below the lowest parts of the earth, moves the tides of the **ocean**, which the lunar rays certainly do not reach then, unless it acts through an "influence" distinct from both light and the heat that follows light.

These matters will be dissolved later: the first in chapter 13, where the changes of lower things by the sun will be treated; the other where the cause of the ebb and flow of the ocean will be widely disputed by us. Here, we will only satisfy those who ask how the moon affects us during the **interlune** <note>The "new moon" phase when the moon is between the Earth and the Sun and invisible.</note>, since it does not illuminate us at all during that time. <margin>Galen</margin> Galen says that just as it does not illuminate, so it does not affect us in any way...

...affirms that it is in conjunction with us; for this reason, he makes the lunar month twenty-six days and twelve hours, which is the number of days the moon’s light reaches us with efficacy, while it remains hidden under the sun's rays for about three days. The moon acts upon us when joining the sun in the same way that something acts by doing nothing; for bodies deprived of its light are harmed, but as it waxes <note>The "adolescent" or waxing moon refers to the period between the new moon and full moon when its visible light increases.</note>, it nourishes them more fully and fills them with moisture. If we believe that the moon possesses its own light, however dim and thin—from which, if it is not entirely overwhelmed and lost in conjunction, one might believe that it retains some efficacy from that light.

### Chapter VI. That the light of the moon, like that of the sun, is life-giving; and that neither produces cold or moisture except by accident.

<margin>
Aristotle
Avicenna
</margin>
**I**f, therefore, as we have said, all these things are brought together, this celestial heat is the vital craftsman of bodily things. Nor is there any reason to believe that other "breaths" <note>Pico uses "flatus" here to mean specific occult influences or "spirits" attributed to the stars by astrologers.</note> are inspired into earthly bodies by the stars, lest we attribute more to those higher bodies or less to these lower ones than is proper. Likewise, let the reader recall this: whatever a better nature rules in a secondary nature, by the very fact that it proceeds from that source and is admitted according to the capacity and condition of the receiver, it must necessarily become something else. Because it is inferior to its first origin and mingles with a foreign and alien nature, it becomes "worse"; since it is affected by many impressions from elsewhere, it is necessarily infected and confused by a collection of many influences, having received them in a better place. 

Accordingly, there is no doubt that this very thing happens to this celestial heat whenever it is received into the sublunary mass: it falls short of its natural action and perfection. This happens in two ways: first, although it is always healthful by its own nature, it sometimes becomes harmful due to the weakness of the receiver. Second, although it produces none of the elementary qualities <note>The four "elementary qualities" in Aristotelian physics are hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note>—being different from them by its own unique property—it nevertheless degenerates in an elementary environment into elementary actions, especially that of heat. This is because it naturally approaches the nature of heat more closely (just as it does at night). Therefore, it often acts not so much as celestial heat, but as fiery and elementary heat is accustomed to act. 

That this occurs not from its own nature but from a defect of the matter is evident (to set aside reason for a moment) because when it finds a matter related to itself among sublunary bodies, it is found to be always beneficial and life-giving, yet heat-producing. For indeed, there is no matter more like it than the <term>spirit: a thin, clear, and mobile vapor arising from the blood</term>, which corresponds in proportion to the heaven, as Aristotle and Avicenna write. The heat of the heaven always nourishes and strengthens this spirit, such that the heat is to the spirit almost what the spirit itself is to the denser body. If the heat harms the spirit at times, it does so for no other reason than the weakness of the receiver; the proof of this is that by the same ray, a weak thing is harmed while a stronger thing is invigorated. So that here it is true that "to him who has, more shall be given, and from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away" <note>original: "hñ tī datū nō hñ tī auferri & id qd hēt"—a reference to the Gospel of Matthew (13:12 or 25:29), applied here to physical health and the reception of light.</note>. Therefore, it is not from the sun that harm comes, for otherwise it would not have benefited the other.

<margin>
Why Aristotle, in the book *On Generation and Corruption*, rightly perceived the power of the sun.
</margin>
Rather, it comes from the debility of the matter, which collapses under the weight of such great goodness due to its own sickness. Otherwise, those things that are equal to the sun’s rays would acquire more life and vigor the more they are exposed to the sun. For this reason, no one should think that either a devouring heat or a life-opposing dryness flows from the sun, just as one should not think that the moon causes suffocating dampness or excessive flux, or a numbing cold. 

Otherwise, the moon's light as it waxes would not aid the innate generative power in things by which bodies flourish and grow along with it. Nor would the full moon be useful for conception, as Hippocrates writes in his book *On the Eight-Month Parturition*, increasing fertility in the female and making the male fertile. Nor would Aristotle speak truly when he says the moon is a principle that—being higher and a "lesser sun"—contributes to all generations and perfections. For how could these things be true if its light were not by nature nourishing, vital, and fertile, just like that of the sun and other stars? For this property belongs to them all, just as the celestial property is common to all. 

But (as we were saying) just as this celestial heat sometimes becomes excessive through the weakness of the patient <note>In this context, the "patient" is the physical object or body receiving the influence.</note>, so too, through the elementary nature into which it descends, it almost turns into elementary heat; thus you would not easily recognize it as celestial, except in those spiritual corpuscles which we have declared to be most similar to the heaven among all bodies. For when infused into these, it perfects every mixture and the works of the soul.

<margin>
Hippocrates.
Aristotle.

Note the effects of the sun.
</margin>

**BOOK THREE**

...the means for perfecting the soul, it serves everywhere; falling upon other hard, rough, thick, watery, and dross-filled bodies, it degenerates from its celestial property and behaves much like elemental heat itself. If this heat is powerful, it burns, dries, and reduces to ash. Conversely, if it is thin and meager, it causes a flux and dissolves moisture. This happens to celestial heat according to the condition of the matter; hence the opinion arose that the sun causes dryness and the moon increases moisture, because the sun's heat is more burning, while the moon's is more lukewarm. 

But in suitable and related subjects, the sun's ray will not dry out healthy moisture, nor will the moon generate useless or harmful moisture. Instead, each star will work according to its own nature, although the moon does more mildly what the sun effects more intensely. However, "by accident" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accidental" effect (per accidens) is one that is not part of an object's essential nature, but occurs due to external circumstances or the specific material it acts upon.</note> and through the infection of foreign matter, it happens differently for them: for the sun to dry and the moon to moisten. For when the sun's rays are closer to us—as in the northern signs—or strike us at more direct angles—as at midday—or when they gather in concave, rough, and stubborn places, being squeezed and repelled, they leap back; by a fiery property acquired through such violence or infection, they dry and scorch the bodies they strike. 

In turn, the moon, with its meager and thin heat, if it touches a moist and fluid body, dissolves the moisture it finds there and makes it more fluid. She does not bring that cold and watery moisture herself, but rather dissolves with her own heat what she finds in a watery and cold body, drawing it out and spreading it. For this is the nature of heat: if it is stronger, it consumes the moistures it draws out of bodies; if it is weaker, it draws them out (because it is the same healing heat), but because it is weak, it fails in the effort and does not consume those it has drawn out. Thus, "by accident," the moon moistens excessively and the sun dries; but both also produce coldness by accident.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
For as Aristotle writes, both are principles of cold and heat, and the movement of these stars holds the limit of both the beginning and the end of those qualities. How this is to be understood, the same author declares elsewhere: for he says the sun produces winter and summer throughout the whole year, and the moon does the same throughout the month. 

<margin>Whence the coldness of the sun and moon arises, according to Aristotle.</margin>
But there is this difference: in the sun, this happens through its approach and departure; in the moon, it does not happen in this way, but rather one occurs in the waxing light and the other in the waning. Thus, when the sun departs far from us, it leaves us to the cold, and so it is said to "make cold." Similarly, the moon, when it is stripped of its light at conjunction <note>Conjunction refers to the New Moon, when the moon is positioned between the Earth and the Sun, making it appear dark from our perspective.</note>, is said to make things cold—not because it brings cold, but because it protects us from the nocturnal cold less than at other times. 

Furthermore, it is worthy of examination that Aristotle, in those same books on the *Generation of Animals*, says the times of the waning month are moister and colder, even though it is commonly agreed that moistures dry up as the moon ages. I would resolve it this way: when the moon is waning, moisture thrives, but it does not come from the moon; rather, it comes from the lower elements which the moon resists less, being weakened in heat and hiding for the greatest part of the night below the horizon. Therefore, that moisture is also watery, unhealthy, and excremental <note>In medieval medicine, "excremental" refers to waste fluids or "superfluities" that the body's natural heat has failed to process or "cook" properly.</note>. 

Hence, as the new moon approaches, many vapors are raised like a harvest of rains, and menstrual cycles often flow more fully, as Aristotle writes in his *Histories* and *On the Generation of Animals*. In the adolescent <note>The "adolescent" moon refers to the waxing phase, from the new moon to the full moon.</note> moon, however, moisture increases—either because the moisture already in bodies is made more fluid, or because a more life-giving moisture is added by the benefit of lunar heat. For in this way, 

<margin>What arises from lunar increases</margin>
Aristotle thinks that from lunar increases, sea urchins <term>echinos (sea urchins)</term> and living things of that kind become fuller for no other reason than that, since they are cold (as they lack blood), they grow warm more vitally when pregnant with the moon's more abundant light, and thus they digest <note>Original: "concoquant." In Galenic medicine, "concoction" is the process by which the body's heat matures or "cooks" food and humors into useful substances.</note> better; hence they necessarily become more succulent and substantial. 

Therefore, moistures flow both when the moon is waxing and when it is waning, but they are of different kinds: good when waxing, and bad when waning. From this it is most clearly evident that the moon does not moisten because it is cold and humid (for such moisture increases when the moon is waning), but because it is healthily and life-givingly warm; for under the abundance of its light, those bodies become moister and more robust—and not moist in any other way than by the power of heat and the help of a nourishing force, and by what is characteristic of the moon: drawing humors from the innermost parts to the extremities. 

<margin>Haly Hamec</margin>
For this reason, bloodletting is also most conveniently performed then; thus Haly Hamec <note>Likely referring to the 11th-century Arabic physician and astrologer Ali ibn Ridwan (known in Latin as Haly Heben Rodan).</note> erred greatly among astrologers when he said that veins should be cut while the moon is waning. Let us, therefore, conclude with certainty...

<summary>Pico argues that the moon's influence on moisture and temperature is a result of its life-giving heat acting differently across its phases, rather than inherent coldness. He differentiates between the healthy moisture promoted by the waxing moon and the stagnant, "excremental" moisture that occurs when the moon's light is absent.</summary>

Having previously argued that celestial influence is primarily light and heat rather than "occult" qualities, he now addresses the contradictions in how astrologers classify planets as 'cold' or 'moist' and critiques the theories of the medieval scholar Abraham Ibn Ezra (Avenazra).</meta>

->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

<margin>Another cause of solar and lunar cooling</margin>
...moisture increases together with the moon: because by its influence, the healthiest moisture is increased, not loosening bodies with flux or killing them with cold, but rendering them firmer and more lively. This is attested by that experience confirmed by the consensus of all physicians: those who fall ill at the start of the month bear the injury of the disease more strongly; and those who are already proclaimed to be dying <note>original: "conclamati iam animam agunt" — a Roman expression for those whose death is so certain that people have already begun the ritual shouting of the name to ensure life has departed.</note> can hardly be deserted by life as the moon ascends. But both the sun and the moon can cool us, not only by withdrawing their light but by affecting us (though this is also an accidental effect). The sun indeed cools when it kills through excessive drying, or draws vital heat outward, or generates rains from marine vaporous breaths which it raises more than it dissolves: or by stirring winds, or for other reasons. The moon, however, with its thin heat, thins and opens the passages of the body more widely, letting the nocturnal cold (also thinned by its rays) enter into us more abundantly. Hence—where many are deceived, thinking the moon cold—comes that torpor and coldness for those sleeping under lunar rays: for which the weaker ray of the star makes a path into the body for the air occupied by earth and water during the night. In this way, they both cool and dry, falling now on hard bodies, now on those dripping with watery thickness: and the rays of the stars, by their own nature only healthily heating, moisten. They are also harmful sometimes, not by their own fault, but by the weakness of the recipient.

## Chapter VII. The dogmas of the astrologers cannot be defended as Avenazra thought, even if all stars are considered hot.

<margin>Opinion of Abraham Avenazra regarding the heat of the stars</margin>
**B**ut someone will say it would be enough for astrologers if, in this way, this star causes dryness, that one moisture, and another other qualities. For Abraham Avenazra <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish polymath, poet, and astrologer whose works were highly influential in Latin translations.</note>, a great man in the astrological profession, contends that stars are only producers of heat, nor can it be believed otherwise of bodies that are bright and in perpetual motion. But some stars are called "cold" because they do not impart as much heat as is sufficient for our temperament; thus Saturn is accused of cold because, placed far from the earth and being smaller than Jupiter, it fosters the lower nature more tepidly than is necessary; and therefore, when it is the lord of a birth <note>The "ruling planet" in a person's horoscope at the time of birth.</note>, it signifies death not because of an impressed cold, but due to a lack of heat. I, for my part, praise Avenazra for thinking correctly about the heat of the stars, but he loved his profession too much, not foreseeing that its dogmas necessarily conflict with that truth.

<margin>Against Avenazra in a specific opinion</margin>
For let it proceed in Saturn as he said—that it be held cold because it is insufficiently hot, and therefore kills—in the remaining stars, this reasoning does not proceed; nor does it proceed everywhere in Saturn. Since when a planet is only slightly hot, it moistens by its approach (as we have declared) and does not dry out; yet the astrologers contend that Saturn is "dry." Furthermore, will it not immediately and evidently follow that all the fixed stars, especially those below the first magnitude, are "colder" than Saturn, since they are both smaller than it and more remote from the earth? And a star is not called "cold" in this theory otherwise than because it is insufficiently hot. Therefore, the "Heart of the Lion" <note>The star Regulus in the constellation Leo.</note> will be a cold star, which nonetheless is decreed by astrologers to be most blazing. Then, among the planets themselves, if we wish to examine which star heats us more and which less according to this principle received from Avenazra, we shall gather nothing consistent with the sayings of the astrologers.

<margin>What factors produce heat in the stars</margin>
For nearly three things produce heat in the lower world: the magnitude of light, density, and proximity. But it is not clearly explored how much magnitude weighs against density, or density against magnitude, or how much proximity itself outweighs either or both in the stars. Therefore, for those wishing to reason, the matter will be in uncertainty, nor can the senses judge, since they do not perceive the rays of the others besides the sun and moon. And this is the first obstacle for the astrologers, whose art is worth nothing if the powers of the celestial rays remain in ambiguity. But for those wishing to follow conjecture, something entirely different will appear than what they themselves determined: for to those considering the mass, the rays of Mars will be thought less hot than those of Saturn and Jupiter; [but others] might reply that they are hotter because they come from closer and from a compaction of light; I say it is in no way credible that these things could do so much. Furthermore, with the smallness of its disk, so that Saturn is almost fifty times larger, should it be numb with cold while Mars is burning? Otherwise, if so little is taken away from the efficacy of the light...

<meta>Catchword: ...of the light of the body (luminis corporis)</meta>

...the smallness of the body. Truly, she adds so much through the proximity and abundance of light that we are warmed more by Venus than by any star besides the sun and moon. When the nurturing heavenly Cytherea <note>original: "citherea" — an epithet for the goddess Venus, who was said to have been born from the sea near the island of Cythera.</note>, laughing with nectar, shines far and wide, she alone among all the stars casts a shadow. Nor is any star closer to the Earth than Venus—though according to common opinion, the size of Venus's orbit does not exceed its vastness—and yet many astrologers count her among the cold stars. Likewise, they do not doubt that all are greatly surpassed in heat by Jupiter and Mars, which is a great falsehood. In this matter, if they refer back to their imagination of the body, it is done with little reason; for since Jupiter's disk is not much larger than Venus's (if that vastness is properly considered), nor is it much closer to the Earth, they nevertheless define it so that Jupiter warms far more than Venus, and Saturn far less. Indeed, they say Venus and Jupiter nurture bodies, while Saturn kills them with that coldness of his.

### Chapter VIII. An objection against what has been said.

<margin>
S
</margin>
But let it be as someone might say: that the differences of the rays are neither known to astrologers nor can they be known; this pertains to another question. Now we must see whether this diversity can exist in the rays: so that while all stars might be naturally hot and life-givingly warm, yet due to the abundance or lack of light—or its thinness or efficacy—one star compared to another might be called "cold" and "contrary to life." And one might be called "dry" and another "moist," whether this happens by its own nature or by contact with elementary matter. For if something prevents this—even though the heaven is a universal cause—since it nevertheless behaves differently through continuous motion, it might cooperate differently with the lower causes through the various dispositions of the stars. Thus, not all the variety of effects would come from the lower things themselves, but would also happen from the various dispositions of the universal cause itself, especially if stars differ from one another not only in the quality or quantity of light, but by their other gifts and peculiar properties (as the fourth reason <note>Referring to an argument likely presented in an earlier chapter or book regarding the "occult" properties of planets.</note> put forward against us). For then it seems possible that through the motion and heat common to all stars insofar as they are celestial, that common efficiency must also be produced. But through the particular <term>influences</term><note>Latin: "influxus" — the "flowing in" of celestial power, a core concept in astrology Pico is critiquing.</note> that follow the specific natures of the stars, something more particular might occur. By this, the same star might vary the works of the lower world considerably, depending on its position and relationship to other stars, to the places in the sky, and to earthly bodies. Thus, the first argument of the astrologers would still stand, referring the very diversity of effects to the celestial bodies.

### Chapter IX. The objection is resolved, and it is shown that neither the specific nor the individual differences of things depend on the movement of the sky.

<margin>
O
</margin>
This is a timely objection, bringing to mind many things that we might object against them in turn; and it is generally true that the more a bad cause defends itself, the more it betrays itself. On the contrary, just as truth shines brighter the more it is shaken like a fire, so we shall satisfy this point. We shall first declare what the diversity in celestial influence is, whether according to the diverse nature of the manifold stars or the various and revolving changes of the same star. We shall say what evidence or natural reason prescribes regarding these through necessary demonstration. For how much our adversaries err on this point requires more work than can be finished in passing. Therefore, it will be treated in the following books. Here, when it has been sufficiently explained how much a constitution can differ from a <term>constellation</term><note>Latin: "constellatíone" — the arrangement of stars at a given time.</note>, we shall see how much authority that diversity has in varying the lower effects. From this, what we ourselves intend will be confirmed: that the primary, substantial, and almost total distinction of things comes from secondary causes. The fallacy of the astrologers, who profess a prediction of this kind of distinction from celestial causes, will be further exposed. We have said the heaven acts upon us through motion and light. Through motion, it is believed to do three things: to move, to heat, and to bring light. This third point must be treated later when light is discussed. But as for what they say—that it heats by its own motion—this is a difficult question and must be discussed separately in the books of philosophy; for it pertains little to the astrological matter. Indeed, we have explained above how it moves by motion: namely, while all motions...
