Having previously discussed light and heat, he now shifts to "motion" as a potential source of astrological influence, citing classical and medieval authorities to argue that the speed or complexity of a planet's movement does not dictate its specific effect on human affairs.</meta>

<page-num>801</page-num>
<header>DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY</header>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

Everything depends on the first motion, just as the movement of an animal depends on the motion of the heart. Let us see, therefore, as far as motion is concerned, whether different stars move in different ways, and whether the same stars move differently at different times; then we shall look at their light.

<margin>
The difference of stellar motion
</margin>
The movements of the stars differ for a triple reason: First, because some move faster and others slower. Second, because some move with more movements and others with fewer. Third, by the position of the region in which they move, because some occupy higher seats than others and traverse larger spaces. 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose physics and cosmology dominated medieval thought.</note> does not believe that the multitude or fewness of motions contributes to the diversity of things produced or moved. Rather, he believes it happens according to the dignity of the movers: a more noble mover achieves its goal with a few motions, while a less noble one requires many. Regarding their speed or slowness, nothing has been sufficiently explored. For Aurelius Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer; his commentary on "The Dream of Scipio" was a primary source for medieval astronomy.</note>, imitating the ancients, asserts that all planets proceed at an equal pace; 
<margin>Macrobius</margin>
<margin>Auenazra</margin>
Auenazra <note>original: "Auenazra" — Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> agrees with this, placing the Sun, Venus, and Mercury in the same sphere, though separated by the positions of their <term>epicycles</term> <note>Small circles on which planets were thought to move while those circles themselves moved along a larger path (the deferent).</note>. However, those who claim the planets are unequal in speed disagree among themselves. 
<margin>Alpetra.</margin>
For Alpetragius <note>original: "Alpetragius" — Al-Bitruji (d. 1204), an astronomer who challenged the Ptolemaic system.</note> argues that those which seem faster are actually slower; others, conversely, observe the time it takes for a planet to return to its starting point. This must necessarily be deceptive unless one examines the proportion of their delays and the spaces they travel with great care. But however the matter stands, if indeed they produce heat by their motion, a faster motion will produce more heat. As for that "primacy" of motions we mentioned, this can produce no variety, since the lower motions depend on the motion of the heavens. Insofar as that first and circular motion is concerned, it matters nothing whether it is slower or swifter. A stone would not move downward, nor fire upward, if the heavens were at rest; but the stone does not descend more quickly, nor the fire ascend more quickly, simply because the heavens revolve more rapidly. It only receives from the heavens the impulse to move, just as any living thing receives its motion from universal nature. A thing's "species" <note>In this context, its essential nature or category.</note> changes according to its own substance; its decrease or intensity comes from the mover, from impetus, from shape, and from other similar conditions. Therefore, Saturn will not move us differently because it moves more slowly, nor will Mars because it is considered faster; for what the astrologers say—that slower planets grant their effects more late—will be refuted later. 

<margin>Note</margin>
For now, we maintain that nothing else is given by them through their motion except that we ourselves are also moved. This certainly happens no differently from them whether they are driven around more slowly or more quickly. Furthermore, concerning the same planet, there is no reason to doubt that we are moved by it in different ways just because it moves differently at different times; for it is a firm dogma of the philosophers that celestial motions are always similar to themselves and equal. It is not permitted for the stars to suppress or turn their course, even if it appears so to us; that appearance is referred by mathematicians to <term>eccentric circles</term> <note>Orbits where the center is not the Earth, used to explain why planets seem closer or further away at different times.</note>, or to various motions struggling against one another, or to other things of that kind. The only diversity that could exist is that those stars brought lower by their epicycles might affect us more favorably because they are closer; but this is more discordant with the decrees of the astrologers than in agreement with them, as will be explained more fully in what follows.

<margin>
Question
Opinion
</margin>
Concerning the dignity and rank of the movers or the bodies that are moved: how is it that they all act together in the things that happen? Does one mover do one thing and another mover another? For there are those who think that everything that happens is done by the proximate <note>The "nearest" or most immediate cause.</note> cause, and that the higher causes do nothing else except move that proximate cause to act. They believe that with so many intermediate causes interposed by nature, it is not that one cause does one thing and another does something else, but that the effect is produced in its proper order. Since an effect cannot occur except from a known cause, and since that cause is too weak due to the bonds of matter (by which lower things are more strictly bound) to move without being moved itself, it was necessary for as many intermediate causes to intervene as there were ranks of dignity in the order of causes. Therefore, these people believe the same thing is done by many causes, not because they each claim one part of the work for themselves while being connected by an essential bond, but because in order to act as the same thing, one is necessarily moved by another in a triple series.

<margin>
Another opinion.
</margin>
There are others, on the contrary, who would have it that the higher and lower causes do *not* do the same thing in the things that are produced. Instead, they believe that because a substance contains degrees of perfection in its work, that work also depends on causes that are ranked step-by-step in their perfection of order. Therefore, the more common aspect in a work belongs to the more common cause—that is, the more excellent the cause, the more universal its effect. Thus, they believe created things have the fact that they *are* from God; that they are *substances* from the next cause in line; and again, that they are *bodies* from the cause following that...

He critiques various astronomical theories of his time, including those of Aristotle, Macrobius, and Ibn Ezra, regarding the physics of the spheres.</summary>

...until it reaches the thing's own specific <term>species</term> <note>original: "spem," a contraction for "speciem," referring to the defining characteristics that make a thing what it is</note> and nature: which refers back to its own and closest cause. Whichever way we look at it, it is clear that not only individual differences but also the specific differences between things do not come from the heavens, at least insofar as we are considering the efficiency of motion.

## Chapter X. That stars other than the sun and moon do nothing, or certainly very little, to affect us.

<margin>From the mover</margin>
We have spoken of motion; what remains is to speak of light. But first, it is necessary to recognize certain differences between the action of the stars on us through motion and the action that occurs through light. The power of the former <note>motion</note> belongs to the mover and the souls of the stars; the latter <note>light</note> is attributed to the stars themselves or rather their spheres. In the case of motion, the lower things depend more on a higher soul, since there is no doubt that the planets are subjects of the first circle's motion, and that the sun is primarily rotated along with the rest. Regarding light, the opposite is thought, with almost all physicists agreeing that not only the moon but also the other planets are illuminated by the sun. Furthermore, things that are higher move us more, since in their power the other movements are directed; but if other things are equal, the influence of light upon us is more powerful from a closer location. 

However, it is not clear—as we shall demonstrate—whether the lights of the higher bodies act upon us at all, or if it is only the moon and the sun, while the others, up to this point, do not reach us with any effect, either because of the smallness of those bodies or their distance. Regarding motion, there is no doubt that the higher bodies are more powerful. From all of this, it can be gathered from what the philosophers say that everything is linked and hangs downward in a certain essential order, a series, and a kind of chain. This efficiency of motion belongs to this chain most of all, since this troop of orders and causes is understood more in the moving souls than in the bodies. Its unique property is that second things depend on the first, and the higher cause has more strength and power than any lower one; indeed, if the higher were to cease, the lower would not act. However, we do not deny that the heat of the sun stands in the relation of a cause to the heat of seeds <note>original: "feminiales calores," likely meaning "seminal" or reproductive heat</note> in the essential order of the higher; but that order does not extend further. Therefore, the connection of causes from the first to the lowest through intermediate steps, of which they speak, is not found here. But in the movers, insofar as they are movers, that series is found more completely. 

Nevertheless, one can observe a nearly fourfold progression in both. In motion, that sphere or the universe which revolves in daily agitation holds the first place; this motion is shared with all others. Then follows the chorus of the planets running in the opposite direction along the poles of the zodiac; in this, there are no further degrees to be distinguished, since they neither move each other nor are they moved by each other. Therefore, as if a single mobile body is snatched by the "first mover" <note>the outermost sphere of the universe in Ptolemaic astronomy</note>, it is moved by its own motion, which <margin>Plato</margin> Plato calls the "motion of diversity." It moves the ether, and the highest air, and so in the fourth step, the motion reaches us and the lower bodies while all the particular motions of natural things are nourished from there.

In light—and when I say this, I always mean the heat flowing from light—the sun is the eye of the world and the source of all influx. <margin>The Inflow of the Sun</margin> Here, the sun illuminates the moon, the moon affects the air, and the air affects all the bodies that live under and in the air. But there is a difference: we are moved by the first mover through the planets, but we are illuminated by the sun in a different way than through the moon. We review all these things primarily so that, before the discourse on stellar "inflows" <note>the supposed streaming of celestial power into the world</note> begins, we may know it is not established whether those higher inflows—whatever they may be—actually reach our region. 

<margin>Opinion</margin>
Astrologers might believe regarding all planets (except the sun and moon) what is believed about certain smaller stars. Since the primary objection to this opinion could be that celestial bodies are the "essential causes" of lower things—an order in which nothing can be idle—I wanted to declare that this order pertains to the moving powers rather than the illuminating bodies. Indeed, the astrologers cannot say that the stars were created by God in vain simply because their "breaths" or influences are not felt, lest they be in vain. <margin>Doubt</margin> Otherwise, perhaps this sublime candelabra <note>the night sky</note> radiating with so many lights was not made primarily so that, bringing light to our nocturnal eyes, it might illuminate the sun-fearing <term>lucifugis</term> <note>original: "lucifugis," meaning light-shunning; used here to describe the dark burrows of moles</note> beds of moles. But why so many huge stars if the sun and moon alone suffice for us? <margin>Solution</margin> This was appropriate to the nature of heaven; the order of things and the perfection of the entire universe demanded it. Nor, if they do not all illuminate us...

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS

<margin>The reasoning of Averroes and Aristotle</margin>
...it follows that no other use or benefit can come to us from there. <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher who reconciled Aristotelianism with Islam</note> argues in this way: The Sun and Moon act upon us; therefore, since all the others are of the same nature, [they must act as well]. This form of argument is pleasing, and it tastes of <term>Aristotle</term>, who also argues thus: the Moon does not move by its own motion but with its sphere, as its spots declare; therefore, the same must be judged of the others, since there is one nature

<margin>See how Pico takes up the argument against the astrologers</margin>
shared by all celestial bodies. Wherefore, following in these same footsteps, we shall conclude as follows: The Sun heats; therefore, the Moon does too, since they are all of the same nature. And we conclude rightly, because reason itself proves that the conditions of all are the same insofar as they are considered absolutely in themselves. But when you compare them to other things, because they are not compared in the same way, reason wavers. For if the Sun is going to do the same thing by its nature as Saturn, it does not follow that both do the same thing toward us, because one is compared to us as near, and the other as remote. Thus, those who would say that only the Sun and Moon act upon us have reasons they might offer for their suspicion, even though the nature in all celestial bodies is the same. For three conditions of a shining body primarily create the effective action of light upon us: size, density, and proximity. All these concur preeminently in the Sun; for it is closest to us—especially if it is placed above the Moon, as the ancients and, after Ptolemy, <term>Geber</term> <note>Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century astronomer</note> and <term>Theon</term> <note>Theon of Alexandria, 4th-century commentator on Ptolemy</note> contend—and it has a body so vast that it exceeds the largest of the stars by more than a <term>sesquialter proportion</term> <note>a ratio of 1.5 to 1</note>. Furthermore, it is seen with the densest light, the most radiant of all.

<margin>Note</margin>
<margin>Geber, Theon</margin>
<margin>The size of the Sun</margin>
The Moon is so close to our regions that it cannot fail to affect them, and consequently its light is necessarily effective, which is almost nothing other than solar light. You will not find these conditions in the other stars such that what you granted concerning the Moon and Sun, you must also grant concerning the rest. But perhaps the very distance will stand in the way of the lights of the eighth sphere and the largest stars; that same distance will stand in the way for the stars of Saturn and Jupiter, which, just as they are closer to the earth than the fixed stars, so they are also smaller than them. For they report that the fixed stars contain the mass of the earth one hundred and seven times; but Jupiter contains it ninety-five times, and Saturn only ninety-one. These things are not said with the utmost precision; and if we follow experience, we see that none of those fixed stars, though of such vast size, are felt by their rays at night. And even if Saturn and Jupiter radiate upon us along with them above the horizon, Mars decreases much more in body than it approaches in proximity;

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
for it has a proportion to the earth a little larger than sesquialter, so that one Sun would contain almost a hundred Marses. For the Sun is one hundred sixty-six times larger than the earth. Therefore, why would he <note>the astrologer</note> say such absurd things? Why, having confessed by the testimony of the senses that the powers of the Sun act upon bodies, would he believe it possible that the powers of the star Mars reach these things, when it is so much smaller and more remote from the earth? He might believe the same of the star Venus, which is perhaps even more remote from us than the Sun and certainly far smaller than the earth itself, of which it is thought to be not even a twentieth part; for Mercury is smaller than the Moon, just as it is also more distant from us. Wherefore, what wonder that the senses feel so little of this star, which is also so rarely seen? To which, nevertheless, astrologers are accustomed to attribute very much. But Aristotle seems to support those who think this way: who indeed, when he deals with motion, mentions all the stars, as in the book *On the Heavens* <note>original: "de caelo"</note>, and especially the supreme motion as in the last book of the *Physics* <note>original: "physicæ auscultatōis"</note>; since, namely, all bodies are moved by these motions. But when he speaks of that life-giving heat that cherishes things, and perfects generations, he makes mention either only of the Sun—as when he said "man is generated by the Sun and man"—or of the Sun and Moon, as in the books *On the Generation of Animals* <note>original: "de aīaliū gñatiōe"</note>. So that if anyone were to contend that this was Aristotle's opinion, he could be refuted by no sayings of his philosophy.

<margin>Pico's Opinion</margin>
We assert not so much that, as this: whatever reaches down from the other stars is so thin and meager that perhaps the air is softened only slightly by the nocturnal lights of the stars so that it becomes more suited for generation. Although if anyone were to credit all generation to the Sun alone, he could so decide: that what the Sun performs by its light during the day, it also performs at night through 그 light reflected to the Moon as if to a mirror, whence it is reflected back to Earth. Nature most wisely disposes these turns, since earthly weakness could almost never endure the Sun's rays continuously; therefore, it receives them at night through the Moon, more broken and weaker, and therefore more accommodated to its own infirmity; so that they are neither plainly deserted by the life-giving light, nor do they fail, as it were, under its full intensity.

<summary>Pico argues that the physical influence of stars depends on size, density, and proximity, concluding that only the Sun and Moon have significant effects on Earth. He uses astronomical measurements and Aristotelian philosophy to demonstrate that the other planets are too small or distant to exert the powers astrologers claim.</summary>

<margin>The Sun colors the world</margin>
...[it shows] how and in what way the Sun returns to us more healthfully in early spring, after it has been far off all winter, than if it had hovered near us continuously. Indeed, our fragility is so pressed by the goodness of heaven, if it be too much,
<margin>most fittingly</margin>
that even the moon herself does not always reflect solar rays back to us in her entirety; but now more
<margin>above a whole</margin> <note>likely referring to the moon's phases or a full measure of light</note>
sparingly, now more abundantly, according to her <term>schematisms</term> <note>original: "schematismeis"; the relative positions or aspects of celestial bodies</note> toward the Sun, which divine care ordained for that utility.
<margin>it was thought</margin>
For this reason, He did not fill the star nearest us [the Moon] with its own light. If, therefore, you look around at all of nature, you will see no evidence given by it that lower things are fostered by any heat other than that of the sun. While we do not stubbornly defend this—and we do not refuse to admit the stars into the partnership of this duty, as many <term>physicists</term> <note>natural philosophers</note> believe—we nonetheless refute those astrologers who think that in any <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genitura"; a birth chart or horoscope</note> (if the nativities of men actually pertain to stars) leadership is sometimes owed to other planets, with the Sun or Moon being neglected, whether it be a day or night birth. They even think the Sun itself can be oppressed by the rays of others and adversely affected, as if it were just one of their number to be reduced to order. But about these things
<margin>Note</margin>
later; for now, we only warn that those who believe other stars have much power after the sun in changing lower things are refuted more by evidence and the senses. Though they believe these stars can do almost nothing, they attribute all this vegetation and illumination of the lower world to the <term>Phoebean lamp</term> <note>original: "phaebeae lampadi"; the Sun</note>, from which the lunar lantern is also lit for us at night.

### Chapter XI. How the same stars can act on us differently at different times.

But let us grant to the astrologers—and we ourselves do not greatly deny it—that something flows from all stars into us. One question remains to be examined, which their objection demanded: whether the same stars always bestow the same thing, or whether they bestow different things. If not the same, let us see whether lower effects vary because of that diversity. That there are powers proper to each star besides motion and light is proven in the fourth reason by the nobility of heaven and the powers of certain bodies thought to come from heaven. We shall resolve those points there; here, we consider the stars according to reason. They [astrologers] claim diversity: since star differs from star, and light and motion are common to all, they
<margin>Paul the Apostle</margin>
must necessarily have certain proper qualities by which they differ from one another. But <term>Paul</term> <note>St. Paul, 1 Corinthians 15:41</note> said: "Star differs from star in clarity." What if, just as circular motion is common to all, they differ
<margin>Opinion</margin>
in motion, so that this one moves faster and that one more slowly? (Although even this is not granted by all.) If they agree on light—for example, concerning light—one star differs by the conditions of its light: while one is more compact and copious, the light of another is rarer or thinner. For there are those who believe that a sphere differs more from its star than one star differs from another; yet they differ in no other way than by rarity and density. If one accepts this, he will consequently think that their action upon us varies only in that those which are denser, larger, and nearer pour out more light and more heat, while those that are rarer, smaller, and more remote pour out less. Ultimately, the "breathing" from all is the same: of warm light and bright heat, from which comes health, life, and nourishment for bodies. They differ only in that some breathe upon us thinly, others more exuberantly, some from nearby, and others from afar. But what shall we decree regarding the same star
<margin>What the Peripatetics felt</margin>
given the perpetual revolving of its motion? Furthermore, the opinion of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>followers of Aristotle</note> is that stars do not change in quality, but only in place—except for the moon, which shines with borrowed light and is illuminated more or less according to its turnings toward the sun. Therefore, according to the turn it makes from the sun, it reflects light to us more abundantly or more sparingly, and with light, its heat. Thus, it almost deserts us at the new moon, when the part facing us is deprived of light; it fosters and heats more at the full moon, just as it does more when waxing and less when waning. This variety cannot exist in the other stars, which shine with a stable and proper light. Therefore, for almost all changes that frequently occur in bodies, the celestial cause is usually said to be the moon, because she, being changeable not only in position but in quality, touches us most closely. For the other planets, only a change of position occurs through their motion, from which comes a variety of influence—nothing other than that they affect us more intensely or more weakly as they migrate here and there.

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

[the planets are] closer to us or farther away. They have a double motion: universal and proper. The universal motion <note>The daily rotation of the heavens from East to West</note> carries a planet to us every day, lifting it above the earth, and snatches it away every day, leading it toward its setting. From this arises the first diversity of action: for from the summit <note>The zenith or highest point in the sky</note> they hurl the strongest rays, which fall more directly and perpendicularly. Therefore, the more they approach the peak, the more powerfully they affect us; the more they descend from there, the more weakly. Whether stars submerged under the earth 
<margin>Whether stars submerged under the earth can have any effect on us</margin>
can have any effect on us or not must be discussed. For when they are near the horizon <note>original: "finitōrē"</note> and are not yet fully snatched from our sight, they can certainly do something, though very little, as their rays still reach us from an oblique angle. But when they are hidden deep in the hiding places of the earth and are removed further from us, if I believe they can do nothing, my senses will support me and reason will not oppose it. Indeed, how can it be believed otherwise? If what we have defended so far is true—that nothing reaches us from heaven except by the vehicle of light.
<margin>Avicenna</margin>
Even **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose medical and philosophical works were foundational in the Middle Ages</note> said this in his books on meteorology, calling light the vehicle of all celestial powers; and **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a German Dominican friar and philosopher</note> confirmed it in his book *On Sleep and Waking*.
<margin>Albertus.</margin>
Therefore, just as light does not reach us then, neither will any power reach us. We say the Sun is present for us even at night for only one reason: because it makes its sister [the Moon] its deputy, shining upon us through the splendor impressed upon her. Unless, perhaps, it could also be said that since this upper air is continuous with the lower air, the presence of the sun there fosters this air in such a way that it would be colder if there were no sun at all to illuminate any part of the air. But if this effect exists at all, the eyes and the sense of touch will report that it is almost nothing. Astrologers—if they did not dream up powers for themselves against which the whole mass of the earth is no obstacle—should at least not be so delirious, even in sleep, as to deny that these powers are poured into us more purely and effectively when they are shed through the air surrounding us, than when the entire densest thickness of the brute earth must be pierced by them. If they do not concede this, who could defend them from insanity? For they think that the powers of the stars in the <term>twelfth house</term> <note>original: "duodecimo loco"; the section of the sky just above the eastern horizon</note>—which, rising above the horizon, is next to the East and yet only one "mansion" away from the summit—are sluggish, ceasing, and weak. Yet they think these same stars have the most vigor and efficacy in the <term>lowest point of the heavens</term> <note>original: "imo terrarum"; the 4th astrological house, or the point directly "under" the earth</note>. But we shall deal with their errors later; for now, we discuss what ought to be decided by reason. We have spoken of universal motion. By their **proper motion**, the planets are carried now to the South, now to the North, which the fixed stars are also believed to do according to the opinion of some. The Sun does the same, not because it deflects from the orbit it once occupied, but because that oblique path makes it now closer to us, now farther away: closer in the North, farther in the South <note>Pico is referring to the Sun's seasonal altitude in the Northern Hemisphere</note>. From this is born another variety of influence: clearly, there is greater efficacy when the rays incline toward us, and less when they withdraw toward the South. Beyond these or similar factors, any diversity imagined in the action of the stars is utterly vain and irrational. Such is the case with astrologers who think the same star is affected differently according to the twelve houses, 
<margin>Intervals of the stars are called aspects</margin>
the signs it runs through, or the fixed and wandering stars to which it is joined by certain rational intervals which they call **aspects** <note>Specific angles between planets, such as a square (90°) or trine (120°)</note>. They believe planets acquire very different powers for influencing us. Against this error the entire sixth book will arm itself. Here, at the beginning of this chapter, we will only cast against them the authority of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note>, who deny any change in the stars except for their position, except in the case of the Moon. For if they only exclude destructive and harmful change, the Moon should not have been excluded, since she is not changed by the sun in that way, nor by harmful influences. As we shall see, astrologers do not free the stars from changes that weaken their powers and faculties, even if they do not change their substance. But more on this later. One might ask whether the Moon receives the rays of other planets just as she does the Sun’s.
<margin>Whether the moon receives rays from other planets just as it does from the sun.</margin>
It seems probable, because by her nature she is a receptacle of incident light rather than being luminous herself; and since she is the lowest of all, she would seem most fit for this. However, neither the authority of the elders nor the senses themselves support this. Indeed, when the Moon is in conjunction with the Sun, if she were then positioned opposite the rays of Jupiter or Mars, she ought to reflect their light more fully to us; yet she is known to have no rays or light at all [at that time]. We touch on this question because if she drew light from the others as well, the planets would become more effective toward us for this reason too: because they would be joined to the Moon, their power being transmitted through her to us...

<margin>
What the Moon's conjunction with the stars signifies, against the troublesome claims of the astrologers.
</margin>
...to us by a power which perhaps by itself would reach here less. But if this happened, it would happen entirely otherwise than the astrologers think. For they think the Moon transfers the rays of that star with which she is found together <note>A "conjunction" in astrology, where two celestial bodies appear in the same spot in the sky.</note> to us most of all. I, however, do not doubt that the further the Moon moves away from a star, the more that star’s light is communicated to us through her; and the less she is distant, the less light [is communicated], or certainly none at all when there is no distance between them. I am moved by evident experience, which shows that when the Moon is joined to the Sun <note>During a New Moon or solar eclipse.</note>, she does not transmit his rays to us, with the bulk of her body especially causing trouble [by blocking them]. Therefore, how much less does she transmit the rays of others, which are far thinner than the solar ones and further removed from the Moon? See how much they are deceived who believe a day or a birth-chart is fortunate when the Moon meets with beneficial stars, or unfortunate when she meets with malevolent ones <note>Astrologers traditionally classified planets like Jupiter as "benefic" and Saturn as "malefic."</note>, since the Moon "meeting" them is nothing other than their influence being intercepted from us by the density of the Moon. Perhaps, however, there is also a reason that in the changing of lower things, a **morning planet** rising near and before the Sun might claim the air for itself before it is entirely occupied by the Sun. But if this is so, it can hardly have great weight. It remains to be examined whether a new power coalesces from a mixture of rays, an effect of some new work which the individual rays apart would not produce.

<margin>
Question.
Plotinus.
</margin>
**Plotinus** <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> denies that this blending can happen to rays so that a new power or a new form springs out from their union. I think this is because rays are not bodies like liquids, nor are they qualities fixed to bodies in the way that they are received into bodies—for example, as a dye or a habit by which they might be changed. Therefore, it is likely that what happens to many qualities—that they are sometimes changed from some combination or mixture into another form coalescing from them all—does not happen to rays. This is especially true since such a change does not usually happen without the "death" <note>original: "interitu," meaning the destruction or loss of the original individual characteristics.</note> of the simple and individual qualities flowing together, which no one would easily imagine happening in rays. If we grant the astrologers that rays or the heats flowing from rays are mixed, we assert that all rays are always mixed, and they are not "asymbolic" <note>original: "asymbolos," from Greek, meaning "not contributing" or "unconnected."</note> as if they did not join together with others except through those angles they now call "aspects." Therefore, the mixture of the present hour, moment, year, month, or day does not vary from the radiant mixture of another time, except for those reasons by which we explained the actions of the stars vary: namely, that there is one temperament for night and another for day; one when the stars recede to the south, and another when they incline to the north; from which alone arises the strengthening or weakening of heat.

# Chapter XII. What variety of effects can be traced back to the heavens and what cannot.

<margin>
In the mixture of rays in the air, what is substantial and what is accidental.
</margin>
Let us consider the mixture of all rays in the air; in it there is something you might call **substantial**, and something as if **accidental**. What is "substantial" is that there is one light or one heat, either gathered or resulting from all the lights of heaven; and this indeed is perpetual and immutable. But it is "accidental" <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "substance" is the essential nature of a thing, while an "accident" is a non-essential quality, like being "tall" or "hot."</note> that this particular ray is now more intense in it, or another is weaker; this changes repeatedly through the constant movement of the celestial bodies. The reason for this distinction of ours is easily apparent. For in heaven, which we know to be the source of this heat, something can be called "substantial": just as we say those things are substantial which follow the substance of a thing inseparably. Such things are the "unfading" body [of the heavens], and the circular figure (the first of all bodies), the orbital motion, and the light with its heat that enlivens all things. And if the stars have their own powers, those are also substantial properties of the stars. Again, there is something in the heavens and stars that is variable and thus "accidental," such as the change of position in all stars, and the change of light in the Moon. Therefore, that which in the mixture of rays follows the "substantial" parts of heaven, we call substantial; and that which follows the "accidental," we call accidental. For example, it is substantial to the mixture that it contains the power of Saturn, Jupiter, the Sun, and the rest; but it is accidental that it has these more intensely or those more weakly due to the variety of the rays. **Socrates**, therefore, was helped by that superior power—which is certainly not a changeable power, otherwise it would not always be present to the causes doing all things as it is seen to be—helped, I say, in that he was generated as a **human** insofar as he is a human, and as **this human** insofar as he was generated from this seed and from this matter. Therefore, if you look at this "substantial" condition of the effect—whether you call it nature or an individual character—it is indifferent...

-> DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY <-

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>Note</margin>
Any constellation is such that from the diversity of the constellation—that is, the various state and relationship of the stars to the earth—it pours more or less heat into the air. Through the mixing of other rays, a new proportion and measure of hot light results. This is what is **accidental** <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change (like being hot or cold) without changing the essential nature of the thing itself.</note> in the heavens, which also creates an accidental diversity in the effects. For instance, if someone says a better conception happens during a full moon, or that a fetus grows more as the moon waxes, or that a woman is better affected under a temperate state of the sky and thus better offspring are produced—this kind of diversity in the substances being generated can exist due to the various positions of the celestial bodies. We call this accidental and "adventitious" <note>Coming from the outside; not innate.</note> because, as we have explained, the specific and **substantial** nature of the conceived fetus depends on its own most immediate principle and its own substantial matter. Furthermore, the "accidents" of the seed and the matter do more to determine these properties; these are more related, more immediate, and more intimate than the extrinsic disposition 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
of the surrounding air. This is what experience shows daily; Aristotle even says that if a son is not shaped according to the seeds of his parents and does not derive his similarity from them, he should be numbered among **monsters** <note>Aristotle used the term "monster" (monstrum) to describe any birth that deviated from the likeness of the parents, even if it was just a minor physical difference.</note>.

Therefore, nothing stands in our way when we make the stars only **universal causes** and look for the distinction of effects in secondary causes. The various positions of stars might vary the disposition of the air or the bodies of those giving birth or those being born in some way through changes in the air, since, as we said, this is a change that comes from the outside and is very general. However, those things that belong to the "substance"—to the more intimate and specific qualities—undoubtedly draw their origin from their own specific sources. Therefore, they can in no way be foreseen from the sky. This is true in physical things which are complete substances, all of which have nearby **efficient causes** <note>The "efficient cause" is the person or process that actually brings something into being, like a builder for a house or a father for a child.</note>, or what corresponds to them in those things generated from rot and inanimate mixtures (which we will discuss in the solution to the fourth reason). But the heavens can produce changes in the air regarding heat, cold, moisture, and dryness without any intermediary. It does this only universally because, from itself, it only produces heat healthily; other effects happen **by accident** according to the condition of the matter. Just as by one and the same heat, clay hardens and wax melts; and under the same sun, linens become white when washed, but the faces of the washers turn dark. However, because this accidental change is most significant, it is what we have called "accidental" in the celestial constellation: that is, the position and relationship of the stars, from which the power of the rays is intensified or weakened. Indeed, because of this very thing, the four seasons of the year vary by the sun’s different path; and the rising, setting, ascending, and descending of the sun produce nearly those same four changes.

Among these primary qualities of bodies and inanimate mixtures, **meteorological impressions** <note>Atmospheric phenomena like rain, snow, or thunder.</note> occupy a middle place. Their efficient cause is the sky and their matter is lower things, which is why their diversity depends more on celestial disposition than do the bodies of "perfect" <note>Fully formed, complex living beings.</note> things. Thus, thunder usually occurs in spring and autumn, hail in summer, and snow and rain in winter—though less so than the four qualities themselves. For when a ray falls upon matter, those things are moved by its power rather than the rays [themselves], but they grow out of the lower matter. For this reason, they vary mostly by the condition of that matter, as we will explain more broadly in the treatise on the third reason.

<margin>Augustine, in Book Five of *The City of God*, inserts the following</margin>
But perfect substances—which have not only matter but also their own specific efficient cause—derive whatever is substantial and specific to them (to repeat this often) from their own specific causes. The sky acts as a **universal cause** cooperating through an unchangeable influx of light, while making some extrinsic and very general change. Astrologers cannot say anything about this, especially since it depends neither on the celestial causes they have invented nor on the hour of birth, but on other principles, as we will show later; for now, we are only investigating what the sky does and does not do. Understanding these things that we have discussed, **Aurelius Augustine** said it could be considered "not entirely absurd" that certain stellar influences have power over bodily differences alone. He did not assert it was so, nor did he accuse those who thought otherwise; rather, he downplayed the fault of those who held such an opinion, pronouncing it "not entirely absurd." To explain what should be understood regarding these differences in bodies, he added: "just as we see the seasons of the year vary by the sun's approach and departure, and by the lunar...

-> BOOK THREE <-

<margin>Sea urchins</margin>
...by the lunar <note>The OCR reads "narib'," a truncation of "lunaribus."</note> waxings and wanings, certain kinds of things grow and shrink, such as **sea urchins** and **shellfish**, as well as the marvelous tides of the ocean. These are his <note>Referring to Saint Augustine.</note> words, in which you see nothing listed that contributes to the generation of any complete substance. Furthermore, he was soon to point out that even those differences which are most physical should not be referred to the stars. Instead, he immediately noted the most proximate causes: even regarding the body and the sex of the body, twins of different sexes could be conceived under the same position of the stars. In that same passage, a little earlier, he had confirmed this same opinion by proving that **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> 
<margin>Hippocrates</margin>
gave a reason from primary and 
<margin>Posidonius</margin>
secondary causes for why two brothers would fall ill and recover at the same time. **Posidonius** <note>A Stoic philosopher who, unlike Hippocrates, believed in astrological influence.</note>, however, had not proved his point by referring this to an equality of the constellation. Augustine says that the medical conjecture is much more acceptable: that the parents, as they were physically affected during intercourse, could have affected the beginnings of the conceived children in such a way that, with the first developments following from the mother's <note>original: "mīno," likely "materno."</note> body, they were born with equal health. Then, being nourished in one house with the same food—where medicine testifies that the air, the position of the place, and the quality of the wine and water have the greatest power for the body to be received well or poorly—and being accustomed to the same exercises, they possessed such similar bodies that they were moved similarly by the same causes to fall ill at the same time. But to refer this to the constitution of the heaven or the stars because of when they were conceived or born, I know not what kind of "insolence" <note>Augustine uses "insolentia" to describe the arrogance of astrologers claiming to know divine or hidden causes.</note> that is. These are the words of Augustine which we have woven in: though many, understanding this from him, have frequently used it to think that our writers—not without reason—believe the differences of bodies pertain to the "stellar breath" <note>original: "afflatus syderos," a reference to the supposed influence or 'emanations' of the stars.</note>, and that Augustine thought every diversity of physical effects came from heaven. Consequently, they believe that with Augustine's consent, astrologers can prophesy, being unmindful that nothing can be called "physical" as deservedly as the temperament of the body itself; yet those who seek the causes of this temperament in the heavens are taxed with the label of **insolence** by Augustine.

## Chapter XIII. The Sun performs many works which astrologers think are done by other stars.

<margin>Sun and Moon</margin>
**R**etorting their first argument back upon the astrologers, we have declared in a long but necessary digression what the heaven and the action of the celestial bodies might do to us, and how the various readings of things are found whether we consider the stars themselves or the matter receiving them. From this, it has been made clear that the heaven is a **universal cause**, and that the distinction of effects—especially the primary and substantial ones—should not be sought there. Now, in a fitting order, as if taking a step forward through those things we have discussed, we shall set our hands to solving the second argument. For they claimed that since the dispositions of lower bodies are observed to vary according to the various relationships of the **Sun** and **Moon** to us, the same must be believed regarding other things and the planets. For they say that the successions of the four seasons vary through the solar circuits, and the status of all bodies varies with those successions, or through the lunar waxings and wanings. Therefore, there are two 
<margin>Arguments</margin>
things they think can be gathered from this. First: that just as we see sea urchins, shellfish, the ocean, and the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) thought to govern health.</note> of the body change according to the cycles of the moon, and the earthly mass in general changes through the annual and daily revolution of the sun, so too should we agree concerning other things—that they are bound to the stars and governed by them. Second: that the manifest power of the Sun and Moon in changing sublunary matter <note>Matter existing below the moon; i.e., the Earth and its atmosphere.</note> compels us to believe the same about the rays of the other stars—that is, that there is also a great, more hidden life in them for changing things and affecting them in multiple ways. We shall make it plain that neither can be concluded. Indeed, these very things which they bring forward on their own behalf actually favor those who suspect otherwise. First, we shall give an account of all those observations from principles already established, so that it may be clear that we are led to a different view of the efficiency of the stars and the change of celestial virtues neither by arguments nor by experiences, other than what we have prescribed so far under the guidance of natural reason. Nor in the meantime shall I cease to mock the many fallacies of the astrologers and their many errors. Let us begin, then, with the works of the Sun: the approach and retreat of the sun varies the seasons of the year; this we shall assert even by swearing an oath if necessary. But the **obliquity** <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis (or the Sun's path along the ecliptic), which creates the seasons.</note> of the zodiac itself does this, not the "nature" of the signs. That is, it does not blaze in **Leo** <note>The constellation of the Lion.</note> because of the Sun being in the Sign of the Lion, or because it is the "House of the Sun," or a "hot sign," as they fabricate.

-> ### DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY ### <-

...astrologers; rather, it is because the Sun, being situated in that sign and most proximate to our air, has already heated it for six months. Otherwise, the Sun is at its most burning when in **Cancer** <note>The zodiac sign of the Crab, associated with the summer solstice.</note>, even though it is not—among them—the **Sun's house** <note>In astrology, a "house" or "domicile" is the sign where a planet has the most influence. Leo is the Sun's house, not Cancer.</note> or its **exaltation** <note>A specific sign where a planet is thought to have a particularly strong effect.</note>. Nor is Cancer a "fiery" sign; it is a **watery** one. Likewise, in **Aries** <note>The Ram, associated with spring.</note>, it restores the world, calling forth flowers and increasing seeds, because returning to us then for the first time, it breathes a fertile and convenient warmth into bodies.

It is indeed a fable of the astrologers that Aries is the Sun's "exaltation," as if it would not do the same in **Libra** <note>The Scales, the sign opposite Aries.</note> for other peoples as it does in Aries for us—namely, when it recedes from here and approaches them. Therefore, the sole cause of all the variety that occurs with time is the greater or lesser distance of the Sun from the lands we inhabit, from which we participate in more or less of its heat. 

<margin>Why thunder happens in spring</margin>
Here too, thunder truly occurs in the spring, because when the Sun reaches Aries, the winter humidity of the air is dissolved by the heat. From this, much evaporation is raised up into the air—a "harvest" of clouds, so to speak—from which thunder and lightning come. If the astrologers also understand this, what is this drowsiness or desire to deceive? They define Aries as a sign that rouses rain and thunder as if the "nature" of that sign—the Ram itself—produced this. 

<margin><term>alphos</term> is called <term>morphea</term></margin>
They would by no means say that the Moon in Aries produces thunder if they were able or willing to notice that this happens not through the power of that sign, but by the action of the Sun reaching that sign. By a similar fallacy, it was written by **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos* (referred to here as the *Apotelesmaton*), the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> in his books on astrology that the Moon in Aries, if it causes disease, causes specifically **vitiligo** <note>A skin condition causing loss of pigment.</note>, which the Greeks call <term>alphos</term> and the common people call <term>morphea</term>. In Cancer, it causes **mentagra** <note>An inflammatory skin disease, typically of the chin.</note>, which the Greeks call <term>lichenas</term> and the common people call **impetigo**. In Libra, it causes **leprosy**; in Capricorn, **freckles**.

In fact, this is drawn from the state of the air when the Sun is carried through those signs: from the quality of spring, when the Sun is in Aries; of summer, when it is in Cancer; of autumn, with Libra; and of winter, when it runs through the sign of Capricorn. Indeed, those types of diseases fit the conditions of these seasons. The vitiligo of spring easily invades and occupies the top layer of skin because of the humors overflowing in that particular part of the year. To summer belongs mentagra, which comes from drier and sharper matter. To autumn, leprosy, since it is considered an infection of **black bile** <note>One of the four "humors" of ancient medicine, associated with melancholy and autumn.</note>. To winter, freckles, which are generated from colder and wetter humors being overcome.

Therefore, it is the height of foolishness to ascribe what is done by the Sun—heating the air more or less according to the variety of its position—to the signs under which the Sun is carried during those times. Or, if they understand this, as if they did not understand it, they think that the other planets in these same signs perform the same things. Let us conclude that the fixed diversity in the times of the year arises from nowhere else than from the setting and receding of the Sun due to the slant of the **zodiac** <note>original: "signiferi," the "sign-bearer," a common Latin term for the zodiac belt.</note>.

<margin>Why not all summers are equally hot</margin>
If not all summers are equally scorching, nor all winters equally freezing, this happens according to the disposition of the matter, which has the greatest momentum in the air, as proven by the senses and by Ptolemy himself. It is not necessary to refer this to the heavens, except as the universal cause of every physical thing, as may be understood from **Aristotle’s** books on **Meteorology**. Likewise, if the heat is more intense on some days and duller on others in the same summer, the position of the Sun alone does not demand this. A change in the lower regions causes it—for instance, a wind stirred up somewhere, or a flood of rain, or something else of this kind that can happen far from us. We might not see the cause itself, yet we nevertheless experience its force overflowing with effect into our own sky.

If some planets are hotter than others, those that are less hot can, by accident, generate rains and cover the sky with clouds by dissolving humors without consuming them. Thus, where heat fails, cold is intensified. Conversely, that those which are more burning lead to dryness and heat is not far from our principles—that the lordship of a varying star may do something toward the change of the air. Only, let us not understand this "lordship" to mean anything other than that a star illuminates us more proximately or with more direct rays. Truly, since we suspect that whatever reaches us from the higher stars is entirely tenuous—especially regarding these sensible qualities—the causes of storms, if sought in the heavens, are for the most part not found, whether we think of the stars according to the opinion of the astrologers or the philosophers, as we have defined it. It seems that this whole matter, which...

# BOOK THREE

<margin>Whence comes the disturbance and tranquility of the sea, and how the observation of the seasons is useful and not superstitious for sailors.</margin>

...of the seas <note>The Latin text reads "narium" (nostrils), but the context and marginal note "marium" suggest this is a transcription error for "marium" (of the seas).</note> is taken away or added; it should rather be referred to the material. As for the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> themselves, one changes things by its position alone, the other also by its changed light. Neither acts according to the nature of the signs they traverse, nor the places where they reside, nor the planets with which they are configured, as will be manifested in what follows. 

Wherefore, the fact that the ancient sea <note>Likely referring to the Mediterranean.</note> is agitated and boils with waves when the Sun enters **Virgo** <note>The Virgin.</note>, and especially when it reaches **Sagittarius** <note>The Archer.</note>; and yet conversely becomes calm and navigable when the Sun is brought to **Pisces** <note>The Fish.</note> and especially to **Gemini** <note>The Twins.</note>—whereas by contrast, the Indian sea becomes tranquil under Virgo and Sagittarius and navigable under Pisces and Gemini—this arises not from the quality of the signs, but from the position of the Sun and the condition of the material. 

Even astrologers admit this. Therefore, the observation of these times held by sailors is useful and not superstitious, taking into account the nature of the sea. For those days on which they must abstain from sailing are predicted for navigators; if these have any cause from the heavens, they can have it from no source other than the Sun. This is because the observation of them is fixed and perpetual, and thus can only be referred to the Sun, whose disposition is almost always the same at these same times. It cannot be referred to other constellations, which are never found in the same positions. 

For example: the days suspected by sailors are always the 1st, 7th, 15th, 17th, 19th, and 21st of **March**; the 5th, 6th, 12th, and 20th of **April**; and the 6th, 12th, 15th, 17th, 19th, and 20th of **February**. They always use this invariable observation, and they say that through these days great changes of the sea usually occur, leading either to tranquility or to tempest. Therefore, since the outcomes are uncertain, those who abstain act more securely, lest by chance the change results in evil. 

This cannot be reduced to the positions of the stars that astrologers note and command to be observed, since those similar positions do not return during the same parts of the year, but rather most dissimilar ones. An astrologer might pronounce those very days—always suspected by captains—to be harmless and most fortunate for navigation, while declaring those which the sailors do not much fear to be most dangerous, according to how the varied state of the hours and the mixed ranks of the planets represent themselves to him.

<margin>There can be a double cause for the malice of those days.</margin>

Wherefore, the sailor will not approve of such rules which are most hostile to his own principles. These rules, confirmed daily by long experience and the practice of a sublime art, provide the most abundant proof of the vanity of astrologers. 

However, there can be a double cause [for these dangerous days]: one from the Sun, the other from the water. Just as the humors of our body have their own periods by which they are moved, so the ocean may have its own. It is recognized by evident proof that the Sun, according to the moments of its approach to or departure from us, changes the disposition of the sea and of all bodies. 

The reader should also be advised that this variety of seasons is denoted by those who write on rural and nautical matters through the rising and setting of the **fixed stars**, such as **Arcturus**, the **Pleiades** <note>original: "vergiliarum"</note>, the **Hyades**, and others similarly. This is not because they believe the influences of the stars themselves are to be feared or sought—otherwise, even the astrologers would not say this, since they claim stars are ineffective unless they hold the "angles" <note>Key points in a horoscope: the Ascendant, Midheaven, etc.</note>—but rather so that there might be a visible sign for those unlearned in those arts to distinguish the season. Nothing better could be found that is both perpetual and conspicuous than the emergence and setting of the stars. 

Furthermore, nothing would command more authority and observation among the common folk. It is written by physicians that winter illnesses are resolved in summer, and summer ones in winter; sometimes those that attack in winter leave in spring, or those of spring depart toward autumn; and finally, those that occur at any time of year are altered by the change of season. This is surely because the quality of these seasons is diverse due to the proximity or distance of the Sun from the lands. 

As for what they say about the Moon regarding **critical days** <note>original: "crisiis diebus"; days when a disease was thought to reach a turning point.</note>, it is vain and irrational. But we shall speak of this later when we discuss the Moon. It is from these same progressions of the Sun that there is a varied affection of things, both those without life and all living things, under different inclinations of the sky. This is why all lands do not produce the same things, and the customs of peoples and the habit of bodies are varied in various regions. Nor should we hope for other constellations, other signs, or other planets under which those places lie, other than the Sun. The Sun is forever borne between **Cancer** and **Capricorn**. Wherefore, whatever is between the circle of the equator...

<margin>
Humans are born everywhere.
Southerners.
</margin>
Those who inhabit the area of the winter and summer solstices necessarily live in the hottest region; whereas those positioned under the North <note>The "Great Bear" or Big Dipper constellation, signifying the North.</note>, being farthest from the sun, live in the coldest; and the region between these is temperate. And since the right side of the heaven, the East, is more effective in the power of the sun than the West, can a reason for all these things not be given here—as far as the celestial cause is concerned—regarding the properties of things? For gems, spices, and everything of this kind that requires more celestial heat are produced toward the East and the South; likewise, lions, tigers, and elephants are produced in those same lands, along with other animals that require powerful heat to be generated, to live, and to remain in their vigor. Only the human being is born and preserved in every part of the earth because of the wide latitude of his nature under a multiform habit. Under this latitude, although one man differs from another by the force of specific differences, this has nevertheless given some philosophers a vain suspicion <note>That these differences are caused by the stars rather than the environment.</note>. Those, therefore, who inhabit the southern part, the hotter the air they breathe, the colder they are internally. For this reason, they are timid, effeminate, and—as ancient and modern experience proves—born for servitude. These things happen because immoderate heat so relaxes their bodies that it evokes and consumes the greatest part of their internal heat; thus, being drawn out to the surface of the body and deserting the inner chambers, it leaves blackness in the skin and timidity in the heart.

<margin>Northerners</margin>
On the contrary, those who live under a cold sky toward the North are spirited, strong, and fair-skinned for the opposite reason. However, both peoples—either those who are most under the sun or those who are removed furthest from it—possess little humanity and are less sociable because of the excess of heat or cold, through which they recede from that moderate temperament in which our nature is chiefly situated.

<margin>
Error of the Greek astrologers
</margin>
But both peoples are also fierce and rustic, both for the common cause we have mentioned, and because one is ferocious while the other is fearful. It is not, therefore, as the Greek astrologers fabricate, that those peoples are more fierce because the harmful planets **Saturn** and **Mars** rule the extreme climates; nor is it because **Saturn** rules the Southerners that they are timid and short-lived; nor because **Mars** rules the Northerners that they are more warlike. This is a fiction in which even other astrologers do not agree, as they do not place **Mars** over the Northerners, but rather the **Moon**. We, using neither **Mars** nor the **Moon**, provide the proper reason for the conditions of both peoples from the sun—a reason which anyone who dreams of anything else is more a trifler than a philosopher. They say **Saturn** also rules in India; and yet there, people are long-lived. Why then do the Southerners have short lives because of **Saturn's** "excessive coldness," and why are they timid? For even there, the most ferocious beasts are born, though Aristotle writes that all animals in the North are more "masculine."

<margin>
Aristotle in his books on animals.
Avicenna.
</margin>
But human moderation suffers the extremes most poorly; and by the same reasoning that stomachs are hotter in winter than in summer, so those people under excessive heat grow cold internally, and have scarcely finished their thirtieth year of life before they are consumed by old age, as **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina.</note> relates. Those in the North, under their frozen seat, burn most deeply within; with heat enclosed in their principal members and with much thicker blood, they are as much more robust than the Southerners as the latter are more clever due to the subtlety of their spirits and blood. The middle nations, being dull neither from a lack of blood nor from its thickness, are thus made wiser and more prudent for the purpose of ruling; and, if I may put it this way, they are "more human." This is the general variety of the inhabitants of the earth based on the celestial circulation. To this, many peculiar traits are added from the sublunary disposition <note>The "sublunary" world is the Earth, beneath the Moon.</note> of lands, air, and water: for instance, one region is half-decayed by marshes in the way or by stagnant waters, besieged by the dark nights of repeated mists; another is open to winds, or rugged, or elevated by mountains.

<margin>Panetius</margin>
I have already held you with these matters longer than is necessary. These things pass from the lands to the air, and the air itself has its own properties in different places—as **Panetius** <note>A Stoic philosopher.</note> says—not sought from heaven, but held from its own principles. Indeed, it is in doubt how much these differences in the air can change the inhabitants in affecting their bodies; but it is clear through the things they eat, which everyone knows can become either harmful or healthy based solely on the condition of the water and the air.

<margin>
Whence comes the variety of talents and character.
</margin>
Here is the specific diversity of bodies due to the celestial impression from the sun, which is immediately followed by another diversity concerning the manner of diet. But the variety of talents and characters [derives] both from the habit of the body...

->## BOOK THREE<-

...[the body’s] habit depends upon and is established by the foundation of education and habit, which is very close to the powers of nature. Laws are added to this, which are of the greatest momentum in this matter, so much so that they can make savage nations most gentle if they are rightly established; and on the contrary, they can weaken the strongest and turn the best into the worst if the laws themselves are bad. From this, the freedom of the will is most evidently declared against all necessity of nature. 
<margin>Example of the Gauls</margin>
The Gauls <note>Pico uses "Galli," referring to the French of his time and antiquity.</note> were once infamous for the love of boys—if we believe Ptolemy and Aristotle—a crime which they now so abhor, by the benefit of Christian law and the most holy Prince King Louis <note>Likely referring to Louis XI of France (reigned 1461–1483), whom Pico praises here for moral reforms.</note>, that no nation under heaven does so more. Nor is it necessary to rely on the examples of a single people, since evangelical preaching, Moses, and new institutions have changed nearly the whole world from the customs that were first established. 
<margin>Quality of the region</margin>
Furthermore, the quality of a region can do much to determine the arts and masteries one undertakes. For instance, a person may devote themselves to trade and navigation if the city is conveniently located by the sea; or to letters if it is near an academy; or to military service if it is troubled by hostile neighbors or internal civil factions. There are those whom fertility and abundance make idle and pleasure-seeking; while scarcity and sterility make others hardworking, industrious, and diligent. 

Truly, perhaps some astrologer will say: "But we do not deny these things! We assert and proclaim them along with you." 
<margin>Response to astrologers</margin>
They contend that there are other properties in places, namely from private influences and a peculiar constellation—arguing for the <term>trigon</term> <note>A "trine" or grouping of three zodiac signs of the same element (fire, earth, air, or water).</note>, for the planet, for the sign under which the region lies, or for the celestial disposition under which the foundations of a city were laid, or under which its empire, king, or tyrant first invaded. 
<margin>Confutation</margin>
Therefore, while it may be that what you say is true, it does not follow that our own views cannot also be true. But I do not believe, based on the things I have mentioned, that it follows (as you "excellent" diviners imagine) that your theories must be correct. Rather, we should understand that through the things we have said, a reason can be so fully given for the manifold diversity of places and peoples that it is not at all necessary to seek other causes. For the following pages will demonstrate that those theories you astrologers introduced are both false and fabulous. 

While we were disputing against the causes to which you refer the diversity of peoples and regions, it was likely that someone would ask: "What, then, is the cause of such great variety?" Therefore, before we overthrew the false causes, it was necessary to demonstrate the true ones, so that your unnecessary ideas might be understood as such—ideas which will later be refuted as fictional and impossible. 

We did not introduce that life-giving heat of the heaven (about which we have discussed so much above), nor the efficacy of the sun, in order to tear down your views; nor did we mention how rays are intensified or weakened by the distance or proximity of the stars. Rather, before we refuted your invented trifles, I wanted to make it known that your "changes of sidereal power" based on places, signs, and aspects are nothing more than absurd fictions. Whatever the force of the heaven effects in us—by the authority of philosophers, the testimony of the senses, and the judgment of reason—all of it can be sufficiently achieved through the common influx of light, which is healthily warm and emanates continually from a perpetually moving body <note>Referring to the Sun and the celestial spheres moving as a physical whole.</note>. Therefore, to imagine other powers or "stellar influences" acting upon bodies is superfluous. It will then be easier to declare that believing what you have imagined is not just superfluous, but insane.

### Chapter XIV. How the power of the moon varies: and that certain days of the moon are observed with true superstition.

<margin>Opinion of Ptolemy</margin>
**W**e have shown from the works of the sun that the dogmas of the astrologers are not necessarily proven. The same must be done regarding the works of the moon. Ptolemy, in his *Apotelesmata* <note>Better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational text on astrology.</note>, says the moon—from the new moon until it is at its half-phase—is more effective in producing humidity; from then until fullness, it produces heat; from fullness, it produces dryness until it returns to half-phase; and then, in its operations leading back to the conjunction <note>The new moon, when it aligns with the sun.</note>, it produces coldness. 
<margin>Operations of the moon</margin>
Thus, he claims it has the nature of spring and air in its first quarter; of summer and fire in the second; of autumn and earth in the third; and of winter and water in the fourth; and that it excites the qualities of these seasons in bodies most strongly during those times. This division is more "beautiful" than it is natural or true; for indeed, the condition of heat is such that when it is weak, moisture...

-># DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

<meta>catchword: that not so</meta>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

[...continued from previous page] moisture, nor should it move it: so that what it scarcely feels when it has some efficacy, it may begin to release, and being diffused, it may release it as much as it is able, unless it grows so strong that it consumes the moisture it causes to flow; for then it dries out and does not moisten. But the **moon’s heat**, being very thin, never intensifies to such an extent that it dries things out; rather, it increases within those limits by which it moistens bodies with heat and does not parch them. Thus, the more light the moon has, the more moisture it produces, just as it produces more heat; conversely, as it lacks light, it likewise moistens and heats less. Therefore, it follows the nature and quality of springtime more from the **first quarter** <note>The "quadrangulum" or quadrature refers to the moon's position at 90 degrees from the sun.</note> to the **full moon** than from the **new moon** <term>interlūnio: the period when the moon is invisible between the old and new cycles</term> to that first quarter, since the nature of spring is defined as moist. Nor can it represent winter from the **second quarter** to the **conjunction** <note>The "coitus," where the moon and sun meet.</note>, or autumn from the full moon to that quarter; for autumn is dry and winter is moist. Indeed, after the moon has been full until it is half-full, it moistens; and from then until the conjunction it dries, so that when its moistening ceases, it is as if that dryness will endure.

<margin>Ptolemy in the Book of One Hundred Aphorisms</margin>
Therefore, **Ptolemy** himself spoke much more correctly in his *Book of One Hundred Aphorisms* <note>original: "libro centū enūciatorum"; also known as the *Centiloquium*, a collection of astrological secrets long attributed to Ptolemy.</note> when he said that from the moon's first quarter (namely, from when it departed its meeting with the sun) the moisture of bodies flows until the second quarter, but in the remaining times it decreases.

<margin>Experiments</margin>
Beyond the reasoning we have stated, **experiments** themselves also testify to this: for as the moon increases, an addition of moisture occurs; as it decreases, a reduction occurs. This is because not only the quality of its light, but also its motion toward increase or decrease, operates in this way. Therefore, when it begins to rise after departing from the sun until it is half-illuminated, it moistens and heats more than when, possessing the same amount of light at the **second dichotomy** <note>The Last Quarter phase.</note>, it tends toward the conjunction; this is because in the former case the light is growing, while in the latter it is failing. This is the whole of **lunar astrology**: usefully and naturally observed by physicians, farmers, and sailors.

<margin>Why the time of the waxing moon is suitable for planting</margin>
For universally, they have considered the time of the **waxing moon** to be suitable for planting, so that the seeds, nourished by more abundant moisture, might themselves grow more quickly.

<margin>Why timber should be cut during the waning moon</margin>
However, **timber** <term>materiæ: specifically wood used for building</term> should be cut during the **waning moon**, because then all wood is drier and thinner; therefore, it does not rot as easily or become consumed by decay. On the contrary, if any is taken when the moon is increased in light, because moisture is then overflowing, it easily putrefies and is ruined.

<margin>Verification of certain sayings of Hesiod and Plutarch</margin>
Wherefore **Hesiod** <note>Ancient Greek poet known for *Works and Days*, which includes agricultural advice based on lunar days.</note> rightly praises the **ninth day** of the moon for planting trees, as well as the **thirteenth**; for as **Plutarch** says, that same force, now fuller in the roots, scatters the light. He makes that same day inconvenient for sowing seeds, because sown seed desires rains more, so that it may rot and germinate. Furthermore, he denies that the **sixteenth day** is fit for planting, because the failing light does not sufficiently draw out the sprouts.

<margin>Explanation of a certain passage of Virgil</margin>
Therefore, what **Virgil** said—*the seventeenth is lucky both for planting vines* <note>Referring to Virgil's *Georgics*, Book I, line 284.</note> and what follows—cannot be understood as meaning the seventeenth day literally; for this day is least lucky for planting vines since the light is diminished. But either he judged the **first seventh** which is after the **best tenth**—that is, the fourteenth—on which day vines are not unluckily planted under a full moon; or, what is more consistent with reason, he praised two days, the **seventh** and the **tenth**, but the tenth more; wherefore he says "after the tenth, the seventh is lucky." For that is how the matter stands. Indeed, the **seventh moon** (at the quarter) supplies enough heat and moisture for the roots of the plant, but the **tenth day** does so even more abundantly. The **seventeenth** could not have been denoted except through ignorance and error, since that day is not suitable for planting trees but rather for **cutting** them, as Hesiod also teaches, for that reason we mentioned: the decreasing moisture. Therefore, at that time, they prepare timber for building ships, which ought to last for a long time.

<margin>Proclus</margin>
As for the fact that the **Greek poet** <note>Hesiod</note> also orders crops to be carried to the threshing floor then, it has this reason (as **Proclus** writes): that winds usually arise after the full moon, by which the chaff itself may be separated from the grain. Just as in these days the cause and reason for the work are easily recognized, so other lunar days can be more suitable for certain tasks...

He attempts to reconcile conflicting advice from Virgil, Hesiod, and Plutarch by analyzing the moon's effect on plant biology.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument that while the moon has physical effects on moisture and heat, these are natural phenomena and do not justify the "divine" or "judicial" claims of astrologers. He transitions from biological reproduction to meteorology and the tides.</meta>
