->BOOK THREE<-

[...continued from previous page] although they are not so obvious, they nonetheless arise from those natural principles we have discussed. Indeed, if a portion of such great light can harmonize with a thing in a fitting proportion, it will likewise be out of harmony with another. This is perhaps why **Hesiod** <note>Hesiod was an ancient Greek poet whose work "Works and Days" contains agricultural advice linked to the lunar calendar.</note> instructs that lambs should be castrated on the **sixth moon**, oxen and pigs on the **eighth**, and mules on the **twelfth**. He says the **sixth** and **sixteenth** are more favorable for begetting males than females, but the **tenth** is better for females. Furthermore, he orders that calves be castrated in the autumn when the moon is waning, for a well-known reason: those performing the castration fear the flow of moisture, and therefore desire a dry time and a dry moon. For the same reason, they prohibit the castrated animal from drinking much. Thus, there is an evident reason why **Hesiod** <note>The original text uses "Heliodus" here, likely a printer's error for Hesiodus.</note> says the sixth and sixteenth are more favorable for begetting males, but the **fourteenth** <note>The text mentions the 10th then 14th for females; these variations appear in different manuscript traditions of Hesiod.</note> for females.

<margin>Explanation of Hesiod</margin>
As we have often repeated, moisture increases with the moon's light. Therefore, at the full moon, the "excrements of generation" <note>This refers to reproductive fluids (semen and menses), which ancient science classified as "surplus" or "excrement" of blood.</note> will drip more moistly, from which female offspring result more often than male. In this manner, you can reduce other traditions handed down by **Hesiod** to natural causes. He does, however, mix in a few things from ancient superstition—though very few—but nothing anywhere that supports the governors <note>The "governors" or "gubernatores" refers to the celestial bodies as interpreted by astrologers.</note> of the astrologers.

<margin>Sailors</margin>
Likewise, from these cycles of the moon’s borrowed light, sailors can profitably observe many days without falling into superstition; for that variation of light is highly effective in changing the state of the air. Therefore, they prudently abstain from sailing at the **new moon** and **full moon**, because storms are usually stirred up during these times.

<margin>Physicians</margin>
The physicians themselves also rightly consult the needs of the sick by observing the days of the moon’s increase and growth, lest the flowing moisture—especially in an afflicted body that is destitute of its own strength—be more exposed to external injury. For example, it may be reasonable to perform <term>venesection</term> <note>The surgical opening of a vein for bloodletting.</note> as the moon waxes, but to prefer <term>ventosing</term> <note>Also known as cupping; using glass or horn "cups" to create a vacuum on the skin to draw out "bad" humors.</note> as it wanes. This is because the incision of a vein expels and draws out gases. When these humors are boiling and expelled toward the extremities of the body, more material might be drawn out than is appropriate unless one says that the works of art are always more successful when they harmonize with the progression of nature. But let these things be left to the judgment of the physician. Whatever they observe beyond this is clearly vanity, as will become plain in what follows.

### Chapter XV. That the tides of the sea can be attributed to a cause other than the moon, and even if they are, astrology is not helped by it.

<margin>See Adelard’s very plausible reasoning</margin>
Regarding the ebb and flow of the sea, which is a complex matter since everyone sees that this proceeds from the moon, **Adelard** <note>Adelard of Bath (c. 1080–1152), a scholar who translated many Arabic scientific works into Latin.</note>—following the opinion of the **Saracens** <note>A medieval term for Arabic-speaking Muslims; Pico is referencing the transmission of Greek and Indian science through the Islamic world.</note>—both narrates and proves this cause for the sea's approach and retreat. For he says that since the "arms" of the sea (namely those masses of water which, being cast between lands, divide them) hasten to meet and flow together with a swift impulse, it happens—due both to the mountains placed between them and the layout of the earth itself—that while they fail in that same course, they are thrown back. Thus, they are called back by the position of the place from where their prior and natural motion impelled them. The moon is not the cause. Otherwise, this same thing would happen in the seas near the **torrid zone** <note>The tropical regions near the Equator.</note>, since they are no further from the moon (so as not to feel its force) nor are the moist waves thought to be less liquid by nature; and yet, there is no tidal reciprocation there. The reason is that the cause we mentioned is missing: the collision of parts through gaps in the terrestrial layout. This opinion of his is not at all far from the likeness of truth, since the parts of every element are carried by a natural propensity toward their own integrity. What wonder is it, then, if the parts of the ocean, separated by intervening lands, strike the shores as they strive to run together, and being repelled by the obstacle, retreat in the same way? Where this cause is removed (as happens in the southern sea), we see that these tides do not appear. Thus, one might say that this mode of approaching and receding is natural to the water, not merely as water, but insofar as it has parts of a principal element that have been snatched away and separated by the obstacle of the earth's mass. If this reason does not satisfy someone, let him hear...

<margin>Another opinion</margin>

### DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS

...another: astrologers admit <note>The text here refers to the "ebbs and flows" or "reciprocations" mentioned in the preceding arguments.</note> that such recurring flows do not happen in all waters, even at sea, but only in those where the earth is deep, hard, and made rugged and uneven by frequent mountains; where the water is plentiful—neither increasing by the addition of rivers nor diminishing by their departure—but has remained there for a long time with a thick density. Because of this, a reservoir is formed (a nursery of vapors, many of which are neither thin nor easily scattered). These vapors derive that famous bitterness and saltiness from their components—that is, from water and "earthy water"—and from the heat of the sky. Because springs and rivers, and even certain seas, do not have these conditions, they say these tides do not appear in them.

Indeed, it might appear to anyone from this that there is a sufficiently apt and adequate cause for the sea's ebbing and flowing: if indeed from such earth and water those same vapors and winds we described are repeatedly stirred up. From this, a "wind" <note>In ancient physics, "wind" (ventus) often referred to any moving gas or spirit, even within water.</note> and turmoil arise in the water, especially because it grows hot from that motion and impulse and the mixing of vapors; for this reason, it seeks a larger place in which to spread itself out. 

There is added, as it were, a third cause of motion: the reflection of winds plucking at the surface of the water toward its lower parts. These winds, entangled with the winds breathing from below, push the waters in an upward effort. Then the waters necessarily overflow, swell, and "eructate" <note>original: "eructant" — literally "to belch"; used here to describe the forceful bursting forth or surging of water.</note> as they are rejected and pushed alike. Having rolled back, they create their own "accession" <note><term>accessio</term>: the rising tide or "approach" of the sea.</note>. Again, when that force burns out as the vapors are dissolved, the waters subside and are leveled; contracting themselves into narrow spaces, they depart from the places they had occupied. This generation of vapor and winds—based on the nature of the sea—seems a sufficient cause for the continuous ebbing and flowing, just as its generation is almost perpetual, so is its dissolution. Thus, the water returns cold, though it had previously arrived warm—as Adelard <note>Adelard of Bath (c. 1080–1152), a natural philosopher known for his work "Natural Questions," which sought physical explanations for tides.</note> indicates to us. 

And those who hold this opinion can indeed give a reason why certain larger seas do not ebb and flow, even though winds and vapors are present. For the same effect certainly occurs in them too, but the vastness of the open sea and the distance of the shores removes the appearance of the "approach" and "retreat" <note>High and low tide.</note>. Thus, it might rather be called "blessed" that the waters seem to alternate in this way—that is, as a fluctuating surge rather than a receding tide. If these things harmonize with natural reason and experience, why should they be judged less probable? Or why is it necessary to add, besides these causes, the motion of the moon—dragging the waters with it, now downward, now on high? Especially since it does not respond in the way it must necessarily respond: such as when the moon is increased in light, when it is faster in its course, when it is closer to the earth, when it is declining toward the North from the sun's path, or when it is positioned in Northern signs—at those times the tides should become more abundant. On the contrary, they are weaker when conditions are otherwise than what we were saying. 

Furthermore, nothing seems to be able to be objected to those who think this way, except for the "concordance" of the waters with the moon in both their rising and falling. Yet if what Abu Ma'shar <note>original: <margin>Aboafar</margin> refers to Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note> confesses is true, I do not see how even that can be sufficiently objected. For he writes that the beginnings of the rising and receding tide are not the same everywhere, even where there is no difference in the horizon. Instead, it sometimes happens in practice that at the same time the waters recede in one place, they begin their approach in another. Nor does he himself hide the fact that this has given many people cause to suspect that those motions do not depend on the movements of the moon. Although he tries to give a reason for this diversity so that he may defend the idea that the moon is nonetheless the cause, it follows from this that an argument cannot be taken in favor of the moon. Rather, it provides an occasion for contradiction. These things are quite distant from each other: for the lunar cause to be evidently confirmed by the times of the tide, and for it not to be evidently refuted by them. 

Al-Bitruji <note>original: <margin>Alpetragius</margin> — a 12th-century astronomer who challenged Ptolemaic models.</note> brought forth a cause for this motion from the heavens—not from the moon, but from the daily motion by which all things are moved, though lower things less so. For the sphere of fire is rotated in a circle; an uncoordinated motion occurs in the air, which in the water ends in the ebbing and flowing of the tide.

...fallacy; for when they have seen certain earthly things, situated among men, moved by the sense and guidance of celestial things—such as how the ocean, like a companion of the moon, grows old and young <note>A poetic way of describing the waxing/waning or the ebb/flow of the tide.</note> along with it—from this they have clearly prepared an argument for persuasion: so that we might believe all human affairs, both small and great, are led and ruled by the stars and constellations as if conquered by them. Now, let there be things governed by the moon which we ourselves freely and easily believe; but what does that prove for the astrologers or against us? For, as some think, the stars are not understood here to act only by motion and light, but by "occult influences" <term>occultis influxibus: a common medieval belief in invisible "hidden" forces flowing from the stars to the earth</term>; for instance, that the moon, when placed beneath the lowest part of the earth <note>Meaning when the moon is on the opposite side of the globe.</note>, might move the waters, even though its light could not then reach those waters.

<margin>The opinion of Roger Bacon</margin>
Roger Bacon, in his letter to the Supreme Pontiff Clement <note>Pope Clement IV, to whom Bacon sent his major works in the 1260s.</note>, wished to explain this movement as resulting from light in this manner. For when, he says, the moon rises above the sea of some region, the lunar rays fall at oblique angles; for this reason they are weaker. Therefore, the vapors raised from the depths of the sea, which the rays cannot consume—these vapors, I say—fill the waters with bubbling swellings, causing them to expand from their channels, just as a fire placed under a cooking pot evaporates the water, causing foam to spill over the rims of the vessel. Wherefore, as long as that attraction of boiling vapors lasts, the water flows from its seat. But when the moon nears the peak <note>The meridian or zenith.</note>, the rays become steadily straighter and thus stronger as the moon ascends further; and finally they grow so strong that they become capable of dissolving the vapors. For this reason, Bacon says, the flow <note>original: "accessus"</note> becomes slower as the moon nears the meridian; when the moon declines, the waters also immediately decline—just as in that same pot: when the heat has grown stronger and the vapors are consumed, the liquid subsides and retreats to the bottom of the vessel. After this, he addresses the following question: in what way, when moving from the west to the bottom of the earth, does the moon retain the power of moving? For then the waters rise equally as the moon hastens from its rising to the summit. And yet, as he himself admits, no force of rays can penetrate through the middle of the earth.

<margin>The explanation of the solution</margin>
Therefore, he himself resolves it thus. The highest heaven, he says—whether the eighth or the ninth sphere—is necessarily dense, since it terminates our sight, which can only be terminated by something dense. Consequently, it is necessary that the lunar rays stretched out there be reflected back to the opposite side. Therefore, if the moon moves from the west to the bottom of the earth, its power will be active in the other opposite quarter of the heaven, and by the reflected ray it does what it did when proceeding from the east to the peak. This is Bacon’s discovery, in which he takes such great pleasure that he boasts of being the first to have rendered an account of the flow and ebb in opposite quarters; and yet, in his words, there are as many shameful errors as there are words.

<margin>Refutation of Bacon</margin>
First, I would say he contradicts not just experience, but certainly Albumasar <note>original: "Aboasari", referring to the 9th-century Persian astronomer Abu Ma'shar.</note>, whose interpreter he makes himself; for Albumasar teaches that the vigor of the flow occurs when the moon has reached the summit of the heaven, and it is not diminished until the moon has begun to descend from our sky.

<margin>First point</margin>
In contrast, Bacon thinks the flow is diminished the more the moon nears the summit, because the vapors are dissolved by the hotter light.

<margin>Second point</margin>
Nor did he see that the moon's light is never so intense that it could consume maritime exhalations—not even to raise such great ones as are needed to move the tides.

<margin>Third point</margin>
But if he should stubbornly deny this, he must admit, even against his will, that for several days around the new moon there would be no tides of the ocean; for at that time there is either no lunar light, or it is so thin that it could not, by any stretch of the imagination, be called sufficient for procreating so many vapors in the sea and then dissolving them.

<margin>Fourth point</margin>
Finally, why are the rays of the descending moon not stronger than those of the ascending moon? Why does the descending moon recall the waters, while the ascending one pours them out? And why are the rays not weaker when slightly declining from the summit than when they are first rising? Why does it cause the ebb there and the flow here? Since, as he himself feels, the vigor of the rays suppresses the flow with more intense heat, while their weakness increases it.

<margin>Fifth point</margin>
Finally, who would believe that in the reflected rays of the moon running beneath the earth there is such great power that they could even consume raised vapors? Or if they cannot do that, what is the cause of the recession once the moon has been carried below the horizon, according to Bacon’s foundation? For which reason the moon dece... <note>The text breaks off mid-word: "dece..." likely for "decepit" (deceived) or "decedit" (departs).</note>

<summary>Pico della Mirandola critiques Roger Bacon's theory that tides are caused by the moon's light heating maritime vapors like a cooking pot. Pico argues this theory is physically impossible and contradicts both observation and the authorities Bacon claims to follow, such as Albumasar.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of astrological theories regarding the tides. ->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

...depart as they set, or arrive as they rise in the east. Therefore, let Bacon keep these inventions of his for himself; as for us, if such an effect pertains to the moon, let us refer it to that motion of hers which the motion of the ocean imitates by a silent consensus of nature: why it rises when she rises, and falls when she falls. 

<margin>The opinion of Thomas</margin>
This view seems to have pleased Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> in his book *On the Secret Works of Nature* <note>original: "de occultis opibus naturae"</note>. Nor should we think that these tides are an increase or decrease of the waters themselves, but rather what the words themselves express: an "approach" and a "retreat" <note>Referring to the ebb and flow of the tide.</note>. It is not a matter of the water growing or shrinking, but of the sea extending itself as it rises and contracting as it falls. We say these things regarding the tides of night and day; for if there are some seas (as has been written by certain authors) that are always in a state of "approach" while the light of the moon increases—that is, from conjunction <note>The New Moon, when the sun and moon are aligned.</note> to the full moon—and again in "retreat" when it diminishes from the full moon until conjunction, those seas do not follow the motion of the moon in its sphere, but rather the motion (so to speak) of the light in the moon, as it decreases or increases within her. This variation can also somewhat vary the daily tide. 

But the observations handed down on this matter do not agree. For both the Egyptians and those who sail to the West used to say that the approach of the tide grew stronger from the noon of the first day of the lunar month until the eleventh day; from the eleventh to the eighteenth and part of the following day, it weakened. Then until the twenty-sixth it intensified again, and was thereafter reduced until the start of the month. Whenever the "approach" [high tide] was greater, the "retreat" [low tide] was smaller, and vice versa. There are some who say this is truly observed in the waters of rivers flowing from springs, which on the aforementioned days are extended on some and contracted back to their sources on others. Regarding the sea, however, it is reported differently by the Easterners, who do not even agree among themselves. For there are those who record that in the first and last "decan" <note>A ten-day period of the month.</note> of the month, the tides are diminished, and in the middle they increase; the reason for this seems to be that they increase with fuller light and decrease with failing light. Others say it is not a continuous process over many days where the tides either increase or fail, but that it happens on only one or two days, whether they are intensifying or slackening. 

<margin>Aboafar</margin>
Aboafar <note>A Latinized name for Albumasar (787–886 AD), a famous Persian astrologer.</note> creates four phases in this manner: first, after the conjunction when the moon begins to move away until it is half-full; then he says the tide is diminished in that proportion by which the moon departs from the sun, so that when it reaches the "quadrature" <note>The quarter-moon phase, forming a 90-degree angle with the sun.</note> they are weakest. Second, from then until the full moon, at which time they are gradually intensified so that they reach their peak at the full moon. Third, from the full moon until it is again divided [half-moon], with the tide decreasing along with the light. Fourth, from then until the conjunction; then, however, he says the tides become progressively more violent, so that they are most violent when the moon is in conjunction.

<margin>Against Aboafar</margin>
But this can have no rational basis: if this difference depends on light (as pertains to the proposal), whether there is much or little light, increasing or decreasing. If the tide is caused by much or increasing light, the fourth observation is wrong; if by little or decreasing light, the second is wrong; if by much but decreasing light, the third is wrong; if by little but increasing light, the first is wrong. Truly, whichever of these traditions is accepted, it is clear we are not forced to devise any "new power" in the moon besides motion and light to explain why it moves the sea, since all the reported diversities in the approaches and retreats of the sea can most evidently have their cause either from the diversity of the motion of the star as it climbs or declines, or from the losses and increases of its light.

### Chapter XVI: The opinion of Galen regarding "critical days," which refers them to the moon, is refuted.

<margin>A dual lunar influence: one from the sun, the other from the signs of the oblique circle.</margin>
**C**ritical days <note>original: "Crísimos" or "dies cretici." In ancient medicine, these were specific days during an illness when a "crisis" was expected to occur, determining if the patient would live or die.</note>, which in Latin you might call "judicial days," are referred to the moon as falsely as they are superstitiously; this must be explained at greater length. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician (130–210 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note>, the author of this opinion among physicians, mentions a dual lunar influence in the third book of *On Critical Days*. One influence is from the sun, from which the moon receives its light; the other is from the signs of the "oblique circle" <note>The Zodiac.</note> which the moon passes through in its own motion every month. Then he posits—as if from the opinion of astrologers and from experience and proof—that great commotions are excited by the moon in the "opposite" and "quadrate" positions. He contends that this is true both in her relationship to the sun and even to the zodiac signs, regardless of the sun's position; regarding the sun, since when she is...

<meta>This page continues Pico's investigation into the moon's influence, transitioning from the physical movement of the tides to the medical and meteorological theories of the "critical days," specifically critiquing the calculations of Galen and Peter of Abano.</meta>

# BOOK THREE

The divided moon <note>The quarter moon, when it appears half-lit.</note> (which occurs in roughly the quadrant positions after conjunction <note>original: "coitu"; the New Moon, when the moon and sun are aligned.</note>) and again when it is full, changes the state of the air and the weather in the opposite locations. Regarding the signs of the zodiac, it works in this manner: whatever change begins when the Moon is, for example, in Taurus, a change in that state always occurs when the Moon subsequently reaches Leo, Scorpio, or Aquarius—which are the locations square <note>original: "tetragona"; an astrological aspect of 90 degrees.</note> or opposite to Taurus. This is confirmed by the authority of the Egyptians, who assert 
<margin>Note the opinion of the Egyptians</margin>
that if lucky stars reside in Aries in someone's birth chart (to use an example), the person will fare well whenever the Moon passes through either Taurus, or the square or opposite signs; conversely, they will fare poorly if the stars are unlucky. From this, Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> believes the cause of <term>critical days</term> <note>original: "cretici dies"; specific days in the course of a disease when a decisive change—for better or worse—was expected.</note> becomes most evident. For the seventh and fourteenth days are particularly "critical"; and the Moon reaches the fourth sign from its starting point on the seventh day (counting from the onset of the illness), and the opposite sign on the fourteenth day, since it completes its full circuit in roughly twenty-seven days and a third part of a day. Therefore, since the Moon excites commotions in these square and opposite locations, it causes the crisis of a disease to be stirred up on these days—namely the seventh and fourteenth—when it reaches those places. If the crisis is favorable, it leads to health; if harmful, to death. However, since Galen thought the twentieth day was critical, rather than the twenty-first as Archigenes <note>Archigenes of Apamea (c. 1st–2nd century AD), a Greek physician.</note> believed, he worked to provide a reason why the twentieth day itself would be the "seventh" day of the third week.
<margin>Archigenes</margin>
And first, he demonstrated this with a proof that was neither absurd nor difficult. For the course of the moon is completed in twenty-seven days with eight hours added. If you divide this into four <term>weeks</term> <note>original: "ebdomadas"; from the Greek 'hebdomas', meaning a group of seven.</note>, each week will consist of six days and twenty hours. Therefore, three weeks will contain twenty days and twelve hours; thus, the twenty-first day—which is the third weekly marker of the lunar course—will fall partly on the twentieth natural day and partly on the twenty-first. For its twelve hours will finish the twentieth day, and the remaining hours will begin the twenty-first. And so, the critical commotion happens on the twentieth day when the moon reaches the second square, namely in the third week. Again, the same logic does not fail if the crisis is deferred to the twenty-first natural day, which usually happens in acute illnesses; just as in longer-lasting illnesses, the crisis runs through even numbers in their cycles, and through odd numbers in others. After Galen himself had said this, he then brought forward a new commentary (which he reported as if it were the specific invention of Peter of Abano <note>original: "Apponensis"; referring to Pietro d'Abano (c. 1250–1316), a philosopher and physician known for his astrological medicine.</note>) through which he would not have to agree with Archigenes regarding the critical influence belonging to both days. Instead, he would conclude that the entire twentieth day was
<margin>Peter of Abano</margin>
critical, and the twenty-first was not. Thus, he devised a period for the time in which the moon returns to conjunction with the sun: twenty-nine days and twelve hours, which is commonly considered a month. Let us subtract the days in which the moon does not appear, being overwhelmed by the rays of the sun, because then she has no power to change lower things; there will remain roughly twenty-six days and twelve hours. For she is hidden for about three days. Let us add these days of the "shining moon" to the days in which she traverses the signs (which he computed as twenty-four days and twenty hours); the sum will be fifty-three days and twenty hours, the half of which is twenty-six days and twenty-two hours. Galen thought this span was a not unreasonable measure for the placement of critical days; for he saw that only half the days in which the moon traverses the zodiac are those in which she is illuminated by the sun, as if the lunar influence then twice enfolded its powers within itself: both that power which comes from the signs, and that which comes from the sun—it being likely that a commotion in diseases would arise from both. This number was later called by those who followed Galen's authority the "medical month"; 
<margin>Who defines the medical month</margin>
just as one calls the period of twenty-nine days a "conjunction month," the period of twenty-six days and twelve hours a month of "manifest vision," and the period of twenty-seven days and a third of a day a "traversal month." From this invention, Galen achieved what he wanted against Archigenes. For if the total month is twenty-six days and twenty-two hours, the individual weeks of this month will each consist of six days, seventeen hours, and a half-hour; therefore, half the month is thirteen days and eleven hours.

Therefore, the hours of the seventh natural day <note>A "natural day" refers to a standard 24-hour period.</note> up to the seventeenth hour will belong to the seventh day of the **medicinal month**; and for that reason, they will be **critical** <note>original: "creticae"; days when a disease reaches a turning point.</note>. The remainder of that day will belong to the eighth medicinal day. The fourteenth natural day will have only its first eleven hours from the end of the fourteenth medicinal day; its preceding thirteen hours will be counted with the thirteenth natural day. Since any given medicinal **week** <note>original: "ebdomada"</note> consists of six days and seventeen and a half hours, it is clear that the third week ends on the twentieth natural day, with only four and a half hours spilling over into the twenty-first. And so, what Galen primarily desired is achieved—and it was for this sake that he fabricated this entire invention—so that the twentieth day would be considered **critical** far more than the twenty-first, by the logic of the succeeding week. Galen took up this labor for himself for no reason. For it was not necessary; the twentieth day was sufficiently defended as critical by the duration of the moon's passage through the **zodiac** <note>The circle of twelve constellations through which the moon travels.</note>, especially since he himself does not deny that the twenty-first is also critical, as it often is in acute diseases. Nor did we report these things so that we might judge between Archigenes <note>A prominent Greek physician of the 1st century AD who often disagreed with Galen.</note> and Galen, overstepping our prescribed limits, but rather lest anyone think I had not fully satisfied the argument when we demonstrated that critical days cannot be referred to the Moon—whether we consider the power she receives from the Sun or from the signs—on the grounds that Galen had introduced a kind of "mixed influence" which specifically excites the critical days. For perhaps Galen did not actually do this, or if he did, he could not have done so reasonably. For if we say with him that the Moon excites movements when it is in **squares** <note>90-degree angles</note> and **opposites** <note>180-degree angles</note> to some original signs, and again [excites movements] when it is illuminated by the square and opposite rays of the Sun, we cannot expect these events from the Moon except at those times when she is in one of those two states—if, of course, one expects the event from those causes. For if at both times she produces such effects according to the condition and **constellation** of each time, and we are to believe that the power of both constellations is mixed at a time when neither of those constellations is found—for no other reason than that the time is the midpoint of the sum of both times counted together—then we do not know if we are even among the sane <note>original: "inter & horestes"; a reference to Orestes, a figure from Greek mythology often used as a symbol of madness.</note>. Therefore, if Galen thinks this exciting force exists in the weeks of this "medicinal month" of his and its midpoint, but not in the weeks or the midpoint of the month in which the Moon is either illuminated by the Sun or passes through the signs of the zodiac, he must explain to us how that force of an invented month can be reduced to any **astrological influences**—that is, neither to the square or opposite signs, nor to the square or opposite configurations of the Moon with the Sun. For it is too absurd and fictitious, as I have said, for the power of these things to be preserved and fused at a time when they do not exist. Those who wished to defend Galen while simultaneously attempting to fit critical days to the Moon's cycles could not stand by their premises; instead, they defend now this point, now that, but never both at once. For let it be asked why the fourteenth day is critical: they will retreat to the Moon's cycles and its month of passage, because on that day the Moon arrives at the opposite signs. This reason fits a part of the medicinal month, since its second week falls back into the thirteenth natural day, and only eleven hours of it remain belonging to the fourteenth. For, as we said, any week of Galen’s month is six days and seventeen and a half hours; therefore, the thirteenth day should be called "more critical" than the fourteenth, since the former has thirteen critical hours and the latter only eleven. Here, then, having abandoned the power of the "mixture" and the manufactured month, they will flee to the spaces of the zodiac traversed. Conversely, to make the twentieth day critical, they use Galen’s month, not the moon's passage. But if someone falls ill the day before the Moon joins the Sun <note>The New Moon</note> and has his seventh day as a critical day, how will that result from the influence of power received either from the Sun or from the signs? Since for the greatest part of those days, just as she was not seen, so the Moon did not affect us with solar power, by Galen’s own admission. It is necessary, therefore, here too for them to turn to the signs, whose influence alone, by virtue of the **square**, would have made that seventh day critical for him. ...struck from the mint of nature. For it is forged as if the Moon were always hidden by the sun for three days. But it is also sometimes seen in the morning before the sun rises, and in the evening of that same day with a **sickle-shaped face**; both experience indicates this and <margin>Al-Farghani</margin> Al-Farghani <note>A 9th-century Persian astronomer, known in Latin as Alfraganus, whose works were foundational to medieval European astronomy.</note> testifies to it. Let Galen have his month to himself; lest he thrust it upon us too conveniently, let us grant it to those whom he prefers to have "critical days," while rejecting those of **Archigenes** <note>A prominent Greek physician whom Galen often criticized.</note>. I firmly assert that these days are governed by no cycles of the moon. Whether we estimate the moon's power as received from the sun or from the zodiac signs: for that power which comes from the sun is indeed solid and natural (as we have declared), but **critical days** <note>original: "cretici dies"; the days on which a disease reaches a turning point or "crisis."</note> cannot pertain to it unless diseases always attacked us during the **new moon** <note>original: "nouilunio"</note>. Otherwise, neither the half-moon of the seventh day nor the full moon of the fourteenth would correspond—those times when the square and opposite configurations of the sun stir the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health.</note>. There remains the power from the signs. But as the following will clarify, there is no such power; even if there were, it would in no way regard what they themselves say about critical days. For if they argue from experience that a commotion occurs on the seventh day, and again on the fourteenth, and that during these days the Moon is in **quadrate signs** <note>An astrological aspect where two bodies are 90 degrees apart.</note> or in opposition, then they claim these commotions follow from this change of signs. <margin>Refutation of the argument.</margin> We, on the other hand, argue thus: a commotion occurs on the seventh day and again on the fourteenth, yet during these days the Moon is frequently *not* in quadrate or opposite places. Therefore, that commotion is not aroused by this change of signs. To anyone not entirely ignorant of lunar motions, there is no doubt which side relies on truer assumptions. For when passing through the lower part of its **epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain planetary speeds in the Ptolemaic system.</note>, the Moon moves faster and reaches the quadrate signs on roughly the sixth day, and sometimes the opposite signs by the thirteenth. But when it is carried more slowly through the upper parts, it does not reach the quadrate position until the eighth or ninth day. If they were to respond that for this reason those days also sometimes become critical, they would have a point—*if* the humors were stirred on the eighth or ninth day when the moon’s course is slow. <margin>The opinion that Hippocrates and Avicenna follow Galen is falsely written. Celsus. Asclepiades. Galen is mocked by Avicenna and Moses the Egyptian; likewise by Averroes regarding the first books of Aristotle. General argument regarding the fourth figure.</margin> But observation shows this is not the case; rather, it frequently happens in practice that the Moon, though slow, brings about a judgment on the seventh or even the sixth day, while when it is swifter, the commotions are deferred to the eighth or ninth. Noting this, many physicians have denied that this order preserved by nature in diseases depends on lunar cycles. Nothing led those who did believe it to report such things except either a love for astrological matters or the authority of Galen. However, we shall soon say how much weight these things carry in this matter. Furthermore, some of the **Moderns** <note>original: "Neotericis"; refers to later medieval or early Renaissance commentators.</note> falsely claim that **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian polymath and physician.</note> and **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> also held this opinion. For Hippocrates never spoke a word on this; rather, he relied on this order as referring to numbers, which nature is accustomed to observe willingly—a point noted by **Celsus** and **Asclepiades**. As for Avicenna, when he recalled the opinion referring these things to the moon, he said "there is much ambiguity in these words." Then he rejected the question, stating that its investigation did not belong to the physician, as it would rather be an impediment to him. Let Galen's authority prevail among us when he determines which days are critical and how a patient should be treated when they appear or are foreseen. For in this medical duty, we—along with the consensus of the learned—approve and admire Galen as truly divine and preeminent in his profession. But when the cause of those days is investigated, which is a work of higher **philosophy**, Galen’s opinion should not only be denied precedence, but should not even be held as a testimony of great weight. Indeed, **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the Jewish philosopher and physician.</note> and Avicenna—great men and great supporters of Galen in medicine—report that he possessed more of the branches of knowledge than the roots. He is certainly ridiculed by logicians for his "fourth figure" of **syllogisms** <note>A form of logical argument; Galen is traditionally credited with adding a fourth structure to Aristotle's original three.</note>, and in philosophy he is so often terrified and fails to perceive the strongest reasons that many find his philosophical judgment lacking. He cannot understand how the soul, being surviving and immortal, could cease from its work while the brain remains intact; he says he was "fatigued" by this question from a certain **Platonist**, as if a surviving sailor would not cease from navigation if his ship were destroyed. ...understands what is demonstrated by the physicists: that universal notions of things are comprehended only by our intellect and not by animals <note>original: "brutis"</note>. Why he hesitates concerning the knowledge of innate time is not a story for this occasion. For we are not discussing Galen’s philosophy here; we have only touched upon these matters so that we might confirm the judgment of Moses and Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard text in Europe for centuries.</note> concerning him, and at the same time take care lest his authority impose a superstition on anyone.

For on this very page where he deals with astrology, the calculation of the lunar motion shows him to be unskilled. Nor does Pietro d’Abano <note>original: "Apponēlis"; a 13th-century Italian physician and astrologer who attempted to reconcile Greek medicine with Arabic astrology.</note> defend him in any other way than by saying that in Galen's age, the logic of celestial motions had not yet been fully explored. Therefore, let his credibility in medicine be as great as it can possibly be; but as far as other doctrines are concerned, let us remember to deal with the man more cautiously. We must examine more diligently what he has passed down, whether it accords with experience, reason, or the opinions of others.

And since we have proved that what he published concerning **critical days** <note>The specific days during an illness, like the 7th or 14th, when the patient’s condition was expected to change drastically.</note> agrees little with the facts themselves, it will become clear to those looking into it that these same ideas lack even the appearance of reason. For what logic is there for the moon to stir up agitation in the **humors** <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to cause disease when out of balance.</note> when it reaches the fourth or seventh sign from the place it occupied when the disease first attacked?

Galen denies that he will give a reason, but instead puts forward the authority of the Egyptians. We shall remind him of his own sixth book *On Simple Medicines*, in which he marks the Egyptians for their madness. Why his authority wavers among us will be made known in the last two books. For now, let us say that changes in bodies through these lunar cycles could not have been faithfully observed by the Egyptians, for whom the moon's course was not accurately known.

<margin>
Hipparchus
</margin>
For Hipparchus, on the island of Rhodes, was the first to observe them more accurately, though he did not reach the full truth. <margin>The reasoning of the moderns</margin> Ptolemy then approached closer to it, although even he did not satisfy the needs of the Spanish astronomers. The **moderns** <note>original: "Neoterici"; likely referring to medieval or Renaissance scholastic astrologers.</note> have devised a reason that not only fails to agree with the truth, but also fails to match the position they defend, nor the sayings of Galen which they follow.

It is of this sort: square or opposite signs have contrary qualities. Square signs differ in both qualities, or at least in the active ones: for instance, **Aries** differs from **Cancer** in both qualities, since Aries is a hot and dry sign, while Cancer is moist and cold. **Taurus** differs from **Leo**, but not in both, for they agree in dryness; however, they disagree in the active quality, Taurus being cold and Leo being hot. Likewise, opposite signs always disagree in at least one quality. Then they say—as is commonly chanted by astrologers—that square and diametrical radiations <note>These are "aspects": a "square" is a 90-degree angle and a "diameter" or "opposition" is 180 degrees.</note> are contrary and fighting. Given these premises, they conclude that when the moon reaches places hostile to those it held when the disease attacked <margin>Opposition of reason</margin>, it follows that a fight arises between the disease and nature.

But we, granting their premises, would address them thus: you think this is the reason why the moon causes critical days: because if, for example, it was in **Taurus** when the disease occupied the body, it ought to produce a contrary effect when it comes to a contrary place. It will therefore cause "nature" to rise up against the disease; hence a fight and a "judgment" as victory leans toward one side or the other. It will be in a contrary place when it comes to **Leo** or **Scorpio**. But it will arrive at Leo on the seventh day, and at Scorpio on the fourteenth. Through these days, then, the war-trumpet sounds for the disease and nature.

But why does it not do the same on the third day when coming to **Gemini**, which differs from Taurus more than Leo does? Why not on the twelfth or thirteenth day when coming to **Libra**, with which Taurus again agrees less than with Scorpio? Why not on the fifteenth when entering **Sagittarius**, which disagrees with Taurus just as much as Scorpio and Leo do? I know what they will answer: that there is no connection of "aspects" between these signs. But I did not wish to lead them elsewhere: not so that I might object that this logic of aspects is worthless (which we shall do in the sixth book), but so that we might show that even if some such thing exists, it does not serve the question at hand. For that logic which is observed between two planets—whose rays they do not think can come together to complete an effect, whether they agree or disagree, unless they are figured by such intervals as the hexagon, triangle, square, and diameter—well, here we are not "figuring" the Moon with other planets. We are only noticing that it is carried to a place contrary to the one it previously occupied. Although a star placed in Gemini [is near] a star placed in

### BOOK THREE ###

Astrologers will deny that Taurus is linked by a geometric aspect <note>original: "aspectum"; in astrology, this refers to specific angles like 90 or 120 degrees between zodiac signs.</note>; yet they will not deny that this place is "contrary" to it. But if the Moon produces an effect contrary to the first state because it has arrived at a place of contrary quality, why—if it stirred up a disease while in a cold and dry sign—does it not stir up nature to fight the disease when it is placed in warm and moist signs? Whether that sign is the sixth, or the second, or any other number you prefer to count? This is entirely ridiculous, and not something that could be said by a man looking at the truth rather than merely defending a position. 

If they contend that the power consists in these **aspects**, they must consequently concede that the Moon will confirm the disease when it reaches the **square signs** <note>original: "tetragona"; signs 90 degrees apart, which were traditionally thought to be "disharmonious" or stressful.</note>; for just as square signs are in discord, so **trine signs** <note>original: "trigona"; signs 120 degrees apart, considered harmonious.</note> are in concord. Why then, if the square signs rouse nature by their contrary quality relative to the sign of the sickness, would not the trine signs excite the disease for the same reason of concord? Since the Moon is carried to these on roughly the eleventh day, the eleventh day would have to be established as harmful; yet it is numbered by physicians among the beneficial **critical days** <term>creticos dies</term> <note>From the Greek "krisis," meaning a turning point or judgment in an illness.</note>.

Finally, it will be most manifest to anyone considering it that the observations of critical days passed down by physicians cannot have a rational basis in the motion of the moon. For they say that bad disturbances happen on these days: the sixth, eighth, twelfth, tenth, sixteenth, and eighteenth. Let them give a reason for these from the moon if they can! For it would be more fitting, as we were saying, for the sixth and eighth to be good, as the moon reaches the **square signs** <note>original: "tetragona"</note> on <term>those days</term>. But why is the tenth or twelfth bad at all, on which days the moon is not in any place linked by an aspect to the sign of the sickness? Why do they count the seventeenth and thirtieth among the healthy days? 

And what lunar logic dictates that four-day cycles have power before the twentieth day, while after the twentieth, it is seven-day cycles rather than four—such as the twenty-seventh, thirty-fourth, and forty-first? And when you exceed those, twenty-day critical cycles are found, such as the sixtieth, eightieth, and one-hundred-and-twentieth. Why then the circuit of months and years? Just as all these things have no cause from the moon, so they can have none from the sun, nor from any other constellation; for the stars are not found to be fixed, similar, or concordant on those fixed days, but vary in a wondrous way. They keep no order that could correspond to the order in the disturbances of diseases, which is for the most part maintained by nature. 

Thus one might marvel at <term>the man from Abano</term> <note>original: "apponensem"; referring to Pietro d’Abano (1257–1315), a famous medical mediator.</note> who says that the malice of the sixth day (which Galen compares to a tyrant) can be reduced to the seventh (which he compares to a king) <margin>See the shameful error of Pietro d’Abano, the "Conciliator," regarding the process of nature through sevens in Avicenna and Galen.</margin> because the moon, by its swifter course, reaches the square. He is too forgetful of himself, having said that healthy changes in sickness happen on the seventh day because of the nature of the **square**—which, naturally, would oppose the sign of the disease. By what logic does he now also render a reason for the malice of the sixth day from the square? 

It is clear, therefore, that all these things have other causes. They were deceived because the seventh and fourteenth days seemed to coincide [with lunar phases]; though, as we said, they do not truly coincide there either. But we see this progression by sevens observed elsewhere in the works of nature where there is no suspicion of the motion of the moon or sun, as in the very periods of diseases. Just as acute diseases end on the seventh day, so long-term ones—as Avicenna writes—are often accustomed to terminate in the seventh month, the seventh year, the fourteenth, or the twenty-first. 

I do not, however, approve of those who superstitiously observe numbers here; rather, I say that the courses of nature are usually fulfilled in things not because of constellations appearing at these times (for none are found), but because of a **hidden property** and condition of those things in which it usually happens this way. For we see it so arranged by nature—as Galen himself writes—that acute diseases move through the odd days, while slower and longer-lasting ones move through the even. Reduce these to the moon, or reduce them to the sun and stars if you can! Why then should we refer the disturbance of the seventh day in acute diseases to the **square signs** through which the moon is carried? Especially since that is not even a universal rule; indeed, some of the younger writers speak against the opinion of Galen and others who flee to the moon for help. If someone falls ill while the moon is positioned in Aries, they ought to have a critical eighth day, because that is when the moon reaches the square in Cancer. He responds that it so happens...

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY #

...should be considered by reason of the lunar motion: but on the seventh day, a "commotion" <note>In ancient medicine, a "commotion" refers to a sudden change or crisis in the body's humors during an illness.</note> occurs because of the nature of the disease, which, when it is acute, moves through the unequal days until the fourteenth day. Finally, those things which have been truly observed by medicine concerning **critical days** <term>creticos dies</term> <note>From the Greek "krisis," meaning a turning point or judgment; days when a disease was thought to be "judged" by nature.</note> not only fail to confirm the astrological case: they weaken it. This serves as the greatest proof that the afflictions of bodies do not depend on the causes which the astrologers introduce. For if there were no fixed order in these days—if now this day were critical and now that one, and if among the critical days one were found harmful at one time and healthy at another—no wonder would rouse us to investigate, as the shifting diversity of the matter alone would satisfy us. But since certain days are not always, but yet for the most part, critical—and some for the most part lead to life, and others to death—it seems this order requires a certain cause that is rarely changeable.

<margin>Galen: Critical days would not be unchangeable if they were caused by the heavens.</margin> Galen concludes from this that the cause must be in the celestial bodies, which are bodies that move in a fixed and stable order and can produce a fixed and stable effect. To me, on the contrary, it seems clear that such a cause *cannot* be from the celestial bodies; for if it were from there, the critical days would be different at different times, and the order that appears in them would not be preserved. For if the Moon were joined to Mars or the Sun, the influx would summon a commotion; if joined to Saturn, it would be delayed. Furthermore, the "conjunction of the luminaries" <note>The meeting of the Sun and Moon, i.e., a New Moon.</note> immediately preceding the day of the disease would have to be inspected: then, if the "Lord" of the place in which they joined held the ascendant <note>original: "orientem"; the eastern horizon or rising sign.</note>, the commotion would happen quickly; if it were in the west, it would happen late. Moreover, stars proceeding in direct motion or placed in "moveable signs" <note>The cardinal signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn; associated with swift change.</note> would sound the battle-cry for the disease and nature more swiftly; conversely, those moving backward <note>original: "retrocedentia"; refers to retrograde motion, when a planet appears to move backward in the sky.</note> or located in "fixed signs" <note>Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius; associated with stability or slowness.</note> would do so more slowly. These things would not happen the same way for every sick person, even if they shared the same constellations, but would differ for each according to the condition of their own birth-chart <note>original: "geniturae"; the horoscope at the moment of birth.</note>.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
I pass over the "figure" whose angles Ptolemy commands us to observe—whether they are derived from fortunate or unfortunate "rays" <note>Astrological aspects or geometric angles between planets.</note> so that we might pronounce a judgment on the disease from them; things which some most ignorant men believe pertain to critical days. If physicians received all these things from astrologers, the critical days would not be for the most part those which the medical art intended, but would change from one to another. Nor would it be a fixed rule that the sixth day would oppress with "tyrannical" cruelty, while the seventh would liberate with "royal" kindness. Rather, the seventh day would be counted among the harmful ones under bad constellations, and the sixth among the healthy ones under good ones. If this does not happen, it should not be said to come from the heavens (where they seek a cause for that which happens with order and almost always), but should instead be attributed to the matter and some particular property of the laboring person.

### Chapter XVII: The periods of the humors are not to be referred to the motions of the stars ###

<margin>The first way.</margin>
**B**ut let no one believe that the periods of the humors in fevers are to be referred to the motions of the stars—as if, for the sake of example, **black bile** <term>bilis atra</term> <note>Also known as melancholy; one of the four bodily fluids or "humors" in ancient medicine.</note> should cease for two days and be roused on the fourth because it is under Saturn, whose motion is slower than the others. For by what reason does **blood**, which is referred to Jupiter by astrologers, putrefy continuously without any pause, when Jupiter is not the swiftest of all? Indeed, if we take the time of its "restitution" <note>The time a planet takes to return to its starting point in the zodiac.</note>, it is the slowest of all after Saturn. Likewise, why is the motion of **red bile** <note>original: "rubræ bilis"; also called choler, associated with anger and heat.</note> ascribed to Mars? It is only a little slower than the motion of black bile: for it ceases for six hours less, since it sleeps for thirty-six hours, while the other lasts forty-eight—yet the star of Mars is much swifter than Saturn. Furthermore, it is a decree of the astrologers that the works of slow-moving stars are more long-lasting the slower they are. Since, therefore, the motion of **phlegm** <term>pituitae</term> returns more quickly than that of red bile—for the former returns after six hours, the latter after thirty-six—because the motion of the Moon exciting the phlegm is swifter than the motion of Mars exciting the choler; why, I ask, if this is true, does the agitation of choler not last longer than that of phlegm? The former lasts only twelve hours, while the latter lasts eighteen. For the works of Mars ought to be more long-lasting than those of the Moon (if we stand by the precepts of the astrologers), since the latter's motions are swifter than the former's. But if, again, we wish to refer all these periods to the Moon alone, as if it were predominant over all humors, the astrological reasoning on which they lean will fail no less. For they say that because phlegm has a kinship with the Moon and water, it almost imitates the motion of the waters; they flow in and flow out with an intervening delay—but a small one, such as necessarily falls between direct motions. <margin>The second way.</margin> Thus, phlegm leaves only six full hours.

<summary>Pico argues that medical "critical days" and the cycles of bodily humors (like bile and phlegm) do not align with the speeds or positions of the planets, proving that astrology is an unreliable basis for medicine.</summary>

...is left behind. But this could better suit the blood, in which, just as in water, a continuous surge is found, where a delay separating the flow from the ebb does not correspond well to the interval of six hours—the time in which the entire flow or ebb itself is driven. But in the blood, there could be a greater similarity, the motion of which is not denied by the proponents of this opinion to be interrupted in sensible delays. But let us pursue the rest. They say that **black bile** <term>Atra bilis</term> <note>One of the four "humors" in ancient medicine, associated with melancholy and the element of earth.</note>, since it differs greatly from the nature of water, moves in a manner contrary to **phlegm** <term>pituita</term>: namely, ceasing for the most part for up to two full days. 

<margin>Pico's opinion</margin>
But it seems to me that it has more in common with earth than with fire, whether you consider its location, quality, or motion—conditions which no other factor can outweigh. Therefore, the same judgment will apply to the humors in relation to the elements: the motion of **red bile** <note>Also known as yellow bile or "choler," associated with fire.</note> ought to be more different from the motion of phlegm than that of black bile. Yet none of the illustrious and ancient physicians traced the cycle of fevers to these causes. 

<margin>The nature of Peter</margin>
The first to attempt this was Peter of Abano <note>original: "Petrus Apponensis"; a 13th-century physician and astrologer known for trying to reconcile medicine with astrology.</note>, a man born to gather more than to digest; indeed, the more unlearned a person is, the more they are accustomed to admiring him when he is talking nonsense.

### Chapter XVIII. The misfortune of an eight-month birth is not to be ascribed to Saturn.

<margin>Abano</margin>
**W**hile we are discussing these things, it comes to mind that astrologers are accustomed to ascribing the misfortune of an eight-month birth to Saturn. This must be discussed here, but briefly, lest by not refuting it we seem to be forced to concede—even against our will—that we are caught by the rays of the most hostile stars. Which I will concede as you wish, provided it is not also conceded that we are caught by them so as to be held bound; for I hold that anything descending from heaven does not arrive as something harmful. 

The sum of the matter is this: astrologers are mistaken if they believe that those born in the eighth month do not live because a single planet presides over each month of gestation, and because Saturn—the same planet as in the first month—rules the eighth. They claim Saturn is a cold and dry planet, and therefore contrary to the qualities of life. 

<margin>The reason given by astronomers for eight-month births</margin>
First of all, those handed-down successions of planetary rule have no basis in reason (as will be said elsewhere in its proper place), and there is an entirely different reason why an eight-month birth does not survive. Some believe the fetus tries to exit in the seventh month and is injured in the attempt; if it comes out in the eighth, not yet having been restored to its health, it is not usually viable. 

<margin>Hippocrates</margin>
But I agree rather with Hippocrates, who, in the treatise he wrote on the eight-month birth, says the reason why it usually does not live is that in that month, the carrying of the womb is difficult. For then, pregnant women feel more heavily burdened and suffer certain heavy and inconvenient things in the matrix; and if they give birth, being oppressed by the double labor of both the birth and the illness, they become extremely weak. Hence, the fetus itself is necessarily made weaker and rarely lives long. 

<margin>Avicenna, Aristotle</margin>
This opinion is supported by the fact that if any women are found to be more vigorous and strong, they are accustomed to give birth even in the eighth month to those who will live—such as Avicenna writes are found in Spain, and Aristotle in Egypt. I have added the Greek words of Hippocrates on this matter, lest, since this book is not commonly available, it might be believed to be a fiction by us: "Concerning births in the eighth month, they say..." <note>original: "περὶ οκταμήνου γενεσιν φασὶ"</note> and what follows.

### Chapter XIX. Why sailors, physicians, and farmers predict the truth more often than astrologers.

**T**here were roughly three objections in that second line of reasoning used by astrologers. The first was from the changes in lower things caused by the courses of the Sun and Moon, from which they gathered that the stars also act upon us and that the change of other things must be conjectured from them. The second was from the testimony of the good arts of medicine, agriculture, and navigation, which employ astrological observations in their work. We have rejected both of these in such a way that we fought back against them with their own weapons, showing (as we said a little while ago) that from the works of the Sun and Moon and from the observations of those arts, it is gathered rather what they deny than what they affirm. There remains the third point, which was taken from the predictions of those same craftsmen and of the common people themselves, as if we were being too unfair by granting no foreknowledge of the future to the astrologers of the entire sky...

He also begins a critique of why practical professions like farming and sailing are more accurate than astrology.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument from the previous page, shifting from the medical nuances of "critical days" and humors to a broader comparison between legitimate expertise (like medicine, farming, and sailing) and the "fictional" science of astrology.</meta>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

...skilled masters rather than crude ones; and even among the common people, some occasionally succeed. Thus, we see many things concerning rains, illnesses, livestock, and daily provisions predicted by the common crowd with credible results. Why then, they ask, would those who know the celestial causes more deeply not be able to predict these things more correctly, and other secrets as well? This is what we must dissolve at present; or rather, as is our habit, we shall push it back upon them, explaining it briefly with no trouble. For if they predict true things without any regard for the precepts of astrology, who would not say that those things they omit or are ignorant of are either light conjectures or unnecessary, but superfluous; not more secret, but more false; not dogmas, but fictions. 

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
Yet Ptolemy says that those who are ignorant of astrology are sometimes mistaken, but that astrologers are mistaken even more often. It is concluded, therefore, that astrologers understand astrological matters less than those who are not astrologers. For it cannot be denied that the physician’s word concerning the sick, the farmer’s concerning the harvest, the sailor’s concerning storms, and the shepherd’s concerning the flock, corresponds more to the truth than what is predicted about these matters by astrologers. 

The reason is immediately at hand: the astrologer looks at signs that are not signs; he looks for causes that are not causes; therefore he fails. For he looks at the celestial disposition, which is only a universal cause and does not produce variety in inferior things except through the condition of the matter and the influence of proximate causes. Furthermore, even that celestial disposition which he looks at is not real, but a disposition **fictionalized** by him in the heavens through the most vain and contrived rules—consisting not in nature, but in the arbitrary choice of astrologers. For, as we will demonstrate, neither the image of man, nor those other images, signs, parts, *antilia* <note>original: "antilia"; likely referring to 'antiscions' or specific degrees/points in a chart</note>, *dodecathemoria* <term>twelve-fold divisions</term> <note>The subdivision of each zodiac sign into twelve equal parts of 2.5 degrees each.</note>, houses, and such things used by them were made in the heavens by that Father and God of gods. Rather, the astrologer, a deceiver of men and a slanderer of the gods, has lied about these things being in the heaven. Therefore, it is no wonder if this art is concluded to know no future thing by any certain reason. 

But the craftsmen we mentioned rely on true, natural, and proximate causes and judgments; and therefore they rarely fall away from the truth. By true foreknowledge of the future, they create faith in their methods, and they practice their arts with successful results and good fortune. Read the books of the *Prognostics* of Hippocrates; you will never find him seeking the future state of the sick among the stars, for he knew these things were sought better from urine <note>original: "lotio"; uroscopy was a primary diagnostic tool in ancient and medieval medicine</note> than from a star, and more certainly from the pulse of the veins than from the motion of the spheres. 

Skilled pilots do not foresee storms from Jupiter, Saturn, Venus, Mars, or Mercury; but from clouds, from winds, and from every observation of the air. This skillful discipline of theirs is confirmed by experience everywhere: from the breath of a tiny breeze or from a barely visible cloudlet, the sailor understands an imminent storm, of which no person had any prior inkling, and no sign was yet visible to the eyes of others. Nor do they only say a storm is coming when they perceive it, but from which direction it will be stirred up, how it can be avoided, and how its force can be overcome—matters upon which all the wisdom of the astrologers will be utterly blind. 

So too shepherds, farmers, and even the uneducated common people often foreknow the state of the air—not from the stars, but from the disposition of the air itself and from those impressions which occur on high. 

<margin>fictions</margin>
Why do they rarely fail? Because they judge the air from the air, just as physicians judge the sick from the sick; that is, from proximate principles. They do not do what astrologers do, who judge from remote and universal causes, or—what is worse—from fictional, imaginary, and fabulous ones. Therefore, let no one think that farming will become better, medicine more effective, or navigation safer if these things are handled by men deeply versed in and observing astrology. On the contrary, this would rather be the decay and destruction of those arts, while they are called away from certain rules to uncertain ones, from true ones to contrived ones; and by the mixing in of false dogmas, the solidity and truth of all proven experience would be undermined. 

This point, even if the reasons by which the vanity of astrology becomes known are not yet understood, can be sufficiently argued from what we said at the beginning of this work: the greatest masters of those arts, who were especially successful in practicing them, not only did not apply astrological observations to their work, but either despised them or even...

<meta>Catchword: or even</meta>

He asserts that astrology actually degrades the quality of legitimate sciences by introducing uncertainty and fictional data.</summary>

<margin>A witty saying</margin>
...or even to have refuted it. Columella—whom we have cited elsewhere—that most exact writer on rural matters, in the place where he is about to deliver precepts for observing the seasons, mentions his own late-night studies against astrologers. He says: "These things which we have treated with <term>plain wit<note>original: "pingui Minerva"; an idiom referring to common sense or practical, unrefined knowledge rather than subtle academic theory</note></term> are true; but those things which the <term>Chaldeans<note>A common historical term for astrologers and soothsayers</note></term> most imprudently promise are false, and have been refuted by us elsewhere." Therefore, if Ptolemy concludes that because farmers foresee many things about the state of the air, we [astrologers] must therefore know more and more certain things insofar as we excel them in knowledge of celestial matters, Columella will deny that there is truth in this conclusion. For if this "astrological wisdom" (by which they supposedly surpass farmers) is not wisdom but folly—that is, if they do not know more than farmers but simply invent more—they are merely covering the mockery of their profession with the magnitude of the things about which they lie. 

Undoubtedly, human life would have welcomed astrology into a most honorable place alongside other arts if it actually made such good and necessary arts as farming, medicine, and navigation better. But its vanity and deceit, having been frequently detected by most prudent legislators, forced them to eliminate it from cities with the severest prohibitions. As we declared in the first book, this was done so that it would not infect both good minds and the arts with its most hidden poisons. How much astrology is surpassed by these common arts we were mentioning—in the foreknowledge of the future—may be known from this: among sailors, farmers, and shepherds, there is a wonderful agreement about their prognostications; but among astrologers, there is such total disagreement that <term>Abu Ma'shar<note>original: "Aboasar"; a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note></term> did not hesitate to start a journey without <term>wearing a traveling hat<note>original: "petaſatus"; the petasos was a wide-brimmed hat used by travelers for protection against sun and rain</note></term> on the very day Ptolemy predicted a flood of waters.

# Chapter XX.
## Not everything predicted by astrologers depends on the primary qualities.

<margin>First reason</margin>
<margin>Second reason</margin>
We now wish to examine what can depend on the <term>primary qualities<note>The four basic physical states: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note></term>, since the third argument of the astrologers seemed to demand it. Ptolemy proves that whatever things happen do not happen from the stars by any other way [than through these qualities], as is declared in his <term>books on effects<note>original: "apoteleſmatici"; referring to the Tetrabiblos, Ptolemy's work on the influence of stars on earthly affairs</note></term>. All astrologers always retreat to this point whenever they defend themselves against the charge of speaking superstitiously, or of not proceeding through the tracks of nature, or whenever they cannot provide a manifest reason for something. For they almost always flee to these qualities whenever they are asked why Jupiter does this, Saturn does that, or another planet does something else. It will be shown in that part of this work where the reasons for astrological dogma are refuted that they speak with little consistency, both with themselves and with the truth. 

Truly, many things besides what we have said demonstrate that they prepare this refuge for themselves in vain. Among these, the first point is that in the "allotment of fate," the time of year in which someone is born would matter more than any other variation of the constellation. This is because the season does more to increase or decrease the primary qualities than any position of the stars or mixture of rays. Thus, summer days are always hotter than winter ones, even if <term>Saturn<note>Associated with cold and sluggishness in astrology</note></term> is as rigid and sluggish as you like in summer. Conversely, winter days are always colder than summer ones, even when <term>Mars<note>Associated with heat and fire</note></term> burns and rages in the middle of heaven. 

If the difference in fate arises from heat, cold, dryness, and moisture being more or less vigorous, it follows that everyone born in winter would necessarily be condemned to a "cold fate" compared to those born in summer—especially if astrologers must defend the idea that humans follow the quality of the air (as affected by the heavens) more than the condition of the seed and the immediate material matter. 

Furthermore, if Ptolemy maintains this principle—which they take as the very foundation of natural astrology—that the rays of the planets act through the primary qualities, he ought not to prophesy character or fortune in human births from anything other than the constellation that creates and demonstrates the physical condition of the body; for all things would follow from this. Likewise, in universal prophecies, only one thing would need to be inspected: the future state of the air. Once this is inspected, the rest would be revealed, since all other things are arranged according to the measure of heat, cold, dryness, and moisture. But neither other astrologers nor Ptolemy himself do this, since they often say that things concerning character in a private birth-chart or concerning accidental events do not correspond to the temperament of the body...

Nor will those things which are predicted concerning the weather of the whole year agree with what they pronounce concerning morals, pestilence, **grain prices**, or wars; for these things are investigated from the most diverse constellations, which will be clearly evident to anyone reading both astrological books and the prophecies of astrologers. Therefore, they should not put on a respectable face or a pretext for their superstition as if it were a natural method—claiming that they subject human affairs to the stars only insofar as the disposition of the air and the body depends on the heavens through the **primary qualities** <note>The four basic qualities of Aristotelian physics: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. For while Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> asserted this when entering upon the art and called it "possible," yet in the process and explanation of his dogmas, he neither observed this rule nor could he have observed it while keeping the claims of his profession intact. Anyone of average intelligence could conjecture the rest for themselves from these very few given rules. But there are countless things in the books of Ptolemy and others which can in no way derive their origin from the primary qualities of matter.
