## Chapter XXI. Neither the harms of the elements nor the damages of our bodies are from the heaven.

**F**rom these things which we have just said, that which was brought forward in the third place for the assertion of astrology can easily be rejected. For when it is said: "if the changes of the air are from the stars, then so too are pestilences, <term>cataclysms<note>original: "cataclismi"; refers here to devastating floods</note></term>, conflagrations, and the high price of grain," we deny it. For it does not follow; rather, he who says this is ignorant of what the heaven is. For what else is the heaven in the whole of corporeal nature, but that same containing force found in any particular body which prevents the whole from flowing away or dissolving? Just as the heart in a living creature is the source of that virtue by which integrity and the order of the mixture are preserved, and by which the injury of invading members is repelled. Let him know, therefore, that he who refers the excesses of the elements—from which fires and floods happen, and from which the high price of food, disease, and pestilence arise—to the heaven, errs no differently than one who refers the diseases, vices, and ailments of our body to the very power of nature that rules the body; whose role is to cure those things, not to cause them; to put them to rest, not to excite them. If these things are true, another point is clear: it is one thing for the primary qualities to exist, and another for the withdrawal and detriment of the primary qualities to be caused by the heavens—unless we deny that the laws and all the magistrates of a city are one thing, and that the crimes committed against them are another, or that they trace their origin to the work of a good prince. Therefore, while a philosopher might grant that whatever is orderly and natural in the elements has the heaven as its author, I do not know by what reason he would grant that those things which fail, or which vary from the prescription and laws of nature, are also from there. For it is rather a dogma of the philosophers that the elements remain within their bounds and, content with their own right, do not cause trouble for the world because the celestial nature rules and moderates the fluid and erratic number of corruptible things.

<margin>Objection</margin>
But you will say: "Since you have granted me that some stars produce cold and others heat, does it not follow that when the cold stars predominate, the cold elements grow strong, and when the hot stars rule, the hot elements do?" If this is said, does it not also happen that by a great gathering of cold constellations,
<margin>First response</margin>
<margin>Second response</margin>
coldness so overflows the waters that the earth is submerged in floods? Conversely, when the hot stars are very powerful, conflagrations occur. The answer is easy, and not just one: First, concerning the "dominion" of planets and signs which the astrologers have invented—it will be demonstrated later that these are false. Why, I ask, should any planet so command the heaven as to produce portents in this world, especially evil ones? Since the work of heaven results from the **conspiracy** <note>original: "conspiratione"; used here in the literal Latin sense of "breathing together" or "harmonious action."</note> of all the lights, that entire superior harmony is always so tempered that, just as all things within it are in consonance, so through it nothing ever sounds discordant in the inferior world. In that world, whenever something inharmonious, harsh, or discordant is heard, it should not be referred to the touch of the heaven, but to these four strings of the <term>sublunary lyre<note>original: "citharae sublunaris"; a metaphor for the four elements (earth, water, air, fire) in the world below the moon.</note></term>. These strings, being in contact with unordered and impure matter, are sometimes found to be stubborn, even though the celestial <term>plectrum<note>The tool used to pluck a lyre; here representing the moving influence of the heavens.</note></term> always moves them according to rhythm and concord.
<margin>Third response</margin>
After this, it must be more subtly considered: if various stars are set over various elements, they are set there so that they might perfect those elements. Therefore, any element will be more perfect when touched by it, insofar as the presiding star is more powerful. But if the perfection of the parts...

## BOOK THREE

...perfection of the parts is not inconsistent with the perfection of the whole; indeed, when the parts collapse along with the whole, it will not pertain to the perfection of an element if nature, overstepping its order, occupies the rest. But it will then be perfect when it has deflected nothing from the order and course of nature; from which it is certain one can deflect as much by exceeding as by falling short. Therefore, if Mars presides over fire, since it is not fitting for anything to occur from a star into a subject quality that does not harmonize with good order and the laws of nature, it would be the duty of the celestial governance to restrain the tumultuous no less than to rouse the sluggish. It can therefore be conceded that the four primary qualities <note>The foundational qualities of Aristotelian physics: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> are from heaven, yet their transgressions and tumults are not from heaven, but from the inordinate motions of matter, which does not everywhere obey the laws of celestial discipline. For this reason, I believe that neither Plato in the *Timaeus* nor Aristotle in the *Meteorology* ever attributed those temporary tyrannies of the elements to any force of the constellations.

<margin>
Plato.
Aristotle.
Harms to our bodies do not have causes in heaven.
</margin>

It is established that not only the harms of the elements, but also, by the same reasoning, the damages to our bodies and other living things do not have causes in heaven. Because that which is the most eminent among all bodies, and distinguished by titles of both order and beneficence, ought not to produce those things which are rather the works of tumultuous or failing matter. Wherefore, what we have said of the elements may likewise be said of the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—once thought to control health and temperament.</note> in our body that correspond to them: if Saturn presides over black bile <note>Original: *atra bilis*, the humor associated with melancholy.</note>, Mars over red <note>Yellow bile, associated with anger.</note>, another over blood, and another over phlegm—the work of these planets is no more than to bridle these qualities and contain them under a harmonious arrangement of life. Nor when Saturn is most powerful will black bile be aroused to destroy the rest and collapse the whole; rather, it will behave more orderly, more composedly, and better. The same must be said of red bile when Mars reigns, since their rays are by their nature beneficent and healthy. They do not act like fire, but just as the vital heat implanted in us, through the hand of the soul, works correctly toward a certain end for the health of the living being, so those vital lights act as the instruments of their innermost mind and soul—never for destruction, but for the benefit and well-being of the subject bodies. Saturn, in influencing black bile (if indeed he presides over it), will never influence anything that is not orderly and life-giving; therefore, he will not excite it to the destruction of the animal but will moderate it for preservation. Nor will the humors receive from their stars, when they prevail, the means to act more violently, but rather more moderately and vitally. 

<margin>
Death is not from heaven.
</margin>

Death is never from heaven, but from matter with its own defect, whenever any quality has so degenerated that it does not sustain the discipline of the presiding star, but either wanders immoderately or fails through slackness. But our diviners <note>A dismissive term for astrologers.</note>, who make themselves both the interpreters and the patrons and defenders of heaven, refer not only diseases caused by an excessive irritation of the primary qualities, but even vices themselves—blindness, deafness—to the stars; and what is more detestable, even monsters <note>Referring to congenital disabilities or "deformities" at birth, which were traditionally called "monsters" in natural philosophy.</note>. Nothing more absurd can be said or thought than this. For what else are monsters but the sins of nature? Yet no philosopher ever referred these to an efficient cause—especially an unfailing one—but all referred them to matter. Nor was anyone ever so delirious as to say that the birth of monsters happens through the fault of the informing power <note>The biological force supposed to shape the embryo.</note>. 

<margin>
For even the whole council of physicians affirms that monstrous births do not happen except from some impediment of nature.
</margin>

Which, being performed by the hand of God, fails in nothing; rather, they accuse the matter as being poorly formable and defiant and rebellious toward its maker, whether by location, quantity, or quality. But it is a far greater insanity to condemn the power of heaven than that of the seed. Which can err and fail so much less as it is more powerful than nature itself, more a mistress, and more joined to the Artificer <note>God.</note>, by whom this inferior seminal power is ruled and formed no differently than the heavens themselves. It is therefore too absurd to think that the motions and configurations of the celestial bodies (if indeed those configurations vary the effectiveness of the planets) ever go or are composed otherwise than the natural tenor and ordered course of the lower world requires. Otherwise, where does that order of nature sit, whose transgression is a monster? Where indeed does it have its origin, if not in heaven? Or how do those things hear its voice well enough, whose...

### Chapter XXII. That the variety of talents and characters does not depend entirely on the primary qualities.

**I**ndeed, if the stars do not cause the harmful conditions of bodies, they at least cause the diversities of bodies—not those that are diseased, defective, or weak, but those within the bounds of natural integrity that differ from one another by the logic of their temperament. It follows from this, as it seems to some, that if the stars are the authors of the four <term>primary qualities</term> <note>The basic building blocks of the physical world in Aristotelian physics: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>, then perhaps bodies are born or conceived drier and colder under Saturn, hotter under Mars, more moist under Venus, and so on for the rest. This diversity of temperament is usually followed by a diversity of talents and affections of the soul—not that we are compelled by them, but that we are provoked by them. But this point will be treated more extensively later. Let us see, however, whether the dissimilarity of talents and characters can be born from this. For while it is true in some way, it is nonetheless false in another. For the manner of the predominant qualities in the body does indeed result in some influence on the affections: for instance, boiling <term>bile</term> <note>Yellow bile, associated with the choleric temperament (anger).</note> makes men more prone to anger; <term>phlegm</term> <note>Associated with the phlegmatic temperament (sluggishness).</note> makes them sluggish; blood makes them more cheerful; and <term>black bile</term> <note>Associated with the melancholic temperament (sadness).</note> makes them sad. 

But this is quite general and does not always correspond to the evidence, nor does it satisfy the more hidden and specifically unique conditions of talents. I said it does not always correspond to the evidence because one can sometimes find men with very similar bodily temperaments
<margin>Error is often conceived from physical appearance.</margin>
who are nevertheless very different in their pursuits—not by choice, but by natural inclination. I myself have seen a wild cruelty under a virginal face; and under a grim and repulsive countenance, a mild and lovable gentleness. I have seen others who, by the grace of their brow and the beauty of their face, present a perpetual joy, while inside they seethe with sorrows and are a disgust to themselves. Others, whom you would judge to be the mere slaves of Saturn <note>That is, naturally gloomy or "saturnine."</note>, brighten everything with cheer and wit. These powers can be followed as seeds from the primary qualities by the general consensus of philosophers—that is, things which are neither those first four qualities, nor their daughters or appendages. We shall shortly declare that many things concerning the diversity of characters cannot be clearly attributed to those qualities about which the astrologers prophesy.

### Chapter XXIII. Neither wars nor external affairs depend on the primary qualities.

**I**t is truly too ridiculous to suggest that if the stars can produce cold, heat, and other qualities, they can also cause wars and seditions, or overturn cities and change empires. Their reasoning is no less ridiculous than their position. For they say that when the bile is stirred up in the bodies of kings and princes, they become more greedy for injury, either to return it or to inflict it, due to a more burning heat of the soul. O blessed Italy, flourishing in perpetual peace, if you were permitted to have phlegmatic princes! This great and divine good could cost very little: a single ounce of a chosen <term>pharmacy</term> <note>A medicinal purge or laxative.</note> that draws out bile, if distributed rightly to those princes who are more warlike, will pacify the whole world for us. Who would bother to refute such things rather than laugh at them? As if this were ultimately the cause of wars—as if it were not greed more than anger, or lust, or the opportunity to seize hope. As if it were not grudges and 
<margin>Causes of wars.</margin>
hatreds, which among the astrologers are attributed to Saturn rather than Mars. Do not the love of justice itself sometimes stir up wars and tumults? As if the soul of kings were not more often "God" than "bile"—now exercising the good toward virtue, now punishing the wicked, often through the ministry of the wicked, whom He employs as executioners in cleansing the state, like visible demons. Truly, here,

[The stars] do not vary at all regarding our humors: how will they relate to these four qualities? <note>The "four qualities" are the building blocks of the physical world in ancient science: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> Poverty, social status, riches, want, children, a wife, friends, enemies? <margin>Ptolemy. Question. Solution.</margin> Ptolemy says they have an "affinity" with the soul and body: such as honor and dignity with the soul, and a wife and riches with the body. What is this affinity of yours, O Ptolemy? That these chance events should follow from the condition of the soul or body? <margin>Refutation</margin> Or is it what you people are accustomed to say: that if an influx from Mars makes someone bilious <note>original: "biliosum" — having an excess of yellow bile, which was thought to cause a fiery, aggressive temperament.</note>, it also inflicts wounds and a violent death upon him? This is because the heat of the bile incites one to quarrels and to arms, in the midst of which death itself familiarly dwells. 

But we usually consider it to be most especially the "work of the stars" when a mild man, living in leisure and insulting no one, is nevertheless drawn into dangers, swords, and enmities by some fatal force, as if against his will. Likewise, a warlike man and a "provoker of hornets" <note>original: "crabronum... irritator" — a classical idiom for someone who stirs up trouble.</note> as the saying goes, may die full of days, unharmed at home among his own people. Why then does the former, though lacking Martian heat, meet his end by the sword (which is the work of Mars), while the latter dies in peace, even though he is himself almost "hotter" than Mars? 

Furthermore, some things of this kind might show a slight connection with what is inside us, and so might be referred to the habit of the body; but those things which are said to follow the distinction of body and soul—a wife, riches, social status, and other things of this sort—one cannot certainly even dream of such a connection. Wherefore even <margin>Ptolemy.</margin> Ptolemy himself, in the first chapter of his book *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "Apotelesmaton" — better known today as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational 2nd-century text on astrology.</note> where he builds his argument for the influence of the stars, concludes nothing other than that, in some way, the diversity of the body and of the soul (insofar as it clings to the body) will follow from the stars. Regarding chance events, he adds nothing in that place. 

For he writes thus: "One might therefore be able to say what the state of the surrounding air will be at any time. Moreover, he will understand the proper habit and temperament of any man by using the argument drawn from the state of the air when that man was being formed. Therefore, he will be able to say what kind of body and soul the man obtained. Then, he will foresee how he will fare through the succession of times; for example, by foreseeing that a future disposition of the air with such a temperature is suitable for the body and will contribute to its health, or that a discordant state will give occasion for disease and sickness." These are Ptolemy’s words there, in which, as is apparent, there is no mention of external things. 

But soon in the very next chapter, where he repeats what was said and connects it to what follows, he also adds external things as if he had proved those as well—perhaps thinking that the reader might be deceived, having already forgotten the reasoning by which he claimed those points were deduced and proven. Therefore, even if we granted to Ptolemy that the primary qualities of matter—moisture and dryness, cold and heat—are changed according to the condition and state of the stars, we are by no means going to grant that the stars are the causes that vary the different chance accidents of men.

### Chapter XXIV. That occult powers do not exist in the heavenly bodies through which they produce the hidden properties of inferior things: but only heat and life-giving light.

<margin>Refutation</margin> **I**t remains to be discussed whether, besides the power of those qualities to produce effects, there are more occult <note>original: "occultiores" — hidden or "extra-sensory" powers that cannot be explained by simple physics.</note> and eminent powers in the stars through which they can do many things that are beyond those primary qualities which aid perishable things. And [whether] in other things there are other powers, both nobler and more effective than the primary qualities of matter themselves. This was the contention of the fourth reason, asserting that the stars could in no way fail to abound in virtues of this kind: thus (as is said by almost all philosophers) by the benefit of the stars, earthly things obtain such endowments; and since the stars are the noblest bodies, they must necessarily be endowed with the noblest gifts. 

But neither the nobility of these bodies, nor the powers of earthly bodies which are said to be the occult and wonderful results of the stars, is an argument by which we are forced to imagine such virtues—that is, that there is anything in the celestial nature beyond that life-giving heat and power which we have already mentioned. For to take up the last point first: they do not correctly understand what is said—that inferior bodies "obtain from heaven" the powers by which they do those things which cannot be done through the four primary qualities. Those endowments and powers flow from the innermost principles of the bodies themselves: that is, from their forms or, if you prefer, their essences. Furthermore, just as heaven gave the form which that motion follows, so to give to them...

-># DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

<meta>Catchword: which between</meta>

...such powers are spoken of. However, whatever diversity exists arises not from the constellation but from the mixture <note>original: "mixtio" — referring to the way the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) are combined in earthly objects.</note>, from whose varying proportions one form or another springs forth. Indeed, this very fact pertains to the dignity of the heavens: since those things which are divided into a multitude among the inferior order are possessed by the superior order, collected into a single and more eminent act. Therefore, if this <term>sublunary</term><note>The "sublunary" region is the Earthly realm below the moon, characterized by change, decay, and the mixing of elements.</note> crowd of falling bodies—so multiform, so numerous, weak, tumultuous, and particular—is compared to the celestial body, which is eternal, indefatigable, simple, ample, and universal, it is then most consistent with reason that whatever strength or perfection is cut up and distributed into parts among the inferior things proceeds from that first body. Yet, the celestial bodies bestow all these things, varied and manifold as they may be, through their one unique gift of light and heat.

<margin>The great dignity of light. God is the true light.</margin>
This gift, communicated more or less through the series of stars, creates their order among themselves rather than a diversity. We have said often enough—and it requires no demonstration, since it demonstrates itself and all other things along with it—what this gift is, what this property is: it is light. Light, indeed, is evident to all; flowing from the celestial body and breathing forth heat, it indicates to us the almost hidden mystery of the Divinity: power in its motion, wisdom in its light, and love figured in its heat. By these, that first God—the first of all, just as the heaven is the first among all bodies—moves, illustrates, creates, perfects, and preserves all things. Besides this prerogative of threefold efficacy <note>Referring to the three effects: motion, light, and heat.</note> hanging from one body, what more do we desire in the heaven? Or what does it seem to lack for the highest perfection of corporal nature and the mastery of the inferior world? To be marked and distinguished by manifold properties is a claim to the dignity of an *imperfect* nature; but it detracts from a *perfect* one, for whom it is proper (as I have said) to possess collected together in one that which inferior things possess divided into parts. 

Certainly, this privilege would not be appropriate to the perpetual motion of the body and its heat-giving light; one would have to seek something else in the heaven that might, by a simple act, encompass and embrace the <term>virtue</term> <note>In this context, "virtue" means an inherent power or medicinal property.</note> of any corruptible bodies whatsoever. But if this is found fully within it, there is no need for the labor of inventing other things. And it is undoubtedly found there, since without it no corporeal thing can either generate or, once generated, carry out its operations. For take away the heaven and its heat, and the peony <note>original: "paeonia" — a plant used in Renaissance medicine to treat "falling sickness" or epilepsy.</note> will no longer help those who fall, nor will the hyacinth <note>original: "iacinthus" — often referring to the gemstone or the flower, believed to have power to stop bleeding.</note> stop blood, nor rhubarb <note>original: "reubarbarum" — used as a purgative.</note> draw out bile. And just as any things that act upon us would cease their efficacy if they were not stirred by the fomentation of our own internal heat, so too would the virtue of those bodies—and the very heat of living things—cease, unless it were both cherished separately and joined together in turn by celestial heat. 

Therefore, the act and perfection of whatever strengths are implanted in earthly things is this very heat-giving light, insofar as it is hot; just as the heat of all things is, in turn, perfection insofar as it shines. And just as colors can neither be seen, nor the eyes see, except by the benefit of this light, so too the gifts of any bodies can neither stand on their own nor affect one another if they are destitute of the help of that motion and heat. Therefore, just as it pertains to the dignity and beauty of the heaven that it gleams with the single splendor of its own native light despite such great diversity of colors, so it is a sign of its perfection to have possessed one virtue in place of a manifold number of material virtues—one more noble than all of them, just as light surpasses all colors. Nor should we think it detracts from the dignity of the heaven if we deny these particular gifts to the stars, any more than we believe the heaven itself to be yellow, or sky-blue, or leek-green, or purple; such variety, while beautiful and necessary in earthly things, is neither possible nor becoming in the stars.

### Chapter XXV. Even if a specific and proper power is granted to each star, it is nevertheless universal.

**If** anyone should contend that, besides this property of motion, light, and heat common to all, each star has its own proper influence, I would not resist him very greatly. But I will remind him that these diverse virtues...

...by which they differ from each other, it nonetheless remains that all are celestial powers. Whatever is in heaven—even if it is something particular when compared to the totality of celestial things—is nevertheless universal when referred to the sublunary <note>The "sublunary" region refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, everything "below the moon," which was thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note> things (no matter how narrow it may be). When I say "universal," I want it to be understood in this way: that it encloses within itself the entire perfection of the corruptible world; otherwise, it would not be "celestial," as has already been declared in part, and will soon be explained more broadly. If this is granted, those peculiar gifts of the stars will be of no help to the astrologer's case. There will indeed be one property of Jupiter and another of Saturn, but Jupiter will not, for that reason, produce anything different among us than Saturn. Therefore, both will be able to do all things equally through this property of theirs.

I will not deny that the power of Jupiter differs from that of Saturn. But there is no power of the inferior bodies that the Jovian power does not contain, generate, preserve, and make effective and perfect just as much as the Saturnian power, and vice versa. I will say first why this is so, and then how diversity of both property and action exists alongside this commonality. The nature of Heaven does not seem to be able to be explained more aptly and briefly than if you were to say that Heaven is the **unity** of all bodies. Truly, there is no multitude that does not depend on its own unity; there is nothing in the universe that does not derive from one source-like head.

<margin>An analogy.</margin>
And just as in an army every legion is referred to its own prefect, and the whole army to one Commander; so any series of things, agreeing with itself through a commonality of kind, has its own principle from which it is led, and by which it is nourished, ruled, and contained. Since these principles are many—forming a kind of manifold unity—they are finally reduced to the simplest unity of the first principle. Moreover, just as every number is in a certain way contained in unity, the whole city in the king, and the whole army in the Commander, so too is every power and perfection of its own "flock" <note>original: "grex" — Pico uses the metaphor of a herd or flock to describe groups of related physical things.</note> (so to speak) contained in its principle. Truly, that which in that "gregarious" condition is divided, maimed, unfinished, and unlimited, flourishes in the head within a singular embrace of a certain unlimited unity: pure, effective, and perfect.

From this it follows that one may say that nothing of the subordinate body is in the head, and yet again that the whole body is in the head. In this way, that which is first among those things which exist is the ineffable God; He is none of those things which exist, and yet again He is all things by a certain eminence of His foundational nature and all-encompassing power. From what principle, then, will the corporeal <note>Physical or bodily.</note> kind depend, if not from the first body in rank and dignity? This, however, is the Heaven. Therefore, what we were saying is true: Heaven will be the unity of all bodies, of which all things that belong to other bodies can be denied, and all can also be affirmed. They can be denied because, while in those other bodies things are formed with various ends—discrete, manifold, and imperfect—in heaven they have neither those characters of form nor that same diversity. They can be affirmed because heaven concludes all those things at once—not by the potential of matter, but by the amplitude of power and the sublimity of its original nature.

If this is the nature of heaven, it certainly applies to every one of the celestial bodies. Nor should it be thought that while the whole Heaven contains the whole perfection of the inferior bodies, a specific part contains only a specific part. That would be no privilege for Heaven; rather, any part of Heaven is the whole inferior world, except for those things which are *in* the world but not *of* the world <note>Pico likely refers to the human soul or divine intellect, which exists within the physical world but originates from a higher, non-physical reality.</note>.

<margin>Note. Allegory. The opinion of the Pythagoreans.</margin>
The Pythagoreans seem to have signified this by a certain allegorical opinion of theirs, by which they were accustomed to affirm that this whole sublunary region is a single star, and that in any star of Heaven there are all the things that are seen in this region of ours. Thus in the Moon, there are both the four elements and the distinctions of valleys, streams, or mountains, as well as plants and whatever animals are among us. So also in Venus, Mercury, and the rest of the stars. By this trope <note>original: "typus"</note>, they certainly declare nothing else to us than what we wished to assert: that there is no star in Heaven that does not encompass the whole of what is under the moon. Otherwise, they would not be of a celestial nature if what was previously supposed and proven is not false: that nothing is more truly called "celestial" in nature than the unity of corporeal nature. Then, because this was a privilege worthy of Heaven: that with such vastness and an innumerable number of lights, it should embrace the goods of the sublunary narrowness. Therefore, in the power of any star, there is every power of bodies...

He uses a Pythagorean allegory to suggest that each star is a complete world in itself, functioning as a universal cause rather than a specific one.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical argument from Book Three. ...of fleeting things. Nor do the powers of different stars differ in that some preside over certain things and others over others, since all stars preside over all things. Nor is a star that is higher superior to a lower one by a broader embrace—that is, by ruling over more things—but by a more noble one: it contains the same things that the lower star contains, but in a much more unified and eminent way.

<margin>Distinction of the equivocal <note>A logical term for things that share a name but differ in nature or power.</note></margin>

This same principle can be seen in the "separate minds" <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "separate minds" refers to angels or pure intellectual beings who exist without physical bodies.</note> and in the knowledge of living beings. For just as every body depends on heaven, so every power that participates in knowledge depends on the Intellect. I am calling "Intellect" not our own faculty (which is called Reason), but rather that of the angels, whom the philosophers call "Minds" and "Intellects." This Intellect is sufficient unto itself for understanding; it looks neither at anything below itself, nor into anything below itself, to understand what it knows. It is not deceived; it does not struggle. And whatever excellence is distributed among various powers in every kind of knowledge, the Intellect possesses that same thing through a single power far more excellently than it exists in those others. In itself, it beholds the truth and touches it with the presence and certainty of a sense. It holds within itself that power which, in fleeting things, belongs to the faculty of imagination; it foresees the causes and forms of things, both bodily and incorporeal, through a "rational foresight"—yet it is not itself rational, or sensual, or imaginary. Rather, through its intellectual nature, it exists in a more noble condition, gathering what is perfect in those lower faculties and rejecting what is imperfect. For in us, physical knowledge is one thing, mathematical knowledge another, and divine knowledge another still.

<margin>The order of the sciences which Aristotle posits in Book 6 of his *Metaphysics* <note>Pico refers to "Theology," which was the traditional title for Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>. To be noted.</margin>

For Reason attains physical knowledge through the senses; mathematical knowledge through the imagination; and divine knowledge through the mind and intellect. Furthermore, there is no Mind so lowly that it does not see all truth in its own light—that truth which we either reach or certainly pant after through those sciences and arts. 

Come then, let us compare these intellectual things to bodily ones. These arts and sciences are within us. In the whole of "knowing nature," there are various types of knowledge, just as in the "crowd of bodies" there are various privileges of different powers. All knowledge is a certain participation in intellectual light; all bodily power is a certain participation in celestial faculty. However, just as that light shines more clearly in Reason, so this power shines more perfectly in the "spirit of the heart." 

These things being established, let us see if anyone would be right to say that if intellectual rays flow down from those Minds, some would be those that make people physicists but not mathematicians; others mathematicians but not theologians; and others theologians rather than physicists or mathematicians. And would this light then be divided—like these studies are—according to a diversity in the nature of the "breathing" Minds? Or rather, would it be that the same Mind sends its rays by its own counsel and will? I think it is more correct to believe that nothing of this sort exists. A Mind does not give these gifts by its own choice (in the manner of the stars), but by its very nature. And if it happens that one receives this gift rather than that one, it is not to be referred to the Giver—who is equally liberal toward all—but to the capacity and condition of the receiver.

If, as we have said, the relationship of a star to a corruptible body is like the relationship of a Mind to our own fallible knowledge, then we must likewise say that any star is able to give from itself whatever a subordinate body is naturally born to receive. Thus, the diversity of the "hidden breath" <note>original: *afflatus occultus*. This refers to the subtle, invisible influence astrologers claim stars exert on humans.</note> is not caused by the star that "breathes" it—as the astrologer thinks—but by the diversity of the matter that receives the breath. I said "hidden breath" because the action of a star through light and heat can be varied according to the intensity or weakness of the ray (as we explained above). But in these hidden properties, through which a star propagates itself and pours out its own "images" (so to speak), just as no variation in intensity is apparent, we are not persuaded to suppose any diversity in their action. 

But you will say, "The power of Jupiter is one kind of power, and its diffused image is certainly different from the power of Saturn." I admit it. But it will not, for that reason, produce a different thing, since there is no thing in the sublunary world <note>The Earthly realm below the moon, subject to change and decay.</note> that either one could not produce.

<margin>That the effect of the stars' power is equal.</margin>

What then is the diversity of action? Each does the same thing, but each does it in a different way: the more noble star does it in a more noble and eminent way. Though I wonder, if we were to decide on these powers, whether perhaps a lower power is more effective upon us—not because it is closer in location, but because it is more related to our nature. But that is an inquiry for another work. Here we only assert that if, besides light and heat, the stars have their own...

# BOOK THREE

...by its own nature, a specific property is granted to each star. In this way, all stars can be defended as universal causes, so that no star by itself creates the diversity found in lower things. We could, however, grant them some particular power—namely, a "stellar power." And even if we granted this, it would not help the astrologers at all. For even if we concede that all stars always perform the same work in all things, but not that all things receive them in the same way, we might use the following example:

It is well known that all bodies consist of **matter** and **form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "matter" is the raw stuff of the world, and "form" is the structure or essence that makes a thing what it is.</note>. Someone might think the matter works like this: the three "lesser" stars—the **Moon**, **Venus**, and **Mercury**—manage what pertains to matter by divided duties. The **Moon** rules the matter itself; it is then disposed toward a "form" by **Venus** and **Mercury**. From **Venus** comes the quantity, including the order, figure, composition, and proper beauty of the parts; from **Mercury** comes the quality, as it applies the appropriate affections for receiving the form through a "shapeable mobility." 

As for the enduring form itself, it would be governed by the three "superior" stars in this manner: **Saturn** provides what the form actually is; **Jupiter** provides existence and life to those things that live; and **Mars** provides the internal movement and the drive to act. 

As for the fact that a thing spreads itself out, and through that spreading makes itself known and propagates, this would be referred especially to the **Sun**, whose work is seen to be the mastery of matter, resulting in both the generation and the manifestation of things like itself.

What if the works of the planets did differ in this way? We might grant this for the sake of argument, though not because of reason, faith, experience, or the authority of Plato or Aristotle. Even then, all the diversity of lower things would still come not from heaven, but from inferior causes. The celestial influence always acts in the same way, but its work varies because of the immediate causes and the particular "disposition" <note>The specific physical state or readiness of a material to be changed.</note> of the matter. To assign more particular virtues to the stars than these universal ones is not persuaded by any reason. One might suspect otherwise regarding certain things without committing a sin, even with the authority of learned men—I do not deny it—but as the following book will show, such powers are not the ones the astrologers describe, nor are we affected by them in the way they believe.

---

### Chapter XXVI. Epilogue of this book, with a rejection of certain arguments (that is, of those making the arguments).

<margin>Argument of the astrologers.</margin>
<margin>Another argument.</margin>
<margin>He first retorts Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>Hippocrates.</margin>

**W**e have examined all the natural changes of sublunary <note>The "sublunary" region is the Earth and its atmosphere, everything below the Moon, characterized by change and decay.</note> things which seem to be works of the heavens. As for the accidental fortunes of men, we shall speak of those in our discussion of "Reason's Solution." We found nothing in those natural changes that would favor the astrologers; instead, they provided an opportunity to raise many objections, so that they may regret having stirred up this <unclear>refreshment</unclear> <note>Original Greek: αναψυχιν (anapsychin), meaning a relief or cooling, likely used here sarcastically regarding the astrologers' "theories."</note>. For we gather nothing from them other than that sublunary bodies are affected by the rays of the lights. Nor are they affected by any influence other than heat—specifically a "vital heat"—nor does its action change anything except through the position of the star, either by its closeness or by its directness in radiating upon us. 

From these principles, we have rendered an explanation for all the effects which the astrologers used to bring forward as evidence for their dogma. It was necessary to show that astrology is not confirmed by those observations, but weakened; and that the astrologers were either being deceived or were deceiving others everywhere we looked. 

Thus, it appeared that they falsely believe the Sun has a "drying power," or that the Moon is "healthily moistening and cold." They falsely imagine an "occult power" in the Moon—separate from its motion and light—that pulls and pours out the sea. It is false that **Saturn** is blamed for the harm of an eight-month birth. It is false to attribute powers to the **Signs** <note>The constellations of the Zodiac.</note>, since they vary in power only by their position and the way the Sun's rays use them. It is false that "critical days" <note>In ancient medicine, specific days when a fever was expected to break.</note> and the periods of fevers are referred to the motions of the Moon or other stars. 

Finally, far from using the changes caused by the Sun and Moon as an argument for the truth of astrological decrees, it led us to a significant suspicion of their falsehood. For they argued this way: "If someone sleeps under the Moon, numbness seizes their limbs, and at the same time, sea urchins fill up; therefore, the Moon makes things cold and moist. Our senses attest the Sun is scorching; therefore, it is dry." 

We, on the contrary, insist: "The Moon fills sea urchins; therefore it is hot." We demonstrated this from **Aristotle**. "People sleep-heavy with cold under it; therefore it is hot." We explained with clear reason how that happens. "In the full moon, it favors conception, nourishes bodies, and as it grows, it strengthens and enlivens; therefore it is hot." We proved this from **Hippocrates** and from evidence itself.

<summary>Pico concludes Book Three by arguing that while stars might have universal roles relating to matter and form, the diversity of life on Earth is caused by earthly conditions. He systematically rejects astrological claims about the specific "temperaments" (hot/cold/dry/moist) of planets, using logic to show that the Moon's effects actually suggest heat, not cold.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>Solution to the second argument.</margin>
Concerning the sun, we likewise appeal to experience; it is evident that by its rays, every **spirit of life** is quickened. This is not the effect of a drying power, but of a healthfully warm one. Nor was it difficult to declare how, either by accident, the sun might dry or burn, or even produce cold; the moon, too, is said to be the cause of cold and moisture, even though both stars are by their nature authors of life-giving light and heat alone. 

<margin>Another argument of the astrologers.</margin>
They likewise inferred: we clearly see our bodies changed by the sun and moon; therefore, we should not doubt the "fluxes" <note>Influences flowing from the stars.</note> of other stars. But this very thing we see regarding the sun and moon draws us into doubt concerning the others: namely, that we find the dispositions of bodies varied by them in such a way that we judge the remaining stars to be *uncontributing* <note>original: "asymbolas"; a term for those who do not pay their share or contribute to a common goal.</note> rather than called to share in the work. For indeed, when the moon’s light decreases, moisture in bodies always diminishes; it always increases when that light grows. Why then, if what the astrologers think about the efficiency of other stars is true—why, I ask, do "moist" planets, when they are dominant, not sometimes compensate for the loss of moonlight and increase moisture? If they did, we might occasionally, by the benefit of the stars, feast on succulent oysters even during a new moon! <note>Ancient naturalists believed shellfish were meatier during a full moon and thinner during a new moon; Pico is mocking the idea that other planets could override this lunar cycle.</note> Why, conversely, when the moon is full, does the dryness of Saturn or Mars—taking control of the heavens according to astrological laws—never desiccate bodies or protect felled timber from rot? Therefore, these observations favor those who remove power from the planets rather than those who affirm it; just as they favor those who attribute no efficacy to the [zodiac] signs. Otherwise, if the sea is moved by the moon (as they claim and we do not deny), why does it not move the sea more when placed in "watery" signs than in "fiery" ones, or no less in "dry" signs than in "moist" ones? 

<margin>The error is uncovered.</margin>
Or why does the moon not create more abundant tides when joined with moist planets than with drying ones? And if what they predict about the **twelve places** (which they call **houses**) were true, how does it harmonize with this: that the moon, rising from its birth, acts more strongly on the ocean the closer it approaches the zenith? Thus it acts more strongly from the **twelfth house** than from the **horoscope** <note>The "horoscope" here refers to the First House or Ascendant. In traditional astrology, the Twelfth House was considered a place of weakness or "bad spirit," yet Pico points out it is physically higher in the sky and thus has more tidal influence.</note>, yet they claim that in that place the power of all stars languishes and becomes the weakest of all. 

<margin>Favorinus</margin>
Therefore, these experiments stand with us against them, rather than allowing their opinions to overrule faith in experience—unless it is as **Favorinus** <note>A skeptical philosopher whose arguments against astrology were recorded by Aulus Gellius.</note> used to say, as we touched upon above: because the ocean, like a companion of the moon, grows old and young along with it, they think this is an argument to persuade us that all human affairs, both small and great, are led and ruled as if bound to the stars. But it is a far cry from the truth; and as the same man, mocking the astrologers, used to cast it: it is excessively inept and absurd that just because the tide of the ocean agrees with the course of the moon, we should think that some man's legal business—perhaps a dispute over a water pipe with his neighbors before a judge—is also governed from heaven as if by a rein.

### Chapter XXVII.

It remains for us to dismantle the final argument sought from human events, in which some things so exceed our powers, or happen so far beyond merit and reason, that they seem to affirm the force of a fatal decree and celestial power. We shall solve this for the present and show that all these things have their causes among us; nothing appears in all of them that requires heaven as its author. This is to say: there is nothing in the course of human affairs from which a suspicion ought to arise that the deeds of men are ruled and governed by fates. For at the beginning of the following book, no longer merely solving but arguing, we will show especially that these things, in which those men seem to recognize the force of fate, cannot possibly happen from heaven. These are finally of two kinds: the great and the bad. Let us speak first of the great: these pertain either to the soul or to external things. For in this way, they cast in our teeth both the **felicity of Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great, often used as an example of someone with "miraculous" luck.</note> and the **genius and learning of his teacher** <note>Aristotle.</note>. 

<margin>Why Aristotle is a consummate philosopher.</margin>
Let us begin, therefore, with those things pertaining to the soul. You admire in Aristotle a consummate knowledge of natural things; I admire it equally with you. "The cause is heaven," they say, "and the constellation under which he was born." I do not agree; and not merely for the common reason that many born under the same star were not Aristotles, but because, besides heaven—under which, as a universal cause, both **Boeotian swine** <note>A traditional slur; Boeotians were considered dull and "pig-like," while Athenians were considered sharp.</note> and **Attic philosophers** equally sprout—there are "proximate causes" proper to Aristotle himself.

<summary>Pico argues that while the Moon affects physical phenomena like tides and moisture, this does not prove the stars control human affairs or legal disputes. He begins a new chapter refuting the idea that the genius of figures like Aristotle or the success of Alexander the Great are caused by their birth horoscopes.</summary>

# BOOK THREE

z ii

...properties and peculiarities of <note>The text likely refers to Aristotle here, following the argument from the previous page.</note> Aristotle: to which we refer his singular perfection. First, as he says, he was allotted a **good soul**: and this certainly not from heaven—since the soul is immortal and incorporeal, as he himself demonstrated and even the astrologers do not deny. Then he was allotted a body suitable to serve such a soul; nor was even this from heaven, except as a common cause, but rather from his parents. He chose to practice <term>philosophy</term><note>original: "philosophiari"; to live the life of a philosopher.</note>: this was the work of those principles we mentioned—that is, of soul and body—and it was of his own <term>free will</term><note>original: "arbitrii"; the capacity for choice.</note>. He reached perfection in philosophy: this was the fruit of his chosen purpose and his own industry. 

But many more have practiced philosophy with equal zeal and labor. The cause in his case was the teaching of his master and the good fortune of the age in which he was born, which was full of ancient monuments—though not so perfect that there was no work left to do in beginning and perfecting the noble arts. Yet he achieved far more than his contemporaries and his disciples. He was allotted not a better star, but a better <term>genius</term><note>original: "ingenium"; natural talent or innate ability.</note>. Nor did this genius come from a star, since it is incorporeal, but from God, just as the body comes from the father, not from heaven. 

We speak of this matter with more honor than the astrologers, insofar as we attribute it to a more divine and eminent cause than your particular [astrological] causes. For if the grasp of human genius exceeded that of either Aristotle or any other philosopher, this would not be due to a cause that is entirely inferior—such as every celestial body—but to one that is superior, that is, divine. Just so, **Socrates**, who in my opinion was the wisest of all philosophers, attributed his wisdom not to his birth stars, but to an <term>assisting divinity</term><note>original: "assitenti numini"; referring to the "daimonion" or divine voice Socrates claimed guided him.</note>. 

Therefore, we give more to heaven than is proper if we derive the divinity of souls from those corporeal rays; and we give less than is proper if we attribute the corporeal differences we receive in private matters to the stars as if they were a particular cause. Indeed, it is altogether less than is fitting when we ascribe our very deformities and the stains of our minds to the stars. This is one of the main reasons people are moved to flee to the stars: because there appear in many men certain absurd desires, contrary to the laws of humanity, which seem to have not an intrinsic (that is, human) cause, but an extrinsic one—and because it is powerful, they assume it is astral. 

But I would ask them: why does a pregnant woman prefer to eat earth and coals rather than every exquisite kind of food? <note>This refers to "pica," a medical condition where people crave non-food items.</note> And if they find the cause of this monstrous desire is not a star but the fetus, I will likewise remind them that the cause of those things they marvel at should be sought in the temperament of the body rather than in heaven. I might say this of the demons in wicked men, but I shall lead them back to corporeal causes. Certainly, beyond the habit of the body—

<margin>
See a monstrous example of lust
</margin>

—I can declare by a most true example how much **habit** <note>original: "consuetudo"; custom or habituation.</note> contributes to these monstrous affections. There lives yet a man known to me of prodigious and unheard-of lust. For he never approaches <term>Venus</term> <note>A common euphemism for sexual intercourse.</note> unless he is beaten; and yet he contemplates this crime in such a way, and so desires the cruel lashes, that he scolds the one whipping him if she acts too gently; he is not fully in possession of his wish unless blood breaks out, and the more violent whip leaves the limbs of an innocent man <note>original: "innocentis artus"; perhaps meaning physically unblemished or unharmed before the act.</note> most wickedly violated. 

That miserable man entreats this service with the greatest prayers from whatever woman he visits; he provides a whip himself the day before, hardened for that duty by being soaked in vinegar, and as a suppliant, he begs to be whipped by a prostitute. The more harshly he is beaten, the more fervently he grows hot; and he hastens at an equal pace toward pleasure and pain. Here is one man found who discovers bodily delights amidst torture! Since he is not otherwise of the worst character, he recognizes his disease and hates it; and since he has been familiar to me for many years, he freely revealed what he suffered. When the cause of such an unusual plague was diligently sought from him, he said: "I have been accustomed to this since I was a boy." And when I asked again for the cause of this habit, he said he had been raised with most wicked boys, among whom it was agreed that they would sell their mutual shame to one another in a shameful exchange, using this license of beating as a kind of price. 

I have not suppressed this fact, though it is heavy for refined ears, so that we might recognize by this very evidence how much **habit** can do in those affections; let us not immediately accuse heaven as if such things could have no earthly cause. For if an astrologer were to hear of this, he would say that "Venus was condemned" in the man’s birth-chart, and perhaps whipped by the warlike rays of **Mars** <note>Mars was associated with violence and iron/whips; Venus with sex. An astrologer would see a "square" or "opposition" between them as causing this behavior.</note> threatening her in some other way.

Let us come to external matters, in which **Alexander** was preeminent; whose great success in affairs...

Here, he addresses the common argument that the extraordinary success of great conquerors like Alexander the Great must be written in the stars, countering it with the concepts of human virtue and Aristotelian chance.</meta>

<header>DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY</header>

<margin>Fortune.</margin>
...so sudden a prosperity: where would it originate if not from heaven? The answer is easy: from the virtues of Alexander, of which he had many necessary for an emperor: <term>fortitude</term><note>original: "fortitudinem"; bravery or moral courage.</note>, liberality, industriousness, endurance, military skill, an excellent stature, and others which it is not necessary to list. It came from the army he obtained, which was highly trained under his father Philip, and by the benefit of their region, most warlike; and because of his liberality and example of virtues, they were most devoted to him. It came from the laziness of the peoples whom he overcame; whence it was said by his uncle that he had fought against women. It came from **Fortune**, which holds the most power in matters of war. Indeed, when I say **Fortune**, I do not mean "heaven," but that cause which <term>Aristotle</term><note>Pico frequently cites Aristotle's "Physics" to argue that many events are "contingent" or accidental rather than predestined by a higher celestial cause.</note> mentions in the second book of his *Physics*; what we commonly call fortune, and are accustomed to express in these words: "so the lot fell," "so the matter turned out," "so the thing happened." It is through this that it happens to those playing at dice: they either throw what they want, or what they do not want. This is that so-called "blind" power which, besides those causes we have mentioned and similar ones, made the Caesars, the Syllas, the Augusti, and the Alexanders. This power, by itself, neither depends on heaven, nor is it the same as <term>fate</term><note>original: "fatum"; here meaning an inescapable celestial decree.</note>, nor does it detract from divine providence. Finally, whether it can "be" or "not be" must be discussed at length in the next book; it need not be said here.

<margin>Thomas</margin>
In this matter, we shall overwhelm the astrologers with no better weapons than those of **Thomas Aquinas**, whom they think favors them most highly. But as for what principally concerns us here: I deny that anything on earth becomes or appears so great that it deserves heaven as its author. For miracles—whatever they are, as we have said—are greater than heaven; whereas **fortune** and the **body** (however great they may be), when compared to heaven, are found to be very small, as <term>Phavorinus</term><note>A philosopher from the 2nd century AD known for his skepticism and extensive learning.</note> rightly said:

<margin>Phavorinus.</margin>
> "Nothing is great on earth except man: nothing is great in man except the mind and the soul; if you ascend to this, you transcend heaven; if you bend toward the body and look up at heaven, you see yourself as a fly, or even something less than a fly." 

Just as in that black column of ants, there are those who surpass others in strength and size; there are victories, wars, peace, duties, labors, poverty, and riches. To us who contemplate them, these are all tiny and, without distinction, are nothing. So too are these little bodies of ours: our fortune, our kings, our provinces, wars, treaties, and marriages—if they are compared to heaven, they are absolutely nothing. To heaven, the entire earth (one tiny portion of which men divide among themselves with fire and sword) is an <term>indivisible point</term><note>original: "individuum punctum"; a standard geographical concept in the Renaissance, emphasizing the earth's insignificance relative to the cosmos.</note>. Therefore, the magnitude of earthly kingdoms is not such that it could not be the work of something other than heaven. If those things which are considered "worthy" among us are not worthy of heaven, how much more unworthy will be those things which are done unworthily by us? Such as the wicked being raised to dignity, or **Socrates** perishing by the judgment of a "star-gazer," and enormous things of that kind, many of which we see and suffer daily. 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>Objection</margin>
In these matters, <term>Maternus</term><note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century author of a famous astrological manual, whom Pico attacks for blaming crimes on the stars.</note> says that fate and the necessity of celestial decree especially shine through. I would gladly ask him, along with the other astrologers: why are they so eager to impute our errors to the stars? And when we ourselves sin, why do they more willingly accuse heaven than us? As if it were a marvel that we should err—we who are of ourselves evil from youth—or as if those heavenly bodies could ever err, serving as they do the commands of the best God in an always unchangeable order. "The innocent are condemned," they say, "and the wicked are bestowed with rewards." By which princes, I ask: just or unjust? If by the just, even heaven will not suffice for such a "miracle" <note>This is sarcastic; Pico implies that a just prince condemning the innocent would be an impossibility.</note>; if by the unjust, why is heaven needed? The malice of man, which despises heaven, is sufficient. Aristotle asks in his *Problems*: "Why are the good almost always poor?" and although he brings forward many causes, both true and clever, 

<margin>Response</margin>
he brings none from heaven: as if he knew that the earth, not heaven, germinates weeds and briers. But a cautious and prudent man, while fleeing a great danger, runs into it; another escapes a peril to which he had often rashly exposed himself. Why should we wonder? These things happen no less often than they do; but if they happen often, they should be considered a marvel. When these things occur, their cause must be sought: first the immediate cause; if that is missing, the more remote and hidden one. When dealing with the rare and the fortuitous, no other cause needs to be investigated, if we remember well what the most wise Aristotle left written for us both in the second book of the *Physics* and the sixth of the *Metaphysics*.

->JOHN<-

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS: BOOK FOUR BEGINS.

## Chapter One: The method observed in disputing and to be observed hereafter: Also, if it is granted to astrologers what the highest theologians grant, astrology is nonetheless nothing.

<margin>
A method of disputing that marvelously convicts the authors.
</margin>

**O**ur method in disputing is almost always this: if an adversary proposes something that can be denied without impiety and reasonably, we prefer to deny it rather than grant it, even if granting it would not further his goal. And when we reach the point where he can demand the most, we show that even if that were granted—which we previously showed could be denied—it still does not follow what he thinks. In this way, the matter under dispute is explored in all its particular parts, and the adversary understands how many things he takes for granted and how poorly he defends a certain and absurd opinion. For though it may be false or at least doubtful on many counts, yet however things may stand, it cannot be entirely false. Observing this custom with the astrologers, we first 

<margin>
The order of the dispute.
</margin>

defended that only the rays of the sun and moon have the power to change inferior things. The other <term>stars</term><note>original: "sydera"; in this context, Pico refers to the planets and fixed stars beyond the sun and moon.</note> have no influence on us because of their rays, or their distance, or their weakness. Secondly, if it were granted to them—not because they prove it, but because they ask for it—that something flows from all of them into us, we showed that it flows from all of them with different intensity and degree; that is, light with life-giving heat. But cold, moisture, and dryness do not emanate from them. Thirdly, even if they produced the four primary qualities, it would not follow that there would be a diversity of impressions made on high by them; or if there were, it would not mean that <term>pestilences</term>, or <term>cataclysms</term><note>original: "cathaclifmos"; referring to universal floods.</note>, or <term>conflagrations</term><note>original: "exustiones"; great fires or droughts.</note> are caused by them. Much less could external matters, subject to chance and fortune, be governed by the stars through the power of those four primary qualities. Fourthly, even if one believed the stars were the authors of those primary conditions—that is, having the power of <term>heating</term>, <term>cooling</term>, <term>moistening</term>, and <term>drying</term>—no other gifts should be attributed to them through which they might effect many things that cannot be done by those primary qualities. Finally, whatever virtues and properties the stars might have, they are so universal that there is none which does not encompass the true condition and power of inferior bodies. Therefore, they act upon all things with all their power, which is the nature of a universal cause. But the diversity of all things that happen and occur takes its origin from proximate causes, whether they be free, natural, or accidental.

<margin>
The weakness of the astrologers.
</margin>

We undertook to defend all these points with the intention that astrologers might understand that when they think and assert otherwise, they are not speaking of things that are conceded and manifest, but of things that are neither confirmed by any certain reasons, nor by evident experiments, nor by the authority of **Plato** or **Aristotle**. Instead, these matters are placed in ambiguity: just as they are defended by some, so they are attacked by many. If the whole of astrology were to rely on these points, and did not place more unreliable foundations for itself, it would not be entirely ruinous to me, but "tottering"—that is, my opinion would not so much fall as it would waver.

<margin>
The authority of Thomas.
</margin>

But even if we grant the astrologers as much as **Thomas Aquinas**, the theologian, contends—along with many philosophers—can be given, without reason greatly resisting, they would still receive far less than is necessary for them to defend that any astrology exists, not only among us but in its own nature, even among angelic minds.

<margin>
Granting that there is no astrology.
</margin>

For Thomas will grant them the most that can be granted without an open slander of the truth: namely, that the outflows of all the planets reach us with power, and that different stars have different properties—not only of heating, cooling, moistening, and drying, but more hidden ones, from which the crowd of earthly things receives various gifts. Even if he does not grant that every property which humans and the rest of inferior corporal nature have is from their own causes...

<sig>z iii</sig>

<summary>Pico outlines his logical method for dismantling astrology, arguing that even if he grants their major premises (like celestial influence), the "science" still fails to prove its specific predictions. He highlights that celestial causes are universal, while specific events on Earth are determined by local, natural, or accidental factors.</summary>

## Chapter II. Fortuitous things are not from heaven.

<margin>The subject matter of predictions</margin>
**F**ortuitous things, through which we call men fortunate or unfortunate by a good or bad outcome, are primarily those which are thought to be fated and dependent on a celestial decree. As such, they are the greatest and most powerful subject matter of astrological predictions. For those things which have immediate causes in themselves—such as the conditions of the soul and body—do not seem to require a higher and more hidden cause. However, we say things happen by "luck" or "chance" when they seem to happen without an immediate cause. <margin>The outcomes of mortals</margin> Such things include sailing happily or unhappily, traveling, engaging in commerce, finding treasure while digging the earth, encountering robbers or wild beasts, pleasing a king, escaping danger, obtaining good or bad servants, entering a house about to collapse, and other things of this kind that happen to wretched and truly weary mortals beyond their planning or expectation. Concerning these things—because they are outside our control and come upon us from the outside—we especially desire the opinion of the astrologers. Otherwise, one might know the condition of one's body from a mirror or a doctor, just as one knows the quality of one's mind from oneself (if indeed one has a mind). Those things we call "fortuitous" are the very things human curiosity most seeks through the divinatory arts. Therefore, we shall prove first of all that these things can in no way be foreseen from heaven. We shall use no other reason than that which <term>Thomas Aquinas</term> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher whose views on astrology were often more nuanced—and sometimes more permissive—than Pico's.</note> uses, particularly in that passage where he seems to favor the opinion of the astrologers: namely, in the third book of *Against the Gentiles*, where he seems to say that men are made fortunate and unfortunate by heaven. <margin>Where St. Thomas showed his prediction and its reasoning</margin> His reasoning is as follows: The power of a celestial body does not act upon the intellect or choice, but acts just as nature acts; and it is the property of nature to tend toward a single end. Therefore, an effect that is not a single, unified thing cannot exist <note original: "per se">directly or by its own nature</note> from a natural cause. But those things which happen by accident and coincide with one another are not truly "one" thing, but only "one" by accident. Therefore, a coincidence of this kind, which we are accustomed to call "fortuitous," can have no direct natural cause; but a celestial cause is a natural cause, as we were saying. And therefore, there can be no direct cause for such fortuitous things. <margin>An example of the same:</margin> He adds an example to this, by which he demonstrates how heaven is not the direct cause of such an outcome, but only an accidental one. He says: someone is incited by heaven to dig a grave; it happens that there is treasure in the grave. Therefore, the one digging the grave finds the treasure. This was not "from heaven" so that he would find the treasure, except by accident: for it is by accident that the same place is both a grave and a treasure site. For to incite a man to dig a grave in which treasure is hidden *so that* he might find the treasure belongs to a rational and intelligent cause, <margin>Note.</margin> whose property it is to relate and ordain one thing to another. It does not belong to a natural cause, which is only carried toward a single end as we have said—and no one will deny that a celestial ray is such a cause.

## Chapter III. How God is the cause of fortuitous things: how angels are, how heaven is, how we are, and how fortune is.

**S**ince mention is made of fortuitous things, it would be worthwhile to explain more deeply what their causes are according to philosophers and theologians. From what we have said so far, one might estimate that we attribute these things only to chance and rashness. Now we must prove that the astrologers are wrong to try to maintain an order and certain causes even in these extraordinary events, as if nothing happened rashly in nature and nothing without a legitimate cause. If any cause is to be considered, that which the astrologers accept—namely, heaven—seems most likely to be chosen, since no such power is judged to exist below heaven over all things that happen under heaven. Nor do they look above heaven, because many things seem to happen unworthily, beyond merit and reason, which suggest a certain necessity of a physical cause rather than the providence of a Chooser. Therefore, to push aside these doubts, it will be useful to discourse more broadly on these matters: so that after it is shown that these things cannot be governed by heaven...

<summary>Pico argues that "chance" events (like finding treasure) cannot be predicted by astrology because stars are natural causes that act predictably toward a single end, whereas chance is a coincidence of multiple factors that only an intelligent mind could coordinate. He invokes Thomas Aquinas to support the idea that celestial bodies do not control human luck or intellect.</summary>

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

<margin>Fortuitous things</margin>
...we have shown that they cannot [be governed by the stars]; nor do we grasp from where or by what they are steered. We say that fortuitous things are those which happen contrary to the intention of the one performing an action. For this reason, <term>fortune</term><note>Latin: *fortuna*. Pico uses the classical definition where "fortune" applies only to rational beings who have intentions that can be frustrated or surpassed by luck.</note> is spoken of only in human affairs, as they are the only ones that happen by deliberation and reason.
<margin>An Example</margin>
The following is an example we have used before: a farmer intends to dig the earth, thinking only of cultivation and not of treasure. It happens that he finds treasure; we say this was done by fortune, and we give no other cause for the discovery of the treasure than "fortune." Truly, by fortune we do not mean a
<margin>Note that fortune is excluded</margin>
divinity or nature, or any thing that is a cause of such an outcome; rather, we use the term to exclude a specific cause, as if we were saying "it happened by chance, not from any [intended] cause." For the digging of the earth cannot be called the cause [of the treasure], nor can the earth itself, insofar as the earth is merely the location. But it happened that the same location was both the earth and the hiding place of the treasure. Therefore, if you ask for what cause it happened that he dug up this treasure, there is none to bring forward, since it was not one cause, but a fortuitous concurrence of many causes that produced this effect. For this reason, those who denied that fortune exists in things were in error. Aristotle agrees with this opinion in the second book of his *Physics* and the first book of his *Metaphysics*.
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
However, they erred not because they thought that things which are unforeseen and fortuitous to us might be known and foreseen by higher minds—for in that sense nothing is absolutely and simply "fortune"—but because they thought such events must necessarily have a direct and inherent cause. They did not understand how a thing that is <term>accidental</term><note>original: *per accidens*. In logic, this refers to a property or event that is not essential or intended, like a "warrior who happens to be a musician."</note> requires no single inherent cause. For example, there is no single cause for the same man being both a musician and a warrior; otherwise, if they were together because of some cause, they would have an order relative to each other derived from that cause. But since they happen to coincide by chance—as a warrior being a musician or a musician being a warrior—it is clear they have no mutual order. Therefore, such a coincidence has no agent acting as an inherent cause, but only an accidental one. Thus the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the covered walkways (peripatos) where they walked and talked.</note> rightly defend chance and fortune in things, thereby banishing <term>necessity</term><note>The idea that every event is inevitable and could not have happened otherwise.</note>. Yet some of them err more detestably than those who remove chance by denying that these things happen in any way other than by fortune—that is, by no counsel of a higher cause and no providence. Indeed, this most pestilential error sprouts from the root of impiety, which believes that human affairs are either not known or, if known, not cared for by the powers above. This will be refuted by arguments elsewhere, where there will be a dispute against the philosophers themselves. For now, let it be rejected as a proven falsehood by the authority of all theologians, the entire family of philosophers, and Aristotle, the prince of the Peripatetics. In his books on ethics, both where he discussed happiness and where he discussed good fortune,
<margin>Another detestable error</margin>
he asserted most clearly that humans, and especially the wise, are under the care of the gods, and that all sensible things, past and future, are known to God, and that we are directed by Him in these matters. He also confirmed this in the book *On the Universe*—a book certainly worthy of Aristotle's wisdom—which he concluded with that Platonic sentiment regarding divine justice as if with a crowning oracle. If, therefore, the gods care for human things (for we speak thus so as to include the guardian angels and the series of intelligent causes serving the counsel and providence of the true God), if, I say, this is true, no one will doubt that men, urged by them, often do things which are unforeseen and unknown to the man himself, but which are arranged by those [higher beings] with the wisest foreknowledge. There is a very common example of two servants 
<margin>How the Intelligences and [angels]...</margin>
sent to the same place by their master so that they might meet, yet they are ignorant of their master's will. Their meeting and concurrence is unexpected and fortuitous to the servants themselves, but it was foreseen and pre-arranged by the master. In this way, a guardian angel, providing for the utility of a poor farmer, can invite him by hidden movements to dig in that place where the angel knows the treasure is. Thus, what was fortune to the poor man was a plan to the angel. Reflecting on this, Aurelius Augustine 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
says in the fifth book of *The City of God*: "We do not say that the causes which are called fortuitous (from which fortune also took its name) are non-existent, but that they are hidden; and we attribute them either to the will of the true God or of certain spirits." He said "of certain spirits" because this can be done by both good and evil angels, although the evil ones cannot do all that the good ones can, nor is their end the same. For the good, the goal is the common good of men; for the evil, it is harm. Yet divine goodness frustrates their malice, while whatever they have perpetrated with an evil will is reduced and ordered toward the good.

He uses the example of a farmer finding treasure to show that while an event may be "chance" to a human, it is "design" to a higher intelligence.</summary>
