<page-num>481</page-num>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>Definition of fortune assigned by Proclus.</margin>
These things are discussed more broadly elsewhere. Proclus the Platonist <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers; Pico is citing his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*.</note>, in his commentaries on the *Timaeus*, defined fortune by the same reasoning as Augustine: that it is a **demonic power** <note>original: "dæmonicā ptātē". In the Platonic sense, a *daimon* is a guiding spirit or intermediary intellect, not an evil "demon."</note> gathering together causes that were otherwise separated from one another. Nor does this differ from the <term>Peripatetic</term><note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> determination, which says that fortune is a cause producing something by accident within the sphere of human choice. One of them [Proclus] looked to a more remote and hidden cause, while the other [Aristotle] looked to a more proximate and known one. For Proclus spoke of a "demonic power," as the Platonists call any minds placed between humans and the higher intellects, which are removed from the particular and immediate knowledge of our affairs.

<margin>Example of the above.</margin>
->Let us clarify by examples how these things happen, and let us understand what the heaven <note>Meaning the celestial bodies or stars.</note> does in them.<-

Lucius was at home and had nothing to do outside; but it occurred to his mind to go out, and as soon as he left the house, the house collapsed. You would call him fortunate for having thus avoided the imminent danger. If you ask a poorly pious philosopher for the cause of this thing, he will reply—as will even a poorly skilled philosopher—that it happened by chance and no other cause is to be sought. But if you ask an astrologer, he attributes this to some benign radiation of a fortunate planet, by whose help he was defended from the ruin. 

He is mistaken for the reason explained above: for to incite Lucius to go out so that he would not perish under the ruins is the work of an **intelligent agent** acting with counsel and reason. No ray from Jupiter or any other star is of such a kind. From the heaven, there could only be an influence making Lucius’s mind more prone to movement than to sitting still; just as this could also come from the habit of his own body, which makes some men sedentary and others walkers. Thus, if any constellation were the cause of this good, it would be from those that make us vigorous and seeking better things—which they call **Martian** <note>Influenced by the planet Mars, associated with energy and motion.</note>—not some benevolent power acting as a defender against evils, a point we have often argued. 

A ray cannot coordinate these things together—namely, the act of exiting and the protection from ruin. Rather, just as it is fortuitous for Lucius, who chose to go out for a walk, that he escaped death; so too, if we suppose such a constellation exists, it is fortuitous and accidental to that constellation that it freed him from ruin, insofar as it merely prompted him to motion. Thus it follows that even if an astrologer knows what the heaven is then influencing in Lucius, he knows nothing else but that Lucius will be eager for movement; but that he would simultaneously escape the house and the danger—neither his <term>birth chart</term><note>original: "thema". The layout of the stars at the moment of birth.</note> nor any reason allows that to be foreknown by him. 

Therefore, only one cause remains for whom this was foreseen and could not be fortuitous: the **Divine**. Namely, God nudging Lucius’s mind from within and instigating the exit, so he would not perish under the house about to fall; for the same Deity understands that the house is about to fall and can coordinate Lucius's exit to that end. Regarding a physical ray from a star, neither can be said. 

Therefore, no philosopher ever defined fortune as a decree of the heavens or an effect of a birth chart, or anything drawn from the dogma of astrologers. Instead, they either referred it to the unexpected concurrence of causes, or to intellectual causes coordinating things by their own counsel which escape our foresight. Thus that great leader of philosophers, Aristotle, distinguishes at great length between good and bad fortune, and being "fortunate" versus "unfortunate." He does this not by decreeing celestial constellations, nor even by entertaining that discussion; for he did not think the opinion of those who cast birth charts was worthy of a philosopher’s doubt. Rather, like the other ravings of charlatans, it should be numbered among fables and stage-tricks rather than philosophical controversies. 

Aristotle himself, in that treatise after a diligent examination of the whole question, defines it thus: when things turn out well for us by chance, it usually happens in two ways. Either we stumble entirely unintentionally into an event that brings a good outcome, or we are led toward it by a mental impulse, though not by counsel or deliberation. We are so ignorant of the reason for this impulse that even though we do not know where it leads, we follow it with the most obstinate "sail and oar" <note>A classical metaphor meaning "with all one's might" or "at full speed."</note>. The first he thinks should be referred to chance; the latter to a **divine motion** which inclines the will itself by hidden impulses. People are accustomed to say of such things: *"My mind has a premonition of I-know-not-what,"* or *"I cannot do otherwise,"* or *"I am swept this way."* Since they can give no reason for their plan, they nonetheless assert that it is their pleasure and a firm prejudice of the mind.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle correctly on God and the soul.</margin>
In this place, the philosopher Aristotle shows that all things are known to God, as we said above; and that nothing is more sublime than God, from whom the will can proceed.

<summary>Pico argues that "fortunate" events, like escaping a collapsing house, are either random accidents or guided by divine intervention, but never caused by the stars. He uses Aristotle and Proclus to show that astrology cannot predict the specific "lucky" outcomes of general physical influences.</summary>

# BOOK THREE

<margin>The ambiguity of human affairs</margin>
...that it is our will that is moved, which he affirms is a great argument for our immortality. From all these things, it can be gathered that among human affairs, some happen by **chance**, some by **nature**, some by **choice**, and some by **divine counsel**. For although nothing happens outside of God’s counsel, we distinguish them in such a way that we say things are done "divinely" which the minds of men, if left to themselves, would not achieve, but which they do when moved by a peculiar impulse of the Divine Power <note>original: "numinis impulsu". Pico refers to a specific nudge from God rather than just general existence.</note>. This is beyond that general assistance of the Supreme Power which is present to all things, without which nothing can exist or happen, even the smallest thing. Thus, although it is characteristic of a human to act by choice, nature sometimes rules when a person, enslaved by the movements of bodily affections <note>Physical passions or urges.</note>, does not wait for the judgment of reason. 

Let us clarify this with a single example: a king declares war on his neighbors. Perhaps the **nature** of the king is warlike, greedy, or restless; perhaps he is led not so much by passion as by **reason**, either by a legal right to claim what is his, or to repay an injury, or for other causes. Beyond all these, a special **divine counsel** may intervene—always just, always rational—even if its justice or reason is not always apparent to everyone. I speak of the counsel of God, both in an animal sense <note>Moving the king as a living being.</note> for the undertaking of war, and in the movement of the armed man toward victory. In this way, God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah: 

-><note>original: "Ecce ego mittā & aſſumā uniuerſas cognationes aqlonis..."</note> "Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, and Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant: and I will bring them against this land, and against its inhabitants, and against all the nations that are round about it."<-

And in Isaiah: 

-><note>original: "Aſſur uirga furoris mei..."</note> "Assyria is the rod of my anger and the staff in his hand is my indignation: I will send him against a deceitful nation, and I will charge him against the people of my wrath, to take the spoil, and to seize the prey: and to trample them down like the mire of the streets. But he will not think so, and his heart will not so estimate."<- 

### Chapter IV: That anything done by us which seems to exceed our powers 
### should not be referred to the heavens, but rather to either angels 
### or God. And therein many things concerning fate, and how 
### divine providence does not take away our freedom.

<margin>The condemnation of popular applause</margin>
**W**hen something is done by a human that seems to exceed his powers, our mortal nature is usually shaken by such unusual and admirable events. Overcome by the magnitude of the matter, we suspect the force of a more powerful cause acting in and through the human, surpassing the capacity of human faculty. And indeed, those who have only **eyes of flesh** <note>Meaning those who only perceive the physical world.</note> are seized by this suspicion and look toward the sky <note>The celestial bodies/stars.</note>, because they see nothing greater than it, nor feel anything more powerful. They are so possessed by a poor mind that they refer the event to a cause that is unloving and lacks knowledge <note>The stars, which Pico argues are inanimate and irrational.</note>—a cause they believe is sufficient for even those things which no counsel of the human mind could achieve. 

But if they should respond that these things are indeed disposed and ordered by God, but fulfilled by God *through* the heavens and the stars (whose power and efficacy they claim is so great), they are easily refuted for speaking most absurdly. For if these causes standing between God and us are lower than God, they must likewise be higher than humans. It is not fitting for the First Author to arrange things that are carried out by reason and counsel (as our affairs are) through **irrational bodies** <note>The planets.</note>. Rather, just as He rules and moderates the <term>elemental mass</term><note>The physical matter of the four elements (earth, water, air, fire).</note>, which is inferior, through the celestial mass, which is better; so it is fitting that human affairs be governed not by the mystery of bodies, but of **angels**, who by their nature and dignity stand as mediators between us and God. 

Therefore, when you descend from God to the earth, descend through the heavens; but when you descend from God to humans, descend through the **angels**. Thus we read in the prophets of the angels of the Persians, the Greeks, and the Hebrews providing for their own peoples. And in Plato and all the Platonists, we find <margin>Angels and humans</margin> "local gods" set over cities, kingdoms, and men. Mention of these was also made by **Aristotle**; and the elder **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD).</note>, and after Isidore, **Clement of Alexandria** in his *Stromata* <note>A famous work of early Christian philosophy.</note> have remembered them. 

Nor should it disturb us that certain things sometimes seem to us to be done unworthily or unjustly, so that we might more willingly run back to a cause acting by natural necessity <note>The stars/fate.</note> rather than by counsel. Truly, it would be ridiculous if the lowliest slaves of a city presumed to judge the counsels of a prince; how much more ridiculous, or rather sacrilegious, is our rashness when it claims for itself the judgment of the events of the First Order and of Divine Wisdom—which is not given for the sake of one man alone.

<summary>Pico argues that while human affairs can be influenced by nature or chance, events surpassing human ability are governed by God or angels, not the stars. He asserts that using irrational celestial bodies to explain rational human actions is a philosophical error.</summary>

He argues that what astrologers call "fate" is actually the unfolding of God’s vast, orderly plan.</meta>

<page-num>181</page-num>
->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS<-

God extends the eye of His providence and the ray of His goodness to the benefit not of a single family or a single city, but of the entire world; not merely for the present age, but for all ages alike. Shall we—mere little humans, <note>original: "homunculi"</note> or rather owls and moles, truly asses and oxen, and indeed the dullest of judges—recall God to an examination? 
<margin>Common rebuke</margin>
For quite often we do not even use the tiny amount of judgment we possess, but rather, judging from a diseased mind, we complain that whatever happens that we ourselves do not want is "unjust." And who would not have persistently exclaimed that God was "dozing" when the righteous Joseph was being sold by his brothers? Who would not have said God does not even exist when that same man received prison as the reward for his chastity? But see him shortly afterward as king in Egypt, or second only to the king. See him redeeming his father and his whole family from famine. See that noble prophecy, and you will not deny that those earlier events were brought about by God, through which he arrived at these later things in their proper order. 

And if you look even deeper, you will understand that from that wicked merchant-trade, the matter was brought to the point where the entire people descended into Egypt and, after being worn down for a long time by the Egyptian kings, were gloriously asserted into liberty by Moses. This power of God was confirmed by so many portents, manifested by so many oracles: in Pharaoh, in Egypt, and among the Hebrew people through the Law; through so many miracles of divine majesty—now through kindness, now through justice—which prefigured the future ineffable mysteries of the divine incarnation under Jesus. 

Indeed, even a madman could not be led to suspect that anything happens in human affairs without a reason. Therefore, you should not believe that things are governed by an "evil demon" (as the <term>Manicheans</term><note>A dualistic religious movement that believed the world was a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note> do), or by the necessity of the "sidereal revolutions" of the body (as the <term>astrologers</term><note>Practitioners who believed the movements of the stars and planets dictated human destiny.</note> do), or by fortuitous chance and rashness (as many who imagine things poorly do). But as often as you understand wars and slaughters to be stirred up, and the devastation of cities, and the overturning of kingdoms, you will not think the cause is a "mixture of two rays" <note>An astrological term referring to the planetary aspects or configurations.</note> or light being interposed between the sun and moon in its natural course, like those tricksters do. Instead, you will see the counsel of God, either punishing the wicked or exercising the good. 

Hence, one man was called the "Scourge of God" <note>A reference to Attila the Hun, famously titled "Flagellum Dei."</note>; and another, closest to our own age, said he was not a man, but the "wrath of God" and the "wasteness of the world." 
<margin>Herodotus.</margin>
That wise man of the Persians in the writings of <term>Herodotus</term><note>A famous Greek historian (c. 484–425 BC), often called the "Father of History."</note> spoke rightly when he sat at a banquet with a Theban. He revealed that he had foreknowledge of the future slaughter of his own race through some sort of premonition. For when the Theban urged him to report this to the commander of the army and warn him away from an undertaking that would have such an unhappy exit, he replied that what God has ordained to happen is inevitable for a human. Therefore, his own words would not be believed even if he warned the commander, since it had been so decreed by God. Thus, both he and <term>Mardonius</term><note>A leading Persian military commander during the Persian Wars.</note> (for that was the prince's name) were bound by necessity. I am pleased that he called this "necessity" not of the stars, but of the **divine counsel**. If anyone calls this "fate," Augustine says he will think more correctly than he speaks. 
<margin>
On fate.
Augustine.
Fate is accepted in four ways.
First mode.
Alexander.
Virgil
Demosthenes
Aristotle
Second
</margin>
Moreover, this name of "fate," as far as can be gathered from the monuments of the ancients, is accepted in a fourfold meaning: 
1. That fate is **nature** itself. 
2. That it is a **series and order of causes** producing all things by a necessary connection. 
3. That it is the **constitution of the stars** at the moment someone is born, conceived, or begins something. 
4. That it is the **execution of divine counsel**, certain and inevitable in its success.

The first meaning is accepted by <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term><note>An influential Greek commentator on Aristotle (late 2nd century AD) who wrote a famous treatise "On Fate."</note> in his book *On Fate* addressed to the emperors Severus and Antoninus. For he concedes that there are "fates" in such a way that fate is nature itself, which is a principle distinct from choice. Thus, by fate, fire heats; water is wet; the sun illuminates. Also, when someone dies because the temperament of their body has dissolved, they die "by fate." If, however, they are thrown from a horse or killed by swords, they do not die by fate. This is the way <term>Virgil</term><note>The great Roman epic poet.</note> speaks of **Dido** as she prepared her own death: *But because she perished neither by fate nor by a deserved death.* <note>original: "Sed quia nec fato debita nec morte peribat." A quote from the Aeneid (4.696).</note> Astrologers, however, would have cast that specific kind of death into the category of fate. So too thought **Demosthenes**. And indeed, no one would deny that "fate" exists in this sense, just as no one denies nature. In this way, **Aristotle**, in the fifth book of his *Physics*, spoke of "fatal generations"—that is, those things which happen according to nature. There is no doubt that when we understand fate this way, many things happen "outside of fate," just as many things happen "outside of nature."

<summary>Pico argues that human history, like the story of Joseph and the Exodus, is guided by Divine Providence rather than the stars. He begins to deconstruct the concept of "Fate," identifying four different philosophical definitions to show that astrological fate is a logical error.</summary>

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

<margin>Alexander of Aphrodisias.</margin>
...beyond nature, whether by chance, by our own choice, or, as <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term><note>A late 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle who wrote a famous treatise "On Fate," arguing for human free will against Stoic determinism.</note> himself says in that same place, by the counsel of the gods. However, those who introduced the second opinion argued that in nature itself nothing happens that is not by necessity, if one were to embrace all causes together at once. For those who say many things happen outside of necessity defend this view in both natural things and in matters of choice <note>original: "arbitrariis"</note>. 
<margin>Refutation of the second mode.</margin> 
In natural things, they argue that not everything that happens naturally happens necessarily, since the work of nature can be hindered. In matters of choice, they argue that our selection and will are free. Those on the opposite side, however, insist that in natural things, if something is hindered, it is hindered *necessarily*, because even that hindrance arises from a natural cause, which must eventually be traced back to the supreme nature—that is, the heavens. They claim those heavens act by necessity; but they are mistaken. For even if a natural cause acted as a hindrance, it was still a cause that could itself either not exist or be hindered while it was acting; therefore, that hindrance was a <term>contingent</term><note>In philosophy, "contingent" refers to something that happens but could have happened otherwise; it is the opposite of "necessary."</note> event and not a necessary one. And if you should press us again regarding that hindrance—claiming it was a natural cause that would necessarily hinder just as nature does—I answer you: if you believe the world is eternal, or in an infinite progress from one contingent cause to another contingent cause (between which the order is always accidental), you will never arrive at a single primary necessary cause from which necessity is imposed upon all subsequent things. This is because no such cause exists among natural things, not even the celestial one, whose works are easily obstructed by both matter and concurrent inferior causes. If, however, you agree with theological truth concerning the creation of the world, you will arrive through that troublesome regress to the first contingent institution of things, by which necessity is removed. 

<margin>The third mode of fate must be refuted with all effort.</margin>
The third mode of necessity is brought in by our choices much more irrationally; they claim the will chooses nothing that is not already judged by reason, and that it is not in our power to will or judge in this way. But they rely on false assumptions, as has been shown by others and will be shown by us elsewhere. Indeed, these matters require their own separate treatises. Nor does this pertain greatly to the refutation of the **astrologers**, whose "third acceptance of fate" must be refuted with all one’s might. This differs from the first opinion because it makes the celestial nature the origin not only of natural things, but also of fortuitous things, as we have seen. It thinks poorly regarding inferior causes in this respect, and worst of all regarding the celestial ones. For although the heavens are natural by their essence, those **constellations** which they invent—based on the position of stars, through places, signs, houses, and other things of that sort—are not natural causes, but fictitious ones. Nor does the operation of the heavens depend solely on that one initial moment <note>The "horoscope" or moment of birth.</note>, nor do they refer the causes of things to those which are proper to inferior things, as we have already declared and as following sections will declare further.

<margin>Approval of the fourth acceptance of fate.</margin>
There remains the fourth, theological meaning of fate, just as the first was more physical; yet both are true. This meaning denotes the series and order of causes depending on divine counsel, under which our liberty is in no danger. Since we are ourselves among these causes, we do not merely "suffer" or endure in this "dance of fate," but we act. Therefore, whether you look to God's foresight or His providence—that is, whether you consider His mind foreknowing all things, or His will disposing all things according to His pleasure—
<margin>From the foreknowledge of God, our liberty is not removed, nor is providence.</margin>
no prejudice is done to our free actions. For if we consider His foresight: why should I not freely do what God foresaw I would do? For if what He foresaw will happen, then surely I shall do it freely, because He foresaw that I would do it *freely*. But also, because what He willed will happen—and He willed that I be free—I shall act freely in whatever I do, unless He Himself should take my liberty away from me. And certainly, God not only foreknew our wills, but also preordained them. 
<margin>Declared according to the opinion of Damascus and Gregory of Nyssa.</margin>
When <term>Gregory of Nyssa</term> and <term>John of Damascus</term><note>Two influential Early Christian Church Fathers who wrote extensively on the soul and free will.</note> denied this, they did not seem to deny it except as a warning. While other things are indeed disposed by the divine will, our choices are disposed through that will in such a way that our own will is included. Thus, not only the outcomes of our thoughts, but the thoughts themselves, the plans, and the purposes—not only of kings, as it is written, but the hearts of all people—are in the hand of God, who alone moderates all things. Now, in those things which pertain neither to vice nor to virtue, He inclines the will wherever He pleases, if the fulfillment of some decree of His requires it; now He begins virtues in us, and perfects those already begun, moving us from virtues toward...

<summary>Pico distinguishes between different definitions of Fate, refuting the idea that nature or the stars impose necessity on human will. He argues that Divine Providence and Foreknowledge actually preserve human freedom rather than destroying it.</summary>

<header>DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY</header>

...changing towards justice or applying the schoolmaster's rod through mercy, or you crush them through justice <note>original: "iustitia." Pico is addressing God or Providence here, describing the different ways divine discipline or justice is administered.</note>; you will always make all things either good or certainly occasions for good. We have said this much concerning fate, providence, and the governance of human affairs, as these things are useful to know in themselves and necessary for uprooting the vanity of astrology. Thus, when we see something happen or occur that seems either greater or more orderly than can be attributed to chance or man, we should understand it not as the power of physical rays <note>Referring to the "astral influences" astrologers claimed stars emitted.</note>, but as the divine plan and the service of angels combined with human freedom and power. It is clear from what we have said how future things can be foreseen and how evils can be avoided by us. For if human affairs happened only by chance, no foreknowledge of the future could exist. But since they occur by human and divine plan, human reason can speculate somewhat about them; yet only those inspired by the divine can foresee with certainty, as the predictions and oracles of the prophets confirm. Those who are prudent are next to the prophets, though at a very long distance. 
<margin>Euripides</margin>
Hence that saying of Euripides: *The one who conjectures well, let him be the best prophet.* <note>Pico translates the Greek playwright’s sentiment into Latin, arguing that "prophecy" is often just a high form of human wisdom or "prudence."</note> Thus, in seeking a happy outcome in our affairs and avoiding misfortunes, the most important thing is to reconcile God to oneself through purity of soul, pious works, and holy vows. After this, a man should consult his own prudence. For although fortune can do much in many things, the disposition of the fixed divine will is the most powerful—indeed, the whole—in all things. Nevertheless, it is necessary that the right way of living carries great weight in these matters, unless we are to say that this gift was bestowed upon us by God in vain. How rightly that man <note>Likely referring to the Roman satirist Juvenal.</note> said that no divinity is absent where there is prudence, but we make Fortune a goddess and place her in the heavens. 
<margin>Plato</margin>
Therefore, Plato, in his letter to the Syracusans, when he remembered that Homeric saying, "The gods took away his mind," argued that men instead "took away the mind that had been added to them." This is confirmed by that sentiment of Euripides, who said that Fortune is the daughter of the soul. Therefore, wisely establishing our lives by natural reason, and preparing divine benevolence for ourselves through true religion, let us avoid all superstitious vanity. Otherwise, he who hopes either to foresee the future or to avoid evils through astrological observations will hear <margin>Isaiah</margin> saying to him: *Evil shall come upon you, and you will not know its rising; and calamity shall fall upon you which you will not be able to ward off.* <note>Quoting Isaiah 47:11, a classic biblical rebuke against Babylonian star-gazers.</note>

### Chapter V. Neither the past nor matters pertaining to others can be foreseen from any constellation.

But if they happen to have anything to say about chance events—though they can have nothing true or even likely—what, I ask, will they answer about those things which precede the hour of birth <note>original: "geniturae horam," the moment the horoscope is cast.</note>? That is, how will they think that an efficient cause can come after its effects? What about things that are not only prior, but also belong to others, and therefore have their causes not in the constellation of this birth, but elsewhere? For instance, when they pronounce on the natures and fortunes of parents, grandparents, and older brothers from the hour a son is born. For these things are both prior to that constellation and foreign to it, as they already have their own order of fate and dependency from their own past constellations (if indeed we think fate comes from the heavens). Likewise, regarding the one who is being born: how does the birth constellation effect that which the child received many days before the day of birth? For they predict from the birth chart whether the one being born is male or female, crippled or whole, beautiful or deformed, and other such bodily conditions, about all of which the die was cast <margin>Lucilius</margin> before the infant was committed from the mother’s "pouch," as <term>Lucilius</term> <note>A 2nd-century BC Roman satirist known for his blunt, often coarse language; "bulga" (pouch) is his term for the womb.</note> says. The astrologers claim the prediction of all these things for themselves by some reasoning, but a cause cannot be later than its effect. 
<margin>Haly Abenragel's imagination regarding births</margin>
Nor can they foresee from the heavens in any other way than the way an effect is foreknown from a cause. <term>Haly Abenragel</term> <note>A famous 11th-century Arab astrologer, author of "The Complete Book on the Judgment of the Stars."</note>, in explaining the <term>Apotelesmatic</term> <note>From the Greek "apotelesma," meaning the effects of the stars; refers to Ptolemy’s "Tetrabiblos."</note> books of Ptolemy, wishing to solve this question of ours, tried to show how the fate of a brother or the fates of parents could be foreseen from the births of sons. He says: "It is not every time a woman joins with a man that she conceives; but only then when it happens at an hour whose..."

## BOOK FOUR

the hour whose constellation <term>constellation: the specific arrangement of stars and planets at a moment in time</term> corresponds with the constellation of the parents; and since those things which agree with a third thing must also agree with each other, if the nativities <note>original: "genituræ," referring to the astrological charts at the moment of birth.</note> of all the children agree with the constellations of the parents, then they themselves will also be in accord with one another. For this reason, they will also mutually signify each other’s fates: thus, the nature and fortune of the parents are shown from the brother's nativity, or from the son’s nativity. But in this astrological subtlety, I truly do not know what I should first refute or mock. It is argued: "A woman does not conceive," he says, "unless at that hour the position of the stars agrees with the stars of the parents." I do not agree. Therefore, the fates of the parents ought to be foreseen from that hour in which the child is conceived, not from the hour he is born. But also, regarding the first reason: <margin>Second [reason].</margin> since the mother of the one who conceives may have been born under a different sky, how will a single constellation be able to <margin>Third [reason].</margin> respond to such diverse constellations? Or if they think this can happen by some diversity of the stars, how will the themes <term>theme: an astrological chart or horoscope</term> of so many sons respond at the same time to the themes of the father and the mother? Since the signification of the parents ought to be sought in all of them from these same stars and from these same regions of the sky. From the fourth and tenth places of the sky, the lot of the father and mother is investigated by them; likewise from the Sun, Saturn, Venus, and the Moon. The arrangement of these in the themes of nativities is almost always varied and manifold according to the variety of the sons: do you then think that all this variety can fail to vary from the constellations of those born? As if a thing could fail to disagree with another when it first disagrees with itself, or as if it would not necessarily follow that the same person is both fortunate and unfortunate at once—namely, because one of his sons has the fourth house illuminated by happy rays, while the other has it occupied by unhappy ones. To avoid this, <margin>The response of the common crowd of astrologers.</margin> the common crowd of astrologers are accustomed to say that the fates of the parents are not foreseen from the nativities of all the children, but only from that of the eldest. But that refuge is immediately taken away from them by the nativities of brothers, which they were showing to be in agreement with each other for the reason that they all harmonized equally with the constellations of those born. But why is it necessary to laboriously refute things that are so evidently frivolous? For by what reason is it defended? That a woman does not conceive unless the one then conceived is to be born at an hour whose constellation will be of such a kind that it can signify the lot and nature of his parents to the astrologer. In this, the heavens and all of nature serve them: nothing can happen in the universe unless it happens in such a way that the astrologer can divine from it. Furthermore, how do they solve that point in which the whole force of our argument lay: that what preceded long before in the brothers and parents cannot be caused by the hour in which the infant is born? For we shall later refute the opinion of those who said that things are not caused by this, but only signified by the stars. Now we are disputing against those who think the sky is the cause of those things which are predicted from the heavens—which both Ptolemy and all the leading masters of this art have believed.

### Chapter VII: Future things cannot be caused by a present constellation a long time afterward.

<margin>An attack on the method of astrological vanity.</margin> Even if we consider correctly, not only past things but also those which are to be in the future a long time afterward cannot be caused by the present constellation; yet this is most familiar and frequent in the predictions of astrologers. For where does one not read among them: that an oriental <note>Planet rising in the East before the Sun.</note> planet provides what it promises in the first part of life; an occidental <note>Planet setting in the West after the Sun.</note> one in the last; that the planet which occupies the horoscope <term>horoscope: here meaning the Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term> or is the ruler of the horoscope gives its gifts quickly; a little later, the one who possesses the rights of the tenth house; the one who is either present at or presiding over the West gives his late; and latest of all, the one who was placed in the bottom of the sky <note>original: "imo cælo," referring to the *Imum Coeli* or the 4th house cusp.</note>; and innumerable other things of this kind. Finally, these things attest that what the constellations are going to do is not done when the constellations themselves exist, but rather many years after they have been. Truly, an example of this wonder appears in no other power or natural action (such as they confess the celestial one to be): namely, that it is thought to be more effective when it is not, than when it is. Nor does the celestial influence remain in the body like <margin>Response.</margin> a medicine. But perhaps they will respond that even if that celestial positioning has passed away, a certain power infused into us from it endures, which in its own time, according to the nature of the agent and the suitability of the material, will finally bring its <margin>Refutation.</margin> effects into the light. I, however, regarding what pertains to the nature of the agent, object to them as I did before...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrological logic. In the previous section, he questioned how the stars at a person's birth could influence their relatives. Now, he addresses the "lag time" between a celestial cause and its earthly effect, and begins a new chapter attacking the practice of "elections"—choosing specific hours for activities.</meta>

<header>DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY</header>

I argued that while effects do indeed vary according to the condition and the various powers of the agents, it is common to all causes that they produce their effects more powerfully while they are active than long after they have ceased to exist. Regarding the "matter" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "matter" refers to the physical subject being acted upon—in this case, the human being.</note>, if they perhaps say that a person is not made a king or a philosopher immediately upon birth—even if the heavens promised it—because their age resists it, this might not seem absurd. However, when they reach an age capable of those duties which the birth stars promised, why then does the effect still not occur? For the sufficient cause has already passed away, and <margin>Note regarding the failure of divination</margin> the matter is now ready and suitable. But they claim either that the effect is delayed for as many years as the planet was distant from a certain place in degrees <note>original: "partibus," referring to the degrees of a zodiac sign used to calculate the timing of future events.</note>, or that because the planet held a certain place in the birth chart, it cannot provide its benefits except late in life. This sounds more like the nature of a rational being, dispensing its gifts by its own choice and will at whatever time it wishes, rather than a natural cause—which it is not, and cannot be. Furthermore, if the heavens provide immediately what they promise, but the <margin>Note</margin> physical condition of the person is the cause of the delay, it will not be the astrologer’s job to foresee the timing of events by looking at the heavens. Rather, it belongs to one who understands the state and condition of the physical matter; the astrologer would have to hear from *him* what is going to happen, rather than the astrologer demonstrating it himself. Likewise, regarding their answer that a power derived from the heavens is preserved even after the constellation has passed, I would like to know from them: where is it preserved? Is it in the matter, or in lower and secondary causes? Whichever they prefer, let them know that neither in the ebb and flow of changing matter, nor in such a varied and mutable multitude of particular causes, can a celestial power remain the same and stable for such a long time.

### Chapter VII: On the "auspices" which they call <term>elections: the practice of choosing a specific moment to begin an undertaking based on the stars</term>; how vain and impossible the opinion of the astrologers is.

It is also worth inquiring about that part of astrology considered most useful for life: the taking of auspices, commonly called **elections**. That is, how do they understand it to be caused by the heavens that what we undertake to do at this hour happens successfully, but what we do at another hour happens unsuccessfully? For while they say all these things easily, and they have a certain appearance of probability at first glance, when they are examined more diligently, they are found to be vain and impossible. If someone, they say, begins a journey under a certain constellation of the sky, they will have a pleasant trip, be kindly received by the king, and increase their family wealth. Conversely, if they mount a horse at another hour, or board a ship, they will experience difficult travels and dangerous sailing. <margin>See by what arguments elections are refuted</margin> Nor will they eventually achieve the purpose for which they undertook the journey or voyage. I confess I do not see how all these things are caused by the sky; let them teach me themselves if they can. Suppose Jupiter from the ninth region of the sky casts his rays upon the earth; they will call this a lucky constellation for beginning a journey. I ask them: does this "outflow" or fortunate influence affect the men themselves who are about to start the journey? Or does it rather affect the very *action* of the traveling men—that is, the mounting of the horse, the leaving of the house, or any of those things that are necessary beginnings of a journey? If they answer the first—that it affects the men—then they would be influenced even if they did not start the journey then, whenever they had the intention of starting; especially since, according to the astrologers' own opinion, a constellation does not provide what it promises most when it is present, but often after a long interval of time. If they answer the second, they will certainly be forced into many absurdities to defend their position, such as explaining how that "Jovian" <note>Influenced by the planet Jupiter, traditionally associated with luck and kingship.</note> mounting of a horse strews a soft path for the feet, drives robbers away from the road, and makes the sky peaceful with diffused light once the clouds are driven off. Nor will they have a small task in explaining how that influence is retained while the journey is being completed over many days. For there is a justified suspicion that no power descends from the sky into that man mounting his horse; by the same logic, when he dismounts, that power should ascend back into the sky, and this traveler would always need a "new Jupiter" whenever he had to jump onto his horse. For to dream of some primordial force, nowhere consistent and nowhere rooted, which...

<summary>Pico argues that astrological "elections" (choosing lucky times) are logically impossible, questioning how a fleeting celestial alignment could physically influence complex human actions like traveling or avoid dangers like robbers.</summary>

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

...that the whole journey should be completed for you softly and happily is the talk of sleepless and even delirious men, who, not weighing what they say, give off a futile and mindless sound. Let us look again at these same men, lest they fall into difficulties in these matters which are our own works rather than mere operations. There is an opinion of Ptolemy <margin>Ptolemy’s example to be refuted</margin> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note>: if Mars occupies the midheaven <note>The highest point of the sky at a specific moment.</note> at the founding of a city, the princes of that state will mostly perish by the sword. Let Ptolemy explain to us: where is that bloody radiation of Mars received, which is meant to kill so many successive princes by the sword in the course of time? If he wants it to be received in the prince who then builds the city: I will ask in what way those stones, cast and buried in the earth by the prince's command—that is, the city's foundations—can bend and derive those celestial rays (or any others tending toward that prince) toward himself? In what way does this harmful power descend to his posterity and the successors of the kingdom, as if by hereditary right, when both the vessel that received it has perished and its origin has passed away? Truly, I do not see what he could answer us when we ask such things without blushing. 

Perhaps he will say that this pestilence is not received in the prince himself, the founder of the city, but rather in the city itself—in those very first <margin>If such a pestilence lurks in the foundations of the city and might eventually emit a foul vapor, then the poor would also be killed.</margin> stones upon which it is to be built; as if by some pestilential breath of Mars, it will breathe upon all the princes of that city. This would certainly be a new invention to be confirmed by the Mosaical testimony, which long ago showed us the purification of a "leprous house" by prophetic inspiration <note>A reference to Leviticus 14, which describes laws concerning "leprosy" or mold in the stones of a house.</note>. But I fear that the earth piled on top, and the nearby stones packed in, might prevent that Martian foul vapor <note>original: "mephitin," a reference to Mephitis, the Roman personification of foul-smelling gases from the earth.</note> from exhaling; or if it exhales at all, would it not rather attack the needy and the poor, who are more susceptible to pestilence, than the prince of the city himself? If the prince happens to live in some suburban villa, I believe he will not perish by the sword—especially if it is many thousands of paces distant from the city, so that the Martian vapor, suffocated on all sides by the rubble of lime, cannot reach there whole or arrive with any efficacy. But the glory of the Academy, Plato, and of the Lyceum, Aristotle, will be at risk here; for in their books on the Republic, where they gave so many instructions on founding and successfully ruling a city and state, they left us nothing written about such a useful and necessary caution. If we consider all these things seriously and not as a joke, we will see that Haly <note>Haly Abenragel (11th century), an Arab astrologer and commentator on Ptolemy.</note>, the interpreter of Ptolemy and a most eminent astrologer, rightly judged this part of astrology—which concerns "elections"—to be frivolous and ineffective.

### Chapter VIII: Astrologers subject our minds to the heavens, though they are clever enough to try to hide it.

Hitherto it has been demonstrated that none of the physical and temporary things, over which the heavens are thought to have the greatest right, depend on the heavens in the way that astrologers imagine. For they do not depend on the heavens in matters of chance, nor those pertaining to others, nor those which are either past or in the distant future, nor even the majority of those things which men begin under the observation of certain hours so that they might turn out happily. If the heavens do not act in such a way that these things can be foreseen from the sky, how much less can they influence those things which are incorporeal? Yet astrological superstition does not blush to pronounce upon these. For this category includes the diversities of characters and natural talents, and whatever works and properties belong to our soul; it includes things pertaining to demons, to superior minds, to God, to the efficacy of prayers, to the secrets of conscience, to the state of the future life, and other things of this kind. Concerning all these, this <margin>The cleverness of astrologers.</margin> "trifle-selling" <note>original: "nugiuendũ" (nugivendum), a derogatory term for someone who sells worthless things or lies.</note> race of men publishes a thousand dogmas with the most arrogant rashness. And indeed, they might begin with "morals," which they think vary in men according to the variety of the birth constellation. But when they are pressed on this point, they are accustomed to hide what they truly feel; babbling much about the freedom of the will, they <margin>Astrologers subject our mind to the heavens.</margin> caution us not to think our liberty is forced by the stars, from which we only have some propensity or invitation, which it is our choice either to follow or decline. I will therefore first detect the fraud of this defense, bringing forward many of their own dogmas from which it is clear that they subject the mind itself to the heavens, even where it does not depend on the body. Afterwards, we shall declare that the diversity of characters and talents cannot be traced back to celestial causes, even in the way they claim.

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS #

Therefore, if the astrologer thinks that differences in the human soul arise from the condition and position of the stars only insofar as the body is affected in various ways, then the soul’s operation should not be changed much at all. How, then, can they contend that Mars, when favorably positioned in the ninth region of heaven <note>The "ninth house" in astrology, traditionally associated with religion, philosophy, and divinity.</note>, can grant us such power that we might expel demons from possessed bodies by our presence alone? 

<margin>Second point</margin> This is a power that belongs not merely to a soul leaning toward the body, but to one living in the body in such a way—being full of God and inhabiting the inner chambers of the mind—that it does not even feel itself to be living in the body. Likewise, how do they presume they can judge, from the position of the Sun, the secrets of the conscience regarding gods and men for one who is being born? 

<margin>Third point</margin> Nothing in these matters is placed in their hand, but rather in our soul and our freedom; these secrets are not even open to angelic knowledge, nor are they subject to celestial power. Finally, if the partnership of the body connects the soul to the heavens, how can they pronounce upon the soul’s state when it is placed *outside* the body based on a celestial constellation? 

For it is a common saying among them that two planets are the authors of happiness: Venus and Jupiter. They assign them different duties: Venus bestows the happiness of the present life, while Jupiter bestows that of the future. 

<margin>Maternus</margin> <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the *Mathesis*.</note> Maternus, after recording many of the things provided by Saturn when it is positioned in Leo, then adds this: "But when they have attained all these things, they will die at a great age, and their soul, having been joined to the gods, will pass to heaven." 

<margin>A hollow dogma from which the beginnings of the dispute are taken</margin> For Saturn, he says, when placed in Leo, recalls the souls of those who lived such a life on earth—now freed from countless anxieties—to heaven and back to the beginnings of their origin. So he says. 

From this, I want it understood not only how far this astrological superstition spreads, even to the point of suspected impiety, but also how much faith can be placed in the writers of this art. When they commit these things to writing, have they been tested and proven by experience? We know beyond doubt that when he was writing, he had no experience of the future life. For if they perhaps learned these things from their deceased followers who had finished their lives, the constellation could more easily be understood as something that sends one to the underworld rather than the heavens. 

Furthermore, although the astrologer thinks he can obtain what he wants from God through supplications at a certain hour, I will not easily believe (unless he changes his dogma) that they will obtain eternal happiness from Him. And certainly, they believe what we have said. 

<margin>Fourth point. Albumasar.</margin> <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), known in the West as Albumasar, a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note> For that most mythical Albumasar writes: whoever supplicates God while the Moon is joined to Jupiter along with the Head of the Dragon <term>Head of the Dragon</term> <note>The North Node of the Moon, considered a point of great increasing power in medieval astrology.</note> will obtain from God whatever he asks. 

And yet there will still be philosophers and theologians who are pleased by these things, thinking that they—and the astrologers they follow—sufficiently understand what God is and what prayer is. This madness is not so much to be refuted in this place as it is to be cursed, since it has been sufficiently refuted by what I have disputed elsewhere regarding prayer against the impious. 

<margin>Peter of Abano. Heraclitus.</margin> <note>Peter of Abano (c. 1250–1316), an Italian physician and astrologer who was eventually accused of heresy and magic. Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.</note> But as for Peter of Abano, whose writings whenever I read, that saying of Heraclitus comes to mind: "Much learning does not bring understanding" <note>original: *polymathia noon ou pherei*</note>. He himself writes that at that hour of which we were speaking, he sought knowledge from God and made great progress in it after that day. 

I have no leisure to measure how much this "new Solomon" progressed in it. I certainly believe that whatever progress he made was no more than what can be accomplished by human effort. But however the matter stands, I would advise this Peter to credit all he achieved to his own industry and talent rather than to that Jove-like <note>Related to the planet Jupiter, associated with success and divine favor.</note> supplication of his. Let him not stubbornly defend it, lest sound judgments be forced to deny that he achieved anything at all in good literature, so that they might never assent to a vain superstition. 

I would also advise all astrologers in common: since Jupiter is so favoring to them, they should acquire such a mass of wealth and riches for themselves by a single supplication at a lucky hour that, needing none of our money hereafter, they might finally stop mocking the minds of the skilled with so many daily lies for the sake of squeezing out money.

For perhaps if we think that neither the rational part of the soul suffers the force of heaven, nor is our freedom compelled, there will be no further reason why either philosophy...

# BOOK FOUR #

<margin>The opinion of some</margin>
It is neither wisdom nor piety to deny that the varied pursuits of men and the many types of talent arise from the different influences of the stars; after all, the stars also shape the condition of the body, while the dignity of the soul and the freedom of choice remain intact. <margin>Refutation</margin> Truly, however, whoever thinks in such a way is far mistaken. For to suggest that even the sensual part <note>The "sensual part" refers to the lower appetites and physical desires, as opposed to the rational mind.</note> of the soul is so bound to the stars that it has a propensity toward some crime—opposing reason and greatly contrary to piety—is a grave error. For whatever things are made by natural causes (especially those that immutably keep the laws prescribed for them by the Creator of nature) must be traced back to the Author of nature who so established them, just as they are traced back to nature itself. Whatever power or property the stars are endowed with, God, the principle of nature, bestowed it upon them—a point on which both philosophers and theologians agree. Scarcely even the foolish deny that God is the best and wisest; yet what goodness or most powerful wisdom of the hand of heaven would bend a man—who, though free, is nevertheless weak—toward that side to which you would least want him to decline? <margin>Second reason</margin> Then, it would make the best servants <note>Pico refers to the stars as "servants" of God.</note> into the authors and ministers of evil; so that while they themselves never transgress the king's commands, they are the very ones who most invite and impel others to transgression. <margin>Third reason</margin> Finally, what kind of order of nature, what consensus, what wise institution is this: that things which the very reason of nature would not want to happen are nevertheless diligently provided for by those who are the great, powerful, excellent, and principal parts of nature? Furthermore, he who sins does not "do" anything; rather, he fails or falls short. <margin>Note the paradox</margin> Therefore, whoever invites one to sin, invites one to fail—which does not suit superior "efficient causes," <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being. Pico argues that higher beings like stars only cause "being" and "good," not the "lack" that constitutes sin.</note> which are always acting and never failing. <margin>Fourth reason</margin> Thus, they think it a most absurd dogma of the astrologers that we have an inclination toward theft from this position of the stars, or toward incest, fraud, and homicide from another; for all of nature, especially the superior part most closely joined to the Divine Mind, can perhaps favor the observation of natural and divine law, but can in no way oppose or hinder it. Therefore, let them stop their insane speech; let them not say that Venus joined to Mars calls us to adultery, or that these same planets placed in "masculine signs" <note>In traditional astrology, certain zodiac signs were classified as masculine (e.g., Aries, Gemini) and others as feminine.</note> excite men to wicked couplings; or that Mars occupying the ninth part of heaven <note>The "ninth house," associated with religion.</note> makes men irreligious; and that other constellations altogether irritate us toward other crimes. Let them impute their crimes to themselves, not to their heaven, nor to "foul matter"; and let them not think the filthy stains of an unjust mind emanate from the purest fountains of nature. <margin>The solution of some</margin> Truly, perhaps that objection can be resolved if (as some think) we were to say that the powers of all the stars are good and healthy, but when they are received in us, they degenerate through the vice of matter; thus, those influences which were beneficial turn out to be noxious and harmful. Thus, from Mars is provided fortitude of soul and Herculean efficacy. But either through a vice of the body in which red bile <note>original: "rubra bilis." In the theory of the four humors, an excess of yellow/red bile was thought to cause anger and violence.</note> boils over, or by the fault of a soul abusing a celestial gift, those impulses are sometimes bent toward cruelty and injustice. Thus from Saturn is poured into us the height of mind, depth of counsel, the investigation of hidden things, and the love of contemplation. Yet these same things, because they find a sluggish recipient, or through the fault of the will in the one who receives it, make the soul deceitful, filthy, unrefined, superstitious, and—to the point of the danger of madness—full of delusions. Thus from Venus we are made prone to cheerfulness, benevolence, and civil elegance; but we abuse that instinct for wickedness, luxury, and dishonesty. We are incited by the Sun toward magnanimity, but we abuse that impulse for ambition; and so it goes for the rest. <margin>Rejection</margin> But truly, someone might say these things as a *defender* of astrology rather than as an *astrologer*. For among the sayings of the astrologers, this is the very first and most confessed of all: that some planets are good and others are bad. But if the things just said were true, then all would be equally good by their nature, or all would be called bad for the same reason. For there is no influence so healthy that the matter and condition of the recipient could not infect, change, and disturb it. But if even they themselves do not want any planet to be so bad that great goods cannot also come from it, nor any so good that great evils cannot also proceed from it, they nevertheless do not refer this diversity of effect to the matter or the recipient of the ray, but to the various state and position of that star in the sky. This is why they say that if Saturn is in his own house...

He also refutes the apology that stars are inherently good but corrupted by human biology, noting that astrologers themselves contradict this by labeling certain planets as naturally "malefic."</summary>

...its own height and held its own boundaries. They say that if it is mixed with good radiations <note>In astrology, "radiations" refer to aspects or geometric relationships between planets that transmit their influence.</note>, and if the birth is diurnal <note>Occurring during the day.</note>, it makes men into contemplators: pious and wise. But truly, if it is received in a less favorable "receptacle," they claim this same planet degenerates into a bad condition. If it is poorly placed, joined to Mars, or in bad configurations with the Sun, they say it makes men demonic, filthy, envious, and liars. Nor do they ever contend that anything good can be expected from Saturn when it is so situated in the sky.

Therefore, whoever defends this astrology clearly ignores what it is they are defending. For what we have said regarding Saturn should be understood as said of all the planets. Indeed, they are also accustomed to say that Mars, when not favorably positioned, stimulates ambition, lack of self-control, and the lust for tyranny—not because the vital spirit of the newborn is excessively hot or cold, or because it makes the good fire of heaven either sluggish or consuming, but because Saturn, Mars, and the Sun, when so positioned in the sky, are thought to influence the newborn with these types of evils out of their own nature and property. This is what astrologers write and believe. Nor does anyone who denies this defend astrology any better than one who "cleans a book with a sponge" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to erase or destroy something entirely while trying to "fix" it.</note>; as we have shown, they take away both the dogma and the truth of every prediction if it does not depend on the observation of celestial influence, and if the disposition of the matter does not merely diminish or increase the celestial influence, but entirely changes and alters it.

### Chapter X. That bad laws, just like good ones, are not subject to the heavens.

<insert>H</insert>ere the opinion of those is refuted who deny that good laws are subject to the heavens (holding instead that they depend on divine power), but concede this point regarding evil laws, since they believe these contain nothing that exceeds the forces and capacity of nature. Yet, just as the sublime nature of truth prevents good laws from being subjected to bodily causes, so too does the wickedness of evil laws prevent them from being attributed to the best causes, which are most obedient to God. 

Universal experience sufficiently demonstrates that religions—both good and bad—do not depend on the heavens. For some refer the origin and variety of religions to the stars ruling over cities and provinces by their own "right," as they believe. Others refer them to what they call the <term>Great Conjunctions</term> <note>The alignment of the "superior" planets, Saturn and Jupiter, which medieval astrologers believed signaled major historical and religious shifts.</note> of the superior planets, especially Saturn and Jupiter; this is the opinion followed by the Arabs and by the Latins who follow in the footsteps of the Arabs.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin> Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> seems to have approached this view, although (as we shall show later) he never made mention of those Great Conjunctions. But in the second book of his <term>Apotelesmaton</term> <note>The original Greek title of Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*, meaning "Effects" or "Prognostications."</note>, he says that those of the Asians who tend toward the East and South worship Venus and Saturn because they are subject to the <gloss>Trigon of dry quality</gloss> <note>Also known as the Earth Triplicity: the zodiac signs of Virgo, Taurus, and Capricorn.</note>, over which he believes Saturn and Venus rule. Conversely, those who live between the South and the West have Venus and Mars for their deities, because they are subject to the humid triplicity, over which he places Mercury and Venus along with Mars.

<margin>No religion is subject to the conjunctions of the stars</margin> Truly, both opinions are refuted by the evidence of the facts and the outcomes themselves. For if any religion is born by the power of some Great Conjunction, that religion ought to be abolished when that power is abolished. Yet there is no conjunction of stars whose power can be imagined—even by astrologers—to last for as many years as the worship of idols, the Mosaic religion, and the Christian religion have endured. The world sat in the darkness of the cult of idols for approximately five thousand years. What conjunction, I ask—what "greatest year" of any star—claims for itself such a span of years? The rites and observations of the Mosaic law are still flourishing among the Hebrews today, and have already flourished for three thousand years or more. What constellation is so strong and so long-lasting that it does not permit a religion to be extinguished even after its empire has perished? The theologian will give the true causes for these things, consistent with his doctrine; the astrologer can give none from the heavens. If the variety of religions were derived from the heavens, we would see them vary daily and change more frequently. Even the astrologers, thinking this and gathering it from the principles of their own science, pre-defined terms for every religion; but since religions have transgressed those limits, the evidence of the facts shows they depend on something else.

He specifically critiques the theories of Ptolemy and Arabic astrologers regarding the celestial origins of regional religious practices.</summary>

Now, that opinion of Ptolemy—which thinks that just as various stars rule different places and nations, so too do they bring about various religious rites in those places—is even more thoroughly refuted by experience itself. For in those provinces lying between the East and the South, the same stars are present which presided over them in ancient times. Yet Venus and Saturn are no longer worshipped there as they once were. For why did these deities rule over them? Certainly, as Ptolemy himself writes, it was because the "terrestrial triplicity" <term>triplicity</term> <note>In astrology, a group of three zodiac signs associated with the same element; here, the "Earth" signs: Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn.</note> consisting of Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn is assigned to those regions, and Venus and Saturn rule that triplicity. Indeed, this is what he believed. But this partitioning of the world and its regions distributed under various triplicities is permanent, not temporary; therefore, the situation will always be the same as it once was.

<margin>Mockery of Ptolemy.</margin>

Why then, O Ptolemy, does the same religion not endure in those same places even today? Finally, let us conclude this entire dispute by asking Ptolemy himself: if, by the varying presidency of the stars, other nations once worshipped other stars, by the power and force of which star is it brought about that no stars are worshipped today in almost any region of the whole world?

### Chapter XI: Physical dispositions are not brought about by the heavens.

If all these things have been sufficiently refuted, there remains only the disposition of the body, about which an astrologer might be able to pronounce—if indeed he can do so regarding things which are brought about by the heaven. But the birth constellation cannot effect even this, since a child possesses both the habit and the form of the body which he carries with him while still in the womb, before he leaves the womb. Therefore, this must also be numbered among those things which we said in the fifth chapter cannot be predicted through the "nativity" <note>A horoscope or birth chart based on the exact moment of birth.</note> they use, because these things precede the birth. Why not, then, through the conception or the disposition of the seed? But the seed is not "made" at that moment. Therefore, the constellation under which the seed was made would instead have to be examined—but more on this later. If, therefore, the disposition of the body could be foreseen and pronounced, it would certainly be possible more from the hour of conception than from the hour of birth (from which it is in no way possible); but whether it is possible even from that hour will be examined in the following books.

Now, this demonstrates that astrologers err when they pronounce—from the hour of birth—whether the one being born will have a short or tall body, be fat or lean, strong or weak, maimed or whole, legitimate or monstrous. For he acquires all these conditions long before he is sent out into the public from his mother's womb, already formed and finished. Therefore, just as these things are not made by that constellation which they followed long ago, so they cannot be predicted from its observation by a mathematician <note>In this period, "mathematicus" (mathematician) was often a synonym for an astrologer.</note>. We have disputed regarding the time of conception elsewhere; for now, we want the reader to know that the greatest astrologers have thought that what pertains to the temperature <note>The "balance of humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determined health and temperament.</note> of the body depends on proximate causes and things lower than the heaven.

<margin>Haly</margin>

Thus, as Haly <note>Referring to Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer whose work was a standard textbook in Europe.</note> writes, they have requested that pardon be given to them if they should fall away from the truth in predicting the disposition of the body.

<margin>Epilogue</margin>

Let us therefore collect this entire dispute concerning the efficiency of the heaven in this way: if heaven is a "universal cause," the variety and distinction of particular things do not come from it. And even if we grant that there are powers in it that produce particular properties, they are nonetheless not of the kind that astrologers prophesy from the heaven. For it seems that by no reasoning can chance events be referred to natural causes; nor can things which are evil be referred to the best authors <note>The "best authors" refers to God and the celestial bodies, which were considered inherently good in the Aristotelian tradition.</note>; nor can things which proceed from reason and counsel be referred to principles acting by natural necessity; nor can incorporeal rays be referred to bodies; nor can things already past, or things far in the future, be referred to the present constellation; nor can things pertaining to others be referred to our own nativity. Finally, it is utterly absurd and most alien to all philosophy to seek the origin in the stars of things for which you see distinct, manifest, and sufficient causes among us: in the powers of inferior bodies, in the diversity of minds, in emotion, counsel, opportunity, and custom, and in the so varied gathering of things and causes flowing together from all sides. For the origin is not there, nor does the nature and condition of the things that happen or of the efficient heaven allow it to be there. Hence it happens (as with all philosophers whose study and labor is occupied in scrutinizing the causes of things) that when from medicine, or from ma...

# Chapter XII. The heavens cannot be a sign of something for which they are not the cause.

<margin>
Refutation.
The first reason.
</margin>
**B**ut someone will perhaps say: even if it is granted that these variations and events in human affairs are not *caused* by the stars, it does not immediately follow that they cannot be foreseen and predicted from the heavens. For indeed, even things that the stars do not cause at all, they can nevertheless signify and portend. For there are those who have held this opinion: that inferior things are not brought about by the power of the heavens (except in the general way that they affect all things), but that since they depend on their own immediate and proper causes, they are nonetheless indicated by the heavens before they happen. Thus, through the transit, station, and retreat of the planets, the future is known—just as birds, either by flying past or by standing still, signify the future by their feathers or their voice, without even knowing they do so. But in truth, neither have the distinguished astrologers themselves ever believed this, nor does any reason permit us to believe it. For whatever is a sign of something else by nature (and not by human institution) and is a physical body, it must either be the *cause* of the thing it signifies, or its *effect*, or it must be that both the sign and the thing signified proceed from the same common cause. If anyone thinks something should be added to this—as if different from what we have said—such as being necessarily and inseparably connected to the cause, he is greatly and far deceived. For such a connection and accompaniment cannot happen for any other reason than that the cause produces the sign from itself before it effects the other thing, or that whatever rouses the cause to action also rouses this sign at the same time; we concede that in this way both are referred back to a common cause. Come then, let us see which of these is more appropriate to the heavens, if the heavens signify the future. Certainly, the motions and arrangements of the heavens are not the *effects* of inferior things; and they [the astrologers] deny they are the *causes*. It remains then to say that the state and arrangement of the heavens, and that which is believed to be indicated by them, proceed from the same cause—just as a rainbow <note>original: "iris"</note> sometimes portends clear weather, not because it *makes* the clear weather, but because the cause of the rainbow is also the cause of the clear weather. But no physical cause will be found that is superior to the heavens and which, for that reason, brings about the arrangements of the heavens and inferior things at the same time.

<margin>
Divine minds are not the causes of inferior events without the action of the heavens.
First reason.
Second reason.
Third.
Fourth.
Thomas.
</margin>
Or will the remaining cause be incorporeal? For perhaps it will seem possible to say that human events are brought about by the divine minds themselves which revolve the heavenly bodies; and while they occur, they are indicated to us by the very state and position of the heavens they move, as if by certain nods of the head. Truly, whoever says this—which is indeed very close to the fables of the poets—how will he avoid the following absurdity: that those things are done by divine minds which men themselves cannot do without the guilt of a crime? For this would mean they urge and impel this man to homicide, that one to adultery, and another to theft. I pass over the fact that all philosophy finds it abominable that physical things should be produced by incorporeal causes without an intervening physical cause. Furthermore, why are those born at different hours born with a different fate, if it is not the position of the heavens (which varies by the hour), but the immovable Author of the heavens—who is always equal to Himself and His children—who is considered the author and cause of fate? Finally, as Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> argues: although the effects of the same cause indicate one another because they proceed from the same principle and in the same manner, the motion of the heavens and the arrangement of inferior bodies and things do not proceed from superior causes in the same way. For the former [the heavens] proceed in an immutable and necessary order, while the latter [human affairs] proceed in a variable order, falling into either side contingently—according to the nature, that is, of the things that are moved and governed. Divine principles do not change these natures but preserve them; otherwise, they would not be guiding nature, but destroying it. Therefore, the heavens cannot signify inferior things except insofar as a cause indicates its effect. Wherefore, those who, being conquered by reason, confess that the heaven is not the cause, but still contend it is a sign, do not understand their own words. This is what Thomas Aquinas—a man of the weightiest judgment who was not accustomed to asserting anything rashly—asserted in his *Theological Summa*.

<margin>Thomas</margin>
This could be said of comets, of "shooting stars" <note>original: "traiactionibus"</note>, and other things of this kind which happen in the heights: that having been stirred up by the stars which effect certain things, they do not cause what the cause is about to do, but signify it. This can in no way be said of the stars themselves, since...

<margin>The second major reason.</margin>
regarding the necessity of fate <term>fati necessitate</term> <note>The idea that all events are predetermined and unavoidable.</note>, whether they wish to or not, bring it in: for if the stars are the causes of inferior things, a reason can be grasped for why that which is being brought about by their influence might not be effected—either due to obstructing matter or a particular cause diverting the common influence elsewhere.
