If indeed it indicates all equally, there will be no remaining causes through which that which was demonstrated could be hindered from happening. Therefore, what was portended will necessarily happen. However, if we say 

<margin>That astrologers denied the necessity of fate.</margin>
this, we will oppose not only the truth (as we have demonstrated elsewhere), but also the astrologers themselves; since the Egyptians, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note>, and every most famous astrologer has always denied the necessity of fate. They declare this to be their opinion especially in the treatise on "questions" <term>interrogationibus</term> <note>Horary astrology, where a chart is cast for the moment a question is asked to find the answer.</note>. For they do not say every question is legitimate, but only those which proceed from an impulse of the mind moved from heaven. Since they concede that many questions are not of this kind—namely, those born from our own reason and counsel—they openly declare they do not admit the necessity of fate. Furthermore, if such necessity were introduced, all the utility of astrology perishes, which is placed chiefly in this: that we might be able to avoid foreseen evils and confirm or increase good things. Finally, if the stars are signs and not causes of inferior things, that part 

<margin>Fifth.</margin>
of astrology which is commonly called "elections" <term>electionibus</term> <note>The practice of choosing the most astrologically favorable time to begin an undertaking.</note> is removed beyond controversy; for in that practice, they seek celestial favor for the sake of *effecting* something, not the indications of signs for the sake of curiosity.

### Chapter XIII. Whether the stars are signs or causes, the part of astrology dealing with interrogations is null.

<margin>The foundation of astrological questions.</margin>
Whichever opinion the astrologers prefer—that is, whether they want the stars to be causes of inferior things, or only signs and not causes—that part which deals with questions [interrogations], and which they use most frequently, would necessarily be fundamentally removed. For the foundation of this part is that our minds are moved by a celestial constellation, at least from the "imaginary" part; and when the mind is instigated from there to the desire of knowing some thing, then if one consults an astrologer, from the configuration of the heaven at the hour of consultation, that which the inquirer desired to know is portended. For this reason, they claim the astrologer can give true answers to those asking about all things concerning which a question is made. Let us therefore ask of those who claim they can resolve every question: are the stars only signs of inferior things, or are they also causes that signify by *doing*? If they are signs only, then the impulse of our desire is not from the stars. But just as others who hold that opinion say other things happen by their own causes (even if indicated by the stars), so too the movement of desire would take its origin and cause not from a celestial constellation, but from the imaginary power itself, our own choice, the appetitive power of the mind, and those things which provoke the senses and the mind from without. If they respond that the stars are causes and that inferior things are signified by them just as an effect is demonstrated from its cause, in what way will they defend the idea that the configuration of the heaven appearing at the hour of consultation is the cause of those things about which the astrologer answers the inquirer? For since those things have either happened long ago, 

<margin>A very witty quibble.</margin>
or because they will never happen, they ought to have no cause. Truly, Mars will be in the west, which will not permit the truth to be answered by them. But if they can obtain from him that they may at least be allowed to hear...

<summary>Pico argues that if astrology is true, it implies a logical necessity that destroys free will—a conclusion even famous astrologers like Ptolemy tried to avoid. He specifically attacks "interrogations" and "elections," arguing that stars cannot logically be the cause of a person's sudden desire to ask a question.</summary>

...turned. I shall reply even to those who do not ask about these questions, which are truly many. It 
<margin>Whence this part of astrology was born</margin>
seemed to astrologers a small matter of glory for themselves—and what urged them more, for profit to be gained—if they only pronounced each person's fate from the time of their birth <term>genituræ</term> <note>A birth chart or natal horoscope.</note>, or from the annual revolution of their year. For to understand these things, it was necessary to visit them either only once in a lifetime, or only once each year. Yet since our curiosity desires to know many things daily, about which they were able to answer nothing, much authority for the art was lost among the unlearned <term>idiotas</term> <note>In this context, laypeople or those without specialized education.</note>, and much money was lost to the professors of the art. Hence they persuaded themselves, or at least others, that they could clearly foresee whatever was asked from the "hour of the interrogation" <term>hora quæstionis</term> <note>This refers to Horary Astrology, where a chart is drawn for the exact moment a client asks a question.</note>, provided that the one who questioned was moved by a "natural impulse" and did not come to the questioning by their own choice; thus, they beautifully cleared themselves of any infamy of falsehood. For if the response was refuted by the event itself, they would say it was not that the astrologer was untruthful, but that the question had not been "effective" <note>Meaning the client didn't ask with the proper spontaneous "spiritual" impulse required for the stars to align with the thought.</note>. If, however, the outcome matched the response, what was to stop them from claiming they held divine oracles on earth? With these arts and deceits, this "trifle-selling" <note>original: "nugiuendũ"</note> class of men mocks the unskilled, since nothing more dissonant with reason can be said or thought than what they have devised concerning this fallacy of interrogating. For even if I were to grant them that my desire to know about a person's absence (for example, how they are doing) comes from the heaven, what kind of logical sequence is it that the constitution of the heaven—at the exact hour I explain this desire of mine to the astrologer—must be such that it shows me the status of that absent person? Whence comes this correspondence or 
<margin>Response. Refutation.</margin>
alliance between both our desire and the thing we wish to know? But if they should perhaps respond that the same celestial power which effects that distant thing also "plucks" at our mind and thus warns us of the event as it happens: First, it would follow then that these desires only strike us at the very moment the event occurs. And yet, they think "effective" interrogations can be made about things that happened long ago, or will happen long after, or even things that will never happen at all.

Furthermore, if we were to say this, we should not look at the constitution of the heaven at the hour we question the astrologer, but at the first moment the craving to ask invaded us. Indeed, if it is the same or a similar constellation that both produces the event and stirs in us the desire to know it—which would be a far more "rational" way to be insane—it would be much more reasonable to say what the astrologers say must be observed is the time of the inquiry, not the time when the care of inquiring first solicited us. Then, as we were saying, if any kinship can exist between these things, if any consensus, it can only be that both the thing which happened and our desire can be referred to the same or a similar constellation. But the hour in which we ourselves consult the astrologer can vary for a thousand reasons, which might make us meet the astrologer later or sooner: such as if his house is far from us, if someone delays us on the road, and other things of this sort occurring by chance, which make the hour of the question (and therefore the configuration of the heaven from which he is to answer) one thing or another. But the astrologers care nothing for these things, for it has long been familiar to them to always say and feel those things which have no reason or firmness at all.

### Chapter XIV. Divine miracles are neither performed nor signified by the heaven, but miracles are indicated by miracles, just as natural things are indicated by natural things.

<margin><unclear>...</unclear></margin>
**B**ut would that they were only insane to this extent, and did not also think that divine miracles—which exceed the capacity of all nature—are performed by the natural rays of the higher bodies. For we have shown above that they are entangled in this error, declaring that divine religion is referred by them to the power of the stars: both that which God once promulgated through **Moses** to the Hebrew people, and that which **Christ** later promulgated to the world through the Apostles. Thus also they have ascribed that flood of the whole world under **Noah**, and other divine miracles of this sort which sacred history brings forth, all to their own constellations. In this matter they undoubtedly seem more insane than those who do not concede that these things ever happened; for he who believes they happened as they...

<margin>Utmost madness.</margin>
...such things as they narrate: and yet they say they were produced by natural causes: though no greater madness can be imagined than to think something done above nature was done by the powers of nature. Moreover, we have proved against the impious that there is a divine law from those things which exceed the powers of nature. 
<margin>Book against the impious.</margin>
Concerning the universal <term>Flood</term> <note>original: cathaclīsmo. From the Greek 'kataklysmos', referring here to the Great Flood of Noah.</note>, the same can easily be demonstrated: since nothing is more repugnant to nature than that she should devise her own destruction. Wherefore she would never inflict such an injury upon herself, from which she could not deliver herself by her own power. But if it could not happen in the natural course [of things]—that when the waters surpassed the peaks of all the mountains by fifteen cubits, <term>Noah</term> <note>original: Noe</note> with his family and every kind of animal, enclosed within a single <term>ark</term> <note>original: archā</note> for twelve months, should escape that shipwreck—then it was also not the purpose of nature to submerge the whole earth with a flood of waters for the destruction of all living things. And if these things were not done by the heavens, they cannot even be foreseen from the heavens. Since what the heaven does not do, it also does not signify, as we proved a little while ago. Although these things have their own specific reason why they are not portended by the stars, even if we were to grant that other things, which do not exceed the capacity of nature, are either done or indicated by the heaven. For as we have declared elsewhere, there is an order of things established by God in a natural course: and so enclosed within its own limits, and separated from those things which are done by divine power and will beyond nature, so that if all these [supernatural things] were removed, there would be nothing in the nature of things that is missing, and nothing that is superfluous. But the heaven, and whatever happens in the heaven in its common course, are among those things which are according to nature. Therefore, if the <term>motion of the stars</term> <note>original: syderum motus</note> or the arrangement which is owed to them by their natural condition signifies anything of the future, this significance and indication must be held and counted among natural things. But if we should say that some of these signs portend those things which will happen above nature, this absurdity follows: that if God were to leave nature to its own conditions and not do anything above it, nature itself would then be found false and lying, in which God would even have established something in vain and superfluously; since there would still be in the stars signs of future things, which nevertheless would not happen, because the things signified are matters beyond nature which we were supposing to be removed. The signs themselves are things according to nature: which, when supernatural things are removed, must be said to be neither removed nor deprived of any perfection due to them. Therefore, if God disposed from eternity to perform some <term>miracle</term> <note>original: miraculum</note>, he did not insert the indications of that miracle into natural things in such a way that this significance belonged to the very logic of nature; rather, he wished natural things to signify natural things, while he signified miracles by preceding miracles. <term>The Flood</term> <note>original: Cathaclīsmum</note>, which was to occur by a miracle of divine justice, was signified to the world by <term>Noah</term> <note>original: Noe</note>, who was divinely inspired and to be divinely saved. The leading of the Hebrews out of Egypt and the giving of the Law to them were attested by miracles performed through the divine rod by <term>Moses</term> <note>original: Mose</note>, rather than by the <term>astrologers</term> <note>original: astrologis</note> of the Egyptians. That the land of promise was to be subjected to the people of God, and the wonders God was about to perform in it above the laws of nature, was indicated not by any natural configuration of the heaven, but by the most rapid motion of the sun restrained by the hand of the Creator—not to mention the crossing of the <term>Jordan</term> <note>original: iordanem</note> on dry feet and the walls of the city destroyed by the sound of trumpets. The life of <term>Hezekiah</term> <note>original: Ezechiæ</note>, prolonged by divine power, was demonstrated not by the benign radiation of Jupiter running its spaces in the right order, but by the miracle of the sun moving backward. The prodigy of the Word made flesh and of the virgin’s <term>Childbirth</term> <note>original: Puerperii. Referring to the Nativity of Christ.</note> was announced when the oracles of minds divinely inspired beyond the nature of the mind proclaimed it; then a thousand prodigies were attested in the celestial and earthly bodies themselves, while that immense new star rose for the Lord; and again, when He was failing on the cross, the Sun failed while the Moon was full, contrary to the order of nature. By these signs, divine miracles are both demonstrated and confirmed, which can neither be performed by the natural state of things nor is it fitting for them to be indicated by it.

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.
<meta>image quality: high; catchword: ri. Is. n. nō</meta>

**N**ow since we have come to the mention of the star that pointed out the birth of Jesus, it would not be out of place to advise the reader not to suspect that this star favors the opinion of the astrologers. It is as if it were nothing other than a celestial constellation indicating the birth of a prophet, supposedly better known and investigated by those from the East because they were thought to be exceptionally skilled in celestial science. However, the very letter of the Gospel most clearly leads us away from this error; speaking of this star, it says: *And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood over where the child was.* No one except a madman would think this should be understood as referring to the stars or configurations of the heavens <note>Pico argues that because the star "stood over" a specific house, it must have been low in the atmosphere, unlike actual stars which are too distant to point to a single building.</note>. It was, therefore, a made and temporary star, not a permanent and natural one, created for this duty by the Creator so that the birth of the King of the Jews might be signified by it. Perhaps the Magi understood it in the same way they were later warned in a dream to avoid Herod and return to their country by another way. 

But we must likewise take care not to be disturbed by certain expressions in the Scriptures, as when we read in <margin>Paul</margin> that the Son of God was sent in the "fullness of time," or in the Gospel when the Lord says: *Now is your hour and the power of darkness,* and elsewhere: *My hour has not yet come.* For a superstitious person will think that constellations of hours and times are being signified. But you should ask him: When a person is hungry, does he think it is the "time for eating" regardless of whatever the celestial arrangement might be at that time? Or when the body has worked enough, the "time for care"? Or when one has slept enough, the "time for waking"? If he says all these things have their own time, it is not because of a constellation of time, but according to the nature of the thing itself which is happening, and according to the occasion and opportunity for doing it. 

So it is likewise for other things which God does above nature, and which men do by their own freedom. Although they require no constellations to occur, it is nonetheless necessary that they happen at some time, and more fittingly or conveniently at this time rather than that. It was fitting for the Son of God to be sent at the time he was sent; before then, it was not fitting. The cause is not in the sky, but in the purpose of God and the requirement of things, about which theologians write much, insofar as they were permitted to penetrate the secret of the divine counsel through the indications of Scripture. Likewise, it was fitting that after he was born, he was not killed immediately, but at the time it was expedient, he permitted himself to be in the hands of the impious, and that was the "hour and the power of darkness." 

The same is to be understood in other matters, which is clearly declared to us from a single passage in the Book of Genesis. There, when God promises the "land of promise"—so called from the event—to Abraham, He says: *Know for certain that your descendants will be strangers in a land not their own, where they will be afflicted for four hundred years, but in the fourth generation they shall return here.* If the writing had ended there, the astrologer might insultingly claim that the divine promise could not be fulfilled until that span of years had passed and a certain disposition of the sky was reached that would produce that outcome. But see what the prophet adds from the person of God: *For the iniquities of the <term>Amorites</term> <note>original: Amorreis. An ancient Semitic people; Pico uses them here as an example of human behavior, not stars, dictating the timing of events.</note> are not yet complete up to the present time.* 

Look, therefore, at what he was waiting for: not a <term>conjunction</term> <note>original: copulatiõ. In astrology, the meeting of two planets in the same degree of the zodiac.</note> of Jupiter and Saturn, or some other stellar constellation, but the "fullness of iniquity" in the Amorites. Through this, divine justice—by whose laws human affairs are governed, and not by fatal necessity—would both justly expel them and introduce the seed of faithful Abraham there.

### Chapter XVI. That things which exceed the powers of nature, even as far as they contain something natural in themselves, cannot be signified by the heaven.

<margin>
What happens to be done.
Girolamo [Benivieni] by Pico.
Response.
The error of [Pierre] d'Ailly.
</margin>
**I**t has now been sufficiently demonstrated, unless I am mistaken, that divine miracles are neither caused nor signified by the heaven. As for what pertains to their efficiency, the very words indicate this, and it needs no proof. However, <term>Girolamo Benivieni</term> <note>original: Hieronimus Beniuenius. A Florentine poet and close friend of Pico who shared his interest in Platonic philosophy.</note>, a man of sharp and penetrating intellect, recently asked: since in those things which happen above nature there is sometimes something natural, could they be signified by the stars from that aspect? For example, if no constellation could indicate the incarnation of God, could a "lawgiver" man and one about to promulgate good laws be shown? But these things can no more be signified by the stars in this way, nor in the way that <term>Pierre d'Ailly</term> <note>original: Alliacensis. A famous 14th-century cardinal and scholar who attempted to reconcile astrology with theology.</note> thought...

<summary>Pico argues that the Star of Bethlehem was a temporary, divine creation rather than a natural astronomical event, and asserts that biblical references to "the fullness of time" refer to moral and divine readiness rather than astrological alignments. He specifically cites the delay in Abraham's inheritance as being due to the "iniquity of the Amorites" rather than planetary positions.</summary>

<page-num>195</page-num>
<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

...d'Ailly <note>original: "Is.n." referring to Petrus de Alliaco, or Pierre d'Ailly, a 14th-century cardinal who argued that astrology could be compatible with Christianity.</note> thought that piety could be defended in no other way than if the causes of these miraculous and divine things were sought in the stars. He argued that these depend on heaven not insofar as they are above nature, but insofar as there is something natural in them. But this says nothing at all: just as it is meaningless to say a man is made by a certain constellation, yet his rational nature is not made by it. For if the star does not produce that which is rational in a man, there is no reason why it should be said to produce a man any more than a lion. If, therefore, you take from divine miracles that which is proper to them—leaving only those qualities they share with countless other things—there is no reason to seek the cause of a singular effect so studiously in the heavens. 

Indeed, those who investigate the birth of Jesus do not strive to know why he was in the womb for nine months like other men, or why he was in good physical health, or had long hair, or was poor, or a Jew; for all the lives of mortals abound with these conditions. Rather, they seek the cause in the stars for those things which were primary and singular in Him, believing those causes to also be primary and singular. Yet those things are already works of God above nature, not of the heavens: that He was born of a virgin; that He was both God and man; that He was Lord in presence and a pilgrim in the flesh; the performer of miraculous works; the rightful Lord of the world; the judge of the living and the dead; the author and dispenser of divine grace; the expeller of idolatry; the safe-triumpher over demons; the author of virtues; the expeller of vices; the peace of the world; and the manifester of truth. If you do not seek these things, you seek nothing; if you do seek them in the stars, you seek impiously.

<margin>
Reduction to an impossibility.
</margin>
Therefore, the refuge prepared by d’Ailly for the astrologers—that they might say divine miracles are performed by heaven, but not *insofar as* they are miracles—is no refuge at all. Such things cannot even be "signified" by the stars for that reason (as our friend Jerome <note>Likely referring to Girolamo Savonarola, Pico’s contemporary and spiritual mentor, rather than St. Jerome.</note> used to ask of us). For if the order of things that come from God above nature were removed, these "signs" in the heaven would remain (as we said above), stretching toward those effects in some part, yet the effect itself would no longer exist. Those signs would therefore be vain and deceptive—and it was demonstrated above that nothing in the celestial nature is of such a kind.

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK FIVE BEGINS.

## Chapter One. That the decrees of astrologers regarding great conjunctions are profitably refuted: and how deceitful those have been found who wished to judge the great changes of lower things through them.

<margin>
The heretical opinion of the astrologers.
</margin>
<margin>
That the trifles of the astrologers are impossible.
</margin>
<margin>
A refutation by reasons and just experience.
</margin>
**B**ut the fallacy of the astrologers leads many away from this truth, persuading the unlearned that there has never been a change of laws, no arrival of prophets, nor any admirable event in human affairs that a "Great Conjunction" <term>Great Conjunction (the meeting of Saturn and Jupiter, occurring roughly every 20 years, which astrologers believed signaled major historical and religious shifts)</term> of the superior stars—especially Saturn and Jupiter—did not precede. Regarding this matter, they discourse in their tables as if about a certain and confessed truth, whether in person or before their more ignorant followers. Running through many thousands of years, they argue: this constellation caused the Flood; this one brought forth Moses; that one preceded the arrival of Jesus; and this one the law of Muhammad. There is almost no one who is not moved by this, and who is not forced either to descend into their science or at least to doubt. 

Therefore, since this profession attacks religion most strongly in this part, I wish to encounter this pestilence before I pull up the very foundations of the whole art. For the astrologers err in this place to such an extent that even if they were right in everything else, they could not be defended here. This is not only because they predict things which it is doubtful are subject to heaven, but because the very rules they use in predicting contain the most manifest errors in both history and astrology. Before I show this by logic, experience itself can make it certain to those who may not see the logic as clearly: for all who have wished to divine anything from these constellations regarding the change or success of sects and laws have been found to be false and liars. In olden times, when the faith of Christ began to sprout, the mathematicians <note>In this context, "mathematicians" refers to astrologers.</note> predicted it would not last more than [365] years...

-># DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

<margin>Now the year 1518 is currently passing <note>This marginal note was likely added by a later reader or editor, as Pico died in 1494.</note></margin> Now, however, they said it <note>The "it" refers to the law of Muhammad/Islam mentioned on the previous page.</note> would last; but from its beginning, the 1494th year has already passed. Albumasar <note>original: "Albumasar," the Latinized name of the Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), whose works were fundamental to medieval European astrology.</note>, either the author or the inventor of this error, said this same law—that is, our first law—would remain for 1,460 years. He claimed these were the "greatest solar years." Those years have passed, yet the law itself did not pass; for indeed, heaven and earth shall pass away, but the words of the Lord shall not pass away. Nor did he predict more truly concerning his own law, that of Muhammad.

<margin>The error of Abraham</margin> Abraham the Jew <note>original: "Abraā iudæus," referring to Abraham ibn Ezra, a renowned 12th-century scholar and astrologer.</note> said, based on astrological observation, that their Messiah would come in the year of Christ 1464; he claimed that the position of the stars under which Moses once led the people out of Egypt and gave them the law would then return for the first time. I was born in the year immediately preceding that one <note>Pico was born in 1463.</note>, and now that I am in my thirtieth year, I have learned by experience the falsehood of that prediction. 

<margin>The error of Arnaldus</margin> Arnaldus the Spaniard <note>original: "Arnaldus Hispānus," likely referring to the famous physician and scholar Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), who was known for his prophetic and alchemical interests.</note>, a noble physician but perhaps too inclined toward superstitions, threatened us with the arrival of the Antichrist in the year of grace 1345, based on astrological vanity and many other added reasons. From that time, more than 148 years have already flowed by, and no Antichrist has appeared yet, except for the many of the kind that existed in the time of the Apostles. 

<margin>The error of d'Ailly and the astrologers of his time</margin> Whenever younger men announced the arrival of a false prophet based on some conjunction of the superior planets, especially from that conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in Scorpio twelve years ago, no false prophet has yet appeared to the world besides themselves. Even Pierre d'Ailly <note>original: "Alliacenſis."</note> writes that in the year the General Council of Constance <note>The Council of Constance (1414–1418) ended the Western Schism, which had seen multiple claimants to the papacy.</note> was celebrated, the astrologers predicted there would be no peace in the Church; instead, they claimed the destruction of religion and dissensions within it were signaled by Jupiter being retrograde in the first house in the chart of the year. And yet, that great schism—the greatest and longest the Church ever saw, which had been confirmed for forty years—was finally extinguished in that very year, and the customary peace and tranquility were restored to the Church. This surely could have moved d'Ailly himself not to place any further faith in such vanity; for he, perhaps persuaded by them, feared that the schism would soon after bring us the Antichrist. There were other predictions of these men concerning laws and sects that were subsequently refuted by the actual event, but I think these suffice, as there are no others in that art of such great authority as these whom we have mentioned, whose predictions we have shown to be refuted by experience itself. Now let us descend to the reasons.

## Chapter II: By what ways astrologers judge greater matters; and the rejection of great orbits.

<margin>The ways in which astrologers especially strive for the investigation of things</margin> **A**strologers usually investigate great matters and the mutations of lower things through four main ways via the superior planets: especially through Jupiter and Saturn when they are together, which they call a <term>Great Conjunction</term> <note>A significant alignment of Jupiter and Saturn that occurs every 20 years, believed by astrologers to signal major historical shifts.</note>; through great orbits; through Saturnian revolutions; and through the access and recess <note>The "access and recess" refers to the theory of "trepidation," a mistaken medieval belief that the precession of the equinoxes oscillated back and forth.</note> of the eighth sphere. We shall show all these ways to be irrational, false, and impassable; from this, we shall not only achieve what we first sought here—that what they publish regarding religion and laws with such temerity is proven false—but also every judgment regarding the great changes of the world will be weakened.

<margin>The opinion of astrologers regarding great orbits</margin> I shall begin from the refutation of the <term>Great Orbits</term> and the revolutions they call Saturnian. Once these are rejected, because they provide less support, the whole disputation of the present book may then range freely against the "Great Conjunctions." They imagine that each of the planets, and likewise each of the signs of the world, holds power for 360 years. When these are finished, they say a new <term>Great Orbit</term> begins, which is governed both by the planet next to the previous one and the sign that follows the previous sign in order. Thus, whatever is the nature of the ruling sign and star, such things occur in that span of years; and when a new orbit begins, many things in the lower world are also renewed and changed according to the nature of the ruler, always regulating our condition. 

<margin>Under which orbit we live according to the astrologer Aoniar</margin> Then, if anyone asks them where or in what orbit we live now—that is, under which ruler—they answer: under Leo and the Moon. They prove it thus: for Aoniar <note>original: "Aoniar," possibly a corruption of an Arabic name like Abū Ma'shar (Albumasar) or another medieval source.</note> writes in his *Book of Nativities* that the new Great Orbit began at the time of that conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn by which they claim the Great Flood was signified. Indeed, that preceded...

...preceded the cataclysm <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note> by 279 years, as he says. Aoniar <note>Likely referring to a specific chronological system or section within Albumasar’s work.</note> claims that Saturn ruled over this cycle among the planets, and Cancer among the zodiac signs—which Albumasar also states in the first book of his *Great Conjunctions*, first difference. Therefore, laying these down as the foundation of their entire calculation, they conclude from the number of years he provided that our Lord Jesus was born when the 141st year of that cycle was turning. This cycle was the fifteenth since the one we mentioned during which the Flood occurred; it is ruled by Leo among the signs and the Moon among the planets, and is set to end in the year of grace 1659. This is the opinion of all astrologers. You will not see anyone making mention of the "Great Orbs" <term>Great Orbs: A cycle of 360 years (corresponding to the 360 degrees of the zodiac) used by medieval astrologers to track historical ages.</term> in their public annual predictions who does not appoint Leo and the Moon as the rulers and governors of the world.

I could object here to how flimsy a conjecture moves them to call a space of as many years as there are parts of the heavens <note>360 degrees/years.</note> a "Great Orb," and that there is no reason why the governing power of a single planet should be said to last through so many years—especially an inferior planet <note>The Moon, being closest to Earth in the Ptolemaic system.</note>. Furthermore, no such thing was ever devised by Ptolemy or any of the ancients, but it is a fiction of the Arabs and the moderns. But setting these things aside, let us first press them with necessary reasons which they cannot avoid if they wish to stand by their own principles and not renounce their dogma. 

<margin>Albumasar</margin>
Let them tell me then: if these Great Orbs are to be established, did they mark the beginning of a new cycle at the very first constitution of the world (upon which everyone agrees), or did they not? If they say they did not, what could they say that is more absurd? If they say they did, I shall now dismantle whatever they determined above regarding the Great Orbs through mathematical deduction, showing it is impossible for what they were saying to be true if the beginning of the new cycle started with the constitution of the world. 

<margin>Reasons: First, Second, Third.</margin>
For Albumasar, whose authority they chiefly lean upon, counts 2,228 whole years from the beginning of the world to the Flood. 

<margin>Albumasar</margin>
<margin>Eusebius</margin>
Granted, the calculation of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a Christian historian whose "Chronicle" set the standard for biblical dates.</note> exceeds this number by sixteen years, but it makes no difference whether we use one or the other; since we are disputing with the astrologers, let us use their own opinions most of all. Let it be established, then, that the number of years from Adam to the Flood according to the opinion of Albumasar (against whom we dispute) is clear: from that conjunction which they say pre-signified the Flood—and with which a new cycle simultaneously began—there remained 1,947 years back to the creation of the world, since the conjunction itself preceded the Flood by 279 years, as we were saying. 

Let us therefore divide that number <note>1,947 years.</note> by the number of the Great Orb—that is, by 360 parts. It will be clear that five whole Great Orbs are produced from it, and then a remainder of 147 undivided years. Therefore, it is necessary to place the beginning of a Great Orb in the year of the world 1,408 <note>Pico is pointing out a mathematical inconsistency: if the cycles started at creation and lasted 360 years, they should align perfectly. The remainder proves the cycles are arbitrary.</note>. If this number of years is part of another preceding cycle, it will necessarily have to be said that 213 years of the cycle passed before there were any years at all—that is, before the very beginnings of the world itself. Nothing could be more delirious than this! 

<margin>How delirious the astrologers are.</margin>
But certainly, there is nothing more thoughtless than this class of men; nothing more inclined by nature or profession toward lying and deceiving. They invent something for themselves so they may cherish their dogma and perform tricks for the unskilled—which is a mark of their malice and vanity. But it always happens by the power of truth that something follows which is either false, entirely impossible, or repugnant to their own sayings and dogmas. Paying the least attention to this, they both perform and spread these things, being equally forgetful and lying—which is a vice of ignorance and sluggishness. 

<margin>The vanity of the beginning of the world's constitution.</margin>
An example is at hand in this matter we are discussing. To persuade whoever they could that the Great Flood of the world was brought about by the heavens, they added a new cycle starting with it, based on a childish fiction of a "Great Conjunction." 

<margin>How delirious.</margin>
And so that nothing should be lacking from the fallacy, they put Saturn and Cancer in charge of that cycle—one of which is a planet and the other a sign regarded as the authors of moisture and cold. And this indeed, as I said, is due to their malice and vanity. But their stupidity, sluggishness, and ignorance also appear...

...they did not see what follows: namely, that since the novelty of the world <note>The beginning of creation.</note> would not have the beginnings of a new cycle, then if Saturn and Cancer presided over that [first] cycle, we would necessarily conclude that Mars and Aquarius presided over the very first whole cycle. They will never be able to defend by any reason why an impious beginning of the world should be inaugurated by these. For if they said this of the Moon, they might offer some reason, as she is closest to the Earth; if from Saturn, for the eminence of his sphere; if from the Sun, for the power of his virtue; if from Jupiter or Venus, for the beneficence of their nature. But in Mars they find nothing why he should deserve the primary rudders of the world. Likewise, there is nothing in Aquarius, since it possesses no initial prerogative. Yet they think both Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn have such status. But why do we wander through so many points? One may see plainly and clearly from this how 

<margin>How lying and forgetful they are</margin>
lying and forgetful they are at the same time. For they say (as we have shown) that Cancer and Saturn presided over that cycle before the event of the Flood, because this confirms their dogma that a great inundation of water is considered to be brought about by a cold and moist planet. <margin>Haly Abenragel. Albumasar.</margin>
planet of the world was the Sun, and the sign was Aries. For this is what Haly Abenragel <note>A 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> writes, and even Albumasar <note>A famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> himself in the first book of his *Great Conjunctions*. And yet these things fight against each other so much that they cannot both be true at the same time. For since there are five whole "Great Orbs" or six imperfect ones from the beginning of the world up to the Flood—whether we count five or rather six—it is impossible that if Aries rules the first cycle, Cancer should rule the fifth or sixth. Or if the solar star ruled the first cycle, that Saturn should fall to the cycle of the Flood. For if Aries and the Sun presided over the first, then Taurus and Venus presided over the second; Gemini and Mercury over the third; the Moon with Cancer over the fourth; but neither in the fifth nor the sixth do Cancer and Saturn appear. Rather, in the fifth, Saturn would be with Leo, and in the sixth, Jupiter with Virgo. Why then do they not blush to leave these writings to posterity—manifest testimonies of such great ignorance or stupidity?

<margin>Another opinion of Oclaton.</margin>
But the authors of astrology are almost always of this character. Thus a certain Oclaton <note>Likely a reference to an obscure or corrupted name of an astrological author in Pico's sources.</note>, inventing other "Great Orbs" for himself, wished to bring it about that both the constitution of the world and the birth of Jesus should have the beginnings of a new cycle, and that the same sign—that is, Aries, the head of the signs—should preside over both. When this would not otherwise work for him, he said that 4,320 years ought to be counted from Adam to Christ. If we count that many, it would clearly be exactly what he wanted. But no history accepts that number; it differs from Greek and Latin writers by nearly 900 years, from the Hebrews by 500, and from other astronomers by even 1,100. But he preferred that what was real should not exist, rather than renounce his own beautiful invention.

<margin>See a most beautiful Aristotelian example.</margin>
They are just like those ancients mentioned by Aristotle <note>Referring to the Pythagoreans in the *Metaphysics*.</note> who, having once established that all things were distributed by the number ten, but finding no more than nine spheres in the universe, said there must necessarily be another Earth <note>original: "antichthon" or Counter-Earth.</note> so that their number ten might be filled. They do this in a certain emulation of Divine Wisdom—which does not form itself to things, but forms things to its own truth. Finally, it must not be overlooked that even if these "Great Orbs" were something necessary (which the astrologers claim), they must be false by the astrologers' own logic, since they err greatly in calculating them. For they think that this cycle which is now revolving—of which they want the 195th year to be passing—is the 19th cycle from the first, and the 14th from the one under which the Flood occurred. By this reasoning, they appoint Leo and the Moon to preside over it. But this cannot be unless we count 6,838 years from the beginning of the world to our time. This exceeds the true reckoning of years by more than 1,400 years, as we have proved in our treatise *On the True Calculation of Times*. Even if we follow other histories—namely, the Latins who compute more years—we still find fewer than those these men scrape together to complete their cycles, since no history exceeds or even approaches that number of 6,700. Yet they are caught adding nearly 140 years just to defend the position of their cycles—a position which I think is sufficiently refuted even to the unlearned.

BOOK FIVE

## Chapter II: That the Saturnian revolutions of Abu Ma’shar are opposed both to history and to reason.

**I**t remains to speak of Saturnian revolutions. It appears that **Abu Ma’shar** alone devised these for himself; and after him, others have not made much use of them. But let us see what they are, what moved Abu Ma’shar to propose them, and how much he has wandered from the truth in these—as he is accustomed to do in other matters. When Saturn has completed ten periods <note>A Saturnian "period" or revolution is the time it takes for Saturn to orbit the sun, roughly 29.5 years. Ten of these equal approximately 300 years.</note>, which are completed in three hundred and six years, he thinks that great things happen in human affairs. He was moved by this conjecture because, in his other histories, he occasionally found that some significant event occurred after this number of years. From this, he founded the dogma that ten revolutions of Saturn bring about a change in the lower kingdoms. 

Yet, by this very historical conjecture, it is first evident how much he has erred. For he says that three hundred years after Alexander, Aielasor <note>Likely a corruption of a name from Abu Ma'shar's Arabic sources, possibly referring to a Seleucid or Persian figure.</note>, the son of Bel Anniab, appeared and crushed the laws; and after another equal number of years, Jesus, our leader, appeared. By this reasoning, there would be six hundred years from Alexander to Jesus. It is established beyond all controversy that this is entirely false; for there is no history that counts four hundred years from Christ back to Alexander, and **Alfonso** <note>Referring to the Alfonsine Tables, the most influential astronomical tables in the Middle Ages, commissioned by King Alfonso X of Castile.</note> himself, in his astronomical tables, counts no more than three hundred and eleven. Let us see, then, upon what foundations these primary authors of astrology support their marvelous dogmas. 

The same Abu Ma'shar says that ten Saturnian revolutions after Jesus, a law arose that is midway between the Nazarenes <note>Christians.</note> and the pagans (for so he calls the gentiles). But we certainly know that no law arose after Christ before Muhammad; I believe these Arabs meant the sect of the **Manichaeans**, whom they also call *Minin* <note>original: "Minin". A Hebrew term for heretics or sectarians used in the Talmud.</note> among the Talmudists. This heresy gained strength not only after ten revolutions were completed, but even before the ninth revolution of Saturn was finished. 

If he had brought all these things from a faithful history, that would still be no reason to make a dogma of the idea that ten periods of Saturn produce such things. Otherwise, I could devise a thousand dogmas of this kind for myself. For even the Hebrews say the first Temple built by Solomon lasted for four hundred or a few more years; then they say that from the time it was rebuilt under Darius, no more than ten years passed <note>Pico is likely being sarcastic here regarding the Hebrew calendar's "Short Chronology," or referring to specific cycles.</note>—that is, four hundred and ten years; from its desolation, they devised their laws in Babylon for the same number of years. Should we then make a dogma from this: that every fourteenth revolution of Saturn always brings a great change to the Saturnian race of the Jews? We would be saying something more probable than Abu Ma'shar, who chooses a number that simply pleases him. I would also like to ask him: from where 

<margin>The beginning.</margin>
do these revolutions take their start? And under what part of the sky will he begin the calculation of this period? I ask him to provide a reason why he placed that point before others. But we must not labor any longer in refuting these trifles, especially since they seem to have satisfied few other astrologers besides Abu Ma'shar. 
<margin>Pierre d'Ailly.</margin>
Indeed, even **Pierre d'Ailly**—who had made great use of these in his treatise *On the Concordance of History and Astrology*—confessed in his *Elucidarium* that they had no foundation, reversing his pen and gnawing away at a great part of his own book with a sharp critique.

**I**t remains to speak of the "accession and recession" <note>The theory of trepidation, an erroneous model of the movement of the stars.</note> of the eighth sphere and the ninth sphere; it remains to speak of the Great Conjunctions. But let the former be examined in the following book. Now let us turn to the Great Conjunctions. It will be worth the effort to first bring forward what they themselves think about these, so that what we bring in refutation may be more easily understood. This narration itself will not be without the utility of refutation, for 
<margin>Opinions on Conjunctions.</margin>
we shall see them disagreeing so much on these matters that it is not yet even settled among astrologers which is the "greatest" conjunction, which is the "greater," and which is the "middle." In this matter, the controversy is not only about the name; from this arises a great diversity of predictions, as some bid us expect events from the greatest, others from the middle, and others from the minor conjunctions. 

The common opinion which **Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and **Leopold** <note>Leopold of Austria, a 13th-century astronomer.</note> pass down, and Abu Ma'shar before 
<margin>Great Conjunction.</margin>
them, is of this kind: a "Great" conjunction occurs whenever Jupiter and Saturn join together, which happens always after twenty years. A "Greater" one occurs when the meeting happens during a migration from one triplicity <note>In astrology, a "triplicity" is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note> into another, at the thresholds of the new triplicity; and this happens...

### Chapter V: Planets joined in great conjunctions are no more powerful than when separated: and these great conjunctions are a new invention born from a bad understanding of Ptolemy.

<margin>First reason</margin>
**I**n the first place, I would like to learn from them why they think Jupiter and Saturn do greater things when they are together than when they are separate, where each one pursues and exercises its own powers. A mixture of the rays of various natures does indeed create something new that a discrete and private influence would not; but why it should create something *greater*, we cannot find a reason. Rather, we are inclined to believe that something *less* occurs than if each of the planets acted separately. This is possible: for if the planets that come together possessed the same property and had the power to produce the same effects, then surely by the addition of a double ray, the effect would also be doubled. But since they are of contrary and repugnant natures—such as Jupiter and Saturn—one necessarily hinders the other. While they mutually restrain and bind their powers by the diversity of the mixture, it happens that we can expect nothing from them except mediocrity, just as all things are which result from a mixture of extremes. Just as they themselves are accustomed to say when Saturn and Mars are together: although both are harmful and both are <term>malefic</term> <note>In astrology, "malefic" planets (traditionally Saturn and Mars) are thought to have a negative or destructive influence.</note>, because they nevertheless have a different power of harming, no greater or more admirable evil arises from their conjunction; rather, the powers of one are broken and weakened by the other. Thus, neither can harm while each strives to harm according to the condition of its own nature. Therefore, it is not fully certain that if the events of lower things are subject to the heavens, greater and more durable things happen when the superior stars are joined than when one of them, perhaps with the others weakened, acquires more strength and power than usual.

<margin>Second reason</margin>
Even if we granted that joined planets do more than separate ones toward the great changes of this world, we would still not grant that this should be referred to the conjunction of Jupiter, Saturn, or Mars. Instead, we shall prove, both by reason and by the authority of the greatest astrologers, that other stars hold the primary power in these matters. For none of the ancients ever judged the universal changes of the world by these which these men call "Great Conjunctions." Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> says nothing of these, though he was a most curious investigator of astrology; nothing is said by Paulus <note>Paulus Alexandrinus (4th century).</note>, nothing by Hephaestio <note>Hephaestio of Thebes (5th century).</note>, nothing by Theophilus <note>Theophilus of Edessa (8th century).</note>, nothing by Astaxarchus <note>Possibly a corruption of Aristarchus or a similar name.</note>, and nothing by Ptolemy himself, whose testimony here will be sufficient for us to use against them as a witness they know well. For he, in the second book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, teaching by what way general and world changes are foreseen, refers them all solely to the eclipses of the Sun and Moon. Nor can anything more reasonable be said; for universal and great effects ought to be referred to those causes which are most universal and effective. It is admitted by all that among the planets, there are only two of universal efficiency: the Sun and the Moon (whose light is nothing other than the light of the Sun brought to the earth through her as if through a mirror, so to speak). Therefore, if any celestial virtue ought to be considered the origin and cause of universal and great effects, none should be considered such more than these stars. For as to what Messahala says—that great things are done by Jupiter and Saturn because they are slower...

Having previously defined what these conjunctions are, he now moves to debunk the claim that the great astronomer Ptolemy supported these theories, arguing instead that astrologers have misinterpreted and mistranslated Ptolemy's works.</meta>

<header>BOOK FIVE</header>

# BOOK FIVE

movement proves rather than denies what he affirms: since it is the unanimous opinion of all that a faster motion is owed to a more noble and powerful body. Wherefore, let those who defend the rank and dignity of the superior stars not think them weaker because they are restored to their place more slowly. They are accustomed to prove, from the proportion of the orbits they encompass, that these stars are much faster than many others, even if they appear slower due to the length of their periods. But I know what they will say: that this was omitted by Ptolemy in his book *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "Apotelesmaton," better known today as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note> lest he betray the mystery. This is indeed what Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy.</note>, his interpreter, writes. 
<margin>Ptolemy's excuse</margin>
But in the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms formerly attributed to Ptolemy, though now considered to be by a later author.</note> (as they call it), he is said to have given many proofs of this matter. In the fiftieth "word" <note>In the *Centiloquium*, the aphorisms are referred to as *verba* (words).</note> of that book, he commands that we should not forget the conjunctions of the planets, in which there is great efficacy. And in the fifty-eighth "word," as well as the sixty-fourth, he warns us of the same things, handing down great precepts about them, and distinguishing between the **greatest**, **middle**, and **smallest** conjunction.

I, however, would wish for nothing more than for them to respond; so that from this it might become clear to everyone that whatever of their dogmas seem greater and more admirable have sprouted either from vain opinions or from a false understanding of ancient authors. 
<margin>Confutation</margin>
For as to their claim that Ptolemy remained silent about this in the *Apotelesmaton* lest he betray the mystery, I am so far from denying it that I do not even believe it was betrayed by him in the *Centiloquium*. In that work, he certainly spoke no more of those conjunctions than he did of the death of Priam or the Trojan War. We shall subsequently reveal how they have perverted many of that author's pronouncements, and how many successive errors have been propagated from a single one. 

The fiftieth "word" of Ptolemy, as it stands in their common edition, is this: *Do not forget that there are one hundred and twenty conjunctions among the wandering stars; for in them is the greatest knowledge of the things that happen in this world, regarding their increase and decrease.* In the Greek, however, it is this: *Lest we overlook the one hundred and nineteen conjunctions. For in these is placed the conjunction of those things that happen in the world, both of generation and corruption.* 

First, the "barbaric" interpretation <note>Pico uses "barbaric" to refer to the medieval Arabic-to-Latin translations, which Renaissance humanists considered linguistically inferior to original Greek sources.</note> attributes more to these conjunctions than Ptolemy does. In his view, it is not the case that there is "no greater knowledge" of world events than that which comes from them. Furthermore, setting that aside, the meaning of the pronouncement is simply that we should not look only at the individual property of each star. 
<margin>Ptolemy's opinion</margin>
Rather, we should know that various and diverse powers for effecting things arise from their conjunction—which no one denies, and which must be conceded by all astrologers. But as to which are the most important, Ptolemy certainly did not say that the conjunctions of the superior stars are responsible for all the greatest internal changes. Rather, if his words are correctly read and understood, they will indicate to us the opposite opinion. For he did not say there were one hundred and twenty (as is commonly read) of these conjunctions, but only one hundred and nineteen. 
<margin>Correction of a passage in Ptolemy's *Apotelesmaton*</margin>
The reason is that he does not count the conjunction of the Sun and Moon among these; because that conjunction holds such peculiar privileges and singular prerogatives in great and universal changes, he groups all the others together in a mass and order, as if none among them surpassed the others by any singular condition. The "barbaric" expositors, not noticing this and thinking it a scribal error, added the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, believing it should read "one hundred and twenty" instead of "one hundred and nineteen," which all the Greek manuscripts have. Thus, not content with a depravation of the sense, they also corrupted the integrity of the text itself.

Let us pass to other matters. Ptolemy writes in the fifty-eighth "word" in this manner: *The place of the conjunction, in which place the degree of the ascendant is in the ear of grain <note>Refers to the star Spica in the constellation Virgo.</note>...* and so forth. And the sixty-fourth "word" is of this kind: *In the smallest conjunction is the difference of the middle conjunction, and in the middle, the difference of the greatest conjunction.* 
<margin>Bad understanding of words 58 and 64</margin>
The Arabs and Latins think that in both places, Ptolemy's "conjunction" refers to the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter. But no one would be so deceived if they had ever read the Greek authors of astrology, and especially Ptolemy, with their eyes open. For what we call a **conjunction**, in Greek is <term>synodus</term> <note>σύνοδος (synodos): literally a "meeting" or "coming together."</note>. When this word is uttered on its own, it is understood as the coupling of the Sun and Moon, unless it is specified whose conjunction it might be—such as of Venus and Mercury, or Jupiter and Saturn, and other planets. Therefore, when in both pronouncements the word <term>synodus</term> is used absolutely...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s detailed critique of the "Centiloquium" (the hundred aphorisms traditionally but falsely attributed to Ptolemy). Pico is systematically dismantling the astrological interpretation of these aphorisms, specifically regarding the "conjunctions" of planets, arguing that the author was actually discussing the cycles of the Sun and Moon.</meta>

->## DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

<margin>The sense of the fifty-eighth aphorism</margin>
<unclear>He said</unclear> <note>original: "Dixit"; the text likely begins with this standard formula for an aphorism.</note> Ptolemy, adding nothing further, clearly shows—at least to those who are not entirely ignorant of Greek reading—that he is speaking of the conjunction of the luminaries <note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note> and not of other stars. And so, the meaning of this prior fifty-eighth "word" <note>original: "verbi"; the aphorisms in the Centiloquium were referred to as "words."</note> is this: when the sign and place where the conjunction of the Sun and Moon occurred in the revolution of the year is carefully observed, and the "perfection" <note>A technical term in astrology for a method of timing events by advancing a point through the zodiac.</note> of the year is distributed through the months—by which one sign after another succeeds to power according to the sequence of the arrangement—when it reaches that place, I should expect the effect which the conjunction of the Sun and Moon at the start of the year's turning signified to us. For Ptolemy uses these meetings of the luminaries above all to investigate the events of the whole year, as anyone knows who has unrolled the volumes of his *Apotelesmatics* <note>Ptolemy’s "Tetrabiblos," the foundational text of systematic astrology.</note>.

<margin>Errors of the common translation in aphorism 58</margin>
Furthermore, in the common translation of this aphorism, many things have been added, omitted, or interpolated. For instead of "conjunction," they read "lesser conjunction," though no distinction of "greater" or "lesser" is added in the Greek manuscripts. Moreover, the term of "perfection" is extended to many years, though Ptolemy makes no mention of this—as we said, he deals only with the events of a single year—but he seems rather to support those earlier points.

<margin>Explanation of aphorism 64</margin>
Finally, there is that statement where "greatest," "middle," and "least" conjunctions are distinguished. Many do not understand this difference regarding the conjunction of the luminaries, but it is easy and fitting for those who have occasionally kept watch by Ptolemy’s lamp without yawning; for since he attributes everything to the conjunctions of the Sun and Moon (as we have said), he then distinguishes these into a threefold genus and order.

<margin>What are the greatest conjunctions according to Ptolemy?</margin>
For those that cause an eclipse of either luminary, they place these in the first rank, through which they can foresee events—not of a single year, but sometimes of many years. We shall therefore call these "greatest" because those stars are then most greatly joined together, neither differing in the longitude of their place nor in their latitude, and they portend the most distant of future events.

<margin>What are the least?</margin>
Conversely, according to him, the "least" are those which occur every single month; these indicate to us the disposition of only one month.

<margin>What are the middle?</margin>
The "middle" ones are those which immediately precede the entry of the Sun into the four tropical signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn. From these, the whole following time of the year is indicated to us, whether it be spring, summer, autumn, or winter. Therefore, since the following particular disposition distinguishes and determines what the universal disposition indicates, he called the difference between the middle and the least a "middle" conjunction. For example: if the conjunction of the Moon and Sun immediately preceding the vernal equinox shows us the future quality of the spring, we know that the whole is then either diminished or increased by the nature of the conjunctions which happen in a fixed revolution in each of the following months.

<margin>In what way the barbarians erred in their understanding of Ptolemy, while Pico has detected it so sharply.</margin>
And whatever relationship those monthly ones have to those four seasonal conjunctions, these three-month ones have that same relationship to the "greatest" and few conjunctions of the ecliping stars. This is Ptolemy's opinion on the greatest, middle, and least conjunctions, which those barbarians <note>Ptolemy's medieval Arabic and Latin commentators, whom Pico often calls "barbarians" for their lack of Greek scholarship.</note>, not understanding, have fabricated for themselves most beautiful dreams about the conjunctions of Saturn and Jupiter. They say the "greatest" of these return after nine hundred and sixty years, the "middle" after two hundred and forty, and the "least" after twenty years. This cannot agree with the statement, beyond what we have already said, because for them, a "greatest" conjunction encompasses the middle and least ones. Therefore, the effect of a greatest conjunction cannot be determined by those lesser ones, through which that greatest one is driven through many revolutions of centuries. Why, then, did Ptolemy say the middle is the difference of the greatest, and the least is the difference of the middle? This is that fiction, born from the false understanding of a single author, in which these men so boast. It is by this that they preen themselves, gloriously thinking that all religion is bound to the stars; by this they subject the most holy laws of the <term>prophets</term> <note>original: "prophetarum"</note>, the advents [of Christ], and divine miracles to the powers of the stars and the fates. Certainly, nowhere do they show themselves more childish, or are they found to be more crude and ridiculous.

***

### Chapter VI: That the principal astrologers used "mean" conjunctions, not "true" ones; and other errors of theirs regarding the same.

<margin>Reasoning.</margin>
<insert>B</insert>ut perhaps some astrologer will say: granted, we have not understood Ptolemy; but what if, just as a storm sometimes drives a ship into harbor, so this error has led us to the truth? Whatever Ptolemy and others thought, experience has confirmed that no great change of laws or kingdoms...

### BOOK FIVE

...that no great change has occurred which was not preceded by some conjunction of the higher stars; nor has any such conjunction ever preceded which was not followed by changes of that kind in lower things. It would be well if they would recognize the storm when they are already in the harbor, as we shall see. For even if they have raved in great matters, they have been forced by experience to see how much those lowest things are consistent. We shall first declare this in general, then point by point: whatever great conjunctions any of the astrologers have noted and related to wonderful events, we shall show—clearer than light—that they are both false and falsely calculated, and falsely related to their effects. To begin with, all authors of this doctrine do not use **true conjunctions**, but **mean** ones—that is, fictional and imaginary ones. So that everyone may clearly understand this, I will explain what "true motion" and "mean motion" are.

<margin>The first reason</margin>
The wandering stars <note>The planets.</note> do not pass through the Zodiac at an equal pace; that is, they do not always traverse an equal portion of it in an equal interval of time. Therefore, those who wished to measure their motions

<margin>What mean motion is.</margin>
and arrange them into numbers **invented** a uniform motion for each planet, so that from this fictional and uniform motion, they might more easily track that unequal and true one. Ptolemy calls that fictional motion "periodic," while younger writers call it "mean," because they use it as a sort of middle ground to investigate the truth. When we seek the location of a planet from a calculation of its motion, we sometimes use mean motion and sometimes true motion—not because that

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
"mean" position indicates to us where the planet actually stands, but so that from it we may seek its true seat by an easier method and reasoning. For a planet is **never** where it is found to be through mean motion, because it never actually moves that way. Rather, as I said, this was devised by astronomers so that they might attain the truth more certainly in a specific order. I was saying, therefore, that those who judge the future by "great conjunctions" use mean conjunctions and not true ones. For when they say that after 20 years Jupiter and Saturn are joined, or after 200 years they meet at the start of the **triplicities** <term>Triplicities: groups of three zodiac signs associated with one of the four elements (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).</term>, or then after 960 years they meet in the borders of Aries—this is most false if we look at their true motions. It is true, however—though not even exactly so—if we look at those "mean" ones, which are fictional and false, and nothing but inventions by mathematicians to make their teaching easier. Indeed, what is called mean motion is so different from what we reach through true motion that the very sign of the conjunction may be changed. For example, a conjunction might be assigned to Pisces which actually occurred in Aquarius; and the time varies so much that if we are discussing conjunctions occurring after 240 years, the true one sometimes precedes the mean one by as much as a hundred years. It is apparent to anyone calculating correctly from the tables that Jupiter and Saturn, in the year 1226, migrating from the Earthy triplicity to the Airy one, met in Aquarius. According to the logic of mean motion, they were to remain in that same triplicity for two hundred and forty years; and yet, after about a hundred and forty years—that is, in the year 1365—the change having been made from the Airy to the Watery triplicity, they met in Scorpio. Having been found together always in Watery signs, they did not afterwards return to the Airy ones. 

<margin>The insanity of astrologers.</margin>
What insanity is this, then, to fight against the evident truth and to use things so shamelessly false and fictional? By the consensus of all astrologers, there is no constellation there at all; yet with blind audacity, they refer the events of human affairs to what is not, has not been, and never will be.

<margin>I will cut this short.</margin>
Lest they think these are just a few who are in error, certainly nothing is more delusional than this vanity, in which nevertheless almost all the principal authors of astrology have fallen. **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note>, the prince of this doctrine, in that book titled *On Great Conjunctions*—which is much celebrated among astrologers—always used mean conjunctions, never true ones. Furthermore, **Abraham** <note>Likely the Jewish scholar Abraham Ibn Ezra.</note>, in that work titled *Redemption*, when he investigates one or two conjunctions from true motion, then always flees back to the mean ones, making no mention of the true ones at all. **Pierre d'Ailly** <note>original: "Alliacensis"; a 15th-century French cardinal and scholar.</note>, in his treatise *On the Concordance of History and Astrology*, in his seven assertions regarding the greatest conjunctions, brings forward only those mean ones and none that are true. Many others, always

<margin>Pierre d'Ailly.</margin>
laboring under the same disease, do the same, about all of whom we shall discuss individually later. And indeed, these things could suffice for us to show that what they say is nothing, if the very constellation from which they predict is nothing. For since these "mean" conjunctions—which are effectively non-existent—do not correspond to the truth, and do not fall at the times they would most wish, they devise another refuge through a new stupidity, 

<margin>A figment of the astrologers.</margin>
defending their prior insanity. For they have invented the idea that what these conjunctions portend does not follow immediately...

-># DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS<-

<margin>Refutation</margin>
Rather, the effect does not come quickly: but after many years, indeed a hundred, or two hundred, or even more. In this matter, see how much they are deceived; for it is not the way of a powerful and effective cause to be late in beginning what it is meant to do. Divine matters, however, act either instantly or quickly. Therefore, the power of these conjunctions is either effective or weak. If it is effective, it cannot cease for a long time without acting; if it is weak, it cannot endure for long. Though it might act at some 

<margin>Another refutation</margin>
point, a great force tames and overcomes whatever prohibits or resists it. A weak force vanishes; it dissolves itself by its own thinness over a long stretch of time. Furthermore, in these intervals of time, new conjunctions always supervene. It is their nature, as even the astrologers say, that the prior ones are forgotten when a succeeding <term>constellation</term><note>Here meaning a specific arrangement of stars or planets.</note> strikes out the preceding one. Hence, if an eclipse of the luminaries occurs at a certain time of year, they are accustomed to say that the <term>fate</term><note>Latin: *fatum*; the predestined outcome dictated by the stars.</note> which was received from the start of the annual revolution ceases. Why then does it not cease with a following conjunction, especially one of a different property and nature? Why does it not expunge that first one? Yet they wish for effects to pertain to that first conjunction which follow it even after three hundred years, with so many various intermediate constellations running between them. No one would say this—neither a philosopher nor even a man of the most extreme slowness of mind. This error is increased in a marvelous way by another inexpiable error: for in the very calculation of dates, they err so significantly that what they think followed a conjunction by two hundred years, for example, actually preceded the time of that event by one thousand and four hundred years. This will be demonstrated in the following chapters of this book; and in these matters, 

<margin>Astrological Cunning</margin>
even the unlearned and the unrefined catch them in lies. But see also how clever these "most fine" diviners are: so that an opportunity for deception would never be lacking, they have so connected their own dogmas that whenever something slightly wonderful happened at any time, they could refer it back to some preceding conjunction. For they said, in order to achieve this, that the force of one conjunction lasts until the very hour of the next; and thus, whatever intervened in the middle could always be referred back to some accepted conjunction. Nor did they see their own ruin in this fallacy: for if, according to them, the relationship is reciprocal—such that there is no great effect without a great conjunction, and no great conjunction appears without an effect—then while they protect themselves by claiming such causes are always present for such events, they necessarily cause such causes to often be exhausted without such events. For great and wonderful things do not always happen because of them; indeed, those things they say are caused by great conjunctions do not even happen frequently. And yet, as they themselves wish, the effective power of these conjunctions remains uninterrupted by the succession of time. This is my general argument against those who speak with impious temerity about future events based on these great conjunctions; now let us examine everything point by point.

***

### Chapter VII. What order is to be preserved, and that d'Ailly felt one thing at one time and another at another.

<margin>d'Ailly contradicts himself</margin>
**L**et us begin with the greatest conjunctions which **d'Ailly** <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a French cardinal and scholar who wrote extensively on the "concordance" of astrology and history.</note> collects in his treatise *On the Concordance of History and Astrology*. From this, the astrologers' claim is confirmed: that such conjunctions never occur without a great mutation of lower things. Yet d'Ailly himself, in his *Elucidarium*, disagrees with this entire "concordance" of his. While in the former work he uses both **Saturnian revolutions** and the greatest conjunctions, in the latter he once aptly confesses that the former have no foundation and that the latter were not calculated by him. It is therefore all the more wonderful that he has a praiser in a matter in which he did not even approve of himself. But because they sometimes bring forward arguments against themselves that are not entirely true—since some are not necessary and some are poorly expressed—let us collect a few but effective points by which that entire treatise may be plainly cut away. Then we shall proceed to refute the other conjunctions which **Abraham** <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra.</note> and **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, the influential Persian astrologer.</note> and many others—including d'Ailly himself, who followed them—presented in the *Elucidarium*. 

<margin>The order to be observed in the process</margin>
Truly, since I must often speak regarding the calculation of dates, I thought it necessary to preface certain things. From these, it may first be shown that when there is doubt about dates, the judgment of this matter is not, as d'Ailly thinks, in the hands of astrologers, but in the hands of **history**. Then, when there is a variety among historical writers, we must determine which of them should most rightfully be followed. Regarding these matters, I will say a few things here in passing, as I have disputed these things at length in a separate work which I wrote concerning the true calculation of time.
