# Chapter VIII: The timing of historical events is not to be sought from astrology, as Pierre d'Ailly thought, but from history.

<margin>Opinion of Pierre d'Ailly.</margin>
**P**ierre d'Ailly <note>Latin: *Alliacensis*; a French cardinal and theologian (1351–1420) who famously attempted to harmonize astrology with biblical history.</note> in his book *On the Concord of Astrology and Theology* thinks that the number of years from the beginning of the world until these present times can be discovered through astrological reasoning and brought back to the truth, more so than what various sacred or foreign histories have provided on the matter. For, he says, if you have investigated the <term>horoscope</term><note>Latin: *thema*; a birth chart or map of the stars at a specific moment.</note> of the world’s birth itself, you will be able to calculate from that the first <term>conjunction</term><note>The meeting of two planets—in this case, Saturn and Jupiter—in the same degree of the zodiac.</note> of Saturn and Jupiter from the world's beginning. If you then search for another conjunction closest to your own years, you can elicit the interval of time that lies between that first <margin>His opinion in the *Elucidarium*.</margin> and the last one from a calculation of the intervening conjunctions. This is what he felt about that time; but in his *Elucidarium*, he clearly confessed that there is no astrological way for us to find anything certain from a doubtful number of years. For this reason, he said, not even the greatest astrologers have ever attempted this or made promises about it from their own art. Yet while he says this, I do not know why he persists again in the opinion that the ultimate question of the calculation of times should be referred to astrologers, and that whatever is found in histories regarding the year of the world that differs from them <margin>Against Pierre d'Ailly.</margin> should be amended and corrected according to their opinion. We shall briefly show that this can be defended by no reasoning. For an astronomer can indeed—if he has some true position of the stars that existed once, and again has another recent one noted—determine by a very certain calculation how much time must necessarily have passed between them. But how will this help him if the time of the event itself is uncertain? For suppose someone says three thousand years have flowed from Christ to us, and another says one thousand and four hundred. In settling this dispute, what will the office of the astronomer be? You will say: he will show that the position of the stars under which Christ was born, and that which is held now, cannot be separated by three thousand years, but rather by one thousand and four hundred. But what sluggishness is this, what dullness, that you do not see what is at issue? For the astronomer does not know <margin>Alfonso. Albumasar.</margin> what position of the stars Christ was born under unless he first receives from history at what time He was born. Let us move to more remote times. Alfonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile (1221–1284), sponsor of the Alfonsine astronomical tables.</note> counts three thousand one hundred and two years from the Flood to Christ. Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note> did the same, whom Alfonso followed. All history contradicts this number; yet Pierre d'Ailly thinks all histories are in error rather than the astrologers. By what reasoning, I ask? Is it because the conjunction that preceded the Flood arrives at Christ through a cycle of so many years? No one denies this to them; but from where did they learn that there was such a conjunction so many years before the Flood as they themselves think? Could they have known this from anywhere else than from history? Truly, this is so manifest that, had I not seen d'Ailly slip here, I would think I was wasting words on a superfluous matter. <margin>Praise of histories.</margin> For how ridiculous was their opinion, I ask, which said we could be made more certain about the years of the world from the first conjunction since the world's beginning? They gathered that first conjunction from the birth of the world—as if, while we might doubt the years of the world, we nonetheless had it fully investigated not only in what year, but even at <margin>From what songs among the barbarians or Arabs.</margin> what hour it began! No one should doubt, therefore, that the timing of events must be sought from the great history of events; in this matter, astronomy is a disciple and cannot be the judge. For I will grant to Alfonso that through so many thousands of years before Christ, there was such a position of the stars as appears from his tables; but I will not grant that the <term>Deluge</term><note>The Great Flood.</note> or any other historical event occurred at those times, unless a faithful history demonstrates this to me. All astrologers, however, have erred vehemently in this calculation of times, which will become more manifest in its proper place; this could have happened to them for no other reason than that they clung to false histories. For the Latin astrologers followed the Arabs, but those men are most full of fables; and when they received histories from Greek or Latin writers, <margin>Of the faithful.</margin> foreign translation violated most of them. This happens easily in every matter among the letters of barbarians; but it happens most easily in the notation of numbers, in which even the most accurate diligence of scribes almost always hallucinates somewhat. One must use true and faithful histories, therefore, among which no Christian will doubt that the Sacred history is to be placed before others—and neither would a Hebrew or a Saracen <note>A common medieval/Renaissance term for Muslims.</note>. Furthermore, in those things which happened before the Deluge, they will have either that Mosaic history or none at all.

If indeed, in the sacred volumes, the Greek edition <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> disagrees with the Hebrew truth <note>Latin: *Hebraica veritas*; a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Old Testament.</note> in this measurement of years, no one of sound judgment can prefer the reliability of the translator over the author himself. <margin>The Hebrew computations are valid</margin> This is especially true since not only does Jerome agree with the numbering of the Hebrews, but Augustine also thinks one should agree with it. ### Chapter IX: A summary of the opinion of Pierre d'Ailly in the book which he titled "On the Concord of Astrology and History."

<margin>Ridiculous</margin>**A**fter we have briefly laid these foundations concerning the true computation of times, let us come to those "greatest conjunctions" of the astrologers—that is, to their greatest madness—beginning with those which Pierre d'Ailly <note>Latin: *Alliacensis*; 1351–1420.</note> collected in his treatise on the concord of history and astrology. In that work, D'Ailly used the following order. He assumes two principles: <margin>Foundations of d'Ailly's concord</margin> the first concerning the number of years from Adam to Christ; the second concerning the <term>horoscope</term><note>Latin: *thema*; a map of the planetary positions at a specific moment.</note> of the birth of the world itself. He says that 5,344 years passed from Adam to Jesus: specifically, 2,242 years from Adam to the Flood, and 3,102 years from the Flood to Jesus. ¶ In the first constitution of the world, he claims the stars were so placed in the heavens that the first part of <term>Cancer</term><note>The sign of the Crab.</note> formed the <term>horoscope</term><note>The Ascendant or rising sign.</note>. The very highest point of the sky <note>The Midheaven.</note> was occupied by the first part of Aries. Mercury was in the fifteenth part of Gemini in the twelfth region of the heaven. Venus occupied the eleventh house in Taurus. Both of the luminaries—the nocturnal one <note>The Moon.</note> being in Taurus, and the diurnal one <note>The Sun</note> in the nineteenth part of Aries—shone forth in the middle and highest point of heaven. Saturn was in Aquarius in the eighth house, the house of death. Jupiter held the ninth place of the heaven in Pisces. Mars lingered in Scorpio <margin>Layout of the figure of the greatest conjunction</margin> and in the fifth seat from the horoscope. In that same place, but in Sagittarius, was the <term>Dragon's Tail</term><note>The descending lunar node, often associated with misfortune in astrology.</note>. ### Chapter X: Pierre d’Ailly has erred in many ways; and even if his premises were granted, he still would not achieve his goal.

<margin>The first reason regarding the "birth" of the world, that it might finally confirm history.</margin>
**F**irst of all, even if we grant his premises regarding the conjunctions, the timing of events, and historical deeds—let us give him everything he asks for concerning the "birth of the world"—how is this supposedly a confirmation of astrology through history? If we were to show any period of nine hundred and sixty-five years <note>The length of a "great cycle" in d'Ailly's astrological system.</note> that has passed, the world would have seen some great change in the cycle of human affairs. I ask you, describe this span of years from other starting points—not, for example, from the year 320 of the world, which

In that long stretch of time, you will find a great variety of wars, laws, prophets, plagues, and diverse events. Why did you not trace the series of these actions back through the two-hundred-year spans from the time of that conjunction of yours? This is a very "clumsy wisdom" <note>original: "pinguis Minerva"; a Latin idiom for a plain, unrefined, or common-sense approach that lacks subtle logic.</note> if this is how we harmonize astrology with history. Furthermore, those conjunctions are not "true" but "mean" <note>In astronomy, a "mean" position is a simplified average, whereas a "true" position accounts for the actual, irregular elliptical orbit.</note>—which is to say, they are false and non-existent; nor should they be referred to those times even if we accepted them as "mean." Nor is the number of years he calculated from Adam to Christ correct; rather, it exceeds the true calculation by more than one thousand four hundred years. Nor did those deeds or events occur at the times he thought they did. Moreover, the "birth of the world" <note>The initial horoscope of the universe.</note> which he describes is demonstrated to be not only doubtful or false, but impossible by astrological reasoning. Therefore, that entire booklet can be corrected with a single strike of the pen. No one is ignorant of the fact that those conjunctions are "mean" and false rather than "true," and he himself does not deny it. ### Chapter XI: On the conjunction of the Flood, that astrologers disagree both among themselves and from the truth.

And even if one grants them whatever they seek, they still do not prove what they contend.

<margin>The discord of astrologers; the common opinion whose author is Aoniar.</margin>
**L**et us move on to other great conjunctions noted with a bit more diligence by others, but not so much that they avoid the mark of madness, let alone error. And let us begin first with that most ancient one to which they refer the occurrence of the universal cataclysm <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note>. Regarding this, we shall first see how the astrologers feel things that are clashing and contrary among themselves, and how one brawls with and reproaches another; then, how they all clearly wander from the truth. Finally, even if their opinion were true, it does not achieve what they want. Indeed, I will clearly confirm this point here: such conjunctions do not happen without a great change in lower affairs <note>Refers to "sublunary" or earthly matters, as opposed to the "higher" celestial realm.</note>. It is, therefore, the common opinion of astrologers that two hundred and seventy-nine years before the universal Flood, Jupiter and Saturn were joined in the fourteenth degree of Cancer, with the beginning of Aries in the horoscope; both stars were placed together in the fourth region of the sky. Aoniar wrote this in his *Book of Nativities*, and the later crowd has for the most part followed his opinion. 
<margin>The opinion of Albumasar, differing from the former.</margin>
Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to medieval European astrology.</note> noted this conjunction eight years earlier—that is, two hundred and eighty-seven years before the Flood—and Henry, his interpreter, is certain of this. But while the same 
<margin>Henry, the interpreter of Albumasar, contradicts him.</margin>

Based on the reliability of the Machlivian tables <note>original: "tabularz machliuíēsīū"; likely referring to the astronomical tables of Henry of Mechelen.</note>, Henry says he discovered through numbers that in the year Albumasar claimed they were joined, there was actually an interval of four signs between Saturn and Jupiter. But, having calculated more diligently, Henry says he 
<margin>The discrepancy of Henry from others</margin>
found that conjunction in the year one thousand nine hundred and fifty-one before the constellation of the Arabs. Likewise, while this Henry says they were joined in the fourth degree of Cancer, others using the Alfonsine Tables <note>The standard astronomical tables of the late Middle Ages, sponsored by Alfonso X of Castile.</note> contend that they were joined in the fourteenth degree of that sign. But let us dismiss these discords of theirs and now show how they all equally disagree with the truth. For whether we use the tables of King Alfonso or those of Mechelen, by taking the starting points of celestial movements backward from Christ, we fall upon that conjunction in the year 
<margin>The discord of astrologers from the truth.</margin>
(as Henry says) three thousand three hundred and fifty-two before Christ; other authors vary from this number by only a few months. For I do not think they would extend the power of that conjunction over so many years. But let us grant them that the Flood preceded by no more years than they wish, and occurred at the times they think; do you believe they will nonetheless achieve what they want? Even if we grant them this, it is nonetheless false, vain, and ridiculous. For suppose Saturn and Jupiter were joined in Cancer: did the world perish immediately, submerged by a flood of water? Indeed, more than ten times since those days they have been together in that same sign, and yet the world did not perish; on the contrary, not even...

First Reason for Refutation.

<margin>
Second: The Jews expelled from Spain.
</margin>
Since this has already been sufficiently refuted by the facts themselves—fifty years having passed since the first conjunction and thirty since the second—the fable concerning Moses could also be sufficiently weakened here. It would show that his kingdom was not given by that constellation, since when that constellation returned to them, their kingdom did not return at all. Nor did it produce anything by the power of Moses; for though those forces returned to us with no effect, they brought us no prophet. Furthermore, the Hebrew people did not begin to live more happily after those conjunctions; on the contrary, they have been overwhelmed since that time by calamities no less than those under Titus or Hadrian. This is seen in the recent expulsion of all Jews from all of Spain by that most Christian King <note>Referring to King Ferdinand II of Aragon, who issued the Alhambra Decree in 1492.</note>—who can certainly never be praised enough—where they were most powerful in number, wealth, and authority. They themselves do not deny that they have never suffered anything more sorrowful or bitter than this ejection: many were lost to shipwreck, very many to plague, and a great part of them by extreme hunger. Even for us Christians, while the glory of divine justice was a delight, the sight of people suffering such extremes nonetheless provoked deep compassion and grief. Is this the Messiah? Is this that redemption which Abraham <note>Likely referring to Abraham bar Hiyya or Abraham ibn Ezra, Jewish scholars who used astrology to predict messianic dates.</note> promised them from the Mosaic constellation?

<margin>
Third [Point]
</margin>
Lest we believe he divined better concerning past events than future ones, let us look at that conjunction to which he attributed the arrival of Moses, and see how clearly false and ridiculous it is. For that conjunction, through which he believed Moses was born, occurred many years after the death of Moses; and even if we grant him the time, it signified nothing of the sort as he imagines. Let us look at the timing; but first, it is necessary to know that in this year—which is 1484 from Christ—the Hebrews count five thousand two hundred and fifty-three years from the constitution of the world (from which they number their years). 

<margin>
Calculation.
</margin>
Therefore, from the [beginning of the] world to Christ, they compute three thousand seven hundred and sixty years. Since that Abraham says that conjunction occurred in the year of the world 2365, and says Moses was born three years after it passed, it follows that it occurred 1395 years before the time of Christ. But in truth, by an accurate calculation, 1,509 years are counted from Moses to Christ. Therefore, that conjunction occurred one hundred and thirty years *after* the birth of Moses. 

<margin>
Calculation of years from Moses to Christ.
</margin>
The number of years is demonstrated as follows: from Moses to the first building of the Temple (from the third book of Kings, which they call the first book of Samuel <note>Pico is reconciling the naming conventions of the Vulgate and the Hebrew Bible.</note>), 479 years are collected. From that first building to the restoration of the Temple under Darius, 512 years are computed. From Darius to Christ, 518 years are numbered. The sum of all these is what we said: namely, 1,509 years. But that conjunction preceded Christ by 1,395 years; and thus it followed the birth of Moses by 130 years. Yet, that constellation was not so wonderful or prophetic that its timing should be so greatly contested.

Fourth [Point]
</margin>
For he says: "Jupiter and Saturn were joined in the year of the world 2365, on the 25th day of the month of Adar—that is, February—in the first part of Pisces." Let him first explain, then, which conjunction he would rather choose to which he might primarily refer the kingdom of the Jews and the Mosaic law: that "mean" one in Pisces, or this "true" one in Aquarius?

What such Conjunctions rather predict.

Such conjunctions, as he himself writes in the same place, do not signify changes of laws or the arrival of prophets, but either the fertility or scarcity of the harvest, or perhaps a transfer of power, but only among relatives and those things within the fortunes of a single nation—indeed, they contain themselves within the boundaries of the same family. 

<margin>
Questioning with refutation.
</margin>
Furthermore, in the <term>house</term> of the conjunction which he describes, Aquarius (in which Jupiter and Saturn were) occupied the seventh place in the heavens, not the ninth or tenth, which are the places where kingdoms, laws, and the beginnings of new wisdom are signified. And if anyone should contend that this Aquarius rained Moses down upon us from his city in the sky, let him say, I pray, why in the year of our Lord 1226, when Jupiter and Saturn were in Aquarius with a change...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the "great conjunctions" theory. He is specifically refuting the claims of the Jewish scholar Abraham Ibn Ezra and the Persian astrologer Albumasar, who attempted to link the rise of religions and prophets to planetary alignments.</meta>

Through the change and <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element: Fire, Earth, Air, or Water.</note> they joined together, which was to be counted among the greater conjunctions; yet no Moses descended from heaven, no people were led out of Egypt, no law was given, and the world saw no miracle at that time among those that occurred under Moses in the desert. But it seems that Abraham Ibn Ezra did not particularly note that <term>conjunction</term> <note>The meeting of two planets at the same degree of the zodiac.</note> which occurred in Aquarius; rather, he called the conjunction in Pisces the "conjunction of the Jewish kingdom and the Mosaic law," wherefore he also makes the conjunction for the Messiah similar to that one, as if he were a second Moses. Why do we bother to refute this in more detail? Since it is among those they call "mean" or "middle" conjunctions—which is to say, they are nothing, but are fictions and imaginary constructs of our own making. I can never sufficiently marvel at the insanity of astrologers, which I have already so often mocked and censured, that they refer the events of lower things to those professional calculations as if they were true causes, when those calculations are nothing, and have never been, nor ever will be.

<margin>Censure of Abraham Ibn Ezra</margin>
And I do not know why Ibn Ezra—who says no faith should be placed in Albumasar because he uses middle conjunctions—did not say the same about his own teacher, who in that whole little book always deals with middle conjunctions that occur after the migration from one <term>triplicity</term> to another every 238 years. And in that initial prophetic conjunction of his, it is incredible how ridiculous he is. For he describes a <term>celestial chart</term> <note>A horoscope or diagram of the heavens at a specific moment.</note> for that hour in which Leo holds the <term>ascendant</term> <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon; originally "horoscopus."</note>, while in the seventh place, in Aquarius, Saturn and Jupiter are guests; the Sun runs through the mid-heaven in Aries. Pisces occupies the ninth region, from which every significance of laws and the lot of prophets is sought; it followed that no planet was found in it. But the astrologer, a man of admirable loftiness, transported both the Sun and Jupiter and that Saturn—one from the tenth place and the others from the seventh—to the ninth. For he says, "by mean motion Jupiter and Saturn were in Pisces; Pisces is in the ninth place; therefore Jupiter and Saturn are in the ninth." And the Sun, although it is in the tenth by the division of the houses, yet if we observe the number and sequence of the signs, it will be in the ninth, and Aries is the fifth from Leo, and the ninth house is the fifth from the ascendant. Do we think even the subtlest thinkers <note>original: "arististas"</note> are more refined than these comments?

<margin>Laughable stupidity</margin>
Whether I should laugh or be indignant at such stupidity, such madness, I do not know; or whether I should rather grieve for the loss of simpler minds who pass down these things to writing as if they were not understood. And they sometimes magnify them, since such people usually go from error into superstition, and from superstition they gradually fall into infidelity. Tell me, I pray, admirable Abraham, at what hour were Saturn and Jupiter in Aquarius, or were they also in Pisces? By "mean motion," you say. But what else is this but saying they were not there? And if he promised the beginning of a kingdom from the tenth house, how could he also indicate the splendor of the law from the ninth, when neither the ninth turns into the tenth, nor the tenth into the ninth, nor can the same planet be in both places at once? But I have said too much about these things, since Aristotle says one should not dispute against stupid opinions.

### Chapter XIII. That the Christian law is ascribed to various middle conjunctions by various people, and even without astrological reason.

<margin>For Aristotle’s Physics teaches that one should not dispute against those who deny principles.</margin>
Thus far, I have not seen the Christian law referred to any true conjunction, but only to middle ones: some to that which occurred in the sixth degree of Aries six years before Jesus was born; others to that which happened in the last part of Cancer, preceding the former by twenty years. There would be much here that would complicate his business, such as if I were to show that Jesus was born not under a fiery or watery triplicity, but under an earthy one, which could be proven both by reason and by the authority of Abraham and others. Furthermore, the prophets do not signify that conjunction in Cancer, since it was not among the "greatest" or even the "greater" ones. Seeing this, a certain author says that if it is said to belong to Leo—for the end of Cancer and the beginning of Leo are neighbors—then it will be the beginning of the fiery triplicity. This is certainly a clumsy invention; for those places are not distant by more than five fingers across. Therefore, no migration can be referred to that which has not yet occurred. But I think we have laughed enough and sufficiently refuted these middle conjunctions. Since we have now clearly removed them all from the discussion, there is no reason to build more defenses against them, as it has been sufficiently declared that calling them "middle" is no different from saying they are nothing. That which is nothing, certainly, can neither act nor indicate those things which are. If after...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological claims regarding religious history. -># DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS<-

...that they assert some true <term>conjunction</term> <note>The meeting of two planets at the same degree of the zodiac.</note> at the birth of Christ; furthermore, I shall wonder at nothing unless we believe the heavens stood still after he was brought into the light. Otherwise, it was necessary for Jupiter, Saturn, and the other planets to both meet and depart from one another quite frequently. But none of the astrologers ever said that these conjunctions had power over things that had already passed; rather, they say their effects proceed for many years afterward. This is never said with any reason: for if they produce an effect, the cause cannot come after the effect; if they are signs, it is pointless for the celestial signs to signify that which has already happened.

### Chapter XIV. That the birth chart of Jesus which is commonly circulated is not true; nor is it indicated by it that he would die a violent death or be a great prophet.

<margin>The godless fiction of Albumasar.</margin>
**C**ertain people are usually moved by the trifles these little diviners babble regarding the <term>nativity</term> <note>A birth chart or "genitura" showing the positions of the stars at the moment of birth.</note> of Jesus. For he was born, they say, when the first "face" of the Virgin (so they call the <term>decans</term> <note>A subdivision of a zodiac sign into three parts of ten degrees each.</note>) was ascending, concerning which <term>Albumasar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer whose works were influential in Medieval Europe.</note> writes that there is in it a beautiful virgin holding two ears of grain in her hand and nursing a boy, whom a certain nation calls "Jesus." Thus they think the miracle of the Word made flesh is confirmed by the science of astrology, which found the Virgin and Jesus among the images of heaven. Here, I am not greatly angry with them, since they are accustomed to confirm their own dogmas with such testimonies; therefore they think we will gladly receive these things by which our own dogmas might be corroborated. But Christian truth does not need these fables and dreams, for among serious and upright men, these are regarded as little more than myths. Who ever saw these images? When the senses were silent, what hidden reason pointed them out? Where did <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational authority on astronomy and astrology.</note> or any ancient author ever make mention of them? These are the purest trifles of the Arabs, who refer them to their idols, against which we shall dispute more extensively in the following book.

<margin>First reason.</margin>
<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Furthermore, the Lord Jesus was not born with that Virgin (as they say) ascending; otherwise, he would have appeared in the light nearly two hours before midnight, whereas we have received from Church tradition that he was born at midnight. Therefore, it was not the third degree of Libra (as some say), but rather the tenth, that occupied the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopum"; here meaning the Ascendant, the specific point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> when the most Desired of all nations was being born. From this, it is also shown to be false what they disseminate with blasphemous voice: that Mars was in the "house of death" <note>The 8th house in an astrological chart, traditionally associated with death.</note> in that nativity, from which he was destined to die by the punishment of the cross. For Mars could not have been in that place unless we make the Virgin the Ascendant, which we have declared to be greatly different from the hour of his birth.

<margin>Mars was not in the eighth house.</margin>
<margin>Objection.</margin>
<margin>Solution.</margin>
<margin>The end of a violent death is not pre-signified by the nativity of Jesus.</margin>
But some might insist that if we remove Mars from that part of the heaven, we will place him in the "descendant" <note>The 7th house, the point opposite the Ascendant.</note> where he also threatens the danger of a violent death. However, without departing from their own decrees, I shall show that the end of a violent death is not pre-signified by that nativity. For although Mars in the seventh place might bring the newborn into the danger of his life, nevertheless, <term>Maternus</term> <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> writes that such misfortune is lessened if it be a nocturnal birth; likewise if Mars were in his own house, or his own terms, or his own exaltation. Furthermore, even if he were found in the eighth place (from which no clearer sign of death exists), the malignity of Mars is nonetheless resisted by the benevolence of Jupiter—whether Jupiter be in the Ascendant, or the Ascendant itself be in the house of Jupiter or Venus, which star joins itself to Jupiter by a favorable <term>aspect</term> <note>The angular relationship between planets; here specifically "radiatiōe," meaning a beam or ray.</note>. From these factors, not just one or two, but clearly all were present in the nativity of Jesus. For he was born by night and not by day, and Mars was in Aries (that is, in his own home), and the Ascendant was Libra, the house of Venus, which Jupiter would illuminate from nearly the same degree. Then, Venus being positioned in Aquarius, a trine aspect <note>original: "trigoni radii"; an aspect of 120 degrees, considered very harmonious.</note> joined them in a friendly fellowship. To these things you may also add the Moon, which rules the night; you will see that in a nocturnal birth, she was happily situated and held the house of death. Necessarily, a "good death" had to be pronounced from that position of the stars. For she was in Taurus—favorable, in her own exaltation, and increased in light—and in the place where she rejoices (that is, the eighth), flowing away from a most happy aspect with the Sun toward Venus, with whom she was a guest, infested by no rays of either Mars or Saturn. She was neither departing from them nor going toward them; that is, she was bound to them by no bond of fellowship. Add that Venus, the lady of both the house of death and the Ascendant alike, was struck by no hostile ray of Mars or Saturn, but was cherished by the rays of Jupiter, promising him a good end. He was offered up, therefore, because he willed it <note>A reference to Isaiah 53:7: "He was offered because it was his own will."</note>, not because the fury of the heavens drove him to the punishment of the cross. But an opportunity for babbling can never be lacking to reckless men of no shame. For imagine...

Indeed, imagine that Mars had been in any location; they would have had no less cause to rave in some way. For if one should place it in the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The Ascendant, or the first house of the zodiac chart.</note>, they would say this refers to a face struck by fists and defiled with blood, and that this "Martian" man brought destruction upon himself by the sword. If in the second house from the horoscope, they would claim it brought poverty and a lack of all things. If in the third, no brothers; if in the fourth, no <term>patrimony</term> <note>Inheritance or ancestral estate.</note>, so that he who was the Son of David nonetheless did not obtain even the temporal kingdom of David. If in the fifth, no children; if in the sixth, that all his servants were given over to death. If in the seventh and eighth places, they would have something to say regarding death. If in the ninth—oh, blessed astrologers!—since he says that he had Mars in less than the ninth region of heaven,
<margin>A blasphemous doctrine in my view.</margin>
in its own house, he would be a man destined to be a terror to evil demons, at whose arrival the spirits of the wicked demon would flee, and from whom he would free suffering men, not by a word, but by his appearance alone. With how much shouting and applause, then, do you believe the astrologers would follow and spread these things, if the star of Mars had happened to be standing there at the Lord's birth? But if it had held the heights of heaven, they would immediately have pronounced the world subject to his laws, especially since Jupiter occupies the first <term>angle</term> <note>The "Cardo," one of the four most powerful points in a chart.</note>. If they had found him in the eleventh place, they would have brought forward the "Charleses" and "Constantines" <note>Referring to Great Christian Emperors like Charlemagne and Constantine.</note> and all the Caesars who fought for the Church of Christ. If in the twelfth, they would seek among the snares of enemies, among whom they would even find themselves—so insane are they that they are called an occasion for a spirit of madness. But hear also what they say about Saturn:
<margin>What the astrologers say about Saturn.</margin>
for it was in the ninth region of heaven in the sign of Gemini; and they say, "It makes prophets and priests." Why does he shrink back? Let them give these promises with all their power: it could make a prophet, but it could not make one greater than a prophet, as was John the Baptist. Could it then make the divine inspirer of all a prophet? Saturn was established in that same place and in the same sign when Eleonora, the niece of Galeotto, was born.
<margin>Refutation by reason.</margin>
She is a virgin who is chaste and of the highest integrity; but she is neither an Anna, nor a Deborah, nor a Cassandra <note>Biblical and mythological prophetesses.</note>. But I ask you, admirable astrologers, persevere in your proposed doctrine, and let us see
<margin>Refutation by example.</margin>
what Saturn would signify there in his nativity. Your Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a Spanish rabbi and astrologer.</note> writes in his *Book of Nativities* that one who had Saturn placed thus—that is, in the ninth region of heaven—would be a "bad Christian." You see how beautifully he has confirmed your doctrine! For who would dare
<margin>The madness of Cecco d'Ascoli.</margin>
to call Christ a "bad Christian," who was not even a "Christian" <note>Pico's point is that Christ is the source of Christianity, not a follower of it; therefore, the label "Christian" is technically a category error.</note>? O ridiculous men, certainly never mocked enough! That superstitious <term>Cecco d'Ascoli</term> <note>Italian astrologer (1257–1327) burned at the stake for heresy.</note>, who was almost a sorcerer, says: "Jesus was born in a stable because Capricorn held the <term>Imum Coeli</term> <note>The "bottom of the sky," the lowest point of the chart, associated with foundations and domesticity.</note>;" and another says he was "King of the Jews" because the horoscope was Libra—for the Hebrews belong to Saturn, and the kingdom of Saturn is Libra. As if many are not born every single month under these same conditions who are neither born in stables nor inscribed as kings of the Jews! But enough now of these rascals.

### Chapter XV. That the things Albumasar said about Muhammad are found to be false by experience.

<margin>Albumasar is false.</margin>
**A**lbumasar the Arab <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), the most influential astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note> relates the arrival of his Muhammad and that law of the Saracens to a <term>conjunction</term> of Jupiter and Saturn which occurred in Scorpio fifty-two years before the publication of that Law. He does not need to be refuted with many words, since the things he prophesied from that same constellation regarding that Law have already been refuted by experience itself. Finally, as we said above, at whatever time either good or evil prophets come, a conjunction cannot be lacking to which their arrival may be referred, since after twenty years—as we said above—Saturn and Jupiter always meet. But that such meetings are neither a sign nor a cause for why prophets of this kind come can be sufficiently proven by this:
<margin>A conjunction similar to that of Muhammad which produced no new law.</margin>
that often at other times, similar or even more effective constellations for that same work return; after which, however, no prophet, no new law, and no change of religion followed. They say Muhammad came after Jupiter and Saturn were joined in Scorpio. Why did another Muhammad not come after the Greek year 1065, at which time Jupiter and Saturn were together under a similar condition, with the <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note> even changed? And what did not happen in that conjunction of Muhammad: Mars in that same year, in the same sign, joined with them by body; and yet, if we consult the histories, no new religion appeared during those times...

### Chapter XVI. On the prophecy of the Antichrist: that some liars have already appeared, and others will appear in the future.

<margin>Arnaldus</margin>
**I**f we catch them as false, vain, and ridiculous in those things they have spoken regarding past religions, we ought not to grant any more faith to their trifles when these scoundrels hold forth with a certain prophetic authority concerning the Antichrist, the end of the world, and other future matters of this kind. For indeed, events have already refuted some of them, such as Arnaldus <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a physician and reformer who famously predicted the world would end in the 14th century.</note> and several others who say that in the year of the Lord 1345, because of that conjunction of the three superior stars in Aquarius, or in the year 1464, because Jupiter and Saturn were joined in Pisces, some were threatening the Messiah of Abraham <note>A reference to Jewish messianic expectations linked to astrology.</note> and others the Antichrist. I do not doubt that others who postponed these things further into the future will be refuted by posterity with the same argument, since the reality itself will refute their prophecy until that day arrives which is unknown even to the angels. Since the Lord Jesus denied that it was our business to know this day, as <margin>Augustine</margin> Augustine says, he "untied the fingers" <note>original: "digitos... resoluit" – a metaphor for stopping those trying to calculate the date of the end times on their fingers.</note> of all the audacious with a single word.

## Chapter XVII. How frivolously the astrologers try to prove that there can be only six religions, and then that the law of the Hebrews ought to be called Jovian or Solar rather than Saturnine.

**B**ut hear with what a beautiful fiction they bind together all past religions and those that will be under the Antichrist under one (so to speak) bundle. Jupiter, they say, signifies religion, and it signifies one or another based on its embrace with various other stars. However, there are six stars besides Jupiter; therefore, there are also six types of religions, of which there will be neither more nor fewer, nor have there been. For with Saturn, it makes the religion of the Jews; with Mars, that of the Chaldeans, who worship fire; with the Sun, that of the Egyptians, who worship the host of heaven—that is, the stars; with Venus, the Saracen religion; with Mercury, the Christian; and with the Moon, that which will be the last of all under the Antichrist. This is that "subtle and profound invention" which, though many others use it, <margin>Roger Bacon</margin> <term>Roger Bacon</term> <note>A 13th-century English philosopher and friar who attempted to integrate science and theology.</note> uses most especially in his letter to Clement, and which <margin>Pierre d'Ailly</margin> <term>d'Ailly</term> <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1350–1420), a French cardinal and theologian who wrote on the "harmony" of astrology and history.</note> also used in his treatise on the harmony of astrology and theology.

<margin>First reason for the assessment of this astrological fiction.</margin> In this, I first marvel that they have so forgotten their own dogma: for while they are always accustomed to say that religions are made or signified only from the conjunction of the superior stars—especially Saturn and Jupiter—they now descend all the way to the Moon to depict some Antichrist for us. And if they want to count the types of religions according to the number of planets, they must either remove one planet from the sky or beg for several more elsewhere; otherwise, the number will not match. For they either treat idolatry as one religion, or they want to treat each species of idolatry separately in that count, according to the various rites and worship of those who served idols. If they prefer the first, they must remove one planet from the set; for there would not be one religion for the Egyptians and another for the Chaldeans, but one and the same: namely, idolatry. In that case, there would only be five religions: the idolaters, the Mosaic, the Christian, the Muhammadan, and (so to speak) the Anti-Christian.

If they command that the species of idolatry be taken separately, there are hardly as many stars in the sky as there are religions on earth. And if they think these can be reduced to "heads," so that one group worships fire and another the sky, they deservedly bring a great evil upon themselves from the demons, who would be indignant at being omitted in this partition, though in idolatry they are the ones primarily and almost solely worshiped. For "all the gods of the nations are demons"; therefore, they must necessarily make at least three types of idolatry: of the sky, of demons, and of the elements. They will be forced to seek one "error" for themselves from their friends—I meant to say a wandering star <note>Pico is punning on the Latin "error" (error/falsehood) and "planeta" (wandering star).</note>—so that they might find eight to match the number of religions.

<margin>Third: Iamblichus</margin>
<margin>Fourth</margin>
But they are also always poorly informed about the things they discuss. For the worship of the heavenly bodies was proper to the Chaldeans, as <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian and Chaldean mysteries.</note> writes, while the Egyptians were more occupied with the worship of demons; therefore, they should give the Sun to the Chaldeans instead of Mars, and they should procure some "diabolical" planet for the Egyptians. I would easily endure them fighting against the truth everywhere, since they have always been friends with falsehood. But why do they so often disagree with themselves? For if they consulted reason, they would not find enough in their own dogmas to explain why the law of the Hebrews should be Saturnine rather than Christian; instead, the former should rather be referred to the Sun or Jupiter, while ours [Christianity] should be referred to Saturn. For Saturn, as some say, does not bestow bodily goods but takes them away; it gives spiritual goods and

...spiritual things and those which are not seen. The Mosaic law <note>The law of the Old Testament / Judaism.</note> promised and bestowed physical goods; our law <note>Christianity.</note> takes these away rather than displaying them, but promises and provides spiritual things which are not seen. Saturn makes kings of the people, emperors of armies, rich men, and nobles with much offspring; nature does not make them effeminate <note>original: "mulierosos" — Pico is contrasting the stern, worldly power associated with Saturn with the humility of the Christian faith.</note> like all the princes of the Hebrew religions: Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Joshua, Solomon, and David. It makes [us] ignoble, poor, hermits, haters of pleasures, meditating on eternal things, and despising physical things. If anyone is to be numbered among such as these, it is our leader and emperor Jesus Christ, as well as the apostles, martyrs, monks, and Christians, by whose life, doctrine, and blood our religion was increased, born, and confirmed. Therefore, if we were to speak in accordance with their decrees, we should be called Saturnians, and the Hebrews should be called Solar or Jovial <note>Relating to the planets the Sun or Jupiter.</note>. But the worship of the Sabbath drew them into that opinion; since that day is considered the day of Saturn among them, it seemed most fitting to them to say that they were a Saturnian people who venerated the Saturnian day above all others. They are also led by conjecture to say our religion is "Solar," because we observe the day of the Sun which we call the Lord's Day. But why are we not rather moved by the day of Mercury, <margin>Albumasar</margin> since they also subject us to Mercury? For they gave Mercury to us just as they gave the Sun to the Egyptians. And Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note> says that Jupiter with Mercury signifies the Christian law, although he said the same thing about the Sun. For it is not a vice among those who are so diligent in the errors and movements of the planets to either err or change their opinion; stunned in that rapid vertigo of the heavens, they hardly ever stand firmly on their feet. But however it may be, they have wonderful reasons with which they confirm these inventions of theirs. Indeed, they did not rashly refer us to Mercury; for, as Roger Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), an English friar and philosopher who integrated science and theology.</note> says, because he [Mercury] has multiple movements and is difficult to know, he claims the Christian religion for himself, whose dogmas are almost incredible and very difficult to recognize. Others more recently have devised I know not what: since Mercury is the "Librarian" of the gods, and since there is a great abundance of books among Christians, he says this religion should rightly be considered "Mercurial." This is the admirable wisdom of the astrologers; they have forgotten the libraries of the Gentiles, and they have seen almost no books of the Arabs and Hebrews yet.

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST ASTROLOGY: BOOK SIX BEGINS.
## Chapter one.
### In what order we must proceed in uprooting the foundations of the astrologers. Likewise, that it is impossible for all the stars to ever be restored to the same positions in which they once were.

<margin>
Aries
Leo
Sagittarius
Cancer
</margin>
**W**e have departed from the order and plan of our commentary, in which the primary roots of the astrologers were to be uprooted, before we cut down these summits of "great conjunctions" <note>An alignment of planets, particularly Jupiter and Saturn, which astrologers believed heralded major historical shifts.</note>, "great circles," and other things of that kind. For once those roots are removed, these summits must necessarily collapse. For who would put faith in those pronouncing through great conjunctions about the change of kingdoms and religions? To whom will it now be certain that those signs—Aries, Leo, Sagittarius, Cancer—in which they think Jupiter and Saturn meeting produce these things, are actually nothing? Or if there are any things of this kind in the sky, they are not in the places where they calculate them? Furthermore, that Saturn, Jupiter, and the rest of the planets do not cause events and the vicissitudes of lower things. And even if they did cause them, nothing is known about their efficiency, nature, or property, by either reason or experience. Since they proceed from one conjunction to another (if anything does indeed proceed from them), these things cannot be judged by those among whom the very rudiments of this art are still in doubt. For we shall see in the disputes that follow that it is not yet agreed which hour of conjunction should be considered: whether the beginning of the year in which it happens, or rather the time when the stars themselves meet. We shall see that they can attain neither of these times, which leaves the horoscope of the conjunction in doubt. Likewise, even if the horoscope were certain, nothing is yet certain regarding the method of arranging the "theme" <note>The structure of a birth chart or astrological map.</note>, but it remains uncertain where the beginnings of the twelve houses <note>term: Twelve Houses: The divisions of the sky in an astrological chart, each representing different areas of life (wealth, health, etc.). Pico argues their placement is arbitrary.</note> are correctly established; and even with those established, concerning their power...

the beginning, middle, and end of the place itself is not clear to them. Since these are unknown—just as it is unknown in which region of the sky they are joined—the nature of the conjunction <note>An alignment of planets.</note> cannot be known, as almost every variety of significance is reduced to the nature and property of the places which they call "houses" <note>The twelve divisions of the celestial sphere in astrology.</note>. And because in these great conjunctions they are accustomed to observe which planet is exalted above the other, we shall see that they still do not know what that "exaltation" is, which they commonly call "elevation." And since it matters very much which planet primarily rules the place of the conjunction of superior stars, or the eclipse of the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon.</note>, we shall see how all these impious laws and "authorities" of the planets are so controversial that there is almost no part of any sign for which there is anything certain among astrologers regarding its prince and lord. But it is not necessary here to enumerate the foundations of this art which will later be torn down. With these (as I was saying before), all those things must also fall which they dare to pronounce regarding divine miracles based on "great conjunctions" and other things of that kind. Truly, since they would especially offend the specific nature of religion with this part, every delay in removing this plague seemed like an eternity—especially because its efficacy seemed to be refuted by logic even while the rest of the astrological system remained intact; if this part concerning great conjunctions were proved false, then they would be defeated in their greatest and strongest claims. Now returning to where we departed, we will proceed to pull out the first foundations of this art by the roots in the following order. Nor should the widespread error among astrologers be passed over in silence, into which <margin>**The error of Albumasar and others**</margin> Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer.</note> and many others fell, thinking that at some point all the stars would be restored to the same positions, so that a completely similar disposition of the heavens and the position and relationship of all celestial bodies to one another would be found as it once was. From this, they think it would result that there would be the same things among us as once were: the same men, the same events, the same animals, and the same condition for all lower things. Some "astrologizers" <note>Those who mix astrology with theology.</note>, examining these things more deeply, are accustomed to whisper in the ear of their fellow-initiates: <margin>**An impious and cursed dogma**</margin> "this is that Christian resurrection which both the Hebrews and the Mohammedans <note>Muslims.</note> hope for; surely those greatest prophets were astronomers, but they hid these mysteries from the common people and the unlearned." For they thought there was a common number of years and days for the world by which the locations of the planets and stars could be certified, and when that number is completed, and all stars have returned to that very same point, because of this, all things will return to how they were. We, however, do not need to refute this insanity with many words, since <margin>**Haly and Ptolemy. Nicolaus Oresme.**</margin> Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer.</note> himself, in his commentary on the first book of the *Apotelesmata* <note>Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, following the opinion of Ptolemy himself saying the same, rebukes that idea with indignation; he says there is no person trained in arithmetic to whom the error of this notion would not be evident. Then, after him, Nicolaus Oresme <note>c. 1320–1382, a brilliant French philosopher and mathematician.</note>, a most acute philosopher and diligent mathematician, in his treatise *On the Proportions of Proportions*, demonstrated by mathematical reasons that this opinion is false and impossible—namely, the thought that the same position of the sky and stars that existed at another time could ever return. Since he has sufficiently fulfilled this task, I have decided to refer the reader to him, lest we do again what has already been done—something we have nowhere done until now.

## Chapter II. By what means astrologers say the influences of the stars vary: and how entirely absurd they are on the whole.

**G**reatly, if I am not mistaken—or to speak more truly—all the foundations of astrology are removed if it has been sufficiently proved that nothing is caused by the heavens, nor indicated by them, of those things which astrologers profess to predict from celestial observation. Among the reasons we used against them was one most powerful concerning the "momentary change" of celestial powers which they invent. We touched upon this in the previous dispute, but we have rightly delayed explaining it until this place, for it requires a peculiar and proper treatise of its own and carries great weight in tearing down astrology. From this, not only is that confirmed which has been proved so far—namely, that particular changes in lower things are not caused by the stars—but also that if those things do come from the sky, they nevertheless come in a way other than can be detected or signified by any observation of the celestial bodies.

He then begins a new chapter attacking the supposed momentary changes in celestial influence.</summary>

# BOOK SIX

<margin>Opinion of the astrologers</margin>
This, then, is what the astrologers say: that there is one power and potency of the constellations and stars at one hour, and another at another moment,
<margin>on the theories</margin>
while they are either in different parts of the sky—which the <term>moderns</term> <note>original: "neoterici"; Pico refers to medieval and contemporary astrologers who expanded on classical methods.</note> call "houses"—
<margin>concerning the variation</margin>
or are found in different signs (the twelve they have imagined); or because the planets themselves, separated by a certain interval of space,
<margin>and the powers</margin>
are joined together through various mutual radiations, which are commonly called the "aspects" <note>Geometric angles between planets, like a square or trine, believed to alter their influence.</note> 
<margin>of the stars.</margin>
of the planets. These are the primary ways (to omit certain newer ones) by which the <term>outflow</term> <note>original: "defluxus"; the supposed streaming of celestial influence down to the earthly realm.</note> and power of the heavens are thought to be changed: namely, by the house, the sign, and the diversity of the aspect. If they did not defend these things, they could not maintain their dogma regarding the efficacy of the stars—namely, that every change and diversity in <term>lower things</term> <note>Earthly affairs and the physical world.</note> originates from the stars. For if those stars were always of the same and immutable power—as we believe of all of them except the Moon—then identical or similar effects would necessarily always proceed from them. For they cannot attribute the diversity of effects to <term>lower causes</term> <note>Physical or environmental factors on Earth.</note> as we do, unless they also admit with us that they can divine nothing from heaven regarding this diversity, since heaven would then not be considered the author or cause. Therefore, they must find in heaven a diversity equal to the variety found in the effects of lower things.
<margin>Variety of things not due to the multitude of stars.</margin>
In this matter, the multitude of stars does not help them at all; for however many stars and planets there are, all are present to everyone being born. For this reason, no reason could be given as to why they would bestow different things on different people, rather than the same on all, unless something were imagined whereby the power and efficacy of the stars were different at different times. From this, it could then be easily gathered what things happen or arise at different times, based on the fact that the state of the stars would then receive a different condition from heaven—about which they themselves might pronounce, provided they have explored and understood the state of the stars at any known time.

***

<margin>General refutation</margin>
This is what we shall refute in the present book, since nothing can be thought more absurd or further from all reason than that there should be such great inconsistency and mutability in the nature of the superior bodies <note>The planets and stars.</note>—such as is not even seen in lower things, which are by their nature extremely fluid and changeable. For what is this <term>skin-shifting</term> <note>original: "versipellis"; implying a deceptive or cunning change of appearance.</note> change and chameleon-like inconstancy, that within a brief interval of time those most divine bodies should never be found similar to themselves or endowed with the same gifts? Let them tell us, I pray, what they think those properties of "sidereal outflows" are: do they proceed from the nature and substance of the stars themselves, or rather from some power sent in from the outside—whether drawn from the twelve places of heaven, from the signs, or from mutual radiations? If they answer the first, they cannot change those properties unless the substance of the stars itself is changed, which they themselves (I believe) will not grant. If they prefer the second, the celestial bodies will be the most ignoble of all bodies, doing almost nothing from their own nature, but doing everything according to a force and influence rushing in from the outside. Indeed, a physical substance is more perfect the more its resulting operation proceeds from the innermost substance of the one acting. And these things I have said generally and universally; for the insanity of this opinion shines out most clearly when we examine in detail the ways by which the powers of the stars are thought to be changed. In examining these, we shall follow the sequence of their errors and fables. Let us now begin to do this, starting from the twelve houses of heaven, for whose diversity they most fabulously devise that the outflow of both signs and stars is not only intensified or diminished, but changed into something entirely and fundamentally different.

### Chapter III. The houses of the astrologers are supported by no foundation: and how astrologers fight among themselves in explaining their powers.

<margin>D</margin>uodecim <note>The initial 'D' is historiated with a woodcut of a scholar at his desk.</note> No one is entirely ignorant of the twelve houses celebrated among astrologers, provided they are not completely unrefined in that art; it seems to me that almost every significance and property of the "outflows" is ultimately referred to these. For if you ask about the nature of any planet—what it might effect, or of what thing it is considered the giver and author—they will answer nothing definite or certain, unless it be according to the nature of the house in which the planet is found. Thus, almost everything they are accustomed to say in general about the properties of the planets seems to fall under those terms which have multiple meanings under a single common word. For what is more general in the logic of a planet than that it be good or bad—that is, the author of happiness, or in...

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>What a good and bad planet might effect.</margin>
...of happiness. And yet even this is not always firm or the same regarding the stars. They believe that a "good" planet harms when in a "bad" place, while a "bad" planet is beneficial when in a "good" place. Finally, to take Jupiter as a single example for all: when placed in the <term>ascendant</term> <note>original: "oriente"; the eastern horizon or First House, considered the most powerful and positive point in a horoscope.</note>, he differs as much from himself as he does when he has migrated a little above the ascendant into what they call the twelfth place <note>The 12th House, traditionally associated with "secret enemies" and misfortune.</note> of the sky, as fire differs from air or water, or as a hare differs from a donkey, or a donkey from an elephant. For in the ascendant he always decrees the greatest goods; yet in the twelfth house, which is adjacent to the ascendant, he often decrees great evils. It is especially characteristic of Jupiter to bestow wealth and riches; nevertheless, when located in the third or eighth house, he frequently dissipates the inheritance, even though by his own nature he makes men noble and wise. If he holds the eighth place, he will make men ignoble, and those whose fury—as <term>Maternus</term> <note>original: "Minus" in text, "Maternus" in margin; referring to Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century author of a major astrological compendium.</note> says—results in insanity. Finally, what is more characteristic of Jupiter than that he be considered a beneficial star, since he is called both the "greater fortune" among planets and the "great happiness of heaven"? But when established in the third place, Maternus says he is neither good nor bad. Located in the sixth place, he even decrees the greatest

<margin>Maternus</margin>
evils. Giving the reason for this, Maternus adds: "For the sixth place has the particular prerogative of malice, and whatever star is in that place—that is, the sixth—will borrow the greatest power for decreeing evils from the defect of the place." 

<margin>Refutation</margin>
Let us therefore ask the astrologers from where such a great, sudden, and perpetual <term>deluge</term> <note>original: "diluvio"; Pico uses this to describe a chaotic flood of changing influences.</note> comes to these divine bodies, which—because of the firmness and immutability of their substance—should rightly be believed to be most tenacious of their own nature and always like themselves. Certainly only two ways can be imagined by which this could happen. One is that we understand various powers and potencies to be implanted in those "places" [the houses], which they then flow into the stars situated within them; this is what the quoted words of Maternus seem to signify. The other is that we consider that the planet itself neither receives anything from elsewhere nor is affected in different ways, but rather that as the star’s disposition is exposed to the Earth through different [angles], the projection of its rays varies. From this, we might believe that the force and efficacy of the rays also vary. Whichever they prefer to say will convict them of insanity. 

<margin>Definition of "Place" from Aristotle’s *Physics*</margin>
For if they reply that powers of this kind flow from the *place* to the planets, we will ask what they think about "place": is it what some of the ancients said—that place is a void space separated from bodies? Or is it what Aristotle said—the "innermost surface of the surrounding body"? If it is space and interval, let them admit along with those same philosophers that such an interval has no powers or properties, since natural forms [essences] do not follow from mere dimensions and bare distance. If it is the innermost surface of the surrounding body, some power could indeed exist in this "place"—namely, the same power as the body whose surface it is, by which the surrounded body [the planet] is then affected. But what are these bodies, the edge of which will be considered the "place" of the stars? Certainly, whatever they say—whether it is the outermost sphere of all, or the one joined and closest to each individual star—there will be no part of such bodies that does not revolve through the East, the West, the top of the sky, the bottom, and the other places in a single day’s revolution. Therefore, if the power comes from those parts [of the surrounding sphere], the power of the East will not always be the same, nor will that of the West. Rather, according to the nature of the body currently located there, the power itself will also change. Finally, this cannot be said by them: because the twelve signs—which they say are in the houses as something different from the houses themselves, just as planets are in houses and in signs—those signs are described by them as being in the highest sphere of all. These signs, I say, in the highest sphere of all, are said by them to borrow their powers and nature from the house in which they are located (just like the planets). For they say that <term>Aries</term> <note>The first sign of the Zodiac.</note> does not do the same things in the East as it does in the West; and they say the same of other signs which are contained in the eighth sphere <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the sphere of the fixed stars.</note> (if there is no higher one) or in that which is considered the highest sphere. Since these highest spheres are surrounded by no other body, there is nowhere for us to imagine this "power of the houses" coming from, except from immobile space and interval occupied by bodies. But that is either nothing (if we believe Aristotle) or, if it is something, it is marked by no character of such efficacy or property. Therefore, to imagine different powers in those places—that is, in the different positions of the signs and planets—by which the stars placed therein are affected, is entirely alien to all reason. Nor will they say things less discordant or ridiculous if they use the second part of their defense: namely, that because of the diversity of position, the planets look at us with a different "face" and send down their rays to the Earth differently, and that the diversity of effects arises from this. For how ab-

->### BOOK SIX<-

...even a dull person who has barely tasted the basics of <term>optics</term> <note>The study of light and vision, which in the Renaissance was a branch of physics used to explain how stars influenced the Earth through their rays.</note> and philosophy will easily understand this: since there is no one who does not know that the quality of an effect is distinguished by the quality of the ray and the nature of the body radiating it, and not by some different circulation of the rays. This positioning can only be the cause of something happening more or less intensely. The Sun’s ray, in whatever manner or position it is cast down upon us, always heats and always illuminates; however, when it is closest to us—even to the point of being direct—it illuminates more and heats more. But when it descends obliquely, or refracted, or from a more remote place, it does the same things a direct or nearby ray does, but it does them less intensely. No other diversity can occur in the effect except that which follows the intensification or weakening of the heat and light itself.

Therefore, the dogma of the astrologers is insane when they think that the twelve signs of heaven and the planets positioned here provide us with brothers, or make us wretched, yet when they have moved just a little from there into the "house of brothers," they have no power and no significance. Or that they either give or snatch away riches, in one place reconcile friends, and in another stir up adversaries against us. In these cases, nothing of the nature of the sign or the planet has changed; only a variety of position has occurred.

But as we have said, whether this variety brings the rays closer to us, or pulls them more powerfully toward the earth, or joins or separates them from the rising sign, or mixes them more or less with the vapors of the earth—this might perhaps sharpen or blunt the force of the ray, but it certainly cannot change its nature. For this reason, neither the thing upon which the ray acts, nor the kind of effect it produces, is changed; it might perhaps dispose the effect to be firmer and more effective, or perhaps weaker, since the virtues and properties—whether they be elemental qualities or more hidden ones—follow the nature and species of the thing. Therefore, as long as that nature is not changed into another, the properties themselves cannot be changed so as to become different from one another.

However, if they could respond that experience proves them right, perhaps some faith would be given to them—either if an experiment could be produced to support these claims (which will be refuted below), or if they agreed among themselves on the same opinion. But since different authors ascribe different properties to the same places, they strip their own observations of the authority of a faithful witness.

The Arabs, and the Latins following in the footsteps of the Arabs, contend that the quality of slaves is indicated by the sixth place. The Egyptians and Ptolemy seek this from the place most distant from the sixth—that is, the twelfth. Regarding adverse health, whether it be a defect or a disease: Ptolemy does not seek it from the sixth place so much as from the seventh and the first, for he never uses the sixth in his <term>apotelesmata</term> <note>original: "apoteleſmatīs"; these are astrological judgments or predictions about the outcomes of a life.</note>, while he always uses the others. This is contrary to the common crowd of astrologers who, omitting those, seek every significance of this kind from the sixth.

As for what kind of children anyone will have: the Arabs and Latins pronounce judgment from the fifth place. Ptolemy uses the tenth and eleventh; and since no part of life is extended for anyone without the fifth, he uses the fourth as well. Paulus Alexandrinus observes the same. Mallius hangs the fortune of children and the prayers of parents upon the "rising" <note>the eastern horizon or 1st house</note>. Porphyry says that children are signified especially by the tenth, because from that part souls are sent down into bodies—and thus he beautifully confirms one fable with another fable. Ptolemy accepts the fortune of parents from no specific place. The Arabs use the fourth and sixth, as does Heliodorus. Others, as Abenzaghel reports, also use the ninth. 

The second place, according to the Alexandrian, signifies especially the <term>logic of business</term> <note>original Greek: "περιπρασεο λογον" (peri praseos logon); concerning the discourse of buying and selling.</note> and sudden hopes. Among the younger astrologers, it signifies almost none of these things, but rather riches; yet no judgment is found for these in Ptolemy's *Apotelesmata*, neither from the second nor from any other of the twelve places. Then Heliodorus takes the significance of those things even from the third. 

Regarding marriage, almost all predict from the west <note>the 7th house</note>; Heliodorus from the mid-heaven <note>the 10th house</note>; Ptolemy neglects both. Travels are judged from the ninth and third regions. Heliodorus, about to explore these, also examines the seventh; Ptolemy treats both this and those with equal contempt. Regarding parents, Heliodorus judges from the fourth place, Maternus from the tenth; Ptolemy judges from neither. They foresee friends in the eleventh; Heliodorus also in the third; Ptolemy in neither the eleventh nor the tenth. The rest take religion from the ninth. Likewise, Mallius takes it from the seventh, which he also calls the "Gate of Pluto." This is the name for the second house among the Egyptians. The same Mallius puts Saturn in charge of the fourth place, against the opinion of the others who assign him to the twelfth. But if we unroll the works of Mallius, who says he follows the ancients...

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>In religion/belief.</margin>
We find that a certain dogma was once imitated—than which no more ancient [account] has emerged among the Latins regarding celestial matters (or, to speak more truly, we have found an orator of fables) regarding the twelve "places" <note>original: "locis.xii." – these are the twelve "Houses" of a horoscope, which astrologers believe govern different aspects of life like wealth or health.</note> which is so different from every opinion reported today that the entire method of prediction is completely changed. For he [Manilius] placed Mars at the setting <note>The descendant or West.</note>, where others have decreed its primary seat elsewhere beneath the setting. What of those other twelve celestial places handed down by <term>Manilius</term> <note>original: "Mallio" – Pico is referring to Marcus Manilius, a 1st-century Roman poet who wrote the *Astronomica*, the earliest major Latin work on astrology.</note>? Are they not different from all the astrology now in our hands? Do they not vary every method of reasoning in prediction?

<margin>First house.</margin>
"The first lot," he says, "is given to Fortune: this is counted 
By that title through art, because it contains within itself 
The nearest foundations of the house and all things clinging to the house. 
What manner of life is in the servants, what agreement in the fields; 
And that it is given to compose great masses of works 
As the wandering stars of the shining heaven harmonize."

<margin>Second [house].</margin>
"After this is the place of military service: where whatever in arms, 
And whatever for those traveling among foreign cities 
One is accustomed to receive: it is encompassed by a single title."

<margin>Third [house].</margin>
"The third station is to be numbered for urban labors. 
This also is a kind of military service in civil acts. 
It holds the composed bonds of parental faith, 
It forms friendships, and shows how many duties often falling 
In vain, and what great rewards of worship might happen 
When the world sounds in harmony with the adjacent stars."

<margin>Fourth [house].</margin>
"In the fourth, nature has located the work of legal judgments 
And the fortune of the forum: the patron <note>A legal advocate or lawyer.</note> pouring out words, 
The defendant hanging on his tongue; and the authority of the speaker 
Placed over the people and stripping bare the hidden laws, 
And settling disputes with his own brow. 
Since a judge truly calls for nothing more than himself, 
Whatever eloquence achieves among the proposed laws, 
He has granted this whole part into one section. 
And however the ruling stars behave, so it flows."

<margin>Fifth [house].</margin>
"The fifth step is dedicated through the signs to marriage. 
It holds partners and companions: and together with the guest 
It is joined, and a similar treaty joining friends."

<margin>Sixth [house].</margin>
"In the sixth seat, a rich abundance is numbered, 
And the health of things joined to it: one of which warns 
How much use might happen; the other [warns] how long-lasting 
As the stars decline their strength and govern the temples."

<margin>Seventh [house].</margin>
"The seventh is judged as dreadful with savage dangers: 
If the stars located through the signs subscribe poorly."

<margin>Eighth [house].</margin>
"Nobility holds the eighth, in which the condition of honor 
Is established: and the measure and kind of fame: and grace 
Under a beautiful pretext." <margin>Ninth [house].</margin> "The ninth place occupies every 
Doubtful lot of the Fates, and parental fears, 
And it nourishes all the mixed words of those entering."

<margin>Tenth [house].</margin>
"Neighboring this will be that which contains the action of life. 
In which the character of servants, and of what kind every..."
