Let the house also be formed with examples in a certain order.
Let the servants, arranged for their own duties, depart.
<margin>Eleventh [house]</margin>
The pre-eminent eleventh part is located in the lot,
Which always governs our sum and our strength.
Which height stands now free from diseases,
Now oppressed; and the stars warn of all things in the world.
Not otherwise does it demand the time or the type of healing 
For itself: or at whose time it provides
Assistance: and to mix the healthy juices of life.
<margin>Twelfth [house]</margin>
The last part, concluding the whole sum in order,
Is the labor for attaining things, which contains every
Effect of vows, and the studies and arts which each man
Proposes for himself and his own, lest these be in vain;
Whether it brings duty: it flatters every nod,
Whether it tries harsh quarrels through litigation in the forum;
Whether one seeks fortune on the sea and follows the winds,
Or seeks a full grain harvest and a crop overcoming the granaries,
Or seeks Bacchus <note>The god of wine, used here to represent the grape harvest.</note> flowing through the rich new wine.
In this part, days and these moments will be given,
If the stars following through the signs will agree well.

Thus far Manilius <note>original: "Mallius" – Marcus Manilius, a 1st-century Roman poet whose work *Astronomica* is the earliest major Latin text on astrology.</note>, whose opinion it is clear differs from all the astrology now in use. But nonetheless, I believe he has been understood by no one yet among those who make themselves Manilius’s interpreters and followers. In such a great variety of opinions, then, what is the reliability of the experiment, especially when another greater problem is added: namely, the beginning and ends of the <term>houses</term> <note>original: "domo℞" (domorum) – the twelve divisions of the sky in a horoscope, each supposedly governing a different life area.</note>? In what way ought one to divide the established knot <note>A metaphor for the difficult problem of calculating where one house ends and another begins (the "cusps").</note>? But some think one way and others another, as we have declared in another book; yet this ought to have been investigated before an observation regarding their properties was established for making the experiment. It is so far from being certain or established that finally some observation can be offered which might compel us and, by reasons leading to assent, cause us to decline. Whatever Ptolemy and others have believed, we conclude—the evidence of reasoning compelling us to this—that it is ridiculous and false either that there are any properties in these "places," or that the flow and efficiency of the planets are changed by their diversity.

### Chapter IV. Concerning the twelve signs, which were devised by mathematicians for ease of calculation. Likewise, that astrologers have erred in multiple ways regarding these same signs.

<margin>Against Albumasar, Haly, Avenazr</margin>
Indeed, they observe that division and the boundaries of the signs as if they were prescribed by laws of nature, so that they think two planets have more in common even if they are twenty degrees apart, provided they are placed in the same sign, than if one should hold the last parts of Aries and the other be found in the beginnings of Taurus, even though they are separated by the smallest space. Between these, however, not even the interval of a finger’s width falls transversely. But if anyone should grant that this number of signs is from nature, and not devised by mathematicians for ease of calculation—but established by philosophical reason such as <term>Albumasar</term> <note>Ja'far ibn Muhammad Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi (787–886), a leading Persian astrologer whose works were highly influential in Medieval Europe.</note> brings forward, namely that there are twelve signs because there are four elements, each of which is divided into three parts: middle, first, and last—I could indeed respond that this reason is no less ridiculous and frivolous than that mathematical one. But the authors of this division were not moved by such a conjecture at all: just as we have declared above by the testimony of <term>Haly</term> <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and <term>Avenazr</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note>, so it can easily be demonstrated by reasons. For even if that conjecture holds for the signs, what shall be said of the distribution of signs into thirty parts <note>The 30 degrees that make up each of the 12 signs of the Zodiac.</note>? What of the portion of parts into sixty minutes? For those who would bring a physical reason for these, or by what...

<summary>Pico concludes his citation of the poet Manilius to demonstrate that ancient and modern astrologers cannot agree on the meaning of the "Twelve Houses." He then argues that the division of the Zodiac into twelve signs is a man-made mathematical convenience rather than a physical law of nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the mathematical foundations of astrology. In the preceding section, he argued that the division of the Zodiac into twelve signs was an arbitrary human invention rather than a physical reality. Here, he explores how astrologers have layered increasingly complex—and, in his view, increasingly absurd—properties onto these imaginary divisions.</meta>

### DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY
<meta>catchword: another.</meta>

In this way, they will justify the actions of the mathematicians <note>In this context, "mathematicians" refers to technical astronomers who calculated planetary positions.</note> who, regarding those places, estimated no natural properties, but sought numbers more convenient for calculation. From this error, or perhaps from a certain opportunity for deception, astrologers began deciding on these matters as if the signs possessed entirely separate powers, and as if nature, rather than human choice, had divided them in turn. It is well known how they ascribe various properties to various parts and even to the individual minutes <note>A "minute" is 1/60th of a degree in the 360-degree circle of the Zodiac.</note> of the same sign. Hence, they declare some parts to be "bright," others "dark," others related to the Sun, others to Mars, and others to different planets. They even tell fables about the minutes themselves,
<margin>Aesculapius</margin>
as when "Aesculapius" <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus or mythical Egyptian wisdom; the *Myriogenesis* was a lost astrological text attributed to him.</note> wrote the *Myriogenesis*, which he hid as if it were a mystery. In it, he handed down the idea that every single minute of the celestial flow possesses a specific property. But just as the calculation was made by mere will according to that second partitioning, 
<margin>Maternus</margin>
so the principal division of the twelve signs of the whole Zodiac itself took its origin from nowhere else <note>Pico is citing Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century astrological writer, to show that even the "authorities" admit these divisions are artificial.</note>. We have already declared that the division of these signs has no efficacy and is void; thus, the insanity of astrologers is refuted here. They claim that a planet is "changed" depending on the condition of the sign through which it travels. For they establish the "houses" and "exaltations" <note>Technical terms for signs where a planet is thought to be particularly powerful.</note> of the planets according to these mathematical signs, not according to the actual <term>constellations</term> <note>The physical groupings of stars. Pico distinguishes between the "sign" (an abstract 30-degree block) and the "image" or "constellation" (the actual stars).</note>, which we showed in the previous book can only be imagined and have no physical solidity. 

Because of this, perhaps the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers.</note>, who did not use these abstract signs, made no "houses" for the planets. Among them, Leo was not the home of the Sun, nor Cancer of the Moon, nor Libra or Taurus of Venus, nor Pisces and Sagittarius of Jupiter, and so on for the rest. They observed only the "heights" of the stars, relating them not to the abstract signs but to the physical constellations. Thus, among the Chaldeans, Saturn possesses nothing in Capricorn or Aquarius, but holds power only in Libra and Scorpio. Otherwise, if Ptolemy and others were to refer the houses of the planets to the physical constellations (which they do not), their reasoning would not square: for Mars has the greatest affinity with the stars that actually form the image of Taurus—so much so that no other planet compares—yet in the astrological system, Mars is said to be "debilitated" or "thrown down" in Taurus. 

Therefore, all these affinities—the houses, exaltations, <term>terms</term> <note>Subdivisions of a sign assigned to different planets.</note>, triplicities, <term>monomoiriai</term> <note>A system where every single degree of a sign is assigned to a specific planet.</note>, decans, <term>faces</term> <note>original: "hydroprosopias," likely referring to the decan faces.</note>, and the rest—receive their supposed power from these abstract signs. It has been sufficiently proven, I believe, that no force can flow to the planets from these things if they are entirely imaginary, not natural, and not effective. One must marvel at those who wish to bolster astrological opinion by a "likeness to plants," saying that planets "smell" of the qualities of the Zodiac in which the seeds of things are dispersed, just as plants reflect the taste of the earth they grow in. 

But this comparison is very dissimilar. Plants are indeed nourished by the earth and therefore reflect its taste, but the planets are not fed by the Zodiac. Although every kind of living thing shines there, the planets are not attached to the Zodiac like the roots and bushes of the earth; they are separated from it by an immense chasm and interval of space. 
<margin>Panætius and Plotinus</margin>
For this reason, Panætius <note>A Stoic philosopher who famously doubted astrology.</note> and Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism, who argued the stars were signs but not causes.</note> especially mock those who think a "contagion" can reach the stars from the Zodiac across such a vast gap. We are moved not so much by the immense space that lies between them, but by the nature of the things themselves: real and natural bodies cannot be affected by imaginary ones, and shining stars cannot be changed by non-shining spaces (not to say by nothingness). 

<margin>Source of the deception</margin>
But it is easy to see what deceived the astrologers here. Because the Sun, when positioned in the constellation of Leo, heats the earth more violently, and when coming to Aries, it "restores" the world (Spring), it seemed to them that the Sun had a "kinship" with Leo and Aries. Because its power is felt more strongly every year when it travels through those signs, they established Leo as the Sun's "home" and Aries as its "kingdom." Led by this conjecture regarding the Sun, they thought they should decide similarly for other signs: that a planet would be more powerful in one and less in another. And with a most "beautiful" reasoning, they distributed two houses to each planet, except for the Sun and Moon, for whom one "royal palace" each was enough. For regarding the Sun, they decided (for the reason given) that it should obtain Leo as its home, where it exercises its greatest strength in the burning heat. It seemed reasonable that the neighboring house should belong to the Moon, which is closest to us. Its circle is indeed most proximate to us, so they assigned Cancer as the Moon's home. Then, according to the order of the spheres in which the planets are carried, they distributed two houses to each on either side...

<summary>Pico argues that astrological "houses" and planetary "affinities" are arbitrary human inventions rather than physical realities. He mocks the idea that planets are "influenced" by the empty space of the Zodiac, noting that ancient authorities like the Chaldeans, Panætius, and Plotinus rejected these concepts.</summary>
<keywords>Zodiac signs vs. constellations, houses of the planets, exaltations, Aesculapius, Myriogenesis, Chaldeans, Plotinus, Panætius, planetary properties, ancient astronomy</keywords>

Having previously argued that the twelve signs are arbitrary human inventions, he now critiques the "dignities" (the assignment of planets to specific signs as their 'houses') and the conflicting systems used by different cultures, such as the Chaldeans, Egyptians, and Greeks. He concludes by introducing the topic of "aspects"—the geometric angles between planets.</meta>

->**BOOK SIX**<-

# BOOK SIX

...on the one hand to Mercury, who is believed to be adjacent to the Moon, they assigned Gemini, and on the other Virgo; to Venus they gave Taurus on one side and Libra on the other; Aries on one side and Scorpio on the other they granted to Mars; to Jupiter they gave Pisces and Sagittarius; and to Saturn, Aquarius and Capricorn. They founded their dogmas upon these persuasive arguments—which lack even rhetorical probability—yet these were handed down by their successors with such great authority that they are received with almost greater reverence than the oracles. 

In these matters, first observe how one remaining point is as criminal as it is full of both ignorance and sluggishness: for the fact that the Sun in Leo warms us more does not arise from the nature of the sign it traverses, but occurs because of its site and position, since from that place it strikes the earth more directly, being closer to our regions. Otherwise, if a quality received from the sign caused this effect, it would do the same among all nations, since the same signs exist for everyone. But in truth, at the time when the Sun scorches the lands situated toward the North <note>original: "Aglonem," referring to the North Wind or the North</note> while in Leo, it is cold for those who inhabit the southern regions; for them, it is hot when it reaches Aquarius, under which it pours out ice, water, and rain for us. This is clearly because the more it approaches us, the further it is removed from them, and conversely, it bends its path toward them whenever it departs from us. 

But what if they contend that they were led not so much by that argument as by other experiments, through which it was observed that a planet has more or less power in one place or another? Perhaps there would be some faith in this if the founders of the true art had handed down consistent findings; however, I tell these new professors that the experiments of the Chaldeans—I mean the Magi who, in the open fields, claim to have observed the celestial bodies for so many thousands of years—never placed any faith in these "houses" <note>The "house" or domicile is the sign where a planet is said to be most powerful.</note> we mentioned above. Why then, in such diligent and long-lasting observations, did they never find Mars to be strong in Scorpio and weak in Taurus, or Saturn powerful in Capricorn and feeble in Cancer? The same should be understood for the rest of the planets. 

Furthermore, although the same sign is divided into so many "terms" <note>original: "finibus," specific degrees within a sign ruled by different planets</note>, so many <term>decans</term> <note>10-degree subdivisions of a sign</note>, so many <term>monomiria</term> <note>individual degrees, from the Greek for "single part"</note> among the Egyptians, and <term>dodecathemoria</term> <note>subdivisions of 2.5 degrees, or "twelfth-parts"</note> among the Chaldeans, there is no agreement among them regarding these boundaries. Ptolemy ignores the decans, which the Indians and Egyptians divide differently; the Arabs do not know the monomiria; the Greeks mock them, yet the Egyptians use them in every prediction. I pass over the use of the twelfth-parts, which are more common among the Chaldeans; yet, as Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century astrological writer</note> writes, a planet performs in its own "terms" what it performs in its "house," and grants in a decan what it would in terms and house, or at least those things that are nearest and most similar. Since these things are so, what faithful and consistent experience can there be regarding which part of the Zodiac a planet travels through as a ruler or as an exile, or whether it be found powerful or weak? 

Add to this the various opinions about the signs: whether they refer to the "new sphere" <note>The moving Zodiac (tropical)</note> or are described according to the eighth sphere <note>The fixed stars (sidereal)</note>; one person wants Saturn to rule a certain part, another wants Jupiter, and another wants some other planet. Moreover, some use those signs which they believe to move, others those which do not move. Regarding these opinions, nothing is so settled or predetermined that 
<margin>Abraham</margin>
Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century scholar and astrologer</note> in his book *On Nativities* commanded that a double chart <note>original: "thema," an astrological figure or horoscope</note> be made: one for the moving signs and another for the fixed ones. By this variety of the chart, the whole reasoning of the predictions is varied. Thus, all authority of experience is weakened; later it will be demonstrated that no experience can be had concerning these matters, or if it could be had, it has not yet been obtained.

## Chapter V. What the opinion of the astrologers is regarding aspects, and what the rational part is.

The <note>Decorative initial C</note> opinion of the astrologers concerning the signs and the twelve houses of heaven has now been refuted; there remains the third way by which they imagine powers and influences are changed, which is commonly called "aspects." For they think that if Saturn, for example, is distant from Jupiter by 60 degrees—that is, by two whole signs—it affects and moves the lower worlds differently than if it were distant by 90 degrees from the same star, which is an interval of three signs. They say that in the former distance, Saturn looks at Jupiter with a "hexagonal radiation," which they call the **sextile** aspect, because the intervening space is the sixth part of the Zodiac; in the latter, they behold each other in a **square**, because they are separated from each other by a fourth of the Zodiac. Similarly, there are other properties for both stars if one is 120 degrees from the other, from which "trigonal radiation" emerges—this is the **trine** aspect. There are yet others if they are simultaneously positioned diametrically opposite...

Having just discussed the arbitrary nature of planetary "houses," he now focuses on why the distance between planets shouldn't logically change their fundamental nature or influence.</meta>

->**DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY**<-

...meet either in the same site or place; and what we have said of Jupiter and Saturn should be understood as being said of all of them: that according to their always-varying distance from one another, their power and efficiency are changed. They claim it changes to such an extent that when they are distant by certain intervals—that is, in a **trine** <note>An aspect of 120 degrees, considered harmonious.</note> or **sextile** <note>An aspect of 60 degrees.</note>—their entire influence is good and healthful. On the other hand, when positioned at another certain distance—that is, either in a **square** <note>An aspect of 90 degrees, considered tense.</note> or **opposition** <note>An aspect of 180 degrees.</note>—they possess rays that are most harmful, or at least never very beneficial. They claim that from this diversity of intervals, not only is the goodness or malice of the influence changed, but also the very type and manner of its effect. These are the ravings of astrologers regarding the "aspects" of the planets, which any upright person will condemn immediately upon hearing them, even without a counter-argument. For it can be defended by no reason that, from the mere diversity of distance and interval, the nature and properties of two causes working together toward the same end could be so radically altered.

But first, I ask them this: do they intend for these things they say about aspects to refer to the planets themselves, or only to the effects of the planets?
<margin>A two-part argument</margin>
That is, when they speak of Jupiter being "provoked" by Mars through square rays, or Venus being "cherished" by the trine radiation of Jupiter, do they mean that the actual bodies of the planets are moved by these kinds of good or evil affections? Or do they mean that the planets themselves suffer nothing from one another and feel no such mutations, but rather that this manner of speaking signifies what they do toward us and in what way they move the bodies subject to them? For whether they answer one way or the other, they fall into a thousand snares and a thousand difficulties from every side.

<margin>That the planets do not harm one another. Job, Aristotle.</margin>
For if they think the planets are moved by one another and, as if exercising friendships and hatreds, now cherish one another in a friendly embrace and now pursue and attack in a hostile manner with the points of their rays, not only will the divine **Job** cry out—in whose book we read that God "makes peace in his high places" <note>original: "deum facere pacem in excelsis suis"; Job 25:2</note>—but so will his own **Aristotle** and the entire family of the **Peripatetics**. Among them, it is certain that the superior celestial bodies are changed only by their variety of place. Those qualities found below the Moon <note>The "sublunary" sphere, where things are subject to change, decay, and the four elements.</note> neither reach up there nor depart from there.

But if they wish to concede that such qualities do exist there—especially regarding harmful qualities—they should be hissed out of every gathering of philosophers. They clearly seem to be entirely ignorant of the nature of the celestial homeland if they think anything can exist within it that could do or suffer injury. Therefore, if any "passion" <note>In the philosophical sense of *passio*, meaning "being acted upon" or "undergoing change."</note> is to be admitted in the stars, it should be called a "perfection" rather than a passion. This is like when the Moon is illuminated by the Sun; she "suffers" from him in no other way than one who receives a benefit suffers from the benefactor. To suggest, then, that a star is harmed by another, or besieged, or infected, or made weaker or worse—rendered harmful instead of beneficial, or weak instead of powerful—is as far removed from all truth as all celestial nature is removed from all evil.

Furthermore, if the stars can suffer injury, surely the nobler and more perfect ones should not suffer it from the less noble. Thus, at the very least, one must conclude that not all things can be mutually affected and moved by all others, but only certain ones by certain others, so that some only act while others only suffer. Otherwise, how are they not ashamed?
<margin>The power of the Sun.</margin>
They reduce the Sun—the ruler and king of the planets, the supreme celestial fountain of both light and power—to such a rank and order that he too might languish, overcome by the rays of others, or turn out to be hardly healthful. Thus, while every power of the planets is derived from him, he is said to "suffer from his own weapon," as the saying goes.

But let us set aside all these things, which perhaps do not seem absurd to them, and let us assume for the sake of the planets that they are affected and moved as they wish. Let them answer this: what reason is there that stars which are very close move each other not at all, but once they have become more distant, they begin to feel one another and suffer mutually? For this is how they usually define things when they speak of aspects. For if Jupiter holds **Cancer** and Mars holds **Leo**, between which signs nothing lies, they say the stars of Jupiter and Mars are *asyndeta* <note>original: "asyndeta," a Greek term meaning "unlinked" or "disconnected." In astrology, signs that do not "see" each other.</note>—that is, joined by no coupling of rays or aspects. But then, when Mars has moved much further away from Jupiter and traveled to **Virgo**, they will think that Mars participates in Jupiter, and Jupiter in Mars. What could be said that is more absurd than this, or further from all philosophy? For it is a most common principle that everything which acts upon another does so more strongly the closer it is...

<summary>Pico argues that the astrological concept of "aspects" is logically flawed, asserting that celestial bodies are immutable and cannot harm or "provoke" one another. He specifically mocks the idea that planets have no influence when adjacent but suddenly exert power when moved to specific geometric angles like trines or squares.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical deconstruction of "aspects" in astrology. Having established that mere distance should not change a planet's nature, he now argues that "aspects" are simply another name for the physical radiation of light and power, which should follow the laws of nature rather than the arbitrary rules of astrologers.</meta>

<page-num>210</page-num>
->BOOK SIX<-
<sig>g iiii</sig>

# BOOK SIX

<margin>Aspect is nothing other than radiation.</margin>
...the less a thing is acted upon, the more effectively it can act. Therefore, this thing which the younger generation calls an **aspect** <note>In astrology, an "aspect" is the specific angular distance between two planets, such as 90 or 120 degrees.</note> is nothing other than **radiation**. It was also called this by the ancients: the propagation of a planet's own light and power into another (an "elucidation," if I may call it that). How can it be that this radiation is ineffective on the bodies that are nearest to it, yet effective on those most remote? What could possibly persuade them that a ray, depending on whether it is poured out from a closer or more distant interval, should turn out to be of one nature or another? If we follow true reason, no other difference can arise from this distance except that the planet's ray strikes the subject either more weakly or more strongly. Why its very property or quality should be changed is a cause that can neither be imagined nor devised. For even if the number of intervening parts varies due to the difference in interval, or if the planets themselves happen to take on a different geometric shape in relation to one another, the power of natural things is not varied by a diversity of numbers and shapes. Natural virtues do not proceed from numbers and figures; rather, they proceed from **natural forms**. It is through these forms that the figures themselves—the stable, native ones, not the accidental ones arising from motion—move and vary things.

No fewer difficulties arise if they think the diversity of radiation should be considered not in the bodies of the planets, but in their effects. For instance, they might say that the stars suffer nothing from one another, but that the varying ratio of distance between them causes the flowing rays to mix differently; and thus, from the various diversities of the mixture, different effects proceed.
<margin>That different radiations do not produce different effects.</margin>
If they answer this way, we could first object on the authority of **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) whom Pico frequently cites.</note> that rays flowing down from heaven cannot be so mixed together as to produce a new virtue or form. This is because rays are not physical bodies, nor liquids, nor qualities fixed to bodies. They do not behave like substances that can be "stained" or changed in their condition by a mixture. Therefore, it is probable to that philosopher that what happens to many qualities—where they coalesce from a certain mass or mixture into a single form—does not happen to rays. Such mixing usually involves the destruction of the simple and individual qualities that flow into it, which is something no one would easily imagine happening to celestial rays.

But let us grant them that rays are mixed. Let them demonstrate how it is that rays mix differently when they flow from stars at different distances from each other. The only difference that could arise (as we said above) is this: rays emanating from bodies that are closer and more joined will mix more intimately and better, while those from stars that are separated and remote will cohere with more difficulty. Yet this does not please the astrologers, for they grant no "commerce" <note>An astrological term for the interaction or "sharing" of influence between planets.</note> between the rays of planets placed in adjacent signs, but they grant a massive interaction between stars separated by vast and immense regions of the sky. 

Furthermore, if the ratio of either a **diameter opposition** <note>180 degrees.</note>, a **square** <note>90 degrees.</note>, or a **triangular** <note>120 degrees.</note> figure creates a diversity in the property of the rays, this cannot be defended unless we say the bodies of the planets themselves change their condition based on that variety of figures. This is because the virtue and property of a ray comes from nowhere else but the nature of the radiating body. 
<margin>Where the variety of figures is located.</margin>
Nor is that variety of geometric figures located anywhere other than among the bodies themselves from which the rays descend to us. The further they recede from those bodies, the less they preserve that geometric relationship to one another, until, upon touching the earth, they converge into a **cone**. Thus, rays which flowed from opposite sources are united into a single point here with us. Therefore, when they mix, they are no longer entangled in triangular or square patterns, such that the nature of the mixture could be changed by that variety of patterns. Astrologers will be forced to retreat to this: they must say either that there is a property in the rays by which the stars from which they emanated were arranged in such a geometric relationship—and thus the stars change their nature based on their configuration (which has been refuted)—or, if the stars themselves do not change, they must admit that the virtue of the rays flowing from them is likewise the same and unchanged.

### Chapter VI. Various theories of aspects are recounted and refuted.

->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>Refutation</margin>
The ancients, whom Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the influential *Mathesis*.</note> imitated, derived the logic of aspects from numbers. They argued that planets are said to be joined if they are separated by a specific number of parts <note>The "parts" refer to the 360 degrees of the zodiac circle.</note> such that, when multiplied, that number accounts for all the parts of the heavens. Thus, they claim an "opposition" radiation occurs at an interval of 180 parts, because that number doubled completes the full number of 360 parts. Likewise, the **trine** <note>An aspect of 120 degrees, forming a triangle.</note> consists of 120 parts, because if you triple these parts, you again account for all the parts of the sky. The **square** radiation <note>An aspect of 90 degrees, forming a right angle.</note> requires ninety parts, which if you double <note>original: "duplicaueris"; Pico likely means "double and double again" or refers to the 180-degree diameter, as 90 x 4 makes 360.</note>, you collect the sum of 360. The **sextile** <note>An aspect of 60 degrees, forming a hexagon.</note> is computed at 60 parts, which are a sixth part of all the degrees. But this reasoning is far too sleepy and lazy; for by that same logic, they should make an aspect at 72 degrees, because multiplied five times they complete 360 degrees. They should do the same at 45 degrees, since this number is an eighth part of all the degrees of the sky. But Aboasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> says those numbers have another privilege: they not only count the parts of the sky, but when multiplied, they also count the number of the signs. For in the sextile, he counts two signs; in the trine, four; in the square, three; and in the opposition, six. For twice six, three times four, four times three, and six times two all complete the number of twelve signs. But this confirmation is also frivolous. For by similar logic, stars that are 30 parts apart would be configured toward each other, because if you look at the number of parts, you have a twelfth of the parts of the sky, and of the signs, you also have a twelfth portion. Finally, the reasons brought by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> regarding geometric figures do not prove his point, since the harmonies of these shapes do not produce different properties in natural things. Rather, those who use them fall into the error condemned by Aristotle: treating physical things as if they were mathematical objects. Perhaps you see, Avenrodan <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and commentator on Ptolemy.</note> says, that Ptolemy, after providing the mathematical reason for aspects, brought another reason from nature.

<margin>
Rejection of
Ptolemy's
mathematical
reasoning.
Avenrodan
</margin>
<margin>Ptolemy's natural reason.</margin>
The reason he brings is of this sort: the sextile and trine radiations are beneficial because they come from signs of the same kind—that is, either masculine or feminine. This means the planets bound together in those patterns are so arranged that if one is in a feminine sign, the other is also in a feminine sign; if one is in a masculine sign, the other is likewise in a masculine sign. Conversely, the square and opposition radiations are harmful because they emerge from signs of different kinds. This reasoning of Ptolemy's is not only weak, but it destroys itself.

<margin>
First reason.
Second reason.
</margin>
Firstly, this is because those signs are truly nothing at all, as we shall reveal in the following books. Secondly, even if they do exist, they are not distinguished by those marks of qualities or sexes, such that some can be called masculine, others feminine, some fiery, and others airy—as has already been sufficiently proven above.

<margin>
Third reason.
Fourth reason.
</margin>
Finally, whatever their condition might be, the planets cannot be changed by them, as we have demonstrated below. For now, I will not make a legal dispute over these points. But let us most clearly demonstrate how these ideas, like all their theories, fight against themselves. For if what he assumes is true, the **opposition** radiation—which is considered most harmful—should instead be granted as good, since it also never occurs except in signs of the same kind. For Aries (the Ram) and Libra (the Scales) are of the same kind; likewise Cancer (the Crab) and Capricorn (the Goat-Horn), and all others that face each other diametrically. It is quite a wonder that Ptolemy did not see this, and that a man otherwise so ingenious should hallucinate in a matter so clear and obvious.

<margin>Fifth reason.</margin>
If he had remembered what he said elsewhere, he would have seen that his reasoning does not proceed but is contrary to his own precepts. For in the third book of that same work, he thinks that between signs not only of the same sex but even of the same quality, the configuration is sometimes not sextile (that is, good) but square (that is, bad)—as when they are signs of "oblique" or "short" ascension. Likewise, those which are of different kinds may have a sextile affinity rather than a square one. Thus, he would compose a square radiation between Gemini (the Twins) and Aquarius (the Water-Bearer), but a sextile one between Taurus (the Bull) and Aquarius. If this is true, how can the goodness or malice of the configurations arise from the affinity or discord of the signs? This is a difficulty that must be faced by all those who measure the spaces of radiations not by the zodiac but by the parts of the celestial equator, which the greatest part of astrologers observe. Yet all of them (since they are marvelously thoughtless) when they speak of malice...

<summary>Pico deconstructs the mathematical and "natural" justifications for astrological aspects, arguing that the selection of specific angles like 60° or 90° is arbitrary and that Ptolemy's gender-based logic for these angles is self-contradictory.</summary>

<meta>Continuing the previous page’s discussion, Pico has just dismissed the numerical foundations of astrological aspects (angles between planets). He now turns to specific justifications provided by the famous Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar and others who try to link these angles to physical phenomena or musical harmony.</meta>

BOOK SIX

When they must account for the malice or goodness of aspects, they derive their reasoning from no other source than the kinship or diversity of the signs. <margin>Another reasoning by Abu Ma'shar.</margin> Abu Ma'shar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), known in Latin as Albumasar, was one of the most influential Persian astrologers in the Middle Ages.</note> offers another reason that he considers "natural" regarding the aspects. He says that the **opposition** <note>An angle of 180 degrees.</note> is confirmed by the fullness of light which the Moon attains when it is opposite the Sun. <margin>Refutation.</margin> He claims the **square** <note>An angle of 90 degrees.</note> appears in the motion of planets from their apse <note>The highest or lowest point in a planet's orbit.</note>, for when they are ninety degrees distant, they change their course. The **trine** <note>An angle of 120 degrees.</note> is seen in the superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> which, when removed 120 degrees from the Sun, begin to move backward if they were moving forward, or forward if they were moving backward. The quantity of the **sextile** <note>An angle of 60 degrees.</note>, he says, corresponds to half the diameter of the circle, as well as the distance of the houses of Venus from the houses of the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon.</note>.

In this way, he has badly stitched together a patchwork quilt from a thousand rags: seeking the opposition from the Moon, the square from the apse, the trine from the superior planets, and the sextile from Venus—and poorly assigning all things to all. For what logic is there that because the Moon is filled with the Sun’s light across a diameter, all planets should be coupled by this same distance, not only to the Sun but among themselves? <margin>Refutation.</margin> And even if the superior planets change their course at the Sun's trine, why should this interval have the power to change the influence of planets—not only the superior ones but the inferior ones as well—and not just in relation to the Sun, but relative to the planets themselves?

What is more, that rule is not even permanent for the superior planets. For Mars, as Paul <note>Paul of Alexandria, a 4th-century astrological author.</note> and Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyros, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> write, sometimes halts to move backward when it is located eighty-four degrees ahead of the Sun, <margin>Paul and Porphyry.</margin> not only without waiting for the trine, but before even completing the square. Furthermore, if they gathered the power of the trine from that change in the superior planets at the Sun's trine, it should have been numbered among the "bad" rather than the "good" radiations; for every superior planet at the Sun's trine is "unhappy" if we believe Paul and Heliodorus <note>Heliodorus, an astrological writer and brother of Olympiodorus.</note>. For they all say: <term>αστερεσ ο στηριζον τεσ κακοι</term> <note>original: "αστερεσ ο στηριζον τεσ κακοι" (asteres hoi sterizontes kakoi)</note>, which means "the stationary stars are bad and unhappy," whether they are in their first station or their second. But all these things are of such obvious shallowness that they hardly need further refutation.

<margin>Another reasoning for aspects devised by certain "moderns."</margin>
Finally, another reason was devised by certain modern thinkers based on musical consonances; they claim that the radiations of the planets either harmonize with one another or clash, following a certain similarity to musical harmonies. They say it is proven among musicians by both reason and experience that the third and fifth voices harmonize with the first, but the fourth and seventh do not. What then, if planets distant from each other by equal spaces are found to be sometimes in good and sometimes in bad harmony? The **sextile** radiation corresponds to the third voice; the **trine** to the fifth; and the **square** to the fourth, since there are as many signs mediating the intervals here as there are voices there.

These things are certainly "pretty" and have a veneer of probability to those who have only "saluted philosophy from the threshold" <note>A Latin idiom meaning those who have only a superficial or amateur knowledge of a subject.</note>. But we, setting aside these similarities between such diverse kinds of things, shall demonstrate that this reasoning has no efficacy and that the comparison and similarity do not hold. Among musicians, if a voice does not harmonize with another, it is dissonant; <margin>Refutation.</margin> but among astrologers, many spaces are (so to speak) "mute" to each other—that is, they neither harmonize nor clash. For example, the second voice is counted by musicians among the dissonant no less than the fourth, seventh, or eleventh. Yet among astrologers, the second sign does not "discord" with the first, but rather emits no voice at all. The fifth and seventh signs emit some voice, but it is not a concordant one. Furthermore, there is an even greater discrepancy: the sixth voice among musicians harmonizes just as much as the third, yet among astrologers, the sixth sign is entirely distinct from the first. Also, in music, the eighth voice harmonizes as if it were the same sound; but the eighth sign does not recognize the first, nor can the eighth voice represent the hope of a conjunction in the way that voices of the same tone do. Therefore, in this "pretty" similarity, one finds entirely more dissimilarity than similarity.

## Chapter VII
## What deceived them: and that no experience was had regarding aspects.

<margin>The reasoning of those deceived by the logic derived from the consideration of solar aspects.</margin>
**V**erily, they were not even led by these kinds of reasons when they first invented that dogma; rather, they were deceived by a certain conjecture drawn from the Moon. For when they saw the Moon borrowing light from the Sun, they observed that it changed its shape according to its different position relative to the Sun—whether it was closer or further away. They then transferred this same principle to the remaining planets...

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the physical justifications for astrological aspects. Having just dismissed Abu Ma'shar's inconsistent logic, he now examines the theory that planetary aspects are based on the phases of the Moon.</meta>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.

<margin>Five configurations of the Moon in relation to the Sun.</margin> ...planets, so that they all would change their condition and state based on their distance not only from the Sun but also from one another. You can easily notice that they were led to this opinion from no other source than this: that they established no more or fewer, nor any other configurations between planets, than those which the Moon is observed to undergo in relation to the Sun with the greatest diversity of signs. There are, moreover, five celebrated configurations <note>original: "schematismi"</note> of the Moon in relation to the Sun: when it is seen either joined to the Sun <note>The New Moon or conjunction.</note>, or crescent-shaped, or divided <note>The half-moon.</note>, or bulging, or full. To these correspond an equal number of configurations devised by them for the planets: when they are either together, or in a hexagonal, or quadrangular, or triangular, or opposite radiation. For conjunction responds to conjunction; then the hexagonal radiation <note>The "sextile" aspect of 60 degrees.</note> corresponds to the crescent shape, which is first seen in the Moon when it is sixty degrees distant from the Sun, and is called <term>conoides</term> <note>Meaning "cone-like."</note> by the Greeks; by which number of degrees the hexagonal radiation between planets is also established by them. Likewise, the Moon is then "divided"—called <term>dichotomos</term> in Greek—when ninety degrees lie between it and the Sun; by which space, when the stars themselves are separated, they are said to be composed in a square configuration <note>The "square" aspect.</note>. They derived the triangular radiation <note>The "trine" aspect of 120 degrees.</note> from the likeness of the bulging Moon, which is first seen in that shape when it is removed 120 degrees from the Sun; it is called <term>amphikyrtos</term> <note>original: αμφικυρΤοσ, meaning "curved on both sides" or gibbous.</note> by the Greeks; we can call it "pre-swollen" or "hump-backed." Everyone understands that the opposition itself corresponds to the full moon. And since the Moon, according to the diversity of its shape, is accustomed to change bodies in different ways, they established the same regarding all the planets: namely, that through this variety of intervals they would also affect inferior <note>Earthly or "sublunary" things.</note> things in various ways.

The conjecture of this consequence (if it is as I think) can easily be understood as to how much they are deceived. If indeed the Moon changes its properties of influencing just as it changes its shape according to its distance from the Sun, it is because, receiving light from the Sun, it is illuminated more or less by it on the side that faces us. And from this it happens by natural reason that through the increase or decrease of light, it not only presents itself to us in a different image, but also changes the physical qualities of our bodies and those of others. For who does not know that the moisture of bodies is dissolved by heat? Who, again, does not know that light is the cause of heat? From which it is aptly gathered that the more light the Moon has, the more the lower bodies (to which it is closest) are heated; and consequently, the moistures within them more greatly liquefy and dissolve. In this way that statement of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> will be true: that from the first quarter of the Moon until the second, the moisture of bodies flows forth, because during that time the parts of the Moon turning toward the Earth possess a more abundant light. Hence those experiments proven by the labors of farmers: that timber, when cut while the Moon is full of light, quickly rots; whereas that which is cut when the Moon is waning remains free from decay and is preserved from the vice of rot. For moisture is most favorable to putrefaction, which, as I said, both increases and decreases in bodies along with the increase and decrease of the Moon's light. 

<margin>A reflection of the argument back upon the arguer.</margin> But truly, to transfer these changes of the Moon—which alone is subject to this kind of light variation—to the planets, which always shine with their own and unchanging light, is utterly insane. One may rather argue from the opposite: if the Moon, because it is more or less illuminated due to its position, changes us according to the measure of its light, it follows that for the planets, just as their light does not change, neither should their property of influencing change. For through their various distances either from the Sun or from one another, they neither grow poor in light nor grow rich, but they always look upon us and other earthly things in the same way. 

<margin>That astrologers cannot appeal to experiments.</margin> Whether, therefore, they were led to this opinion by these conjectures (as we suspect) or by those we first approached, it is clear that they rely on the flimsiest and most ridiculous reasons. If perhaps they trust these reasons less and allege the evidence of experience—which is the only refuge for those destitute of reason—we can equally appeal to experience, by which their <term>apotelefms</term> <note>Astrological outcomes or predictions.</note> are daily refuted. But let them answer this one thing: what true and faithful experiments have they had regarding these matters?

<summary>Pico argues that the five astrological "aspects" were baselessly modeled after the phases of the Moon. He refutes this by noting that while the Moon's light physically affects Earthly moisture, the planets shine with constant light and thus cannot be judged by the same logic.</summary>

# BOOK SIX

...about which there is such great controversy among them: that where one establishes a square, another contends it is a trine. And what one here makes a hexagon, another would have be a square; indeed, what is a trine to one will be a diameter <note>The "opposition" aspect of 180 degrees, where planets are directly across the zodiac from each other.</note> to others. Concerning this matter, since it will be discussed extensively below, we refer the reader to that place. For now, we are advising this: not only in prescribing the boundaries of these radiations, <margin>Discord between Paul and Heliodorus.</margin> but they differ on many points regarding the nature of the radiations themselves. This goes so far that Paul and Heliodorus write that a hexagon <note>The "sextile" aspect of 60 degrees.</note> which is between signs not equally distant from either the equinoxes or the tropics has the nature of an opposition. Furthermore, they claim that an opposition is not necessarily "malefic" <note>In astrology, "malefic" refers to an influence that causes harm or misfortune.</note> but mediates between good and bad aspects. Similarly, Ptolemy thinks that neither is the square "bad" nor the trine "good." Thus, it is clear enough that no authority of experience supports them, since each master contends with equal faith and equal authority for a patronage of such diverse opinions that favors himself.

### Chapter VIII. What they say about "enclosure" conflicts with those things said about aspects.

<margin>Enclosure <note>original: "εμπεριχεσις"</note></margin>
**B**esides these figures and aspects which we have mentioned, there are other positions of the stars—both among themselves and in relation to the Sun—by which they think the stars' powers are affected and their properties of things changed. Among these are some that seem to contradict those earlier points. For they say a planet is "besieged" <note>Also known as "enclosure."</note> whenever the rays of malefic stars <note>Specifically Mars and Saturn, considered the "greater" and "lesser" misfortunes in traditional astrology.</note> stand around it on both sides, a condition which the Greeks call <term>emperihesis</term> <note>original: "εμπεριχεσις"</note>. For example, if Jupiter holds Libra, while Mars holds Virgo and Saturn holds Scorpio; or if, with Jupiter placed there, Mars hurls rays from Taurus into Virgo and Scorpio, then they will call Jupiter "besieged." I therefore ask them: do planets move and affect one another when located in adjacent and neighboring signs? If they say no, then "enclosure" <note>original: "empicheſis"</note> is abolished, because a ray touching Virgo will not harm a star placed in Libra. <margin>Response.</margin> Just as one sent to Scorpio will not, since Scorpio and Virgo are signs neighboring Libra. If they concede it, then the entire theory of "aspects" is worthless, which depends entirely on our belief that planets affect one another from certain intervals, but suffer nothing from each other from other distances. If they respond that it happens differently in "enclosure" because there are rays on both sides, it is from this point especially that their insanity is made manifest. It is as if they think stars are like men: an enemy following from behind does not hurt a man who is fleeing, <margin>Refutation.</margin> provided a free field lies open in front of him to escape; yet he is captured by the pursuer if another stands opposite him, blocking his way. For example: if Mars occupies Virgo, he does not touch Jupiter located in Libra; yet he will touch him if Saturn stands in Scorpio opposite Jupiter. What then is this kind of discipline, so inconsistent with itself, that you call neighboring signs "disconnected" <note>original: "asindetę apostrophę," referring to signs that do not "behold" or aspect one another.</note>—in which stars placed have no communion with each other, nor does anything flow from one into the other—and yet you say a planet is "besieged" because malefic rays press upon it from neighboring signs? For if Saturn were removed, you would concede that Jupiter is not harmed by Mars; but with Saturn added, you would concede it—especially since Saturn arrives in such a way that he himself cannot even harm Jupiter. But it is certainly as we were saying: the similarity of a surrounded man, who has no exit to safety with enemies standing around him, led them to this idea.

### Chapter IX. Planets positioned under the Sun’s rays are not badly affected, nor "combust" as astrologers say.

<margin>The first reason.</margin>
**A**re they not also raving regarding the planets compared to the Sun? They want those placed under its rays to be ineffective and badly affected, as if the stars themselves cannot bear the light of the Sun, and like weaker heads, they grow sick if they are in the sun too much. And yet, all celestial light—and especially solar light—is beneficial. Even if it is sometimes hostile to earthly things, this happens only through a defect in the matter <note>Pico argues that while the Sun's heat might wither a plant on Earth, the "matter" of a star is perfect and cannot be damaged.</note>; but there is no such defect of matter in the stars. Therefore, the more they enjoy the light of the Sun, the more vigorous and effective they should become, especially since the Sun, compared to the stars, holds the status of a "universal cause," whose nature is not to weaken but to confirm the particular nature of things. <margin>The second reason.</margin> What if, when the Moon is silent <note>The "New Moon," when it is between the Earth and the Sun and therefore invisible.</note>, lower things seem to be deprived of its benefit? That is for another reason: because the part that faces us is stripped of light when joined to the Sun. But the same does not happen to the other planets, which possess their own light; therefore, when the rays of the Sun are poured around them...

<summary>Pico criticizes the inconsistencies between astrological authorities regarding planetary aspects and refutes the concepts of "enclosure" and "combustion," arguing that solar light should strengthen rather than weaken other planets.</summary>

<margin>Third [point]</margin>
...the lower planets are less capable. But if one stubbornly defends this idea that a planet's power is oppressed and exhausted by a star, this ought to happen more intensely the more powerful they are and the closer the planets are to the Sun—yet they usually deny both. For if a planet joins the Sun at the exact same degree and minute, they claim it becomes most effective. Furthermore, when a star is occupied by the Sun's rays in Aries or Leo, they say the Sun does not harm it, even though they decree the Sun is most powerful in those places. For they say the Sun "receives" the star into its own home, since Aries is his exaltation <note>A point in the zodiac where a planet is thought to have maximum influence.</note> and Leo is his house; and no good host brings injury to a guest. This treats celestial matters in a human fashion—a mistake they make everywhere—as if the Sun pours out light and heat outside itself by some personal choice rather than by natural necessity.

### Chapter X. If we wish to follow the logic and even the authority of certain astrologers, retrograde planets appear stronger than those in direct motion.

<margin>Where the error of astrologers is most especially found.</margin>
**F**inally, whoever examines the decrees of the astrologers will see that everything has been derived either from some human similarity (which, as we said, is contrary to the nature and dignity of celestial things) by poetic license rather than sound reason; or from mere fables and arbitrary inventions, such as what they pass down regarding the "images" <note>The constellations or zodiacal figures.</note> which we shall discuss below; or by the occasion of certain mathematical positions, which, while used correctly by mathematicians, are perversely transferred by "genethliaci" <note>Astrologers who cast birth charts (horoscopes).</note> to this profession of divining. They have erred most especially in the division of the Zodiac. But regarding that division, I will dispute in its proper place later. For now, there is that category of things where they think the effectiveness of planets is either diminished or strengthened—and even that the nature of the effects is changed—by those diversities of motion which mathematicians devised: such as when they now proceed in a direct course, now move backward <term>retrograde: the apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky</term>, and now stand still in stationary slowness. For they say a planet acts weakly when it is retrograde, but effectively when it proceeds forward. They even say it is favorable when moving forward, but the same planet becomes harmful if it moves backward. Regarding this matter, Heliodorus, seeing what could be said against the astrologers, raised the question against himself in his book of commentaries on Paul of Alexandria. I shall explain his solution in no other words than his own, adding the answer by which he thought he solved the question (though he rather increases it); his words in Greek are as follows:

<note>Pico omits the Greek text here, moving directly to his translation.</note>

We have translated it into Latin, rendering it almost word for word: "It is necessary to know that although planets are said to move unequally, in truth, there is nothing unequal or disordered in the heavens; rather, all order and all equality are found in them. But it appears to our estimation that they move unequally and sometimes even stand still. In reality, they neither stand still nor ever slow down or move backward. But it happens that they appear to do so because of the positions of the eccentrics and epicycles <note>Components of the Ptolemaic system used to explain why planets appear to change speed or direction.</note> upon which they move, as Ptolemy 
<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
taught us in his *Composition*. And if someone objects: 'How then are the *apotelegmata* <note>original: "αποτελέσματα" — the astrological outcomes or predictions</note> diverse?' 
<margin>Objection</margin>
meaning that because of their motion something is either added or taken away, or because they are said to stand still, even though they truly neither stand still nor move unequally. We respond that the *apotelegmata*—that is, the astrologers' 
<margin>Response</margin>
answers—do not occur properly because of that inequality of motion or station. Rather, it is because it happens then that the planets, carried in their epicycles, either become closer to the Earth or are moved further away from the Earth." These are the words of Heliodorus, from whom we take it as not only granted but attested and confirmed 
<margin>Heliodorus</margin>
that the stations of the planets do nothing insofar as they are stations—that is, they do not change the effectiveness of the planets. Likewise, neither do the retrogradations nor the direct motions do anything insofar as they are such. Instead, diverse things are pronounced because of what happens during these differences of motion: either the planets draw closer to the Earth or move further away. If he says this has a natural reason, then they should affect us differently when they are close and differently when they are distant. We would certainly concede this to be true; but if they observe the direct, stationary, and retreating planets for that reason, then the opposite doctrine ought to be established: namely, that retreating <note>retrograde</note> planets should be more effective than when they are carried in a direct course, and weaker when they are direct.

<header>BOOK SIX</header>

<margin>Haly</margin>
...distance. In these matters, a greater or lesser distance from the earth is observed. For as Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> writes when explaining Ptolemy, every reason certainly testifies: that the closer a planet is to the earth, the more strongly it changes us and affects us more powerfully. Every planet, when it is retrograde, approaches closer to the earth; conversely, when moving direct, it becomes more distant from the earth. Therefore, a retrograde planet ought to have been considered stronger—not weak and feeble, as they [the astrologers] have decreed.

### Chapter XI ¶ That the Head and Tail are intersections of imaginary circles endowed with no natural power, which the ancients did not use in prediction; nor do the moderns agree on their powers.

<margin>What the head and tail are.</margin>
**W**ho would not see that the Dragon's Head and Tail <note>The lunar nodes: the points where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic</note>, to which the crowd of astrologers attributes so much, are empty and fictional things? But as we said before, here astrologers often slip into error: because whatever they find recorded by mathematicians as necessary methods for measuring motions, they misuse all of them in predicting—as if they were equally natural and endowed with the power of influencing—when in fact the reality is far different. For they [the mathematicians] both devise and invent many things in the heavens to serve mathematical numbers and measurements, which are otherwise founded on no stability of nature. We showed this in the signs which Ptolemy considers non-movable <note>The "fixed" signs or the tropical zodiac tied to seasons</note>, intercepted by the solstices and equinoxes; we shall show it in the division of the minute parts of the signs. Now the same will appear in the Head and Tail: for they are nothing other than the intersections of two circles—mere points—the meeting of two lines conceived in the mind, introduced by mathematicians so that ecliptic locations <note>Points where an eclipse can occur</note> may be discerned. Yet there is no power there, no quality or natural efficacy that can be transferred to natal astrology <term>genethlica: the branch of astrology dealing with birth charts</term>. Certainly, they can do nothing unless some planet placed there decides something better or worse according to the advantage or disadvantage of the location; but noted by themselves and separately, they can have no power to rule or change bodies. The astrologer Abraham Ibn Ezra <margin>Abraham Ibn Ezra</margin> <note>A 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer</note> also saw this regarding the signs, writing in his first book of *Astrological Reasons*: "They also said the Dragon's Head is exalted in Gemini, and the Tail in Sagittarius. But this is empty, because the Head and Tail signify neither good nor evil. For they are connections of two circles; however, the Moon is observed when she is in them: because when placed in the Head, she is more invigorated for that reason, as she is closer to us. Conversely, she is weaker in the Tail, because in it, turning toward the south, she is distanced from us. The same happens to the other planets when they are found in the Head and Tail, except for the Sun, which has no declination in either part. When you see the Head and Tail noted separately in the tables of the law <note>The authoritative astronomical tables used by practitioners</note>, know that they neither harm nor help, although many think otherwise." Thus he spoke. But neither does Ptolemy ever use them in predicting, nor will you find the ancients used them in Maternus <margin>Maternus</margin> <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer</note>, in whose work there is no mention of the Dragon's Head or Tail. If the ancients ever speak of them, it is only as a certain place and position. Hence, there was also a differing opinion among them: for to the older ones, both places seemed evil because of the "ecliptic"—that is, the path [of eclipses]—and for that reason they established both equally among the unlucky places. Heliodorus <margin>Heliodorus</margin> <note>Likely the philosopher and commentator on Paul of Alexandria</note>, in the treatise *On Children* <note>original: "peri gen[eseos]"</note>, says: "If the places signifying children are free from the unfortunate planets and the ecliptic nodes—that is, the Head and Tail—it is happy." The moderns <margin>Moderns</margin>, if the Head is in the place of children, will announce children like "olive plants around the table" <note>A biblical allusion to Psalm 128:3</note>, led by the other conjecture which we related above from Ibn Ezra: that planets in the Head are closer to us and thus more effective. Truly, that third reason proceeds when some planet is in the Head; although a planet declining toward us even before the Head ought to be considered stronger for the same reason. But when no star is found in it, what can it either give or take away? For it is designated only by our minds. As for the fact that some suspect a certain power is left there by the Moon, no astrologer has said this; moreover, it is not physical if you consider the nature and light of the heavens, nor is it astrological, since the Moon travels through the Tail just as much.

<summary>Pico argues that the Dragon's Head and Tail (lunar nodes) are mere mathematical points used for calculation, not physical entities with astrological power. He cites historical authorities like Ibn Ezra and Maternus to show that even within the tradition, there is no consensus on their influence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of the "Dragon’s Head and Tail" (the lunar nodes). Pico argues that these are merely mathematical points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path, having no physical substance or power. He then transitions to Chapter XII, where he attacks the concept of "antiscia"—zodiacal points mirrored across the solstice line—arguing that astrologers like Firmicus Maternus misunderstood their origin and falsely attributed their use to Ptolemy.</meta>

<page-num>312</page-num>
<header>DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY</header>

<margin>
The disagreement of the astrologers: Alchabitius.
</margin>
Therefore, it is merely a site and a pure position, about which both the Arabs and the Latins have finally decreed as if it were some kind of star, even going so far as to believe that this "Head" <note>The North Node of the Moon</note> adds years to one's life, governs a certain portion of one's age, is exalted in Gemini, and possesses the nature of Venus and Jupiter—whereas they claim the "Tail" <note>The South Node of the Moon</note> acts against Mars and Saturn. In this matter, we see how far they deviate from the truth. But it is astonishing how much they also disagree with themselves when they sometimes call the Head the "bond and link of all celestial happiness." Yet elsewhere, they say it is good with the good and bad with the bad, increasing whatever it finds. In other places, they speak of it as something entirely evil. For Alchabitius <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note>—in whose work we find the rules I just recounted—mentions this among the "misfortunes" of the planets: if they should be with their "heads." For every planet has its own "head" and "tail," called *genzauar* <note>from the Persian 'jawzihr', referring to the nodes</note> among the Arabs. Just as when they are with the Head and Tail of the Dragon (the specific names for the Moon’s Head and Tail), they are considered to be in as bad a state in the Head as in the Tail. The same author, in his *Book of Nativities*, makes the Moon "climacteric" <note>referring to a critical or dangerous turning point in life</note> when it approaches the Head. In the principal places of life, he counts this Head and Tail together. Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish scholar</note>, as we have mentioned, asserts that the Moon is strengthened when located in the Head. We saw Heliodorus above counting these among the "unfortunate" stars. Yet, in his treatise on the climacteric, he counts them alongside the Sun, the Moon, the Ascendant, and the Part of Fortune. Thus, what they have put forward concerning this "Head" seems to have been produced by men with no head (or certainly no heart) of their own. Everywhere, however, these malicious men call it the "Dragon's Head" so that it might sound in the ears of the credulous with greater reverence, as if possessing the authority of a deity.

### Chapter XII The origin of antiscia: that Ptolemy did not use them in predicting, and how much Maternus and Haly erred in these matters.

<margin>
Where the antiscia come from: Hipparchus.
</margin>
<margin>
Rejection of the antiscia.
</margin>
<margin>
Maternus, most ignorant of all mathematics, as shown elsewhere.
</margin>
<margin>
Ptolemy does not use antiscia in judging.
</margin>
**A**strologers have likewise erred concerning the "antiscia" <note>Antiscia are points in the zodiac that are equidistant from the solstice points (0° Cancer or 0° Capricorn), mirroring each other in terms of day-length</note> on account of a saying by a certain mathematician. For since Hipparchus and the ancients called those degrees in which the Sun is positioned "antiscios"—meaning "opposite-shadowed" or "equal in shadow"—because the days are equal to days and nights to nights on both sides, our "diviners" claimed these degrees were equal in power and potency. This is a display of such profound ignorance that no one could fail to recognize it: they have transferred an equality of light and darkness (which occurs when the Sun passes through them) to an equality of astrological power. But I wish to accuse Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer</note> above all others as the propagator of this error, although pardon must be granted to him as one most ignorant of the entire mathematical art. He claims that Ptolemy gives the highest weight to decrees and antiscia. This does not surprise me, for although I have read through all of Maternus diligently, he has nowhere given me any indication that he himself had actually read Ptolemy. As far as antiscia are concerned, Ptolemy never uses them in his judging or pronouncing of outcomes, whether you look at his *Centiloquium* <note>The "Hundred Sayings," a collection of aphorisms formerly attributed to Ptolemy</note> or his *Apotelesmata* <note>The Tetrabiblos, Ptolemy's main astrological work</note>. Only in the first book of the *Apotelesmata*, where he narrates the opinions of others <term>περὶ τῆσ συμπαθείας τῶν ζωδίων</term> <note>original Greek: "about the sympathy of the zodiac signs"</note>—that is, concerning the affinity and consensus of the signs—among the various institutions, does he use these words: "Again, they say that whatever points are equally distant from either of the tropics are equal in power, because the Sun, placed in them, makes days equal to days and nights to nights." Having said this, it is as if he then forgot it; because he did not approve of it, he never brings it up again. He never mentions the name "antiscia" (which is found nowhere in his work), nor the thing itself—that is, this affinity and consensus of parts equally remote from the tropics. For as to what he says in a certain place in the *Centiloquium*, that a planet often extends its powers to a place where it is not physically present, to want to transfer this to the antiscia and the *dodecathemoria* <note>The twelve-fold subdivisions of a sign</note> is too forced and reckless. This is especially true since, in his entire discipline, Ptolemy laughs at the one (the *dodecathemoria* and other things of that sort) and ignores the other (the antiscia we are discussing). By that precept, he intended to indicate nothing other to you than the <term>σχηματισμὸν φάσεων</term> <note>original Greek: "configuration of phases"</note>—that is, the power of configuration and radiation, by which, according to the opinion of astrologers and especially Ptolemy, the planets act effectively in places where they are least present. For he himself observes almost nothing else in constellations other than phases and schemes—or certainly nothing more than those. But not even...

<margin>
What antiscia are.
</margin>
