<meta>This page continues Pico’s systematic dismantling of astrological concepts, moving from the lunar nodes (Dragon’s Head and Tail) to "antiscia"—mirror points in the zodiac. He specifically targets the misunderstandings of Firmicus Maternus and medieval Arabic authorities like Abēzagel.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE

<margin>Maternus did not understand what antiscia are.</margin>
Our Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer and author of the *Mathesis*</note> did not understand what the "antiscion" <note>An "antiscion" (plural: antiscia) is a point in the zodiac mirrored across the solstice line (the Cancer/Capricorn axis). Planets at these points are thought to share the same amount of daylight.</note> meant for himself; he promised that he would explain the hidden reasoning elsewhere, as if it were a matter not already explained to any mathematician, or something that could not be explained in three words. But his ignorance is caught right there, in the way he uses the term so unskillfully. He speaks of Mars, positioned at a certain degree in Gemini, "sending" an antiscion into Cancer—a way he would never speak if he understood what an antiscion actually was. For an antiscion is neither a ray nor a light that is "sent"; nor has it ever been said by anyone that an antiscion is "sent" by a planet, other than to say a degree is "sent" into another where there is equality. Therefore, one should speak more physically: the "epoch" of Mars—that is, the part of the zodiac it occupies—is the antiscion to such a part of Gemini; or, what amounts to the same thing, that Mars is in the antiscion of Gemini. Those who say Mars "hurls" an antiscion into Gemini will be hissed at and mocked by mathematicians.

<margin>The error of Abēzagel.</margin>
But Abēzagel <note>Likely referring to the medieval Jewish scholar and astrologer Abraham ibn Ezra</note> also slipped up in many ways. In the first book of his commentaries, while explaining certain aphorisms, he writes that degrees equally distant from the equinoxes <note>The points where day and night are equal (Aries and Libra)</note> have the same power as those equally distant from the tropics <note>The solstices (Cancer and Capricorn)</note>. Yet the ancients never said this about the distance from the equinoxes, but only from the tropics, to which the name "antiscia" was given. Nor should Abēzagel have failed to see this: although circles drawn on both sides of the equinoxes are indeed equal—for parallels equally distant from them must be equal to each other—they do not form equal hemispheres <note>halves of the celestial sphere</note> relative to each other, which only happens at equal distances from the tropics. From this comes that "agreement" of the antiscia.

<margin>The error of both our and barbarian astrologers.</margin>
He also errs, along with many others, by counting the relationship of a degree to its antiscion degree among those they call "aspects" <note>The specific geometric angles between planets, like a square or a trine</note>. From this, they conclude that a star placed in one of these points has power in the other as well, as if it were in a hexagonal, tetragonal, trigonal, or opposite position. This error arose because what the Greeks call **figures** <note>original: "schēmata"</note>, the barbarians and our own people call **aspects**. Among the Greeks, however, signs are said to "look at" each other not just because they form geometric configurations (which is how our people use "aspect"), but what they call in Greek **from the equinoctial lights** <note>original: "ek tōn phōtōn isēmerōn"</note>. This means they rise and set at the same points. Because this happens in signs equally separated from the tropics (since they are on the same parallel), a large part of the astrologers call these signs **beholding** <note>original: "bleponta"</note>. The Arabs and then the Latins adopted this meaning, but they misused the word "aspect" to describe it.

<margin>Often an error in words gives birth to an error in facts.</margin>
And so it happens: often an error in wording gives birth to an error in the facts themselves. This sufficiently demonstrates how varied the observation of antiscia is among astrologers in explaining fates (if any fates were granted at all), and how much both the Arabs and Latins have dreamed up on these matters contrary to the opinion of the ancients.

### Chapter XIII. How astrologers are equally deceived regarding "commanding" and "obeying" signs.

<margin>E</margin>X Of this same kind is that observation—clearly one of pure dullness or deception—concerning "commanding" and "obeying" signs. For mathematicians called those signs in which the Sun makes the days longer than the nights **commanding** <note>original: "prostattonta"</note> when compared to signs where light is conquered by darkness in equal proportion. These opposite signs, which portend darkness over day, they called **obeying** <note>original: "hypakouonta"</note>. Moved by the mere sound of these names, the horoscopic astrologers decreed that a person whose birth had a "commanding" sign on the horizon would be one who commands; whereas one who has an "obeying" sign on the horizon would be a servant. It is as if that naming of "commanding" and "obeying," established by mathematicians, pertained to such a thing, rather than merely indicating the inequality of days and nights occurring under those signs!

### Chapter XIV. Refutation of the reasons some astrologers assigned to the exaltations of the planets.

<margin>Praise for Pliny, Book 2, Chapter 16.</margin>

<margin>S</margin>ED But regarding this opinion of the altitudes or "exaltations" <note>Specific degrees in the zodiac where a planet is thought to be most powerful</note> of the planets—where it emanated from and how they rushed headlong into it based on a certain mathematical occasion—I was reminded by that most diligent writer of natural history, to whom all antiquity and all posterity owe a debt, for he rescued the one from death and the other from barbarism. He, therefore, in his second book, treating the question of why the same stars appear higher at some times and lower at others...

He begins to address "exaltations" by citing Pliny the Elder as a superior authority on natural phenomena.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

...adds some of these lofty matters as follows: "Another cause of heights <note>original: *sublimitatum*; referring to the 'apogee' or the point where a planet is furthest from the Earth or the center of its orbit.</note> is that they have their highest apsides <note>The 'apsis' is the point of greatest or least distance of a planet from the center of its orbit.</note> from their center in those signs: Saturn in the twentieth part of Libra; Jupiter in the fifteenth of Cancer; Mars in the twenty-eighth of Capricorn; the Sun in the nineteenth of Aries; Venus in the twenty-sixth of Pisces; Mercury in the fifteenth of Virgo; and the Moon in the fourth of Taurus." So says he. From this, anyone who is not slow-witted may easily gather that either it was once so, or it was thought to be so by those then devoted to the science of the stars: that the stars placed in those aforementioned parts were moved at the highest point from the center of their apsides. For this reason, those degrees or parts were called the "heights" of the planets. From this, an opportunity was given to the casters of birth charts <term>genethliacis: practitioners of natal astrology who predict a person's fate based on their birth moment</term> so that, while keeping the name of "height," they might abuse it as if it were not a height of place, but of nature and power. For astrologers do not say planets are "exalted" in any other parts than those where we have shown that, according to ancient astronomy, they were thought to be at their furthest distance from their centers.

However, the reader should know that a mistake is found in the common manuscripts of Pliny, and the words that are placed thereafter have become established with the numbers swapped, when the mark for ten <note>original: *nota denarium*; likely referring to a Roman numeral transcription error</note> due to Venus was transferred to the Sun—so that in the Sun, the twenty-ninth part is wrongly read instead of the nineteenth, and in Venus, the sixteenth instead of the twenty-sixth. For there is also a flaw in Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, the 4th-century Roman astrologer</note>, where we read that Venus is exalted in the twenty-seventh part of Pisces.

<margin>**Error in Maternus and Porphyry.**</margin>
It should be written as the twenty-sixth, according to Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and scholar whose astrological works Pico views as more reliable than later Roman sources</note>. There is also some variation in that ancient astrology assigns the fourth part of Taurus to the Moon, while a later age assigns the third. This is either a difference of opinion or the fault of librarians who very often hallucinate in the notation of these numbers. Similarly, in Saturn, one ought to read the twentieth, not the twenty-first, on the authority of the same Porphyry. Now, I do not doubt it has been made clear to sound minds how the "exaltations" of the planets crept into divinatory astrology. But when the dogma reached posterity, and that astronomical reasoning for the dogma had been made obsolete by changes in the theoretical discipline of the stars, posterity devised other reasons for itself by which they thought the earlier ones were persuaded—and some devised one thing, others another, which, as happens most often with a lie, are truly trivial and ridiculous. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note> says: "In Aries,

<margin>**Ptolemy's Reason and its Refutation**</margin>
the Sun is exalted, because when it reaches it, its power begins to appear more." But (as we said above when speaking of the "houses"), that is not caused by the quality and nature of the sign, but by the location. It does not begin to be stronger because it travels through Aries, but because it begins to approach us <note>Referring to the Sun moving north of the celestial equator during the spring equinox in Aries, making the days longer and warmer for observers in the Northern Hemisphere</note>. Therefore, if it pours into your gardens at that time, one should not hope that by coming to that sign it is also elevated to a kingdom because it is placed in its own "height." For in other regions, it would surely be cast down, since it is further away in Aries and happens to be closer to them under Libra. But let us see about the remaining planets as well. The height of the Moon is Taurus: "because if she is joined with the Sun in Aries, her power first appears in Taurus." What a most effective reason! As if, if she were joined with the Sun in Taurus, the same would not happen in Gemini; and if joined in Gemini, the same in Cancer; and if in Cancer, the same under Leo, and so on with all the rest. One can only marvel at Ptolemy, who was not ashamed to write such things.

<margin>**Refutation**</margin>
Indeed, there are also other reasons given: "because the Moon is close to the Sun and is in the lateral trine <note>A 'trine' is an aspect of 120 degrees, considered harmonious in astrology</note> of the Moon." But Ptolemy does not think the Moon is closest to the Sun; nor should we conjecture a "height" from a trine, nor from a house, nor a trine or altitude; nor from any of those, the "terms" or the "decan." For these things are so mixed up that each should have its own proper authority in its own matter. Furthermore, if the trine moves the argument, why will Mercury not rather be exalted in Gemini than

<margin>**Aboafar**</margin>
in Virgo? Where it would also fit that it be closest to the exaltation of the Sun, from which it is usually not far removed. This is what Aboafar <note>Abu Ma’shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer who was a major authority for medieval Latin scholars</note> attempts to preserve in the reasoning for these exaltations. But Ptolemy says: "Virgo suits Mercury because it is dry, and under Virgo the autumnal dryness

<margin>**On the exaltation of Mars.**</margin>
appears." However, we have already said that this change of the four seasons does not proceed from the nature of the signs. Therefore, the Sun placed in Virgo will do for other regions what it does not do for us when placed in Taurus. Furthermore, if this was being observed, why was it not established that Mars should reign in Cancer? Under...

<meta>catchword: which.</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that astrological "exaltations" are merely misunderstood astronomical apogees, corrupted by scribal errors and faulty reasoning by authorities like Ptolemy and Abu Ma'shar. He refutes the idea that signs possess inherent qualities like "dryness" or "power," noting that seasonal effects are geographical rather than zodiacal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of "exaltations"—specific zodiac signs where planets are supposedly most powerful. On the previous page, he argued that these positions were originally just the "highest points" (apogees) in ancient astronomy, which later astrologers misinterpreted as signs of mystical power. Here, he exposes the logical inconsistencies astrologers use to justify why certain planets are assigned to certain signs.</meta>

### BOOK SIX

->**DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY**<-

...by which the world seethes, just as it already withers under Virgo. Moreover, Mars is a most burning planet, which they nevertheless wish to be "exalted" <note>In astrology, a planet is 'exalted' in a sign where its influence is supposedly most harmonious and powerful.</note> in Capricorn—a sign under which we are constricted by cold, frost, and ice. But, the astrologers say, Capricorn turns toward the south, and the southern part of the world is hotter. This is exactly what we object to: this levity and inconsistency of your reasoning (if indeed these can be called "reasons"). For you argue concerning the same sign however it suits your whim—now as if it were hot, now as if it were cold. Soon you will call that same sign neither hot nor cold, but rather "moist" or "dry" in your classification of the signs. You make Capricorn an "earthy" sign, and therefore dry; yet when it relates to Mars, it is counted among the burning things. <margin>On Jupiter and Mars' nature.</margin> And when it is called the home of the star Saturn (which is the highest and coldest of planets), snows and rains are recorded as occurring under it.

But if Capricorn grants Mars its power as a supposedly "hot" sign, then by the same logic Cancer should be numbered as the coldest sign. Therefore, Cancer should certainly not have Jupiter as its "king," for Jupiter is very powerful with a life-giving heat, as they say. <margin>*Ptolemy*</margin> But a hiding place is at hand into which they may retreat. For Ptolemy says that Jupiter stirs up northern winds; therefore, a sign positioned toward the north is suitable for him. Yet, other astrologers cannot flee to this excuse, because they deny that winds of this kind are stirred by Jupiter at all. Furthermore, not even Ptolemy is excused: by similar reasoning, he ought to have assigned Mars to the west, not to the south, since he thinks westerly winds (not southern ones) are excited by Mars. I pass over the fact that Gemini and Leo incline toward the north; why then is Leo not rather the exaltation of Jupiter? Averroes <note>A famous 12th-century Islamic philosopher and polymath who commented extensively on Aristotle and science.</note> says the heat of Leo does not suit Jupiter; but actually, it suits him far more than the coldness of Cancer. Add to this that Leo is the "trine" <term>trigonus: an astrological aspect where signs are 120 degrees apart, usually sharing the same elemental nature (Fire, Earth, Air, Water)</term> of Jupiter, as well as a daytime and masculine sign; Jupiter likewise is masculine and diurnal. Cancer, meanwhile, is designated among the feminine, nocturnal, and aquatic signs, all of which are removed from the nature of Jupiter. Therefore, Leo is entirely more suitable for him than Cancer.

<margin>On the exaltation of Venus and Saturn.</margin> Regarding Venus and Saturn, they rave no less: claiming that Libra is the height of Saturn because Saturn is "contrary" to the Sun; and that Venus is exalted in Pisces because she is moist, and the moisture of spring begins under Pisces. But as we have already often said, these qualities of the seasons do not follow the nature of the signs themselves, but rather the position of the approaching and receding Sun. Regarding Saturn, they speak as usual for their own convenience. For what they here claim is "opposite" to the Sun, they elsewhere declare to be "sharing the same nature" <note>original Greek: *synoreuon* (συνορεύον)</note>; that is, they declare it to be of the same condition. For this reason, they say the "father" is signified by both the Sun and Saturn, and that both are "eastern" planets. 

But both are masculine; both are diurnal. Surely we would say far too much if we pursued all other such details individually. For these details, others of little wisdom have devised a new reason—shorter, perhaps, but entirely ineffective: namely, that the exaltations of the planets are "trine" <note>120 degrees apart</note> or "sextile" <note>60 degrees apart; original Latin: *exagona*</note> to their "homes" <note>The 'home' or domicile is the sign a planet naturally rules.</note>, except in the case of Mercury. But if you ask why they preferred the "sextile" for the Moon, Venus, and Mars, but the "trine" for the others, they reply that the trine is more suitable for the daytime and more powerful planets; but for the nocturnal ones, which belong to the "sect" <note>original: *haeresi*</note> of the Moon (which the Arabs call *aiz* <note>Referring to *hayz*, an Arabic astrological concept of dignity and planetary strength.</note>), they use the sextile "because of the weakness of the ray" <note>original Greek: *dia to asthenes tēs aktinos* (δια τὸ ἀσθενὲς τῆς ἀκτῖνος)</note>. 

<margin>Rejection.</margin> But they are mistaken regarding Mars. He is not numbered among the nocturnal planets because he is "weak," but rather so that the vigor and heat of the "Martial ray" might be restrained by the cold of the night. Nor can he be said to belong to the "sect" of the Moon, since he is a masculine planet and disagrees with the Moon in both qualities. He is considered nocturnal for an entirely opposite reason than the Moon is: she is so because of her similarity to the night's nature, but Mars because of his dissimilarity. He is opposed to the Moon and Cancer while in Capricorn, just as he is opposite to Taurus while in Scorpio. 

But even if we let that conjecture stand, let this be answered: why a right-hand trine rather than a left-hand one? Why a left-hand one rather than a right? Indeed, why for Jupiter is it left-handed, but for Saturn and the Sun it is right-handed? And since planets have two "houses," why is the trine taken from one rather than the other? For instance, since Jupiter has both Sagittarius and Pisces as his homes: why should he be exalted in Cancer rather than in Leo? Especially since he has more affinity with Sagittarius, as astrologers say—and also (as we said before) Leo suits him far more than Cancer. Finally, I will show you that all such conjectures were invented by later writers, and did not exist at all for those who first...

<summary>Pico criticizes the arbitrary and contradictory logic astrologers use to assign "exaltations" to planets, arguing that their elemental and geometric justifications (like trines and sextiles) are modern inventions rather than consistent physical laws.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic dismantling of astrological foundations. Having previously argued that "exaltations" were merely misinterpretations of astronomical apogees, he now moves to the "triplicities" (groups of three signs) and the arbitrary assignment of elements (Fire, Earth, Air, Water) to the zodiac.</meta>

<page-num>112</page-num>
->**DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY**<-

...the founders of this dogma laid their foundation; from this you may recognize that they give no reason why a planet is said to be exalted in such a sign, but rather in such a part of that sign. We have already demonstrated the cause of this from ancient astronomy. <margin>Aboasar</margin> <note>Aboasar refers to Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note> For this reason, Aboasar says that it was difficult for the whole community of astrologers to find this reason; and he himself, lest he say nothing at all, anxiously distorted many things with an overly perverse and fabulous subtlety regarding this matter. Therefore, it is undoubtedly clear that this dogma regarding the "heights" <term>altitudinibus: here used as a technical term for planetary exaltations</term> of the planets was received by the genethliacs <note>Genethliacs are astrologers who cast horoscopes based on a person's birth.</note> from the occasion we mentioned: that ancient discipline which thought that planets were at their maximum distance from their centers at these degrees. No one now fails to understand how vain that observation is—not only because they transferred to "nature and power" what was merely a naming of "place and position," but also because ancient astronomy was perhaps deceived in that matter. <margin>Apogees</margin> <note>The apogee is the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> It was a discipline too deceptive in its beginnings and poorly explored; and even if they had decreed a true ratio then, it would not fit posterity now, since the apsides and what are called the "apogees" of the wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" (stellae errantes) are the planets.</note> have shifted.

### Chapter XV. The arguments of astrologers regarding trigons and their rulers; and, in passing, the sex of the signs are refuted.

<margin>That elementary qualities cannot be ascribed to the signs.</margin>
Nor should we think that astrologers, having taken the opportunity of the trines <note>A "trine" or "trigon" is an astrological aspect where signs are 120 degrees apart, forming a triangle.</note>, are more clear-sighted, as if they could not go astray without a guide. They prevaricate most often where there is no one to lead them astray. Indeed, they ought to be considered almost as insane regarding these "triplicities" as they are concerning the mathematical exaltations—though perhaps they are more insane toward themselves, lest we do them any injustice by defrauding them of their due. For they themselves gave birth to what the common people call "trigons" or "triplicities." Mathematics did not help them in this place at all, since the matter depends on this: that they make some signs fiery, some earthy, some airy, and some watery. We shall first compel them to give a reason for this, and then we will examine how they define why this trigon belongs to this planet and that one to another.

Tell us then, you "wisest men" and "interpreters of the heavens," by what reason did you distribute those qualities of the elements to the signs in the sky? Auenrodan, <note>Auenrodan refers to the 11th-century Egyptian astrologer and physician Ali ibn Ridwan.</note> a great man in your discipline, refers the nature of the signs either to the Sun or to the stars. To the Sun, such that the nature of a sign is said to be whatever the work of the Sun is while passing through that sign; in this way, the "movable" signs are called equinoctial or solstitial, and the rest "fixed" or "common." Or to the stars, if the virtues of the stars dwelling therein are attributed to the sign. I see neither reason squaring with your partition. For if we follow the works of the Sun, Cancer will be fiery, not Aquarius; just as Sagittarius would be watery rather than fiery. Aries would not be fiery but airy; Taurus would abound in moisture and heat rather than cold and dryness; and thus the condition of almost all the signs would change—which do not wander but are perpetual (as you yourselves wish). 

If we refer to the stars, which are constantly migrating from their seats <note>Pico is referring to the precession of the equinoxes, which causes the stars to shift relative to the zodiac signs over centuries.</note>, do you think the reasoning of Al-Kindi <note>Al-Kindi (c. 801–873 AD) was a pioneering Arab philosopher and scientist.</note> is better? Since there are four principal signs in the Zodiac—two equinoctial and two solstitial—he assigned to these four the four primary qualities of the elements: Fire to Aries, Water to Cancer, Air to Libra, and Earth to Capricorn. <margin>Against the reasoning of Al-Kindi</margin> Then, because the radiation of the trigons falls upon congruent places, the signs forming a triangle on either side of any sign are rightly established as having a similar nature. 

But even this reasoning does not square. For in assigning the four properties of the elements to the signs, there could have been two types of order: one based on the kinship of the sign and the element, and the other based on the position of the elements themselves, so that he would assign the first to the first, the second to the second, and so on. If they observed the first, so that hot things corresponded to hot and cold to cold, they ought to have given Fire, as I said, to Cancer <margin>Refutation of Al-Kindi's reasoning</margin> and Air to Aries. If they followed the second, they should have given Air to Cancer, which is second from Fire. 

"But," says Al-Kindi, "opposites—heat and cold—must be given to the sign of a fruitful time, that is, to Cancer." On the contrary, it should therefore be given to Libra, which is opposite to Aries. If they say Water should be placed before Air because it is "more effective," they are making themselves wiser than nature itself. Furthermore, if an active quality like coldness—not a passive one like moisture—belongs to Cancer, why is it counted by them among the feminine and nocturnal signs, rather than the masculine and diurnal ones? This is something they observe even in the planets, for no more rational reason...

<meta>catchword: rationally</meta>

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the arbitrary "physics" of astrology. Having previously dismissed the logic of planetary "exaltations," he now turns his attention to the classification of zodiac signs as masculine or feminine, and diurnal or nocturnal, arguing that these designations are contradictory and lack any consistent basis in natural philosophy.</meta>

<page-num>216</page-num>

## BOOK SIX

...reasonably acknowledging sex in the heavens based on active and passive qualities: for this reason, they called Jupiter, the Sun, and Mars males, in which heat excels; and Saturn male, in which cold excels <note>In ancient and medieval humorism, heat and dryness were considered "active" (masculine) qualities, while cold and moisture were "passive" (feminine).</note>; the Moon and Venus they called females, since they are moist. Thus, therefore, water and fire were also called males by the Egyptians for the stated reason; yet air and water were also called females. <margin>Astrology is not a science: it subverts itself.</margin> So, the signs that they established as watery, the astrologers ought to have counted among the masculine, not the feminine: yet they did this in all cases: <term>Cancer</term>, namely, <term>Pisces</term>, and <term>Scorpio</term>. They decreed the others to be masculine contrary [to this logic], even though moisture is the proper quality of air. Therefore, astrology fights with itself in these matters: and it subverts itself as if raving everywhere. 

But lest we wander from the matter proposed, let us consider these lightest trifles: the discernment of sex in the heavens, especially by such a conjecture as that which moved them to establish six masculine signs and six feminine ones, so that the first is male, the following female, and thus by turns always one man, the other woman. Now, if this had to be done, it ought to have been done according to the nature of the signs: not by a fatal and vain consequence of this sort—namely, of first and second, and so on. 

<margin>See the reasoning of Ptolemy.</margin> Hear what reason this has from <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), whose *Tetrabiblos* was the foundational text for Western astrology.</note>. Night, he says, follows day, and wives cling to husbands: therefore, a feminine sign ought to be placed next to a masculine one. Against which reason one must not dispute but rather laugh, unless it is perhaps serious that we should see whether day comes before night or night before day; perhaps nocturnal signs ought to have been placed first, because day follows night rather than night following day. For it is written: *and evening and morning were made one day* <note>original: "factum est vespere et mane dies unus" (Genesis 1:5). Pico points out that in the Hebrew tradition, the day begins at sunset.</note>, wherefore the Hebrews established the beginnings of times from the night. But we are too busy to be allowed to trifle with many words. Although among <term>Ptolemy</term> himself this diversity of sexes has great weight, as he claims it matters quite a bit whether planets are found in masculine or feminine signs.

But if they contend that the dogma is proven by experience, I ask: by whose? Their own, or that of the ancients? If their own was lacking, many made the order from the horoscope <note>The "horoscope" here refers specifically to the Ascendant, the sign rising on the eastern horizon.</note> so that the rising sign was always masculine and diurnal; they divided the rest by turns in the following order. Others made four signs diurnal: <term>Aries</term>, <term>Cancer</term>, <term>Leo</term>, and <term>Sagittarius</term>; four nocturnal: <term>Gemini</term>, <term>Libra</term>, <term>Capricorn</term>, and <term>Aquarius</term>. Four promiscuous <note>Meaning of mixed or neutral gender.</note>: <term>Virgo</term>, <term>Pisces</term>, and <term>Scorpio</term>, a classification which antiquity eventually rejected. Whence that verse from ancient astrology:

> There are those who like to say signs are diurnal which rise as masculine.
> That feminine signs rejoice enough in the shadows of the night.
> Concerning which many things the books speak with no one showing the way.

In which place it is a wonder how much a certain trivial interpreter of that poet raves; far more reasonably than him (if one must ever be insane with reason) are those who called all things equally fiery and watery "diurnal": the remaining six nocturnal being earthy and airy. Likewise, if anything pleases <term>Ptolemy</term>, masculine and diurnal follow each other; those will be masculine, these feminine. Thus he sang:

<margin>This verse is read incorrectly here, which Politian corrected, as he did many other things; his faithfulness in emending books is proven: the greatest diligence and rare erudition. <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Renaissance humanist and close friend of Pico, known for his philological accuracy.</note></margin>

> For the sign of Sagittarius and of the swift Leo
> And [Aries] looking back at its own back with a golden fleece
> Then Pisces, Cancer, and the sting of Cancer's Scorpio
> Either neighboring in place or with equal parts
> All are said to be diurnal under a similar lot
> The others, not sharing in number nor turn, are carried
> As nocturnal, cast between in just as many foul places.

There were also those who felt otherwise, wherefore he adds:

> Nay, they even said six continuous signs are diurnal.
> To be the turns of Castor <note>The constellation Gemini.</note> which are from the leading sign
> Of the Wool-bearer <note>The constellation Aries.</note>; six from the Scales <note>The constellation Libra.</note> are seen to be nocturnal.

He highlights how different authorities—including Ptolemy and various ancient poets—contradict one another, suggesting the entire system is based on arbitrary whims rather than natural law.</summary>

<header>DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY</header>

Let [astrology] therefore stop citing faith and ancient observations, from which it often differs as much as all of astrology differs from the truth. It could also be objected that if they judged a masculine sign should be placed in the first position, it remains uncertain which sign is first and masculine, just as it is uncertain which sign is the initial one, as we declared above. For to some, **Cancer** seemed first; to others, **Capricorn**; yet both are considered feminine among these people. But perhaps it was not necessary to mock these fables with so many words, although it is worthwhile to have refuted in passing this fable of distinguishing celestial signs by sex. We turned aside for this reason: to show that they contradict themselves regarding Cancer, which they make watery and feminine, even though coldness is counted among the active, not passive, qualities <note>In the physics of the time, "active" qualities were typically associated with the masculine, and "passive" with the feminine. Pico points out that if cold is active, a "cold" sign like Cancer should be masculine.</note>. But if their first division fails in the <term>tropical</term> <note>The signs of the solstices (Cancer and Capricorn).</note> and <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The signs of the equinoxes (Aries and Libra).</note> signs, the reasoning for the distribution in the other signs will not proceed. For they demonstrate in a circle—which is a crime in logic—whenever they prove in this place that the signs of a <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (fire, earth, air, or water).</note> are of the same nature; they assume the argument that a triangular radiation [aspect] comes from places that agree with each other, and conversely, it is proven that the triangular radiation agrees because they assume it falls on places of the same nature. 

<margin>The reasoning of Abraham ibn Ezra.</margin>
Let **Al-Kindi** <note>Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi (c. 801–873 AD), a prominent Arab philosopher and astrologer.</note> now be silent. What remains is the opinion of **Abraham ibn Ezra** <note>A Spanish Jewish scholar (c. 1089–1167) known for his astrological works.</note>, who derives the reason for these qualities from the figures of the images and likenesses: specifically from the properties of the animals therein. Thus **Pisces**, **Cancer**, and **Scorpio** are called cold because they represent the names and likeness of aquatic creatures. The sign of **Leo** is hot because of the nature of the Lion; and so on for the rest. But this reasoning is also either non-existent—if there are no actual images as we have demonstrated—or false if there are some images in which the images are confused with the signs, something we also rejected above. Finally, since the figures vary by location <note>Due to the precession of the equinoxes, the physical constellations no longer align with the astrological signs.</note>, this distinction of signs will be temporary, not what all astrologers (including Ibn Ezra himself) want: something immobile and perpetual. Nor will **Aries** be a fiery sign in our time, since the image of **Pisces** has now occupied almost the whole sign, up to its twenty-fifth part, the image of Aries having already shifted away. 

<margin>That the triplicity rulers, whom they call lords of triplicities, are nothing.</margin>
If there are no triplicities, there are also no <term>trigonocrators</term> <note>From the Greek *trigonokratōr*, meaning "ruler of a triangle" or triplicity.</note>; that is, the "lords of the triplicities," as they say. Although, even if those were granted, they have nevertheless defined these things—as is their habit—without reason. For they will not deny that if a planet is well-placed in some sign, it is poorly placed in the sign that opposes it diametrically. This is evident in the "houses" of the planets and evident in their "exaltations." But if this is widely admitted among them, how have they forgotten their own astrological dogma and willed that the same three planets should rule in opposing triplicities? Namely, in the Earthly and Watery ones: **Mars**, **Venus**, and the **Moon**. **Taurus** is opposed to **Scorpio**; **Virgo** is set against **Pisces**; **Capricorn** resides opposite the region of **Cancer**. And yet, those who rule in Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn likewise all rule with triplicity power in Cancer, Pisces, and Scorpio. Nor, if you ask astrologers why **Mars** is <term>debilitated</term> <note>Original: *deiiciatur*, meaning "thrown down" or in its "fall," a position of weakness.</note> in **Cancer**, will they answer otherwise than because it is exalted in **Capricorn**; and why it is harmful in **Taurus**, they will say it is because it has its domicile in **Scorpio**. 

All these things, therefore, fight against each other and prove themselves false through mutual contradiction. Add to this that in the first triplicity, 

<margin>Abū Maʿshar, Al-Qabisi.</margin>
**Abū Maʿshar**, **Al-Qabisi** <note>Also known as Albumasar and Alchabitius, respectively; two of the most cited authorities in medieval European astrology.</note>, and all the Latins decree that **Saturn** rules with **Jupiter** and the **Sun**; yet in that triplicity, Saturn is "in exile" in **Leo**, is in its "fall" in **Aries**, and in **Sagittarius** it recognizes nothing of its own. "But," they will say, "[Saturn] is diurnal just like Jupiter and the Sun." But it is also cold, while both of those are considered hot. And if, when they were dealing with exaltations, they assigned **Libra** to Saturn only for the reason that it was opposed to the nature of the Sun, why then give it rule in **Aries**? Why is it associated with the Sun as a lord of the triplicity, contrary to the nature of the signs themselves, as if it were most congruent with the Sun's nature? There are more things of this kind, but to follow each one would perhaps be superfluous and certainly annoying and nauseating to me. 

If one appeals here to the proof of experience, I point again to the discord among such "experiences." For at one time the Egyptians make only two triplicity rulers, as can be understood from the <term>monomeria</term> <note>Astrological systems that assign individual degrees of a sign to different planetary rulers.</note>. 

<margin>Abū Maʿshar, Al-Qabisi, the Latins.</margin>
Others establish things that then conflict among themselves. For in the first triangle, **Abū Maʿshar**, **Al-Qabisi**, and the Latins want **Saturn** to rule; **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*.</note> wants **Mars**. On the other hand, in the second, Ptolemy wants **Saturn**; almost all the Arabs and Latins want **Mars**; in the fourth...

He specifically highlights the conflicting traditions between authorities like Ptolemy, Abū Maʿshar, and Ibn Ezra as proof of astrology's unreliability.</summary>

<header>BOOK SIX</header>

Ptolemy makes him <note>Ptolemy, the famous 2nd-century astronomer, is Pico's frequent target for critique.</note> the lord. Namely, [he makes] Mars [the lord of the fourth triplicity], while assigning two almost secondary lords: the **Moon** by night and **Venus** by day. Others equate Mars with Venus in leadership; nor do they grant Mars anything but an unequal share except by night. They also fly to Venus by day, then the Moon as a second by night and day. This is the authority among them. More recent authors say the opinion of the **Arabs** and the experiments of the **Latins** are confirmed. <margin>Ptolemy.</margin> **Averroes** <note>original: "Averro..." (Ibn Rushd), a major medieval philosopher.</note> and **Avenrodan** <note>original: "Avenrodan," likely the commentator Ali ibn Ridwan.</note> <margin>Recent authors, Averroes.</margin> himself (not to mention the Greeks) affirm that all effects support the opinion of Ptolemy. I pass over the many points on which they clash over these same triangles <note>Pico uses "triangles" to mean triplicities, groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (fire, earth, air, water).</note>, since they have been discussed above. It is clear from this that even the "great conjunctions" <note>Rare alignments of Jupiter and Saturn believed by astrologers to signal major historical shifts.</note> are dissolved, insofar as they depend on the movement through the triplicities—not to mention other dogmas of the astrologers that derive their faith and origin primarily from these triangles.

### Chapter XVI: On faces, bounds, Babylonian dodecathemoiria, ninths, and monomoiria, which are poorly supported even by the testimony of Ptolemy himself.

**I**t remains to refute the "faces" <note>Also known as decans, these are 10-degree divisions of a zodiac sign.</note> and the "bounds" <note>Unequal divisions of a sign assigned to different planets.</note> so that everything regarding the affinity of the planets with the signs may be addressed. For we have already overturned the houses, cast down the exaltations, and obliterated the triplicities; there is no trouble in refuting these remaining ones. For even according to Ptolemy, there are no "faces." The Greeks also called these "decans." But while there are decans of the signs, "faces" belong to the planets. <margin>In Ptolemy there are many faces.</margin> Ptolemy rejected these faces, deeming them unworthy of mention or of ever being used in <term>apothelesmata</term> <note>Astrological predictions or calculations of effects.</note>. Since they cannot support these with any reasons, they might perhaps pretend they are based on experience—if only their own consistency did not desert them in this place as well. For the **Indians** want one thing to be the faces of the planets, while the **Babylonians** (whom the **Arabs** imitate) want another, and **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century astrological writer.</note> yet another. <margin>Various faces of various authors.</margin> The first decan of **Taurus**, according to the Babylonians, bears the face of **Mercury**; according to the Indians, **Venus**; according to Maternus, **Jupiter**. <margin>First decan of Taurus.</margin> The second, for some, belongs to the **Moon**; for others, **Mercury**; for others, **Mars**. The first of **Gemini** is **Jupiter’s** for the **Chaldeans**, **Mercury’s** for the Indians, and **Mars’s** for Maternus. <margin>First of Gemini.</margin> Not to follow them all in detail, the Babylonians followed this method: they gave the first decan (the beginning of **Aries**) to **Mars**, since that is the house of Mars. Then, following the order of the spheres, they gave the first ten-degree section of any sign to the "head of the family" (that is, the lord of the house), and the remaining two to the lords of the signs of that same triplicity. Maternus’s invention is entirely arbitrary and only pretends to be an ancient tradition. <margin>Babylonian dodecathemoiria.</margin> When anyone examines it closely, they will know these dogmas were not decreed by true observations or the reliability of experimenters, but by weak and light conjectures of this sort, which they call the "certainty of experience"—about which, and about the experiments themselves, we shall dispute most extensively further below.

Just as the Egyptians devised the decans by dividing a sign into three parts, so the Babylonians devised <term>dodecathemoiria</term> <note>Divisions of a single zodiac sign into twelve smaller parts, each 2.5 degrees long.</note> by dissecting a sign into twelve parts. They used this dodecathemoirion—not the one Maternus ascribes to them, which the authors **Manilius** <note>original: "Mallius," likely referring to the Roman poet Marcus Manilius.</note> and **Porphyry** mention, and which Ptolemy also mentions, though mockingly. These dodecathemoiria are called <term>topon</term> <note>original: "τόπων," meaning "of places."</note>, that is, "places." <margin>Porphyry, Albumasar, Avenazra, John of Seville.</margin> **Albumasar**, **Avenazra**, and **John of Seville** <note>original: "Hispalensis."</note> mention only this dodecathemoirion, not the one handed down by Maternus, **Alchabitius**, and **Heliodorus**, which we will discuss in its own place later. **Leopold of Austria** <note>original: "Saxoniensis," referring to Leopold’s origin.</note>, in his commentaries on Alchabitius, was deceived by the similarity of the names and confused the two. <margin>Error of Leopold.</margin> The Indians, also making up their own fictions, divided any sign into nine parts <note>Known in Vedic astrology as Navamsas.</note>. They established that the first part belongs to the lord of the sign which is "movable" <note>Equivalent to the modern "cardinal" signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn.</note> within that triplicity. Thus, the first ninth part of Aries belongs to Mars, for Aries is a movable sign; but the first part of **Leo** is also Mars’s, because Aries is the movable sign of that small triangular group. <margin>The Demonian [method].</margin> They place the following parts in the series of the following signs: if the first is Mars's (whose house is Aries), the second is Venus's, and the third is Mercury's, because Venus has her house in Taurus and Mercury in Gemini. <margin>Of the Egyptians.</margin> The Egyptians, again, numbered each single degree, which they called <term>monomoiria</term> <note>A system assigning a specific planetary ruler to every single degree of the 360-degree zodiac.</note>. They assigned these to the planets by the order of the triplicities: so that the first part of any sign was the monomoiria of the planet that ruled that triplicity—a nocturnal planet if the birth was at night, or a diurnal one if by day. The second part belonged to the lord of the second sign of that same triplicity, and so on. <margin>Refutation of all these by the words...</margin>

...the lordship of the following triplicity sign and so on in order; yet in such a way that the same planet would not obtain the <term>monomoiria</term> <note>A system assigning each of the 30 degrees of a zodiac sign to a specific planetary ruler.</note> twice in one cycle. All these "anatomies" and "dissections" of the signs I shall refute with no other words than those of **Ptolemy** himself, who said that all these things have <term>no physical basis but are empty reasoning</term> <note>original: "οὐ φυσικὸν ἀλλὰ κεδόξον λόγον"</note>. Indeed, they have no physical rationale, but are a vain ostentation; nor could he have defined them more correctly. For the more these things possess of rashness and the greater the license with which they are made up, the more wonderful and great they seem to the unrefined and unskilled. Nor was there any other reason why **Abu Ma'shar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), known in Latin as Albumasar, was a leading Persian astrologer.</note> was held as a great man in astrology—though otherwise ignorant of mathematics—except that nothing seemed unreasonable to him. Instead, he heaped together the fables of everyone at once, rejecting nothing and despising nothing. Thus, he seems to have produced more secrets than others because he recounted more fables.

It remains to speak of the **bounds** <note>Also called "terms" (termini); these are unequal subdivisions of a zodiac sign assigned to the five non-luminary planets.</note>, which I shall refute just as briefly by the very discord among those who are still litigating about these bounds among themselves. For **Ptolemy** prescribes some; the **Egyptians** others; the **Babylonians** others; the **Indians** others; and others still by some astrologer mentioned by Abu Ma'shar.

<margin>
Abu Ma'shar.
</margin>
In his *Great Introduction*, Abu Ma'shar says it is remarkable how much the younger astrologers adhere to the **Egyptians**, while the **Greeks** follow **Ptolemy**, and with them **Avenrodan** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer who commented on Ptolemy.</note>. Others also have their own followers. These affinities of the planets with the signs—as if one had a house here, a kingdom there, and bounds elsewhere—are not only unsupported by the signs themselves, but are frivolous, fabulous, conflicting, and fabricated. Nor do the Latins alone disagree on these points, but they also clash in their comparisons of them. For the common crowd gives the first rank to the **house**, the second to **exaltation**, the third to **bounds**, the fourth to **triplicity**, and the fifth to **face** <note>Also known as decans; ten-degree subdivisions of a sign.</note>. **Ptolemy** puts the house in the first place, the triplicity in the second (as **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, a 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> prefers), the exaltation in the

<margin>
Ptolemy.
Haly.
</margin>
third, and the bounds in the fourth; he omits the "face" entirely. The **Chaldeans** do not have houses; the **Egyptians** add *monomoiria* to everything; the **Indians** use **ninths** <note>Known as *navamsa* in Indian astrology.</note>; the **Babylonians** use **twelfth-parts** <note>dodecathemoria.</note>; and they do not place triplicity with the houses. **Firmicus Maternus** attributes more to "altitude" <note>Exaltation.</note> than to bounds, and more to bounds than to

<margin>
Maternus
</margin>
houses. For he says: "The stars rejoice in the first place when positioned in their altitude; in the second place in their bounds; in the third place in their houses." These are the most vain dogmas of the astrologers, which they strengthen neither by reasons nor by experiments; for in the former they talk nonsense, and in the latter they do not agree.

### Chapter XVII. Regarding feminine, bright, and dark degrees, and others of that kind, which Ptolemy ignores, nor do other astrologers agree on them.

**W**e have refuted those divisions of the signs that they refer to the planets: such as that **Mars** is exalted here, the **Sun** there; that this is the "face" of one, that of another; this is the *monomoiria* of this one, that of that one. Similarly for triplicities, bounds, ninths, and twelfth-parts. Now we must treat those things which they have handed down concerning the **degrees** themselves in an absolute sense: such as that some are **bright**, others **dark**, others **fortunate**, others (as they say) **pit-like** <note>Degrees thought to "sink" a planet's influence.</note>, others **sickly** (which they call <term>al-zamana</term> <note>Arabic term for "maimed" or "chronically ill" degrees.</note>), some **masculine**, and others **feminine**. But these were largely satisfied above; now we will add this: **Ptolemy** also despised all these things, and his interpreter **Avenrodan** seems to concede to the astrologers only that they may observe these if they find truth in them through experiments.

But what faith can there be in experiments when six different opinions are offered regarding **masculine and feminine degrees**? For you will read them described one way in **Firmicus**, another in **Abu Ma'shar**, and another

in **Avenrodan**. **Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note> differs, and **Abraham** <note>Abraham ben Ezra, a 12th-century scholar and astrologer.</note> varies in many points. Moreover, they entirely disagree with all those who make the twelfth part of each sign now masculine, now feminine by turns, establishing the first parts based on the gender of the sign. I pass over those who place twelve degrees out of thirty in the sex of the sign, the next twelve in the opposite sex, and then divide the remaining six into equal portions. Regarding the **bright**, **dark**, and **obscure** degrees, another opinion first existed among the ancients based on the **position of the stars**; for they called that part "bright" in which there was a star. They believed this was permanent because they thought the stars did not move. Therefore, they were in error if we agree with **Hipparchus**, **Ptolemy**, and the rest of the later scholars, as the origin of the dogma was not perceived; for even though they contend the stars move, they nevertheless [assign] those same degrees...

...concerning the shining degrees and those dark ones which the ancients determine. In this matter, how much confusion arose among them, and how much childishness of both things and words was present, has been explained above; truly, nothing could be less true than their supposed experience in these matters. The same error was made by them regarding the degrees they call "increasing fortune," which we have also pointed out there. You will find these noted one way in **Al-Qabisi** <note>original: "Alchabitium," a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note>, another way in **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: "Albumasarem," the most influential Persian astrologer of the Middle Ages</note>, and yet another in **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Auenazram," a 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer</note>.

<margin>The Lying Egyptians</margin> There is the same diversity regarding the "wells" <note>specific degrees in which a planet was thought to lose its influence, as if it had fallen into a pit</note>, which none of the ancients established. Nor can **Aboafar** <note>A variant of Abu Ma'shar</note> help but lie when he claims to follow their opinion while describing them, since he makes several of them into "wells" which others do not. 

<margin>Theban</margin> While Aboafar creates these wells, **Hephaestion of Thebes**—an expert in all Egyptian astrology—lists the "shining degrees" differently than Aboafar. He identifies the 6th degree of Aries, the 5th of Taurus, the 30th of Gemini, the 22nd of Cancer, and many others in different signs. Furthermore, a certain Eastern astrologer who called himself the "Searcher" <note>Likely referring to Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), who frequently used the title "Perscrutator"</note> feels entirely differently about these degree properties than all the ancients. He offers no other proof for his dogma than the "reliability of experience"—namely, that the sayings of the ancients do not match reality, but his own do. This observation of various degrees is therefore vain, unfaithful, and inconsistent, condemned not only by us but by **Ptolemy** as well.

## Chapter XVIII. Where the "Lots" originated and how much astrologers conflict with each other in calculating them.

Since the three methods they use in every prediction are nothing but a fiction of the mind—a vain thing and a voluntary dogma—they say: "Count the degrees intercepted between this planet and that, and when you have counted as many degrees starting from the <term>Ascendant</term> <note>original: "horoscopo," the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment</note>, the place where the number ends will be a <term>Lot</term> <note>original: "pars" (part). These are mathematical points in the zodiac used to signify specific life areas like wealth, marriage, or death.</note>." They treat this Lot as an indicator of some matter, observed no differently than a planet or a star. What greater delirium can be imagined than this precept? No natural power exists in the heavens where there is no star, no light, nor any other natural quality—just as there is certainly nothing in that specific degree where the count ends.

<margin>Refutation</margin> But because this enumeration is fashioned according to their whims, it cannot have any physical rationale. **Aboafar**, the most trifling of men, wanted to provide a reason for these Lots, which none of the ancients had done. Yet, despite his great loquacity, he said nothing of substance. 

<margin>Aboafar's Logic</margin> For the sum of his words is finally this: when two planets signify the same thing, the distance between them also has the power of signifying that thing. But this must be measured from the Ascendant, because whether coming events are good or bad is known from the location where the significator of those things arrives from the Ascendant. For example, since the Sun and Saturn are the stars of parents, the interval by which they are separated from each other should be counted from the ascending degree. The degree where that number ends will hold the future significance regarding parents, as if the power of the Sun and Saturn were, in a way, joined there. 

This is the "subtlety" of Aboafar, in which he assumes what he denies, and which we primarily mock: namely, that a distance has such power that the end of a similar interval drawn from the Ascendant possesses a power of effect. He ought to have explained the reason for this, but since he does not, it is not a rational opinion but a mere story. As we have seen, this is not only ineffective (as it proves nothing about the matter in question) but is also false and repugnant to the principles of astrologers. For the creators of the Lots—as we just said—made the primary Lots those of the planets themselves, not of things and events; that was a later invention by their successors. 

What place can Aboafar's logic have regarding the Lots of the planets, when he says Lots are taken from the interval of two planets signifying the same thing? This is especially true since, according to **Hermes**, the distance of no planet except the Sun and Moon is taken by itself. 

<margin>Hermes, the first author of the Lots</margin> Hermes was the first author of these Lots, in that book he titled *The All-Virtuous* <note>original Greek: "πανσαρελω" (Panaretos)</note>. But he derives the Lot from the planet whose Lot is sought and the Lot of one of the two luminaries [Sun or Moon]. For he takes the Lot of Venus from the Sun and Venus; here we noted in the first book that Aboafar and Al-Qabisi were deceived. 

<margin>Aboafar Al-Qabisi</margin> They also erred regarding the Lot of Mercury (taken from the Lot of Fortune and Mercury itself), the Lot of Mars (from Mars and the Lot of Fortune), and the Lot of Jupiter (from the Sun and Jupiter). The Lots of the Sun and Moon are taken from each other, as is manifest to everyone. Nor does he intend for other things to be signified through the Lots than what each...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrological "Parts" or "Lots"—mathematical points calculated from the distances between planets and the Ascendant. He is currently arguing that the assignment of these Parts is arbitrary and inconsistent with the planets' own traditional meanings.</meta>

-> ## DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY <-

<sig>A</sig>

the planet whose part it is said to be signifies that matter. Add to this that the "parts" <note>technical term: *partes*, often called "Lots" in modern astrology</note> of things are not actually derived from the planets that signify those same things among astrologers. For instance, while everyone agrees that Mars signifies brothers, the "Part of Brothers" is derived from Jupiter and Saturn, and never from Mars. Furthermore, all the ancients demand the "Part of Marriage" from Saturn, a planet they intended to have no association with weddings or unions. Therefore, the invention of that **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: "Aboasaris"</note> is not only trivial and nonsensical—presupposing the very thing under dispute—but it is also alien to the opinions of the original authors of this dogma. Something else entirely moved them than the dreams this trifler had after so many centuries. 

Indeed, the first occasion for this error was as follows. It seemed to the ancients that the rising degree—that is, the "horoscope" <note>In ancient astrology, the *horoskopos* specifically meant the Ascendant or rising sign, not the entire chart</note>—corresponded to the Sun. Therefore, since the Moon exists almost as a secondary Sun above us, they wanted there to be a second "horoscope" responding in proportion to the Moon. They judged that this spot should be placed no elsewhere than at the same distance from the rising point as the Sun is from the Moon in any given birth. They called this place the **Lot of Fortune** <note>original: "κληρον τυχησ" (*klēron tychēs*)</note> for a reason we shall mention shortly. **Ptolemy** himself teaches this in the third book of his *Apotelesmatika* <note>Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*</note>, reminding us also that all antiquity agreed that the Part of Fortune should be distant from the Ascendant by the same amount the Moon is from the Sun. Nor does the opinion of those who, in nocturnal births, calculate from the Moon to the Sun vary from this; for they simply turn from the ascendant toward the preceding signs. Thus, they define the location in the same way as those who, calculating from the Sun to the Moon, count through the sequence of the signs. 

<margin>Whence the name of the Lot and of Fortune</margin> I suspect the reason for the name is this: since they had made two "horoscopes," as it were—one for the Sun and one for the Moon—they attributed the Lot of the body and soul to the former (the true and solar horoscope), but to the latter (the lunar and adventitious one) they attributed the "Lot of Fortune." This refers to those things which are outside of ourselves, so that we might receive our very selves from the first, and our circumstances from the second. This is why the lunar horoscope is called the "Lot of Fortune," and Ptolemy judges fortunes from no other source more than this. For these "Parts" are commonly called "Lots," but in **Firmicus Maternus**, they are called "Places." 

<margin>Here Hermes the Egyptian is censured in the book he titled "The All-Virtuous"</margin> When this practice had already been accepted, a certain **Hermes the Egyptian** <note>The legendary Hermes Trismegistus</note>, having little regard for the logic of the original institution, thought that Lots should be made for all the planets by following this example. Thus, he established the Lots of Saturn and the rest in a book titled **The All-Virtuous** <note>original: "παναρετοσ" (*panaretos*)</note>. He called the Part of the Sun the **Good Spirit** <note>original: "αγατον Δαιμονα" (*agathon daimona*)</note>, which is to say the "Good God" or "Spirit"; that of Jupiter, **Victory** <note>original: "νικην" (*nikēn*)</note>; that of Mercury, **Necessity** <note>original: "αναγκην" (*anagkēn*)</note>; that of Venus, **Love** <note>original: "εροτα" (*erōta*)</note>; that of Mars, **Boldness** <note>original: "τολμαν" (*tolman*)</note>; and that of Saturn, **Retribution** <note>original: "νεμεσιν" (*nemesin*)</note>. In arranging these, he observed a method where each part was taken from the distance of the planet itself to the Part of either the Sun or the Moon. Specifically, he used the Sun’s Part for Venus and Jupiter, and the Moon’s Part for the others. Where the Sun's Part was to be used, the calculation was made from the planet to the Part in a daytime birth, but in a nighttime birth, from the Part to the planet. He did the opposite where the Part of Fortune was used. However, he commanded that the starting point for all calculations be the Ascendant, because he saw that this was done by the ancients for the Part of Fortune, and he followed their example for the rest. 

<margin>Paulus of Alexandria added four parts. An infinite number of parts. The Chaldeans did not use parts, according to Porphyry.</margin> He failed to notice that the conjecture—whatever its worth—that moved the ancients to establish a Lot for the Moon does not apply to the other planets. There is no such parity or kinship between the other planets and the Sun that would require something to correspond to them in place of a horoscope, just as the rising point corresponds to the Sun. 

Would that this license for invention had contained itself within these boundaries! But **Paulus of Alexandria**, who lived some centuries after the aforementioned Hermes, added four parts to the planetary parts: not of stars now, but of things—namely parents, children, brothers, and marriage. This discovery provided the occasion for further raving, so that they fashioned an infinite number of "Parts" to designate almost everything in the heavens. For you can read of the "Parts" of chickpeas, beans, lentils, barley, onions, and a thousand things of this sort in all the Arabian and Latin authors. 

I am not so moved as to believe these were an invention of the Egyptians, since **Porphyry**, when writing his *Introduction to Astrology* <note>original: "Apotelesmaticas"</note> based on the opinions of the Chaldeans, makes no mention of them anywhere. Ptolemy abhors all of them except for the Part of Fortune—though he would have been more correct to despise that one as well, since the "Lunar Horoscope" and everything they devise regarding it is vain and arbitrary. But those errors may be considered pardonable when compared to those into which the license of astrologers, with futile temerity, has slid down from the example of a single ancestor.

...has fallen away. The reason why he maintains the distances between two planets, and why they count it from the horoscope <note>In this context, "horoscope" refers to the Ascendant, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note>, is now clear: namely, it was found in the **Part of Fortune** <note>original: "fortunæ pte"</note>. In this, according to the ancients, it was sought as if it were a horoscope, which is why it had to be placed at that distance toward the east where the Sun was moved by the Moon. Later, those who were ignorant of the origin of this dogma made up such fables as **Abu Ma'shar** <margin>Abu Ma'shar</margin> <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD) was a highly influential Persian astrologer known in the West as Albumasar</note> recounts there. If they say they were moved by experience rather than reason, I will respond—as I have always done—that there is no authority in "experiments" <margin>Astrologers cannot rely on experiments because of the disagreement among authors</margin> upon which men of equal authority do not agree.

This also happens with the "Parts" as in every astrological dogma. First, almost every author places the **Part of Fortune** itself in a different spot. For **Ptolemy** instructs it to be calculated from the Sun to the Moon, whether the birth <term>genitura|A birth chart or the moment of birth</term> was by day or by night. Others affirm that for a nocturnal birth, it should be calculated from the Moon to the Sun. <margin>Opinion of Heliodorus and Minus</margin> **Heliodorus** and **Minus** calculate the **Part of Venus** from the **Part of the Daemon** <note>The Part of the Daemon, or "Lot of Spirit," is the spiritual counterpart to the material Lot of Fortune</note> to Venus during the day, but the reverse at night. **Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note>, following Abu Ma'shar <margin>Opinion of Alchabitius and Abu Ma'shar</margin>, goes from the Part of Fortune to the Part of the Daemon at night, and from the Daemon to Fortune during the day. **Abenzagel** <note>Likely the astronomer Al-Zarqali</note> takes it from Venus to Fortune, both day and night alike. <margin>Another by Abenzagel</margin>

For the **Part of Parents**, the Arabs <margin>Opinion of the Arabs</margin> take it from the Sun to Saturn in a diurnal birth, and from Saturn to the Sun in a nocturnal one. **Heliodorus** says that if Saturn is hidden by the Sun's rays, whether it be night or day, one proceeds from Mars to Jupiter. For the **Part of Brothers**, **Minus** goes from Jupiter to Saturn at night. The Greeks do the same at night, but during the day they go from Saturn to Jupiter. Regarding **Marriage**, they disagree immensely: for if you seek the **Lot of the Husband**, Alchabitius always counts from the Sun to Venus; Heliodorus goes to Venus as well, but starting from Saturn. **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer</note>, following the opinion of the ancients, commands that during the day we go from Saturn to Venus, but at night we begin from Venus. He testifies, however, that he himself—as others also prescribe—has proven in many nativities <margin>Another by Heliodorus</margin> that one should always calculate from the Sun to the Moon in both day and night births. If we examine the birth of a woman, Maternus orders the calculation from Mars to Venus by day, and from Venus to Mars by night. Others always go from Venus to Saturn, which Abenzagel prefers; Alchabitius says this is the opinion of **Hermes**. Abenzagel proves it should always be taken from the Moon to Mars. Others always go from the Sun to Mars. They differ similarly in the rest, but it would be tedious to follow them all. For the **Part of Travel**, the Arabs go from the Lord of the Ninth House to its first minutes; the Greeks go from the Sun to Mars. For the **Part of Inheritances**, the former go from Saturn to the Moon, while the latter go from Saturn to Venus. For **Slaves**, the former go from Mercury to the Moon, the latter from Mars to the Moon. All the ancients calculate the **Part of the Mother** from Saturn to the Moon, then reckoning the number from the horoscope, as the ancients were accustomed to do in all things. The Arabs seek it from the Moon to the first minute of the Eighth House, and they add as many degrees as Saturn has traveled through the sign in which he is located; and whatever sum the calculation makes, they follow that amount from the beginning of the sign where Saturn is, and through the following signs. But we are not so idle as to record all their fables; it is certainly clear to anyone that these are not based on faithful experiments, but rather that each man has fashioned dogmas for himself according to his own whim.

## Chapter XIX. The opinion on the Twelfth-parts is exploded, and their Egyptian authors, along with their climacteric years, are rejected.

<margin>What is being discussed here regarding the Twelfth-parts</margin>
**T**he insanity regarding the **Twelfth-parts** <term>Dodecathemoria|A system where each 30-degree sign of the zodiac is subdivided into twelve 2.5-degree sections</term> is equal to that of the "Parts," and should be hissed away for the same reason. I do not mean that "Twelfth-part" we mentioned above, which is simply the 12th part of any sign. Rather, I mean what is handed down by Maternus and the Greek writers in this manner: regarding whichever planet you wish to find the Twelfth-part, they say you should multiply the degree you are calculating by twelve—whether that planet is in the tenth degree, the fifth, or any other number of the sign it occupies. You divide the total sum of that calculation into thirty parts for each sign. But you take the starting point from the beginning of the sign in which the star is whose Twelfth-part you seek; and in whichever sign the final number falls, that indicates to you the position of the Twelfth-part. <margin>Example</margin> For example, place the Sun in the 5th degree and 5th minute of **Aries**. If you multiply five by twelve, there will be sixty degrees; the minutes will make one degree, and thus there will be [sixty-one] parts...

<summary>Pico catalogues the contradictory methods used by various astrologers (Ptolemy, Abu Ma'shar, Alchabitius, etc.) to calculate mathematical "Lots," arguing their disagreement proves these are made-up fables. He then begins a similar refutation of the "Dodecathemoria" or Twelfth-parts system.</summary>

<margin>Refutation: Paul of Alexandria, because he saw this part was false, thought up another calculation.</margin>
...sixty-one parts. You will give thirty to Aries, in which we said the Sun was; thirty to Taurus; and they will find the <term>dodecathemoria|The division of a single zodiac sign into twelve equal parts of 2.5 degrees each, often used to refine a horoscope's meaning</term> in the first part of Gemini. What can be thought up that is more empty or futile than this finding? Since through these numbers, no power of a planet and no quality is transmitted into that part. But if someone objects that it has been observed to correspond to events, I will put forward Paul of Alexandria, a most serious author among the Egyptians—whose invention this was originally—who testified that such an observation was found to be false.
<margin>Against the Egyptians.</margin>
For he himself introduced a new method against the ancients: he argued that the parts of all things should not be multiplied by twelve, but by thirteen. If the ancient calculation did not work for him, it was surely because it was false and fabricated. And because sometimes by multiplying by thirteen he happened upon what he was looking for, he established a dogma from a single success, after the fashion of astrologers. These are those "Egyptian mysteries" whose opinions the superstitious common folk adore as if they were oracles. Yet their doctrine not only lacks anything divine, but is ridiculous even to the half-learned. For if there were any such thing as astrology, the Egyptians would deserve the name of astrologers least of all, since they were ignorant of the true and natural things in the sky—that is, the motions of the constellations and stars—as we shall say below. In their predicting, they made more use of these deceptive dreams than of the stars and planets. Heliodorus writes that **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>Heliodorus was a 4th-century astrologer; Hermes Trismegistus is the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and astrological texts were attributed</note> had already revealed the finding of the "Parts" of the planets; for by those parts alone, with no other thing considered, one could pronounce on everything equally—all the <term>monomeria|The system of assigning a specific planetary ruler to every single degree (1/30th) of a zodiac sign</term> and dodecathemoria—just as much as they attributed to the whole of prediction. From this, Ptolemy, the most prudent of astrologers, noting them indirectly, says that he will hand down his own dogmas **not through lots and numbers without physical cause** <note>original: "ου δια κληρων και αριθμων αναιτιο λογητων"</note> because they are all **superfluously babbled about by many and have an unbelievable explanation** <note>original: "περιττωσ υπω των πολλων φλυα ρουμενα και απισιανον εχοντασ λογον"</note>. That is: not through parts and numbers that are ineffective and have no rational cause, which many people fabulously talk about with no reason for persuasion. Moreover, when he says "numbers," he also marks the dodecathemoria which we find fault with, as well as those who create <term>climacteric years|Cycles of years in a person's life—specifically every 7th or 9th year—thought by astrologers to be periods of great risk or change</term> from numbers by observation alone, such as the ninth-year and seventh-year cycles. From this comes the superstition that is troublesome to many old men concerning their sixty-third year; for they fear it more than a snake or a tiger. But the common people sin in these things with a pardonable error; yet for those who wish to be philosophers, who shall excuse them?
<margin>Ptolemy, the most prudent of astrologers</margin>

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS. THE SEVENTH BOOK BEGINS.

## Chapter I. What has been disputed so far, and what must be disputed in this book.

<margin>Continuation of this book with the preceding ones</margin>
Hitherto, we demonstrated that astrology is nothing, having stripped away the influence of the stars. This we showed by what was said by us reasonably from philosophy, from the dignity of the stars, the condition of lower things, and the reliability of experience. Then, we proved that even if the stars did effect what the astrologers think, they would nevertheless do it differently than has been devised by them; and consequently, no knowledge of this influence or of future things is possible for them. Now we must act so that, even if we concede that these things happen by the heavens, and that they are arranged by them—that is, that all things receive their fates from the sky at their primordial hour—we may nevertheless declare that the "fate" of each thing cannot be known by them. For this is the first necessity for them: if they are to succeed, they must have most certainly explored which fatal hour belongs to each person. In the disputation of the present book, we shall teach that this cannot be known, or at least is not certainly known by them. And since they establish various principles for various things, we shall first dispute the principle of man: declaring it to be in ambiguity, and that whatever it may be, it is certainly not what is thought by the astrologers.

## Chapter II. That the fatal hour is ambiguous, if any exists, in all things which are not completed in a moment but in time, and especially in humans, in whom the birth chart seems to have little strength.

He then begins Book Seven, arguing that even if stellar influence existed, the exact "fatal hour" of birth is impossible to determine precisely.</summary>
