# BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>
A question concerning the beginning <note>original: "initium." The OCR suggests "uitium" (vice/defect), but context confirms "initium" (beginning).</note>.
A thing acquires its fate when it begins to be made.
Which hour was fatal; the various beginnings of a human being.
Aristotle, the interpreter of nature.
</margin>
**N**ow, in determining the beginning of any thing—which is not completed in a single moment but over a period of time—it is an inextricable question whether the fatal time for that thing is when the craftsman first sets out to make it. For whatever "efficient cause" <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; in this case, the force or person that brings something into being.</note> it might obtain, one must ask: is fate determined at the start? Or rather, since the whole thing is not completed at the beginning, but is built part by part, are there different fates for these different parts? For whatever we might say, there is a reason to support it. Indeed, if the craftsman's hand moved successfully, how can the work be unsuccessful when the craftsman works successfully? For the "success" of both the maker and the thing made is simply when the work turns out well and according to the maker’s wish. Furthermore, if fate is efficiently caused by the stars and not merely designated by them, when should a thing more rightly receive its fate than when the stars, through the intervention of other causes, actually produce it? Therefore, the fate of the finished product would depend on that hour in which the craftsman first set about making it. On the other hand, how can a thing receive a fate before it even exists? Or how shall we say it exists when it first begins to be made so that it might one day be? Finally, a thing is what it is because of its species <note>The "species" or "form" is the philosophical essence that makes a thing a member of its category (e.g., what makes a chair a chair).</note> and the form that arrives in an instant to complete it. Therefore, what moment is more fatal to it than the one in which it first begins to be what it is? At that point, it can stand by its own nature and stability, separate from the cause that was making it. Therefore, we shall more reasonably search for the fates of things not from the hour they *begin to be made*, but from the hour they *begin to exist*.

Again, if different parts are finished at different times, why should each part not receive the decree of its own fortune from its own time? This is especially true since experience proves that things happen differently to various parts of the same object. For even in the body of the same human being, some members will sometimes be healthy while others are diseased. Similarly, one part of the same city will be subject to ruins and fires, while nothing of the sort happens to the remaining parts. Why, then, is it not more reasonable for each thing to be moved and governed by its own private constellation, rather than having subsequent events draw their "condition of fate" from some past and perhaps forgotten beginning?

Let these things be said in general regarding all things. Now let us examine the same issues specifically in the human being, regarding whose "fatal origin" (if such a thing exists) a great and necessarily inextricable ambiguity arises. For what shall we establish as the beginning, when so many of its "beginnings" appear, all of them seemingly worthy of primacy? Shall we judge that fatal point of time to be the one which is first in time among all others: the moment when the man and woman join? Or is it not that, but rather when the human seed from the male is added to the womb? Or are these merely "preludes" and necessary antecedents? We might instead establish the first beginning of human formation as when the seminal power itself attacks the purest part of the female discharge and establishes it—that is, curdles it into a fetus—just as milk is joined and thickened by rennet <note>original: "coagulo." Pico uses the classical analogy of cheese-making to describe early embryonic formation.</note>. Or is it not yet a human beginning even then, but rather when all the parts of the body are present in the conception? Or when it is already wrapped in membranes or the afterbirth? Does nature begin the human being when the heart is first distinguished in actuality? By the power of the heart, the thing being born is now like a son emancipated from his father, beginning to be governed by himself, as Aristotle, the interpreter of nature, taught. Indeed, great authority and power must be granted to this beginning, since the heart is the first thing formed, and in the distinguishing of the other parts, the movement and growth of all are distributed from the heart. Thus (if we must spin tales with the astrologers), just as the power implanted in the heart subsequently unfolds the whole human being as the other parts join together, so the solar virtue <note>The "solar virtue" refers to the life-giving influence associated with the Sun, which astrologers and ancient biologists often linked to the heart.</note> first drunk in by the heart might subsequently unfold the entire power of fate. 

Or is it rather that this heart-moment is the "principal" fate of life, but the disposition of any particular limb depends mostly on the hour in which it is formed, thereby undergoing its own private condition of fate? For to those who consider and penetrate all things correctly, it seems highly reasonable that if, for example, the "luminaries" <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> preside over the eyes (as is said), the condition and mixture of the eyes should depend on the disposition of the luminaries at the time the eyes are formed, rather than on what happened earlier when the seed filled the womb, or what will follow later when the eyes are already finished and the infant is about to emerge from the mother's womb. This same reasoning should be understood to apply to the other limbs. 

But if, setting aside all these things we have mentioned, another beginning more outstanding in authority and efficacy is sought, what can we propose more reasonably than the moment in which the soul is shared with the fetus? For it is then that a human being begins to be; having attained the full rationale of substance, he then consists of his own matter and form. And if fate comes from...

the hour proceeds, in which the thing first exists; certainly no other hour will be considered more fatal for a human being.
<margin>A new way of considering the beginning from several mixed factors.</margin>
But if we must depart from this opinion, it will have great probability to suggest that things belonging to the body are referred to the seminal principle <note>The "seminal principle" refers to the moment of conception, when the physical seeds of life are first joined.</note>; those belonging to the soul to the moment of animation itself; and those which are external or matters of fortune to that moment by chance when the human being, having left the enclosures of the womb, first enters this field in which fortune plays. Finally, from this so varied and knotty ambiguity concerning the human beginning, perhaps those who are divine spirits will extricate themselves; it can in no way be correctly explained by relying on reason. If reason is to affirm anything, it will affirm nothing less than what the astrologers have decreed—namely, that the fates of a newborn human depend on the hour of birth—an opinion into which the astrologers were led by no sound reason. But because they saw they could better track this beginning <note>Meaning the birth hour is easier to record than the moment of conception.</note>, they granted it the primary role. Therefore, they are even accustomed to attribute something to the conception after the birth has occurred, because they hope that sometimes something can be known about it. The remaining principles, which are certainly the most powerful—especially the animation of the fetus—they have rejected entirely. Therefore, if these are completely unknown to them, even if they conceded that human fates depend on them, they would not be able to claim any power of divining fate for themselves. But to pass over the rest, by what reason do they prefer birth to conception and the animation of the fetus? For if we give the primary role in establishing fate to that beginning which is first in time, there is no earlier principle than the seminal principle from which all others proceed. If a moment is preferred not so much for being first in time but for its efficacy and dignity, then the time of animating the fetus should be preferred above all. Birth is both the latest of all and has little or no efficacy; it neither begins, nor makes, nor completes the human, but only shows what has already been begun and completed.

### Chapter III. That Ptolemy attributed more to conception than birth, and Ptolemy’s own reasoning proves that nothing should be attributed to birth either.

<margin>Ptolemy gave more weight to conception than to birth.</margin>
**B**ut if the words of Ptolemy himself are weighed carefully, we will see that he was led by the force of reason to give more weight to conception than to birth—even though, to favor his profession, he attempted to build up many arguments about the efficacy of birth. His words in the third book of the *Effects* <note>original: "apoteleſmatũ." This refers to Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos* (The Four Books), often called the *Apotelesmatika* or "Effects" of the stars.</note> are as follows: "When a temporal beginning of a human is established, the natural beginning will indeed be when the seed is admitted to the genital womb; but potentially and accidentally, it is the hour of birth when the infant comes forth. Therefore, for those who have grasped the hour of the admission of seed by chance or observation, it is more fitting for them to follow that moment in discerning the properties of body and soul, considering the configurations of the stars at that time. For once the seed is disposed from the beginning with a certain quality from the state of the surrounding air, although it varies through the times of the subsequent formation, yet since it naturally takes to itself only its own and related matter, when it is brought to action it will be assimilated even more to the disposition of its first quality." These are Ptolemy’s words verbatim. Here it seems to me that he pronounces most expressly and assertively, without any doubt, that the first and natural and most effective principle of a human is the admission of seed; and this should be followed most of all when identifying the turns of human life, both those pertaining to the body and those pertaining to the soul. And once he asserted this, he then accurately and anxiously addressed what might be objected regarding the changes the seed undergoes. But because he knew the art of astrology would be endangered if he denied that human fate could be pronounced from any other source, he added the following to what we have said: "But for those who are ignorant of the hour of the seminal beginning, which is mostly unknown, it is necessary for them to follow the principle of birth." Let us weigh these things before we add others: he says the hour of birth is to be used only when the hour of conception is unknown. Concerning the hour of conception, he said it is "fitting" <note>original Greek: "προσηκει" (prosēkei), meaning it is appropriate or the proper way.</note> to adhere to it. Of the hour of birth, he did not say it is fitting, but "necessary" <note>original Greek: "αναγκαιον" (anankaion), meaning forced by necessity or a last resort.</note>: that is, it is "necessary" for those who do not know the hour of conception but still wish to divine fate to flee to the birth, as if to a light...

<summary>Pico argues that the moment of birth is the least important "beginning" of a person, following Ptolemy's own admission that conception is the true natural starting point. He claims astrologers only use the birth hour out of convenience and "necessity" because they cannot track the more significant moments of conception or animation.</summary>

...so that it may appear clearer than light that he descended into this opinion not willingly, but forced by necessity. Ptolemy uses the hour of birth as if it were (as he says) a **second plank after a shipwreck** <note>original: "secunda post naufragium tabula"; a classical idiom for a last-resort or fallback plan.</note>. And while he has spoken reasonably enough thus far, he soon tries as much as he can not to desert his profession, attempting to demonstrate that this moment of birth is also a valid principle. Regarding this, he adds: "And this is also a very great principle, 
<margin>The words of Ptolemy: regarding the inception <note>original: "καταρχήν" (katarchēn); the Greek term for the start or inaugural moment of an event.</note>.</margin>
falling short of the first only in this: that through conception, those things which happen before birth can also be foreknown." Furthermore, if someone should call this the "principle" and that other one the "inception" <note>original: "καταρσην" (katarsēn); likely a variant or OCR error for "καταρχήν" (katarchēn).</note>—that is, what follows the principle—that second one would indeed be following this time, but perhaps it will be more perfect in its priority. For almost by right, this generation of the human seed will not be denied, but that of the **man** will be; since the infant then receives many things which it did not have before while in the womb, and those things are proper to the nature of man. Likewise, although the hour of birth may seem to contribute nothing to making the one who is born such or such a person, it nevertheless makes him come forth into the light with a configuration closely related to the surrounding heaven. For after nature has perfected him, it gives the impulse to exit only when the disposition of the heavens is similar in figure to that which formed the fetus from the beginning. Wherefore it is reasonable that this disposition of the stars at the hour of birth also has a significance for things—not because it is the cause of them, but because by natural necessity it is similar to that prior cause which did effect them. 

These words of Ptolemy have been faithfully recited by us, in which the first thing to see is that what the commentator Averroës <note>Averroës (1126–1198) was a famous Andalusian philosopher and commentator on Greek science, whose interpretations Pico often contests.</note> says is entirely false: 
<margin>The error of Averroës</margin>
that Ptolemy speaks hesitantly in his earlier words where he discusses the efficacy of conception, but speaks assertively in these last words where he demonstrates that the hour of birth has the power of signifying. On the contrary, in the former case he affirms everything, excepting nothing and doubting nothing; whereas here, he speaks with no part of his speech lacking an added particle of doubt—now inserting "almost," now "perhaps." And finally, when he is about to conclude his entire dispute, he has no other reason to defend the hour of birth as a signifier of fate than to persuade us that it is similar to the seminal principle. He is so far from denying that the authority for deciding what kind of person is to be born exists in the conception, that he concedes no more to the birth-hour than that it be found similar and in agreement with the conception. 

For that common opinion among astrologers, 
<margin>A common opinion is rebuked.</margin>
believed even by the commentator on Ptolemy—that the hour of conception signifies only those things which happen to the fetus in the mother’s womb—is born from a false understanding of Ptolemy’s words. It is easily understood that he did not say *only* those things are signified through conception, but *also* those things which the birth-hour cannot signify. "The conception," Ptolemy says, "excels the birth-hour in this: that through it, even those things which occur before birth can be foreseen." But if it signified *only* those things, it would never have been necessary to add that, nor should the first principle be considered superior to the second, since the span of an entire life is far greater than the task of governing the first, unformed rudiments of a still-developing nature.

Therefore, if Ptolemy trusts in those words uttered so doubtfully and hesitatingly—that the power of the second principle is perhaps more effective than the first, and that this is "almost" the principle of the human being while the other is merely of the human seed—he disagrees not only with reason but clearly with himself. With himself because (as I was saying) he could not defend the authority of fate at the beginning of birth without devising an affinity between the birth and the seminal principle; and when he later hands down precepts for foreseeing sex and other conditions of the newborn, he says these are better foreknown from the conception than from the birth. He disagrees with reason both because of many things we have said above, and because it is utterly beyond reason for us to say that conception is the principle of the seed and birth the principle of the man. For indeed, when the seed has filled the womb, it does not "become" itself, but begins to be abolished as nature applies its hands to fabricating the man. Therefore, that moment is the principle of generating the man, just as it is the principle of the seed’s destruction. 

But if you call birth the "principle of the man" because he then first has many things he did not have in the womb, those things do not pertain to his **substance** (which was already made and completed), but only to the carrying out of certain actions. Some of these are not even unique to humans; if we were to date a man's fate from these, the fate would begin long after his origin—such as when the fate of a human (not just an infant) begins: when he starts to think, deliberate, and reason. For immediately upon being born, he has nothing uniquely human except his **wailing**. Therefore, Ptolemy, the most prudent of astrologers, would not insist on such false and frivolous arguments...

Neither are these things alone, by which the birth-horoscope is placed before the conception, but those which attribute some power in decreeing fate to the birth-horoscope can have little firmness. For the sum of the whole virtue 
<margin>Haly is refuted.</margin> 
is referred to the **consensus** <note>agreement or alignment</note> that exists between the birth and the conception; but what is this consensus, or what is the similarity? Haly <note>Referring to Ali ibn Ridwan, a prominent 11th-century Arabic astrologer and commentator on Ptolemy.</note> responds that the Sun at the hour of birth is always found in a sign which is either the seventh, ninth, or tenth from the sign it was in at the hour of conception. Is this then that "similarity"? O ridiculous vanity! As if any time does not "agree" with another time by this reasoning—namely, that the Sun, at whatever time, is necessarily distant by some number of signs from the sign in which it was at another time. Or is it more probable what they assert about the Moon? That its position when we are born was the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The "horoscope" here refers specifically to the Ascendant, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of an event.</note> of conception; and whatever the Moon's position was then [at conception] becomes the horoscope of the birth. Yet, this is false and a fiction of the astrologers, as will be demonstrated later. And Haly Abenrodan, explaining Ptolemy in a treatise on this present question, says that he has found this to be sometimes true and sometimes false. But come now, let us say it were true: there is no better way that faked "consensus" of both hours will be more clearly disproven than if you investigate the hour of conception using that rule of the astrologers: if you establish a <term>theme</term> <note>A "theme" is a technical term for a natal chart or astrological map of the heavens.</note> for that time, you will find the disposition of the heavens and stars to be always different from it, and a signifier of entirely other things than those which will appear to those calculating for the hour of birth. But why do we waste more words in refuting such trifles?
<margin>Haly says the efficacy of fate is in the hour of conception.</margin>
Haly, the distinguished astrologer, in the book he wrote on *Elections* <note>Astrological "elections" involve choosing the most auspicious time to begin an endeavor.</note>, aptly confesses that the efficacy of decreeing fate is in the hour of conception. But because these things are unknown, he says the astrologers have fled to the hour of birth. And when they themselves are pressed regarding the birth of twins, whose fortune is disparate, they are accustomed to say that sometimes the diversity of their conceptions varies their fortune; whereas, if the hour of conception only disposes those things which happen within the womb, it follows instead that their conception could be disparate while their fortune is similar, but the birth could in no way be the cause.

<margin>Chapter 4.</margin>
## By what ways astrologers track universal fates, and how they are everywhere unreasonable.

<margin>The threefold way of astrologers for foretelling universal things.</margin>
We have spoken of the beginning of particular fate—that it is uncertain and established by astrologers upon false reasoning. It remains to speak of universality: namely, from whence the fates of cities, nations, kingdoms, and the world in general proceed. This also (if it be granted that such a thing exists) is in doubt and uncertainty, and is wrongly defined by our astrologers. They are accustomed to proceed toward predicting universal changes by roughly a threefold way: either from the great <term>conjunctions</term> <note>The meeting of two or more planets in the same degree of the zodiac.</note> of the superior stars or eclipses of the luminaries [the Sun and Moon]; or from the disposition of the heavens when the Sun enters the first minute of Aries, which they have established as the beginning of the year; or from the particular principles of cities, kingdoms, and nations—that is, from the hour in which a city was built, or a kingdom instituted, or a law given to a nation by which it lives and is governed. That all these things are 
<margin>The insanity and impiety of astrologers.</margin>
frivolous was shown for the most part above: not only where the entire influence of the stars was driven out, but also when we weakened the whole reasoning of predicting from great conjunctions; and (whether from those, or from the failures of the luminaries) we declared it vain to expect anything a long time after they occurred. Then we uncovered the impiety and insanity of the astrologers in subjecting nations to the fate of the heavens and the fate of their own laws; and also how vain it is to decree a "birthday" for a built city or an accepted kingdom 
<margin>The fates of a city are not reasonably inaugurated from the throwing of the first stone.</margin>
as if it were a natural thing. Now, even if we grant that there is some fate for all things, we are going to show that nothing certain can be defined concerning the fatal principle of these things, nor has it been defined by astrologers thus far. First, by what reason are they moved to inaugurate the fate of a city from the "throwing of the stone"? Although they search for the fates of the "citizenship" rather than the "city," that moment should rather be observed when the built city began to be inhabited, and to be ruled and contained by its own laws. Likewise, regarding the fortune of a king, there is great discord among them, as some think it depends on that hour in which the king is instituted or chosen. Others think the enthronement or coronation should be inspected.

### Chapter V. That an astrologer cannot predict in which region of the world some fate will occur: since it is uncertain among them which region is subject to which sign or planet.

<margin>
Great discord among astrologers regarding the fortune of a king, or arguments passed over.
</margin>
**I**f those which they call "great <term>conjunctions</term>" <note>original: "coniunctiones"; the alignment of major planets, particularly Jupiter and Saturn, which astrologers believed heralded new historical eras or religions</note>, or those eclipses of the Sun and Moon, stir up the changes that astrologers babble about, I now contend this: that truly nothing can be predicted about them by astrologers. Nor indeed can it be known from those conjectures which may be raised—whether the horoscope of a great conjunction is its own, or belongs to the very year in which it happened to occur. For they are arbitrary in observing the beginning and middle in an eclipse of the <term>luminaries</term> <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>, while the remaining times go unobserved; then, having taken account of only the beginning, let us grant them all these things, nor let us make any dispute over them; we can press them more effectively elsewhere, where the total uncertainty of such predictions may be demonstrated. 

<margin>
Four main heads of the method of predictions.
</margin>
For there are four main heads of these things: first, that it will be in the future; second, in what kind of thing; third, at what time; fourth, among which peoples and in which places and regions. But if there is almost no change in affairs, no event either prosperous or adverse, which does not happen in some part of the world among some peoples at whatever time it comes, then every prediction of this kind will be vain and futile, unless they have this last point explored: namely, in what place and what part of the earth those wonderful changes are to happen. 

<margin>
By what means, according to the astrologers, it can be known in which part of the world the effect is to be expected.
</margin>
Concerning this, they define it so that it is expected in those regions which are subject to the sign in which such a conjunction of stars or eclipse of the luminaries occurred: and not only those which are entirely under the same sign, but either the same sign or at least a sign of the same <term>triplicity</term> <note>original: "triplicitatis"; a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element—Fire, Earth, Air, or Water</note>. This is the certain opinion of all astrologers on this matter. From which it is gathered that nothing can be truly predicted about the fate of any region unless it first remains settled: to which sign and to which planet that region is subject—just as the fate of a man cannot be foretold if the time of his birth is unknown. 

<margin>
Discord of astrologers concerning such an astral matter: on the lordship of planets and signs over the regions of the world.
</margin>
But if the distribution of lands under different signs and planets is such that everything is uncertain among astrologers, it is most clearly evident that their predictions about such things must necessarily be most uncertain. Truly, he who has read the books of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos* (Apotelesmatika)</note> and <term>Albumasar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar, the most influential astrologer of the Islamic world in the Middle Ages</note> accurately will easily understand this, since there is no dogma in which astrology agrees with itself less. <term>Ptolemy</term>, in his book on <term>apotelesmatics</term> <note>original: "apotelesmatū"; the study of the stars' effects</note>, says that the fire <term>triplicity</term> presides over the North; the earth over the South; the air over the East; and the water over the West. This was followed by <term>Julius Firmicus</term> <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer</note>, an emulator of ancient opinions. Yet the same <term>Ptolemy</term>, in the second book of the same work, seems either to explain differently or to change the division, assigning the fire triangularity not so much to the North as to those lands which are situated between the North and West; the earth to those between the East and South; the air to those between the Sunrise and North; and the water between the Sunset and South. 

<margin>
Opinion of Albumasar.
</margin>
From all of these, that which <term>Albumasar</term> writes is as distant as the East is from the West. For he, in the sixth book of his *Great Introduction*, did not want the fire <term>triplicity</term> to rule the North, as <term>Ptolemy</term> did, but the East; while over the North itself (to which <term>Ptolemy</term> assigns Fire), he contends that Water rules; and where <term>Ptolemy</term> assigns Air to the East, he conversely assigns it to the West. <term>Paulus Alexandrinus</term> <note>A 4th-century Greek astrologer</note> holds the same in his *Institutes of the Apotelesmatic Art*. 

<margin>
Another opinion of the same Albumasar.
</margin>
But this same <term>Albumasar</term>, as if having forgotten himself, in the first book of his *On Great Conjunctions*, writes things as different from those he wrote in the *Introduction* as those were different from the dogma of <term>Ptolemy</term>. For in that place, he assigns Air to the <term>triplicity</term>—not Fire like the Greeks with <term>Ptolemy</term> and <term>Mino</term> <note>original: "Mīno"; likely an abbreviation or corruption for Manilius or another classical authority</note>, nor Water like he did elsewhere and many Arabs; and where he had given Water to the North, he then ascribes it to the opposite region, that is, the Southern; and for the West, he says it is ruled by neither Water (as <term>Ptolemy</term> says) nor Air (as he himself says elsewhere) but by Earth. What can be more conflicting than these opinions? Since no reason can make a judgment here...

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.

Whether Henry <note>Henry of Mechelen, a 14th-century commentator on astrological works</note> can show the truth through experience. Henry of Mechelen says this last opinion of **Albumasar** <note>original: "Albu."; refers to Abu Ma'shar, the most influential Persian astrologer of the Middle Ages</note> is the truest and is confirmed by a great many experiments. On the other hand, **Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note> and **Zael** the Israelite <note>Sahl ibn Bishr, a 9th-century Jewish astrologer and mathematician</note>, and **Abraham ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abraā auenazra"; a famous 12th-century Spanish scholar</note>, and **Saphar** in his *Introductory* works, and **Messahala** <note>Mashallah ibn Athari, an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer</note> approve of that which he wrote in his introduction. **Haly Abenrudan** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician</note>, rejecting both, places the opinion of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational figure of Western astrology and astronomy</note> above all others. I pass over how even the ancients disagreed among themselves on these matters: the **Egyptians** from **Hipparchus**, and **Ptolemy** from **Hipparchus**.

I shall declare this with some examples. For to **Aries** <note>The sign of the Ram</note>, the **Egyptians** subjected ancient **Babylon** and **Arabia** bordering **Egypt**. **Ptolemy** subjected **Britain**, **Galatia**, **Germany**, **Bastarnia** <note>An ancient region in Eastern Europe</note>, and **Palestine**. **Hipparchus** and the most ancient astrologers, following a more exact reasoning, subjected different regions to different parts of the sign: thus to the left shoulder of **Aries** they gave **Babylonia**; to the right shoulder, **Thrace**; to the thighs <note>original Greek: "Τοῖσ Τήβει"</note>, **Armenia**; to the ribs <note>original Greek: "Τοῖσ ωλευραίοισ"</note>, **Arabia** bordering **Egypt**; to the neck <note>original Greek: "Τοῖσ Δερα"</note>, **Persia** and **Cappadocia** and **Mesopotamia**; and to the hands <note>original Greek: "Χεικαιν"</note>, **Syria** and the **Red Sea**. 

And thus in the other signs there is similar discord: the **Egyptians**, **Hipparchus**, and **Ptolemy** disagree no less than **Albumasar** disagrees with **Ptolemy**, or even with himself. From this it is clearer than light that nothing certain can be foretold by astrologers regarding where in the world some event might happen, since they have nothing certain or explored concerning the very division of nations and lands under the signs.

## Chapter VI. That a single beginning cannot be established upon which the fates of the entire year depend; then, that various beginnings are set for the year by different people, and that according to the Hebrews the year begins in autumn rather than spring.

**I**t remains for us to speak of the beginning of the year, which **Ptolemy** himself expressly confirms cannot be established as a single point from which the state of the entire year is predicted; I shall prove this using no words other than his own. He therefore writes thus in the second book of his <term>Apoteleſmata</term> <note>Also known as the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational textbook of astrology</note>: "In a circle, no one can simply conceive of a beginning. Yet in the <term>Zodiac</term>, one might rightly establish those points as beginnings which the <term>equinoxes</term> and <term>solstices</term> determine: which are four—namely, two <term>equinoctial</term> and two <term>solstitial</term>. Truly, this place wavers as to whether any one of these four should be preferred. For if you look simply at the nature of a circle itself, none of them will obtain the privilege of being the unique beginning. Yet those who have written on these things use them by making some assumption; they are moved in various ways by each of those four as if by a beginning, some by their own natural reason and others by consensus. For each of those parts has something peculiar and excellent about it, whereby they seem to claim for themselves the authority of the beginning and the New Year." 

He continues: "The <term>vernal equinox</term> <note>Spring</note> is favored because then, for the first time, the day begins to become longer than the night, and because that time of year abounds in moisture—a quality and nature which (as we said above) is most necessary for generating things in every beginning. The prerogative of the <term>summer solstice</term> is this: that then the day is extended to its greatest height and completion; furthermore, among the **Egyptians**, the **Nile** then floods and the <term>Dog Star</term> <note>original: "canícula"; the star Sirius</note> rises. In the <term>autumnal equinox</term>, all fruits are gathered and the seeds of the earth are cast. In the <term>winter solstice</term>, after the decrease, the day then first begins to increase. But what seems more suitable to me and more in harmony with nature is this: that in the observation of the events of the year, we use those four beginnings, observing the <term>conjunctions or oppositions</term> of the **Sun and Moon** that occur nearest to them, and especially the <term>eclipses</term>; so that from the beginning taken at **Aries**, we may foresee what the **spring** shall be; from that at **Cancer**, the **summer**; from **Libra**, the **autumn**; and from **Capricorn**, the **winter**." 

These are **Ptolemy's** words, verbatim. From which it appears that he both believed and proved that no single true beginning can be established from which the fate of the entire year may be foreseen. Thus, I cannot sufficiently marvel at both **Haly Abenrudan**, his interpreter, and the younger astrologers, who repeatedly proclaim that **Ptolemy** attributes more to the <term>vernal equinox</term> in starting the year than to either the beginning of autumn or the <term>solstice</term>. For just as he shows the <term>vernal equinox</term> has no unique reason to deserve the privilege of being the beginning, he does exactly the same for the others. And after he has shown that there is initial authority in all of them, then...

<margin>
Error of Haly Abenrudan and the moderns.
</margin>

Indeed, each has its own reason why it might rightly be considered the beginning of the year. Thus it has happened that different nations began the year from different starting points. The **Egyptians** from the <term>equinox</term> <note>original: "æqnoctiali ſolſtitio"; Pico likely means the spring equinox here</note>; the **Romans** from the winter <term>solstice</term>; others from the autumn; that is, from the entry of the **Sun** into <term>Libra</term>. If it is a common sign, they 
establish two beginnings for the year; if a mobile sign, four. These ideas are utterly vain and arbitrary; as they lack reason, so too are they unsupported by the authority of the ancients or by experience. 

But if someone should perhaps wish to confirm the opinion of the astrologers by the creation of the world—arguing that one should know future fortune from the entry of the **Sun** into <term>Aries</term> because God created the world at that time, so that the successions of years are nothing other than the revolutions of the world's own birth-chart—he will truly be refuted most easily. For if we follow the birth of the world, it is as uncertain when the beginning of the year should be established as it is uncertain at what time of year the world was instituted. For even among the **Hebrews**, from whom we received the account of the world's creation, nothing on this matter is certain or defined; some contend it began in spring, others in autumn. And if one opinion is to be preferred, they lean rather toward believing it was founded in autumn. For regarding what is written—that the same month in which the <note>original: "phaſe"; refers to the Passover (Pesach)</note> **Passover** was celebrated would be the first month among the months of the year—they hold that this was 
<margin>The year [considered] more reasonably</margin>said for the sake of celebrating solemnities. Therefore, if that was the greatest and primary solemnity—their exit from **Egypt**, which was the first of God's benefits to the people, followed by the others—yet in all other matters, the **Hebrews** made the beginning from **September**. This seems to be proven both by many expressions in the <note>original: "ſacraꝝ Iſag."; likely referring to sacred introductions or scriptures</note> **Sacred Introductions** and by the ancient customs of the **Jews**. It is written in Exodus that <term>scenopheigia</term> <note>The Feast of Tabernacles or Sukkot</note>—this is the feast of booths celebrated in autumn—is at the end of the year; but that is celebrated in mid-September. 

And in the book of **Nehemiah**, it is written: *And it happened in the month of Chislev*—which is December among us—*in the twentieth year*. Then: *It happened in the month of Nisan*—which is April—*in the twentieth year*. If the month of **Nisan** (April) were the head of the year, it should have been written as the twenty-first year, not the twentieth. Furthermore, since the Law warned that in the seventh year (which was the Sabbath of years), they should neither reap the fields nor sow, if the head of the year were April, it would follow that what they sowed in October of the sixth year could not be reaped in the following summer; for that summer would belong to the seventh year if its beginnings were taken from spring. If that were so, the seeds entrusted to the earth in the sixth year would perish. This inconvenience did not follow for those establishing the year from September. I pass over what the **scholar of Lérida** <note>original: "Lerſienſis"; likely a reference to a calculator from the school of Lérida</margin> 
<margin>Lérida</margin>wrote in his computation, and **Bede** in his *Book of Times*, and **Josephus** in the first book of *Antiquities*, and **Jerome** 
<margin>Bede, Josephus</margin>in his *Epistle on Solemnities*, who also, in explaining **Ezekiel**, says that **October** is the 
<margin>Jerome</margin>first month and **January** the fourth. From all of these things it is clear—whether we conjecture something from the creation of the world, or whether we follow the reason and authority of the ancient astrologers—that the astrologers who contend they can pronounce the fate of the whole year from the entry of the **Sun** into <term>Aries</term> are entirely in error.

### Chapter VIII. On directions and other methods by which they define the times of future events, [showing] how little consistency they have, and how astrologers disagree among themselves in these matters.

<summary>Pico argues that the astrological practice of using the Sun's entry into Aries to predict the year's events is baseless because there is no historical or religious consensus on when the year actually begins. He cites Hebrew, Roman, and Egyptian traditions, as well as biblical texts, to show that the "start" of time is a matter of convention rather than celestial law.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<a>

<margin>A prior concession based on the astrologers' own premise.</margin>
<margin>The arguments of the astrologers.</margin>
**J**ust as they err in predicting the fates of the year (if any such prediction of fate were to be granted), so too do they err in defining the time when that which the initial hour promised will come to pass. For in this matter also, they employ frivolous, false, and vain suppositions and methods that in no way agree with natural science. Among these, the first and most powerful is the technique concerning the "directions" of the planets and the parts of the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs</note>. (We call them by this name so that we may be better understood by those with whom we are disputing.) We shall briefly expose those theories which rest upon false and ridiculous foundations, after first explaining the opinion based on the astrologers' own premise. Let us suppose, therefore, that the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopus"; here meaning the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note> of some <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genituræ"; a birth chart</note> is at the fifteenth part of Leo, and Saturn is placed in the sixth part of Virgo. It is clear that Saturn is joined to the horoscope neither by sight <note>aspect</note> nor by any other means; therefore, it ought not to harm it. Yet, they have an ancient belief that eventually, through "direction," the horoscope will move toward Saturn, and in the year it reaches it, the person born will face the danger of disease from Saturn. They say it reaches it by this reasoning: because for each individual year, individual parts of the signs are attributed to us—though in proportion to their <term>ascensions</term> <note>original: "anaphorarum"; the time it takes for a zodiacal sign to rise above the horizon</note>—but this is irrelevant to the matter currently at hand. They say, therefore, that in the first year of life, the degree in which the horoscope is located is assigned to us; if a good planet is in that degree, either by its body or its rays, it bestows its benefits in that year; conversely, if a bad planet is there, it bestows evils. In the second year, the second degree from the first corresponds; in the third, the third, and so on. Therefore, if Saturn, for example, occupies the twenty-first part from the horoscope, since that part corresponds with the twenty-first year of life, it would follow that that year will be infested by the rays of Saturn. Thus, when they wish to foresee in which year some good or evil will happen to the one born, they measure the degrees between the principal places of the birth chart and the body or rays of a good or evil star intercepted between them. Based on the number of degrees, they prescribe the number of years after which that event should be expected. This is their position on "directions," from which both **Ptolemy** determines the span of life and the crowd of astrologers pronounces all the falls and turns of fortune. What could be more trivial than these? What could be imagined more irrationally? For first, that distribution of degrees to years—can it be fashioned more out of mere whim? It is conceived with no foundation of scientific reason, especially since sometimes they say years are indicated by these degrees, and sometimes days (depending on what happens to suit them). This might perhaps hold some probability if the partition of the degrees themselves were from nature; but that is entirely dependent on the will of the mathematicians, who divide the signs into thirty parts rather than twenty for no other reason than that the number thirty is more convenient for arithmetic divisions, as will be demonstrated to us by the testimony of the astrologers themselves in the next book.

<margin>Response</margin>
But how could Saturn, located in the sixth part of Virgo (as was assumed), harm me when I was a newborn, even if we grant them that its influence pertains to me in the twenty-first year of my life? For when Saturn pertains to me, it will not be there; and when Saturn is there, that part of the sky will not pertain to me.

<margin>Refutation: First argument</margin>
If they should say—perhaps like clothes infected by a plague do not lose their poison for some time—that it happens to parts of the heaven that they retain the contagion received from an evil star for a long time, and therefore that degree, which was already infected by Saturn when I was born, pours back that noxious power into me even after many years: they would be proposing a very pretty and subtle defense.

<margin>Avicenna in *Meteorology*.</margin>
Indeed, if this discussion were with philosophers, I would bid them remember that the quality of light does not cling to a subject but departs with the body from which it is diffused. And of all celestial impressions, as **Avicenna** says in his *Meteorology*, light is both the vehicle and the fuel.

<margin>Second [argument]</margin>
But let them answer me themselves: since the transit of other planets occurs at that same degree during so many intervening years, could that ingrained power be abolished or diminished by the arrival of the healthy light of other stars?

<margin>Third [argument]</margin>
<margin>Fourth [argument]</margin>
Furthermore, if the qualities received and taken up from the planets endure in the regions of the sky, and are not preserved for only a short space of time, then in judging events one must not only observe which planet is found in which place of the sky, either in the revolving year or at the hour of birth, but also those which preceded in those same places...

<summary>Pico attacks the astrological theory of "directions," arguing that the practice of equating one zodiacal degree to one year of life is a mathematical fiction without any physical or natural basis. He mocks the idea that a planet's "influence" can linger in an empty point of space like a contagious disease on clothing.</summary>

...the places they traveled through in the preceding years. Finally, that invention of "directing" is nothing other than subjecting things not only to those constellations that exist, but to those which *could* be. For what else is it to say: "At my birth, the Moon was struck by rays of a <term>sextile</term> <note>original: "exagonis radiis"; an aspect where planets are 60 degrees apart, usually considered harmonious</note> from the Sun; yet it will at some point produce misfortune from a <term>square</term> <note>original: "quadrato aspectu"; an aspect of 90 degrees, considered harsh or challenging</note> aspect of the Sun"? Under this aspect, it was not present when I was born, but it *would have been* if more parts of the heaven had been placed between them farther from the Sun—parts which, when the Moon has traveled through them after so many years, it will inflict that calamity. But that constellation did not exist at my birth; and if it is to be at some later time, it is nothing to me, for if I have any fate, the past disposition of the heavens ought to declare it. It is clear, therefore, how absurd, how false, and how inconsistent is the practice of "directing" which astrologers use every day. For what foundation do they have from which it is derived? They have perhaps not yet, I think, brought it back for consideration and examination.

Besides directions, they also use in predicting the times of events the "dominion of the planets," whom they have fixed to take up the rule of life in a certain order.
<margin>Other ways in which astrologers believe the times of events can be foreseen.</margin>
From this come the "centers" of the Chaldeans, the <term>Firdaria</term> <note>original: "fridariæ"; a medieval Persian system of planetary periods</note> of the Persians, the "ninths" of the Indians, the <term>profections</term> <note>original: "tecates"; likely referring to 'aphetes' or points that "release" influence</note> of Ptolemy, his "aphetic" points and "intersectors"; from this come the "decennials" of the Egyptians, the <term>chronocrators</term> <note>original: "cronocratores"; literally 'time-lords,' planets that rule specific periods of a person's life</note> of the Arabs, and whatever other things of this kind others have invented according to the whim of their dreams. All of these err in this unseemly way: they define the stars such that one planet rules us for so many years; when that time is consumed, it hands over the "rudder of government" to the succeeding planet, as if by hand, according to the order of the spheres or the climate. This planet, in turn, having administered its jurisdiction for the time granted to it, entrusts the right and power to the next star—which is entirely foreign to all natural reason.

For why should this planet rather than another rule the lower things at this time? No other reason can be rationally assigned than either the disposition of the matter is more suitable for the impressions of one rather than the other, or because of a more effective relationship of the star itself to us—such as when it is carried above the earth while others are placed below the earth, or when it becomes closer to our regions as it turns toward the north, or casts more direct rays onto the earth. We might agree with the astrologers regarding the good or bad condition of things based on the diversity of places, signs, and radiations of that planet which holds more authority and power in the sky than others during that time; this is the only thing that can be said based on natural method. 
<margin><unclear>note a singular opinion concerning Saturn in Taurus</unclear></margin>
But the rest are fictions and fables, such as saying that Jupiter now presides over earthly things because in preceding years Saturn presided (whom Jupiter follows in the order of the spheres), and that Taurus rules this year because Aries ruled the preceding year—as if they had found successions of earthly offices and magistracies among the stars.

If they say that this has been proven by experience, there might be some faith in it if they agreed among themselves about this distribution of times. But since one attributes the same years to the Moon, another to Mars, and another to Jupiter, should not faith in "experience" be rejected by everyone, since each person offers it according to their own choice among such a variety of options? The Egyptians (whom Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer</note> follows) give the administration of life to each of the stars in an equal partition of ten years and nine months, in this order: 
<margin>Opinion of the Egyptians and Firmicus.</margin>
in a daytime <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genitura"; a birth chart</note>, the Sun receives the first decennial; in a nighttime one, the Moon. After that decennial, the one found in the second place in the nativity through the course of the signs takes over, then the third who follows the second, and the others in a similar way. But whoever has been allotted the decennial, although he is the lord of the whole time, nevertheless divides the entire substance of the ten-year period among all the stars, beginning with himself and then handing it over to those placed in order after him. First, however, to whoever was found second in the <term>theme</term> <note>original: "themate"; the layout of the astrological chart</note>. The sum of the years which the seven planets govern, according to their opinion, is seventy-five, with three months added; when these are completed, there is a return again to the first planet.
<margin><unclear>Opinion of the Persians</unclear></margin>
The Persians collect the same number of years and similarly start from the Sun if someone was born during the day, or from the Moon if born at night. They also make one principal lordship of the times, but make others participants in the lordship by vicarious succession, which distribution...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the various, often contradictory, systems astrologers use to divide a human life into periods ruled by different planets. Having dismissed the "method of directions" on the previous page, he now examines the systems of "time-lords."</meta>

<page-num>481</page-num>
->### DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.<-

They call this <term>fridaria</term> <note>original: "fridariam"; a medieval system of planetary periods used to predict the different stages of a person's life</note>; hence the common saying among the younger astrologers that someone is a "partner in the fridaria of Jupiter." However, they disagree greatly with the Egyptians; for in the sequence of the planets, they do not observe the locations of the birth chart but rather the order of the celestial spheres, placing the Sun in the middle. Furthermore, they do not assign an equal amount of time to each planet. Instead, they give ten years to the Sun, eight to Venus, thirteen to Mercury, nine to the Moon, eleven to Saturn, twelve to Jupiter, seven to Mars, three to the <term>Head</term> <note>original: "capiti"; the North Node of the Moon</note>, and two to the <term>Tail</term> <note>original: "caudæ"; the South Node of the Moon</note>. Even <term>Avenazra</term> <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer</note> confesses in his *Book of Astrological Kingdoms* that he does not know what reasoning could justify this. Conversely, in choosing a "ruling partner," the Persians give an equal portion to each of the planets, so that the presiding planet governs the first seventh of its time alone, the second part with the planet following it, and the third part with the third. The Egyptians, however, make this distribution unequal, decreeing nineteen months for the Sun, thirty for Saturn, twelve for Jupiter, fifteen for Mars, eight for Venus, twenty for Mercury, and twenty-five for the Moon. These they subdivide again: for example, from his thirty months, Saturn imparts six days to the remaining planets, and the others do the same from their own months, as <term>Hephaistion</term> <note>Hephaistion of Thebes, a 4th-century astrologer</note> teaches and <term>Maternus</term> <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer</note> was ignorant of. But there was another dispute between the Persians and Egyptians: the former include the "Head" and "Tail" among the <term>chronocrators</term> <note>original: "cronocratoris"; from the Greek for "time-lords," planets that rule a specific period of life</note>, while the Egyptians do not. From all of this, it is clear that after the first ten years, the governor of the years will rarely be the same among the Persians as among the Egyptians.

<margin>Ptolemy's Opinion.</margin>
Ptolemy, however, dissents from both, creating "lords of the ages": he has the Moon govern the first four years, and Mercury the following ten. Following that order, Venus governs eight, the Sun nineteen, Mars fifteen, Jupiter twelve, and Saturn the remainder of life. Yet, when he seeks an exact and specific distribution of times for each individual birth, he adds annual, monthly, and daily rulers to those principal "time-lords." In these matters, the entire "hinge of fate" for Ptolemy turns; there he censures those who make only one time-lord for life—finding fault with the Egyptians and <term>Dorotheus</term> <note>Dorotheus of Sidon, a 1st-century astrological poet</note>. If anyone follows this opinion of Ptolemy, they will find definitions for distributing time that are always utterly different from those of the Egyptians and Persians. This makes it all the more pleasant to mock the astrologers of our age who, not understanding that Ptolemy’s <term>tecates</term> <note>likely referring to "decennials" or specific time-divisions</note> and time-lords are the same thing as the Persian *fridaria* and Egyptian <term>decennials</term> <note>original: "decénia"; ten-year cycles</note>, have wanted to use all of them at once—as if they were not diverse and contrary opinions about the same thing.

<margin>Notable error of the astrologers of our age.</margin>
But these opinions are by no means consistent with one another. Indian astrology knows neither *fridaria* nor decennials, nor *tecates* nor time-lords; instead, it divides life into nine parts, not seven like the others. Regarding these, it pronounces an order arranged by the houses of the birth chart: the first part of the years is ruled by the constellations belonging to the twelfth house, the second by those in the <term>ascendant</term> <note>original: "horoscopum"; the sign rising on the eastern horizon at birth</note>, the third by the second house, the fourth by the ninth, the fifth by the tenth, the sixth by the eleventh, the seventh by the sixth, the eighth by the seventh, and the ninth by the eighth. They disagree with others not only in this dispensation of time, but in the very partitioning of the houses by the degrees of the zodiac (which they call "equal"). The Arabs, imitating <term>Abrugazarem</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer</note>, judge the three parts of life by the <term>trigonocrators</term> <note>original: "trigonocratores"; lords of the triplicities or planetary triangles</note>—as if you were to say "triangulators," that is, the lords of the triplicities. From these, they judge the state of things signified by each of the twelve houses: they judge the first and future status from the first lord of the triplicity, the middle status from the second, and the final status from the third. Yet, as I mentioned in another book, if there are only two lords for one triangle, or if perhaps there is only one disposer for a particular birth (because one is for a day birth and another for a night birth), a large part of life will be left without a governor. But these "triangulators" do not even exist; and even if three thousand were granted to exist, this vicarious succession in ruling a life is utterly ridiculous.

<margin>Opinion of the Chaldeans</margin>
But far different from all these are the inventions of the Chaldeans, who use neither *tecates*, nor decennials, nor *fridaria*, nor the "nines" of the Indians, nor the "triangulators," but rather the "angles" (cardinal points) of the birth chart. They take the first part of life from the first...

<meta>catchword: ex primo (from the first)</meta>

<summary>Pico catalogues the conflicting systems used by different cultures (Egyptian, Persian, Indian, Arab, Chaldean) to divide a human life into planetary periods. He uses these contradictions to argue that astrology lacks a consistent or logical foundation.</summary>
<keywords>fridaria, chronocrators, decennials, triplicity lords, Ptolemy, Ibn Ezra, Abu Ma'shar, astrological houses, planetary periods, history of astrology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the various, often contradictory, systems astrologers use to divide a human life into periods ruled by different planets. Pico now moves from the "time-lords" to how astrologers divide a human life based on the "angles" of the sky—the Ascendant, Midheaven, and Descendant—before beginning a broader critique of their technical errors regarding fixed stars.</meta>

-># BOOK SEVEN.<-

## BOOK SEVEN.

...investigating from the first cardinal point <note>The "angles" or cardinal points of a birth chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note>: the middle part of life from the peak of the highest heaven; the last part from the west; then truly concerning death; and concerning those things which happen after death, they pronounced from the fourth place of the birth chart. But they also divided that earlier three-part division again, so that the <term>apoclima</term> <note>original: "apoclima"; a Greek term for a "cadent" house, one that "slopes away" from a cardinal point</note> of the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopi"; here referring specifically to the Ascendant or first house</note> (which you might call the "decline") would indicate the pains of birth and what happens to the mother while she carries the womb; the horoscope itself would indicate the birth itself and the very first years from it; and the <term>epanophora</term> <note>original: "epanophora"; a "succeedent" house, one that "rises up" toward a cardinal point</note> of the horoscope would indicate what remains of the final part of the first age. Again, they did the same in the fourth house: the house declining from it would signify the things immediately preceding death; the fourth house itself would signify death; and its *epanophora* would signify what might happen after death. I have set out to explain these opinions so that the contradictions between them might be recognized, and likewise so that it would be clear that there is no faith in their "experiments," and that the vanity of their arbitrary dogmas, resting on the flimsiest conjectures, might be exposed. For how shall we give the first part of life to the East [the Ascendant] and the middle to the highest heaven, when the middle age follows the first, yet the Midheaven does not follow the East, but precedes it? <note>Pico is pointing out a logical flaw: in the daily rotation of the sky, a star reaches the Midheaven before it reaches the Ascendant, so using the Midheaven for "middle age" is chronologically backwards</note>. But one should not labor in refuting these opinions which refute and destroy themselves. If I were to fight against all their dreams, there would be no end to it.

<margin>Opinion of Messala</margin>
**Messala** <note>Masha'allah ibn Athari (c. 740–815), a prominent Persian Jewish astrologer</note> governs the first half of life from the oriental Sun, and the second from the occidental. 

<margin>Opinion of Hemus</margin>
**Hemus** <note>Likely a reference to a classical or Arabic source, possibly Hermes Trismegistus</note> assigns life differently: one part to the planets located in the upper hemisphere, whether they are in the east or west, and the other to all those which are under the earth. **Vellius** <note>Vettius Valens, a 2nd-century Greek astrologer</note>, by another fiction, ascribes the first part to the Moon and the other to the lord of the second house. **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), one of the most influential medieval Islamic astrologers</note>, the most fabulous of all, says the first part should be referred to the <term>Lot of Fortune</term> <note>original: "partem fortunae"; a mathematical point in a chart used to predict prosperity</note> and the other to the lord of that part. Others say otherwise, but it is not necessary to pursue them all; read **Hephaistion** in his book of *Apotelesmatics*. Read **Ptolemy**. Read **Avenazra** <note>original: "Abēzagelē"; Abraham Ibn Ezra</note>; and besides those we have mentioned, you will find many other opinions there, all fighting amongst themselves on this matter. Therefore, each man composes his own fable according to his own whim. To these men, those who are too credulous grant their faith as if to oracles and true prophets, and we entrust our hopes, fears, anxieties, joys, and—what is more ruinous—the very instruction and governance of our whole life to these most trifling and deceitful hucksters.

### Chapter VIII. Just as they adopt fictitious things for their efficacy, so they omit necessary ones; and how much they err regarding the fixed stars.

<margin>The error of astrologers in omitting almost infinite fixed stars</margin>
Just as they adopt many fictitious things such as we have mentioned—which, having no nature, have no influence, such as the signs, the houses, the "images," the **Tail** and **Head** [of the Dragon], the **Parts**, the <term>dodecathemoria</term> <note>original: "dodecathemoria"; the division of each zodiac sign into twelve 2.5-degree segments</note>, the <term>novenaria</term> <note>original: "nouenaria"; the division of signs into nine parts</note>, and others of this kind—so they omit many things that are primarily necessary, and they decree many false and contradictory things regarding those they do use. For just as things lacking light are ineffective, so no light in the heavens is ineffective. Yet while almost innumerable stars shine in the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>, they use only a thousand, with twenty-two added. When this is objected to them, different men answer differently. **Pietro d'Abano** <note>original: "Petrus aponensis" (1250–1316), an Italian philosopher and astrologer</note> says in his *Elucidarium* that this shows the difficulty of the art, but demonstrates that it is not impossible. In so responding, he seems to concede that those stars are indeed necessary if a fatal constellation is to be perfectly understood; and because this is difficult, he claims the art he professes is difficult. But we contend that it is impossible for all of them to be grasped; and even if it were possible, the astrologers who have not yet accomplished this will not truly predict future things from the heavens.

<margin>Defense and Reproof. The first reason.</margin>
Others, hiding in a safer refuge, say that those stars they omit are ineffective. They claim that all the larger ones, which have the power to discern fate, have been explored by astrologers, and the rest were omitted because, due to the smallness of their bodies, they have almost no importance. But they are easily flushed out of these hiding places: for if they have never observed these stars, what can they assert about their nature?

-># DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

<margin>Second [argument]</margin>...whether they act rarely or not, whether they change things or not; and if they respond that they are convinced of the smallness of the [star's] body: what body in the heaven will be considered small when compared to the Earth? Or, to put it more correctly, compared to those things placed on the Earth which are thought to be governed from heaven? Likewise, what is ineffective and weak if you compare the nature of celestial and terrestrial bodies to each other? For in the former, there is nothing that is not sublime, powerful, and great; in the latter, nothing that is not humble, weak,
<margin>Third [argument]</margin>and tiny. Add that perhaps many of these stars, which they say are neglected because of their smallness, are not surpassed by the globe of either Mercury or the Moon. For the smallest of these stars which they 
<margin>Fourth [argument]</margin>observe, they consider to be larger than Mars and Venus. Furthermore, if perhaps individual stars, being smaller,
<margin>Fifth [argument]</margin>do not have great powers, nevertheless a gathering and concourse of many of that kind will have the greatest amount of power; just as if those stars which make that Milky Way dense with so many lights
<margin>Sixth [argument]</margin>were to have little power individually, in what way will they think they have little power all together? Moreover, often in a musical melody, if one small little voice is withdrawn, the harmony is dissolved, while that which by itself would be heard but little, makes it so that all the other parts of the modulation are heard. The whole adornment of the heavens is mutually linked and in agreement; it has nothing that ceases, nothing that is superfluous, or that is useless. Therefore, whatever part you take away, even the smallest, that which the whole integrity created perishes at once. Among <term>helciarii</term> <note>original: "helciarios"; workers who pull boats or heavy loads by rope</note>, just as it can happen that a man who is not strong takes away from the pull so that if his hand is missing, the load is not pulled; so can the ignorance of just one star undermine the truth of fate—and we have not even mentioned how they bypass a nearly innumerable number [of stars] without any sense of religious dread. <margin>How lightly Bonatus speaks of astrology</margin> **Bonatus** <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), perhaps the most famous and influential astrologer of the 13th century</note> perhaps fearing these things (if indeed he saw them clearly), says: "The astrologer uses all the stars; let no one explain them all by name. For he uses the twelve signs <margin>Response / Confutation</margin>under which almost all the stars are contained." And he must have said this not as an astrologer but as one who is frantic! Since the signs, as they call them, have a width of twelve degrees, outside of which there are innumerable stars on both sides. But if he should respond that those which are between the same lines, co-extensive with any sign, possess the same power as the stars of that sign: I will ask first, on what basis does he assert things that are unknown? But if he says this is the "proper way" for astrologers, I will not fight him, but I will call upon the astrologers themselves, among whom the <term>images</term> <note>original: "imagines"; here referring to the actual constellations as opposed to the mathematical zodiac signs</note> themselves rising with the signs claim one thing, while the signs with which they rise claim another. Otherwise, if those [signs] which they use are immobile, the images change their place <note>Pico is referring to the "Precession of the Equinoxes," where the constellations slowly drift out of alignment with the zodiac signs over centuries</note>. There will therefore be one nature after another for the same image, corresponding repeatedly to different signs by both location and sign. But I think **Bonatus** himself, noticing the madness of his response, immediately turned to something else. And when he perceived it could not be denied that the knowledge of all stars pertains to the matter of astrology—yet astrologers did not have knowledge of all of them—what then, he asked, "if we do not know the whole of astrology? Christian preachers do not know all divine things, about which they nevertheless preach daily to the people." In this matter, see how little "good" this **Bonatus** is deceived <note>A pun on the name "Bonatus" and "bonus" (good)</note>. For if someone investigates the nature of the stars for the sake of knowledge—which is the task of the philosopher—once one star is known, he has achieved something. But if, as the astrologer professes, he seeks not so much the stars as the future through knowledge in the stars, he will have accomplished nothing unless he first has knowledge of those stars from which the future can be foreseen. But they foresee from those things from which they happen; they happen, however, from all [stars]. Therefore, they also foresee from all. Therefore, anyone who has not known all—though he may perhaps know some—will never foresee future things from the stars. <margin>Example in philosophy and medicine</margin> Take an example in medicine and philosophy: the philosopher seeks the powers of herbs so that he may understand them; the physician seeks them so that by their virtue he may heal diseases. If the philosopher discovers even one, he will be a philosopher of some sort, though imperfect, since whatever knowledge of things he seeks, he has some. But let us suppose ten species of herbs—or whatever number you prefer—necessary for repelling all diseases, such that if one is missing, no flaw of the body can be cured. If someone knows nine of them and is ignorant of one, he is not only an incomplete physician, [but he cannot cure at all]...

<summary>Pico criticizes astrologers for ignoring the vast majority of stars, arguing that if the heavens act as a unified "harmony," missing even one star makes a prediction of fate impossible. He specifically rebukes the medieval astrologer Guido Bonatti for comparing the incomplete knowledge of astrologers to that of Christian preachers.</summary>

...absolved, but he will be no doctor; for when he can provide some knowledge but no cure, he cannot claim the profession of a doctor. Likewise, he cannot be called an astrologer who cannot speak of the fate of even one man after inspecting his birth chart <term>genitura|The astrological map of the heavens at the moment of birth, used to predict a person's life.</term>. But if fate is composed from the mixed influence of all the stars, how will he foresee it? He who does not know what each individual star effects, nor what their combined temperament produces. Regarding theology, however, there is a different reasoning, because just as perfect knowledge of it is not possible, so it is not necessary: so that we may believe, know, and persuade many things about it. It is almost impossible to know nothing about it, just as it is to know everything; for it is no less denied to those with eyes not to see the Sun than it is to look into it thoroughly. ### Chapter IX. The dogmas of astrologers concerning the fixed stars conflict both with themselves and with the truth.

**B**ut astrologers do not only err in being ignorant of most of the stars; they have also established most conflicting and false dogmas concerning those they think they have explored. For there are times (as I shall demonstrate) when they judge the stars to be more effective than the planets, and times when they judge them less powerful and effective. In this matter, they both conflict with themselves and deviate from the truth on both sides. They promise what I might call "ordinary" happiness according to the capacity and condition of the person being born from a good state of the planets; but from the non-wandering <note>The "fixed" stars, which do not move relative to one another unlike the planets.</note> stars, as Ptolemy says, they expect *fortunes beyond expectation* <note>original Greek: παρὰ δόξασ α Τυχίασ (para doxas tychas)</note>—that is, happiness greater than any opinion. I, however—following both Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* and reason—contend that greater things can be provided by the planets than by the fixed stars. For a more sublime seat does not indicate a more sublime nature for the non-wandering stars, since the Sun, the moderator of all things, certainly has many stars placed above it, if not all except the Moon. <margin>First reason</margin> Furthermore, let this be the argument for why we judge the planets to surpass the fixed stars: because many spheres serve each individual planet, whereas only one sphere serves the many fixed stars; thus the very army of stars together does not overcome the power of a single wandering star. Nevertheless, individual stars cannot surpass individual planets. <margin>Second [reason]</margin> If you look at the magnitude of their bodies, the Sun is beyond controversy larger than all; likewise, Jupiter and Saturn are larger than all others if you except certain principal stars—though a greater power is not understood solely from the vastness of the bodies. <margin>Third [reason]</margin> For it is not established that Saturn is more powerful than Jupiter even though it is larger; and although Mercury is the smallest of all the heavenly bodies, it nevertheless has (as they themselves wish) the most power in every birth chart. Likewise, they do not place Venus before the Moon, even though she is exceeded by the Moon's body in vastness. <margin>Fourth [reason]</margin> Finally, that bright star situated at the "Heart of the Lion" <note>The star Regulus.</note>, which is called the "Queen" by the Latins and the "Basilisk" <note>original: "basiliscus," meaning "little king" in Greek.</note> by the Greeks: although it is not of the first magnitude, they nevertheless judge it to be of the first authority and power. They certainly make it more noble because it does not deviate from the path of the Sun; by that same reasoning, the planets are more noble than the stars, as they deviate less in either direction from that same path. <margin>Fifth [reason]</margin> Added to this is the testimony of antiquity calling the planets *world-rulers* <note>original: "cosmocratoras", from the Greek κοσμοκράτορας</note>, a title they did not deign to give to the stars. But would that they at least maintained their dogma, and did not more often speak of those same stars—which they make the effectors of wonderful works—as if they were weak and feeble. For they say the stars effect nothing unless they occupy the "angles" <term>cardines|The four cardinal points of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</term> or the beginnings of the houses, or are joined to one of the two luminaries <note>The Sun or the Moon.</note>. And thus, to those to whom they previously attributed so much, they here detract from their virtue to such an extent that the stars effect nothing by themselves unless they are bolstered by the vigor of their location or the support of a most powerful heavenly body. They offer neither a cause nor any probable reason for this thing, but have perhaps slipped into this through a false understanding of a certain ancient saying. <margin>How they slipped</margin> For the ancients, as Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer.</note> teaches, said regarding the signs of the zodiac that when they were found bare of stars, they had no effectiveness except for those occupying the four angles. This teaching, which the ancients gave concerning the signs, the mansions, and the lodgings of the stars, they have also transferred to individual stars—unless they instead craftily established this dogma so that, if the account of fate had to be explained by all the stars...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is logically inconsistent, specifically critiquing the contradictory importance astrologers assign to fixed stars versus planets. He provides five reasons why planets should be considered more influential than stars, refuting the astrological claim that fixed stars grant extraordinary fortunes while planets only grant ordinary ones.</summary>
