they would be tortured by an almost inextricable anxiety: that this art could be mastered by man; nor would they easily persuade the credulous of it. Otherwise, what is the reason for their opinion? Is it because a star is in a more remote location? But how much closer to us is Saturn? Or what is such a great prerogative of the "cardinal point" <note>The cardinal points or "angles" (Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli) are considered the most powerful positions in a horoscope.</note> that in it, stars not only do not fail to act, but <margin>The error is made manifest by reasons</margin> perform wonders, despite the vastness of the distance? Yet soon, when they have declined a little from it, or have not yet reached it, they do absolutely nothing, even though the eleventh house, rising toward the heights of heaven, would seem more powerful for acting than the fourth house situated deep under the earth. But it is certainly as we were saying: the labor deterred them, and they did not want the art to seem so difficult that it could easily be judged impossible. For the "slowness of motion" which they are accustomed to cite as a cause does nothing to help their case, since the ray of a star is fixed all the more strongly and clings more constantly the longer the star itself lingers in the place from which it is sent down. How these things fight against themselves! For concerning a slower star <note>original: "sidere tardiori"; referring to Saturn, the slowest of the visible planets.</note>, the dogma is that it gives whatever it gives late, but that what it has given lasts and remains for a long time. Conversely, they decree concerning the fixed stars <note>original: "non erraticis"; literally "the non-wanderers."</note> that they, being of the slowest motion, usually bring the greatest happiness, but they eventually close these with calamities; therefore their gifts do not last long, just as they are not long preserved. But just as they are always far from the truth, so they disagree with themselves everywhere—though we do not follow up on all these points. For someone could also ask them why they do not consider the intervals and aspects <note>The geometric angles between celestial bodies, believed to determine their influence.</note> between the fixed stars themselves, just as they do among the planets. Johannes Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a celebrated German mathematician and astronomer.</note>, noticing this, says that the aspects of the fixed stars might perhaps be more perfect than those of the planets, because they are not fleeting and momentary like the latter, but rather stable and perpetual. Other objections could be made on these points, but let us run through the consequences.

### Chapter X. That astrologers are also deceived regarding the planets; and a repetition of those things which have been disputed so far.

**F**or it has been sufficiently demonstrated above that they are deceived in many things concerning the planets themselves. They think the properties and powers of the planets (a point on which they err regarding the fixed stars) are not only intensified or diminished, but actually become different or even opposite from time to time, depending on the variety of locations, the condition of the signs, the configurations, and the manifold relationships among them all. They also rely on the various names of their motions—whether standing still, proceeding, or regressing—all of which, unless I am mistaken, we have most clearly shown to be said far from any truth, far from reason, and far from the dignity and nature of heavenly things. We also censure the fact that they assign certain provinces to be ruled by planets and signs beyond those twelve, and prescribe a sort of impious administration of various things and prices passed down, as if by hand, through the right of succession. Clearly, they are measuring—or rather, lying about—the heavenly things themselves based on human affairs. Furthermore, we have laughed at and, along with Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who argued that stars are signs, not causes, of earthly events.</note> and his contemporaries, struck out the idea of waiting for the effect <margin>Plotinus also contends against the astrologers</margin> of some planet for as many years as it was distant in degrees from some place in a sign; they devise a thousand such false things conceived on no foundation of knowledge. Let us thus summarize this entire preceding disputation: it seems indeed that astrologers say probable things when they say inferior things are ruled by the celestial ones; but they are soon caught as false, vain, and detestable—that is, neither pious nor prophetic—when they contend that particular things can be produced from universal causes: evil from good, tiny from great, reckless from orderly, incorporeal from corporeal, arbitrary from necessary, artificial from natural, and things already past or present from one another. Even if all these things were done by the heaven, the astrologers would nevertheless assign the least celestial causes for them, since they remain silent about the true powers of the stars and constellations that are in the heaven, yet accept many properties from things that are not true. And although they hold a small part of the truth, they themselves add many invented things, such as those we mentioned in the preceding book: "places" <term>loca|In astrology, the twelve "houses" of the sky that govern different areas of life.</term>, "houses," "images," "nodes," "antiscia" <term>antiscia|Points on the zodiac that are mirrors of each other across the solstice points.</term>, "dodecathemoria" <term>dodecathemoria|The division of each zodiac sign into twelve smaller parts of 2.5 degrees each.</term>—fictional, ineffective, and imaginary things with no solidity of nature. If any wise man can place his faith in these things as if they stood with the true solidity of nature and therefore ruled over us, I confess that I have undoubtedly not yet understood what it means to be wise.

He concludes by listing several technical astrological concepts as purely "fictional" inventions that lack any basis in natural science.</summary>

->BOOK EIGHT.<-

# JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S DISPUTATIONS AGAINST
# ASTROLOGERS. THE EIGHTH BOOK BEGINS.

## Chapter One: That the number of the superior bodies—in whose hands the power of decreeing fate lies according to the astrologers—is uncertain.

Among all the things that he who professes a knowledge of the stars must know, that which we were just discussing might be thought almost the easiest: to judge, namely, what the fatal hour <note>The "fatal hour" refers to the precise moment of birth or inception used to calculate a horoscope.</note> of each individual thing is. But if astrologers have neither grasped this nor are able to grasp it, how shall more difficult things be hoped for? For how much more difficult and requiring of greater labor is it to have a complete understanding of the number of the superior bodies from which the force of fate reaches us? This is necessary so that, in describing a fatal constellation, nothing fictitious is introduced and nothing true and effective is omitted. Otherwise, while this knowledge is useful and necessary for them, we shall reveal through the disputations of the present book that it cannot, in fact, be known. Thus, not only can they fail to predict the truth because they do not clearly foresee the motions and positions of the stars, and because they have by no means explored all of them (which we shall object to in the following books), but also because it is not even established among them yet what those very bodies are whose positions must be inspected and whose properties must be investigated. Indeed, they are so far from achieving all that their profession promises that they do not even know what those things are which it is necessary for them to know. For if they say we are mistaken or are driven by malice to raise these objections, I shall compel them by the divine voice <note>A rhetorical appeal to reason or perhaps a reference to the complexity of God's creation as described in scripture.</note> and ask them to tell me something about the number of the stars. When I question them, I realize not only that the stars which are visible are not grasped by them in number, but that it is not even certain whether, besides those we behold, there are others in heaven that escape both our senses and our reason.

<margin>Favorinus against the casters of horoscopes. Gellius. Alpetragius.</margin> Favorinus, in that elegant speech of his against the casters of horoscopes <note>original: "genethliacos"; from the Greek 'genethliakos', referring to those who cast birth charts.</note> found in Gellius, said he wondered how it could be clear to any teacher that the planets—which Nigidius calls "wanderers" <note>original: "errones"; a Latin term for planets, literally 'wanderers'.</note>—cannot be more numerous than is commonly thought. For it could happen, he said, that there are certain other planets of equal power which men cannot see due to an excess of either brightness or distance. Certainly, as Alpetragius says—a man most wise in celestial matters—if there is a motion in heaven that is still unknown, there may also be a body therein to which that motion primarily belongs, which has not yet been detected by any observation of the art. This is attested by the many and various motions of the superior bodies devised by more recent thinkers which were unknown to the ancients (as they themselves believe) and finally detected by a long duration of observations. By this example, it is made manifest that other motions might still lie hidden from mathematicians due to their slowness, obscurity, or some other appearance, which posterity itself will one day come to know through even longer observations. I do not wish to speak here of epicycles and eccentrics <note><term>epicycles and eccentrics</term>: geometric models used by ancient astronomers to explain the irregular paths of planets while maintaining circular motion.</note>, nor of the multitude of spheres serving the planets, which are uncertain among all astronomers, since perhaps they will deny that the power to decree fate resides in these bodies.

<margin>The opinion of the Egyptians and Chaldeans.</margin> Regarding the spheres above the planets, and how much ambiguity exists there—and how much this makes this divining astrology uncertain—one must by no means remain silent. For some make the eighth sphere, which they illuminate with the non-wandering stars, the outermost; others have placed a ninth above it; others even a tenth. The astronomers of the Egyptians and Chaldeans <note>Ancient groups traditionally credited with the invention of astronomy and astrology.</note> believed there was nothing above the eighth sphere; they were followed by Plato, Aristotle, Hipparchus, and Ptolemy. Perhaps more recent thinkers did not believe this, but such is the case. There is no ninth sphere in Ptolemy’s work, which can easily be understood from his *Great Composition* <note>original: "magna compositione"; referring to Ptolemy’s *Almagest*.</note>. Many are deceived because they think that all those who have explored the fact that the eighth sphere moves from west to east must necessarily fall into the opinion of a ninth sphere. Therefore, since both Ptolemy and Hipparchus...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is fundamentally flawed because practitioners cannot even agree on the number of celestial bodies or spheres that influence human fate. He cites historical authorities like Favorinus and Alpetragius to suggest that many planets or motions may remain invisible or undiscovered, rendering any "complete" horoscope impossible.</summary>

<header>DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY</header>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>
The cause of the error of the moderns.
</margin>
Since the components of their error are many, they themselves hesitate at nothing; for the discovery of the ninth sphere <note>Ancient astronomers originally believed there were eight spheres (seven for the planets and one for the fixed stars). Later medieval astronomers added a ninth sphere to account for the slow "precession" of the equinoxes.</note> was the invention of those by whom that motion was first recorded.

<margin>Another cause.</margin>
It is added that Ptolemy uses both "movable" and "immovable" signs: since he makes the constellations of the eighth sphere movable, and is said to locate the planets at the immovable signs. For this reason, it seems indubitably certain to them that besides the moving signs of the eighth sphere, there are other signs in Ptolemy’s work which do not move except by the motion of the whole world; and they imagine these to be nowhere else than in a ninth sphere above the eighth. But they are greatly and widely mistaken; for the motion of the stars from West to East does not necessarily lead to the conclusion of a ninth sphere.

<margin>
Ptolemy describes the immovable signs in the eighth sphere.
</margin>
And that he is speaking of immovable signs in the eighth sphere is most clearly shown by the fact that Ptolemy was content with only the eighth sphere; I marvel that this was not understood by those men. For Ptolemy describes these "immovable" signs in the eighth sphere itself; which he would not have done if he had devised another one above it. His words in the second book of the *Great Composition* <note>original: "magnae compositionis"; this is the Almagest, Ptolemy's definitive work on astronomy.</note> are these: "We shall use the names of the signs for the twelve parts of the oblique circle <note>The ecliptic, or the path the sun appears to follow across the sky.</note> as if their beginnings were taken from the tropics and the equinoctial points. Thus we shall call the 'dodecathemorion'—that is, the twelfth part—which extends from the spring equinox toward the following parts of the whole sphere, 'Aries'; the second, 'Taurus,' and so on according to the order of the twelve signs handed down by us." Ptolemy says this, and he also teaches the same in the first book of the *Apotelesmatika* <note>original: "apoteleſmatū"; this refers to Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos, his primary astrological text.</note>: that the parts of the zodiac to which the planets are referred begin and are determined by the solstices and equinoxes as starting points. Since these four points are fixed and unmoved, therefore the partition of the signs established from them is also fixed and immovable, even though the constellations from which those names were borrowed move constantly, and their beginnings and ends are found in various places over the course of time. Therefore, these "immovable" signs are not, according to Ptolemy, in a superior sphere; rather, they are described by the four fixed and immovable points of the eighth sphere. If he had imagined another sphere above it, he would never have kept silent about such a great discovery in his *Great Composition*.

<margin>
John of Saxony is mocked.
</margin>
Furthermore, one might laugh at John of Saxony <note>A 14th-century astronomer known for his commentaries on the Alfonsine Tables and Alchabitius.</note>, who in his expositions on Alchabitius <note>An 10th-century Arab astrologer and astronomer.</note> strives to prove that one should use the signs of the ninth sphere according to the opinion of Ptolemy. To confirm his opinion, he brings forward certain words of Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, a famous Arab commentator.</note>, the interpreter of Ptolemy, concerning the "bright and dark degrees." John thought these were the words of Ptolemy himself, not Haly; but they are the words of the commentator, not the author. Anyone can easily understand this not only from the Greek manuscripts but even from the common translation. See what faith can be placed in these men regarding celestial matters, when they are caught reading their own authors with such sleepy and blinking eyes! What of the fact that not only Ptolemy, but no one for more than a thousand years after him, is found to have used a ninth sphere?

<margin>
Alphonso was the first to calculate the positions of the planets according to the ninth sphere.
</margin>
King Alphonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile (r. 1252–1284), who sponsored the "Alfonsine Tables," which became the standard astronomical data for centuries.</note> was the first to calculate the positions of the planets according to the ninth sphere, to which all the moderns have adhered; the ancients used only the eighth. Even Leo the Hebrew <note>Also known as Levi ben Gershon or Gersonides, a prominent 14th-century Jewish polymath.</note> and Proclus the Platonic <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist who wrote on the construction of the world.</note>, most excellent mathematicians, contend that the eighth is the highest of all.

<margin>
The reason why the younger ones were moved.
</margin>
The younger astronomers support the different opinion that there is another sphere superior to the eighth by a conjecture that is not entirely vain: because two motions in completely opposite directions cannot exist in the same body. Therefore, since it has been discovered by true observation that the fixed stars move from West to East, and yet that sphere with the rest is rolled from East to West, they think it necessarily follows that the former motion (which completes one revolution in many thousands of years) follows the proper nature of the sphere of the stars; while the other motion (which is completed in the space of a single day) is communicated to the eighth sphere from another and thus superior globe, just as it is to the planets, sweeping with it from East to West all the stars which are carried by their own proper motions from West to East. This suspicion, though not born of nothing, is nevertheless refuted by others in many ways.

<margin>
Various solutions.
</margin>
For there are those who deny that the stars move from West to East; indeed, they are observant men and mathematicians who say there is a daily motion of the ether, which is thus one, not divided into spheres, but continuous; and that all the stars, both fixed and wandering, are carried by their own motions from the West...

<summary>Pico argues that the "Ninth Sphere" is a modern invention misattributed to Ptolemy, who actually located his fixed reference points within the eighth sphere. He critiques medieval astronomers like John of Saxony for misreading their sources and explains the mechanical reasoning (opposing celestial motions) that led "moderns" to adopt the ninth sphere theory.</summary>

Here, he highlights the internal contradictions among various authorities like Leo the Hebrew and King Alfonso, arguing that if the foundations of astronomy are this uncertain, the "science" of astrology built upon them must be a house of cards.</meta>

<header>BOOK EIGHT</header>

carried by chance into the east. <margin>First.</margin> Leo the Hebrew <note>original: "Leo hebraeus"; referring to Levi ben Gershon (1288–1344), a prominent Jewish philosopher and astronomer.</note> attributes this motion to an inferior sphere rather than a superior one. <margin>Second.</margin> Others say there is another way: they constitute the whole heaven as a kind of living creature made of all the spheres as if they were limbs; they say there is one way for the whole heaven to move by a certain universal motor, and another for the individual spheres. <margin>Leo the Hebrew.</margin> This motion is distinct from the specific and diverse motors belonging to the spheres themselves. Therefore, that which we call the "daily motion" <term>diurnus motus (the apparent rotation of the sky every 24 hours)</term>, since it is common to the other spheres and not more to the eighth than to any other, exists from a certain common motor of the celestial universe. <margin>Third.</margin> On this account, it is not necessary to imagine another orb to which that motion specifically belongs, <margin>Fourth.</margin> nor does it follow that the same sphere has two motions belonging to it; for one arises from what it has in common with the other parts of heaven, and the other from its own nature, not assigned by the same motor. We place all these views in the middle, asserting only this: that nothing indubitable or certain can be affirmed concerning these matters. Instead, the whole dispute returns to probable and metaphorical arguments which, being ambiguous on both sides, leave us in uncertainty. But if we think reason must grant what the ninth orb confirms, then we must also agree with those who devised a tenth above the ninth, since the reasoning for both dogmas is nearly the same. For while the former stubbornly defend the idea that more than one motion cannot suit a single sphere—and thus introduced a ninth when they detected a double motion in the eighth—the latter, having detected a triple motion, introduced a tenth led by the same conjecture. <margin>Alfonso, Campanus, Leopold, Messala</margin> This is what Alfonso <note>King Alfonso X of Castile, sponsor of the Alfonsine Tables.</note>, Campanus, Leopold, and Messala <note>Masha'allah ibn Athari, an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer.</note> believed; they also refer this opinion (however falsely, as Albert <note>Albertus Magnus.</note> followed them in doing) back to Ptolemy.

# Chapter II. If another sphere exists above the eighth, ancient astrology is false; if none exists, modern astrology is false; and even if it is modern, it must necessarily collapse entirely.

<margin>All ancient astrology will collapse if there are two [extra] spheres.</margin>
**F**rom this diverse and manifold variety of opinions, it is easy to see how uncertain the art of divinatory astrology is rendered. For if there are two other spheres above the eighth, all the astrology of the ancients is false, for they relied on useless and imperfect observations while ignoring the most powerful parts of the heaven. Indeed, those spheres cannot be ineffective: the highest surpasses the others in the rapidity of its motion, and both surpass the rest in the sublimity of their location and the vastness of their mass. If, on the other hand, there is no sphere besides the eighth, then all the astrology of the moderns is void, for it describes the twelve signs in a ninth orb. If that orb is nothing, what authority will it have in decreeing fate? Furthermore, whether there is a ninth sphere or not, all the astrology of our age is known to waver; it speaks not only with inconsistency but with controversy and conflict. For let them answer me this: do they think that celestial influence <term>afflatus (literally 'breath' or 'influence' flowing from the stars)</term> comes to us from the whole heaven, or only from those parts which flash with visible light? First, if they grant the former, then not only the planets but also the orbs that carry the planets will be admitted into the participation of the fatal decree. Yet the astrologers do not observe these orbs, as they think they have no efficacy in changing things below. Second, if they respond that this power exists only in the stars shining with the radiance of visible light, they must also admit that no flowings from the ninth sphere reach us here; for it is distinguished by no visible light, nor by any variety of stars or luminaries. It is either entirely transparent—whence it is called the "Aqueous" or "Crystalline" heaven <note>Medieval cosmologists often identified the "waters above the firmament" from Genesis with a transparent ninth or tenth sphere.</note>—or it diffuses a thin and rare light, such as might also exist in the other globes, as many believe. Therefore, either every sphere must be observed, or that ninth one (even if it exists) must be held in contempt. This is what **Bonatus** <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century.</note> believed when he affirmed that nothing placed above the eighth sphere pertains to the astrologer. And yet, they all describe the twelve signs within it—signs which have not just some, but the greatest authority in the constellation of the year. This is not only because of what they bestow by their own power, but because the primary roles in exchanging the powers of the planets are delegated to them. Therefore, whichever way they turn, they fall into inextricable snares: they either omit many spheres that should not be omitted, or, by admitting one that is ineffective, they corrupt the truth of every constellation.

<summary>Pico argues that the fundamental structure of the heavens is a matter of debate among astronomers, citing conflicting theories about the Ninth and Tenth spheres. He concludes that if the basic "map" of the sky is contested, then astrology—whether ancient or modern—cannot claim any certain authority.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY #

<meta>catchword: of images likewise | image quality: ink bleeding from the back of the page</meta>

Even if they should happen to extricate themselves from this point, they will be entirely held by an unresolvable knot. Even if we were to grant that power and efficacy are attached to the ninth sphere—as much as you might wish to claim—and if no further dispute were raised concerning the other spheres, the prediction of all the modern practitioners <note>original: "iuniorum"; referring to the astrologers of Pico's time who followed newer astronomical models.</note> would be proved nothing less than utterly false. For it cannot be denied that the power and property of that ninth sphere is different from the influences of the eighth; yet they, treating them as if they were the same, have handed down nothing regarding the signs of the ninth sphere other than what was handed down by the ancients regarding the signs of the eighth. This is surely a result of either great dullness or malice: either they did not see that different spheres cannot have the same nature, or, seeing this, they wished to persuade others otherwise. It seems likely enough that they took care to deceive others. Once the ninth sphere was devised, if they had to discuss the influence of a different orb, their profession would necessarily have had to cease for many ages, until the nature of this newly discovered orb could be proven through many experiments. This is something that these boastful and ambitious men <note>original: "eruscatores"; literally "beggars" or "swindlers," here used to disparage the integrity of astrologers.</note> could by no means endure. Therefore, by transferring the same names to the parts of the ninth sphere that the ancients called the parts of the eighth—as if nature itself were shared along with the name—they put forth exactly the same dogmas about them as their predecessors did concerning the eighth sphere. Thus they describe Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and the rest of the signs in the ninth sphere, and they claim they do the same things that the ancients recorded were done by signs of the same name, but in a different sphere. Indeed, they defend their entire imposture by the mere association of names. If they deceive in this matter, it is a disgrace; if they are themselves deceived, it is madness. They err no differently than if, having transferred the name of Jupiter to Saturn, they were to believe that Saturn had become Jupiter, and when a prophecy regarding Saturn was required, they were to pronounce those things which the ancients taught that Jupiter portended.

<margin>
The difference
between the ninth
and the eighth
is no less
than that
between
Jupiter and
Saturn.
</margin>
For the difference between the eighth and ninth orb should be thought no less than that between Jupiter and Saturn, if we consider their motions, their light, and the quality by which celestial things are primarily distinguished. For between those two planets, the only apparent difference is that one is slower than the other, and that the light of one is either darker or brighter than the light of the other. But how much greater is the distance between those orbs where one is carried by its own nature with the slowest motion, while the other is carried with the swiftest motion of all? <term>slowest and swiftest motion (in the Ptolemaic system, the outer spheres moved faster to complete a rotation in 24 hours, while the inner ones had slower "proper" motions)</term> Furthermore, the one is radiant and conspicuous with a manifold army of stars, while the other, with either no light or invisible light, does not fall under our gaze or eyes. Finally, if they say that the efficacy of parts of the same sphere, and even of tiny fractions, is extremely diverse, how then can the nature of different spheres be the same? And if two spheres had the same nature, would not the God who is the craftsman of nature have made the second one in vain? And if, as I have said, they agree neither in motion, nor in light, nor in position, nor in mass, what other communion of nature is there for them? Let the machine of the universe be inspected on all sides, and in all the globes of the elements or the heavens, a manifest diversity will always appear. Therefore, if some ninth orb has been devised, it is necessarily of a different nature from the eighth; and thus, what Ptolemy and other ancients taught about the signs and parts of the eighth cannot be ascribed or suit the signs of the ninth sphere. Since all the moderns do this, however, their prophecies—even if they profess a true art—can only strike upon the truth by chance.

***

### Chapter III. Images differ from signs, even if their names are the same. ###

**R**egarding the number of the spheres, whatever may be decided, there are twelve signs themselves to which both the ancients and the moderns have attributed so much that the sum and pivot of the entire astrological prediction turns upon them. We shall briefly demonstrate that these signs are fictions and are nothing at all. Then, even if they were real, we shall show that astrologers have handed down false and conflicting dogmas about them; therefore, those divinations which depend on them (and indeed all of them do) are utterly fallacious. But the reader must first be advised that the twelve signs are one thing, and the images <note>original: "imagines"; here referring to the actual constellations or groupings of stars, as opposed to the abstract "signs" or 30-degree mathematical divisions of the zodiac.</note> are another, even though they agree in number and name. I say that these are entirely different things, even among those who, through ignorance or neglect of the ninth sphere, make the same division of signs as they do of images likewise...

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers are fraudulent because they apply ancient rules for the stars (the 8th sphere) to a theoretical "9th sphere" purely to save their profession from obsolescence. He notes that different celestial bodies must have different natures, and thus recycling names like "Aries" for different spheres is a logical fallacy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's critique of the mathematical foundations of astrology. Having previously argued that the "Ninth Sphere" is a baseless invention, he now focuses on the "Eighth Sphere" (the sphere of the fixed stars) and the discrepancy between the physical constellations and the mathematical signs of the zodiac.</meta>

-># BOOK EIGHT<-

...of the images likewise, whose forms are contemplated. For they establish the signs as unmoved and fixed, beginning from the equinoxes <note>The points in the year when day and night are of equal length, marking the start of spring and autumn.</note> and the solstices, so that the sign of Aries always takes its beginning from the vernal equinox. However, they may calculate the beginning of the *image* of Aries <note>Pico distinguishes between "Signs" (mathematical 30-degree arcs) and "Images" (the actual groups of stars/constellations).</note> at another time and elsewhere, just as the stars from which it is formed are continually carried from the west to the east. In this matter, a great many astrologers have slipped up, thinking that those who refer the planets to the eighth sphere <note>The celestial shell containing the fixed stars.</note> must necessarily use "movable" signs. Nor did they understand the words of **Ptolemy** in the first book of the *Tetrabiblos* <note>original: "apotelef."/Apotelefmatika; Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note> to mean the opposite; his words in Latin are as follows: "Let us not omit this, which is worthy of note: that it is reasonable to make the beginnings of the twelve-fold divisions <note>original: "dodecathemorū"; the 12 signs of the zodiac.</note> or boundaries from the tropical and equinoctial points. This is what the greatest writers have especially indicated. For from those things which we said above, it is clear that both their natures and powers and relationships have their cause from the tropical and equinoctial beginnings, and not from any other. Therefore, if we were to establish other beginnings, we would either be forced not to use their natures in predictions, or, if we did use them, we would stray from the truth of the zodiac, the intervals from which their powers proceed having been omitted and changed." These are the words of **Ptolemy**, whose opinion had to be revealed before being refuted, since it has been either misunderstood or ignored by so many.

<margin>The second difference</margin>
The first difference between images and signs is therefore clear: that the former are moved, while the latter are not. Even if they are described in the eighth sphere, there is another very evident difference: that the images have unequal sizes, while the signs are equal to one another. For each of the signs contains thirty parts <note>degrees</note>, whereas some images extend through smaller spaces and others through larger ones. Since, therefore, signs are one thing and images are another, we shall refute both by their own specific reasons.

<margin>It is demonstrated by no reason that they are distinct in twelve powers.</margin>
And first, we shall inquire of them concerning the signs: what reason has demonstrated to them that there are twelve natures there, distinct in powers and properties, and neither more nor less than these? **Abraham ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abraam auenazra"; a famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> at the beginning of his *Book of Astrological Reasons* says that some things are said about the signs which are proven, and some things are stated by arbitrary choice. Immediately declaring which of these are primarily brought forward as arbitrary, he mentions the division of the zodiac. For they say: why is the division of the signs only into three hundred and sixty parts? Because this number is more convenient for divisions. The same is also written by **Ali ibn Ridwan** <note>original: "Haly Auērodan"; an Egyptian Muslim physician and astrologer who commented on Ptolemy.</note> when explaining the predictive books of Ptolemy: "We have divided the circle into twelve parts which are called signs, and each of the signs into thirty parts which are called degrees, and any thirtieth part into sixty minutes, because these numbers are found to be more suitable for divisions." By what words, therefore, could you better refute them than by their own? They are so ignorant of the nature of things and the consequence of reason that, because those who measure the movements of the stars divided the circle into twelve parts for the convenience of dividing the number, they then established a dogma that those twelve parts have diverse powers and properties—as if their distinction arose from the nature of the heavens rather than the choice of mathematicians! It follows that if they were described in the eighth sphere—as **Ptolemy**, the Egyptians, and all the masters of the signs wished—nothing of a solid nature would correspond to them; instead, they could only be thought of and conceived in the mind.

<margin>Origen</margin>
For this reason, **Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) who studied Greek science and philosophy.</note>, imbued with the doctrine of the Egyptians, called those signs "intelligible" and perceptible only by reason. For there is no part of the eighth sphere which always becomes either the equinox or the solstice; rather, one part after another does so, just as that sphere is carried by its own motion from west to east. Therefore, the points in which we understand the equinox or solstice to always occur depend on no physical reality, but solely on our own thought. These points can certainly serve mathematicians for finding movements and calculating the locations of the planets, but to suggest they are the origins of virtues and influence is an argument whose principles cannot be established. Perhaps the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonians, often regarded as the founders of astrology.</note>, considering this, used the images and signs in their predictions with some inconsistency.

<margin>The greatest weakness of this art</margin>
From this, the greatest weakness and inconsistency of this art is clearly recognized; for those things which are thought by the consensus of astrologers to be its primary and strongest foundations are in fact... <unclear>tis</unclear>

<summary>Pico argues that the twelve signs of the zodiac are arbitrary mathematical constructs rather than physical realities with natural powers. He points out that even famous astrologers like Ibn Ezra admit the 360-degree system was chosen for its mathematical convenience rather than discovered in nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s Book 8 of his "Disputations Against Divinatory Astrology." In the preceding text, he began challenging the notion that the twelve mathematical divisions of the zodiac (the signs) possess any inherent power separate from the actual physical stars (the constellations).</meta>

->### DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.<-

...for the followers of the Chaldean <note>The "Chaldeans" was a common term in the Renaissance for astrologers, referring to the ancient Mesopotamian origins of the practice.</note> profession, who are most famous for their predictions of the future, considered these things to be nothing. **Haly Abenrodan** <note>original: "Haly auērodan"; Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote famous commentaries on Ptolemy.</note>, noticing this in part, said: "The signs are merely mansions <note>stations or zones</note> which perform nothing; however, it is the fixed stars within them that act." Then why does the sun run through them all every year? And they receive their names from the effects the sun produces while positioned in them. Similarly, regarding the fixed stars that are in that same part of a sign—whether they are one hundred as the ancients thought, or seventy as the more recent writers claim—if their power remains, then for that whole time the force of that sign will be the same as the power of the star dwelling there. If that star is moved to another part, its power will also be transferred to that part. 

These are his words. Indeed, his opinion—both from what has been cited and from his words elsewhere—is known to be this: the parts of the zodiac themselves, if the influx of the stars is excluded, have no power of producing effects. However, when they say that one sign has such a property and influence, and another has a different one, they claim this truth is based on two reasons: either because the stars coming together in that part of the sign at that time are endowed with such power (so that the efficacy belongs to the "guest" rather than the "host," as they say), or because the sun produces such effects when it reaches that sign. It is by this logic that the equinoctial and solstitial signs—namely Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn—are called "movable" <note>Now usually called "cardinal" signs.</note> because the sun, when positioned in them, changes the season of the year. Conversely, those next to them are "fixed" because at the time of year when the sun traverses them, the state and quality of the air do not change.

<margin>Haly Abenrodan: By what reason thunder and lightning occur, according to Ptolemy.</margin> Similarly, **Ptolemy** says that Aries causes thunder and lightning, not because of any power located in that part of the zodiac, but because when the sun is positioned in Aries, it is the vernal equinox <note>The start of Spring.</note>; this season of the year, by its own quality, stirs up such changes in the air. For the heat of the sun, approaching us closely and dissolving the moisture of the preceding winter, lifts many vapors upward. When these form into dense clouds, they emit flashes of lightning when they collide with one another. This is the opinion of **Haly Abenrodan** concerning the power of the signs. Nothing could more strongly confirm our own point: namely, that the parts of the zodiac intercepted by the equinoxes and solstices (in which **Ptolemy** says the principal power resides, and which all astrologers except the Chaldeans use) have no power of producing effects.

For while **Abenrodan** desires to explain and declare the opinion of **Ptolemy**, he—even if unwillingly—completely obliterates and erases it with a pen already dipped in truth, so to speak. For he asserts that the parts of the circle effect nothing, and that the things thought to be done by them are actually stirred up by the operation of either the sun or the stars acting in those parts. But in truth, the Egyptians, **Ptolemy**, and the whole crowd of astrologers ascribe perpetual and immobile properties to the signs, which do not fade or change even when the sun or the stars depart from them. Otherwise, **Ptolemy** ought to have handed down a different nature for the signs than what had been previously declared by the Egyptians. 

Furthermore, even later writers would have had to write differently than **Ptolemy** if the power of the signs changes as the stars migrate. Yet, without a single syllable being altered, the same things regarding the nature of the signs are preached by those who wrote just yesterday as were found in the works of **Petosiris** and **Nechepso** <note>Legendary founders of Hellenistic astrology, supposedly an Egyptian priest and a pharaoh.</note>. This is despite the fact that a shift ought to have occurred: what were once the properties of Aries should now sometimes be those of Taurus, and what were Scorpio’s should at some point be Sagittarius’s, and so on for the rest. This is because the stars that once ran their course in Aries are now passing into Taurus, and those that once occupied Scorpio will, in the passage of time, migrate to Sagittarius.

Now, as for what is said about the sun—good Jesus, how vain and trifling it is! To attribute to a sign an effect that proceeds from the power of the sun positioned there, rather than the sign itself. This is almost the same as if someone were to say that a chair inspires the power of debating because a philosopher is accustomed to debate while sitting in it; or if they expected syllogisms from a footstool because someone was sitting on it. Thus, because the sun, when placed in Aries, stirs up thunder and changes the frost of winter into the mildness of spring, the "planet-mongers" <note>original: "planetarii"; a derogatory term for astrologers.</note> decree that when the moon is in Aries, thunder is to be expected, and that in all things Aries is the author of mobility. They do not notice that if thunder occurs when the sun is in Aries, the same does not follow for the moon and the rest of the planets. This is because that effect does not come from the nature of the sign, but from the heat of the sun lifting vaporous matter—the material of clouds—into the heights, from which thunder and other such things are later produced; which power...

<summary>Pico argues that the mathematical "signs" of the zodiac have no inherent power, as the seasonal effects attributed to them are actually caused by the Sun's physical heat. He mocks astrologers for maintaining ancient definitions of the signs even though the stars have physically shifted into different constellations due to precession.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's critique in Book 8, where he dismantles the logic behind astrological "signs." He is currently arguing that the properties astrologers assign to signs (like being "movable" or "fixed") are based on faulty reasoning and a confusion between the sun's seasonal effects and the inherent nature of the zodiac divisions.</meta>

<page-num>230</page-num>
<header>BOOK EIGHT</header>

...the power found in the heat of other stars <note>original: "syderum"</note>, since it is not the same as the Sun's, will not produce what is produced by the Sun, even if those stars are placed in the same sign. For the fact that the Sun does this more in **Aries** <note>The first sign of the zodiac, marking the spring equinox.</note> than in **Aquarius** is not due to the properties of the signs themselves, but the position of the place; namely, because in Aries it is closer to us. Therefore, things here on earth are more affected by its rays during that time. For this reason, even when placed in the same sign, it produces different effects in different regions during that same time. 

But these men are ignorant of the first rudiments of **logic** <note>original: "dialectices"</note>, in which we are taught to distinguish what exists **by its own nature** <note>original: "per se"</note> from what exists **by circumstance** <note>original: "ex accidenti"</note>. I only wish they were not merely illogical, and did not rave plainly like children. For who would not call it insanity rather than error when an astrologer claims that because the time of year changes when the Sun is in Aries (to stay with the same example), any project you begin when the **Moon** is positioned there will not be firm or lasting, but "childish" because it is fleeting and changeable? 

And because the quality of the air does not change but remains the same during midsummer when the Sun occupies **Leo**, they claim Leo is a "fixed" sign. Therefore, they say whatever one undertakes under it will be long-lasting and immovable. From this comes that marvelous dogma: when the Moon is traveling through Leo, one should neither put on new clothes for the first time nor cut the fabric; for, due to the quality of the "fixed" sign, those clothes will last too long. By this "signification," it seems either a disease or some other misfortune is implied, because of which you would be unable to use them, since clothes that are actually used cannot help but be worn out and cannot last forever. Who, hearing these things, could not think they were either invented for a laugh by storytellers or are the ravings of the mad? By what skills can those men now be led away from error, to whom such things can seem not only not absurd, but even true? 

Philosophers, when disputing with those who feel no shame and resist even the most obvious truths with a hardened face, are accustomed to forcing them into their own self-destruction—that is, to show that the things they say do not prove their point so much as contradict it. Let us, therefore, attack these men in the same way. Since it does not seem absurd to them that Aries has the power to make things "movable" because the Sun, approaching it, changes the season of the year, let us at least obtain this much from them: let those born under Aries not move from their place, but let them hold to and defend their dogma. 

But if they do this, we ask them: are these signs which they call **movable, fixed, or double** <note>In astrology, signs are categorized by their "modality": Movable (Cardinal) signs start seasons, Fixed signs are in the middle, and Double (Mutable) signs end them.</note> themselves immovable, or do they move along with the **images** <note>original: "imaginibus"; the actual constellations of stars as opposed to the mathematical 30-degree "signs."</note>? If they answer that they are movable, then they themselves are moved away from their own signs; for initiating spring, summer, autumn, or winter is the role of immovable signs, not movable ones. And the properties they give to the signs—that they are movable, fixed, or double—are derived from the aforementioned variety of the seasons. Therefore, these properties do not belong to any signs except those which are imagined to be always unmoved in specific places on the circle. 

If they say they are immovable, it follows that they do not coincide with the location of the "images," which are repeatedly shifted in location along with their stars <note>Pico is referring to the **precession of the equinoxes**, where the physical constellations slowly drift away from the mathematical signs used by astrologers.</note>. If this is the case, by what logic are properties derived solely from the *shape* of the images attributed to the signs as well? They call **Aries** "movable," "equinoctial," and "of short duration"—which are conditions of an immovable sign—and then immediately call it "four-legged," "with drooping eyes," and "lustful," which are not properties of the sign, but of the **image** <note>i.e., the shape of a Ram</note>, even if it shares the same name. They differ in nature, location, and properties.

And so as not to pursue every detail, the whole crowd of astrologers, when they divide the signs—declaring these to be common, these fixed, these movable; and again, some "straight" and others "oblique" (which are, as I said, conditions of the immovable signs)—they also use these differences: some are **human**, some are **wild**, some are **aquatic**, others **earthly**, some **mute**, others **vocal**, some **sterile**, and others **fertile**. All of these belong to the *images*, not the *signs*, because these follow the form, effigy, and nature of the image, not any position of the circle. 

<margin>
See the exclamation!
</margin>
What is this great sluggishness or sleepiness? That they seem to see things so diverse mixed and confused together, deceived only by the shared names and not by their nature? For even that idea—that this sign is **hot**, that one **earthly**, another **airy**, and another **watery**—is taken from the images and transferred to the signs with the same recklessness. For if the state of the circle were considered from the "movable points" <note>the equinoxes</note>, Aries should be judged to be **Air**—that is, hot and moist—rather than **Fire** (hot and dry), since spring is opened with it, which is of a hot and moist quality.

<summary>Pico critiques the logical inconsistency of astrology, specifically how it erroneously applies seasonal characteristics (like "fixed" or "movable") and physical imagery (like animal traits) to mathematical divisions of the sky.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the logical inconsistencies in astrology. # DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

...Furthermore, Ptolemy gives a reason why, in a circle where there is no inherent beginning, we are accustomed to taking the start of the year from **Aries** <note>The Ram, the first sign of the zodiac.</note>. He answers that in the first age of all things, there is an abundance of moisture, which is the quality of spring that we begin with Aries. So then, O Ptolemy, if Aries is the first sign, and you think moisture is owed to the first age, do you think Aries is a dry sign or a moist one? If it is dry, then it is not the first; if it is moist, why do you call it "fiery" <note>original: "ignitum". In astrology, Aries is a fire sign, which is traditionally hot and dry.</note>? 

In short, those differences of cold, dry, hot, and moist distributed among the signs—which I intended to prove—seem to be taken from the condition of the **images** <note>The actual constellations of stars.</note> rather than from the **signs** <note>The mathematical 30-degree divisions of the ecliptic.</note> themselves. <margin>Abraham ibn Ezra</margin> Even **Abraham ibn Ezra** <note>A 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer, often cited by Pico as "Auenazra".</note> confesses this in his *Book of Astrological Reasons*. For instance, they established **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces** as cold and moist because they considered the nature of the creatures for which they are named. For the same reason, they called **Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius** hot. They called **Gemini and Aquarius** "airy" because of their human form, since that quality <note>The "sanguine" or airy temperament.</note> dominates most in humans. Likewise, they made **Taurus, Capricorn, and Virgo** "earthy," partly because of their gender <note>In traditional astrology, these are "feminine" signs, which were associated with the element of earth.</note> and partly because of the ear of grain <note>The star Spica.</note> that the Virgin holds in her hand. Therefore, they attributed this power to the signs by taking it from the various properties of the images. 

In this matter, the "good" Ptolemy is not only nodding off but is fast asleep, as in the same passage he shifts himself from the sign to the image. I shall demonstrate this clearly, along with the inexpiable error of **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, a famous Arabic commentator on Ptolemy.</note> in explaining Ptolemy’s words. 

His words in the second book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>Also known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note> are these: "The twelfth-part <note>original: <term>dodecathemorion</term>; the 30-degree division of a sign.</note> of Aries is, universally speaking, <term>thundering and hailing</term> <note>original: "βροντῶδες καὶ χαλαζῶδες"</note>, <term>but specifically its forward parts are according to the property of the star standing over them</term> <note>original: "ἰδίως δὲ τὰ μὲν ἔμπροσθεν αὐτοῦ μέρη κατὰ τὸν ἐφεστῶτα ἀστέρα ἰδιότητος"</note>." That is to say: individually, these effects occur more or less according to the nature and property of the stars that are within it. And he adds that the preceding parts cause rains and winds; the middle parts a temperate air; the final parts heat and plague. Furthermore, the parts that turn toward the north cause heat and corruption, while those toward the south are icy and somewhat cold. 

I understand these words of Ptolemy as follows: what he pronounces about Aries in general, he refers to the **immobile sign** <note>The fixed 30-degree coordinate in the sky.</note>—which cannot be denied, since that is where the equinox occurs. For that reason, Ptolemy said it was <term>thundering and hailing</term> <note>original: "βροντῶδες καὶ χαλαζῶδες"</note>, because all these things usually stir up before the springtime. Then, what he adds subsequently regarding the different efficiency of its parts according to the nature of the stars existing therein, Haly believes refers also to the parts of the sign, as I will soon show. But I shall demonstrate more clearly than light, from Ptolemy himself, that this was said of the **image** <note>The actual constellation of stars.</note>. I will also show how much Haly erred in explaining Ptolemy, as much as Ptolemy erred in establishing the doctrine. 

Haly thinks Ptolemy’s words should be taken to mean that the stars he says are in those parts were in those parts of the sign he speaks of at the time he was writing; and that such was the property of the sign then, which would be transferred to another place as the stars moved over time <note>A reference to the precession of the equinoxes, where the stars slowly shift their position relative to the mathematical signs.</note>. This interpretation by Haly might seem plausible if Ptolemy had done for other signs what he does for Aries, and if he had not provided the names of the stars he places in those parts. But since, in the case of **Taurus**, he explains certain stars by name, he reveals both his own error and the error of his translator. For those stars were not in that part of the sign in Ptolemy's time where he places them, but rather in the part of the image, where they are, and will be, and have been. 

<margin>Words of Ptolemy: Pleiades, Hyades, Vergiliae</margin> His words regarding Taurus are these: "The sign of Taurus universally brings both qualities of air, even being somewhat warm. Specifically, however, its preceding parts, and especially where the **Pleiades** <note>A famous star cluster in Taurus.</note> are, stir up earthquakes, winds, and clouds; the following parts, where the **Hyades** <note>Another star cluster near the "eye" of the Bull.</note> are, cause lightning and thunder." 

Come now, who does not see that these things are said by Ptolemy about the **image**? In its preceding parts are the Pleiades, which our people call the *Vergiliae*; in the following parts are the Hyades (for which "Aldebaran" is read in the common translation). For although the Hyades are in the vertex, the horns, and the whole head, and the Pleiades are between the end of its body and the tail of Aries (a place they call the "severing" <note>original: "abscissionis"</note>), the former occupy the following parts and the latter the preceding parts...

<summary>Pico argues that the physical qualities astrologers attribute to zodiac signs are actually based on the physical appearance of the constellations (the images) rather than any mathematical or logical basis. He highlights a contradiction in Ptolemy's work where the astronomer confuses the fixed mathematical signs with the shifting stars of the constellations.</summary>

# BOOK EIGHT

...since **Taurus** sets and rises backwards. But truly, if these things are referred to those signs <note>The mathematical divisions of the zodiac.</note>, there will be no truth in the sayings, since in the time of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose works formed the basis of medieval science.</note> the **Pleiades** <note>A prominent star cluster in the constellation Taurus.</note> were not in the sign of Taurus, but in **Aries**: as is easy to recognize from his *Great Composition* <note>original: "magna eius compositione", referring to the *Almagest*, Ptolemy's most famous work.</note>. Since **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> ought to have read this, and would not have doubted that the same man was the author of both works <note>The *Almagest* and the *Tetrabiblos* (an astrological work attributed to Ptolemy).</note>, I cannot marvel enough that he hallucinated in so obvious a matter. He explained Ptolemy's sayings regarding the places of the stars in the signs, yet left it written that the Pleiades during that time were in the first points of Taurus. This error was followed by Haly, **Leopold** <note>Leopold of Austria, a 13th-century astronomer.</note>, and **Ascadelis** <note>John of Aschenden, a 14th-century English astrologer.</note> in the summary they call "English," and finally by later writers like **Bonatti** <note>Guido Bonatti, the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century.</note>. But the error of those who follow Haly is greater; they say Ptolemy spoke of stars placed in those parts of the sign, yet they do not change them, but say the same as Ptolemy, even though since that time they have changed by more than twenty degrees <note>Referring to the precession of the equinoxes, which causes the stars to slowly shift position relative to the calendar signs over centuries.</note>. It is clear, therefore, what we wished to prove: that astrologers imprudently contradict themselves, mixing together the properties of signs and images—if there are any—as if they do not differ in location, nature, or parts.

### Chapter V. That the images of the Chaldaeans are mere fictions, what led them to invent them, and how the error of artificial images and many others sprouted from there.

**C**ome now, let there be no power in the signs; but are the **images** <note>The constellations (the shapes stars make), as opposed to the "signs" (the 30-degree mathematical sectors of the zodiac).</note> themselves anything? For perhaps here the astrologers will not seem to rave, nor to lean on fictional and arbitrary things, when they deny that anyone could have the greatest power through the nature of the stars, unless they hold those images by their own lights, stars, and rays? Truly, I do not doubt that astrologers rave here too. For even if the stars from which the images are fabricated are both true and natural, nevertheless the constitution of the images from the stars is neither true nor natural, but false and fabricated according to whim, entirely imaginary and without any hope of probability. For who will not judge immediately that if the power of one star is great, the power of many conspiring together would not be greatest? But returning to the point: no "conspiracy" of stars is seen there except one feigned by us. For there is certainly no mixture there through union. By what means, then, do many stars—distinct in nature and separated by the immense vastness of great spaces—combine into one property? 

I know what they will respond: that they agree in the likeness of a single image, which is evidence of some hidden affinity; just as a figure is outlined from a single species, so there is one native property in these stars from all of them together. But truly, this might be something—even if it did not achieve what they want—if those images were seen there expressed and finished with the truest marks. But since they are fashioned according to our whim (as I shall declare), and it is just as convenient for anyone to form for himself **tigers and elephants** there as it is for them to see **dogs and hares**, it is clear that the argument taken from the figure is, like the rest of the astrologers' tools, vain, arbitrary, and fabulous. But if they contend that those figures exist there not by the whim of the viewers but by nature, I will not call upon the faith of experience so much as the reasons and testimonies of the astrologers themselves. For **Abraham ibn Ezra** <note>A 12th-century Jewish scholar often cited by Pico.</note>, a man of great authority among them, in his second edition of *Astrological Reasons* (for he wrote two books on the same subject), intending to give a reason for these images, writes in these words:

<margin>Abraham ibn Ezra wrote two books on the reasons which astrologers use.</margin>
Which we have translated thus into Latin according to the sense: "What Ptolemy calls the **Lyre**, others call the **Falling Vulture** <note>original: "vulturem cadentem... lyram". In Arabic astronomy, the constellation Lyra was often depicted as a vulture or eagle.</note>; and it is no wonder, since anyone may change the figure and name placed upon it for himself. For the heaven is spherical, wherefore there is no reason in it why you should establish the beginning of anything in this place rather than another. But just as some stars are joined to others according to the whim of the eyes, so diverse images are made. We, therefore, shall relate them in the manner they were handed down." Thus he speaks. Nothing could confirm my opinion more truly or effectively: since there is no beginning or end in the parts of a circle, you can begin an image for yourself from whatever star you prefer, and in whatever...

<summary>Pico argues that constellations (images) are arbitrary human projections rather than natural groupings, citing the shifting positions of stars like the Pleiades and the subjective naming of constellations like Lyra to prove astrologers rely on fiction.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>
That he fabricated various images for himself in the same place.
</margin>
...rise and set. Nor is it doubtful that by the diversity of beginnings and ends which you have prescribed for yourself, and by the number of stars you have either included or excluded, it is certain that you have established various images therefrom. This is especially true since different people imagine different forms for themselves from these same stars: as **Abraham** <note>Likely Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish scholar whose astrological works were widely read in the Renaissance.</note> declared regarding the **Vulture** and the **Lyre** <note>The constellation Lyra was often depicted in ancient and medieval maps as a "falling vulture" (Vultur Cadens).</note>; and you can demonstrate the same in other cases. For they do not even agree on the number of those more celebrated zodiacal images; for while others counted twelve, the **Chaldeans** <note>A term often used by Pico to refer to ancient Mesopotamian astrologers.</note> made only eleven of them, forming one out of **Libra** and **Scorpio** <note>In older Greek astronomy, the "claws" (chelae) of the Scorpion were later separated to form the scales of Libra.</note>. For what prevents everyone from daring anything in this celestial painting, since equal power is granted to all? Even
<margin>Albumasar</margin>
**Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer and the most influential authority on the subject in the Middle Ages.</note> himself, who professes to give reasons for all the dogmas of astrology,
<margin>Aratus</margin>
when he comes to the images, brings forward no other reason than that **Aratus** <note>A Greek poet (c. 315–240 BC) whose poem "Phaenomena" fixed the shapes of the constellations for centuries.</note> described them thus—
<margin>Cicero</margin>
as if Aratus were not the most legendary of poets! As **Cicero** <note>The Roman orator who translated Aratus into Latin.</note> says, he wrote on astrology while being entirely ignorant of the science. If you compare the sphere of Aratus with the **Barbarian Sphere** <note>The "Sphaera Barbarica" referred to non-Greek astronomical traditions, such as those of the Egyptians or Babylonians.</note>, you will see they are often at odds and dissonant with one another. This shows that they are fashioned according to whim and rest on no solidity of learning or reason.
<margin>
They paint the Hebrew alphabet in the sky.
</margin>
The masters of the **Hebrews** contend that they find their own alphabet—that is, the marks and elements of their language—among the stars, just as astrologers find their images. If they find credulous eyes, they can persuade people of this no less plausibly than the astrologers do with their images. The truth is that all forms and all effigies are there, and for that same reason, no forms or effigies are there at all, except by the whim of men; in nature and in actual truth, there are none. If only our little diviners had fashioned some likenesses of majestic and more sublime things, I might more easily be led to believe they were the works of God rather than human fabrications against nature. But when I consider His counsel and wisdom, I do not see
<margin>
See this extraordinary madness.
</margin>
why He would not or could not have adorned that temple of divinity, those halls of heaven, with better images than those of irrational animals, monsters, or even lifeless things. For what is there besides bears, dragons, hares, dogs? And those things that are inanimate, like arrows, ships, triangles? Add to these the severed heads, dripping with gore and rot <note>original: "tabo sanieque", likely referring to the head of Medusa held by Perseus.</note>, and the maiden banished to punishment <note>Andromeda.</note>—to say nothing of the **Hydra** and the **Centaur**. If nature does not permit such things on earth, why did she describe their patterns for herself in the sky? Indeed, I think it is the greatest madness to be led to believe that these things were formed there by the institution of nature and divine counsel. A good priest or a magnanimous king would be ashamed not to have better paintings in his temple or palace. Otherwise, what purpose would you claim nature had? Is it so that she might govern lower bodies of the same kind through these superior images? That she might breathe musical melody into whatever men she wished through the celestial **Lyre**? That she might generate and preserve those animals among us which are born and perish every day through the animals that are there? Are our animals not necessary, since none are found there? Why are those animals not described there, since none are described? For what "privilege" do dogs and bears have that they should have two rulers or priests in heaven, while elephants, tigers, and innumerable species of animals have no divinity in heaven by which they are ruled? But I have said too much about these things with those for whom it is not only shameful to believe such things, but even unworthy to refute them.

But if someone should ask me why, in this license of invention, the supporters of astrology descended to these images rather than others, I will reply that he seeks a reason here which is sought in vain in things established by no reason. Yet it is easy to see what led them to most of these. I believe the names of the images ascribed to the parts of the **Zodiac** are derived solely from the activities that most often occur when the sun is found in those parts. For example, **Cancer** <note>The Crab.</note> received its name because in that part of the sign-bearer the sun is placed and begins to move backward like a crab. **Leo** <note>The Lion.</note> follows because of the excessive heat. **Taurus** <note>The Bull.</note> is the name of another part because when the sun arrives there, the earth is plowed by oxen. **Gemini** <note>The Twins.</note> follows because then, by doubling everything, all things are doubled. Under **Virgo** <note>The Virgin.</note>, the earth, scorched by the heat of the sun, bears nothing. Under **Aries** <note>The Ram.</note>, the "fleece" of flowers with which the fields are clothed; or because of the likeness of the head and hair, they fashioned that animal. **Libra** <note>The Scales.</note> balances the nights and days against each other like a pair of scales. When the sun arrives at **Scorpio**, the air first stings with cold. Soon, under **Sagittarius** <note>The Archer.</note>, it goads us with the stings of more vehement cold and winds. In **Capricorn** <note>The Goat.</note>, the reason is manifest: from there the sun begins to "climb" back up like a goat. In **Aquarius** <note>The Water-Bearer.</note> and **Pisces** <note>The Fish.</note>, the rains...

He mocks the idea that God would fill the heavens with images of monsters and severed heads while omitting noble creatures like elephants.</summary>

# BOOK EIGHT

...you will pour out rains, having addressed the fish <note>A reference to the constellation Pisces, traditionally associated with rainy weather.</note>: led by such similarities, they were able to fabricate these images in various parts of the sky rather than others, drawing the stars into the likeness of that nature whose name they were going to impose on that part for some other reason. <margin>What Conon the Egyptian mathematician saw</margin> The fictions of the poets were added for pleasure or for favor, inventing many things: just as Conon the Egyptian mathematician first "saw" monsters and then a lock of hair from the head of Berenice <note>Conon of Samos was a 3rd-century BC astronomer who claimed to find a new constellation, Coma Berenices, to please Queen Berenice II after she sacrificed her hair for her husband's safe return.</note>. But it is not worth the effort to investigate more diligently or to explore the insanities of others; it is enough and more that it is established that these are not the works of nature, but the trifles of inventors or the delusions of dreamers. Thus we may finally rightly define these inventions as having arisen from corrupted philosophy and the fables of poets. Nevertheless, all astrologers grant so much to these things—as if they were most likely truths or things pointed out with a finger (so to speak)—that it is scarcely credible into what superstitions this madness has led them. They say: "Do not give medicine when the Moon is positioned in Taurus, because that animal ruminates <note>The Latin text here has a likely contraction for 'ruminates.' The astrological belief was that because a bull chews its cud, the patient would vomit up the medicine.</note>; therefore the medicine will cause one to vomit." Or: "When you have built a house, beware lest Scorpio occupy the fourth place; for many scorpions will abound in that house." Another says that he who is born when the Crown <note>The constellation Corona Borealis.</note> is rising will be a king; he who is born under the Lyre will be a musician. There are a thousand other things of this kind by which you may see that they are most thoroughly persuaded that the true likenesses and natures of all these things exist in heaven, from which a wonderful power flows down to us in determining fate. Finally, that whole superstition of fabricating images has sprouted through this same madness: namely, that by piercing a similar image into some metal, they think the metal is breathed upon by that celestial power. These things, however, are not in heaven; nor, if they were, would they descend there because of that carved image; and even if they did descend, as **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note> proves against **Al-Ghazali** <note>The 11th-century Persian theologian Al-Ghazali; Pico refers here to their famous debate on the limits of philosophy and causality.</note>, it would benefit us nothing. But we shall discuss these things more extensively later in a special treatise.

### Chapter VI. Invisible images are known neither by sense nor reason, and their authors—who were not Chaldeans or Indians, but only Arabs—fight among themselves.

**A**nyone might truly marvel at the insanity of astrologers in fabricating those most fabulous images we have attacked so far, were it not for the fact that they have dreamed up others far more ridiculous. For they report that in every single decan <note>A 'decan' or 'face' is a subdivision of a zodiac sign, spanning 10 degrees. There are 36 decans in the zodiac.</note> or "face" of any sign, there are certain images that are indeed invisible, but which consist of the solidity of a most true nature. Those who hear these things cannot keep themselves from laughing. They are of this sort: they say that in the first face of Cancer there rises a handsome young man, well-clothed, yet having some crookedness in his face and fingers, with the rest of his body like a horse and elephant, with white feet, hanging various kinds of fruits and leaves of trees above himself. In the first face of Leo, there rises a tree with a very deep root, on whose branches a dog sits, and a man clothed in noble but dirty garments, weeping and sad about his parents. Others similar to these are described by them in other decans of the signs, all of which—as if they were the most effective things—<margin>Abu Ma'shar</margin> **Abu Ma'shar** mentions in the sixth book of his *Great Introduction* <note>Abu Ma'shar was a 9th-century Persian astrologer whose work was the primary source for Western medieval astrology.</note>. <margin>Ibn Ezra</margin> **Ibn Ezra** mentions them in that book which he titled *The Beginning of Wisdom*. <margin>Peter of Abano, Michael Scot</margin> **Peter of Abano**, **Michael Scot**, and many Latin and Arab astrologers mention them. I once thought, having heard something of these matters, that they meant to indicate by these images what the nature of each decan of a sign produced, not that they actually thought there were such figures there in the sky. But reading their books, I recognized it was far otherwise. For they think, and assert, and contend that these images are most truly in those decans, and are the workers of miraculous effects among us. As **Abu Ma'shar** says: "They sometimes produce things similar to their own forms, but often other things entirely different." And indeed, if they had established this dogma by reason, it might lead me to wonder in some way if these things had been visible to their eyes while escaping our sight. But I find no faith in what these men can claim while they reveal such "wonderful mysteries," since they have no other eyes than those men usually have—and men do not see such things. We do not read in the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, who in 2 Corinthians 12 describes being "caught up to the third heaven."</note> that they were snatched up into heaven, nor could any reason demonstrate these things to those located on earth. Let those who call themselves philosophers blush; yet they are not ashamed to write down such trifles, which an old woman could hardly persuade a two-year-old child of in fables. Add to this that they do not all imagine the same images, but some invent one thing and others another. This man says that in the first face of Aries there rises a woman...

<margin>Abraham's mockery</margin>
You see that Abraham the Jew <note>Referring to Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar whose astrological works Pico often cites, sometimes to highlight Ibn Ezra's own skepticism of certain myths.</note> and astrologer, in his *Book of Nativities*, confesses that these images are ridiculous rather than true. Indeed, I find no one besides the Arabs—men always most prone to fables—and those Latins who followed them, who have put any faith in these things. The Egyptians, Chaldeans, Greeks, and ancient Latin writers of astrology say nothing of them. For when Albumasar <note>The Latinized name of Ja'far ibn Muhammad Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi (787–886), one of the most influential Persian astrologers in the Middle Ages.</note> claims that the Indians, Egyptians, and Babylonians passed these things down, he is easily caught in a lie. Regarding the Egyptians and Chaldeans, we have sources to understand that no such delusions existed among them; from this, one can guess that he is lying equally about the Indians, although he cannot be refuted as easily as with the others, since no monuments of the Indians have been handed down to us by trustworthy authors. But this is a peculiar habit of the Arabs: whatever commentaries they invent, they prefix them with the names of illustrious authors—many of which instances we mentioned in the first book of these Disputations. 

Since there still exist the works of a certain Petosiris <note>A legendary Egyptian priest-astrologer often cited in Hellenistic texts.</note>, a master of astrology among the Egyptians; and since there are, besides Maternus, Hephaistio of Thebes

Regarding Greek authors, only those who have not read Greek can doubt it, for there is no mention of these images in any Greek writer. We must greatly accuse Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy.</note> for ascribing this error to Ptolemy. He indicates this same meaning in the second book of the *Effects* when discussing the types of things that "rise together."
