Furthermore, Porphyry in his *Introductions* says that the type—that is, the figure and form—of <term>the zodiacal signs</term>, which means the animals in the zodiac <gloss>that is, the things rising together</gloss>, is composed of stars. From this, we understand that these "co-rising" things they speak of are no other images than those constituted by the stars. 

I have been quite lengthy in explaining this because I hear that George of Trebizond <note>A 15th-century Greek scholar who translated and commented on Ptolemy; Pico is critiquing his reliance on Arabic interpretations over Greek ones.</note>, though a Greek, followed Haly's interpretation in his commentaries on Ptolemy’s *Centiloquium*. From this error, even the barbarian Albumasar could have steered them away, for he recognized no images besides the visible and established ones...

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST ASTROLOGERS. THE NINTH BOOK BEGINS.

## Chapter One: A summary of what has been accomplished so far; and what must be done in the following books and where to begin.

**W**e have traversed enough so far to show that there is no astrology except that which does not depend on heaven for its pronouncements, except by accident, or as if from a remote and universal cause; neither of which produces particular knowledge of events. It has likewise been declared that even if these things were done from heaven, it is not in the way astrologers think: that is, from a certain initial moment. Then, even if we granted this, it certainly would not be from these causes which they use in predicting, which are neither true nor natural if we have a certain examination. For although they use the intelligences and planets, their increases and decreases, their changes by place, sign, intervals, and the rest of that kind, we have declared them to be false and ineffective. Whether they introduce bad causes—that is, fabulous ones—or make good ones bad by mixing them: now we must act to declare that even if all those things stood firm, they could not be known by them; or if they could be known, they have not yet been grasped by human knowledge. Three things are necessary for knowledge if true things are to be predicted about future matters. First, that the initial hour of each thing be faithfully held. Second, that we exactly comprehend the state of the heaven and the stars in relation to that hour. Last, that we understand through experiments observed what that position of the heaven and stars produces in true, or at least non-deceptive, ways. We will grasp in the two following books that none of these can be known, or that no one who knew them has existed so far. We shall begin, however, from the primordial hour <note>The exact moment of beginning, such as birth or the founding of a city.</note>, the knowledge of which is primary and necessary, nor can the rest be correctly established if anything in it is either ambiguous or erroneous. Whether it be of men—that is, births—or of cities and kingdoms, or the constellations of the year, let us take our start from births.

## Ch. ii. That the astrologer can neither know the certain hour of birth himself, nor can it be explored through any true rule.

**A**n astrologer cannot have the moment in which someone is born explored, unless perhaps by accident when he is present and, as it were, insane, he measures the celestial bodies with an astrolabe <note>A complex historical instrument used by astronomers and navigators to measure the inclined position of a celestial body.</note>. But this happens very rarely; nor can it always happen when we wish it, such as at night, when the air is cloudy, or when no mathematician is present. Furthermore, it is very easy to slip: as Averroes <note>Original: *Auē.* Referring to the 12th-century philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd).</note> testifies in his commentaries on Ptolemy. For if the instrument is not most exact—the likes of which perhaps never exists—so that it responds clearly to the inspection at the moment of emergence, then the whole calculation of the horoscope will falter. But even if the search for the hour through the astrolabe were true, it happens very rarely, as we were saying. The frequent and almost perpetual occurrence is that parents or the masters of the birth tell the astrologers that the hour of birth was such-and-such. They should not be trusted, nor do the astrologers deny it; for it is generally deceptive. Therefore, it is called among them the "expired" or "suspect" hour: regarding which, naturally, there is suspicion and no certainty. For they measure by sun-dials and clocks which, although they might not fail in themselves, nonetheless do not distinguish the intervals that fall in the middle hours. Add to this that the common hours do not take their beginning from the setting of the Sun: which the mathematicians...

<summary>Pico opens Book Nine by arguing that astrology is impossible because the exact moment of birth—the essential starting point for any horoscope—cannot be measured with the necessary precision by parents or instruments.</summary>

->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS.<-

mathematical calculations: reason demands it. For when the air begins to be obscured by darkness—which happens when the sun has long since sunk beneath the horizon <note>original: "sole subfinitore"</note>, especially when the sun is positioned in oblique signs <note>Signs of the zodiac that rise or set at an acute angle to the local horizon, such as Libra or Scorpio in the northern hemisphere, causing longer durations of twilight.</note>—because they linger longer in the west, sometimes night may have already passed for one hour before the air grows dark. Finally, the astrologers agree with us on this; but they have applied a remedy lest their divination be endangered. For if that which they call the "exact hour" <note>original: "horam extiatam." In astrology, this refers to the precise moment of birth required for an accurate horoscope.</note> is not true, unless it is very far from the truth, they say they have a method for finding the true one. Therefore, that prior uncertainty does nothing to hinder them. If they could often object to us that an art or science could not be given by which a particular thing could be known to be so or not, then there would be no method by which we could be made more certain of the moment at which John or Paul was brought into the light. But if these things seem absurd to them, perhaps there is no such method for any particular minute of time, let alone an hour, at which no one can be born in a certain region; they demonstrate this quite easily. 

For if I am said by my parents to have been born at the first hour of the night, and the astrologer, through his "method," denies that hour, I ask: why might someone else not have been able to be born at that same first hour of the night under the same inclination of the heavens? If they deny that this could happen, it follows (as I was saying) that there are many parts of any hour in certain places where a human being cannot be born. I say "many parts of any hour" because no certain time of a birth chart <note>original: "geniturae"</note> is given by those consulting the rules that satisfies the astrologers; instead, it is always changed by them into either a preceding or subsequent part of the hour. If they admit that someone else could have been born during that time in that region, even though I was not born then, let us say that Anthony was born at the first hour of the night. I then ask: if we now establish that as the true hour of Anthony's birth and present it to the astrologer, will he judge it to be true or false? If he judges it true, he ought by the same reasoning to have judged mine to be true when it was offered, since his method is no more consistent now than when John offered his. If he judges it false, then he would be establishing that the hour Anthony was born was false; therefore, it is a false dogma through which a most true hour is reputed to be false. Furthermore, those who handed down this precept say the sign ought not to be changed from the one shown by the "exact hour," but that a specific part of that sign should be declared by the method as the most significant in the horoscope. Truly, the "exact hour" often lies about the sign, especially when a person is born with the very last or very first parts of a sign ascending; in that case, the method will not correct the error but will confirm it. It is clear from these reasons that there is no way of tracking down the horoscope when it is uncertain. Now let us show that if such a method could perhaps be devised, those which the astrologers have handed down are most aptly described as deceptive.

### Chapter III. The dogma of Ptolemy, which they call *Almuseli* or *Aiodar*, is refuted both by authorities and by reasons.

<margin> ⁜ </margin> <margin> Aoniar <note>Likely a variant spelling of Animodar or a reference to a specific astrological authority.</note> </margin> **P**tolemy, in the third book of the *Apotelesmata* <note>Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology, also known as the *Tetrabiblos*.</note>, hands down a dogma of this kind. He commands that the new moon or full moon immediately preceding the birth be observed. Then, one must find the planet having more authority <note>In astrology, "authority" or "dignity" refers to a planet's strength based on its position in the zodiac.</note> over the degree of that conjunction or opposition. Finally, once the chart <note>original: "themate," the astrological figure or map of the heavens.</note> is arranged, one must establish that place as the cardinal point <note>One of the four main angles of a horoscope: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, or Imum Coeli.</note> where that prior planet was, according to the number of the degree of the sign which that ruling planet held. They fashion this cardinal point for the entire birth chart; all astrologers decree this to be the foundation of all astrological prediction <note>original: "apotelesmaticae."</note>. This is the decree they call *Almuseli*, or sometimes *Aiodar* <note>Known more commonly in Latin as the *Animodar*, a method used to "rectify" or correct the recorded time of birth to match planetary positions.</note>. In this, the younger astrologers err greatly, having misunderstood Ptolemy’s opinion above. 

Now Ptolemy himself is examined, against whom I can first oppose the great weight of authorities. For Abraham the Jew <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> says that he observed many birth charts with very exact astrolabes in these regions whose longitude and latitude were confessed and explored; yet he never found any of the planets whose degree and minutes (among the signs they occupied) corresponded to the degrees and minutes of the Orient <note>The Ascendant or rising sign.</note> or the Midheaven, nor varied by less than half an hour from the hour of birth already discovered to be most true by the senses. It is truly ridiculous that they say Avenaz <note>Another name for Abraham Ibn Ezra.</note> did not write these things with sound judgment—as if he had a dispute with Ptolemy over a kingdom, even though he lived nine hundred years later—and as if he does not prefer Ptolemy's opinion in establishing the year, the giver of years, and many other things. But Alchabitius <note>Al-Qabisi (died 967), an influential Arab astrologer and mathematician.</note> also writes in his own commentary that he has demonstrated that the true rising degree can by no means be found by that reasoning. Henry Bate <note>Henry Bate of Mechelen (1246–1310), a scientist and astrologer.</note>, a disciple of Albert the Great, while examining his own birth chart—naming himself "a servant of God" to conceal his identity—says: "let us dismiss the *Animodar* of Ptolemy as rejected by wise men." Others do not expunge the dogma but correct it, as Aoniar does not...

...nothing dissenting from Ptolemy. Others fight over the understanding of it <note>Referring to a specific astrological rule or method mentioned on the previous page</note>, as it is asked to which place a planet is closer; some want discrete quantity to be observed, while others prefer continuous quantity, such as Antonio di Montulmo <note>A 14th-century Italian physician and astrologer famous for his "Judgment of Nativities."</note>. But leaving aside the authorities opposing Ptolemy, I am accustomed to declaring the falsehood of the dogma in this way. Suppose Lucius is born in Rome and Fabius in Florence at the same hour and same moment; it is clear to astrologers that there will not be the same horoscope <note>The Ascendant or rising sign.</note> for both because of the different inclination of the sky under which they are born. And yet, if we follow the reasoning from Ptolemy’s precepts, we will make the same horoscope for both, since in both regions the preceding full moon or new moon occurred in the same part of the sky; wherefore the same ruler, possessing a degree of the sign in both themes <note>An astrological chart or horoscope.</note>, will define the cardines <note>The four "angles" or most important points of a chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note> with the same numbers in both nativities. But the evidence of the matter and the senses refute this; therefore, it is a false dogma, which I am surprised Ptolemy—a supreme mathematician—did not see through.

### Chapter IV. That the investigation of the specific horoscope through conception is falsely ascribed to Ptolemy by the Arabs; it is irrational and rejected by many astrologers.

<margin>Another dogma of the moderns</margin>
<margin>Occasion of error: A faulty translation of Ptolemy</margin>
Among the moderns, another way of investigating the horoscope from the hour of conception has been found, to which they attribute much. It is of this sort: they take it as granted from the tradition of the ancients—especially from the fifty-first aphorism of Ptolemy's *Book of One Hundred Sayings* <note>Known as the *Centiloquium*, this was a popular collection of 100 astrological rules; though attributed to Ptolemy in the Middle Ages, modern scholars consider it pseudo-Ptolemaic.</note>—that the position of the Moon at birth was the horoscope at conception. Conversely, they hold that the position of the Moon at conception is the horoscope of birth. With this established, they pass down a method by which they think the place of the Moon can be apprehended when the seed filled the womb. Once this is found, they gather that a similar degree ascends at the hour of birth. But the occasion for their error was a faulty translation of Ptolemy’s books; for he wrote nothing about this *degree*, but spoke only of the *sign*. His words in the place mentioned above are these "notable opinions" <note>original: "ἔνδοξα" (endoxa)</note>, and what follows.

<margin>No one of the ancients handed down this method of investigation</margin>
<margin>Hephaestion, Porphyry, Petosiris</margin>
In Latin, the word-for-word translation is: "Where that sign was at the time of birth, establish that as the horoscope of conception; where the Moon was at conception, make that the horoscope of birth, or its opposite." Therefore, Ptolemy did not think that the horoscope could be found to the specific degree in this way. For this reason, in the books of the *Apotelesmatica* <note>Ptolemy's primary work on astrology, also known as the *Tetrabiblos*.</note> where he inquires into this, he makes no mention of this decree. Indeed, if he had understood it to be about the degree (which we have shown to be false from his words), he would have also considered it very easy to find the hour of conception, which today the moderns provide with no great trouble to anyone who desires it, using the method they wish to be Ptolemy’s. How is it, then, that Ptolemy himself, in the third book of the *Apotelesmatica*, says the seminal principle is "mostly" <note>original: "επιπλεου" (epi to pleon) - meaning for the most part or usually.</note> unknown? And when it does come to our knowledge, he says it is either "by chance" <note>original: "συνπτοματι" (symptomati)</note>—that is, by a fortuitous accident—or by observation. He certainly ought to have added "by art" <note>original: "εν τεχνωο" (en technō)</note>—that is, skillfully—if indeed he believed that by some art or way this could be apprehended. But how it is known by chance or by observation, the Greek interpreter declares: "by chance" when it happens that a woman feels the reception of the seed, as Cleopatra <note>Refers to the medical writings attributed to Cleopatra, which were common sources for gynecological information in the Renaissance.</note> teaches; "by observation" if the man carefully notes the time when, having once had intercourse with a woman, he then abstains from her, and her missing her periods thereafter declares the intercourse was fertile. Besides these, none of the ancients recorded any other way of exploring that time with clarity, let alone wanting to investigate the hour of birth from it. For what the Arabs say, that Hermes commanded this, is a fable; just as they most lyingly attribute many other things to the same author (as we noted in the first book). For what the Egyptians handed down on this matter, Hephaestion <note>Hephaestion of Thebes, an Egyptian astrologer from the 4th century AD.</note> relates, and Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote an introduction to Ptolemy's astrology.</note>, who says that this very precept which is read in Ptolemy was an invention of the Egyptian Petosiris <note>A legendary priest-astrologer of ancient Egypt.</note> in these words: "But Petosiris [says]..." <note>original: "ὁ δε Πετοσε ιρισ" (ho de Petosiris)</note> and what follows.

Petosiris, however, says that the sign in which the Moon was at the time of conception is the horoscope at birth, or its opposite.

<summary>Pico critiques the "Trutine of Hermes," a method used to find a birth time based on the moment of conception, arguing it is based on a mistranslation of Ptolemy and is logically flawed. He cites ancient authorities like Porphyry and Hephaestion to show that the method was originally about general signs, not precise degrees.</summary>

-># DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.<-
->iiii .3.<-

...held that the place of the Moon at the time of conception was the horoscope <note>In ancient astrology, the "horoscope" refers to the Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note> of the birth. But in the same passage, Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on astrology.</note> mentions two other ways of tracking the sign, based on the opinion of Antiochus and certain others: namely, identifying the sign in which the Moon was at the hour of intercourse, though no mention is ever made of the specific degree. Indeed, they even title this chapter <term>concerning the seminal sign of the Moon</term> <note>Original Greek: περι σπορασ ηουσιπειου (peri sporas...)</note>; that is, concerning the seminal sign of the Moon, because they mark the sign the Moon held when the seed was released into the genital place. Ephestion of Thebes also recounts three other methods, different from these, which Porphyry mentions; these were Egyptian methods by which they tracked the same thing: namely, which sign was ascending at the hour of intercourse. In those writings, Ephestion expressly warns us that we do not arrive at a useful horoscope through these paths, but that the search is conducted <term>roughly</term> <note>Original Greek: παχυμερωσ (pachymerōs). This implies a lack of precision.</note>—or as is commonly said, with a "crude Minerva" <note>A Latin idiom meaning a rough, unrefined, or common-sense approach rather than a precise scientific one.</note>. He claims there is only one true method for determining the degree, which Ptolemy handed down in the third book of the *Apotelelesmaton* <note>Known today as the Tetrabiblos, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>. It is the very method we refuted in the previous chapter; however, as we have said, the modern astrologers fell into error because in the Arabic translation followed by the Latins, the translators mistakenly put "degree" instead of "sign." Furthermore, whatever these authors may have written, what is the reason for this dogma? Or what could have been grasped through such observation? They answer, he says, with a calculation: since the number of days the infant was in the womb is understood from the position of the Moon at the hour of birth; if you count these days backward, you arrive at the hour of conception, and for that time you will find the Moon's position to be the same degree that ascends at the time of birth. But I ask: who taught us to define the duration of stay in the womb based on the Moon's position? Not Ptolemy, nor any of the ancients, nor even your Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of Hermeticism and astrology.</note> recorded this. There is no other answer but this: that those stays in the womb must be defined in this way *if* the dogma about the exchange between the Ascendant and the Moon’s place at conception and birth is true. Therefore, they prove the truth of the dogma by arguing in a circle; they claim it arrives at the truth once the durations are observed, yet they say the durations must be observed in that specific way *because* the dogma is true—otherwise it wouldn't work. Thus, it is quite easy for anyone to "confirm" their dogmas.

The dogma is rejected by experiments.

But if perhaps you dare to verify this by experiment—observing and comparing the time of birth and conception together—you may lie with impunity, as the act occurs without witnesses. However, even those among you who most strongly claim to be experienced deny that this precept matches the truth. For Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note> is said to have observed this many times, and it failed three times; he blamed this now on Mars, now on Venus, now on Mercury. I think if he had observed it ten times, he would have accused the other planets as well. For Emanuel the Hebrew, a follower of Ibn Ezra, tested it twice; once he found it varied from the true time of birth by seven days. Aboafar <note>Likely Abu Ma'shar, a prominent Persian astrologer.</note>, the prince of astrologers, believes this method can be off by five degrees, as his disciple Sedis relates; if that is the case, it does not help us at all, as we are concerned with the specific degree. Likewise, Avenrodan <note>Haly Abenrudan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer.</note>, a great commentator on Ptolemy among these people, testifies that it is often deceptive. John of Saxony, the interpreter of Alchabitius <note>A 14th-century astronomer known for his commentary on the 10th-century astrologer Alchabitius.</note>, considers it utterly false, vain, and useless, affirming it is impossible that an uncertain degree of the horoscope could ever be made certain through it—which he demonstrates extensively using the example of a proposed birth chart.

### Chapter V. The fiction of Messahallah is refuted, along with five other methods for investigating the horoscope recounted by Paul of Alexandria.

<margin>
The fiction of Messahallah.
</margin>
<margin>
See the beautiful derivation of the astrologers' folly.
</margin>

**H**hese are almost the only methods accepted by astrologers; Messahallah <note>An 8th-century Persian Jewish astrologer and astronomer.</note> thought up another fiction, but it is rejected by everyone and seen as a transparent vanity. For he ordered that the time of the Moon from the new moon to the full moon (or conversely from the full moon to the dark moon) be considered as one hour; whether that period preceded the birth, the interval between it and the time of birth should be compared to the whole distance of the Moon’s cycle from start to finish. Whatever the proportion of the intervals, one should take that portion of the temporal hour—but only so long as we observe that a male is not born in an even hour, nor a female in an odd one. The following age laughed at this, having learned by experience that males and females are born at the same hour. I, however, do not merely consider the vanity of this one decree; rather, I judge the whole of Messahallah by it. For while it is the nature of man to slip, to err, and to be deceived, yet to write such shameful things, to rely on ridiculous matters, and to present fables as if they were dogmas—to speak of things which the evidence of reality everywhere...

...evidence confutes it. It is certainly not within the nature of man—if indeed reason is the proper gift of man—to accept this. But I do not judge Messalla <note>Messahallah (c. 740–815 AD), an influential Persian Jewish astrologer and astronomer.</note> alone, but rather all astrologers alongside him, among whom he is of the highest rank; you will not easily find anyone wiser in that guild. For those wonderful Egyptian high priests of this sacred discipline—what fables they have devised on this matter! Paulus of Alexandria <note>A 4th-century astrological writer whose *Introductory Matters* was a standard textbook.</note> relates 

<margin>Five other Egyptian methods recited by Paulus.</margin>

five different methods, aside from the three already mentioned, which they use to profitably track the truth of the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>. Good God, how vain, crude, futile, and false they are! The first is of this kind: they say, look at the position of the Sun in a daytime birth, or the Moon in a nighttime one; whichever planet holds the <term>monomoiria</term> <note>A technical system where each of the 360 degrees of the zodiac is assigned a planetary ruler.</note>, make that same planet’s *monomoiria* the true horoscope by choosing the degree closest to the suspected one. The second method, whether it be day or night, looks only at the position of the Moon, but is otherwise similar. The third, which gave Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most famous astronomer and geographer of antiquity, whose *Tetrabiblos* codified ancient astrology.</note> the occasion for his own doctrine, 

<margin>First</margin>

considers the full moon or new moon closest to the birth; then it looks at the 

<margin>Second</margin>

<term>despotes</term> <note>Original: "despotem," meaning the lord or ruler of the astrological house.</note>, that is, the master of the house in which it occurred, and the <term>onocrator</term> <note>Original: "onocratorem," a term for the ruler of the "bounds" or specific subdivisions of a sign.</note>, that is, the ruler of the limits. 

<margin>Third</margin>

It sees which of the two is stronger in the birth constellation and which possesses more 

<margin>Fourth</margin>

authority; from that, it calculates the ascending degree. The fourth method looks only at the supreme ruler of the degree—namely, the degree in which the Sun and Moon either meet or oppose each other after the infant actually comes forth; however many "limits" <note>Subdivisions of a zodiac sign assigned to different planets.</note> that planet possessed in the ascending sign, they think that many degrees of that sign have already appeared in the east. The last method observes not only the birth but the 

<margin>Fifth</margin>

conception; that is, which time—either the full moon or the new moon—preceded it. Then it orders the <term>dodecathemoria</term> <note>A division of each zodiac sign into twelve parts of 2.5 degrees each.</note> of the degrees where that occurred to be calculated and observed, seeing which of the planets' *monomoiria* they fall into; whichever planet is better situated in the chart has the judgment for measuring the horoscope. Heliodorus <note>Likely Heliodorus of Alexandria, a 5th-century philosopher and astrologer.</note> wrote on how he would investigate the 

<margin>Heliodorus</margin>

time of conception: they would go backward from the birth, he said, through nine months as if for the gestation of the womb. He assumed the time was always equal, so that these "most divine" Egyptians might be found to be the most ignorant everywhere. I could, however, object to many things in which these doctrines are specifically in error. But this one reason is enough for those who study brevity, by which we also rejected Ptolemy's doctrine: for whichever of the aforementioned methods we follow, we will always produce the same horoscope for those born at the same time but in different regions—even though it is established among all mathematicians, beyond any controversy, that these horoscopes must be different.

## Chapter VI. The beginnings of cities, kingdoms, factions, and laws are unknown, and astrologers have provided no art by which they can be investigated.

L<gloss>iquit</gloss> It is clear from these things that the natal hour is never known with clarity except by chance; furthermore, because it wanders, it cannot be restored by any art. But when the truth of the time is not certain, the truth of the prediction cannot stand. Therefore, nothing true can be said by the "genethliacs" <note>Astrologers who cast birth charts (nativities) for individuals.</note> who testify with one voice that the specific degree of the horoscope is the hinge of the birth, the joint of all fate, and the foundation of the entire <term>apotelesmatic</term> <note>The branch of astrology dealing with the practical effects or "results" of planetary positions.</note> art. Nor, indeed, is there better reliability in the beginnings of cities and kingdoms; the knowledge of these is far more difficult and meticulous than that of individual births. For who has recorded these? Which writer of histories has observed them? If the reliability and diligence of such writers provided the day a city was restored, or the day a city was founded, it would surely be considered an exceptionally great feat. At Rome, it was the custom to celebrate the city's birthday; but from this, nothing more is certain to astrologers than that the Moon was in Libra when it was being founded. In the notebooks of Paolo Florentino <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous Florentine physician, mathematician, and cosmographer.</note>, 

<margin>Paolo of Florence</margin>

the physician and mathematician, I found two different times noted for the restoration of the city of Florence: one in the year of grace 801, and the other in 802. From this, the constitution of the stars is entirely different. I would believe that many of the constellations of various cities that are commonly circulated are faked based on later results; just as Julius 

<margin>Julius Firmicus</margin>

Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Latin author of the *Mathesis*, a massive astrological compendium.</note> invents those for Paris, Plato, and others—and even the birth chart of the world itself which he provides...

He then transitions to Chapter VI, asserting that the founding times of cities and kingdoms are historically unknown, making political astrology impossible.</summary>

...also testifies. Furthermore, they wish for that moment to be of great significance when something new happens among the common people: when civil discord is born: when a foreign nation invades a kingdom: when new laws are established or new decrees are promulgated. Who, if not a diviner, shall provide the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopum"; here referring to the Ascendant or the exact timing of the celestial configuration for an event.</note> for these things? For it is necessary to have these timings before we can divine anything. Finally, so that some moments of these times might be obtained: surely they will not deny that these are perhaps less exact and less certain than those of particular <term>genitures</term> <note>Individual birth charts.</note>. Therefore, if they think that those individual charts require "correction" and are otherwise not to be trusted, it will be much more necessary in these historical cases. They teach no method for correcting these, for the methods we have mentioned are applied only to the births of men. Thus, their entire prediction regarding the fates of cities and kingdoms was crippled and deceptive, since they want these to depend on those primordial moments which they either completely ignore or have received through traditions that are neither faithful nor precisely rendered. Therefore, let men no longer fear death, exile, poverty, or destruction; let cities no longer fear plague, even when these most audacious triflers threaten such things in their annual pamphlets published everywhere.

### Chapter VII. It is still uncertain among astrologers how the houses are to be divided: how far their powers extend: and which signs should be used.

**R**egarding the remaining matters, we must speak of the beginnings of the year, great conjunctions, and eclipses; for it is by observing the moment these occur that they prophesy the fates of public and universal affairs. It must be declared, therefore, that such times cannot be grasped by them without falling into error. Indeed, this will become clear from what follows, when we show that the motions of the planets are still uncertain and have not been captured by any blameless calculation. Thus far, we have said how uncertain the "fated hour" of any thing is—if indeed there are fated hours for things as astrologers mostly believe—for we demonstrated above that there are no such fated hours, or if there are, they are different from what astrologers think.

<margin>Discord among astrologers regarding the division of houses.</margin>
Now let us make it clear that even if they could obtain the correct times for a suspected prediction, they still cannot know the position of the stars that exists at that hour. First, it is necessary to arrange the "theme" <note>An astrological chart or diagram.</note> into twelve predetermined places which they call <term>houses</term> <note>The twelve divisions of the sky, representing different areas of life (e.g., wealth, siblings, death).</note>. No one who has touched the books of the mathematicians <note>In this context, "mathematicians" usually refers to astrologers who calculated planetary positions.</note> is unaware of how much darkness the astrologers pour over this, or how much they clash with one another over this completely unproven matter. Some distinguish these places by six circles, one of which, revolved through the point of the East, makes the seventh <term>cardine</term> <note>An "angle" of the chart; the four main points: Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note> and the horoscope; another, the meridian itself, outlines the highest and lowest points of the heavens. Others say that the arcs of the semi-diurnal and semi-nocturnal periods are intercepted in four middle places by four points, and divided into three equal portions.

<margin>Abraham</margin>
But all these circles pass through the poles of the world; an opinion widely accepted which we refuted above. Abraham Avenazra <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar, poet, and astrologer.</note> teaches in his work *On the Composition of the Astrolabe*, and elsewhere, that the houses should be divided by designating six circles: one of which is the horizon, another the meridian, by which the four cardines are immediately established. He orders the other four to be drawn through the points of intersection of the horizon and the meridian, and by dividing the parts of the <term>equator</term> falling between the East and the meridian into three equal portions.

<margin>Johannes de Regio Monte</margin>
Johannes de Regio Monte <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), known as Regiomontanus, the most influential astronomer of the 15th century.</note>, a man of lofty mind and the most learned mathematician of our age, strongly approves of this method, though he suppresses the author’s name. However, he did not satisfy Campanus <note>Campanus of Novara (c. 1220–1296), who developed a competing system of house division based on the prime vertical.</note>, because he himself brought a new reasoning to this inquiry; in other respects he is similar to Avenazra, but differs greatly in this: that he uses a certain "fictitious" circle on the equator which he called the "vertical circle," from which a different measure and different boundaries of the places emerge. Johannes wrote copiously in confirmation of this dogma, relying on many mathematicians and the authority of ancient astrologers.

<margin>Ludovicus the Hermit, a most exact calculator.</margin>
Others divide them in different ways: and our friend Ludovicus the Hermit, a diligent and most exact calculator, used to prove that none of the methods we have mentioned agree with the sayings of Alchabitius <note>A 10th-century Arab astrologer whose *Introduction to the Art of Judgments* was a standard textbook.</note>. What of the fact that many believe these same places should be divided according to the degrees of the zodiac which they call "equal," either using only this way (which we warned above that the ancients often did) or using both divisions...

<margin>Abraham of Seville, Henry</margin>
...and you would equally accept that division, as well as the one that varies according to the <term>ascensions</term> <note>original: "anaphoris"; the time it takes for a sign of the zodiac to rise above the horizon.</note>, yet which nevertheless corresponds to the degrees of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi"; literally the 'sign-bearer', referring to the ecliptic belt.</note>. This is what Abraham the Spaniard <note>Abraham bar Hiyya, a 12th-century mathematician and astronomer.</note>, the teacher of Ibn Ezra (<term>Auenezra</term>), and Henry of Mechelen <note>original: "Henricus valentis"; likely Henry Bate of Mechelen, a noted medieval astronomer.</note> observe, pronouncing their judgments no less from the place in which a planet is located by a distribution of equal degrees than from where the divisions are marked in the common manner. Furthermore, if it were certain where the beginnings and ends of these places [the houses] were to be established, there remains another doubt which again calls everything back into uncertainty: for they do not agree whether the power and efficacy of a "place" is enclosed within the space designated for it. Rather, Ptolemy would begin five degrees before that point into the preceding parts of the signs; others extend it by only three parts. The wise men of the Egyptians wanted the beginning of a place—which is commonly called the <term>cusp</term> <note>The line or point that marks the beginning of an astrological house.</note>—to be not the beginning, but the middle, as if it were the center of power. Therefore, they spread it fifteen degrees above that point and as many degrees below it. If we consider all these varieties of opinion—nearly all of which are supported by similar reasons or authorities—we must confess that the entire system of pronouncing judgments through the stars (if such a system even exists) is held in ambiguity by this uncertainty alone. For when the divisions of the places are varied, the entire constellation [the chart] is varied; since (as we rebuked above) the stars change their nature, influence, and properties in the eyes of the astrologers simply by a change of "place." And what is most significant: those places which are joined and coherent in position are judged to be primary in their fighting and contrary conditions. For in the first place and the twelfth, which follow one after the other, what could be more different? Or in the sixth and seventh? Again, in the fifth and the sixth? Likewise, the eleventh and twelfth, or the ninth and eighth, and so with the rest. It often happens that one mathematician will place a planet in the sixth house, while another will contend it is in the fifth, which will utterly change the entire prediction; and one will judge a planet to be in the ninth, while another says it belongs to the eighth. This entire distribution of places, the very root and foundation of all <term>apotelesmatic</term> <note>original: "apoteleſmaticæ"; the branch of astrology concerned with predicting effects or outcomes.</note> art, remains in uncertainty. There follows the concern regarding which signs we ought to use, where there is a complex and inexplicable question regarding moving and immobile signs, and concerning the eighth, ninth, and tenth spheres—a matter we need not speak of in this place, as it has been treated abundantly above. 
<margin>Abraham the Jew makes a double chart.</margin>
Abraham the Jew <note>Ibn Ezra.</note> instructs that a double <term>theme</term> <note>original: "thema"; an astrological chart or horoscope.</note> be made, as if he did not believe the controversy could be decided. Not only will there be uncertainty from this doubt as to which signs are owed to the planets, but also from that which we treated before regarding which "places" they occupy. But since every astrological pronouncement hangs on this, everything is therefore doubtful, uncertain, and unproven.

### Chapter VIII. That it is most difficult to attain the true locations of the planets, and concerning the deception of instruments.

<margin>Andreas Summarius</margin>
**O**nce the places have been divided and the signs distributed, there remains the labor of establishing the <term>epochs</term> <note>original: "epochas"; reference points in time used to calculate the positions of celestial bodies.</note> of the constellations and stars. This is the task of indicating at which degrees and minutes both the fixed and wandering stars [planets] may be found. The unrefined and unskilled think they can perform this duty very easily; the most learned hesitate and despair. To them, it is known how great the difficulty is in truly attaining the locations of the planets—a task judged by many to be not only laborious but impossible. Andreas Summarius, a serious mathematician, begins his book thus: "Whether the motions of the stars can be known, I know not; that they have not yet been known, I hold as most certain." He offers this reason for his opinion: because those who measure the motions of the constellations must necessarily first define the location of the constellation, in which they behold it by the help of an instrument. Having found the location of the star, they use it as a sort of assumption to organize the calculation of its course. If the location is truly grasped, the future calculation of the motion will be true, for they rely on mathematical reasoning, which is least likely to fail. However, the apprehension of the location is not faithful in every respect, as the instrument simply fails. For no matter the vastness of a mechanical instrument, it cannot be sufficient for divisions perceivable by action and sense, which are necessary to avoid error—especially if the distance of any star from the observer’s location is considered, as well as the ratio by which the circumference of the universe exceeds the circumference of the instrument. Therefore, since the sense cannot attain the relationship of the parts of a tiny instrumental body to the parts of the whole (as if to immense things), the location of the constellation cannot be observed without deception. To be sure, the error will perhaps remain hidden, but with the passage of time it will become more evident, as the constellation always moves further from its true location with each cycle...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is foundationally flawed because authorities cannot agree on how to divide the sky into "houses" or where a house's influence begins. He also cites mathematicians who claim that mechanical instruments are too small and imprecise to ever truly measure the vast movements of the heavens.</summary>

<margin>
Confirmation
through the
opinion
of Haly.
</margin>
He confirms <unclear>that it</unclear> deviates. Ptolemy confirms this when, for the sake of correcting the fallibility of instruments, he orders astronomical numbers to be renewed every hundredth year. He does this because, over that period of time, the faults of old observations are uncovered; for this reason, they must be corrected by new observations. Yet even these new observations will not be entirely faultless, but they may be free from errors that can be perceived by the senses at that time. When, after many rotations have passed, they again wander significantly, they must be brought back to the truth by a new correction, as accurate as can be made. Thus, the tables of Ptolemy, the prince of astrologers, maintained for many years in the past, have become useless. Indeed, the studies of more recent men repeatedly correct these observations, because—as we have said before—no manufacture of any instrument is so skillful or so subtle, nor is any size so vast, that it can report the location of a star with faultless reliability.

<margin>

Astrolabes

palms.
</margin>
Abraham the Jew <note>Abraham bar Hiyya, a 12th-century mathematician and astronomer.</note> reports in his book on the *Work of the Tables* concerning two astrolabes constructed with the greatest logic, of such great size that the diameter of each extended nine palms <note>A "palm" was a historical unit of length based on the width of a human hand; nine palms would be roughly two meters wide, an enormous size for a portable instrument.</note>. When the two Bersechit brothers <note>original: "Bersechit"; likely referring to the Banu Musa brothers, famous 9th-century scholars in Baghdad.</note>, who were makers of instruments, simultaneously observed the altitude of the Sun as it was entering Aries, each instrument did not report the same thing; rather, they varied from each other by two minutes <note>A "minute" in this context is 1/60th of a degree of arc.</note>. Henry Baten of Mechelen <note>Henry Bate (1246–1310), a renowned astronomer and philosopher.</note>, who was as eminent in this art as in all mathematics—for he wrote a noble treatise on the composition of the astrolabe—thinks it is either impossible or, as he says, nearly impossible to make an instrument that is in no way deceptive. He also reports that while in Paris, he saw the maximum altitude of the sun observed at the midday of the summer solstice using two very large quadrants <note>A quadrant is an instrument for measuring angles up to 90 degrees.</note> arranged with miraculous skill.

<margin>
An error of
forty-
two
minutes.
The eyes
can be
deceived in
many ways.
</margin>
With one instrument, the measurement was found to be sixty-four parts <note>degrees</note> and forty-two minutes. With the other, it was the same number of parts, but with zero minutes. Therefore, there was an error in one or the other of forty-two minutes. See how those who gather the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The specific point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> of a newborn using an instrument can also be deceived—a fact about which we testified above that we were also warned by Averroes <note>original: "Auenrodā"; the Latinized name for the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note>. Baten, whom I just cited, proves in his *Mirror of Natural Things* <note>original: "naturaliū reꝝ speculo"; referring to Bate's *Speculum divinalium*.</note> through many thousands of verses that neither Ptolemy, nor Geber <note>Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century mathematician.</note>, nor Al-Battani <note>original: "Albategni"; a 9th-century Arab astronomer.</note> could investigate the size of the diameters of the Sun and Moon more certainly than through eclipses; for the reliability of instruments regarding that matter would be suspect. I pass over the fact that in his *Great Composition* <note>The *Almagest*.</note>, Ptolemy teaches—as does Pierre d'Ailly <note>original: "Alliacen."; a 14th-century French cardinal and scholar.</note> in his seventh book on vision—that the eyes can be deceived in many ways when observing the locations of stars. For even if the air is held to be clear and cloudless—which is often prevented—winds might blow that are not felt. Yet the philosopher Aristotle writes that when the east wind blows, the stars appear larger. Leo the Jew <note>Levi ben Gershon (1288–1344), also known as Gersonides.</note>, a distinguished man and celebrated mathematician, because he had little faith in the ancients, devised a new instrument <note>The "Jacob's Staff" or "Cross-staff," used to measure the angle between two celestial bodies.</note>, the mathematical rules of which we have seen to be of surpassing subtlety. Nevertheless, when he had observed two fixed stars with it twice in the same year, he says the first observation differed from the second by two degrees, which he thinks should be attributed to the state of the atmosphere.

### Chapter IX. Various opinions on the movements of the planets, the inequality of the year, and the maximum declination of the sun.

<margin>
On the [views]
of the ancients.
Another opinion.
Opinion of Hipparchus.
Opinion of Ptolemy.
Opinion of Al-Battani.
</margin>
**F**rom this, perhaps, was born such a great diversity of opinions among authors concerning the movements of the stars. For if they had grasped the true locations with instruments that do not deceive, they would not have wandered or disagreed with one another in measuring the time of the <term>return</term> <note>The "restitution," or the time it takes for a planet or the sun to return to the same point in the sky.</note>. Ptolemy, in his *Great Composition*, calls the movement of the sun the most manifest of all, by which we ought to measure the others as if they were better known. Yet how little it has been certainly explored is shown by nothing more clearly than the fact that the traditions written about it by the princes of astronomy are so utterly conflicting. The ancients before Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BC) considered the founder of trigonometry.</note> wanted the return of the sun, which constitutes a year, to consist of three hundred sixty-five days plus a quarter part of one day. Others, however, added more than a quarter part. Hipparchus, writing in the one hundred seventy-eighth year from the death of Alexander [the Great] based on his own and the Chaldeans' observations, calculated that less than a quarter part of a day should be added; however, he did not determine exactly how much was lacking to reach the clear truth. Ptolemy, two hundred eighty-five years after him, defined that missing part as the three-hundredth part of a day. Al-Battani, observing the heavens 743 years after Ptolemy, found the movement of the sun to be swifter, for it fell short of that quarter part by a hundred and sixth... <note>original: "& sextā"; this is the catchword for the next page.</note>

<summary>Pico argues that astronomical observations are fundamentally unreliable due to the physical imperfections of instruments and the limitations of human sight, citing discrepancies among famous astronomers like Ptolemy, Al-Battani, and Levi ben Gershon. He concludes that if even the length of a solar year cannot be agreed upon, astrology's foundations are crumbling.</summary>

->BOOK NINE<-

...and a sixth part of a day. Thabit <note>Thabit ibn Qurra (9th century), a Sabian astronomer and mathematician who worked in Baghdad.</note> stated that the year consists of 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 12 seconds.
<margin>The work of Thabit.</margin>
Then there is that great diversity because some think all years are equal, such as Ptolemy and Alfonso <note>Referring to the Alfonsine Tables commissioned by Alfonso X of Castile.</note>. Others think they are unequal, such as Azarchel <note>Al-Zarqali (11th century), an Arab astronomer from Al-Andalus.</note>, Al-Battani, and Isaac the Israelite <note>Isaac Israeli ben Solomon (c. 832–932), a Jewish physician and philosopher.</note>, whom others among the younger writers follow.
<margin>Ptolemy, Alfonso, Azarchel, Al-Battani, Isaac.</margin>
Therefore, they say the Sun returns to the place from which it departed sometimes sooner and sometimes later. They claim the cause of this inequality is that the "eighth sphere" <note>In the geocentric model, the sphere of the fixed stars; this refers to the theory of "trepidation," a supposed oscillation in the precession of the equinoxes.</note> does not always move from west to east—as Ptolemy and many others think—but is sometimes carried from east to west. Because of its motion, when it moves toward the same part to which the Sun reflects, the Sun's motion becomes faster; when toward the opposite part, it becomes slower. Thus, at different times, the year is observed to be now longer, now shorter. And that Isaac whom we cited, in the book titled *Yesod Olam* <note>original: "iesodola"; This is the *Foundation of the World* by Isaac Israeli ben Joseph (14th century).</note>—which you might say is the *Foundation of the World*—wrote in the year of grace 1310, which was the Hebrew year of the world 5070. 
<margin>Isaac's opinion on his years.</margin>
He thought the years were then at their shortest, so that they could not be shortened further; but he believed the time was already appearing where, by the motion of the eighth sphere, they would begin to lengthen gradually. Between the longest possible duration and the shortest, he claimed the average delay is 365 days and 5 hours.
<margin>The average year.</margin>
Then, dividing the hour into 1,080 parts <note>This refers to the *helek*, the traditional Jewish unit for time calculation.</note>, he says the year has 996 parts, then 48 minutes, each of which is a 1/76th part of one of those 1,080 parts.
<margin>See in the average [years].</margin>
I remember reading this scrupulous calculation also among the most ancient Hebrews. Eclipses show that they precede the time noted in the tables by more than half an hour, which 
<margin>Adaba is most true.</margin>
Andreas Sumarius also reports, and sensory evidence daily declares. Henricus Machivensis also, in the book titled *Mirror of Natural Things*, asserts that in detecting eclipses—whether one looks at the place, the hour, or the quantity—one errs if one follows the numbers of motions of either Ptolemy or Al-Battani. Paulus Florentinus <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous Florentine mathematician and cosmographer.</note>, a distinguished mathematician, when he had observed the entrance of the
<margin>Paulus Florentinus.</margin>
Sun into Aries with most diligent annotations, found it to be faster than the time defined in the tables by a third of an hour. Alliacesis <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1350–1420), a French cardinal and scholar whose astronomical work *Elucidarium* Pico cites here.</note> also reports in his *Elucidarium* that when the entrance of the
<margin>Alliacesis.</margin>
Sun into the vernal equinox was observed in Paris in the year of our Lord 1364, it was discovered that the Alfonsine Tables had fallen away from the truth. But if they are blind in such bright light—that is, in the motion of the Sun, the most manifest of all—where if any error is made, it is necessary to err in the rest as well, what will become of the motion of Mercury, which almost never shows itself to mortal eyes? Sosigenes, the teacher of Alexander of Aphrodisias, reports that it cannot be more than 22 degrees distant from the Sun.
<margin>Various opinions on the distance of Mercury from the Sun.</margin>
Theon, Paulus, Heliodorus, and Porphyry say 23 degrees; Ptolemy even says 28. Concerning the motion of this planet, a certain distinguished mathematician confessed that nothing had been discovered by him. Furthermore, he claimed Mars was about one part in thirty slower than they thought; he himself discovered the difference, yet in this matter he said the studies of later men should be more exactingly watched over. The same man reported the maximum declination <note>The angle between the celestial equator and the ecliptic (the Sun's path).</note> of the Sun from the equator observed by him to be 23 degrees and 30 minutes; whereas Ptolemy reported the same degrees but 51 minutes, Al-Battani 36 degrees and 30 minutes, and Azarchel more than 23. 
<margin>Ptolemy, Al-Battani, Azarchel, Abraham Ibn Ezra.</margin>
Finally, Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraam Auenazra"; a prominent 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note>, the supreme mathematician, in the sixth book on *Revolutions*, affirms that a point cannot be found that is on the horoscope <note>In this context, the "ascendant" or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> when the Sun enters the first part of Aries. For that reason, the time when it reaches Aries is discovered neither by a certain calculation of motion, nor by any kind of instrument. This Averroes <note>original: "Auerrodan"; referring here to the commentator Ibn Rushd.</note>, also explaining Ptolemy, aptly confesses.
<margin>Averroes.</margin>
The same often-cited Ibn Ezra, whenever he was about to calculate anything by exquisite reasoning, would employ three types of canons <note>Standard tables or rules for calculation.</note>: those of Ptolemy, the Persians, and the Hindus, which all varied among themselves and determined the planets to be in different locations. Plutarch, who lived after Ptolemy and was a contemporary of Emilius the Roman, the supreme mathematician
<margin>Plutarch, Emilius.</margin>
under Trajan, says in his *Roman Questions*: "Even at this time when the summit of astrology has been reached, the inequality of times has nevertheless conquered the skill of mathematicians, and very often deceives and escapes their numbers and calculations."

He concludes that if the most obvious celestial motions are subject to such uncertainty, the predictions of astrologers are necessarily fraudulent.</summary>

->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

### Chapter 10. That the error of a single degree, or even of a single minute, sometimes produces many errors; and that the astrologer cannot judge through annual revolutions, nativities, or great conjunctions.

<margin>
The boundaries change.
Exaltation.
Monomoiria.
Decans.
The Sign of Aesculapius.
</margin>
**F**rom this uncertainty of celestial motions, who does not see that the entire art of divining astrology is undermined? For if it wavers by even one degree, it must necessarily fall away from the whole truth. Indeed, if the part of the sign where the star is found is changed, the "boundaries" <note>Also known as "terms," these are specific degrees within a zodiac sign ruled by different planets.</note> are often switched; these boundaries are considered by some to have power equal to the "houses," by others greater power, and by everyone the greatest. Furthermore, the "exaltations" <note>Specific degrees where a planet's influence is said to be most powerful.</note> which they have prescribed for determined parts will be lost; certainly the *monomoiria* <note>original: "monomiriæ"; the division of each sign into 30 individual degrees, each with its own planetary ruler.</note> will always vary, and sometimes the borders of the decans <note>Divisions of a zodiac sign into three parts of ten degrees each.</note>. And if a planet occupies the final parts of a sign, it is possible that an error of a single part transfers the planet from one sign to another; thus, the Moon which would have been in Taurus might become the Moon in Gemini—being fortunate in Taurus but unfortunate in Gemini. Likewise, it will change from masculine to feminine, from bright to dark, from dark to shadowy, from a "pit" <note>Degrees considered particularly weak or debilitating for a planet.</note> to a "height," and from "full" parts to "empty" ones, or from "diseased" parts to the most fortunate. Finally, since among astrologers every single degree has a different property from the next—and even the minutes have distinct properties, as Aesculapius <note>A legendary figure often cited in Hermetic and astrological texts as a source of ancient wisdom.</note> handed down in the *Myriogenesis*—how can the power and influence of a star not be greatly changed by error when the planet's location is varied by a degree or even minutes? And just as an error of a degree sometimes changes the sign, so an error of a minute sometimes changes the degree. Even the "houses" <note>The twelve divisions of the sky relative to the horizon.</note> are sometimes deceptive because of a slip of a single degree: what might actually be in the west [the descendant] could be placed below the earth, and the planet belonging to the horoscope <note>Here referring specifically to the Ascendant, the degree rising on the eastern horizon.</note> might be thrust back into the darkness of the twelfth house. In the *dodecatemoria* <note>The division of each sign into twelve sub-sections of 2.5 degrees each.</note>, an error of one degree will cause a mistake of twelve degrees; nor, if the "epoch" <note>The reference point in time used for calculations.</note> of the star is held incorrectly, will any of the "Lots" (which they call "parts") be correctly established. Add to this the deception in the "radiations" <note>Aspects or angular relationships between planets.</note> arising from the variation of only a single part; for it makes one difference if a radiation is "partile" <note>Exact to the same degree.</note>, another if it is "applying" <note>Moving toward an exact aspect.</note>, and another if it is "separating." Add the most serious error of all in "directing" <note>A complex calculation used to predict the timing of life events.</note> the rays of the planets; if the astrologer slips by a single degree, an error of an entire year will result. But these are the greatest and nearly the most shameful outrages in that profession; yet if you compare them to other errors, they will seem small—errors which they must necessarily incur when they take the initial hours from the motions of the planets, a topic we postponed earlier to this place.

<margin>The beginning of the year.</margin>
Let the beginning of the year be set, therefore, at the Sun's entry into the first minutes of Aries; furthermore, if they are mistaken there by more than half an hour (as we have seen), the constellation will be entirely different, and such a great variation will result.

<margin>The error of Avenezra and Avenrodan.</margin>
The same will happen no less if they do not begin the year from the Sun's entry into Aries, but from the preceding full moon or conjunction [new moon]. I do not see why Avenezra <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> and Avenrodan <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian Muslim physician and astrologer.</note> think error can be avoided in the latter case but not the former, since the hour of the "union" [conjunction] cannot be clearly grasped unless the motion of both stars is correctly held—a point which Avenezra of Messina also objects to. Likewise, regarding the "revolutions" <note>The annual return of the Sun to its position at birth.</note> of nativities: when they are organized by the return of the Sun to the exact same place, how can they fail to be defined incorrectly when the time of that restoration is unexamined?

<margin>The Saxon.</margin>
How will they correctly establish the Ascendants of "great conjunctions" <note>The meeting of Jupiter and Saturn, which astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts.</note> if the motions of Jupiter and Saturn are not exactly understood? Abraham [Ibn Ezra] thinks we are so far from knowing these that he pronounces it a "great thing" if we even know the *day* on which they should meet. The "Saxon" <note>Johannes de Saxonia (14th century), a commentator on the Alfonsine Tables.</note> agrees with this opinion, though he is said to have made a mistake: he says the Ascendant of a great conjunction should not be the one that rises at the hour of the conjunction, but the one that was rising at the start of the year in which it occurred. Thus they defend one error with another error. But the Ascendant of a conjunction does not cease to be what it is simply because it is unknown to us; therefore, it should rather be said that we cannot know what the conjunction will produce because the horoscope cannot be known—not that we should invent another false one because the true one is ignored. For what does the conjunction have to do with the horoscope of a year that perhaps began so many months earlier? Or what reason is there that we should observe the Ascendant of the eclipses (the "failing lights") but not observe that of a conjunction? Finally, though power is granted...

<summary>Pico argues that because astronomical measurements are imprecise, even a tiny error of one degree or minute renders astrological predictions impossible. He critiques various famous astrologers for using "false" charts to compensate for their inability to calculate exact planetary positions and conjunctions.</summary>

In the preceding text, he argued that even a minute error in calculating the "ascendant" (the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon) invalidates an entire horoscope. Here, he extends this critique to the motion of the "eighth sphere"—the firmament of fixed stars—and highlights the deep disagreements among the greatest astronomers of history.</meta>

->BOOK NINE<-

...granted that they have the ascendant of the year in the conjunction; <note>The "ascendant of the year" refers to the specific point of the zodiac rising at the moment of the sun's entry into Aries.</note> they will nonetheless not deny that the year’s own ascendant is of equal or greater importance. Since a completely different constellation arises from this—of which they are ignorant—they must necessarily waver in predicting the effects of the conjunction. I will pass over the fact that the ascendant of the year is equally uncertain, according to the author <margin>Ibn Ezra</margin> <note>original: "Auenaz." referring to Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> Ibn Ezra himself. From all of this, the shameful error of Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboasaris," referring to the Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi (787–886).</note> is evident; for in the first book of his *Greater Introduction*, he said it does not matter if the astrologer errs by a single degree. In saying this, he clearly showed he did not understand the very astrology he was defending. Thus, it is not true, as many say, that astrology is accused out of ignorance; rather, it is only condemned when it has been thoroughly examined, and it is only loved when it has been greeted from a distance and from the threshold.

### Chapter XI. Conflicting opinions on the motions of the eighth sphere: the distance of the head of Aries of the eighth from the head of Aries of the ninth: and the apogee of the sun. <note>The "eighth sphere" is the celestial sphere containing the fixed stars. The "ninth sphere" was theorized to account for the wobbling motion called precession. The "Head of Aries" is the zero-point of the zodiac (the vernal equinox). "Apogee" (auge) is the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note>

**W**e see that until now we were speaking only of the motion of the planets, which is perhaps more thoroughly investigated; but who will faithfully render the motion of the fixed stars? <note>original: "hærentium syderum," literally "clinging stars," a common term for fixed stars.</note> All astrology confesses that these stars possess great, indeed primary and wonderful power. Who among them will correctly place the fixed stars in a birth chart? Or who will deny that an error of a single degree is of no consequence, since there is only one degree in which they are believed to be effective—that is, either at the "cardinal points" <note>The four most powerful points in a chart: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note> or with the "luminaries"? <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> "But," they say, "we have all this in our astrolabes and in the tables of numbers widely and commonly written down." This is exactly what I was warning about when we began to dispute these matters: these things seem very easy to trivial astrologers whose doctrine is drawn entirely from a few pamphlets. But to the learned and the skilled, they are inextricable. For when they approach slightly more distant writings, they are ashamed that masters of equal authority disagree on these matters as much as the east is distant from the west. The Egyptians, the Chaldeans, and indeed the entire ancient consensus <margin>Opinion</margin> think that the "wandering stars" <note>The planets.</note> are moved by only one motion, which we call the "diurnal" <note>The daily rotation of the sky from east to west.</note> motion. Hipparchus <margin>Hipparchus</margin> <note>Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) credited with discovering the precession of the equinoxes.</note> introduced another motion that carries them, like the planets, from west to east. Thus, let this first controversy be raised: whether they move by their own motion or not. The moderns will say there is no controversy, since it is no wonder that things were observed by later men which the ancients could not yet have detected. But there are also those among the <margin>Proclus, most skilled in all theoretical mathematics</margin> moderns who defend the opinion of the ancients, and who do not doubt that those who thought otherwise were deceived. Proclus, who lived long after Ptolemy, was most skilled in all mathematics, as is easily declared by his astrological suppositions, his treatise on the sphere and the construction of the astrolabe, his commentaries on Euclid, and many other things he wrote. <margin>Proclus censures Ptolemy and Hipparchus</margin> In his commentaries on the *Timaeus*, as he also does elsewhere, he censures Hipparchus and Ptolemy for thinking that the non-wandering stars revolve around the poles of the zodiac toward the east, completing one degree every hundred years. Instead, he argues we should agree with the Egyptians and Chaldeans, who through long-lasting observations discovered nothing of the sort—especially since the senses testify to the ancient tradition in such a way that Ptolemy could not have agreed unless he had lost his eyes. For if they moved above the poles of the zodiac as Hipparchus and Ptolemy think, it would be necessary for the "Bear" <note>The constellation Ursa Major.</note> to sink significantly toward its setting in these locations; yet it has been called "never-setting" since the time of Homer. And it would be necessary for Canopus to no longer be visible, since that star makes a brief circuit above the horizon for those living in the third "climate"; <note>A geographical division of the Earth based on the length of the longest day.</note> <margin>Posidonius</margin> but for those who inhabit Rhodes, it grazes the eastern horizon, as Posidonius writes. Since, therefore, the Bear now appears the same—never setting, as it has appeared for so many centuries—and Canopus has preserved the same position, the falsehood of the motion of fixed stars introduced by the moderns is detected by the evidence of the senses. And if they should perhaps object that the calculations of the motions of the planets are correctly gathered by the testimony of the senses by those who assume the motion of the fixed stars in arranging numbers and in the exposition of the rules, <margin>A double response</margin> we dilute this objection in two ways: First, because those who omit that motion of the fixed stars also give results consistent with appearances when calculating the motions of the planets; and while they establish rules for the revolutions of the stars as if the fixed stars were immobile, they nevertheless arrive at a very true competence of reason. Secondly, it is well known that the truth can be gathered from false premises; <margin>Abraham Ibn Ezra</margin> therefore, the fact that a calculation corresponds to the senses does not prove the truth of the underlying assumptions. The most learned philosopher and mathematician Abraham ibn Ezra often mentions these things...

He cites Proclus’s critique of Ptolemy and Hipparchus, arguing that observational evidence of constellations like the Great Bear and the star Canopus contradicts the theory of stellar precession.</summary>
