# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS

...both opinions: one that they are mobile but not wandering <note>In ancient cosmology, the "wandering stars" are the planets, while the "fixed stars" move together as a single unit.</note>; the other, which he ascribes to the Indians, that they are comfortably immobile. He never pre-judges, but leaves the matter in the middle, just as in his book on nativities <note>referring to a work on birth charts</note> he commands a double theme <term>theme</term> <note>A "theme" or *thema* is a technical term for an astrological chart or horoscope.</note> to be made: one as if they moved, and the other as if they did not move. And although I define nothing regarding these matters except this one thing—that nothing certain can be defined—it is nevertheless most true that this favors the opinion of the ancients, for the proponents of the opposite dogma agree on nothing among themselves.

<margin>
Ptolemy
Hipparchus
Arzachel
Isaac
Thebit
</margin>

For Ptolemy, following Hipparchus, thinks they are moved always from the west toward the east. Arzachel the Moor <note>referring to al-Zarqali (c. 1029–1087), an Arab mathematician and astronomer from Al-Andalus.</note> says that when they have proceeded a certain distance, they return from the east toward the west—an observation Isaac the Israelite <note>referring to Isaac ibn Sid, a 13th-century astronomer.</note> follows, saying it was observed through the most true experiences. Thebit ben Chorat <note>Thabit ibn Qurra (c. 826–901), who proposed the theory of "trepidation," an oscillation of the equinoxes.</note> strikes out this motion with another thought-out theory: that they lean toward the south and the north. The more recent writers, approving of Thebit’s invention, admit Ptolemy's opinion by tearing the eighth sphere apart into three separate motions.

Then, those who agree with Ptolemy that they progress toward the east without changing course still clash over the speed of that course, thinking it false that one degree is completed in a hundred years (as had been handed down). For Ibn Ezra <margin>Ibn Ezra</margin> <note>original: "Auen." or "Auenazra," referring to Abraham ibn Ezra.</note>, Moses the Egyptian <note>referring to Moses Maimonides (1138–1204).</note>, and Avenazra report that the space of one degree is passed after seventy years. 

<margin>
Albategni
Paulus of Florence
</margin>

Albategni <note>al-Battani (c. 858–929), a famous Arab astronomer.</note> says they passed after sixty-six years, making them faster than Ptolemy by nearly a sesquialter proportion <note>A ratio of 3:2.</note>. Paulus of Florence <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous Florentine mathematician and astronomer.</note> asserted that they turned even more quickly than Albategni said. Who will judge these opinions? "We have detected their locations with more faithful instruments," say the younger men, "so we cannot be deceived." Why then did it deceive those ancients, who did not lack instruments, nor had less skill in the art than you?

<margin>
Ibn Ezra
</margin>

It is commonly said in this season that the "mobile Aries" <note>The point of the vernal equinox.</note> is distant from the "immobile Aries" <note>The actual constellation of stars.</note> by twenty-five degrees. But Ibn Ezra, in his *Book of Astrological Matters*, records that the distance was eight degrees when he was writing; for he wrote in the year of grace 1153, which preceded our times by about 340 years, more or less. Therefore, if we follow the motion handed down by Albategni (which is faster than the others), the stars would have proceeded no more than five degrees in the years since Ibn Ezra's time. Thus, the distance today would be thirteen degrees, not twenty-five as they say. Was Ibn Ezra then deceived? He for whom both reason and instruments were available.

<margin>
Moses the Egyptian
</margin>

Moses the Egyptian, in that book titled *Mishneh Torah* <note>original: "miſmethora"</note>—which you would call in Greek *Deuterōsis* <note>original: Δευτερωσιų, meaning "repetition" or "second telling"</note> and in Latin "The Second Law"—says near the beginning of the first part that at the time of the Cataclysm <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note>, the mobile Aries coincided with the immobile. Then, afterwards, the eighth sphere moved always toward the east by one degree every seventy years. 

<margin>
Time of the Flood
Years from the beginning of the world
</margin>

Since, therefore, the waters flooded the earth in the year of the world 1656, and now there have passed since the founding of the world—as a truer calculation teaches (for it does not matter here to demand a perfectly precise account)—five thousand years plus nearly three hundred, there will be nearly 3,600 years or thereabouts from the Flood to us. Therefore, in all those years, the eighth sphere will have moved fifty-two degrees, more or less, by which distance the mobile Aries would be removed from the immobile.

Isaac the Israelite writes that both signs coincided in the year that was for us 560 years from the birth of Christ. Pierre d’Ailly <note>Petrus Alliacensis (1351–1420), a French theologian and astrologer.</note> in his *Elucidarium* records that this happened in the year of Christ 260, which calculation disagrees with the former by 300 years. 

<margin>
Angelus of Mantua
Isarith
</margin>

Angelus of Mantua and most of the more recent writers contend it was in the year of the Greeks 515, with a few months added. The same Isarith <note>likely referring to a specific astronomical table or author</note> reports that when a certain younger man had calculated the locations of the Sun and Moon in the eighth sphere, he found the New Moon of the month of March—after 5,224 years had passed from the beginning of the world—at nearly the fourteenth part of Pisces. 

<margin>
Tables of Emmanuel
</margin>

But he found that Angelus, calculating that same New Moon according to the immobile signs—since he was using the Tables of Emmanuel, which he inscribed "Baal Cuaphaim"—found it in the twenty-eighth degree of Pisces. If he followed the Alphonsine Tables <note>The *Tabulae Alphonsinae*, a standard set of astronomical data sponsored by Alfonso X of Castile.</note>, it would be in the twenty-seventh part and fourteen minutes. From this, it would be gathered that the mobile signs were distant from the immobile by thirteen or fourteen degrees. Now, he wrote this a few years before our age; wherefore he says it is a marvel to him that the Oxford Tables record that the star located between the horns of Aries—which is the beginning of the mobile Aries—is distant from the immobile Aries in the year of the Greeks...

<summary>Pico highlights the radical lack of consensus among history's greatest astronomers regarding the motion and position of the fixed stars (the eighth sphere). He demonstrates that different authorities, using different calculations for the speed of precession, arrive at wildly contradictory dates for when the zodiac signs were last aligned.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the "eighth sphere." Having previously mentioned the conflicting views of Arzachel and Thabit ibn Qurra on the movement of the stars, he now brings in more recent authorities like Roger Bacon to show that the confusion has only increased over the centuries.</meta>

<page-num>239</page-num>
<header>BOOK NINE</header>

<margin>At what time Isaac and Roger Bacon flourished.</margin>
In the year of our Lord 1360, at twenty-four degrees and fifty-seven minutes: at which times I find—or nearly forty years earlier—that both the famous Isaac <note>Isaac ibn Sid, a 13th-century Spanish-Jewish astronomer who helped compile the Alfonsine Tables.</note> and Roger Bacon flourished. Both of them thought that in their own age, the immobile Aries <note>The theoretical starting point of the zodiac that remains fixed.</note> had varied from the mobile Aries <note>The actual constellation in the sky, which appears to move due to the wobbling of the Earth’s axis.</note> by no more than ten degrees. For each followed Arzachel <note>Al-Zarqali, an 11th-century Arab mathematician.</note>, who previously estimated that the maximum distance that could occur between them was exactly ten degrees; Isaac reported that this limit had been reached in his own time. Therefore, they claimed the time would come when they would begin to approach each other again, with the motion rolled back toward the west <note>This refers to the theory of "trepidation," an incorrect historical belief that the stars moved back and forth like a pendulum rather than in a continuous circle.</note>. So then, let us conclude: either the mathematical instruments do not fail, or they do fail. If they do not fail, how did Isaac and Roger, observing the stars, judge that the mobile Aries was removed by no more than ten parts from the equinox? Yet, if the opinion of the Oxford tables <note>original: "tabularum ozoniensium", likely referring to the astronomical tables used at Oxford by Bacon and his peers.</note> or the moderns is true, they were moved more than twenty-three parts from there. Thus, an error of thirteen degrees is made evident. If the instruments do fail, how do our contemporaries know they are not failing, when the leading men in this art disagree with such a great variety of opinions? Among these opinions, if anyone thinks he can judge between them, he does so with a brutish judgment <note>A judgment based on instinct or whim rather than science.</note> rather than one fit to judge celestial things. Therefore, whoever offers an opinion on the positions of the non-wandering stars <note>The "fixed" stars of the constellations.</note> might by chance not err, but he will by no means be able to attain the truth through reason.

<margin>Proclus. Ptolemy. Leo the Hebrew agrees with Ptolemy.</margin>
But we must not overlook the fact that Proclus and Ptolemy deny that the apogee <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in the Sun's orbit where it is farthest from the Earth</note> and the perigee <term>perigee</term> <note>the point where it is closest</note> of the Sun move at all. However, more recent authors want what they call in their barbaric tongue the *auge* <note>original: "augem", a medieval term derived from Arabic for the apogee</note> and the opposite of the *auge* to move; the Hebrew Leo <note>Levi ben Gershon, also known as Gersonides, a 14th-century philosopher and astronomer.</note> refutes them, defending the true opinion of Ptolemy. I pass over what they do not know and how they clash concerning the "equation of days" <note>the correction needed to account for the fact that solar days are not all exactly 24 hours long</note>, from which arises the greatest uncertainty in casting horoscopes.

## Chapter XII. On "directions," about which there are manifold opinions among astrologers.

<margin>The opinion of the moderns. A reason against the method itself.</margin>
**T**hese things being considered, there remains the inextricable work of arranging "rays" and what Ptolemy calls *aphetes* <term>apheta</term> <note>The "giver of life," a specific point in a birth chart used to predict a person's lifespan.</note> and what are commonly called "directions" <term>directions</term> <note>A complex calculation where the astrologer "moves" a planet forward in time to see when it will meet another point, used to predict the timing of future events.</note>, which must be exactly calculated. For the mathematicians stab each other with mutual wounds on both sides; nor can they rely on any equal authority, or decide any matter by the experience of so many ages. The opinion of the moderns is that the most exact "radiation" is composed from right, oblique, and mixed ascensions <term>anaphorae</term> <note>The way signs of the zodiac rise over the horizon.</note>, according to the variety of locations. But the result is that if someone is born in a region where the pole is exalted forty-eight degrees above the horizon, and the first part of Capricorn is rising on the horizon, the trine <term>trine</term> <note>An aspect where two points are 120 degrees apart, usually considered harmonious.</note> radiation will occur in the parts of Cancer; yet we know that Cancer is diametrically opposed to Capricorn <note>Pico is pointing out a mathematical absurdity: a "harmonious" 120-degree angle is falling exactly where a "clashing" 180-degree opposition should be.</note>. Henry Bate <note>original: "Henricus batelis", a 13th-century astronomer and astrologer.</note> observes that configuration of the planets by reason of their physical places, such that a trine is whatever occupies the fifth house of the horoscope, with no regard for the sign itself; and likewise for the rest.

<margin>The opinion of Albategni.</margin>
Albategni <note>Al-Battani, a 9th-century Arab prince and astronomer.</note> counts the intervals by the degrees of the zodiac, which he calls equal, unless a star has declined to one side or the other; and the number varies little because of that.

<margin>Johannes Regiomontanus.</margin>
For it varies by no more than thirty minutes even if it has declined by ten parts. Johannes Regiomontanus followed this method, which was also taught by Abraham, the prince and teacher of Ibn Ezra. But if you say that experience has shown that these charts must be composed through "ascensions," Ibn Ezra will resist for a long time; he will say that through many observations it has been noted infinitely many times that they must be established by equal degrees.

<margin>Abenzagel. Albumasar.</margin>
There are those who always use "right ascensions," which we have already shown above that Ptolemy falsely objects to. Add to this that Ptolemy does not observe latitude <note>The distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic line.</note> except in conjoined planets. Abenzagel <note>Likely referring to Al-Zarqali.</note>, however, observes it in every radiation except in the diameter. Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, the most famous Persian astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note> observes it even in the diameter, for which they criticize him. I pass over how much they disagree on how far the power of a radiation extends:

<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
some say from three degrees, some prefer five; the Moon, some say up to twelve parts, and some say up to thirteen, as Porphyry says. There is an equally inexplicable disagreement among mathematicians regarding "directions" (to speak with them in their own manner). For the Egyptians always used the ascensions of the specific region.

<margin>Dorotheus. Abraham. Ptolemy.</margin>
Dorotheus, in "directing" the first part, always used right ascensions—which Abraham testifies that experience very often confirms. Ptolemy and almost all later authors, when a star is placed in the east or west, use the ascensions of the region; but when placed in the fourth or tenth house, they use the equator...

me <note>Catchword for the next page, beginning the word "mentis" or similar.</note>

<summary>Pico demonstrates the profound lack of consensus among history's greatest astronomers regarding the movement of the stars and the Sun. He argues that if these experts cannot agree on basic measurements or the correct way to calculate "directions," then the entire foundation of astrological prediction is built on guesswork.</summary>

<margin>

Another [opinion of] Ibn Ridwan.

...but in various places through mixed <term>ascensions</term> <note>Methods used to calculate the movement of planets across the sky over time.</note>. Almeon feels the same in chapter seven of the fourth treatise on directions; Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboafar"</note> directs degrees through the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs.</note>. For thus, in the eighth difference of the second treatise of the *Book of Great Conjunctions*, he directs the Moon to the place of the conjunction of the malefic stars. Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazra"</note> feels the same in the book titled *The Beginning of Wisdom*, confirming it also with the authority of Al-Battani <note>original: "Albategni"</note>. There are those who think that both the <term>rays</term> <note>Aspects or influences sent from one planet to another.</note> must be extended and the stars directed in both ways: namely, through the degrees of the zodiac and through the ascensions <note>original: "anaphoras"</note> by proportion; this is what John of Seville seems to have intended in his *Isagoge*. For in the second part of his *Quadripartite* <note>A common title for four-part astronomical works, likely referring here to a specific commentary.</note> in the chapter on the first house, he performed the same thing. Others extend the rays indeed through the degrees of the zodiac, but direct them through the ascensions, which Ibn Ridwan <note>original: "Auerodan"</note> seems to have ascribed to Mashallah <note>original: "Messalae"</note> and Ptolemy. On the other hand, Abraham the Jew <note>The same Ibn Ezra mentioned above.</note> brings forward the same reason for both works, why the <term>charts</term> <note>original: "schemata"</note> should be composed by equal degrees and directed through them. 

I will pass over how they disagree on which direction the planet should be led; where Ptolemy seems to dissent from others in his *Apotelesmata* <note>Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, with Ibn Ridwan explaining not a little. But neither do we treat in this place how great a difficulty there is for those who think "mixed ascensions" should be used in the execution of the doctrine. For the most learned have judged that Ptolemy taught this neither correctly nor sufficiently. Paul the German <note>Paul of Middelburg, a famous 15th-century mathematician and advisor to the Pope.</note>, a distinguished mathematician who now lives with Guido, Duke of Urbino, a most learned prince, wrote once that he had never seen a star correctly directed to a <term>trine</term> <note>An astrological aspect of 120 degrees, usually considered harmonious.</note> position, and (what should have been said earlier) he denies that the tables commonly circulated regarding the <term>latitudes</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic.</note> of the planets are reliable. 

From all of which it is clear how wide a door is opened to errors—whether in capturing the "initial hours" <note>The exact moment of birth or a city's founding.</note> of <term>births</term> <note>original: "geniturarę"</note>, or of cities, or of constellations; then in arranging the <term>theme</term> <note>The layout of an astrological chart.</note>, whether the <term>angles</term> <note>original: "cardines", the four most powerful points in a chart: Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note> are established, or locations defined, or signs divided, or seats assigned to the stars—either the fixed or the wandering <note>Planets.</note>—or charts are composed, or the <term>hyleg</term> <note>original: "aphetes", the planet or point in a chart that supposedly determines the length of life.</note> is calculated. All this is uncertain since the truth and mathematical certainty concerning these things still lies unexplored in Heraclitus's cave <note>An allusion to the philosopher Heraclitus, who said that truth is hidden in the depths.</note>.

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK TEN BEGINS.

## Chapter One. An epilogue of those things which have been accomplished so far, and what must be done in the following books.

<margin>
What he has
done so far
in the
disputation.
</margin>
**B**y many steps now we have cast down the astrological business. We have declared that the fates of all lower things neither hang from heaven, nor are signified by it; nor, if they did depend on it, would they do so otherwise than through natural kinship. Both of these points were confirmed by the perpetual and stable condition of the celestial bodies, which, always equal to themselves and like themselves, do not change like a chameleon by the force of locations or distances. 

Next, because I denied that what the heaven might do or indicate could be understood by us; then because it is beyond our human weakness to know which those fatal hours might be, or in the celestial choir with whom the power of decreeing fate is placed. Certainly, whatever they have handed down on these matters wanders utterly from reason. For they have made "beginnings" of things which are not beginnings, while the true ones are omitted; and, either ignorant or negligent of the most powerful celestial factors, they use imaginary and fabulous causes in predicting, in which, just as there is no truth inherent, so there is no power to effect anything. 

After these things, it was thirdly declared that even if they stumbled upon nothing in these matters we discuss, not only has what was hoped for not happened, but rather it is revealed how impassable and untraversable by human footprint is the task they must accomplish: namely, that they investigate the initial hours and follow every state and position of the celestial houses they have invented at every single moment; we argued in the last book that neither of these can be known. But even if they had provided these things, it is so far from...

<meta>This page transitions from the technical disputes of various astronomers on the "directions" of stars to a more philosophical critique of the very foundations of astrology. It challenges the logical consistency of astrological "houses" and the "angles" of a horoscope, arguing that their definitions are physically and rationally baseless.</meta>

->BOOK NINE<-

...fulfilled their own duty: so that they have not yet even approached their own office. For that labor proper to the astrologer, once the <term>theme</term> <note>original: "themate"; referring to the casting of a horoscope or natal chart.</note> has already been established (which is the work of the <term>mathematician</term> <note>In this era, "mathematician" usually referred to those who calculated planetary positions, including astronomers and astrologers.</note>), is to investigate what the explored constellation may do. Among all things, this is the most difficult. If these things were granted to be consistent with reason, astrology would be a science; if by experiments, it would be an art; but if it is supported neither by reason nor by experiments, it is certainly neither an art nor a science, but rather a reckless and unstable deception: a most fabulous fiction of quacks. First, therefore, we shall strip from the astrologers the authority of reason, and then the reliability of experiment.

### Chapter II. The arguments of astrologers are empty and ridiculous.

**A** certain general doctrine concerning the stars was handed down by Aristotle, Plato, and the other philosophers who relied on reason, concerning their eternal substance, their circular motion, and other things of that kind. But they nowhere handed down the specific properties of the stars, nor did they indicate anything about them by way of reason which could be called a physical demonstration. Otherwise, regarding the corruptible things that we deal with and perceive most closely, and which we know most intimately, we only know their peculiar gifts by their outcomes and effects. <margin>The stars</margin> But as for the reasons the astrologers have devised to prove their dogmas, they are so far from reason that nothing more irrational can be imagined. For they are not only non-demonstrative, or even inferior to rhetorical <term>enthymemes</term> <note>A type of rhetorical argument or syllogism that is only partially stated, relying on common knowledge.</note>, but they are false, futile, conflicting, flawed, and ridiculous; by examining them, let us make each one clear in order.

### Chapter III. The double principle by which astrologers decide which house is stronger is false: and even if it were true, that which they want does not follow from it.

<margin>The order of the process.</margin>
**W**e shall begin with the reasons by which they prove the properties of places; though we have declared above that no properties exist and that the intervals between them cannot be known. We shall treat first the quantity of the power of these places. Second, the quality, declaring everywhere that the principles on which they lean are false; and yet, even if they were true, that which they want cannot be concluded from them. There is a kind of double discourse by which they define which star is stronger in which place, and which is weaker. One is that those places prevail which are connected to the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopo"; the Ascendant or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> by the affinity of radiation, whether it be a <term>trine</term> <note>original: "trigone"; an aspect of 120 degrees.</note>, a <term>square</term> <note>original: "q̃drãgulæ"; an aspect of 90 degrees.</note>, or a <term>sextile</term> <note>original: "sexãgulæ"; an aspect of 60 degrees.</note>. Conversely, those places are "sluggish" or "cast down" which are not so joined. The other principle is that the <term>cardines</term> <note>original: "cardines"; the four pivotal points of a chart: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note>, which they call "angles," are of primary importance; second are the places succeeding the angles; third are those which decline from them, which in Greek they call *apoklimata* <note>original: "αποκλιματα"; cadent houses.</note> and the barbarians call "falling." First, therefore, those principles are false; or if they are granted, most of the things they understand from them are repugnant both to each other and to these principles. 
<margin>Demonstration of the falsity of the principles.</margin>
The falsity of the principles is demonstrated thus: the efficacy of places cannot be referred to anything other than the relationship of a place above the <term>horizon</term> <note>original: "finitorẽ"; the line that separates the visible sky from the invisible earth.</note>, such that in that position any star is thought to be more effective in which, being placed above us, it acts more strongly. A philosopher, persuaded by natural reason, will immediately grant this. The astrologer is also forced to grant this, since that power of places is sought either from the nature of the space itself or from that relationship to us which we mentioned. It cannot be derived from the space alone, because there is no natural power in that space, as we showed above. Furthermore, if he should say this, the horoscope and the division of places would be the same in every region, provided that the determined parts of space had their own properties by which they affected the stars placed therein. Therefore, they would not vary according to the sky but would be the same for all. But this entirely contradicts astrology, which decrees that the same star placed in the same part of space is in the ascending sign for me, in the second place for others, in the twelfth for others, in the third for others, and in the eleventh for others, according to the different inclination of the sky. This inclination should not be considered if it were the nature of the space from which these properties followed, rather than its relationship to us; for by the slope of the sky, the space is not changed, yet the relationship is always becoming one thing and then another. But if a place is granted to be more effective in which a planet, being situated, acts more strongly upon us, those foundations concerning the angles and the horoscope immediately collapse. First, every place under the earth will be weaker than all those above the earth; neither the fifth nor the fourth house will be preferred to the twelfth or the eighth. Then, among those above the earth, whichever rises higher above the horizon will be judged more powerful; wherefore the twelfth will prevail over the first...

<summary>In this page, the author begins a rigorous logical assault on the foundations of astrology, arguing that the system of 'houses' and 'angles' is rationally inconsistent and physically impossible. He specifically critiques the idea that planetary power depends on a star's geometric relationship to the horizon or the observer's location.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's systematic dismantling of astrological theory, specifically targeting the inconsistencies among major authorities like Ptolemy, Masha'allah, and Ibn Ezra regarding the strength of the "houses" or locations in a birth chart.</meta>

->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

<margin>Eschenden</margin>
...let him be Eschenden, the astrologer and author of the work they call the *Summa Anglicana*, who believes more in an absolutely indissoluble reason than in the authority of all other astrologers. But Ptolemy also saw a reason which, having followed it in the first book of the *Apoteleſmata* <note>original: "apoteleſmaton"; referring to Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, he established that the strongest place of all is the Midheaven <note>The highest point in the sky at the time of birth.</note>, because the rays of planets placed there affect us most powerfully. 
<margin>The opinions of Masha'allah, Firmicus, and Abu Ma'shar on the primacy of the East.</margin>
He considered the eleventh house next in virtue for that same reason, but claimed those planets are weakest which lie between the West and the bottom of the earth <note>The *Imum Coeli*, or the lowest point of the chart.</note>. However, these points are rejected by other astrologers, the majority of whom place the East <note>The Ascendant or rising sign.</note> before all other locations—such as Masha'allah, Firmicus, and Abu Ma'shar—although Ibn Ezra agrees with Ptolemy. For this reason, he does not make all the <term>angles</term> <note>original: "cardines"; the four most powerful points in a chart: the East (Ascendant), West (Descendant), Midheaven, and Nadir.</note> equal in priority, but prefers the eleventh place to all others except the highest point. Finally, if they maintain these sayings, he makes a planet in the fifth house weakest when it is midway between the fourth and seventh houses. 
<margin>Ptolemy and Ibn Ezra disagree.</margin>
Also, in his book concerning the span of years, while speaking of how everything above the earth is preferred to those below the earth, he forgot what he said earlier and placed the East ahead of the eleventh house. 

Then, following the astrologers, he rejects the twelfth house for a surely futile and false reason: because, he says, a thicker and darker vapor of the earth, exhaling from moistures, disturbs and weakens their descending power. Certainly, if this reason holds, anyone born in foggy weather would always be born unhappy, as all the planets for them would be under darkness, just as if they were placed in the twelfth house. Furthermore, why should a star placed in the East not suffer this more? Or has the present exhalation, once light has been created above, which could lift the vaporous fumes, not yet been able to dissipate them? Truly, this might proceed in the case of the Sun; but at noon, what star residing in the twelfth house will be hindered by vaporous air? 

Therefore, it was more correct that in his first book he only considered that the Midheaven would be the most powerful among other places, being more or less intense depending on whether it was closer or further from the summit. This is the only thing that can be said naturally, if we weigh only the efficacy of natural forces. For perhaps a place in the West might have a property of some influence that the Midheaven does not have (if there are indeed such differences). But as for what a planet is going to do, what else will cause it to act strongly except the power of diffusing its rays toward the observer? 

It is therefore too foolish that a fixed star in the fourth house—that is, hiding beneath the bottom of the earth—should be considered powerful, yet if it were shining in the evening sky but not quite touching the "angle" of the chart, it would have no strength at all. No one will ever be persuaded that a planet in the twelfth house is not "vital" while one in the fifth is, when it is far more reasonable to call the fifth house a seat of darkness than the twelfth. No one will be convinced that we are affected more strongly by the Sun when it is still twenty-five degrees away from the East than when, having slipped by a single degree, it is merged into the setting—even though in the latter case it belongs to the Ascendant, and in the former to the sixth house. Much less will they persuade anyone, unless they lack all sense, that a planet is more powerful in the fourth house (that is, in the middle of the night) than if it occupied the eighth or twelfth house. 

For the <term>trine</term> <note>An aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart, usually considered harmonious.</note> connection with the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoiſcopo"; here used technically to mean the Ascendant degree.</note> is rejected based on what we said above regarding the intervals of rays. If we wish to follow straight reason, the <term>anaphora</term> <note>The "rising" or "following" house; here referring to the house immediately following the Ascendant.</note> relates more to the horoscope than "Good Fortune" <note>A traditional name for the 11th house.</note> which is distant by so many spaces. If such a connection has weight, 
<margin>A second demonstration of the disagreement between principles and decrees.</margin>
why will the house not be more powerful when joined to a better angle? However, with reason teaching it and various astrologers supporting it, the highest angle is better than all others. Therefore, the sixth house, which is in a triangular relationship to it, ought to be counted among the good ones; by the same logic, the ninth house should be favored for its affinity with the Ascendant. 

Thus far we have seen how the decrees disagree with the false principles. For the eighth house is not always "evil" simply because it is disconnected from the Ascendant, since a planet located there often supports the East with a trine ray. Similarly, a <term>sextile</term> <note>An aspect of 60 degrees.</note> radiation sometimes comes to the horoscope from the second house. Therefore, what they conclude is by no means a universal rule...

They likewise promise that since the affinity of the ascendant and the <term>angle</term> <note>The four most powerful points in a chart: East, West, Midheaven, and Nadir.</note> makes a good location, one privilege should suffice; or is there a need for both? ## Chapter IV. The arguments of the astrologers by which they strengthen their dogmas are reduced to about five kinds; which are indeed weak and ineffective.

<margin>The arrangement of the refutation of the Astrologers, and where it is resolved.</margin>
<margin>The first kind of reasoning.</margin>
**L**et us now examine the errors by which they prove the properties of the "places" <note>In astrology, "places" refer to the twelve houses of the birth chart, each governing a different area of life.</note>: how this one signifies brothers, another parents, another friends, this one death, and another enemies. But lest I frequently repeat the same criticisms, I shall first refute certain types of argumentation which astrologers use to prove whatever they wish. Then, overturning the foundations of each dogma piece by piece, we will merely point out from which already-censured category the argument is drawn; this will be done in the appropriate places so that, once the principles and the form of reasoning are granted, we may show that what they believe does not actually follow. There are generally five heads to which you may reduce every astrological proof. The first kind can be called "from the order of numbers"; the second "from parabolic similarity"; the third "from mathematical principles"; the fourth "from astrological principles"; and the fifth "from dialectic." They argue from the "order of numbers" in this way: The first climate is subject to Saturn, the second to Jupiter, the third to Mars; because Saturn is the first planet, Jupiter the second, and Mars the third. There are twelve locations and twelve signs. Therefore, the first sign corresponds to the first location, the second to the second, and so on. 
<margin>The second kind.</margin>
Since the third sign is of the **Gemini** <note>The Twins.</note>, the third location signifies brothers, as if they were twins. Similarly, the first planet corresponds to the first location, the second to the second, and the third to the third. But Jupiter, the second star, signifies riches; therefore, there was a signification over riches in the second location. This method derived from numbers is easily refuted. Indeed, if the conversation were with philosophers or logicians, it not only fails to compel, but it doesn't even persuade or suggest anything. First, it is a futile and quite insane supposition that the first of one genus should harmonize with the first of another genus by some kinship of nature. Fire is the first element, and Saturn the first of the planets; yet what is more different from fire, according to the astrologers themselves, than Saturn? Mars is the third of the planets, and water the third element; does not Mars differ from water as much as fire differs from water? Aries is the first sign, and Saturn the first planet; yet astrologers do not give Aries a proportion with Saturn—he does not reign in it, nor rule it, but rather is "depressed" <note>A planet in its "fall" or "depression" is considered weak and poorly placed.</note> there. Thus, the supposition is deceptive, crude, and unskilled. Even if it were true, it would be no less uncertain: not so much because it is uncertain whether one should ascend from the Moon toward Saturn, or rather descend from Saturn to the Moon, since by its own reasoning, any planet could be "first" in order, while the positions and order of the middle planets are entirely ambiguous. 
<margin>The question of the Sun: whether grave authors define it as the middle or secondary. The Summary.</margin>
For the ancient dispute still remains under the judge’s consideration: whether the Sun is second or rather the middle. It was believed by the Egyptians to be closest to the Moon, but placed in the middle by the Chaldeans. Ptolemy and the crowd of more recent writers also think it is in the middle. However, not only Geber <note>original: "Ieber"; likely Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century Andalusian astronomer who critiqued Ptolemy.</note>, a most sharp mathematician, but even Theon <note>Theon of Alexandria, a 4th-century commentator on Ptolemy.</note> himself, the Greek interpreter of Ptolemy, disagreeing with his master, thinks it should be placed immediately above the Moon. Plato and Aristotle also affirmed this. It is no wonder that the greatest authors disagree on this matter; since many arguments are brought forth on both sides, no certain one can be conceived. For once you remove the "parallaxes"—that is, the differences in vision—mathematics indicates nothing about which of two stars is higher. This is not only debated regarding the Sun, but also Venus and Mercury; for although the *Summary* <note>Referring to the *Summa Anglicana* by Richard Eschenden, mentioned on the previous page.</note> says it is established that Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are all above the Sun, yet in what order is neither known nor can it be known. For there is much "difference of aspect" (as they say), and whatever reasons you construct will be vain and dialectical, not certain and mathematical.

<summary>Pico criticizes the "order of numbers" argument in astrology, pointing out that assigning planetary influences based on numerical sequence is arbitrary and mathematically unproven. He highlights long-standing astronomical disputes over the physical order of the planets, specifically the position of the Sun relative to Venus and Mercury.</summary>

<header>DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY</header>

<margin>
Ptolemy's reasoning is frivolous and Alpetragius's is weak.
</margin>
Thematic reasoning. Such is that of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> concerning the sun, which he places conveniently in the middle of the planets because certain ones are removed from it by a great distance—as are Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—while others always follow it, such as Venus and Mercury. This is a frivolous and unproductive conjecture, because the Moon departs from the sun as much as the "superior" <note>Planets further from the Earth than the Sun: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> planets do; therefore, the sun is not truly "in the middle" between those that depart from it and those that do not. The reasoning of Alpetragius <note>Al-Bitruji, a 12th-century astronomer from Al-Andalus who proposed an alternative to the Ptolemaic system.</note> is equally weak, suggesting that the lower planets are faster. Although those who are seen to be faster he proves to be slower. In this way, the position of Venus, the Sun, and Mercury would be higher than the other places; because they do not all resist equally, he seems to strive more for the evidence of the reasoning of the ancients who decreed the Sun was closest to the Moon, because the sun is never snatched from our sight by the intervention of Venus or Mercury <note>Pico is discussing why Venus and Mercury don't seem to cause solar eclipses like the Moon does.</note>. But this is also solved in many ways: what happens with Mercury may be due to its smallness; what happens with Venus may be because it is occupied and intercepted by the sun’s rays due to its proximity. Therefore, it cannot block the path of the rays descending to us as the more remote Moon can. Furthermore, perhaps being thin and lacking the earthy density of the Moon, they do not block the rays. Likewise, they may have their own light which they return in place of the snatched solar light; they do not take away the light but exchange it, which is why a defect <note>An eclipse or "transit."</note> is not perceived. Averroes <note>The famous 12th-century Islamic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> in his paraphrase of the *Great Composition* <note>The *Almagest* of Ptolemy.</note> says that he once noted two blackish spots on the Sun, and when he had calculated the numbers, at that time Mercury was found to be positioned opposite the rays of the Sun.

<margin>
See the Great Note of Averroes.
</margin>
<margin>
Moses the Egyptian
</margin>
Rightly, therefore, Moses the Egyptian <note>The Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204).</note>, also by the testimony of Abubacer <note>Ibn Tufail, a Moorish philosopher and physician.</note>, pronounced the position and order of the planets to be uncertain. For we know indeed that the Moon is the lowest of all and the "vestibule of heaven" on account of its greater <term>parallax</term> <note>The displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight; a larger parallax indicates a closer object.</note>, which necessarily indicates a smaller relationship of the earth's radius to the sphere's radius. But how the other three—the Sun, Venus, and Mercury—relate to each other is uncertain. Similarly, it is known that these four stars are closer to us than the other three, but reason does not demonstrate the position and order of those three among themselves. Therefore, when the <term>genethliaci</term> <note>Casters of birth horoscopes.</note> strive to find a principle of consequence for an order of this kind, they strive first upon something false, and then, even if it were true, upon something uncertain. One might object to the same regarding the "signs" <note>The signs of the Zodiac.</note> when (as we have sufficiently demonstrated) there are either no starting points in the zodiac, or four equal ones.

<margin>
The second kind.
</margin>
Having spoken of the first kind of argumentation, he proves the following from a "parabolic similarity" <note>An argument based on metaphor or analogy rather than physical or logical proof.</note>: the tenth "place" <note>The 10th House, the Midheaven.</note> lies open at the high summit of heaven; the fourth lies hidden at the bottom of the earth. Since, therefore, more is known to everyone about their mother than about their father, it is fitting that the mother be judged through the tenth place, and the father through the fourth. This method is to be refuted by nothing other than its own title <note>i.e., its own absurdity.</note>.

<margin>
The third kind.
</margin>
For whatever arguments seek similarities from these things are not only unworthy of those who teach, but are neither fit for logicians nor useful for those who dispute; indeed, they are not even convenient for the persuasions of a rhetorician. They offer the play of vain poetry rather than the suitable authority of any serious proof. I said they argue from mathematical principles when they wrongly turn the decrees of mathematicians toward their own predictions, such as what I said above regarding the division of the zodiac into signs, signs into parts, and parts into minutes.

<margin>
The fourth kind.
</margin>
<margin>
The fifth kind.
</margin>
Likewise, because certain signs are called "straight" and others "oblique" <note>Based on the time they take to rise over the horizon (ascension).</note> due to the unequal delays in their rising, they transfer this to a nature of "straightness" or "obliquity" in human morals. They gather from astrological matters whenever they make some astrological dogma the principle for confirming another dogma. They use the methods of logicians if they ever assume certain common and probable propositions from nature or first philosophy—but that is very rare. For I do not remember reading any reasoning among them that brought the credibility of logical probability.

### Chapter V. Arguments derived from parabolic similarity, by which they prove the properties of the houses, are refuted.

We have said these things in general; now let us descend to recounting the fables in detail (for I would more truly call them that than "arguments") by which they have asserted the properties of the "places," beginning with those they take from the position and conditions of the signs. It is, however,

<header>BOOK TEN</header>

# BOOK TEN

The argument from metaphorical similarity works in this way: a father loves his sons. And since the fifth house is joined by a friendly ray—because it forms a triangle <term>trine</term> <note>A trine is an aspect of 120 degrees, considered the most harmonious and beneficial connection between two points in a horoscope.</note> with the ascendant—the fifth house therefore signifies children. To show that this method of arguing, while clearly ridiculous, is also poorly constructed, let us demonstrate that their conclusions do not follow correctly.

The first house, they say, signifies the newborn himself because he emerges from darkness into light. Likewise, the ascendant is used as a metaphorical similarity to explain why the same house represents short journeys: such as when one goes from one neighborhood of the same city to another, from the city to the suburb, or from a house to the boundary line. For they wish the cause of these movements to be in the stars, which the arrangement of the first house portends, as Bonatti says.
<margin>Bonatti <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), one of the most famous Italian astrologers of the 13th century.</note></margin>

Furthermore, let us see if this similarity holds in the remaining houses. The property of the second house concerns wealth, because they say nothing is more "neighboring" or "next" to a man than his possessions. Therefore, the second house, clinging to the first, will signify riches. A "necessary" reason, indeed, for those who value nothing more than wealth! Yet many things are more neighboring and intimate to a person: the gifts of the mind and body, wisdom, and health. Why then should these not be signified by the second house rather than by the sixth or ninth? Moreover, external things like a wife, friends, children, glory, and money are often preferred as more important or "closer"—except among that single race of men who call themselves astrologers. This same house also denotes letters/correspondence, as Zael the Israelite says, unless perhaps it is noted in the horoscopes of notaries, to whom the pen and writing tablets are always clinging.
<margin>Zael the Israelite <note>Sahl ibn Bishr (c. 786–845), a Jewish Persian astrologer and mathematician whose works were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note></margin>

Now let us proceed to the rest. They want brothers to be indicated by the third house, and as we said, sons by the fifth. The reason why sons are treated similarly to brothers is that the third house is joined to the ascendant by a hexagonal <term>sextile</term> <note>An aspect of 60 degrees, also considered harmonious but less powerful than a trine.</note> ray. Since a hexagonal connection is friendly, but a triangular one is better, the trine is given to children (whom we love more) and the sextile to brothers. For the same reason, the eleventh house is for friends, as the ascendant regards it likewise with a sextile. But I ask them: why should the ninth house not signify children, since it also forms a triangle with the ascendant? They will answer because it "falls" <note>In astrology, houses are classified as Angular (strong), Succedent (medium), or Cadent (weak/falling). The 9th house is a cadent house.</note>. I ask then: which is better, the third or the eleventh? A father would say the eleventh is preferable, because the third "falls." Why then was the third house not for friends and the eleventh for brothers, unless they think the order of nature is inverted and friends should be preferred to brothers?

The matter of children is further disturbed by another claim: for they say parents are to be judged by the fourth house. But between the fourth and the ascendant there is a square <term>tetragon</term> <note>A 90-degree aspect, traditionally considered tense, difficult, or hostile.</note> aspect, which is the ultimate judge of enmity. How then can they connect the newborn and the newborn’s children with a friendly ray, yet connect the same child with his own parents with a hostile one?

Furthermore, Ptolemy, all the Greeks, and Averroes <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd, known in Latin as Auenroda.</note> prefer that children be judged from the tenth house rather than the fifth. Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> approves of this as correct because from there souls are sent down into bodies.
<margin>Ptolemy, Averroes, Porphyry</margin>
<margin>The descent and ascent of souls.</margin>

But we can oppose Porphyry's fable with another fable: because they claim souls slide downward through Cancer and ascend through Capricorn. Cancer, however, is a northern sign, which in Ptolemy's system corresponds to the "bottom of the sky" <note>The Imum Coeli, the lowest point of the chart, associated with the 4th house.</note> rather than the top. Yet they begin predictions about children from both the fourth and eleventh houses. What of the fact that Al-Qabisi <note>Known in Latin as Alchabitius, a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and the Hebrew Andragazar want ambassadors to belong to the fifth house? And they add what Vettius Valens says about rumors, news, and posthumous fame. Adla adds that clothing is signified there. By what reasoning? They give none.
<margin>Al-Qabisi, Andragazar, Vettius, Adla</margin>

It is truly irrational that they attribute the sixth house—which they call *aprokton* <note>original: "$\omega \pi \rho \omega \kappa \tau o \nu$" (aprokton), meaning "unfruitful" or "not acting."</note>, as if you were to say torpid, ceasing, lazy, and ineffective—to servants, whose labor and industry nevertheless nourish the leisure and laziness of their masters.
<margin>*aprokton*</margin>

But see the "most beautiful" reason Averroes makes for this dogma. "The first house," he says, "signifies equals; but subjects are elegantly distant from equals" (his own words) "just as much as the sixth house is distant from the seventh." Therefore, they placed the sixth as the house of subjects. This is to be laughed at rather than refuted, lest we be too heavily rebuked by Aristotle. For regarding what they say of the seventh house—that "equals" are signified—see how they themselves think it is least truthful and least consistent. For they refer to the same house the wife, partners, and open enemies. What is there between...
<margin>Mockery of Averroes' position</margin>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer whose "Book of Reasons" Pico frequently critiques.</note></margin> Abraham, however, defends the seventh house in this way: since the seventh house is opposite the first, it signifies lawsuits and wars. Then again, because it descends while the <term>horoscopus</term> <note>The "horoscopus" or ascendant is the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> is rising, it signifies the wife. Finally, since the time of its descent is equal to the time of the first house’s ascent, it possesses some kind of "suitability"; therefore, it signifies equals and partners. In this way, anything can be easily "proven," since there is nothing so unique that a similarity or dissimilarity to something else cannot be fabricated for the sake of an argument. For where does this logic *not* succeed, if they can assign meanings based on opposite things just as easily as they do for similar things? 

But they agree, he says, by this reasoning: that the time of emerging in the ascendant and falling in the descendant are equal. I admit that is well said—if you also concede, by the same example, that water is similar to fire because water possesses as many degrees of coldness as fire has degrees of heat. For I think that descent and ascent are perhaps just as opposed (to speak as precisely as possible) as heat and cold. 

Would it not be more certain that the wife belongs to the second house? She is always closest to the man, succeeding him as a near-equal and "second"—especially since they even want one of the signs to be male and the other female, because, as <margin>Ptolemy, Vettius <note>Vettius Valens, a 2nd-century Greek astrologer.</note></margin> Ptolemy says, women are attached to men. 

Furthermore, let them give a reason why the same house signifies thieves and fugitives (as Vettius pleases), as well as buying and selling, and—as others teach—moderately long journeys. Then there is what <margin>Bonatti, Ibn Ezra <note>Guido Bonatti (13th century) and Abraham Ibn Ezra.</note></margin> Bonatti writes: that it signifies the worship of pure divinity and the foreknowledge of the future. Certainly, death ought to have been assigned to this place more rightly than to the eighth house, since here one descends from light into darkness, just as in the ascendant one goes from darkness into light. 

But Ibn Ezra says this was not pleasing because the seventh is not entirely unlike the ascendant; namely, by that same kind of "similarity" by which we just proved water is like fire. Yet <margin>Dorotheus <note>Dorotheus of Sidon (1st century AD), author of an influential poem on astrology.</note></margin> Dorotheus also used to judge death from this house rather than the eighth, by observing the lord of the house for that purpose. 

Likewise, let them answer why the eighth house signifies wars according to <margin>Abu 'Ali, Al-Khayyat <note>Abu 'Ali al-Khayyat (c. 770–835), a student of Mashallah and a major source for medieval astrology.</note></margin> Abu 'Ali, while Al-Khayyat writes it signifies <term>stewardship</term> <note>The management of a country estate or villa.</note>. Others want it to signify usury, and they say inheritances are also foreseen here. I do not see how an heir and a dead man are "suitable" to one another. Therefore, it would be better if the eighth house judged death and the ninth house—which follows the eighth—signified inheritance. 

But <margin>Ibn Ezra</margin> Ibn Ezra says inheritances are related to the eighth house because it corresponds proportionally to the second house, which governs wealth. Truly, this is that "harmony of opposites" that has been mocked so often. For what similarity will there be between opposite houses except for their dissimilarity? If they always spoke of them as similar, the error might perhaps be forgiven; but now they use them sometimes as similar, and sometimes as most dissimilar and truly opposite—whenever it helps their case. 

Thus, houses are taken as "contrary" when the second and fifth portend that we are nourished and life is preserved, while the eighth signifies death and exile. Yet soon, that same eighth house signifies inheritances and wealth, as if it were similar and related to the second! Surely those who die make heirs; they do not *become* heirs (unless perhaps "heirs of heaven," which certainly is not subject to the sky). 

<margin>Well said!</margin> Other objections should be raised, but I fear that by refuting trifles, I may become a trifler myself. However, what they say about the ninth house cannot be omitted, as it offers the reader so much to laugh at that it might relieve the boredom of this long-windedness. The ninth house, they say, signifies long journeys. Hear the reason: because the sun, placed in the tenth house, moves by descending toward the ninth. <margin>Ibn Ezra</margin> Ibn Ezra wrote this in the first and second <note>original: "lib. rationum"</note> *Book of Reasons*—a work that requires cackling laughter rather than logical syllogisms. As if the sun, passing from one house to another in every single location, were not always moving! 

What if, because the sun "descends" with that motion, the ninth house should therefore signify journeys where we *climb* mountains and high places? Who would not joke when arguing with such ridiculous people? Add to this that story about the twelfth house: they say animals used for transport are signified by it because it is joined to the ascendant whenever the same sign stretches across both houses. Elsewhere, however, they say darkness and prisons are portended by the same house because it is as far as possible from the ascendant (from which, indeed, it is the twelfth). Thus, remembering neither themselves nor the truth, they measure things

->in whatever way<-

<summary>Pico mocks the contradictory logic used by astrologers to assign meanings to the "houses," such as the sun's movement supposedly making the ninth house represent travel. He argues their system is so inconsistent that any house could be made to mean anything through arbitrary metaphors of "similarity" or "opposition."</summary>

...in whatever things. But if they say that place is joined to the ascendant only when the same sign occupies both positions, and is "disjoined" when the signs are different, it follows that neither the "other soul" by which we are carried, nor prisons, will always be indicated by that place. In fact, that place would never signify the soul and the prisons at the same time; rather, it would signify the soul only when the sign is the same in both, and the prisons only when the signs are different—a distinction that no astrologer actually makes.

### Chapter VI Refutation of the arguments of Ibn Ezra <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a Spanish-Jewish polymath and astrologer whom Pico refers to as "Auenrodan."</note> concerning the properties of the houses, which are derived from the order and sequence of the signs.

<margin>Ibn Ezra</margin>
**T**hese are arguments drawn from the location and condition of the places by a kind of metaphorical similarity. Ibn Ezra, in the first book of his *Apotelesmatics* <note>original: "apotelesmaton"; a term for the study of the effects of the stars on human affairs.</note>, argues from the order and sequence of the signs: that the first sign corresponds to the first house, the second to the second, and that the nature of the house should be judged according to the nature of the lord of that corresponding sign. Thus, through the third house, brothers and short journeys are judged, because Gemini is the third sign, and its lord is Mercury. Likewise, he says that Mercury has influence over "mixed things," which is why he signifies brothers; and he always clings closely to the path of the Sun, which is why short journeys pertain to him. 

<margin>Refutation from the greater premise</margin>
But no other astrologer, nor even Ptolemy (whom Ibn Ezra follows), makes Mercury the significator of brothers. Nor is there any reason why he should preside over short journeys just because he "imitates the course of the Sun." For if he does this because he revolves with a swift motion, this would pertain no more to Mercury than to the Sun or Venus, since the courses of all of them are roughly equal. 

Let us come to the fourth house, to which Cancer corresponds. He says it signifies the father, because the Sun presides over fathers, and the power of the Sun appears most strongly in Cancer <note>Cancer is the sign of the summer solstice in the northern hemisphere, where the Sun reaches its highest point.</note>. See what vain and frivolous conjectures they seize upon! For while in other cases a house always uses its own "lord" <note>In astrology, every zodiac sign has a "ruling planet" or lord.</note>, here he flees to one who has no authority in that sign. For the Sun in Cancer has neither kingdom, nor hospitality, nor triplicity, nor decan <note>These are "essential dignities," various ways a planet is said to have strength or rights in a specific sign.</note>. Because neither the mistress of the house, the Moon, nor the king of the sign, Jupiter, served the meaning of "fathers," he turned to the Sun—simply because the Sun, being positioned in Cancer, is at its hottest. As we have often said, this happens not from the nature of the sign, but from the Sun's physical relationship to the Earth. Otherwise, if we follow the principles of the astrologers, what kinship does the Sun have with a sign that is moist, cold, and feminine? In that sign, as we noted a moment ago, the Sun holds no prerogative of any dignity. 

Furthermore, since Saturn rules in that same place—as Ibn Ezra says in the same passage—how will the Sun also rule? They consider the natures of these two planets to be opposite, and they even make their houses and kingdoms opposites. Or how is it consistent with what he says there, that the nature of Saturn corresponds to that place? For that reason, the house is extended to cover inheritances and hidden things; yet the sign of Cancer (fitting the fourth house) is a place where Saturn suffers "exile," far from his own home.

Regarding the eighth and ninth houses, he invents no less false and contradictory things. Scorpio, he says, is the eighth sign, whose lord is Mars, because it signifies death. Yet it is not the kind of death Mars produces according to astrologers, but rather the kind Saturn produces. For, as they say, it signifies poisons, sluggishness, and idleness, as Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboafar"; a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> says. 

<margin>Abu Ma'shar</margin>
<margin>lazy/idle <note>original: "αργοσ" (argos)</note></margin> 
For this reason, it is even called *argos* <note>Greek for lazy or slow.</note> by the Greeks, which least of all suits the nature of Mars. 

The ninth house refers to Jupiter; therefore, the ninth sign is Sagittarius, because he is the lord of religions, a judge, and wisdom, according to the nature of Jupiter. But why, by the same reasoning, is the twelfth house (to which Pisces corresponds) not also a "house of Jupiter" just like Sagittarius? Even if the house of Sagittarius is more pleasing to Jupiter, if this theory is true—that the nature of the planet ruling the corresponding sign should match the nature of the house—

<margin>
Ibn Ezra 
recognized 
the weakness 
of this 
doctrine.
</margin>
then the twelfth house ought not to be the most miserable of all, given that the sign ascribed to it is the home of the most fortunate of all planets <note>Jupiter is traditionally called the "Greater Benefic" or most lucky planet.</note>. Ibn Ezra himself sufficiently confirms the weakness of this method; when he saw that it did not work for all of them, he used it for only five houses, and for the rest, he fled to the arguments we refuted in the previous chapter. We, however, have shown that his thinking is not to be followed even in those five.

<summary>Pico critiques the inconsistency of Ibn Ezra's system, which attempts to link the twelve astrological houses to the twelve zodiac signs in order. He points out that this logic is applied selectively and results in contradictions, such as the lucky planet Jupiter being associated with the traditionally "miserable" twelfth house.</summary>

### Chapter VII Against the justifications for these same properties which Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboafar"; the Latinized name for Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi (787–886), one of the most influential medieval Persian astrologers.</note> derives from the order of the planets.

<margin>Inconsistency from Abu Ma'shar’s doctrine</margin>
**A**bu Ma'shar gathers these properties of locations <note>i.e., the "houses" or "places" of the horoscope.</note> from the sequence of the planets: so that the first is given to the first, the second to the second, and the third to the third. He decrees that the property of the house is determined by the property of the planet of the corresponding number. But a most heavy absurdity immediately arises: that the same planet is assigned to places that are diametrically opposed. To Saturn, the first and the eighth; to Jupiter, the ninth and the second; to Venus, the fifth and the twelfth. For the first house is the place of life, while the eighth is the place of death; how, therefore, can Saturn preside over both the first and the eighth? For after the seven locations have been run through according to the number of the seven planets, they return to the first; thus Saturn falls into the eighth, which everyone admits. Likewise, the ninth house is the indicator of faith, wisdom, and religion, while the second is the indicator of riches; but God and Mammon <note>original: "mamona"; a biblical reference to the incompatibility of spiritual devotion and the pursuit of wealth (Matthew 6:24).</note> do not agree. Add to this that <margin>Abu Ma'shar.</margin> in other places Abu Ma'shar says that Jupiter signifies the happiness of the future world—which is acquired through faith and wisdom—while Venus signifies the happiness of *this* world. Therefore, since riches belong to the happiness of this world and not the one to come, they should be signified by Venus rather than Jupiter. Nor should they be referred to the second house, which falls to Jupiter by number, but to the fifth, which is given to Venus. This is especially true since they themselves are accustomed to saying that the houses of Jupiter and Mercury are opposites, because the wisdom of which Mercury is the author is opposed to the dignities and riches of Jupiter. From this, they sometimes repel the slander by which they are frequently attacked: namely, that although they are the masters of almost all nature through their foreknowledge of the future and their derivation of celestial virtues, they nevertheless usually remain poor and obscure. They claim it is the fate of the wise not to grow rich, because Jupiter is opposed to Mercury. How, then, can they now make Jupiter the author of wisdom as well as of riches? 

But in the case of Venus, the absurdity is even more evident. Just as she falls into the fifth house, she likewise falls into the twelfth. The former is called the house of joy and pleasure; the <margin>Irony</margin> other the house of prisons, sorrow, and darkness. What could be more conflicting than these? Some have devised a most beautiful defense: for since repentance <note>original: "pœnitentia"; implying the regret or pain following worldly pleasure.</note> usually follows pleasures, they say both places are appropriate for Venus—that is, both joy and sorrow. I suppose they will defend it likewise this way: that since death follows life, both are signified by the same planet. <margin>Note</margin> Nor do I doubt that by the same reasoning they will say that war and peace pertain to Mars, because peace always follows war, just as serenity follows rain, and rain follows serenity. But—lest they think they must always grieve without any joy—let them grieve for once: I wish to remind them that sorrow is not the companion of *all* joy, but only of that which has been beyond measure and reason. However, they will not say these sorrows are signified by the fifth house if they follow their own principles; for they refer these things to the fifth because they help, nourish, and revive, just as the fifth house joins the ascendant <note>The "ascendant" is the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth, considered the primary indicator of the life of the newborn.</note> through which the life of the person being born is signified. Indeed, immoderate pleasure, which repentance and pain follow, is not the nourishment of life, but its ruin; but we speak too seriously in refuting trifles. 

Regarding Mars, let us see Abu Ma'shar’s reasoning. "And it signifies brothers," he says, "and sisters, because they are from the same parents." The reason for this dogma is this: because Saturn is assigned to the first house where the lord of the birth is judged, so Jupiter is assigned to the second, being the second planet. Mars is third, following the order of the spheres. But Mars and Saturn are of the same kind, because both are evil and harmful <term>malefic<gloss>Astrological term for planets like Saturn and Mars believed to have a naturally negative or destructive influence.</gloss></term>. Therefore, the third house will signify those who are of the same kind as the one being born; hence, brothers and sisters. Abu Ma'shar <margin>Accusation of Abu Ma'shar</margin> does not know that if he did not write these things while drunk, he certainly wrote them while insane. For what planets are more dissimilar than Mars and Saturn? One is fire, the other earth; one rages with heat, the other is numb with cold; one is nocturnal, the other diurnal. If you run through them all, you will find no influence of Mars that agrees with the influences of Saturn. Furthermore, since children are also similar to their parents, they should not have [remained distinct]...

<summary>Pico critiques the astrologer Abu Ma'shar for arbitrarily linking the twelve houses of the horoscope to the seven planets in a repeating sequence, leading to logical contradictions where the same planet signifies both life and death, or joy and imprisonment.</summary>

<header>BOOK TEN</header>

...should have been signified by the fifth house, to which Venus is assigned. Or, one would have to say that Saturn also agrees with Venus. We have recounted the reasons of the astrologers by which they attempt to prove the properties of these locations; perhaps it should be argued that we have examined them too diligently rather than too little. Truly, we have assessed them as being guided by a certain thin thread of similarity; but although they can be refuted with no effort, they nevertheless possess an authority derived from the tradition of the ancients and the testimony of writers, which should be refuted rather than ignored.

## Chapter VIII. The joys of the planets fall along with the houses.

From this, everything concerning the **joys of the planets** <note>The "Joys" (Latin: *gaudia*) are specific houses where a planet was thought to be particularly well-placed or "happy" because the house's purpose matched the planet's nature.</note> is overturned, since they are designated by the properties of the locations. For they want each planet to "rejoice" in that place whose property is similar to the property of the planet. Thus, they place Venus in the fifth house because Venus signifies joys, children, and pleasures, just as the fifth house does. They apply the same reasoning to the others in other places, as can be understood from the third book of **Ibn Ezra’s** <note>original: "Auenazræ"; Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> *Book of Reasons* and from **Abu Ma'shar’s** <note>original: "Aboafaris"; Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi.</note> *Introductory Treatise*. Yet, if we were to follow this intention, the third or sixth house would suit **Mercury** better than the Ascendant; the Ascendant or the Descendant would suit the **Moon** better than the third; the tenth house would suit the **Sun** better than the ninth; the ninth and the second would suit **Jupiter** rather than the eleventh; the seventh house would suit **Mars** better than the sixth; and the fourth would suit **Saturn** better than the twelfth. Anyone comparing the "gifts" of the locations with the conditions of the planets will be able to notice this.

<margin>Abenzagel.</margin> **Abenzagel** <note>Probably referring to Ibn Zarqal (Azarquiel), an 11th-century Andalusian astronomer/astrologer.</note> says that some parts of any sign are hot and dry, others cold and moist, others cold and dry, others hot and moist, and others middling or mixed; therefore, any planet is invigorated by the parts that match its own nature. He says that the middling or mixed parts suit Mercury. Truly, **Ptolemy** and others—who maintain that Venus is hot and moist—would not accept this reasoning, for then the cold and moist parts would suit no planet at all. Furthermore, since Mars possesses only five parts <note>referring to "terms" or "bounds," which are sub-divisions of a zodiac sign.</note> in Aries, if Abenzagel is correct, there will be only five hot and dry parts in Aries; the remaining parts would be of another condition and different from the nature of the sign, insofar as the nature is determined to be hot and dry. Similarly, there would be many more "airy" parts in Taurus than "earthy" ones, and so it would happen in others. Therefore, Abenzagel's reasoning is fallacious; even if it were true, it does not explain our question, because it remains uncertain which parts are hot and which are cold, as it is not certain which should belong to which planet.

## Chapter IX. Ptolemy's reasons regarding the houses of the planets are destroyed.

Now we must deal with the signs. Indeed, we have already overturned many of their reasons regarding these, such as those by which they prove there are twelve signs—neither more nor less. Nevertheless, we must address why the beginning of the signs is established at **Aries**; furthermore, that division into water, earth, fire, and air; and why this sign is the <term>exaltation</term> <note>A specific sign where a planet’s influence is said to be most powerful, distinct from its "home" sign.</note> or <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three signs belonging to the same element.</note> of one planet and that of another. Other matters remain, of which we shall now speak, beginning with the **houses of the planets**. Even if it were granted that planets have an affinity with different signs—such that a planet placed under one sign is weakened and under another becomes stronger—we still cannot follow the distinctions of these signs by any logic, because this cannot happen except through the nature of the stars and the sign, as we said above. But reason does not demonstrate the nature of the stars to us. Therefore, it does not demonstrate the affinity of signs with the stars; and if it is said that we follow the spaces of the heaven rather than the stars, it will be no less unprovable by logic than the hidden properties of the rest of the celestial realm.

<margin>Three reasons of Ptolemy regarding the houses.</margin> Ptolemy relies on only one reason regarding the houses of the Sun and Moon, but on a threefold reason for the houses of the rest. The **first** is taken from the nature of the signs. The **second** concerns the proportion of the configuration <note>i.e., the "aspects" or geometric angles between the signs.</note> to the houses of the <term>luminaries</term> <note>The Sun and Moon.</note>. The **third** concerns the sequence and number of the spheres. Let us first examine the first. It is of this sort: **Capricorn** and **Aquarius** are winter signs because they are cold; the planet **Saturn** is also cold; therefore, they rightly suit him.

<margin>Ptolemy's reasoning errs in many ways.</margin> This argument, however, errs in many ways. But first, because one ought to look at what belongs to a sign by its own nature rather than what...
