# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

...by accident. However, coldness happens to coincide with those signs <note>Aquarius and Capricorn</note> only accidentally; therefore, they are considered cold only for the reason that the sun, when positioned in them, is the cause of cold by accident—namely, because it is moving at its furthest point from us. But when those signs are judged according to their own nature, the astrologers themselves define one as earthy <note>Capricorn</note> and the other as airy <note>Aquarius</note>. This quality of "air" fits Jupiter much better than Saturn, who is cold and dry and thus opposed to all the qualities of Aquarius. Furthermore, when astrologers associate different things with different stars, they are accustomed—if the stars are "malefic" <note>Evil-acting or harmful planets</note>—to give them things that differ from their nature rather than things that agree with them. This is done so that their "bad" nature might be tempered by a mixture of the opposite. In this way, they make Saturn a **diurnal** <term>Diurnal: A planet belonging to the day "sect," supposed to be tempered by the sun's heat.</term> planet and Mars a **nocturnal** planet. Yet, a cold night does not agree with the heat of Mars, nor does a hot day agree with the cold of Saturn. They claim this is done so that the harmful quality of each might be restrained: the fervor in Mars and the torpor in Saturn. Let them say, then, whether they wish to follow this same reasoning when assigning signs to "bad" planets, or rather the opposite? Indeed, <margin>Ptolemy</margin> Ptolemy seems to follow a contrary opinion here compared to the method he observed above in defining the nocturnal and diurnal planets. Truly, he may be permitted to hold different views in different places, provided he does not contradict himself within the same line of argument. But if he makes a sign a "house" because it is consonant with Saturn’s nature, then Aquarius is excluded <note>because Aquarius is airy/warm and Saturn is cold</note>. If he makes it the house because it is dissonant, then Capricorn is cast out. <margin>Response</margin> Ptolemy will say that he looks to those qualities of the signs which are owed to the works of the sun: both the sign of the Goat <note>Capricorn</note> and the Water-Bearer <note>Aquarius</note> are numbered among the cold signs, which accords with Saturn’s quality. We contend that this is done without reason, but let us admit it for a moment; even then, we can show that his conclusion does not follow. <margin>Confutation</margin> For he will perhaps answer this regarding Saturn, but it will not succeed for the other planets. For the houses of Venus are **Libra** and **Taurus**. Libra is an autumnal sign; therefore, it is dry and cold, just as Aquarius is a cold winter sign. Therefore, Libra is repugnant to Venus, who is defined by most as hot and by all as moist. Nor am I slightly amazed at Ptolemy, who said these signs suit Venus because they are

of a sort that you might call generative and especially fruitful. For while this can be said of **Taurus**, it can in no way be said of **Libra** <note>Libra, as an autumn sign, marks the beginning of the "death" of the year's growth</note>. In what way does the reasoning square for Jupiter? He has no commonality with **Pisces** and **Sagittarius**. If the season of the year is reckoned under those signs, one finishes the winter and the other is the end of autumn. Therefore, the former will be repugnant to Jupiter because of its coldness, and the latter because of its dryness; moreover, the watery moisture of Pisces does not suit the vital humor of Jupiter. <margin>Ptolemy</margin> Ptolemy refers himself to this "concord": that both of those signs create winds and also possess a "genital power," which is why the temperate planet Jupiter harmonizes with them. While I refute these things, I would think I was performing a superfluous task, had these things not been produced by Ptolemy, whose authority can easily impose itself upon the unlearned. Otherwise, things like these—which literate men sometimes say in jest while playing among themselves—"arouse the winds." Therefore, they say they are "similar to Jupiter." <margin>Averroes</margin> **Averroes** <note>original: "Auẽrodã"; refers to the 12th-century philosopher Ibn Rushd</note> gives the reason: because Jupiter presides over the generation and seeds of living things, whose vapors and breath are somewhat similar to winds. <margin>On the delirious minds of the astrologers.</margin> Oh, what marvelous wisdom, by which even dry things can be defended as similar to moist ones! For all philosophers (unless I am mistaken) make the winds dry, contrary to all moist generation. But they also call these "fruitful signs" because, when the Sun is placed in them, seeds germinate and things arise. Oh, if only this could have been applied to human seed! It would have fallen much more conveniently to them from **Aries**. But they could not give Aries to Jupiter because Mars had already occupied it—though entirely by injustice. For what does Mars have to do with the first of spring? His heat and parched dryness share nothing with the "genital humor" and prolific nature of that season. Audacity also invaded through **Scorpio** without any right; for it is a cold and autumnal sign. Therefore, if we follow reason, this partition of the houses will not be sufficiently fair. Let us examine the other assignments taken from the configurations of the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note> and the number of the spheres. But since they gather these by relationship to the houses of the luminaries, that reasoning must be examined first.

He mocks the attempts by Averroes and others to find biological or physical justifications for these symbolic links.</summary>

<header>BOOK TEN</header>

### BOOK TEN

<margin>Ptolemy’s reasoning</margin>
...whereby the houses of the luminaries <note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note> themselves are established. For this is the nature of the reasoning which Ptolemy offers: among the twelve signs, Cancer and Leo turn most toward the north and come closest to our zenith <note>The point directly above an observer's head.</note>; for this reason, they were given to the two greatest and principal stars—that is, the luminaries. Leo was given to the Sun because it is a masculine sign, and Cancer to the Moon because it is feminine. 

Firstly, however, the premise he assumes is false; for the signs closest to us are Cancer and Gemini, not Cancer and Leo. Furthermore, even if it were true—as his reasoning suggests—that the signs of the larger stars should be those closest to us, the ancients could have argued this by a similar logic: that those planets are also closer to us. But Ptolemy cannot say this, for he places the Sun in the middle of all the planets. Or was it done because the Sun heats more intensely when in Leo? It has been said often enough that this happens because of the Sun's position <note>The angle of the sun's rays in summer</note>, not because of a property of the sign itself; otherwise, the Sun would produce for other nations in Libra what it produces for us in Leo. Indeed, if we could experience the true senses and reasons for the powers of the other stars as we do for the Sun's heat, we would find the same regarding the rest as we do for the Sun: that we are affected more by them as they approach Leo simply because they are found closer to us there than in other signs. Does the Sun then harmonize with Leo for other reasons? To be sure, that it is a hot and dry sign, and likewise masculine, is not unique to Leo, but is shared with Aries and Sagittarius. There remains one condition mentioned by that most serious author, Aboafar <note>Aboafar refers to Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a famous Persian astrologer known in the West as Albumasar.</note>.

<margin>Aboafar’s reasoning</margin>
For just as the Sun is the "middle" of the planets, he says, so Leo is the middle sign of summer. Had I not been bound by this reasoning, I would not have conceded that Phoebus <note>A poetic name for the Sun.</note> is better hosted in Leo than in the other beasts of the heavens. But Aboafar truly serves as a safeguard and "sweet glory" of the astrologers <note>This is likely a sarcastic reference to a line from the Roman poet Horace: "O et praesidium et dulce decus meum."</note>; he also reconsidered a most beautiful kinship between the Moon and Taurus.

<margin>His other reason why Cancer is the house of the Moon, and Averroës’ view</margin>
Ptolemy attributed it to the distance between the signs closest to us being feminine. Not content with this, Aboafar added another reason: that the Moon signifies the beginnings of things, and let Cancer be the beginning of summer. Who would not concede to such a demonstration? Averroës <note>A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and polymath who wrote commentaries on Aristotle and Ptolemy.</note> did not see this, using a different reason: namely, that the house of the Moon is rightly placed next to the house of the Sun because the Moon always follows the Sun. But he should see that this is more correctly said of Venus and Mercury, whose houses nature made closest to the Sun—if we believe Ptolemy, whom Averroës (whom we have cited) interprets. 

But as for those houses of the luminaries, this is the reason Ptolemy offers for distributing the others: primarily so that the houses of the "malefic" stars <term>Malefic: Planets traditionally thought to have a harmful influence, specifically Mars and Saturn.</term>, such as Mars and Saturn, might gaze upon the houses of the luminaries with hostile radiation <note>Astrological "aspects" or angles; certain angles were considered "hostile" or "friendly."</note>. Meanwhile, the houses of "benefic" stars, like Jupiter and Venus, should be placed in a friendly way, with Mercury established closest to them. 

Rightly, then, was Scorpio and Aries given to Mars, which are "quadrangular" <note>An aspect of 90 degrees, known as a "square," traditionally considered stressful or hostile.</note> to Cancer and Leo. To Saturn were given Capricorn and Aquarius, which are opposite to them. To Jupiter were given the "triquetra" <note>A "trine" aspect of 120 degrees, considered very harmonious.</note> signs, Pisces and Sagittarius; to Venus the "hexagonal" <note>A "sextile" aspect of 60 degrees, considered friendly.</note> signs, Libra and Taurus; and to Mercury the closest signs, Gemini and Virgo. But neither is the premise he assumes true, nor is the conclusion correctly drawn from what he assumes.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
For we say a house is reasonably established as that in which a planet is well-situated when placed there. But "quadrangular radiation" is equally harmful to Mars and the Sun; likewise, "opposition" is harmful to Saturn, both because of the adversity of the opposition and because of retrogradation <note>The apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky.</note>. But if that which Ptolemy himself teaches were true—that all planets are "happy" at that distance from the Sun which their houses are from the Sun’s house (which the Greeks call *apopiropon* <note>original: "αΠοΠιροΠιαn" (apopiropon), referring to a planetary distance from the sun.</note> and the Arabs *alhugea* <note>original: "alhugeā," likely from the Arabic 'al-awj,' meaning apogee or height.</note>)—it would follow that Saturn in opposition to the luminaries and Mars in a square aspect to them would be "happy." This goes against the opinion of all astrologers, who decree great misfortunes and calamities from such configurations. Finally, it is evident that the conclusion does not square with the principle: for when they say these or those houses are "trine" or "square," they only arrive at this by comparing them to Leo in one sequence (from Leo to Capricorn) and to Cancer in a reverse order (from Cancer to Aquarius). Otherwise, the houses of Venus could be called both square and trine at once.

<summary>Pico disputes the traditional astrological assignments of "houses" to planets, arguing that the geometric and elemental reasons provided by Ptolemy, Aboafar, and Averroës are inconsistent and contradictory.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.
<meta>image quality: excellent. clear typography with visible show-through.</meta>
<meta>catchword: That likewise [Quod itẽ]</meta>

<margin>Avenrodan <note>Also known as Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer whose commentaries on Ptolemy were standard textbooks.</note>. Reason.</margin>
<margin>Ptolemy, taken according to the number of the spheres.</margin>
<margin>Avenazra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer whose "Book of Reasons" Pico cites here.</note></margin>
...since Libra is square to Cancer/Leo, and Taurus is square to them; and the houses of Mars would be in trine <note>A "trine" is an astrological aspect of 120 degrees, usually considered harmonious.</note> if Scorpio were to Cancer and Aries to Leo. Therefore, the house of each luminary <note>The Sun and Moon.</note> ought to be compared to a collateral house and located as if placed under the dominion of that star. But if this is done, it will be found to be most false that the houses of Saturn are opposed to the luminaries, as Ptolemy says; for neither is Aquarius opposed to Cancer, nor is Capricorn opposed to Leo. Therefore, no one would say these are the houses of Saturn because they face the luminaries from a diameter <note>Meaning a 180-degree opposition.</note>, since they hold the sixth place from the Sun or the eighth from the Moon; which Avenrodan also confesses. Another reason is taken according to the number of the spheres: as when it was defined regarding Leo and Cancer, then the houses nearest to them were assigned to the planets closest to the Sun and Moon in the order of the spheres. Thus they decree that Mercury is given Gemini on one side and Virgo on the other; then Venus receives those which follow; then the signs next to Mars; then Jupiter; and finally Saturn. We have declared that all these arguments drawn from the sequence of the spheres are false, and even if they were true, they would be uncertain. Rightly therefore does Avenazra say in the second book of his *Reasons*: "I have sought," he says, "in the books of the wise for the reasons for the houses of the signs, nor have I found in them anything good; they turn only to the trust of experiments." Thus says he: in this book we shall weaken their reasons, and in the next, the experiments of the astrologers.

### Chapter X. That the reasons for Faces and Bounds have already been rejected.

<margin>Division of the faces</margin>
<margin>Another division of the Indians.</margin>
**T**he faces <note>Also called "decans," these are 10-degree subdivisions of a zodiac sign.</note> of the planets, which everyone uses, are similarly divided from the sequence of the spheres. For assigning the first parts of Aries to the lord of the house, they give the following parts to those following, according to the order of their position and the spheres of the Sun: that is, the first to Mars, the second to Venus, and so on. The Indians gave the first parts to the lord of the house; the other two to the lords of the signs of the same trigon <note>A "trigon" or triplicity is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note>. If we have sufficiently refuted the trigons and the arguments based on the number of the spheres, there is no need for new reasons against such reasons as these. Regarding the bounds <note>The "bounds" or *termini* are specific unequal degree-segments within a sign assigned to different planets.</note>, they disagree so much that they have produced five different opinions on them. Therefore, the reasons of one man are argued against and mocked by another. Indeed, they are all so weak and infirm that each person, by some new law, changes his neighbors' boundaries and invades those of others. The Chaldeans <note>A term often used for Babylonian or ancient Mesopotamian astrologers.</note> arranged their bounds according to the order of the trigons, so that they divided the signs of the trigons similarly. The method of division was that the lord of the trigon occupied the first parts, then the subsequent parts were held by those who have power in the following signs of the trigon, with the numbers always decreasing from eight down to four.

<margin>The Egyptians and Ptolemy.</margin>
The Egyptians, whom Ptolemy criticizes for this, maintain no steady method: sometimes they go by trigons, sometimes by "kings," sometimes by "heads of families"; sometimes beginning from those who possess no authority in the sign, such as starting from Mercury in Capricorn. Ptolemy approves another division, the reasoning for which anyone may read in the first book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>The *Apotelesmaton*, also known as the *Tetrabiblos*, is Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>. It depends, however, on the lords of the house, the exaltation, and the trigon; yet Ptolemy ought not to have approved this unless he were refuting himself, since the author of that division prefers exaltation to the trigon, and the trigon to the house. Ptolemy, however, prefers the house above all, and puts exaltation last—whereas in that other division, it is preferred before all.

<margin>Afotol <note>Possibly a reference to a specific Arabic source or a corruption of a name like Al-Fadil.</note>.</margin>
The Indians divide masculine signs similarly through all things, and feminine signs likewise by the same example; but no reason for the example is recognized in either. Afotol even gave bounds to the luminaries, with as many parts to each planet, but the first parts to the lord of the house in the order of the "prophets," and the rest to the remaining ones. Since we have already removed this foundation—and similarly the houses, exaltations, and trigons—or proved that if they do exist, they are uncertain, the entire reasoning for defining the bounds collapses (even if it were conceded that bounds exist). Furthermore, even if the truth concerning trigons, houses, and altitudes <note>Exaltations.</note> had been explored, it would not follow that bounds should be decreed in this way rather than that. From this has been born the variety of opinions, while one way seemed more probable to some than to others.

### Chapter XI. That which sign rules which member [of the body] is determined differently by different people and by all of them with little reason.

<summary>Pico critiques the arbitrary nature of astrological "houses," "faces," and "bounds," pointing out the logical contradictions between various traditions (Egyptian, Indian, Chaldean) and Ptolemy's own systems. He argues that these subdivisions lack a consistent rational basis and are often self-contradictory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrological foundations. Having previously questioned the logic of "houses," he now turns his attention to the "melothesia"—the traditional practice of assigning specific parts of the human body to the twelve signs of the zodiac.</meta>

# BOOK TEN

<margin>Aristotle makes seven parts of the body. Nicolaus ten. Note on medicine.</margin>
The fact that they likewise assign the head to Aries, the neck to Taurus, and similar members to the other signs, also takes its origin from that order of numbers which has already been frequently mocked: namely, so that the first sign is placed over the first part of the body, the second over the second, and the third over the third. Yet they err even in this division: not so much because they make Aries the first of the signs, but because they accept twelve signs as a proven fact for a matter so ambiguous, if not to say utterly false. For no reason persuades us that there should be exactly as many principal parts of the body; Aristotle made seven <note>Aristotle's division of the body usually included the head, neck, trunk, two arms, and two legs.</note>, and Nicomachus made ten. Why twelve, unless they can provide a reason? They seem to do something quite absurd when they force the shoulders, arms, and hands into a single part subject to one sign, while they separate the feet from the shins, the shins from the knees, and the knees from the thighs as four large parts to be subjected to four different signs. Furthermore, those making such a distribution ought to have compared hot things with hot, and cold with cold, rather than simply matching the second to the second and the third to the third. This commonality of nature is more to be observed than a mere enumeration of position and order. Perhaps they would not be laughed at for subjecting the feet to Pisces <note>The sign of the Fishes.</note>, which alone among the celestial figures lack feet. Therefore, let physicians beware lest, being persuaded at some point by such a futile dogma, they fear to open a vein in the arms when the situation requires it, simply because the Moon is traversing Gemini <note>The Twins, traditionally ruling the arms.</note>; let them not delay a healthy remedy led by such empty superstition.

<margin>The studies of all learned men disagree with this.</margin>
Neither Hippocrates, nor Galen, nor Avicenna <note>Famous Persian physician (980–1037).</note>, nor Paulus, nor Oribasius <note>Greek medical writers of late antiquity.</note> did this themselves, nor did they decree that others should do it—not even those who, in our own time (as we have said elsewhere), have practiced this art successfully and prudently. Therefore, let all insane superstition of this kind cease; for if it is proved to have no rational basis, it can have no strength from experience. This is partly because no truth harmonizes with a lie, partly because of the many things we shall prove in the following book, and partly because of the very contradiction among those who propose these things.

<margin>Abu Ma'shar, Al-Qabisi, Porphyry, Heliazer.</margin>
For Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazra"</note> gives the testicles to Sagittarius; Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboaſar," a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> gives them to Scorpio; Al-Qabisi <note>original: "Alchabitius," a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note> gives the diaphragm (which is called the *septum transversum* in Latin) to Virgo. Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist who wrote on astrology.</note> gives the belly to Leo, which the Arabs give to Virgo. There are some who give the knees to Sagittarius, which both Arabs and Latins usually give to Capricorn. Heliazer of Gargon <note>original: "Heliazer garnozenſis," likely referring to Eliezer of Worms or a similar medieval Hebrew authority.</note>, a Hebrew man, in his book *On the Soul*, assigns the hands and feet to Cancer, even though others give the hands to Gemini and the feet to Pisces. Again, that same author subjects the shins and feet to Libra, but for a different reason than those who subject them to Cancer: for they give them to Cancer insofar as they fulfill the function of walking, but to Libra because of a certain similarity, because during the gait they are raised and lowered like a balance <note>original: "libra," the Latin word for a weighing scale.</note>. Others say nothing of the sort regarding Libra, but subject the shins to Aquarius and the feet to Pisces; they subject the buttocks as well as the kidneys and loins to Libra. Heliazer says the nature of Scorpio corresponds to Sagittarius, but others give the private parts to Scorpio.

<margin>Heliazer</margin>
But if anyone should say that astrologers have observed that the blade is never safely applied to a limb whose sign the Moon occupies at that time, I say first that in such great uncertainty, no constant and agreed-upon experience can be had as to which sign governs which limb. Nevertheless, however it may happen, a wise man has observed the opposite.

<margin>Nicole Oresme.</margin>
For Nicole Oresme <note>original: "Nicolaus orem," a 14th-century philosopher and mathematician who was a famous skeptic of astrology.</note>, a serious philosopher and mathematician, writes that he has frequently seen bloodletting performed healthily in the foot when the Moon was in Pisces, and likewise in the arms when it was traversing Gemini.

## Chapter XII: The reasons of the astrologers by which properties belonging absolutely to the signs are asserted: and why the aforementioned reasons are rejected.

<margin>The first kind of proof.</margin>
We have spoken of the properties by which the signs relate to us and to the planets; there remain those which belong to them simply and absolutely, which they assume from a threefold kind of proof. The first is derived from the affinity with the planets, which has already been refuted; the second from the figure of the animal for which it is named; the third from those things which the Sun performs when positioned under them. From the affinity with the planets, they argue when they make the nature of the sign the same as the nature of the planet that rules in that sign; for example, when they say Aries signifies the hiding places of thieves and wicked men because it is the house of Mars, which signifies that kind of person. From the work of the Sun, they determine which signs are "movable," "fixed," and "common." From...

He cites Nicole Oresme to argue that medical procedures like bloodletting are not affected by the Moon's position in the zodiac.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological principles. Following his critique of the "houses" and the bodily associations of the zodiac signs on the previous page, he now examines the physical and elemental qualities attributed to the signs and planets, specifically targeting the foundational theories of Ptolemy.</meta>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>The second reason</margin>
The second [reason] by which the Sun either changes or confirms the seasons of the year, or tempers them with a mixed quality, [is based on] the figure. They say that some figures breathe gentle characters into those being born, while others breathe wild ones, because these signs carry the likeness of all things: such as Aquarius, Gemini, and Virgo [which are human]; and others of beasts, such as Leo, Taurus, and Capricorn. Likewise, they claim some are beautiful and others deformed; for they call "beautiful" whatever is conceived under a human likeness, except for Aquarius, because it is the dwelling of old Saturn—as if an old man, even if deformed, might not benefit from or delight in a beautiful home. Similarly, those with a brute likeness, such as Taurus and the like, they call "half-voiced," while the human ones are "vocal," and those that resemble aquatic creatures are "mute," because that genus of living things has no voice. Again, they say the aquatic signs produce much offspring, while the human-shaped ones are sterile. The remaining signs they place in a middle condition, according to the nature of the animals whose likenesses they are generally believed to be.

<margin>These things have been refuted.</margin>
The arguments discussed above have sufficiently overturned these modes of positioning. For when they make a conjecture about a planet's houses and character, they argue from astrological [principles] which we refuted a little while ago. When they argue from <margin>The third reason</margin> any specific effect, we have shown how much they either deceive or are deceived; for the effect is not to be thought of as the nature of the *sign*, but rather the work of the Sun located in that sign—acting not because of the sign’s nature, but because of its position and distance relative to the Earth. Furthermore, what occurs in the seasons of the year and atmospheric changes is transferred by a most deceptive inference to other things: for instance, because the "mobile" sign of Aries <note>Aries is a "cardinal" or "movable" sign because it marks the start of a season.</note> varies the weather, they claim it also makes the character of one born under it "mobile"—not persevering, but better suited for beginning things than finishing them. Not only do they err by turning the quality of the air into diverse events and properties of characters, but they imagine that what is observed in the Sun also happens in other stars regarding atmospheric changes. Therefore, if the Sun placed in Aries, creating the vernal equinox <note>The spring equinox, around March 21st.</note>, stirs up lightning and rouses thunder, we are expected to believe the Moon placed in Aries will do the same. They fall into no other error than this: referring to the "nature of the sign" that which actually proceeds from the Sun's variation.

<margin>The images had no natural origin</margin>
Regarding the shapes of the [celestial] images, we spoke abundantly in the eighth book, showing that they are non-existent, vain, and fictional. They are not the works of God but of men; not perfected by the reason of nature, but fashioned by the rashness of the poetic mind. But as [that author] most truly said, astrologers are never more false than when they elicit the properties of signs from these images. As we demonstrated extensively above, even in the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the "fixed stars" in the geocentric model.</note>, the images differ not only in position and mobility, but also in the dimension and quantity of their parts. Finally, they struggle against a force of inert, futile, and listless slowness when they seek the condition of these signs from both the Sun’s work and the image. For that [distinction] is openly [made]: these [qualities] belong to the "immobile" signs by common consensus, and those to the "mobile" ones.

->Chapter XIII. Ptolemy is censured for speaking of planets as if they consisted of elements, and the reasons of others by which they prove the qualities of planets are likewise refuted.<-

Thus far concerning the logic of the signs, which is remarkably irrational; in the planets, the same falsehood—indeed, a greater one—and greater rashness is found. Intending to show that Ptolemy philosophized poorly regarding the "wandering stars" <note>original: "erronibus," referring to the planets (from the Greek 'planētes' meaning wanderer).</note>, we have indicated those points especially by which they investigate the nature of the planets. For Ptolemy speaks of them as if the planets consist of elements, or consist of the "passions" <note>In ancient physics, 'passions' refer to qualities like heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> of elements—not only changing each other by heat or cold, but also being changed by the vapors of the Earth. <margin>Ptolemy’s discourse</margin> The Moon, he says, is moist because, being nearest to the Earth, she becomes damp from the vapors of the Earth ascending toward her. The star of Saturn is primarily cold and moderately dry; it is cold because it is placed far from the Sun, and it grows parched because it is exalted far from the vapors of the Earth. Mars, scorched by its proximity to the Sun, is dried out. Jupiter, being in the middle between the cold of Saturn and the heat of Mars, turns out temperate. Since it is indeed above the hot spheres of Mars and the Sun, it does not heat excessively. Venus is moist like the Moon; for by the abundance of her light, she draws many vapors of the Earth to herself. Likewise, she has a power of heating from the Sun, to which she is near. Mercury also has a property of drying from the Sun, to which he always clings...

<summary>Pico attacks the symbolic and elemental foundations of astrology, arguing that the "qualities" of zodiac signs are merely human poetic fictions and that planetary characteristics described by Ptolemy are based on flawed physical reasoning.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the physical justifications for astrology. Having previously dismissed the symbolic associations of the zodiac, he now turns to the arguments made by Ptolemy and others regarding the elemental qualities (heat, moisture, etc.) and colors of the planets, arguing that these are based on flawed physics and optical illusions.</meta>

# BOOK TEN

...and the powers of moistening from the vicinity of the Earth and the borders of the Moon. Thus, in the first book of the *Apotelelsmatika* <note>original: "apotelelsma ton"; Pico is referring to Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of systematic astrology.</note>, Ptolemy reasons. 
<margin>Note.</margin>
If he cannot be persuaded by the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed the heavens were made of a "fifth element" (aether) and were exempt from the changing qualities of the four earthly elements.</note> that the heavens are free from these types of influences, he should at least understand this from the very things he himself demonstrated: that the Earth is further from the Moon than would allow earthly vapors and breaths to reach it. For physicists believe that these vapors are not raised even sixteen stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of length; sixteen stadia is roughly two miles. Pico is arguing that atmospheric moisture doesn't go high enough to reach the planets.</note> upward, let alone being lifted intact to the Moon, to Venus, or to Mercury. 

<margin>Conflict of the physicists.</margin>
Add to this that Venus, by its proximity, would be more dried out by the Sun than made moist by the clouds of the Earth, since it is closer to the Sun than to the Earth; nor can the power of earthly moisture be compared with the power of the Sun. Add also that Mercury, being closer to the Earth and therefore more distant from the Sun, would be more dry than moist. How then is [Ptolemy] consistent with himself when he assigns moisture to Venus, given that the Lunar fire is so close and provides so little heat that the Moon is considered cold by many? And if Saturn is frozen because it is so far from the Sun, wouldn't the wheel of fixed stars, being even more distant from the Sun, be bound by the numb ice of cold? Yet among these stars, they proclaim many to be of a fiery nature. 

Therefore, Ptolemy's reasoning is not only false but also inconsistent with itself, which is what usually happens with false arguments. Others argue from the colors of the planets, a point which Ptolemy also touched upon regarding Mars. These people say that the philosophers lie who think the elements partake in no color or flavor. They claim that a white color and a sweet flavor belong to water; a dark color and a bitter flavor to earth—though others deny this, contending it is sweet, for if it were bitter, the earth would sprout nothing. 

Then they admit no flavor in fire, but a red color. They say air is devoid of both color and flavor, but admits various external and changing colors. They claim that in the planets there are no flavors, but there are multiple colors, from which we can easily investigate their natures. For they say the darkness in Saturn shows an earthy property, suiting <term>black bile: or "melancholy," the humor associated with earth, cold, and sadness</term>. In Mars, the redness bears witness to a fiery quality and <term>red bile: or "choler," the humor associated with fire and anger</term>. Venus radiates with yellow and white: from the yellow she is understood as hot, and from the white as moist; since these qualities are not equal, they indicate a tempered nature like that of blood. A similar conjecture is made for Jupiter. In the Moon, its whiteness shows moisture, and its touch of darkness demonstrates cold. The color of Mercury changes repeatedly, appearing now green, now dark, now turning to another appearance; yet it favors the dark more, and is thus more conformed to earthly dryness. 

So they reason, quite beyond all reason, for colors follow the mixing of elements, of which there is none in the celestial bodies. 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Nor does Aristotle say the heavens partake in color, except insofar as light is a kind of color. Truly, even if color indicates some property of a mixture, light will not indicate the nature of the shining body, since conjectures about color are thought to arise from the variety of mixtures. Therefore, since color is nothing other than the evidence of light, more or less bright, flowing not from a composite but from a simple body, it will give us no indication of the body that illuminates. 

Furthermore, no certain inquiry for exploring the heavens could come from their colors, even if they were endowed with true colors, because the intervention of such a vast and—what is more disturbing—multifarious space utterly takes away the reliability of the color. Nor did I wish to object to them with Plato, 
<margin>Plato</margin>
who writes in the *Phaedo* <note>Pico refers to Plato’s description of the "true earth" seen from above, where colors are more vibrant and the atmosphere is different.</note> that what we see are not the bodies of the stars, but certain reflections of rays in the air, bringing back an appearance similar to a star; just as fish living in the depths see on the surface of the water not the stars, but images of the stars—what I might call "radiant shadows." Whether we look at this or the stars themselves, no one initiated into the sacred mysteries of philosophy is unaware that colors vary in a marvelous way and things are seen through the intervention of multiform [bodies]...

<meta>catchword: multiform</meta>

<summary>Pico critiques the astrological theory that planets derive their "qualities" (like moisture or heat) from their proximity to Earth or their visible colors. He argues that atmospheric vapors do not reach the heavens and that planetary colors are optical illusions or properties of light rather than indicators of elemental composition.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic debunking of the physical "proofs" used by astrologers. After questioning the influence of atmospheric moisture on the planets, he now addresses the claim that a planet's astrological "nature" (hot, cold, wet, or dry) can be determined by its visible color.</meta>

-># DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

<margin>Galen</margin>
<margin>Averroes</margin>
...nus. Finally, it is doubted among physicians whether the powers and properties of herbs can be known from their smell, color, taste, or touch, as Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; he believed physical traits like taste and color revealed a plant's medicinal qualities.</note> believes. This is shown to be false by Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd, known as Averroes (1126–1198), was a philosopher who often critiqued the limits of sensory perception in science.</note> through many arguments and experiments. Furthermore, no one has even suggested that we could determine such things from color alone—even for things that we can keep under our gaze for entire days, where our study is not interrupted by motion, distance, or a confusing multitude of lights.

<margin>The error of Averroes.</margin>
Who, then, would listen to such a promise regarding the celestial bodies? This is true even if the colors of those bodies were reported to us in their most sincere and pure state. The whiteness of lime is surpassed by that of clear snow, yet there is a great deal of heat in lime and, conversely, a great deal of cold in snow. <note>Pico is referring to quicklime, which creates heat when mixed with water, proving that two things can look white but have opposite "temperatures" or qualities.</note> Averroes errs too shamelessly here: he believes we are deceived by color in earthly things, but not at all in celestial things, because he argues that earthly things are "mixed" from elements while celestial things are not. In fact, it is for this very reason that we know color should not be trusted regarding the nature of the heavens: since they are not made of the four elements, color cannot indicate their nature in the same way that a mixture of elements indicates a substance's state to us.

Besides (as we were saying just now), the vast region of space lying between us and the stars contains a multitude of bodies that must pervert and interrupt any colors one might imagine to be there. This is proven by the sheer variety of opinions that have arisen concerning those colors.

<margin>Various opinions on the colors of the planets</margin>
For Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboasar"; a famous Persian astrologer (787–886 AD) whose works were fundamental to medieval European astrology.</note> denies that the colors of the planets are what we described above (which was the belief of those who judged stars by their colors). He claims that the star of Saturn resembles the color of lead rather than the darkness of earth. He says there is no whiteness in Jupiter, nor is brightness proper to Venus. Furthermore, if Mars is called "hot" because it is red, then a red color should be attributed much more to the Sun, which is hotter than Mars.

No one who is not blind would think the Moon is white. Indeed, the accounts of the planets' colors found in the records of the ancients in natural history are quite diverse: there, Saturn is called white, Jupiter clear, and Venus is called "shining" when she is the Morning Star <note>original: "Lucifer"</note> and "flashing" when she is the Evening Star <note>original: "Vesper"</note>. Mercury is described as radiating and the Moon as having a mild color. It is said that Mercury varies in all colors; for this reason, the idea that its nature is multiform and changeable is born from deceptive evidence. This does not happen because Mercury is actually like that, but because it is always very close to the sun and is seen near the horizon. In that part of the sky, as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the "bible" of astrology.</note> testifies, the multiple vapors and earthly moistures create a shifting appearance and represent the stars in many-wandering colors.

Therefore, Abu Ma'shar says that none of that commentary on colors is colored with the credit of probability—yet, as he admits, the entire community of astrologers depends upon it.

<margin>Confutation of the error of Abu Ma'shar, Al-Zarqali, Al-Qabisi, and Ptolemy.</margin>
Abu Ma'shar himself, rejecting those reasons, thinks their nature can be known from the "primary qualities" <note>The four basic qualities: Hot, Cold, Wet, and Dry.</note> that the planets produce; a view Ptolemy also suggested. Thus, Saturn is discovered by "experience" to be the author of cold and dryness; for these qualities are said to flourish in bodies when Saturn is the governor of the year <note>The "ruler of the year" is the planet designated by astrologers to have the primary influence over a specific 12-month period.</note>. The same is observed for Mars and the others: whichever elementary affection each influences upon earthly bodies. From these effects, they conjecture about the whole nature of the planet. Since cold and dryness (the works of Saturn) are adverse to life, Saturn is decreed to be an evil and unhappy star. Mars is also called evil because of its parching heat and immoderate dryness. On the other hand, Jupiter and Venus are beneficial stars because of their nature of heat and moisture, which are the qualities that preserve life. He argues similarly for the others, referring everything to those four qualities: cold, moisture, heat, and dryness.

But this type of reasoning is shamed by the actual experiments. He does not prove by reason that Saturn produces cold rather than heat (which those we refuted earlier tried to do), but relies on "experience," as if it were a fact proven by the senses. Many philosophers think this is completely false, asserting that no star produces cold or dryness. There is no certainty among them as to which star produces which quality; this is especially ambiguous regarding the Moon and Venus. For Al-Zarqali <note>original: "Abenzagel"</note> and Al-Qabisi <note>original: "Alchabitius"</note> think Venus is cold, while Abu Ma'shar and Ptolemy think it is hot. Ptolemy thinks the Moon is hot, but others call it cold. They do not even agree on Mercury...

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers cannot determine the physical nature of planets through their color or perceived temperature, noting that even the most famous authorities like Ptolemy and Abu Ma'shar contradict one another on whether certain planets are hot or cold.</summary>

Having previously questioned the physical properties of the stars, he now addresses the lack of consensus regarding the "Lord of the Year" and challenges the fundamental astrological classification of planets as "malefic" or "benefic."</meta>

-># BOOK TEN<-

...come: Then if the observation is made regarding the planet governing the year (as Abu Ma'shar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), known in the West as Albumasar, was a leading Persian astrologer whose works were central to medieval astrology; Pico frequently targets him as a primary authority on the subject.</note> wishes), how can they agree on it? For there is such great ambiguity of opinion in choosing the Lord of the Year that there will be nearly as many future "Lords" as there are astrologers to pronounce them.

## Chapter XIV. Even if we grant that the planets produce the primary qualities, it should not therefore be granted that some are harmful and others beneficial.

Furthermore, whether we grant what they say about the primary qualities <note>The four primary qualities are hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note> through such experiments or through the first reasons brought forward, they will achieve nothing more than that the explored influences of the stars change the state of the air, not of bodies, through these kinds of primary affections. Truly, these stars are neither "beneficial" nor "harmful," nor can the proper and peculiar gifts of the stars be gathered from this. First, if the star of Saturn represents the nature of Earth, and Mars represents Fire: why is either the former or the latter considered "evil"? Neither Earth nor Fire is evil; from them come innumerable uses for life, without which nature could not exist. For even in the bodies of living things, black and red bile <note>original: "bilis atra rubraque." These are the humors of melancholy and choler. In the medical theory of the time, health depended on the balance of four humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and red bile.</note> are not harmful but necessary, and no less useful for performing certain duties than blood or phlegm. If they are said to harm by excess, then in that way blood and phlegm also harm if they increase beyond measure.

If the reasoning of the "particular world"—which we call Man <note>This refers to the "Microcosm," the idea that the human body is a miniature reflection of the "Macrocosm" or the universe.</note>—is properly investigated regarding the universal world, we will recognize it as an injustice to ascribe the excess of any quality in the human body to the stars. For it is believed that the elements remain within their boundaries and content with their prescribed law, doing no harm to the business of the world, because the celestial nature is ruling and moderating the fluid and wandering matter of corruptible things. Why then, by the same reasoning, should it not rather be the role of heaven to contain and restrain the qualities in our body under a continuous disposition of life, rather than for the leftovers of one to be excited to excess and ruin the whole and weaken it entirely? 

Therefore, if Saturn presides over black bile, since nothing emanates from heaven that is not ordered and life-giving, he will not excite it to the destruction of the animal, but will moderate it for its preservation. Nor will black bile receive from its star that which makes it act more violently, but rather that which makes it more moderate and vigorous. For the matter of these things is a certain heap of elements, with heaven acting as the efficient cause; but the efficient cause gathers into one those things which are mixed, and tempers all things under the peace of a single union, moving one thing from one part of heaven and another from another—if indeed these things are subject to different stars. In truth, they all act together with the stars conspiring unanimously <margin>Death is not from heaven</margin> toward the harmony of the whole. 

Accordingly, let no one be deceived into suspecting, when he hears that Saturn is placed over red bile, that anything happens to the quality subject to it from the star that is harmful, or which does not agree with good order and life. For the duty of the celestial prefecture should be understood as no less to restrain what is tumultuous than to rouse what is sluggish. Death does not come from heaven, but from <margin>None through</margin> nature; it occurs when, by its own defect, a quality has so degenerated that it cannot sustain the discipline of its presiding star, but either wanders immoderately or fails through slackness. 

This is what I have warned the reader more than once: no profession does more injury to heaven than astrological superstition <margin>Injury to heaven by astrology.</margin>, which seeks to impute to the stars everything we do contrary to reason through the fault of the will, and everything that happens in nature contrary to order through the fault of reckless and failing matter. It does not think the dignity of the stars is safe unless we credit them with every most unworthy thing. Thus, let the reasoning be gathered: the four qualities do not harm bodies but benefit them when they are moderate and tempered; and they proceed from the stars in no other way. Therefore, even if they do proceed from them, the stars cannot be called "harmful." First, neither Mars nor Saturn can be called "evil" because the latter excites black bile and the former red bile in bodies; for neither is harmful to life if it does not exceed its limits and measure, but is rather necessary. Indeed, it is so far from being the case that they overflow fatally by the author of heaven, that they are kept within their prescribed limit and measure by no other source; a matter of which we spoke abundantly in the third book, where we proved that the evils of the body do not come from heaven. For if heaven invigorated such qualities beyond measure, it would not immediately follow that Mars and Saturn are "evil" for everyone; rather, for some, these excesses would be healthy. For the cold seed would be tempered by the rays of Mars. And...

Therefore, an astrologer could not judge that someone in whose birth chart <note>original: "genitura"</note> they saw a powerful Saturn would suffer from the discomforts of black bile; nor could they pronounce that someone whom Mars had breathed upon more than others would be prone to the heats of choler—unless nature had written these traits into those planets, or experience had proven it. Since the astrologer neither knows nor investigates this, but only examines good and bad fortune based on these excesses of qualities, it is clear he is always dealing in doubt. 

It is also clear that what they say—that a "fortunate" planet is sometimes changed into an "unfortunate" one, and an "unfortunate" into a "fortunate" one—is problematic. For Jupiter sometimes harms and Saturn sometimes helps; they say this happens only because of the condition of the material, not because of the distance of the places or the variety of the signs. If those things were the cause of such a change, the astrologers would have decreed most poorly concerning them, at least when maintaining the position regarding the primary qualities. For as Mars in Aries will heat more, so it will harm more; yet they deny this, for they say "Mars does not overthrow his own house." <note>An astrological principle stating a planet is beneficial when in the zodiac sign it "rules."</note> Universally, they consider a star to be "happy" <note>i.e., "benefic" or lucky.</note> if it possesses either a <term>house<note>The zodiac sign where a planet is most "at home."</note></term>, a <term>term<note>Subdivisions of a sign; a planet in its own "term" gains strength.</note></term>, or an <term>exaltation<note>The specific sign where a planet's influence is considered most dignified or powerful.</note></term>. 

But who can doubt that Mars will heat more in Aries? Since Aries, as they wish, is a fiery sign; likewise, Saturn in Capricorn should be thought harmful, but in Aries, he should be thought "happy"—contrary to their opinion. For in Capricorn, Saturn's cold and dryness (by which they do harm) are intensified, while the heat of Aries will moderate that rigor. Indeed, he will be "happier" when in retrograde, which they do not believe; <margin>Al-Kindi</margin> for as Al-Kindi <note>Abu Yūsuf Yaʻqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī (c. 801–873), a prominent Arab philosopher and scientist who wrote extensively on astrology.</note> says, when a planet moves backward, it heats more. 

By the same reasoning, Mercury in Virgo will harm us with excessive dryness; and the Sun's heat will invade us more violently than is proper from the heat of Leo. Truly, they will affect us more moderately and healthfully if their rays are spread upon us tempered by the mixture of a cold sign. Thus, this reasoning, accepted in many ways regarding the primary qualities, is repugnant not only to truth but to the dogmas of the astrologers themselves.

For there are, besides what we have said, many things yet to object to them: such as if we ask why no star is found ruling over phlegm <note>In the humoral system, health required a balance of blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm.</note>, just as Saturn commands black bile, Mars red bile, and Jupiter blood. If they say the Moon or Venus rules it, then Venus and the Moon would have to be numbered among the "unfortunate" planets, since an excess of phlegm harms life no less than black or red bile. 

Furthermore, if the Moon is as <margin>Ptolemy</margin> Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), whose *Tetrabiblos* was the foundational text for Western astrology.</note> defines it, it will be seen as the most "unhappy" of all the stars by reason of its nature. For it is (as he pleases) of little heat but much moisture; no temperature is more subject to putrefaction <note>decay or rot</note> than this. Therefore, if a harmful or healthful planet is judged by the influx of its primary quality, the Moon will be harmful, being the producer of a dissolving and corrupting mixture; and it would be far more harmful than Mars and Saturn, which, if they do not instill the best natural qualities, at least instill qualities that only harm when not moderated. But what descends from the Moon is itself, by its very nature, <margin>Ptolemy</margin> immoderate through the weakness of its heat, flowing with moisture that is neither "cooked" <note>original: "cocto," referring to the biological process of "concoction" or maturation of humors.</note> nor sufficiently thickened. 

Yet Ptolemy himself numbers it among the "fortunate" stars, leaning on the authority of the ancients; and <margin>Abu Ma'shar</margin> Abu Ma'shar <note>The Latin text uses "Aboafar" for Abu Ma'shar.</note> even contends that it is more "happy" than Jupiter. From him I would also like to ask: since the Sun is hotter than Mars, and joined with dryness, why is Mars considered "unfortunate" while the Sun is considered the first among the "fortunate" stars? For thus Abu Ma'shar defines it, placing the Sun in the leading position among the authors of happiness, the Moon second, Jupiter third, Venus fourth, and Mercury fifth—concerning which he seems to disagree with himself, since he wants Mercury to be dry by its own nature, often more so than the nature of the others. Therefore, if he follows his own principles, he ought to number it among the harmful things. 

Others, however, disagree much both among themselves and with Abu Ma'shar himself; for a great part make the Moon, Sun, and Mercury "middling" between the harmful and the beneficial; all of which, as we have seen, Abu Ma'shar makes "beneficial." <margin>Heliodorus, Paulus</margin> Heliodorus <note>A 4th-century commentator on astrological texts.</note> and Paulus <note>Paulus Alexandrinus, a 4th-century astrological author.</note> also number Mercury among the healthful. Ptolemy makes the Moon healthful, but the Sun and Mercury of a "middling" condition, so that even this discord among themselves is no small...

overturns that opinion and makes the uncertainty of the art obvious. Furthermore, what would happen if that supposition about the primary qualities were true: that out of the twelve celestial signs, six are—without controversy—unhappy and unfortunate? Namely, all the fiery and all the earthy signs, since they abound in those qualities for which they accuse Mars and Saturn of being unfortunate. Indeed, nine signs rather than six would be unfortunate, since in the watery signs there is also an exitial <note>Deadly or destructive.</note> humidity along with coldness (as they believe). This humidity is not like the air of the <term>signs of air<note>Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius.</note></term>, such as is found in Jupiter, Venus, and the "aerial" planets—which is vital and prolific—but rather an aquatic and fluid quality that dominates. 

This is absurd for a double reason. First, the heavens—the first of all bodies and the most beneficial—would be condemned in their greatest part. Second, unfortunate signs would be the "houses" for fortunate stars: such as Pisces and Sagittarius for Jupiter, and Taurus for Venus; yet these ought to be distributed according to a kinship of nature. Finally, if they call these planets "fortunes" and those "infortunes" because more vital primary qualities come from the former, while corruptive and harmful ones come from the latter, they would still achieve no more (granting them the most generous conclusion) than to say this happiness or unhappiness pertains to the state of the body, which is tempered and regulated by those primary qualities. But how will they defend the idea that this also derives into external and accidental successes <note>i.e., "luck" or external events like wealth or social status.</note>? Unless those arguments we brought against that opinion above are not already incredibly weak. 

Lastly, even if all we have just said were nothing, there is no doubt that those who wish to give an account of the influences of the stars based on these primary qualities act with too little skill and too little consideration. Yet there is no astrologer who does not do this; nor do those who boast they can provide the "natural causes" for the dogmas of this art turn to anything else but these elemental affections <note>Physical states or qualities like heat or moisture.</note>. But in truth, if there are any proper and particular "breathings" <note>Influences or emanations.</note> of the stars, these do not follow such qualities, but rather the occult and truly celestial properties of each individual star. It is to these properties that people are accustomed to refer whenever things in terrestrial matters seem to rise above elemental nature, yet remain within the limits of the body. In these things, we sometimes see many gifts and virtues that not only do not arise from a mixture of elemental qualities, but even disagree with it. 

Just as the <term>myrobalan<note>A plum-like fruit used in medieval medicine; Pico uses it as an example of a substance whose physical properties (cold/dry) shouldn't be life-giving, yet it was believed to have a "hidden" restorative power.</note></term>, with its cold and dry temperament, seems to work more toward death than life; yet, by the privilege of a more secret nature, its efficacy is believed to be wonderful for prolonging and invigorating life. Much more so must Jupiter and Saturn and the whole superior nature be thought to act—if they influence us as the astrologers believe—not through these qualities, even if this planet is judged cold and dry and that one hot and moist. Rather, they must be thought to perform many of their principal works through other occult powers of their rays. This is both because it is more consistent with their nature, and because the works attributed to them by astrologers cannot be referred to those qualities and affections, as we have demonstrated. If this is the case, it is clear by reason that those qualities cannot be grasped—which is what we undertook to prove in this section. There remains the path of experience, about which we will dispute at length in the following book.

## Chapter XV: The reasons of the astrologers regarding the lords of the days and hours and the years of the planets are ineffective; also, astrologers often use circular demonstration.

There remain the arguments by which they gather certain more particular conditions of the planets. These are elicited either from a parabolic similarity, or from astrological principles, or from the order of the spheres—from the spheres, as in the lordship of the days and hours. ...[of the supre]me grace as examples, they give to the **Sun** alone; they give the remaining [portions] to the **planets**, which then follow according to the position of the spheres. From this, the distribution of days is born, so that a day is ascribed to that planet which, by the preceding order of <term>hourly division<note>This refers to the "Chaldean order" of planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon), which astrologers used to determine the "ruler" of each hour and subsequently each day.</note></term>, falls upon the first hour of that day. These claims are amply refuted by what was said above: where we declared how futile that mode of arguing is, how the order of the spheres is still placed in ambiguity, and how the succession of command in the heavens is a vain imagination. Besides these points, we can also ask the astrologers: what reason showed the **Chaldeans** and **Egyptians**—the authors of this superstition—the first day of all time? For they cannot use the authority of the **Mosaic law** unless they also believe that, according to that same law, astrologers and every type of diviner must be utterly exterminated.

<margin>Refutation</margin> They also calculate from astrological reasons when they say that a certain planet grants so many years of life because it possesses so many <term>bounds<note>In astrology, "bounds" (Latin: *fines*) are specific degrees within a zodiac sign assigned to a particular planet, which allegedly increases that planet's influence.</note></term> in the **Zodiac**. Indeed, what is taken from the "bounds" is just as uncertain as if it were a confessed fact, just as what is proven from those years is uncertain. Nevertheless, even if what they want regarding the bounds were true, **Ptolemy** states there is no logical reason for the consequence: that the span of our living should be decreed through so many [bounds]. 

<margin>The beginning of the year.</margin> Moreover, they often err in these matters as well: in one place, they prove the number of bounds from the number of years, and in another, they gather the years from the bounds—reasoning in a circle. They begin the year from **Aries** because it is the first of the signs; yet they are then accustomed to show that it is the "first" in a continuous circle because we begin the order of time from it. Similarly, they argue that the second place corresponds to **Jupiter** because he produces and portends wealth, and then argue that Jupiter produces and portends wealth because he corresponds to the second place. You will find many such examples in their books, but far more ridiculous ones, especially if you happen upon the books of **Aboafaris** <note>original: "Aboafaris"; a Latinized name for Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note>.

<margin>Why the Moon grants 108 years and the Sun 120 according to Abu Ma'shar. Why the "minor years" of the Sun are 19.</margin> I was recently reading in his works that the **Moon** grants one hundred and eight years, while the **Sun** grants one hundred and twenty. He claims the Moon falls short of the Sun’s life by twelve years because she has no power until she has been elongated from the Sun by twelve degrees. Thus, it is no wonder that **Abu Ma'shar** boasts that he has fully rendered the logic of astrological dogma, since nothing is so irrational that it does not seem like "reason" to him.

There is equal insanity when they say the <term>minor years<note>In ancient astrology, each planet was assigned "great," "mean," and "minor" years, which were used to predict the length of various life events.</note></term> of the Sun are nineteen because, through this number, the luminaries are joined in their mean motion. In this, there is nothing at all in common, nothing connected, and the subsequent parts do not follow from the antecedent ones; yet they argue thus: "After this number of years, the Sun and Moon meet in mean motion; therefore, the Sun gives that many years when it gives the fewest." It is exactly as if one were to say a human is born with two eyes, therefore he is also born from two parents.

They use "parabolic similarity" in this way: "The **Moon** is the gate of heaven; therefore, it signifies the **mouth**, for a gate is like the mouth of a house, and the mouth is the gate for food and speech." Likewise, the **beard** pertains to the same celestial body because, like the Moon, it is renewed time and again. The **ears**, however, are subjected to **Saturn** because they hold the high parts of the head, just as Saturn himself is high in the heavens. By the same logic, because he is the highest, he produces tall men—even though this does not fit his nature, since he is decreed to be "dry and cold" <note>In ancient medicine and astrology, cold and dry qualities were thought to stunt growth rather than encourage it.</note>.

These are the "reasons" of the astrologers by which their celestial dogmas are propped up. I would not call these reasons, but rather occasions for either wandering or playing. When these are heard, the vanity of the dogma is as obvious as the firmness of truth usually becomes when it is heard. Therefore, it would have been better for them to cover these things with a veil or a chest like <term>secret rites<note>original: "orgia"; refers to the ancient mystery cults whose rituals were hidden from the public.</note></term>, leaving behind a suspicion of mystery. Instead, while they wish to appear rational, they sign the indictment of their own case with their own hand through their "reasons." To hear these reasons is nothing other than to understand what led the astrologers into error.

# BOOK ELEVEN

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS. BOOK ELEVEN BEGINS.

## Chapter One
### It is clear from what has been proved so far that astrology has not been confirmed by experiments; then the same is proved by many reasons.

If they could not grasp the nature of the heavens through reason—as we have already demonstrated—could they have done so through experience? And although they are ignorant as to *why* a thing happens, have they nevertheless learned *that* it happens through observation? If so, then even if astrology cannot claim the name of a "science," it might still hold the prerogative of being an "art" and a "true tradition." For it would still be able to predict the truth, whether it achieved this through logical arguments or through experiments.

Astrologers, like all practitioners of the prodigious <note>The Latin *prodigiosa* here refers to arts claiming to work wonders or deal with omens.</note> arts, are accustomed to defending themselves first and foremost under the title of "experience." This is the asylum to which they retreat whenever they speak or promise something that goes beyond credibility or reason; they think they can immediately untangle themselves from all the snares of logic if they simply say they have "experienced it" to be so.

We shall therefore take away this refuge from them—a refuge they are more accustomed to speaking of with their lips and hearing with their ears than understanding with their hearts. For if anyone has carefully meditated upon what "experience" actually is, and by what means it can be obtained regarding the influence of the stars, he will certainly not doubt that the specific powers and proper operations of the stars are just as inscrutable to human experience as they are to human reason.

Indeed, this can be made clear enough from what was said above: for if there is either no fate from heaven at all, or if what is called "fate" depends not on the initial hour of birth but on the "kinship of matter" <note>This refers to the biological or environmental conditions of the parents and the physical world, which Pico argues are more influential than the stars.</note>, it is clear that no path is left for experiments. For at the moment when any particular star breathes its influence upon you, it will be just as uncertain to you as the singular condition of that material heritage is entirely unknown. 

But even if someone were to claim that the "seminal hour" <note>The moment of conception.</note> is the fatal one, the astrologers themselves would not deny that the opportunity for observing such a hidden moment is far too difficult. Yet, let us grant that the time of birth is sufficiently observed. How could that observation ever be considered reliable? As we have declared, one would need to know how many and which celestial causes must be observed. They do not possess a true grasp of these; they cannot determine with any certainty the shapes, the conditions, or the positions of the stars at every single moment. Furthermore, they can neither obtain the exact hour of birth from the "lord of the birth" <note>A technical term for the planet deemed most influential in a birth chart.</note>, nor can they correct errors in their timing by any reliable method. 

If they fail in these matters (and we have shown they always fail), then the authority of their entire observation necessarily collapses. Now, we shall demonstrate in this present book that no experiments regarding the heavens are even possible. Let us grant the <term>natal astrologers<note>Latin: *genethliaci*. These are practitioners who specialize in casting horoscopes based on a person’s birth.</note></term> their premise: let them hold the hour of birth faithfully, and the state of the heavens at that hour just as faithfully. I ask you: by what means do they think they have attained through experience the knowledge of what such a constellation decrees or signifies? 

For if experience is gathered from the manifold and frequently repeated observation of the same thing, then consider this: the exact same constellation either never returns (as the more learned scholars prove) or, as the ancients believed, it will not return except after many thousands of ages <note>This refers to the "Great Year" or Platonic Year, the time it takes for all the planets and stars to return to the same relative positions—estimated by some ancients at 25,000 to 36,000 years.</note>. 

<margin>Example.</margin> Perhaps they will reply that *particular* constellations return and are repeated frequently, even if the restoration of the total and absolute constellation does not occur. They might claim they can acquire knowledge of those particular configurations through repeated observations, so that they might announce the future reliably from collected experiments. 

This can be explained by an example: Someone is born with **Aries** as the <term>horoscope<note>In this context, the "horoscope" (Latin: *horoscopante*) refers to the "Ascendant," or the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note></term>, with the star of **Mars** placed therein, and with **Saturn** occupying the seventh "cardinal point" <note>The four "angles" or cardinal points of a chart: the Ascendant, Descendant (7th house), Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note>. Then, another person is born later; their birth chart is different in other respects, but similar regarding **Mars** and **Saturn**. The astrologer could then make an observation of that particular part, even if it is not the whole constellation, twice. When this happens more often, the repeated observation creates an "experiment." This is how they perhaps defend themselves. But it is done with little truth and little consistency with their own principles.

<meta>This page continues the argument from the beginning of Book Eleven, where Pico challenges the claim that astrology is based on reliable empirical observation. He argues that because the heavens are never in the same configuration twice, "experience" is impossible.</meta>

...the same constellation operates quite differently within a different whole. For the substance of the entire decree <note>The "decree" or "judgment" refers to the astrologer’s final prediction based on a chart.</note> arises not so much from the individual parts as from the whole—that is, from the harmony of all parts together, producing a peculiar and specific effect that no part achieves on its own, nor even all the parts if they are considered separately. Indeed, the sum of all parts is one thing, but that which springs from the proportion of their mixture is quite another. Therefore, any observation by which astrologers collect their "experiments" will be imperfect. For it is imperfect because it fails to grasp the whole; it is deceptive because it considers the same part but not within the same whole. 

This reasoning draws its strength from the very precepts of the astrologers themselves, who assert that everything happens due to the **mixtures of the stars**, and that the lot of fate arises not from their individual powers, but from the complex of all stars together and their social union. Therefore, if in one or two birth charts <term>genitures; a birth chart or horoscope</term> you have seen the lord of the chart distracted by calamities when **Mars** and **Saturn** were in opposition <note>original: "ex diametro"; a 180-degree aspect considered highly stressful or malefic in traditional astrology.</note> at the primary angles, you cannot—as if having performed a reliable experiment—denounce future calamities when the same thing happens again. For nothing prevents that constellation from combining with a different tempering of other stars in such a way that it either does no harm at all, or perhaps even produces something entirely different from what it had done in other birth charts through various mixtures of rays. 

If we were to agree with the astrologers that human affairs happen by fate, we might point to what experience discovers every day: that the birth charts of the most unhappy people appear to be the "happiest," and conversely, those of the happy appear most "unhappy." Why is this? Because although particular constellations might seem to portend a good or bad fate based on past observations, the actual harmony of the total mixture—never before seen, known, or explored—can now produce an effect entirely different from what those stars portended elsewhere, whether individually or in a different mixture. 

Noticing this, the most ancient astrologers did not hand down the dogmas of this art in any other way than by explaining in detail the individual birth charts they had observed and finally comparing them with the actual outcomes. Their goal was not to judge what **Saturn** or **Jupiter** did, but what 
<margin>Maternus</margin> 
such a total constellation had produced. **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note>, following the example of the Egyptians, attempted this in some way in the sixth book of his commentaries. 
<margin>Ptolemy</margin> 
However, **Ptolemy** accuses those ancients of failing to reduce the art to a systematic method, even though they were pursuing a subject that is infinite and incomprehensible. Therefore, Ptolemy turned himself toward explaining universal precepts and the simple powers of the stars, 
<margin>Ptolemy is to be accused</margin> 
thinking that once these were known, a practitioner of birth charts could finally judge a specific mixture by his own conjecture. 

But although he rightly accuses the ancient astrologers, he himself is no less rightly to be accused. For the ancients saw correctly what needed to be done, but they erred in thinking it was something that *could* be done; since the matter is infinite, it can be reduced neither to an art nor a method. Furthermore, there is no use for it, since the exact same constellation is never restored. 

Ptolemy, however, thinking rather of what *could* be done than what *ought* to be done, wandered too far from the truth if he believed that true predictions could be made from those general precepts. Perhaps this is why **Avenazra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a celebrated 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> 
<margin>Avenazra</margin> 
writes that Ptolemy’s precepts never agree with actual outcomes and experiments. Yet Ptolemy is perhaps less to be blamed because, as we showed in the second book, he plainly confessed that this art is based on opinion, conjecture, doubt, and is prone to deception. 

Therefore, let us press the astrologer by bringing a chart into the open. "Is there here, O Astrologer—even if everything else were granted to you—some potent and primary thing in the production of an effect? Namely, the specific effect of the **total harmony**, upon which the fortune of the newborn most properly depends? Since neither reason nor observation has given you knowledge of this, how can you explain the truth of fate?" 

For you are deceived if you think the efficiency of the whole is nothing other than a collection of what the individual parts produce. This would only be true in a heap of sticking bodies or qualities, but not where they are mixed and grow together into another form—which is what all astrology believes happens with the rays of the stars. 
<margin>Example.</margin> 
Just as a man has not truly experienced the property of **theriac** <note>thæriacæ; a famous ancient medical compound consisting of dozens of ingredients, believed to be a universal antidote.</note> simply because he has observed the powers of the individual things from which it is made, so too he does not understand what the present army of heaven produces who only knows...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology cannot be an experimental science because the "whole" of a birth chart is more than the sum of its parts, and since the exact celestial configuration never repeats, no valid "experience" can be gathered.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, Firmicus Maternus, Ibn Ezra, theriac, birth charts, celestial harmony, empirical observation, planetary mixtures</keywords>
