<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of astrological "experimentation." He argues that because the stars act as a collective whole, it is impossible to isolate the influence of a single planet to claim it as the cause of a specific event.</meta>

<page-num>251</page-num>
->BOOK ELEVEN<-

# BOOK ELEVEN

...has had another experiment regarding its parts. For it is not only the relation of part to part—that is, star to star—but the state and condition of all stars together that produces the effect which is specific to the person being born. Just as there are specific individuals who are not born by nature from a mere confluence of accidents, but possess an incommunicable or private allocation of a peculiar substance. What is more, they cannot even obtain knowledge of a single star through experiment, since nothing

<margin>Reason.</margin>
can be defined by its condition relative to others in such a way that it can be discerned by a cognition separated from the rest. For from the whole constellation, you will indeed see the course of such a life, and see such events coming to pass; however, with all the stars acting upon all those things, you will not be able to know which star was the author of which thing, unless you have first grasped the nature of each individual star by reason or some other 

<margin>Solution</margin>
path. But if you say that you will observe in this way: that whenever you see some similar fates among men, you will argue that the matter arises most from that part where their astrological decrees harmonize—judging those things specifically through frequent observation—

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
I respond <margin>Refutation.</margin> that this way of conjecturing is far too deceptive. Firstly, because a similar state of a star can produce a different result in a different mixture, and a dissimilar state can produce the same result. Secondly, because the same chance can occur without having the same cause, since according to the opinion of the astrologers, the causes of the same effect in the sky are nearly innumerable. This will all be clearer by an example: Peter is born with **Jupiter** <note>original: "Ioue"</note> placed in **Pisces**; Paul is born with **Jupiter** in a similar position. With the rest of the constellation being entirely dissimilar, they live with a different lot: in character, talent, and health; they are equal only in their fortune in accumulating wealth. From this, is one permitted to conjecture that **Jupiter**, located in the second house in **Pisces**, is the giver of riches? Certainly not. For that which was common in their fate—namely, wealth—could have come from different celestial causes, not from common ones. Perhaps in one man’s birth chart <term>genitura; a horoscope</term>, the lord of the ascendant <term>horoscopi; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term> bestowed power upon the **Sun** occupying a pivot <term>cardinem; one of the four most powerful points in a chart: East, West, Zenith, and Nadir</term>, while for the other coming into the light, the **Part of Fortune** <note>A mathematical point in a chart used to predict prosperity.</note> held the east, joined to its lord by a favorable radiation. Or in one birth chart, a fortunate planet shone in the first pivot, while in the other, **Mercury** situated in that place was changed into the power of a fortunate and pivotal planet. But even if **Venus** was residing in the fifth house at Peter’s birth, but at Paul’s birth the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon.</note>—unweakened by any debilities—looked upon each other amicably, it will be, according to the opinion of astrologers, not from the same face of the stars. Wealth might come to both by the same fortune, yet the lot of these things is varied and happens from different causes, even though the star responsible for it <note>Jupiter, in this example.</note> was in a similar position in their birth charts. Furthermore, the same condition of a single star cannot exist at all unless the entire constellation is completely the same. Also, in another’s chart, a contrary force could be present to either overwhelm or dull the effectiveness of such a star. It is clear, therefore, that from the union and the mixed influence of the stars, we cannot discern through any observation what any specific star especially bestows. Therefore, neither can the natural powers of the stars be defined as known through experiments. 

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
There is another reason <margin>Third reason.</margin> for this insurmountable difficulty, even if each star acted individually. Since the condition of another star, or of lower circumstances, can in many ways invert, alter, or frustrate their effects, no one—unless they are reckless and hasty in judgment—will assert: "these things happen while this star is in this state; therefore, when it is in that way again, a similar event is to be expected." For that star might have been about to produce a different thing by its nature, but the work was changed by the power of a private fate, or the universal fate of a region, a year, a prince, a city, a family, or a fellowship. Or by preceding factors, such as parents, grandparents, or ancestors; or the free will of the person born; or the disposition of the air through which the celestial influences are transmitted; or stubborn matter; or a nearby cause that is inconvenient or unsuited to the higher motions. Since all these things, as they wish, can change the effectiveness of the stars, how will astrology be safe?

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers cannot claim their craft is based on "experience" because it is impossible to isolate the effect of one star from the complex whole of a constellation. He uses the example of two wealthy men (Peter and Paul) to show that identical outcomes can stem from entirely different celestial configurations.</summary>

->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY<-

<margin>Refutation of a silent solution.</margin>
<margin>Favorinus.</margin>
<margin>Paulus of Alexandria.</margin>
<margin>Hippocrates.</margin>
The argument will be secure if we interpret what has happened by the nature of the stars: especially since those things we have mentioned are always so linked to the operations of the stars that an event cannot be referred back to a single star as if to a primary cause—something we have noted happens quite often. They <note>The astrologers.</note> seem to be inexpiably deceived in this: that they think those things which they have observed for the sake of their own examples—whether in the regions of the Egyptians, or the Chaldeans, or the Arabs—hold the status of a universal dogma. That is, they think these rules will be equally valid in every region, when in fact it is necessary that things happen entirely differently, if indeed those things are true which are handed down by them and which the reliability of experience and life itself demonstrates. For in the changes of the air, we see quite clearly that from the same constellation different weather is stirred up in different places: here calm, there violent; here snow occurs, there clear skies; in another place winds, in another rains. It is therefore far too inconsistent that in the birthing of human bodies, or in the successes of business—if indeed these things come from heaven—the same stars would not act differently in different places due to the diverse curvature of the sky. Favorinus <note>A philosopher of the 2nd century known for his skeptical arguments against astrology.</note> also objected to them on these grounds, which we shall confirm by the authority of Paulus of Alexandria <note>A 4th-century author of an introductory text on astrology.</note>. For he writes in his *Introduction to Effects* <note>original: "isagogis apotelematum"</note> that births in Egypt are especially happy when <term>Aquarius</term> <note>The eleventh sign of the zodiac.</note>, holding the principal positions, is well-disposed, because the region of Egypt is subject to Aquarius. Thus, perhaps Mercury in Aquarius breathes fortunately upon the talents of the Egyptians here, while in truth Mercury is humbled in every house of Saturn <note>Both Aquarius and Capricorn were traditionally ruled by Saturn.</note> and is poorly disposed, as claimed by Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note>. It is clear, therefore, by the testimony of a singular astrologer, that the same observations will not be valid in every region equally—even if any reliable observations could be made in a specific region, which we have already demonstrated by many reasons does not happen. And if Hippocrates, the father of physicians, said that "experiment is deceptive" <note>A reference to the famous first aphorism of Hippocrates: "Life is short, art is long, opportunity fleeting, experiment deceptive, judgment difficult."</note> in medicine, no one but the most unlearned would deny it is most deceptive in astrology.

### Chapter II. If any experience of astrological dogmas could be held, it has not yet been obtained.

<margin>Favorinus.</margin>
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
<margin>Plato.</margin>
<margin>Varro.</margin>
**W**e have dealt with this point until now: to prove that by no length of time, and by no industry or learning of any men whatsoever, can an experiment be acquired regarding the more secret powers of the stars. Now, if perhaps that has not been fully persuaded, we shall at least demonstrate this most evidently: that if any such experience could be acquired, it has not yet been acquired. For by the prior reasons, this much is certainly established: that knowledge of all such things is most difficult to grasp, and it cannot be perfected through many revolutions of ages. Therefore, we shall first refute those lies of the astrologers by which they—not very skillfully and not very truly—proclaim that they possess observations of many thousands of years; then we shall declare that whatever they do have from their sayings is deceptive. The philosopher Favorinus, as recorded in Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, author of the "Attic Nights."</note>, says: "The discipline of the Chaldeans is not of such great antiquity as they wish it to seem." And Cicero, following the authority of Panaetius <note>A Stoic philosopher who, unusually for his school, rejected astrology.</note>, says: "For what they say—that the Babylonians have recorded forty or seventy thousand years in testing and experimenting on whatever boys were born—they are lying." For we have no author who says it can be done or knows it to have been done. These are his words. We, beginning from a deeper point, shall prove their impudence: and whether the world is eternal, as some philosophers wish, or created in time, as divine truth teaches, let us leave this most well-attested fact: that no observations older than four thousand years could have reached those who handed down the science of the stars. For it is certain even to those philosophers who believed in the eternity of the world that, through certain great mutations of the elements, seas have receded and lands have been inundated; with the habitations of lands and men changed, the ocean appeared where there was land, and land where part of it was ocean. Not only sacred historians, but also the philosopher Plato and foreign writers have often mentioned such floods and conflagrations. It matters nothing whether it is the novelty of the world or the change of past things that takes away the memory of events from us. Let us therefore examine from histories how old these observations of the heavens could be. Varro, the most learned of the Romans, when about to weave together a most ancient history, began from the kingdom of the Sicyonians <note>The Sicyonians were traditionally considered the oldest kingdom in Greece.</note>; to this kingdom, or a little before it, was contemporary...

He also dismisses the "ancient" records of the Chaldeans and Babylonians as fraudulent, noting that natural disasters would have erased any truly ancient data.</summary>

<page-num>252</page-num>
### BOOK ELEVEN

Trogus <note>Trogus Pompeius, a Roman historian from the 1st century BC.</note> took his starting point from Ninus himself, who fought against Zoroaster. This Zoroaster lived only a few years before the patriarch Abraham. Thus, those who write that Zoroaster flourished five thousand years before the Trojan War are revealed as tellers of fables, 
<margin>Note on the calculation of times.</margin>
since not even that many years are counted from Abraham down to our own time. What, then, was the reason why both Trogus and Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a renowned Roman scholar known for his immense learning.</note>, though they professed to write the most ancient histories, did not begin any earlier? It was either because of the novelty of the world—or at least its renewal—or because any previous events were either non-existent or completely obliterated. For although those men wished to write ancient and indeed primary histories, they nevertheless wished to write *true* ones, not mythical ones like Herodotus and Diodorus. The most reckless storytellers are accustomed to bolster their observations of so many thousands of ages by the sayings of these two, 
<margin>Herodotus and Diodorus.</margin>
as if Diodorus were not considered the greatest fabulist by the very title of his work, and Herodotus the same by the consensus of all literature. 

<margin>Noted by Porphyry.</margin>
But let us <term>pass over</term> <note>original: "praetermittamus"</note> these things; there is a most evident testimony of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of the 3rd century AD.</note> regarding our subject. He says that the observations of the stars which Callisthenes <note>The court historian and relative of Aristotle who accompanied Alexander the Great.</note> sent from Babylon into Greece at the time of Aristotle and Alexander—observations of the Chaldeans—comprised only one thousand nine hundred and three years. If you count those years backward from Alexander, you will find they end at the time of the patriarch Abraham, or only slightly earlier. 

<margin>Hipparchus and Ptolemy.</margin>
Hipparchus and Ptolemy, the princes of astronomy, when establishing a doctrine, assert that there are no older observations than those which took place under King Nabuchodonosor <note>Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon.</note> among the Egyptians or Babylonians. Hipparchus flourished nearly six hundred years after that king’s reign, and from his time down to our own, no more than one thousand six hundred years or thereabouts have passed. Therefore, they lie and speak fabulously when they boast of having observations from so many ages; and it is easily demonstrated that those observations they *do* have are necessarily false. For they either began at the time of Ptolemy, or they fell away from those who preceded Ptolemy. If the course of such observation began after Ptolemy, there was not enough time to complete the observation, which they themselves would not deny. But if it rests on the experiments of the ancients—namely, what the Egyptians or Chaldeans handed down—who can doubt that it is deceptive? Faithful observation of the heavens cannot exist among those who did not correctly grasp the celestial movements. And that the Chaldeans and Egyptians alike erred greatly in these matters, no one is ignorant who has touched the books of the mathematicians. 

Ptolemy censures them everywhere in his <term>Great Composition</term> <note>Better known by its Arabic title, the *Almagest*, the most influential astronomical text of antiquity.</note>; Hipparchus censures them too. Nor would anyone easily believe that the world only began to understand something correctly about the movements of the heavens quite late. 
<margin>Eudemus and Callimachus.</margin>
According to Eudemus <note>A student of Aristotle and historian of science.</note>, Thales was the first to predict a solar eclipse. Callimachus <note>An influential Greek poet and scholar at the Library of Alexandria.</note> says that Thales was the first discoverer of the Little Bear, by which the Phoenicians sail. He also divided the year into three hundred and sixty-five days. 

<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
Plutarch asserts that the obliquity of the Zodiac—the first rudiment of stellar science to be devised—was found by Pythagoras; 
<margin>Chian</margin>
although Euripides the Chian, who was younger than Pythagoras, boasts that it was first discovered by him. Before Solon flourished in Greece—and he flourished nearly six hundred years before the time of Christ—everyone thought the lunar month was exactly thirty days. 
<margin>Proclus.</margin>
Solon was the first to correct this error, as Proclus writes in his commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*. 

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
Now, if they erred so remarkably regarding the movement of the moon, which is so easy and familiar to us, what should we think of the movements of the other stars, which are more hidden and slower? But there is no need for conjecture here. Let Ptolemy’s book titled the <term>Great Composition</term> be read; it will be clear beyond suspicion that all the ancients were "out by a whole heaven," as the saying goes, regarding the celestial movements. You will learn there that regarding the movement of the closer star <note>The moon.</note> which we were discussing, nothing was discovered by the ancients that was not only untrue but not even close to the truth. 
<margin>At what time Hipparchus lived.</margin>
Hipparchus was the first, on the island of Rhodes about two hundred years before Christ, to observe the course of the moon more truly. But even he did not reach perfect clarity, which is why he is corrected by Ptolemy, who followed him...

He highlights the frequent errors made by "ancient" authorities like the Egyptians and Chaldeans concerning basic celestial facts like the length of a month or the tilt of the zodiac.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY <note>original: "ADVERSVS ASTRO." - likely "Adversus Astrologos" (Against the Astrologers) or "Adversus Astrologiam" (Against Astrology)</note>

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
Hipparchus indeed came closer to the truth, but in such a way that he was not reached by the Spanish <note>Likely referring to the medieval Alfonsine tables produced in Spain, which sought to correct astronomical data.</note>, and was subsequently corrected by later astronomers. Regarding the motion of the Sun, by which they measure all other things, they are still to this day struggling to see clearly <note>original: "cercutiunt"</note>, nor did antiquity ever fully grasp it. Furthermore, the Egyptians wandered excessively from the path, thinking that the solar restoration <note>The completion of a full solar cycle or year.</note> happened after three hundred sixty-five days and a quarter part of a day, with a thirtieth part added <unclear>moreover</unclear>. Yet more recent observations have taught us that not even the quarter part is fully completed. How then could the wisdom of the Egyptians have produced reliable experiments regarding the fate of the year, when they failed so greatly regarding its very beginning? In this matter they were even ridiculous, for they inaugurated the year—as Theophilus <note>An ancient historian or chronographer.</note> records—as soon as the Nile first began to flood Egypt. Anaximander, as Favorinus writes in his *Universal History*, was the 
<margin>Favorinus.</margin>
first to invent the <term>Gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow, used here to measure the solstices and equinoxes.</note>, with which he might mark the turnings of the sun and the equinoxes. Everyone who has read his books knows that the astrolabe was the invention of Ptolemy. Pythagoras was the first 
<margin>Parmenides.</margin>
to say that the Evening Star and the Morning Star <note>Hesperus and Lucifer; both are the planet Venus.</note> were the same celestial body, on the authority of Parmenides. Pythagoras did not precede Christ by even five hundred years. But let us return to the motions of the stars, which were so little explored by the 
<margin>Hipparchus.</margin>
ancients that Hipparchus said there exist so few observations of the five planets (excluding the sun and moon) by the ancients that he could not affirm anything certain about them that would inspire confidence. Ptolemy was the first who seemed to say something certain about these things, though the following age, by the benefit of time, has corrected <note>original: "castigauerit" - literally "chastised" or "reproved"</note> him in many places. Regarding the counting of the "ascensions" of the signs—which the Greeks call <term>anaphoras</term> <note>The rising of zodiacal signs above the horizon.</note>—how far those who practiced divination by the stars in Egypt fell from the truth 
<margin>Ptol. Apollinarius.</margin>
is testified by Ptolemy in the first book of his <term>Apotelesmatika</term> <note>original: "apotelesmaton"; Ptolemy’s work on the effects of the stars, commonly known as the Tetrabiblos.</note> and by Apollinarius in his commentaries. Likewise, Apollonius of Laodicea, in a work dedicated to the subject in five 
<margin>Apollonius.</margin>
books, mocked their errors. Who, then, considering these things, could doubt? No true experience regarding the influences of the stars could be held among the Egyptians or Chaldeans, since they had not even explored the ascensions of the signs—upon which the greatest part of this art depends—nor the motions of the planets. How could they faithfully experience what a planet did in a certain place when the planets were always in a location other than where they thought they were? This is to say nothing of the "wandering stars" <note>The planets.</note> whose motions, if we believe Ptolemy, were entirely unknown to them. But if they were in error, as is undoubtedly clear, then the Greeks err who follow them; the Arabs err who follow the Greeks; and the Latins err who follow the Arabs and the Greeks. It is from their rules, lacking in experience, that they pronounce what is to come. For they do not think to put forward anything with greater authority than that which they confirm by the authority of the Chaldeans and Egyptians. From this they scatter various names like mists <note>original: "nepulas" for "nebulas"</note> before their readers—names such as Aesculapius, Hermes, Nechepso <note>original: "Notepsos"</note>, and Petosiris—as if these men were not the most ignorant of the science they professed, if Hipparchus and Ptolemy, the chief authors of astronomy, have passed down the truth to us. Why then did Ptolemy, in the first book of his *Apotelesmatika*, as if to grant credit to his words, turn to the experiments of the ancients? He himself could scarcely begin to find the truth in the science of the stars in his own time, when it was 
<margin>Peter of Abano. Time of Galen and Ptolemy.</margin>
first tolerably investigated. Peter of Abano <note>Petrus Apponensis, a 13th-century physician and astrologer.</note> excuses Galen’s errors regarding the motions of the moon in this way: "Galen did not write these things exactly because they were not yet understood." Yet Galen was not prior to Ptolemy, but a contemporary. Therefore, let us conclude our whole discussion thus: if the astrology which has been written down relies on the experiments of the ancients, it is deceptive, because they lacked a method <note>original: "ratio"</note>; since these things are also ambiguous to the moderns, as we have shown above, they were hardly manifest to antiquity. If the astrology of the younger men is even more deceptive, it is because they lacked both method and time.

He concludes that because the mathematical foundations of astrology were wrong, the entire tradition of astrological prediction is built on a "chain of error."</summary>

<meta>This page begins Book 12 of Pico della Mirandola’s Disputations. Having previously critiqued the physical and mathematical failings of astrology, he now turns to the claim that astrology is a "revealed" wisdom passed down from the patriarchs.</meta>

# THE TWELVE BOOKS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS BEGIN.

## That no faith should be given to astrology as if it were revealed.

<insert>Chapter One</insert>

<margin>First Reason</margin>
If there can be neither support nor faith in the fables of the astrologers based on experiments—as has already been shown—what remains? Why should a wise man surrender himself to them? Will they consider them oracles? And shall we receive as divine those things which we have refuted as purely rational? Shall we imitate the astrologers who, if something is done by men beyond reason, refer it to the stars?
<margin>Second Reason</margin>
Shall we then, by the same example, refer the delusions of men to the stars? But if by chance this persuasion has taken hold of someone, let him know that divine revelations of this kind are of no use to him, since, as we have seen, there is such great disagreement in the decrees of astrology. Nor has it yet been revealed whether it is the astrology of the Chaldeans, or rather of the Egyptians, or the Jews, or of Ptolemy, or of the Arabs, which the gods, by a singular gift, inspired for us as well-deserving people. Therefore, that divine beneficence helps us not at all while that most true wisdom received from heaven lies hidden in the filth of our lies. Nor has any Lydian stone <note>A "Lydian stone" or touchstone was used in antiquity to test the purity of gold; here, Pico means a standard for truth.</note> been sent down from there by which the legitimate can be distinguished from the counterfeit.
<margin>Third Reason</margin>
But if I am speaking with Christians, I would ask whether they think it was revealed by God, or rather by a demon. It cannot be said to be from God if the interpreters of the divine voice in Sacred Scripture forbid it. 
<margin>Fourth Reason</margin>
If they respond that it is from a demon, then no faith is to be given to a demon, whom God called the father of lies. From this, the insanity of those is refuted who fabricate the story that this science, like all others, was conferred divinely upon Adam, from whom it passed through hands down to Noah. 
<margin>Methodius</margin>
Whose son, Ionicus <note>A legendary figure in medieval tradition, often called the fourth son of Noah, to whom hidden wisdom was attributed.</note>, Methodius records predicted many future things through this art. Then, through the sons of Noah who survived the Deluge, it passed to the patriarch Abraham, who taught it to the Egyptians, as Josephus witnesses; and from the Egyptians to the Greeks, and from the Greeks handed down to the Latins. Thus they invent this "beautiful" succession, convenient for ensnaring the unrefined, but everywhere false and lying to the more learned. For what they say about Adam—unless this too was revealed—by what testimony do they prove it? Or because we believe that by God's gift he was skilled in all sciences, does it follow that he knew this one too? Certainly, it would follow if this were also a science—if it were not vain, false, ridiculous, and repugnant to the principles of true doctrines; and not, as we were saying, unworthy of God, or even of man as an inventor. 
<margin>Methodius the author</margin>
Let us come to Ionicus. Methodius writes about this, but he is a hardly suitable author. For he is not the one whom Saint Jerome mentions among illustrious men—that one was from Patara <note>original: "parcharensis," a common corruption of "Patarensis," referring to St. Methodius of Patara.</note>—this one is entirely different, cited sometimes by Peter Comestor <note>A 12th-century theologian; Pico is distinguishing between the genuine Church Father and the "Pseudo-Methodius" whose writings contained these legends.</note>, in whom no person of even moderate education would fail to notice a lack of selection of good authors. But Methodius does not say that he said anything except empty things; moreover, what weight can the authority of an ignoble writer have regarding this Ionicus, when even the prophet Moses himself numbers only three sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth? Neither Josephus names any other besides these, nor Philo, nor any Hebrew, whether a composer of annals or an expounder of the Mosaic law. 
<margin>Philo</margin>
<margin>Josephus</margin>
Let us believe Josephus that Abraham handed down astrology to the Egyptians; but not this superstitious divinatory kind, which is more frequent among idolaters than among worshippers of the true God (who is called the "God of Abraham"), and which was rebuked by Moses and the prophets, who nevertheless professed to follow the traditions and precepts of Abraham. 
<margin>What kind of astrology the Hebrews had</margin>

-> DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY <-
<lang>English</lang>

[astro]logy: which Abraham first indicated to the Egyptians, having received it from the Chaldeans. However, it is clear from what was said above that the Egyptians created their own version of astrology for the purpose of prediction, which has almost nothing in common with the dogmas of the Chaldeans. Moreover, Ptolemy <note>Original: "Pro." referring to Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer.</note> teaches in his *Great Composition* <note>Original: "magna compositione," the *Almagest*, the most influential astronomical manual of antiquity.</note> that few Chaldeans practiced the part concerning the motions of the stars, and that it flowed from them to others without their involvement. Therefore, Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the Jewish historian, who claimed in *Antiquities of the Jews* that Abraham taught the Egyptians arithmetic and astronomy.</note> understood this to be nothing other than mathematics. 

<margin>Ptolemy, Aboafar, Fifth reason.</margin>
Furthermore, Aboafar <note>A Latinized name for Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer often cited by Western scholars.</note> is to be laughed at; he says in his own work that the sons of Noah disseminated this science when they came into Chaldea—an opinion he himself rejects regarding the boundaries of the planets, claiming it was held by the Chaldeans through divine gift. But one should not spend so much effort in refuting these trifles, since no one, unless they are most dull-witted, fails to understand that these are the ravings of a man so enslaved to his own dreams that he confirms things produced with no reason by citing authority traced back to Adam. For let them answer this: why did other arts and sciences not descend to us through that same succession, but were instead thought out by the talents of later men and brought to perfection through diligent study? Or did we receive a gift of divine providence in astrology alone, as if it were more useful? Truly, that providence would have been uncharacteristically asleep if it failed to notice that it was preserving this divinatory art for us in vain unless mathematics was also preserved, without which we cannot rightly use astrology. 

<margin>What the study of astrology ought to involve.</margin>
For it is of no use to have discovered the powers and natures of the stars unless you can note, by exact calculation, the habits, form, and position of the stars at every hour. Since mathematics alone provides this, it too should have devolved to us from our first father by hereditary tradition, if divine providence did not wish the use of such "salutary" divination to be missing from our lives.

## Chapter IIII: What manner of people the Egyptians and Chaldeans were, among whom astrology was born.

<margin>The Chaldean and Egyptian nations, and what they studied diligently.</margin>
**S**o those are rejected who venerate these trifles—so unworthily and falsely fabricated about the heavens—as if they were received from heaven itself. When anyone reads these things and looks closely, they see the nature of it so clearly that no suspicion of celestial inspiration remains; I think this is evident enough even to the most thick-headed by what has been said. Nevertheless, it will not be useless, reader, to consider under a single view how this "pest" was born and spread through the world: that is, by which authors it arose, by what persuasions it was received, by what authority it was confirmed, and by what nourishments it has increased and persisted to this day. For this will also be not entirely ineffective in stripping away its credit and exposing its vanity. It was born, then, from Chaldean and Egyptian parents, about whom something must be said before we speak of their vanity. 

Each nation was primarily studious and skilled in two things: idolatrous religion and mathematics. The convenience of their location invited them to the latter; for they inhabited open fields and wide plains, from which an easier and truer view of the stars was possible. As for the former—that is, why they, before other nations, were occupied with and honored vain and superstitious ceremonies—this happened because of their antiquity, on account of which they practiced the first cults of the gods as if they were parents to others, and were necessarily the masters of religion. Furthermore, as we have shown elsewhere, this was due to their ignorance of physical reasoning and the rudeness of their talents. For mathematics does not make men wise; which is why, among the ancients, it was a study for boys. Rather, just as mathematics, when tasted moderately and with reason, builds a path to philosophy, so too if anyone gives themselves entirely to it, it produces the greatest occasions for error in philosophy, as Aristotle testifies. 

<margin>What mathematics contributes to philosophy.</margin>
The Egyptians and Chaldeans were, therefore, as far as I can follow by conjecture and fact, of a talent suited for wisdom, just as is seen in the men of those regions even now; though chance might have taken away their education and study, it should not have taken away their nature. 

<margin>Solution to the doubt.</margin>
Nor indeed should we be deceived by what once deceived me as a youth: the celebrated wisdom of the Egyptians and Chaldeans among the ancients, including Plato. It is recorded in memory that Pythagoras, Democritus, Eudoxus, Plato, and many others visited them for no other reason than to acquire wisdom. For that celebrated and divine name of wisdom was claimed for itself from ceremonies alone...

<meta>This page continues Pico's historical critique of the ancient Near Eastern civilizations. Having previously discussed Abraham, he now addresses the reputation of the Egyptians and Chaldeans as the supposed "fathers" of wisdom, arguing that their contributions were limited to mathematics and religious ritual rather than true philosophy.</meta>

# BOOK TWELVE

...they claimed the knowledge of ceremonies and the worship of the gods, which was a common belief among all nations and even among all good philosophers: that the highest wisdom consists in religion. For this reason, Plato, Pythagoras, and many others, rightly seeing that the truest philosophy lies in the knowledge of divine things, traveled down to the Egyptians because of their reputation for being especially skilled in these matters. They were driven by an eagerness to learn whatever seemed most hidden and sacred among them. They also went down to learn mathematics, which those we just mentioned—Pythagoras, Democritus, and Eudoxus—drank in greedily.

<margin>Wisdom has indeed claimed the highest name for itself, both in Plato and in Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* <note>The branch of philosophy dealing with first principles, including the nature of being and the divine.</note>—that is, the human inquiry into such things.</margin>
However, that title of wisdom and the privilege of "secret discipline" came to the Chaldeans and Egyptians from no other source than their mastery and teaching of how to worship the divine powers. Whether or not the good philosophers approved of what they heard from them, we have discussed elsewhere. Nevertheless, we assert this: it is demonstrated by the principles of natural and first philosophy <note>term: "First philosophy" is a traditional name for Metaphysics, the study of the ultimate cause of all things.</note> that the Greek philosophers—whomever among them philosophized correctly—received nothing from the Egyptians except what pertained to ceremonies and mathematics. A proof of this is that whenever the subject is mathematics or "mysteries," we see the Chaldeans and Egyptians cited and their opinions always brought forward; yet in the logical reasoning of philosophy found in Plato and Aristotle, their names are nowhere to be found.

<margin>Plato, Pythagoras, Democritus.</margin>
Now, if you say that Thales <note>The first of the Greek philosophers, known for predicting an eclipse and proposing water as the fundamental substance.</note> philosophized in Egypt, I will not deny it, as he learned from them that water is the beginning of all things. I believe the Egyptians were led to this opinion for no other reason than seeing their region blessed and made fertile by the flooding of the Nile. Indeed, they even began their year from the conclusion of that flood. They were, in truth, quite unrefined minds and therefore prone to superstitions.

<margin>Iamblichus.</margin>
Nothing is rejected and scorned more by a vivid and vigorous intellect than these superstitions; yet they were so susceptible that they were led by demons into every kind of madness. If they had no religion other than superstition—as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> largely confesses by confirming they were most occupied with the cult of evil demons—it follows that since their name for "wisdom" came from the name of their religion, the more "wise" they were reported to be, the more foolish they actually were. Furthermore, as has been said, the Greeks' commerce with them was more profitable in mathematics than it was in their superstitions.

<margin>Thales.</margin>
Thales, in a letter to Pherecydes, says: "I and Solon <note>The famous Athenian lawmaker.</note> traveled to Egypt to see the priests and astronomers"; he mentions nothing of philosophy. He also says he learned geometry from them.

<margin>Demetrius.</margin>
Demetrius says that Democritus <note>The philosopher famous for his atomic theory.</note> went to the Egyptians to learn geometry. Occasionally, Democritus, Plato, and the wise Pythagoras are called "monstrous" <note>note: original: "monstrousus," used here to mean extraordinary or marvelously strange in their depth of knowledge.</note>. But that unblemished genius of Plato, which was sufficient and necessary for his age, showed honor to antiquity and the title of religion; otherwise, he never tainted his own "dough" with the Egyptian "leaven." <note>Pico uses a baking metaphor: Plato respected their age but didn't let their ideas change his fundamental philosophy.</note> And so Eudoxus <note>A Greek astronomer and student of Plato.</note> also followed the Egyptians in true astronomy, but did not agree with them in the divinatory <note>term: "Divinatory" refers here to astrology, the practice of foretelling the future via the stars.</note> part.

<margin>Conclusion of what was said.</margin>
So as not to wander too far, we conclude this: the Egyptians and Chaldeans were most occupied in idolatrous superstition and very much devoted to mathematics, but they exercised themselves very little in the rest of philosophy.

<margin>Averroes. In that book, Averroes says it is most likely that philosophy has been corrupted many times.</margin>
Nor should anyone be moved by what Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain, known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says: that philosophy was once perfect among the Chaldeans. For he is not speaking of the Chaldeans whose memory or monuments have reached us, but from that opinion which, believing in the eternity of the world, says these arts have been both abolished and restored infinite times among different nations. Nor should it be held against us that we do not approve of the Chaldeans as a whole, from whom Abraham, a man of God, came. For Abraham was not a "Chaldean" <note>Meaning he did not share their superstitious practices.</note>, though he is sometimes called a Chaldean because of the proximity of the regions. There is a saying of Plato: "In a nation that is mostly bad, if a good person is born, they are the very best." Nor did Abraham obtain his privilege so much by nature as by divine grace. But let us return to astrology: it is easy to see what led the Egyptians and Chaldeans into this matter, now that we have said enough about their studies and characters.

->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.<-

# OF DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.

**I**t is customary for those who have immersed themselves entirely in any discipline to refer everything to it most willingly: not so much out of ambition, so that they might seem to know everything through it, but because it appears so to those to whom it happens, much like those traveling through snow; for everything else usually appears white to them, the habit of whiteness having already been received into the eyes and transforming everything else into itself. Likewise, for those desperately in love, whatever they encounter reflects the face or some aspect of the beloved, the entire imaginative faculty of the lover being surrendered to the dominion of that single image. He who is a Theologian refers everything to divine causes; the Physician to the condition of the body; the Physicist to the natural principles of things; the Mathematician to figures and numbers, as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed that the structure of the universe was based on numerical ratios.</note> used to do. By this same reasoning, since the ancient Chaldeans <note>Inhabitants of southern Mesopotamia, famous in antiquity for their astronomical observations and their association with magic and astrology.</note> were constantly and diligently occupied in measuring celestial motions and observing the courses of the stars, and their minds were held by nothing more than these things, everything to them was "the star." That is, they willingly referred everything to the stars—which should be understood as being equally true of the Egyptians. Since, therefore, they approached this specific inclination, the conjectures 

<margin>Note.</margin>
which we described and refuted in the third book—such as that lower bodies are moved by superior ones, or that stars must have the greatest power of influence—seemed to be confirmed when they observed in the sun and moon how much they rule over our bodies and the air. When such things occurred to minds already inclined in that direction, they were easily led to believe that whatever happened to men—whether pertaining to the body, the soul, or 

<margin>
As it is said by
Aristotle in the
*Ethics*,
happiness
consists in these
three things.
<note>Aristotle identified three types of "goods": those of the soul (virtue), those of the body (health/beauty), and external fortune (wealth/status).</note>
</margin>
fortune—proceeded from celestial causes. They believed that by knowing and exploring these causes, the future events of all things could be foreknown. For they did not have such a clear perspective on physics that they could sufficiently understand how a universal cause differs from particular causes, or what the function of each might be; what was appropriate to celestial substance and what was contrary to it; what was "essential" <note>original: "per se"</note> or what was "accidental" <note>original: "ex accidenti"</note> among logicians; or how great a dissimilarity exists between the works of nature and the works of art. Nor did they understand what could be a sign of another thing without being its cause. Thus, driven by these reasons, they did not ascribe particular differences to a common cause (as if the immediate causes were idle), nor did they—as if to a god from whom little good comes—impute their own faults to the stars, deriving the punishments of both the evil soul and the body from them. Nor did they refer the accidental meeting of causes to the nature of the body as if it understood them; nor did they imagine new powers flowing from heaven into the works of art, as if art could penetrate the innermost substance of a thing. Or, if these things were not produced by heaven, they still believed they could be signaled by it, even if they were neither effects nor causes of one another, nor proceeded from the same origin in the same way. Since they were ignorant of all these things—philosophy being as yet imperfect and little investigated by them—is it any wonder if they were led into error by so many pulling forces? First, by those conjectures we mentioned, which were indeed ineffective but possessed great probability for the common people and those uneducated in philosophy; then, by that constant habit and a kind of familiarity with the stars; to all of which was added the innate 

<margin>
Hence Aristotle
says in the first

*Metaphysics*:
All men by
nature desire
to know.
</margin>
curiosity of men for knowing the future. For what we desire to be possible, we easily believe to be possible. There was also the vice of the age: a deeply held persuasion toward divination <note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</note> in the minds of men at that time. They greedily followed a thousand modes and types of divination far less probable and more insane than this, such as pyromancy <note>divination by fire</note>, geomancy <note>divination by earth or sand</note>, astragalomancy <note>divination using dice or knuckle-bones</note>, and other such old wives' nonsense, among which the error of the astrologers could be considered the highest wisdom. Add to this that it agreed marvelously with the idolatry to which they were subject: they considered the gods they worshipped to be the authors of all things, not only the good but also the bad. For in the discipline of idolatry, there was also this: that some gods were beneficial and others harmful; thus, even here, contrary to the reason of philosophy, they considered some stars to be good and others evil. Add the opportunity for glory and profit which astronomers saw prepared for them if it were thought that the courses of the heavens—which they investigated perhaps with great labor but for little reward—could foresee the future. To all these things, add the frauds of wicked demons, then ruling the world most powerfully, who, through more hidden instigations, drove their minds (already inclined toward this error for the reasons mentioned) even further.

->BOOK TWELVE<-

...impelled them with [demonically induced] thoughts: since, perverting their judgments, they <note>Pico is referring here to demons or malevolent spirits, a common explanation in Renaissance thought for how people were led into superstition.</note> completely enslaved their minds to themselves: then by sometimes confirming the predictions of those people, or by moving them to predict what was going to happen: or by carrying out what had been predicted by them. I do not doubt that all these things together were the cause why, first among the Egyptians and Chaldeans <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia, famous for their early developments in astronomy and astrology.</note>—men devoted to superstitions and idolatry, most occupied in the motions of the heavens, yet little skilled in philosophy—the opinion was born that future events could be foreseen from the state of the stars. The age easily accepted this opinion out of curiosity and lack of skill; astronomers confirmed it most willingly in the hope of profit and the acquisition of glory.

### Chapter IV. How they happened upon those things which they established to be observed in predictions.

<margin>Where the conjectures of prediction were born.</margin>
**W**e have seen among which nations and how this error was first born—that human affairs are either caused or indicated by the heavens; it is easy to see how astrologers again arrived at these dogmas which they use in predicting. They were not, as we have demonstrated, led to these things by true reasons; for how could they be, since there is no true reasoning for a lie? Furthermore, we do not investigate the properties of things more closely joined to us in place and nature except by their operations. But they were not led by experiments either; otherwise they would have had to cease from predicting for at least many ages, since experiments of this kind are perfected only by long-lasting and quite often repeated observations, which are beyond controversy. What then? They followed conjectures, partly from the mathematical tasks <term>mathematicis</term> <note>In this context, 'mathematici' refers specifically to those who calculated planetary positions, often synonymous with astrologers in the late medieval period.</note> upon which they were intent, and partly taken from certain parabolic <note>Meaning metaphorical or based on symbolic similarities rather than physical evidence.</note> similarities than which nothing more deceptive could be imagined. Either they themselves, being rude in philosophy and logic <term>dialecticae</term>, were deceived, or they thought the unlearned common folk could be deceived; and for those rushing toward the profit and glory of divining, no way was so satisfying as the one that was more plausible, easier, and more ready. Thus they first established that the fates of men depend on the hour of birth <term>natali hora</term>, both because it commonly seems that a man is "made" when he is born, and because other principles—either of the conceiving of the fetus or of its receiving a soul—were too uncertain to be observed for prediction. From the mathematicians they first accepted this: since in measuring the motions of the stars they had divided the slanted circle <note>The Ecliptic or the Zodiac.</note> into twelve parts for ease of counting, and again 
<margin>The reasoning of divination</margin>
by the same reasoning they took each of the parts into thirty [degrees], and each thirtieth into sixty [minutes]; they noted this rule here as if this division were made by nature and not by choice. And since they had fashioned so many parts for themselves, they decreed that the powers of influences and their properties were diverse. Then, according to the number of signs, they divided twelve "houses" <note>The twelve divisions of the sky in an astrological chart.</note>, six above the horizon and six below, just as six signs are always beneath the earth and six revolve above. Thus it was defined with great error that it must be observed first under 
<margin>Signs are observed.</margin>
which place and which sign a planet was located; for they believed that, due to the variety of the place and sign, the planet acquired different powers for influencing. After this, whatever diversities they noted in the motions, they judged those also in the operations of the stars to be noted, as if the power of efficiency also varied according to the appearance. Thus they decreed that a planet did one thing when it moved forward, another when it moved backward <note>Retrograde motion, an optical illusion where a planet appears to move backward in the sky.</note>, and another when it stood still. Then, they believed that different things happened because of either the conjunction or the distance of the stars from one another. They observed especially certain distances, which they had found to be more significant for changes when they measured the motions: such as the trine interval <note>Trine: an aspect where two planets are 120 degrees apart (one third of the circle).</note>, because in that configuration Saturn and Jupiter always moved backward; just as sometimes Mars in the square <note>Square: an aspect of 90 degrees (one fourth of the circle).</note>, and they never saw Mercury and Venus removed from the Sun beyond the sextile <note>Sextile: an aspect of 60 degrees (one sixth of the circle).</note>. They thought, therefore, that these distances of the stars were to be observed when they were placed in trine, sextile, or square radiation; but also in opposition, for which there is an evident reason, especially because in these configurations they saw the phases <term>schemata</term> of the Moon change in relation to the Sun: becoming a crescent in the sextile, half in the square, gibbous in the trine, and full in the diameter <note>Opposition (180 degrees).</note>. Just as they had imagined the intersections of certain circles at the path of the sun <note>The nodes of the moon or planets.</note> to be a necessary thing for measuring motions, but a vain thing for influences, so they also treated these...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic deconstruction of the origins of astrology. Having previously argued that the practice was born from superstition and demonic influence rather than reason, Pico now turns to the specific mathematical and physical errors that underpin astrological doctrine, specifically the arbitrary division of the zodiac into elements and aspects.</meta>

### DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

the decrees of the fates, they added what they call the head and the tail <note>original: "caput caudaque." These refer to the North and South Nodes of the moon, points where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic, often called the "Dragon's Head" and "Dragon's Tail" in Renaissance astrology.</note>; as if, finally, the powers and influences of the rays followed these mathematical quantities, positions, locations, points, and distances, rather than the qualities and natures of the rays themselves. But they did not notice this error due to their ignorance of physics; nor could they avoid it if they wanted there to be different constellations in the sky at every single moment, which would vary the life, fortune, character, and talents of men being born one after another.

### Chapter V. What those things to be observed indicated; and by which conjectures they defined them.

Thus, they received from the "mathematicians" <note>In this period, "mathematici" (mathematicians) was a common term for astrologers, as their work relied on calculating planetary positions.</note> what was to be observed with a perverse intention, which—if we believe Aristotle—was also the occasion for error among the ancients: namely, when they judge natural things as if they were mathematical. It remained, after these things, to investigate what these signs, stars, motions, and aspects themselves would signify or effect when they were found arranged in one way or another; here they proceeded with the most trivial and deceptive conjectures, which we shall relate.

<margin>Regarding composition and the mixture of elements, I have argued that [he] previously doubted. Plato.</margin>
Regarding the signs, they first devised this: it was an undisputed fact for the Egyptians that all things consist of the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>. Since, therefore, they had already received twelve signs by the occasion we have mentioned, a convenient and beautiful division seemed possible to them: to distinguish these also by the four elements, so that when these were applied three times, the number of signs was filled <note>12 signs divided by 4 elements equals 3 signs per element, known as a "triplicity."</note>. And because they thought the first bodies were fire and earth—as it were, the center and the circumference (for fire was to them the highest body)—then the intermediaries, air and water, arrived, as Plato also shows in the *Timaeus*. Therefore, they established the first sign as fiery, the second as earthy, the third as airy, and the fourth as watery. Then, returning with a similar consequence, the fifth was fiery, the sixth earthy, and so on. From this it happened that those signs which are distant by a "trigon" <note>original: "trigonum." A trine or triangular aspect of 120 degrees.</note> interval—that is, with three signs intercepted between them—were judged to be of the same nature, because the fifth sign returned to the nature of the first. However, those in a hexagonal aspect <note>A "sextile" aspect of 60 degrees.</note> would be partly related and partly discordant, but more related, since the first was fiery and the third was airy. But those in a "tetragon" <note>A square or "quadrature" aspect of 90 degrees.</note> were utterly opposed, just as fire and water are utterly discordant. Thus it was a fabrication that the triangular radiation would be good, the square bad, and the hexagonal nearly neutral; but that the square would be a better opposition, and the direct opposition would also be bad, because stars so placed look at each other from the opposite side. Yet some also want this [opposition] to be neutral, looking at the qualities of the signs in it as in others. For there are among the signs those which agree in one quality but disagree in another. It is evident from this how these dogmas gave birth to one another; and while they leave some suspicion of reason when heard in isolation, they immediately become contemptible once their origin is revealed. For if that first foundation is shaky and weak—namely, the number of twelve signs introduced by the judgment of those calculating (as astrologers admit)—everything they build upon it is ruinous, or rather, many things sprouting from that one root. For even the "trigons" come from there, which claim a great part of astrology for themselves.

<margin>From where the "Trigonocratores" come.</margin>
From this come the "trigonocratores" <note>Greek: <term>trigonocratores</term> meaning "rulers of the triplicities." These are the planets that "rule" the groups of three signs associated with an element.</note>—that is, the lords, as they say, of the triplicities—from whom the later Chaldeans received the theory of "terms" <note>original: "de finibus." These are sub-divisions of signs ruled by different planets.</note>; the Egyptians received the "monomoiria" <note>original: <term>monomiriās</term>, referring to a system where each individual degree of a sign has a specific planetary ruler.</note>; and the Arabs derived their greatest dogmas from the "great conjunctions." Ptolemy and all others (though some differently than others) derived the distribution of the parts of the world and its regions under the signs: so that, clearly, they gave this triplicity to the east, that one to the west, another to the south, and another to the north. From this, predictions about the fate of the year greatly depend, so that we may know what will come to which region. But let us return to the other properties of the signs: for we have sufficiently uncovered the mystery of the distinction into elements, having drawn back the veil to find only the most unadulterated nonsense there. They therefore devised other things from the effects that the Sun, sliding beneath them, produces in those figures. From this, they divided them into fixed, movable, and common <note>In modern astrology, these are called Fixed, Cardinal, and Mutable qualities.</note>; others [they named] from the name of the parts of the circle, as if they were similar in nature not just to the image of those things but to their powers. Thus they called some signs "human" and others "brute" <note>Animal-like.</note>, because this sign, Aquarius, is figured as a youth himself, while that one is called Aries. Thus almost all dogmas born concerning the signs come either from the work of the Sun, or from the name of the images, or from the division by elements—which one immediately judges to be...

-> refuted <-

<summary>Pico argues that the fundamental structures of astrology, such as the elemental triplicities and the "strength" of different planetary aspects, are arbitrary mathematical inventions rather than physical realities. He traces these "nonsense" doctrines back to ancient Egyptian and Greek misapplications of natural philosophy to the zodiac.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, elements, triplicities, trines, aspects, Ptolemy, Plato, Aristotle, zodiac signs, lunar nodes, planetary rulers</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the "conjectures" used by astrologers to build their system. He moves from the general mathematical errors discussed on the previous page to the specific, often poetic or visual, associations astrologers made between planets, signs, and human life.</meta>

# BOOK ELEVEN

...have been refuted. They judged the nature of the planets from their colors, as Abu Ma'shar <margin>Abu Ma'shar on where the nature of the planets comes from and other notable things</margin> <note>original: "Aboasar." Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD) was a leading Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to European medieval and Renaissance astrology.</note> testifies, saying this was the conjecture of the "universality of astrologers." This was also applied to the fixed stars; for they said all reddish stars were of the nature of Mars, such as the Eye of the Bull <note>Aldebaran</note> and the Heart of the Scorpion <note>Antares</note>. But it has already been sufficiently demonstrated how irrational and false this is. 

They introduced the affinities of the planets with the signs gradually. The "exaltations" <note>Points in the zodiac where a planet is thought to have its maximum power.</note> were first invented, I believe, among the Chaldeans, concerning which we wrote in Book Eight: that the stars placed in those degrees were at the furthest points from the centers of their orbits <note>original: "absidum." Pico argues the choice was based on orbital geometry rather than celestial influence.</note>. 

Then the Egyptians added the "houses," first accepting the conjecture regarding Leo, under which the power of the Sun was seen to increase. Making a beginning from that sign, they distributed the remaining signs to the other planets according to the order of the spheres, as we have seen. We have already discussed the "triplicities" <note>original: "trigona," groups of three signs belonging to the same element.</note> which they introduced. 

The division of the signs produced "terms," "decans," "twelfth-parts" <note>original: "dodecathemoria."</note>, "ninths," and "individual degrees" <note>original: "monomirias."</note>. Since the signs seemed too vast to be granted entirely to the jurisdiction of a single planet while excluding others, they marked them out into various parts in many ways. They wanted some parts to be the "terms" <margin>A very great question regarding the "terms" of the astrologers.</margin> of one star and others to belong to another. Because each person decided this by a different conjecture, five different opinions arose concerning these "terms," over which they still fight without end. 

Some divided the signs into "decans," which is into three parts; others into nine; others into twelve. But they all did so at their own whim, with no reason. For who could call it "reason" that any sign must be divided into twelve parts simply because there are twelve signs? Or into three parts because of the perfection of the number three? Or into nine because the ninth sign matches the first in quality—namely, Sagittarius with Aries, Capricorn with Taurus, and so on? Even the astrologer Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most famous authority on astrology in the ancient world.</note>, when he had read these things, laughed at them. Yet those "divine" men—the Egyptians, Indians, and Chaldeans—embraced them as if they were first philosophy.

Let us come to the "places" <note>The twelve "houses" of a birth chart, representing different areas of life.</note>, <margin>From whence the properties of the places come</margin> whose properties they defined by a certain similarity. For example: because the "Midheaven" <note>The highest point in the sky at a given moment.</note> is a sublime place, they thought it should signify sublime things: honors, kingdoms, and powers—as if a man does not descend within himself rather than ascend. 

They said the "Rising" <note>The First House or Ascendant.</note> indicates the person being born coming forth from the womb. The Seventh House signifies adversaries because it is opposite the first. The Twelfth House signifies prisons and darkness; for when the Sun reaches that place, the vapors it raises are not yet dissolved, and the air becomes dark, as it were. 

But it is not necessary to follow everything we mentioned above; it is enough to recall to memory how the oracles of this starry and celestial discipline came forth step by step. They are wonderfully connected to each other, with one fable always lending a hand to the next. 

Thus, when they had determined that the "trine" and "sextile" intervals <note>Harmonious aspects of 120 and 60 degrees respectively.</note> were good, and again that the planets Venus and Jupiter (and also the Sun and Moon) were good—since good things rejoice in other good things—they said that <margin>Note the "joys" of the planets</margin> Jupiter "rejoices" in the eleventh place and the Sun in the ninth. One of these is a sextile and the other a trine from the "horoscope" <note>In this context, the Ascendant.</note>. They placed the Moon in the third and Venus in the fifth, which are distant from the Ascendant by similar intervals. They gave the better and more powerful places (those above the earth) to Jupiter and the Sun, but the weaker places (those below the earth) to the others. 

By the same reasoning, they wanted Mars to "rejoice" in the sixth place and Saturn in the twelfth, because these are bad places, just as those planets are bad. Nor do I doubt that many properties were then assigned to these places by them based on the nature of these planets: 
* To the Ninth: prophecies, which the Sun is believed to give. 
* To the Third: short journeys, just as the Moon completes her circuit in a shorter space than all other stars. 
* To the Twelfth: sorrow (due to the condition of Saturn) and hidden enemies. 
* To the Sixth: slaves and diseases, due to the nature of a harmful but effective and agile planet <note>Mars</note>. 
* To the Fifth: joys, children, and pleasures because of Venus. 

They established Venus as the ruler of these things for no better reason than the brightness, rays, and beauty of the star. From this comes that image of her: "gracious from above, laughing with nectar" <note>original: "alma supne nectareũ ridens." Pico is likely quoting or paraphrasing poetic descriptions of Venus/Aphrodite.</note>. Why was she believed by the ancients to be the goddess of elegance and beauty? 

Using such demonstrations, they wove a deceptive web like the daughters of the spider. If you look at it from afar, it might deceive you with the feigned magnitude of its threads and the charm of its novel texture; but if you look closely, it is flimsy; if you touch it with your hand, you break and dissolve it. The grandchildren increased the invention of the fathers, and it was a fiction of the ancients that became more robust because it was more hidden by the fraud of its origin—and because, as always happens, authority is gained through age. Nor have we even said everything.

<summary>Pico deconstructs the arbitrary and metaphorical foundations of astrology, arguing that assignments like planetary "houses," "joys," and "terms" are based on poetic associations and visual metaphors rather than physical reality.</summary>
<keywords>Abu Ma'shar, planetary color, exaltations, houses, decans, Ptolemy, twelve houses, midheaven, planetary joys, Venus, spider's web metaphor</keywords>

--- Page 511 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic dismantling of astrological "conjectures," moving from the physical appearance of stars to the logic of their movements. He transitions into a historical and psychological analysis of why such a flawed system became so popular among both the common people and the ruling elite.</meta>

->DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS<-

However, we have already demonstrated that this "method of invention" is actually a slippery slope of error. Their remaining rules are based on that same pattern of the flimsiest things—namely, they are all built on conjectures and lean on a weak and very dissimilar resemblance to earthly matters. <margin>Retrograde motion.</margin> Such are those ideas that planets are "happy" when they move forward and "unlucky" when they move backward, or even when they are believed to stand still <note>The "station" of a planet, when it appears to stop moving in the sky before changing direction.</note>. It is as if, while moving backward, they deny what they previously granted; while moving forward, they carry out what they promised; and while staying still, they delay the gifts they bestow. <margin>Eclipses of the luminaries.</margin> They claim that an eclipse of the Sun or Moon produces great calamities. Indeed, these events terrify people primarily because their cause is unknown, making it seem as if the gods were either deserting us or being abolished. They claim that when stars are positioned in the apogee <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note>, the person being born is "exalted," simply because that location is physically the highest. Then there are the "parts" of the Moon, then of the others, then of the stars, and finally even of the oats and the beans which some astrologer introduced. <note>original: "auenae: & fabae." Pico is likely mocking Haly Abenragel or other Arabic astrologers who created complex "Lots" or "Parts" to predict specific agricultural yields.</note> This error was explained in Book VIII. 

After they founded these dogmas on such conjectures, they began to observe the "genitures" <term>geniturae: the specific alignment of stars at the moment of a person's birth; a birth chart</term> of those being born. If once or twice by chance their dogmas happened to correspond to the outcome, no faith was thereafter greater, and no authority more certain. For example, if someone happened to be born while Mars occupied Scorpio and later became famous in war, it was held as an absolute certainty that Scorpio was the "house" of Mars; for they reasoned that if Mars was positioned thus, something warlike must be born from it. As we have said, this allowed them to claim they were acting on "experience" while failing so significantly in their understanding of celestial motions. They therefore noted what occurred in the life of someone with a particular birth theme and from there established rules and "canons." Because this was not a path of true experimentation, but rather relied on chance and rashness, different observers saw different things at different times. The result was that there emerged almost as many versions of astrology as there were observers; this led to the confusion and conflicting opinions that we discussed at length in the previous book.

### Chapter VI: By what fuels it was increased and how it was propagated.

Thus, having arisen from trifling conjectures, astrology grew through deceptive "experiments." It was encouraged by the vice of the age and nourished by human curiosity, for there is no one who is not greedy to know their own future. People believe such knowledge is most truly sought from the heavens. After all, how few among the common people—or even among scholars—recognize that these things cannot be rightly sought from the sky? Added to this were the pursuits of princes <note>Rulers and monarchs.</note> who, out of ignorance, believed everything, and out of greed, hoped for everything. If a happy future was announced to them from the heavens (and it was *always* being announced), they were as unwilling to see astrology overturned as they were to lose that promised happiness. 

The astrologers occasionally predicted true things: sometimes by chance, sometimes by cunning, and sometimes with the support of a demon, in the ways we have already explained. For who could fail to succeed occasionally if they predict enough things? In those cases, there are cheers and applause; yet the thousand lies of astrology are immediately buried in oblivion. But they also gained much credit and authority from oracles, which not only approved of this art but practiced it. <margin>Astrological dogma confirmed through Apollo.</margin> When Apollo was asked whether a female would be born, he replied "a female," because at the time of conception the Moon was being carried toward Venus. What greater testimony could there be for a profession than to have the gods as its authors? For the wicked demons knew—and they are so named not only by our people <note>Christians.</note> but by the Platonists as well <margin>The name of the demon.</margin>—they knew, I say, how much poison they were serving the world under this one superstition. 

Once this poison had penetrated deeply into minds, it would first take away faith in religion, the greatest good of mankind; for if everything depends on a fatal necessity from heaven, there would be no miracles and no divinely foreknown future events. Instead, everything would happen by the force of the constellations. <margin>He shows that all liberal arts, such as theology, medicine, and religion, are contaminated by this superstition.</margin> Then, it would provide a defense for vices by claiming they descend upon us from the heavens (and perhaps even for "good" things, if indeed they are good when they come from nature). Finally, it would infect the good arts: medicine and philosophy. While it might not entirely overturn them, as it tries to do with theology, it nonetheless contaminates them. It turns philosophy from true reasoning toward fables, and medicine from natural and effective remedies toward vain observations and the ravings of old women. It would become a single plague of perverse superstition, fatal to both body and soul at once. It saw prudence go to ruin, for people now consulted astrology on what to do, at what time, and by what reason; thus, a most stupid vanity held the tiller of life in its hand. Finally, it was hoped that what did happen would occur: that through this one "mathematics" <note>In the Renaissance, the term "mathematicus" often specifically meant an astrologer.</note> of the heavens and its intricate calculations, it would gain authority, and the fraud of other superstitions would be less noticed, their weakness better hidden. Nor would those other superstitions be thought vain, since they would appear as followers, appendages, and foster-children of celestial doctrine.

<summary>Pico argues that astrology's "rules" are based on poetic analogies rather than science, and that its popularity is driven by human curiosity, royal greed, and demonic influence. He warns that astrology corrupts religion, philosophy, and medicine by replacing reason with "celestial necessity."</summary>
<keywords>retrograde motion, eclipses, apogee, Scorpio, Mars, demons, Apollo, fatal necessity, corruption of medicine, prudence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico's historical critique of astrology, transitioning from its internal logical fallacies to its historical origins and the mechanisms of its spread through "demonic" influence and bad scholarship across different cultures.</meta>

->BOOK ELEVEN<-

<margin>
Porphyry
</margin>
<margin>
Necipsus: The source of superstitious medicine
</margin>
Indeed, would harmful demons not make themselves out to be astrologers? They would leave nothing untried to ensure that, day by day, a pestilential flood might possess the senses and studies of men. Even Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who was often conflicted about the validity of theurgy and astrology.</note> must have doubted whether demons used the rules of astrologers in their oracles specifically to deceive—that is, to create a false sense of trust—since Porphyry himself said that oracles based on astrological dogmas often lied about things that never came to pass. If astrology truly showed the future, these demons, who are most skilled in natural things, could hide nothing. Drawn in by these lures and protections, this vanity deeply occupied the Egyptians and Chaldeans, and it immediately gave birth among them to a superstitious form of medicine. For Necipsus <note>A legendary Egyptian pharaoh to whom many early astrological and medical texts were attributed.</note> wrote in Egypt about which <term>Decan</term> <note>A subdivision of the zodiac into ten-degree segments, each ruled by a specific spirit or deity.</note> caused which disease, and which Decan’s power would, in turn, cure it. This matter was held in secret and among the "mysteries," as if it were not an arbitrary invention—though we have already shown that this division of Decans is a sham, and it was entirely mocked and neglected by Ptolemy. From this root, magic immediately grew, which is nothing other than the embrace of idolatry, astrology, and superstitious medicine—subjects which I have already refuted individually in my books *On the True Faith* against the seven enemies.

### Chapter VII: How Astrology Passed from the Egyptians to Others.

<margin>
What Magic is. The Greek schools did not perceive this kind of superstition.
</margin>
<margin>

Abu Ma'shar's disgrace.
</margin>
<margin>
Note. By what path this art reached the Italian realms.
</margin>
<margin>
Note.
