**A**strology passed from the Egyptians and Chaldeans to the Greeks, but through ignoble authors. For except in the houses of street-performers and charlatans, it did not enter the Lyceum or the Academy <note>The famous schools of Aristotle and Plato in Athens.</note>. Nor did it enter the Stoa, although Thales <note>The first Greek philosopher, often (perhaps wrongly) credited with introducing astronomy/astrology from Egypt.</note> is said to have looked into it; even Epicurus, who could believe in atoms and the void, could not believe in astrology. The first to cultivate it with a good reputation in literature was Ptolemy, in the 140th year after Christ, but he did so more sparingly than the others. He seems not so much to favor this insanity as to want to set a limit upon it; thus, the authority of a single man—always a mathematician and rarely a philosopher—is set against the many prejudices of the most famous men in both mathematics and philosophy. Ptolemy's name snatched some Greeks into error who were otherwise prone to superstition, such as Porphyry, whose excessive care for the cult of demons and superstitions was condemned by his teacher Plotinus and his disciple Iamblichus. From the Greeks, it devolved to the Arabs with even greater authority, as they marveled at whatever they found written by the Greeks and looked with a vain hope of antiquity upon the names of the Egyptians and Chaldeans. But just as Ptolemy, the most prudent of astrologers, had purged and cut back the version received from the barbarians with his own strength, so did a certain Grammarian and historian named Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboasar." Known in the West as Albumasar, a highly influential Persian astrologer (787–886 AD).</note> receive the Greek version and fill it with innumerable trifles and fables. He made astrology almost as much worse than Ptolemy’s astrology as astrology itself is worse than the good arts. He was a man made for empty talk, almost entirely ignorant not only of philosophy but of astronomy as well, and he was mocked by every learned astrologer; yet he was pleasing to the common crowd, among whom a man is "great" if he says more, not if he says better. 

However, through those times, the study of mathematics grew, as did the discipline of all philosophy, throughout Spain. There, while Alfonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile, "The Wise" (1221–1284), who sponsored the "Alphonsine Tables" of planetary motion.</note> reigned—a man most diligent in mathematical numbers and the calculation of celestial motions—he also loved this divinatory vanity, being otherwise unlearned in the studies of philosophy. For his sake, many monuments of that art from the Arabs and Greeks reached us, primarily through John of Seville and Michael Scot <note>A 13th-century scholar and "wizard" figure known for translating Arabic science into Latin.</note>, a writer of no weight but much superstition. Albertus Magnus <note>One of the most important medieval theologians and scientists; Pico claims he outgrew his youthful interest in magic.</note> first embraced these things as if they were new, for he was born in those times; but I think he approved of them not as an old man, but as a youth. Just as he published magical things as a young man, in his mature age he detested them, living a most holy and blameless life in the monastery. Yet it happened as time went on, both through the long duration of the tradition and the multitude of writings, as well as the affinity of name and subject matter with mathematical astronomy, that it has now almost come into dispute whether it is a science without deceit or merely superstition. Truly, even though it has been accepted for so many centuries by the multitude (whose nature is to know nothing), and by the superstitious...

<summary>Pico traces the "genealogy of error" for astrology, claiming it moved from Egyptian demonic medicine to the Greeks, was briefly moderated by Ptolemy, but was later corrupted by Arabic writers like Abu Ma'shar and eventually introduced to Europe through figures like Michael Scot and the young Albertus Magnus.</summary>

the knowledge of which is to rave: sought out by curious men with no judgment, so that from the very beginning—as we have warned—it was mocked, refuted, and driven out by prudent and most holy philosophers. For at the time when the worship of idols in Egypt and Chaldea was growing along with the madness of all vanities, among the Hebrews—the worshippers of the true God—it was condemned by

The Platonists and Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> did not even think it worthy of being discussed, regarding it as one of the itinerant juggling arts <note>original: "artes circulatrices" – deceptive or fraudulent practices often associated with street performers.</note>. Eudoxus of Cnidus, a most prudent lawgiver (for he wrote laws for his citizens) and likewise a great philosopher under Plato—indeed the prince of mathematicians of his age by everyone's consensus—affirmed that astrologers should in no way be believed, and he left this in writing. Thus under Tiberius, Vitellius, Diocletian, Constantine, Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, they were

Soon after, under Ptolemy, when it seemed briefly to be honored, it was immediately brought into infamy by the judgments of Plotinus (the great Platonist), Alexander of Aphrodisias (the distinguished Peripatetic), and Origen (eminent in all disciplines). When it came to the Arabs, it did indeed occupy Abenzageles <note>Likely Abu Ma'shar.</note> and Aboafares—men who were neither dialecticians nor philosophers—but it did not occupy Averroes and Avicenna.
